It was a perfect day. Three days later, the family would be rocked by the sudden death of Joel who was hit by a lone bullet that came into his car and struck him in the neck.

Couho had brought Joel from Mexico when he was 2 months old. He was with her throughout the entire journey to the United States and just like that he was gone.

“I learn to live, I learn how to live with this, and it took me 10 years to put myself together, and start to do things for people,” she said. “Some days I’m down, some days I’m up, but I learned to live and that new process in my life.”

Beatriz Couho works on an initiative of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute called “Pan con Café,” where she works with Spanish speakers dealing with the death of loved ones due to homicide, overdose, and suicide.

The organizer of this walk for nearly three decades has been Chaplain Clementina Chéry, mother of Louis. In 1993, Louis was a 15-year-old straight-A student at West Roxbury High School. In the most deadly of ironies, a bullet to the back of his head ended his promising life right before Christmas as he was on his way to a gathering of Teens against Gang Violence.

While the killing was still under investigation, Chéry didn’t stop to mourn. The next year she formed the peace institute and became what she has described as a “wedding planner for funerals” — helping suffering neighbors deal with reporters’ loaded questions, plan a meaningful service, and figure out how to go on. In the 30 years since, the institute has become the most important support system in Boston for families of the victims of violence. Today, it’s become a national anti-violence model and is halfway toward the $25 million needed to build a proposed center for healing, just blocks from where Louis was killed.

Three years after Louis’s murder, police arrested a suspect. Charles Bogues was, by his own account, in the neighborhood to do a drug deal armed with a .45-caliber handgun. At some point, he acknowledges, he fired it during a shootout. When his lawyer told him that police had proof he was responsible, Bogues assumed it was true. He later told me that his father, a Boston police officer, said to him, “if you think you did it, do the right thing and plead guilty.” So, based on that advice and his attorney’s dubious representation, he did. What Bogues says his lawyer didn’t tell him was much more consequential than what he did.

But given the chaos of that night, how could police know he fired the deadly shot? From the outset, Chéry was skeptical about the police narrative. The day of the plea, Chéry says she turned to her then-husband, Louis’s father, and said: “God said he didn’t do it. People will think I’m really crazy, but he didn’t kill Louis.” Evidence is emerging that her instincts might have been right.

In 2012, after about 16 years in prison, Bogues was granted parole after Chéry and prosecutors declined to oppose it. Not long after, he appeared onstage with Chéry at the Mother’s Day walk. Together, they joined me for an interview on GBH 2 later to discuss their budding relationship. I asked Chéry why she sought to connect first with Bogues’s mother, Doris, then with Bogues himself. She replied: “It could’ve been my son on the other end of that gun. … No winners here.” Bogues, who more than once told me he hoped his own son would grow up to be like Louis, said he’d asked the chaplain for forgiveness.

In late 2021, Chéry, who relentlessly continued to fight to reform a system she argues revictimizes and retraumatizes survivors, suggested that I watch a nearly hour-long video titled “I didn’t kill Louis Brown.” In it, Bogues convincingly contends that he did not receive effective legal representation and that if all the facts had come out, there would have been more than reasonable doubt that he was guilty.

He maintains that the police and prosecutors were guilty of misconduct for a host of reasons. First, they failed to tell the grand jury there were at least two guns involved — that is, there was more than one .45-caliber shell casing with a unique marking at the scene. They did not ask their own witness about a photo lineup in which she picked out someone other than Bogues. And they failed to call an eyewitness who identified the shooter as someone who looked very different than Bogues.

These are not simply the assertions of a man seeking exoneration; they were also confirmed through rigorous investigation by a team of Northeastern law students.

“I just want to know who killed my son,” Chéry said when I called her after watching the video. Why, she wondered, was Bogues the only one from the multi-person shootout who had been arrested?

Every attempt to reopen the case has failed. Most recently, in 2022, the office of the Suffolk County district attorney wrote Chéry saying it was not persuaded that Bogues’s plea was “either unreliable or unjust.”

If history is prologue, when Chéry, a force of nature, takes the stage on Sunday in Dorchester, she’ll make a deep connection to people like her who have suffered unimaginable loss, while giving a special shout-out to people with a loved one whose killing remains unsolved. Most will think she is not in that group. She would disagree.

While the legal system remains resolute in saying justice was done, the people most intimately involved make a compelling case that it was not. Here’s hoping the mother of Louis D. Brown and the son of Doris Bogues finally get the fair hearing they deserve.

In January of 1975, a Black hospital janitor named James Bowden was fatally shot by two white Boston police officers. The Police Department exonerated the officers, but a federal jury found them at fault and awarded the family a settlement of $250,000 five years later. Mayor Kevin White refused to pay the damages, allowing some $600,000 in interest to accrue by the time his successor arrived at City Hall.

In March 1984, Ray Flynn — sworn into office weeks earlier — hand delivered the overdue check to Bowden’s widow, Patricia, in Roxbury. For Flynn and the city he was leading, it was a defining moment. “I hope in a small way this is a symbol of Boston’s commitment to deal with this tragedy,” Flynn told Patricia Bowden.

It also signaled a commitment to fairness, justice, and equality that I saw up close while serving in Flynn’s administration for nearly 10 years. Though sometimes misunderstood, his tenure laid the foundation for the city to become the progressive bulwark it is today.

Revisiting his time in office for my book, The Battle for Boston: How Mayor Ray Flynn and Community Organizers Fought Racism and Downtown Power Brokers, I was reminded of how deeply rooted his principles were. When, in a public housing development, he announced his candidacy for mayor, he signaled his focus would be on poor people. This went beyond policy: When he encountered a homeless person, he would sometimes bring them to a shelter or his own home, he told me.

As a community organizer, I was tapped to lead community engagement for the integration of Charlestown’s all-white Bunker Hill public housing development. Within weeks of Flynn taking office and through collaboration with tenants, religious leaders, community members, and police, Black families began moving into Bunker Hill without incident. This was a sign of what could be accomplished by working with the community. Similar progress occurred several years later in his home neighborhood of South Boston.

Flynn took office during a period of racial unrest, which stemmed from the 1974 federal court-ordered busing. Flynn said his anti-busing stance echoed the concerns of many Black and white parents regarding safety and their authority over their children’s education. He saw schools as a pathway out of poverty, believing they were failing all students.

His position upset his critics, but the racial tensions struck a personal chord. Flynn had grown up in South Boston playing basketball, including on the Roxbury Moulton basketball team, on which he was the first white player. In 1969, he helped launch the Boston Neighborhood Basketball League, which continues to foster peace in the city to this day. Amid the busing crisis, he helped facilitate meetings among leaders of youth sports leagues.

As mayor, he visited the victims of hate crimes reported to the Community Disorders Unit, which was established to address the racial turmoil, and fostered public dialogue through regular reports detailing the unit’s work. With consistent enforcement of civil rights by the police and courts, Boston saw hate crimes drop from 607 in 1978, the year the CDU was created, to 150 by 1987.

Flynn also confronted the downtown power brokers who wielded influence in City Hall: developers, real estate agents, landlords, and bankers. He required developers to fund hundreds of affordable housing units and challenged banks to eliminate racially discriminatory lending practices. He gave neighborhood leaders a seat at the table, and brought down a $40 million deficit and balanced the budget, allowing the city to focus on parks, playgrounds, police, and fire stations. Additionally, he constructed a new Boston City Hospital and renovated public library branches.

At a time when such services were rare in cities across America, Flynn also led by creating an immigrant rights unit, which provided free health care and legal advice to the city’s growing immigrant population. In one case, he provided refuge for 13 Polish defectors fleeing oppressive conditions, a couple of whom slept on couches in the mayor’s office.

No mayorship is without challenges, and Flynn faced criticism for his handling of the Charles Stuart case, which once again heightened racial tensions in the city. Stuart, who killed his pregnant wife, blamed the act on a Black man, setting off a manhunt in the Black community. In 2023, Mayor Michelle Wu would issue an apology to two men falsely linked to the slaying. (Flynn did visit the family of one of those men to apologize, but the meeting did not go well.)

Flynn’s overall legacy, however, has been particularly relevant in the era of Donald Trump, who has sought to rewrite our history as a nation of immigrants. Mayor Marty Walsh fought against Trump’s threats to the immigrant community. More recently, Wu issued a fiery challenge to the federal administration to protect Boston’s immigrant families.

Some may take Boston’s progressivism for granted, but we must not forget how far we’ve come. Mayor Flynn helped establish its enduring foundation, and subsequent leaders have carried the torch. Today, the city embodies equity, fairness, and equality. Let’s keep it that way.

Don Gillis’s book, The Battle for Boston: How Mayor Ray Flynn and Community Organizers Fought Racism and Downtown Power Brokers, was released by Fordham University Press on May 6. Gillis will give book talks at Boston library branches in June. For more information, visit battleforboston.com. Send comments to magazine@globe.com.

Last month, Andrew Owens stopped by the Roxbury headquarters of Josh Kraft’s mayoral campaign to sign up as a volunteer. A few days later, Owens, 38, died from gunshot wounds, incurred around 11 p.m. in Nubian Square, according to Boston police.

The April 19 shooting of Owens and a second victim, who suffered non-life-threatening injuries, drew scant attention — just a brief police report and the listing of Owens’s name in the running tally of homicides reported by Universal Hub, the community news and information site managed by Adam Gaffin. There was no official mayoral response to that loss of life.

Kraft shared the story of the shooting during a recent meeting with the Globe editorial board when he was asked about Mayor Michelle Wu’s description of Boston as the safest big city in America, a framing that is largely attributed to last year’s homicide count. In 2024, there were 24 killings, down from 36 the year before, and the lowest number of homicides in the city since 1957. While it’s “awesome” that the homicide rate is down, Kraft said, “a lot of people feel a lot of fear.”

No mayor can prevent every act of gun violence, and Wu has said that any life lost is one life too many. But celebrating the historically low homicide statistics of last year leaves her open for criticism should they start heading in the opposite direction. So far in 2025, there have been eight homicides, according to Universal Hub. At this time last year, there were four.

As GBH’s Adam Reilly reported last October, whether Boston is the safest city in America depends on how you analyze the numbers and on which cities are used as comparison points. If people feel less safe, that may also be due to reports that some crime is spreading to areas such as Downtown Crossing and the South End, a scenario that is linked to the breakup of encampments at the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard. That spillover effect from Mass. and Cass — what has long been the epicenter of the city’s opioid and homelessness crisis — is something Kraft is pledging to address.

I asked the Wu administration for response to the uptick in homicides, as well as to Kraft’s contention that two youth outreach programs have been disbanded on Wu’s watch. I also asked the administration what the city’s plans are for the upcoming summer months, when gun violence has increased in past years. A spokesperson told me they are working on a response.

Whatever the statistics, for some Boston neighborhoods, violent crime is still a reality. Of the eight homicides so far in 2025, two were in Mattapan, two were in Roxbury, two were in Charlestown, one was in Dorchester, and one was in Allston.

Police are still investigating the April 19 shooting that killed Owens. Through the Kraft campaign, I connected with two people who knew him.

According to Garrick Thames, executive director of Lives Are Meant to Be Changed, a nonprofit that helps people break the cycle of addiction, unemployment, and recidivism, Owens was about to get custody of a daughter. To help make that happen, he had been attending a weekly father’s group meeting, Thames told me in an interview. Owens was known as “Goofy” because of his friendly, outgoing personality, and that’s why he thought he would be a good fit on a campaign.

He said he referred him to the Kraft campaign because he knows Josh Kraft through his work with the Boys & Girls Club, where Kraft worked for three decades.

At Kraft campaign headquarters, Owens met with Dana Jackson, a Kraft supporter who also knows the candidate through his community work. In an interview, Jackson said he talked with Owens about joining other volunteers on April 30 to gather signatures needed to put Kraft’s name on the ballot. Both Thames and Jackson said Owens was excited to be part of that effort. But he never got the opportunity. A door that was opening for him closed when he was fatally shot in Nubian Square. Thames and Jackson both contend that Owens was caught in crossfire and was not a gang member.

When it comes to dealing with gun violence, “we still got work to do,” Thames said. The city could “absolutely” be doing more, he said, especially with more outreach programs to young people. Jackson said that while programs “are not the end-all, be-all, if we’re going to talk about the city being the safest city, how do we explain taking them away?”

Thames told me that Kraft attended Owens’s funeral and memorial service — something Kraft did not mention at the Globe meeting but which a Kraft campaign spokesperson confirmed afterward.

It may not fit the narrative, but not everyone here is safe. In the safest city in America, Owens wasn’t.

Worried the witness would choose not testifying over removing the niqab, the Suffolk district attorney filed an emergency petition with the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court asking that she be allowed to wear it on the stand. Otherwise, Fiandaca’s ruling would be “tantamount to a dismissal” of the case, prosecutors argued.

The request exposed a deep tension between the constitutional rights of religious expression and a defendant’s right to confront an accuser. Both are ingrained principles of the Constitution, and there are rarely easy ways to balance them.

Last Thursday, the woman, whom the Globe is not naming as she says she is a victim of domestic violence, returned to the courthouse as word trickled in that a ruling from a single justice of the high court was imminent.

Minutes ticked by as the sun beamed into the quiet, stuffy courtroom. The defendant sat quietly. He wore a black suit and tie, and only spoke to his attorney next to him.

The ruling landed shortly before noon: Justice Serge Georges Jr. sided with the prosecution and the woman would be allowed to testify.

“The right to confrontation is not absolute,” Georges wrote. He said other courts have “recognized limited and exceptional circumstances in which a defendant’s rights under the Sixth Amendment” to confront his accuser may “appropriately yield to competing constitutional interests.”

Fiandaca acknowledged the ruling and proceeded with the trial. It was the woman’s turn to take the stand.

She entered from the rear of the courtroom. A black covering shrouded the top half of her body with a slit around her eyes. She spoke so quietly that a juror raised a hand, indicating they couldn’t hear. She calmly testified for about one hour, describing the alleged assault by her ex-boyfriend, whom she dated for more than a year until about May 2022.

She testified that about one month after she broke up with him, a noise awoke her around 4:30 a.m. She said she found him downstairs in her Dorchester townhouse, acting belligerent and mumbling incoherently, seemingly drunk.

She urged him to leave but he grabbed her by both arms, hard, she said.

“I could feel his nails digging into my arm,” the woman testified. She clutched her biceps where she said he grabbed her.

The struggle continued as they made their way out the front door, she said. The woman’s boyfriend — now husband — was woken up by the noise. He tried to get between them, she said. Amid the fracas, the ex-boyfriend grabbed her near the neck and punched her in the face, she testified.

“I felt like I was being choked,” she said. “I just felt the hand hitting my mouth.”

An attorney for the defendant, Andrew Lloyd, argued to jurors that the woman’s testimony contradicted evidence that police observed at the scene. Officers, for instance, found no sign of a break-in, he told jurors during his closing arguments.

Lloyd also noted the defendant had been found stabbed and bleeding badly after the confrontation with the woman’s boyfriend. The woman had told police she thought he had arrived at the home already bleeding.

“It’s simply not possible that [he] had arrived with those injuries,” Lloyd argued.

After just over an hour, the six-person jury found the defendant not guilty. He bowed his head.

The woman left the courtroom immediately after the verdict was announced, walking quickly to her car. She was upset, she said, and needed to process it.

Prosecutors did not address the verdict, but in a court filing said the woman had the religious right to testify with her niqab all along. Preventing her from doing so would have dissuaded other victims of assault from wanting to testify.

“This would no doubt embolden those who would commit violence against such persons to do so with impunity,” they argued.

In 2020, Susan Collins looked like an endangered species.

Collins, Maine’s senior senator, was the last Republican member of Congress from New England. Donald Trump was in the White House. Collins, a moderate, had broken with him on major legislation. She faced a well-funded Democratic challenger. And polls suggested that after decades in office, she might actually lose.

Yet Collins ended up winning by nearly 9 points — even as Trump lost Maine to Joe Biden by a similar margin.

Many of the same dynamics still pertain ahead of Collins’s expected run for a sixth term next year. Her staying power seems to have made prominent Maine Democrats wary of challenging her and Maine Republicans content with a senator who sometimes defies Trump. Today’s newsletter explains Collins’s strengths and potential weaknesses.

Collins, first elected in 1996, has survived all kinds of political environments. She’s won in good years for Democrats, like 2008, and in good years for Republicans, like 2014. She’s won after outspending her opponent (2002) and after her opponent outspent her (2020). She’s won under presidents of both parties (Clinton, Bush, Obama, Trump), in midterm and presidential elections alike.

That’s an intimidating record. It may help explain why, even as several high-profile Maine Democrats angle to run for governor next year, no major challenger has yet announced against Collins. (Jordan Wood, a 35-year-old staffer for a former California congresswoman, and a candidate who briefly ran for Senate last year are the only declared contenders so far.)

Senator and governor are different jobs, and seeking an open seat — Governor Janet Mills, a Democrat, is term-limited — is easier. But at least one Maine Democrat who wanted to be a senator in the past — Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who lost to Collins by 37 points in 2014 — is running for governor instead.

Charlie Dingman, chair of the Maine Democratic Party, argues that it’s still early and that challengers will emerge. “I’m aware of and have been talking with a number of folks in the Democratic Party in Maine who are very interested in the opportunity and are exploring it,” he said, declining to name names. “I expect we’ll have a very strong field.”

The most eagerly anticipated entrant may be Mills, 77, who easily won re-election in 2022 and gained national attention when she clashed with Trump earlier this year over transgender athletes. Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, has reportedly talked with her about running. Yet Mills sounds noncommittal.

Chellie Pingree, a US representative who lost to Collins in 2002, sounded similarly undecided when asked about a rematch last November. The state’s other representative — Jared Golden, a fourth-term Democratic moderate — used to work for Collins and seems unlikely to challenge his old boss. Some think he may seek the governorship instead.

Even if Democrats do field a strong challenger, Collins has at least three advantages going for her this year.

One is experience. Nearly 30 years in office have bred a deep connection to voters in a small state where personal touch can transcend partisanship. “It’s the most successful political machine the state of Maine has ever seen,” said Lance Dutson, a strategist who worked on Collins’s past three campaigns.

Another, ironically, is Maine’s blue lean. In 2020, despite having voted to block Trump’s repeal of the Affordable Care Act, Collins faced only token primary opposition — an acknowledgment that she may be the best Maine Republicans can get.

“Collins is somebody that votes with Republicans more than she doesn’t vote with Republicans, supports the Trump administration more than she doesn’t support the Trump administration,” said Nicholas Jacobs, a political scientist at Colby College in Waterville. As other GOP senators face serious threats from more Trump-aligned challengers, no similar movement has yet emerged against Collins.

Collins’s third advantage may be plausible deniability. She chairs the Senate appropriations committee, giving her a powerful perch to break from Trump and other Republicans over tax policy and government funding if she chooses. “It’s a chance to prove her independence,” Jacobs said.

Still, Collins may yet end up with a real race on her hands.

Past polls have underestimated her, but recent surveys find her approval rating underwater and that most Mainers feel she doesn’t deserve another term. That could be because Maine has become a target in Trump’s second term. His administration has sued Maine over trans athletes and tried to withhold federal funding. (Collins said her state should get funding but that Trump was right to scrutinize its gender policies. A spokesperson for her campaign called it “absurd to be polling at this point in the cycle.”)

Next year’s electorate may also complicate her path. Split-ticket voters who backed a Democrat for president and Collins for Senate helped her win in 2008 and 2020. But voters who increasingly support Democrats — whiter, older, and more educated — have been more likely to turn out in recent midterms. That means Collins may face a substantially bluer electorate than in prior cycles.

Her record also offers Democrats plenty to criticize. Collins voted to confirm four of the six Supreme Court justices who struck down Roe v. Wade and controversial Trump nominees like Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Russell Vought, an architect of Project 2025.

For now, Maine Democrats’ best recruiting pitch may be that past isn’t necessarily prologue. “We are seeing such an extraordinary eagerness on the part of the president to dismantle our government wholesale and to do so in a lawless fashion,” Dingman, the state party chair, said. “I just don’t believe that the results of an election in a past cycle are going to discourage people from taking on that challenge.”

RAUW ALEJANDRO “Cosa Nuestra,” the latest full-length from this San Juan-born dynamo, threads salsa, tropicália, and old-school reggaeton through its dancefloor-ready mix of modern música urbana’s heavy beats and insistent hooks. May 17, 8 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

LOS AMIGOS INVISIBLES The long-running Venezuelan funk act throws a Sunday-night rager. May 18, 7 p.m. Brighton Music Hall. 617-779-0140, crossroadspresents.com

SWIRLIES The locally grown shoegaze pioneers play an all-ages show—and given their chosen genre’s recent revival, it’s a perfect opportunity for fuzz aficionados of all generations to come together in the name of blissing out. May 22, 6 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

THE WOLFF SISTERS They describe themselves as a “gritty and raw folk-rock outfit,” and that description fits this Boston-area sister act to a T. And with a musician father and poet mother, you could say that both words and music run in the family. May 17, 7 p.m. $25. The Burren, 247 Elm St, Somerville. 617-776-6896. www.burren.com

MARK SCHATZ AND BRYAN MCDOWELL The weekly Bluegrass Tuesdays event brings a duo with plenty of bluegrass pedigree to Cambridge this week. Both have lent their talents to a multitude of players, including, to name just a handful, Bela Fleck, Tony Rice, Jerry Douglas, Sierra Hull and Alison Brown. May 20, 7 p.m. No cover. Lily P’s, 50 Binney St., Cambridge. www.bluegrasstuesdays.com

PEPPINO D’AGOSTINO Sicilian by birth but American by residence for the past forty years, in that time Peppino D’Agostino has made his mark in the world of fingerstyle guitar, incorporating a gamut of influences and styles to produce what he calls“minestrone music.” May 21, 8 p.m. $30. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. 617-492-7679. www.passim.org

STUART MUNRO

DUKE ROBILLARD BAND New England’s own jump-blues guitar maestro helped found the legendary Roomful of Blues and has played with everyone from Big Joe Turner to Tom Waits. And no less an eminence than B.B. King once called him “one of the great players.” May 17, 8 p.m. Tickets: $33-36. Spire Center, 25 1/2 Court St. Plymouth. spirecenter.org

CONTEMPORARY JAZZ ORCHESTRA EAST Saxophonist and bandleader Christopher Pitts – who’s collaborated with such orchestral jazz avatars as Dizzy Gillespie and Thad Jones – debuts his 16-piece CJO East big band, exciting equal to its original San Francisco iteration, featuring an extraordinary lineup of internationally renowned jazz musicians. May 20, 7;30 p.m. Free. Newton City Hall/War Memorial, 1000 Commonwealth Ave., Newton. jazznation.com/contemporary-jazz-orchestra

MARK ZALESKI’S MIXTAPE SESSIONS The accomplished alto and soprano saxophonist interprets 1990s popular music – top 40 to metal to punk – from a jazz perspective with a distinguished cast: trumpeter Jason Palmer, tenor saxophonist Jon Bean, guitarist Caio Afiune, pianist Peter Vazquez, bassist Matt Dwonszyk, and drummer Jonathan Barber. May 22, 8:30 p.m. Tickets: $18-$34. The Mad Monkfish, 524 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. themadmonkfish.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

MUSIC FOR VIOLS AND FRIENDS Early stringed instrument specialists Olav Chris Henriksen and Carol Lewis are the longstanding Duo Maresienne; they perform an evening of virtuoso pieces from the early Italian baroque period with countertenor and cornetto player Michael Collver. May 16, 8 p.m. Lindsay Chapel, First Church in Cambridge. www.duomaresienne.com

SARASA CHAMBER MUSIC ENSEMBLE Sarasa takes inspiration from three literary figures – Soviet/Russian poet Anna Akhmatova, Japanese author Yukio Mishima, and French poet Charles Baudelaire – in “The Muse,” its final program of the season, which includes pieces by Florence Price, Philip Glass, and Emilie Mayer. May 17, 7 p.m., Friends Meeting House, Cambridge; May 18, 3:30 p.m., Follen Community Church, Lexington

BOSTON PUBLIC QUARTET The Public Quartet and flutist DeShaun Gordon-King offers two performances of “Source Code: Music She Wrote”, featuring music of five women composers including Gabriela Lena Frank, Eleanor Alberga, and Boston’s own Amy Beach. May 18, 3 p.m., First Parish of Milton; May 22, 7:30 p.m. Strand Theatre, Dorchester. www.bostonpublicquartet.com

A.Z. MADONNA

JAJA’S AFRICAN HAIR BRAIDING Directed by Summer L. Williams, with a 10-member cast skillfully navigating rapid-fire crosscurrents of conversation and conflict, this vibrantly alive production offers a showcase of ensemble acting at its finest. Jocelyn Bioh’s play takes place in a Harlem salon on a scorching summer day in 2019. Most of the characters are immigrants — meaning that, for them, the past is often commingled with an increasingly uneasy present — and their individual narratives are strands within a larger story. Through May 31. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, SpeakEasyStage.com

LEARNING HOW TO READ BY MOONLIGHT Natsu Onoda Power directs the premiere of Gaven D. Trinidad’s drama about the struggles of an undocumented Filipino family in 2017-2018 as they try to stay afloat in a hostile political environment shaped by two presidents: Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines and Donald J. Trump in America. We see the story through the eyes of a six-year-old boy who is learning English from an imaginary friend. Coproduction by Company One Theatre and CHUANG Stage features original songs composed by Trinidad. At Plaza Theatre, Boston Center for the Arts, from May 16 – 25. Then at Pao Arts Center, Boston, from May 29 – June 1. Then at the Umbrella Arts Center, Concord, from June 5-8. www.companyone.org

DON AUCOIN

DAVID DORFMAN DANCE Nearing its 40th year, the company is known for lively, engaging dance theater that tackles socially relevant themes in a personal, humanistic way. The Bessie Award-winning Dorfman’s 2024 “truce songs,” which Global Arts Live presents at the ICA/Boston, is an evening length work about healing and peace with text by the choreographer and an original score by Lizzy de Lise and Sam Crawford. May 16-17, $63. Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET SCHOOL NEXT GENERATION This one-night-only performance provides a glimpse of aspiring stars of tomorrow while highlighting the possibilities of the artform moving forward. Featuring dancers of Boston Ballet II (BBII), Graduate Program dancers, and students of Boston Ballet School’s Professional Division at Walnut Hill School for the Arts, the program includes classical excerpts as well as the premieres of Jorma Elo’s “Five Etudes” and Adrienne Canterna’s “Hold Me Tight,” plus works by Paul Craig and Helen Pickett. May 21, $25 and up. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

(JUST) 33 In this Boston Dancemakers Residency Showcase, Nailah Randall-Bellinger / RootsUprising presents a multimedia dance narrative celebrating the life and inspirational music of the late performing artist Donny Edward Hathaway. Using Hathaway’s music and archival documentation, including recorded interviews and photographs, the choreographic work explores the intersection of artistic expression and mental health. May 22-24, $25. (Free video access May 26-30.) Boston Center for the Arts’s Martin Rehearsal Hall. https://bostonarts.org/

CONTINUUM DANCE PROJECT The company presents its immersive dance-theater work “Not Eye, Us,” which explores diversity and the power of perspective. The work aims to create an interactive journey that plays off Michael Alfano’s sculpture “Cubed,” which allows the manipulation of nine moveable pieces, each hued with a different skin tone. May 22, $0-$20. Brookline High School Tappan Street Gym, Brookline. https://continuumdance.org/

KAREN CAMPBELL

EDVARD MUNCH: TECHNICALLY SPEAKING I know, I know: “The Scream,” right? There’s no getting around the cultural oversaturation of Munch’s most famous work, but recent efforts have done much to broaden our understanding of Norway‘s most-loved artist beyond his all-time smash hit. In the summer of 2023, “Edvard Munch: Trembling Earth,” the Clark Art Institute‘s voluminous presentation of the artist’s deep affinities with — and anxieties for — the natural world opened a universe of difference for all but the most devoted Munch fan. “Technically Speaking,” at Harvard, takes a different tack, exploring the artist’s material genius and almost manic enthusiasm for media across painting, drawing, and every manner of printing. With it, a view of an artist too long seen as one-note broadens further. Through July 27. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400,harvardartmuseums.org

HUGH HAYDEN: HOME WORK Hayden‘s first solo exhibition in New England brings with it a decade‘s worth of work centered on his prickly vision of the American Dream – a school desk studded with thorns, un-sittable chairs sprouting thickets of branches, and, in a holistic metaphor of unattainability, cookie-cutter tract homes so tangled with overgrowth that entering is an impossibility. Hayden‘t work, which ranges from the sculptural to the architectural, portrays that dream as “seductive but difficult to inhabit,” a bald truth in this era of housing inaffordability that seems to grows worse by the day. Through June 1. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434,www.brandeis.edu/rose

SOVEREIGN MEMORY: PHOTOGRAPHY, REMEMBRANCE, AND DISPLACED HISTORIES Photography and modernity go hand in hand — the upheavals of a world remade first by colonialism and then industrialization ran right into the new technology, able to capture it firsthand. This exhibition seizes on the medium’s ability to record, but also deceive and reshape collective memory — and, finally, through these artists’ various pieces, be stitched together into something resembling whole. Through June 1. The Davis Museum at Wellesley College, 106 Central St., Wellesley. 781-283-2051,www1.wellesley.edu/davismuseum

MURRAY WHYTE

FRANK POOR The artist grew up in the small town of Woodstock, Georgia. He goes back to the South often to photograph the spaces – details of houses, churches, barns. Back home in his Rhode Island studio, Poor sculpturally builds out from an image of a door, window, or wall, crafting works that mix two dimensions and three dimensions. The vivid visuals of the photos play against the physicality of the spare structures that support them. They pose a question: “what’s real here?” As with a lot of art, the answer is both … and neither. Through June 7. Krakow Witkin Gallery, 10 Newbury St. 617-863-0952, (cq)www.krakowwitkingallery.com

CATE McQUAID

EUGENE MIRMAN SPECIAL RECORDING It has been ten years since Mirman’s last special, “Vegan On His Way To the Complain Store,” came out on Netflix. The Boston comic, who voices Gene on “Bob’s Burgers,” is recording his new hour with two shows Friday, tentatively slated for a fall release through his Pretty Good Friends. Early show is sold out. May 16, 7 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. $37.75. Crystal Ballroom at Somerville Theatre, 55 Davis Square, Somerville. 617-245-2900, www.crystalballroomboston.com

DANAE HAYS: THE FIRST TIME TOUR She was a social media star first, creating country-flavored characters and singing funny country songs on TikTok and IG during the pandemic, but her rise in live comedy has been lightning quick. Hays’s first time doing stand-up was February of 2024, and now she’s touring theaters, and made her Grand Ole Opry debut in March. May 16, 8 p.m. $49-$74. Boch Center Shubert Theater, 265 Tremont St., Boston. www.bochcenter.org

AAPI COMEDY FESTIVAL The second edition of the AAPI Festival kicks off at the Rozzi Square Theater to celebrate Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month with four shows over three days. Nora Panahi, Steph Dalwin, and Courtney Pong serve as hosts with lineups that include Shruti Datari, Peter Liu, Tien Dao, and other stand-ups, magicians, and storytellers. May 22-23 at 7:30 p.m. and May 24 at 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. $22. Rozzi Square Theatre, 5 Basile St., Boston. 617-318-6376, www.rozzisquaretheater.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

GREENWAY SPRING FEST Stop by Spring Fest, formerly the Food Truck Fest, for a variety of free, family-friendly activities. Fitness classes like yoga, pilates, HIIT, and more will be offered from 11 a.m.-2 p.m. (be sure to register ahead to secure a spot). Snag a bite to eat at several food trucks from 11 a.m.-2 p.m., including Mi Corazon Taqueria, Cookie Monstah, and Butter “UR” Biscuit. Visitors can also ride on the Greenway Carousel, as well as check out the Greenway Artisan Market, featuring over 50 local vendors and artists. May 17, 11 a.m.-5 p.m. Free admission, additional vendor costs. Rowes Wharf Plaza, Atlantic Ave. and High St., rosekennedygreenway.org

NEWTON FAMILY FUNFEST Enjoy live performances, food, vendors, and artists throughout the day at the Newton Family FunFEST. The festivities will also include a carnival, the unveiling of the SHINE 2025 student-made art mural, and free community paint and dance parties. Live performances will start at 10:30 a.m. with the O’Shea Chaplin Irish Dancers, and will close with local teen band RedWire at 2:30 p.m. May 17, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Free admission, additional vendor costs. Newton City Hall, 1000 Commonwealth Ave., Newton Centre. newtonma.gov

ESPLANADE COMMUNITY DAY This event will kick off the 2025 Groundbeat Concert Series with “Love Conquers All,” featuring performances by DJ Z.O.O.M, Amanda Shea, Dreion from NBC’s “The Voice,” and more. Food sponsor Bocadillos is giving away its first 100 empanadas free to hungry attendees, who can also enjoy bites and drinks courtesy of Polar and Culture Pop Soda. May 18, 4-7 p.m. Free admission, RSVP encouraged. Hatch Shell Lawn, 47 David G Mugar Way. esplanade.org

HALEY CLOUGH

Despite threats both to the value of downtown office towers and to federal research funding that flows through the city, Boston’s economy is among the strongest in the country and the city has a stable financial outlook, two premier credit rating agencies said this month.

For the 12th consecutive year, Boston has maintained AAA bond ratings from both Moody’s Ratings and S&P Global Ratings — an achievement Chief Financial Officer Ashley Groffenberger likened to winning the “finance Super Bowl.”

“As the current federal administration sows economic chaos and targets the very industries that Boston relies on — health care, life sciences, higher education, climate technology — Boston remains determined to fight back against illegal attempts to undermine our economy and our communities,” Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said Wednesday. “Our AAA bond rating today is proof that despite this federal administration’s best attempts to tear down the pillars of our economy, Boston is well positioned to weather the storm.”

The AAA ratings come amid Wu’s reelection campaign — she faces off this fall against Josh Kraft, a Dorchester nonprofit leader and son of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft — along with ongoing concerns from the business community and elsewhere about the city’s fiscal health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on office values.

Moody’s noted Boston’s “sound fiscal management” and economic resilience, driven by a diverse mix of industries and anchored by world-renowned health care and educational institutions. However, analysts noted that uncertainty regarding tariffs, immigration, and cuts to the National Institutes of Health funding and other federal support for research and education could lead to higher unemployment, slower economic growth, and demographic shifts.

“The city’s resiliency will be challenged over the next several years,” Moody’s Ratings analysts Nicholas Lehman and Thomas Jacobs wrote in a May 8 report.

Another challenge could come from declining values of commercial real estate. Last year, the city’s commercial property tax base fell in value by 2.9 percent — its first such decline in 14 years.

Multiple office properties have recently sold at prices far below their assessed values. The 36-story One Lincoln St. tower, for example, sold at foreclosure auction for $400 million earlier this year after a $1.1 billion refinancing in 2022. The property’s current assessed value is $588 million.

And the 32-story office tower at 99 High St. sold last month for $227 million, some $100 million less than its assessed value.

“We are very concerned and monitoring the ongoing transition that cities across the country and downtowns, in particular across the country, are experiencing with macroeconomic trends that are really reshaping the purpose of commercial office buildings and the occupancy of them,” Wu said Wednesday.

Though some 71.1 percent of Boston’s $4.8 billion budget for fiscal 2026 is generated by property taxes, declining office values shouldn’t translate into a “major revenue disruption” for the city, Groffenberger said. State law restricts how much a city can raise property taxes in any year, and after trying unsuccessfully to do so last year, Wu has again filed a home-rule petition seeking to exceed that limit on commercial property to avoid a steep increase in residential property taxes.

The city’s assessing department has started the process to determine property values for fiscal 2026, Assessing Commissioner Nick Ariniello said Wednesday. That includes asking property owners for information on vacancy, asking rents, and other transactions that the city can use for its fiscal modeling.

“Individual data points kind of help key us in on areas that we maybe want to ask more about, but they don’t define the market for this,” Ariniello said.

What’s more, despite last year’s 2.9 percent commercial property value decline, Moody’s noted it would take a multiyear decline of 10 percent or more in the assessed value of commercial properties to lead to a downgrade in the city’s bond rating.

The AAA ratings have been granted as the city prepares to issue a nearly $500 million general obligation bond next week, which Groffenberger said will fund close to 200 projects, including renovations at schools, parks, and playgrounds, along with new libraries, community centers, and pools, and energy improvement and infrastructure projects. The AAA rating helps Boston sell those bonds at lower interest rates, saving up to $250,000 annually, or $5 million over the life of the bond, that would have otherwise gone to debt service, Groffenberger said.

“This means we can spend more of our taxpayer dollars on the critical services and priorities that residents expect, instead of the costs associated with financing,” Groffenberger said. “It should also give residents the confidence that city leadership is acting in a strong, responsible way with their resources.”

Visit with your canine companion from 6 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 5 p.m. on Friday, and 11 a.m. on weekends (when they have breakfast pizza specials).

Time Out Market Boston (401 Park Drive) welcomes South Boston-based Lulu Green and Café Lulu, serving a vast vegan menu: breakfast sandwiches with scrambled plant-based eggs and fig jam; grilled cheese; a hot honey, plant-based chicken sandwich; cakes; and lattes.

Lens, a student at UP Academy in Dorchester, was hit by the bus just after being dropped off on Washington Street, police said shortly after the crash. At the time of the crash, Lens was with his 11-year-old cousin, who had also just gotten off the bus, according to a family attorney.

The revelations, coming 16 days after Lens was killed, were the most comprehensive accounting of the crash and the first time officials publicly identified Charles as the driver. On Tuesday, Mayor Michelle Wu said the driver had been placed on leave after the crash, which had been the first update since the crash occurred.

Those updates also came after the Globe reported Friday that the bus that struck Lens also struck two parked cars in Wellington Hill in Mattapan before fleeing that scene, according to recordings of Boston police radio calls reviewed by the Globe. And after striking Lens, the driver tried to leave that scene, police reported in those recordings.

Attorneys for Lens’s family, in a statement Wednesday, said the tragedy in Hyde Park “could have been, and should have been, completely avoided.”

“We are dedicated to pursuing justice for the families involved,” said attorneys Matthew Fogelman and Alan Klevan. “We are also dedicated to making changes to any policies and procedures to ensure that something as senseless as this never happens again.”

City and school officials who spoke Wednesday said Charles drove BPS buses for two years and was an employee of Transdev, the district’s transportation contractor.

Officials said Charles underwent drug and alcohol testing, and no sign was found immediately after the Hyde Park crash.

But officials declined to comment on Charles’s driving history, whether he was involved in any other crashes while driving buses for Boston Public Schools, or on the ongoing investigation by Boston police and the Suffolk District Attorney’s office.

Boston police did not respond to questions Wednesday, and a spokesperson for Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden declined comment.

Neither Charles nor Emmanuel Marcellus, the president of the union for Boston’s school bus drivers, could be reached for comment Wednesday night.

A spokesperson for Transdev, which signed a five-year contract with BPS in 2023, did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Transdev, based in France with US headquarters in Illinois, said it operates in 46 states, Washington D.C., and Puerto Rico, as well as 19 countries, according to its website.

Superintendent Mary Skipper, who spoke during a School Committee meeting Wednesday night, mourned the death of Lens as well as that of another BPS student who also recently died. Skipper did not provide details about what happened to the second student, a 14-year-old.

“Anytime we have a student that’s injured or loss of life, we work really directly with the families to try to support them as best we can, and I think, for both of our students, that’s been our focus,” Skipper said.

Skipper said the district is working with Transdev to ensure bus drivers have been appropriately trained and supported following the fatal crash.

In Boston on the day of the crash, Charles was driving a Bluebird Type C71 electric bus that entered the BPS fleet in February 2023, city and school officials said. Charles was a substitute bus driver that day — UP Academy Dorchester had an early dismissal on the first day back from April break, and the route was reassigned to Charles, officials said.

Charles had apparently never driven that route before, they said. No bus monitor — an adult assigned to assist a student as part of their special education plan — was onboard the vehicle at the time, officials said.

But for months, Charles was driving Boston school buses with an expired school bus certificate, which he needed as part of the requirements to drive a school bus in Massachusetts, they said. Under the terms of the contract with Transdev, the company employs the city’s bus drivers, and is responsible for their hiring and training, city and school officials said.

Transdev had notified Charles he needed to renew that certification, but he did not, officials said. Transdev notified the city and school officials about the expired certification following the crash in Hyde Park.

Officials said Charles struck another vehicle on Goodale Road in Mattapan, and the collision was reported in a 911 call to Boston police. Charles, who was transporting Lens and other children at the time of that Mattapan crash, was supposed to report it to the Transdev safety desk at the district’s Freeport bus yard, school and city officials said.

There are five safety supervisors available to respond to accidents across the city, and it is their responsibility to determine whether a school bus involved in a crash can resume its route, officials said. Families of students on a bus involved in a crash are also notified, they said.

Drivers are not authorized to unilaterally decide to leave the scene of a crash, they said.

School officials learned of the Mattapan crash after the one in Hyde Park through Boston police, they said. They shared the information with Transdev so they could investigate further.

On Goodale Road this week, a car with significant front-end damage was parked on the street, and its owner said he had been hit by a BPS bus. He declined to comment further.

According to police radio calls reviewed by the Globe, Charles hit two vehicles in Mattapan before leaving the scene. The Hyde Park crash occurred about 20 minutes after the incident in Mattapan, those recordings indicated.

City Councilor Edward Flynn called the revelations in the case “a troubling development” and called for a City Council hearing to investigate transportation safety protocols and compliance.

“We must immediately review the certification and safety records of every driver to ensure 100% compliance,” Flynn said in a statement. “This must be a top priority.”

City Councilor Erin Murphy said investigators should have released more information about the case sooner.

“When we’re not transparent, and we don’t share the facts, it just allows for rumors to start to take over, and I think that this tragedy, and this family deserve way better,” Murphy said.

Marcela Rodrigues of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

And so, in a move Joseph Stalin or Victor Orban would love, the president took over the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in D.C., the nation’s storied cultural center, installing himself as chair. The old programming was all drag shows and anti-American propaganda, President Trump ludicrously claimed, decreeing that now, “There’s no more woke in this country.” Whatever that means.

Now, art must be about satisfying Dear Leader, and reflecting his vision of Great America. What does that look like? To a president who has slammed the door on almost all refugees except poor, persecuted Afrikaners — the white minority in South Africa who created the brutal system of apartheid — the answer is obvious. So if you want your work to actually reflect what the country looks like, serve everyone, or accomplish some other anti-American, DEI nonsense, no federal funding for you!

Trump is trying to kill outright the National Endowment for the Arts, which funds cultural organizations all over the country. Meantime, his lackeys have pulled back already approved NEA grants from hundreds of groups across the country.

To small outfits like Urbanity, a dance company based in the South End and Roxbury, that has been a sucker punch.

Urbanity runs community dance classes and programs to help improve mobility for people with Parkinson’s. And for a few years now, its performers have worked with student dancers at Boston Arts Academy and others to create “Call of Courage,” a show designed to teach kids about standing up to bullies.

Urbanity won a $15,000 NEA grant to fund this year’s performance, which played before a packed house at the school on March 28. The company fronted expenses, as it has in the past.

“I didn’t have a question in my mind that we would get reimbursed,” said Betsi Graves, who founded the company 15 years ago.

But earlier this month, Urbanity was one of hundreds of recipients of an NEA email pulling the grant. By that point, Graves wasn’t entirely surprised: All of the dance administrators at the NEA had left, and when she had asked for the money, she couldn’t get clear answers. Still, when the grant was pulled, it was a sucker punch, she said.

On top of that, it made no sense. The letter said the NEA was acting to “focus funding on projects that reflect the nation’s rich artistic heritage and creativity as prioritized by the President.” It offered a list of those priorities that reads like a random, AI-generated poem: “projects that elevate the Nation’s HBCUs and Hispanic Serving Institutions, celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, foster AI competency, empower houses of worship to serve communities, assist with disaster recovery, foster skilled trade jobs, make America healthy again,” and more.

Graves could make a convincing argument that preventing bullying keeps America healthy, but what would be the use? It’s impossible for her, or any arts leader, to satisfy this administration. Just as it’s impossible for Harvard, or Canada, or any target of Trump’s senseless tariffs, to do so. The aim of the president and his toadies is chaos. Trump’s ethos is destruction. There is no clear set of demands that could be satisfied, no logic that could guide his many targets through disputes and negotiations. He will always, always move the goalposts. Instability is where his power lies.

There’s nothing for a small arts group like Urbanity to do but try to plug that $15,000 hole somehow.

“Our existence is always precarious,” Graves said. “But it’s especially so now, with regards to the government funding, and just the state of the economy, and not knowing how many donations we’ll receive.”

She worries donors will be chilled by Trump’s crusade against the arts, that their support for Urbanity might make them, too, targets.

But she is not backing down.

“We are not losing sight of our mission,” she said. “All of us artists really have to band together and find new funding structures that will support our values.”

That’s how you stand up to bullies.

The deadly collision killed Lens A. Joseph after he was dropped off on Washington Street on his way home from UP Academy in Dorchester on April 28. On the day it happened, Mayor Michelle Wu said she was “completely heartbroken.” But then it took 15 days for Wu to say the bus driver was suspended. That update, which came on Tuesday, followed a Globe report based on recorded police calls that the same bus had previously hit two other vehicles before striking and killing Lens.

Of course, every investigation is different. But on May 13 in New Orleans, a school bus driver crashed a bus carrying 27 students into an abandoned home. No child was injured. On the same day, the New Orleans Police Department said the bus driver was cited for failing to yield to traffic. In Boston, two weeks after a child was fatally hit by a bus, the public knew little about the circumstances.

According to the Globe’s John Hilliard, around 2:20 p.m. on April 28, a police dispatcher told a cruiser that a caller from Goodale Road in Mattapan saw a school bus hit two parked cars. The dispatcher gave the identification number of the bus — BO15 — and said it “took off.”

City officials, however, said they believe that the bus driver hit only one vehicle and afterward spoke to the owner — but also that the driver did not follow protocol and report that accident to a supervisor.

According to the calls reviewed by the Globe, shortly after the crash involving Lens in Hyde Park, a dispatcher contacted the same cruiser and said, “It’s a completely different incident but that same school bus just ran over a child in Hyde Park.”

On a subsequent recording, a police department member said, “It’s bus number BO15. The driver did try to take off.” Another vehicle blocked the bus in. According to city officials who spoke to the Globe on Wednesday, however, it was unclear if Charles attempted to flee. They said he was talking at the scene of the accident about the need to finish his route. In Massachusetts, leaving the scene of an accident that results in death is a felony.

There are still many unanswered questions. What was his past driving record? City officials said they were not the right source to provide that information. How long did it take Boston police to respond to the first call about the bus hitting the cars? If the police had responded more quickly, could the bus have been intercepted before it struck the child?

“While we grieve this profound loss, we have to confront the serious questions surrounding the circumstances of this incident,” City Councilor Erin Murphy told me in an interview given before city officials provided new details. “When things go wrong, we need to have oversight and accountability. We can’t just ignore it. We can’t allow the administration to not give us information.”

She’s right. But Wu was not pressed very hard for answers by other elected officials.

On April 30, City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune opened the council meeting by asking for a moment of silence to honor Lens. That’s fine, but why not also demand transparency on behalf of all the Boston schoolkids who get on a bus every day?

Of the circumstances surrounding the tragedy, City Councilor Enrique J. Pepén, whose district includes Hyde Park, told the Globe, “I think that it is concerning, just because I know that the community is looking for answers. They’re looking for an explanation as to what happened.”

It’s hard to ignore that this tragedy happened as Wu is running for a second term. Louijeune and Pepén, along with several other Boston city councilors, have endorsed Wu in her bid for reelection. So has Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden, whose office is investigating the incident. That shouldn’t stop anyone from asking tough questions.

On Wednesday, Wu held a press conference to announce that for the 12th year, Boston got a triple-A bond rating. That’s good news, the kind that mayors like to talk about. But sometimes a mayor has to talk about sad and bad news. This is one of those times.

FRANKLIN — An MIAA Board of Directors meeting that began Wednesday with 40 minutes of executive session to discuss ongoing litigation concluded with two approved conferences, a couple of rule tweaks, and possibly a new process for adding member schools.

The two new leagues — the Massachusetts Charter School Athletic Conference and the Central Massachusetts Athletic Conference — were both approved by unanimous 19-0 votes. The charter conference vote had been tabled at the March meeting, but after Pioneer Charter School athletic director Phil Signoroni allayed concerns Wednesday, namely that every school has an AD, is already an MIAA member, and none will be departing other conferences, it breezed through.

“The idea of getting everyone into the MIAA and following their rules takes a lot off our plate,” Signoroni said. “Now, we’re not regulating. All our schools are 100 percent expected to follow all MIAA rules and requirements.”
