Everett had been studying mending in 2018 when she met Vernée Peacock Wilkinson, of Boston, and the two felt a strong bond. Both lifelong sewing practitioners, they teamed up to teach an online sewing course early in the pandemic, when they began to ruminate on the historic role of mending as “women’s work,” and how that was emphasized in early COVID times through mask-making. Together, they founded Mending Church as a way to formalize sharing what Everett called the “embodied practice” of mending with others.

“The world can be breaking. My heart can be breaking. My relationships can be breaking,” said Everett. She said that for white people who attempt to think about racism and social justice, it can be common to intellectualize the practice without — especially in New England — feeling that gravity in their bodies. “I know my prayers are stronger when I can see the pin-pricks and feel them on my fingers because I’ve been stitching,” she said.

Around Boston, practitioners attend repair workshops at public library-based Fix-It Clinics, and in Somerville, Homme Repair offers “bespoke mobile tailoring” and denim repair clinics. To help assess whether something can — or even should — be repaired, Mending Church guides its participants through a “discernment process.”

Using a University of Kentucky checklist, the questions can be seen as tenderly personal as they are textile-inspired, said Wilkinson. Is the object worthy of repair? How extensive is the damage? And do I have the skills to take on the process?

“I really love where it’s asking, ‘Am I going to be putting this back into use?’” she said. “When you evaluate a relationship and you’re working on some form of repair, is it a healthy relationship that has the foundation and can rebound from a misstep or a misunderstanding, or has the damage come to a point where it needs to be assessed?”

In addition to mending workshops, the duo also works with indigo plant dye as a way to point to reparations work. Indigo was used as a slave trade crop, and it has also has been used in medicinal practices. Mending Church hosts circles for Black women to work with indigo as a means to acknowledge that history, and to help return its knowledge and history to those in connected ancestry, said Wilkinson.

The group aims to go deeper than a traditional crafting social.

“There’s lots of places in life where someone can go and learn how to stitch,” said Wilkinson. “But there’s not many spaces where people are coming together to think about what that also means internally.”

The metaphors flow beyond the mending process itself, especially when using intentionally visible mending methods. Some mending styles aim to be seamless, but visible mending may showcase stitches by using contrasting colors, for example.

“Repair doesn’t mean perfection,” said Peacock. “There still might be scars on the other side; that doesn’t mean we didn’t do repair.”

Mariko Sugimori, a Brookline-based visible mending educator, is the child of parents she describes as crafty and frugal, who inspired her own love of the practice.

“It shows a history of the garment, and maybe you have more of a relationship with it, rather than thinking of it as something you just discard,” said Sugimori. “It’s something that is worth maintaining and keeping.”

How might something be deemed unworthy of repair? For Sugimori, sustainability is a motivator, so “downcycling” a garment might be a way to find a new use without tossing it completely. For example, a pair of bicycling pants too full of holes to function could evolve into patches for something else, and in doing so, allow sentimental connections to the garment to live on.

“Is that repairing, or is it re-creating something new?” she posed.

Mending can inspire resilience during turbulent economic and political times, suggested Lisa Graustein, who leads mending workshops in Dorchester.

“In the current context, where it seems like many things are going to get more expensive, there’s going to be more disruptions in in the economy and the supply chain, the ability to fix what we already have access to, to share what we have and be able to alter it in ways that work for other people is going to be increasingly important,” she said.

She loves visible mending because it can appear defiant.

“In a culture that really demands and expects perfection, that expects our bodies to look a certain way, [visible mending] says, ‘Oh no, I’m gonna put a bright orange patch on this purple sweater,’” she said.

In Providence, artist Zoë Barbano Grinder expanded her improvised patchwork and began offering on-demand mending at public markets, including darning, zipper repair, and other fixes.

“People bring me really loved things that they would otherwise just throw into a landfill,” she said.

(While Massachusetts banned textiles from landfills in 2022, clothing waste remains a major environmental problem in the United States.)

“People have relationships with their clothing,” she said. “I like to think clothing is kind of like our second skin, and our bodies age, and our skin gets older, and it changes and it grows.”

Grinder points to a sweater that was given to her by her father years ago.

“Every time it gets a new hole, I get really excited because I get to add another patch to it, and I get to look back and see patches that I did when I was as early as, like 16, 17 [years old],” she said. “It’s kind of like a wearable testament to my age.”

Grinder, who has worked in clothing manufacturing, said there is no clothing made without human hands in some way, despite the prevalence of machines.

“To me, it is respecting not only my time and handiwork, but respecting the handiwork of other people who I don’t know, but I know made my clothes,” she said.

And over time, other threads can emerge.

“I think it’s made me consider how I approach problems,” she said. “It’s made me rethink, from what point do I begin fixing an issue?”

Her repair work has inspired Grinder to slow down and not rush for a solution in interpersonal conflicts. And it’s just like patching a sweater.

“You can’t just start patching at the corners, at the little frayed edges,” said Grinder. “You have to take a step back and really think through your actions. . . . I have at least one old man at the market who comes by and asks me if I can mend his broken heart, too.”

It is probably true that not everything can be fixed. But for the things — and people — we deem worthy of our devotion, some argue that learning to repair is a worthwhile and necessary practice. And while what we fix may no longer be the same, it might, after all, become better.

It was the latest reminder that, each summer, dozens of beaches in Massachusetts close because of pollution from downpours that wash stormwater and sewage into swimming areas. This year, several new initiatives by advocacy groups and legislators are aiming to make the state’s water bodies more swimmable.

The Charles River Watershed Association has spearheaded a campaign called “Cut the Crap” to address sewage connections to street-level stormwater systems, state legislators have filed bills to set targets to reduce discharges and eventually eliminate those connections, known as combined sewage overflows, while two municipalities are piloting a UV light system to kill bacteria on some of the state’s most notoriously polluted beaches.

Portions of sewer systems in Massachusetts that were constructed in the late 1800s allow sewage from homes and businesses and stormwater runoff to move through the same pipes. Normally, these flows are sent to treatment plants, but during heavy rains and storms, the systems become overloaded and release excess flows into the nearest body of water so that sewage doesn’t back up in homes and streets. The heavy rain also draws bacteria from surrounding areas into the river.

Back in 1987, there were a total of 84 active sites discharging combined sewage flows into Boston Harbor and the Charles, Mystic, and Neponset rivers, according to the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority; around 46 of these are still active, according to a December 2024 report.

The MWRA has a long-term control plan for most active discharge sites. There are 10 locations along the Charles in Cambridge and Boston where sewage overflows are discharged during storms.

“That rain flushes out whatever’s dripping from dumpsters, bacteria from city streets, and stuff from our pipe network,” said Max Rome, stormwater program manager at the Charles River Watershed Association. Heavy rain also draws pollution from areas upstream, such as the Watertown Dam, Rome said.

Combined sewage overflows have long been an issue, but there is renewed energy around making public waterways in Massachusetts safer. The Charles River Watershed Association has been advocating for bills that would require municipalities and other operators to eliminate combined sewage overflows by December 2050. Rome said legislative action was needed to finally “finish the job” because the federal Clean Water Act of 1972 largely encouraged incremental progress on eliminating pollution in rivers.

For example, rather than eliminating all combined sewage overflows, MWRA’s long-term control plans focus on reducing discharges below to meet minimum levels set in 1985. Of the MWRA’s active discharge sites, there are six in particular that present “significant challenges,” according to the agency’s December report.

“We’re very worried about those six sites, especially in wet years because there’s no clear plan,” Rome said. “Legislative efforts would speed that up and clarify goals.”

In June, advocates and members of the public testified at the State House in favor of a bill that would require municipalities and other operators to eliminate combined sewage overflows by December 2050. The bill, sponsored by Democratic State Representatives Greg Schwartz of Newton and David Rogers of Cambridge, would set more stringent reduction targets for combined sewage overflows within six months of becoming law.

Mark Jacobson, vice president at Charles River Recreation, which rents paddle boats on the Charles and Mystic Rivers, said pollution from those overflows routinely shuts paddling for his customers.

“It’ll look like a nice Saturday that’s perfect for paddling, but the water quality is just not good enough,” Jacobson said.

He’s also worried about cyanobacteria blooms in the Charles. Excess phosphorus from stormwater runoff and warmer temperatures cause the blue-green algae to explode into a toxic “bloom” that can cause skin rashes, irritation of the nose, eyes, and throat, gastrointestinal distress, dizziness, and even more serious problems. Warmer temperatures caused by climate change have made these blooms more frequent.

This year would have been the eighth iteration of City Splash, which was started by the Charles River Conservancy in 2013. Laura Jasinski, executive director of the Conservancy, said the cancellation offered an opportunity for people to learn and discuss the health of the river.

She is pleased with the work so far to remove some sewage overflows along the Charles, but wants people to be more cognizant of how new construction contributes to the pollution problem. Jasinski is especially concerned about the project to realign the Massachusetts Turnpike in Allston that will free up space near the Charles for new development that could potentially increase stormwater pollution.

“If we put down lots of pavement instead of more parkland in the I-90 project, there will be more pollutants in the river,” Jasinski said.

Swimmers looking to cool off along the coast have had to make other plans, too. Constitution Beach in Boston and others in Winthrop and Swampscott were closed for swimming as of Tuesday, July 29, because of high levels of bacteria. The state’s Department of Public Health provides an online list of beach closures that is updated daily.

Some beaches in Boston and Lynn have a history of elevated bacteria levels. But the frequency and timing of closures of other beaches can fluctuate dramatically based on rainfall and environmental conditions, a DPH spokesperson said.

The department tests the water at around 1100 public and semi-public beaches across the state for the bacteria Enterococci. At Donovans Beach in Winthrop, bacteria levels were more than 14 times the allowed limit as of the last test on July 23.

In June, officials in Lynn and Swampscott began a three-month pilot program to use ultraviolet light to treat the water near King’s Beach, one of the most frequently closed for high bacteria levels. Seawater is pumped through a system that exposes it to UV light to kill bacteria and then discharged back into the ocean. The water is sampled daily to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment.

Swimming in unsafe waters can cause nausea, diarrhea, skin rashes, and ear aches, according to the Department of Health’s website. The department tests water every two to three days for many beaches and closes beaches to swimmers when bacteria levels exceed the limit for two consecutive days. Beaches with a history of multi-day exceedances are required to close to swimmers after just one test result that exceeded the allowed limit.

And while Morrissey’s office has a high rate of resolving homicide cases compared to the national average, it trails its State Police peers in Massachusetts with the lowest clearance rate of murders among the state’s 11 district attorneys: investigators in Norfolk County solved 82 percent of 57 homicides, a Boston Globe review of cases between 2015 and 2024 found.

In Massachusetts, homicide investigations in all but four cities are handled by State Police units attached to the local district attorney, an elected position.

Homicide clearance rates at the other State Police squads ranged from 88 percent at the Essex and Plymouth district attorneys, to 91 percent or higher in the remaining offices, the Globe found. Combined, the State Police units at the 11 offices had a clearance rate of 92 percent for the 848 homicides they investigated during those years. (Clearance in this circumstance means a case has been solved, though it does not mean there has been a conviction.)

All of those results are much higher than elsewhere: The average nationally hovers around 57 percent. The clearance rate in Worcester, one of the four Massachusetts cities that conduct their own investigation, was 71 percent from 2015 to 2024. Rates for the other three cities, Boston, Pittsfield, and Springfield, were not immediately available.

Morrissey has faced mounting scrutiny, particularly over his investigation of Read in the death of her boyfriend, Boston police Officer John O’Keefe, and his handling of the death of Birchmore, a young pregnant woman.

Morrissey’s office declined to make him available for an interview. In an email, a spokesperson said its homicide clearance rate is “well above the national average” and in line with district attorneys serving similarly sized populations.

He also said the term unsolved is “misleading,” because it “implies that the case is done and there are no further leads.”

“That is not the situation with a majority of those cases,” the spokesperson said. “A majority of the ‘unsolved’ cases are active and ongoing and are being investigated.”

State Police consider cases solved or “cleared” if investigators make an arrest, obtain an arrest warrant, or “can determine the responsible party with certainty,” an agency spokesperson said.

In a statement, State Police Colonel Geoffrey Noble, who joined the agency last year, said the department has implemented “advanced training, oversight, and accountability to improve outcomes.”

“Under my leadership, we will continue to strengthen our partnership with each district attorney’s office and invest in investigative services that deliver answers, secure justice, and serve the people of Massachusetts,” Noble said.

In July, , a new commander, State Police Detective Lieutenant Jeffrey Perry, took control of the detective unit in Morrissey’s office, the State Police spokesperson said.

Morrissey’s office has faced a public reckoning over its job performance with demonstrators gathering outside its Canton headquarters, courthouses, and elsewhere to protest the prosecution of Read and its finding — with the state medical examiner’s office — that Birchmore killed herself.

A jury in June acquitted Read of any responsibility in O’Keefe’s death. Separately, federal officials last year concluded Birchmore was murdered and the FBI arrested former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell, who had a sexual relationship with her. He was charged with strangling her and has pleaded not guilty.

State Police said the investigation into the fatal shootings of Porter and Santos-Andrade is active. Some relatives of the victims also kept tabs on Read’s case as it wound through the courts.

Porter’s father, Les, said he sought a meeting with detectives last year after Michael Proctor, the lead investigator in both his son’s case and in the Read trial, was suspended over misogynist texts he wrote about Read, which became a central factor in her trial. Proctor was ultimately fired.

“I am the father of a child that was murdered,” Les Porter said. “I wanted to make sure Proctor was no longer on the case, and I wanted to meet the new person who was.”

In Morrissey’s jurisdiction, all 10 unsolved homicides involve shootings that occurred outdoors, and in all but one case, the victims were Black or Latino males. Two occurred in Weymouth, two in Randolph, and the others in Norwood, Sharon, Holbrook, and Foxborough.

In general, outdoor shootings that kill Black people tend to have lower clearance rates than other murders, experts said.

In many outdoor shootings, there’s no DNA evidence and, if the violence was related to gang or other criminal activity, witnesses sometimes refuse to cooperate, they said.

Police distrust among some in the Black community is also considered a factor in lower clearance rates in killings of Black people, said Philip J. Cook, professor emeritus at Duke University.

“There may be more difficulty in conducting a successful investigation with a community that is inclined to wonder whether the police really care about them and whether the police have their best interest at heart,” Cook said. “It can be a vicious cycle.”

Norfolk County’s suburban settings produce other challenges for investigators. Unlike their urban counterparts, suburban neighborhoods may not have as many surveillance cameras, and emergency responders may take longer to reach crime scenes, said Christina Miller, associate clinical professor at Suffolk University Law School.

Thaddeus Johnson, a senior fellow at the Council on Criminal Justice, a nonprofit in Washington, D.C., said solving homicides and other violent crimes is the best way to make communities safer.

“It sends a message that you will be caught,” he said. “Making arrests also proves to the public that police can do their damn jobs.”

Les Porter and Santos-Andrade’s mother, Edna, said investigators have hinted at the possibility someone suspected in the shooting may have died before charges could be brought, but didn’t reveal details.

Rodriguez, Jahzier Les Porter’s mother, said she and two of her daughters were sitting by a window overlooking her street when her son, a Braintree High School student, and Santos-Andrade were shot at 1:30 a.m. on June 25, 2023. Porter and Santos-Andrade were seated in a vehicle with two others, who escaped.

Home security video viewed by the Globe captured the drive-by shooting, but the recording is too dark to identify anyone.

Santos-Andrade became a father shortly before the shooting, his mother said, but he was consumed by thoughts of death and recorded rap music about his fears.

“All he talks about is him dying, and people [wanting] him dead,” Edna Santos said. “It’s as if he predicted his own destiny.”

At the time of his murder, Santos-Andrade himself had been charged with shooting a former friend in Dorchester in January 2023, court records show. That spring, he relocated to Braintree to live with his girlfriend, Porter’s sister. Santos said she thought leaving Boston would be good for her son.

She said she met with an investigator. They have suspects, he told her, but no evidence, she said.

Meanwhile, four years after her son was killed, the mother of another shooting victim in Norfolk County said she’s losing hope investigators will solve his murder. Eric Small Jr., 30, was killed attending a birthday party in Weymouth in January 2021.

Troopers made an arrest on a related gun charge in 2021 and the investigator in Small’s case is “focused on achieving the best outcome,” the State Police spokesperson said.

“There’s a lot of things for me that are left unanswered,” Annie Small said. “It seems as though this might be a cold case.”

Inside the meaty mass that science classifies as the human brain, there typically comes a moment, probably several, when the meat will stare at an expanse of water and tell itself that it should buy a boat.

They are all good reasons, those wishes and whys. Ancient. Curious. Independent. Perhaps fleeting. But sometimes they become yearnings, returning, until you execute a before-and-after moment for your life and bank account and become the captain of your own vessel.

Don’t do it. Listen to what everyone who has ever lived with a boat will warn you. You don’t want a boat. You want a friend with a boat. Or, better yet, a dad with a boat. A role I now find myself in because I didn’t listen.

My oldest turns 16 on Saturday, and to celebrate, he wants to take our boat, my boat, a 25-year-old Boston Whaler, by himself for the first time, with his friends, into that predictable body of water we call the Atlantic Ocean.

He’s responsible, has been hustling digging clams this summer, and deserves to have his maiden voyage with the fellas be everything he wants it to be. Because that’s how they get you, the boating gods. The day you buy it and the day you sell it are the only good days they guarantee.

He will feel infinite, I’m sure. The horizon is yours. That quickly drains, like so many such feelings, leaving behind a reality that being in charge of a boat, and the lives on board, involves long periods of stress that something bad or expensive is going to happen, interrupted only by bills when they do.

I’ve had two boats since 2018 — moving from an old 13-foot Whaler to an old 18-foot Whaler — and didn’t listen to Louis C.K. when he said you can’t afford a boat unless you can afford 10 boats. They weren’t expensive boats, but all boats are expensive, and in the time I’ve had them I’ve had unforgettable nautical events like blowing an engine off the backside of Crane Beach, and a trailer wheel bearing exploding on I-95 in Needham at 5 p.m. on a Friday.

Yes, I have found magic on rivers and oceans, but each time there is less I don’t know, and what was once just a river or an ocean is now currents and tides and rocks and sandbars, not to mention other boaters who may or may not be under the influence of a Jimmy Buffett-level of tequila. Everything is seeking to destroy you at the wheel, while your passengers work on their tans and think idyllic thoughts like, “I should buy a boat.”

I’ve always been an ocean guy, but never a boat guy. Then my sons were born obsessed with fishing — the one water activity that never interested me — and they soon infected me. And there’s only so much time you can spend scrambling across wet rocks with a long surfcasting rod chasing striped bass before they convince you that this would be much better from a boat.

Have you ever backed a boat down the town ramp on a Saturday before an impatient audience of other boaters? Then imagine your battery dies, but not before having just enough juice to lower the engine so you can’t pull the boat back out, and now you’re just blocking the ramp. It’ll make you feel like Jacques Cousteau.

I’d give anything to be free of the trailer, keep the boat in the water where it belongs, but a slip at a marina in my town will run me about five grand for my small center console. Who has that kind of money? A lot of people, apparently, because there’s a long wait to get one. But nowhere near as long as for one of the moorings owned by the town. You need to put your kids on the list for their kids to get one. Maybe. No one ever gives them up.

In truth, the whole thing is hard to give up, because of all the wishes and whys that do come true on the water. I’ve had Technicolor moments, like when my younger son was 11 and caught a striped bass so big he couldn’t lift it, so he laid down next to it for a photo. Or those early mornings when the Great Marsh is waking and flocks of birds dive-bomb the surface, telling you exactly where to cast your rod.

Or the other night, when I was cruising through Gloucester Harbor just as the golden hour arrived and a sweltering hot day felt cool on the ocean, lounging in the bow, beer in hand, on my friend’s boat. Most I did was take off my sunglasses.

And it was there that I willed into being a third category of nautical freedom: a son with a boat. That’s what’s got to happen here. I don’t let him use my boat. I let him have it.

So Happy Birthday, buddy. I got you a boat. It’s in the driveway. The horn and GPS aren’t working for some reason. And it sometimes smokes when you’re idling. And don’t forget to put the plug in. And you’re going to have to share it with your brother when he’s older. But it’s yours now.

My son has a boat. It’s a foolproof plan. My meaty mass is never wrong about these things.

It’s made Pelton’s portfolio that much more challenging too.

With $1.7 billion in assets, The Boston Foundation is a multifaceted organization, Pelton told The Boston Globe, and it’s using all its tools to “meet the moment.” In the last several months, the foundation hasdistributed over $2.6 million in safety net grants to over 75 local organizations facing economic uncertainty due to federal funding cuts.

“We’re different than most foundations in the breadth of what we do,” he said. “Grantmaking is a part of what we do, but it’s only a tiny fraction. We convene, we bring people together. We advocate, and we spend a lot of time in the community meeting community needs and listening to the community.”

And among the most urgent crises, he said, has been responding to the needs of community organizations experiencing a pullback in funding for emergency food benefits.

“I’m appalled at this mean-spirited federal administration that would deprive hungry people of food by cutting their access or diminishing their access,” Pelton said. To respond, the foundation raised $1 million from donors to support the Greater Boston Food Bank. An additional $500,000 will be awarded to other local and regional food organizations.

“The secret sauce for us is that we’re able — our community is able — to catalyze additional dollars" quickly to respond to urgent needs, Pelton said. “Our hope is that our community will contribute even more.”

The Boston Foundation also conducts research on issues critical to Boston’s future, and uses those findings to inform its advocacy and grantmaking. “An important aspect of the Boston Foundation is this wonderful research center called Boston Indicators,” he said. “They provide the direction and insight on big topics not only for us but for the city.”

One striking example, he said, was the foundation’s work on the housing crisis. As Boston Indicators has been tracking the various factors that make living here so challenging, the foundation has designed funding programs to address those needs.

“We’re working with the Massachusetts Housing Partnership on a down payment assistance program that will help families who might not otherwise be able to afford to actually get into [homes],” he said. “If we invest $25 million in the down payment assistance program for 500 families, we can create [between] $155 to $170 million of asset growth equity over the next ten years. And that’s wealth that’s not only for those individuals and families, but it’s intergenerational because it will be passed on.”

Pelton says the legacy of the foundation has been being there for Bostonians at critical moments and helping them improve their status in life. But it’s also about helping neighborhoods move forward too.

Standing outside the Bruce C. Bolling Building in Nubian Square, Pelton recalled arriving in Boston from Kansas nearly 50 years ago to attend graduate school at Harvard University. During the summer, he used to take the Number 1 bus from Cambridge to work in a coat factory in Roxbury. As he wandered the neighborhood one recent afternoon, he marveled at the changes underway, and said he’s proud of the work the foundation is doing to support a renaissance there.

“I could not have imagined, first of all, that I would be back here as the president and CEO of the Boston Foundation,” he said, grinning.

Pelton pointed around the square at various projects sprouting up: The Jazz Urbane nightclub is under construction. The Franklin Cummings Tech Center is moving in nearby, relocating its campus from the South End. The Haley House Bakery Cafe is reopening soon with affordable housing units stacked above it. He said the foundation will have a hand in supporting each of these endeavors.

“To come here and help revitalize this very important part of Boston,” was a personal mission for him, Pelton said, but one that couldn’t have happened without the resources of the foundation. “The important thing to remember, we’re in the center of Boston,” he said. “Symbolically it is, I think enormously important.”

After Pelton earned his PhD at Harvard, he went into academia and eventually climbed to serve for a decade as president of Emerson College. That experience offered him unique insight into the challenges his alma mater is facing today, he said.

“Alan Garber has been just absolutely heroic. The way in which he has stood up and spoken out against this, really outrageous, mean-spirited actions that the federal administration has taken against higher education,” he said. “This is a time to be strong. This is the time to speak out and to speak up. And for those presidents and those institutions that don’t, shame on them.”

Assessing the gauntlet of challenges facing the city, Pelton believes the foundation can use its levers to help navigate the uncertainty.

“We’ve had other moments in our history that were really challenging. And this is one of them,” he said. “I have great faith in this city. I have great faith in the people who live in this city.”

It may take a while for uncertainty to subside, he said. “But it won’t be forever,“ he continued. ”And of course we’ll be stronger for it.”

HomeBASE has become a go-to option to move people from shelters, but shelter operators, nonprofits, and volunteer groups said they have had to get creative to make the program money stretch during a years-long process to help families become self-sufficient.

Nadine, an asylum-seeker who asked the Globe to withhold her last name because of deportation concerns, moved to her three-bedroom HomeBASE unit last year after sharing a shelter apartment with other families. She initially was able to make rent comfortably on her wages as a home health aide, despite using HomeBASE for her broker’s fee and first and last month’s rent. But after her boyfriend moved out and she lost her job in April, Nadine struggled to pay her third of the roughly $3,000 rent.

She has now turned to a volunteer refugee resettlement organization for rehousing.

“HomeBASE had to pay a bigger share, so the money went out a lot quicker,” Nadine said in a Zoom interview with the Globe on Thursday.

Nadine’s path through the emergency shelter system into a HomeBASE apartment and, now, out of it, captures the concerns of many advocates at housing nonprofits and refugee resettlement agencies who help homeless parents get on their feet.

More than 1,500 families have left the state’s hotel shelters since November, following Governor Maura Healey’s announcement they would close by July 31, six months ahead of schedule, according to a housing office spokesperson. Twenty-four hotel shelters were shuttered by June 30, and the last four are scheduled to close this week.

Some parents, like Nadine, had to alter their plans after the state canceled third-year extensions of the program in June.

Families in the program must dedicate at least 30 percent of their monthly income toward rent; HomeBASE pays the rest directly to the landlord. Secondary expenses, such as moving expenses, which can amount to upward of $10,000, are deducted from the total subsidy.

The less a family makes in income each month, the more of their HomeBASE money is used to cover rent and the sooner it runs out.

A housing office spokesperson said HomeBASE is a “cost-effective” affordable housing program at a time of state budget constraints, federal cuts, and a housing shortage.

“HomeBASE has been critical in helping thousands of families leave the shelter system in the past year alone, which is an important part of how we have been able to reduce the size and cost of the shelter system,” the spokesperson said in an email to the Globe on Monday.

Kyrenecia Casterlow, a HomeBASE stabilization manager for the nonprofit Metro Housing Boston, said families sometimes do not understand how long HomeBASE money will last.

“‘I understand that this is what you thought you were going to get, but let me tell you how your funding broke down,’” Casterlow said she tells parents.

Leaders of nonprofit organizations working with shelter families said they found work-arounds to these shortfalls. Some workers rented U-Haul trucks for families from hotel shelters to “shop” at large warehouses full of donated furniture.

Nonprofit leaders also said they raised funds for rent payments, negotiated rent and fees down, and in many cases, explained HomeBASE to landlords who had never heard of the program.

Making matters more challenging for service providers is the expensive and competitive housing market. Nonprofit workers who spoke to the Globe described scouring the internet daily for apartment listings and racing to make inquiries wherever they popped up. Casterlow even directed her team to reach out to developers as soon as they saw a building foundation being laid to reserve spots on the tenant waitlist.

Some experts are concerned Massachusetts is not allocating enough money to ensure families cross the finish line. HomeBASE received $57.3 million in the budget for fiscal 2026, the same amount as last year, despite increasing housing costs.

The program now faces budget constraints, with its funds hovering below the $59.4 million it received in 2023, more than double its budget the year previous as new arrivals of foreign migrants spiked. In August of that year, Healey declared a state of emergency in the shelter system, as the state’s caseload hit 5,500 families — 2,000 more than it typically serves, according to a November 2024 report by a special commission on the emergency housing system.

“At some point, we were just running out of space to put folks,” Mark DeJoie, CEO of shelter operator Centerboard, said. “This system is a shelter system, it’s not an immigration crisis system, that’s what it turned into on a dime.”

More than 1,100 families in long-term shelter as of July 24 — or about 35 percent of all families — entered as migrants, refugees, or asylum-seekers, according to the most recent update by the housing and finance offices.

Many of them are racing to secure work permits before their HomeBASE funds run out.

At the Immigrant Family Services Institute, Elizabeth Davis-Edwards, the founder and CEO of the volunteer refugee resettlement organization WelcomeNST, ran through a documentation checklist with Nadine: asylum status, work authorization, driver’s license.

When Nadine pulled out her driver’s license, providing the final proof of qualification for rehousing, the interviewers broke out in cheers and applause. Her family is one of 10 who have been matched so far to a volunteer resettlement team, which will raise rent money and help Nadine find a job to eventually support herself and her son.

Nadine smiled with relief as she stood up to hug Davis-Edwards.

“NST was really my only option,” she said Thursday. HomeBASE “was a dead end for me.”

Rodriguez, who grew up in Boston and played at West Roxbury High, will never reach that point. The 5-foot-10-inch guard — scrappy, relentless, and unflappable by nature — uses setbacks and lowered expectations as fuel.

Five days after a round of chemotherapy, and two days before another, the 30-year-old Rodriguez took the court with the same fearlessness he’s had his entire life.

“Something about me just doesn’t allow me to watch and sit. I can’t,” Rodriguez said. “That’s the love of the game. I love basketball. If I’m going to die, I’m dying on that court.”

Born in the Bronx, Rodriguez moved to Boston as a kid and began to develop his love for basketball with the Boston Spartans.

As a freshman at West Roxbury, he garnered early college interest. He transferred to Redemption Christian Academy in Troy, N.Y., where he learned the value of discipline by eating, showering, and sleeping on a regimented schedule.

Rodriguez, who didn’t have much of a support system growing up, evolved from a kid who did whatever he wanted to someone who mapped out a blueprint and stuck to it.

“If basketball failed for me, I felt like I was going to fail in life,” he said.

He sharpened his skills through playing for BABC under founder Leo Papile, who advised him to go the junior college route to improve his grades and build toward his Division 1 dream.

Rodriguez ranked eighth in the nation in scoring (22.8 points per game) at Marshalltown Community College in Iowa, which sparked interest from West Virginia, Colorado State, and others.

“My life changed,” Rodriguez said. “I became exactly who I felt like I was supposed to be.”

He decided on Southern Illinois, where he started every game for two seasons and led the Salukis in scoring (12.9 PPG), assists (4.0), and steals (45) as a senior.

Rodriguez then launched his professional career with stops in Canada, Colombia, Iceland, the UK, Puerto Rico, and the Dominican Republic.

Puerto Rico was his favorite, Colombia made him feel like a star with an “Ole, ole, ole, ole, Speedy Rodriguez” chant, and Canada treated him like he was LeBron James.

But seven days after he signed with St. John in Canada, Rodriguez’s life changed forever. While working at Papile’s restaurant in November 2024, Rodriguez went home, tried to use the bathroom, and wasn’t able to do so.

“My stomach started hurting like someone stabbed me,” he said.

In his family, the expectation is that sancocho, a stew, and ginger ale can cure everything, but he couldn’t digest anything so he went to the hospital.

They asked if he could stand up straight, and when he said no, they declared it was his appendix. Morphine stopped the pain temporarily, but it quickly returned and led to a three-plus-week stay in the hospital.

Doctors sent him home, but he couldn’t use the bathroom once again, so he rushed back. They sent him for a colonoscopy on Jan. 26, and almost immediately the surgeon spotted a tumor.

“She told me I had cancer,” Rodriguez said. “I was like, ‘What are you talking about? I have a game tomorrow.’ ”

The months since have tested Rodriguez’s patience. He smiles in public, and finds freedom on the court, but in private he has been the victim of panic attacks.

He minimizes his condition to keep others uplifted, then weeps in solitude and wonders why this happened to him.

“I’d rather get shot. I’m going to be honest, it’s the hardest thing in the world,” Rodriguez said. “I never know when I have to use the bathroom. I never know when I’m about to start crying. I never know when I’m about to be in pain. It’s hard to live like that.”

As agonizing as his journey has been, Rodriguez has had Boston behind him. That includes NBA players Terance Mann and Bruce Brown, two close friends who are always in his corner.

People call him “The Mayor of Boston” because of all his connections. One supporter told him that he was the right person in his community to get cancer. The comment confused him at first, but the more he thought about it, the more he understood it.

“I’m resilient,” Rodriguez said. “I’ll run through a wall to make sure the task gets done.”

After five rounds of chemo, some people thought he was faking because he was still playing like himself. The weeks since have been worse, but that hasn’t deterred him.

When Boston vs. Cancer and Fisher College coach Anthony Leonelli reached out about playing in TBT, he had no idea Rodriguez was battling cancer. Rodriguez struggled through practice the week prior, with his health deteriorating, but he wasn’t going to let his team, or his city, down.

“The beyond superhuman ability to deal with the physical and emotional trauma from his chemo treatments, and still compete at an elite level of basketball, transcends anything I’ve witnessed in sport,” said Papile.

Boston vs. Cancer teammate Mason Madsen, a former Boston College catalyst, said he never would have guessed what Rodriguez was going through.

“He carries himself with so much joy and humor, it naturally lifts everyone around him,” Madsen said. “The fact that he’s doing all this while battling stage 4 colon cancer really puts things in perspective.”

Rodriguez believes basketball is saving his life. It gives him purpose, structure, and motivation.

“You could tell me I have stage whatever. You could tell me I have six months to live … I’m going to play basketball,” Rodriguez said. “That’s just what it is, no matter how much pain I’m going through. I’m Mikey Rodriguez. I’m Speedy. I’m always going to find a way.”

“Mentally, it’s very challenging to keep going for two hours straight,” MacDonough said. “All I kept saying to myself was, ‘Positive mind-set, you got this, be confident.’ I just kept my shot going.”

MacDonough, a South Burlington, Vermont, resident and Worcester Academy graduate who will play at St. Bonaventure next year, shot a blistering 87.4 percent to defend her title as the best shooter in Massachusetts.

Rising junior Maddie Keough, also a Worcester Academy catalyst, placed second (72.9 percent), while Medfield junior Naya Annigeri took third (70.9) at the Starland Sportsplex.

On the boys’ side, Lynn native, Phillips Academy standout, and Northeastern-bound guard Xavier Abreu won at 86.4 percent.

Abreu shot for his grandmother, Cristina Medrano, who beat breast cancer twice. He planned to call her afterward to savor the moment together.

“It meant everything,” Abreu said. “I know she’d be proud of me regardless, but the fact that I could come out here and win it and dedicate it to her means a lot.”

Archbishop Williams junior Jack Olinto earned second (83.3), and Roxbury Latin sophomore Jackson Perri was third (80.9 percent).

MacDonough thought of her grandfather, Paul LaBonte, who is currently dealing with a health scare that may be cancerous. She just learned that his situation took a turn for the worse earlier this week, which gave her even more incentive.

“I’m just trying to be as supportive of him as he’s been for me,” MacDonough said. “Doing this for him really meant the world to me.”

John MacDonough credited his daughter for living in the gym and relentlessly chasing her dream. He works in digital pathology at Philips, and seeing his daughter play for a larger purpose with so much meaning feels like a full-circle moment.

“Her mind-set is what sets her apart,” John MacDonough said. “When I miss one, I’m going to get the next one. Resilience is the biggest piece. She figures out how to win.”

Alana Hogan, an Ursuline Academy graduate who will play at Kenyon College, honored her late aunt and godmother, Margaret Nelson, who died of a brain tumor three years ago.

“I play for her every day,” Hogan said. “She wore 15, so now I wear 15. It’s special to me to be able to represent her in that kind of way and make her proud.”

In New England, 63 of those grants, worth $126 million, are set to be restored, according to a Globe analysis based on the Grant Watch database. But researchers say the process of restoring their funding and restarting their projects remains clouded by confusion and delays.

The grants were restored as the result of a lawsuit filed by the American Public Health Association and 16 state attorneys general arguing that the NIH improperly ended funding tied to topics like gender identity, health disparities, vaccine hesitancy, and DEI efforts. The judge in the case ruled in June that the terminations were “illegal and void” and ordered the government to immediately make the funds available. The Trump administration has appealed the decision.

The grants are a fraction of the more than $3.1 billion in funding from the National Science Foundation and the Department of Health and Human Services that the Trump administration has canceled across New England.

At a status hearing on the case Monday, attorneys representing the public health association said that more than 50 of its roughly 300 affected research grants across the country have not been reinstated, and that the NIH has not provided a timeline for when all grants will be restored. Researchers face other obstacles as well.

At Harvard, virtually all federal funding remains frozen as part of the administration’s broader assault on the university. Others face reduced staffing, due to layoffs, and shortened deadlines to complete their research. And funding at the federal level remains subject to sudden reversals, as shown Tuesday night when the White House issued and then rescinded a broad NIH funding freeze within a matter of hours.

In a statement Thursday, the NIH told the Globe it “has been working to reinstate grants to comply with the court’s order.”

Scott Delaney, a Harvard scientist and co-creator of Grant Watch, said many researchers remain wary despite the win because of further appeals and reviews.

“Every indication is that NIH will continue to cut research on trans health and on DEI. They still remain hostile to broad bodies of research, and they continue to ask researchers to rewrite their grants to avoid certain topics,” said Delaney, who lost his own NIH funding and received a layoff notice effective in October.

But many are pressing ahead despite the obstacles and hoping for the best.

Nancy Krieger, a professor of social epidemiology at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, learned this month that her funding would be restored. She said that despite feeling vindicated by US District Court Judge William G. Young’s ruling, she cannot access the funds due to the federal freeze on funds to Harvard.

Since 2019, Krieger and her team have been working to measure the impact of six types of discrimination — including racism, sexism, and ageism — on health. The researchers enrolled 699 patients who completed two study questionnaires online and at three Boston community health centers — including Fenway Health, Mattapan Community Health Center, and Harvard Street Neighborhood Health Center in Dorchester — to test how discrimination contributes to psychological distress and sleep disorders.

“We can resume the work because we had completed all data collection and we were in the phase of data analysis and manuscript preparation,” Krieger said. “Whether or not the funding ever truly gets reinstated for my grant — and I would like that it is — it’s important, given the complexities, to make sure these things go from a court order to reality.”

At Tufts, the school lost and then suddenly regained a pipeline for young talent, though several young scientists lost out in the process. The university hosts one of just 22 NIH-sponsored programs in the country that trains a diverse group of postdoctoral scholars in both research and teaching. The program, called the Institutional Research Career and Academic Development Award, or IRACDA, focuses on underrepresented groups.

“We were ramping up for another five years after earning highly competitive funding last fall,” said Mitch McVey, program director and professor of biology at Tufts. “Then the new administration came in, and everything changed.”

When the NIH terminated funding, four incoming applicants had their offers rescinded just one day after receiving them.

Marissa Maroni, 28, celebrated the news with her husband and prepared to move back to her home state.

“It felt like the right next step, personally and professionally,” said Maroni, who is finishing her PhD at the University of Pennsylvania. “But just a day later, I got an email saying the program was canceled. It was incredibly disheartening.”

The loss also affects Bunker Hill Community College, University of Massachusetts Boston, and Suffolk University, where IRACDA scholars like Maroni were slated to teach next year.

McVey said Tufts might extend the offers again to the four applicants but, “We’re trying to balance the risk involved here, which would be that if the government wins the appeal, the funding will likely be terminated again. We don’t want to put the scholars in a position where their job security is always in jeopardy, so we’re trying to figure out how to best navigate this situation. It’s not easy.”

At Yale, nine NIH grants that were terminated are in the process of reinstatement. Four of those belong to John Pachankis, a Yale School of Public Health professor who has spent the past 20 years investigating why people in the LGBTQ+ community are at higher risk for depression, anxiety, and suicide.

The sudden March terminations not only disrupted years of research but also halted the rollout of promising mental health interventions.

One of Pachankis’s halted trials aimed to train front-line mental health providers working at 90 LGBTQ+ community centers across 35 states in cognitive-behavioral therapy to treat depression, anxiety, and substance use.

“Right before the funding termination, we learned that our trained mental health providers had started delivering our cognitive-behavioral therapy to over 4,000 LGBT people in just four months,” he said. The funding cut prevented them from studying the longer-term impact of the therapy and ways to sustain it in local communities.

Restarting the work has been slow and resource-intensive, he said. It requires updating ethics approvals, reconvening data safety review boards, updating clinical trials registries, drafting now-overdue progress reports, and restarting trials enrollment while no longer having sufficient staff to do this work.

“The research infrastructure took years to build, was collapsed in a day, and will take months if not longer to rebuild,” Pachankis said. “My confidence in future federal funding for this research remains shaken, but my team’s commitment to asking and answering important scientific questions isn’t going away.”

Meanwhile, at Brown, Moitra is figuring out how to move forward with his research. Between 2022 and early 2024, he and his team recruited 240 LGBTQ+ participants, offering two counseling sessions to study the mental health impacts from the pandemic. After funding was pulled, Moitra said, they lost 40 participants’ worth of data that had timed out after those participants received just one counseling session. Now that the grant has been reinstated, Moitra’s team is left racing against the clock as the deadline for the funding to be used remains Aug. 31.

The researchers are applying for a no-cost extension to allow them to complete the work without requesting additional funds.

“After five-plus months of uncertainty, we were moving on,” Moitra said. “It’s hard to scramble it all back together.”

More commuters than ever in Greater Boston are embracing Bluebikes on their daily trips to work, driven by a growing network of pickup stations, the introduction of e-bikes, and expanded discount programs. In just four years from 2020 to 2024, annual ridership increased by 2.7 million.

“We’ve seen the Bluebikes program explode in popularity, almost exponentially,” said Mandy Wilkens, a spokesperson for the Boston Cyclists Union, a local cycling advocacy group.

But the rising popularity isn’t as evident outside of the Boston city center and major college hubs. There are still gaps, particularly in less dense neighborhoods, such as Roxbury and Dorchester, which logged far fewer trips in comparison.

To understand how the bikeshare program has impacted the region, the Globe analyzed trip-level usage data from Bluebikes. The analysis was limited to where riders left in the morning and returned in the evening to better capture commuter patterns.

Across the 13 municipalities served by the Bluebikes network, managed by the rideshare company Lyft, riders logged more than 4.7 million trips in 2024. Boston, Cambridge, and Somerville were among the top use areas.

Bluebikes launched in 2011 with just 600 bicycles parked at 60 stations in a limited section of Boston. Now the program has more than 3,000 bikes at over 400 stations across the metro area.

Wilkens said one reason the trip numbers have surged recently is the addition of e-bikes, which have made the program more accessible to residents with disabilities or other mobility issues.

Despite the program’s rapid growth, stations in neighborhoods such as Dorchester and Mattapan logged surprisingly few commuter trips. Multiple stations reported fewer than 500 commuter trips in those areas from January 2024 through May 2025.

The map below shows how many commuter trips each Bluebikes station logged in that period. Many areas with robust public infrastructure and high population density, like Cambridge and Somerville, had significantly higher ridership.

In contrast, areas with lower urban density and fewer nearby Bluebikes stations have been slower to see upticks in usage.

“If you have to walk 15 minutes to go get a bike share, you’re less incentivized to do it,” said Galen Mook, executive director for MassBike, a cyclist advocacy organization.

Boston is about halfway through a two-year initiative to construct 100 new stations, said Kim Foltz, the bikes director at Boston Streets Cabinet, a division of the City of Boston that oversees transportation infrastructure.

The ultimate goal is to make the stations so common throughout the city that no one lives more than a five-minute walk from a pickup, she said.

The three busiest stations during peak commute hours were in the dense city of Cambridge, clustered near Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. All three of those stations recorded more than 40,000 trips during commute times.

That high use number is driven in large part by Harvard and MIT students, who are offered steep discounts on Bluebikes memberships by their universities, advocates said.

Boston also offers a $60 membership for residents during their first year in the program and a $5 annual membership to low-income residents, suggesting that price isn’t the sole factor behind the disparities.

Advocates point to more systemic issues that continue to deter residents in low-use areas from signing up.

“What’s the bigger issue is there is not as much safe infrastructure,” in areas such as Roxbury, Mattapan, and Dorchester, Wilkens, the cycling advocate, said.

Safe biking infrastructure can include everything from separated bike lanes and protected intersections to well-maintained road surfaces.

They added that those neighborhoods are too far from central commercial hubs for commuting by bike to be practical.

Mook, of MassBike, said Boston’s broader cycling strategy needs continued coordination and funding to close the remaining gaps.

“We definitely need to connect networks of safe cycling corridors,” he said. We must make sure “that we’re accelerating the puzzle pieces to make it a fully contiguous network.”

Police arrested a woman in Dorchester last week for allegedly stealing eight boxes of ice cream after she pulled a knife on a CVS employee, police said.

Shortly before 1:30 p.m. on Tuesday, officers responded to reports of a person armed with a knife inside a CVS Pharmacy on Blue Hill Avenue, police said.

Omaila Michelle Medina, 41, of Boston, was arrested without incident, police said. She pleaded not guilty to a charge of armed robbery at her arraignment on Wednesday, according to court records.

She was ordered held without bail.

There were nine outstanding warrants for Medina’s arrest, police said. At least six were for shoplifting or larceny, court records show.

As of Monday, Medina did not yet have an attorney, according to court records.

Prosecutors are also asking that Medina’s bail for her outstanding charges be revoked, the Suffolk district attorney’s office said.

“Focusing on repeat offenders is a major tenet in our initiative to keep workplaces safe for employees and consumers,” James Borghesani, a spokesperson for the district attorney’s office, said by email.

Luis Mendoza, the manager of the CVS on Blue Hill Avenue, said Medina and her friends have been stealing from the store for years.

“It’s not just the eight boxes,” he said. “She steals everything.”

Nobody was injured in the alleged robbery, officials said.

Joe Hale, the former president of the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum, will be in charge of managing development, capital campaigns, gifts, and donations, the institute said in a statement Monday.

“I’m honored to join the Kennedy Institute and help support its critical work to inspire bipartisan civic engagement and strengthen our democracy,” Hale said in the statement. “America needs to return to a place of civil discourse. Senator Kennedy believed in the power of public service and citizen participation, and I look forward to building a community of supporters who share that belief.”

The institute celebrates the career of the late Senator Edward M. Kennedy, the Massachusetts liberal who served from 1962 until his death from brain cancer in 2009.

The institute opened nearly 10 years ago in Dorchester, on land next to the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, named for the late senator’s brother.

The EMK Institute is dedicated to educating the public about the importance of democratic participation and the governmental role of the Senate.

The institute plans to honor former president Joe Biden with a Lifetime Achievement Award in October, during the 10th anniversary celebrations. Biden, also a former vice president, served for many years as a senator from Delaware alongside Kennedy.

Hale’s resume includes raising hundreds of millions of dollars for nonprofits.

As president of the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum, Hale led a $200 million campaign, renovated the museum, and added $100 million to the museum’s endowment, according to the institute’s statement.

“Joe’s experience and success in spearheading large-scale capital campaigns is a testament to his strategic vision and leadership,” said Adam Hinds, chief executive of the EMK Institute. “We are thrilled to bring that expertise to the Kennedy Institute as we prepare to celebrate our 10th Anniversary.”

Hale was also the vice president and chief communications officer of Cinergy Corp., now Duke Energy, the executive director of Nantucket’s Dreamland cultural center, and the president of the Global BrightLight Foundation, famous for providing off-grid families with solar lanterns in developing countries.

Hale was president of Cincinnati Gas and Electric Company and the former executive director of the Arts Council of Indianapolis.

Hale and his wife, Linda, have contributed large donations to philanthropic efforts, including raising $250 million for different nonprofits, and raising more than $300,000 for the March of Dimes, where Joe Hale was also a trustee and board chairman.

Hale is a graduate of Hanover College in Indiana and of the Harvard Institute in Arts Administration. He also holds honorary degrees from the College of Art and Design in Columbus, Ohio, and from Hanover College.

Ahmed said if elected he would push to make the lottery systems that distribute affordable units in private developments more transparent. Miniard Culpepper, a lawyer who previously worked for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, supported giving tenants in public housing more ownership rights.

Community activist WaWa Bell supported the idea of creating a more localized area median income that would better reflect the demographics of District 7. Area median income is the standard used for determining income eligibility for affordable housing projects. Such a change would require the Legislature’s approval.

Mavrick Afonso, who works for the state’s Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, also supported the idea of a localized area median income for the district, noting that areas like Waltham are included in the region for which HUD calculated the area median income.

“Locally in Roxbury, that median income is a lot lower,” Afonso said, “we’re not making housing for Waltham in Roxbury.”

The candidates are running in the only open seat on this year’s ballot, and would represent a district that encompasses parts of Roxbury, Dorchester, Fenway, and part of the South End. Fernandes Anderson officially resigned on July 4, more than two months after she agreed to plead guilty to federal corruption charges.

The District 7 race is crowded, with a total of 11 candidates on the Sept. 9 preliminary ballot. Only the top two vote getters in that election will move on to November’s general election. The organizers of the event only invited the first four candidates who responded to them so that each candidate would get around 30 minutes to answer questions. The other candidates will be interviewed at future events.

When asked by an audience member about how he would make sure that Black people from Roxbury could afford to stay in the neighborhood, Bell said reparations were the solution. Community organizations like Roxbury Rising envision reparations in the form of restoring property to Black people who were forced out during urban renewal, as opposed to just cash payments. Bell, a cofounder of the nonprofit Nubian Square Foundation, said that if elected to the City Council, he would support a policy not based on race, that is targeted toward the descendants of slaves in Boston, not all Black people. Bell, who was formerly incarcerated, also said he would set up an American Freeman affairs office for reparations.

“I think I can go a step further and establish the infrastructure,” Bell said, “so that if reparations does happen . . . we have a dedicated office that will be able to deliver those resources properly.”

On reparations, Culpepper said Black students at Madison Park Technical Vocational High School should be able to attend nearby Northeastern University tuition free if they are admitted.

“The little white kids are paying cash right from the money that was made from the slaves on our back,” Culpepper said.

Culpepper said the university developing the land in the area has limited access to students of the long-underinvested high school to facilities like Carter Playground. The high school was set to get a new building, but funding for the project is now uncertain.

“Look at the disparity,” Culpepper said, “it’s amazing how we’ve given up the city to Northeastern University.”

Afonso, who previously worked for the city’s Parks and Recreation Department, said a public discussion about past injustices like redlining was needed before deciding on how reparations may be implemented.

“The first step for me is to really do the work to try to understand the damages that happened at the time, a model that was set forth in South Africa with the Truth and Reconciliation trial,” Afonso said, “I can’t tell you I have a solution for all of that right now, because we don’t know how deep it’s gone and how much it’s infected and hurt families over generations.”

Ahmed did not directly voice his opinion on reparations, but said he supported efforts to keep Roxbury residents in the neighborhood. Ahmed, who came to Roxbury at the age of 12, as a refugee from Somalia, went on to become a member of the USA Track & Field national team and later, work in the Boston Public Schools system.

He works as a supervisor of attendance for the schools system. Ahmed said he became passionate about advocating for Black and brown families when he saw those families were disproportionately involved in truancy hearings. He said he began working with students, particularly those from low-income and immigrant families, to address attendance issues before the issue escalated to a court hearing.

“No one wins in court,” Ahmed said, “The judge might not make the decision that’s good for our community.”

The candidates were also asked about how they would maintain transparency while in office given that Fernandes Anderson resigned after she plead guilty to violating state ethics laws by hiring immediate family members as paid staff and receiving a $7,000 kickback from a staff member’s city funded bonus.

All four candidates said they would host regular town halls, Ahmed said he would set up a district office in Roxbury for easier communication and Bell said he would continue the advisory council Fernandes Anderson set up where community members would meet weekly. Culpepper favored setting up an ethics commission for the City Council, an effort that has previously failed. Afonso said he would support more participatory budgeting events.

“I know single mothers that make more prudent decisions than some of these [city] departments in their own homes,” Afonso said, “I’m sure they can handle some of our budget issues.”

There will be another forum with the remaining District 7 candidates Thursday at 6 p.m. at the same location, One Westinghouse Plaza, in Hyde Park, also hosted by Speak Boston. Thursday’s forum will also be live-streamed on Facebook.

The city has historically struggled to give contracts to minority-owned businesses. In 2018, less than one percent of the money the city was putting toward city contracting was going to businesses owned by people of color. In 2024, that number increased to 12 percent, following the implementation of new legislation aimed at supporting those businesses, Wu said.

“We are on track to continue that positive momentum,” she said. “When businesses like these are working for Boston, it works for all of Boston.”

Hansy Better Barraza, the cofounder of Latino-owned Studio Luz Architects, said immigrant-owned businesses struggle with stability, and city contracts offer a solution.

“By allowing us access to city-owned contracts, we don’t necessarily have to ride the highs and lows,” Barraza said.

SCALE provides an avenue for companies to build wealth in the future, Wu said. The city, she said, needs to ensure that local businesses can benefit from upcoming global events, such as the FIFA World Cup, which will be held at Gillette Stadium next summer.

While developing the program, Andrea Caruth, the director of supplier diversity at Boston, said her department surveyed people and asked: “What are the gaps? What are the barriers?” The department found that one of the biggest challenges facing minority- and women-owned businesses was capacity, she said.

Entrepreneurs from underrepresented backgrounds have to find time to squeeze in a phone call and spend hours on a laptop — while balancing familial commitments, officials and grantees said.

Recipient Shonté Davidson, CEO of Better Together Brain Trust, a climate-focused electrical contractor, said that “capacity was a theme of the day.”

Davidson said SCALE will help her business increase its operational capacity. The company currently has a contract with the city of Boston to install curbside EV charging stations. Davidson plans to use the grant to secure more capital, collateralize the money, and increase her line of credit.

Better Together Brain Trust has received $50,000 of the grant money so far. After Davidson completes the six-month program — which requires weekly meetings and classes, she hopes to receive up to another $150,000.

“We’re going to use [the money] to scale — pun intended,” Davidson said.

Irene Li, CEO of Prepshift, is working with six grantees in the food and dining industry as a consultant in developing their business plans. Restaurants deal with expenses, like tariffs, insurance, ingredients, and labor — all of that adds up, she said.

“Most mom-and-pop and independent restaurants are barely surviving,” Li said.

After reviewing more than 180 applications, the city chose 27 grantees from a spectrum of industries to receive money through funds from the American Rescue Plan Act, totaling up to $6.5 million.

Of those applicants, about a third were food and dining businesses, according to Li. “We have a lot more to do. We’ve made a great start,” she added.

The Ancient Bakers, a baking company dedicated to plant-based and allergen-friendly goods, is one of the recipients. Mother and son duo Tonya Johnson and Bennuamen McCormick Johnson started the business because, as an infant, Bennuamen was diagnosed with acute malnutrition and severe allergies, meaning he couldn’t eat eggs, milk, and dairy.

“It was a call to action,” Tonya Johnson said. “I had to do something as a mother to save him.”

The business worked out of a shared kitchen and sold products at farmers markets, hospitals, and colleges — a “grassroots kind of growth,” Johnson said.

Now, the Ancient Bakers is in the middle of a “pivot,” trying to focus on e-commerce, offering multi-purpose bakery mixes and finished cookies to customers. The business is working on building its online presence, which the grant money will help go toward.

“[The grant] is the fuel that is going to help us come back to a marketplace strong,” Johnson said.

Over two nights, on Monday and Tuesday, Boston police were joined by firefighters, emergency workers and city leaders to celebrate in 12 neighborhoods.

On Monday, celebrations were held in Roxbury, Brighton, Roslindale, Hyde Park, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain. On Tuesday, the celebrations were held in the Dorchester, South Boston, Chinatown, the South End, the North End and East Boston.

In the North End, on a breezy night, law enforcement showed no signs of fatigue as members of the police, fire departments and emergency services, welcomed families to the festivities.

Free pizza, ice cream, balloon art, face painting and was part of the fun. Children took turns playing with animals in a mini petting zoo.

“Officer Copper,” the Boston Police Comfort Dog, greeted visitors.

A deejay blasted music and residents stopped at booths to get information about healthcare, children’s music lessons and other services availabe in the neighborhood.

It was also a chance to speak with local police.

“They’re part of this community,” John Pregmon, president of North End Cares, which helped to organize the event. “We’re both focused on the same thing, how can we make the North End better and safer.”

In a speech, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden thanked first responders but emphasized the importance of community partnerships and collaboration.

“You’re the reason we do what we do,” Hayden said, speaking to dozens of residents. “But you’re also the reason we’re successful in what we do.”

In an interview, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said National Night Out is an opportunity to acknowledge residents who help law enforcement keep the city safe.

“We ask them for so much, to partner with us to provide public safety.” Cox said. “This is an opportunity to go around the city and say ‘Thank You,” to all the residents that work so hard to keep the city safe.”

Danny Coakley, who has lived in the neighborhood for four years, said the North End “full of passion.”

“You won’t meet a group of individuals more invested in their community,” Coakley said.

“An engaged community is a safe community,” Cox said.

Coakley believes police in the North End help the community as much as neighbors help each other.

“They really do a good job of making themselves visible and really want to make sure that they are available to any of the community organizations,” Coakley said.

Mayor Michelle Wu arrived to greet residents. The city’s National Night Out celebration brought together kids, seniors and others to get to know their neighbors.

“Boston is a city that sees safety not only as numbers and statistics and charts, but as community,” Wu said in an interview. “We’re all in this together to keep our communities safe.”

Sharon Verrocchi, who was born and raised in the North End, attended to show her support for law enforcement.

“I love the cops. They do a great job,” Verrochi said.

Michelle Topor chatted with her friend, Mary Ann D’Amato, about the joys of seeing the neighborhood come together.

Topor, who has lived in the North End for 54 years, said “I’m blessed to be able to be here. I could never be anywhere else.”

D’Amato, who’s lived in the neighborhood for 62 years, agreed saying she feels “very safe here.”
