“[SNAP] is not enough because I have my grandkids,” Brown said. “They’re hungry. We don’t have time to fight over the piece of chicken.”

Even on cold or rainy days, the line at the pantry snakes down the sidewalk. Brown and other patrons hope for meat, bread, milk, and fresh produce . But recently, as the number of peopleseeking food assistance has increased, the bags have been lighter.

Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 limited eligibility and benefits of SNAP, a program many low-income families and individuals rely on for groceries. Earlier this year, Trump cut 94 million pounds of food aid, leaving food banks scrambling to scrape together enough for their increasing numbers of patrons.

These problems, which many food bank workers in Greater Boston described as an impending crisis as the holiday season approaches, are expected to be exacerbated by the government shutdown, which, on Oct. 18, entered its 18th day.

“We’ve seen a 30 percent increase in the distributions that we’ve handed out over the past three months,” said Jonathan Tetrault, vice president for basic needs at Catholic Charities Boston, a nonprofit organization that provides community support, including food services, child care, and healthy families programs.

“So what that tells us is, not only are more people needing support, but the people that have been coming to us are needing to come more frequently.”

MaryAnn Laughlin, a volunteer at the Yawkey Center food pantry, said that recently, it has sometimes had to start closing earlier. Having to turn away the hungry is her least favorite part of the job, she said.

“There’s not enough food because sometimes...as you could see, the bag is not that full,” said Laughlin. Bags are still packed with a variety of foods, including dried beans, rice, and canned fruits and vegetables, but they often include fewer fresh products and less meat, which volunteers and employees have said have been more difficult to get.

Catherine D’Amato, Greater Boston Food Bank president and CEO, said the USDA cuts in March meant that the food bank needed to raise more money “to keep providing the healthy food that our 600 food pantry partners rely on to serve their community.”

“Our donors and the food acquisition team at GBFB rose to the occasion and we never had to change the amount of food going to our food pantry partners,” she said in a statement to the Globe.

She also said any government shutdown will only exacerbate the already growing problem of hunger and emphasized that while exact numbers are not yet available, prior shutdowns have shown that the need for additional assistance is clear.

“What we’ve experienced in previous shutdowns is that when federal workers don’t get paid, many of them turn to the food pantry system to keep food on the table, some of them will likely be visiting a pantry for the first time,” she said.

Jennifer Lemmerman, the chief policy officer at Project Bread, a nonprofit group that helps connect people in Boston with food sources and advocates for food security policies, said that she is worried about the Massachusetts hunger crisis being exacerbated by the government shutdown.

During the last government shutdown in 2019, which lasted 35 days, Lemmerman said thousands of government employees who were furloughed or working without pay experienced food insecurity for the first time. Now, she predicts the same will happen.

“We’re in a crisis in Massachusetts. Food insecurity rates right now are the same as they were at the height of COVID,” she said. However, with the government shut down, the government programs that were implemented during COVID to help with food insecurity are not available, causing further stress to a system already burdened by heightened food insecurity rates.

David Waters, CEO of Community Servings, a nonprofit organization based in Jamaica Plain that provides meals to people experiencing critical and chronic illnesses, said he is worried about the looming impact the cuts will have on the organization, which relies heavily on federal funding.

Waters said Community Servings has already felt the effects of increased food insecurity in the Boston community, with the wait list for its program growing longer and longer.

“Community Servings in February had a waiting list of about 100 people. Yeah, that’s close to 300 people now, and some of them could be waiting six months,” he said. “And, if you’re dealing with a critical illness and you’re food insecure, you can’t wait six months.”

Eric Lindsey, a director and food pantry manager with Omega Men in Action, a nonprofit organization that helps families in need in Greater Boston, said he has seen an influx in families visiting the monthly food bank, and anticipates that number will keep growing.

“Two years ago, when I took over the position, we were probably looking at, like, on average, 30 to 40 families a month. And [now] we’re at like 90 to 100, so we [have] definitely more than double, close to triple, the amount of families we’re seeing,” he said.

Brown, the Yawkey Center food pantry patron, was able to take some fresh fruit and vegetables, including tomatoes and apples, and add them to her bag. It’s a luxury that the Yawkey food pantry can sometimes give people when they have fresh food.

Brown said she is grateful for the food that she can get at the pantry, even with less being offered at times.

“I can survive. But there’s certain things, you know, there’s certain things that you need,” she said. ”You [can’t] to go to sleep [when] your stomach is growling."

In April, our financial adviser did something new: He put my wife and me in gold.

I’d always dismissed gold as a fringe asset — something for investors who are 1) obsessed with inflation; 2) don’t trust paper money; 3) are convinced the world is about to fall apart, or 4) all of the above.

But I’m quite pleased our adviser made the move. It’s turned out to be the best year for the yellow metal since 1979.

The price of gold on the spot market closed Thursday at $3997 a ounce after ending Wednesday above $4,000 for the first time. It has gained 51.5 percent this year and nearly 150 percent since 2022.

Gold has outshined bitcoin, another don’t-trust-the-government asset, US stocks, and play-it-safe funds that mix stocks and bonds.

After such an extended run-up, it’s fair to ask whether the Great Gold Rush is nearing an end. The general consensus is no.

Goldman Sachs just raised its gold forecast to $4,900 an ounce for the end of next year. That would mark a gain of more than 21 percent from Wednesday’s record close of $4,042.

“Even when adjusted for inflation, gold is at an all-time high,” Jack Ablin, chief investment strategist at Cresset Capital Management, said in an interview. “But it’s still not too late” to add gold to your portfolio.

No investment is a sure thing, but here are three reasons many experts think gold is a prudent play right now.

Insurance: Plenty of investors speculate in gold by betting on short-term price swings.

But the metal is mostly used as a hedge against inflation, a drop in the value of the US dollar, and financial or political turmoil. Right now, investors are anxious about all three.

As the impact of tariffs kicks in, forecasters see inflation remaining elevated at about 3 percent, one percentage point above the Federal Reserve’s target.

The dollar is on track for its worst year in five decades. Morgan Stanley blames the decline in part on slowing US economic growth, falling interest rates, and foreign investors reducing their exposure to the greenback.

Tensions are running high over the federal shutdown, mounting government debt, and the Trump administration’s threats to Fed independence.

For these reasons, investors are starting to view gold as safer than the dollar, according to Ken Griffin, the billionaire hedge fund manager.

“People are looking for ways to effectively de-dollarize, or de-risk their portfolios,” Griffin told a Bloomberg conference this week.

Silver is also on a run, mostly for the same reasons.

Diversification: Gold can add balance to a conventional portfolio heavy in stocks and bonds.

The metal often appreciates when equities fall or when fixed-income returns wane. Because gold is priced in US dollars, it often rises in value when the dollar weakens, since it takes more dollars to buy the same ounce of gold.

A weaker dollar also makes gold cheaper for buyers using stronger currencies, increasing global demand and driving prices up.

My adviser, Alex Burke of Financial Solutions Associates in Dedham, bought shares in April of an exchange traded fund that invests in gold. The price has appreciated 28 percent since.

The ETF is a small slice of our IRA — about 6 percent. Burke recommends being judicious.

“Don’t put all your eggs into one golden basket, use it as a small part of a well-diversified portfolio,” he said in an email. “Even if you are entering at the top, if you limit the allocation to a small part of a portfolio you will limit your potential losses, but still have plenty of upside if gold soars.”

Market trends: Gold prices have been on an upward slope since the Great Recession as central banks sought to diversify their reserves beyond the dollar and protect against financial shocks.

The buying accelerated after Western countries froze Russia’s foreign currency reserves as punishment for its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. That triggered a flight to safety and concerns among some emerging market governments that their dollar holdings might not be so safe.

Analysts expect central banks to continue buying gold to reduce their exposure to the US. Falling interest rates, federal deficits, and fears of an AI stock bust will increase the metal’s appeal to investors.

Final thought: Gold supply increases only about 2 percent a year, so even a modest rise in demand can send prices sharply higher.

In June, JPMorgan Chase analysts forecast that gold would top $4,000 by the third quarter of 2026. It was off by almost a year.

Of course, financial markets reverse course all the time. Gold’s surge could lose steam due to an unexpected rise in interest rates, an easing of geopolitical tensions, or a rebound by the US dollar.

Gold isn’t always effective as a hedge.

Still, a modest allocation makes sense — not because gold is going to beat stocks or bonds over every stretch, but because its appeal as an inflation hedge and diversification tool, combined with strong demand, make it a reasonable insurance policy in tumultuous times.

“I doubt there’s an opera recording made between 1930 and 1980 that he didn’t have,” said Stephen Dyer, the critic’s nephew, who is managing his uncle’s estate.

The younger Dyer, a lawyer for the city of Columbus, Ohio, has been regularly flying to Boston while he puts his uncle’s affairs in order. He said he saved the vinyl for last because he “knew there was historical significance in it, and that [his uncle] loved it.”

“I just wanted to take some time to find a good place for it,” he said.

To that end, he plans to open the condo, located at 61 Garfield St., Unit 3, for a pay-what-you-can sale on Saturday between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. and again on Sunday from 10 a.m. to noon.

Stephen said he has been in touch with several universities and archives about donating the records, but wants to give interested local listeners first pick.

“He cared so much about the Boston music community. I saw it firsthand when I went to school here,” said Stephen. “He just promoted the heck out of the local arts scene. He really believed in it. He loved it. . . . I thought I’d give the Boston music community first crack at taking something out of here that they’d like.”

Richard Dyer was the Globe’s classical critic between 1976 and 2006 and was considered an influential voice nationally, “a dean of the profession,” as fellow critic Alex Ross of The New Yorker once said. Composer Ned Rorem allegedly introduced Dyer to a friend in the 1980s by saying that he “runs Boston.”

Stephen said he has kept a single record for himself, a 1953 recording of “Tosca” starring Maria Callas, whose oeuvre Dyer delightedly shared with him as he began to study singing in high school: “Over time, he just gave me all of her live stuff on CD.”

The collection contains more music than anyone could have reasonably listened to, especially someone who spent as much time out of the house as Dyer did. Stephen found a few sealed LPs still in plastic bags from local music store Stereo Jack’s, which was previously located on Massachusetts Avenue a short walk from the condo.

But simply owning the records was a source of comfort and joy for Dyer, who had an encyclopedic knowledge of classical music. “He was as much a collector as a listener,” Stephen said.

CDs supplanted vinyl as the best-selling medium for recorded music in the late 1980s, and when Stephen recalls visiting his uncle while studying at Tufts University around then, he “only really heard [Dyer] listen to CDs at that point.” He kept on buying vinyl nonetheless.

By the end of Dyer’s life, he also stored records at the house he kept in Western Massachusetts, and there was also a storage pod in Dorchester, where Dyer had been living with his longtime companion. The Cambridge condo had not been his home base for roughly two decades at the time he died, but he still used almost every room to store records, with still more in the basement.

Many of the records Dyer collected were made during his lifetime, but he also pursued a significant number of recordings that were already vintage when he was born: for example, 1920s-era Soviet records, and an anthology of recordings of the early-20th-century soprano Nellie Melba. His personal favorite singer, Stephen said, was the Croatian dramatic soprano Zinka Milanov, who recorded prolifically in the mid-20th century prior to her retirement from performance in 1966.

Dyer’s opera obsession began at an early age. “In Oklahoma, his grandfather would listen to the Met broadcasts every Saturday. When he turned 10, or 11, his grandfather looked at him and said, ‘Dickie, you’re big enough — it’s time to come in and listen.’ ” said Stephen. “He fell in love with it. . . . I think a lot of this is remembering those days. He was just chasing that feeling all the time.”

In recent years, vinyl sales have reached heights they have not approached since the 1980s, even overtaking CDs as the best-selling physical medium in the United States in 2022 and 2023. Surveys conducted in the United States and the United Kingdom have documented a surge of interest in vinyl among Gen Z listeners born in the late 1990s through the 2000s, when the medium seemed to have settled into a niche as collector’s item, hipster novelty, or tool for DJs. But now Stephen’s own 16-year-old son, a budding saxophonist, has his own record player and enjoys listening to jazz on vinyl; in the meantime, he doesn’t own a CD player. “He has to play [CDs] through an Xbox or something,” Stephen said.

There might be some valuable items hidden among the records, but Stephen said he’s not concerned with making money off the collection — “it’d be nice if I made up the airfare,” he said, as he unpacked some of the boxes recovered from Dorchester in preparation for the opening sale. “I just know he loved this collection, so I’m doing my best to find it a home, or many. Whoever appreciates it, I certainly want them to have it.”

One box yielded a clear vinyl edition of Talking Heads’ “Speaking in Tongues,“ seemingly unopened with a yellowed price sticker still attached. “I don’t know why he had this. He never talked about the Talking Heads,” Stephen commented. “He’d probably remember where he got all this stuff. . . . I wish he could tell me.”

He emphasized that he was referring only to Keith McDermott, the former director of the Reggie Lewis Track and Athletic Center, and Robert Lewis Jr., the president of the Boys and Girls Clubs of Boston.

Ahmed said both have endorsed and donated to his campaign. State campaign finance records show McDermott contributed $100 to Ahmed’s campaign in February. Ahmed said Lewis donated to his campaign this month.

“They have been mentoring me,” Ahmed said. “They are supporting me, and I have their support and confidence 100 percent, but if someone else in that image reached out to [the Globe], I wanted to apologize that they are included in the picture.”

The photos at issue were taken at an apolitical event for the Boys and Girls Club months before Ahmed posted them, Bodrick said.

“It was really a celebration of Black history in a moment where many of us wanted to centralize and celebrate the history of our community in Roxbury,” Bodrick said of the event.

Bodrick said he has not yet endorsed a candidate in the race, and has been fielding calls from people who saw the post and were “taken aback” by it.

“I’m thankful for the great relationships I have in community, because folks knew that they could call me and ask, ‘Was this true?’, and I operate in integrity and honesty, and I could tell them that wasn’t true,” he said.

Joseph Feaster Jr., who appears in two of the photos, said he, too, was surprised by the post and took offense to what he saw as an implication in the caption that he is backing Ahmed in the race.

“If you want to ask me for my support, that’s one thing, but when you infer that I’m supporting you, I know that’s a problem for me,” said Feaster, an attorney with decades of experience as a civic leader in Boston, including as former chair of the city’s Board of Appeals, and current chair of the city’s reparations task force.

He emphasized that he is supporting Reverend Miniard Culpepper, an attorney and pastor who, along with Ahmed, advanced from September’s preliminary election in the race to represent District 7 on the council.

Bruce Bickerstaff, who also appears in one of the photos, called the post and the caption “upsetting.”

“It’s disingenuous at best, and totally untrue,” said Bickerstaff, a longtime Roxbury resident and former member of the city’s Zoning Board of Appeals.

He said he sees the post as an inappropriate and “disconcerting” misstep for a candidate running for public office.

“It decries that the approach is not honest or sincere, and if that is the way that he feels that he has to comport himself, it’s worrying,” Bickerstaff said. “I would not be in support of him in any fashion or form.”

Ahmed was also recently accused of harassment by another District 7 candidate, as well as a Healey administration official, who filed two police reports about Ahmed’s alleged behavior during early voting in the lead-up to Boston’s preliminary municipal election in September. A municipal court judge later terminated the harassment prevention order the official had requested against Ahmed.

Ahmed, a former track star and current coach who previously ran a failed campaign for the State House, was the top vote getter in the District 7 race in September’s preliminary election, with Culpepper coming in second. Third-place finisher Mavrick Afonso formally requested a recount in the race, but it did not ultimately change the outcome of which candidates will advance to November’s general election.

The District 7 council race drew the most crowded field of candidates of any race on the ballot, with eleven candidates vying to replace disgraced former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson in the preliminary election. The seat is the only open position on the November ballot.

Despite Massachusetts’ reputation as deeply blue, the vandalism at Russ and Mimi’s represents one of seven instances so far this year of Pride flag symbols being targeted in the state, according to GLAAD. Most of this year’s incidents happened in June, which is LGBTQ Pride month, and two involved arson, with flags being set on fire, GLAAD data show.

The incidents are part of an unmistakable national trend, according to researchers of anti-LGBTQ extremism. Targeted attacks against LGBTQ Pride symbols have risen in recent years, and point to a paradox the gay and transgender communities face, according to GLAAD. As the country’s LGBTQ population grows, the communities’ symbols have become more common and visible, which in turn leaves them vulnerable to attack.

“It’s a crime of opportunism,” said Sarah Moore, senior manager of news and research at GLAAD.

At Russ and Mimi’s, community members rallied to support Walsh after the incident, with many sending messages on Facebook condemning what happened and offering to pay for a new flag. The original, which had been flying since the start of June, was discovered in a nearby alley on the next day.

That day, Oct. 5, during the Roslindale Day Parade, Councilman Enrique Pepén and Mayor Michelle Wu met with Walsh to show their support, the local blog Universal Hub reported.

“Acts like this don’t represent who we are,” Pepén told the Globe. “We stand with Russ and Mimi, and with our LGBTQ+ neighbors, today and every day.”

Still, the incident — and others targeting flags, painted crosswalks, and banners — is part of an overall trend, Moore said. GLAAD recorded a slight decrease in attacks on Pride symbols from 2024 to 2025, but researchers believe the drop could be due to more LGBTQ people being afraid to display flags in the first place, Moore said.

There’s been a greater prevalence in recent years of Pride flags being targeted in blue bubbles, according to GLAAD. Where liberal communities border more conservative ones, LGBTQ-friendly establishments or residences that display rainbow Pride flags can become easy targets for vandals who are more hostile toward gay and transgender people, said Moore,

“This can really happen anywhere, and it’s often an expression of the broader community’s debate over LGBTQ rights and the existence of trans people,” Moore said.

In Boston this July, someone set fire to a Pride flag hanging outside a West Roxbury salon, then placed the damaged flag on a bench. The month before, two Pride flags displayed at a Jamaica Plain home were torn down. In July 2024, two men tried to set Pride flags on fire outside a private home — also in Roslindale.

“There have been cases where these attacks over the symbols will escalate into some really scary acts of harm against both the property and potentially the lives of the people,” Moore said.

A police detective was assigned to investigate the incident at Perfect 10 salon in West Roxbury, but they have not shared any updates with owner Kanessa Alexander, she said on Friday.

“They said things like this are pretty tough to look into,” Alexander said.

In most cases, attacks on Pride flags lead to misdemeanor charges, if a suspect is apprehended at all, Moore said.

So far this year, California has seen the greatest total number of attacks on Pride flags, and in August 2023, a shop owner in Cedar Glen, Calif., was shot and killed in front of her business over a dispute tied to the storefront’s flag.

After California, Ohio has had the most instances of Pride flag vandalism this year, with Pennsylvania and Massachusetts tying for third, GLAAD data show.

The Russ and Mimi’s Pride flag included rainbow colors and stripes representing the transgender community, people of color, and the lives of people who died during the HIV/AIDS crisis. The now popular design debuted in 2018 and is known in the LGBTQ community as the Progress Pride Flag.

“So they offended a lot of people,” said Walsh, nodding to the different identities the flag includes.

The pole’s damage looks like someone would have had to make a concerted physical effort to knock it down, possibly with a baseball bat, Walsh said. When she discovered it on the morning of Oct. 4, the metal brackets and anchors had been torn out of the wall, Walsh said.

Walsh said she planned to report the incident to police on Friday, Oct. 10, and that staff from the nearby restaurant JJ Brannelly’s offered to reinstall the flag pole next week.

Nearby businesses don’t have any security cameras that could provide footage of what happened, Walsh said. It’s possible that drunk teenagers or someone with mental health problems could have knocked the flag down without intending to send a hateful message, she said.

Regardless, other LGBTQ owners of new businesses in Roslindale are speaking up in support of what the Pride flag represents.

Midnight Morning, a restaurant a couple of doors down, opened in July 2023 and identifies on Google Maps as LGBTQ-owned and LGBTQ-friendly. Owner Virginia Brown, who also opens up her business early in the morning, was among the first people Walsh texted after she saw the flag pole on the ground.

“I love that she put that up there, and I’m proud of it,” Brown, 43, said. “I’m glad it’s back up. I want everyone to feel like they’re supposed to be there.”

Ana Crowley, an owner-worker at nearby bookstore co-op Rozzie Bound, which opened at its South Street location in 2023, said that despite the flag being attacked, the positive response has been overwhelming.

“The neighborhood has really rallied in support of Russ and Mimi’s and everyone wants them to feel like they’re not targeted in any way,” Crowley said.

“We’re not hanging those images to celebrate them, but to recognize a chapter in the gritty story of our neighborhood,” Osherow said during a telephone interview, insisting they weren’t meant to glorify the gangsters. “We’re acknowledging the history of this very spot.”

But the mugshots have outraged neighbors who are demanding their removal, not only because Bulger and Flemmi killed people while running a sprawling criminal enterprise and secretly working as FBI informants. One of those victims was Edward Connors, who ran a tavern, Bulldogs, in the same spot that is now Savin Bar, when he was murdered decades ago.

“It’s extremely disrespectful and distasteful,” said Tim Connors, who was a baby when his father was killed in a barrage of gunfire inside a telephone booth on Morrissey Boulevard in Dorchester on June 12, 1975. Tim Connors waited decades for Bulger and Flemmi to finally be convicted of his father’s slaying. “Absolutely they should take them down,” he said.

Connors, citing news accounts of how Osherow himself was the victim of a brutal stabbing in New Hampshire in 2009, asked during a Globe interview, “How would Ken’s family feel if he died from those wounds and I owned that restaurant and put his killer’s pictures in there?”

Evelyn Cody, who was Edward Connors’s girlfriend and the mother of Tim Connors, said she was “sick to my stomach” when she heard the mugshots were hanging on the walls of the former Bulldogs.

Bulger “had nothing to do” with Bulldogs, which was a neighborhood hotspot, and never frequented the bar, Cody said. “It was Eddie’s place.”

She added that Bulger’s photo “doesn’t belong in there ... put him over in Southie,” a reference to the South Boston neighborhood where he was based.

On Monday, during a meeting of the Columbia-Savin Hill Civic Association, several members proposed starting a petition urging Savin Bar to remove the images of Bulger and Flemmi, according to the Dorchester Reporter, which first reported on the controversy. The group agreed to take up the issue at a general membership meeting in November.

Donna McColgan, a lifelong Savin Hill resident who proposed the petition, said she was appalled by the mugshots and had asked the restaurant owners to take them down, but they refused.

“I think members of this community feel affronted and disrespected by putting Whitey Bulger as a theme,” McColgan said during an interview. “Are we so far removed from that kind of world when there were mobsters and gangsters all over the city that we think it’s pure entertainment?”

For McColgan, 71, the exploits of Bulger and Flemmi are still raw. She said the restaurant owners should be sensitive to the fact that the gangsters ruined families and terrorized the community.

“To say that Whitey Bulger is part of our history is false,” she said. “He has nothing to do with the community other than he brought in drugs. He maimed and murdered so many people who live here.”

The death of Connors, a 43-year-old former New England middleweight boxing champion, shook the neighborhood. Gruesome photos of his bullet-riddled body slumped in the telephone booth appeared in newspapers across the region.

The slaying, like many others, would go unsolved for decades, until Bulger fled Boston to evade a federal racketeering indictment in 1995. His former associates began cooperating with authorities after it was revealed during court proceedings that he, and his sidekick Flemmi, were longtime FBI informants. The remains of some victims who disappeared in the 1970s and 1980s were recovered from secret graves in Dorchester.

In 2004, Flemmi pleaded guilty to killing 10 people, including Connors, and implicated Bulger in all of them. He was sentenced to life in prison, where he remains. Seven years later, Bulger, who was a fixture on the FBI’s 10 Most Wanted list, was captured in Santa Monica, Calif., after 16 years on the run.

Bulger was convicted in 2013 of killing 11 people, including Connors, while running a racketeering enterprise from the 1970s to the 1990s that participated in drug trafficking and other crimes. Five years later, the then-89-year-old was beaten to death by a fellow inmate at a federal penitentiary in West Virginia, where he was serving a life sentence.

During Bulger’s federal racketeering trial in Boston, hitman-turned-government witness John Martorano testified that members of the Winter Hill Gang decided to kill Connors because they believed he had been bragging about helping the gang kill James “Spike” O’Toole, who was shot by Martorano in 1973 as he crouched behind a mailbox in Savin Hill.

Detailing Connors’s slaying, Martorano told jurors that he dropped Bulger and Flemmi off near the telephone booth, where they waited for Connors, knowing that he would go there to take a prearranged phone call. Martorano said he heard the shooting from a distance, then Bulger and Flemmi got back into the car and said, “He’s gone.”

Prosecutors played a taped conversation for jurors in which Bulger mimicked the sound of machine gun fire, saying “rat-a-tat-tat” as he mentioned Connors’s slaying to his nephew and niece when they visited him at the Plymouth County Correctional facility.

Osherow, who opened the Savin Bar and Kitchen in 2010 with his partner, Driscoll DoCanto, said Ramsay and his production team “played off the history of the place” when including the mugshots of Bulger and Flemmi as part of a redesign and revamping of the menu featured on an episode of Ramsay’s television series “Secret Service.”

“I actually thought the concept was kind of cool because it is the history of the place,” said Osherow, a New York native who moved to Dorchester in the 1980s. “It wasn’t meant to offend anybody.”

Osherow said the mugshots have been hanging in the restaurant since March and he was “caught off-guard” when a resident asked him to take them down a couple of months ago. Instead, he tacked a flyer onto Bulger’s framed mugshot, stressing that it’s not an “homage,” with a QR link to more information about the gangster.

He said a lot of patrons have urged the restaurant not to remove the images.

“We talked about taking them down,” said Osherow, adding that it is still a possibility. “We don’t want people to be upset.”

In a time when there is no longer a happy political medium in America, Pearl stands on the right, which led some media members to celebrate his departure. Pearl told the Globe he has no plans to run for US Senate and instead will remain an ambassador at Auburn.

His newly found free time allowed him to visit the Nova Music Festival Exhibition in South Boston, a moving remembrance of the attack by Hamas on the Nova Music Festival in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. It marked the beginning of the Israel-Hamas conflict.

“I’ve been to Israel a dozen times,” Pearl said. “There are two sides to every story. Unfortunately, this is a side of good vs. evil. And that’s hard to explain when there are good people on both sides. The Jews in Israel have tried since Israel was born in 1948 to be willing to live next door to their neighbors. You get off the plane and there’s people of every color, every shape, such incredible diversity. There’s so much freedom. It’s an incredible democracy. You’ve got 6 million Jews living with 2 million Arabs, and peace and prosperity in Israel. It works.

“But you’ve got neighbors all around Israel, including 2 million Palestinians who have been told and taught that somehow the Jews stole their land.”

To protect their image, to continue to flourish in the recruiting game, to thrive in a sport that pays high-seven-figure salaries, some coaches have chosen to keep their political beliefs to themselves, at least until they finish coaching. Not Pearl.

He is open about his thoughts, and combine that with his political beliefs and two particular NCAA violations ― as an assistant at Iowa in the late 1980s (where he secretly recorded a conversation with a recruit) and 15 years ago at Tennessee (where he invited a recruit to a family barbecue) ― and the coach has been labeled as conniving and untrustworthy. Others believe he is misunderstood, passionate, and perhaps a man of too many words.

That’s where Pearl’s legacy and reputation become confounding. He led Auburn to two Final Fours in a seven-year span. His players adored his openness and honesty. They didn’t have to agree on politics or the state of the world.

”In recruiting some families, because of my opinions, I was told I’m a racist,“ Pearl said. ”I’m not afraid to talk about race, not afraid to talk about faith. I’m not afraid to talk about politics. We don’t have to agree.

“What happens is families will come visit and go, ‘Wow, you’re not at all who they said you were,’ and we break down barriers.”

Pearl has been shaped by his experiences, especially growing up Jewish in Boston in the 1970s and seeing racism and discrimination firsthand in a city that has taken decades to shake its intolerant reputation.

“I know the METCO program,” he said. “I knew what forced busing was. I was here in 1972. I saw real race riots. As an athlete and as a kid, I didn’t get it. I knew that when I would go from Southie to the North End, while there was great ethnicity and great pride in those neighborhoods, you weren’t always welcomed.“

Pearl will be remembered as a passionate, controversial, opinionated, charismatic, and brash coach who was successful in his stops but also sometimes messy. But he says his desire to teach and to relate will never dissipate.

“Having been a head coach for 30 years, my players had come first, over my family, because it’s what was required in order to be successful,” he said. “I just got to the point where I didn’t want that to be my priority. And once I recognized that, that I couldn’t give it 100 percent, I didn’t want to do it.

“I’m not retired. I’m going to continue to lead in areas of education, faith, family, traditional values in our country. I’m going to continue to be an advocate for the State of Israel and fight antisemitism.

“I got to a point where the pressure, the anxiety, winning became a relief, and then just living up to the expectation. We have graduated over 150 kids as a head coach, and just 51 alone in the last 11 years. And I’m really very proud of that. But it’s just time.”

It’s OK to like Bruce Pearl, to be captivated by his words, lulled by his amiable personality and engrossed in his storytelling, but disagree with his politics. Those conflicting sentiments will be part of his legacy. He is at peace with that dichotomy and perhaps we all have to accept that.

In 2024-25, it reached another level, as the Dragons (284-97-7) won a whopping 74.1 percent of their 388 regular-season games to garner the Globe’s Division 2 Holmes Award, with Patriot League rival Hingham (68.6) placing second.

Duxbury was one of 10 divisional winners for the Globe Scholastic awards — now in their 53rd year — in which schools are ranked based on their regular-season win percentage. Scores are compiled and updated daily during the season through the Globe’s database.

Capturing its first Globe trophy since garnering Dalton Division 3 honors in 2001, Duxbury posted the third-highest winning percentage of any school in Eastern Mass., behind only perennial powers St. John’s Prep (76.7) and Bishop Feehan (75.3).

“I’m most proud of the embrace that this community has for athletics,” said Duxbury athletic director Jeff Maidment. “It’s such an important role and identity. It’s what I’ve always believed in.”

It was the Year of the Dragon in the Chinese zodiac calendar in 2024, and the 2024-25 school year made the cycle look prophetic.

The girls’ soccer, girls’ volleyball, girls’ golf, field hockey, girls’ crew, boys’ crew, boys’ swimming/diving, wrestling, girls’ indoor track, boys’ tennis, boys’ golf, and girls’ lacrosse teams all captured league titles.

For longtime boys’ tennis coach John Bunar, whose team cemented another Division 2 state championship last spring, it’s strong leadership, parenting, and, most of all, highly motivated student-athletes who ultimately make the difference.

“We get kids that are driven to be there, driven to succeed in school, how they treat other people, and on the athletic field,” Bunar said. “As coaches, we benefit from that.”

Coaches and players credit the consistency in large part to the foundation established through youth sports.

Senior Cole Martin, a hockey and lacrosse captain, developed his drive from a young age while watching the high school teams that came before him and dreaming of one day donning that same jersey. Senior cross-country, track, and lacrosse captain Addie Slimbaugh believes having that continuity from youth through high school pays off.

Girls’ lacrosse coach Colby Bartro’s daughters, third-grader Nell (8) and kindergartner Cece (5) are mesmerized by what they see on the field. Nell asks Bartro if she can tag along to 7:30 a.m. Sunday morning practices and sets her alarm to ensure she’s ready.

“Seeing our high-school athletes as role models really sets the tone for the younger kids,” Bartro said. “I know in the back of Nell’s mind, she’ll always think, ‘I want to be the next Lili Fisher or Maggie Slimbaugh.’ ”

Another component is the overlap and intersection between sports at the school. While athletes enjoy defeating nemeses Hingham and Marshfield, they also take pride in friendly competitions with one another. Track coach and lacrosse assistant Tony Fisher has noticed that once one team has achieved something, every other team is eager to match that feat.

“The team doesn’t want to be the first team to lose,” said Hailey Flynn, a basketball and golf captain. “Everyone wants to win, everyone wants to succeed, and we all want to be to the Duxbury standard, which is winning.”

That camaraderie and continuity extends to coaches, where girls’ hockey coach Dan Najarian explains that leaders from different teams bounce ideas off one another.

For instance, football coach Matt Landolfi’s daughter, Grace, was on Najarian’s hockey team. The two go way back, and will often text each other before a big game.

“It pushes us in the same direction to make it the best you can for the kids,” Najarian said.

In Duxbury, walking into the grocery store with a jersey or jacket carries great weight. The student-athletes serve as a liaison between the school and the community. Maidment said teachers and administrators constantly stop him in the halls and ask how specific teams are doing.

His formula isn’t a complicated one — building a positive culture is the key, a place where athletes can be themselves, make mistakes without fear of failure, and collaborate to compete at the highest level.

When they feel welcome, they feel empowered, which facilitates the notion of executing their role for the greater good.

Said Maidment: “It’s really about allowing the kids to be kids.”

“Everyone was very happy, because they knew the hostages were about to be released,” he said.

Many in his community, Berechman said, stayed up overnight to watch it unfold online: Aspart of a cease-fire in Gaza, the remaining living hostages were returned to Israel Monday morning.

“I am feeling relieved knowing that all 20 hostages who are alive have since been returned,” he said, though he added, ”It’s going to take a very long time for all the families to heal."

Like many in Greater Boston who have been watching the conflict in Gaza closely, Berechman was happy Monday that the cease-fire was stabilizing. He watched videos of Palestinian families returning to their destroyed homes in Northern Gaza. Other residents, including Palestinians, praised initial steps by Israel to keep the peace as well.

But Berechman, like others, was not ready to call it a lasting peace. Many also shared in enduring grief over Oct. 7 and the subsequent war.

Just rebuilding Gaza, Berechman noted, will take a very long time.

“I hope that Israelis and Palestinians can live together one day,” Berechman said. “There are many people in Israel’s government that want to restart the war after all the hostages have gone home.”

The cease-fire put on pause a two-year war that devastated Gaza and killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. Both sides in the conflict began carrying out key components of the peace deal Monday. Just as families cheered the return of the 20 Israeli hostages, crowds in Gaza and the West Bank Monday welcomed thousands of prisoners released by Israel. Still, many details remained to be resolved, as President Trump and other world leaders gathered in Egypt Monday to discuss the US-proposed peace plan, which includes an international body in Gaza overseeing Palestinian technocrats.

Berechman’s mixture of hope and trepidation was a common theme connecting many of those across Greater Boston closely watching the news from the Middle East Monday.

Sammy Nabulsi, a Palestinian American lawyer in Dorchester, was also optimistic about what he’d seen so far, including the return of Israeli hostages and the resumption of aid distribution in Gaza.

“Most importantly, it does seem that the carpetbombing of Gaza has stopped for the time being,” Nabulsi said. “So in that respect I’m very hopeful.”

But he, too, had concerns for the future, regarding the vagueness of Trump’s peace plan, its silence with respect to the West Bank, and in particular whether the United States will put sufficient pressure on Israel.

“Many of us are holding our breath,” he said. “I don’t see how this agreement can be a basis for peace if the US is not ready to enforce it to our quote-unquote ‘partner’ without conditioning our foreign military assistance.”

Nabulsi also emphasized how much it will take to rebuild Gaza, destroyed during the war, and said building materials and contractors must be allowed into the Strip.

Jason Greenberg, a Needham attorney who lost two family members on Oct. 7, 2023 and had three taken hostage and since released, said hostages “never should have been part of the equation in terms of the negotiations,” and was hopeful their release would pave the way for “something good to come out of this.”

Greenberg’s cousin Ofer Calderon and his two children were taken by Hamas on Oct. 7. The children were released the following month, and Calderon was released in February after more than a year in captivity.

“They are reunited and have been all recovering,” said Greenberg. “My cousin has expressed to me his profound awe and gratitude at the huge wide net of people who have been in his corner.”

Still, Greenberg called the situation “very, very tenuous” and called for international actors like Arab states and the United States to ensure the cease-fire doesn’t collapse in response to a breach by either side.

“Now I think meaningful negotiations can take place because lives of innocents aren’t hanging in the balance anymore,” he said. “The achievements that have been accomplished today could be unwound very easily and the fighting could resume on a moment’s notice. We want to avoid anything like what happened on October 7 but also in the last two years.”

Lea Kayali, a Palestinian-American and organizer with the Palestinian Youth Movement, was less hopeful. She said she didn’t feel confident the cease-fire meant permanent peace.

“I think all of us as Palestinians have 77 years of collective lived experience of Israel breaking promises,” she said.

But as she watched videos of Palestinians returning to their homes in Gaza and Palestinian prisoners being released, Kayali said she was moved by the steadfastness of her people.

“The scenes of embrace of the prisoners by their families this morning — I feel like they’re love notes to a Palestinian future. They’re glimpses of Palestinian freedom,” she said.

For Noe Caplan, an organizer with the Jewish activist group IfNotNow Boston, feelings of joy at the cease-fire news were equally tempered by grief for the thousands of lives already lost.

“We recognize that every life is a universe. So the end to the nonstop barrage of bombs and bloodshed is cause for relief and celebration,” he said. Still, concerns remain for Caplan about whether the cease-fire will hold and if the peace plan will sufficiently rebuild Gaza.

“The cease-fire, while urgently needed, is only a first step,” he said. “True safety will come when there’s freedom and equality for all who live between the Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea, Palestinians and Israelis.”

Among the aspects of the cease-fire that remained unresolved Monday was the release of the bodies of two dozen dead hostages; the cease-fire called for their return but only four of 28 bodies were immediately released.

Bonnie Polin, a Newton resident whose nephew, Hersh Goldberg-Polin, was killed in Gaza last year, said in an email she was “pained by 24 families that are still in limbo.”

“It is bittersweet for many people but so thankful 20 came home and reunited with their families,” Polin said. “I am relieved for 4 of the 28 families that can have closure and can start to recover.”

Shachar Horovitz, a survivor of the Oct. 7 attack on the Nova music festival who was in Boston Monday for an exhibition on the festival attack, said she was happy about the hostages being released, and struck that she could have been one of them.

“I’m thinking about the last two years, and what happened to me personally, and all the healing I’ve been through,” she said, adding that others, “They didn’t have those two years.”

Then, last year, Color, Inc. was acquired by another company, which prompted McClurkin to consider her next move. “I didn’t see myself working for somebody else any longer,” said McClurkin, a Roxbury native who now lives in Lynn.

Friends convinced her to use her years of retail experience to open a store, and her relationships with Faneuil Hall management led her to a roughly 3,000-square-foot space in the marketplace, where Beantown Flair opened in September. The South Market Building storefront, located between the Coach outpost and a new footwear store, was previously occupied by John Fluevog Shoes, which closed in 2023.

Now, McClurkin is putting her own stamp on the souvenir shop genre. Yes, there are still the requisite baggies of Boston baked beans ($5.99) and copies of “Make Way for Ducklings” ($10.99). But there’s also a hearty selection of locally made fare that McClurkin hopes will appeal to townies and tourists alike: Bags of coffee beans from Peabody-based Capito Coffee ($16.99), irreverent greeting cards made by Lynn artist Jennifer Adler ($4.75), and displayed on the back wall, paintings and prints by artist Raheem Jamal, a friend of McClurkin’s ($25-$600). The plan is to feature a new artist every two months.

The way she sees it, this concept has been a long time coming for Faneuil Hall, where she is the only Black woman operating a brick-and-mortar store in a marketplace named after a slave trader.

“As complicated as it is, it’s important that everybody knows [who is] from this city or from the surrounding communities, that they have a place here,” she said.

It’s also a new era for Faneuil Hall. The marketplace got a new landlord last year, J. Safra Real Estate, which took over the lease from Ashkenazy Acquisition Corporation, which faced frequent criticisms over its investment in the property and its preponderance of out-of-state chains.

The new landlord, McClurkin said, is “really making an effort to bring this place back to life.” Next door to Beantown Flair, woman-owned footwear retailer MaraK Shoes recently opened its doors, and Flourish & Foundry, a home decor and gift shop, is another nearby addition.

“As we think about the next generation of retail, dining, and cultural experiences that we can offer residents and visitors, we are committed to honoring the legacy of Faneuil Hall Marketplace while creating a thriving gathering place that reflects Boston’s culture, vibrancy, and diversity,” said a spokesperson for Faneuil Hall Marketplace in a statement.

Beantown Flair, meanwhile, is just getting started. McClurkin is constantly on the hunt for more products from vendors throughout New England, and by the end of the month hopes to start bringing in more foot traffic by hosting live music and open mics at the dedicated performance space in the back of the store.

“The vision is grand,” she said.

South Market Building in Faneuil Hall Marketplace, Boston; instagram.com/beantownflair

Last October, the massive redevelopment of Suffolk Downs debuted its first residential building, the 475-unit Amaya. A year later, those tenants have a place to drink, just downstairs.

Twisted Fate Brewing opened its second location earlier this month on the ground floor of the Amaya, near the Beachmont MBTA station. It is the first retail tenant on the 161-acre site, a former racetrack spanning Revere and East Boston, which local developer HYM Investment Group purchased in 2017 and is transforming into a mixed-use community with housing, retail, office, hotel, and public space.

“We’ve been waiting so long to open our doors, but something tells me HYM might have felt like they’ve been waiting even longer to have a retail tenant open,” said Erica Tritta, one of the owners of Twisted Fate, which debuted in Danvers in 2022. The other owners are Tritta’s husband, David Pinette, his sister, Kim McNamara, and her husband, Bill McNamara.

Rachel Ottley, HYM’s vice president of retail, said the firm was drawn to Twisted Fate because of its local ownership, as well as its proven track record and loyal following; a customer from Danvers was actually the one who connected the Twisted Fate team with Blackline Retail Group, the project’s leasing agent. HYM also liked the idea of introducing a community hub to the site early on — another gathering spot, The Point Barre and Yoga, is slated to open later this month.

“This is a development that has no retail kind of surrounding it at all,” Ottley said. “My goal in the first lease-up in these first few buildings is building a city within a city.”

For the Twisted Fate crew, the Suffolk Downs development presented an opportunity to design a taproom, essentially, from the ground up, bringing to life their vision of “brewery chic,” as Kim McNamara puts it.

The roughly 2,000-square-foot brewery boasts plenty of comfortable couches, TVs, and a 16-tap bar, carrying suds popular with the Danvers crowd, like the Match Made in Heaven stout, as well as the Paul Revere, a New England IPA exclusive to the Revere taproom. Soon, small bites will join the menu — think pretzels, empanadas, and small pizzas — and come next spring, an approximately 400-square-foot patio will add outdoor seating to the mix.

Twisted Fate’s grand opening in early October coincided with Revere’s annual fall festival, which brought thousands of revelers to their doorstep. In addition, plenty of devoted customers from Danvers made the trek down Route 1, where they mingled with the building’s tenants.

“We got a decent amount of feedback just saying, like, ‘We’ve been waiting for this,’” Kim McNamara said.

64 Salt St., Revere; twistedfatebrewing.com

At its latest store in Burlington, David’s Bridal is marrying couture with computing.

Earlier this month, in the Wayside shopping center, the wedding dress juggernaut opened its second location of Diamonds & Pearls, a new retail concept that debuted in Delray Beach, Fla., in May.

“It was by far the next stop we needed to make,” said Kelly Cook, David’s Bridal chief executive, of New England.

Unlike a typical David’s store, which offers around 200 gown styles, Diamonds & Pearls is “more curated,” Cook said, carrying about 50 to 100 options, many of them by high-end designers such as Marchesa and Oleg Cassini.

Meanwhile, large wall-mounted digital touchscreens contain everything the store doesn’t, displaying the brand’s full inventory of dresses, jewelry, and accessories.

“It’s not tech for tech’s sake,” said Cook, who stepped into the top job in April. “It is technology to romanticize this experience so much in a way that she completely forgets that she’s stressed about planning the wedding.”

It’s part of the Pennsylvania-based company’s tech-focused “Aisle to Algorithm” strategy, which was announced about two years after David’s Bridal filed for bankruptcy and was subsequently acquired by a new owner, CION Investment Corporation. These days, “the vision of the company is to be the largest AI-enabled retail, media, and planning marketplace serving weddings,“ Cook said.

To that end, just in the past year, David’s has launched Diamonds & Pearls, acquired the wedding-focused media company Love Stories TV, and rolled out Pearl Planner, an AI-powered tool meant to help couples tick off everything on their to-do list, from picking out an engagement party outfit to writing vows to booking honeymoon lodgings.

The Diamond & Pearls store is getting ready to host an official grand opening in Burlington later this fall, but Cook is already looking ahead.

“We’ve got 100 more locations around the United States that we think that we’ve got an opportunity to expand,” she said.

No one likes rain on a parade. Still, as holiday storms go, nor’easter that struck Southern New England over the Indigenous Peoples/Columbus Day weekend was relatively mild. The storm dumped more than 6 inches of rain and brought gusts of up to 65 miles an hour to Cape Cod. But there have been few reports of major damage, power has mostly been restored, and the storm is set to peter out today.

The recovery hasn’t always been so swift. Here’s a look back at seven other storms that dampened, damaged, or delayed New England’s holiday spirit over the years, with a little help from the Globe’s archives.

This storm holds the record for dumping the most snow on Boston, ultimately depositing more than 27 inches. Yet as a front-page Globe story at the time put it, the storm “was more disruptive than destructive.” Because of the holiday, many residents were already at home and off the roads.

April Fool’s may be more joke than holiday, but this powerful nor’easter was no laughing matter. It started as heavy rain before rapidly intensifying off the coast, dropping more than 2 feet of snow on Boston. Winds roared to over 70 miles per hour, knocking out power to 700,000 people in New England and snapping one of the USS Constitution’s masts in the Charlestown Navy Yard. See photos of the aftermath.

A low-pressure system stalled over coastal New England over Mother’s Day weekend, unleashing months’ worth of rain in just a few days. Rivers in Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts overflowed, damaging buildings and roads. York County, Maine, alone got more than 15 inches of rain, doing more than $12 million in damage in today’s money.

Globe meteorologist Dave Epstein has called it one of his worst forecasts. While working in Hartford, he predicted a dusting of snow. It ended up being the region’s biggest Thanksgiving snowstorm in 64 years, with more than a foot accumulating on Cape Cod. The storm created treacherous driving conditions for holiday travelers and canceled high-school football games across Eastern Massachusetts.

In Dave’s defense, Thanksgiving weather is notoriously unpredictable. In 1938, sleet, hail, and ice killed 11 people across the region. Three years later, the year Congress made Thanksgiving a federal holiday, temperatures in Boston reached 71 degrees.

Initially called the No-Name Storm, this nor’easter and hurricane combo canceled trick-or-treating and flattened hundreds of buildings across the region. The storm is now better known by the nickname Sebastian Junger gave it in his 1997 book about a Gloucester fishing vessel that sank during the storm with all hands. See photos of the devastation.

This March nor’easter did its worst damage on the first day of Lent, giving rise to its holy-day moniker. Although it caused the most havoc across the mid-Atlantic and the South, the storm also sent big waves crashing into Southern New England.

Normally a good thing, a snowy Christmas can come with costs. A freak snowstorm on Christmas Day in 1974 made “dreams come true and holiday traveling a nightmare,” the Globe reported, snarling traffic and causing at least eight deaths in Massachusetts. In 1947, a surprise storm deposited another few inches on top of the 17 already on the ground in some places. In 1909, a windy snowstorm reached hurricane force and flooded coastal areas.

For more on the weekend’s nor’easter, read my colleague Ken Mahan’s updates and see photos from the storm.

Five men have been charged in connection with the assault of a gay couple in Mattapan last month, the Boston Police Department said Wednesday.

All five men pleaded not guilty to various assault and battery charges, according to court records. The case was investigated by detectives in the department’s Civil Rights Unit, though no civil rights charges are being pursued at this time, the police department said in a statement.

Woopenson Morrisset, 30, of Boston; Maurice Payne, 37, of Brockton; and Patrick Fanfan, 53, of Hyde Park, were each charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon resulting in serious bodily injury, the statement said.

Franklin Francois, 51, of Randolph, and Gardy Exantus, 33, of Mattapan, were each charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Exantus also faces an additional charge of assault and battery.

The men were arraigned in Dorchester District Court between Oct. 3 and 10. All except Payne were released on their own recognizance, with orders to avoid contact with the victims or any witnesses, court records show. Payne was ordered held without bail and is scheduled for a status review hearing on Oct. 17.

The assault took place Sept. 13 near 550 River St. One of the victims was struck in the head with a baseball bat and his partner was attacked after confronting the men, according to a police report.

The man who had been struck by the bat was bleeding from the back of his head when officers found him on the ground in a River Street parking lot, the report said.

The violence followed a verbal dispute between the couple and their alleged attackers in front of a liquor store on River Street at about 7:45 p.m., the report said. As the couple approached the store, the men allegedly directed anti-gay slurs at them, including some in Haitian Creole, a witness told the Globe last month.

Police have not provided an update on the condition of the man who was struck with a bat and did not immediately respond to a follow-up inquiry from the Globe Wednesday evening.

A virtual press conference and rally to discuss the attack was held last week, the Globe reported. Both state and local officials as well as leaders of local LGBTQ+ advocacy groups condemned the incident, reaffirming their support for queer people in their communities.

Culpepper is highly qualified for the job; indeed, it would be hard to find a candidate with deeper roots in the district and the city. His grandparents were the first Black homeowners on Seaver Street in Roxbury. Culpepper graduated from Boston English in 1971 and Brandeis University, worked in local politics, and later served as senior pastor at Roxbury’s Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church. His work as regional counsel for the US Department of Housing and Urban Development included a successful discrimination lawsuit against the Boston Housing Authority that resulted in new civil rights protections at the agency.

If elected on Nov. 4, Culpepper said he will focus on housing. While he supports preserving public housing and subsidized rental housing, he said his main priority would be to encourage homeownership as a safeguard against gentrification. “In terms of really stabilizing neighborhoods, I think you really need homeownership,” he said in an interview earlier this month with the Globe editorial board. His plan for doing so would include pushing tenant first-right-to-buy policies and the use of Section 8 vouchers for home purchases.

Culpepper said he would support the planned renovation of White Stadium, which is located in District 7, as long as the community benefits are sufficient and enough of the money spent goes to local businesses. “One of the things that I think this community desperately needs is private investment,” he said.

Looming over the election is the legacy of Fernandes Anderson, who was praised as a trailblazer but whose ethical lapses ultimately led to her downfall. She hired relatives to city jobs, drawing a state ethics commission fine, and ultimately pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges after taking a $7,000 kickback. She was recently sentenced to a month in prison.

Everyone deserves elected officials who are looking out for voters, not themselves, and who understand the common-sense ethical guidelines that seemed to elude Fernandes Anderson. Culpepper said “integrity is not going to be an issue” if he’s elected, pointing to his own record managing the church and working in government. Part of his role at HUD, he said, was providing ethics guidance to the agency’s employees in New England. “Folks know that they can count on Miniard Culpepper to do what’s right and what’s in the best interest of the residents of District 7,” he said.

Culpepper and his opponent, Said Ahmed, emerged from an 11-candidate field after receiving the most votes in the September preliminary election. The district covers Roxbury, parts of Dorchester and the South End, and a sliver of Fenway. Ahmed, a Somali refugee and running champion, graduated from Boston English, competed as a professional athlete, and has worked in the Boston Public Schools as a coach and attendance officer. While his candidacy is strong — he finished first in the preliminary — the Globe’s recent reporting on Ahmed’s misleading campaign materials raise questions about whether he is the right choice to represent a district still reeling from controversy.

Since the preliminary, Culpepper has picked up endorsements from several of the candidates he defeated. It’s not hard to see why. The district includes some of the neediest parts of the city, which in turn require an effective advocate and leader. Based on his long history in Roxbury, Culpepper is the candidate who best meets those needs, and the Globe enthusiastically endorses his candidacy.

At night, you can hear them before you see them. Beneath piled trash bags comes the faint rustle and scratch that makes every Bostonian’s skin crawl — then the slick blur of fur and a long tail slipping into the gutter.

“The rats in our neighborhood are getting worse it seems every day,” one disgruntled Roxbury resident reported to 311 last week: “Fifteen years and I can’t remember it ever being this bad.”

Run-ins with rats are becoming more common as the chorus of complaints grows louder across Boston. A Globe analysis of 311 data shows rodent reports climbing steadily over the past four years, with 2025 on pace to be the rattiest year yet. Residents filed more than 5,000 reports in 2024 — about 1,000 more than the year before.

It’s been more than a year since the city of Boston launched the Boston Rodent Action Plan, which includes a slew of anti-rodent measures: rat-resistant trash bins, sewer traps, and new cameras and sensors placed around the city to track where rodents are most active.

But change comes slowly. City officials say it’s still too early to tell the results. In August, City Council also floated a proposal for a “rat czar” in Boston after New York City appointed one, but that effort fizzled.

“The goal was: how do we become more proactive,” said John Ulrich, assistant commissioner of the city’s Inspectional Services Department. “It’s really addressing … the supportive environment that allows rodents to thrive, mainly trash.”

Rodents can pose a serious public health risk. A Tufts University study published in April found that rat populations in Boston carry leptospirosis, a type of bacteria that can spread to humans, and in rare cases cause severe illness or death.

In the absence of an official “rat czar,” Viviano Cantu, a 12-year Boston resident who works for the tech company WHOOP, has taken up the mantle. He runs a website called rats.boston, which maps rodent and other critter complaints across the city.

For Cantu, the problem was personal.

When he and his wife were apartment hunting while expecting a baby, they nearly signed a lease on a place that seemed perfect — until they opened a closet and found a giant rat trap. A quick search of 311 data revealed dozens of rodent complaints about the restaurant next door and trash piling up in the alley.

“With a baby, that’s not gonna fly,” he said.

Using city data, his website helps identify rodent hot spots. Without the data, he said, “it’s not easy to understand where these problems are.”

Nowhere is the chorus of complaints louder than in the North End, where some residents are truly smelling a rat. The neighborhood tops the city for rat reports per square mile, with 619 reports since 2021 packed into less than a quarter of a square mile.

Its dense housing, narrow streets, and restaurant-lined blocks make it an irresistible haven for Boston’s most reviled neighbors.

“They’re everywhere,” said Yuri Jimenez, 42, who works in the North End and lives in neighboring West End. “It’s scary. You walk by the trash and they run out.”

The North End is followed by Beacon Hill, South End, and Back Bay in rodent complaints. Despite long being known as “rat city,” Allston didn’t crack the top five.

A 2-year-old girl was found safe after a five-hour search in Dorchester, N.H., last week that began when the child went missing from her yard, authorities said.

Shortly after 4 p.m. on Oct. 10, the child’s mother called 911 to report that her daughter, who was playing in her fenced-in backyard with the family’s two dogs, was gone, Christopher McKee, a conservation sergeant with the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department, said Wednesday.

The dogs, a black lab and a golden retriever, were also gone, evidently through an opening in the fence, McKee said.

“Looks like the lower section was pushed open, probably by the dogs, and they went out to play, and she probably followed right along,” McKee said.

Upon receiving the report, McKee immediately marshalled rescue services in the area, including the New England K9 Search and Rescue team and the State Police.

“We knew we were heading in the right direction,” he said.

“It was very clear that the dog had a scent,” Corson said. “We went ahead and called out for the child, and as the dog was pretty much right on top of her, she ended up yelling back to us.”

Corson said the toddler was freezing cold and lying down in the dark, but was still “very excited to see people” and initially thought Corson was her father.

“I’m right here!” the toddler said, Corson recalled. “Hi Dad!”

“I asked her if she was cold, and she told me she needed a bath,” Corson added.

The girl was found less than a mile from her house, Corson said.

Corson picked up the girl, bundled her in warm clothes, and brought her to a waiting ambulance, where she was taken to the hospital as a precaution.

“She was clearly excited to be going home,” Corson said. “She was very excited to be home and see mom and dad and her dogs.”

Proudly or infamously, South Boston was the most insular community in Boston in those years. Bulger was embraced as a native son, even as he exploited and destroyed those who lionized him.

Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police log books (a.k.a. blotters) in our communities.

At 8 p.m. Oct. 9, a 39-year-old man from Boston attempted a bold move while driving when he tried to squeeze by an MBTA bus in Andrew Square. It didn’t go as he had planned. In fact, if he were trying to save himself some time, it backfired in a very big way, as his car hit the side of the bus and became wedged between it and the curb. MBTA Transit Police determined he was impaired, took him into custody, and had his vehicle towed. Thankfully, no injuries were reported, and police shared a video of the debacle on social media along with this timeless bit of advice: “Don’t Drink & Drive!!!!”

A moose got a police escort in Keene, N.H., on Oct. 5. Police said the animal “made its way through downtown” and video footage shared on social media showed cruisers following behind the animal as it galloped down the street. Police reported that they guided the moose out of downtown safely and away from residential neighborhoods.

At 2:41 p.m. Sept. 14, Medway police got a call from a resident of Fisher Street who reported that his Boston Globe mailbox had been “thrown from its post.” Police responded and lent a hand with “getting the box back together.” According to the log entry, the caller was satisfied by the police response and didn’t want to take further action.

At 8:53 p.m. Oct. 3, Norwood police got a call from someone walking a dog and heard yelling in the area of Hampden Drive. According to the log entry, the caller “thought it was possibly a Halloween decoration but was not sure.” Police checked the area and didn’t see or hear anything suspicious. They spoke to a man, however, who said he had also heard something, but he, too, thought it sounded like one of those audible Halloween decorations.

A harrowing event took place recently in Dorchester — not the neighborhood in Boston, but the tiny New Hampshire town with a population of 339. It started around 4:07 p.m. on Oct. 10, when New Hampshire State Police and the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department were informed that a 2-year-old child there was missing. When they got the call, the child had not been seen for over 45 minutes, and first responders quickly swung into action. Conservation officers, state troopers, and firefighters from Canaan, Rumney, and Grafton responded along with area search and rescue teams to look for the toddler. All told, over 90 volunteers showed up to help. Several K-9 teams searched along drainage areas and in thickly wooded spots near the the toddler’s home, and drones and a state police helicopter were used to search a large swamp from the air. Almost four hours later, at about 7:52 p.m., the mission ended happily when the child was located safe and sound (albeit a little chilly). WMUR reported that when Jeremy Corson and his dog Freya from New England K9 Search and Rescue found the toddler, she said: “I’m cold, I think I’m ready for a bath.”

Ahmed painted himself as a “young, energized fighter,” saying his approach to elected office would be rooted in his lived experience as a Somali refugee and former professional athlete, along with his years of working with youth in Boston Public Schools and as a coach and cofounder of the Boston United Track and Cross Country Club.

Culpepper, a Dorchester native, emphasized his decades-long track record as a grass-roots community advocate, including his nearly 30 years as an attorney in the US Department of Housing and Urban Development, as well as his tenure as a well-known senior pastor at the Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church.

The two also offered different policy strategies to address the range of challenges in the district.

When asked how they would spur investment in Roxbury’s economy and support local businesses, Ahmed focused on pushing developers to include affordable commercial space in new developments, and increasing education and awareness for how to apply and qualify for Community Development Block Grants.

Culpepper said he would seek to get the district designated as an “empowerment zone,” a federal program that offers tax incentives and grants to spur economic development in particular areas, and that he’ll also work closely with the mayor’s Office of Economic Opportunity and Inclusion to funnel more funding to the district.

On housing, Ahmed emphasized his support for rent control, while Culpepper outlined his “gentrification neutralization plan,” which would aim to increase homeownership options for people with Section 8 vouchers or residents of public housing developments.

The two also committed to being “independent” representatives, but Ahmed indicated he would be inclined to “be aligned” with the mayor and work in partnership with her, while Culpepper offered a specific example of an issue on which he and the mayor do not agree. He would fight her administration’s effort to put a bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue.

The debate turned tense on a few occasions when Ahmed opted to question and request a fact-check on Culpepper’s record. Ahmed also emphasized the age difference between himself and Culpepper, referring to himself as a “young, go-getter.”

Culpepper brushed off the attacks, and later told the Globe he is “confident” in his decades of experience advocating for Roxbury residents, which he said “speaks for itself.” After the event, Ahmed said he felt it was appropriate to question Culpepper’s background working on housing issues, particularly when residents are still suffering from rising housing costs and facing being pushed out of their neighborhoods.

Toward the end of the debate, the moderators asked how each candidate will demonstrate “integrity, transparency, and ethical leadership” considering recent scandals that have plagued the district. Both candidates painted themselves as role models poised to earn the trust of their constituents.

“When folks look at Miniard Culpepper, they look at someone that has fought for the community all of his life, someone that grew up in the community and fought when it came to housing,” Culpepper said. “They look at somebody they can trust, someone that cares and someone that will fight for them.”

“This neighborhood took me in, this neighborhood gave me home, access, and opportunity,” Ahmed said. “We need someone that’s a go-getter ... and I will be there fighting for you day and night.

The District 7 position is the only open seat on the November ballot, after Fernandes Anderson stepped down from the role earlier this year after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges for taking a $7,000 kickback while in office. Fernandes Anderson was ordered to pay $13,000 in restitution, and sentenced to one month in prison.

She is set to self-report to an as-yet-to-be designated federal prison on Friday.

Ahmed has also faced some controversy and accusations of misconduct during his District 7 campaign.

Another District 7 candidate previously accused Ahmed of harassment, as did a Healey administration official, who filed two police reports about Ahmed’s alleged behavior during early voting in the lead-up to the preliminary election in September. A municipal court judge later terminated the harassment prevention order the official had requested against Ahmed.

Several longtime civic leaders also criticized Ahmed last week over a recent Instagram post, which they said misleadingly and incorrectly implied they are supporting and have endorsed his political campaign.

Ahmed later deleted the post from his Instagram and told the Globe he did not intend it to be misleading, or imply that all the men pictured in the post had endorsed him.

District 7 voters will choose between Ahmed and Culpepper in November, after the two advanced from a crowded field of 11 candidates in the September preliminary election, with Ahmed receiving 1,170 votes and Culpepper winning 1,112, according to the city’s official election results.

Mavrick Afonso, who came in third place by a tight margin, had formally requested a recount in the race last month, but it did not ultimately change the outcome of which finalists will compete to fill the District 7 seat in November.

District 7 comprises some of the city’s most diverse and historically disenfranchised neighborhoods, including Roxbury, and parts of Dorchester, Fenway, and the South End.

Both Ahmed and Culpepper have previously run for office. Ahmed ran a failed campaign for the State House last year, and Culpepper unsuccessfully ran for a state Senate seat in 2022.
