Those three homicides are among approximately 1,800 murders in the city that remain unsolved and are now posted on the Boston Police Department’s website.

Investigators are publicizing them in an ambitious effort to enlist the public’s help in solving them.

Boston’s unsolved murders are now listed by year, going back as far as 1963.

Sergeant Detective Nick Moore said the effort to document every case is a work in progress, and the department will update the listings as necessary.

Moore, a member of the department’s homicide unit, said detectives are seeking information and tips that can help solve these cases.

“People want justice, obviously. They want closure. They want convictions,” Moore said. “But they also want to know that we are actively looking at their loved one’s case, and we’re actively seeking information on it.”

Police are also asking relatives and loved ones to contribute photos of the victims by sending them to unsolved@pd.boston.gov.

Clementina Chery, president and CEO of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, said listing the unsolved homicides online is a “great step” that represents “just one part of the broader support families of unsolved homicide victims need.”

By publishing individual cases online, police hope to increase public awareness and generate new leads. Information from witnesses, family, friends, and the community is their greatest resource to solve these homicides, investigators say.

“These cases are unsolved for a reason,” Moore said. “There’s always something that somebody’s been withholding over the years.”

He said people with that kind of knowledge may not have wanted to get involved before or were scared to talk to police. But as time goes on, circumstances can change. They might have a change of heart, want to clear their conscience, or are no longer afraid.

Police hope the photos will jog their memory and motivate them to “come forward with information that they’ve been withholding,” Moore said.

The list of unsolved murders can be found on the homicide unit’s webpage: police.boston.gov/homicide-unit.

The oldest case currently featured is the murder of James Smith, who was wearing women’s clothing when he was fatally shot in Roxbury on March 1, 1963.

Smith was shot to death in his apartment at 2:45 a.m., the Globe reported at the time.

“At the time of the shooting two women, friends of Smith, one 22 and the other 21, were chatting in the kitchen,” the Globe wrote. “Witnesses said they heard four shots, and a stranger ran out through the kitchen. He entered a parked car and drove off.”

Moore wants to make sure that every unsolved homicide since 1963 is remembered.

“That is exactly why I want them all up there,” he said. “So they know that we are seeking information ... and that they’re not forgotten.”

Mariellen Burns, the police department’s chief of communications, said the goal of the project is to keep the victims’ memories alive and inspire people to share their knowledge about these homicides, no matter how long ago.

“This is still somebody’s baby. This is still somebody’s child,” Burns said. “Or their father, or their boyfriend, or husband, or girlfriend, or mother.”

Chery knows this all too well: her 15-year-old son, Louis D. Brown, was murdered in 1993. She founded the Peace Institute, which is named in his honor, the following year.

The institute has long advocated for family members of homicide victims, promoting legislation to establish an office of unsolved homicides within the attorney general’s office, create a statewide database of unsolved homicides, and allow relatives to petition to have a case reviewed if it remains unsolved after three years.

Chery said she would like to see a “frequently asked questions” page on the police department’s website that provides guidance for families and loved ones of homicide victims, and for police to have a clear communication schedule with family members during the investigative process.

Chery said she also wants to make sure the police department’s homicide unit has enough resources.

“We know the detectives are busy,” she said. “If they say it’s a manpower issue, what can we as survivors do to advocate [for] more funding?”

Anyone with information about any unsolved homicide is urged to contact the homicide unit at 617-343-4470. Tips can also be submitted anonymously by calling the Crime Stoppers Hotline at 1-800-494-TIPS.

That’s the key for the Redhawks (8-5), ranked eighth in this week’s Globe Top 20 poll. Brooke Barnett, a 6-foot-1-inch junior, and Dottin, a 5-11 senior, form arguably the best middle duo in the state.

“We work on blocking at practice a ton because it’s such a key to our defense,” said first-year coach Bob Harless. “Having two big blocks on six rotations is unheard of. It frustrates other teams.”

Barnett, the team leader in kills and blocks, didn’t initially enjoy volleyball. Her parents, Brettany and Clifton, encouraged her to finish what she started, and though her father died of COVID in 2021 before she got into the sport, she thinks of him when she gives that extra effort.

“I know that my dad would want me to play some type of sport,” she said. “The more I got into it, the more passion I got for it and the more that I want him to be happy for what I’m doing.”

For Dottin, second on the team in kills and blocks, the sport has been “a new happiness” since she started playing in eighth grade. Harless said it is a “testament to her commitment” that she is a vital member of the team despite having limited time due to travel from her home Boston as part of the METCO program.

“It’s like a blanket in a way. It’s safe in here,” Dottin said of the Natick gym. “With my team, it’s like a family. It’s tough being away from my actual family, but I have the family here, so I love it.”

Facing each other in practice makes them both better. Dottin thrives with quick dishes in the middle, and Barnett sometimes wants a setup that draws her closer to the left pin. As they improve their hitting, they improve their blocking.

“I’m always trying to go around her,” said Dottin, “Doing different shots, that also help in games, when you’re seeing that higher block or multiple blocks.”

It’s rare for a team to have two star middles. Though it presents mismatch opportunities, it requires timing, and timing requires chemistry.

Natick’s two-setter system helps with that. Senior Ruby Jasper connects with Barnett and sophomore Lily Chung operates with Dottin.

“Me and Brooke, I’ve never had a connection like that with a hitter before,” said Jasper, who is best friends and club teammates with Barnett. “Our connection is so phenomenal, and I think the same for Lily and Aiya.

“Only practicing with that person, really getting the reps with that person, and doing the extra things like having the extra outlets, having the extra plays, every single play is so important because whenever a ball gets thrown out of system, how do you set the middle on that?”

Chung and Dottin don’t have Jasper and Barnett’s three years of development together, but seeing that cooperation has hastened their synergy.

“Whenever we get off a point, me and Aiya, we’ve always had a chance to talk,” Chung said. “I know when I go wrong, she knows when she goes wrong, and we can communicate really well so we can get the next point.”

The dual system allows for the setter-middle partners to also observe what the other pair does from either the sideline or the back row. However, it costs Harless some of his 18 substitutions per set. He has to be prudent with his lineup changes when matches go point for point.

“I chew through a lot of subs against the good teams,” he said. “It’s all about the game situation, matchups.”

Last year in Division 2, Billerica had a similar composition. The Indians’ kills leader, Ella Quin took sets from Meghan Downs, and their blocking leader Nyrah Joseph received feeds from Emma Johnson.

Billerica rode the senior middles and junior setters to an undefeated regular season and advanced to the state semifinals, navigating frequent substitutions when games went point for point.

“I really utilized matching each of the middles with the setter they connected best with, along with lining them up in the front row with a blocker who can complement them or by themselves,” Billerica coach Brittney Apostolakes said.

Natick made a statement with the win over Newton North, and look to carry that confidence into the Division 1 tournament.

“If we compete, stay focused, I think we can make it to the final four,” said Harless. “I really do.”

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Saturday’s rally concluded after a performance by the Boston-based rock band The Sheila Divine.

Attendees began heading off the Common, still waving flags and holding up signs.

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Several members of the state’s Washington delegation took the stage and fired up the crowd with more chants and calls to resist the Trump administration.

Senator Elizabeth Warren called Trump “a bully” and “weak.”

“When we don’t bow down to kings or bullies, they start to lose their power,” she told the crowd. “The American people do not bow down.”

Senator Ed Markey and Representatives Katherine Clark, Ayanna Pressley, and Seth Moulton also spoke to the demonstrators from the stage.

“I want him to hear this down in Washington, DC, that freedom is knocking on Donald Trump’s door,” Moulton told the crowd. “Ding Dong, Donny! Freedom is here.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As demonstrators began heading towards the exits, vendors at tables piled with “No King’s” merchandise struggled to make their final sales. Others wove through the thinning crowd with stickers and flyers, handing out protest paraphernalia to anyone willing to take one.

“I think it’s a good message,” said John Leonard, 68, as he passed out laminated stickers that read “President Chump” in bold block letters. “I even sent some to my friends to put up around Mar-a-Lago.”

Leonard said the crowd was just what he expected — peaceful and joyful. He was glad to see both older and younger protesters in attendance, and said the turnout represented “all kinds of people.”

“People may be depressed, but the solution is getting out and being counted,” said Leonard, who lives in Hingham. “People have to stand up right away. We can’t hesitate.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As the demonstration neared the three-hour mark, there was no sign of waning energy from the crowd. Dozens of protesters climbed the Soldiers and Sailors Monument to lead chants. Cheers grew louder and views of the stage were hard to find.

“Our democracy is melting away,” said Trish McClean, 75, of Dorchester. “It’s heartbreaking and very frightful.”

McClean said that the Trump administration has no respect for the US Constitution, and she worries that people will lose their health insurance.

Saturday’s sizable crowd made her more hopeful than she’s been in some time, but she said the rally still doesn’t feel like an adequate response to the world’s atrocities. “I can’t believe there’s not more people here, and that this isn’t happening every day. ... We can all make a difference.”

By Amanda Gokee, Globe Staff

Among the eye-grabbing costumes and outfits were many people dressed up as frogs.

Barb Brunelle, a 65-year-old retired math teacher, said the inflatable full-body frog suit she wore was a symbol of solidarity with protestors from around the country, including those in Portland, Oregon. She said a viral social media post of a person in a frog costume hexing an ICE official inspired her attire.

She said she ordered the $60 inflatable suit on Amazon last Saturday, and by the next day, she said, they weren’t available until after Halloween. She said she hopes the costume brings a bit of levity to a “dark” time.

“If we can bring some joy to all the insanity that’s happening, even for a few minutes, why not?” she said.

By Amanda Gokee, Globe Staff

For Corrine Jones, a 31-year-old mom of four, protesting President Trump was a family affair. She had all four of her children, from ages one to 10, in tow during the “No Kings” protest in Concord on Saturday.

“I think it’s really important that my kids don’t get used to the insanity of the last nine or 10 months,” she said. “I want them to realize that everything that’s going on now is abnormal.”

She said she’s also disappointed in how Democrats are responding to the Trump administration.

“I’m really worried about the fact that both parties seem to serve the same masters,” Jones said. “They’re both really bought out by corporate interests. It feels like the Democrats can’t launch an effective and credible resistance because they’re paying homage to the same billionaires that the Republicans are.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As the Common continued to fill with people, families dotted the crowd. Some parents hoisted toddlers onto their shoulders, and others followed teenagers weaving toward the stage.

“They were the people who introduced me to protesting and marching, so I wanted them to come with me,” said Amina Castro Jacobs, 19, who suggested the family attend Saturday’s demonstration together. “And we hate Trump.”

The family, active in Boston’s immigrant community, said they’re deeply worried about the future of their neighbors. But protesting together, said Jenny Jacobs, Amina’s mother, serves as a way for parents to pass down important political values while learning from young people.

“Our child’s generation has created a new energy,” said Jacobs, 50, who lives in Jamaica Plain. “There’s a lot of things to be angry and frustrated and depressed about right now, but following their lead has been really hopeful.”

By Amanda Gokee, Globe Staff

Protesters gathered in front of New Hampshire’s State House on Saturday afternoon for a “No Kings” rally.

Speakers addressed people on the State House lawn, with the crowd extending along the surrounding streets, where they were met with the honking horns of passing cars and live protest music.

“I came here specifically because I wanted to stand up for my state in my capital,” said Pebbles Sillars, 61, who donned a handmade outfit representing a “wolf in sheep’s clothing.” She wore an actual sheep’s skin on her back and a hand-felted wolf’s head over her face.

She said the outfit is meant to represent President Trump, who she sees as a wolf in sheep’s clothing.

“I think that a lot of people were misled by Trump and his promises,” she said.

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Some who came out to the Common were dressed in costumes ranging from unicorns and dinosaurs to lobsters and frogs.

Many stopped to take pictures with Richard Saunders, 69, of Newton, who was dressed as Pope Leo XIV. Saunders said he bought the costume after friends remarked on his close resemblance to the pontiff.

Saunders, who was raised Catholic, carried a sign quoting the sonnet inscribed on the Statue of Liberty pedestal that symbolizes the country as a beacon of hope for immigrants.

“This is what made America great,” he said.

He said the country was built “on the backs of immigrants, like my Irish ancestors who came over during the potato famine.”

“People are losing sight of that,” he said.

He said he felt inspired by the large turnout in Boston on Saturday.

“It gives me so much strength,” he said. “When you get cynical for the future, come to something like this if you want to get your faith restored in humanity.”

By Steven Porter, Globe Staff

Among the throngs of protestors who descended on Market Square, many bobbed about in colorful costumes, including one man who wore an inflatable suit depicting President Trump as a giant baby.

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell touted the approximately 40 lawsuits she’s filed against President Trump.“They will keep coming, and we will keep fighting,” Campbell said. “And if they want to come for Massachusetts, I say: Bring it on.”

The crowd cheered.

Campbell ran through the lawsuits over funding cuts, attempts to end birthright citizenship, and more.

“We are here to send a message: In America, we have no kings, we have the people,” she said.

As they did with Mayor Michelle Wu, a small group of hard-left protesters in the front row, waving Palestinian flags and ones with the Soviet hammer and sickle, attempted to yell over her.’

“You’re not going to out-noise us,” Campbell told them. And then she added: “We’re with you.”

By Carlos Munoz, Globe Staff

From the steps of the State House, Providence Mayor Brett Smiley spoke to the need for people to be around “like-minded people” to know they are not alone in their frustration, and to send a message “this is not the direction we want our government to be going in.”

He estimated more than 2,000 people in attendance at the city’s “No Kings” rally.

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As hundreds of people pressed toward the stage, others spread out across the southeast corner of Boston Common, chatting with friends and clapping along to a live rendition of Yankee Doodle.

“We thought it would be fun to bring a little humor,” said Elizabeth Barry, 50, who came dressed as a calico cat after her first-choice raccoon costume didn’t arrive in time. “I think it’s really important to make this feel safe.”

Inspired by demonstrators who wore inflatable animals at protests in Portland, Ore., Barry said the costumes are meant to make rallies feel more welcoming for people who might otherwise be nervous to attend. The unicorn beside her nodded in agreement, adding that the pair is meeting President Trump’s absurd decisions with their own showing of absurdity.

“Fascists hate when you laugh at them,” said Rosy, Barry’s friend, who lives in Somerville. “This is a way of saying we’re out here protesting and we’re wearing funny costumes because they’re ridiculous and we can be, too.”

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Ingrid Geis, 65, said she was surrounded by fellow demonstrators on their way to the protest in Boston as she boarded a train in her hometown of Winchester on Saturday morning.

She said she has participated in local protests regularly, where a few hundred people attended, but she wanted to join thousands of others at the big protest on the Common.

“I wanted to see thousands of people, I wanted to be with the thousands,” she said.

Geis said she is the daughter of German immigrants who came to the US after World War II. She said she sees parallels between the authoritarian uprising her parents witnessed in Germany in the 1930s, and what is happening in the US today.

“People ask me what were average Germans doing during that time, and I say, ‘What you’re doing now. They were listening to the news and saying it’s awful, and then they’re just leading their normal lives, not doing anything about it.’ That’s why I’m here today,” she said.

Geis carried a sign that read, “A king is only a king if you bow.”

She said she is “embarrassed” by the institutions in media and academia that she said have capitulated to the Trump administration, noting her alma mater, Columbia University, among them.

“I can’t believe how quickly they bowed,” she said. “If you bow, bad changes can happen.”

The other side of her sign read, “Democracy is not a spectator sport.”

“You’ve got to get out here and make your voice heard,” she said.

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

A stage with a huge American flag as a backdrop and an LED screen above. A riser 50 feet in front of the stage for TV cameras to capture what’s on it. A sound team, under a canopy, keeping tabs on the full rig of speakers on the sides and base of the stage.

The “No Kings” rally on the Common diverted from some of the ad-hoc nature of many of the protests that have raged here in recent years. It was a festival atmosphere that included various sing-alongs, as well as an appearance from Mayor Michelle Wu.

This one began with a brass band pumping out a jaunty tune.

One of the members began a rap verse that quickly churned through references to “free Palestine,” rent control, white supremacy, and capitalism.

Later, the lead singer of the 2000s band Dispatch sang a few songs, including their main hit, “The General.”

As is common with progressive protests, organizers wearing orange vests identified themselves as the “safety team.” There was a sizable police presence around the Common, with dozens of officers in yellow vests, but they stood at ease, chatting as they looked around the area.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

Jaden Leegeary, a Canadian visiting the country, who attended the “No Kings” protest wearing a MAGA hat, called the protesters “clueless.”

Leegeary said that when he arrived and began confronting demonstrators, several organizers reacted by asking him to move to a less crowded area. “I said, this is America. I’m gonna use my free speech right here,” he said.

He said he came “to call these people’s hypocrisy,” arguing that Trump is not a fascist.

By Steven Porter, Globe Staff

Retired public school teacher Jayne G. Winsor gathered with demonstrators Saturday in this town of fewer than 10,000 residents to publicly express disapproval with the nation’s trajectory under President Trump.

“It’s time for all of us to be loud and clear, get the message across not only to everyone in our country but the world that the direction that our country is being led in right now is not the direction we want it to go,” she said, holding a protest sign in one hand and the leash of her miniature golden doodle, Acadia, in the other.Her dog wore a sign that said, “I bark at kings.”

Winsor said the list of issues that have her unhappy with the Trump administration is long: there is the immigration crackdown, the deployment of military forces on domestic soil, and the shift in federal health care policy. One topic of particular worry is the dismantling of the US Department of Education, she said.

“I’m concerned for kids who have any kind of challenges. I’m concerned for all kids. I’m concerned for staff. I’m concerned for educators,” she said. “I’m concerned about free thought.”

Winsor said she is a registered Democrat and never misses an election, but she’s feeling more like an independent lately as she’s “rather disappointed” in many elected Democrats.

“I don’t think they’re doing enough,” she said.

“Every day it’s something new. The Democrats need to be out there having press conferences, making their voices heard,” she said. “I really don’t get where many of them are.”

By Lylah Alphonse, Globe Staff

Protesters gathered in the town common in Middlebury, Vermont, for the “No Kings” rally organized by the pro-democracy group Indivisible Middlebury.

They chanted “USA! USA!” and sang along as a small band played “This Land Is Our Land.” At noon, cowbells started clanging and the crowd cheered.

Little kids colored in pictures of butterflies and the Liberty Bell, which were hung on a line with colorful clips. A couple wore matching rubber chicken heads and carried signs calling President Trump a “motherclucker.” People in their 50s and 60s, some wearing daisies in their hair, others dressed in Colonial-era costumes, carried a Revolutionary flag, upside-down American flags, and signs that read “Let Freedom Ring.” A golden retriever with a small “No Kings” sign around his neck drew a cluster of college students.

Elizabeth Melican, a freshman at Middlebury College, stood with friends, holding a handmaid sign adorned with a monarch butterfly that read “the only orange monarch we want. No kings in the USA.”

This wasn’t her first protest — she’s from Manhattan and has participated in walkouts in support of Roe V. Wade and gun control — but came to the” No Kings” protest because Trump’s policies are “impacting our education and our ability to protect people.”

“It’s important that we stand up for that as young people,” she said.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

Sue Doherty joined the “No Kings” protest with members of the grassroots group Quincy4Palestine, carrying a red sign that read “End Zionism. Arms Embargo Now. Free Gaza.”

Doherty, 65, a retired educator, said she wished the “No Kings” movement centered pro-Palestinian causes more directly.

“I think they leave it out,” she said. “People are still afraid of the issue. There’s still this kind of fear that it’s antisemitic to stand up for Palestinians.”

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

Mayor Michelle Wu told a roaring crowd, “Boston doesn’t back down,” during a “No Kings” protest at Boston Common.

“What scares them about Boston is that we are the America they say is impossible,” Wu said.

She said America is a nation of immigrants and laws, and “both make us stronger.” She continued that Trump mistakes “cruelty for greatness.”

Trump, she said, is “counting on us going quiet.” She said Boston will “stand with LA and Portland,” where Trump has tried to send in the National Guard.

When she took the stage, Wu was greeted by cheers, but someone in the front row, amplified by a bullhorn, began chanting criticism of her from the political left. The man was shouted down, but loud arguing continued as she spoke, even as a couple of police officers walked over to stand nearby.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

“Donald Trump wants to be a tyrant,” said Claire Fitzmaurice, 64, of Quincy, who arrived at the “No Kings” protest in hand-sewn colonial attire beside her friend Mimi Balsamo, 78.

Fitzmaurice’s sign read “Same Shite, Different Century,” while Balsamo’s read, “Democracy Needs Your Courage.”

Fitzmaurice said their outfits were meant to symbolize how Trump’s politics represent a return to an era of tyranny.

“It’s not just women’s rights,” she said. “Donald Trump wants to be a tyrant, and we’ve beaten tyrants before. The Massachusetts Constitution is against tyrants, and so are we.”

Both women are members of Quincy’s United First Parish Church, where John Adams once worshiped and where he and Abigail Adams are now buried.

“This church has been standing up for social justice since the beginning of the American Revolution,” Balsamo said.

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

It took an ugly two-year fight, but Shannon O’Brien is back at the helm of the Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, an agency so poorly run that Cheech & Chong could do a better job.

Now comes the hard part: fixing the CCC’s dysfunction and addressing deep-rooted problems facing the state’s marijuana industry, where many companies struggle to make a profit despite bringing in more than $1.6 billion in retail revenue last year.

Back up: O’Brien was reinstated last month after Suffolk Superior Court Judge Robert B. Gordon ruled that she had been wrongly fired by state Treasurer Deborah Goldberg. Goldberg, who appoints the agency’s chair, alleged O’Brien had bullied colleagues and made racially insensitive remarks. Gordon said that while she may have made “concededly ill-considered remarks,” her behavior didn’t meet the legal bar for “gross misconduct” required to dismiss her.

“I’m thrilled to be back,” O’Brien said in her first interview since returning to the commission. “There’s a lot of work to do.”

In an hourlong conversation, she didn’t seek to relitigate the past. O’Brien instead wanted to talk about an agenda focused on tightening up the agency’s internal controls, cutting costs for cannabis companies, expanding access for consumers, and setting consistent product safety standards.

But one of the first steps she took was to ask the state attorney general’s office to weigh in on whether votes taken during her involuntary absence were valid — a move that sparked concern she might try to undo prior commission decisions such as license approvals.

O’Brien sought to dispel the speculation, telling me that the move was simply an effort to ensure that past commission business remains legally valid.

She contends there wasn’t a proper transfer of authority to an acting chair when she was suspended by Goldberg in 2023 and then fired a year later.

“I’m just buttoning things up, dotting the I’s, crossing the T’s, and making sure that we’re not open to potential lawsuits,” she said.

Zoom out: O’Brien, a former state treasurer who lost the 2002 governor’s race to Mitt Romney, said she’s “thrilled” to have the opportunity to finish the job she started in 2022. She sounds determined to show up her critics.

While O’Brien was fighting Goldberg in court, Inspector General Jeffrey S. Shapiro and Auditor Diana DiZoglio released reports that found widespread mismanagement at the CCC.

The agency failed to collect millions in license and extension fees, permitted procedural inequities that created an appearance of favoritism, and lacked strong internal controls and oversight, according to the state watchdogs.

O’Brien, whose one year as boss partly overlapped with the periods covered by the reports, said her first obligation is to fix the shortcomings identified by Shapiro and DiZoglio.

Their recommendations are many but boil down to this: For the CCC to serve the industry and consumers, it must run a tighter ship with better systems for collecting fees and fines, reviewing agreements between cannabis businesses, and holding staff and leadership accountable.

Just as important: The watchdogs said the agency needs to clarify the roles of the chair, commissioners, and executive director — gray areas not spelled out in CCC founding law.

Up next: O’Brien also has priorities of her own.

Cutting red tape. She’s putting together a task force to explore ways to reduce regulatory and operating costs for cannabis businesses.

Last year, commissioners voted to do away with a rule requiring delivery companies to have two employees in the vehicle on every run. Now, O’Brien would like to streamline the training courses that cannabis company employees must attend.

Lowering costs is critical because federal restrictions on banking and business deductions “make it very, very hard for this billion-dollar industry to be profitable,” she said.

Approving social consumption regulations. After many delays, the CCC in July okayed draft rules for pot cafes and other public locations for cannabis use.

Once a final vote is taken, the rules would create three new license types — for existing marijuana vendors, for non-cannabis businesses partnering with a licensed operator, and for temporary events.

For the first five years, social consumption will be restricted to disadvantaged businesses in the commission’s equity programs, giving them a head start on tapping new revenue streams beyond dispensary sales, delivery, and cultivation.

Establishing independent testing lab standards. Massachusetts still lacks uniform testing standards, leading to wide discrepancies in lab results for potency and contamination.

Turnover among testing experts has left consumers and businesses uncertain about product quality and safety.

One issue O’Brien declined to discuss, saying she needed to do more research, is whether she’d consider curbing oversupply. Some states have slowed production by limiting new cultivation licenses or reducing growing space.

“It’s on the table, but I’m just not comfortable answering that right now,” she said.

Final thought: Massachusetts has built one of the nation’s largest cannabis markets. The state has invested heavily to help small and disadvantaged businesses gain a foothold.

But the nearly decade-long experiment in recreational pot ushered in by voters has been hampered by uneven regulation.

O’Brien’s term as CCC chair ends in August 2027. That gives her less than two years to prove that winning her job back was more than a personal victory — and that she can finally make the commission something more than a bad weed joke.

House Speaker Mike Johnson and other top Republicans have called the “No Kings” protests that swept the country over the weekend “hate America” rallies. They might have felt differently if they’d visited the rotary at the intersection of West Roxbury Parkway and Centre Street on Saturday.

Under a blue fall sky, more than 100 protesters ringed the roundabout holding signs and symbols associated with American patriotism. Some displayed messages like “Save the Constitution” or waved American flags. The story was similar elsewhere. In thousands of communities nationwide, protesters critical of President Trump and his actions carried signs like “Resistance is patriotic,” “Nothing is more American than opposing a tyrant,” and “I’m here because I love America.” They dressed up like the Statue of Liberty. They chanted “USA!” and sang “America the Beautiful.”

Using patriotic symbols is a tactical choice for protest movements, and some of the most successful ones in US history have. During the 1960s, civil rights activists carried American flags and quoted the country’s founding documents. The Tea Party protesters who pushed the Republican Party rightward during Barack Obama’s presidency dressed up in colonial garb and took their name from the 1773 protest in Boston Harbor.

Here’s what a few No Kings protesters told me about why they chose to demonstrate as they did — and what it could mean for their movement.

One reason protest movements adopt patriotic symbols is obvious: It associates their cause with the country’s core ideals. “He is destroying this document that our country was founded upon,” Hathaway Norman, a legal assistant standing by the rotary in West Roxbury, said of Trump while holding a sign that featured the US Constitution and an image of George Washington’s face.

For others, patriotic signs were an argument about which side’s values better align with the country’s founding ethos. “True America stands for free people and freedom of speech and freedom of religion,” said Megan Reilly Padilla, a public school teacher who held a handwritten poster that said “Defend Democracy” alongside her dog, Maple, whose collar bore a “Dogs for Democracy” sign.

Patriotic symbols can also give unlikely allies a way into a political movement. Andrew Padilla, Megan’s husband, said he knows many longtime Republicans — including members of his family — who disagree with Trump but aren’t easily swayed to protest him. “You hear often there’s a lot more that we have in common than we have to disagree about,” he said. “Getting some of those people engaged in this and standing up and saying ‘This is not okay,’ that’s what we can hope for.”

It’s also possible that No Kings will start to shift perceptions about who patriotic symbols belong to. Polls show that self-identified Republicans are more likely than Democrats to describe themselves as proud to be American and associate the flag with their political party. In 2021, the New York Times ran a story about the perception that people who conspicuously display the flag on their lawn or bumper are conservative. Trump, whose walk-on song during last year’s campaign was Lee Greenwood’s “God Bless the USA,” made headlines after he hugged the flag — literally — on stage during a 2019 conference for conservative activists.

With that in mind, I asked Ralph Tisei, who stood by the rotary waving a medium-sized version of the Stars and Stripes, whether his protest emblem of choice had anything to do with Republican remarks associating No Kings with hating America. “That’s why I brought it,” he said. “We need to take back the flag,” said his sister Joanne, a retired Boston Public School teacher, adding that she’d recently hung one outside her house.

Patriotism, of course, wasn’t the only thing on protesters’ minds on Saturday. “He’s so awful I protest for free,” read one sign, ridiculing conservative claims that the rallies featured paid protesters. Other signs lamented Trump’s policies or poked fun at his trademark tan. (Trump, speaking to Fox News over the weekend, rejected the claim that he’s ruling like a king.)

But overall, the No Kings marches have hewed toward patriotic symbols more than any other Trump-era protest so far, from the Women’s March to Black Lives Matter. Said Norman, the protester who carried a copy of the Constitution: “It’s important to all of us to remember that this is what we are all here for.”

After winning office in 1983 by defeating Mel King, the first Black mayoral candidate to make it to the final election round, Flynn worked hard to unify Boston. He confronted the racial conflict that tore neighborhoods apart during court-ordered school desegregation and took on difficult issues, including the desegregation of public housing. With humble roots — his father worked as a longshoreman and his mother was a cleaning lady — Flynn also found common ground between working-class voters and progressive activists.

“That was Flynn’s success,” Gillis told me. He had “organizers and working-class neighborhood leaders … all working together despite and in spite of difference.”

With today’s Democratic Party struggling to bridge a yawning gap between the working class and the elite, surely there’s a lesson in Flynn’s success on that score. But only if people can get past the Charles Stuart debacle, and some won’t be able to.

When Stuart, a white man, killed his pregnant wife in October 1989, he said a Black man did it. Flynn accepted Stuart’s story, and the police manhunt that was launched in the aftermath turned every young Black man into a potential suspect. That was wrong. In 2023, Mayor Michelle Wu formally apologized to two men falsely linked to the murder, and the city recently paid $150,000 total to them.

Since his book launch last spring, Gillis has spoken at many events, including one that I participated in last June as a co-panelist in Roslindale and one I attended on Sunday at the Dorchester home of Joyce Linehan, a well-known convener of political guests, who also worked for former mayor Marty Walsh. The Gillis answer to the Stuart question is basically that mistakes were made, but they shouldn’t define Flynn’s entire legacy. “What defined Ray Flynn was uniting Boston racially against all odds,” he told me after Sunday’s event.

Flynn, who is 86, has attended some of Gillis’s book events, including the book launch. He was supposed to be at Sunday’s event, but missed it because of health issues.

As a reader, I wish the book had more detail about what it was like to be in the room where tough policy decisions were made, including those involving the Stuart case. If it reads like an academic journal, that’s because it began as research for a doctoral dissertation and continued in that vein.

Even so, it does raise important questions about the role of government when it comes to sharing the benefit of wealth and, by doing that, easing racial tensions. In the book, Gillis concludes that Flynn “is a progressive — a term he never used to describe himself — having steered Boston’s economy toward greater fairness and opportunity for poor and working-class citizens while embracing the city’s racial, ethnic, and cultural diversity.” He sees Flynn as a bridge to Wu, and even to Zohran Mamdani, the progressive candidate and Democratic nominee for mayor of New York City, who calls Wu his role model.

The leap from Flynn to Mamdani may be one too far. But overall, I think Gillis is right.

Flynn is accountable for everything that happened between 1984 and 1993, his years as mayor. That includes his mishandling of the Stuart case. But it also includes moving the city in a positive direction during difficult times and building a foundation for progressive change by putting the issues of economic inequality and social justice front and center.

“We’re better on race than we were,” Gillis said in an interview after the Sunday event. “There’s more racial equality and more class inequality.”

If everyone who believed Stuart back in 1989 raised their hand, there would be a lot of raised hands. And yes, they would be white. But people learn and grow. Today, Boston is not at war with itself. There is still racial inequity and much work to be done. But today, Stuart’s story would be subject to much more scrutiny from everyone, and especially from the mayor.

Now, what does it take to change the economic inequities that still break down along racial lines?

Three decades after Flynn left office, that’s the question a progressive mayor must answer.

The Archdiocese of Boston had owned the property, then a vacant lot near St. Augustine Church, since 1955. The church and a neighborhood committee collaborated to turn it into a so-called “vest pocket park,” the first of its kind in a non-urban renewal area of the city in 1968, the Globe reported.

It was named for Mary Greene, “a South Boston girl,” who joined the Catholic religious order of nuns in 1939 and died in 1960, the Globe reported.

Over the decades, residents came to care for the small park they looked after with pride.

“While the archdiocese owned the land, they had almost never done anything with the park,” said resident Vicky Shen.

When the archdiocese listed the property for sale in 2023, surprised residents formed the “Save Sister Mary Veronica Park Committee,” said Shen, the committee’s spokesperson.

Last month, the city formally acquired the 4,675-square-foot park from the archdiocese for just over $200,000, saving the park from any future development.

It was a neighborhood committee in the late 1960s that turned the lot into a park, Shen said, and the newest generation of neighbors ultimately saved it.

Every other week, one neighbor uses their own leaf blower to move leaves and debris away, Shen said. Another neighbor wheels the park’s trash cans to the curb every Wednesday for pickup.

The park has five benches around its perimeter and is surrounded by tall trees with Dorchester Avenue is just a few blocks away.

South Boston has the second-lowest tree cover in the city, making every foot of green space “precious,” said Donna Brown, president of the South Boston Neighborhood Development Corporation.

“It has touched newcomers to South Boston as well as long-term residents because it is a rare open space in a really dense part of the neighborhood, and that’s why it means so much to people,” Brown said.

Brown said people walk their dogs in the park, kids ride their bikes, and neighbors talk. That’s why it was essential to save.

“It was really just neighbors talking to neighbors and then trying to figure out what we could do as citizens to get visibility and try to do something to prevent the sale of it to a developer,” Shen said.

At a public hearing on July 28, the Boston Parks and Recreation Commission voted to approve the purchase of the park, the city said in a statement.

The property was placed under a Conservation Restriction held by the South Boston Neighborhood Development Corporation, which ensures the space will not be converted to another use, Brown said.

“It was really inspiring and made you realize that a neighborhood and a community matter,” Shen said. “It was saved because people who live in the community came together to try to fight for something important to us.”

With extension of the subsidies at the heart of the stalemate behind the government shutdown, specifics on the size of the premium increases could add new pressure on Congress.

The subsidies were introduced in an expansion of the ACA in 2021. Democratic leaders want to make the subsidies permanent, but Republicans have declined to consider that until Congress authorizes new funding to reopen the government. The expanded tax credits doubled participation in the ACA exchanges over the past four years, and while their expiration wouldn’t end all of federal subsidies for health insurance, it would reduce support back to 2021 levels.

The 2021 legislation made subsidies more generous and extended them to a larger number of people. In Massachusetts, some 337,000 people benefited from the federal subsidies that made health insurance more affordable through the connector.

Losing the subsidies could play a role in increasing the number of uninsured people in Massachusetts by roughly 300,000 over the next decade, officials have said.

On average, the loss of the expanded subsidies will trigger double-digit increases in for people in most eligible income brackets, according to the connector. Those averages, though, obscure a wide range of increases that vary depending on location, family size, and type of coverage. Almost 20,000 Massachusetts residents would no longer get any subsidized insurance at all, said Alex Sheff, senior director of policy and government relations at Health Care For All, a Boston-based health advocacy organization.

“There are particular groups that are going to see these really astronomical cost increases,” Sheff said.

Judith O’Gara, a part-time editor at community newspapers, and her husband, a self-employed computer animator and mural artist, were notified this week that their monthly premium would increase by $435. A cheaper plan would likely offer higher copays or premiums and would still be $200 more. It’s less than she feared, but still a burden. She hopes, but isn’t certain, that she could get insurance through her employer if she works more hours. If not, she must make difficult choices.

“It’s not great to be presented with rising costs and $200 to $400 a month at the same time the cost of food was rising, the cost of oil is rising, the cost of electricity is rising,” O’Gara, 56, of Millis, said.

The premium notifications in Massachusetts may give some exchange customers sticker shock, said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a centrist Washington policy think tank. They may decide they can’t afford to renew their insurance, and stick with that decision even if the subsidies are saved.

“We are getting to the point where the fact that the subsidies have not been extended will have actual consequences for who has health insurance and who doesn’t,” Fiedler said.

Lidia Pruente, of Dorchester, recalled first receiving her notice from the connector this week.

“My first reaction was definitely dread, but I think things might not be as bad as I currently feared,” said the 35-year-old.

Her premiums would increase by $70 a month in 2026, she said. The increase comes as she also faces higher costs for compression leggings and shorts and bandages she needs to manage swelling in her legs and abdomen caused by lymphoedema, a chronic condition that causes fluid to build up in parts of her body, she said.

“$70 plus a ton more in durable medical equipment, that would be a challenge,” said Pruente. “It’s very stressful to know this is what health insurance costs.”

But for some, the rate increase looks to be manageable. Sara Hamlen, a Boston resident who works in catering, was notified that her premium would increase by just $12 a month.

The 61-year-old said the subsidized insurance is a lifesaver as she manages a year of bills with seasonal employment.

“I’m just treading water,” she said.

The White House did not reply to a request for comment Wednesday.

The notifications drive home the point that, “nobody is coming out ahead as a result of the Republican cuts,” said Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren in an interview Tuesday. “The only question is how much higher people’s insurance premiums will be.”

Insurance through ACA exchanges nationwide is expected to increase by a median of 18 percent next year, KFF, a health policy analysis foundation, reported. That is in part driven by the expected end of the expanded subsidies, but also increases in medical costs and prices in general due to the Trump administration’s tariffs.

Massachusetts began sending out notifications of premium increases last week, and will continue notifying customers through the end of the month, according to the Connector. The state is one of 19 that, along with the District of Columbia, run independent ACA insurance exchanges, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The other independent exchanges are expected to send similar notifications, Fiedler said.

Nationally, about 70 percent of people insured through the exchanges use a federal marketplace operated by CMS, said Fiedler. They may have to wait until that agency posts rates for 2026 on its website before Nov. 1, when the open enrollment period for insurance begins, CMS said in a statement Wednesday.

Until now, the government shutdown has been driven by estimates of the cost of the expiring subsidies. The information released now by Massachusetts is among the first to put a number to premium increases, said Fiedler, of the Brookings Institution.

“It hasn’t necessarily been individuals being told, ‘here’s what’s happening to your premiums next year,’” he said. “The conversation is about to change.”

Last week, the family learned that Molea, 61, had been killed in a shooting not far from the women’s shelter in Roxbury where she often stayed. Police have released few details, including whether they believe she was an intended target. No arrests have been made.

Officers found Molea lying facedown next to a bus shelter on Washington Street, according to a police report. She was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

It was a horrific ending to an already painful story.

“We knew we’d get a bad phone call someday, but we didn’t think it would be this,” her first husband, John Calnan, said. “A tragedy.”

The shooting unfolded around lunchtime on a rainy Monday, marking the city’s 27th homicide of the year. It left residents uneasy and upset, especially members of the homeless community around Roxbury and the South End. Like many others, Molea relied on nearby shelters and service organizations.

Her killing underscores the inherent risks that often come with homelessness, said Jose Colon, an unhoused resident of the area.

“You’d think a bus stop would be safe, but this happened in broad daylight,” said Colon, 46. “That’s how you know people don’t care about human life.”

Long before receiving the news, Molea’s family witnessed her descent into mental illness, which began more than two decades ago. In their memories, her life is starkly divided into a before and after. There’s the vibrant young mom whose world revolved around her children. That’s the era they remember fondly — before she became distracted and delusional, left the workforce, and lost her housing.

“We just don’t know what happened,” said her daughter Krysta Calnan, 35. “It plagued everybody for years, and then I guess you just kind of accept it.”

A newspaper clipping from 1981 shows Molea in her high school cheerleading uniform, clapping enthusiastically despite the team’s impending loss. Another shows her as homecoming queen, standing next to Lynn’s mayor with a huge bouquet of flowers. A 1982 article in the Lynn Daily Item said Molea was voted most school spirit for her senior class superlatives.

After college, she quickly passed the exam to become a registered nurse, according to the Daily Item. She later worked at a Lynn elementary school and a local hospital, among other places.

In 1996, she ran the Marathon to raise money for a childhood leukemia patient, the paper reported. Her neighbor wrote a letter to the editor about a close call on race day: Molea accidentally left her number in the car when her then-husband dropped her off at the starting point that morning, but he realized the mistake and rushed back just in time to deliver the forgotten envelope.

“In spite of the hour of anxiety she had just gone through, Marie ran the marathon and crossed the finish line at 4:32:50,” the letter read.

That was a happy time, John Calnan recalled. The couple met in elementary school and dated as teens. After getting married, they bought the house next door to Molea’s parents. Many weekends were spent shuttling their four kids to baseball, football, and Irish step dance.

It was hectic, but that’s “the stuff you live for,” he said.

They divorced in the late 1990s, but he stayed in touch with Molea through the years and helped her out when he could.

Their two adult daughters visited his house last week and looked through old family photo albums. The pictures show Molea hugging her children, dancing at a wedding, and flashing a radiant smile. In each image, she looks confident and carefree.

Her daughters said Molea was an attentive mother who fully embraced the role. She would dress them in matching outfits and throw big birthday parties when they were young.

Even after the paranoia set in, her concern for her children was paramount, they said. She would sometimes call 911 to report bombs planted in their house and other imagined dangers.

Molea’s family wants her to be remembered as a whole person, despite her complicated history and the circumstances of her death.

“She never would have been in that situation otherwise, if not for her mental illness,” said Keara Calnan, 38. “I think that’s what bothers us the most . . . that she was alone.”

Molea also suffered from lupus, an autoimmune disease that can impact mental health. She discussed her diagnosis with other women who frequented Rosie’s Place, a shelter and community center in Roxbury.

Molea was a familiar presence in the area. Neighborhood residents described her sweet nature and generous spirit that persisted even when things looked hopeless. With her training and experience as a nurse, she often came to people’s aid.

“If someone was on the ground, she was the first to run to help,” said Andrea Corin, 62, who considered Molea a close friend. She said Molea supported her through the death of her husband and a recent overdose. Molea would bring her little presents and pick up her prescriptions whenever Corin couldn’t make it to the pharmacy.

Corin said she stayed in bed the day Molea was killed, which she regrets. The women relied on each other to help navigate a precarious existence.

“Homelessness, substance abuse, mental illness — it’s like a round robin. Once you get on, it’s so hard to get off,” said Shari Delgiudice, 61, who also knew Molea from Rosie’s Place.

She said there’s a dire need for more robust services to help people like Molea: “If she had been housed, everything would have been easier.”

John R. Ellement and researcher ​​​Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

So it isn’t hard to understand the shock waves triggered when the owners of a Dorchester restaurant, embarking on a revamp of the place, decided to adorn its walls with oversize photographs of the two notorious killers.

“The first thing patrons see when they walk into Savin Bar and Kitchen is a poster-sized mugshot of the late notorious South Boston gangster, James ‘Whitey’ Bulger,” reporter Shelley Murphy wrote in a recent Page 1 story in the Globe. “A mugshot of his partner in crime, Stephen ‘the Rifleman’ Flemmi, hangs on another brick wall of the Dorchester restaurant.”

The owners of Savin Bar — which is located on the same block where Eddie Connors’s tavern, Bulldogs, once stood — were encouraged by celebrity TV chef Gordon Ramsay to play up the neighborhood’s link to the infamous serial killers. When Kenneth Osherow and Driscoll DoCanto opened the eatery in 2011, they promised to make it a place “where people feel comfortable going a few times a week.” Now, apparently, they have other priorities.

“We’re not hanging those images to celebrate them, but to recognize a chapter in the gritty story of our neighborhood,” Osherow told Murphy. “We’re acknowledging the history of this very spot.” In a letter to the Globe, he reiterated that claim: “The images displayed are mug shots, reminders of accountability, not admiration,” he wrote. “By acknowledging this past, we honor Boston’s resilience and evolution.”

But serving brunch and cocktails beneath poster-sized portraits of murderers, elegantly matted and framed, is not how you acknowledge history; it’s how you romanticize evil.

If the proprietors of Savin Bar had truly wished to meaningfully convey the neighborhood’s history, the framed photographs would be of Connors or Davis or some of the others whose lives were destroyed by Bulger and Flemmi. True remembrance centers the victims of murder, not the perpetrators.

Perhaps Ramsay and his production team believed that turning mobsters into wall décor was an appropriate way to showcase Boston’s “gritty” past. Maybe it never occurred to them or to Savin Bar’s owners that what might come across as edgy and stylish on a chef’s TV reality show would feel like desecration to neighborhood residents.

But many of those residents have been vocal in their outrage.

“How can you go into a restaurant that says it’s a community restaurant,” Donna Blythe-McColgan, whose family has lived in the neighborhood for generations, said in a WBZ interview, “with photos of the very people who murdered and maimed many of the people in this community?”

To be fair, Savin Bar’s obtuseness isn’t unique. It’s merely a local variant of a larger cultural sickness — the glamorization of evil. From Hollywood movies that portray mass killers as sympathetic, to T-shirts and mugs emblazoned with the faces of communist butchers, to Mafia-themed party decorations, depravity is treated as charisma.

This perversity has become ubiquitous. Think of Rolling Stone’s cover photo of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, which rendered the Boston Marathon terrorist as a brooding rock star. Think of Manhattan’s KGB Bar, a watering hole named for the Soviet Union’s grim security network of secret police and torture sites that features Soviet propaganda posters and a hammer-and-sickle flag. Think of President Trump’s 2024 campaign promise to restore the names of Confederate generals to the Army bases from which Congress had ordered them removed.

The same moral blindness runs through it all. Making images of evil fashionable doesn’t sanitize what they stand for. Defending monuments to slavery and those who fought to preserve it on the grounds that they are emblems of “heritage” is equally dishonest and dishonorable. And hanging framed mugshots of Whitey Bulger and his partner in a Dorchester restaurant is a homage to murderers, no matter how piously the owners deny it.

Particularly feeble is Osherow’s excuse that because the images featured on Savin Bar’s walls are mugshots, they serve as “reminders of accountability, not admiration.” The power of a mugshot depends entirely on context. Some police photos have indeed become icons of esteem — think of Rosa Parks’s mugshot, taken during the Montgomery bus boycott, or that of Martin Luther King Jr., arrested in Birmingham in 1963. Other mugshots have been turned into symbols of defiance or martyrdom. A mugshot isn’t inherently a rebuke; it can just as easily become a banner.

In a restaurant, wall hangings are meant to set the mood. Guests read the space before they eat or drink anything. When the first thing they see is the framed face of a gangster, elegantly lit against a brick wall, the message isn’t accountability — it’s atmosphere. No dining room displays mugshots to emphasize shame. They do it to signal edge, swagger, attitude. If you doubt that, ask yourself why no one proposes lining a dining room with mugshots of drunk drivers, wife beaters, or child abusers.

There are ways to confront a painful past with dignity and truth.

In Europe, the Stolpersteine Project marks the doorways of Holocaust victims with small brass plaques — “stumble stones” — embedded in the pavement, each engraved with a name and fate. Passers-by are reminded that real people once lived there until they were destroyed by the Nazis.

In Montgomery, Ala., the National Memorial for Peace and Justice pays tribute to the thousands of Black Americans lynched to death; each victim is honored by a rust-colored steel column hanging in a quiet, somber space. There are no statues of the killers, no nostalgic murals of Southern heritage — only the unflinching recognition of what was done and to whom.

In Boston, the 9/11 Memorial at Logan Airport honors the passengers and crew of the two flights that took off from Boston on that awful morning, only to be hijacked by terrorists and crashed into the World Trade Center. The memorial is a glass cube, inscribed with the names of the victims, and accessed by two walkways that mirror the flights’ paths.

That is how history should be remembered: with humility for the dead, not glamor for their tormentors.

Boston has never lacked for grit. What it needs, always, is moral sense. Those Dorchester residents who have spoken out against the mugshot motif understand that difference. They know there’s nothing trendy about hanging killers’ portraits on a restaurant wall. That isn’t history; it’s a cynical attempt to refashion one of Boston’s darkest chapters as ironic interior design.

Bulger and Flemmi weren’t colorful rogues or local celebrities. They were cruel, violent men who left a trail of corpses and broken lives. To turn them into décor is to strip that truth of all its gravity.

Boston once trembled before Whitey Bulger. It shouldn’t now dine beneath his gaze.

“Can You Stand the Rain” sounded a little different in Fenway Thursday night, with a member of New Edition joined on stage by Boston high school students.

The performance was a part of the Boston Arts Academy Foundation Honors, the foundation’s annual awards ceremony and fundraiser at MGM Music Hall. Johnny Gill, a member of the Roxbury R&B and pop group, was the music honoree this year, according to a statement from the public arts school and its foundation.

“The power of this night lies in what our students show us — that art is not just a subject, it’s a lifeline,” BAAF President and CEO Denella Clark said in the statement. “Tonight’s performances remind us that when we invest in arts education, we invest in Boston’s future leaders, creators, and changemakers.”

Michael Bivins, New Edition member and Roxbury native, introduced Gill to the stage, officials said.

Gill performed the song alongside seven students from the academy who are from Hyde Park, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, according to the statement.

The event raises money to support the academy’s “robust academic and arts curriculum, bridging the gap between public funding amounts and the total cost of delivering a world-class arts education to more than 500 students,” according to the statement.

Actor and New Kids on the Block member Donnie Wahlberg received the foundation’s lifetime achievement award, officials said.

Wahlberg, now starring in the new CBS police drama Boston Blue, was not in attendance, but recorded a video for the event.

“This is why we go to school and why we put all the effort into these endeavors…so when the opportunity comes, you can make the most of it,” the Dorchester native said on the video. His brothers Paul and Bob Wahlberg were in attendance to accept it on his behalf, according to the statement.

Other honorees included internationally recognized tap dancer Dianne Walker, designer for fashion David Josef, and former actress Eliza Dushku, officials said.

The fundraiser also included performances from dancer Leah Pires, salsa musician Sebastian “SBM” Medina, and Gospel singer Jason Price — three Boston Arts Academy alumni, according to the statement.

Wyland’s first season was the 2021 Fall II campaign, when the program earned its first Middlesex win over Reading. That fall, Wakefield beat Lexington and Burlington for the first time en route to its first postseason appearance and win. In 2022, the Warriors got their first win over Arlington, then Woburn in 2023, and Belmont last season.

This year’s Warriors feature 10 seniors, and some of them played as sophomores on the first team to make the Division 3 semifinals in 2023. Last fall, the Warriors were the only team to win a set against D3 champion Weston.

“It’s so emotional because of all these seniors. I’ve seen them in the youth clinics when I took over, trying a new sport and seeing what it is,” Wyland said. “Seeing them sophomore year [in the] final four, now seeing their development and growth, confidence and gameplay. I feel like a proud mom. That’s one of the biggest moments of their lives, if not the biggest to date.”

This year’s team is 15-4 and 19th in the Globe’s Top 20 poll. With a win Friday, the Warriors would clinch at least a share of their first Middlesex League title. For a senior core that has been achieving firsts regularly, the postseason presents further opportunities.

“We have a goal: To make it to the championship and win the championship,” said libero Cara Carangelo, a senior captain whose sister, Lea, was the setter during the semifinal run two years ago. “To have that goal brings us together. Keeping positive attitudes with each other makes us closer.”

Arkinstall (2.7 kills per set this season) and Kenny (2.4) were two of the team’s top three hitters as sophomores. Kenny said every win in the playoffs two years ago was “surreal.”

“It was a lot of pressure, but I think having coach Kayla, she really helps on and off the court,” she said. “She’d talk to me if I’m down or if we have a big game ahead of us. She’d say we trust you. That really helps.”

It’s a special combination for these teammates — to have a team with all these milestones and firsts to achieve, and have the skill on the roster to check them off.

“I’m just so grateful for the opportunity I’ve had to play with this team,” said Grace. “I love making memories with them. I love to conquer these milestones with my teammates.”

“There are other girls who don’t have the opportunity to play club and I want to be a role model for that,” the senior said. “You don’t have to pay thousands of dollars. If you put in the work, you can play. I hope that gives hope and inspiration that there’s a chance.”

In Massachusetts, more than 1 million people are at risk of losing their benefits next month if the federal government shutdown continues and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program runs out of money — an unprecedented lapse in benefits that advocates say the already strained network of food pantries can’t come close to compensating.

The US Department of Agriculture has posted a notice on its website saying federal food aid will not go out Nov. 1.

With food insecurity increasing to COVID-era levels and resources declining, the loss of SNAP benefits could press low-income families already reeling from rising costs related to inflation and tariffs to a breaking point.

Advocates have been pushing the state to dip into its “Rainy Day” fund, which has a balance of some $8 billion, to make up the difference in SNAP benefits until the shutdown ends, but the Legislature has traditionally been reluctant to tap into this fund. Both Governor Maura Healey and Massachusetts House Speaker Ronald Mariano said the state can’t replace the roughly $212 million in federal SNAP funds received by Massachusetts residents every month. Instead, the United Way is launching a fund for private donations to help SNAP recipients across the Commonwealth, the governor announced Friday.

“Donald Trump is the first president in US history to cut off SNAP benefits to people in America,” Healey said recently.

A few states, including Virginia and Hawaii, have committed to providing state funds to residents who rely on SNAP, and Vermont is also set to do so. In New Hampshire, officials announced a plan to provide mobile food pantries open to SNAP recipients with $2 million in public funding.

In Roxbury, the 46-year-old Otero said her family will rely more on rice and beans, pancakes with protein powder, and McDonald’s $6 meal deals: a double cheeseburger, four chicken nuggets, small fries, and small drink, which Otero sometimes splits with one of her children.

“I’m low-key terrified,” she said. “I’m heartbroken, not just for myself but for little ones [whose] families may be experiencing way worse than I am economically.”

The Department of Agriculture, which oversees the nation’s largest antihunger program, distributing $8 billion a month to about 42 million Americans, has a contingency fund that advocacy groups say could cover much of the shortfall. But on Friday the agency said it couldn’t tap into that money, as it must be used for emergencies such as hurricanes and other disasters, according to a memo first obtained by Axios.

The USDA didn’t respond to questions from the Globe but sent a statement referencing the partisan fight over extending health insurance subsidies that led to the shutdown, including an inaccurate claim that undocumented immigrants are entitled to them.

“We are approaching an inflection point for Senate Democrats. Continue to hold out for healthcare for illegals or reopen the government so mothers, babies, and the most vulnerable among us can receive timely WIC [Women, Infants & Children Nutrition Program] and SNAP allotments.”

In Massachusetts, 665,000 households rely on SNAP benefits, at an average of $323 a month, and more than one in three households have reported not having enough to eat, according to a recent study by the Greater Boston Food Bank.

“One in six Massachusetts residents simply just cannot be the consequences of a political football,” said Victoria Negus, senior economic justice advocate at the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute.

The need has been growing, even with SNAP in full effect, as resources shrink.

The Trump administration has cut food aid by 94 million pounds, according to ProPublica, and with the government shut down, food insecurity programs implemented during COVID aren’t available either. Furloughed government workers, and those working without pay, could soon also find themselves in greater need.

If Congress doesn’t approve a budget to keep federal agencies running, the USDA can’t issue new benefits beyond those that are already funded. On Friday, the USDA instructed states to notify SNAP recipients that November benefit allotments have been suspended. When federal funding is available, the agency said, it will notify state agencies to immediately resume issuing benefits.

For the state’s four food banks to make up for missing federal benefits, they would have to provide up to 56 million additional meals next month, according to a letter sent to Healey and the state Legislature by local antihunger organizations. That would be four times what is currently distributed each month — “an impossible outcome,” they wrote.

Other federal food assistance programs, including WIC, which provides food aid to pregnant women, new moms, and young children, and school lunch and breakfast programs, are also at risk if the shutdown continues.

The nonprofit Food For Free has seen a rising need from almost all the food pantries, schools, and other groups it works with in Eastern Massachusetts, said Alex Gladwell, associate director of programs and partnerships. Boxes of food that previously took up to two hours to distribute are now gone in 15 minutes, she said.

“We’re being hit from all fronts,” Gladwell said, noting the cuts to government programs alongside shrinking private grants and donations.

On a recent morning at the East End House in Cambridge, more than a dozen people were lined up in the rain before Dominic Carter arrived with a delivery from Food For Free.

“You see a line like that? Before it even opens,” Carter said. “It will probably be wrapped around the corner soon.”

SNAP also accounts for 20 percent of grocery sales in the state, according to the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute, and the loss of that spending would have a significant impact on the small grocers that fill a big need in low-income communities.

“We need every penny … to continue to serve the community,” said Michael Valente, general manager at the Dorchester Food Co-op.

Customers are already starting to pull back on buying produce in anticipation of SNAP funds coming to an end, said Keisha Oneal, the co-op’s grocery store manager. And with Thanksgiving approaching, it’s the worst time for people to worry about feeding their families.

“People are nervous,” Oneal said. “They’re not buying in the quantity they used to.”

Even before the potential SNAP cutoff, Renée Dingman has been trying to eat all her meals at Mount Holyoke College, where she goes to school, so that she can focus on feeding her 13-year-old son. If the cuts go into effect, she may skip meals to make sure he can eat.

“It makes me wonder, am I going to fight for food, or am I going to fight for my apartment?” Dingham said. “Because that’s how I became homeless five years ago. I chose to feed my son over paying my rent, and I don’t want to have to make that decision again.”

In addition to families going hungry and grocery stores losing revenue, farmers who sell food to SNAP recipients will also lose customers. Liz O’Gilvie, who leads the Springfield Food Policy Council and the urban farm Gardening the Community, said 90 percent of the people who shop at its store rely on SNAP.

“Everyone gets nervous about the state’s Rainy Day fund: ‘Let’s save it, what if we need it?’” she said. “Well, I think a tsunami is coming. I think some people are looking outside and maybe seeing clouds, and I can see the big waves offshore that are going to hit us and slam people in ways that will be very hard to recover from.”

November is also when new eligibility rules start kicking in for SNAP recipients, a result of the so-called Big Beautiful Bill that passed this summer, which also included the largest cuts to SNAP funding in history. More than 150,000 Massachusetts residents are at risk of losing some or all of their food stamp benefits due to expanded work requirements and termination of benefits for immigrants here legally who fled persecution, many of whom are on a track to get a green card.

All told, the threats to the SNAP program are “horrifically short sighted” for residents and for the economy, said Negus of the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute: “There are massive human cost implications.”
