Her struggle mirrors a trend documented in recent federal employment data, which show the unemployment rate for Black women rising for three consecutive months.

On Monday, Inniss joined a roundtable and press conference hosted by congresswoman Ayanna Pressley in partnership with YW Boston, bringing together impacted Black women, economists, civil rights leaders, mental-health providers, and community members to highlight what Pressley called a “five-alarm fire” in the labor market.

The Democratic congresswoman from Boston has raised the issue of high unemployment among Black women in recent months, writing to Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, as well as questioning him during congressional hearings on the Civil Rights history of the Fed policies.

Pressley Monday continued to press the central bank and federal agencies to address what she calls a “growing pushout” of Black women from the workforce.

“The feds have a statutory mandate of full employment. We need you to study the data, we need you to come up with a plan,” she said, speaking at the YW Boston Kuumba Library.

According to September’s jobs report, the unemployment rate for Black women remains almost twice the national rate of 4.4 percent.

Black women make up 12 percent of the federal workforce, nearly double their share in the overall labor force. Pressley said recent federal layoffs by the Trump administration have eliminated many jobs historically held by Black women, including roles in student aid processing, fair housing enforcement, and consumer protection.

“Nearly 70 percent of Black women are the primary breadwinners in their households,” she said. “When we lose work, it reverberates far beyond ourselves. Black women are economic ecosystems.”

Pressley also stressed how stark the crisis would appear if another demographic were affected at the same scale. “If white women were being pushed out of the labor force at the rate that Black women are, we’d be looking at the equivalent of three million white women unemployed — the entire female workforce of Pennsylvania,” she said. “If that were happening, the country would be paying attention. That’s exactly why we are calling on the fed to do their job.”

Other speakers detailed the barriers Black women face in the current job market — delayed unemployment benefits, shrinking grant and contract opportunities, and hiring processes they fear may rely on algorithms that replicate bias. Inniss said the speed of her rejection emails made her question whether automated systems were screening her out before a human ever saw her résumé.

“We all know that it’s not legal for companies to engage in racist hiring practices when the decision is happening on a human level, but my sense is that AI is playing a role in discrimination with the algorithms,” she said.

Aba Taylor, president and CEO of YW Boston, said the 7.5 percent unemployment figure only scratches the surface of what many Black women are experiencing.

“We are America’s expendables,” she said. “Overlooked, pushed down, exploited — and yet we still show up, anchor our families, and hold our communities together.”

Economist Anna Gifty Opoku-Agyeman warned that the crisis does not stop with Black women. “Don’t ignore your neighbor when their house is on fire,” said Opoku-Agyeman, a doctoral candidate at Harvard. “What’s happening to Black women economically is now reaching all women. It’s only a matter of time before it reaches other groups.”

Mental-health providers said the economic instability adds to longstanding stressors. Helen Joseph, a licensed mental-health counselor, urged employers to create trauma-informed workplaces and invest in mental-health care rooted in cultural understanding. “Everything happening in this country is creating trauma,” she said. “Our communities will feel these impacts for generations.”

For Inniss, the loss is also personal. Her great-grandmother owned a laundry service in Roxbury in the 1920s and managed to buy two homes. Today, despite multiple degrees, Inniss is still struggling to find stable work. “I look at my life and think, how is it that I have less opportunity than she did in 1926?” she said.

In court papers, Suffolk prosecutors alleged that Reed learned she was pregnant in September 2024 and delivered the baby, identified as G.R.W., in her Dorchester apartment on Dec. 5, 2024. She gave birth two months early, according to prosecutors.

On Jan. 9, Reed called 911 reporting the child wasn’t breathing. She was rushed to Boston Medical Center and later pronounced dead, prosecutors said.

She weighed 2.5 pounds at the time.

“During the five weeks of her life, G.R.W. failed to gain or maintain weight and was severely malnourished,” Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Laura C. Drohan wrote in court papers. “Despite knowing that their baby was born at least two months premature and observing the newborn was unable to gain or maintain weight, the defendants never sought any medical care for the infant as her health continued to significantly deteriorate.”

The baby’s cause of death was acute intoxication from the combined effects of fentanyl and cocaine in a premature infant with malnourishment and sepsis, according to the autopsy by the state medical examiner’s office.

Prosecutors alleged Reed and Winn “used illegal substances in the infant’s presence, resulting in her exposure to these substances.”

Reed’s court-appointed defense attorney, Paul J. Davenport, said she has struggled with fentanyl addiction. But she’s spent the past six months in a residential treatment program and “largely turned her life around,” Davenport said. He asked for a lower bail, saying her progress could be lost if she’s forced to leave the program for jail.

“It would just seem tragic, in my humble opinion, to derail this sobriety that she’s managed to achieve,” he said.

Winn’s court-appointed attorney, Christopher M. Kenney, said Winn has been cooperating with law enforcement throughout the investigation. He was arrested Monday after showing up to court, handcuffed and taken into custody after sitting through Reed’s arraignment in the public area of the courtroom.

“He’s maintaining his innocence. He’s cooperated with police up until now,” Kenney said. “He showed up on his own two feet.”

Kenney said Winn has other children he wants to have contact with while the case proceeds.

But Suffolk First Assistant Clerk Magistrate Edward J. Curley ordered both Reed and Winn to stay away from anyone under 16.

In a statement, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden said the child died from “sheer neglect.”

“It’s difficult to conceive of something more tragic than a child being born and then ignored to the extent it leads to death by malnourishment and sheer neglect,” he said in the statement. “The allegation that the parents were using dangerous drugs in the newborn’s presence only adds to the terrible aspects of this crime.”

PROVIDENCE — A UMass Boston student was arrested after he allegedly took part in a fraud scam targeting Rhode Island seniors, according to federal prosecutors.

Samyag Uday Doshi, 25, a citizen of India residing in Dorchester on a student visa, was arrested on Nov. 17 and charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud. He appeared before US District Court Magistrate Judge Amy E. Moses in Providence that day.

“It is alleged that he participated in a scheme that caused a Rhode Island resident to turn over $54,000 in cash, with an attempted loss amount totaling more than $385,000,” the Rhode Island US attorney’s office said in a press release.

According to a criminal complaint filed in court, police in Newport, R.I., received a call earlier this month regarding an elderly resident “who may be the victim of an elder abuse financial fraud scam.”

“The individual also made multiple inquiries about purchasing hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of gold bars,” prosecutors said. “These inquiries are believed to have been directed by members of the conspiracy.”

Moses ordered Doshi detained, noting there was serious risk he could flee if released, filings show. Moses also cited that Doshi lacked stable employment and strong ties to the community, and noted the evidence against him is strong.

Doshi’s family is also looking to travel to the United States to help support him as the case moves forward, Fitzgerald wrote.

Doshi has been in the United States for nearly two years while studying at UMass Boston, and had been living with five roommates, who “were fairly shocked when they heard he had been arrested,” Fitzgerald wrote.

“Mr. Doshi is charged with a serious felony offense,” Fitzgerald wrote. “While the evidence has been deemed strong, there is no question that his part in the charged conspiracy is as a cog in the machine rather than the control panel.”

Responses to the motion are due by Dec. 5.

There are differences between the Boston colleges. Roxbury is smaller than Bunker Hill and serves students who are more likely to be low-income, Black, or entering college as an adult. The schools offer different academic programs. But are there lessons Roxbury can learn from Bunker Hill about how to better support graduates in entering the workforce?

Amid an ongoing debate over the value of higher education, the Department of Higher Education for the first time released data on post-graduation earnings of public college graduates. The data is available through the state’s Performance Measurement Reporting System and in a report released Nov. 19.

As Americans are increasingly questioning whether college is worth the money, the answer provided by this report — a resounding yes — is important. The report finds that five years after graduation, the typical Massachusetts public college graduate with an associate’s degree will earn approximately $20,000 more a year than a typical high school graduate, while a bachelor’s degree holder will earn $30,000 more.

As Governor Maura Healey said at a State House press conference, college degrees can be tools of economic mobility. “They’re equalizers, tickets to the middle class and far beyond,” Healey said.

But equally important is the report’s nuances, which suggest the value of a degree also depends on what you study and where.

Higher education leaders and policy makers should dig into the data to figure out where improvements are needed. How do colleges ensure more students complete, not just start, college? Do universities adequately inform students about the wage implications of their chosen major? How do schools expand course offerings in high-wage and high-demand majors while doing a better job connecting students in low-wage majors to jobs? Colleges can learn from one another about what works.

Unsurprisingly, one predictor of post-graduation wages is field of study. Someone who earns an associate’s degree from a Massachusetts public college who majored in health sciences will earn a median salary of $76,480 five years after graduation, while the median salary of someone with an associate’s degree in education is $45,400. The median salary for someone with a bachelor’s degree in health care or a STEM field (science, technology, engineering, and math) is more than $85,000, while those with bachelor’s degrees in arts and humanities or education will earn a median salary under $60,000, the report found.

Of course, high wages aren’t the only reason someone enters a field. Massachusetts desperately needs more early educators and special educators, and someone who loves teaching children should be encouraged to study education. But it’s also important that students choosing a major know the wage data and can make an informed decision.

Additionally, the data could be a tool for colleges to shape their programs. Perhaps colleges seeking to be engines of economic mobility could expand programs in health care, the trades, and STEM. College administrators running programs in arts and humanities could redouble their efforts to craft experiential learning experiences, allowing students to gain real-world skills and connections that make it easier to find jobs.

Bunker Hill Community College, for example, got a grant to fund internships for 300 liberal arts students. Bunker Hill president Pam Eddinger (who holds a degree in Japanese literature) said there is a need for students trained in both sciences and liberal arts. “The goal is not that you choose one or the other but how to get the liberal arts grads connected into career in a more meaningful way,” Eddinger told the editorial board.

Massachusetts Maritime Academy has the highest median wage five years after graduation for all public colleges, $98,418. The college is unique because of its focus on maritime trades along with engineering, emergency services, and STEM. Mass Maritime President Rear Admiral Francis McDonald said every degree is aimed at making students employable upon graduation. Every student does a six-month work experience, and they participate in military-style leadership training.

Beyond that, the University of Massachusetts, which is more selective in admissions than other public colleges, generally has the highest post-graduation wages, ranging from $73,000 to $81,000 depending on the campus. The other colleges’ post-graduation earnings range from a median salary of around $54,000 five years post-graduation at the Massachusetts College of Liberal Arts, Holyoke Community College, and Bristol Community College to a median salary of more than $70,000 at Berkshire and Bunker Hill community colleges and Worcester State University.

The report also found that simply enrolling in postsecondary education doesn’t drive a meaningful gain in earnings; only completing a degree does.

As this board has argued previously, public colleges and universities must do more to help students graduate. In addition to the significant financial aid Massachusetts already offers, schools should provide services like academic advising, tutoring, and help with unexpected financial expenses. Colleges can work to schedule classes at convenient times for students and ensure students can easily enroll in required courses.

The new data suggest that attending public college can provide a strong return on investment. But colleges should always be seeking ways to enhance that payoff.

Graduates of the Massachusetts Maritime Academy earned more than their counterparts at the state’s other public colleges and universities, according to a new study.

A report released earlier this month from the state’s Department of Higher Education culled data from public college graduates in Massachusetts between 2014 and 2018.

The median salary for a Mass. Maritime alum five years after graduation was $98,418, according to the report. That was followed by the University of Massachusetts Lowell at $81,050, UMass Amherst at $80,441, UMass Boston at $74,042, and Bunker Hill Community College at $73,433.

The report found that graduating from a public college or university often served as a springboard to a solid profession.

“Our data suggests that postsecondary pathways may play a significant role not only in improving earnings outcomes for all graduates, but also in reducing income gaps across lines of economic and racial/ethnic backgrounds,” the report said. “For example, gaps in median earning levels across races/ethnicities are roughly half as large among those holding associate degrees from a Massachusetts public college as compared to those holding only a high school diploma.”

Governor Maura Healey, a Democrat, emphasized that finding.

“The data is clear — Massachusetts degrees deliver,” Healey said in a statement. “When students graduate from our community colleges and public colleges, they get paid more, they have more opportunities for upward mobility, and they provide a skilled workforce for our employers.

“This is why, working with the Legislature, we have prioritized making college more affordable in Massachusetts,” the statement continued. “When we lower barriers to pursuing higher education, our students succeed and our economy succeeds.”

Ranking at the bottom of the list of the state’s 28 public postsecondary schools was Springfield Technical Community College at $59,721, Roxbury Community College at $58,807, Bristol Community College and Holyoke Community College at $53,932, and the Massachusetts College of Liberal Arts at $53,627, according to the data.

There are gaps in the data, according to the report. Information about graduates who work out of state, part time, or are in the military is not included.

“Our earnings data and analyses are not without limitations,” the report said. “As examples, the data to which we have access does not include self-employed individuals, military personnel, federal government workers, or persons employed out of state, nor does the earnings data source include hours worked.”

The report omitted graduates who worked part time, and noted that surveying salaries at the five-year mark “may not fully account for varying, long-term earnings growth trajectories by field of study.”

One factor that could explain Mass. Maritime’s leading position could be its focus on STEM-related fields, which are typically more lucrative.

“Massachusetts Maritime Academy is a top-ranked university with seven undergraduate degree programs focusing on science, engineering, technology, math, and business,” the school says on its website. “Our unique blend of academics and experiential learning allows students to learn theory, put that theory into practice, and graduate with both the knowledge and experience needed for a successful career.”

The Bourne academy offers undergraduate coursework in emergency management, energy systems engineering, facilities engineering, international maritime business, marine engineering, marine science, safety and environmental protection, and marine transportation, according to its website.

“Our 14:1 student to faculty ratio and average class size of 20 allows for personalized and direct access to our amazing professors,” the site says. “State-of-the-art labs and simulators create an immersive teaching experience that replicates real life scenarios within practice environments.”

This year it’s easier than ever. What is unusual is that, when I sit down to think about the year in food, my first response is one of anger. For the first time, SNAP funds were held hostage from those who need them, the bulk of whom are children, senior citizens, and people with disabilities. After 43 days, the government shutdown ended and the benefits were issued. But not before the country learned that those now in power will treat hunger not as an urgent problem to be alleviated but as a weapon, the suffering of the citizens who elected them a convenience, for they can use it as a bargaining chip.

I’m angry that a country that can afford whatever it wants chooses not to afford this. Those responsible can fight over who gets to borrow Melania Trump’s hideous jacket, emblazoned with the message “I really don’t care, do u?” For the rest of us, the answer is yes, always yes. We really do care, very much.

So, gratitude: I could not be more grateful for the community that stepped up to care for neighbors, to make sure that friends and strangers had access to food. Allandale Farm set up a free weekly farmers’ market for November in Jamaica Plain, giving away produce and bread donated by Iggy’s. Watertown restaurant Ritcey East, known for its comfort food, offered real comfort: free prepared meals, plus a food drive. Roslindale butcher shop and Italian grocery Tony’s Market “adopted” families, providing them with meat, eggs, and prepared foods.

In Newton, Blacker’s Bakeshop leaned into the Jewish mitzvah of maakhal revi’im, feeding the hungry, through its Community Table initiative; they gave away loaves of challah, which community members could also sponsor, alongside Inna’s Kitchen’s donated soups. East Boston’s EBO & Co. Grocery set up a “take what you need” stand outside the shop, offering everything from diapers and formula to oatmeal and mac ’n’ cheese; neighbors contributed money and groceries to keep supplies stocked. In Taunton, Kinfolks BBQ offered $6 dinners, first-come-first-served free meals, and free Thanksgiving dinners.

These are just a few of the examples we heard — on top of the increased, tireless efforts of food banks, food pantries, soup kitchens, and their volunteers and donors longtime and new.

So, to the powerful few who have long perverted “welfare” into a word of shame and scorn rather than compassion and concern: no thanks to you. Everyone else, hell yeah: You make me proud to be a human.

Beyond that, I was thankful for so many smaller things that make life brighter every day:

Like tacos! The local supply of good ones continues to grow, at places such as Esquite in Revere, Pátzcuaro Taqueria & Bar in Newton, Plazita Mexico Tacos in Watertown and Wakefield, and Taqueria El Amigo in Waltham. This year’s big news was a second Taqueria Jalisco in East Boston, with a branch in Orient Heights joining the well-loved Day Square branch. The place is wonderfully festive, and the birria tacos are as good as ever.

I’m always grateful for the Boston area’s strong Asian food scene, from pho in Dorchester to dim sum in Malden to Chinatown’s vibrant assortment of restaurants and bakeries. It was nice to see that recognized by the Michelin Guide, in its first pass through this area. Michelin gave one star to 311 Omakase, serving chef’s tasting menus focused on sushi and sashimi in the South End. The recognition reached from the high end to the more affordable, from the traditional to the innovative — designating Jahunger, Mahaniyom, Pagu, and Sumiao Hunan Kitchen as Bib Gourmand restaurants and recommending Nightshade Noodle Bar, Somaek, Wa Shin, and Zhi Wei Cafe. Mahaniyom also won an award for its cocktails.

In addition to 311 and Wa Shin, I’m grateful for omakase restaurants with unique local flavor that surprise and delight — places like Akame Nigiri and Sake in Lexington, Sushi Sang Lee in Gloucester, and Washoku Renaissance in Charlestown.

I was also glad to see Korean cuisine expand in interesting, thoughtful, and delicious ways ­— at places like Damgeuda in Haverhill, where husband-wife chefs Walter Gorrell and Yu Gin Kim continually re-create their tiny menu of hand-hewn, seasonal gems; Nine Winters Bakery in Cambridge, where Marissa Ferola crafts Korean-American baked goods (gochujang-citrus sticky buns, peanut butter chile crisp cookies) and more (milk bread finger sandwiches, galbi pot au feu); and Somaek, Jamie Bissonnette’s ode to the cuisine he married into, falling in love with the flavors while cooking alongside his mother-in-law, Soon Han, who is consulting chef at the restaurant.

In these days of Instagram and influencers, I sometimes feel that emphasis is placed on how a restaurant looks over how its food tastes. So when Jody Adams’s new Italian restaurant, La Padrona, opened — equal parts style and substance — I was thrilled to ascend its glamorous staircase and quaff fancy martinis and slurp down handmade noodles and tiramisu. Time to do that again soon.

Boston’s Italian food always shines. I was thankful for Little Sage, chef Tony Susi’s new-again restaurant, on its own strengths (those delicate, pillowy gnocchi!) but also because it’s wonderful to have a North End restaurant ready to recommend when people ask, “Where should I eat in the North End?”

Dorchester got the Irish pub it deserves with McGonagle’s, serving perfectly pulled pints of Guinness alongside gorgeous fish and chips and more. The place is named for owner Oran McGonagle, also behind the Dubliner and others; executive chef Aidan McGee worked in London at places such as gastropub the Truscott Arms and the Michelin-starred Dinner by Heston Blumenthal before bringing his excellent pub fare to Boston.

And Jamaica Plain got the cafe/wine bar of my dreams in Jadu, a winning little hangout that brings us chai, savory oatmeal, and brothy beans by day, fancy snacks and glasses of nice wine by night.

One of the best meals I experienced this year was not in Boston at all but on the Cape, at the extremely charming Lune in Dennis Port. I met up with great friends; sat at the counter and watched the chefs do their thing; ate mind-blowing foie gras tarte topped with glowing green chartreuse gelee, confit halibut with fava bean ragout, and house-made sourdough bread with cultured butter; and felt fortunate, fortunate, fortunate.

Perhaps the best part of the year was revisiting places that endure, excel, and enrich our lives — from Slade’s, sometimes called “the Black Cheers,” open since 1928, to Brookline tapas legend Taberna de Haro, now stewarded by new ownership and as wonderful as ever, to — yep — the Ground Round, that nostalgic favorite, reincarnated in Shrewsbury. In Harvard Square, Harvest marked its 50th anniversary this year. Fifty! I’m thankful for everything that makes the food scene wonderful and new, and also for the restaurants the community respects and supports for the long haul.

King, who sells popcorn at TD Garden in the evenings, cooks like many home chefs raised on hearty New England comfort food. Meatballs with gravy are a Sunday night staple. But he’s enjoyed the cooking classes and plans to keep coming back.

“I like this a lot,” he said, shaping patties with purple-stained gloves. “I learned something new, and it wasn’t as hard as I thought to make a vegan meal — and it smells good, too.”

King is one of a growing number of patients in Greater Boston who are being “prescribed” cooking classes as part of their medical care. From Revere to Chelsea to Roxbury and the South End, hospitals and nonprofits are leaning into the idea of “food as medicine,” teaching people with diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and other chronic conditions how to cook healthy, affordable meals, often using only what they can get from food pantries.

At MGB Revere Community Health Teaching Kitchen, two free classes a week draw a diverse group of patients, with interpretation in Arabic and Spanish. All the recipes are designed for people receiving food pantry produce — a pantry just off the kitchen serves only plant-based food and currently supplies about 150 families a week.

About 15 patients gathered for last Thursday’s class, taking turns shredding beets, chopping onions, and turning soaked cashews into a creamy garlic aioli. When the cooking was done, they sat and ate together at long tables, swapping stories like old friends.

Food insecurity is surging in Massachusetts. The Greater Boston Food Bank’s latest Food Access Report found that about 2 million adults — over 1 in 3 residents — struggled to afford food in 2024. An estimated 37 percent of households faced food insecurity, nearly double the 19 percent rate in 2019. The most severe form, where people skip meals or go a whole day without eating, has nearly quadrupled in that time, rising from 6 percent in 2019 to 24 percent in 2024.

Dr. Elsie Taveras, chief community health and equity officer at Mass General Brigham, said screening for food insecurity is becoming standard practice at doctors’ offices. She said it’s essential as food insecurity is linked to higher rates of chronic conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.

Across the room from King, Saida Mahjoubi said she comes as much for the camaraderie as the recipes. Participants know each other by name, and they listen as chef Elliot Kephart, a hospital dietitian, teaches about probiotics, prebiotics, and gut health.

Mahjoubi often cooks Moroccan food at home, but she has embraced unfamiliar ingredients like tatsoi, a leafy green vegetable similar to kale and bok choy.

“We’ve learned how to cook squash in the oven and use different ingredients,” she said. “If we don’t normally use it ... in Moroccan food, that’s OK. It gives us ideas that we take back home and make our own.”

Across town, Boston Medical Center’s Teaching Kitchen has become a hub for hands-on nutrition education with produce from the hospital’s expansive rooftop garden, which yields more than 5,000 pounds of food each year. There are 14 monthly in-person and eight virtual classes, free and open to any patients wanting to learn how to turn what the garden produces into soups, stews, and simple sides that can stretch for several meals.

The teaching kitchen launched in 2008 and has grown significantly as physicians focus more on treating the root causes of chronic disease through nutrition, said Olivia Thomas, a dietitian and BMC’s director of nutrition innovation and implementation.

“We have food that’s appropriate for people who are managing their blood sugar, blood pressure, and especially, those who are pregnant,” Thomas said. “We have to give people confidence to eat healthy foods we provide, because the alternatives are ultra-processed foods that are just so cheap but not as nourishing.”

Patients are typically connected through BMC’s social needs screener, which flags food insecurity and refers them to services. The hospital’s food pantry requires a prescription, and patients can visit up to twice a month. The rooftop garden supplies the food pantry, the teaching kitchen, and BMC’s cafeteria.

Beyond the hospital system, the local soup kitchen Haley House has a similar model through its Take Back the Kitchen program, where community cooks teach participants ages 9 and up everything from basic knife skills to preparing meals with produce from the organization’s one-acre farm in Roxbury. Some classes are offered for free at the Roxbury Library and the Hawthorne Community Center, while others are held in the group’s former bakery café in Nubian Square at a cost of $500 per class.

Each two-hour class brings 12 to 15 people into the kitchen to cook, share a meal, and talk about where their food comes from.

“We ask for people’s favorite recipes, and make them in a much healthier way,” said Alexander Bezek, operations director at Haley House.

Earlier this year, Mass General Brigham and La Colaborativa Community Care launched Bridge to Health/Puente a la Salud, a partnership based at La Colaborativa’s Survival Center on Sixth Street. The initiative is designed to link health care with the free, market-style food distribution and cooking support the organization already offers.

That includes expanding its teaching kitchen and inviting families to practice making affordable, culturally familiar dishes. Classes often double as community gatherings, where participants exchange recipes, swap ingredients, and leave with the groceries they need to recreate the meals at home.

“It’s food as medicine — and what does that mean in a food desert or without access to a refrigerator or kitchen because you’re subleasing?” said Dinanyili Paulino, executive vice president at La Colaborativa.

Meanwhile, back in Revere, King was planning his Thanksgiving. Although he enjoyed his first class at MGB, he grinned and said that he still planned to make meatballs and gravy part of his holiday meal. “But now I know I can do things a different way, too,” he said.

The housing program through Women’s Lunch Place is a short-term solution for women like Debbie experiencing homelessness in the Boston area. Unlike some other shelters, it’s designed so each woman can have their own room, and they’re paired with an advocate, or social worker, who helps them find permanent housing. The Globe is not naming the specific location of the shelter because some of the women living there have been victims of domestic violence.

So far, 13 women have moved from the Women’s Lunch Place shelter to permanent housing. The wraparound services — including meals, access to a kitchen, laundry machines, and a social worker — give women experiencing homelessness more stability than they’re used to in typical nighttime shelters, said CEO Jennifer Hanlon Wigon.

Many women experience homelessness as a result of physical or sexual assault, Hanlon Wigon said. Between 22 and 57 percent of all homeless women report that domestic violence was the immediate cause of their homelessness, according to the National Network to End Domestic Violence.

“Having safe gendered spaces is a real key to their ability to turn off that fight or flight aspect of their trauma,” Hanlon Wigon said.

Women’s Lunch Place opened its pilot housing program in response to a spike in homelessness last winter, she said. The number of people experiencing homelessness in Greater Boston peaked in 2024 at over 20,000 people, and fell to around 19,600 in 2025, according to a report from Boston Indicators, the research arm of the Boston Foundation. Women in Greater Boston experience homelessness at slightly higher rates than men — 30 per 10,000 women compared to 27 per 10,000 men — in contrast to the national trend, the report said.

Women’s Lunch Place increased the shelter capacity by 50 beds for women experiencing homelessness in Greater Boston. Now, thanks to a new grant from the Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, the pilot program will be expanded to 65 beds.

“The first night that we were up to capacity, the shelter system had a bed for every woman,” Hanlon Wigon said.

In addition to adding 15 beds, the $760,000-plus grant will extend the shelter program from November through April.

Because of Massachusetts’ unique right-to-shelter law — which means state officials have to provide housing to families with children and pregnant women — shelters in Greater Boston are often overburdened. At overnight shelters, women may have to carry all their belongings if they can’t get a locker, and sleeping arrangements are in flux.

Marcia Fabiola Davis, 65, remembers her time living in other shelters. When she stayed in a safe house in Florida after escaping domestic violence, local restaurants would send leftovers when they closed, but she couldn’t always keep her young daughter awake until 11 p.m. to eat.

When her daughter, now married, asked Davis how the food was at Women’s Lunch Place recently, she said, “Not the same as the safe house in Florida.”

“That makes me more calm,” Davis remembers her daughter saying.

Davis has lived in the Women’s Lunch Place shelter program since November. Originally from Brazil, Davis moved to the US to take care of her sister in Florida, who has liver problems, and eventually became a citizen in 2018.

While in Florida, Davis worked at a grocery store on-and-off — a job she loved despite having to pause work to navigate multiple health crises — before eventually following her daughter to Boston.

“This year, in May, [my daughter] married, and it’s time that I go,” Davis said, insisting to her daughter that she should have her own private life.

Davis said she had been working on housing applications since 2023. Earlier this year, she stayed in the Missionaries of Charity shelter in Dorchester, where she had an early curfew and shared bedrooms. Now, she loves having her own key and access to laundry.

“The mission is nice, too, but in here, it’s five stars,” Davis said.

Through the daytime programs at Women’s Lunch Place, Davis takes crochet and English classes. After she finds an apartment, she plans to go back to school and finish the political science degree she started in Brazil.

Finding permanent housing has gotten more difficult as affordable housing grows scarce in Greater Boston, said Doris Romero, senior director of housing and advocacy at Women’s Lunch Place. She leads a group of 11 advocates who help guests fill out apartment applications and address barriers to housing. Last year, advocates held 11,830 meetings with 1,275 guests, including visitors to the Women’s Lunch Place daytime program and the shelter.

Jackeline Dixon, 59, moved from a shelter to her own apartment in May. In her own place, she’s able to rest when her sciatica flares or cook whenever she wants.

“When you’re homeless, it’s a different kind of stress,” she said.

Dixon, who lost her housing after a fire in her apartment complex in 2023, credits the staff at Women’s Lunch Place with helping her fill out applications every day.

Staff at Women’s Lunch Place said they still hear from women who have since moved to permanent housing because of the community at the shelter. Debbie G. promises to come back and help volunteer in whatever way she can.

“You know Cheers? The place where everybody knows your name?” Debbie said. “That’s what the Lunch Place is. Everybody knows your name.”

On Dec. 6 and 7, Boston’s For the Children toy drive takes over Big Night Live for two all-day, all-ages shows. It’s a big leap from the Middle East in Cambridge, where the first local events took place: Big Night Live can accommodate as many as 2,000 people. (Two-day passes are currently sold out.)

More than a dozen bands, including Haywire, Fiddlehead, Bane, Colin of Arabia, and Twitching Tongues, will take the stage each day. Each attendee is expected to bring a new, unwrapped toy for the toy drive. (Two-day attendees are required to bring a toy for each concert.) Volunteer members of the hardcore community will distribute the toys at an event at the Roxbury YMCA on Dec. 10.

The Boston FTC shows are the brainchild of Austin Sparkman, frontman for Haywire. That band has been on a roll of late: Following the 2024 release of their frenetic “Conditioned for Demolition” (11 songs in 19 minutes), they’ll be on tour in early 2026 with the Dropkick Murphys.

“Kudos to Austin,” said Pat Flynn, the high school history teacher and frontman for Fiddlehead. “He’s really kind of revived the Boston hardcore scene in a lot of ways.”

As a young man growing up in small-town Ohio, Sparkman went all-in for hardcore, booking shows out of his home. When he moved to the Boston area 13 years ago, he was adopted by the local scene, as he explained on the phone from a tour stop in the Netherlands. On the day he arrived, 30 members of the community threw a dinner to welcome him.

For a few years, Sparkman helped run Anchors Up, a hardcore venue in Haverhill. In 2015, the city shut it down after a violent incident.

Hardcore, with its rigorous mosh pits and strong-willed, sometimes warring ethical codes, might seem an unlikely community to host an annual toy drive.

“I find it so fascinating from an anthropological and sociological standpoint,” said Flynn, who counts his own band as one of the “softer” hardcore groups in Boston (“I wear, like, sweaters”). “The ethos [of hardcore] is, there kind of is no ethos.”

Sparkman agrees, noting that there are different factions that coexist under the “hardcore” umbrella — punks, skinheads, metalheads. As it has been in LA for years, For the Children is an annual opportunity for them all to come together for a good cause.

Not that they love the idea of being congratulated for doing “charity.”

“We’re not trying to be ‘do-gooders,’ at least in my interpretation,” said Flynn. “We try to stray from moral sanctimony.”

Nevertheless, two years ago Sparkman launched a fund-raiser for the family of Jimmy Flynn, the beloved Quincy hardcore promoter who died after an illness at age 40. The effort raised nearly $50,000.

In July, Haywire headlined the Back to School Skate Jam, a live music event and skateboard competition at the Lynch Family Skatepark in Cambridge. Admission was free with a donation of school supplies.

“We’re all not great people by any means,” said Sparkman of the hardcore community. “But when there is an objective, everyone can come together and make something like this happen.”

Toy donations from the FTC shows will be distributed at an upcoming event at the YMCA and members of the hardcore community will be wearing reindeer outfits, Sparkman said. Brockton’s Colin Campbell, the burly frontman for Colin of Arabia, is scheduled to dress as Santa Claus.

Campbell has had plenty of practice. For years, he said, he has “ho-ho-ho’d over the phone for my friends’ children.”

“I love Christmas, and the spirit of giving,” said this snarling hardcore singer, an Army veteran who named his band’s latest EP “Trauma Dump.” “I’m almost there with my hair and beard combo.”

The current “home-based” method has not met its goals for academics or racial diversity, and its confusing and complex design likely hurts the city’s most needy families. The mayor and Boston Public Schools should scrap the current assignment system, consider a return to “neighborhood schools,” and focus their energy on providing access to more high-quality schools, rather than a lottery for a few.

The current system dates back more than a decade. The late mayor Tom Menino inherited a system based on “zones” for elementary and middle schools, a legacy of court-ordered desegregation starting in the 1970s. But in 2012, at the height of his political power, Menino pulled together a committee and charged it with creating a new student assignment system. After years of analysis and public meetings, a novel solution — designed by an MIT graduate student — arose.

Rather than using large zones, families would receive school lists based on where they lived and how closely they lived to schools that were deemed high-quality. Assignment, however, was still up to fate, as families ranked their schools and awaited lottery results. Coined the home-based assignment system, families were promised “higher-quality schools, closer to home,” and shorter bus rides to boot.

It was a bold move then — but that system hasn’t worked as its creators hoped. A rigorous study by MIT’s Blueprint Labs, involving Nobel Prize-winning researchers, found that the changes in assignment did not lead to a boost in test scores, graduation rates, or college access. Nor did the system make a meaningful dent in diversity: 86 percent of Boston children still attended a segregated or intensely segregated school (defined as a population of at least 71 percent white or non-white students) in 2024.

Meanwhile, busing has only gotten more expensive. Boston school transportation spending is the highest in the nation, $189 million this year even though there are 9,000 fewer children riding buses than 10 years ago. Whatever gains the home-based system captured in shortening bus distances have been lost to the snarl of Boston’s traffic, which studies place as among the worst in the country.

The city is spending a lot of money supporting an approach that simply has not worked.

So it is time to radically rethink how our schools are enrolled to deliver on the promise of high-quality schools. The city should start by creating a commission to study the best ideas and generate public engagement to build political support for a final plan.

Here is one approach worth considering: Boston could assign elementary school students in their neighborhoods (secondary schools, grades 7-12 and 9-12, could remain citywide), similar to other big cities like Chicago and Washington, D.C. “Neighborhood schools,” as they are known, is a loaded term, conjuring images of racism and strife, and of a time when schools were built to exclude children.

But a new vision of neighborhood schools is quite different and potentially progressive, allowing the system to invest more heavily in areas of greater need, literally meeting families and students where they are. It also has the added benefit of enabling children and families to develop or deepen relationships where they live, which has proven elusive in a fractured school-choice environment.

A move to neighborhood schools would result in some Boston schools becoming less racially diverse. This could be ameliorated through voluntary magnet programs or strategic siting of new buildings. But we must also be clear-eyed about the data. The fact that about 75 percent of students in the district are Black or Latino makes the math impossible to create a large number of schools balanced across all races. That was a factor cited when the federal desegregation order was lifted from Boston four decades ago.

Although research indicates that racial diversity does have positive impacts on student achievement, it is not a required ingredient for school success. Some of the most successful schools I have worked in or visited, or that operate in Boston today, have an overwhelmingly Black and/or Latino student population. Whether it is the Brooke charter network, the O’Bryant, or the Henry Grew, there are many examples of schools in the city proving that students of color can achieve at the highest levels. Implying that students of color need to be proximal to white or Asian students to be successful is incorrect and dangerous thinking.

No assignment plan can retire busing completely. State law and special education requirements will still demand a daily fleet, but even a diminished one could save tens of millions of dollars annually — money that could be reinvested in schools. Fewer buses would also reduce traffic and carbon emissions.

Critics will argue that some families will not have access to high-quality schools because all the schools in their neighborhood are deemed low performing. That is a problem. But students under the current system also attend low-performing schools. The answer is not to stick with that status quo system but to find ways to improve those schools. We should stop offering families algorithms as a substitute for what they really want.

One approach is to expand seats in high-quality schools. In my decade at Boston Schools Fund, we helped to open thousands of high-quality seats in schools in every neighborhood in Boston. Whether it was supporting the expansion to middle school for New Mission High School in Hyde Park, helping smaller but very effective elementary schools like the Nathan Hale in Roxbury add sixth grades, or working with all neighborhood schools to create a high-quality pre-K-12 pathway for every family in East Boston, the path to more quality school access was simply more quality schools.

With talented educators and a commitment to overhauling facilities, this goal has never been more possible. With a mayor who has experienced this assignment system as a parent, and with a city councilor, Ruthzee Louijeune, who served on the assignment committee in 2012, we have many political leaders with the experience and expertise to tackle this issue.

This is a deeply complex and political topic, with trade-offs and real potential benefits. Who wouldn’t want less time and money spent on buses, more money spent on academics and after-school programs, and the opportunity to go to school with your friends and neighbors?

Even the few high-level suggestions offered here will spark responses and would require immense study and debate. So let’s have it. Surely, all of the public schools in Boston deserve just as much attention for how they are enrolled as the city’s three exam schools.

We may end up back where we are, but at least we would not have accepted a status quo that we know is not working.

Higher education institutions can, and should, learn from each other. This is particularly important for community colleges, which are crucial engines of opportunity.

To that end, quantifying earnings outcomes can be useful in identifying top performers. The Massachusetts Department of Higher Education recently released a report doing just that, and a Globe editorial focused on the fact that Bunker Hill Community College graduates earn, on average, $15,000 more than Roxbury Community College graduates. This is a striking comparison, but it’s only part of the story: In a broader analysis, Roxbury outperforms Bunker Hill in student earnings.

The biggest piece of the puzzle is which students’ earnings are counted. The DHE report compares the earnings of graduates. To make the key point that earning a degree matters, that’s sound. But if you want to compare which institution is doing a better job, one should look at everyone who enrolls, as does the American Council on Education’s Access and Earnings Classification.

If you include only graduates, an institution would look better even if most students drop out while a few graduate to high earnings. When you look at earnings for everyone who enrolls, Roxbury emerges as a strong performer.

Boston is fortunate to have both of these robust community colleges, and no one benefits from a misleading comparison. But everyone can benefit by examining the practices of colleges that are serving most effectively as levers of economic mobility, which is why the organization I lead, Public Agenda, has been sharing research findings on exactly that question.

For example, someone living in an apartment building with a package drop-off area may avoid using mail order because their package could get stolen. Someone who lacks internet access or doesn’t speak English may struggle to order prescriptions. Someone with strep throat can’t wait three days for an antibiotic to arrive.

A 2019 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association found that adults over 50 taking cardiovascular medications were less likely to take their medication consistently after the pharmacy where they previously filled a prescription closed. That drop persisted a year after the closure. A 2024 JAMA study in Colorado similarly found that patients filled fewer prescriptions for anticonvulsant medications — which are prescribed to treat epilepsy, some types of chronic pain, and other illnesses — after their pharmacy closed.

Additionally, amid a shortage of primary care doctors, many people rely on pharmacies for vaccinations. For older residents with Medicare Part D insurance plans, physicians may encourage patients to get vaccinated at a pharmacy because it simplifies billing.

In Massachusetts, pharmacists can also prescribe birth control and order medication-related lab tests.

“They are central health hubs and are arguably one of the most accessible health care providers,” said Kaley Hayes, associate director of Pharmacoepidemiology at Brown University’s Center for Gerontology and Healthcare Research. When pharmacies close, Hayes said, “It’s taking another health care provider out of the equation.”

The largest proportion of Massachusetts pharmacy deserts (47 percent) are in urban areas, and deserts created since 2019 include neighborhoods in Boston, Springfield, Worcester, and New Bedford. Generally, urban pharmacy deserts are in areas where people have lower incomes. But pharmacy deserts are spread throughout the state, including in some rural parts of Western Massachusetts, the Health Policy Commission found. The commission defines a pharmacy desert as a census block that’s more than one mile from a pharmacy in an urban area, two miles in a suburban area, or five miles in a rural area, with an adjustment for areas with low vehicle ownership or low-income households.

One way to prevent closures is through payment reform to ensure that insurers compensate pharmacists — regardless of whether they are independent or part of a chain — a fair amount for dispensing drugs.

The Federal Trade Commission issued a report last year that documented ways in which pharmacy benefit managers (middlemen that negotiate drug prices and formularies with insurers, drugmakers, and pharmacies) negotiated higher prices for the same drug for pharmacies affiliated with the benefit managers than for unaffiliated pharmacies. The companies also use tactics like offering lower copays to steer customers to affiliated pharmacies.

Todd Brown, executive director of the Massachusetts Independent Pharmacists Association, estimated based on anecdotal reports from pharmacists that independent pharmacists lose money on about 70 percent of the drugs they dispense. “They’re left to try to eke out enough money to stay in business with the remaining amount of claims that are over the acquisition cost, but that’s becoming smaller and smaller, and PBMs are steering more claims to their own pharmacies,” Brown said.

Congress has been considering ways to regulate pharmacy benefit managers, including through an outright prohibition on the companies or insurers owning pharmacies. The Massachusetts Independent Pharmacists Association is pushing state legislation that would require insurers and pharmacy benefit managers to pay all pharmacies for drugs at a rate no lower than the rate paid by Medicaid. New York passed legislation prohibiting pharmacy benefit managers from penalizing consumers for not using pharmacies affiliated with the companies. Some states set rules around the rates that pharmacy benefit managers in Medicaid managed care programs can use to reimburse pharmacies.

But payment reform can’t be the only solution, since the decline in pharmacies is not unique to independent pharmacies. There have also been closures of chain pharmacies, retail-based pharmacies, and grocery-based pharmacies.

The Health Policy Commission research didn’t delve into the reasons for closures. Mike Tocco, president of Integrated Pharmacy Solutions, which provides pharmacy management services, said causes can include reimbursement challenges, a switch to mail order, the proliferation of shoplifting in inner cities, and the overwork of pharmacists in chain stores, which causes pharmacists to leave the field and fewer to enter.

Insurers could be part of the solution by expanding “preferred pharmacy” networks so consumers have more options to find a new pharmacy. Insurers could also cover medication for a larger number of days if a prescription is filled at a pharmacy that’s about to close, so that patients have more time to find an alternative. Community Health Centers could contribute by expanding pharmacy services in underserved communities.

One open question is whether there’s a systemic way for an insurer, pharmacist, or medical provider to reach out to customers who have filled prescriptions with a closing pharmacy to help them transition to a new pharmacy or method of ordering medication.

Legislation passed in 2024 established a state Office of Pharmaceutical Policy and Analysis. Its priorities should include figuring out how to support customers when pharmacies close — and how to shore up pharmacies so fewer close in the first place.

It’s not as splashy as groundbreakings and ribbon cuttings, but the shift has defined the economic development strategy of Wu’s first term. That work begins in Boston Public Schools with a push to guarantee a summer job for every student, and it extends into training and placing thousands of adults in skilled jobs. Administration officials say Wu has poured more city dollars into workforce development and secured more than $100 million in public and private grants to support it.

That focus has served Wu well, with Hasbro and other marquee companies drawn by Boston’s ability to attract, retain, and develop talented people. From early 2022, when Wu took office, through early 2025, the number of jobs in the city grew 2.7 percent, according to the most recent data from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, a pace that is faster than the rest of Massachusetts if slower than the United States as a whole.

“It’s a recognition that human capital is the bedrock on which urban success in the 21st century rests, and it is also the most plausible path to make sure that we have a more economically inclusive city,” said Harvard economist Edward Glaeser, who is known for his research on urban economies. “We don’t just want people who have PhDs from MIT or Harvard or Stanford to be able to thrive in those places. We want these to be places where lots of other people can work.”

Perhaps the emphasis on workforce development comes out of economic necessity: High office and lab vacancy rates, coupled with high interest rates, have stalled new construction. Jump-starting development would likely require giving out more tax breaks, which Wu is not apt to do. Instead, she leaned into her comfort zone: building an equitable economy, one resident and one family at a time.

While Wu’s predecessors have championed youth jobs and offered workforce training, she has gone bigger — creating a record number of summer jobs and devoting more resources to help 20- and 30-somethings who’ve felt shut out of growing industries including health care, life sciences, and clean energy. That’s led to two new signature programs: Good Jobs Metro Boston Coalition and the Life Sciences Workforce Development Initiative.

“She sees education and workforce development as a continuum,” said Neil Sullivan, the longtime executive director of the Boston Private Industry Council who has worked with six mayors. “It’s grounded in the public schools, but the commitment has to extend beyond.”

Her administration has been able to deftly tap federal money and philanthropy to create workforce development programs. In 2022, during Wu’s first full year in office, the city won a three-year, $23 million federal grant to train and place people in about 4,600 jobs in Greater Boston. The city expects to meet that goal by August; some 3,250 individuals have already trained or landed jobs as child care teachers, HVAC technicians, and EMTs, with many earning anywhere from $18 to $36 an hour.

Then, in June 2023, during the BIO convention that brought thousands of biotech executives and investors to Boston, Wu unveiled a life sciences initiative to get 1,000 city residents trained and hired at area research labs by the end of 2025.

Since then, the city has invested over $5.7 million in that effort, including a new collaboration with the Massachusetts Biotechnology Council, the state’s life sciences trade association. But the life sciences slowdown means Wu won’t meet her goal this year. Only 126 residents have completed training, with 73 placed in jobs; the city is now retooling the program to offer additional training and educational opportunities so that residents can find similar roles in health care, where labor shortages still exist.

“We have to make sure that all Bostonians have access to those jobs up and down the pipelines,” said Trinh Nguyen, the city’s chief of worker empowerment, a Cabinet-level position Wu created. “And if they don’t, we have to create ramps for them.”

Still, the heart of the mayor’s workforce development will always be with BPS students.

Since coming into office, Wu has tripled the amount of money for youth summer jobs to about $21 million annually and raised another $10 million from philanthropy. In her 2024 State of the City address, Wu promised to “guarantee a summer job offer to every BPS student who wants one.” And this past summer, a record 10,511 students enrolled in the program, up from 6,455 in in 2022.

Summer jobs are a start, but the goal is to help young people build careers. That’s why the city has been working to develop stronger partnerships between employers and schools such as Roxbury Community College, Bunker Hill Community College, and University of Massachusetts Boston.

Perhaps the best example has been the expansion of the Edward M. Kennedy Academy for Health Careers, a BPS vocational high school that prepares students for health care jobs. Early last year, the city won a $37.8 million grant from Bloomberg Philanthropies that will pay to double the number of students it enrolls to 800. It is the largest philanthropic donation ever to BPS, and the money will allow EMK Academy to expand career pathways to include medical imaging and biotech lab sciences in roles that earn upward of $100,000 annually.

Some students, in their EMK maroon scrubs, are already a regular presence at hospitals such as Brigham and Women’s and Massachusetts General, where they have paid internships. A few times a year, students visit the hospitals for hands-on training, from how to insert intravenous lines to how to deal with patient falls.

To Taveras, the MGB executive whose community health portfolio includes working with EMK Academy, the expanded partnership “is a perfect coming together of solving a pain point” that addresses labor shortages for hospitals and helps “some students see themselves in a career that can break the cycle of poverty.”

Whether Wu can maintain momentum on her workforce development initiatives remains to be seen.

Hiring has started to slow, a trend that is expected to continue amid economic headwinds. Grant money for some programs is running out, even as commercial property taxes — a key source of revenue for the city budget — slump. That may ultimately force Wu to reckon with her rocky relationship with developers.

“With housing starts slowing, cranes scarce, and too many local businesses expanding in places other than Boston, it is not clear that the right balance has been found yet,” said Dan Dain, a Boston attorney whose firm focuses on the commercial real estate industry.

The through line for Wu has been creating a city that is a desirable place to live and work — not just for the best and brightest, but for everyone. Companies will need talent at all levels to grow, and it’s that growth that ultimately will fuel the need for more office towers and housing.

That’s the case she made in victory-lap speech at a Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce forum shortly after winning the September primary.

“They’re choosing Boston because of our people,” Wu said. “Competitiveness in this economy and in this moment means working together to nurture, recruit, and promote top talent, building up the community and workforce that any company would want to consider relocating to join,” she added. “So when I say I’m fighting to make Boston a home for everyone, I’m talking about making Boston the human capital of the world, the talent capital of the world.”

Do that, she believes, and the cranes will follow.

The parent mentors are one of many strategies Boston Public Schools is using to address a serious shortage. One-third of the district’s 47,000 students primarily speak a language other than English, but the schools don’t have nearly enough bilingual teachers to offer them support in their native tongue.

Research shows English language learners do best when they receive at least some instruction in two languages.

In Boston, the district has only 13 such programs, mostly in elementary schools, and they have long waiting lists. Last year, only 7 percent of English learners — or about 1,200 students— were enrolled in dual-language programs. For the most part, other English language learners are simply integrated into regular classrooms.

The result has been lower test scores for English learners. Almost three-quarters of English learners and former students who were English learners failed to meet or exceed MCAS scores for math and science in 2024. And over the past four years, more than 15 percent dropped out, twice the dropout rate of other students, according to state education data.

“Most of these kids are being dumped into general education classrooms and are pulled out for 45 to 90 minutes a day to take English as a second language classes,” said Rosann Tung, an education researcher who resigned from a BPS task force on English learning after criticizing the district’s approach.

Tung and seven other task force members left in protest in late 2023 after the district announced it could not keep up with an influx of new English learners and would not guarantee instruction in their native language. Instead, the district doubled down on an “inclusive education plan,” integrating English learners into general education classrooms.

“We are implementing inclusive classrooms, so multilingual learners and students with disabilities can learn close to home, in the same room as their peers,” said Mayor Michelle Wu at the first ever State of the Schools address this fall.

Wu did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

In Boston, where students hailed from 139 different countries, the district last year promised to add 1,060 students to bilingual classrooms by the 2032-2033 school year, while hiring 40 new bilingual teachers over almost a decade. After this story was published, BPS said in an email that it had increased its hiring plan to 54 teachers and that it “currently offers over 2,500 seats” to students wanting dual language bilingual programs.

Four out of 10 new teachers hired this year were fluent in a second language, BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper said in an interview.

“We’ve had more bilingual programming approved by the state and operationalized in the last couple of years — and will continue to do that — than we have had in decades,” she said.

For the upcoming school year, the city invested $123 million, nearly 8 percent of its total school budget, in multilingual programs.

Of that funding, $4 million will go toward adding or expanding multilingual programs in seven elementary schools and two secondary schools.

The district is also in the process of planning a new bilingual program taught in Cape Verdean creole.

The growth of those multilanguage programs won’t come close to keeping up with the growing need, as half of pre-K and kindergarten students entering the district don’t speak English as their first language. Only five new bilingual teachers will be added for the next school year districtwide, according to the district’s budget.

St. Stephen’s parent mentors are filling in the gaps where they can.

Since 2017, the youth program at the church in the South End has been training mothers who hail from Haiti, Mexico, Morocco, Somalia, Ecuador, Paraguay, and other countries to work in kindergarten classrooms. The moms help with academic development and provide social, emotional, and language support by stepping in when a child can’t communicate.

Backed by BPS, the program also aims for some of the bilingual parent mentors to eventually become professionals, with 40 percent of all participants going on to work for the district.

“We are building a pipeline for bilingual people who come from the same communities as our students to enter education,” said Ari Branz, director of organizing at the St. Stephen’s youth program.

Kayra Amador, a Dominican parent mentor who provides support at the William Monroe Trotter Elementary school in Dorchester, said she is striving to become a lead teacher so she can have a positive impact on children’s lives.

“The kids who don’t speak English are always more isolated and lonely,” Amador said. “When I am there in the class with them, I feel like I can help them.“

A grant provided by the City of Boston pays for Amador and 19 other parent mentors to enroll at Urban College, where they take courses required to become certified lead teachers. After that, they can choose to pursue an associate’s degree in education.

A 2002 ballot campaign led by a conservative Silicon Valley millionaire eliminated bilingual instruction in schools in Massachusetts until it was lifted in 2017.

The 15-year-ban has left a hole in the state’s teaching workforce, Branz said.

“There is a whole generation of students who graduated without learning a second language,” said Branz, who previously worked with the Boston Teachers Union. “Those are the people who are now entering the workforce as teachers.”

Since 2017, the number of districts statewide offering dual language programs grew from 15 to 25, across 62 individual schools, according to the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.

Experts said initiatives like the mentorship program at St. Stephen’s will help, but not enough to address the shortage.

“The parent mentorship program is a very positive step,” said John Mudd, a former member of the School Committee’s task force on English language learners. “But in no way can it substitute for broader reform in the education of multilingual learners.”

Meanwhile, mothers who participate in the St. Stephen’s mentorship program continue to do their part.

Every Friday, they gather at the church to talk about what they have experienced Monday through Thursday in the classroom and to receive training from educators. About 40 parents participate in the program this year.

In a crowded meeting room adjacent to the church, they sit at round tables and scribble in notebooks, as a team from the nonprofit Boston Partners in Education offers a presentation on the best ways to provide support.

”When one of our mentors shows up, [teachers] are relieved to finally have someone to help them communicate," said Rafaela Polanco, director of parent organizing and engagement at the church. “So at least for 2½ hours, four days a week, we are helping to bridge that gap.“

“It was like watching the sunrise,” Brown, 25, said about moving into her apartment on Nov. 1.

Giving Tuesday — a national day of philanthropy held on the first Tuesday after Thanksgiving — has leaders of Boston-area nonprofits hopeful for the donations they need this year to help people in the community, such as Brown.

Amid cuts to critical federal funding, the high cost of living, and rising fear among immigrants facing possible deportation, nonprofits have carried a heavy burden. Staff, such as the social workers who worked for months to help Brown find a home, have witnessed the upheaval first-hand.

”We’re seeing a surge in demand for our services just as federal resources are being cut,” said Catholic Charities Boston CEO Kelley Tuthill.

Boston-area nonprofits said support on Giving Tuesday doesn’t have to come in the form of money.

People who themselves may need extra help paying bills often give in other ways, such as volunteering, they said.

No matter what form it takes, giving to others has psychological benefits, experts said.

“People call it warm glow giving, you get a hit of joy from giving to other people or helping others,” said Paige Amormino, a post-doctoral researcher at Pennsylvania State University who studies moral psychology.

Catholic Charities Boston started their Giving Tuesday campaign earlier than ever this year, toward the beginning of November, Tuthill said.

The decision came after months of rising demand for emergency aid and shelter spots, such as the one Brown and her daughter were able to access earlier this year.

When donors write a check on Giving Tuesday or later this holiday season, they will be helping the approximately 100,000 people across Eastern Massachusetts that the nonprofit serves, Tuthill said.

“I think right now, many people are feeling powerless,” Tuthill said. “They feel like they don’t agree with some of the things happening right now in our country. They think, what can I do? And I say to them, ‘You can do a lot.’”

Brown said her worst moment living unhoused came early one morning when her family’s makeshift sleeping area in a storage unit was almost discovered by a staff member doing a walk-through.

“I had to jump up real quick and deconstruct our set-up,” said Brown, who knew that living in a storage facility could get her in trouble with police. “That was a really scary point, almost getting caught, and thankfully, I managed to make it look like we were just there super early going through stuff.”

Now, Brown said, she feels like she can persevere through anything to take care of her kids, ages four and three months.

“Even when you feel like nothing is going right, any effort you give is your best,” she said.

In East Boston, some people who fear possible encounters with federal immigration agents have been too afraid to go to the drug store alone, said Neenah Estrella-Luna, who helps run Mutual Aid Eastie. The group gives emergency aid to residents in the form of grocery store gift cards and toiletries. In many cases, cash is the most dignified form of aid, Estrella-Luna said.

“We don’t judge what people need; we let them decide what they need,” she said.

People who give monthly are the top factor keeping Mutual Aid Eastie’s work “sustainable,” Estrella-Luna said, including those who can give only $5.

Donors benefit from the group’s resources too, Estrella-Luna said, even if simply by knowing that a safety net will be there to catch them if they lose their job or get sick.

“It’s not charity, I think that’s a really key piece of it,” Estrella-Luna said.

While many on Giving Tuesday may feel more accustomed to writing a check for their favorite cause, plugging in to a hyper-local network could come with unique psychological benefits, Amormino said.

“There’s this bigger theme of reciprocity ‐ you’re helping me right now, and it might take a couple months or even years for me to get back on my feet and be able to help you ‐ but there’s a motivation to give back once you’re able to," Amormino said.

In Boston, some are worried about funding changes the Department of Housing and Urban Development proposed in November that could push 170,000 formerly homeless people back onto the street nationwide, said Philip Mangano, founder and president of the American Round Table to Abolish Homelessness.

“When a Bostonian sees a wrong, they want to right it. When they see an evil, they want to end it,” said Mangano, whose group is based downtown.

Mangano’s group solicits donations on Giving Tuesday, he said. The inflow of cash helps his advocacy work preventing and ending homelessness, which increased by 53 percent last year in the state, he said.

In Somerville, a group of low-income residents cook food and get a steady stream of donations from farmers markets, which volunteers place inside free sidewalk refrigerators for anyone who needs them, said Crystal Huff, who has helped manage three fridges across Union Square, Tufts, and East Somerville since 2020.

Lately, there are almost always people waiting at the fridge to see if there will be a food delivery, Huff said. She said she hopes that Giving Tuesday raises awareness for the fridges and that people know anyone can get food from them.

When Huff was on a late-night cooking kick that resulted in an enormous batch of cardamom-ginger applesauce, there were people waiting outside by the fridge when she brought a surprise delivery at 2 a.m.

“It’s hard to see how much food insecurity there is in Somerville, and it’s hard to be part of a household that’s experiencing food insecurity, but the community fridges give me hope that we can help each other get through this,” Huff said.

Globe Santa hears all these reasons (except, happily, the one about feeling guilty saying “no”.) When donors write to Globe Santa, they typically express empathy for struggling families, and gratitude for their own good fortune in life. As one donor wrote in an email this year: “I’m so very fortunate and so many are not. It’s the least I/we can do.”

But many people donate to Globe Santa for a reason that’s unique to this charity, one that would never show up on any survey. They want to give because they themselves were Globe Santa recipients as kids. And they remember how much that big box landing on their doorstep transformed a potentially dismal time of year into something indelible.

“My sister and I were Globe Santa recipients, back in 1964,” Stephen Factor of Hyde Park emailed Globe Santa this year. “I never, ever forgot about Globe Santa.”

Factor was born in 1956, the same year the Globe Santa program started. His father was “not a stable man mentally,” he said in an interview, and after his parents divorced, Factor moved with his mother and sister to the Franklin Field housing developments in Dorchester. “It was tough, mostly for my mother,” he said. “She would always fly off the handle. I got the brunt of that.”

His memories of those years are hazy. He vaguely recalls the family was on welfare and that his mother had no money for presents. But he distinctly remembers that Globe Santa brought gifts to his sister and himself.

“One thing I’ll never forget is what it was like to feel like as a kid; I’m very, very sensitive to kids’ needs,” he said. “Kids want things, too. They watch TV. They dream. And then they go back to school [after Christmas] and they hear ‘I got this’ and kids are showing everyone their new laptop. And then there’s this poor kid who didn’t get anything.”

His philosophy is that “life is about doing the best you can and taking some time to help others whenever you can. Donating to Globe Santa is one of the things I do that puts a smile on my face this time of year, and hopefully others do too. “

Mary Ann Sperandio, 75, a retired school teacher living in Franklin, was also a Globe Santa recipient.

She grew up in housing developments in Jamaica Plain with her mother, sister and brother. Her father was out of the picture, she said in an interview. “My mother left my father when I was three because he’d beaten her up nonstop for seven years.”

She describes a childhood spent in cheerless surroundings. They had no car. No telephone. When she was seven years old, she saw her first gun. (“It was domestic abuse outside our window. The man was waving a gun because his wife had left.”) She acquired the knack of getting herself to school without being beaten up by gangs.

At Christmastime, her mother tried to compensate for their meager means by filling red mesh stockings with oranges and candy bars, and hanging them from the doorknobs. But young Mary Ann saw right through this ploy.

“I knew it was from her because Santa doesn’t give out oranges,” she remembers thinking. “Why would he give me an orange and a candy bar?” Also, she knew from watching TV that Santa came down the chimney and put presents under a tree.

“Does Santa just go to rich people’s houses?” she’d ask her mother. “Is it because we’re poor?” Her mother told her it was because they didn’t have a chimney.

But Globe Santa came to their house, with the intervention of a social worker. “I knew the presents were coming from the Boston Globe, but I didn’t care,” she said. “I knew Globe Santa was a charitable foundation for poor kids. I knew that at a very young age. But I was just happy to get the big box.”

Among the gifts Globe Santa delivered to her home was a jewelry-making kit with “little tiny plastic beads in different shapes that fit one into the other.” She coveted it, as she did the metal roller skates Globe Santa brought “that you put under your shoes with a key to tighten them. Zipped all through the projects on them.” They also got paper dolls and games like Checkers, Pick-Up Sticks, and Jacks.

“Every year we waited for that box,” she said. “It made such an impression.”

The deprivation of her childhood years left a deep impression. “It made me who I am today,” she said. “I really feel for the underdog.”

Happily, as the years went on, her family’s situation improved greatly. Sperandio taught school, mainly 7th grade, for more than 30 years. As for her mother, “The first half of my mother’s life was hell, and the second half was absolutely wonderful,” Sperandio said. “She was surrounded by family. She saw her grandchildren grow up.” And she became an artist, a passion she’d long wanted to indulge.

When Sperandio donated to Globe Santa this year, it was in memory of her beloved mother, Mary Boyajian, who died at the age of 96.” Sperandio sent a note accompanying her donation, saying: “When that package arrived each Xmas, it brought such joy to us. Thank you!”
