Last year, Nigerian artist Burna Boy made history when he became the first African artist to sell out TD Garden. “Boston is now a part of me, Boston is now my home,” he announced at his concert on March 2, 2024, which Boston City Council declared “Burna Boy Day” throughout the city.

Now, amid his ongoing “No Sign of Weakness” tour, it’s apparent that those strong ties to Boston haven’t faded.

Burna Boy — born Damini Ebunoluwa Ogulu — made a surprise visit to the Boston Arts Academy on Tuesday, one day before his next show at TD Garden.

“If you don’t know, I’m from Boston now, because Boston is the first place to show me the kind of love that I have never seen from any city,” Burna Boy said to the crowd of over 100 students, most of whom were seniors. “I intend to give that love back 100-fold.”

Burna Boy briefly addressed the students, and announced that he planned to sponsor BAA’s community bodega, a free, donation-based store within BAA that launched in November as a way to manage food insecurity among students. This is not Burna Boy’s only initiative to fight food insecurity; he is also a partner with Reach Every Available Communal Household (R.E.A.C.H.) Nigeria, a nonprofit that distributes food and hygiene products to vulnerable populations in Burna Boy’s home country.

“Talent is evenly distributed, but opportunity is not,” he told the crowd at BAA. “So I’ve taken it upon myself to, you know, do as much as I can to make sure we all get to where we need to be.”

“It’s important for students not to feel insecure asking for help,” said Edily Perez, 17, a senior at BAA and president of BAA’s student government. She and BAA’s student government facilitated the opening of the bodega.

Perez called herself a huge fan of Burna Boy’s music. As a 13-time Grammy nominee, and one-time Grammy winner for his 2020 album “Twice As Tall,” Burna Boy is one of the most globally-recognized artists from Nigeria. His most recent album, “No Sign of Weakness,” and his song “Love” have been nominated at the 2026 Grammy Awards.

“With an international star’s support, people might feel comfortable asking for what they need,” Perez said.

Burna Boy also gave students 20 free tickets to his TD Garden show, took pictures with BAA staff and students, and restocked some items in the bodega.

Roxbury-based DJ duo SuperSmashBroz and Boston City Council president Ruthzee Louijeune facilitated the school visit.

“Burna Boy means a lot to the Nigerian community — and the Black community — in Boston,” said Louijeune. She will attend Wednesday’s concert, and noted that it will be her fourth time seeing Burna Boy perform.

According to Louijeune, Massachusetts has one of the largest Nigerian populations in the country, and the UMass Donahue Institute estimates that there are approximately 14,300 people from Nigeria living in the state.

But Burna Boy and his music represents more than just one country, Louijeune said.

“There is a diverse Black population at [Burna Boy’s] concerts,” she said. Louijeune recalled fans touting flags from Nigeria, Ghana, Haiti, and more at Burna Boy’s 2024 Boston concert, noting how the crowd felt unified by African heritage and Burna Boy’s music.

“Everyone who has stepped foot in the CASH has seen and felt how well we play the cards we are dealt,” Miller told the committee, referring to the school by its nickname. “We do not lose because of our efforts. We lose because you stacked the decks for us.”

The demonstration came just over two weeks after Mayor Michelle Wu and Superintendent Mary Skipper announced the latest round of closures and reconfigurations of school buildings. The proposal called for closing the CASH, ACC, and Lee Academy.

The proposal would also cut the high school grades at the Henderson K-12 Inclusion School, converting it into a pre-kindergarten through eighth-grade school. The seventh and eighth grades would be eliminated from the Tobin Elementary School.

The closures and reconfigurations would be in place by the 2027-2028 school year.

The plan also called for the William E. Russell School, a pre-K through Grade 5 building, to add a sixth grade starting in fall 2026.

“We will ensure that every student affected by this set of recommendations has a pathway to a high-quality seat at a welcoming school community,” the statement said.

BPS’s building footprint is too large for the number of students enrolled in the district. Enrollment as of Oct. 15 was 46,824, a steep drop from the 53,000 students attending BPS in 2019.

And while new migrant students helped level off the decline in recent years, with about 48,000 attending schools last year, enrollment has fallen further amid federal ICE crackdowns.

The district has a long-term facilities plan that includes a goal of shuttering nearly a fifth of BPS school buildings by 2030. BPS currently operates 109 schools, down from 114 in 2023-2024.

An earlier round of closures — approved by the School Committee in March — will reduce the total number of BPS facilities to 104. The goal is to reach around 95 by 2030, according to the district.

That facility plan serves as the district’s roadmap to 2030 by matching the number of schools in BPS to enrollment projections, the district said in its statement.

“Each of these recommendations aligns with our vision of building a district where all our school facilities are delivering the high-quality educational experience our families and students expect and deserve,” the district said.

More than three years since her daughter was killed in a Dorchester triple shooting, Deniquaa Ellison is doing everything she can to prevent the case from going cold.

A young mom, business owner and singer, Quaaneiruh Goodwyn, 24, was helping her friends film a music video when gunfire broke out. No arrests have been made in the October 2022 shooting.

At a breakfast Thursday morning in Dorchester to honor the families of local homicide victims, Ellison said she wants to keep her daughter’s memory alive — in hopes of someday getting justice.

Despite the statistics placing Boston among the safest major cities, the roomful of grieving families was a stark reminder that the problem hasn’t gone away. Dozens of people attended the ceremony, where speakers commended a range of local programs and services aimed at reducing gun violence and supporting victims.

“There shouldn’t be this many people,” Ellison said. “It’s still happening. Where is the prevention?”

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said his office organizes the annual gathering to recognize the unimaginable grief experienced by homicide survivors and highlight their ongoing efforts to promote peace. It takes place during Survivors of Homicide Victims Awareness Month, a nationwide initiative to educate the public and appeal to policymakers and grieving families.

Hayden said the message remains as important as ever amid the city’s relative peace.

“When you truly believe that one homicide is one too many, when you say that because you mean it, when you say that because you’ve experienced it, the numbers just don’t seem to matter,” he told the crowd.

Nonetheless, he said in an interview after the event, “We should be proud of where we are.”

Ellison wore a pin featuring her daughter’s name and photo. As organizers read off the names of homicide victims, Ellison filmed the ceremony on her phone. After hearing her daughter’s name, she ended the recording, bowed her head, and wiped away tears.

Denella James Clark, whose only brother was shot and killed in 1989, said that even decades later, the pain still sometimes feels fresh.

“It never goes away,” she said, recalling how her father fell to his knees upon hearing the news. “I often wonder what my life would be like if my brother was still here.”

The shooting took place not far from her family’s Mattapan house. Clark said her mother never moved — just in case her son’s killer ever decided to come apologize.

“Well, that apology never came. But we as a family forgave in our own hearts,” she said. “Carrying that pain is just too much to bear.”

Clark, the CEO of the Boston Arts Academy Foundation, said she pursued a career in the nonprofit sector because she wanted to do something positive for her community. She’s working on a campaign to raise money for the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, which supports families and communities impacted by violence. The organization is planning to build a new headquarters in Dorchester.

The ceremony concluded with a song by Janet Connors, whose son, Joel Turner, was stabbed to death in 2001.

“We did not come here alone; we carried our ancestors in our bones,” she sang, her voice filling the banquet hall. “We did not come here alone; we carried beloveds in our souls.

“We carried each other in our hearts.”

MBTA officials said investigators are interviewing an Orange Line train operator after a man was injured when he stepped off a train that had stopped just outside the Roxbury Crossing station on Wednesday.

Train doors opened on the platform side even though the train had not fully reached the station around 3:45 p.m., the MBTA said. The train did not move while the doors were open, the agency said.

Officials said they are investigating what caused the door to open but have ruled out an issue with the train itself or a mechanical problem. It is not clear why the train stopped short.

Two people got off the train as it sat in place, the MBTA said. That section of track is outdoors.

An MBTA spokesperson said they did not fall out but exited on their own.

One man was taken to a local hospital with minor injuries, officials said.

“The train door opens and an adult male intentionally steps/jumps off the train,” said Richard Sullivan, superintendent of the MBTA Transit Police.

The second person who got off the train was not injured, according to the MBTA.

One passenger, Dioni Acosta, 14, said he saw the man on the ground lying “motionless.” He did not see him get off the train.

The man was not trapped beneath the train and did not require a technical rescue, Sullivan said.

According to a Globe reporter who was on the train, it was stopped for about an hour before proceeding to Roxbury Crossing, where the remaining passengers got off. The train was then sent to Wellington Yard for inspection, the MBTA said.

The Globe reporter estimated the drop from the doors to the ground was about five feet.

Orange Line service was paused during the incident. Trains were back in service by about 5:15 p.m., according to an MBTA alert.

I started watching because I wanted in on the joke. So I clicked on a Hallmark Christmas movie, and sure enough the most formulaic, sappy, saccharine story I’d ever seen played before my eyes for one hour and 24 minutes. I clicked on another one. Then another one, all trying to figure out the strange feeling coming over me. Was it ... satisfaction?

That was two Christmases ago. For a while, I pretended it was a joke, my Hallmark-ness, but I wasn’t fooling anyone. So this year, I found myself becoming so excited for Christmas that I had to install a brake, which was: no Hallmark movies until after Thanksgiving.

Which is now, and I’m frankly out of control. On Black Friday, I immediately signed up for the new Hallmark-Plus streaming channel and entered the predictable-feelings factory that always ends with the main characters sharing a kiss.

Soon, I was deep in subreddits trying to find the best ones from the past, parsing the various genres, where I discovered Hallmark movie factions. Was I a time-travel romance kinda guy? Or a royal princess who finds Prince Charming in flannel in a small town kinda guy? Or the career woman who finds magic and romance in a small town after she comes to shut down/write about/redevelop the local Christmas fair/Christmas tree farm/Christmas whatever kinda guy? I think the latter, but really all of them.

It’s hard to keep up, because they drop a new one every day in December, perhaps every minute. Just this week, I’ve plowed through “Christmas Land” and “Christmas Getaway,” which were aaaamazing, as well as “Melt My Heart This Christmas,” which I thought was just so-so until everyone got all nice and kissy at the end and I clapped.

Then came the nostalgia hit of “A 90’s Christmas,” where an overworked, lonely big city lawyer gets transported back to her childhood home, and, wouldn’t you know it, realizes she should have married the guy next door; and the adorable “Holiday Touchdown: A Bills Love Story,” because nothing is more adorable than Bills fans.

Kurt Vonnegut said that a good story should have an ending that is both surprising and yet inevitable. Hallmark movies skip the surprise; you’re just waiting for the inevitable, which is that the holiday festival will be saved, the couple will fall in love, and it will be the best Christmas ever.

Sure, the characters are caricatures. The women wake up in perfect makeup and manage to stay trim despite subsisting on fresh-baked cookies and hot chocolate. The men wear flannel and drive vintage pickups and, oh, hey miss, do you need help with that flat tire? Why yes, I am the owner of the hardware store that you’ve come to foreclose on, but that’s no matter, I’ve got a wrench in the truck next to my dog and we’ll get you back on your way.

It feels like this is the part where I’m supposed to say it’s indefensible to watch such cookie-cutter shlock when there are so many other things I could be doing with my time, so many truly great films I could be enjoying. But those require an effort that a Hallmark movie does not. I can pop one on at night when I’m winding down, that window when I would typically tell myself I’m going to read a book but instead end up doom-scrolling on my phone, and that soft Hallmark nostalgia will lull me into feeling all is right, that everything I need already surrounds me, and a princess could suddenly appear from Zelarnia (not a real place, I checked, but definitely the real plot of “A Royal Montana Christmas,” which I also just watched) to change everything in one hour and 24 minutes.

And yes, when I recently mentioned to my wife that I wanted to get a sherpa-lined coat, she thought she was calling me out when she accused me of wanting to look like a Hallmark guy. Wanting to? No, honey, I am a Hallmark guy.

Now let me help you with that flat tire. By calling AAA.

FIFA on Saturday detailed the day, time, and place of every group-stage match-up for next year’s World Cup.

The announcement capped off an exciting two days of news for Greater Boston’s soccer fanatics. FIFA on Friday bundled competing nations into 12 groups of four, finalizing which countries will compete to advance to the elimination rounds (a few World Cup slots have yet to be filled). Some fans filed into local pubs to watch the procession live.

The World Cup will unfold across three countries over the course of about a month next summer.

Seven games will be played in Boston, one of 16 cities hosting matches. (To be precise, teams will play at Gillette Stadium — rechristened “Boston Stadium” — in Foxborough.)

Besides Haiti, Ghana, England, Scotland, Morocco, Norway, France, and either Iraq, Bolivia, or Suriname will compete in group-stage games at Gillette. The venue will also host two knockout games.

For soccer’s heavyweights — the likes of Spain, Brazil, Germany, and others — the World Cup is a quadrennial chance for the world’s elite players to showcase their brilliance and jostle for the sport’s ultimate prize. It’s also a source of immense national pride for the World Cup’s infrequent attendees, for soccer-obsessed countries rarely associated with the highest echelons of the game.

Two such countries — Haiti and Cape Verde — have sizable and vibrant diasporas in the Bay State. Haiti has participated in the World Cup only once before, in 1974. Next year’s World Cup will be Cape Verde’s first.

“We have been dreaming of being in this World Cup for a long, long, long time,” said Hudson Julsaint, who said he’d immigrated to Boston from Haiti in 2023. “It’s a really, really big deal for Haitian people.”

Manny Coleta, a Cape Verdean immigrant who watched the group unveiling at a Dorchester bar Friday, says he still hasn’t fully grasped the fact that his home country will be competing among the world’s best.

“It hasn’t sunk in yet,” he said. “Maybe after I watch the first game I’ll actually believe it.”

Cape Verde, grouped together with Uruguay, Saudi Arabia, and world number one Spain, will play its group-stage games in Atlanta, Miami, and Houston.

“It doesn’t really matter whether we play here, Canada, or Mexico,” he said, a scarf with Cape Verdean colors draped over his shoulders. “I’m going to catch at least one game live.”

For many, the pride and exaltation of a World Cup appearance offer an uplift that extends well beyond the realms of the sport.

Such is the case for many Haitians, Guillaume, the Hyde Park restaurant owner, said.

“We have been through so much,” she said — vicious gang wars and cataclysmic health crises at home, and demonization in the places they’ve sought refuge.

Julsaint hopes the World Cup will help other nations form a richer, more human picture of his home.

“It’s a good opportunity to make people know better about our culture,” he said. “They’re gonna say, ‘Where is this country?’ or, if they know it, ‘Let me try to learn what they have.’”

Many Haitians, Guillaume and Julsaint observe, have, over the years, developed a fondness for other national teams.

“The Haitians love the Brazilians,” Guillaume said. Julsaint says he’s followed Argentina since childhood, and will be rooting for the defending world champions — as well as Haiti — next year.

Other Bostonians born and raised in the States are also overcome with anticipation.

“I’m rooting for the US,” said Steve Cherenfant, a Massachusetts native. “I don’t think they’ll go that far, but it’s the opportunity to prove the doubters wrong.”

Cherenfant, sporting a black, sheen-finished US Soccer jacket and a scarf printed with the gold World Cup trophy, sat with friends at The Phoenix Landing, a Cambridge bar and popular gathering spot for soccer junkies.

The US national team will face off against Paraguay, Australia, and either Turkey, Romania, Kosovo, or Slovakia in the group stage. The Americans will play their first (and perhaps only) matches of the competition in Los Angeles and Seattle.

The United States finished third in the 1930 World Cup — the inaugural tournament, hosted in Uruguay — but hasn’t advanced past the quarterfinals since.

Whether he’ll attend a match depends on ticket prices, said Cherenfant, though he plans to be part of the moment in some way.

“If you want to meet people who are supporters, come to a bar for a big game,” he said. “You’ll find somebody, make connections, and you can be friends for a long time.”

It’s market intelligence.

For years, companies treated inclusion as a moral gesture instead of an economic reality. They argued about ideology while ignoring the most important force shaping their future: the customer. But diversity, equity, and inclusion never needed rescuing — it needed better analytics.

Business runs on metrics — profits, market share, viewership. And for years, many companies refused to measure the economic power of Black and brown consumers, even as we shaped the very markets they relied on. In a 2021 McKinsey Podcast, McKinsey partner Shelley Stewart III stated that businesses were missing out on a $300 billion market. Outside of Black Enterprise magazine, few bothered to count our dollars or track our influence with the rigor applied elsewhere.

Contrast that with the blockbuster data fueling the rise of women’s sports — sold-out stadiums, soaring ratings, and investment flowing into everything from women’s rugby to softball and baseball. Metrics drove belief. Metrics drove investment. Metrics are driving change.

The same economic power has always existed in Black and brown communities, but stereotypes kept companies from seeing it. Tiger Woods was treated as an anomaly. And despite Serena Williams’s undeniable dominance, her white counterparts long earned more endorsements and higher appearance fees. The star power and profitability of Black and brown audiences were were obvious; the industry simply refused to acknowledge them.

The awakening started after the police killing of George Floyd in 2020. From Misty Copeland redefining ballet to Coco Gauff electrifying tennis to Black snowboarder Zeb Powell winning gold at the 2020 X Games, companies are no longer guessing. They’re following the culture, the viewership, and the purchasing power of Black and brown communities.

I have lived the shift from an industry that once struggled to imagine me — or people who look like me — as part of their customer base. I am a proud member of the National Brotherhood of Snowsports, a 50-year-old movement that rewrote who belongs on the mountain. My first ski outfit was a canary yellow one-piece Bogner — bought when the brand’s aspirational image was European, white, and exclusive. Yet there we were: thousands of Black skiers nationwide, not asking permission to participate but expanding the market and looking good.

Timberland tells a similar story. Its boots became iconic in cities with large Black populations in the early 1990s, long before the company understood why. Biggie, Nas, Tupac, and the Wu-Tang Clan took them far from New England construction sites. Only later did Timberland follow the culture that had already embraced them.

Nike grasped the economic potential of Black and brown communities early. It built an empire around Black athletic excellence — from Michael Jordan to Williams to LeBron James — and didn’t flinch in backing Colin Kaepernick, who took a knee in 2016 to protest police brutality. Critics warned Nike to stay out of politics; Nike simply followed the market. Culture drives consumption, and culture has long been led by Black and brown consumers.

My friend Ross captured it perfectly, telling me: “Black folks don’t wait for a sale. Status is having it first.”

That is not vanity. That is predictable market behavior — the kind companies pay consultants millions to understand.

Boston has its own version of this evolution. In 2016, New Balance faced backlash after its vice president of public affairs came out in support of Donald Trump in the presidential election, and a neo-Nazi website called New Balance sneakers “the official shoes of white people.” Many of us stopped buying. The business felt out of step with the city we live in.

Fast forward eight years. New Balance now sponsors Gauff — brilliant, bold, beloved — whose presence electrifies every tennis court she touches. It sponsors Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone, an Olympic track and field marvel. It has invested in Historically Black Colleges and Universities. It has expanded its designs. And now it is supporting Sportsmen’s Tennis, a community where Boston’s athletic, cultural, and demographic future is already vibrant and visible.

New Balance didn’t change its politics. It changed its marketing to be in sync with the marketplace, because inclusion is simply the work of seeing, engaging, and honoring all the customers who shape your future.

This is not a diversity initiative. This is a business pivot — toward the consumers who shape the culture and drive the market.

The company I stopped buying from is not the company I see today. It’s following the market. It’s following the money. And it’s smart to do so.

Customers first. Profit follows. Inclusion isn’t charity. It’s reality.

Companies can rebrand DEI, reorganize it, or declare it over. It doesn’t matter. The sneaker companies know who is buying. The apparel companies know who sets the trends. The entertainment companies know who creates cultural gravity.

There’s no need to rescue DEI. It’s alive and well in the customers who are buying products. The market has already moved, and the companies that follow their consumers, not the politics, will be the ones that win.

Hopping back into the director’s chair for the first time in 15 years, Brooks wanted to take viewers to an era when we “weren’t divisive,” according to the 85-year-old mastermind behind hits like “The Mary Tyler Moore Show,” “The Simpsons,” “Terms of Endearment,” and more, seeing the 2008 political landscape as a time before “we lost our way about being together as a people.”

“To me, the most powerful thing the picture says is in the first 30 seconds: we still liked each other,” said Brooks, referencing the film’s opening narration by Julie Kavner, with the voice of Marge Simpson appearing as Ella’s feisty secretary.

Explaining that, in his view, there was nothing to get out of naming the film’s setting outright as any particular state, Brooks just wanted to showcase the “heartland” of America — which he found in Rhode Island.

While finding filming locations for “Ella McCay” seemed like easy enough lifts, casting the right person to play the main role was a bit more difficult, according to Brooks.

The Oscar and Emmy winner wanted to channel the fast-paced, “screwball comedy energy” of films that Katharine Hepburn and Audrey Hepburn would star in, but “combine that with enough real-life crap that we all have to go through to make it real and to make it relatable.” After an exhaustive search for an actress, Brooks admitted he was a bit worn down. That was, until Mackey auditioned, where she impressed him with her take on a monologue scene.

“I almost didn’t believe my eyes, because I was beaten down a little from looking [for the right actress]‚” said Brooks, who also praised Mackey’s ability to play the character’s younger self in flashback scenes. “People think we did something with technology or something. It’s all acting.”

Mackey, who’s perhaps best known for her four seasons of work as teen troublemaker Maeve Wiley on “Sex Education” and will soon reteam with “Barbie” director Greta Gerwig in next year’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” calls landing the role of Ella “a big step” and cherishes the feeling she got while making a comedy icon like Brooks laugh during her audition.

“To be championed by someone like that, and to be able to make him laugh ... like, I love this feeling. I want to do this again all the time,” said Mackey. “It was quite addicting.”

The actress praised Brooks for his continued enthusiasm for the craft and for being so open to collaboration.

“I feel like we were really each other’s buddies,” said Mackey.

“He’s still so proactive and so buoyant and so curious and has such incredible experience that I had everything to learn,” she added. “But I really felt like we were learning from each other, and that we both were in this thing together.”

“Ella McCay” has plenty of laughs to go around, with Dorchester native and “The Bear” star Ayo Edebiri making a brief appearance as the love interest of Ella’s brother Casey (Spike Fearn). Brooks noted that Edebiri “was one of the first ones cast” and hailed the actress for her improv comedy talents.

“She’s a dream and she trusts her impulses, and her impulses are great,” said Brooks.

Curtis also showcases her comedic skills as Ella’s aunt, with their relationship serving as the heart of the film. The veteran actress proved to be just as caring and supportive off set when Mackey briefly fell ill during shooting.

“When she found out, 15 minutes later, there was a basket on my front door with hair things for me, broth and graham crackers and a book, and I cried,” explained Mackey. “That’s so wonderful, when you’re far away from your family and you’re on your own ... to have someone like that who’s able to bring you a bit of comfort and reassurance in a moment, is so lovely.”

For Brooks, even after all these years, he still loves working with actors and enjoys seeing the magic of a scene come together. But he’s not resting on his laurels and knows just how hard it is to get a movie made, especially now.

“There’s no high horse here,” said Brooks. “It’s always a struggle. It’s always human beings coming together and trying to make it work. ... Everybody sweats and gets dirty and tries to do the damn job.”

Mackey said making “Ella McCay” was “really a labor of love” for Brooks, praising him for fighting to get it made and seeing his vision through with the same passion that Ella brings in the film.

“[Ella is] someone who works consistently, achieves her goals with some struggle, but keeps going,” said Mackey. “That’s all we can do, is keep going.”

A small religious college on the border of Jamaica Plain and Brookline is moving toward selling a portion of its campus as conservation land.

The board of directors of the Hellenic College Holy Cross Greek Orthodox School of Theology on Tuesday voted to explore the sale of up to 25 acres of its campus overlooking Jamaica Pond to The Lyme Timber Co., a New Hampshire real estate investment management company that owns 1.3 million acres of forestland across the country.

The property under consideration is mostly a wooded area called Hellenic Hill. Lyme Timber would pay up to $30 million, or $1.2 million per acre, for the property, college president Demetrios S. Katos said in a recent letter to faculty, staff, and students. That money would then be invested into the college’s endowment, generating up to $1.2 million per year as “a stable recurring revenue for scholarships, faculty support, facility upgrades, and operational sustainability,” Katos said.

The potential sale follows financial challenges at the Greek Orthodox school. Its state accrediting agency placed the college on a two-year probation from 2019 to 2021.

“This proposal is the result of years of deliberate study and exploration of all feasible options, including sales to developers, joint ventures, and leases,” Katos wrote. “Conservation emerged as the optimal choice, offering alignment with our values, improvement to the student experience, and a strengthening of HCHC.”

Lyme Timber declined to comment prior to the vote.

If the board ultimately agrees to a deal, the goal is to eventually sell the property to local conservation organization The Trustees of Reservations, which would partner with the Emerald Necklace Conservancy to steward the land. The groups would “create the vision and plan for the property,” Katos said, and the Trustees would eventually steward the land as part of a broader collection of protected property around Jamaica Pond.

That process would incorporate feedback from both outside partners and community members, Katos said. It would, meanwhile, be “contingent upon raising the necessary funds to make this a reality” and “may take up to five years.”

In a joint statement, the Trustees and Emerald Necklace Conservancy said Lyme Timber and Hellenic College are actively outlining the “several steps needed to acquire the property for conservation with private philanthropic support.” Lyme Timber and the Trustees have previously partnered on land conservation in Massachusetts, most recently with 2,000 acres of forest in Pelham and Belchertown.

“This wooded drumlin that overlooks Jamaica Pond has long been on the City of Boston’s Lands of Interest list for preservation,” the groups said. “This potential acquisition would forever protect an important part of the historic Emerald Necklace.”

Hellenic is the latest example of small colleges and universities in Greater Boston leveraging their real estate to financially support school operations. In 2023, Simmons University in Boston’s Fenway neighborhood signed a 99-year ground lease with Swedish development giant Skanska for a chunk of its campus, while the board and building authority of the University of Massachusetts in 2019 agreed to a $235 million ground lease for the former Bayside Expo Center site in Dorchester.

Katos said Hellenic had considered developing the forested area but chose conservation instead after considering the myriad “zoning, regulatory, and community hurdles that would take years to address and may have never been resolved.” Preserving the property will instead protect Hellenic’s core campus and operations as an Orthodox Christian college, seminary, and graduate school of theology.

He stressed that Tuesday’s vote is nonbinding, and the board hasn’t yet reached a final decision.

“If realized, it would serve as the cornerstone of a transformational plan that aims to fortify our institution’s future,” Katos said. “We remain focused on outcomes that honor our heritage and secure our legacy.”

“There are so few voices that seem to come out and say ‘no’ to this administration,” Josoma, 70, said Tuesday in an interview at St. Susanna’s rectory. “I don’t get that. I don’t understand that.”

Outside the church’s doors, the nativity scene does not include the centerpiece figures of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph. In the empty space they ordinarily occupy are these words: ‘’ICE WAS HERE.“

“The Holy Family,” the sign’s text continues, “is safe in the sanctuary of our church.” A phone number to report activity by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents is listed at the bottom of the sign.

The Archdiocese of Boston has asked that the sign be removed because of its “divisive political messaging,” according to a statement issued last week by spokesman Terrence Donilon.

But in Josoma’s view, “any divisiveness is a reflection of our polarized society, much of which originates with the changing, unjust policies and laws of the current US administration,” the pastor said at a news conference Monday.

Josoma said he is waiting for an opportunity to discuss the issue with Archbishop Richard Henning.

In the meantime, disparaging calls and emails, many of which Josoma described as “disturbing,” are being received at the rectory and on his personal phone, the pastor said. But if he is rattled, Josoma didn’t show any signs of it Tuesday.

Dressed in a sweater and smiling broadly, Josoma recalled his upbringing in a two-family home in Brighton and how he found role models among the priests in St. Columbkille’s Parish. As a seminarian in 1976, he said, Josoma cycled across the country with a fellow student.

Along the way, “I realized anyone can be a priest, just like anyone can run a marathon. But I said to myself, ‘I want to be a good priest,’ ” Josoma said. “If it’s meant to be, it’s meant to be. Go and find out.”

The liberalizing reforms of the Second Vatican Council for the Catholic Church in the 1960s also played a key role in his path toward the priesthood, Josoma said.

Calling attention to the plight of fearful immigrants is an organic outgrowth of his mission, Josoma said. Moments before he spoke with the Globe, the pastor wrapped up a meeting about a refugee Ukrainian family that will arrive in the area this week and needs support.

The family will be the latest of many helped by St. Susanna’s and other local churches as part of an interfaith effort in Dedham.

“It’s always about compassion,” said Josoma, who decided on the nativity display after consulting with the Parish Council.

In 2017, he used a wall of the nativity scene to decry gun violence by listing locations of mass shootings and the numbers of deaths at each. Killings at Newtown, Conn.; Virginia Tech University; San Bernardino, Calif.; and the Washington Navy Yard were among them.

“This can’t be a way of life,“ he said of his motivation for the display.

The following year, he placed a cage around the infant Jesus to call attention to the detention and separation of migrant children from their families at the southern border.

“How do you feel when they put human beings in a cage?” Josoma said of the message. “I just don’t think that people like to see that acknowledgment. It’s easier to deny a reality.”

Outside the rectory Tuesday, parishioners stopped by to view the crèche in subfreezing temperatures. The parish attracts worshipers from dozens of ZIP codes, Josoma said, adding with a laugh that “we’re like the Island of Misfit Toys.”

As parishioners from Needham, Watertown, and West Roxbury dropped by, all expressed support for Josoma’s ministry.

“He’s a wonderful pastor,” said Pat Ferrone, a local leader of the Pax Christi peace movement. “He listens to everyone. He participates in everything. You can say what you need to say.”

Jeannie Connerney recalled Josoma’s kindness after her mother died in January. The pastor organized the funeral, and continues to keep in touch with her father, who is in his 90s.

Concerning the crèche, “this in my mind is what a parish should be doing,” she added.

Phil Mandeville, a parishioner and friend of Josoma’s, said the display “is not a stunt,” adding the figurines are not sacred artifacts, in any event.

“We feel compelled to make this statement. How can you sit back?” Mandeville said.

When Josoma preaches, Mandeville said, he usually ends his sermons with a challenge. One frequent theme, he said, is, “How can you remain quiet when you see people suffering?”

To Josoma, being a good priest itself comes with a mix of challenges. Among them, he said, are these: “Be true to your vocation. Be true to the Gospel. The call, I think, is from God.”

Prosecutors said Fernandes Anderson arranged the kickback when she was struggling financially, missing rent and car payments, and facing bank overdraft fees and a $5,000 fine from the state Ethics Commission for previously hiring relatives to her council staff.

Fernandes Anderson, a 46-year-old Democrat who came to the US From Cape Verde at age 10, was once a rising star in city politics. She made political history in 2021 on multiple fronts. She was the first Muslim, the first formerly undocumented immigrant, and the first African immigrant to serve on the city’s legislative body. On the council, she represented District Seven, which covers neighborhoods including Roxbury, Dorchester, the South End, and Fenway.

Her political rise came with a compelling backstory, punctuated by stints of homelessness, an eviction as a teenager, racism at school, and immigration complications.

But her political career came crashing down last year when the FBI arrested her at her Dorchester home.

She attended her final council meeting in June, and officially resigned in July of this year.

On Monday night, she spoke at an event hosted by New Beginnings Reentry Services at the Bruce C. Bolling Municipal Building. Among the crowd were local luminaries including former Boston mayoral candidate Josh Kraft, City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, and Fernandes Anderson’s elected successor, the Rev. Miniard Culpepper.

Known for calling out racism on the City Council floor during the days as a lawmaker, Fernandes Anderson on Monday railed against the perpetuation of “intentional, systemic oppression.”

“We think about how do we defend ourselves?” she said. “We never think of the offensive plan, and we’re never ready. We’re always chasing the carrot.”

She also described her political style.

“To every battle, you need a barbarian and you need a diplomat,” she said. “And I’m no diplomat.”

She continued, “I just don’t fit in that stage, in that place where we still believe in politics and we still say ‘We should lobby the politicians’ or ‘We should go to Mayor [Michelle] Wu and tell her to move money.’ Well, there isn’t enough money, when you do the math.”

She lamented that too many people in Boston are beholden to a “government that holds the purse.” She described the city as a place “where no one dares to speak, where pretty politics take place.”

“No one will open their mouth and say ‘This is [expletive]. This is not working,’” she said.

The crowd applauded.

“If you have a contract with the city, you’re not going to say anything, if you work for the city, you’re not going to say anything,” she said. “If you are cousin, wife, son, whatever of somebody that works for the city you’re not going to say anything.”

Black people, said Fernandes Anderson, need to organize.

“We’ve just been so inundated by our stressors, by our headaches, by our problems, that we can’t organize. And then we wonder why they won’t listen,” she said.

Fernandes Anderson featured on a panel that included others who were formerly locked up, including Sean K. Ellis, who served 22 years in prison before his murder conviction was overturned because of police and prosecutorial misconduct.

The discussion was emceed by Rickey “FuQuan” McGee, who was released in October from prison after prosecutors declared he did not receive a fair trial for a 1997 murder.

During the discussion, Fernandes Anderson appeared to allude to her recent legal troubles.

“I’m very grateful for my journey,” she said. “There ain’t no shame in this game,” meaning there’s no shame in taking accountability.

She added, “It’s a book some day.”

Those dual actions shook both Somali communities around the United States and those who’ve tracked Trump’s history of embracing xenophobic commentary.

Trump, they said, has already adopted a mass deportation agenda, pursued a more autocratic approach to governance, and surrounded himself with fewer people willing to challenge him. To then cast an entire ethnic group as “garbage” is “just beyond the pale,” said Thomas Whalen, a Boston University professor and presidential historian.

“This is a whole new ball game,” Whalen said. He added that Trump is “sounding more authoritarian,” the very type of freedom-limiting governance that many immigrants fled in moving to the United States.

“And this plays into it,” Whalen said, “this extremist rhetoric, because all authoritarian types want scapegoats. People of color are so vulnerable, he can say, ‘This is why we have a bad economy, it’s them.’ That, to me, is concerning — and a little frightening.”

The Trump administration has defended the president’s remarks, pointing to reports about social services fraud rooted in parts of Minnesota’s Somali community, which has spurred dozens of convictions. The state is home to roughly 80,000 people of Somali descent; most of those residents are US citizens.

“President Trump is absolutely right to highlight the problems caused by the radical Somali migrants,” said Abigail Jackson, a White House spokesperson. “While the media feigns outrage, Americans who have suffered at the hands of these schemes will celebrate the president’s comments and strong support for American citizens.”

Somali immigrants represent only the latest group Trump has criticized while his administration carries out mass immigration raids in Minnesota and beyond. In public and private life, the president has routinely made racist comments and at times adopted prejudiced policies dating to the 1970s, when the federal government sued Trump for discriminating against Black people seeking to rent apartments.

Presidents in the modern era have tended to keep discriminatory remarks behind closed doors, Whalen said, such as Lyndon Johnson using racial slurs in private.

But upon entering the political arena, Trump embraced not being “politically correct,” especially on race, using his first 2015 campaign speech to accuse Mexico of sending criminals and “rapists” to the United States.

After he took office, his first administration attempted to ban travel from several Muslim-majority countries. He at times referred to groups of immigrants as “animals.”

William Roberts, senior vice president for rights and justice at the left-leaning Center for American Progress, said Trump has already shown a “pattern of egregious, outright racist statements.”

But his comments attacking Somalis felt “different and dangerous,” he said, in part because he believes “the rhetoric is coupled with a really authoritarian crackdown across the government.”

“Donald Trump has always said [things] previously under the guise of ‘I’m not going to be politically correct.’ He has always wanted to push the envelope on racism,” Roberts said. “He is feeling free to go as far as he wants to go.”

Trump has directly attacked Omar before. In 2019, he suggested that she and three other Democratic congresswomen of color, including Massachusetts’ Ayanna Pressley, should “go back” to “the totally broken and crime-infested places from which they came.” All four women are American citizens, and all but Omar were born in the United States.

Trump again targeted her last week, saying in his Cabinet meeting that she is a “real terrible person.”

Omar has repeatedly defended Minnesota’s Somali community, telling reporters on Wednesday, “We are not, and I am not, someone to be intimidated, and we are not gonna be scapegoated.”

Pressley has also come to her defense, saying that while Trump’s attacks aren’t new, “they are no less dangerous.”

“This vile hate speech toward women, people of color, and immigrant communities puts lives at risk,” Pressley said in a statement to the Globe.

Trump criticizing immigrants without American citizenship is “a very old pattern” for which “each iteration is worse,” said Jennifer Hochschild, a Harvard University political science professor. But his comments on Somali immigrants appear to be more overt, which she attributed in part to his being term-limited and surrounded by more allies.

During the Cabinet meeting when Trump attacked Somalis, Vice President JD Vance banged on the table in support. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters afterward that Trump’s remarks were an “epic moment.” And Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem later claimed without evidence that half of Minnesota’s immigration visas are fraudulent.

“There were enough people in the room during his first term who he could plausibly expect not to approve of what he was saying, so there may have been a little bit of self-discipline as a consequence of that,” Hochschild said. “Now you’ve got Vance and Noem saying the same stuff.

“There’s a very deep continuity here of real hatred,” she added of Trump, “but there’s an increasing willingness or an increasing capacity to make that explicit verbally.”

She likened Trump’s attacks on Somali people, along with recent comments about immigrants “poisoning the blood of our country,” to those used by Nazi Germany to dehumanize groups of people in the 1930s.

Trump is unlikely to see backlash over his comments from his Republican base, which has long supported his views on race and immigration, public surveys indicate. Fewer Republicans this year than last said they believed there was discrimination against racial and ethnic minority groups, according to Pew Research.

But it’s less clear how Trump’s remarks may affect gains he made among Latino and Black voters during the 2024 election, many of whom said they turned to him for his economic promises.

Whalen, the Boston University professor, said Trump’s Cabinet speech “causes all sorts of problems domestically for the Republican Party, who showed signs in the last presidential election of expanding beyond the white and Southern male base they’ve enjoyed now for several election cycles.”

Democratic elected officials have quickly rallied around the Somali community in places like Minnesota, as Somali residents have responded to the president’s latest attacks with anger and frustration.

Abdirahman Yusuf, director of the Somali Development Center in Roxbury, said in an email the organization is a “non-profit macro-social service provider” that does not engage in national politics. But, he added, “from my experience, Somali people are far from ‘garbage.’”

“Most of those I know are decent, hardworking, law-abiding citizens,” he said, “and permanent legal residents of the United States.”

Which is why when he attends the Boston Music Awards this Wednesday at Big Night Live and hears his name announced as a nominee in the Afro/Caribbean artist category, the moment will feel like its own sort of victory.

“Now, Afrobeats music is a worldwide phenomenon and people are speaking our various languages word for word,” says Echezona, whose most recent album, “Ényì,” includes lyrics in both English and Igbo, one of the most widely-spoken languages in Nigeria. (The album’s title is the Igbo word for “friend.”)

The Afro/Caribbean artist category is one of five additions to this year’s awards ceremony, which honors standout artists and industry professionals from the Greater Boston music community every December. In the last decade, the BMAs have mushroomed to include over a dozen new categories, namely ones that recognize behind-the-scenes industry personnel: managers, talent buyers, journalists, live audio engineers, and lighting technicians, to name a few.

Other new titles for 2025 include honors for local festivals, radio DJs, graphic designers, and music-focused nonprofits (titled the Margaret Stewart Lindsay Music Non-Profit of the Year award). The inclusion of the new Afro/Caribbean category is unique, as it replaces the previous Reggae/Ska category.

Echezona calls the switch “historic,” noting that “I am now among folks who have broken the door down for people in the city to have to say, ‘We need to make room and recognize this whole other music lane taking shape.’”

The shift not only recognizes the growing global influence of genres like Afrobeats, but also refines the category to include acts that are more closely culturally associated with Afro-Caribbean music. That distinction is especially important for category nominees like Roots Alley Collective, a Caribbean group who strive to bring traditional music to communities throughout the diaspora.

Drummer Shaquan Gabriel was born and raised in St. Lucia, and moved to Massachusetts as a teenager, while keyboardist RJ Walters and bassist Christoff Glaude are the first-generation children of immigrants from Barbados and St. Vincent, respectively. Gabriel says that Roots Alley Collective’s shows are a key link to traditional music for folks of Caribbean descent who “were born here [in the US] but don’t really get to have that full effect of being raised in the Caribbean.”

Gabriel also says that the boost in visibility from the BMAs nomination helps the group’s goal of bridging a “generation gap” between Caribbean performers in the region. In Gabriel’s experience, Roots Alley Collective — whose members are in their late 20s and early-to-mid 30s — is the youngest Caribbean music act in the Northeast. Most groups are in their 40s and older, he notes.

“We have to get our generation to support and learn about what we’re doing,” Gabriel says. “We’re trying to really craft that same kind of model that the older guys had — the community coming out to see shows, and buying the records and the vinyls.”

“I think [the nomination] gets everybody more involved in what we’re doing,” Gabriel adds, “and that makes it 10 times more important to us.”

“Failure and success can be measured in different ways,” said Scully, sitting in the back room at McGonagle’s Pub in Dorchester, where he’d performed solo the day before. “The community we built — total success. Trying to tour nationwide and crack that — not a success.”

Over three albums, several live releases, and a slew of singles, Scully’s band grew from regulars at the Bell in Hand to headliners at Leader Bank Pavilion and MGM Music Hall at Fenway. They’ve opened for Jason Aldean, Sam Hunt, Thomas Rhett, and other Nashville stars, and they stepped in as a last-minute replacement for TLC at this year’s Boston Calling.

But they haven’t been able to gain enough traction outside of their hometown.

“We’re a rock band, but we tell pretty ‘country’ stories,” said Scully, a burly, bearded father of three teenagers in a crisp new Notre Dame cap. “I think we sound like what a country band that was born and raised in Boston would sound like.”

The rest of the current version of the band — Jay Tagg and Joe Pantaleo on guitars, Dennis Walsh on bass, and Dan Vassallo on drums — have day jobs and other music projects to focus on. Tagg owns Matt’s Music Center, a guitar shop in Weymouth, where Pantaleo works.

Scully, meanwhile, plans to regroup by performing his solo shows, which are a mix of Dalton songs and covers. Working closely with his wife, Kate, he calls himself a full-time “barroom hustler.”

Last year the band released a cover version of Zach Bryan’s “Oklahoma Smokeshow,” and they’ve covered Eric Church’s “Springsteen,” the Wallflowers’s “One Headlight,” and many more. Scully said he grew up with grandparents who loved “the whole Irish cable-knit sweater” folk scene of the 1960s.

“I could play three hours of Clancy Brothers music at the drop of a hat,” he said. “That was my entry into country music.”

Some of his current bandmates joined the group after attending shows as fans. Walsh said he and Tagg convinced each other to sign on together about a half-dozen years ago.

“Make no mistake — Dalton has put the five of us on stages that we only dreamed of,” Walsh said. (There is no actual “Dalton” — the band’s name comes from Patrick Swayze’s bouncer character in 1989’s “Road House.”)

“It’s weird to have to count how many times we played House of Blues or the Pavilion, places we never thought we’d play once,” he continued. “Walking on the field at Fenway doing the [National] Anthem. So many pinching moments.”

On a phone call, Walsh explained that the band members had been anticipating changes. The younger guys are starting families; Scully’s oldest son is about to head to college.

“We knew coming out of this year that something drastic had to change, and it hadn’t yet,” Walsh said. “Basically, we’ve been running as fast as we can since 2020.”

For Scully, the fact that he felt compelled to put the band on hold doesn’t necessarily mean it’s the end.

“There’s no animosity. I know we have the right guys,” he said. If the right deal came along, “the band’s ready.”

“At the end of the day, you really have to be lucky with certain things rolling your way at the right moment,” Scully said. “We’ve been lucky with the relationships and the community we built, the people we got to make music with. And that’s pretty remarkable.”

ARSHILE GORKY: REDRAWING COMMUNITY AND CONNECTIONS Just open: The Armenian-American artist Arshile Gorky arrived in the United States in 1920 as a teenager, having survived the Armenian genocide in 1915 and then a dark period in Russia where his mother died of starvation. RITUALS FOR REMEMBERING: MARÍA MAGDALENA CAMPOS-PONS AND ANA MENDIETA María Magdalena Campos-Pons and Ana Mendieta never met, which seems odd on many counts: Of similar age, both were exiled dissidents from Cuba living in the United States, making art about the alienation of displacement, often in the elemental language of earth, air, water, and fire. Mendieta, born in 1948 (she died in 1985) was a key member of a cadre of artists in New York who used performance to communicate visceral truths; in her “Silueta Series,” she embedded female forms — and sometimes her own body — in the landscape, emphasizing human connection to something larger than ephemeral political systems. Campos-Pons, born in Cuba in 1959 and now working in Nashville, works with a myriad of materials, from ceramic and clay to video and sound, to conjure deep cultural connection that endures political trauma; her “A Town Portrait,” 1994, now installed at the MFA, evokes the legacies of the colonial sugar industry. The 116-bed building, to be located on the over 10-acre campus of Franciscan Children’s, will house several services beyond inpatient psychiatric care. Those offerings include a partial hospital program and intensive outpatient program, a 14-bedroom acute treatment program, a dental suite, four operating rooms, a pharmacy, outpatient rehabilitation programs, and five outdoor play spaces. The first building is expected to break ground in 2026 and open by 2029, an executive said.

The hospital system will relocate inpatient units from Waltham to Brighton, though medical psychiatric beds will remain in Longwood. In all, the project will nearly double Children’s inpatient psychiatric capacity, hospital officials said.

The Hales’ donation, which includes naming rights to the building, materializes a vision that hospital executives have had for the campus since Children’s announced its acquisition of Franciscan in 2021. This project is only the start.

“We envision, ultimately, over the next 10 to 20 years, continued development of that site,” said Dr. Kevin Churchwell, chief executive of Boston Children’s Hospital. He touted the project as both an expansion of clinical services and a place to teach the next generation of pediatric caregivers and clinicians.

Hospital leaders also envision new research opportunities to develop objective measures of when children are improving or worsening as they grapple with mental illness.

There has been a longstanding shortage of mental health care availability for children, which was exacerbated by the pandemic. Pediatric patients were sometimes spending days to weeks “boarding” in emergency rooms as they waited for an inpatient psychiatric bed to open up. At one point in May 2023, Children’s saw more than 90 children in its emergency room in one day needing psychiatric care.

“That was our pandemic,” Churchwell said.

The hospital and the state have worked to better care for those children, triaging them and sending them to the right kind of care sooner. But still there is a need for more services, hospital officials say.

A state snapshot of surveyed hospitals in November showed there were 48 pediatric patients boarding at hospitals throughout the state. In November 2024, that number ranged from 48 to 71 in weekly reports.

Even as Children’s has worked to improve access to care, Churchwell said the volume of children needing psychiatric support has remained high.

Dr. Stacy Drury, psychiatrist in chief at Boston Children’s, said suicide is the second-leading cause of death in children. And despite increased recognition of psychiatric illness and treatment, she said, there is often a gap of eight to 12 years before parents recognize symptoms in their children and act to get them care.

“Mental health services in Massachusetts are fractured,” Drury said. “This will allow us to have kids go between different intensities of treatment faster without going to ERs.”

“By building a beautiful campus centering mental wellness, it will be one of the most powerful tools we have against stigma,” she added.

Danna Mauch, chief executive of the nonprofit Massachusetts Association for Mental Health, welcomed the news of Children’s investment. She said pediatric psychiatric services see a lot of seasonal fluctuation, which can be hard for smaller institutions to manage. Additionally, the size of Children’s operation could help it retain a talented team of clinicians, whereas other programs have struggled to recruit.

Having a mix of inpatient and outpatient care is also key.

“What they are doing is the right thing, in terms of what we know about kids and families, of their needs, and what we know from research literature about what is optimal,” Mauch said. “And not everyone can pull that off.”

The donation is the latest from the philanthropic couple, who have given regularly to Boston Children’s in particular for years.

In 2018, the Hales announced two donations totaling $100 million to Boston Children’s and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Before that, they also gave $5 million in 2013 to establish the Hale Family Center for Families at the hospital.

In 2022, the couple gave away $1 million a week in surprise donations to nonprofits across the state, including one to Children’s.

All told, inclusive of this recent donation, the couple’s given away $500 million of their wealth, amassed through Rob’s successful Quincy-based company Granite Telecommunications, which manages telecommunication services for large businesses.

In an interview, the couple said that at least a dozen friends reached out during the pandemic, asking the Hales to help connect them with hospital resources for mental health care. As Boston Children’s and Franciscan came together and embarked on a larger project, the couple was keen to get involved.

The Hales, who have three children, are particularly loyal to Children’s. Rob recalled touring the hospital in 2011 and seeing a child the size of two tennis balls in the neonatal intensive care unit. He teared up recalling the visit, and the fact that because of the hospital’s care, the child would survive.

“We thought then, and now, that if you help Children’s Hospital, you’re helping the world,” Rob said. “Like, hey, is it going to help your kid, our kid, some kid in Roxbury, some kids from Western Mass. and everywhere? Yes, which is wonderful. But as you learn more about Children’s Hospital, is it going to help kids from Bangladesh and Bangalore and everywhere between? Yes. So it’s the idea that you can help not just your community, but the whole world.”

The project, and the donation, comes at a perilous time for health care. Looming federal funding cuts will significantly reduce the money the state receives for Medicaid, the government insurer for the poor and disabled, which insures nearly half of all children in Massachusetts.

“We do think that America needs help right now, perhaps more so than ever,” Rob said. “And, yes, hopefully we can catalyze other leaders [to give].”

Simultaneously with pending cuts, the wealth gap in the United States has only grown.

The Hales are aware of their own fortune. Rob ranked 630th on the Forbes list of the wealthiest people, with a net worth of $6 billion. The couple plans to give away the majority of their wealth.

Karen said giving publicly motivates other people to join a fund-raising campaign. The Hale name already adorns the awning of the front of the main Children’s building and is emblazoned throughout the lobby, the Hale building is an entire section of the hospital, and the Hale Family Center for Families offers a place for families to relax between appointments or find hospital resources.

Karen said the Hales receive emails from friends and acquaintances who come into the hospital and see their name, thanking them for their support. As they embarked on the biggest donation they’ve made to any institution, it felt good to give more, they said.

“Helping this institution gives you joy,” Rob said. “When you sit here, you see the kids coming in, and it tugs at your heartstrings. But you see the kids going out, and you know a bigger percentage of them are going to go out because you’re able to help.”

One grandmother wrote that she is raising her 11-year-old grandson on her own. The boy has autism, ADHD, PTSD, trauma, and depression.

“[He] is a loving, outgoing boy who loves school and sports,” she wrote. “I am very proud of [him].”

He lost his mother when he was only 2 years old. He receives Social Security survivor benefits but no disability or child support.

The recent government funding cuts, she wrote, means there are “no longer outside options for our family.” Still, she tries to be positive at this time of year.

“As many others on Christmas Day, my gift to myself is his child[‘s] smile [and] excitement,” she wrote. Being remembered by Globe Santa “is the most precious gift you could give to my family.”

US Census Bureau Data from 2024 found a decline in the number of grandparents living with and caring for their grandchildren in the first part of the 2020s compared to the last part of the 2010s, the Associated Press reported.

Many grandparents have written Globe Santa asking for help for their families over the years — and this year is no different.

“It’s very rarely for positive reasons that grandparents find themselves in this situation,” Susan Kelley, a professor emerita at Georgia State University, told the AP. “Usually, it’s a tragic situation in an adult child’s life, either a death, incarceration or mental health issues which correlate with substance abuse. Many grandparents thrive in that role, but there are still socioeconomic and emotional burdens on the grandparents.”

These burdens include their own health struggles and navigating their own well-being while also looking after grandchildren who may have complex medical issues, other grandparents wrote Globe Santa.

One grandmother wrote that she adopted her now 8-year-old granddaughter “who has a lot of her own health issues.” The granddaughter has recently had to get X-rays and MRIs, in addition to physical therapy twice a week, “for as long as insurance will have her.”

“[My granddaughter] is a happy, smart child who loves music [and] books and dance,” she wrote to Globe Santa.

They live on her disability income. The grandmother had a stroke in 2013 — but is “OK as long as I keep my stress level down,” she wrote.

“With all the above, low-income, health issues with both of us, we are grateful to have what we have,” the letter continued. “Anything Globe Santa can bring is much appreciated for this little girl.”

Another grandmother wrote of her myriad health issues — lupus, COPD, emphysema, a major heart attack — “the list goes on.”

Nevertheless, she is the sole provider for her family, including her 5-year-old grandson whom she has custody of.

To make matters worse, the grandmother had to take a leave of absence from work to care for her grandson whose short life has already been marked by neglect, child abuse, custody “battles” between his parents, and witnessing domestic violence.

Traumatized by these events, he is now in therapy and speech therapy, and she is working to help him get “on the right track of where he should be with speech, potty training, and many other milestones he had not reached yet due to [not] being taught.”

The stress of the bills prevents her from providing the holiday season any grandparent would love to give.

“I’m not asking for much,” she wrote. “Just something to give this little angel a Christmas he deserves after all that he has been through.”

These families will join thousands of others across the state in receiving gifts for the holiday season thanks to those who donate to Globe Santa, allowing them to focus on what matters most — their health and each other.

In a text message prior to the hearing, Hawes wrote, “While claims have been made, they are not supported by facts.”

Hawes’ attorney has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, which will be addressed at the Jan. 7 hearing.

Demay, of Middleborough, Mass., could not be reached for comment, and Nuñez did not return requests for comment. Attorneys for Greenhalgh did not respond to an inquiry from the Globe.

The lawsuit also names Hawes’s real estate attorney, Jonathan Lynch, and the firm that employs him, Percy Law Group, as defendants. Lynch did not return a message seeking comment.

The lawsuit is the latest in a series of controversies that have shrouded the historic home — made famous by “The Conjuring” horror movie franchise — over the past year and a half.

Last year, Nuñez faced allegations of harassment from Hawes, and accusations from former employees who say she owes them money; she allegedly fired one after claiming a spirit told her he was stealing from the business.

In November 2024, the Burrillville Town Council opted not to renew the house’s business license after Nuñez — who bought the 1677 Round Top Road property for about $1.5 million in 2022 — was arrested and charged by local police with allegedly driving a Lexus SUV while intoxicated and leading officers on a chase through town.

The home was headed to foreclosure auction in October of this year, but the event was abruptly canceled after Needham Bank sold the underlying mortgage to YouTuber Elton Castee, through his Summit & Stone LLC, a corporation formed in Rhode Island in September.

Castee, who touts more than 4 million subscribers on his “TFIL” (Traveling to every country in A-Z order) channel on YouTube, along with comedian Matt Rife, purchased the former Connecticut home of paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren earlier this year, with its vast collection of allegedly haunted objects. (Castee’s LLC was named as an “interested party” in the lawsuit. Castee declined to comment when reached by email.)

At the urging of Andrea Perron — whose family was supposedly haunted in the 1970s at the Burrillville home where the Warrens were called in to investigate — Hawes launched a GoFundMe to try to raise money to purchase it at auction.

Hawes has said his effort is not about making a profit, and the goal is to raise as much money as possible to keep costs down for visitors, and to keep the house in the hands of people who want to preserve it, not exploit it.

The GoFundMe has continued despite the sale of the mortgage; Hawes said in an interview in November, “It doesn’t change our path.”

Is it likely that if we held on to the first pick of the 2024 NFL Draft, Drake Maye would have been the pick?

— Sheila McVay, West Roxbury

Tough call. I’d lean toward yes, but you’ve got to keep in mind that a large part of the success or failure of a young quarterback depends on those around him, both personnel and coaching. To that point, it’s a safe bet that we know he would have been very good, but there’s no way of telling how things would have turned out for Maye in Chicago or Washington. (You could argue the growth of Maye and Caleb Williams was stunted in their first seasons because of coaching.) In New England, the coaching staff and personnel around Maye has allowed this season for an organic development that has proven beneficial for all involved.

Why do the Patriots ground and pound in the middle of the line at the goal line? This is far from one of their strengths. What are their strengths? Wheel routes? QB rollouts?

— Edward Hozubin, Northborough

Addressed some of this last week, but it’s worth reiterating that a lot depends on the opponent and defensive scheme, as well as your roster. I’m still a little puzzled as to why there aren’t more jump balls offered to pass catchers such as Hunter Henry, Austin Hooper, and Mack Hollins. Or leaning on Maye’s athleticism with designed rollouts or bootlegs.

In the end, it can come down to a question of efficiency and execution, particularly having all 11 guys on the same page. Over the last couple of weeks, Mike Vrabel and Josh McDaniels have addressed this topic, and I was struck by how they both stressed that execution and precision remain paramount. “Precision is critical — that space is limited,” Vrabel said Monday. “Things happen so much quicker down there.” Regardless of how you do it, it’s something that needs sharpening between now and the playoffs.

Maye’s knack for the long ball is the best I’ve seen in a while. This was one of the few areas Tom Brady did not excel in. How do their numbers compare on passes over 20 yards?

— Bob Granese, Chino Hills, Calif.

Tried to comb through some advanced stats, but there was little definitive information. So I turned to my favorite numbers guy, Aaron Schatz.

“I can tell you Maye, this year, is third with 16.3 yards per pass on passes of 20-plus air yards behind Sam Darnold and Jayden Daniels, and he has a 50 percent completion rate (not including defensive pass-interference calls), which is also second in the league behind Darnold,” said Schatz, who created Football Outsiders and is now the chief analytics officer at FTN Fantasy.

“For Brady, it’s tough to gauge over the breadth of his career, so I decided to look at his peak, which I defined as 2007-12. Obviously, he had plenty of other good seasons, but that’s right at his peak, plus you get two seasons (part of the third) with Randy Moss, who might be the greatest deep-ball receiver ever.

“Clearly, 2007 was Brady’s best season; he had 17.6 yards per pass on passes of 20-plus air yards, and had a completion rate of 44 percent. The numbers for Brady did fall off from 2009-12, eventually bottoming out at 31 percent in 2012. Ultimately, we’re only talking about Maye for one season, so the sample size needs to be taken into consideration.”
