Kouame’s essay, which recounts how she learned to thrive as a low-income student of color “surrounded by classmates whose lives felt worlds apart from mine,” is about overcoming adversity.

That’s a theme the White House has identified as a problem in its campaign against diversity, equity, and inclusion. Over the past year, the federal government has flagged “cues” such as personal essays, along with narratives about “overcoming obstacles” and “diversity statements,” as being potentially unlawful: a stand-in for talking about race.

More than two years have passed since the Supreme Court ended race-conscious affirmative action, and the Trump administration has since demanded colleges submit data proving they don’t consider race in admissions. It has also expanded what it sees as “discriminatory admissions processes” to include considering a student’s sexual orientation, gender identity, ethnicity, nationality, political views, and religious associations.

For Kouame, not writing about her identity felt “impossible,” she said in a Zoom interview, “because the things that I’ve gone through in life make me who I am now.”

Other students are weighing the pros and cons, said Ethan Sawyer, founder of College Essay Guy, which offers one-on-one coaching and free online resources through the admissions process. He added the key is “to step back and take stock” of what colleges are actually looking for. Essentially: “How will you be a valuable, contributing member of the community?”

Navigating the college admissions landscape has never been easy, but for the class of 2030 it’s particularly fraught. Plenty of advisers can be hired for a fee: Private consulting is a $3 billion industry, with parents paying tens and even hundreds of thousands of dollars to give their kids an edge. Community organizations, college-prep programs, and high schools are also on hand to assist students.

There’s no question it’s an uneven playing field, though this year there is one equalizer in the college admissions game: No one really knows what’s coming next.

In 2024, one year post-affirmative action, Black first-year student enrollment plunged at many prestigious colleges, and this fall Harvard enrolled fewer Black and Latino freshmen. Meanwhile, the Crimson reported that Harvard banned alumni interviewers from commenting on an applicant’s race, ethnicity, or national origin in their written evaluations.

College consultant Sara Harberson, in a blog post on her website, warned of a future where students are reduced to test scores and transcripts and admissions staff are replaced by AI.

For now, it’s still a human process with human workarounds. Many colleges and universities encourage applicants to submit video introductions using platforms such as Glimpse. It’s a way for students to talk “more authentically and off the cuff,” said Rachel Rubin, the Brookline-based founder of Spark Admissions, noting that, in some cases, video can convey information about race and ethnicity.

Essay questions nudging students to describe their “lived experience” or their “community” proliferated after the Supreme Court ruling and became known as the Chief Justice Roberts Loophole‚ said Jayson Weingarten, a senior admissions consultant with the Manhattan-based Ivy Coach.

“A lot of students might read [a community prompt] and think, Oh, I’m in the band, I’m the editor of the paper, and I’m going to write about an activity,” he said, but other students “read between the lines of what admissions officers are asking — and they’re going to talk about their race, culture, ethnicity, heritage, socioeconomic status, anything like that.“

Weingarten said that after the flurry of executive orders and other memos targeting DEI earlier this year, “there was widespread speculation that many of America’s top universities would be desperate to avoid the crosshairs of the Trump administration” and abandon such prompts. However, most elite institutions have preserved them, he noted.

“It’s a quiet signal, but it’s an unmistakable act of resistance,” said Weingarten.

Sara Barber-Just, an English teacher and chair of the department at Amherst-Pelham Regional High School, said many of her students are answering a Common App question touching on identity. Their topics range from the strengths of being autistic to the musical influences of their Puerto Rican grandparents to accessing gender-affirming care as a transgender person.

“They write really beautiful essays about the experience of being human,” she said. “No president can stop adolescents from writing about their identity.”

And federal policies can’t stop adults from helping them. This spring the tutoring nonprofit 826 Boston rejected $250,000 in funding rather than comply with President Trump’s demands to eliminate DEI programming.

“By not accepting the money, we are able to continue to support students about anything that they want to write about, particularly their identities or historical oppression,” said 826 Boston executive director Corey Yarbrough, who hopes students will see “their perspectives matter, and someone out there cares and will listen.”

Some schools have added prompts to get at themes of viewpoint diversity.

Harvard and Columbia asked students to recall a time they disagreed with someone, and how they handled it. Kouame wrote about going to Ivory Coast in West Africa, where her family is originally from, and meeting a woman selling skin-bleaching cream.

“You’re not trying to change somebody’s point of view,” she said. “You’re just trying to inform them about what you think.”

Kouame worked on her college essays with Thrive Scholars, which assists high-achieving students from under-resourced communities. The Boston-based nonprofit Steppingstone also provided essay and college-prep support and helped her get into the prekindergarten-12 Buckingham Browne & Nichols School, a private school in Cambridge. When she started there, her family lived in Dorchester (they later moved to Belmont). She commuted to Cambridge, doing her homework on the bus ride in and contemplating outer space on her ride home on the T.

“The blur of city lights outside the window reminded me of distant constellations,” she wrote in her college essay, “and in that moving train car, my fascination with space was born.”

She submitted her college applications through QuestBridge, which has a full four-year “Match Scholarship” with various partners.

Other seniors are still finishing their applications before regular-decision deadlines in January.

Ella Daillie, a senior at Northampton High School with Iraqi and Yemeni heritage, marked herself as “white” and “Middle Eastern” on the Common App, which has an optional race and ethnicity question for research purposes.

She had a harder time deciding whether to mention her leadership in her school’s Students for Justice in Palestine club, following campus crackdowns on pro-Palestinian protests. Daillie, who is Jewish, ultimately decided it was too important to omit from her applications to schools such as the University of Wisconsin and Grinnell College in Iowa.

“Like one of my friends says: ‘I don’t want to go somewhere that doesn’t want me there,’ ” she said. “I want to go to a school that wants me for who I am.”

“Thank you to the MSBA for this momentous decision to partner with us for a transformational investment in Madison Park that will redefine the opportunities for our students and the trajectory of our economic future,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement. “This is long overdue to deliver nation-leading facilities to train and support the next generation of our workforce, bringing our entire community into the opportunities of world-class vocational education.”

The city estimated in January that the project could cost as much as $700 million.

That exceeds even the $660 million high school rebuild Lexington voters recently approved and Revere’s $500 million high school project.

Boston is not alone in facing potentially record-breaking costs. Brockton is facing a similar estimated cost for its hoped-for high school replacement. School building costs have surged in recent years due to rising material and labor costs and higher interest rates. President Trump’s tariffs could raise costs even more.

The state’s School Building Authority provides partial reimbursement of construction costs, with the percentage of costs covered based on factors such as the property value and demographics of a school district.

For example, the authority agreed to reimburse Boston about 64 percent of eligible costs, or about $30 million, for the Carter School, which opened this fall. In an effort to rein in costs, the authority limits payments for some features and excludes expenses for features it considers optional. The Carter School’s total cost was more than $100 million.

The proposed new vocational school could be more than a half-million square feet, and serve 2,200 students, according to a prior city planning study. That would include about 800 students enrolled in newly added Grades 7 and 8, doubling the overall enrollment. The expansion would also allow the school to add additional state-approved vocational pathways.

Currently, the school has 20 such programs, from carpentry to nursing. Wu in May signed an agreement with the Greater Boston Building Trades Unions to create a direct pathway for the school’s graduates into the unions’ Building Pathways pre-apprenticeship program.

The campus would feature new facilities and include an auditorium, performing arts spaces, and a media center. The current school, built in 1972, is in terrible condition, with out-of-date facilities and an energy efficiency score of 0 out of 100, according to BPS data.

Madison Park, the district’s only vocational high school, shares a campus with the O’Bryant School of Math and Science. The MSBA application applies to Madison Park; the future of the O’Bryant remains up in the air.

Whether the district renovates existing structures or builds a new Madison Park school on the same campus, the cost would be about $700 million, according to earlier city estimates. Initially the city undertook years of planning and community engagement as part of plans to fund the school without aid from the state agency, but officials switched gears once the potential costs came into view.

The next step for the city will be a feasibility study, where the district and the MSBA explore options for the school’s design. That could partially duplicate work done before the city opted to seek state funding.

Long term, Boston has not been a major recipient of MSBA assistance, as suburban school districts have tended to get a disproportionate share. Under Wu, the district has done better: This is the third year in a row the city has won initial approval from the state agency, after the Ruth Batson Academy last year and the Shaw-Taylor elementary school merger the year prior.

Both of those projects are still in planning stages, and none of the three is likely to be completed until the 2030s.

“We are proud of our ongoing collaboration with the City of Boston on multiple facilities and look forward to continuing our partnership with the invitation of the Madison Park High School project into the MSBA’s Capital Pipeline,” said Mary Pichetti, executive director of the authority, in a statement. “We are pleased to support this investment in the City’s vision for the transformation of Madison Park project which will directly benefit students pursuing career and technical training.”

The MSBA Board also approved funding agreements Friday for BPS on several smaller projects. The agency will pay up to almost $5 million for windows, doors, and roofs at four schools.

The good news on the school building front comes as school officials are also grappling with the less-pleasant task of closing schools. On Wednesday, the Boston School Committee is set to vote on a proposal to close three schools serving about 850 students.

But for us, parents at a Dorchester school in receivership, UP Academy Holland, and a board member at UP Education Network, the nonprofit school manager that runs the Holland, it has meant transformation. It has meant empowerment. It has meant hope.

And today, we’re desperately clinging to that hope.

As soon as this week, the state education commissioner could elect to take our students’ school out of receivership, jeopardizing all of the gains of the last several years.

We implore state officials to keep a good thing going.

And more broadly, we call on the state Legislature to reject a teachers union-led push to eliminate receivership across the board. Families all over Massachusetts deserve a shot at better schools.

Massachusetts’ receivership law, which dates to 2010, allows the state to step in when a school or district has struggled and to appoint a receiver with the authority to make significant changes.

The law, to be sure, has a mixed record. Receivership hasn’t always worked. But we’ve seen, up close, how it can be done well.

A little over a decade ago, the Commonwealth appointed the UP Education Network to take over the struggling John P. Holland Elementary School in the Bowdoin-Geneva neighborhood of Dorchester. The school became UP Academy Holland.

UP Education was already at work nearby, turning around the old John Marshall Elementary School through a separate partnership with Boston Public Schools. That school was renamed UP Academy Dorchester. Both of these UP academies have turned into schools that the neighborhood can be proud of.

Before UP began its work, the schools struggled with leadership turnover, staffing shortages, and inconsistent academic results. None of these challenges reflected the strength of our community or the potential of our children. We witnessed firsthand what can happen when students benefit from clearer routines — routines established by teachers, staff, and school leaders who have had significant coaching and additional training, and are powered by stronger, more consistent use of data. That’s how UP has instilled in our students a spirit of belonging.

One of us, Christina Qualls, a parent in our community and a school principal, tells the story of her younger sister entering UP Holland significantly behind in reading after time in foster care. As she explains, the family was prepared to request an IEP, or an individualized education program for a student with disabilities, but her sister’s teacher asked for time to understand her as a learner before labeling her needs. Within a year, her sister was reading on grade level. Today she is thriving in high school honors classes. Her experience reflects what’s possible when a school leads with skilled instruction, careful attention, and a belief in students’ potential before anything else.

Now students go home talking about books they are reading and math problems they can solve, and they describe teachers who encourage them. The culture has shifted, and so have the results.

Today, UP Academy Dorchester and UP Academy Holland have risen to the 25th and 20th percentiles, respectively, on a statewide accountability measure of how a school compares with other schools statewide that serve similar grades. The previous iterations of the schools were at the bottom of the rankings. The UP schools are now among the best performing public schools in Dorchester. UP students show some of the strongest academic growth in Boston. They rank first and second statewide in English language arts growth among schools serving high-needs populations, and they outperform the district and the state in English and math growth. The percentage of high-needs students meeting or exceeding standards has doubled since COVID, even as district and state rates remain largely unchanged. Teachers report more substantial support, families report greater trust, and our children show more confidence in their learning.

We also recognize that there is more work ahead. Achievement gaps still exist, and our schools must keep focusing on the needs of students who need extra support. Ongoing improvement will require consistent commitment, stronger collaboration with families, and fair distribution of resources.

These local gains matter, but they also reflect national patterns. Research shows that improving outcomes in high-poverty schools typically rests on the sort of strategy UP has pursued — sustained, targeted investment in leadership, teacher professional education, and schoolwide systems rather than ad hoc fixes. A meta-analysis of 35 turnaround studies found associations between turnaround efforts and gains in attendance, test scores, and graduation when structural changes (leadership, human capital, governance) were implemented.

Our greatest concern now is that our progress could be disrupted by decisions made outside our schools. But UP’s work in Dorchester is exactly the kind of partnership that national research identifies as successful. It is targeted, sustained, grounded in community, and built from the ground up on the belief that improvement is not only possible but measurable. What can often get lost in the worthy debates about schools and their governance and management is the perspective of families who rely on these schools every day.

Massachusetts, like states across the country, has a responsibility to support what works, not disrupt it. When the state decides the fate of UP Academy Holland, it should keep that in mind.

The urgency we feel is shaped not only by the approaching decision — if UP Academy Holland is taken out of receivership, it’s unclear that UP will still be able to run the school — but also by a broader movement in Massachusetts to eliminate receivership entirely. Teachers unions across the state have testified in favor of the so-called THRIVE Act, which would end receivership and require every district currently in it to transition out within a year. As the Boston Globe editorial board recently noted, this push is being led by the Boston Teachers Union, the Massachusetts Teachers Association, and the American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts, all of which argue that receivership is a “failed approach” and advocate for removing the state’s ability to intervene. If that effort succeeds, the partnership that has supported our children’s progress at UP Holland could end by statute, regardless of the outcomes our students are achieving.

This decision determines whether our students’ progress continues or is put at risk. The performance of our students serves as living proof that improvement amid challenging circumstances can be real, that children from communities that have long been underserved can excel, and that families can trust public education when the structures around it are strong.

We ask for the chance to protect what has worked so well.

With the New Year approaching, Boston leaders touted the city’s low crime rates in 2025 and pledged to redouble their public safety efforts.

While gun violence has increased slightly this year after reaching a historic low in 2024, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said the numbers are still a significant accomplishment.

During a news conference Monday morning at a new Boston EMS training center in West Roxbury, he said the city has recorded 31 homicides so far in 2025, compared to 24 the same time last year. The 2025 tally represents a 16 percent decrease from the city’s five-year average, Cox said.

Other big cities have also seen declines in gun violence following a widespread pandemic surge.

Aside from ongoing violence reduction efforts, Cox said the department has focused on organized retail theft, quality of life crimes, especially around the downtown area, and traffic safety issues involving the reckless operation of scooters.

“The Boston Police Department continues to rely on community policing as our most valued partner in public safety in the city,” Cox said. He praised the agency for building relationships with residents and taking their concerns seriously.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu thanked local first responders, calling the city a “shining example for the rest of the country” when it comes to public safety.

“This is what it means to be a home for everyone, and to be fighting every day for the residents in every single neighborhood to live in the safest city in America,” she said.

She also acknowledged recent mass tragedies, including the weekend shooting at Brown University.

“It is unthinkable that we live in a world where you don’t even have time to process one major, horrific incident of violence before the next takes place,” she said. “And all the more reason why it is important for us to focus on safety.”

Wu said ongoing efforts will continue as Boston looks forward to hosting a number of large events in the coming months, including the 2026 World Cup games.

Elected officials have sought to reassure residents that local and state law enforcement agencies have things under control in the Boston area, especially after President Trump cited a recent series of so-called “street takeovers” in criticizing the mayor’s leadership. Trump suggested he could move the games elsewhere because of public safety issues, a familiar talking point for the president as he often attacks Democrat-led cities.

Boston officials announced a key arrest in the street takeovers earlier this month. A man from Connecticut was charged with throwing a firework at a Boston police cruiser in an October incident in the South End. The car meetups unfolded in several Massachusetts cities and towns, with large groups of drivers blocking traffic and performing dangerous stunts.

Still, officials said Boston’s overall crime trends are positive.

The recent drop in homicides follows decades of work involving city leaders, police, and community organizations. In 1990, Boston’s most violent year on record, there were 152 homicides.

Officials said they’ll continue taking a public health approach to reducing violence. That means tackling the problem from all angles, including a new initiative that trains hairstylists and barbers to recognize signs of domestic violence and human trafficking, said Isaac Yablo, the city’s senior advisor for community safety and director of the Boston Public Health Commission’s Office of Violence Prevention.

“The main goal will be primary prevention, preventing the violence from happening in the first place,” Yablo said.

Massachusetts education officials announced on Tuesday that the state would end a more than decade-long receivership of UP Academy Holland in Dorchester next year, handing control of the school back to Boston Public Schools.

Many parents and school officials welcomed the news at a board meeting of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, as they also pleaded with local authorities to continue state support for the school, which improved its test scores and other state accountability measures over the last few years.

The kindergarten through sixth-grade school went from being ranked worse than 99 percent of similar grade schools in 2014, a year into the receivership, to reaching the 20th percentile this year.

Under receivership, the school received coaching and professional development for teachers and school leaders, got help implementing its curriculum, and put in place assessments to track student progress. State oversight also included data platforms to allow the school to track student progress more accurately. And the school implemented strategies to improve attendance and streamline budgeting.

“We ask for the commitment to ensure that those things continue,” Amelia Massoud-Tastor, principal at UP Academy Holland, said at the state board meeting. “We know this work is best done with adequate resources,” she added.

“The school has done a phenomenal job over the last 11 years,” said Daisy Stanley, a parent at Holland. “Now we need to make sure that we continue to get the support that the school had to ensure that this transition goes smoothly,” she added.

Jessica Tang, president of the Massachusetts chapter of the American Federation of Teachers, supported UP Academy’s transition out of receivership.

“Allowing more local input and collaboration is a step in the right direction to ensure the voices of parents and the community are heard as well,” Tang said at Tuesday’s meeting.

Holland’s improved results under the state takeover were an “anomaly in the receivership landscape,” according to Massoud-Tastor. A Globe analysis of test scores, graduation rates, college enrollment, and a dozen other metrics in Lawrence, Holyoke, and Southbridge found that the state failed to meet almost all its stated goals for those districts.

Wary of changes if Boston takes over, however, some parents had gone so far as to request that the school, with more than 600 students, stay in receivership indefinitely.

“Our greatest concern now is that our progress could be disrupted by decisions made outside our schools,” parents Sachia Debrosse, Amanda Nelson, Christina Qualls, and Larae Robinson said in an opinion article published by the Globe.

School officials at Holland warned that the state needed to ensure a smooth transition to Boston’s oversight.

“How we exit matters a lot,” Mike Bower, chief operating officer for Education Network, the nonprofit school manager that runs the Holland, said at the board meeting. “It almost matters as much as how we entered. And unfortunately, we have seen exits happen in the past that did not go very well.”

The goal should be to work together to “ensure that Holland does not lose the progress it has made that it continues to thrive,” he added.

Officials at the state agency said they would sit down with Boston Public Schools Superintendent Mary Skipper to develop an exit strategy.

“I expect the plan will maintain essential flexibilities, autonomies, and the district will commit the necessary resources as the school transitions back to local control,” said Department of Elementary and Secondary Education Commissioner Pedro Martinez.

The state plans to keep monitoring how the school develops through the transition phase, he added. State officials will use a series of “academic milestones and benchmarks” to measure progress.

Addie Wyman-Battalen is director of counseling at Brandeis University in Waltham. She knows that this news makes parents feel helpless, because she is one. Talking with your child about campus resources — downloading campus safety apps, reviewing a school’s medical amnesty policy (useful if a student is in danger from binge-drinking but peers are afraid to call for help) can impart a measure of control in risky situations.

“I would encourage parents to begin discussing with their children before they get to campus who is or who can be part of their support team if needed, such as counseling on campus or spiritual life,” Battalen says. “We live in a world that is scary, and we can’t control everything, but identifying what you can do to help keep your kid safe can be a good start.”

Meanwhile, seniors eagerly awaited admissions news from Brown, which had originally planned to release decisions on Monday. That process has been delayed up to 48 hours.

“I feel sadness and understanding of the delay. As a parent, I think I’m more anxious than my son. It’s a strange place to be, holding the knowledge of the awfulness of what happened with the anxiety of the results release. It feels a bit surreal,” says one parent of a Brown candidate, requesting privacy for her son.

I talked to parents of college students, and those who are in the application process, about their dual senses of excitement and dread. Though the sentiments varied, one message was universal: Nobody feels completely safe.

Innocence has been taken away, one more time

“I live on Martha’s Vineyard and am the mom of a 13-year-old boy. I went to the Wheeler School on the East Side of Providence for high school, and this latest shooting feels too close to home. Many friends share the mind-set that the Vineyard is a safe place to raise children. What has become abundantly clear is that no community is safe or immune to this type of massacre. Nowhere. A friend’s son attends Brown and happened to be home during the shooting. Was it luck? I don’t know how to resolve this issue but I know that it is not possible to shelter our son from the potential of gun violence, and that feels too vulnerable.” - Kate, Vineyard Haven

“I feel like I’m drowning after this news. My daughter was accepted into Wellesley at 10 a.m. on Saturday. She found out during a debate tournament. We were with her when she opened her email, and we were all ecstatic.

“The next day was the anniversary of Sandy Hook. When that tragedy occurred, she was in preschool in Providence. We routinely played on the Brown campus on nice days, and the East Side is so near and dear to us. I can’t believe we have made no progress since then. She will be studying political science at Wellesley, and while I’m so hopeful for her future and so glad she’ll be on a women’s college campus near us, I am darkly shadowed by these events. - Keri, Winchester

“I’m the parent of a Providence College freshman as well as a lecturer in a program at MIT that offers English Language Studies courses to both undergraduate and graduate international students.

“This weekend’s horrific events in Providence hit even closer to home than all the other school shootings of the past few decades because the PC campus, where my daughter is a freshman, is only a six-minute drive from Brown University.

“I’m lucky because my daughter was actually on her way back home from Rhode Island when the shooting happened on Saturday, and, as of now, she’s still back home, debating when to go back to campus …

“It makes me absolutely mad and incredibly sad that our kids grow up with active shooter drills at their schools, and we all have to live in constant fear. As a parent, the loss of our children’s innocence and an entire generation’s childhood taken away feels just devastating. I also find living with the frequent occurrence of mass shootings draining as an educator, and it’s often hard to explain to my international students that this is our reality, and as a consequence of them having decided to study in the US, now it’s theirs, too.” - Olivia, Arlington

We need put down our phones and look out for one another

“My daughter just started her freshman year at Brown. I am a Brown alum myself. She is safe, and we picked her up last night.

“I know the university will likely respond in many ways prior to student return, likely enhancing building security and video coverage. I find that reassuring. I know my daughter will benefit from the support the university will provide.

“The Brown community is strong and engaged in picking up the vulnerable and marginalized in our society. We know we need to look out even more vigilantly for each other, but we must continue the mission.

“My daughter is a fiercely independent person. She thrives in communities and has completely been absorbed into Brown. She has already told me she knows things haven’t sunk in quite yet, but she will not let this event define her, and she wants to really make the most of the education and experience Brown is giving (and already has given) her.

“How to better look out for each other? By caring. By realizing your fellow students are your family, like your brothers and sisters. By talking to people, by listening to people, especially those who are different from you. By looking up from your phones and the sidewalk to see the people around you.” - Patty, Acton

This has now become routine

“I have a freshman at college at Endicott. We lived in Tucson when [Gaby] Giffords was shot and knew the judge who was killed. A college friend, her first year of teaching, was at Columbine. [She] still talks about hiding under her desk. My kids have also lived through bomb threats at the Tucson JCC and at their then-school.

“What’s exhausting isn’t one incident — it’s the accumulation. Lockdowns. Bomb threats at Jewish schools and JCCs. Active shooter drills that my kids now treat as routine. Now the Brown shooting. Each one adds another layer. - Erin, Somerville

Our kids never knew true safety

“I personally went to Brown, so now I’m feeling acutely the reality that really nowhere is safe. It leaves me, of course, completely without recourse. You can’t not live life, and you can’t not go places. And yet a study hall for finals is not safe. A college kid riding his bike across campus is not safe. College students expressing their right to free speech and political discourse are not safe.

“Do my sons feel the same? I don’t think they do, sadly. I don’t think they can experience the same loss because they grew up post-Sandy Hook, so they don’t know that churches and schools used to be safe.” - Amy, Lexington

“My daughter returned last night from her sophomore year at Lafayette. I’ve never felt more relieved to have her home. The shooting at Brown hit me hard — maybe because it’s close to home, my father went to Brown, and it’s a school, like Lafayette, where you just can’t imagine something like this happening. But it is increasingly obvious that no place is safe. My daughter was a first-grader during Sandy Hook, and I couldn’t stop crying over the loss of children the same age. Now, here we are again.

“There is so much to worry about when you send your child out into the world. We can’t control what happens. We trust her. But this kind of situation is not something we should have to worry about. The government is failing us by doing nothing about gun control.” - Mary, Concord

This is a problem growing out of control

“I know my child is nervous about going away to college and might choose a place closer to home where she could live at home while attending school. However, this really doesn’t make it much safer.

“Truth be told, gunmen are shooting up movie theaters, churches, and shopping malls, to name a few, so I’m not sure that I have a specific concern about college versus any other venues where people are vulnerable. And a lot of these guns have been acquired legally, so I don’t even know what to say about tighter gun control laws or security protocols. This seems like a problem growing out of control, and we are not adequately addressing it. When I was a kid, we had bomb scare drills because it was the Cold War. This is the new danger. But it’s everywhere and from within. - Laura, Falmouth

This is the new normal

“I’m part of Grassroots for Gun Violence Prevention, an organization I cofounded here in Massachusetts. I have a junior at Arlington High School, and although she’s not applying yet, Brown is her top pick and we were hoping to go visit soon. I think we’ll delay a bit. I could talk for days about gun violence prevention because I’ve been doing this for nine years, but even doing this work on a regular basis, sometimes it hits particularly close to home like this weekend.

What’s really sad is that my daughter is not even fazed by school shootings anymore. She’s got her plan for if it happens to her, and it’s sad that our young people have to plan for it. I admire that she won’t be deterred from going to college, and probably will still consider going to Brown, but we shouldn’t have to live this way. We all deserve better, no matter what school you go to. Schools should be safe places to learn.

It’s just devastating that my daughter’s dream school, Brown, is now marred by senseless violence and fear. I felt like I had to take her aside and let her know about the shooting and be prepared to console her. But, again, the sad part is she wasn’t even fazed.” - Angela, Arlington

“I have a child who is currently studying at UMass Boston and living on campus as a freshman. It is scary. This past fall, the school actually had a shelter-in-place and evacuation notice for the campus because of a suspected shooter. No one was harmed, and I don’t believe there was actually ever a threat, but it was one of the scariest days I have experienced. As parents, we found out via the news and then reached out to our child. He barely knew what was going on, only one text saying to shelter in your dorm.

“It lasted about an hour or two but eventually everything was cleared and he seemed totally unfazed. Can you imagine?! Kids are being trained for this now, and it’s totally unreal. We were in full panic but he was calm and just stayed quiet until police gave the all clear. I’m thankful he was calm but it’s irritating we live in a world where this is the new norm.

“We just try to remind our kids to be kind and respectful of everyone, but always know your surroundings. That day with the UMass Boston situation was very scary. We’re grateful it turned out to be not a real threat to the campus, but it puts things in perspective. Just because you’re in a surveillance area does not equate to a safe area anymore.” - Bea, Andover

“I am sad to say that the incident at Brown does not make me any more worried than I already am about various things to do with college kids — parties, unfortunate decisions, learning to be in the audience rather than the director of their lifetime plays. There’s a general feeling to me of it being all a terrible, horrible crapshoot: who is having a bad day and carrying a gun, who has a grudge and takes it out on your kids.

“The sad fact is that all of our kids in their teens and 20s have been dealing with ALICE drills and the constant terror for all their lives. They all know how to react. - Kristin, Weston

Home is safer than a campus

“My daughter is a student at a college in Providence, and we are very nervous about next steps. We went and got my daughter back home for Christmas break because of our anxiety around the situation.” - Caren, Medfield

“College is supposed to be the first time kids can really spread their wings and fly a little. Campus shootings make me wonder how far I really want them to fly.” - Sarah, Belchertown

We need to address mental health

“I’m feeling helpless and worried. This can happen anywhere, and unless we as a society address mental health, help men learn how to express themselves without violence, and do something about the insane number of guns available (and the ease of getting them), we really won’t be able to prevent this from happening. So I will hug my sons tighter, encourage them to be vigilant, and pray.” - Samantha. West Roxbury

Two Brown students were killed and nine others wounded in the attack on Saturday by a lone gunman. On Tuesday, Providence police released an enhanced video of a person of interest, after the FBI offered a reward of up to $50,000 for information leading to the identification, arrest, and conviction of the person responsible for the shooting.

While some private schools near Brown canceled school on Monday or for the entire week, Providence public schools remained open. The district canceled all after-school activities and field trips for the rest of the week, “out of an abundance of caution.”

Providence schools added “additional law enforcement support,” Superintendent Javier Montañez said in a letter to families Tuesday. The support included State Police troopers at 10 schools during arrival and dismissal, on top of Providence police deployed around schools near Brown’s campus.

Still, one out of five public school students in Providence were absent on Monday and 16 percent on Tuesday, School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said in a statement.

The absences underscored “the importance of ensuring that families feel safe and confident sending their children to school,” Stephens said.

Governor Dan McKee said he would continue to provide State Police coverage to the schools for the rest of the week. Winter break starts Monday.

“We don’t see anything on the horizon that shows there is another action coming our way,” McKee said. He directed Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green to review K-12 school safety plans.

Providence Mayor Brett Smiley also said parents who are comfortable should send their children to school.

Across New England, teachers, students, and families were still processing news of the shooting and said they felt feel a heightened fear of becoming victims in the future.

Colleges around the area tightened security, as well.

Harvard has begun requiring a university ID swipe to enter campus buildings that were previously open to the public. At Yale, officials increased the presence of campus security and required IDs to enter more gate entrances and doors. And at Emerson College, the school said it was reviewing all safety and security protocols.

High school and elementary teachers went to school this week — the last of the year — worrying about their own students and classrooms, often unsure of how to address the subject with children.

“I saw Brown and I saw Providence in the headlines, it definitely hit me in a little bit of a different way,” said Sydney Chaffee, a Dorchester ninth-grade teacher. “That’s just one state away.”

As Chaffee went about her workday on Monday, the news about the shooting was in the back of her mind, she said. The English and history teacher wondered if students would bring up the news, and how she should address their questions. This time, they didn’t.

“My kids didn’t even mention it,” Chaffee said. “We have become so used to the horror and the tragedy and the inaction, that it just keeps happening and we just keep moving forward because that’s all that we know how to do.”

Chaffee said she was thinking about a new teacher in her school. She thought about the enthusiasm of being new to the profession, and how she didn’t want the news and fear to ruin that experience. At the same time, Chaffee felt the responsibility to ensure new teachers were ready for the reality that they could experience a shooting.

“Our kids shouldn’t go to school and fear that they’re going to be killed,” she said.

On Tuesday, before heading to school, Chaffee checked the news first thing in the morning to see if authorities had found the shooter.

“We don’t dream of lockdown drills. We don’t get into the profession and say, ‘Oh, I can’t wait until I can step into my first classroom and figure out which furniture I’m going to use to block the door,’ ” she said. “We don’t dream of, ‘I can’t wait to be able to console my kids when they’ve lost someone’ or attending our students’ funerals. That’s not why we’re in this field.”

Many teachers across New England followed the news about the Brown shooting on Sunday morning, on the anniversary of the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, when a gunman entered an elementary school in Connecticut and killed 26 people.

For Abbey Clements, it was a “tragedy” for another shooting to take place on the same weekend as the anniversary. The retired Connecticut teacher is a survivor of Sandy Hook. Ever since, she has advocated for gun control legislation and created a crisis intervention help line to support educators who survive school shootings.

“Every single teacher in this country worries that gun violence will come to them at any point,” Clements said.

There’s a “look” teachers give one another in the aftermath of school shootings, she said. She experienced it herself after the Uvalde shooting in Texas, which happened in 2022 when she was still teaching.

“It’s like, ‘Can you even believe this continues to happen over and over?’ And without talking, teachers know what that means,” Clements said. “When teachers see these heinous acts of violence happen, they think, ‘Oh my God, this could happen to me and my students.’ ”

Parents also had to decide how to explain to their children what happened at Brown.

Nicole Eaton, a Providence resident whose 7-year-old attends the French American School of Rhode Island, said her daughter felt scared as the family first learned about the shooting.

Eaton, a history professor at Boston College, decided to show her some news coverage.

“I showed her pictures of the police at the campus,” she said. “I showed her the picture of the ambulance. I showed her the picture of the mayor talking. And I talked to her about how they catch people, and how they use evidence to find people, and how this doesn’t happen very often, and that’s why we’re so frustrated and upset.”

Her daughter’s school, which is close to the Brown campus, hired an additional security guard in addition to the local police already patrolling the area. Her school closed on Monday, but reopened on Tuesday.

“Under the circumstances, they’ve done an excellent job,” Eaton said.

“The complex criminal investigation of this tragic incident has many layers, and involves various investigative partners,” the sheriff’s office said. “The investigative process in these type of incidents can take time to develop, and we ask for your patience as the investigation proceeds.”

The bus was operated by Maine’s Bonny Eagle School District, which operates the largest public sector bus fleet in the state, according to the district’s website.

One student was onboard the bus at the time of the crash, officials said. Cumberland Sheriff Kevin Joyce told WMTW-TV that the other student was Gonzalez’s half-brother.

Edna Libby Elementary School dismissed students after a half-day on Tuesday, and canceled classes on Wednesday, according to district superintendent Clay Gleason.

“In this difficult time please keep those directly impacted in your thoughts — first and foremost the family of the student, as well as the students and staff of Edna Libby," Gleason wrote in a message to parents on Tuesday.

Though the elementary school remained closed Wednesday, Gleason said counselors were on site there and at other schools to support students and other community members.

“The Bonny Eagle community has been deeply impacted by this tragedy and while we can’t change the past, we must move forward together,” he wrote.

Gleason said the district was cooperating with law enforcement and had also opened an internal investigation.

“While I can’t share specifics related to this case, it is standard protocol that any employee would be put on administrative leave while an investigation is underway,” he wrote.

Residents of Standish, roughly a half-hour west of Portland, took to social media to mourn Gonzalez.

“Our hearts are with the family who has suffered the heartbreaking loss of their child,“ Standish town councilor Lisa Struebing said in a Facebook post. ”Please respect their need for privacy while offering care and compassion when welcomed."

Struebing also urged “kindness and support for all impacted, including students, the bus driver, EMTs, faculty, and staff.”

“Let’s support one another with understanding, care, and compassion,” she wrote.

The Second Congregational Church in Norway, Maine, wrote that, just as Maine is a state where “everyone knows someone,” it’s also a place where “when one community is devastated by loss, the pain ripples out to the rest of us.”

“With the painful loss of Simon Gonzalez, a small child who was deeply loved, we pray,” the church wrote. “This has been a hard week for many. Take care of yourselves and each other. Love hard.”

Gonzalez is the second Maine student to die after being hit by a school bus in less than a month. 12-year-old Brayden Callahan was killed on Nov. 25 in Rockland, a city on Penobscot Bay.

Earlier this year, another 5-year-old was struck and killed by a school bus in Boston’s. Hyde Park. Lens Arthur Joseph was on his way home from UP Academy Dorchester when he was struck by his school bus just after it dropped him off.

The memories endure: The sound. The smell of smoke. The people screaming and running. The dumb luck that kept someone from harm’s way — or the happenstance that put someone else in it. Then the creeping fear, the sheltering in place, when killers remained at large.

These images come from survivors of an attack in New England more than a dozen years ago, but eerily echo in the aftermath of Saturday’s shooting at Brown University — and as we again watch the frustrating hunt for a killer. For four days in April 2013, police struggled to track down the two men behind the bombings near the finish line of the Boston Marathon. And here we are again, four days later, waiting for an arrest.

Back in 2013, a nervous public asked: “What is this world coming to?” Added security worker Guy Dixon, “This is too close to home.”

On Monday, “The sooner we can identify this person, the sooner we can blow this case open,” Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha said.

In the past days, the violence has piled on. The massacre at a Hanukkah celebration on a beach in Australia. The fatal stabbings of a beloved Hollywood icon and his wife, possibly by a troubled adult son. The shooting death of an MIT professor in his Brookline home.

We’re on guard, much like the people of Utah were days after the slaying of conservative activist Charlie Kirk in September, much like people in Manhattan and elsewhere following last December’s point-blank shooting of health care CEO Brian Thompson.

A killer at large is terrifying, and the wait is harrowing. For four days in 2013, New Englanders were glued to the TV news, staying indoors, checking in on relatives, peeking in their boats in the backyard. After the attack at Brown, we wait to see what happens next.

Varied methods have led to the capture of other suspects. After Kirk’s killing, in which another “person of interest” was released, a man surrendered to authorities late the following night. Five days after the slaying of the CEO of UnitedHealthcare, a tip led to the arrest of the suspect at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pa.

But until those arrests? New videos and new information don’t quell a fear compounded by the cancellation of afterschool activities and university events.

Since the Marathon Bombing, we’ve seen a lot of horror beam across our TVs and phones: school shootings, George Floyd’s murder on a street in Minneapolis, the attempted assassination of a presidential candidate. Readers, we ask: How have you come to live with this? If you made it through the Marathon Bombing and manhunt, please let us know how you endured another time while killers were at large. Did life end up sliding back toward normal little by little, or with a whoosh of relief once the last Marathon bomber was captured?

We could use a whoosh of relief now.

“This means the world to us,” Brennan said while accepting the award at Wednesday’s ceremony, noting in his speech that “Boston is such a huge part of who we are.”

Dropkick Murphys, who haven’t secured any titles at the Boston Music Awards since 2012, also picked up wins for video of the year and song of the year (1 million+ streams) for the band’s politically-charged track “Who Will Stand with Us?” from the new album “For the People.”

While Dropkick Murphys led the field with three wins on Wednesday, Boston band Couch, who were nominated in five categories, took home two trophies, including live artist of the year and pop artist of the year.

Rising women hip-hop and R&B performers continue to dominate the new artist of the year category, with Lawrence artist ISHA! taking the 2025 title, shouting out “the Dominicans and the Haitians in the building” while accepting the award (she also performed at the event). The 2024 crown went to Dorchester R&B act Yanna G, while Mattapan rapper Nay $peaks won new artist of the year in 2023.

Rap also dominated the best album categories, with Boston rapper EXITFAME, who also performed at this year’s awards, winning album/EP of the year for “Last Shall Be First.”

“I grew up in Dorchester, Roxbury. And what makes you stay here is the pride of that,” EXITFAME told the Globe backstage at Wednesday’s event, noting how he wants “to bring an eye on the city” with his work.

Meanwhile, Salem rapper Token won the award for album/EP of the year (1 million+ streams) for “I’m Not Supposed to Be Here.”

“I was always insecure about growing up outside of Boston and being an internet kid,” Token said during his acceptance speech. “But where I’m from means a lot to me, and this means a lot to me.”

In a statement from Paul Armstrong, owner and producer of the Boston Music Awards, he praised this year’s nominees and winners for reflecting “the full spectrum of who makes music in Boston right now.”

“It’s been a difficult year in many ways, for a lot of people, and nights like this matter,” said Armstrong. “When things feel heavy, art is often what helps us see a way forward.”

He added, “Our hope is that the Boston Music Awards offered a little light, a sense of connection, and a reminder of the strength that comes from a creative community that truly represents everyone.”

The 2025 edition of the ceremony featured five new categories this year, including the inaugural Margaret Stewart Lindsay music nonprofit of the year award, which honors organizations supporting the creative community. The honor went to the Boston Music Project, a nonprofit that aims to support “the long-term social-emotional and musical success of Boston youth,” according to its website.

“The arts truly are the cornerstone of humanity, and especially right now,” said Chris Schroeder, executive director of the Boston Music Project, while accepting the award on stage. “They play a vital role in helping us to express, amplify, and shape the future that we all want to see.”

Also new for 2025 was the Afro/Caribbean artist of the year category, which took the place of the reggae/ska category. The award went to hip-hop and Afrofusion musician Echezona.

Additional genre-specific winners included Token (hip-hop); Yanna G (R&B); Lia Nicole (Latin); Megan From Work (rock); Hallelujah the Hills (alt/indie); Ezra Furman (singer-songwriter); GA-20 (blues); Samantha Rae (country); Freezepop (dance/electronic); DJ Real P (DJ); Jared Sims (jazz); TREE (metal); Haywire (punk/hardcore); Kier Byrnes & The Kettle Burners (Americana); Tiny Habits (folk); and Miranda Rae (vocalist).

BEST COMMUNITY PERFORMANCE — Noah’s Flood, Boston Lyric Opera

Benjamin Britten’s children’s opera gathered musicians of all ages from several area ensembles into the Ark of Symphony Hall — pint-size beginners who were just learning to read music, poised teenage soloists and string players, masses of children in between, and a warmly enthusiastic audience that joined in with the hymns as taught by music director David Angus. Though it wasn’t without technological stumbles, “Noah’s Flood” was completely unpretentious and genuinely heartwarming, as a community performance should be.

MOST RESTORATIVE CONCERT — The Secret Trio, presented by Ashmont Hill Chamber Music

It seems that to most of the world the Secret Trio’s existence is, in fact, a secret. The group, comprising Macedonian clarinetist Ismail Lumanovski, Armenian oud player Ara Dinkjian, and Turkish kanun player Tamer Pınarbaşı, has a very limited online presence, and the group may never have appeared on my radar if Ashmont Hill Chamber Music hadn’t booked them for an afternoon this past fall. But on my radar they’ll stay; the trio alchemized one part jazz, one part Balkan and Near Eastern traditional music, and a healthy pinch of rock ‘n’ roll, making for an energizing and joyfully virtuosic performance that chased the Sunday scaries away.

BEST OPERATIC PERFORMANCE IN A LEADING ROLE — SeokJong Baek, “Tosca,” Boston Symphony Orchestra

I wrote in July: In Puccini’s “Tosca,” the painter Cavaradossi “often seems more like a plot device and a dispenser of high B-flats than a real character,” especially in contrast to the vain but virtuous Tosca and the preening villain Scarpia. But that wasn’t the case when South Korean tenor SeokJong Baek performed the role opposite Kristine Opolais and Bryn Terfel at Tanglewood; through his supple and searing tenor voice, he conveyed love, pain, and grief that needed no translation.

BEST BREAKOUT PERFORMANCES — Richard Pittsinger, tenor (“Ariodante,” Boston Baroque; “Octavia,” Boston Early Music Festival; “Stellidaura’s Revenge,” Boston Early Music Festival)

On their own, this recent Juilliard graduate’s performances in town this year might not have been star-making. But to each of those, he brought an elegant mode of expression and compelling clarity, and three times makes it a pattern. Things look very promising for this young singer, whose inclination toward the music of Handel might help land him a few more gigs in this Baroque-loving town.

VALKYRIE AWARD FOR WEATHER SYNCHRONICITY — “Symphonie-Fantastique,” Tanglewood Music Center Orchestra with conductor Andris Nelsons vs. Berkshires thunderstorm

The sky was blue as the idyllic third movement began, so when Tanglewood staff ordered the lawn audience to shelter in the Shed because of incoming inclement weather, there were a few confused grumbles. But there was reason to take cover: the wind gradually picked up throughout the ominous “March to the Scaffold,” the limbs on the trees lashed to and fro as “Dream of a Witch’s Sabbath” began — and the instant the lower reaches of the orchestra intoned the first notes of the “Dies Irae,” thunder rattled and the rain came down in sheets, hammering the Shed’s roof as giant church bells tolled backstage. You’d have thought Mother Nature was reading from her own part in the score.

BEST SURPRISE GUEST — Michelle Wu, piano, with Yo-Yo Ma, cello

When Yo-Yo Ma was toting the complete Bach solo cello suites around the world in the late 2010s, the cellist often invited local musicians onstage for an encore. So it wasn’t exactly shocking when, after his performance of the Bach suites at Symphony Hall, Ma announced that a local pianist would be joining him for one more piece. But few if any expected that local pianist to be Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who accompanied Ma in Bach/Gounod’s immortal “Ave Maria.”

PEANUT BUTTER AND PICKLE AWARD FOR UNEXPECTED COLLABORATION THAT ACTUALLY WORKED Víkingur Ólafsson and Yuja Wang, pianists, presented by Celebrity Series of Boston

In the red corner, representing Iceland: Víkingur Ólafsson, one of the more understated and cerebral pianists on the performance circuit, aficionado of Bach and Glass. In the blue corner, representing New York City by way of China: Yuja Wang, a consummate entertainer and connoisseur of sparkle who once performed all four Rachmaninoff concertos — plus the “Rhapsody on a theme of Paganini” — on the same day. What do these two have in common, besides the 88 keys? As it turns out, quite a lot, especially when it comes to 20th century music, and when the pair teamed up for a playful and adventurous two-piano recital at Symphony Hall, they didn’t miss.

MOST FUN NIGHT OUT — Puerto Rico Symphony Orchestra, presented by Boston Symphony Orchestra and Inquilinos Boricuas en Acción

The San Juan-based orchestra celebrated the music of its island home in its first-ever visit to Boston, and the Puerto Rican community showed out in force to do likewise. Flags waved from the balconies, applause between pieces was punctuated with chants of “¡Yo soy Boricua, pa’ que tu lo sepas!” and the orchestra’s musicians hit the stage during intermission to take selfies in the gilded hall.

JOHN C. REILLY AWARD FOR THAT PERSON YOU’RE ALWAYS HAPPY TO SEE ON THE CAST LIST — Dima Slobodeniouk, conductor

Formerly music director of orchestras in Spain and his home country of Finland, Slobodeniouk now seems to be a free agent — and he’s using that freedom to show up with even greater frequency at Symphony Hall and Tanglewood, where he has led performances that consistently rank in the top tier of evenings I spend at the symphony. This calendar year alone, his highlights on the podium included a blazing run at Arvo Pärt’s “Tabula Rasa” with BSO violinists Lucia Lin and Alexander Velinzon, a balanced take on Mozart’s oft-unwieldy “Requiem,” and Roberto Sierra’s roof-raising Concerto for Saxophones and Orchestra with soloist James Carter. Heads up: he’s scheduled to come back this spring for the subscription season’s final program, featuring Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9. Wait, am I actually psyched to hear Beethoven’s Ninth?!

A century ago, nearly one in three Bostonians was under the age of 17. Today it’s barely one in eight. While Boston has added nearly 60,000 residents in the last 15 years, the number of children has fallen by about 10,000.

“A big motivating factor in why I ran for mayor in the first place was that exact statistic,” said Wu. “The population was growing, but the number of kids was going down. Moms and dads everywhere across the city can feel why that is true, right?”

From scarce housing to sky-high child-care costs to basic city services that too often seem to make life harder, the deck can seem stacked against parents.

It’s not just in Boston. High-cost cities from San Francisco to New York have seen their child populations decline in recent decades. Nationwide, the number of children under 5 has shrunk since the start of the pandemic. The number of school-age children here ticked up last year, but remains below 2022 levels, and anyone trying to make a big-city more family-friendly is fighting some big trends.

Wu thinks about several “momentous milestones” in a young parent’s life. The first is having the baby, and bringing the child home. The second is when the child starts day care, and parents start paying for it. Then there’s the day you enroll them in school and — you hope — that financial burden lifts. And finally, if your family grows, there’s the day when the stars align and your kids attend the same school and you finally have just one drop-off. It’s a moment, she said, when parents’ quality of life dramatically improves.

Those four moments, Wu said, shape her family policy. So do the concepts of “cost, convenience, and community” — concepts that, as a mom, she lives by too.

Wu said she gets how hard it is to be a parent in the city because she’s been doing it herself for 11 years. But she’s also been mayor for the last four. And things haven’t gotten much easier.

So it’s worth asking: If a millennial mom mayor can’t make Boston better for families, can anyone?

Ironically, over the last 25 years, Boston has become a city for the young.

From 2000 through 2015, the population of 20-to-34 year olds in Boston surged, to become 40 percent of the city’s total makeup. That’s thanks in part to our universities, of course, but also a flood of young people drawn to urban living and good jobs.

Scores of apartment and condo buildings cropped up to house these young professionals. They had amenity rooms and dog spas, but few were designed with children in mind. The newly built Seaport is chock-a-block with brunch spots and venues for “competitive socializing” but has no library, no arts venue, no ballfields.

“There’s this real divergence of Boston really rebounding over the last couple generations,” said Luc Schuster, the head of Boston Indicators, the research arm of The Boston Foundation. “The economy’s thriving. There has been some population growth, but at the same time, we’ve lost kids.”

Now many of those urbanites are in their 30s and 40s, finding it harder to live in Boston with children. Families, of course, have long beat an exodus to the suburbs. But for young people who are committed to city living, it’s been frustrating to watch friends struggle to make it work, or leave altogether.

They’re people like Julia Tutko-Balena, who grew up in Dorchester and now lives in Charlestown with her husband and two kids. She’s thrilled that the city is safer than it was when she was young — “Dorchester used to be very ‘stabby’,” she jokes — and believes Boston is a great place to raise her family. But she says she wishes that more middle-class people like her could find a way to stay.

“They’re people who have lived in the neighborhood and literally helped build the neighborhood,” she said. “They’re getting pushed out because they can’t afford to live [here anymore].”

Growing up in Chicago, Wu moved a lot, her immigrant parents always hunting for the smallest house in the best public school district they could afford. And since Wu first took office, housing, particularly housing for families, has been among her biggest priorities.

It’s also one of the hardest to fix.

She admitted recently that her housing efforts so far have only earned a B+, slowed by standoffs with developers and stymied by sky-high building costs. Rents keep climbing, with the average two-bedroom in Boston now going for $2,495 a month, according to real estate website Apartmentlist.com, up 9 percent since January 2022.

And people are frustrated. A recent poll by advocacy group Abundant Housing found 70 percent of Boston residents say Wu has done just a fair or poor job on housing.

“We have this reputation as this progressive city,” said Abundant Housing executive director Jesse Kanson-Benanav. Most people outside of Boston “don’t understand why we haven’t adopted policies that will accelerate the creation of reasonably priced, moderately-sized, family-sized homes.”

Wu has made some progress on income-restricted units, with more than 5,000 completed or in construction, and 4,000 more in the pipeline — more than have been built in Boston than in any three-year period since the late 1990s. Wu, too, has bolstered programs that help Section 8 voucher-holders buy homes, said Stephanie Ettinger de Cuba, the executive director of Children’s HealthWatch at Boston Medical Center.

Those are real successes, Schuster said, but the need remains for housing that middle-income families can afford.

”A subset of the lowest income families actually is able to remain in the city and attend our schools,” he said. “The big challenge is for families above those income thresholds. Many of them are the ones getting squeezed and moving away.”

For parents that decide to live in the city, securing day care is a major hurdle.

It’s an emotional one too, Wu said. “I remember crying,” she said, even though her sons were at the on-site child care at City Hall. And then there’s the cost. Massachusetts has some of the highest early child-care costs in the country — $22,000 a year, double the national average.

In New York, Democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani won this fall’s mayor’s race this fall in part on an audacious promise of free, high-quality child care for all New York City under age 5. It’s the sort of ambitious progressive policy that one might imagine Mayor Wu rolling out.

But Wu doesn’t go that far, focusing, instead, on a pragmatic approach to the realities of getting child care right for parents who face “the exhaustion of having to juggle everything” — something she knows firsthand. Wu said she kept Mira at her side during the election campaign not for optics but because she and her husband couldn’t figure out “a stable and predictable” child-care situation.

“The mayor is able to see the people who often feel unseen,” said Amy O’Leary, executive director of Strategies for Children, a statewide advocacy group. “Their approach is solutions-based in a world where a lot of things are reacting to problems.”

O’Leary pointed to Wu’s creation of the Office of Early Childhood, one of a handful of municipal-led agencies in the country to focus exclusively on a city’s youngest residents.

The office provides training and financial support to early child-care providers and says 77 new businesses have been licensed as a result. In 2022, Wu changed zoning ordinances to mandate that large developments must include child-care facilities; over 200 sites have opened since. Wu has also expanded paid parental leave for nearly all unionized city employees.

One small but significant solution is Great Starts, a new city website that simply maps all the available child-care options in Boston, allowing parents to filter by who took vouchers and hours they were open.

“It’s hard to over-express how much of Wild West it is for families to even to figure out what is available,” said Elizabeth Leiwant, vice president of public policy and research at Neighborhood Villages, an early education systems change organization. “It was revolutionary for a family to just have a single, easy-to-navigate place where they could go and start to figure out what their options are.”

Since its launch, Great Starts has expanded to become the onboarding site for parents to register for early education slots and public schools at BPS, replacing a trek to register in-person. But simply having an easy-to-navigate website isn’t enough to persuade parents to commit to public schools. The programs have to make sense.

Wherever she can, Wu says, she uses her own lived experience as a parent to shape city policy when it comes to kids. One of Wu’s sons wasn’t able to get a pre-K slot, but under her watch, the city has expanded pre-K programs at BPS, which now serve 53 percent of 4-year-olds in Boston, and 23 percent of 3-year-olds.

Even with that expansion, not all the available slots are full, something Wu ascribes to the practicalities of what parents and young children need: Is the pre-school close to home or a job? Do the hours work? She said she’s pushing to expand offerings to get more families to enroll.

“The data shows that when families get a spot in the Boston pre-K program, they are significantly more likely to stay and enroll in the Boston Public Schools,” Wu said. It’s a “pathway to building a sense of predictability and trust.”

As kids get a little older, the quality of schools starts to matter more, too. Wu’s two sons attend Boston Public Schools, and so when she talks education, it’s personal. More than a third of BPS students attend schools ranked in the bottom 10 percent of Massachusetts schools.

That’s a major sticking point for parents, one evidenced in the demographic data. The number of children in the city drops dramatically — by nearly half — when they turn 5, and the number in BPS schools has fallen by 17,000 in the last quarter-century, to just 46,000. Of those, many are “high-needs” meaning they’re lower-income, have disabilities, or are non-native English speakers. The BPS population has risen slightly in the last three years, which shows modest progress, Schuster said.

In a sign she wants to push harder to strengthen schools in her second term, Wu this fall hosted her first State of the Schools address, announcing more before- and after-school programming, and a goal to have all BPS students learning at grade level by the end of next year. She’s also introduced new math enrichment programs – of which her oldest son is now taking part.

“We are the oldest public school system in the nation,” she said. “And together, it’s time that we make it the best.”

Advocates – and parents – remain in wait-and-see mode. Wu has agitated families by pushing for school closures and consolidations, which she argues have been done to improve the facilities and efficiencies within the sprawling system. (Wu’s sons’ school was part of that consolidation — they now attend the Sarah Roberts Elementary School, which got a $91 million facelift this year).

That frustration stands to continue. Earlier this month, over a hundred protesters chanted “Save Our Schools!” during a Boston School Committee meeting.

But while many parents leave the city for the burbs, that wasn’t the case for Paula Silva, who is from Cape Verde and lived in Brockton and Somerville before moving with her daughter to Boston to take advantage of the city’s academic opportunities.

Silva’s daughter is a strong student at the Mather School in Dorchester, and Silva said her teachers have helped enroll her in leadership and performing arts programs. Now, she said, she’s getting help as she thinks about applying to exam schools.

“I believe here, you have a chance to have a very good education,” Silva said.

In a time when so many parents don’t have extended family nearby to help them raise their children, Wu hopes the city can help combat isolation and build community too. “It’s just too hard, even as two working parents, to make all the pieces fit together,” she said. “You need a larger village.”

It’s the thinking behind Wu’s “Connect Learn Explore” initiative, a free program that’s taught 9,000 kids to bike and nearly 12,000 to swim. And it’s also behind one of Wu’s proudest accomplishments: Boston Family Days, which grants all city residents with children free access to Boston’s cultural institutions on the first two Sundays of the month.

“We’re making it so that you just don’t have to worry about whether you can get into certain programs or find certain opportunities for your kids,” Wu said. “And then finding lots of ways to bring people together.”

Tutko-Balena loves Family Days, and used it to take her kids to the Children’s Museum last month. She said she wants more opportunities to connect with all of the city’s neighborhoods, so that people feel less segregated.

“I think if the city takes care of its people, the people will take care of it,” she said.

Making Boston more family-friendly can pay economic dividends, too, said Jason Kelly, cofounder and CEO of Ginkgo Bioworks. The 44-year-old entrepreneur has a 13-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son. He’s raising them in Beacon Hill, and says having a mother of three as a mayor matters when it comes to encouraging people to stay, and start companies, in Boston.

“I tell founders all the time ‘remember, you’re going to have kids some day. You should think about the city you want to raise your kids in,’ ” he said.

But for some, the decision to have children can mean making hard choices.

A lifelong Bostonian who works in biotech, Nya grew up in Dorchester and inherited her family’s home in Melville Park (her father paid $178,000 for it in 1988). Nya, who asked for her last name to be withheld to protect her privacy, is 37 and hopes to start a family soon. But even with housing secured, she’s struggling to see how the math can work.

She and her partner have contemplated moving to Washington, D.C., or perhaps Georgia, somewhere they can envision their money going further. She’d love to stay in the city where she grew up, but worries she won’t be able to raise her child here.

“You work really hard to earn your six-figure salary and now it’s become obsolete,” she said. “People at the state and city level lack a true understanding of the Boston economy and what is fueling it.”

Wu says she does, and she’s trying everything she can to make it easier for people like Nya to stay. But she knows it’s an uphill battle. She’s had enough hard conversations with friends telling her they’re leaving the city.

“It’s such a consequential choice to make,” she said. “A lot goes into it. I think sometimes people try to tell me after it’s too late.”

It was December of 1985 and four-year-old Reggie Nguyenwas adjusting to his new life in Dorchester. It was radically different from anything he had ever known, with snow falling from the sky, and other instances of what felt then like magic.

Reggie and his family were among the third and final wave of “Boat People” to flee Vietnam in the aftermath of the Vietnam war. His strongest memory of the weeks they passed in limbo in a Philippines refugee camp was of a food delivery truck. Every week it came around and the drivers would hand out food with nothing asked in return.

One day that winter, the doorbell rang. There on the doorstep sat a cardboard box. Reggie did not know what to think of this unexpected delivery, except that it was “a gigantic box for a four -year-old.”

Part of him was apprehensive. Just a week earlier, some neighborhood kids had thrown a brick through a window of their home.

But excitement and curiosity won out and Reggie brought the package inside. Opening it, he found action figures, toy trucks and cars, and a strange object that he later learned was a model space shuttle. Being unable to read the letter that accompanied the presents, all Reggie knew then was that he was thrilled.

He especially loved the space shuttle. The Voyager 2 spacecraft was about to make history with its exploration of Uranus and the boy would develop a fascination with the cosmos. The toy fed his sense of wonder, and allowed him to interact with American popular culture. When he started school the next year, he already had shared interests with his classmates.

Back then, his mother worked as a seamstress in Chinatown, where his parents eventually opened a clothing store. Reggie had no concept of Western holiday traditions. The sudden appearance of this mysterious collection of playthings seemed truly a miracle. But it was Globe Santa, made possible through intentional acts of kindness.

Reggie suspects that the Catholic charity that sponsored his family’s immigration applied to Globe Santa on his and his little brother’s behalf. Open-hearted donors sent in money. The Boston Globe was dedicated to ensuring that kids like Reggie had moments of holiday magic.

Nearly 40 years later, Reggie Nguyen, now 44, is a full-time manager for the Brookline Food Pantry. His career is centered on helping struggling families access food and other essential resources.

The pantry serves over 700 households each week—families who, like the Nguyens 40 years ago, are navigating financial hardships. Through Brookline Thrives, a subsidiary of the Pantry, more than 500 students bring home weekend food bags throughout the school year.

When Reggie told pantry volunteers that he was a former Globe Santa recipient, it came to light that many of them were donors. “They told me that they were glad it went to someone; that it made a difference. And oh, it did.”

For Reggie, Globe Santa was more than just “a very fond personal memory” from his first ever Christmas. In retrospect, he knows that Globe Santa’s impact on him lasted much longer than the actual presents.

School scholarships allowed Reggie to pursue his education. He went on to earn a bachelor’s degree in English Literature from UMass Boston.

Before joining the team at the Brookline Food Pantry, Reggie worked at Rosie’s Place, a women’s shelter in Boston. His conviction that helping others matters more than accumulating wealth has been constantly reaffirmed ever since he was just a boy excited about outer space.

The older he gets, Reggie reflects, the more he appreciates that Globe Santa “was something genuinely sweet that happened to me as a young person...bringing joy to a child is precious and that in itself is worth supporting.”
