Hall’s family was one of 300 receiving free holiday gifts at the Teen Center Wednesday. At the event, top city and religious officials spoke about the importance of charity, especially during the holiday season.

“What’s most important is people and making sure that everybody is taken care of,” Mayor Michelle Wu said. “If government can be there to help people, if [the] community can come together to help each other ... then the city of Boston is always going to be OK.”

“It’s a beautiful thing to do in a beautiful place, to act with compassion and solidarity, one for another,” Boston Archbishop Richard Henning said.

The event was hosted by Catholic Charities Boston, with support from the Boston Police Department and the Mayor Thomas M. Menino Fund for Boston.

Menino served as mayor from 1993 until January 2014. He died on Oct. 30, 2014. Two of his grandchildren, Samantha and Taylor Menino, now run the toy drive.

In 1993, it began when Menino, Boston’s then newly-elected Mayor, decided to load up his truck with toys for kids in Dorchester on Christmas Eve.

“At that time, the whole Bowdoin and Geneva [area] was not a very good place for people to live,” said Menino’s widow, Angela. “He would pass out the toys to the kids ... he wanted to assure the people that he would be taking care of and helping them.”

“It started off in the back of a Tahoe ... and now it’s grown to this,” said Thomas Menino’s son, Tommy Menino.

The families receiving gifts previously filled out “wish list” forms provided by the Teen Center, according to Samantha Menino.

“They give an age, and they ask like a desired toy, and then they usually put their size for clothes and shoes,” she said. “A lot of kids ask for bikes, Legos, board games.”

On Wednesday, a few dozen brand new bicycles lined the back of a gymnasium and white bags full of gifts dotted the sides. Police officers spoke jovially to one another and smiled against the wind as snow began to fall in the parking lot outside the center.

“I got a 14-year-old here, he attends the teen center,” said Maria Rivera, 63, of Dorchester. “You know they’re safe here. They get fed, they do activities, get help with their homework.

“They’re mentors for our community,” she added.

Rivera, who was picking up headphones, video games, and clothes for her grandchildren and foster children, said she relies on the support of the community to make sure her loved ones get gifts.

“Our community, we’re together, we’re united,” she said. “We’re caring about each other.”

His effort has made him not only a fixture of his neighborhood’s holiday season, but also one of the longest-serving volunteer bell ringers in Massachusetts.

Nearly every year, Hennigan stands outside the Roche Bros. supermarket on Centre Street in West Roxbury. The location was his idea — he approached the store years ago, knowing it had a history of supporting community efforts, including food drives for Mary Mulvey Jacobson’s Families in Need, another organization with which he has long volunteered and now coordinates.

“They lean over backwards to make it work for us,” Hennigan said. “It’s a good partnership.”

But Hennigan didn’t set out to build a tradition.

Nearly 30 years ago, he was watching television when a news segment aired about the Salvation Army struggling to find volunteers.

That struck him.

“That shouldn’t be the case,” he recalled thinking.

At the time, Hennigan was juggling a full schedule. He was running his own insurance business in West Roxbury, serving on the board of the local YMCA, and raising two young children, both under the age of 3, with his wife.

Volunteering was always part of his life, he said — something he grew up with.

“I was always told by my parents that you do things for your community, for your neighbors, because it’s the right thing to do,” Hennigan said.

So when he saw the call for volunteers, he said, it wasn’t a question of whether he could help, but how — and how soon.

“It’s a natural instinct that I have, truthfully,” he said. “There wasn’t even another thought.”

The next day, Hennigan called the Salvation Army and offered to coordinate volunteers from West Roxbury.

When they asked him what days he wanted to help, he said he’d work every day of the season.

And he did.

That first year, Hennigan began making phone calls across the community — to friends, family members, neighbors, business owners, church leaders, and local officials — asking if people could give just one hour of their time and whether they knew others willing to do the same.

In the early years, Hennigan often filled in himself when volunteer slots went unclaimed, sometimes ringing the bell for multiple hours a day while still running his insurance agency. Today, still running his company, he continues to ring, but much of his time is spent coordinating others.

The red kettle season begins the first week of December and runs through Christmas Eve.

But for Hennigan, the work begins in November, when he pulls out his binder of names and phone numbers and begins making calls.

“If someone sees my name pop up in late November, they already know why I’m calling,” he said. “I’ve had people answer the phone and say, ‘What day do you need me?’ before I even ask.”

The ringing itself is simple. There are no scripted pitches or pressure tactics. Holiday music plays through a speaker, and a sign lists the volunteer on duty for each hour.

The daily setup and breakdown are Hennigan’s responsibility. Each morning, around 8:30 am, he heads to the Roche Bros. customer service desk to retrieve the kettle and stand and place them outside. Smaller items, including the speakers that play Christmas music, the signs, and bells, he stores at his home. At the end of the day, around 6 p.m., he returns to put everything away.

Among the volunteers Hennigan has recruited is Barbara Van Dyke, 70, a retired nurse practitioner who has volunteered at the kettle for more than a decade. Van Dyke first heard about the opportunity through her involvement with the West Roxbury Library, but she said it was Hennigan who kept her coming back.

“He’s always been an important person in the community,” Van Dyke said. “He’s generous with his time. Lots of energy. There’s very little that he doesn’t do.”

Over the years, Hennigan estimates hundreds of volunteers have filled shifts at the kettle. According to the Massachusetts division of the Salvation Army, Hennigan has raised more than $800,000 during his time, through his own shifts as well as ones that he’s filled with other volunteers.

Captain Shakai Drigo, 37, a social services supervisor and pastor with the Salvation Army’s Boston Kroc Center, said coordinating volunteers for the Red Kettle Campaign is often one of the most challenging parts of the holiday season. Hennigan’s long-running, community-based approach, he said, has made the Roche Bros. site the only one in West Roxbury to be consistently staffed year after year.

Earlier this year, Hennigan’s efforts were recognized with The Salvation Army’s Al MacLeod Outstanding Volunteer Award — an honor he insists belongs to the community rather than himself.

“They recognize me, but it’s really all the volunteers,” he said.

Some of the most memorable moments for Hennigan come not from large donations, but from conversations. He said people frequently stop to donate and share stories about receiving help from the Salvation Army.

“They tell me their families got food or clothing when they needed it,” he said. “That’s happened many times over the years. It makes your day.”

Hennigan’s now four children, all adults, grew up volunteering with him.

His daughter, Maeve Hennigan, 26, of Denver said some of her earliest childhood memories are of her and her siblings putting on their Santa hats and ringing the bells at Roche Bros.

“We were born into this organization,” she said, referring to the Salvation Army.

She said she can’t recall a time when her dad wasn’t doing something to help others. “He is never sitting still if he’s not working. If he has a spare second, he’s dedicating that to helping others. He’s always up and at ‘em. He strives to make the world a better place.”

Hennigan’s earliest memories of Christmas are also connected to the Salvation Army. He would visit downtown Boston before Christmas Eve with his family, and his mother would hand him and his sisters change to place in the red kettles.

Now, every Christmas, when the final bell rings and the kettle is packed away, Hennigan returns to his normal routine. But the break is temporary.

Come November, the binder comes back out — and the phone starts ringing again.

Harnois is an elementary school teacher in Boston Public Schools; together she and her husband make $175,000 a year. And their monthly rental costs are modest, considerably less than the typical household around here.

“If homes here cost $400,000, we’d be homeowners,” said Harnois, who is 32.

Such is reality now for Greater Boston’s next generation, particularly younger and middle class people.

The cost of buying a home has been steadily rising for decades, and recently it has exploded, growing far faster than incomes.

The typical house in Greater Boston sold for $833,900 in the second quarter of 2025, more than 7.5 times the region’s median household income. Five years ago, a household needed to earn $126,519 a year to afford the median-priced single-family home in this region, according to an analysis by Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Today, that figure has more than doubled, to $259,648.

The result is people who 20, 10, or even 5 years ago would have been able to purchase a home — teachers, nurses, and academics — can hardly even conceive of it.

“The door to homeownership in the Boston area has really been shut,” said Daniel McCue, a senior research associate at Harvard’s housing studies center. “There are hundreds of thousands of people here staring at these numbers saying, ‘Who can actually afford this?’ ”

The consequences are being felt by an entire generation, forced to make a choice their parents did not: Stay in Massachusetts, and rent forever, or leave, and put down roots somewhere less expensive.

“We work really hard, and we feel like we’ve done everything right,” said Harnois. “It is difficult to accept that there is no pathway for us to own a home in the neighborhood I’ve spent my whole life in.”

Since the 1940s, when the 30-year mortgage emerged and made home buying more accessible to many workers, owning a home has been a symbol of success. To achieve the American dream was to work hard, save up, and buy a house, which would serve as both a stable home and a valuable asset that would appreciate with time. For many working class families in Massachusetts, homeownership was the ticket to the middle class.

It was exactly that path that Ben Watts hoped to follow.

Growing up, Watts’s parents did not own their home, a fact he became aware of when he visited friends’ houses as a kid. As he got older, he came to assume that he, someday, would.

“It was ingrained,” said Watts. “That’s what you’re supposed to do, right?”

Now his goal has collided with economic reality. Watts, who is 33, works three jobs — as a bartender and for a French spirits company — and earns nearly $90,000 a year. His rent for a two-bedroom apartment in Belmont, which he splits with his fiancé, is $2,850.

Watts has effectively given up on owning a home. He can hardly find any listings on Zillow for less than $700,000, at least not ones that look like they wouldn’t require tens of thousands of dollars in maintenance. At that cost, Watts would be more than doubling his monthly housing payment, and likely paying at least half of his income toward a mortgage. And that’s after a six-figure down payment, cash he simply does not have.

The prevailing feeling, he said, is resentment.

“I’m being priced out because I’m working to try and make the city that I love better with great bars and restaurants,” said Watts, who grew up in Arlington. “It feels like I’m being told that there’s no place for me here anymore.”

Perhaps what is most frustrating to people like Watts: They know it wasn’t always like this.

Home prices have been on the rise for decades. But the biggest shift in housing affordability began in the aftermath of the pandemic, as home prices rose even faster, and mortgage rates more than doubled, leaving prospective buyers to pay both sky-high total price tags and huge monthly payments.

In 2010, for example, the median home price was $360,800, but the average on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 4.75 percent, meaning the mortgage payment on that median-priced house was only $1,816 a month, almost the same as it was in 2000. Now, with a median house price of $833,900, and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage around 6.79 percent in the second quarter of the year, the monthly mortgage payment on that median-priced house is $5,240 a month — before homeowners insurance, property tax, and mortgage insurance, which can tack on $1,500 more each month.

The shift is pricing a startling number of would-be homeowners out of the market. Roughly 100,000 people who made enough money to afford an entry-level home in 2021 could no longer afford that home in 2025, according to data from Boston Indicators.

“Tell me how many people can afford to buy an almost million dollar single-family home?” said Gail Latimore, executive director of the Codman Square Community Development Corporation. “Tell me how many people can afford to buy an $800,000 house and pay $5,000 a month for the mortgage? We’ve always been an expensive area, but this is unmanageable.”

What happens when so many people are priced out of homeownership all at once?

Right now, a generational wealth divide is emerging, said Albert Saiz, an associate professor of urban economics and real estate at MIT.

While 50 years ago, nearly half of young adults age 25 to 34 in Massachusetts owned a home, today barely one-third do, and a recent analysis by Boston Indicators suggests the true rate is even lower, roughly 24 percent. Those people who were able to buy in the 1970s, ’80s, and ’90s have seen their investments turn into a launching pad for generational wealth: Those homes, in many cases, are now million-dollar nest eggs that have double or tripled in value, particularly in Boston and its suburbs.

“Unless we do something about housing stock — building, building, building — this is a dangerous situation for working class folks who used to depend on housing as their main way to accumulate wealth,” said Saiz.

Take Coire Jones, 38, who makes almost $50,000 doing administrative work at a real estate law firm. Jones sets aside roughly $200 a month, mostly by cutting out extraneous spending, and by choosing to rent a small room in an apartment in Somerville for just $750 a month.

This is not how he pictured things going. Jones’s family has been in Massachusetts for generations, and he loves it here. He graduated from college with a history degree in 2009, in the middle of the Great Recession, and struggled to find a job.

He’s now switched career paths and found stable income. But Jones can do the math. He knows that at his current income, he’ll never be able to afford even a tiny home of his own.

“We millennials were told that you could be whatever you wanted to be and if you went to college you’d be in the middle class,” he said. “I don’t mind renting for the rest of my life. But the foundation of the American economy is that everyone buys a house, and that equity allows you to do a lot of different things and achieve financial stability. And that no longer exists for my generation.”

That doesn’t stop people from trying.

Every year, 200 to 250 people enroll in first-time homebuyer classes at the Chinatown-based Asian Community Development Corporation, one of countless groups that aim to teach would-be buyers the ropes of mortgages, property inspection, and other intricacies of the biggest investment most people will ever make.

In previous years, it was common for 20 to 40 people who took the class to purchase a home, said Angie Liou, the Asian CDC’s executive director. Last year, only six did.

Latimore, of the Codman Square CDC, said a lucky few are able to purchase with the help of down payment and mortgage assistance programs sponsored by the city and other public entities.

Those who aren’t able to buy are left to grapple with what it means that they may never access homeownership.

Some, like Harnois, are willing to stick it out as renters. She is too connected to the neighborhood where she grew up and today works in to consider leaving.

And then there are people like Lillian Rotondo, an East Cambridge resident who works in biotech sales. She said she can’t quite believe the prices of the homes she sees on the market.

She has a familiar story: She and her husband, a chef who works in the Seaport, make good money — roughly $240,000 a year. But it still doesn’t feel like enough to afford a $600,000 or $700,000 place, especially because Rotondo is pregnant with their first child, which they know will be expensive in its own way.

Rotondo’s parents migrated to the US from El Salvador with $20 to their name, she said. Years later, they were able to save up enough to buy a home on Long Island.

It’s important to Rotondo, who is 40, to do the same. And because they cannot afford it here, Rotondo and her husband are going to move, most likely to Rhode Island, somewhere near Providence.

“We have worked hard our entire lives,’ she said. ”We should be able to afford a two-bedroom. So we’ll go somewhere we can.”

Her grandfather lived in China during the Great Chinese Famine, she said, and he witnessed extreme hunger and starvation.

“He would always make sure at the dinner table [that] I finished every last grain, and that’s something that I think is really instilled in me,” Sun said.

His words inspired her to volunteer at First Baptist Church in Jamaica Plain in 2022, where she cooked meals twice a week.

Along the way, she made a startling discovery: community businesses tossing out unsold goods at the end of the day.

“It just felt really rough to me, because I just spent so much time making food, but there was just perfectly fine food being thrown away on the same exact street, so I wanted to try to do something about that,” she said.

Sun and Hennessy, both 17, are seniors at Boston Latin School. Their campaign against food waste began when they were sophomores. The pair asked local businesses to give them the food instead of throwing it out at the end of the night.

They first approached Dunkin’ on Centre Street and then The Real Deal, a family-owned restaurant. And with those willing partners, NoVasta, Latin for “no waste,” was born.

It started out as a small school club whose members volunteer to collect food waste from local businesses and bring it to a drop-off center, such as the church. The club also organizes food drives and raises money to buy items in bulk from wholesalers like Costco.

Over the past two years, NoVasta has become part of the national Zero Waste Coalition. Club chapters have been started at other US schools and abroad.

NoVasta embraces the global goal of reduced food waste and passing legislation to halve food loss and waste by 2030.

“It’s given us a lot of hope to see that even though it’s such a big problem, there are a lot of people — whether it’s students or city councilors or people our age or restaurants — that are willing to work and find ways to contribute to this cause,” Hennessy said.

Nuvana Ivory, who has worked front of house at The Real Deal for two years, has seen Sun and Hennessy come in often to pick up food at the end of the night. The restaurant usually gives any excess food to staff or to homeless people in the area. But the girls’ initiative to eliminate food waste makes her feel good.

“I don’t like to see food go to waste,” she said. “To see the food go to a good cause and not be thrown in the trash is a good opportunity for us to help out.”

Food insecurity is a growing crisis in the United States, with approximately 13.5 percent of US households being food insecure in 2023, up from 12.8 percent in 2022, according to the USDA.

However, while food insecurity is on the rise, millions of tons of food are being thrown away each year, data show.

According to the US Department of Agriculture, food waste makes up between 30 and 40 percent of food supply. In 2019, 66 million tons of food waste were generated in the United States, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

The growing problem prompted Boston City Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata and others to propose an ordinance in 2023 to create a citywide food recovery program.

“More or less of what [is] safe to consume could go to neighborhoods such as East Boston, Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, High Park that remain underserved by a lack of grocery stores or forcing residents to travel to food pantries on their days off or when they have work,” Zapata said.

Programs to address food waste have been adopted in other cities, such as Washington D.C. Zapata has been working with Sun and Hennessy to try to implement a city-wide food recovery program, which would be established with the ordinance that councilors are working to pass.

“It would compel some of these large food generators to compile their edible leftovers, and then as an effort to utilize what is safe to consume at its highest possible use before it’s sent to be recycled or sent to the landfill,” Zapata said.

While NoVasta started as a school club, it has grown into an international initiative to “turn excess into access.” Through online forums and social media, Sun and Hennessy were able to connect with other high schoolers who noticed the same patterns in their communities: food going to waste while people were going hungry.

“[Students] saw the same overflowing dumpsters in their community, and they saw the same like empty hands on the street that were always just [a few] feet away. So every single student we talked to noticed the same issue in their own city, and they’ve sort of just been waiting for a catalyst to start it. And so we’re really happy that we were that catalyst for them,” Sun said.

Big players like Aman aren’t all out of tricks, however, and in fact such established brands are still the options consumers trust most when they’re visiting a less familiar destination or planning a once-in-a-lifetime trip. The group’s opening in Mexico will help cement the rise of the eastern cape of Baja California, about 90 minutes from Los Cabos. It’s away from the thumping clubs on a less developed section of coastline that claims a rare amenity in this corner of Mexico: swimmable beaches. Meanwhile, Singita, the most renowned luxury safari camp operator in Africa, is finally planting its flag in one of the most desirable private concessions of Botswana’s wildlife-rich Okavango Delta at the end of 2026, a dream combination for safari connoisseurs.

When big brands come to big markets, they have to pull out all the stops. So in London, Waldorf Astoria will transform the landmark Admiralty Arch into the latest jewel in its crown — just one year after wrapping a jaw-dropping $2 billion, eight-year renovation of its New York flagship. But even then it may not be the biggest opening in town. The smart money is on Cambridge House, a Georgian gem overlooking Green Park that’s currently being converted by Auberge Collection. With so much early buzz, snagging a room the minute reservations open may be your best odds at getting in.

When: January

Where: Palm Beach, Florida

Palm Beach has its fair share of luxury hotels. But the Vineta is the American debut from Oetker Hotels, the European group behind Parisian palace Le Bristol. It’s a brand known for continental elegance, old-world glamour and impeccable service — qualities that aren’t typically native to South Florida. Now it’s setting up shop blocks away from the posh boutiques of Worth Avenue, in a Mediterranean-revival-style building that’s been standing for a hundred years.

Its extensive renovation has made for 41 spacious suites, with bedrooms decorated in soft pastels to fit the building’s heritage and pale-pink exterior. In a touch of whimsy, staffers will wheel bar carts around the hotel’s public spaces. One is dedicated to Champagne and another to poolside scoops of gelato. A third will be stocked with Barbara Sturm beauty products, delivering creams and serums to guests’ rooms so they can leave the hotel with not just a tan but also a radiant glow. Rooms from $1,497.

When: March

Where: Kyoto, Japan

It’s been three decades since homegrown Japanese luxury company Imperial opened a new property. That changes in spring 2026, with its update of a 90-year-old former theater in Kyoto’s famed Gion district. The main building has been respectfully preserved, with elements from the former performance space, including its distinct pillars and window frames, retained as visual focal points. A guests-only rooftop bar offers sweeping views of the cityscape and the lanterns’ glow on the streets below.

The Imperial’s 55 rooms use traditional materials such as Japanese cedar columns and tatami flooring, with design by local firms rather than imported big names, as has become the norm in town. The result is something more subtle, and more faithfully and authentically Japanese than the area’s shiny competition. From around $1,100.

When: Spring

Where: South of France

When French spirits entrepreneur Paul Ricard purchased Île de Bendor — off the coast of rosé capital Bandol — in the 1950s, it was just an empty plot. He transformed the stony island into a socialite playground where Russian cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin and artist Salvador Dalí would visit. Now the Ricard family is turning its vacation home into a destination for modern luxury travelers. There will be a 93-room hotel but also a little village with three restaurants, four bars, an art gallery and artisan shops open to the public.

Days on the 17-acre island can be spent playing pétanque, relaxing at the 1,200-square-meter (12,900-square-foot) spa or scuba diving (the hotel will have a dive center run in partnership with the Cousteau family). A ten-minute ferry will take guests to the mainland to explore Provencal vineyards, cobblestone villages and the region’s famed farmers markets. From around $600.

When: Spring

Where: Baja California, Mexico

Ultraluxe Aman is making a splash with its first Mexican hotel, with 18 casitas on a hillside along the quiet east cape of Baja California. Because Aman loyalists are often somewhat reclusive, choosing to hide away in their posh digs, each casita will include expansive views of the Sea of Cortez and the Sierra de la Laguna mountains, plus private pools flanked with plush loungers. The spa, one of the highlights of any Aman resort, will feature a modern temescal (sweat lodge), in a nod to local traditions.

One of the benefits of being here versus bustling Cabo is that the beaches of the east cape are very swimmable, with less strong currents, ideal for days spent exploring the gentle waters. Nearby is a golf course designed by the renowned Robert Trent Jones II, as well as 18 acres of organic farms and orchards to explore. Rates not currently available.

When: Second quarter

Where: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

The futuristic overwater bungalows in Saudi Arabia’s glimmering new Red Sea development are getting fresh competition in an unlikely location: the busy, traffic-clogged capital. It’s here that the kingdom’s royal residence — built in 1943 as the home of the country’s founding father, King Abdulaziz Al Saud, and famous for its art deco architecture — will open to the public as a 70-room hotel. Historic spaces that hosted royal celebrations and state banquets will become reception suites, each one scented with King Saud’s favorite flower, the native Taif rose.

In another display of discretion, the spa is also made up exclusively of private suites, with each treatment room sporting its own changing area, sauna and steam room. And as part of the royal experience, guests will have palace hosts who cater to their every request, within reason. Rates not currently available.

When: March

Where: Charleston, South Carolina

Charleston has long been beloved for its gracious Southern architecture, miles of white flowering magnolia trees and rich Lowcountry cuisine — but now it’s one of the top 2026 destinations for the ways in which it keeps raising the bar. The Cooper, for instance, will be the first hotel in town to marry all the amenities of an urban resort with a waterfront location, making it feel almost like a beach retreat within the city itself.

Among its draws will be a 7,000-square-foot wellness center, five restaurants and a rooftop infinity pool, plus preferential access to a yearlong chef’s residence by Daniel Humm (of Eleven Madison Park fame) at sibling hotel Charleston Place. And of course, seeing the city from the water will be a unique experience worth prioritizing too: Guests will have access to a private marina with cruising vessels to tour the shoreline, as well as a water taxi to Daniel Island. From $950.

When: Spring

Where: London

London’s wildly competitive hotel market is getting a stellar new entrant, in a landmark building in Mayfair that was formerly home to a prince and a prime minister. The design of the 102 rooms and common spaces will channel the opulence of the Georgian era with intricate original ceiling designs, 19-foot-high ceilings and ornate fireplaces. They’ll overlook King Charles III’s current residence, with windows facing the greenery of the parks.

In keeping with its knack for decadent spas, Auberge is adding a wellness area inspired by ancient Roman bathhouses that’s set to span two floors, including a pair of heated swimming pools — a rarity in central London — and a relaxation area with a firepit. A new Major Food Group restaurant might not be the deciding factor in a booking for New Yorkers, but it will likely make Cambridge House a hot spot for Londoners in a similar way the new Carbone at the Chancery Rosewood has elsewhere in Mayfair. Rates not yet available.

When: May

Where: Cartagena, Colombia

Cartagena’s hotel scene — mostly composed of boutique spots in the new city, plus one stunning Sofitel behind the historic ramparts — is getting a big luxury upgrade this spring. Four Seasons, a brand still riding its White Lotus high, is taking over (and unifying) eight buildings including a 16th century San Franciscan temple and the 1920s Beaux Arts Club Cartagena, an old social hotbed. Inside will be 131 rooms and eight bars and restaurants, including a speakeasy and a steakhouse.

Guests can sign up for salsa lessons led by professional dancers, then cool down in one of the rooftop’s two swimming pools. As for the rooms, they’ll start at a spacious 388 square feet, many with balconies overlooking the old cloisters. Consider it the best of both worlds: old Colombian charm and all the modern creature comforts. Rooms from around $800.

When: June

Where: Florence, Italy

La Réserve’s first Italian hotel is located on the Via Santo Spirito, a street lined with Renaissance-era buildings and artisan workshops. It took a meticulous four-year renovation and a collaboration with celebrated designers Gilles & Boissier to transform the 600-year-old palazzo into a luxe hotel, but the result includes frescoed ceilings, ornate tilework, arched windows and the best of Italian craftsmanship, in a nod to the history and art-world heritage that defines Florence.

There are just six standalone apartments in one- to three-bedroom configurations. All have full kitchens and separate living areas, plus access to a gym, library and lounge. There’s also a roof terrace where you can sip on the region’s wines, as well as a “secret bar” to explore in the heritage building. Experiences will include Tuscan culinary adventures and the opportunity to play tennis at the owner’s Florentine house, truly making guests feel at home on the city’s storied streets. Rates not yet available.

When: Fourth quarter

Where: Oman

Rather than a single hotel, this is a trio of ultraluxe lodges forming a circuit — giving guests an easy way to explore an entire country in the most streamlined and amenity-rich way possible. (We’ve noted these circuits as one of the most compelling trends in travel right now.) The Malkai will have one tented camp in the sweeping sands of Oman’s desert and another in the coastal farmlands; the final lodge will be up in the jagged Al Hajar Mountains. The camps include spas and marble swimming pools in dramatic shades of dark red and beige. And unlike most hotels, these can’t be booked individually. Instead itineraries spanning all three lodges will last 4 to 10 days.

In a unique twist, guests will get paired with a personal so-called murshid, a butler who doubles as a driver. They’ll guide guests on every leg of their big Omani sojourn, shuttling them from lodge to lodge in Land Rover Defenders and arranging all sorts of adventures along the way, be it dune-bashing in the desert or snorkeling off Oman’s coast. Rates not yet available.

When: December

Where: Botswana

Singita has made its reputation as the king of five-star safaris without a lodge in Botswana, one of Africa’s most coveted destinations. So safari insiders are eager to see what the company can achieve now that it’s planting its flag in the famed Okavango Delta, a region made up of wildlife-rich islands, lagoons, grasslands and swamps. The specific area Singita has taken on — the privately managed, 400,000-acre Abu concession, where Wilderness Safaris long ran the iconic Abu Camp — teems with herds of elephants, lions and cheetahs. And its topographical diversity lets guests appreciate the animals from many distinct vantages, including wooden mokoro canoes as well as traditional open-top jeeps, offering a wider range of wildlife adventures.

Now, Culpepper is getting ready to add a new line to his resumé. In January, he will be sworn in to elected office for the first time, representing Roxbury-based District 7 on the Boston City Council.

It’s one of the city’s most diverse and historically marginalized districts, and has faced immense turmoil in the last year. The council seat has sat vacant since July, when former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson resigned after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges.

The council is often a launchpad for young politicians with ambitions for higher office, but Culpepper, 72, appears to be flipping that script. The council’s only new member will also be its oldest sitting member, and he comes to the body with decades of advocacy, legal, ministerial, and political experience.

Culpepper said his longstanding community work won him voters’ support.

“The community wanted a voice that they have heard and they can support and that they have confidence” in, Culpepper said.

Representing a council district is similar to leading a parish: They’re both 24/7 jobs, he said.

“Constituents, they call you when they have emergencies. Same thing with church folks,” he said. “What happens now is I don’t stop doing what I’ve been doing, in terms of helping people.”

The mission to serve has been a driving theme throughout his life, and is a thread of his family history, Culpepper said in a recent interview at his home on Seaver Street.

The house is a piece of history itself: His grandparents faced racism when purchasing it in the early 1950s, and were the first Black homeowners on the road, he said. In the 1960s, his mother and grandmother used the small building in the backyard as a day care. This year, it served as Culpepper’s campaign headquarters.

Culpepper remembers his grandfather sitting in the living room when he heard that Martin Luther King Jr. had been killed. The two had protested together, Culpepper said.

Hearing those stories as a child had a profound impact on him.

“How could you be part of a family that fought for civil rights and not have it as part of who you are?” Culpepper said.

Culpepper wants to bring those values to City Hall. He said he plans to push for an ethics committee on the council, a separate city agency focused solely on homelessness, and increased homeownership opportunities for Section 8 voucher holders.

After graduating from Boston Public Schools’ English High School in 1971, Culpepper earned his undergraduate degree from Brandeis University and got involved in politics while getting his law degree from Suffolk University.

He worked on Senator Ted Kennedy’s 1980 run for president and Bill Clinton’s White House bid in 1992. In Washington, D.C., Culpepper worked on Capitol Hill and earned a divinity degree from Howard University in 1988.

By 1995, Culpepper had moved from Washington to Milton with his wife and two young sons, and taken a job as a top lawyer for the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. He also became the senior pastor at the Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church, which his grandfather founded in 1939.

Contentious divorce proceedings between Culpepper and his wife briefly divided the church community in 1999, with some parishioners filing a lawsuit to bar Culpepper from church property, while others fiercely defended him, according to a Globe report from the time.

Culpepper’s ex-wife accused him of verbal and emotional abuse, while Culpepper got two restraining orders against her. A judge dismissed the parishioners’ lawsuit against Culpepper less than a month after it was filed.

In Boston’s Black communities and in many political circles, Culpepper is known for his work at HUD and for his civic leadership.

“He’s a very visible person; he’s out in the community a lot,” said Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a native Roxbury resident and political consultant who’s known Culpepper for decades. “He brings a wealth of experience ... [and] has shown his love for the community.”

At HUD, Culpepper sued the Boston Housing Authority for alleged discrimination against tenants of color in the 1990s. It led the city to adopt new civil rights protections.

Culpepper also worked to curb youth violence, particularly after the death of 20-year-old Jahmol Norfleet, a onetime gang member who was shot to death in 2006. Norfleet was killed just months after he and other youth leaders, with the help of Black ministers, including Culpepper, brokered a peace deal between two rival gangs. Norfleet’s death inspired Culpepper to start the Trotter Park Peace Program, which provided activities and paid job opportunities for at-risk youth.

Antoine Goforth, now 39, was Norfleet’s best friend and also involved in a local gang. He said the Trotter Park Peace Program, and his relationship with Culpepper, changed his life. Not only did Culpepper work to get kids jobs and keep them out of trouble, he also developed relationships with them, listened, and earned their respect.

“Whenever we need help with something, he’d be the first person we’d call,” Goforth said. “If Reverend Culpepper wasn’t around, I’d probably be in jail or dead or something like that.”

Cedric White, a close friend and former colleague of Culpepper’s at HUD, said his dedication to advocacy and his community have not waned in the more than two decades they’ve known each other.

“He’s not one to sit around and be idle,” White said. “If there’s an issue that’s not right, he wants to be there to help the cause and stand up for the people.”

In recent years, Culpepper has rallied Black ministers to encourage their communities to get the COVID-19 vaccine, and started a small church farm to grow and distribute free fresh produce. He led protests against the closures of several Walgreens pharmacies in Black neighborhoods, and organized support for migrant families when the state had to temporarily house them in Roxbury’s Melnea Cass Recreation Center.

He also stayed involved in politics, praying over Senator Elizabeth Warren before debates during her presidential run in 2020. After weighing a run for mayor in 2013, Culpepper lost a race for state Senate in 2022.

He said he had no plans to run for office again, until community leaders urged him to run for the District 7 council seat last year.

Joseph Feaster Jr., who has known Culpepper since they worked on Kennedy’s 1994 Senate campaign, said Culpepper’s experience in politics and housing policy, plus his care for the community, will make him an effective councilor.

“Politics requires the ability to oftentimes compromise in order to get what you need to get done for the greater good,” Feaster said. Culpepper’s “going to be able to state his position, he will be able to articulate it well, but he’s also prepared to listen, and that’s the quality many don’t have.”

On Sunday, Nigerians living in Greater Boston said the sentiment at home is split. Some think the United States is intervening for its own economic and political interests.

“It’s not genuine,” said Kamalu MacPhilips, a devout Christian from eastern Nigeria, standing outside St. Katharine Drexel Parish in Dorchester.

“Trump did not do this because he wants to save Christians, he wants something for himself,” he said. “His mind is always on money, and somehow, he thinks he’s going to get something.”

The United States coordinated with the Nigerian government to launch a series of airstrikes late Thursday against what it called “ISIS terrorists” in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto state where the Lakurawa, a small jihadist group, operates. The number of people injured or killed is unclear, but the US Africa Command said in a statement that initial assessment showed “multiple ISIS terrorists were killed in the ISIS camps.”

Other Nigerians here said that violence affects all residents of the country — and the Nigerian government hasn’t done enough to stop it.

“I’m not a fan of Trump, but people are dying, so he bombed,” said Ifeyinwa Izuchi, who left eastern Nigeria in 1977. “Maybe now the Nigerian government will do something.”

Victoria Awogboro, a Newton resident originally from western Nigeria, said the attack might give Nigerians in the United States a greater sense of security when traveling home.

“The help is needed because this has been going on for a long time and our military seems overwhelmed,” said Awogboro. “If the help is coming now and it’s channeled properly in collaboration with the [Nigerian] government and the military, then that’s a welcome development.”

Standing to her left, Izuchi nodded in agreement, adding that safety concerns while visiting Nigeria have grown in recent years.

“If I want to go home, I’m afraid of kidnapping and terrorists,” she said. “In a country that doesn’t allow its people to carry arms, you have [extremists] walking in the streets with AK-47s and nobody’s stopping them.

“At least now the world is paying attention.”

Trump initially claimed terrorists in the region were targeting Christians in November and threatened military action if the Nigerian government failed to address the alleged religious persecution.

But Trump’s assertion of widespread Christian persecution belies the complicated reality on the ground in Nigeria, one expert said.

“The claims there are that many Christians are specifically targeted for their faith is very, very exaggerated,” said Ladd Serwat, an Africa senior analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, which has monitored the expansion of jihadist groups across Nigeria since 1997.

Data show that 507 Christians died from political violence since 2020, out of a total 53,000 Christians and Muslims since 2009, according to the group.

“Insurgent groups such as Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa often present their campaigns as anti-Christian, but in practice their violence is indiscriminate and devastates entire communities,” Serwat said.

Some of the violence in the region also stems from both economic and religious tensions. Christian farmers and Muslim herders compete for scarce resources, noted Judd Devermont, an Africa Program senior adviser for the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The epicenter of violence in Nigeria is in the northeast, Devermont said, whereas most Nigerian immigrants to the United States hail from southern Nigeria.

While some local groups in Nigeria have direct ties to global extremist organizations, including Al Qaeda and ISIS, others are unaffiliated but embrace the goals of international terrorist organizations, Devermont said.

One of the most prominent terrorist groups in the region is Boko Haram, which has expressed solidarity with Al Qaeda, according to the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

The extremist group Lakurawa — which is increasing ties to both the Islamic State and Al Qaeda — is known to operate in Sokoto state, where the United States carried out the strikes.

Devermont called the location of the strikes “a little strange” given Trump’s stated motivation.

“It’s in an area where it’s 90 to 95 percent Muslims,” said Devermont, a former senior director of African affairs at the National Security Council. “It’s not the epicenter of extremist violence.”

MacPhilips said the location of the strikes also raised his suspicions.

“In the north, where the bomb fell, those guys had not seen Boko Haram or anything at all,” he said.

Nimi Wariboko, Walter G. Muelder Professor of Social Ethics and director of the Africa Studies Center at Boston University, said he doubts Trump carried out the attack for “altruistic purposes.”

The nation, and Western powers in general, have economic and strategic interests in Nigeria, he said.

Beyond that, Trump can use messaging that he is protecting Christians around the world to curry favor with his supporters.

“Trump is playing to the evangelical base at home here. He is playing the strong hand of the global defender of Christians and Christianity, and this plays well for his domestic politics,” Wariboko said.

It’s unlikely last week’s strikes alone will help curb terrorist activity in the region, experts said, as such military interventions rarely root out the issues that cause radicalization in the first place.

“Strikes in and of themselves are insufficient,” Devermont said. “It has to be paired with efforts to address what the drivers of extremism are.”

Wariboko said the strikes are “just the beginning.”

“Intelligence and news accounts suggest that the United States may strike again,” he said.

As another year winds down, forecasts for what comes next are everywhere.

But for the economy, 2026 is shaping up less as a fresh start than as a sequel. The big storylines from 2025 — about jobs, artificial intelligence, and tariffs — have yet to be resolved. Mounting frustration with the high cost of living is poised to be a pivotal issue in November’s midterm elections.

When the ball drops in Times Square on Wednesday night, the TV chyron should read “To be continued.”

Where things stand: Government data released this month after shutdown-related delays offer a snapshot of an economy that looks strong on the surface but fragile underneath.

Gross domestic product expanded at a 4.3 percent annual rate in the third quarter, the fastest pace in two years. Solid gains in consumer spending and exports offset a decline in residential and business investment.

But the top-line numbers mask signs of cooling.

Unemployment is rising and inflation remains elevated. Wage growth is easing and households are saving less than they did earlier in the year, suggesting that incomes aren’t keeping pace with rising costs.

“While top level growth of 4.3 percent looks good prima facie, there are some troubling signs when you pop open the hood,” Boston College economist Brian Bethune said in a note.

Still, the probability of recession remains low — 30 percent, according to economists tracked by Bloomberg, down from 40 percent after President Trump rolled out his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April.

Jobs: The labor market has been sluggish and is expected to remain so next year.

Employers added more than a million fewer jobs in the first 11 months of the year than they did last year. That’s despite GDP growth running near its top sustainable pace.

While layoffs have remained relatively tame, an influx of job seekers nudged US unemployment up to 4.6 percent in November, the highest since 2021.

Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell doesn’t see the jobless rate climbing much further, an assessment shared by most private forecasters.

“We won’t see any kind of a sharper downturn” in employment, he told reporters earlier this month.

The Fed’s optimism stems from its belief that interest rates are now low enough to steady the labor market. (Policymakers have cut their benchmark lending rate by 1.75 percentage points to a range of 3.5–3.75 percent since September 2024.)

AI: Artificial intelligence promises to reshape the economy, but its impact on workers remains a big unknown.

Products such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini improved dramatically, speeding adoption by businesses and consumers. Spending on AI hardware, software, and data centers accelerated economic growth. And AI exuberance spilled into the stock market, raising concerns that a bubble is about to burst.

More importantly, AI poses the threat of massive job losses. Many firms have already curtailed hiring as they assess how they will deploy the technology. Some have laid off workers in anticipation of more widespread AI use.

“Despite concerns about widespread job losses, AI adoption is expected to have only a modest and relatively temporary impact on employment levels,” Goldman Sachs researchers wrote in an August report.

At the other extreme, Dario Amodei, chief executive of AI-maker Anthropic, has said AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10–20 percent within five years.

“Without intervention, it’s hard to imagine that there won’t be some significant job impact there. And my worry is that it will be broad, and it will be faster than what we’ve seen with previous technology,” Amodei said in an interview that CBS News’ “60 Minutes” aired in November.

Tariffs: All of this — a cooling labor market and a fast-moving AI transition — is unfolding against the backdrop of disruptive trade policy.

Economists initially warned that Trump’s tariffs — a 10 percent baseline import tax plus rates of up to 40 percent on nearly all US trading partners — would light a fire under inflation or cause a recession. It didn’t happen. The president backed off some tariffs and postponed others, and companies rushed to build up inventories while absorbing some or all of their increased costs.

In 2026, tariffs are expected to be a modest drag on GDP. The Conference Board forecasts that year-over-year growth will slow to 1.3 percent in the fourth quarter of next year, down from 1.7 percent this year.

Tariffs will also keep inflation higher than it would otherwise be as US firms pass on more of their increased costs to customers. In September, the Fed projected that its preferred inflation gauge — which excludes often volatile food and energy costs — would rise 2.6 percent next year, up from a June estimate of 2.4 percent. The central bank’s target is 2 percent.

Final thought: A weak labor market, AI disruption, and tariff headwinds are a recipe for uncertainty but not an imminent recession.

But they may well leave Americans frustrated with a slow-moving economy and high prices, especially if tariffs don’t yield the gains in US jobs that Trump promised. If so, the midterm elections could deliver a harsher-than-usual rebuke to Republicans as the party in power.

It’s been a good year for stocks, though not quite as good as 2023 or 2024.

Going into the final three trading days of 2025, the Standard & Poor’s 500 index had returned 19 percent including dividends. The tech-heavy Nasdaq’s return was 23 percent. For all of last year, the indexes returned 25 percent and 30 percent, respectively.

But even with all the focus on the AI-fueled stock rally, the big gains were found elsewhere this year.

Silver soared 174 percent through Friday, outshining gold, which gained 73. Investors have plowed into both metals as a hedge against political uncertainty and inflation. Silver’s surge also reflects demand from industrial users.

On the downside, the spot price of crude oil at the Cushing, Okla., hub dropped 18 percent. Supply has been steadier than forecast and demand has been weaker than hoped.

After setting a record in October, the bitcoin rally — sparked in part by demand from new exchange traded funds — has faltered. The cryptocurrency was off 6.3 percent for the year as of Friday as investors moved their money to gold, silver, and other better-performing assets.

Is the recession finally here? It is if you take CNN at its word that knee-high sneakers from Boston-based Converse are “possibly the most obvious recession indicator of them all.” CNN linked to a TikTok video showing these too-tall shoes in a shop window, with the caption: “this has gotta be a recession indicator.” One commenter wrote: “If I’m paying for a shoe, I’m getting as much shoe as possible.” The CNN report also mentioned the return of canned goods, coupons, and Lady Gaga. With those indicators in mind, CNN somehow missed the latest release of Kowloon-themed sneakers, designed by Tagz Footwear, and what they say about the state of things.

The hoopla leading up to the supposed launch of a Boston Monopoly game may have exceeded the hype for Monopoly owner Hasbro’s decision to move its headquarters to Boston. But manufacturer Top Trumps USA still doesn’t list a Boston game among its 47 city-themed Monopoly editions. No word on why. For now, we’ll have to be content with the 1990s Boston edition (available on eBay), created when BayBank and Filene’s were still around. Strangely, there’s no space for Dunkin’ Donuts, Boston’s closest thing to an actual monopoly.

The Trump-era tariffs made life tough for those in the logistics and shipping industry. Good thing we have drug companies like Takeda around to lighten the mood. Takeda announced plans to be the first biopharmaceutical business to use French boat maker Vela Transport’s wind-powered cargo vessel to ship treatments from Europe to the United States. The trips will take two weeks and help Takeda meet its greenhouse gas emissions goals. Test runs start next year on trimarans that look like racing boats but are in fact something else entirely.

Hasbro wasn’t the only company on the move. Welch’s inked a deal to relocate to Waltham from Concord. The fruit-juice cooperative also set its sights on Manhattan by opening a speakeasy in the West Village to highlight its zero-sugar drinks, with ad agency Superdigital. The space was fitted out to look like a New York City bodega, complete with an analog TV on the counter and an animatronic “bodega cat.” This was purely promotional: The pop-up shop “sold” Zero Sugar-themed lip balm and lunchboxes for zero dollars apiece.

Fall in New England means pumpkins, football, foliage, more pumpkins, hayrides, apple-picking, and now “Spidey D.” Just when you thought it was safe to venture into your local Dunks, the ads reappeared on menu boards and social media accounts featuring the spider doughnut character with random misspelled musings. The ad industry swooned over this “unruly spokes-dessert,” and the purple doughnut sold out at many shops. Next year, let’s see if Dunkin’ can get Ben Affleck in the room with this absurd arachnid.

The first year of the second Donald Trump presidency brought upheaval to federal food programs, universities, and vaccine policy. A surge of ICE arrests and mass deportations have created fear for immigrants and their families. In March, Tufts University graduate student Rümeysa Öztürk was swarmed by masked agents on a Somerville street and arrested, despite holding a student visa.

Restrictions outlined in President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” mean that over 150,000 Massachusetts residents could see their federal food assistance, also known as SNAP, reduced or cut. Harvard University and the Trump administration went toe-to-toe, with Trump accusing Harvard of pushing liberal ideology and antisemitism and Harvard saying the issue is part of a broader pressure campaign against the school.

Meanwhile, research grants from NIH, NSF, and the Department of Energy were abruptly cut, leaving New England scientists scrambling. And when decades-old federal vaccine guidance changed under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s CDC, Massachusetts published its own recommendations and required insurers to cover the cost of those vaccines.

Tragedy at Brown, Brookline

Two students were killed and nine were injured after a gunman opened fire at Brown University just days before winter break. Scheduled holiday celebrations turned into somber vigils for the slain students, Ella Cook and MukhammadAziz Umurzokov. Then, an MIT physics professor was shot and killed in his Brookline home. A frantic manhunt — in which police pleaded for public assistance in identifying a person of interest — lasted days. Finally, a flood of information led police to a storage locker in New Hampshire, where the gunman, Claudio Manuel Neves Valente, was dead. He was believed to have committed both crimes.

A nightmare in Fall River

On July 13, a pleasant evening was shattered when a fire broke out at Gabriel House, an assisted living facility with 69 residents in Fall River. Flames, heat, and dense, dark smoke quickly tore through the building, killing 10 individuals in the deadliest fire in the state in 41 years. Former residents have since filed wrongful death lawsuits against the facility, its embattled owner Dennis Etzkorn, and the safety equipment provider. And the fire raised questions about the living conditions at Gabriel House, which has a spotty regulatory record and lax emergency procedures.

New Hampshire mom does the unthinkable

Emily Long was open about her struggling on TikTok. Her husband had been diagnosed with glioblastoma, a brain cancer, and she alluded to money concerns in her videos. On Aug. 18, Long shot and killed her husband, two of their children, and then herself. The only survivor was their toddler, 3-year-old James, who was found near his family physically unharmed. After her death, records revealed that Long’s employer had accused her of embezzling more than $600,000. But the Long family, now caring for James, don’t expect to ever understand why she did it.

Skating dreams cut short

An American Airlines midair collision over the Potomac River on Jan. 29 took 67 lives, including six people connected to the Skating Club of Boston. The jet collided with an Army helicopter near Washington, D.C., killing everyone on board. Figure skaters Spencer Lane and Jinna Han were rising stars in the highly competitive sport, traveling with their parents Christine Lane and Jin Han. Veteran coaches Evgenia Shishkova and Vadim Naumov, who represented Russia in the 1994 Olympics, also died in the crash. Months later, grief hangs over the grind of daily training in Norwood.

Retrial draws crowds then acquits Karen Read

Karen Read’s case was retried in Norfolk County Superior Court, drawing a sea of pink supporters outside the courthouse. After a weekslong murder trial, a jury ruled Read was not guilty of murdering her boyfriend, John O’Keefe, a Boston police officer, and not guilty of manslaughter. She was convicted of driving under the influence and sentenced to one year probation. Now, the drama persists, with trial followers speculating about what actually might have happened.

Wu cruises to next term, greater national prominence

Mayor Michelle Wu took a decisive victory in the city’s preliminary election for mayor, winning about 72 percent of the vote and easily securing her second term. Her skills as a politician were tested and proved in Boston and on the national stage. When Wu was called alongside three other Democratic mayors to a congressional hearing on immigration enforcement, Wu appeared at ease, nursing her newborn daughter and firing back at attacks from Republicans. In Boston, Wu was endorsed by the largest Boston police union and her allies filled City Council leadership.

Climate concerns muddy New England waters

As climate change continues to accelerate, New Englanders are feeling the effects. A Boston Globe project chronicled the risk of rising floodwaters in small town, coastal Massachusetts and behind inland levees. The promise of rising seas threatens the buoy that the Seaport gives Boston’s property tax base. Home insurance premiums have surged in coastal communities from Connecticut to Maine as scores of policies have been abruptly dropped. And a new proposal in Boston — dismaying clean river advocates — would allow continued sewage release into the Charles by changing the water quality classification of the river.

An anniversary approaching

As the 250th anniversary of America approaches, the state is planning for a celebration. Already, Lexington and Concord marked the 250th anniversary of the opening battles of the American Revolution with daylong battlefield reenactments. And in Bunker Hill, descendants of veterans from around the country gathered for a parade and battle reenactment, swapping stories of bravery and sacrifice. But organizers fear the planning will be too little, too late. Some lawmakers and historians said Massachusetts has fallen behind other states in local grants and grass-roots programming.

Search for accountability after boy killed by school bus

In April, a Boston Public Schools bus struck and killed 5-year-old Lens Joseph. The bus driver had been in several prior crashes and lacked proper state credentials, city officials announced in May as they launched an independent investigation into the busing contractor. After warning BPS to improve driver training and safety measures, commercial transportation insurer National Interstate refused to renew the district’s coverage because of a rising number of crashes, according to reports obtained by the Globe. Joseph, the Hyde Park kindergartener, was remembered as older than his years, dedicated to his schoolwork and his love of Spider-Man.

Frequenters of Cambridge brothel ring identified

Authorities have sought charges against at least 28 men who they say most frequently exchanged text messages with the Cambridge brothel hot line and made multiple appointments. The brothel network operated for three years in Cambridge, Watertown, and the suburbs of Washington, D.C. After months of judicial delay, some of the men were publicly identified in court, including Paul Toner, a Cambridge city councilor, and James C. Cusack Jr., a local surgical oncologist.

Boston police officers disciplined after Dorchester crash

Three teenagers were killed in a 2024 rollover crash on Morrissey Boulevard, which occurred after accelerating to speeds that reached 106 miles per hour as police continued to follow them. Reports and related video obtained by the Globe show that officers continued to follow the car with lights flashing even after being told to stand down by a supervisor. This year, an internal investigation found the chase to be a violation of department policy: one of the officers was suspended for 30 days, another has since resigned, and a termination decision was pending for the third officer.

Amid the mayhem, some bright spots

After more than nine months in space, Needham-bred astronaut Sunita Williams came back to Earth to an honorary degree and a warm welcome from her dogs. Williams was originally sent to space for an eight-day test flight to the International Space Station, but her stay was extended due to technical difficulties. The first American pope, elected in May, blessed a South Boston baby. The Chicago native also adorned a White Sox cap donated by a newlywed Haverhill couple — diehard Red Sox Fans.

A Dorchester man, charged with murder in connection with a triple shooting in Mattapan earlier this year that killed an 18-year old woman and injured two men, was arrested early Tuesday morning. An arrest warrant has been issued for a second suspect, authorities said.

At approximately 6 a.m., members of the Boston Police SWAT Team along with homicide detectives, served an arrest warrant at 260 Ruggles St. in Roxbury and took Dkhari Wornum-Brown, 22, into custody, according to a statement from Boston police.

He was arraigned in the Dorchester division of Boston Municipal Court Tuesday on charges of first-degree murder and carrying an unlicensed firearm, police said.

Judge Rebeca Figueroa ordered that Wornum-Brown be held without bail. His next court date, a probable-cause hearing, was set for Feb. 5, according to the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office.

Wornum-Brown was not the shooter, prosecutors said. An arrest warrant has been issued for the alleged gunman. Authorities did not disclose that person’s identity.

Wornum-Brown’s arrest stems from an afternoon shooting in Mattapan on Oct. 11. Police responded to a ShotSpotter activation at 2 Hiawatha Road and found three people suffering from gunshot wounds; all three were taken to local hospitals, authorities said.

According to prosecutors, five people were hanging out on the front porch when two men rode up on a scooter. Wornum-Brown drove the scooter, and the other man hopped off and fired off at least 21 rounds, striking three people. The shooter got back onto the scooter and the two men fled the scene.

Two of the victims were men who suffered nonlife-threatening wounds. But a third victim, 18-year-old G’Kiyah Lewis of Malden, eventually died of her injuries weeks later, police said.

“The violent death of G’Kiyah Lewis is a societal tragedy,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement Tuesday. “I’m grateful for the great investigative effort that brought someone forward to answer for this terrible crime and I urge the second suspect to turn himself in before he or anyone else gets hurt.”

Hayden extended his “deepest sympathies to G’Kiyah’s family and friends.”

Investigators used video, GPS tracking, and other circumstantial evidence to identify the alleged suspects, according to the district attorney’s office.

Lewis was a Malden High School senior who loved fashion, the beach, and having her photo taken, her mother, Rehema Grayson, had told The Boston Globe. She was hanging out with her boyfriend and other friends, her mother said, when a bullet went through her arm, grazed her heart, and lodged in her head.

She leaves behind two younger sisters, aged 7 and 15, her mother said.

After her death, Lewis’ organs were donated to three people, a 60-year-old woman and two men in their 40s, her mother said.

Faith leaders and community activists had demanded police action and urged residents to come forward with any information about her killing.

“None of our children should die in the streets,” said the Rev. Kevin Peterson, a community minister and public theologian at Grace Church of All Nations. “No blood should be in the streets of our community.”

The backstory: This space was long the Blarney Stone, an Irish pub that was a Dorchester institution. Now business partners and longtime friends Freddy Ureña (chef), Yancarlo Fernandez (general manager), and Anthony Cruz (front-of-house manager) have created Acapella, which soft-opened in November and will see its grand opening in January. The “X” is Dorchester native Fernandez’s business group, which also includes a car wash, liquor stores, and Dominican fast-casual PikaloX. Ureña, who grew up in East Boston and attended Le Cordon Bleu in Cambridge, went on to cook in Spain, as a private chef in Dubai, and at area hotel restaurants including Zuma before pivoting to biotech during the pandemic. Acapella is a family affair for him: Wife, Joanna, is also in the kitchen, with daughters Emma and Brianna working as floor manager and bartender, respectively. In opening a venue with an upscale atmosphere, the business partners hope to fill a niche in Fields Corner. “We felt like the community needed something like this,” Ureña says.

What to eat: The menu draws from Ureña’s travels, offering Spanish tapas (patatas bravas, pan con tomate, blistered shishito peppers), tacos, a Turkish salad, and dumplings, along with the likes of steak tips and lobster ravioli. Start with the ceviche, featuring the fish of the day in a bright, refreshing Peruvian leche de tigre marinade, with onions, cilantro, radish, and crunchy toasted corn kernels. Pork and chive dumplings come in a ponzu-soy sauce. Scallops glazed in citrusy butter are delicate bites served on toothpicks for easy hors d’oeuvres-ing. Those who love a cheese-and-charcuterie board will appreciate the generous fried truffle burrata, surrounded by arugula, sliced tomatoes, folds of prosciutto, and toasts, with a ramekin of guava glaze. Grilled skirt steak comes sliced thin with chimichurri sauce, flavorful and nicely cooked, with coarse salt for sprinkling. For the kids: chicken tenders and sliders, both served with fries. Dessert brings the likes of pineapple upside-down cake and Dubai chocolate tres leches.

What to drink: The beverage program is focused on cocktails, with classics (mojitos, margaritas, pisco sours, espresso martinis) alongside house creations like the Fresa Picante (strawberries with mezcal and ancho chile) and La Flor (hibiscus and rum). Perhaps of extra Dry January interest, the mocktails are worthy, not mere afterthoughts: The balanced Felinas (lemonade, apple, ginger beer, and spices) and fruity Citrus & Tonic (grapefruit, guava, rose, and mint) are goblets garnished with fruit and herbs.

The takeaway: A priest, a baby, and a group of women dressed to the nines walk into a bar… A recent midweek visit to Acapella is both perfect setup to a joke and lovely snapshot of the neighborhood. A Berklee student is singing at the front of the room, with its mood lighting, stylish bar, and brick walls painted white. When the weather warms, there will be a patio seating about 80 people. Valet parking is slated for the future, and weekends have been wild, Ureña says, with birthday parties and private events. It seems Fields Corner is ready for its own nighttime scene, and Acapella by X is here to provide.

1505 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester, 617-286-4620, www.acapellabyx.com. Appetizers $9-$24, tapas $7-$20, main dishes $26-$45, cocktails $17-$20.

Rios has been attending First Night Boston for the last 38 years and makes a full night of it — after the parade and 7 p.m. fireworks over the Common, dinner at Faneuil Hall follows, and then more fireworks at midnight over Boston Harbor.

“This night is just for me,” Rios said, explaining that it’s a night of solo festivities for her, since she can’t get anyone else to brave the cold. “I love it. We have to celebrate a new year.”

First timers Jon Lutke and family — including his wife, daughter, and son — came from Wisconsin to celebrate the New Year and son Micah’s eighth birthday.

On winter break, they were skiing in New Hampshire when they decided to check out Boston’s celebration. It was the family-centric vibe that attracted them.

“We had heard that this was a pretty good family-friendly event,” Lutke said. “And they had always wanted to come to Boston. So it just worked out.”

For Kim Cook and her four children, ages 7, 10, and two who are 12, it’s “the family time” that makes First Night Boston “special for us,” she said.

Their annual New Year’s Eve trek from Dorchester to downtown Boston for the revelries has become “a family tradition,” she said.

With temperatures in the low 30s descending into the 20s, First Night Boston marked a cold opening to 2026.

As of late Wednesday night, there had been no arrests or any major disruptions related to the festivities, according to Sergeant Detective John Boyle, a spokesperson for Boston police.

Soon after the festivities started at noon, Copley Square was crowded with Bostonians bundled in winter coats to attend celebration, a series of free events and musical performances that, for 50 years, has marked the start of the new year for the city.

Lines formed outside Boston’s landmark Trinity Church to relish musical performances from an orchestra and choir that performed hymns under the church’s majestic golden arches about the day the United States put an end to slavery. The concert, in its 12th year, is held on the same day that President Abraham Lincoln declared the end of slavery in the US in 1863.

This year, the concert marked an important cornerstone in American history as the country turns 250 years old.

“During this significant anniversary, it feels like we are taking a step back as a country because we are taking away so many people’s liberties,” said Allana Matthews, a singer and member of the Unitus Ensemble, which performed during the concert. “Now is the time to show that we will fight for our freedom of speech and our liberty.”

The First Night celebration has come a long way since it first brought together a small group of local artists to ring in the new year in 1976.

Diverging from most New Year’s festivities that centered on loud parties and alcohol, First Night built upon the tradition of elevating community-based initiatives that celebrate culture and American diversity and history instead.

This year’s celebration is occurring during the second Trump administration, which has been widely criticized for challenging free speech protections by deploying federal agents to target protestors supporting Palestinian rights and Black Lives Matter. Trump also came under scrutiny over the past year for restricting civil liberties through an immigration crackdown which the government says has led to the deportation of over 2.5 million people and for nixing federal funding for diversity initiatives.

Still, at Boston’s First Night celebration, diversity was alive and thriving.

People came from all over Greater Boston and beyond to attend Trinity Church’s Emancipation Proclamation event. The pews, which take up every corner of the majestic church, can hold up to 1,400 people. They were so packed that people had to be turned away at the door. Hosted by the Handel and Haydn Society and the Museum of African American History, the event featured orchestra and chorus performances of hymns about the liberation of the slaves and a reading by Massachusetts poet laureate Regie Gibson.

Even in 30-degree weather, the Greater Boston Chinese Cultural Association put together a series of performances in Copley Square that drew dozens of people from all over the city to watch.

Mira Rifai, an analyst from Allston who carries out technical and administrative reviews at a hospital, was taking time off from work and decided to come watch those performances unfold.

“There are so many different cultures in Boston and it’s so cool to see what the city has to offer,” Rifai said. “Events like these remind us that we are all stronger together.”

The celebration featured a traditional fan dance carried out by a group of students from the Angel Dance Company in Weston, and a group of kids from a martial arts studio in Watertown mimicking a lion’s movements in a colorful costume.

Michelle Lin, who owns the Wu An Martial Arts studio that led the Lion dance, said that in China it is typically performed during the lunar new year to usher in good luck for the coming year.

“I want to be hopeful and optimistic for the new year ahead,” Lin said. “There are a lot of people right now that are fearing for their safety for being different. So its important to celebrate diversity right now and maintain an open mind and an open heart.”

Optimism for the year ahead echoed in the minds and hearts of others who came to see the shows.

For 75-year-old Sandra Harris from South Boston, events like First Night are all about bringing people together. Harris is the cofounder of the Coalition to Build Community & End Loneliness and is constantly looking for ways to make people feel included.

She attended an event hosted by A Trike Called Funk, a Boston-based mobile DJ unit, at which street dance performers taught the audience how to move to the beat of the African diaspora in the Americas, swaying to rhythms of hip-hop, salsa, and samba.

“It’s opportunities like these where we get to meet our neighbors and come together to celebrate that we build community,” Harris said, “and I am optimistic that this is a new beginning for all of us and that we will continue to come together in the new year.”

Local artists who thrive on elevating their communities also took center stage at First Night celebrations.

Latoria Boyd, who performs R&B and soul music with the stage name ToriTori, played songs to a crowd of more than 50 people at the Boston Public Library.

The Dorchester native, who now lives in Brockton, said one of her main goals is to give back to the community that has supported her by offering free shows.

“I really feel like I would not be where I am today if it wasn’t for the support of the community,” she said. “I just want to give back.”
