“We will not appease or abet any threat to our city, and we will not wait for permission to build the world our families deserve,” Wu said. “Boston will be the proof that the nation we fought for is possible — a place where we take care of each other and take on the challenges that matter the most.”

Wu’s second inauguration, following a decisive reelection victory last fall, reaffirmed her considerable influence over Boston politics on a day that kept the face of city leadership largely unchanged and saw one of Wu’s allies elected City Council president. Wu was sworn in at Boston Symphony Hall by Sarah G. Kim, an associate justice of the Massachusetts Superior Court, as her two older children, sons Blaise and Cass, held a Bible beneath her hand. Wu then administered the oath of office to the 13 members of the council, 12 of them incumbents returning to office.

Wu’s remarks — which echoed her past pledges to improve Boston’s education system, tackle its affordability crisis, and protect the job sectors that power the city’s economy — underscored that continuity. Wu said she will spend the next four years continuing to improve school facilities and better city services. And, as the nation prepares to celebrate its 250th anniversary, Wu evoked American history as she promised to continue standing against a Trump administration that has repeatedly targeted the Democrat-run city.

“Right now, in some ways, the world feels helplessly stuck — like we know what problems need fixing, but we’ve lost faith we can fix them," Wu said. “Today, the forces we face aren’t British troops on the Common or ships in our harbor, but they demand no less ingenuity.”

Much of Wu’s speech centered on what her administration has already done. Wu said during her second term, she would continue to use “local government as the bedrock for getting results.”

Wu also took some shots at a Trump administration she said has “plundered our economy, ravaged our reputation, and destroyed the lives of our people.” She pledged to defend higher education, life sciences, hospitals, and clean energy — all sectors that the Trump administration has explicitly targeted or defunded.

Wu in the last year has earned support locally and attention nationally for sparring with the Trump administration. Still, her tone on Monday sounded somewhat milder than in some of her election year speeches, when she painted Boston as the defiant vanguard of the Trump resistance.

“God save whoever messes with Boston,” Wu warned in a speech last year. Her message Monday, though, sounded less provocative than defensive — guarded against economic uncertainty and threats from an unpredictable federal administration.

“This is certainly a moment where we have to make some tough choices about what comes next, and be clear that Boston and every community is having to do more with less. But we are going to keep doing more,” Wu told reporters.

Wu in Monday’s address said she plans to expand on some initiatives from her first term, but she did not propose major new programs. She pledged to make the country’s oldest public school system its best by “rightsizing our district” and investing in school facilities. Wu also said the city would “revisit school assignment” to make the process “simpler and more predictable.”

“We refuse to accept that accessing high quality education means crisscrossing our children all over our city rather than ensuring that, in every corner of Boston, the best school is just down the block,” Wu said.

She also touched on the city’s housing production and cost-of-living challenges, though she did not detail any specific new plans for tackling those challenges.

This week marks the official start of Wu’s second four-year term as mayor, and a new two-year term for the council. Monday’s event kicked off a week of planned community gatherings, including story times at libraries around the city, a gathering of faith leaders, and a celebration of small businesses.

Wu, the first woman and person of color elected to lead the city, sailed to victory in November. She appeared unopposed on the general election ballot after challenger Josh Kraft dropped out of the race following a dismal performance in the September preliminary.

A former city councilor who has long wielded influence over the body, Wu also helped council allies secure reelection in November. The panel appears likely to remain friendly to her policy agenda: Every incumbent councilor who sought reelection won in November.

Following Monday’s inauguration ceremony, the council elected Councilor Liz Breadon its new president, in a narrow 7–6 vote that followed a contentious debate. A 66-year-old physical therapist and immigrant from Northern Ireland, Breadon is the first openly gay female councilor and has been an outspoken advocate for LGBTQ+ rights.

Councilor Brian Worrell of Dorchester narrowly lost the election. The contest had been thrown into uncertainty over the weekend after a front-runner for the role, Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata, said she would not seek the presidency after all.

There is just one new face on the council this year: Rev. Miniard Culpepper, a longtime Dorchester activist, pastor, and former attorney for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, who was sworn in Monday. He represents Roxbury-based District 7, a seat that had sat vacant for months after former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges last year and resigned from the position in July.

While Wu has yet to detail her full agenda for the next four years, she has indicated one of her top priorities is making Boston Public Schools the “best major city school district” in the country.

It’s an ambitious goal and a daunting challenge: BPS’ persistent problems — including dropping enrollment numbers, decades-old facilities, and stubbornly low test scores — have vexed many of Wu’s predecessors.

Wu insists the district in her first term has made notable progress, while acknowledging that more work is still needed. However, Wu has not identified specific benchmarks or timelines she is targeting to determine success when it comes to improving academic outcomes.

While Wu focused many of her remarks Monday on Boston’s rich history, she closed on a more recent development:her daughter Mira’s first steps. Wu said Mira, who turns one next week, had tried to take a few steps on stage Monday morning, after her first attempt to walk last month ended in a fall.

“Some part of her already knows that progress takes courage — the willingness to take the next step when the ground isn’t certain,” Wu said. “Every one of us, from our earliest days, is living proof that last month’s impossible can become this morning’s milestones — that if we are only willing to try, with a little help from each other, we can build the future our families deserve.”

A Roxbury teenager was arraigned Monday in Boston Municipal Court in connection with a violent group assault and robbery aboard an MBTA Orange Line train earlier this month, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Wednesday.

Mannice Mitchner, 18, pleaded not guilty to charges of unarmed robbery, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, and disorderly conduct on a public conveyance stemming from a Dec. 15 attack on an 18-year-old passenger, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Mitchner is one of four teenagers who have been arrested in connection to the attack, prosecutors said. The other three are minors and their names were not released.

Judge Richard Sinnott revoked bail on several open cases involving Mitchner and ordered him to stay away from the victim as well as all MBTA stations and stops, Hayden’s office said.

Mitchner is due back in court Jan. 22 for a probable cause hearing, according to court records. His attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Wednesday.

Prosecutors say Mitchner was allegedly part of a group of seven teens who confronted the victim during the evening rush hour and participated in the assault while recording it on a cellphone.

The incident occurred about 5:45 p.m. after the group boarded an Orange Line train at Downtown Crossing. MBTA surveillance video allegedly shows the teens initiating a verbal confrontation with the victim that escalated into violence.

According to prosecutors, five of the teens allegedly punched the victim with closed fists, threw him to the ground, and continued to punch and kick him in the face and stomach. Mitchner is accused of approaching the scene with his phone out to film the attack and kicking the victim in the head.

Prosecutors said the group stole the victim’s shoes and cellphone before fleeing the train at the Massachusetts Avenue station. Two of the seven teens did not physically assault the victim, authorities said.

The victim told police he did not know any of the attackers, officials said.

“This was a frightening experience for this young man and for all the riders who witnessed it,” Hayden said in a statement, adding that surveillance cameras throughout the transit system play a key role in identifying suspects.

Prosecutors said Mitchner has open cases in multiple courts, including West Roxbury, Fall River, Roxbury, and Dorchester, involving charges such as breaking and entering, malicious destruction of property, attempted larceny, and receiving stolen property.

Three of the five juvenile attackers, along with Mitchner, have been arrested, Hayden’s office said.

Transit Police identified suspects through MBTA video footage and prior contacts with some of the juveniles. Additional arrests were made Dec. 16 and Dec. 19 with help from the Boston Police Department’s Youth Violence Strike Force, officials said.

The remaining juveniles are expected to be arraigned at a later date, Hayden’s office said.

“I think 2025 was the year of transition,” said Ricardo Rodriguez of Coldwell Banker in reference to the political and economic environment, as well as the dust settling around new rules over real estate agent commissions. “What we have is just a new landscape of not only how the business operates, but how the market itself operates. It’s just the new normal.”

The wait-and-see era is officially over. Driven by life events — from marriages to growing families — and a begrudging acceptance of a new economic baseline, the market is poised for a psychological thaw. The question for 2026 is no longer when rates will drop to historic lows (they likely won’t), but how buyers will compete in a landscape where inventory remains critically scarce.

“If you look at the stock market or commodities markets, they’re swinging,” Rodriguez added. “The only one that is not swinging is real estate.”

That stability is a double-edged sword. While it protects property values, it has cemented a barrier to entry that is nearly insurmountable for the middle class. According to Luc Schuster, Executive Director of Boston Indicators and coauthor of the "Greater Boston Housing Report Card 2025," the starter home has effectively vanished.

The report shows that in 2015, 57 municipalities in Greater Boston had a median single-family sale price below $500,000. By 2025, there were only three: Brockton, Halifax, and Wareham. Conversely, Brookline, Wellesley, and Weston now see median prices topping $2 million.

“This shows the entry-level homeownership squeeze,” Schuster said.

While sub-3 percent mortgages are in the rearview mirror, experts envision a critical tipping point.

“If rates get below 6 percent — and stable at 6 percent — you are going to see an increase in buyers rush to the market. You’re also going to see the increase of sellers get on the market,” said Shant Banosian, president at residential mortgage lender Rate. “You can only stall your life to protect your interest rate for so long.”

For those who can’t wait for the Federal Reserve, the 2026 strategy shifts from waiting to creative structuring. Banosian noted a significant rise in the “Bank of Mom and Dad,” fueled by record highs in the stock market.

While cash offers have dipped slightly from their 2024 highs, down payments are rising, a reflection of growing affluence, according to Redfin.

“There is a lot more wealth in the country,” Banosian said. “The parents of first-time homebuyers have a lot more access to capital, and they are willing to gift it to their children.”

For those without a trust fund, the strategy is speed. Cash buyers often demand a discount, leaving an opening for the financed buyer who can move fast. Banosian points to the rise of the “power bid” — a fully underwritten pre-approval that allows buyers to close in as little as two weeks — as a necessary equalizer.

“The two things that we’re trying to combat cash buyers with is certainty and speed,” he added.

Yet, the Greater Boston narrative inevitably circles back to one root problem: supply.

Walk from Back Bay to the Seaport, and you might think Boston is in a building boom amid all the residential projects that are either underway or recently opened. The Greater Boston Housing Report Card highlighted Census Address Counts data showing Greater Boston added more than 70,000 units of housing in the last five years — a “meaningful increase in completions.”

But, those openings are the final delivery of projects permitted years ago. The pipeline for future housing is drying up.

“Permits for future construction are way down in 2025,” Schuster said. “There is real reason to believe we are not going to keep up that pace of new home building in the coming years.”

New housing permits as of July 2025 were down 44 percent from July 2021 levels, according to the Housing Report Card. High interest rates didn’t just scare off buyers; they paralyzed developers, creating a looming supply cliff for 2026 and 2027.

With the supply crunch expected to continue, Kristen Keegan, the 2026 President of the Massachusetts Association of Realtors, suggested buyers look for expanded options, specifically in the condo market. Furthermore, the recent passage of the Affordable Homes Act could allow accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, to squeeze out more inventory, though a construction boom there has yet to materialize.

While the middle market walks a tightrope, the top end occupies a different stratosphere. In 2026, luxury buyers are motivated by a flight to safety.

“Boston has historically been such a stable market, and real estate really is that one place in which people feel comfortable putting a lot of those liquid assets,” Rodriguez said.

However, the era of the glass tower, defined most recently by Winthrop Center and South Station Tower, may be pausing. With construction costs soaring, the math for building 60-story skyscrapers no longer works.

For buyers priced out of the city, the 2026 strategy is geography. Sarah Gustafson, the 2025 president of the Massachusetts Association of Realtors, points to a changing map redefined by infrastructure. The arrival of South Coast Rail has turned Fall River and New Bedford into viable commuter hubs.

But for the true bargain hunter, the compass points west. Gustafson identified Western Massachusetts as perhaps the last stable housing market in the Commonwealth.

The average home value in Springfield is just under $288,000 compared to a little more than $755,000 in Boston, according to Zillow.

“They have just about as much supply as they do people looking for it,” Gustafson said. “Things are moving, but it’s not a frenzied pace.”

Back in Boston, there are reasons for concern heading into the new year, but also reasons to be optimistic about future fluidity. Sellers are listing, buyers are bidding, and the stalemate is being replaced by a pragmatic drive to get on with life.

“I would dare to say [Boston] is the most stable real estate market in the country,” Rodriguez said. “It’s the silver lining to the inventory levels.”

Amid so much economic and political uncertainty, that might be the best news we could hope for.

Some of the region’s real estate agents weighed in on where they forecast the best opportunities for buyers in the new year:

Zechariah Cook, a broker with Douglas Elliman, advises buyers to focus on areas within a 15-minute walk of the Red Line, especially from Savin Hill to Neponset. These pockets offer beaches, parks, local restaurants, grocery options, and quick commutes — all amenities that drive long-term value in a neighborhood that’s continually evolving.

Buyers are drawn to Sherborn for the generously sized homes, larger lots, privacy, and proximity to Boston. Medfield offers similar appeal, with a walkable downtown and a community-driven feel. Parts of Natick, Dedham, and Westwood also stretch buyers’ dollars further while keeping them within a 20- to 35-minute drive of Boston..

Worcester’s rail service, new ballpark, and growing restaurant scene are drawing a new wave of buyers. The South Coast Rail extension is boosting interest in the communities it serves.

Dover, Rochester, and Somersworth, N.H., provide walkability, newer homes, and lower prices while sitting close to Portsmouth and the Massachusetts border.

Douglas Elliman agent Mia Parsons said Woodstock and Quechee remain two of Vermont’s most stable markets. Woodstock saw a significant surge during COVID and continues to grow, while the Quechee Club attracts buyers to its four-season amenities and proximity to Boston.

According to the T and the city, rush hour bus trips are quicker, cars speed less, and bus riders are pleased — proof that the lanes have been a “successful and impactful project,” in the words of a project summary published last February.

Attitudes among Roxbury residents and workers remain split. Some lane defenders welcome the prioritization of transit and find the lanes convenient. Some critics, however, said the lanes have sown confusion along the street, worsening safety.

Available data paint an ambiguous picture of safety improvements along the segment. The city says the number of crashes that caused injuries declined markedly. Boston police tallies indicate that vehicle collisions overall also declined on average, but only marginally. The T, meanwhile, said its buses have gotten into far more “major” collisions since 2021, an upswing that surprised some experts.

The T faulted the dangerous and illegal maneuvers of nonagency drivers for most of the crashes over the past couple of years. Only one incident, in 2023, “was considered preventable by the bus driver.”

“We are currently exploring updates to the bus lane design to make it more difficult for drivers to enter or cross the bus lane illegally,” the T said.

The agency said it’s already made some tweaks — enhancing physical barriers around platforms, banning left turns, and adjusting signal timing at some intersections, among other changes.

The T and the city plan to spend $37.3 million extending the lanes about a mile north to Ruggles. They intend to break ground in 2026, the T told the Globe.

Boston and the T also intend to carve out bus-exclusive street space along Blue Hill Avenue, in a not-yet-designed overhaul at one point priced at $44 million. The T said construction would begin in 2027 at the earliest, assuming the agency secures a still-pending Small Starts federal grant from the Trump administration worth about $80 million.

Columbus offers a rough template of how Blue Hill Avenue’s lanes may take shape.

From the sky, the lanes give the impression of a blood vessel, bound on either side by gray arteries of street and sidewalk.

There are eight stops in total, four in each direction — narrow islands wedged between the bus and general purpose lanes. The stops, outfitted with shelters, seats, barriers, and digital trip displays, are separated from the sidewalks by the shared lanes, much like some street-level Green Line stations.

Proponents promised that center-running bus lanes would free buses from thickets of traffic, improving their speed and reliability for a bus-reliant neighborhood.

Drivers bearing witness to the buses zipping by would, in time, ditch their cars and hop aboard. Confining the cars that remained to fewer lanes would enhance the street’s safety, according to advocates and some experts.

Stringing the bus lanes through the middle of the road, instead of connecting them to the curb, offers the added benefit of removing parked or turning vehicles from a bus’s path.

“It helps tremendously” with bus operation and reliability, said Zhan Guo, an urban planning and transportation policy professor at New York University.

Cities around the country have explored their potential benefits — from New York City to Eugene, Ore.

Bus lanes have recently attracted the scrutiny of the Trump administration, which this fall pumped the brakes on a bus lane project in New York City over its supposed impacts on freight traffic and emergency vehicles.

The Columbus Avenue rebuild cost $14.5 million, according to the MBTA. The corridor services three routes — the 44, 29, and 22, one of the T’s most popular, according to the agency.

The census estimates that about 30 percent of workers living in the 02119 ZIP code — encompassing much of Roxbury and Columbus Avenue — use public transit to get to work, about four times the state rate. About 28 percent of 02119 residents live below the poverty line, more than double statewide rate.

Expanding bus-specific street space is a pillar of the MBTA’s push to improve the popular service’s speed and reliability. Boston has publicly backed the effort, despite walking back bus lane installations in some parts of the city.

“The best bus-priority systems in the US have center-running lanes,” said Annie Weinstock, president of a New York consultancy specializing in bus infrastructure. “So it’s a very positive step that Boston has done that.”

Some in the Roxbury neighborhood greeted the revamp with skepticism that has only hardened since the lanes opened.

Working the checkout counter at Pina’s Grocery Store, a few yards from the dark red lanes, Maria Martinez griped about their impact on her car commute.

Martinez said she drove to work from Dorchester, a short journey that has been beset with “more traffic” since the buses ate up one lane along Columbus.

“We get to school late, we get to work late,” Martinez said in Spanish.

A city report from 2023 concluded that car trips along the nearly mile-long corridor took, on average, 20 to 40 seconds longer than they did prebus lane. Meanwhile, the study determined, bus lanes shaved around three to four minutes off bus trips during rush hour.

LivableStreets Alliance, a Cambridge transportation advocacy nonprofit, surveyed more than 150 Columbus Avenue bus riders in December 2021, shortly after the lanes went live. Around three-quarters of respondents reported faster and more consistent trips, according to a report summarizing the group’s findings. Just under one-quarter of respondents said they took the bus more frequently after the lanes were introduced.

It’s difficult to definitively pinpoint how exactly the Columbus lanes have impacted bus ridership.

“There is some evidence that with all things equal, [bus] speed increases can result in ridership increases,” said Weinstock, the bus infrastructure expert. “However, there are so many factors here and in other places that you really need to look at a lot [of] data before you can say definitively what caused what.”

Bus ridership plunged across the entire MBTA system during the pandemic — the early heights of which partly overlapped with the lanes’ construction — and has yet to fully recover. The T said the ridership recovery rate of the 22 bus has outpaced the agencywide average, but other lines without center-running bus lanes have also showcased strong rebounds. The 29 and the 44 buses, the other, less popular lines passing through Columbus, have shown weaker recoveries, according to data from TransitMatters, a research and advocacy group.

Still, some in Roxbury appreciate the bus lanes.

“They work well for what they’re meant to do,” said Sol Martinez Guevara, an employee at the Boston Public Library’s Egleston Square branch, a short stroll from where the bus lanes cease at Walnut Avenue and traffic begins to mingle again.

Despite typically biking to work from another part of Roxbury, Guevara appreciated what the lanes signaled about the city’s priorities.

“I feel like that’s just what makes more sense for being more of a public transit oriented city,” Guevara said.

Guevara’s colleague, Dorchester native Mikayla Willingham, largely agreed. She had, for a time, commuted by bus after the lanes were installed, she said.

“I feel like it’s convenient,” Willingham explained, acknowledging that confused or unconcerned drivers will sometimes trespass into bus zones.

For resident Luis Peña, that confusion feeds chaos.

“Boston City Hall’s worst expense has been to spend money on that,” Peña said in Spanish.

Vehicles barrel past the bus stops far faster than speed limits allow, he complained. Impatient drivers habitually veer into the bus lanes to slip around vehicles stationary in the right lane.

On a recent December day, some short bendable posts marking the lane-splits near bus stops were missing, snapped, or bore the marks of frequent beatings.

“It’s very unsafe,” said Peña, as he stood outside his friend’s store by the Weld Avenue stops, at times gesturing toward the road with his cane. “I don’t know why they did that and spent that money.”

The Police Department documented an average of 35.4 crashes annually along the corridor between 2015 and 2019, according to data shared by the agency. There’ve been, on average, 34.7 crashes annually along the stretch between 2022 and 2024. (BPD didn’t detail the types of crashes or their severity.)

The MBTA, meanwhile, documented 13 “major collisions” involving its buses along the Columbus corridor in 2023 and another 13 in 2024. The agency recorded only eight total major collisions between 2018 and 2022, four of them occurring in 2022.

The Globe in late November asked the T and the Transit Police for copies of the crash reports for each incident. Both agencies told the Globe to file a public records request for the documents. The Globe on Dec. 1 requested documentation for all crashes along the segment involving an MBTA bus between 2018 and 2024. The Globe later agreed to narrow the scope of its request to reports relating to the 34 collisions identified by the MBTA, but has yet to receive the reports.

More proactively identifying and punishing scofflaws could help reel in the rule-breakers, some experts said.

“More automated enforcement is a particularly powerful tool,” said Jeffrey Tumlin, a former director of transportation at the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency.

The agency, during Tumlin’s tenure, unveiled center-running bus lanes spanning a long stretch of Van Ness Avenue, a wide thoroughfare running through the heart of San Francisco. Buses experienced markedly fewer collisions along the segment once they began traveling through the lanes, according to an agency report published in April 2025.

Some drivers defied the rules of the new format, Tumlin said, but bus-mounted enforcement cameras helped keep them in line. The T plans to rollout a similar program in 2026.

Boston, meanwhile, maintains Columbus got safer. A July 2023 evaluation concluded that, on average, a larger share of vehicles — about 10 percentage points more — obeyed the corridor’s speed limit after the bus lanes came online.

It noted in a March report that the number of crashes resulting in injuries tumbled across the city in the years before and after the lanes opened. The decline in injury-causing crashes along the Columbus corridor was about 7 percentage points greater than the drop recorded on similar roads citywide, according to the report.

To Maha Aslam, a transit advocate in Greater Boston and bus lane believer, doubt and frustration and concern are understandable responses to drastic changes in a person’s environment.

“We see a lot of resistance from community members, because it changes the way they experience their neighborhood,” Aslam said.

She went on, “In general, people are antichange.”

As Ahern helped extract the machine, broad smiles and compliments from movers and school staff greeted the press as it slowly emerged from its hideaway.

“Very cool,” cooed Ahern, who said the press will receive star treatment among the museum’s displays of printing’s centuries-long evolution.

“It’s really exciting to see a press like this pop up,” Ahern said. “In its day, this was printing technology. Our mission is to keep this kind of thing out of landfills.”

Its recent discovery at Franklin Cummings Tech, which is moving to Roxbury for the spring semester after 117 years in the South End, is a reminder of the school’s close association with Benjamin Franklin, the Boston-born printer and Founding Father whose generosity led directly to the college’s creation.

Franklin left 1,000 pounds sterling in his 1789 will to “the inhabitants of the town of Boston,” specifically for trade education, and noted that “good apprentices are likely to make good citizens.”

More than a century later, steel baron Andrew Carnegie matched Franklin’s gift on the condition that it be used for an industrial school and that the city donate the land. In 1908, with those conditions met, the school was dedicated as the Franklin Union.

Jackie Cornog, chief of staff at the college, said the press had been forgotten as Franklin Cummings prepared for its move to Nubian Square.

Amid the bustle, the press appeared — unmarked, untended, and unobtrusive — tucked into a corner of a small, cluttered space at the bottom of the college’s four-story main building.

The Museum of Printing soon showed interest. And Dana Thomson, Franklin Cummings’s facilities director, began hammering away to open a space wide enough to remove the heavy press from the basement.

The work culminated in its departure for the Merrimack Valley when four people, bending and straining, provided the muscle to lift the press into the van.

During a break in the move, Ahern noted that its hybrid design of wood and iron bridged a brief transition between completely wooden presses, which had been used for centuries, to machines made entirely of metal.

“Ramage was an innovator, and he was fine-tuning and tweaking the wooden presses, starting to change the design,” Ahern said.

The discovery of the press, which had been loaned to the college by the Bostonian Society many decades ago, is a reminder of Franklin Cummings’s educational mission, Cornog said.

“Being tied to history is so interesting, because this is just a building and we’re moving on,” Cornog said. “But in a sense, we’re still doing the same thing that we’ve done since the very beginning.”

Franklin’s presence is everywhere inside the main building’s expansive, marble-floor lobby. Murals of Franklin’s life ring the high walls, including one of Franklin at a printing press. Below them, a bust of Franklin, with moving tags attached, faces what once had been a steady stream of passers-by.

Franklin’s beginnings as a printer are what make the discovery so meaningful, Cornog said. More than 1,000 students a year gain skills in disciplines as varied as electricity, automotive repair, HVAC, and opticianry, which is the grinding and fitting of lenses for eyeglasses and contacts.

Franklin Cummings officials say they believe the school offered the nation’s first college-based auto-repair program, soon after Henry Ford introduced the Model T in 1908.

The college also was the scene of the first conference call, linking Boston, San Francisco, Chicago, Atlanta, Philadelphia, and New York in 1916, school officials said. And the first “telephoto” fax was sent from there in 1927.

Now, the printing press brings the school’s origins back full circle, she said.

“Franklin wanted other folks to have opportunities to become entrepreneurs in the trades,” Cornog said. “It’s something that started him out.”

Although Franklin moved to Philadelphia as a young man after a falling-out with his brother, his will showed he retained a lifelong affection for his hometown, where he was born in 1706.

The affection goes both ways. Cornog recalled with a laugh that when she placed the moving tags on Franklin’s bust, the building’s fire alarm suddenly began screeching.

“It seemed he was saying, ‘Either get the heck out or don’t leave,’ ” Cornog said.

The next chance to accelerate that change comes this year, with every legislative seat on the ballot in November. Candidates of color have made huge strides since redistricting in 2021, growing their caucuses to record numbers, and rising in the Legislature’s leadership ranks.

Still, those gains haven’t changed a firmly ingrained fact on Beacon Hill: The Legislature is 83 percent white in a state where just 68 percent of residents are. Advocates say the Legislature needs more lawmakers who share the lived experience of Massachusetts’ growing Black and Latino populations, particularly as amped up immigration enforcement, the state’s housing crisis, and the stratospheric cost of living are hitting those communities particularly hard.

The imbalance is not in race alone. Women make up a slight majority of Massachusetts residents, but are outnumbered by men more than 2-to-1 in the Massachusetts House and Senate.

“To no fault of a legislator in most cases, it’s hard to create all-encompassing policy when you yourself are not reflected,” said Celia Canavan, executive director of the Massachusetts League of Women Voters.

Of the state’s 198 sitting lawmakers, just five are Black women, said Miranda, who co-chairs the Legislature’s Committee on Racial Equity, Civil Rights, and Inclusion.

Miranda represents the progress candidates of color have made. In the 2022 election, she was one of a dozen lawmakers of color who won their seats for the first time. Now with 26 members, the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus has never been bigger.

But that caucus makes up just 13 percent of the Legislature, while Black and Latino residents make up 24 percent of the Massachusetts population, according to Census data.

If candidates of color realize new gains only after each decennial redistricting effort, Miranda said, it’d take decades to “get parity, to build the political infrastructure, to have more people stepping down and opening doors.”

“It will never be just about redistricting,” she said. “We have to actually change culture. . . . It actually takes grassroots support.”

Many of the obstacles are no secret. Massachusetts has some of the least competitive legislative elections in the country, meaning incumbents often face few, if any, challengers, and opportunities to run for an open seat are rare.

New candidates, regardless of race or ethnicity, have to quickly learn the basics of running a campaign: how to fundraise and navigate the state’s campaign finance rules, and also determine where to begin building support. That’s even more difficult when facing an incumbent who often enters the race with more money and experience.

For Black candidates in particular, “there’s no one there telling us how to do it,” said Reynolds Graves, founder of the 1866 Action Fund, which has run a super PAC supporting candidates of color. That has consequences, he said.

“Let’s use the [example of a] single Black mother in her mid-40s: When you don’t have that person in the Legislature advocating for her kids’ school funding, the community that might already have a skittishness about government or policymakers or politicians will feel even further out of place,” he said.

In the Latino community, there’s also the “complexities of that diversity” to consider, said Lorna Rivera, director of the Gastón Institute at UMass Boston, which is focused on issues affecting the state’s Latino population. In Massachusetts, that includes immigrants from 20 different countries, she said, all with distinct political and social histories that help shape voters’ choices at the ballot.

“We’re not a monolith,” Rivera said. “Let’s say there is a Latino running for mayor — it’s going to matter if [the candidate is] Dominican or Puerto Rican. And people don’t get that.”

The state’s last redistricting effort aimed to empower new candidates of color to win seats. After lawmakers redrew the map, voters sent the first Brazilian American women and the first Central American lawmaker to Beacon Hill. Last session’s legislative class was the most diverse in the state’s history, according to one state report. The State House added more lawmakers of color after the 2024 election.

The Black and Latino caucus alone has grown by more than 50 percent in less than four years.

“That was a direct result of intentional redistricting,” said state Representative Andy Vargas, the caucus’ president and the first Latino elected official in Haverhill.

Vargas also chairs the Joint Committee on Community Development and Small Businesses, alongside state Senator Adam Gómez, a Springfield Democrat who was the first Puerto Rican elected to the chamber. The panel’s first meeting in May was a “historic moment,” Gómez said. Vargas later said they are the first Latinos to co-chair a legislative committee in Massachusetts.

Policymakers warned then and now that redistricting alone is no panacea for diversifying legislative bodies. Out of Massachusetts’s 200 state legislative districts, there are now 39 so-called majority-minority districts, where most constituents are people of color. Many of those redrawn districts were intended to offer opportunities for new candidates of color to join the Legislature. Today, half are represented by white lawmakers, many of them incumbents who held the seats when the map was remade.

In some cities, the disparities are clear. In Lynn, where a plurality of people identify as Latino or Hispanic, four members of the city’s five-person State House delegation are white and none are Latino. Brockton, New England’s only Black-majority city, in November elected a Black mayor for the first time, but voters are still not represented by a Black state lawmaker. The city’s four-member delegation to the State House includes just one person of color, state Representative Rita Mendes.

“It takes time to mobilize and build political power within a district,” said Rahsaan Hall, president and chief executive of the Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts and a Brockton resident.

That said, at a time when the Trump administration has attacked diversity and inclusion initiatives and escalated immigration enforcement, “it’s all the more important to have people to speak truth to power and speak out to injustice because of the particular [lived] experience of those people,” Hall said.

Of course, lawmakers’ race or ethnicity doesn’t determine whether they can represent a community’s interests. In Chelsea, a small city where two-thirds of residents are Latino or Hispanic, voters since 2022 have sent Judith García to the House, where she is the chamber’s first Honduran American, and state Senator Sal DiDomenico, who is white, to the Senate.

DiDomenico has served in the chamber since 2010, though it wasn’t until the 2021 redistricting cycle that his already diverse district officially became majority-minority. The Everett Democrat said regardless of who’s living in his district, “my job is to show them that there are people in government who are fighting for them.”

Gladys Vega, head of the Chelsea-based La Colaborativa, said DiDomenico has done just that.

“He’s like a brother to me,” she said. “Redistricting is important because it reflects diverse communities, but most importantly, it’s who the leader is who represents your community, who sees you, regardless of your skin color. ... You also have to have leaders who get it. That’s what we’ve got.”

Murphy teamed up with The Community Builders, a housing developer, and architectural firm Isgenuity to plan a new health center on nearby city-owned land. The 49,000-square-foot facility would be roughly twice the size of Harvard Street’s current location.

Murphy and his team settled on a final design and received city approval. Then there was a not-so-small matter of figuring out how to pay for the $57 million project. Harvard Street will borrow $20 million from South Shore Bank and will use $5 million of its own cash, as well as $8 million from the state’s allocation of federal pandemic assistance funds.

Murphy has been busy fund-raising to pay for the rest, and has all but $4 million accounted for. The biggest private gift, $1.5 million, came from Moderna chief executive Stéphane Bancel and his wife Brenda Bancel, through Bancel Philanthropies. Boston Medical Center, meanwhile, gave $500,000. Murphy hopes to have enough money to close the gap and start construction within the next three months.

“This building has reached the end of its life, so to speak,” Murphy said. “The patients and my staff deserve a better facility.”

Eventually, Murphy is aiming for a phase two that involves leveling a rundown theater on Blue Hill Avenue and working with The Community Builders to replace it with up to 100 apartments across two buildings, and health care space on the ground floor.

One reason Harvard Street has run out of room: Murphy has been on a concerted push to grow the patient base. After rejoining in 2021, he set an ambitious goal of growing that number to 10,000 patients a year, from 7,200.

In early December, Murphy and his roughly 130-person staff pulled it off. Murphy posted a photo on LinkedIn with chief medical officer Tom Karson and a surprised Sissi Maldonado, who was handed flowers to celebrate the moment as Harvard Street’s 10,000th patient in 2025.

Murphy’s not quite ready to hold a similar celebration for Harvard Street’s fund-raising.

“I’m very happy where things are,” he said. “but we’re not there yet.”

Co-managing director Michelle Porter said her colleagues at Goulston & Storrs did consider shortening the name, much like other firms have done over the past two decades.

“We thought about it for sure, but ultimately decided it’s important to who we are, our partnership and our collaborative model,” Porter said.

Aviation fuel startup Lydian has touched down in Charlestown with a new headquarters in Hood Park.

The venture-backed firm announced it recently left the Engine incubator in Cambridge to open a 25,000-square-foot office and research lab in Charlestown. The 20-person company’s main focus now is developing a low-emissions jet fuel that can be created from carbon dioxide, electricity, and water. Chief executive Joe Rodden says he hopes to double his workforce in 2026. Lydian joins other so-called “tough tech” companies in Hood Park, a complex owned by the Kaneb family, such as ArkeaBio and Indigo Ag.

Rodden, formerly with Form Energy, formed Lydian in 2021 by teaming up with Branko Zugic, who previously led research and development at a battery-tech firm called Open Water Power that was sold to L3 Technologies, now L3Harris Technologies.

Lydian’s tech uses an electrolyzer to break out hydrogen from water, and combines it with carbon dioxide to make jet fuel. The riddle that Rodden’s team is trying to solve is how to create this fuel in an efficient and cost-effective way, with a goal of commercializing it by 2028. The company is backed by VC firms such as Congruent Ventures, Galvanize Climate Solutions, and Union Square Ventures.

While Lydian has already announced a temporary pilot demonstration project in North Carolina, Rodden says Boston is a perfect place to develop this technology because of the region’s universities and research labs.

“For the majority of our hiring, we’re able to pull from the talent here in the Boston area,” says Rodden, who splits his time between San Francisco and Boston. “It’s been a big advantage in that regard.”

Plus, Rodden argues that Lydian and similar startups will draw talent to Boston from other metro areas.

“It’s a great thing to be able to pull those people into Boston,” Rodden says, “and to start to plant the seeds around industrial climate-tech in this area.”

Follow the money: It’s the tried-and-true maxim for getting to the bottom of complicated or deliberately obscured events.

In the case of President Trump’s attempt at regime change in Venezuela, the money trail passes through Boston’s Kenmore Square, where the Citgo sign — an unofficial landmark and touchstone of city life — is planted atop 660 Beacon St.

You see, Trump used the sign’s owner, Citgo Petroleum Corp., as leverage in his extended campaign to oust Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela’s authoritarian leader.

That effort began with sanctions during Trump’s first term, including a freeze on the US assets of Venezuela’s state oil company, which owned Citgo, a Houston-based refiner and pipeline operator. The freeze has not affected the sign, but combined with other sanctions, it crippled Venezuela’s oil-driven economy, formerly the richest in Latin America.

But Maduro clung to power despite increasing US pressure, leading to Saturday’s stunning raid by US Army commandos that captured him and his wife, Cilia Flores, in Caracas. They were whisked away to New York to face charges related to cocaine trafficking.

The latest: Trump doesn’t intend to stop there. He and administration officials made clear over the weekend that steering a substantial chunk of Venezuelan oil revenues toward the US was a key objective behind Maduro’s removal.

The US will continue a military blockade of the country’s oil exports until the government stops drug trafficking and opens up the oil sector, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday. “What you’re seeing right now is an oil quarantine that allows us to exert tremendous leverage over what happens next.”

Trump’s view: The president left no doubt about what he wants to see next.

“We’re going to have our very large United States oil companies, the biggest anywhere in the world, go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken. . . oil infrastructure, and start making money for the country,” he said during a Saturday news conference.

“We’re gonna be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground, and that wealth is going to the people of Venezuela. . . And it goes also to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country,” Trump said.

What’s at stake: Venezuela estimates its proven crude reserves at more than 300 billion barrels, the most of any country in the world.

The country was pumping about 3 million barrels a day in the mid-2000s. But after years of mismanagement under former president Hugo Chávez and Maduro, his successor, production has fallen to less than 1 million barrels, or about 1 percent of global output.

Oil prices were up slightly on Monday morning as investors weighed the fallout from Maduro’s capture. Shares of US energy companies, including Chevron, the only American company operating in Venezuela, jumped in trading.

Step back: When Venezuela nationalized its oil sector in 1976, it created Petróleos de Venezuela, or PDVSA, as the state oil company. The government opened up the sector in the 1990s to attract more foreign investment, but an exodus ensued after Chávez clamped down again.

While US sanctions took a toll, the state oil company, PDVSA had already been severely weakened by underinvestment, corruption, and the exodus of technical expertise.

Chevron held on — it’s been in Venezuela for more than 100 years. Operating with a special license, it accounts for about a quarter of the country’s output, with about half its production exported to the US.

Citgo’s role: PDVSA, seeking refining and distribution capacity in the US, bought a 50 percent stake in Citgo from Southland Corp. in 1986 and took full ownership four years later.

Trump’s first-term sanctions cut off Venezuela’s access to Citgo’s US operations, a reliable source of US dollars whose refineries were configured to handle PDVSA’s heavier grades of crude.

The US company’s parent, PDV Holding, has inhabited a legal netherworld: It’s been owned PDVSA but the US government recognizes a board of directors organized by the opposition-led National Assembly of Venezuela in 2019 after Maduro claimed reelection in a vote widely viewed as fraudulent.

After a series of mind-bending legal maneuvers — triggered when Venezuela and PDVSA stopped paying off debt and arbitration awards tied to nationalization — US courts ruled that creditors could go after the shares of PDV Holding. A Delaware judge then oversaw an auction of the shares, with proceeds going to creditors.

Amber Energy, backed by hedge fund Elliott Investment Management, won the bidding, but Citgo has appealed the decision.

The Iraq lesson: Trump’s plan to resurrect Venezuela’s oil sector echoes what happened after the US invaded Iraq in 2003 and toppled dictator Saddam Hussein.

Iraq’s crude production had fallen dramatically under sanctions and Saddam’s neglect. It took billions of dollars in investment and eight years to get output consistently back above pre-war levels.

In Venezuela, returning to peak production levels of the 1970s could require US companies such as Chevron and Exxon Mobil to invest about $10 billion a year over the next decade, Francisco Monaldi, an expert in Latin American energy at Rice University, told Bloomberg.

But before spending that kind of money, oil companies will want assurances of political and economic stability in Venezuela. Moreover, there is an oil glut and prices are near a five-year low.

Final thought: Cities Service, Citgo’s predecessor, put its sign up in Kenmore Square in 1940. The Citgo name appeared 25 years later with a new installation marking a rebranding.

The LED-lit sign is a reminder that oil still generates massive wealth despite political upheaval, environmental challenges, and real estate deals. (After 660 Beacon changed hands in 2016, a long-running lease deal was reached to keep the sign in place.)

Trump senses opportunity in Venezuela. Whether US oil companies will follow the money is another question.

A Democratic state lawmaker from Roxbury spent nearly $6,500 out of her campaign account last year on personal expenses — including at a salon and on food deliveries — in violation of state law, according to public records and campaign finance regulators.

State Representative Chynah Tyler must pay the state $6,000 under a settlement agreement released by the Office of Campaign and Political Finance on Tuesday.

State regulators said they identified $5,664 in campaign money Tyler used for her “personal use.” That included at least $4,500 in spending last spring and summer that the five-term Democrat failed to document even after regulators asked for bills, invoices, and other records.

In addition, Tyler has already reimbursed her campaign account for $830 in other “erroneous personal expenditures” that she herself admitted to, including $223 at a hair-braiding salon, $100 on a AAA membership, and several Uber Eats orders, campaign spending records show.

The personal spending accounted for a significant share of her campaign costs in 2025, a nonelection year during which she reported spending just under $40,000. And between April and June, when officials said Tyler did not account for $4,500 in expenses, her campaign reported spending $6,190 in total, records show.

Elected officials and candidates are allowed to use their campaign accounts for a range of purposes as long as they can show it’s for the “enhancement of [their] political future” and is not “primarily for personal use.” Under those rules, state lawmakers have used campaign funds to pay for swanky dinners, visits to cigar lounges, and luxury car leases.

Campaign finance regulators said that Tyler’s failure to document thousands of dollars in purchases “creates a presumption that the expenditure was made for personal use.”

Officials said Tyler also broke a series of other campaign finance rules when she filed late disclosures, took donations exceeding state-mandated limits, and failed to “keep detailed records,” according to the settlement.

Tyler did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. In a response included in the six-page agreement with state regulators, Tyler said she gave birth to a child in “winter 2025 and experienced limited mobility during that time, which impacted my ability to personally oversee certain campaign finance activities.”

She said that during that time, however, she continued to meet with constituents, “community leaders and other qualified professionals,” though she did not say how those meetings related to specific expenditures by her account.

“These meetings were in compliance with [campaign finance law], consistent with my commitment to transparency and adherence to all legal obligations related to campaign contributions and expenditures,” Tyler said in the statement.

Tyler was first elected in 2017 to succeed longtime representative Gloria Fox in a district rooted in Roxbury. She is currently the House vice chair of the Legislature’s committee on state administration and regulatory oversight, and in the past led the growing Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus.

But it only takes a moment with a handful of those watercolors to see what he means. Immediate, breathless, and intense, they often feel like stray thoughts captured and committed to paper in the brief moment before they flit away. Homer’s thoughts were rarely without gravitas — the curse of a life lived alongside conflict — and so, too, the watercolors, the largest collection of which is owned by the MFA. January is a time to celebrate fresh beginnings, and one way to embrace that spirit is by visiting new restaurants. There are a number of enticing openings off in the distance to anticipate. For instance, Michelin-starred chef George Mendes will open the tasting menu-focused Agosto in the South End in the summer, with bakery-cafe Baby Sister to follow (named after his son and daughter), while Danny Meyer Italian restaurant Ci Siamo expands from New York to the Seaport.

But in the here and now, diners can choose from sushi, Ethiopian cuisine, American comfort food, and beyond. In Back Bay, for the next month only, the lounge at Uni has been declared Lower Uni, offering four- and 10-course tasting menus. Korean mom-and-pop Park’s Kitchen, which offered takeout and delivery in Roxbury, has closed — to become a brick-and-mortar opening soon: Stay tuned for all your spicy rice cake and handmade dumpling needs. (In the meantime, check out the new Gangnam Spice, specializing in Korean fried chicken and more in Jamaica Plain.) And is it too soon to declare this the year of the neighborhood seafood restaurant? Lobster rolls are surfacing everywhere from Allston (at nouveau New England seafood shack Holdfast) to Watertown (read on).

Here are some restaurants to try in the coming days.

Acapella by X

In the longtime Blarney Stone space, something new for Fields Corner: a nightspot with good food and live music, with a generous patio and valet parking coming down the road. Longtime friends Freddy Ureña (chef), Yancarlo Fernandez (general manager), and Anthony Cruz (front-of-house manager) are behind the venture, which offers a menu inspired by Ureña’s travels. Ama at the Atlas

Three years ago, Comfort Kitchen arrived in Dorchester, with a menu that connected cultures, traced trade routes, and brought diners into its expansive worldview. Now, founding husband-wife team Nyacko Pearl Perry and Biplaw Rai and their Pearl & Law Hospitality group expand to Allston. At the Atlas Hotel, Ama is a salute to mothers and others who nurture us through food. (Rai is from Nepal; the restaurant’s name is Nepali for “mother.”) Ama, slated to open this month, features a menu that spans the globe, and the day. Breakfast might bring French toast flavored with Nepali spiced tea, lunch Senegalese-inspired yassa chicken salad sandwiches, dinner tamarind-glazed trout and Berbere-spiced fried chicken.

Atlas Hotel, 40 Western Ave., Allston, www.ama-boston.com

Black Cat Eatery at Wink & Nod

Chef Valentine Howell won a following at modern Greek restaurant Krasi in the Back Bay, then at his Black Cat popup at Jamaica Plain’s Vee Vee, which ended last March. Now Black Cat is on its second life, at South End culinary incubator-slash-speakeasy Wink & Nod. From shrimp ceviche to jackfruit empanadas to red snapper rundown in tomato-coconut broth, Howell’s Afro-Caribbean cuisine is bright and flavorful, a delight to eat and a wakeup for the palate.

Boxfish

When chef Manita Bunnagitkarn moved her popular Cha Yen Thai Cookery across the street in Watertown, it opened up possibilities for the former space. Now it is Boxfish, where Bunnagitkarn offers a seafood-focused menu notable for its originality. Of course there is a lobster roll, the meat poached in brown butter and served on brioche with lemon aioli, as well as clam chowder, a fried fisherman’s platter, and linguine with clams. From there, it goes freewheeling with dishes such as grilled octopus with ube mashed potatoes; fettuccine with uni, brown butter, and nori; and an elegant pan-seared fillet of the day with tomato concasse and beurre blanc. If you’re feeling more surf than turf, try the Boxfish sandwich, featuring shaved ribeye with fontina and caramelized onions.

613 Mount Auburn St., Watertown, www.boxfish.food

If you vaguely remember ripping it up at the Cactus Club on Boylston Street back in the day, don’t get excited. This is not a reincarnation of that. Cactus Club Cafe, which is on Boylston Street, is a Canadian export. It looks luxe, it opens for lunch and closes at midnight, and it has a crowd-pleasing menu comprising sushi, rigatoni Bolognese, miso caramel sea bass, burgers and steaks — and somehow much more, plus fun cocktails. If you want to get your OG Cactus Club on, don’t worry, there are tacos and margaritas here too.

Cafe Sushi, beloved in Cambridge, shuttered for dine-in service during the COVID era. Now it has reopened as Cafe Sushi Nisei (“second generation”), with a renovated dining room and sake bar. Brothers Seizi and Kenshi Imura continue to operate the restaurant, along with Seizi’s wife, Mindy Imura; the Imuras’ parents opened it in the mid-’80s and handed it down in 2007. Although the popular omakase menu Cafe Sushi once offered is no longer, the restaurant makes up for it with a focused menu of small plates, sashimi, nigiri, and rolls. Don’t miss the beautiful citrus salmon sashimi, with blood orange and fennel, or the madai nigiri with preserved yuzu.

Restaurateur Jason Doo is a nostalgist. His Harvard Square spot, Wusong Road, is an homage to classic tiki bars and Chinese-American restaurants like the one his parents ran, Bobo’s in Malden, when he was a kid. His new foray also reaches back to his childhood — spent hanging out at the very mall where he recently opened Gato Exotico. The CambridgeSide restaurant features a menu of guacamole, enchiladas, and tacos from chef Sergio Enriquez, plus drinks with names like the Tijuana Taxi and the Tres Leches Colada.

Just a few blocks from the Eritrean Community Center in the South End is Mesob, featuring Eritrean and Ethiopian cuisine and named for the traditional woven basket on which shared meals are served. Start with sambusas, then move on to an array of fresh salads and platters of kitfo, timtimo, shiro, and more, served with the flatbread injera. Mesob also offers wine, beer, and cocktails.

1746 Washington St., South End, Boston, 857-305-3468, www.mesobrestaurantboston.com

Moona

For dreamy Middle Eastern fare — platters of labneh, hummus, and olives with pita; feta fritters; lamb kefta; grilled branzino — diners flock to Moona in Cambridge’s Inman Square. Now owner Mohamad El Zein has opened a new branch of the restaurant, nearby in Central Square: It is bigger than the cozy original, with more and new dishes to try. After you’ve feasted on monkfish shish and date molasses-glazed lamb shank with freekeh, try Arabic coffee and rose crème caramel or orange blossom labneh frozen yogurt with kumquat jam for dessert. Cafe service is coming soon.

750 Main St., Central Square, Cambridge, 617-665-5915, www.moonarestaurant.com

The last week of December saw a “very high” spike in flu cases, according to the Department of Health.

In the span of a month, flu cases in Boston rose from 133 cases at the beginning of December to 672 cases the last week of the month, according to the Boston Public Health Commission. During the same timeframe, the percentage of flu-like illnesses in emergency department visits jumped from 2.7 percent to 11.1 percent.

Those totals dipped slightly at the beginning of 2026, with 652 reported flu cases, 20 fewer than the previous week, and 10 percent of total emergency department visits, down by a percentage point less.

However, the totals for the beginning of the year are still above those during the same time in 2025, when there were 326 flu cases reported in the city, and 5.2 percent of emergency department visits due to flu-like illness.

Last year, flu cases statewide spiked around February.

The clinic on Wednesday, inside a room on the eighth floor of City Hall, was staffed with registered nurses from LCG Boston, a nurse staffing agency that runs vaccination sites across Boston. There were almost 30 people already registered within the first 30 minutes.

For Jordan Bordner, a city employee, the convenience of the City Hall location influenced his decision to get vaccinated.

”Everyone should get a flu shot,“ Bordner said. ”It helps you and also everyone that you work with and everyone that you live with.”

There are three more clinics planned for this month:

10 a.m.-2 p.m. Saturday, Josephine A. Fiorentino Community Center, 123 Antwerp St., Brighton

3-7 p.m. Wednesday, BCYF Hyde Park Community Center, 1179 River St., Hyde Park

3-7 p.m. Thursday, BCYF Perkins Community Center, 155 Talbot Ave., Dorchester

The registered nurses have been working in these clinics since September, vaccinating more than 2,500 individuals around Boston as of Dec. 23.

“It’s been quite a long, long season,” said Glendaly Avalo-Valdez, registered nurse with LCG Boston.

Since September, the city has held 27 clinics. Avalo-Valdez said individual clinics typically serve between 30 and 100 people. She has been operating vaccination clinics throughout the city, including Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Brighton.

Other people getting vaccinated, like Maya Lazar, had personal experiences that motivated them to get vaccinated. After Lazar lost her brother because of the flu, she believes annual flu vaccinations are essential.

“I suggest getting your flu shot every single year,” Lazar said. “Specifically, with the strain that’s going around this year, which is pretty bad. So everyone should get their flu shot, it just helps keep other people safe.”

The clinic is also an opportunity for those who weren’t able to get their vaccinations earlier in the season. Zoe Davis, a mom of 11-month-old twins, dropped into the clinic to get both her flu and COVID-19 vaccinations.

“I don’t have either shot so far, I’ve just been busy with my twins,” Davis said.

Worrell, who with his brother Chris, a state representative, is one half of what constitutes a prospective political dynasty in Boston, a natural bridge builder in a city that needs more bridges. And I wouldn’t be surprised if Brian Worrell becomes Boston’s first elected Black mayor some day, and he’d be a good one, for myriad reasons.

He comes from a terrific family, who have been an integral part of one of the city’s great traditions, the annual Hewins Street block party in Dorchester, which for more than a half-century has brought together one of the most vibrant, diverse group of people in the city.

But for reasons that seem more political than personal, with Mayor Michelle Wu’s fingerprints all over it, Brian Worrell wasn’t elected City Council president.

Liz Breadon was. And, despite all the politics and wheeling and dealing, that is a good thing.

It is a good thing, some will say, because as the first openly gay president of the Boston City Council, she shows glass ceilings are being shattered in centers of power all over town, even City Hall.

That said, identity politics without substance is just shallow sloganeering. But Liz Breadon is a woman of substance. And her identity, not just her sexuality but where she comes from, is key to understanding what kind of person she is and what kind of leader she could become.

Breadon grew up and came of age in rural Fermanagh, one of the six counties that make up Northern Ireland. While most of the attention during The Troubles — as the Irish, in their penchant for understatement, called their civil war — was focused on urban areas in Belfast and Derry, some of the most pernicious sectarianism and unspeakable atrocities occurred in rural areas like Fermanagh.

Breadon’s father was a farmer, her mother a nurse, and the family also ran a small country store. The civil unrest that launched The Troubles in the late 1960s began when Breadon was about 10 years old.

The ensuing violence led many people to retreat to their tribal enclaves. But Breadon was lucky in that her Protestant family counted many Catholic friends among the customers of their store. And, unlike the vast majority of students in Northern Ireland who attend schools that are segregated by religion and national identity, she went to school with Catholics.

When she embraced her sexuality in her early 20s, she also acknowledged the Protestant and Catholic churches which most people in Northern Ireland called their spiritual homes were irrevocably hostile to gay people.

She came to Boston in 1995, experiencing a liberating, life-affirming personal freedom that was not attainable in her homeland. Years before she joined the council, she and her spouse, Mary McCarthy, who Breadon likes to call “a nice Irish Catholic girl,” were supporters of two women who launched the campaign to bring marriage equality to the Republic of Ireland, which in 2015 became the first country to legalize same-sex marriage by popular vote.

The ballot question came after Katherine Zappone, a native of Seattle, and Ann Louise Gilligan, a native of Ireland and former nun, who fell in love while studying at Boston College, legally challenged the Irish government’s refusal to recognize their marriage in Canada. Breadon and McCarthy held a fund-raiser for the campaign in their Oak Square home.

Unlike most politicians, Breadon knows what it’s like to be told you can’t be yourself.

And, perhaps more than any politician in Boston, past or present, she has seen what happens when incivility takes root, and people retreat to echo chambers, dehumanizing the other side while civil society slides off a cliff.

After Charlie Kirk was assassinated, I wrote a column expressing unease with those who cheered his murder, lamenting, while not excusing Kirk’s divisive rhetoric, that the growing polarization in this country uncomfortably reminded me of what I observed during the more than 20 years I covered the conflict in Northern Ireland.

“I’ve seen what happens when people are so convinced of the righteousness of their side that they dehumanize the other side to the point that not only are they unmoved when someone from the other side is murdered, they actually celebrate it,” I wrote. “I’ve seen this movie before, and have no desire to see it again.”

Not long after that column was published, I heard from Breadon. She noted that her upbringing informed her views and that she was appalled not just by those cheering Kirk’s assassination, but by President Trump’s baselessly and irresponsibly blaming it on Democrats.

“Violence has no place in civil society and it is frightening to hear the President throwing fuel on the fire by openly calling Democrats domestic terrorists,” she wrote in an email to me. “Charlie Kirk was no angel, he profited from peddling misinformation, mistrust and hate, but he did not deserve to die by gun violence.”

Where Liz Breadon comes from, they have a phrase for getting people off their high horses and, as the Irish say, stop acting the muppet. It’s called, “putting manners on them” — not by shaming them as much as emphasizing the importance of empathy, respect and civility.

Here’s hoping she can put some manners on the Boston City Council, and, while she’s at it, the rest of us, too.

In large part, that’s because the prevailing public notion of “Boston music” seems to be set in stone, as if its legacy is predetermined — and done. That — curses! — talent and opportunity are in limited supply here, and folks such as the Cars, Donna Summer, New Edition, and that sweet spot of alt-rock a lá Buffalo Tom, Letters to Cleo, and the Lemonheads, must have gobbled up most of it. Then the paltry scraps were just enough to fuel a few aughts success stories, like cabaret-rock outfit the Dresden Dolls, esteemed jazz bassist and Berklee alum esperanza spalding, and shimmering electro-pop act Passion Pit. In 2020, the Globe even published a story asking “where has all the music gone?,” which amplified this alleged death knell.

As a music columnist whose 4-inch boots are regularly sticking to the weathered floors of local clubs and dives, I know this is all bogus. Yet it’s a perspective I’ve often heard repeated in bar conversations, social media posts, and comment sections, to the point that it’s dangerously close to becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy.

In 2026, the concept of Boston music is overdue for a complete reimagining. The current implications of the phrase — that Boston’s mainly a rock city, and one with waning influence, at that — is outdated and incorrect. It also immediately tees up disappointment.

There are few cities with internet access (if any) where music consumption hasn’t become streaming-forward and algorithm-steered. Record label representatives often look for fresh faces on TikTok, judging an artist’s potential based on a viral hook instead of full performances and in-person panache. Certain acts monopolized the Billboard Hot 100 to the point where the chart had to change its rules to make room for new entries and force turnover. Releasing umpteen album variants — editions with bonus tracks, free autographs, alternate cover art, the blood of the artist’s first-born, you name it — is now one of the only ways musicians can move a significant amount of physical records. If Boston doesn’t “make ’em like we used to,” it’s because the 20th-century roadmap to success went out the window, nationwide, years ago.

Usually, the local music conversation — if it even gets that far — ends there, on a note that’s at best nostalgic, and at worst embittered about an issue that’s far larger than Boston. But the outlook gets better if you keep talking, and consider the reality that Boston just makes ’em differently now.

The newest roadmaps to success start in Boston and stretch to locales far beyond the city and its neighboring suburbs. The Mass Music & Arts Summit (organized by Boston nonprofit Beat The Odds) brought representatives from Warner Records and the streaming platform Audiomack directly to the Seaport last fall. Professionals from every pocket of the state’s music industry continue to pursue membership in the Recording Academy to forge connections with each other and the national music community.

Brockton’s a hotbed of activity, rooted in the success of Soundlab Recording Studios and Van Buren Records, a hip-hop collective comprising members like FELIX!, who seems poised to follow the path of recent Massachusetts hip-hop standouts such as BIA and Cousin Stizz. (He currently boasts more than 1.3 million monthly Spotify listeners.) In Salem, the nonprofit MOON is bringing together the North Shore music scene with its sober and all-ages venue Moon Base One, which you might recall from my coverage of its nifty “cassingle booth” last year.

There’s countless more examples that won’t fit here, although you’ll find a steady supply of them in my weekly music column, Sound Check (a shameless plug but a pertinent one nonetheless).

I’m not proposing that we paint over the past for this rebrand. Quite the contrary — the best boons for the scene’s morale come from juxtaposing different eras of the city’s music history, without one overshadowing another. Done right, that looks like R&B sensation New Edition and modern emcee Joyner Lucas receiving honorary streets in their respective hometowns of Roxbury and Worcester, less than two weeks apart last year.

Another prime crossroads of the city’s past and present: the Rock & Roll Rumble, the longest-running battle-of-the-bands-style competition in the country. The annual event has changed hands over the years, starting as a WBCN project, and is now helmed by Anngelle Wood via her online radio program, “Boston Emissions.” Every spring, a fresh crop of area bands who have never Rumble’d duke it out over the course of one month.

Founded in 1979, the Rumble is a true continuation of Boston music history, which has given rise to everyone from ’Til Tuesday (1983) to the Sheila Divine (1999), to Weakened Friends, the pride of Portland (runners-up, 2016). The Rumble took a break in 2025, but mentioned “a plan to return in 2026″ on social media last year. I sincerely hope it returns this spring.

There’s a saying that often surfaces in my work covering underrepresented communities: “If you can see it, you can be it.” The meaning, of course, is that representation in mass media reminds us that our aspirations aren’t impossible. If we can’t see Boston music — however you wish to define it — as something that’s still alive, then we’ve basically already closed the coffin.

And I really don’t want to write the obituary.
