The following is a lightly edited transcript of the Jan. 8 episode.

Kusmer: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Anna Kusmer, filling in for Shirley Leung.

Boston is a very diverse and dynamic place, but in Hollywood, a certain vibe often dominates: scrappy, working class, Irish American. I think today’s guest was one of the first people to really paint that picture for the public.

Dennis Lehane is a writer who grew up in Dorchester and wrote some popular books about the neighborhoods of his childhood. There’s “Gone Baby Gone,” “Mystic River,” and many more. More recently, he wrote “Small Mercies,” a book set during busing. His current focus is writing for television. His latest show is called “Smoke” on Apple TV, it stars Jurnee Smollett and Taron Egerton.

It’s a crime show about arson and fire. Dennis said his fascination with fire goes back to when he was in one.

Lehane: I was living in a building where the roof caught fire and the fire alarm system was broken — here in Boston, Charlesgate West overlooking the Charles. There were these homeless people who lived under the off ramp for Storrow Drive, and they came in, they rang all our doorbells, and they banged all these trash cans together. They woke us up and they saved our lives. So, yeah, I’ve stared fire in the face a little bit.

The show is inspired by real things. It’s a real arsonist named John Orr who lived and worked in Glendale, California, in the 1980s.

I just saw it as a way to look at chaos. Like I think our country is in a state of just total chaos right now. I think most people are chaotic in general. It’s just my personal belief, and so I wanted to look at chaos in every shape and form. And then once we came up with, once we leaned into this idea of fire, the big directive I gave to my team was, I’ve seen so much crappy fire out there. Fake fire. And I don’t want one bit of this to look fake.

Kusmer: You mentioned chaos, but what other ideas are you tackling with this new show?

Lehane: Oh, I think there’s a lot in there about, kind of like white grievance politics. You know, there’s two arsonists in this show. And they’re counterpoints for each other. One of them believes himself to be a victim.

The other one truly is a victim of society. That’s not making an excuse for him, but it’s saying that this guy literally had no chance.

The other guy had plenty of chances. He just chose not to take ‘em. And then he wants to sit back and whine about it. So I think that’s in there. We just wanted to look at people who were just really on a collision course with the consequences of hiding who they really are.

Kusmer: Right. And there’s a lot in there about sort of being in and out of control, and how that affects your behavior, and how it changes your personality.

Lehane: A hundred percent. I mean, that’s all to the end of the day. That was my favorite thing about what I do. The Greeks called “in extremis.” And so it’s like in extreme circumstances people are revealed. Nobody knows who they are until they’ve been in a really extreme circumstance. I love this phrase that Comac McCarthy had, which is he believes in “fiction of mortal event.”

I’m not a writer who can write like Henry James about like a crack in the Golden Bowl. Okay. I could care less. You’re rich. Go buy another bowl. I want to write about extreme circumstances with people in extremis. That’s what I’m into.

Kusmer: I think one thing that’s very Lehanian, if I can say, is humor and dialogue. There’s so much banter on your new show, but I think that’s true of your books in general. It’s dark, but it’s also funny. Can you talk to me about the connection between darkness and humor for you?

Lehane: Oh, it’s just how I grew up. I’ve never met a comedian half as funny as at least five people I knew growing up in Dorchester. And you know, my dad was part of a bar culture. He used to bring me into bars all the time and pretend, tell my mother we were at a farmer’s market so he could sneak in and have a drink on a Saturday. So I grew up listening to people talk and tell stories.

The point of any working class story is I got screwed, but I got a little bit of vengeance. Like, I keyed his car. I slept with his sister. So it’s a tragic story — “I got screwed” — but it’s got a little bit of levity in it.

Because the idea is, I think in Irish culture — and that’s where Dorchester and Savin Hill where I grew up and Southie, that’s where we get our sense of humor — they believe that God is a prankster and we’re the joke. We’re the butt of the joke, you know? And so I think that’s something that just goes into my work and I can’t not be funny, as much as my stuff is really dark.

Like the funniest thing is when — “Mystic River” was the first book I wrote that doesn’t seem to have many jokes in it — but when I read it out loud, people almost look for permission because they start to laugh. The voice is actually very funny. But the story is so dark, you’ve got to hear it to laugh.

Kusmer: I always think of Boston humor as like, there’s a lot of like defense mechanisms. It’s sort of like a way of processing pain. I know it’s true everywhere, but I think it’s particularly true here.

Lehane: Oh, it’s particularly true here. I mean, I’m sorry. I went to school down south, and irony and sarcasm dies at the Mason-Dixon line. I mean,I got so tired of people staring at me like they just didn’t, I left. I think I left the South because I got tired of people not getting my jokes

Kusmer: One of many things I found really funny about the new series is that one of your main characters is an aspiring crime writer, but he’s a bit of a hack. What do you think separates good crime writing from mediocre crime writing?

Lehane: No, it’s good writing. It’s just good writing. It’s not crime writing, or romance writing, or anything. I believe that all writing is just either good writing or not good writing. You have to have depth, you have to have depth of character, you have to have depth of language, you have to have depth of story.

I think it has to be honest. Honest writing can get over some real clunky writing. Like if you feel like you’re reading somebody’s authentic experience, even if they don’t choose maybe the best word, you don’t mind. But if I feel inauthenticity in what you’re reading, I throw the book away again. There’s no way I’m reading it. There’s no way I’m watching the show.

Kusmer: How do you train yourself in that way? Like, you know, make sure that you’re staying true and authentic in your own writing?

Lehane: You build, you train. It’s a muscle and it takes, I don’t care what anybody says, the bottom line is it takes 10 years. It takes 10 years to master it. That doesn’t mean that you might not be publishing. I published my first book, eight years in, but I didn’t know what I was doing until I wrote my second. Then I was like, “Oh, okay. Phew. Okay, I think I got this.”

And you gotta be hungry and you gotta be willing to park your vanity at the door. You can have a strong ego about the work, but if you are there, just so people will praise you — like when I go into writer’s classes or I teach and I see somebody who’s in the room basically to be praised — just leave.

That was one of the great training experiences [while writing on] “The Wire.” They had no respect for anybody who needed to be treated with kid gloves. None of us were like that. I mean, I would literally have somebody look at me and say, “I don’t like that idea.” Why? “‘Cause it sucks.” Oh, okay. Well thanks a lot. You know, it was literally like that.

I work almost exclusively with three women in my writing teams. And we washed out all the weak people, and they were all guys. We just got sick of dealing with their egos. I can’t deal with your needs, man.

My head writer will look at me now and say, “That sucks.” And I’ll be like, “Okay. Fair enough. Well, and your idea sucks too.” We’ll go back and forth with each other. You can’t be sensitive. If you’re looking for a safe space, a writers room ain’t it. Let me just put it that way.

Kusmer: We’re in the era of the anti-hero. I feel like that’s almost its own cliché. It’s not just that your characters are anti-heroes. It’s just that they’re really messy people.

Lehane: They’re messy people. How many non-messy people do you know? ‘Cause I don’t. I get so tired of it when I read the bad guys who are so bad, and the good guys who are so good. You know, it’s like I’m bored already. I’m bored saying it, you know? I know messy people.

One of the things I think is the biggest delusion is that we know why we do things. You’ll get to my age. You look back on your life, and the most common thing that you’ll say about most of the major decisions you made is, “What was I thinking? What was I thinking? For God’s sake? I guess it seemed like a good idea at the time, but it was a terrible idea.”

We do things all the time out of instincts, and often those instincts are bad. I think, you know, Taron’s character says it near the end of the show. He says, “You know, all these things we give different names to, it’s just appetite. I’m hungry and I want to eat, and that’s it. There’s your morality.”

And I do believe that pretty, pretty hard.

Kusmer: I wanna talk about Boston now.

Lehane: Yeah!

Kusmer: So you grew up in Dorchester? Savin Hill?

Lehane: Yeah. St. Margaret’s Parish — a little bit below Savin Hill. Edward Square. Those are our stomping grounds.

Kusmer: Did your upbringing look and sound at all like a Dennis Lehane novel?

Lehane: Yeah. Inside my house did not. The tribute to my actual life is Sean’s parents in “Mystic River.” That’s my actual life, except for the fact that his parents aren’t immigrants. My parents are immigrants. You went into my house and you felt safe, and you felt like you weren’t in 1980s Boston — you felt like you were in 1940s Ireland. That was the vibe. I liked that a lot and I felt safe in my home. Without a doubt.

The streets outside were kind of rough. I was 9 when busing happened. I mean, there was just a lot of violence in the streets, a lot of racial violence. Boston was a dirtier town back then.

It wasn’t like now. I mean, I can’t even write a crime novel in Boston anymore because nothing ever happens here, you know? Um. What’d you have one murder last year? It was ridiculous.

Kusmer: Mayor Wu is proud…

Lehane: No, I love it. I love it. It’s a great city. I’d love to have raised my kids here. Yeah. But I’m a homer. I just love it, warts and all.

Kusmer: I can imagine that living, especially living in California, that a lot of your work is kind of rooted in nostalgia for the streets of your childhood?

Lehane: Yeah. It’s a vanished world. That world doesn’t exist anymore. And I write a lot about that with great love and a jaundiced viewpoint. Sometimes it’s like, people say, “Aren’t people angry about your writing?” For the most part, no, because I think I do warts and all.

Kusmer: Yeah.

Lehane: And so yeah, you’ll see the warts. You also see all the wonderful things about it. I loved growing up in a working class town. I loved the feeling of it. I loved the loyalty. I loved the jokes. I loved the sense of family bonds. I loved all of it. I don’t find that in a lot of the rest of the world.

Kusmer: You really capture the character of a certain era of Boston, particularly, you know, those neighborhoods where you grew up. A lot of times people will say that books are like a love letter to a place.

Lehane: Yes.

Kusmer: I’m not sure your Boston based stories are a love letter per se, but because they’re so open about the ugly side of people here, there’s so much abuse, tribalism, prejudice in your books. How do you go about capturing all the different sides of a place?

Lehane: Boston is unlike any other place. It just is. And, and you know, it’s a little bit like Chicago. It’s a little bit like Philly, but it’s its own place. And people are — and I say this as with pride — we’re all just at least a can short of a six pack. We’re all just a little bit off. You know? And I don’t know if that’s the Irish influence or what.

I was in Miami for graduate school, and I remember worrying that I was losing the Boston voice. Right? So I went back home and I ran into a guy and I said, “How you doing?” He’d been kind of a brawler.

And he said, “Uh, I’m good. You know, I got stabbed a couple months ago,” and I was like, “What happened?” He tells me the story. He says, “I was in Faneuil Hall and, and I got into beef with this guy. And anyway, he stabbed me.” And he said, “I dunno what you’ve heard, but it really takes the fight out of a guy.”

And I thought that’s it. That’s the voice. That right there, it’s, “I don’t know what you’ve heard.” Like you may have heard that, you know, getting stabbed is kind of like a hot stone massage, you know? And then the incredible understatement — not “I was praying for my God,” not “it hurt so much.” No. “It kind of takes the fight out of a guy.”

Like that’s the Boston I know. That’s the Boston that is always in my head when I write, and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that my personal favorites — that I think my three best books are written in that voice. There’s only three books I wrote specifically in that narrative voice and it’s “Mystic River,” and “The Drop,” and “Small Mercies.”

And they’re all the same narrator. It’s the same person telling the story, and it’s a guy in a bar. That’s the way I’ve always pictured him. He’s a guy in a bar and he has a really cool story to tell you, and he’s not sentimental and he’s kind of funny, and he’ll take the wind out of you if you are remotely pretentious.

And that’s that voice. And I love writing in that voice, but I’ve only done it three times.

Kusmer: Yeah. I want to talk about “Small Mercies.” After a long hiatus from book writing, you release “Small Mercies” in 2023. It takes place during the Boston busing crisis. What motivated you to set this book during busing and take on these themes: racism, tribalism, in that way?

Lehane: I think it’s the story of the city. I don’t think you can understand the city until you understand busing and what happened. I grew up in it. I was 9. And I saw it firsthand. My neighborhood bordered South Boston.

I had a front row seat for it, and I saw KKK graffiti. I saw “kill all the ‘n-word’” graffiti. I’m 9 years old and I’m like, “What the hell is going on here?” You’re 9, you’re supposed to be a child. And I feel like after that, I wasn’t.

And so I had a lot of anger built up in me because the one weird thing was — and I don’t say this with any pride or anything — I just wasn’t a racist.

And I grew up with racism everywhere. I mean, it was in my house. It was out on the streets. It was in my friends’ houses, it was everywhere. And I just didn’t have it. It was just, I don’t know why. I mean, I probably should have. But I think it’s because my dad constantly would talk against it.

He would just say, you know, “I don’t care if you’re Black, white, green, or purple. You have a place at this table.” I loved my dad and I took all my cues of what to be a man from my father. And so I think I took that from my dad. But what I also saw on the other side was — I very much had a very adult concept very early on, and I believe this to this day — that it is, “Why are we fighting each other? Hmm? We’re both poor.”

Why the hell are we throwing rocks at each other? Why are we fighting each other in the streets? Oh, because it’s in the best interest of the people who actually control this country to keep the poor fighting amongst themselves because if the poor ever figured it out, they could do some damage.

And so it’s very important that the poor never realize that they have much more in common than they have in differences. And that’s why you always see, at times of economic disparity or economic insecurity — I don’t care if it’s Nazi Germany or it’s America — you will always see people playing the race card. Always.

Kusmer: Do you feel like those early memories of feeling so alienated — the kind of emotional imprint that that had on you — how did writing about it help you process what you witnessed?

Lehane: I think that’s what it was. I felt like a spy in an enemy camp, you know? Because I had to listen to all this. It wasn’t like you could stand up and say, “No, no, don’t use the ‘n-word.’” You know, like, you’re gonna beat down, you know? I wasn’t picking any fights, essentially. And so I think I just, I began to bifurcate as a person. And that turned me into a writer.

The two things I think that are most important in my maturation as a writer are coming from Dorchester and busing.

Kusmer: Did writing the book make you realize anything that you hadn’t realized before?

Lehane: Yeah. I finally realized why I was so angry. I’d been walking around my entire life with this pit of rage in me, and it’s very hard to get through, but when you get there, it comes out. And I was like, why? I had great parents. You know, I was never abused. I don’t have any traumatic stories from my childhood. You know what I mean?

Like what? That’s what puts rage in people. Oh, finally, as I’m writing the book, it’s all pouring out of me. And I was like, you’re pissed off about that that summer.

Kusmer: What you were exposed to.

Lehane: Yeah. At 9, what you saw, 9. It’s not fair. And I looked at my own kids and one of whom was around 9 when I started writing the book, and I was like, man, if anybody exposed her to this, you know, I mean, it would be criminal. I would consider it criminal. You know, you’re taking a kid’s innocence away.

And so I’m one of one kid in the city at that time. How many other kids never got it? How many other kids never had a childhood? In some ways because they were watching the adults who they were supposed to look up to throwing bricks at buses with kids in them. I mean, what are you supposed to do with that?

Kusmer: Yeah. So, I don’t need to tell you this, but you know, there’s this national stereotype about Boston, people think of movies like “The Departed,” you know, Affleck movies, obviously your books and movies as well laid the foundation for how people see the city in popular culture. Irish American, insular, working class, sassy, violent. Do you take some credit for sort of how much Boston is seen that way in popular culture?

Lehane: Oh yeah. No, I can’t wash my hands of that one. That’s on me. We even shot “The Drop” in Brooklyn because we just didn’t want to do one more Irish gangster story set in Boston, you know, so we moved it to Brooklyn. Yeah, it’s on me.

Kusmer: How do you feel about sort of being so responsible for how the rest of the country and the world, frankly, see Boston?

Lehane: Well, it’s not just on, I mean, it’s on “The Departed” and…

Kusmer: But I think of them as your successors.

Lehane: I know, I know. Here’s a crazy thing. If there’s a book or a movie, and there’s a bar in it — it happens in Boston, and there’s a gun — people think I wrote it. It doesn’t matter. The number of people who have come up to me and thanked me for writing “The Departed” or “The Town” is, I mean, it’s endless. I’m talking Bostonians. I’ve gotten fan letters for “The Departed,” I’m not kidding. I got a fan letter from a very famous person for “The Departed,” thanking me for how much they loved it.

I can only tell you, I was watching this documentary on Martin Scorsese, and he’s a big idol of mine. And somebody said, “Well, how do you feel about people who say you use too much music in your movies?” And he said, “Then I use too much music, and I probably move the camera too much.” Like you can live with it, I can live with it. What I set out to do when I set out to be a writer, I have far exceeded that, and so I am just grateful as hell

Kusmer: In LA, are you basically “Boston guy”? Like you get a call whenever anyone is setting anything in Boston so they don’t look like an idiot?

Lehane: No. Sometimes I get a little offended. I’m like, “Wait a minute you guys, I’m right here, guys. You guys did ‘The Equalizer’ with my favorite actor? You set it in Boston and nobody called me?” I was a little bit offended, like, “What the hell?” No, they do Boston without me. Plenty of times. Plenty of times.

Kusmer: Do you have any advice for capturing the Boston accent? It’s endlessly talked about. Bad Boston accents in movies.

Lehane: Oh, It’s so bad. It’s so bad.

Kusmer: What, what are the common pitfalls?

Lehane: The biggest one is dragging. It’s not an elongation. It’s an amputation. People don’t say “nevaaahh.” They say “neva.’” You know, they say “foreva,’” you know, it comes out fast, and it’s when you drag it that you get into trouble. And so I think, um, you know, Paul Walter Hauser, who did “Blackbird” with me, he went and did a Matt Damon movie with Matt Damon and Casey Affleck that was on Apple, I think a year ago. I’m forgetting the name of it, but he was like, “Should I do the accent?” And I’m like, “If anybody gives you a look, stop.”

Kusmer: Right. A lot of people would benefit from that advice. Who do you think’s done it best? Non-Bostonians.

Lehane: I’ll tell you who I think is the best and nobody’s seen the movie is the entire cast of “Monument Ave.”

Kusmer: Haven’t seen it.

Lehane: It’s a movie from the ‘90s. Ted Demme made it with Dennis Leary and it’s really wonderful. It’s this very dark crime drama, and I think Leary must have been coaching everybody because Billy Crudup is great. Famke Janssen’s great. I mean, people who are not Bostonians crushed it. Absolutely crushed it. And so that one sticks out to me.

The worst of them is “A Perfect Staaahm.” Diane Lane’s accent is so bad that it affects Mark Wahlberg’s accent, and he grew up here. That’s pretty bad.

Kusmer: It’s a domino effect.

Lehane: Yeah. There was one Mel Gibson made that nobody remembers, called “Edge of Darkness.” And I think they called it “Edge of Darkness” just so they could say “dahkness.” And that was really bad too.

I tell actors: Call the Land Rover dealership in Norwood. Because there’s a woman who answers the phone there. It’s a phone recording — at least she used to be 10 years ago. I loved it. You would call up and she would say, “Thank you for calling Land Rover of Norwood.” You’re like, that’s all you need, man. That’s it. Land Rover of Norwood. You know?

Kusmer: They’re probably like, “We get a lot of calls. We don’t know why. A lot of calls from California.”

Lehane: Yeah.

Kusmer: That’s really good. So in Boston we have a poet laureate, but I would like to name you our crime writer laureate. Do you accept?

Lehane: You’re so kind. I accept. Thank you. Okay, so I’ll be the, I’ll be the the writer laureate, the novelist laureate, the whatever laureate, crime fiction laureate.

Kusmer: We’re honored.

Lehane: Good stuff kid.

A leader of a Dorchester based gang pleaded guilty to racketeering and drug charges Friday in federal court in Boston, the Massachusetts US Attorney’s office said.

Anthony Centeio, also known by the street name “Wheezy,” 37, of Boston and Rehoboth, is charged with conspiracy to participate in a racketeering enterprise; conspiracy to distribute 500 grams of more of cocaine, cocaine base and methamphetamine; and being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition, US Attorney Leah B. Foley’s office said in a statement.

The next court date for the Centeio is May 7, at which time sentencing will be discussed, court records show.

Centeio was a leader of Cameron Street, a gang based largely in Dorchester that uses violence and threats of violence to preserve, protect and expand its territory, promote a climate of fear and enhance its reputation, prosecutors said.

In 2022, Centeio was one of 19 alleged Cameron Street members charged in a 39-count federal indictment with crimes that include gun and drug trafficking, illegal gun possession, racketeering conspiracy, and possessing guns in furtherance of drug trafficking , the Globe reported.

Centeio and another Cameron Street member, Daronde Bethea, also known as “Freeze,” tried to shoot and kill a NOB/Wendover gang member in Dorchester in June 2018, prosecutors said. Bethea was sentenced to nearly 24 years in prison for his role in Cameron Street, including the attempted murder in June 2024, the statement said.

Law enforcement recorded controlled purchases of a firearm from Centeio between February 2021 and March 2022, prosecutors said. They also recorded purchases of more than 500 grams of cocaine and cocaine base from Centeio directly or through his cousin and co-defendant Michael Lopes.

Lopes was sentenced to more than four years in prison in May 2024, prosecutors said.

Authorities searched Centeio’s home in Rehoboth in April 2022 and found $25,760 in cash, a Glock .45 caliber semi-automatic pistol, 21 rounds of .45 caliber ammunition, and clothing and jewelry associated with Cameron Street, prosecutors said. Centeio was encountered at Lopes’ residence in Pawtucket, R.I., where hundreds of grams of cocaine, cocaine base and methamphetamine, packaging materials for street level sales and cash were seized.

But some skeptics said they’re wary of carving gaps into environmental guardrails, even in the name of greener transportation. They question whether environmental regulations are such a substantial hindrance to getting projects over the finish line.

“There are a lot of agencies who simply don’t want to do things, don’t want to spend money, don’t want to make major investments, and they use the environmental process as an excuse for not making them,” said Fred Salvucci, the Massachusetts secretary of transportation under former Governor Michael Dukakis.

Public environmental reviews, codified by the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) and related regulations, are triggered when projects meet specific thresholds, such as if they alter a certain amount of land, generate a certain volume of pollutants, add a certain length of road, and so on.

Projects with a bigger expected environmental footprint can require more thorough environmental impact reports that flesh out in detail what a project might do to the environment and what would be done to mitigate those effects.

State law also mandates impact reports for any potentially damaging project within a mile of an environmental justice population, historically overlooked areas with large concentrations of low-income households, non-English speakers, or minority communities.

The impact reports can be exhaustive, demanding portraits of a work site’s topography, habitats, and soil, among other minute details. The draft environmental impact report for the Allston Multimodal Transportation Project, a behemoth effort to reorient part of the Massachusetts Turnpike, spanned more than 600 pages (without appendices).

This process can hamper projects that could greatly benefit the environment, said Crighton, who last year put forward a bill that aims to exempt zero or low-emission rail projects from the need to “produce environmental impact reports.”

“When you look at these diesel commuter rail train locomotives that are spewing out diesel fumes and particulate matter into environmentally sensitive areas, into our backyards, I think most folks would recognize that there is a benefit there, and one that’s worth expediting the process for,” Crighton said.

The T is in the early stages of electrifying its commuter rail service in the hopes of slashing emissions and improving service. It plans to deploy battery-electric locomotives along the Fairmount Line in 2028.

In recent years, the T has undergone MEPA reviews for track improvements in Billerica and a commuter rail maintenance facility in Hyde Park, according to the state’s MEPA database. MEPA analysts have also scrutinized a pedestrian and bike path in Williamstown pitched by MassDOT.

A related bill, presented by state Senator Cynthia Stone Creem, seeks to exempt other types of transit projects from MEPA review, including new bike facilities and light rail and transit lanes within existing rights of way.

These types of projects “are all things that we should be able to help and move along,” said Creem. “Having a better and cleaner transportation option allows us to reduce vehicle emissions that pollute our waterways and harm natural habitats.”

Costs and timelines of the review process can vary, experts said.

“Each project is so context specific,” said Seth Gadbois, a clean transportation staff attorney at Conservation Law Foundation, a Boston-based environmental advocacy group.

According to state rules, the public has 30 days to review the first round of environmental assessments. Environmental impact reports, the next, more intensive review stage, are subject to a 37-day public review period.

The process can get prolonged by the state if it’s dissatisfied with the reviews, or by legal challenges filed by those displeased with a report’s approval.

Working through impact reports can take a minimum of nine to 12 months, and cost $350,000 to $1 million, housing developers and development experts told a state housing commission, according to a February 2025 government report.

The state enacted MEPA in the 1970s. Bearing a nearly identical name to its federal cousin, the measure was born amid a burgeoning public consciousness about the well-being of the environment, and the government’s role in protecting it from the most destructive byproducts of human industry.

“MEPA exists to make sure that decision makers, communities and the proponents of any given project are aware of all the potential consequences, positive or negative, and that we have that view so that we can address negative consequences accordingly,” Gadbois said.

That information, some advocates said, is vital.

“The neighborhood that you live in should have information [about] how different developments impact their public health. That’s something that we advocated and fought for, for a very long time,” said Dwaign Tyndal, executive director of Alternatives for Community and Environment, an environmental justice advocacy group based in Roxbury.

Massachusetts is confronting the potentially cataclysmic consequences of a warming climate. The state government in 2021 pledged to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

Achieving that goal, experts and advocates said, hinges on changing the way Massachusetts moves. The transportation sector is responsible for 37 percent — the largest share — of the Bay State’s emissions, according to government assessments. Light duty passengers vehicles — cars, SUVs, and other four-wheel vehicles below a certain weight threshold — generate the greatest portion of those emissions.

State political leaders have sought to slacken MEPA’s rigor before. This past fall, the Healey administration announced tweaks to the MEPA process designed to speed up housing construction. The amendments allowed some types of housing projects to forego the more strenuous stages of MEPA review.

Some doubt doing away with MEPA assessments for some transportation projects would speed up much at all. Pete Wilson, senior policy director of Transportation for Massachusetts, suspects the time savings from a MEPA exemption would be relatively meagre, not nearly enough to justify foregoing valuable public discussions.

“Removing the MEPA requirement,” Wilson wrote in an October letter to the legislature, “would have minimal impact on streamlining the permitting process,” given all the other state and federal regulations projects must clear to move forward — the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, Massachusetts Historic Commission rules, among others.

“Time is money,” Wilson acknowledged. But, he added, “faster doesn’t always mean they’re better.”

Crighton said he’s speaking with advocates to adjust the bill’s language. He said he knows his bill isn’t a “silver bullet.”

But, Crighton said, “you have to chip away” at reform.

Since its founding, TransMedics has grown into a publicly-traded company worth more than $4.7 billion. And now, the Andover-based firm has finalized plans to move its headquarters to Somerville, leasing a vacant lab building just outside Assembly Row and planning to hire for at least 600 new positions by 2032.

The nearly 500,000-square-foot lease at 188 Assembly Park Drive is the largest lab deal in Somerville’s history, and the second-largest lab lease in Greater Boston in the past 12 months, following Biogen’s new headquarters in Kendall Square.

Beyond leasing the lab, TransMedics has also bought 5 acres of land next door from BioMed Realty for $30 million. BioMed had planned to develop two additional lab buildings — up to 1 million square feet — on that land, said Colleen O’Connor, the developer’s executive vice president and East Coast market lead.

The lab and adjacent property gives TransMedics ample room to keep growing, Hassanein said.

“There’s more growth opportunities in front of us, and we want to make sure that we have at least secured our growth and location, rather than worrying about it in the future,” he said. “We want to be in that area for a very long time.”

The headquarters move is accompanied by a $36 million tax incentive package from both Somerville and the Commonwealth. Somerville in October agreed to give Transmedics $18 million worth of property tax breaks over 10 years, while the state has proposed a matching $18 million package through the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center. The incentives require TransMedics to hire 600 new jobs, have 900 at the headquarters by 2032, and include clawbacks if it doesn’t meet the hiring goals.

“Massachusetts is a global leader in life sciences because of the investments we make in life-saving, innovative companies like TransMedics,” Governor Maura Healey said in statement. “Their expansion into Somerville is a powerful example of how cutting-edge medical innovation and economic growth go hand in hand.”

The deal follows a pitch for a “very creative tax package” by New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte for TransMedics to relocate from Andover to neighboring Salem, N.H., Hassanein said. North Carolina officials were also actively recruiting, he said.

While New Hampshire’s pitch of building a new lab campus exactly to TransMedics’ standards was compelling, that construction process would have taken at least three years — time Hassanein said TransMedics doesn’t have. Going with an already developed building means the company can start moving in as early as the end of this year.

“For us, we could not wait three years. We’re dealing with some exponential growth,” he said.

All 300 employees at TransMedics’ existing campus in Andover will have the chance to come into Somerville — and the company will work with them to find other positions if they’re not interested in relocating. Hassanein is also exploring relocating the headquarters of TransMedics’ aviation unit from Bozeman, Montana, to Massachusetts, and has met with the Massachusetts Port Authority to pitch the move, he said.

Organ transplantation has historically been a decentralized, regional practice, said Brian Johnson, president of state medical device trade association MassMEDIC. TransMedics, meanwhile, combines both advanced manufacturing and medical device technology with a national logistics network; the company maintains its own fleet of airplanes that it uses solely for transporting organs.

“You can have a donor in California and get it to a recipient in Massachusetts — used to be no way you could do that," Johnson said. “If we make this move now, and we’re partners with them, we’re taking ownership of a whole new industry that combines aerospace and advanced machine learning and regenerative medicine.”

Bringing 900 jobs to Somerville in fields ranging from manufacturing, research and development, administration, and youth internships — not to mention filling a hole in Somerville’s lab market — is a huge win, said newly elected Mayor Jake Wilson. Somerville officials expect the 10-year, $18 million tax increment financing package to generate $75 million in new revenue for the city.

“This is going to open doors for our residents across a wide range of career paths and entry levels, from manufacturing to research to tech and administration,” Wilson said. “This is really just the start.”

Michael Resnick, an attorney representing Greenhalgh, said “the cause of action that we pled is really aimed at Miss. Nuñez’s legal capacity.”

“There is no claim or count in this lawsuit asserting that [Labonte’s] clients put Miss. Nuñez under undue influence or duress. We have not made that claim,” Resnick said. “Our claim is aimed at Miss. Nuñez’s mental capacity to enter into contracts and other such obligations.”

The lawsuit is the latest development in a string of controversies over the past year and a half surrounding Nuñez and the house made famous by “The Conjuring” horror movie franchise.

In 2024, Nuñez faced allegations of harassment from Hawes, and accusations from former employees who say she owes them money; she allegedly fired one after claiming a spirit told her he was stealing from the business.

In November 2024, the Burrillville Town Council opted not to renew a business license related to the house after Nuñez — who bought the property for about $1.5 million in 2022 — was arrested and charged by local police with allegedly driving a Lexus SUV while intoxicated and leading officers on a chase through town.

According to Greenhalgh’s lawsuit, since January 2024, Nuñez has been “experiencing serious mental health issues that have impaired her judgment and rendered her incapable of understanding the nature and consequences of her actions.” She has been committed to at least three hospitals for psychiatric care, the lawsuit states.

The “Conjuring” house was slated for a foreclosure auction in October 2025, but the event was abruptly canceled after Needham Bank sold the underlying mortgage to YouTuber Elton Castee, through his Summit & Stone LLC, a corporation formed in Rhode Island in September.

Castee, who touts more than 4 million subscribers on his “TFIL” (Traveling to every country in A-Z order) channel on YouTube, along with comedian Matt Rife, purchased the former Connecticut home of paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren earlier this year, with its vast collection of allegedly haunted objects.

Castee’s LLC was named as an “interested party” in the ongoing lawsuit. Castee declined to comment on the matter last month.

At the urging of Andrea Perron — whose family was supposedly haunted in the 1970s at the Burrillville home where the Warrens were called in to investigate — Hawes launched a GoFundMe to try to raise money to purchase it at auction.

Hawes has said he is not seeking to make a profit, and the goal is to raise as much money as possible to keep costs down for visitors, and to keep the house in the hands of people who want to preserve it, not exploit it.

The online fundraiser has continued despite the latest developments, and as of Monday had garnered more than $323,000 in donations.

Protests are a cacophony of signs, slogans, and chants. But at the anti-ICE demonstrations that took place around Boston and across the country over the weekend, one name and face rose above the rest.

In the days since an ICE agent fatally shot her, Renee Good, a 37-year-old Minneapolis woman, has become a rallying cry for Americans’ opposition to the Trump administration’s deportation policies. The network of pro-immigrant groups that organized a demonstration outside Boston City Hall on Saturday, LUCE, gave out signs with a drawing of Good’s face framed by pastel-colored flowers.

“She’s another martyr,” said James Adams, a substance abuse counselor from Townsend who carried a placard that read “Say her name!” Martyr comes from the Greek for “witness.” According to Pietra Adami, a LUCE organizer, that’s exactly what Good was doing. “She saw injustice happening in her neighborhood,” Adami said. “She died trying to protect the community.”

The United States has had political martyrs since before it was a country, and some of Saturday’s protesters sought to summon that history. One held a sign featuring six coffins. Five reproduced a 1770 Paul Revere engraving memorializing the colonists killed in the Boston Massacre. The sixth was labeled with Good’s name.

“In my mind, these two events are linked,” said the protester, a local high school history teacher who identified herself as Michelle, comparing British troops occupying Boston to the thousands of immigration agents the Trump administration has dispatched to Minneapolis.

People who become symbols often fit a sympathetic mold. Activists challenging segregation in Montgomery, Ala., deliberately elevated Rosa Parks, a seamstress who nonviolently refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, as a living embodiment of the civil rights movement. On Saturday, protesters similarly drew on aspects of Good’s biography.

Her citizenship status was one of them. At least 32 people died in immigration detention last year, a two-decade high, and an ICE agent fatally shot a Mexican man named Silverio Villegas González during a September traffic stop near Chicago. But Good “was an American citizen,” said one Cambridge protester, who declined to give his name. “Any of us could have been in that situation.” He carried a sign featuring a still from a cell phone video of Good in her car, speaking kindly to an ICE agent seconds before her death.

Does it help that Good was young, white, and blonde? Possibly. But George Floyd, a Black man murdered in 2020 by a police officer just blocks from where Good was slain last week, also became immortalized. “Charlie Kirk is a face, too,” said Miguel Gomez-Ibanez of Weston, referencing the right-wing activist many conservatives have called a martyr since his killing last year. “It doesn’t have to be a white woman.”

Others noted that Good leaves behind three children. Alanna Floyd, a 28-year-old speech-language pathologist, held up a cardboard sign that read “Then they came for… a mom of three.” It was, Floyd explained, a reference to the poem “First They Came,” which lists groups victimized by the Nazis — socialists, trade unionists, Jews — and condemns Germans’ failure to speak out. “I wanted to highlight who she is,” Floyd said.

Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and others have cast Good as a far-left agitator who tried to run over an ICE agent, but video appears to show her trying to drive away. According to loved ones, Good was a Christian, a poet, and no activist. “We stopped to support our neighbors,” her wife told local media.

Martyrdom can be cynical. The Nazis, fascist Italy, and other autocratic regimes sanctified the dead to buttress their causes. Trump’s allies have bestowed the label on Ashli Babbitt, a 35-year-old QAnon conspiracy theorist who was fatally shot by a police officer while storming the Capitol on Jan. 6.

But even before Good’s death, a growing share of Americans saw the administration’s immigration policies as too extreme. Most disapprove of ICE and say the agency is being “too forceful,” according to a poll released the day Good was killed. Abolishing ICE remains unpopular, but support has spiked since last year.

Still, until now, that opposition has lacked a galvanizing face. “Maybe she’s the first,” said Gomez-Ibanez. “‘Cause you need a face. You gotta personalize it.”

When Rai and Perry opened Comfort Kitchen in 2023, the city had just about run out of free licenses unless another restaurant returned theirs. The couple was lucky to get one, and they learned just how much their bottom line depended on beer, wine, and cocktails: Alcohol can be twice as profitable as food.

“Without a liquor license,” Rai added, “we would not have survived.”

Rai and Perry got lucky again when groundbreaking legislation in 2024 created 225 new liquor licenses for Boston. Suddenly, the city finds itself flush with licenses in what could be the biggest expansion of alcoholic permits since the end of Prohibition. The city released the last batch of those licenses on Jan. 1.

Unlike the old system that required restaurant owners to fork over hundreds of thousands of dollars to buy a license from a shuttered restaurant, the new licenses are given out for free. And most are tied to 13 ZIP codes that could use the economic boost of sit-down restaurants including Mattapan, Roxbury, and Hyde Park. These so-called restricted licenses can’t be bought or sold and must be returned to the city after a business closes.

So far, 64 liquor licenses have been approved across 14 neighborhoods, according to the Boston Licensing Board. Fourteen licenses landed in Dorchester, followed by 11 in East Boston, 10 in Jamaica Plain, 6 in Roslindale, and 5 each in Roxbury and the South End.

The new licenses allowed mom-and-pop restaurants and community organizations that had long been priced out of buying a liquor license to get one for free, while others with beer-and-wine permits could upgrade to ones that allowed them to pour cocktails.

Perhaps most exciting: The flood of licenses has unleashed a wave of creativity among restaurant owners and entrepreneurs. They no longer have to open pricey places that cater to the masses to recoup the cost of their license. Concepts that aren’t just Italian cuisine and steak houses will have an easier time getting off the ground now.

With free-flowing licenses come spots like Comfort Kitchen and Ama with inventive global food inspired by Nepal-born Rai. And in Dorchester, there’s JustBook-ish, a bookstore on Dorchester Avenue that serves beer and wine, and Sorrel & Lime, a Caribbean-inspired modern event space on Blue Hill Avenue.

Then there are coffee shops that are becoming vibrant spots at night, too, like Jadu in Jamaica Plain and Gracenote Coffee’s The Listening Room in the Leather District.

Had Gracenote founder Patrick Barter not received a free license, he was preparing to close his popular experiment, The Listening Room, which opened in 2024 in an empty space behind his coffee shop. Barter, who studied jazz drumming at Oberlin College & Conservatory, wanted a place modeled after Tokyo’s jazz kissas, intimate bars where people listen intently to curated vinyl set lists and talking is discouraged.

To operate The Listening Room, Barter had been relying on a series of one-day liquor licenses, but the administrative burden was onerous.

“It wasn’t sustainable,” he said.

Then he heard about the influx of free licenses being offered by the city. The Leather District is not among the designated neighborhoods eligible for licenses, so Barter’s only shot was to win one of the 12 unrestricted licenses, or so-called golden tickets, which can be used anywhere in the city and do not have to be returned.

So far the city has awarded only three unrestricted licenses: The Listening Room, Ama in Allston, and Merengue Express in Mission Hill.

In getting such a valuable license for his tiny backroom club, Barter felt seen by the city. The 50-seat Listening Room is small by design; it doesn’t create a lot of jobs nor generate much tax revenue. That’s in stark contrast to how the city gave out unrestricted licenses a decade ago in what felt like a first-come, first-served basis with permits landing at well-connected, deep-pocketed owners in the Back Bay and the Seaport.

“The motivation for giving us one of the licenses doesn’t seem like it could be financial,” Barter said. “It has to be for what seems to me like the right reasons: supporting interesting and unique, culturally valuable things that are in the process of making Boston a cooler place to live.”

For decades in Boston, demand for liquor licenses has outstripped supply because the state caps the number of liquor licenses the city can have. When the city doesn’t have any free licenses to give out, restaurateurs must buy one from another place that closes, with the scarcity driving prices up over $600,000. That, in turn, has driven young chefs out of Boston to Brookline, Cambridge, and Somerville and other places where liquor licenses are cheaper.

The 2024 infusion of licenses has helped lower the cost of licenses to about $525,000 for those that still need to buy them, said Charlie Perkins, president of the Boston Restaurant Group, who brokers sales of both restaurants and liquor licenses.

“It’s a good thing,” he said.

Perkins still thinks the cost of opening up a restaurant in Boston is too high, making it much harder for young chefs to launch new ideas the way that Gordon Hamersley, Todd English, Jasper White, and others did in the 1980s.

“So all you’re getting are chain restaurants in new developments,” added Perkins. “It’s taking the heart out of the young chefs.”

That is something the city wants to work on, said Segun Idowu, the city’s chief of economic opportunity and inclusion.

While the city has reached out to current restaurant owners about the availability of licenses, Idowu said that now it wants to get the word out to developers, encouraging them to include restaurant spaces in new projects now that liquor licenses are easier to come by.

And some neighborhoods, notably Mattapan, still haven’t had many applicants for liquor licenses. Mattapan has only gained one new place to grab a drink — Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant.

That’s something the city wants to stay on top of, making sure the communities that have many licenses left know to take advantage of the opportunity.

“As more and more of these restaurants open as a result of these licenses, then we’ll see a lot more interest from folks because they’ll see that it’s possible,” said Idowu, “and the city will be shaking off that reputation of ‘we’ve got no licenses to give out.’ ”

The announcement triggered bitter reactions from members of the community at Monday’s meeting.

“This is, fundamentally, taking agency away from the Black community, and frankly, it’s just racist,” said Rodney Singleton, a Roxbury resident and community leader. “It’s not just land. It’s economic power as well. And to bereft that of the community is good old Boston racist politics, and we should not be in that business.”

The market for life science development has cratered since 2023, when the development rights on the parcel known as P3 were awarded to the HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace, which were set to expire at the end of this month.

Instead of renewing those rights — as is often done in these situations — Boston’s planning chief, Kairos Shen, told a Roxbury neighborhood group Monday that the city will let the designation lapse and take the site back.

Separately, Boston recently won state approval to help finance new construction or renovation of Madison Park, at an estimated cost of around $700 million. So rather than extend the “false expectation” of a life-sciences lab campus on P3, Shen said, the city will instead examine putting Madison Park there.

“Rebuilding Madison Park as a world-class vocational school for our community is a generational opportunity that is now within reach for the first time in decades,” a Wu administration spokesperson said Monday. “Now our top priority is to deliver the best possible school project in the most cost-effective way, on the fastest timeline.”

HYM and My City at Peace first explored a project in 2018 and eventually won rights for a five-building mixed-use development. The proposal was developed in partnership with multiple minority- and women-owned businesses, and won broad support from the Roxbury community.

In a joint statement, HYM and My City at Peace said the team was “deeply saddened” by the decision and remains “fully committed” to the parcel and the Roxbury community.

“For too long, Roxbury has been left out of Greater Boston’s sustained economic growth,” the statement said. “We are determined to help change that trajectory.”

The decision also shocked and surprised many at Monday evening’s meeting of the Roxbury Strategic Master Plan Oversight Committee.

“It just does not sit right with me,” said Dorothea M. Jones, a committee member. “It’s almost like the land is being taken back a second time from people in this community.”

Meanwhile, Singleton said it was galling for Boston to ask for state funding to build a high school when the city had already planned to funnel $91 million in public funds to the renovation of White Stadium in Franklin Park.

HYM and My City at Peace’s proposal included more than 600,000 square feet of lab space and 466 apartments and homes for sale — many of which would be at deeply discounted prices — along with retail space and a nonprofit center and museum for Embrace Boston, an organization that honors the legacy of Coretta Scott and Martin Luther King Jr.

But progress has been slow. In the three years since HYM and My City at Peace won development rights, the life-science lab market has fallen on hard times, with vacancy rates at record highs. Finding financing for a lab campus, which would then subsidize the affordable housing, is challenging, Shen said.

“It’s not news to anybody that we are at a dramatic downturn of development of all kind throughout the city,” Shen said. “It’s affecting all of the neighborhoods of the city, and Roxbury is not immune to that economic condition.”

Meanwhile, using the site instead for a new Madison Park could help contain costs of that project, said Trish Cafferky, the city’s deputy chief of operations. Rather than putting students in a “temporary swing building” on adjacent sports fields, they could stay in place as new facilities were under construction.

The estimates of between $680 million and $720 million to build a new school or renovate the existing one are “massively higher than what we had budgeted for,” Cafferky said. “This is expected to be, likely, the most expensive school project in the history of Massachusetts, let alone Boston.”

Madison Park is the city’s only technical vocational school, and includes a wood shop, cosmetology lab, and dental hygienist training facility. A new Madison Park could include added programs like early childhood education, robotics, biotechnology, and veterinary science, among others, Cafferky said.

“Imagine that the culinary shop actually also has a bakery that community members could walk into,” she said. “Imagine that there’s a veterinary clinic, and you can bring your animals in to get checked.”

The state process to rebuild a high school takes several years. It would kick off this summer with a roughly nine-month “eligibility period.” The City Council would have to vote on the project, and the city would aim to hire a consultant team next summer before designing the school in 2028 and building it by 2030 — if all goes according to plan.

Shen did acknowledge the “significant time and effort” HYM and My City at Peace have put into developing P3.

“The dedication . . . will put them in a good position to continue this work once the feasibility study for Madison Park is completed,” Shen said. “They will be well-positioned to participate in a redevelopment of what remnant parcel might be available at the end of the feasibility study.”

For Ricardo Louis, a Roxbury resident and chief executive of Privé Parking, the de-designation is both surprising and heartbreaking. The 500-space underground parking garage that his company would have helped develop at P3 would have been Privé Parking’s first project as parking and transportation consultant, and the company would have both operated the garage after it opened and had an equity stake in it.

“Having equity stake is a game changer,” Louis said. “There has never been someone Black, local, that has equity stake in any public garage in the city of Boston.”

Losing the planned future home of an Embrace Boston museum and cultural center is unfortunate and disappointing, especially heading into the MLK holiday and at a time when communities of color are under attack nationwide, said Imari Paris Jeffries, the chief executive of Embrace Boston. Part of why “The Embrace” monument is located in Downtown Crossing was so the organization could build a center that would spur economic development in a historically Black neighborhood, he said.

In a statement Monday, Embrace Boston said it was “profoundly disappointed and deeply concerned” at the decision to let HYM and My City at Peace’s designation lapse.

“This project was built on years of community input and Black-led leadership and vision. That history should matter,” the statement said. “To see this vision abruptly altered without meaningful engagement with affected partners undermines the very principles the city has publicly committed to upholding, particularly when years of trust, participation, and coalition-building are at stake.”

“There is a crisis,” the Rev. Brian M. Flatley, an archdiocesan official, told Dr. Edward Messner, a psychiatrist at Massachusetts General Hospital, on Dec. 30, 1994.

Messner’s notes from that day convey the gravity of the situation: “A priest had admitted abusing minors in the past and has been acting out again recently . . . police and the district attorney are involved . . . The allegations mirror what has come up before.”

Six hours later, the Rev. John J. Geoghan and Messner began regular therapy sessions in which Geoghan admitted to being “drawn by affection and intimacy with boys” and, as an MGH psychologist wrote, “pointed out that his misconduct occurred, `during a time of sexual exploration for this country.’”

In 1995 and 1996, according to court records examined by the Globe Spotlight Team, Geoghan explained why he preyed on children from poorer families: “The children were just so affectionate, I got caught up in their acts of affection. Children from middle-class families never acted like that toward me, so I never got so confused.”

Moreover, court documents that include Geoghan’s psychiatric records contain starkly contradictory assessments of his danger to children from different therapists. He received at least four clean bills of health between 1980 and 1990, a period when the Archdiocese of Boston assigned him three times to parishes despite his record of abuse; but prompted declarations that he was an incurable pedophile after he became a public embarrassment to the archdiocese in the mid-1990s.

For example, Messner’s notes show that Geoghan told him that Flatley, whose job was to deal with priests who had molested children, had branded him “a pedophile, a liar, and a manipulator.”

Collectively, the publicly filed church documents add detailed clinical evidence to what the Globe reported yesterday: Although the 1995 and 1996 psychiatric reports diagnose Geoghan with a deep-rooted sexual perversion, there were ample signs years earlier that he was unfit for parish work.

Yesterday, the Globe reported that Cardinal Bernard F. Law, during his first year in Boston in 1984, assigned Geoghan to St. Julia’s in Weston even though Geoghan had been removed from his two prior parishes for molesting children. In one of those cases, in 1980, Geoghan asserted that his repeated abuse of seven boys in one family, which was disovered that year, was not a “serious” problem. That is according to a church timeline of Geoghan’s career - six parish assignments in 34 years with accusations that he molested more than 130 children.

Law, after celebrating Mass yesterday at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, reiterated the archdiocese’s statement of Friday that he would not comment on Geoghan.

The documents also contain evidence that Geoghan’s false denials of past sexual abuse through the 1960s and much of the 1970s helped justify a critical church decision that freed Geoghan to abuse even more children. In 1989, Geoghan was forced to take a six-month sick leave from St. Julia’s after more accusations of abuse surfaced. But Law soon signed off on a decision to return him to the parish, according to church documents.

The Spotlight reports of today and yesterday are based on public documents filed in connection with 84 civil lawsuits pending against Geoghan and two criminal cases, the first of which is scheduled to go to trial in Middlesex Superior Court next Monday. The archdiocese, Law, and five other bishops are defendants in many of the pending lawsuits, charged with negligence for not properly supervising Geoghan. Already, the archdiocese has settled 50 other lawsuits, paying more than $10 million to Geoghan’s victims.

The multiple accusations against Geoghan represent the largest scandal involving an American Catholic priest since the 1992 disclosure that former priest James Porter had abused more than 100 children in the Fall River Diocese in the 1960s.

The massive number of documents compiled by lawyers handling the 84 remaining civil suits have been under a confidentiality seal sought by the archdiocese. But based on a motion by the Globe, Superior Court Judge Constance M. Sweeney ordered that all the documents be made public. They are scheduled to be released on Jan. 26.

The documents already on public file detail the extent of Geoghan’s lengthy treatment history and make clear the church’s longtime knowledge of his misconduct.

The psychiatric documents offer added insights into Geoghan’s troubled mind and the motivations behind his aberrant actions - often as explained by Geoghan himself.

Geoghan was, by his own assessment, a heterosexual. But he told Messner during his treatment sessions that his victims were usually young prepubescent boys. He said he “avoided girls,” explaining, “I picked the boys because in some way they were the safest, the girls and the mothers would have been more dangerous.”

The records suggest there were early warning signs.

Geoghan, who is 66, attended St. John’s Seminary after graduating from Holy Cross College and was ordained in 1962. Deposition transcripts refer to correspondence from Geoghan’s seminary days in which his superiors conclude he has “pronounced immaturity.”

In an April 1995 session with Messner, Geoghan said that even as a newly ordained priest he would “experience arousal when there was physical closeness” with children.

In a June 1996 psychological assessment, Dr. Mark Blais, a Massachusetts General Hospital psychologist, concluded that Geoghan has a “powerful sense of emotional deprivation and emotional loneliness.”

Medical evaluations of Geoghan, which repeatedly cleared him to return to parish work after incidents of sexual misconduct in the 1970s and ’80s, changed dramatically in the mid-1990s. By then, complaints against Geoghan were being made with unsettling frequency, and it was clear he risked becoming an embarrassment - and financial liability - to the Church.

In December 1984, for example, a month after being reassigned to St. Julia’s in Weston following his removal from St. Brendan’s in Dorchester, Geoghan underwent evaluations by two separate Boston-area psychotherapists. Dr. Robert Mullins declared Geoghan “fully recovered,” and Dr. John H. Brennan advised “no . . . restrictions to his work as a parish priest.”

Not everyone was comfortable with the assignment. Bishop John M. D’Arcy, a popular cleric whose forthright manner rankled Law, according to a friend of D’Arcy, wrote to Law in December 1984 to question Law’s decision assigning Geoghan to St. Julia’s because of his history of sex abuse. He warned that placing Geoghan there might result in further scandal.

Two months later, D’Arcy was gone, transferred to a diocese in Fort Wayne, Ind., which he has headed ever since.

New allegations against Geoghan surfaced within two years, and again in 1989. But Geoghan told Bishop Robert J. Banks in March 1989 that he had “no more sexual attraction to children” and had been “chaste for five years.”

But the church’s own timeline of Geoghan’s misconduct suggests Banks did not believe him. Within weeks, Geoghan was sent to the St. Luke Institute in Suitland, Md., where he was diagnosed with “homosexual pedophilia.” The result: “Told by Bishop Banks he had to leave ministry,” according to a church record.

Instead, Geoghan was put on sick leave the following month, and in August was hospitalized for three months at the Institute of Living, a Hartford treatment center, where he was discharged in November 1989, as “moderately improved.” Banks agreed to send him back to St. Julia’s, subject to approval by another bishop and “BFL” - Cardinal Law.

But during 1995 treatment, psychologists at St. Luke concluded that during the 1989 treatment in Hartford, Geoghan did not tell the truth about the extent of his sexual abuse of children. He denied any incidents before the late 1970s, to include long-running instances of abuse dating to 1962. And the Institute of Living’s report to the archdiocese reflected Geoghan’s lie.

Moreover, the records state that Bishop Banks was “unhappy” with the Institute of Living’s discharge summary because it was “different from what he had understood and based his decision to allow Fr. Geoghan back to work.”

A reply letter from the institute reports: “The probability that he would act out again is quite low. However, we cannot guarantee that it could not reoccur.”

Yet the archdiocese was hit with more complaints in 1991, 1992, and 1994, although the 1992 accusation was dismissed by church officials as “hearsay and vague.”

Law finally removed Geoghan from parish duty in January 1993.

Midway through his treatment with Messner, Geoghan was returned to St. Luke in January 1995. His diagnosis after that 10-day stay was far less optimistic than earlier judgments. “It is our clinical judgment that Father Geoghan has a longstanding and continuing problem with sexual attraction to prepubescent males,” his evaluation reads. “His recognition of the problem and his insight into it is limited.”

Therapists at St. Luke advised that Geoghan have no unsupervised contact with minor males and return for residential treatment, although Geoghan resisted the latter recommendation. Instead, he was sent in July 1995, to Southdown, an Ontario treatment facility, where he stayed for four to six months.

In 1996, Blais, too, submitted a pessimistic evaluation. “Treatment of such a chronic and deeply ingrained condition would need to be lengthy,” he wrote.

Geoghan was removed from the priesthood in 1998.

Massachusetts has taken a nationally leading step by requiring more detailed race and ethnicity data collection across state agencies, helping illuminate the distinct needs of communities long hidden by overly broad categories (“New year, new laws from pot to privacy,” Metro, Jan. 2). Realizing the promise of data equity now depends on strong, intentional implementation.

Since the law’s passage, the Asian Pacific Islanders Civic Action Network and partner organizations have been working closely with the Healey-Driscoll administration to help guide implementation. This collaboration matters, and important groundwork has begun. But as the law now takes effect, it is clear that implementation must move forward with greater urgency.

For Asian, Pacific Islander, Black, Latino, immigrant, and other marginalized communities, data disaggregation is not abstract. It directly affects access to food, health care, education, and economic opportunity. Without timely, consistent implementation across agencies, the law risks falling short of its promise.
