Now, you may think this happens all the time. Plans change. No big deal. There’s some truth to that. The difference is that there have been so many promises made — and broken — on this stretch of Tremont Street known as Parcel 3 that to drop a bombshell like this is stunning — and frankly disrespectful of the community process in general and Black voices in particular.

“You’re making a pronouncement right now,” said Tito Jackson, the former city councilor turned cannabis entrepreneur, during the virtual meeting. “You’re telling people what you’re going to do, not asking them what we should do. That’s not how we rock here in Roxbury.”

Wu did not attend the two-hour community meeting on Monday night. She left it up to her planning chief, Kairos Shen, to deliver the shocking news.

This from a mayor who throughout her political career has vowed to blow up the top-down planning process in favor of a more community-oriented approach.

Apparently that was then, this is now.

Shen will have you believe that the sudden about-face is related to the timing of two things: In December, the Massachusetts School Building Authority gave initial approval to help pay for a new Madison Park, which could cost $700 million and make it the most expensive school project in state history. And this week, the Boston Planning & Development Agency is the last chance for the board to renew the designation for the current project on P3, which, at close to 8 acres, is the largest city-owned parcel that’s undeveloped anywhere in Boston.

The planning agency awarded the project, which sits across from the Boston Police Department headquarters and abuts Madison Park’s existing campus, to a team led by HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace in January 2023, but it hasn’t been able to secure financing because of the current glut of lab space and the high cost of construction.

I can understand why Shen, who spent two decades at the planning and development agency under former mayor Tom Menino, is eager to get behind Madison Park. Shen was at the agency when Roxbury leaders began working on a master plan; he has seen over the decades how plan after plan for P3 has evaporated, from a soccer stadium for Robert Kraft’s New England Revolution to a shopping mall anchored by BJ’s Wholesale Club, to offices for Mass General Brigham (then Partners HealthCare), and a new headquarters for the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

That history may help explain why Shen and the city are sprinting toward a project that can get funding at a time when many other developments in Boston are stalled.

But c’mon, has Wu not learned anything from her experience redeveloping White Stadium in Franklin Park or her controversial plan to move the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science to West Roxbury?

In both instances, there was a community uproar and a sense that City Hall just wanted to steamroll projects through. After only eight months, Wu had to pull the plug on her plan to move the O’Bryant across town.

Through sheer political will, she has made headway on White Stadium. Construction has started on the $200-plus million project, but not without riling up residents of Roxbury and Dorchester and drawing a lawsuit from the Emerald Necklace Conservancy that is now before the Supreme Judicial Court. Some of those same opponents showed up at Monday night’s meeting, again saying they’ve been shut out of the process.

Here’s what I fear will get lost in the bungled rollout at P3: Putting Madison Park there is an idea worthy of serious exploration. If anything, Wu and Shen aren’t thinking big enough.

The school, after all, would only take up a portion of the 8-acre site, leaving other parts of it for future development. Maybe HYM and My City of Peace won’t be able to build their full project — 700,000 square feet of life sciences space, 466 units of housing, and a museum and policy center for Embrace Boston — but they could still put something there.

And that’s what the HYM and My City of Peace development team proposed in a statement Monday night. Not an either/or, but a both/and.

“This is a false choice — one that unnecessarily pits education against community investment,“ the statement said. ”This site can, and must, do both."

I’ve been following P3 closely because of the project’s potential to spread the wealth of Boston’s development boom not only to Roxbury but also the people of color who are partners in the project. The city has been taking a page from the so-called Massport model ― which makes diversity a major factor in awarding development rights on agency properties ― and P3 was supposed to be the shining example of that in Boston.

I’m not worried about HYM chief executive Tom O’Brien, who is white and has other projects on his plate, like redeveloping Suffolk Downs in East Boston and Revere. And perhaps cutting O’Brien out of P3 is political payback for contemplating a mayoral run against Wu last year.

But it’s O’Brien’s partners of color — including the Rev. Jeffrey Brown, Dream Collaborative managing principal Greg Minott, and Privé Parking chief executive Ricardo Louis — for whom I feel bad, as well as the people who would have a chance to purchase affordable homes. To them, the current P3 project represented a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

Now what?

I’m sure the Wu administration will continue to make diversity and inclusion a priority in the way it awards development projects. Still I can’t help but think there’s a missed opportunity here to forge a public-private partnership the way Wu did with White Stadium, and create something bigger and better than the city can by going it alone.

What’s more, it didn’t go unnoticed that the fate of P3 is suddenly up on the air in the week leading up to preparations to celebrate Martin Luther King Jr. Day. At the end of Monday’s meeting, Imari Paris Jeffries, chief executive of Embrace Boston — a nonprofit that exists to honor the legacy of King and his wife Coretta Scott King and their time in Boston — reminded us how we shouldn’t forget their commitment to economic justice.

“This holiday is about making good on a promise, especially in a moment where they’re trying to minimize the memory of this holiday, deprioritize this holiday and deprioritize Black History Month and Juneteenth,” said Paris Jeffries. “There is still an opportunity for us to find a solution where the community gets a win, students of Boston get a win, and that we take advantage of the building opportunity in this moment.”

He’s right. We can’t keep telling Roxbury to dream big and then come up short. This history should matter.

So at the same time the city is closing schools, it must also build new schools and renovate other buildings to ensure students have access to a quality education in modern facilities. It all adds up to a massive task for Mayor Michelle Wu, who just promised to make the public education system the best urban district in the country.

Starting in 2022, shortly after she took office, Wu pledged to work toward the goal of overhauling the schools, with $2 billion dedicated to improving BPS facilities, including $605 million for 14 major school construction or renovation projects in fiscal years 2023 through 2027. Only three renovations have been completed so far, with no other projects under construction, and finishing the rest will require billions more dollars.

In a parallel process,the School Committee has approved a dozen closures and mergers since Wu took office. They have proven largely unpopular with many impacted families and educators, in part because Wu has made so little progress on the 14 major projects she announced in 2022.

“We have too many school buildings, and most of them are old,” said Will Austin, a former public school teacher, principal, and founder of Boston Schools Fund, a nonprofit working to improve BPS. “Those are just the facts, and so it is very difficult to navigate those two things at the same time.”

Martin J. Walsh, a former US labor secretary who served as Boston mayor from 2014 to 2021, said delays in school construction are not about a lack of expertise, but a lack of funds.

It can take about five years to work with the state to obtain school funding assistance, Walsh said. And Boston also has far more schools that need to be replaced or renovated compared with other districts in Massachusetts.

While mayor, Walsh spearheaded BuildBPS, which had a similar goal of building new and renovated school buildings by investing $1 billion in city and state funding.

“It’s easy to criticize from the sidelines,” Walsh said. “Of course, you want to build new schools every year. . . . It’s about the capital, and your ability to have the revenue to do it.”

The three schools that have opened since Wu took office — the Boston Arts Academy, Quincy Upper School, and Carter School — were planned or under construction already when she became mayor, thanks to efforts when Walsh was in office.

Of the 14 projects Wu prioritized in 2022, there has been no progress on eight, according to the district’s website. In two of those cases, the Otis and Blackstone schools, the state rejected requests to help pay, and the proposals were quietly shelved.

A ninth project to renovate the building that houses the Community Academy of Science and Health also appears abandoned: The school will instead close next summer, the district decided.

Three renovations have been completed: East Boston’s PJ Kennedy School, the Irving building in Roslindale, and the Edwards in Charlestown.

And two major school building construction projects are in the planning and design phase required for state funding aid: the Madison Park Technical Vocational High School, which is estimated to cost $700 million, and the Shaw-Taylor Elementary School. It will take years, likely after the end of Wu’s term, before the two projects are completed.

Building the Ruth Batson Academy at Columbia Point, which was announced after Wu’s initial list of 14 projects, is also in the planning stage.

BPS did not respond to questions about the status of the eight projects that Wu announced in 2022 and have not been updated since. The district provided a list of smaller-scale school projects, including new boilers, windows, bathrooms, doors, heat pumps, and building roofs. The district is also providing working air conditioning in 92 percent of schools, up from 32 percent in 2021.

Still, some advocates, such as Mary Tamer, a former School Committee member who served under Mayor Thomas Menino, argue that the city needs to be more aggressive in getting school projects underway and publish a detailed, long-term timeline.

The district’s current facilities program under Wu was a required part of a state improvement plan. In 2024, the state’s K-12 education department reported the city’s plan lacked specific details in some areas, including enrollment projections, and details of the size and number of buildings BPS would need in the future.

“When we’re not putting forth a comprehensive facilities plan, you are creating a level of uncertainty in the district. And that is really unfair to families and to students,” said Tamer, who leads the education policy group MassPotential.

Paul Reville, a former Massachusetts secretary of education, said the district needs more urgency in improving schools if parents are going to accept closures.

“The general strategy on behalf of the school system has got to be, there’s a value proposition for parents who are moving,” Reville said. “It’s painfully slow.”

Boston’s schools were built for a far larger district.In 1940, when many of the current facilities were new, the student population exceeded 110,000. By 2003, there were just about 61,000 students in BPS. Enrollment fell to 53,000 by 2019 and dropped to 46,500 this school year, according to state data.

There was a 30-year period when no new schools were built in Boston. That ended in 2003, with the opening of three buildings. Since then, just four more schools opened, including this fall’s opening of the Carter School, which serves students with disabilities.

Meanwhile, the latest round of closures came in December, when the School Committee approved closing Lee Academy, Community Academy of Science and Health, and Another Course to College, plus eliminating high school grades from the Henderson K-12 Inclusion School, after the 2027-2028 school year.

The closures were part of a plan the district announced in late 2023 to cull the number of school buildings from 114 in 2022-23 to 95 by 2030. Boston now operates 109 schools.

At the time, BPS rated its buildings based on the state of their facilities and other metrics, with an average building score of 38 out of 100 possible points.

Since then, the district has announced a handful of closings once a year, much to the dismay of many residents.

Hundreds of students, parents, and educators demonstrated before the December vote, arguing that they were left out of the decision-making process and that the outcome threatened to rend tight-knit school communities.

“What are you saying to our communities when you say, ‘No, we’re just going to close you,’ with no discussion?” said Jason Lambright, the parent of three children who have attended Lee Academy. “These buildings, maybe they’re not great, but maybe you can still figure out ways that you can fix and help renovate them, versus just trying to push us around.”

The Boston Teachers Union has argued BPS should commit to opening at least three new or renovated school buildings each year until all of its facilities are updated.

Erik Berg, the union president, said the union supports a bill to add funding to the Massachusetts School Building Authority, which distributes state funds to help support school projects. The bill would prioritize districts with buildings with high needs.

“There are definitely some projects happening that are making a difference,” Berg said. “But the unmet need after decades of deferred maintenance is so great that our students deserve more and faster.”

Looking out at the bay, the group of 30 guests attending the celebration at Victory Point Restaurant awaited Woodhouse’s arrival. As he strolled in with his wife, Stella, he shouted greetings and hugged his friends.

“Command, I’m waiting for your honors,” Woodhouse called out.

The cities of Quincy and Boston both proclaimed Jan. 14 as Brigadier General Enoch “Woody” Woodhouse II Day. Beth Veneto of Ginger Betty’s Bakery surprised him with a giant gingerbread man, vibrantly adorned with a US Army hat and frosting medals on his uniform.

William Gross, who made history as Boston’s first Black police commissioner, joked that when he first met Woodhouse, he asked, “Did you play dodgeball with Jesus?”

Gross went on to commend Woodhouse for his perseverance that allowed future generations of Black Americans to break more glass ceilings, adding that Woodhouse “made me the first Black chief, the first Black commissioner.”

“You paved the way so people could exercise their First Amendment rights,” Gross told Woodhouse. “When you still came back [from the war] to a segregated America, you continued to educate people about what it means to be a human being.”

George Rollins, a retired US Army colonel living in Wilmington, is part of Mission Hill Post 327 with Woodhouse, and they have been friends for nine years. Rollins joked about Woodhouse’s long-windedness. But Rollins had a Rolodex of stories to share from the general’s life, such as the time he took a break from classes at Yale University to listen to Thurgood Marshall as the chief counsel for the NAACP in the Brown v. Board of Education case.

Michael Wabrek, 60, a retired lieutenant colonel in the Marine Corps, has been Woodhouse’s “protector, but also best friend and roommate” for over 30 years, despite their nearly-40-year age gap. Wabrek travels with Woodhouse and takes care of his needs for public appearances.

“We really yuk it up,” Wabrek said, noting Woodhouse’s “infectious laugh” as he watched the general mingling across the room.

Woodhouse is a “golden lion,” Wabrek said. When Woodhouse receives accolades, he added, he is representative of the airmen who ”did not make it this far."

“When kids and other people meet him, they’re awestruck,” Wabrek said, tearing up. “To stand 10 to 15 feet in the back and see the sheer reaction and human interaction that he has with people ... that’s my reward, just to witness and help that.”

Looking back on his 99 years, Woodhouse said he is proud of himself for “sticking through and being persistent” as a person of color in a segregated military.

He said his best advice for younger generations is to not seek revenge but to survive, which is how he overcame racial discrimination and achieved high military honors. He hopes to be remembered as, simply, a nice person.

Breadon insists she’s well positioned to bridge the gaps between her colleagues. But some in the Boston political scene said the recent debacle was shameful.

“Unfortunately, this is nothing new,” said Annissa Essaibi George, a former councilor and mayoral candidate. “Just when you think things might calm down, and the body becomes sort of refocused or re-engaged in the very important work that it should be doing for the people of Boston, we’re back to just more chaos.”

The turbulent start to the year is “unacceptable,” she added, and only reinforces the negative public perception of the council. Essaibi George said she hopes Breadon can reverse the tides.

As the council launches into its new term, it falls to the new leader — who was elected president by a margin of just one vote, less than 24 hours after deciding to run — to restore order, civility, and cooperation. Already, she has struggled with her first administrative task of selecting a vice president. Her first choice, Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata, declined the job, as did her second choice, before Coletta Zapata ultimately reversed course to accept the offer.

Breadon acknowledged the events surrounding the presidency vote were “unorthodox” and “messy.” But her goal is to ensure that doesn’t continue, she argued.

“Our constituents deserve a City Council that’s functioning and collaborating and working together, and not just sniping and undercutting each other,” Breadon said in an interview. “I’ve got my work cut out for me, but I am selling my intention to build a more collegial and more collaborative City Council in Boston.”

Dramatic divisions and dysfunction on the Boston City Council have plagued the body in recent years.

In 2022, the council’s once-a-decade redistricting process — which Breadon led as committee chair — sparked enormous tension, heated clashes, and even a lawsuit against the council that was funded by several of its own members. Personal and political scandals have derailed the careers of several councilors, including one, Tania Fernandes Anderson, who recently served time in prison after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges.

The Boston City Council is also fighting the perception that it is merely a rubber stamp for the mayor’s agenda. Though the council has newfound powers to shape the budget, it has often ceded mostly to the mayor’s vision, and only rarely advances legislation of its own.

Meanwhile, pressure is growing to address major issues — bring housing costs down, improve lingering challenges in Boston Public Schools, and preserve essential city services in a budget season that could prove especially challenging due to inflation and the threat of further federal funding cuts.

Against that backdrop, Breadon’s last-minute ascent to the presidency took many councilors by surprise, and inflamed existing rifts.

Coletta Zapata of East Boston had been considered the front-runner in the race since November, when she announced she had enough support from her colleagues to secure the presidency. Councilor Brian Worrell, though, continued to campaign for the position. The night before the scheduled vote, Coletta Zapata announced she was withdrawing from the race after three of her original supporters — Breadon and Councilors John FitzGerald and Enrique Pepén — told her they planned to defect and vote for Worrell, according to City Hall sources.

In a last-ditch effort to salvage Coletta Zapata’s original coalition, Councilors Sharon Durkan and Pepén, both close allies to Mayor Michelle Wu, paid Breadon a late-night visit to persuade her to run as a “compromise candidate,” Breadon said . She won with the backing of Wu allies, while Worrell had pitched himself as an “independent” leader, though he is often aligned with Wu. His supporters included Wu’s most vocal critics on the council.

The vote left some councilors disappointed and angry — and, in a few cases, suspicious of the mayor for meddling, though Wu said on the radio she did not direct her allies to orchestrate Breadon’s candidacy. Breadon has put Wu allies in many of the council’s most influential posts, including as the chairs of the powerful government operations and ways and means committees.

Fernandes Anderson, the embattled former councilor, has accused some of her former colleagues of undermining Worrell’s candidacy to preserve Wu’s influence on the council — a concern shared by some sitting councilors as well.

“The fact that colleagues moved in the darkness of the night before the vote to reverse course and block [Worrell from winning] says far more about a power grab than about leadership or putting the council first,” said Councilor Erin Murphy, an outspoken Wu antagonist who backed Worrell.

For many observers, the chaos surrounding the presidency vote was incredibly frustrating.

Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a longtime Roxbury resident and political consultant, said she’s disappointed the council did not elect Worrell as its leader, but now it’s time for the body to put any lingering personal grudges aside.

“Enough of this back and forth. What’s done is done,” Ferriabough Bolling said. “Let’s get busy on the work of the people, because I believe that the city is going to have a lot of challenges.”

On a body as small as the 13-member Boston City Council, collegiality makes a big difference for effective policy making, said former city councilor Josh Zakim. If councilors can’t work together, it will be harder for them to tackle major city issues.

Having a contested council presidency is “healthy,” he said — “but if people are going to carry over resentment because their preferred candidate didn’t win, that’s not going to be helpful for the term,” Zakim said. “A climate of pettiness just doesn’t serve anyone.”

It’s not unusual for councilors to engage in this sort of political maneuvering, though experts said it typically happens behind closed doors, with alliances sewn up weeks before the actual vote.

“Drama in this isn’t new, but it sounds like it’s been playing out in a more public fashion — that’s new. They haven’t been able to keep the lid on it to the same degree," said Erin O’Brien, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

Those negotiations — candidates offering their colleagues desirable committee assignments in exchange for their support — have long been controversial.

Whether the council can overcome its differences will largely depend on Breadon’s leadership, said David Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College.

“Maybe things are a little raw right now, but in the months and years to come, will it improve, and will Breadon find success in smoothing it over? Or will these things kind of fester?” Hopkins said.

Breadon said despite a rocky start, she is up to the task.

“People are sick and tired of this bickering, and they want us to work together,” Breadon said. “It’s the first week of a long journey, and I’m hoping that people will give me the grace to let me have a chance to do that.”

In a bid to revive Wu’s measure, state Senator Michael Rush, a Democrat from West Roxbury, filed an amendment that largely mirrored Wu’s proposal, tacking it on to a separate property tax relief bill. But Rush’s amendment failed 5-33 after senators debated it for roughly 30 minutes.

In addition to Rush, the amendment was backed by three Democratic senators who represent parts of Boston — Sal DiDomenico, Lydia Edwards, and Liz Miranda — as well as Senator Pat Jehlen, a Somerville Democrat.

State Senator William Brownsberger, who also represents parts of Boston and voted against the amendment, argued it would set a bad precedent to give the city a temporary exemption from the state law that allows municipalities to tax commercial properties only at a rate up to 175 percent of the residential rate.

“This is a ceiling, this is a guardrail. This is saying we’re not going to go further away from that fundamental principle of everybody pays the same,” Brownsberger said on the Senate floor Thursday. “If we voted for this amendment and passed it today, the result would be that we would have this request from every other city” with a similar tax structure.

Instead, the Senate debated and passed several alternative tax relief measures Thursday.

The Senate voted 37-1 to pass a bill filed by Brownsberger, which would allow municipalities to offer property tax credits to certain vulnerable homeowners to prevent a dramatic spike in their third and fourth quarter tax bills in years when residential property taxes are poised to increase more than 10 percent. Under the legislation, those credits would have to be funded by the municipalities themselves; the state would not offer any funding.

The Senate also approved a bill filed by state Senator Nick Collins, one of Wu’s chief antagonists on Beacon Hill. Collins’s legislation would allow cities and towns to offer uniform tax rebates to homeowners who received a residential exemption in their tax bills and meet certain other qualifications. Those rebates would also be funded locally — a prospect Wu has not embraced. The bill advanced with several amendments, two of which would let municipalities expand the personal property tax exemption as well as the senior property tax exemption. Another amendment would extend the deadline for homeowners to appeal their property valuations.

Both bills now head to the House.

The Senate on Thursday also passed two other property tax relief bills, which would loosen eligibility requirements for seniors who want to defer their property tax payments, and make it easier for municipalities to offer tax exemptions to seniors in need.

In a statement Thursday morning, a spokesperson for the mayor indicated Wu is skeptical of using city funds to offer tax breaks and slammed the proposals by Brownsberger and Collins as “costly” alternatives to the city’s pitch.

“As sky-high housing costs continue to push families out of Boston and Massachusetts, we can’t afford to burden residents with continued double-digit property tax increases while commercial properties get significant tax breaks under state tax laws,” the spokesperson said.

The Senate proposals passed Thursday would “require sacrificing needed funding for city services,” the spokesperson said.

In a statement after the Rush amendment failed, Wu thanked the senators who backed her proposal. The measure has received approval from the City Council and state House several times since 2024.

Wu first sought Beacon Hill’s permission nearly two years ago to shift more of the city’s property tax burden onto commercial properties in order to soften coming tax spikes for homeowners.

More than 70 percent of Boston’s budget is funded by property taxes, and the city already taxes commercial properties at 175 percent the residential property tax rate, the highest differential allowed by state law. But in recent years, residential property values have risen while commercial values have fallen, largely due to increasingly empty office buildings downtown, as companies pivoted to remote work policies after the COVID-19 pandemic.

That’s meant that homeowners have seen significant increases in their tax bills to make up for the lost revenue from commercial properties, whose taxes, on average, dropped. This time last year, the property taxes for the average single family home in Boston went up 10.4 percent year-over-year, and this month, homeowners saw another 13 percent increase, on average.

The lawsuit filed Thursday said Baker and Victor were denied the right to use a women’s restroom at the hotel on May 3 by a security guard “because of what Ms. Baker looks like and because they are in a lesbian relationship.”

When the women objected, “the security guard threw them out of the hotel,” the lawsuit stated. The hotel later “panicked” when the pair took to social media to recount their experience, it stated.

“Instead of simply acknowledging its employee’s discriminatory conduct and apologizing, the Liberty Hotel executives agreed to craft a defamatory statement, knowing it was false, suggesting Ms. Baker and Ms. Victor were kicked out of the Liberty Hotel because they had been engaging in obscene conduct in a stall,” the lawsuit said.

Leonard H. Kesten, a lawyer for the women, said the pair were never in the same restroom stall. Despite the previous MCAD settlement, Kesten said, his clients still don’t know who specifically made the false claim against them.

“We’ve always said that we are not going to settle until we know who did it and why,” Kesten said.

In a statement, the hotel’s general manager, Mark Fischer, said the establishment has “apologized several times to Ms. Baker and Ms. Victor about their experience and has spent months working with the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination (MCAD) to address what occurred and strengthen its practices.”

“We’ve been candid that we can do better, as it has been and remains that all guests should feel welcome at the Liberty Hotel,” he said. “We recognize that they have a right to bring a lawsuit, but we unequivocally deny discriminating or retaliating against them in any way.”

MCAD brought the complaint against the hotel in June, one month after Baker, of Dorchester, and Victor were ejected from the hotel, where they were attending a Kentucky Derby-themed event.

A security guard questioned Baker about her gender in the women’s restroom, and when she showed her ID indicating that she’s female, “the guard failed to remedy the situation and instead, continued to eject the couple from the premises,” the commission said in its ruling.

The commission said the hotel had retaliated against the couple by issuing “a false statement to the media implying that the women were somehow in violation of the Liberty Hotel’s policies.”

When MCAD initiated its complaint, a spokesperson for the hotel said a review of the incident found that “the employee was in the wrong and his actions were well beyond regrettable.”

“No guest of ours should ever be treated in a manner that is anything other than respectful and welcoming,” the statement said. “We apologize to our guests, and to our community particularly the LGBTQ+ community. We continue to work on making amends with Ansley and Liz while we have taken corrective action and sensitivity training.”

Fischer, the Liberty’s general manager, said after the MCAD settlement that “we deeply regret that our initial statement may have created unintended impressions about the actions of Ansley and Liz.”

In the lawsuit now pending in Suffolk Superior, the women allege they suffered damages “in excess of $10 million,” according to the civil complaint’s cover sheet.

The complaint itself said the women are seeking “to recover actual damages, punitive damages, and reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs.”

The hotel hadn’t responded in court to the suit as of Thursday afternoon. No hearings have been scheduled.

Speaking to reporters in June, Baker said she has faced “comments” and “looks” when using the women’s room in the past, but the incident at the Liberty Hotel was her “worst nightmare coming true.”

Not unlike today, January 15, 1919, dawned unseasonably warm in Boston. In the early afternoon, North End residents felt the ground shake. Then, with an enormous crash and the squeal of tearing steel, they saw it: A 25-foot wave of molasses. Having shredded the towering tank that once held it, the viscous mass flowed freely through the streets at 35 miles per hour, ensnaring people, destroying buildings, and pushing aside cars as if they were toys.

Disasters, like the deadly industrial accident 107 years ago that became known as the Great Molasses Flood, stick in our imaginations. “Titanic,” about a ship that sank almost 114 years ago, remains among the highest-grossing movies ever. I’ve personally torn through recent bestsellers about the Chernobyl nuclear meltdown, the Challenger explosion, and the Edmund Fitzgerald, a Great Lakes freighter whose loss during a 1975 storm inspired a popular song. Other headline-making catastrophes have spawned documentaries, podcasts, and even video games.

What explains this fascination? There are certainly less-upstanding answers — including a morbid prurience not unlike America’s guilty obsession with true crime. But Stephen Puleo, the author of “Dark Tide,” a 2003 book about the molasses flood, has a more charitable theory.

“These events are so random that almost every person has the reaction ‘There but for the grace of God,’” Puleo said by email. “It’s impossible to truly protect yourself from a disaster — flood, fire, earthquake, shipwreck, and yes, a molasses tank that disgorges 2.3 million gallons of molasses on a random January day.”

Boston no longer stockpiles molasses, which the company that owned the ill-fated tank was storing to ferment into industrial alcohol for munitions. But to mark the flood’s anniversary, I sent Puleo some questions. Here’s more from our (lightly edited) exchange.

Ian: Many disasters feature common themes, from hubris (the company’s failure to properly inspect the tank) to bad luck (mixing warm and cold molasses may have ruptured it). What’s different about the Great Molasses Flood?

Puleo: There are two things that really capture people’s imagination. One, the unusual nature of the substance itself — drowning in or becoming asphyxiated by molasses seems almost incomprehensible. And two, the fact that so many issues that America was dealing with in the early 20th century quite literally touch the flood: World War I and munitions production, the anarchist movement, immigration, and the relationship between government and big business.

A sign on Commercial Street memorializes the 21 people killed. But have you encountered people who treat the flood as a punchline?

I did earlier, but not so much now. When people ask me why it took until 2003 for a full-scale book on the flood, one of the reasons is the molasses itself. It does initially produce almost a giggle of disbelief. If this tragedy was fire, flood, tsunami, earthquake, pestilence, or famine, it would have been written about long ago.

The tank was hastily built and leaky. Could something similar happen today?

It’s very unlikely. With the requirements and regulations imposed on construction projects today, there are many checks and balances. There always will be mistakes and opportunities for fraud and corner-cutting — but all of those would involve breaking the law. In 1919, the tank didn’t even require a building permit because it was considered a “receptacle.” A grand jury did sit on the molasses flood case, but returned no indictments — which I believe was justified because there was no law broken. Today is vastly different.

How has the working-class North End of “Dark Tide” changed?

There is much more money and wealth in the North End, and the neighborhood is much more civically and politically active than it was 107 years ago. It would be hard to imagine siting the tank on the Commercial Street waterfront today.

What happened next might be one of the most catalytic moments in Boston’s urban cultural history, though it’s not as well known, or as much celebrated, as it ought to be. The end of Chandler’s South End studio also marked the beginning of the African American Master Artists in Residency Program (AAMARP) at Northeastern University, though even Chandler himself didn’t know it right away. A chance meeting, an empty factory, and a kindly gesture from a university dean coupled with Chandler’s fiery determination is the short version of the story; the much longer one, finally and for the first time, will get its clearest and most comprehensive treatment at the Institute of Contemporary Art when it opens “Say It Loud: AAMARP 1977 to Now” on Feb. 12.

An airing of decades of determination by an energized community of Black artists, inflected by activism, righteousness, and joy, the show features dozens of artists in the AAMARP orbit, now vital to the city’s cultural history: Ellen Banks, Marlon Forrester, John Wilson, Allan Rohan Crite, Benny Andrews,and of course, Chandler himself, who died last year at 84. Jeff De Blois, the ICA curator of the show, worked closely with Chandler as he pieced the story together, gathering personal histories, archival materials, and a lot of art. “One of the things that I was really drawn to was Dana’s idea that AAMARP is for everyone,” he said. “He wanted people to bring their families. Everything was a party. It was a joyous celebration.”

From the wreckage of Chandler’s studio to a squat former factory building in Jamaica Plain where AAMARP artists in residence still work today, there’s a long, unbroken line of continuous making, convening, celebrating, and doing, always centered on an active cohort of Black artists. The line has zigged and zagged, surely, from three locations and a standoff or two with the university. But today, on Atherton Street, 13 artists continue to carry the torch for a loose organization that honors its founder’s legacy as an activist, an advocate, and a champion for culture left on the city’s margins.

Its start sprang from a happenstance meeting in 1974 between Chandler and Gregory Ricks, then dean and director of the African American Institute at Northeastern University. Hearing of Chandler’s plight, Ricks offered him storage space in an unused building on campus, and then studio space, too. Chandler, mightily prolific, filled every inch offered, and quickly needed more. So Ricks took him to an unused college building at 11 Leon St. with 32,000 empty square feet and asked him how much he might require. Chandler, sensing the opportunity, replied quickly: All of it.

Official designations would come later. But with that answer, the program was born.

“He’d been thinking about how, in the name of Black self-determination, people could become organized; this was the opportunity to live up to those values,” said De Blois. “He convinced them to not only let him use the whole space but to give him a budget, and the budget then became the seed money for the founding of the residency program.”

Had Chandler’s South End studio not come to destruction, would it have happened at all? It’s hard to think not. Chandler was uniquely, irrepressibly resolute. In 1970, after years of agitating, he had finally goaded the Museum of Fine Arts into reluctantly dipping into the surging Black Arts movement that was seizing the country. Enlisting Edmund Barry Gaither, the newly-installed director of the fledgling National Center for Afro-American artists in Roxbury, Chandler pushed the famously non-confrontational MFA into an apex moment in the culture wars.

In the years after the murder of Martin Luther King Jr., the Black rights movement fractured into more militant strains, notably the Black Panthers. Running alongside that political disquiet was the Black Arts movement, a burgeoning cultural imperative to challenge polite society in music, in writing, and of course, in visual art. Unabashedly political, the Black Arts movement was breaking through and being seen at major museums around the country. But in Boston, staid, conservative, and famously racist, that moment had not come.

Chandler set out to change that. In January 1970, he sent a document to Perry Rathbone, then the MFA director. Its title: “A Proposal to Eradicate Instititional Racism at the Boston Museum of Fine Arts.” Among its many demands was an exhibition representing the Black Arts movement, which he shared with the local press. Under growing public pressure, the museum acquiesced. That spring, “Afro-American Artists: Boston and New York,” curated by Gaither, opened at the MFA, to immediate widespread acclaim.

Black artists, of course, had been working in Boston for decades. Allan Rohan Crite’s South End home was an informal artists’ club house, and John Wilson would become a major figure on the national scene. But AAMARP gave bricks-and-mortar permanence to a community of working artists whose place in the city was always precarious; it was their place to stand on, a home to be handed down through the generations.

In later years, AAMARP faced challenges. In 1993, after years of being funded as a program of Northeastern, its funding fell victim to severe budget cuts. The space would be maintained, but further funding, including Chandler’s pay as the program’s de facto head, were cut off. AAMARP would move twice, first to another underused Northeastern-leased building on Huntington Avenue in Roxbury, and finally to Jamaica Plain, to its current home on Atherton Street.

That’s not been without its challenges, either. In 2018, Northeastern moved to close that space down and issued eviction notices to the artists working there, citing liability concerns. A public spat ensued, quelled only when the school acquiesced and AAMARP was allowed to remain, though it remains in negotiations with the school to find a permanent solution.

Without funding and official affiliation with the school, AAMARP survives as it always has, through the sheer force of will of the artists and the community that surrounds it — in a way, an ongoing tribute to its founder, whose no-quit approach lit a fire that burns still.

“There was an entire Black art infrastructure across the country that existed separate from museums,” De Blois said. “We know its story in New York, in Chicago, in Detroit. AAMARP was a huge part of Boston’s story.” Finally, it’s being told.

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO’s spring calendar at Symphony Hall is chock-full as usual; highlights in the near future include an all-John Williams program (Jan 22-25) and the world premiere of BSO composer chair Carlos Simon’s gospel-infused “Good News Mass” (Jan 29 & 31), both conducted by music director Andris Nelsons. Symphony Hall. (April 30-May 3) 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

VIVO PERFORMING ARTS The organization formerly known as Celebrity Series of Boston offers a substantial orchestral bill this season, bringing the Budapest Festival Orchestra with Iván Fischer, (Feb. 10), the Chicago Symphony Orchestra with Klaus Makela (March 1), and two days later the Vienna Philharmonic with Andris Nelsons. Smaller scale but no less notable options include dynamite Baroque band Ruckus with bass-baritone Davone Tines (Jan. 31), a debut series recital by French soprano Axelle Fanyo (Feb 3), violinist Itzhak Perlman with the Klezmer Conservatory Band (Feb 15), the reliably excellent Danish String Quartet (Feb. 27), and solo piano programs by Conrad Tao (March 15) and Vikingur Olafsson (March 20). Various venues. (617) 482-2595, www.vivoperformingarts.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY Artistic director Jonathan Cohen leads H+H’s remaining two mainstage concerts this season; the first has Handel’s “Water Music” as its centerpiece surrounded by music of Bach, Rameau, and Lully (April 10 and 12); the next month brings a program of cantatas and concertos by Bach and Telemann (May 15 & 16). Finally, the H+H Chorus takes its own spotlight concert at Jordan Hall. (May 29 & 31) Various venues. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

A FAR CRY The musician-directed orchestra mounts several concerts with the full group around town this spring, including a program in collaboration with string education program Project STEP (Jan. 31), a Valentine’s Weekend meditation on the shapes of love (Feb. 13 & 14), Copland’s pastoral “Appalachian Spring” alongside Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6 (March 14 & 18), and an evening featuring award-winning tenor Karim Sulayman in composer Karim Al-Zand’s song cycle “The Strangers’ Case.” (May 9) Various venues. 617-553-4887, www.afarcry.org

BOSTON BAROQUE The period instrument orchestra continues its first season without founding director Martin Pearlman on the podium, first with Haydn’s “Lord Nelson Mass” conducted by Bernard Labadie (March 6 & 8), then a staged production of Mozart’s “Idomeneo” directed by Bill Barclay and conducted by David Bates, with David Portillo in the title role opposite Hera Hyesang Park as Ilia and Wendy Bryn Harmer as Elettra. (April 24 & 26). The X-tet chamber ensemble also sorties twice, first for a “Sounds from Spain” program curated by concertmaster Christina Day Martinson and featuring repertoire from the baroque through contemporary periods (Feb. 7), then a Turkey and Ottoman-focused program in collaboration with ensemble DUNYA, with a new work by Mehmet Ali Sanlikol. (May 30 & 31) Various venues. 617-987-8600, www.baroque.boston

ISABELLA STEWART GARDNER MUSEUM Weekend concerts in Calderwood Hall continue apace, bringing in artists including baroque violinist Rachell Ellen Wong with collaborators from her fledgling ensemble Twelfth Night (January 25) the Attacca Quartet (Feb. 22), lutenist Hopkinson Smith with an all-Dowland program (March 8), and guitarist Paul Galbraith, who performs on an eight-string “Brahms guitar” held like a cello (April 5). The museum is also hosting the first event in a new, supposedly more experimental “Thursday Night Music” series, with Signal Ensemble making its Boston debut with Steve Reich’s “Music for 18 Musicians.” (Feb. 26) Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. www.gardnermuseum.org

BOSTON PHILHARMONIC Benjamin Zander leads the Philharmonic first in a twofer of Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 20 (featuring Kristian Bezuidenhout) and Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7 (Feb 13); the season then concludes with Mahler’s ecstatic Symphony No. 3, with British contralto Sarah Connolly and three local choruses. (April 11) The youth arm of the Philharmonic also presents two concerts, the first one of Ives, Debussy and Mahler (Feb. 27) and the second and all-American bill of John Harbison, Gershwin and Copland (May 3). Symphony Hall. 617-236-0999, www.bostonphil.org

LORELEI ENSEMBLE Sometimes it feels like Boston audiences most frequently hear the homegrown Lorelei Ensemble as contributors to larger Boston Symphony Orchestra pieces, so the group’s two-night run in the spotlight at the Institute of Contemporary Art, featuring the world premiere of Christopher Cerrone’s new eight-voice oratorio “Beaufort Scales,” is very much worth marking the calendar. March 20 & 21. Institute of Contemporary Art. www.loreleiensemble.com

ASHMONT HILL CHAMBER MUSIC Local luminaries are the name of the game this spring at Ashmont Hill. New England Conservatory ensemble-in-residence the Borromeo String Quartet throws down a program of Haydn, Britten and Dvořák (Feb. 8), then Harvard University freshman and 2025 National Chopin Competition finalist William Ge plays a solo recital (March 22); finally, the Boston-grown wind and string quartet Hub New Music rolls out an afternoon of contemporary chamber music. (April 12) Peabody Hall, All Saints Church, Dorchester. www.ahchambermusic.org

BOSTON LYRIC OPERA BLO plans to throw open the doors to its new Opera and Community Studios in Fort Point with March’s performances of Mahler’s “Song of the Earth” featuring mezzo-soprano Raehann Bryce-Davis, tenor Brandon Jovanovich, and actor Ellen Lauren (March 20-29); a fully staged American Revolution-inspired production of Donizetti’s “Daughter of the Regiment” brings the company to the Emerson Colonial Theater (April 24-May 3). The Boston Lyric Opera chorus also joins the Budapest Festival Orchestra for Mahler’s Symphony No. 3 as presented by Vivo Performing Arts (Feb. 10), and Bryce-Davis offers a one-night only solo recital at the Opera and Community Studios (March 24). Various venues. 617-542-6772, www.blo.org

GRAND KYIV BALLET’S “SWAN LAKE” This touring Ukrainian ensemble returns with the engaging, spontaneous, well-danced “Swan Lake” it brought to Boston last February. Distinctive touches include the role of the Jester, a quartet of black swans in the final act, and a happy ending; running time is just over two hours, but nothing essential is omitted. Bigger, in other words, is not always better. This time out, Viktor Tomashek and Kateryna Malkovich will be featured in both performances. Jan. 24 at 7 p.m. $54-$69. Huntington Theatre. Feb. 15 at 4 p.m. $48-$108. Emerson Colonial Theatre.www.grandkyivballet.com.ua/en/

TRISHA BROWN DANCE COMPANY Brown, arguably the dean of modern dance, passed away in 2017, but her company, which last appeared here in 2011, continues to celebrate her legacy. The program for the troupe’s Vivo Performing Arts debut spans her career. “Glacial Decoy” (1979) was her first work for a proscenium stage, its five women costumed in long diaphanous dresses designed by Robert Rauschenberg and dancing against a backdrop of his black-and-white photos. “Son of Gone Fishin’” (1981) was Brown’s first proscenium work created to music, a score for computerized organ by Robert Ashley drawn from his opera “Atalanta (Acts of God).” “Rogues” (2011) is one of her last works, a male duet that she created at age 75. Feb. 13 at 8 p.m.; Feb. 14 at 2 p.m. $62-$99. Boston Arts Academy Theater. www.vivoperformingarts.org

“TANGO AFTER DARK” Former World Tango Champions Germán Cornejo and Gisela Galeassi head up a cast of eight tango dancers, two singers, and a seven-piece band playing the music of Argentine tango king Astor Piazzolla. Cornejo and Galeassi have been dancing together since 2011 and were featured on Jennifer Lopez’s reality television series “¡Q’Viva! The Chosen One.” The show comes to Boston from sold-out performances in London. Feb. 20. $45-$76. Berklee Performance Center. www.globalartslive.org

LES BALLETS AFRICAINS In 1949 Paris, Guinean artist Keita Fodeba founded a poetry group that evolved into the African Theater of Keita Fodeba, a dancing, drumming, and storytelling troupe. In 1952, the company took its current name and performed at the Théâtre de l’Étoile; in 1958, it became the national dance company of the Republic of Guinea. It had a run of 48 performances on Broadway in 1959 and subsequently went on to the Edinburgh International Festival. Today the 35-member troupe is an ambassador for African culture as it fuses music, dance, and theater. Feb. 28. $45-$76. Berklee Performance Center. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET: “WINTER EXPERIENCE” Both halves of this program have a seasonal component. Crystal Pite’s “The Seasons’ Canon” premiered in 2016 at the Paris Opera Ballet; Boston Ballet first performed it in the fall of 2024. Set to Max Richter’s 2012 recomposition of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons,” Pite’s ambitious piece calls for 54 dancers. Boston Ballet resident choreographer Jorma Elo created “Le Sacre du Printemps” for the company in 2009; set to Igor Stravinsky’s groundbreaking 1913 score, his version is both original and arresting. March 5–15. $36-$239. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

BALLET RHODE ISLAND: “CURTAIN CALL” Ballet Rhode Island pays a rare visit to Boston with a DanceVisions-curated program of works by Ballet Rhode Island artistic executive director Kathleen Breen Combes, Ballet Rhode Island artistic curator and resident choreographer Yury Yanowsky, independent choreographer Naoko Brown, independent choreographer Ruth Fentroy, Janelle Gilchrist Dance Troupe artistic director Janelle Gilchrist, Dance Currents artistic director Kathy Hassinger, DanceVisions artistic director Margot Parsons, and Boston Liturgical Dance Ensemble artistic director Robert VerEecke. March 7 at 7:30 p.m.; March 8 at 2 p.m. $30. Boston University Dance Theater. balletri.org

GIBNEY COMPANY The New York–based company that Gina Gibney founded in 1991 made its Boston debut at the Institute of Contemporary Art in 2023 with an engaging trio of pieces by Johan Inger, Yue Yin, and Sharon Eyal and Gai Behar. The program this time out begins with “Trio (of six),” William Forsythe’s 2024 reconfiguring of his 1996 “Trio.” Israeli choreographer Roy Assaf’s “A Couple” is a duet excerpted from his 2020 work “Figure No. 16.” Finally, there’s Lucinda Childs’s “Three Dances (for prepared piano) John Cage,” which got its world premiere last year. Set to Cage’s 1944-’45 composition “Three Dances,” Childs’s piece for eight dancers addresses Cage’s minimalist aesthetic. March 13–14 at 8 p.m. $70. Institute of Contemporary Art. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET: “THE DREAM” Over the past 40 years, Boston Ballet has done versions of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” by Bruce Wells and George Balanchine, but this will be the company debut for Frederick Ashton’s one-act, one-hour creation from 1964. The score is drawn from Felix Mendelssohn’s incidental music for Shakespeare’s play. Rounding out the program is the world premiere of former company artist My’Kal Stromile’s “The Leisurely Installation of a New Window,” whose three movements — “Thesis,” “Antithesis,” and “Synthesis” — propose to examine “how individuals and societies live inside systems that no longer resolve cleanly.” March 19–29. $36-$239. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

BALLET RHODE ISLAND: “PURE DANCE” Headlining this bill is “Allegro Brillante,” which George Balanchine created in 1956 to the first movement of Tchaikovsky’s abandoned Third Piano Concerto. Christopher Wheeldon’s “Liturgy” follows; set to Arvo Pärt’s “Fratres,” this duet premiered at New York City Ballet in 2003 with Wendy Whelan and Jock Soto. Closing the program is Yury Yanowsky’s “Fading Creatures,” which he made for Richmond Ballet last year and which was inspired by Salvador Dalí’s “The Persistence of Memory.” March 20–29. $42-$72. Woodman Center, Providence, R.I. balletri.org

SOMETHING IN THE WAY FEST Indie stalwarts Run For Cover Records launched this festival 10 years ago in New York; it’s now a co-production between the label and local promoters Bowery Boston. SPRINTS Dublin has been a launching pad for some great rock acts over the last decade, and these punkers, whose most recent album “All That Is Over” came out in September, scrambled to the top of the heap quickly; vocalist Karla Chubb possesses the righteous fervency of a preacher-poet, while her bandmates’ perpetual motion adds to the urgency. Feb. 3, 7 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

MESHELL NDEGEOCELLO In 2024, this jazz and neo-soul visionary released “No More Water: The Gospel of James Baldwin,” a musically shape-shifting look at the titular writer-activist and his legacy that will be the focal point of this concert. Feb. 7, 8 p.m. Berklee Performance Center. 617-747-2261, berklee.edu/BPC

MIGUEL “CAOS,” this SoCal polymath’s first album in eight years, grinds and grooves as its central figure grapples with the dark sides of himself and the world around him. This is a Valentine’s Day show and Miguel is one of modern pop’s best live acts, so expect the newer album’s hard-edged tracks to be counterbalanced by sumptuous love songs like the effervescent “Adorn” and the devotion-minded viral hit “Sure Thing.” Feb. 14, 8:30 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

NEW EDITION Roxbury’s original boy band comes home with all six members in tow for a post-Valentine’s Day show featuring Michael Bivins proteges Boyz II Men and soul belter Toni Braxton. Feb. 15, 7 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

JADE Freed from the constraints of girlband drudgery, this former member of “X Factor”-spawned Little Mix made a sweeping statement last year with her solo debut “THAT’S SHOWBIZ BABY!,” a thrill-and-chill ride through modern fame that shows off her powerful voice and deep appreciation of pop’s fringe. Feb. 18, 7 p.m. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

JANE INC. In a short period of time, Toronto synth-pop auteur Carlyn Bezic weathered a car accident, a cancer diagnosis, and a breakup; she channeled those intense experiences into “A RUPTURE A CANYON A BIRTH,” which vibrates with the sort of energy that can only come from winning a staring contest with the abyss. Feb. 18, 7 p.m. Middle East Upstairs, Cambridge. 617-864-3278, mideastoffers.com

ALOFOKE Santo Domingo-born Esmelin Santiago Matías García is known to music aficionados in the Dominican Republic as Alofoke, whose championing of reggaetón, dembow, and hip-hop in the ‘00s led to him becoming one of the country’s most influential media executives. At the Agganis, he’ll be helming a massive dance party as he goes about “reimagining the live event experience.” Feb. 28, 8 p.m. Agganis Arena. 800-745-3000, agganisarena.com

CHARLEY CROCKETT This Texas troubadour has released 15 albums since 2015, including his major-label debut “Lonesome Drifter” and its follow-up “Dollar A Day”—both of which were produced by Shooter Jennings and released last year. Crockett’s honky-tonk-ready tunes are catchy and poignant, with his resonant voice burnishing his tales of everyday people. March 8, 8 p.m. Roadrunner. roadrunnerboston.com

DROPKICK MURPHYS The local punk heroes, who released the rousing “For the People” last July 4, set up shop on Lansdowne Street for their annual St. Patrick’s Day Weekend celebration. The three-evening run at MGM Music Hall at Fenway will be supplemented by a kid-friendly Saturday matinee benefiting their foundation the Claddagh Fund; on the holiday itself, they’ll take over House of Blues. March 13, 7 p.m.; March 14, 2:45 and 7 p.m.; and March 15, 7 p.m. at MGM Music Hall at Fenway. Also March 17, 6 p.m. at the House of Blues Boston. dropkickmurphys.com

KEVIN KLING: UNRAVELED The Minnesota-based performer has said: “There’s the trip you plan … and the trip you take.” In his solo show, Kling delivers his personal take, laced with humor, on his own trip. It’s a life journey that has included a congenital birth disorder and a near-fatal motorcycle accident. Directed by Steven Dietz. Jan. 21-Feb. 8. Merrimack Repertory Theatre, Lowell, in partnership with the Contemporary American Theater Festival. 978-654-4678, tickets.mrt.org

SOME LIKE IT HOT A musical adaptation of the 1959 Billy Wilder classic starring Marilyn Monroe, Tony Curtis, and Jack Lemmon. Two musicians, Jerry and Joe, are unlucky enough to witness a mob hit in Prohibition-era Chicago. So they take it on the lam, disguising themselves as women — Joe becomes Josephine, Jerry becomes Daphne — and join an all-female jazz band that is touring the country by train. Joe falls in love with a singer, Sugar Kane. Meanwhile, the gangsters are in hot pursuit. “Some Like It Hot” boasts a blue-chip creative team, with a book by Matthew López (“The Inheritance”) and Amber Ruffin, music by Marc Shaiman, lyrics by Shaiman and Scott Wittman, and direction and choreography by Casey Nicholaw (“The Book of Mormon”). Jan. 28–Feb. 8. Broadway In Boston. At Citizens Opera House, Boston. broadwayinboston.com

THE MODERATE A drama by Ken Urban (“A Guide for the Homesick”) about a content moderator named Frank Bonner (Nael Nacer) who is ground down by the often-unpleasant material he faces on a daily basis. Frank’s gloomy state is further compounded by his estrangement from his wife, Edith (Celeste Oliva), and son during the COVID lockdown. A chance to revive his spirits presents itself when Frank sets out to help Gus (Sean Wendelken), a teenager who has been creating troubling content about his own home and family life. Directed by Jared Mezzocchi. With a cast that includes Greg Maraio, and Jules Talbot. Feb. 5-March 1. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. 617-576-9278, centralsquaretheater.org

PENELOPE Aimee Doherty stars in a one-woman musical that reimagines Homer’s “Odyssey” from the point of view of Penelope, wife of the long-absent Odysseus, who needs to find ways to cope as Odysseus makes his way back home after the Trojan War. “Penelope” is the brainchild of Alex Bechtel, who told the Globe that he was inspired by his feelings of isolation during the pandemic while he was home in Philadelphia and separated from his romantic partner in Boston. With lyrics and music by Bechtel that ranges from folk to jazz to indie rock, and a book by Bechtel, Grace McLean, and Eva Steinmetz, “Penelope” is directed by Courtney O’Connor, with music direction by Dan Rodriguez. Feb. 6-March 1. Lyric Stage Boston. 617-585-5678, lyricstage.com

WE HAD A WORLD Joshua Harmon is one of the most interesting playwrights of the past decade-plus. Boston theatergoers have been able to experience his work via local productions of “Prayer for the French Republic,” “Bad Jews,” “Admission,” and “Significant Other.” In the autobiographical “We Had a World,” Renee, a dying woman (Amy Resnick), calls her grandson, Joshua (Will Conard), with an odd request: that he write a play about their family, and that it be “as bitter and vitriolic as possible.” Also featuring Eva Kaminsky as Ellen, Joshua’s mother. Directed by Keira Fromm. Feb. 12–March 15. Production by The Huntington at the Wimberly Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

ZABEL IN EXILE R.N. Sandberg is a dramatist of note, and his daughter, Megan Sandberg-Zakian, is a director of note who heads Boston Playwrights’ Theatre. The two have teamed up for the first production of Sandberg’s “Zabel in Exile,” about Armenian feminist writer and activist Zabel Yessayan. Set in 1937 in a Soviet prison where she is awaiting execution, “Zabel in Exile” flashes back to episodes in Yessayan’s life, from her upbringing in Constantinople to the Armenian genocide she witnessed as a reporter. With a cast consisting of June Baboian, Danny Bryck, Sarah Corey, Grace Experience, Anelga Hajjar, and Robert Najarian. Feb. 19-March 8. Boston Playwrights’ Theatre, Boston. www.bostonplaywrights.org

THE BALD SOPRANO and THE LESSON The works of avant-garde playwright Eugène Ionesco, an important figure in what became known as the Theatre of the Absurd, are seldom produced in the Boston area. Hub Theatre Company is attempting to fill that vacuum with a double bill of one-acts. In “The Bald Soprano,” which Ionesco described as an “antiplay,” an evening conversation between two bourgeois British couples degenerates into incoherent gabble. In “The Lesson,” the power imbalance between a middle-aged male professor and a young female student takes a deadly turn. Directed by Bryn Boice. Feb. 20-March 8. Plaza Black Box Theatre, Boston Center for the Arts. Tickets are “Pay-What-You-Can.”www.hubtheatreboston.org

THE THINGS AROUND US A solo musical composed, written, and performed by Ahamefule J. Oluo. Presented at Williamstown Theatre Festival last summer, “The Things Around Us” blends personal stories with a soundscape created live onstage by Oluo, using looping technology to layer in clarinet, trumpet, vocals, and percussive sounds. Feb. 20-22. Presented by ArtsEmerson at the Emerson Paramount Center, Robert J. Orchard Stage, Boston. 617-824-8400, artsemerson.org

THE ANTIQUITIES Jordan Harrison’s exploration of the perils of technology, structured as a journey through multiple time periods, including a near-future in which AI curators at The Museum of Late Human Antiquities reconstruct humanity’s past. Directed by Alex Lonati, with a cast that includes, among others, the always-compelling John Kuntz, Kelsey Fonise, and Jesse Hinson. March 6-28. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion at the BCA, Boston. 617-933-8600, www.speakeasystage.com

WAIT UNTIL DARK An adaptation by Jeffrey Hatcher of Frederick Knott’s suspenseful drama about Susan Hendrix, a blind woman in 1944 Greenwich Village who is terrorized by three hoodlums searching for a doll stuffed with heroin. “Wait Until Dark” premiered on Broadway in 1966, starring Lee Remick, and was revived in 1998 with Marisa Tomei making her Broadway debut. But it’s best known for the 1967 film version with Audrey Hepburn. Jenny S. Lee and Eliza Barmakian, who is legally blind, are splitting the role of Susan and will rotate performances. The hoods will be played by Paul Melendy, Bill Mootos, and Mamadou Toure. Directed by Weylin Symes. March 6-22. Greater Boston Stage Company, Stoneham. 781-279-2200, greaterbostonstage.org

MASAKO MIKI: MIDNIGHT MARCH Miki, born in Osaka, is a maker of fantastical felted worlds not entirely of this earth. Using brightly colored fabrics stretched over vaguely humanoid forms set loose in a star-filled universe of her own making, the soft-and-fuzzy sci-fi scene also gives way to a deeper suggestion of a kinder, gentler way to embrace what is different and strange, and to see what’s really universal. Jan. 29 - May 31. MassArt Art Museum, 621 Huntington Ave. 617-879-7333, maam.massart.edu.

DIVINE COLOR: HINDU PRINTS FROM MODERN BENGAL The mass printing industry in India has been alive for decades with wild color and flights of fancy depicting centuries of myths and deities that still play a central role in Indian life. Dismissed as art for their pervasive, throwaway ubiquity, this exhibition reexamines them in the context of not what they are as things, but what they represent, a dynamic culture rushing headlong to the future while holding on to its deep ties to the past. Jan. 31–May 31. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300,www.mfa.org.

AARON T STEPHAN: MURMUR Thousands of cast-concrete cinder blocks will fill the Center for Maine Contemporary Art, the fullest expression of Aaron T Stephan’s long-standing fascination with the rugged, prosaic form. The echo of 1960s Minimalists like Sol LeWitt and Carl Andre, who stacked blocks and fire bricks in neat stacks or straight lines is obvious and intentional. But where those artists pursued precision, Stephan plunges into controlled chaos. Arrayed in heaps, his bricks perform a dizzying perspectival trick: The whole scene is embued with a vanishing point perspective — a trompe l’oeuil sleight of hand seriously at odds with the rough and ready material. Jan. 31 - April 5. Maine Center for Contemporary Art, 21 Winter St., Rockland, Maine. 207-701-5005, www.cmcanow.org.

YINKA SHONIBARE: SANCTUARY Shonibare, a celebrated British-Nigerian artist known for his heady formal engagements with the messy, often brutal entanglements of colonial history, debuts a new installation in the U.S. this winter with “Sanctuary City,” a suite of 18 tabletop architectural models of buildings with known histories as refuges for the vulnerable and persecuted. With inequity always buzzing in the background of the post-colonial world, the piece would never not be relevant; in the current roar of the American mass-deportation experience, it will be more resonant here and now than ever. Feb. 11-Jan. 3, 2027. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434, brandeis.edu/rose

EDMONIA LEWIS: SAID IN STONE Edmonia Lewis studied art in Boston in 1863 and then moved on to Rome a few years later — a feat for a woman artist in an era where few were taken seriously. But it was doubly so for Lewis, who was of mixed race, Black and Indigenous, a set of disadvantages in her time and place that could have sunk her career before it started. That it did not says a lot about her, and this show is a showcase for her gift of sculpting hard stone into flowing, lifelike effigies of a personal slate of concerns: Abolition and social reform, and a dignified representation of Black and Indigenous people most often reduced in art of the time to cliche and disdain. Feb. 14–June 7. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500,

PERSONA: PHOTOGRAPHY AND THE RE-IMAGINED SELF Photography, by its very nature, captures fact: The camera, as they say, doesn’t lie. But it only captures what’s put in front of it, and for at least a century artists have been finding ways to use it to bend reality to their liking. This show, an exploration of performative deception, helps unpack an issue more and more prevalent in our image saturated world: How we can use the camera to capture not who we are, but who we want to be seen to me. Feb. 19-May 10. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org.

BOTH SIDES OF THE LINE: CARMEN HERRERA & LEON POLK SMITH Friends, neighbors, and collaborators, Herrera and Smith, masters of crisp hard-edged abstraction, never quite got the recognition in life that they’re garnering post-humously. (Herrera, all but unnoticed much of her career, was a late life “discovery” for the cognoscenti. She enjoyed her first major museum show at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2016, when she was 101.) This show puts them together for the first time, and conjures a little of the deserved glory that eluded them while they were alive. Feb. 21 - July 31. Addison Gallery of American Art at Phillips Academy, 3 Chapel Ave., Andover. 978-749-4015, addison.andover.edu

TECHNOLOGIES OF RELATION Depending who you talk to, the deepening integration of digital technology in our everyday lives has either brought about a utopia of ease and amusement, or a smoking hellscape of invasive despair. And for some, it’s both. This exhibition and its dozen artists purports not to judge — as if that were possible — but rather attempt to demystify its deep insinuation into the everyday, as a means to both understand it, and coax its more noble uses. On view beginning Feb. 21. Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, 1040 Mass MoCA Way, North Adams. 413-662-2111, www.massmoca.org.

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Spanning almost three millenia, 800 BCE right up ‘til now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across era to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. March 6-Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400,www.harvardartmuseum.org.

FRAMING NATURE: GARDENS AND IMAGINATION A cross-cultural, collection-wide display of natural lushness to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the MFA’s “Art in Bloom” celebration, this show promises a gamut of garden-forward glory, both flora and fauna. But because I know you’re wondering: There will be Monets, so plan accordingly. March 15–June 28. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300,www.mfa.org

DERRICK ADAMS: VIEW MASTER Adams is a jubilant polymath with a very specific mission: “What can I reveal that has not been shown?” he told the ICA. “Black people — not entertaining, just being, living. Letting people deal with that as reality.” This show, his first-ever career survey, spans more than 20 years of painting, sculpture, installation, performance, and collage, all of it with a signature ebullience that celebrates the lives of his subjects and captures the joy of the everyday. April 16–Sept. 7. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

Planning Department chief Kairos Shen stunned a community meeting in Roxbury Monday night with the news that the city plans to abandon a deal with a development team led by HYM Investments and My City At Peace to build commercial laboratory space, affordable housing, and a cultural center on the site.

Building a new Madison Park is a great idea, and kudos to the city for moving it forward. It’s one of the best things the Boston Public Schools could do, a potentially transformative project.

It’s everything else that’s driving the controversy.

Community leaders have cried foul, accusing Wu of walking away from promises to bring economic development to Roxbury, and disrespecting the neighborhood by discarding the results of a years-long public process. The city maintains that rebuilding Madison Park offers significant community benefits of its own, and that development on the unused portions of the parcel will still be possible.

The developers’ proposal, approved by the city in 2023, was to use the proceeds from newly built lab space to fund its community-oriented projects, including deeply affordable home ownership and a cultural center to house Embrace Boston, the social justice organization responsible for the sculpture of Martin Luther King and Coretta Scott King on Boston Common.

In the city’s judgment, that project had become, as the bureaucrats say, unfeasible. Which is to say, the development team, led by veteran developer Tom O’Brien (HYM) and Rev. Jeffrey Brown (My City My Peace), was struggling to raise the cash to fund their ambitious plan.

It’s undeniable that this proposal — like lots of ambitious development plans around town — is stalled for lack of capital. But the developers say they thought the city was willing to be patient and work with them for a vision that promised sweeping benefits for the community.

They and their supporters find it especially galling that Wu has turned away from them while the Madison Park proposal is still in the early stages of a lengthy state approval process.

Wu said she understands the criticism, especially its timing. But it’s pretty clear that she believes the development plan that’s been approved is unrealistic, now and perhaps forever. And she said placing the new Madison Park on a parcel the city already controls could knock as much as $200 million from the cost of replacing the school — on land where nothing seems to be happening. She stopped just short of saying O’Brien’s proposal promises more than it can possibly deliver.

“I don’t want the city to wait around for another eight years, 12 years, seeing nothing happen here because the financial realities aren’t being acknowledged,” Wu told me.

She said she believes there will be plenty of room for economic development once the layout of the new school is established, which she estimated will take two or three years. (New schools in Massachusetts take as long as a decade to approve and build.)

“Once the layout is finalized, that’s when parallel planning for the economic development parcel can happen,” Wu said. “To say it can happen at the same time would be confusing and complicate the school planning process for a project that is not economically viable.”

But that would mean restarting the whole development process, years from now. And, what about the team that was already picked?

The loss of the parcel has to be especially stinging for Rev. Brown, a celebrated community activist. He’s been a Wu stalwart, traveling with her delegation to Washington last year when she testified before Congress, and figuring prominently in a video that played at her inauguration just last week.

Brown and O’Brien told me they are still hoping the city will work with them on an economic development proposal, which they insist the community wants and needs.

“The community has suffered through win-lose prospects for too long,” Brown said. “They deserve a win-win, and we want to deliver it for them.”

Almost everyone outside City Hall believes this process needs to slow down. And that Brown’s group should be part of any final project.

But we’re talking about a parcel that has been a political football for decades. Yes, building big things is a challenge now. But in boom times or bust, big projects in Roxbury always seem to be the ones that don’t materialize.

“I believe our community wants to see things done,” Wu said. “We’re going to see it through, so we’re going to have a brand new Madison Park and an economic development plan.”

If Wu really wants to make Boston “a home for everyone,” to quote her ubiquitous campaign tagline, she needs to do more in Roxbury than replace an existing school. I don’t think Wu is wrong: Parcel 3 needs rethinking. But there has to be a clearer timeline and process for deciding what will happen. Something a lot better than even more vague promises for someday.

MIT urban studies professor Karilyn Crockett wrote the definitive history of the community protests of the late 1960s and early ‘70s that killed the proposed highway project through Roxbury — and created Parcel 3 in the aftermath.

She told me Wu simply does not seem to grasp the history of city and state government overruling community desires in favor of their own judgment.

Crockett said there needs to be a true collaboration between City Hall and Roxbury residents on a path forward.

“Mayor Wu, you have some people who are trying to walk with you, instead of having this heavy-handed decision that just gets handed down,” Crockett said. “You don’t have the history to know that this is a decision that doesn’t feel like it’s meeting the moment.”

The event’s emcee, WBZ-TV reporter and anchor Courtney Cole, said that choosing to come together across differences not only honors King’s legacy, but creates a “living symphony of purpose and possibility that will resonate for generations.”

State Senator Liz Miranda, born and raised in Roxbury, said King’s work reminds us that the “arc of the moral universe bends toward justice.” She said strength comes from community.

“As we move forward through 2026, let us do that with not only confidence but care for one another,” Miranda said. “Let us meet the challenges with more courage, meet the controversy with more compassion and the uncertainty with collective action.”

In her appearance last March before the Republican-led US House Oversight Committee, Wu lauded Boston’s record as one of the safest cities in the country.

Wu said moments like that remind her that the fight for equality is not over, and it comes “from people who like to talk about Dr. King’s work like it’s finished.” Wu clarified, it isn’t.

Jason Price got the crowd on its feet, clapping and singing along to his stirring rendition of “A Change is Gonna Come,” before newly elected City Councilor Miniard Culpepper delivered the keynote address.

Culpepper reminded the audience of a question King once asked: “Where do we go from here: chaos or community?”

While victories have been won, Culpepper said, justice is still unfinished. People, not laws, can change society, he added.

“Community doesn’t happen by accident,” he said. “It happens because people make community happen. In a city where inequality still shapes life outcomes, the YMCA stands as a living example that we can choose community over chaos.”

US Representative Ayanna Pressley and Boston City Councilors Ruthzee Louijeune, Henry Santana, and Julia Mejia were also in attendance.

Three awards were given out during the event: the Roxbury Legacy Award to Arnita Cooper, a longtime water aerobics instructor at the YMCA; the Community Champion Award to Mike Kozu, co-director of Project R.I.G.H.T. Inc.; and the Corporate Leadership Award to Comcast, which was accepted by Becca Fracassa, director of government and community affairs.
