Getting this far wasn’t easy, and neither is it all rosy right now for the African American Masters Artists in Residence Program, currently resident in a disheveled Jamaica Plain warehouse owned by its apparently-grudging, founding patron, Northeastern University. But let’s not let a relationship gone south sour a moment to be savored. There’s a story here, of determination, resilience, and no small amount of joy, and that’s where it starts.

“Dana Smiles,” a photo portrait of Dana Chandler — sun-drenched, mouth wide in toothy exuberance, eyes closed in genuine contentment, which hangs alongside the title wall, a tribute to the group’s founding firebrand. A living keeper of its history, he died late last year, after working closely with the ICA’s Jeff DeBlois putting the show together.

The photo, by Reggie Jackson, a member of AAMARP’s founding cohort in 1977 and now its executive director, is a direct line to the promise of early days: taken in 1976, when AAMARP was about to be born. Chandler, fast becoming the face of a rising community of Black artist-activists, was on the verge of willing it into being. An alliance with Northeastern’s Gregory Ricks, the director of its John D. O’Bryant African American Institute, would lead to many thousands of square feet in a university-owned warehouse, where AAMARP began its journey on Chandler’s foundational principles: to create space for Black artists in Boston, and to nurture a culture largely ignored by the city’s major institutions.

But Chandler — brash, gregarious, tireless, charming — found alliances all over. The early galleries establish the broad stage he set. One of the first pieces in the show is his “Pan-African Man‚” a sparse 1970 painting of a Black man in silhouette. Inside his head, his brain is neatly portioned into the three colors of the Pan-African flag: red, black, and green. Right next to the painting hangs Arnold Trachtman’s “Spirit of ’76 (Louise Day Hicks and Ted Landsmark),” from 1979, a kaleidoscopic, dark pop-art vision of the clash between Black and white during the city’s busing crisis. Hicks, a zealously anti-school-integration politician, looms crone-like over the scene. Landsmark, now a distinguished professor of public policy at Northeastern and a long-time civil rights champion, was the victim in the famous flagpole-lancing photograph taken at Boston City Hall in 1976. Trachtman was not Black, but his allegiance was clear. For Chandler and the AAMARP, the price of admission was radical politics and a hunger for justice. That much remains: L’Merchie Frazier’s “Ericka Huggins: Liberation Groceries,” 2019, is a recent take on a Black Panther Party luminary, cast in silky synthetics.

AAMARP has always toggled smoothly between art and politics; the exhibition is a vivid frame for turbulent local civic and political history across at least a couple of generations. One of the best works here is by Wen-ti Tsen, a Chinese-American artist and AAMARP confrere; called “Peaceable Kingdom,” 1971, its epic unfolds in multiple scenes across three hinged wooden panels. Inside, his take on the Quaker artist Edward Hicks’s famous vision of earthly harmony between man and beast. Framing it are eruptions of violent unrest: a murder suspect in the killing of three civil rights workers in Mississippi; American soldiers brutalizing a Vietnamese commando; another Vietnamese soldier, captured, confined, and howling in pain.

The piece first showed at the AAMARP because, really, where else? Tsen had lost his job teaching at the School of the Museum of Fine Arts because of his political bent, a reminder that within a city that prided itself on a veneer of gentility and intellectual heft, rougher notions of dissent were simply not welcome.

The city’s counter-cultural community found a home at the AAMARP where it could not anywhere else. For years, it thrived, holding exhibitions, performances, lectures, gatherings, and hosting Black luminaries from all over. Artmaking was its constant. Established senior artists like John Wilson and Allan Rohan Crite offered support and guidance. In a lovely moment here, Crite, a beloved painter of the everyday of Black Boston in Roxbury and the South End, lends his no-nonsense social realist style to a quilt-making collaboration with Susan Thompson. “Freedom, Justice, Equality,” 1989-2012, a bright scene of a street protest, is a marriage of their priorities and talents. Jackson, too, looked up to Crite; as the older artist made “An Artist’s Sketchbook of the South End: A Walking Tour about Black People” in 1977, Jackson photographed the same scenes and later superimposed them with images of sacred African objects to confer history and connection.

In art as in life, there’s a rupture here. In 1993, when Northeastern slashed AAMARP’s budget and fired Chandler, he made a 5,000-edition newsprint piece making a case for its value. It’s on view here too, its yellowed pages simmering with accusation and rage. In one glaringindictment, Chandler accuses the school of using AAMARP as a way to burnish its image among communities of color.

Northeastern left the program with free space but little else. In 2018, it changed the locks overnight and moved to evict them. Only an intervention by Mayor Marty Walsh stopped it, and the group remains in the building. But a palpable unease lingers, and a path forward together seems unlikely.

“Say It Loud” overflows with compelling, captivating, overlooked cultural history here. Remarkable works from its stored past are too many to count, and pull at the threads of a Boston that once was. A gathering of ebony-black felted soft sculptural figures in tribal finery by Barbara Ward have been revived here from their debut in a shop window at Filene’s Basement in the 1980s, put there as an anti-racism statement by the city’s Young Woman’s Christian Association. The epic scale of Bryan McFarlane’s “I Dream of African Souls,” 1986, is a somber ode to the ruptures of diaspora that were at the time just becoming fertile intellectual ground for artists and scholars both.

Even so, it all made me worry for its future. McFarlane has been a member of AAMARP since 1983, when a parallel cultural world was still much needed for Black artists mostly ignored by the mainstream. AAMARP “played an invaluable role in healing our communities of color,” reads a quote from McFarlane on the wall near his work. But what about now? That’s what AAMARP, in 2026, needs to figure out. In the exhibition’s last phases, next generation members of the group like Marlon Forrester and Khalid Kodi are on view, a hint at a future obscured by uncertainty.

Forrester makes powerful mixed-media work; his “Warrior Dance,” 2014, sets a sword-wielding figure amid a prismatic storm of abstract fields. Kodi’s work here is brand new, and makes a case: “Excessive Narrative: Echoes of Eden,” he calls it, made in 2025, a vibrant tableaux of bodies in fluid communion with rivers of shadow and color. It seethes with unease, but is just as certainly vital, dynamic, alive. The show may cover AAMARP, 1977 to now, but the question it asks is the real issue, hanging heavy in the air: What next?

Revolution 250, the organizing committee of the state’s celebration, has partnered with multiple community groups, including Boston 250 and Unitarian Universalist Urban Ministry, to celebrate Knox.

The event is part of Knox Trail 250, a statewide observance that has made its way across Massachusetts. Local communities have held celebrations on the date that Knox marched through, such as Feb. 8 in Framingham.

In the winter of 1775-76, Knox, a 25-year-old Boston bookseller, hauled away British cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston. The cannons were positioned at Dorchester Heights, ultimately forcing the British troops to evacuate the city on March 17, 1776.

“You don’t get to declare independence without first commemorating Evacuation Day,” said Jonathan Lane, executive director of Revolution 250. “And you don’t get to Evacuation Day without telling the story of Henry Knox and his Noble Train of Artillery.”

Knox’s ties to Roxbury are significant. Before his expedition, he built fortifications in the neighborhood that caught the eye of Washington, launching his role as an officer in the artillery.

“Within a year, he was the Brigadier General of the artillery,” Lane said. “He has a meteoric rise, but that was Washington’s style.”

The events Saturday will begin at 2 p.m. with a procession from Fenway High School to John Eliot Square. Marchers will include colonial militia reenactors, patriots of color, a fife and drum unit, and the Hamilton-Garrett drumline. Two teams of Clydesdale horses will pull sleds and cannons, echoing Knox’s original winter trek.

Organizers said the event will stand apart from other Knox Trail events across Massachusetts and New York.

“We … wanted it to really feel true to what Roxbury has been and what it continues to be today as a the hub of Black Boston and a center of revolutionary thought and action,” said Alex Meadow, deputy director of partnerships in the mayor’s office.

Formal programs will be held at the Dillaway-Thomas House. Alongside Knox’s story, the programs will highlight Black patriots who fought in the Revolutionary War and explore the experiences of free, enslaved, and Indigenous people during the Siege of Boston. Black reenactors from the Living History Company and local historians, artists, and poets will participate as well.

A speaking program is planned to begin at 3 p.m. at the First Parish Church, recently reopened after a multiyear renovation. Mayor Michelle Wu is expected to attend and announce the launch of the Boston Historic Markers Program.

The event will conclude with a 15-minute light projection show as a part of the Boston Beacon initiative.

The Roxbury event is one of two Knox-related observances in Boston this month, alongside the annual Dorchester Heights ceremony on March 17. Both are part of Boston 250, the city’s public-private effort to mark its role in the nation’s founding. For Meadow, the theme running through Boston 250 is “everyday revolutionaries.”

“Henry Knox was a bookseller who went to Boston Public Schools,” Meadow said. “An important piece of this for us is through our events and through our programs, helping people realize that they hold power themselves.”

Heartbroken by Hillary Clinton’s defeat in 2016, composer Shaina Taub kept working on a play to inspire, as Clinton put it in her concession speech, “all the little girls who are watching this.”

A decade later, Taub is bringing to Boston “Suffs,” her stirring Tony-winning Broadway musical of women suffragettes’ hard-won, century-old victory at getting the vote.

Surprisingly relevant

The story’s struggle seems fresher than ever these days, she tells James Sullivan, mentioning the Roe v. Wade reversal and up-to-the-minute, state-by-state struggles for maternal and reproductive rights. (Yesterday, Texans voted on a proposition that each person has the right to make their own health care decisions, including reproductive rights).

The Vermont native was raised on raucous, rebellious musicals like “Hair,” “Rent,” and “Les Misérables” — and summoned that spirit for the spirited song “How Long” after Trump took office in 2017.

“It’s an elegy that becomes this rallying cry,” Taub tells Sullivan.

A war on women?

While the national tour prepares to play Emerson’s Colonial theater from March 17-29, President Trump is trying to gear up support for a law, already passed by the House, that could strip tens of millions of American citizens of their right to cast a ballot.

In particular, the SAFE Act seeks to throttle mail-in voting and will make it harder for married women who have changed their last name to vote.

An estimated 69 million American women and 4 million men do not have a birth certificate that matches their current legal name.

Last year, the Pentagon had to clarify that Pete Hegseth supported women’s right to vote despite sharing a video that said otherwise.

The message of ‘Suffs’

“I’m not sure that Shaina could have known just how relevant her musical would become more than 10 years after she began working on it,” Sullivan tells me.

Sullivan was struck by Taub’s drive and uplift.

“She has taught herself to find energy in the fact that all movements for social progress are constantly subject to backlash and the frustrations of ‘one step forward, two steps back,’” he said. “I think it has been a conscious decision on her part not to give into despair.”

In the Globe’s coverage of the Boston Public Health Commission’s new life expectancy data (“Boston moves to close life expectancy gap,” Metro, March 2), Mayor Michelle Wu observed that “a beacon that only shines for some is not a beacon at all.” The widening gap in Boston — nearly seven years between Black residents and other racial and ethnic groups, and 23 years between residents of Roxbury and those of Back Bay — is more than a public health statistic. It is a measure of whether our policies reach everyone.

Boston has earned recognition from AARP and the World Health Organization as an “age-friendly” city. This designation reflects thoughtful planning and engagement. But the health commission data demand a harder question: Friendly for whom?

An age-friendly label rings hollow if Black men in Boston can expect to live to only 72 — more than nine years less than men in other groups — and if preventable cancers, cardiometabolic diseases, and drug overdoses continue to cut lives short in neighborhoods long shaped by structural inequities.

What Boston needs now is not simply to be age-friendly, but age-responsive. Age-responsive governance would set measurable benchmarks, require transparent reporting, and commit to sustained investment beyond announcements. It would connect housing stability, addiction services, environmental justice, food access, transportation, and primary care into an integrated longevity strategy — with clear accountability for closing life expectancy gaps by 2035.

Boston is home to world-class medicine. The challenge is ensuring that excellence is not bounded by ZIP code or race.

If we truly aspire to be a beacon, the light must reach every neighborhood — and stay on.

Richard T. Moore

In mid-February, Damas told personnel at the Florence facility that he had a toothache, but he was not sent to a dentist, his brother Presly Nelson said in an interview.

Damas was seeking asylum and had entered the country legally through a Joe Biden-era humanitarian parole program for Haitians in 2024, Nelson said.

Damas died Monday at a Scottsdale hospital, after the family chose to take him off life support. He had been receiving treatment for more than 10 days, his family said. The detention center had only given Damas over-the-counter medication for his pain, according to his family.

Damas had two sons in Boston, the youngest of whom is a 13-year-old in seventh grade.

“It’s like treating a human being like they’re nobody,” Nelson said. “As an American, I’m very ashamed, I’m very disheartened.”

Over the weekend, Nelson rushed from Boston to Arizona to see his brother after receiving a call from the hospital that Damas was in critical condition and might not have much time left. In the hospital, Nelson found his brother on life support. Still, Damas was handcuffed to the hospital bed, had a chain on his body, and two security officers were stationed by his room, Nelson said.

“He could barely blink his eyes — he was in a vegetative state, motionless, on life support,” Nelson, 47, said. “But he still had handcuffs on . . . it was so hurtful.”

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement Friday that it alerted Damas’ family about his worsening conditioning as well as Congress after his death. The statement confirmed Damas was held to be deported, though he had appealed. The department also said it provided adequate medical care.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments,” the statement said. “At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.”

But Damas’s death sparked outrage among lawmakers in Massachusetts and Arizona. On Thursday, Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, along with Representative Ayanna Pressley, wrote a letter to homeland security Secretary Kristi Noem and ICE acting director Todd Lyons demanding a full investigation. They also called on the DHS to provide proper medical treatment care to detainees as a matter of standard.

The letter was sent the same day Noem was fired by President Trump amid mounting criticism of her leadership of DHS. Damas is at least the 10th person to die in ICE custody this year, the lawmakers said.

After Damas first informed staff of his nagging tooth pain, he visited the health clinic at the detention center over the course of Feb. 17 and Feb. 18. He was given over-the-counter medications but was reportedly denied dental treatment, according to the lawmakers. Several days later, Damas told his family that his condition had worsened and he could no longer speak properly. He informed them he would finally be taken to a hospital, the letter states.

On Feb. 20, staff at the HonorHealth John C. Lincoln Medical Center told his family that Damas was suffering from pneumonia and had been placed on life support in the intensive care unit, where he remained in critical condition, according to the letter. But for days after that, neither family nor lawmakers received clear updates on his medical condition and whereabouts, they said.

As the family continued to press for updates, Markey reached out to ICE on the their behalf. “ICE did not provide satisfactory answers,” and officials said they could not release information unless a privacy form was signed, lawmakers say in the letter.

“Senator Markey had made clear that a Privacy Release Form was impossible given that it was unclear where Mr. Damas was located and if he was even alive,” the letter says.

Several days later, the family learned that Damas had been transferred to a nearby hospital, and was scheduled for surgery on Feb. 26. He died on March 2.

Damas, who worked as a mechanic in Haiti, and his sons had fled gang violence in their native country, his family told the Globe. Nelson had sponsored Damas to come to the US in February 2024, and the family lived in Dorchester. Damas and his sons thought they had reached safety here, Nelson said, and they were excited for the 13-year-old’s education in Boston.

“It was like a dream come true when they came,” Nelson said. “It was a relief, considering all the turmoil that’s been going on in Haiti.”

Now, the family, and the boys, are left devastated.

Massachusetts District Court records show that Damas was arrested in September and charged with assault and battery, a misdemeanor. His family said that police took Damas to the station after he gave what they characterized as a slap on the back of the son’s head following a misunderstanding.

Damas was quickly released after the family posted bail, but ICE officers had arrived to the police precinct to detain him. “An officer came out and said, ‘I’m sorry, he was picked up by a federal agent,’ ” Nelson said.

Nelson and his twin brother, Presner Nelson, said they were in close touch with an immigration attorney to try to get their brother out of detention. Damas called both of his brothers, his children, and his mother back in Boston often, remaining positive about his chances to reunite with them, his family said.

“He was hopeful that one day he was going to come back home,” said Presner Nelson.

His family alleges that ICE did not provide Damas with timely medical care. This allowed the untreated toothache “to become a deadly infection,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter. And from Boston, the brothers, and their mother, spent their time constantly calling the detention facility and the hospital trying to get more information. And they were often stonewalled, they said.

Damas‘s death, the lawmakers said, was “a tragedy and likely, a highly preventable one.”

His death comes amid growing concerns about the conditions inside federal immigration detention centers, with last year marking the deadliest in ICE history in over two decades, lawmakers said.

The Florence detention center where Damas was held is operated by CoreCivic, a massive private prison operator, which contracts with ICE across the country.

Presly Nelson has lived in the US for almost three decades, and became an American citizen after first moving here on a scholarship to study in Wisconsin. He had hoped his brother and his nephews would be able to experience the America he had come to love — a country that embraced people from all over the world.

“That was the compassionate country that I’ve come to appreciate and respect,” Nelson said. “This country is great because of its diversity, and without it, I think we become weaker and weaker.”

Now, Nelson wonders: “If he [Damas] were still back in Haiti, he would not have died like this.”

After his brother passed away, Nelson received a call from an official at ICE, he said. The agency was requesting his address, so they could send him a letter of condolence. While he appreciated the call and passed along his address, he felt it was too little, much too late.

“What’s that going to do for me,” Nelson said. “Is the letter going to bring my brother back to life?”

Before the Khmer Rouge’s reign of terror, Mr. Ly had worked in Cambodia for The Associated Press. Then he began assisting reporters from the Globe and Chicago Tribune as an interpreter and as one of the local “fixers” — invaluable colleagues who guided and supported foreign correspondents through dangerous reporting assignments and unpredictable negotiations.

“I know that they educated us, or Ly did, on how to deal with soldiers,” recalled Matthew V. Storin, then a Globe reporter in Phnom Penh and later the newspaper’s editor-in-chief. “We had to buy [soldiers] bottles of Remy Martin brandy just to get information sometimes.”

Mr. Ly, who chronicled his family’s journey from Cambodia’s notorious Killing Fields to Boston in Globe newspaper articles and a memoir, died Feb. 26 in South Shore Hospital in Weymouth, about 13 months after suffering a major stroke. He was 83 and had lived in Quincy for many years.

In 2000, he published “Heaven Becomes Hell: A Survivor’s Story of Life Under the Khmer Rouge.”

“Unless you see something like this through the eyes of someone who’s experienced it, you really can’t begin to grasp it,” John S. Driscoll, a former editor-in-chief of the Globe who edited the memoir, said when the book was published.

During the genocide of the Khmer Rouge regime, led by the dictator Pol Pot, about 2 million people — roughly a third of Cambodia’s population — died between 1975 and 1979 from forced labor, mass executions, starvation, and the lack of basic amenities.

As a journalist before the genocide, Mr. Ly was valued for his intelligence and experience.

“My dad spoke four languages: Cambodian, French, English, and Thai,” said his son, Johnny Sim Ly of Woodcliff Lake, N.J.

But when the Khmer Rouge took over, Mr. Ly was forced into menial labor. He had to lie about his background to avoid being killed at a time when soldiers targeted intellectuals and those who had worked with Americans.

Interrogated by an official one day, “I pretended to neither speak nor write any foreign language,” Mr. Ly wrote in a December 1980 Globe article, after his family had arrived in Boston.

The genocide took an enormous toll on Mr. Ly’s family. In “Heaven Becomes Hell,” he wrote about the joy his family had felt, just before the Khmer Rouge regime, when Prasat, his first child, was born.

Mr. Ly wrote that his son “was precious to me. He was the only hope for my future. I could see in his eyes that he would be thirsty for knowledge.”

As a toddler, Prasat was among many who became very ill. Mr. Ly wrote about how the family struggled without success to care for him with almost no medicine.

After Prasat died, Mr. Ly wrote that he carefully placed him “in a tiny grave, a cubic meter big, and I did not forget to plant a piece of wood there as a marker, so that I could come back to pray for him again. That is an image that I shall never forget. Then I said goodbye in silence.”

Mr. Ly was born on May 18, 1942, in Reap, in Cambodia’s Prey Veng Province. His mother was Cheng Sim. His father, Y Heng, had been a district chief and was reduced to menial farm labor during the Khmer Rouge regime.

In Cambodia, Mr. Ly was known as Y Ly, his birth name. Johnny said that when his father immigrated to the United States, he was told that for purposes of official records here he could not use a single letter as his first name, so his name was reversed from Y Ly to Ly Y.

Foreign correspondents in Cambodia had turned to Mr. Ly for his fluency in languages and for his expertise in many other matters.

“The greatest value of Ly was that he knew everybody, he knew the territory,” Storin said. “He knew where to go, he knew what was safe and what was not safe.”

When Storin returned to the United States, he lost touch with Mr. Ly during the Khmer Rouge regime, but he didn’t forget his friend.

“I had a black and white photo of Ly that I literally kept on my dresser for five years, it just was lying there,” he said.

Mr. Ly had married Chantra Try in 1971. During the genocide, they were forced to leave Phnom Penh and walked for days to villages where they were enslaved.

When the Vietnamese military invaded Cambodia in 1978 and overthrew the Khmer Rouge, Mr. Ly “was the one who had the vision, the courage to try to escape,” Johnny said. “He said, ‘If we stay, we’re definitely going to die.’”

Mr. Ly led his family on a days-long trek by foot to a Thai refugee camp, bringing with him his wife, her three brothers — Hak, Huot, and Heng Meng — and their father, Chour L. Chheng.

Meanwhile in Boston, Storin had lunch one day in 1980 with Sydney Schanberg, a New York Times correspondent who had won a Pulitzer Prize for his Cambodia reporting, and Dith Pran, a photojournalist who had worked with Schanberg in Cambodia much in the way Mr. Ly had worked with Storin.

At the end of the lunch, Storin showed Dith – who had escaped Cambodia’s Killing Fields – the photo of Mr. Ly that he had kept on his dresser. Dith recognized Mr. Ly and said he was in a refugee camp in Thailand.

Storin then arranged for Mr. Ly and his family — which by then included Mr. Ly’s two children — to move to Boston, where they initially lived in Dorchester.

“They came in November 1980 with the clothes on their back, one kilo of rice, and a few trinkets they had used to trade with the people along the way of the refugee trail,” Storin said.

In the United States, Mr. Ly worked for a time at the Globe and became a leader of Greater Boston’s Cambodian community.

“He helped to bring a lot of people from Cambodia over,” said Johnny, who added that his father also helped launch and wrote for the Bodhipriks News, published in Greater Boston and circulated among New England’s Cambodian immigrants.

Along with “Heaven Becomes Hell,” Mr. Ly wrote other books, including the memoir “Becoming American.”

“It was a heroic life in certain ways,” Storin said.

In addition to his wife and his son, Mr. Ly leaves a daughter, Outtra Sim Ly of Woodcliff Lake, N.J.; a sister, Y Sokkom of Phnom Penh; and a brother, Y Leng, of Cambodia’s Kandal Province.

“I applaud the city on those efforts, but definitely more work needs to be done,” Boyd said. “We can’t be caught off guard in future winters like the city seemed to be this year.”

Curb cuts, sloped ramps built into sidewalks at intersections, are especially critical because they allow people using wheelchairs and other mobility devices to move safely from the sidewalk to the street.

“When we find curb cuts not shoveled out or sidewalks not with a wide enough path, it makes it feel like our needs aren’t as important,” Boyd said.

Councilor Ed Flynn called snow cleanup a civil rights issue.

“You judge a snowstorm on how accessible the streets and sidewalks are for persons with disabilities and seniors,” Flynn said.

The city did not respond to an interview request to address complaints from residents with disabilities. However, it defended its snow removal operations.

“We recognize the major impact that snow has on people with disabilities,” Disability Commissioner Kristen McCosh said in a statement. “We make every effort to maintain accessible paths of travel by ensuring that City resources are focused on sidewalks, curb ramps, and crosswalks.”

During the two major snowstorms, the city conducted targeted snow removal in priority areas, including Boston Public Schools locations, major thoroughfares, intersections, curb ramps, and public squares, according to Boston Public Works.

Crews have removed 10,444 truckloads of snow from city streets this season, 6,566 loads in January and 3,878 in February, according to Public Works. The Public Works Code Enforcement Division has issued 5,870 snow removal violations across both storms, the department said.

Of the 311 cases reported to the city each month, 59 percent in January and 53 percent in February were related to snow, according to Public Works.

“Every winter storm presents a unique set of challenges,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said in a statement. “We remain open to feedback and will continue to iterate on our snow removal strategies within our fiscal and staff constraints.”

Osaghae said the Boston Code of Ordinances requires property owners to clear snow, slush, and ice from sidewalks and curb ramps around their property. The ordinance requires a minimum 42-inch-wide path to be cleared for people using wheelchairs and pushing strollers.

“We need to have a finalized ‘who to go to’ when this situation is happening,” said Daniela Depina, 45, who is wary of stepping out of her Dorchester home and onto the icy, snow-ridden sidewalk.

Depina, who is visually impaired, has rescheduled medical appointments, skipped grocery store runs, and even paid someone to take her 11-year-old daughter, Mariah, to school, because the ground outside her home was not fully shoveled, she said. She called 311 after the January storm and said she didn’t get answers about who was responsible for clearing her sidewalk.

“I had to sit on my butt to get down my stairs, because that’s how bad it was,” said Depina, a disability peer advocate at the Boston Center for Independent Living. “If everywhere you call you’re getting the runaround, it’s almost feeling like the door is being shut.”

Gabrielle Mondestin, chief communications officer for the MBTA, said in a statement that its RIDE service is affected “even after the snow has stopped falling.” Drivers may struggle to pull over or park near a customer’s destination, and it can be difficult to deploy vehicle lifts when piled snow blocks the curb, she said.

Crystal Evans, 45, of Braintree, who has a neuromuscular disease and uses a ventilator to breathe, travels to Boston three to six days a week for health care. She gets medical transportation through her insurance company, but it has been unreliable, so Evans opts for the buses and trains.

Evans, who shoveled Braintree sidewalks using her motorized wheelchair in 2015, said piles of snow made the curb cuts inaccessible and crosswalk buttons impossible to reach from her chair.

“When we’re dependent on a sidewalk plow, then things like signs and light posts, the plows can’t navigate,” Evans said. “Then they just stop, back off, go into the street, and we don’t have that continuous path of travel.”

She said snowbanks left at traffic islands were another concern for her as she crossed intersections.

“As a wheelchair user, you don’t know if a car is going to come around the corner or not,” she said. “I’m lower than the snowbanks.”

William O’Donnell, 42, a peer support leader who lives in Quincy, was particularly fearful of having to walk into the street with Juno, his guide dog.

“The dog is trying to guide you around obstacles,” O’Donnell said. “Often, there’s not a straight way you can go, and then they have to dodge traffic, worry about getting you around the cars.”

When he walked in the street, O’Donnell said he could feel the heat of the cars traveling next to him, less than an arm’s length away. He suggested that if municipalities have to build snowbanks at the edges of the streets, they can keep them off of curb cuts or use melting machines to eliminate them.

Casandra Xavier, a 36-year-old disability advocate who was born with blindness and hearing loss, said city officials should take accessibility into account when clearing snow because they never know when they might need it.

“No one is exempt from acquiring a disability in this life,” she said. “We are not asking for a favor. We’re just simply reminding everyone of our rights as persons with disabilities, that we too should have access to our environment freely and comfortably.”

Over the last year, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has quietly slowed the implementation of much of the street safety agenda of her first term. Residents deserve to know whether it’s a temporary pause or a longer-term shift in the administration’s priorities. Many Boston streets are still dangerous for motorists, pedestrians, and cyclists, and it would be unfortunate if Wu allows rancor over street projects like bus lanes or flex posts to block the kind of safety upgrades that are still needed across the city.

The dangers remain as clear as ever: Through the first half of last year, there were six road fatalities in Boston, according to the city’s dashboard. That includes four pedestrians.

In her first term, Wu spent serious political capital upgrading streets and intersections, through interventions like speed humps that slow down traffic and road reconfigurations to improve safety. For instance, she pushed through the stalled “road diet” on Centre Street in West Roxbury, addressing known safety hazards on a road where a pedestrian was killed in 2019 and many crashes involving pedestrians, cars, and bicycles have been recorded.

The inclusion of bike and bus lanes, however, has been a sore spot in many neighborhoods and a potential political liability for the mayor. The bungled installation of speed humps on Allandale Street in Jamaica Plain and West Roxbury, which the city subsequently removed, created additional headwinds. So last year, facing a reelection battle against an opponent determined to make bike lanes a campaign-defining issue, Wu ordered a 30-day review of all street projects. Then she slowed the work of designers and planners in her Streets Cabinet, which since then has seen the steady departure of staff with street-safety expertise.

In an interview with the Globe editorial board, Wu denied adopting a more cautious approach and said street safety was a “constant focus” of her administration. “Ultimately, this is about balancing the tools that we have for the different uses of our streets,” she said. “We need more context-sensitive design, more engagement beyond just an individual street, but to the surrounding neighborhoods at large.”

The departures include former Chief of Streets Jascha Franklin-Hodge, who announced his exit in November; former Deputy Chief of Infrastructure and Design Julia Campbell, who stepped down from her role a month later; the Cabinet’s Chief of Staff Sarah Anders, who left in January; and Director of Transportation Policy and Planning Vineet Gupta, who retired this month.

Notably, the city has also stonewalled a public records request from the Globe editorial board originally filed in October that requested internal emails from the Streets Cabinet. The Globe appealed to the state supervisor of Public Records, who said in December that the city “must provide responsive records,” which it has not done. But the Globe has been told by people familiar with Streets Cabinet operations that many projects are now in indefinite limbo and that there is poor communication and a singular focus on uncontroversial day-to-day operations like street repaving rather than long-term street safety initiatives.

For example, 2024’s “Safety Surge” initiative, which aimed to install more than 2,000 bumps along Boston’s streets, has dramatically slowed. A series of traffic-calming projects for Lower Roxbury, which began its community outreach process back in 2019 and was supposed to be completed last year, has not yet been built. Egleston Square’s redesign is in a similar limbo. The Columbia Road Transportation Action Plan final designs were promised last year, but the website still lists the project in an early planning phase and lacks any upcoming events. Improvements from Boylston Street, between Brookline and Ipswich, were just delayed another four years.

Another project on ice is Hyde Park Avenue’s multimodal corridor. In 2024, after a pedestrian was killed near Forest Hills station, hundreds of residents and safety advocates demanded changes on that dangerous stretch of road. But since February 2025, despite comprehensive designs that have been ready for months, there has been no movement on Hyde Park Avenue’s transit upgrades. An SUV hit another pedestrian in September 2025. The victim sustained life-threatening injuries.

The election is over, and however much some residents may despise street safety interventions, Wu’s transit-friendly first-term record didn’t prevent her from winning reelection by a landslide. The 30-day review that kicked off this cautious approach ultimately recommended slowing down and building consensus. But the city applied this advice indiscriminately, hamstringing projects with years of community input alongside newer ones. Even if street upgrades change in priority and schedule, the mayor should let her specialists in street safety get back to work — or explain to constituents why she’s ignored their advice for more than a year. Above all else, if this change is permanent, Wu must articulate her new strategy to manage the dangers of Boston’s streetscape.

Welcome to The Jar. Executive director Guy Ben-Aharon says the mission of the nonprofit organization, which he founded in 2019, is to inspire individuals to connect to folks like them and not like them through the arts. To that end, The Jar presents a variety of events designed to bring together disparate demographics into one another’s orbits in a way that invites curiosity and connection as a means of driving social change. It’s not just a way to understand differences, but to appreciate them.

“It’s intentionally joyful, a real moment of human connection at a time of real discord,” says Ben-Aharon. “The Jar is for adventurous, open-minded, direct humans who are longing for connection. And that comes in many shapes, sizes, beliefs, backgrounds, genders, sexualities — it crosses everything.”

The Jar’s prescriptive format quickly reassures skeptics and introverts. Each evening starts with a casual meet-and-greet over drinks followed by an artistic offering. Large performance-oriented programs might be held in area theaters. Other happenings are more akin to intimate salons, with smaller groups gathering in someone’s house for dinner and conversation, often provoked by a piece of visual art, a poem, or a reading. For this night of samba, led by former Boston Ballet dancer Irlan Silva, the theme is dance and how we relate to our bodies.

“I think of the small group salons as intimate and uplifting, while these larger events are all about this big communal energy,” says Samantha Tan, an executive leadership consultant who is the organization’s board chairman.

The structure is simple. The Jar’s signature “Convener Model™” was devised so that no one attends an event alone. You are either invited by someone you know (convened), or you are the one doing the inviting (a convener). Conveners buy a Jar of six tickets — all tickets are $10 for a three-hour evening of art, drinks, and food. Each convener invites a plus-one, two “usuals” they often experience culture with, and two “unusuals” intentionally chosen because they “may look, pray, love, or earn differently but who you would like to know better,” according to the website. That methodology creates a deeply diverse room of people open to experiencing a cultural journey together.

With an operating budget of $800,000 (98 percent philanthropy), The Jar presents roughly 25 programs a year in the Boston area with a slow rollout of events beginning in Los Angeles and New York as well. Programming ranges from new play readings to visual art, embracing both emerging artistic voices from around the world and esteemed superstars, like internationally-acclaimed cellist Yo-Yo Ma.

For the samba night, Silva led the group in a lively samba lesson, with most of the participants gamely trying the loose-limbed swings and fast footwork for the first time. After sharing his own personal journey from Rio to Boston, Irlan set the tone for what is the heart of each program, the “facilitated mixer,” an opportunity to share life experiences and reflections through three sets of provocations. Participants divide into small rotating groups of 4-8 people for conversations relating to the event’s theme, this night including: “What was a time your body betrayed you? Surprised you?” The experience requires a level of openness and vulnerability that can be both daunting and rewardingly cathartic, revealing and creating personal connections and understanding.

“People got to experience art and a story of someone’s life in the arts, they got to dance themselves, to feel first before they thought, then were invited to share more of themselves with folks like them and not like them,” says Ben-Aharon. “If there’s some magic sauce to The Jar, it is to go deep fast. People often share and hear stories they normally wouldn’t, and that’s a real gift at a moment when people feel so protective of themselves.”

He adds, “Everybody lives in a bubble. How can we expect to live and thrive in a multi-ethnic democracy by doing the same thing that has led to its destruction?”

Roxbury resident Courtland Townes III, who advocates for disability rights and access as deputy director for Boston Center for Independent Living, has been coming to The Jar events since the beginning and says he is always blown away by how open people are.

“I brought a friend I’ve known over 20 years and she talked about her struggles with ADHD. I did not know that about her, but she felt comfortable enough to share that at The Jar.” He cites upward of 20 new active social connections he’s made through The Jar, including friends he comfortably confides in.

In a divisive era fragmented by tribalism and isolation, Ben-Aharon says The Jar is an invitation for people to step out of their bubble and expand their worldview. “It is like an adventure for people willing to go somewhere they’ve never been. The reality is that it’s in their backyard. You meet people you ride the train with but never talked to. We reintroduce ancient social norms of gathering. It’s the most basic human thing.”

“One of my friends says Bow Market’s the center of the universe,” said regular patron Sam Farnsworth on a recent Friday.

Somewhere between a small business incubator, a food court, and a European-style piazza, Bow Market stands as a bright spot in the Boston area’s brick-and-mortar landscape — a stark contrast to the struggling food halls and shopping malls dotting the region. But even in a region desperate for fresh retail and commercial real estate concepts, Bow Market remains just about as singular as it was when Baum and Boyes-Watson — two local thirty-somethings who run the market full time — pitched it a decade ago. That’s because all the things that make Bow the draw that it is, from its quirky use of real estate to its unique vendor mix, are also what can make it so challenging for homegrown projects like it to get all the “yeses” they need to come to life.

“There are people like us in every neighborhood and every downtown,” said Boyes-Watson. “All of these projects dance on a knife’s edge. All of them do. If you made it slightly easier, you might trip someone over into saying, ‘I’m doing this,’ versus not doing it.”

In the years since the pair founded Bow, construction costs have gotten pricier, and the financing environment is tougher. But the Bow Market founders said the far more crucial and elusive ingredient is flexibility from city hall on jumping through the legion of regulatory hoops.

“Something like this does need a champion in the local government, I think, to get it done,” said George Proakis, Somerville’s former planning chief and now the city manager of Watertown. “It’s not the thing your average zoning officer has seen.”

Proakis worked with Baum and Boyes-Watson to jigsaw the project into being, while still ensuring it wouldn’t be “locked in amber,” Baum said, and that it could evolve over time.

But that sort of municipal patience for projects that aren’t one-size-fits-all can be fleeting, the pair said.

In 2023, Bow said it would expand by about 6,000 square feet, spilling out onto Somerville Avenue. By the time it announced the expansion, Somerville had revamped its zoning code, and both Proakis and former Somerville mayor Joseph Curtatone, another supporter of Bow, had left City Hall. Baum and Boyes-Watson got the expansion done, but the whole process felt more complicated than just a few years earlier, they said, in a way that they believe would be all but impenetrable for others aspiring to create similar projects without the deepest of pockets.

“I think if we tried to do it today,” said Boyes-Watson of Bow, “we would have a way harder time.”

Part of the goal of Bow, its founders say, is for the markets’ triumphs to ripple outward to the local economy. Since opening in 2018, Bow has seeded the area with a bevy of its “alumni” who have graduated to their own standalone storefronts. But without the regulatory wiggle room granted to Bow’s owners, some of those businesses might never have opened in the market.

“I actually had absolutely no interest in opening a brick-and-mortar,” said Lauren Friel, the owner of Bow’s Rebel Rebel wine bar.

Vendors have been drawn to Bow by a few different factors: the relatively affordable rent (from about $1,300–$5,000 a month for most spaces); the manageable amount of inventory it takes to fill the storefronts (as small as 155 square feet); and the lease length (as short as a year, compared to five-year commitments common at other commercial spaces).

What ultimately sold Friel, however, was the fact that the market vendors were able to share a liquor license.

“There was just no other opportunity that existed anywhere in the city that didn’t require a half-a-million-dollar investment,” she said.

Three James Beard Awards nods and two new wine bars later, she still maintains she never would have become a proprietor had it not been for Bow, which she described as “a total unicorn situation.”

Those unicorns don’t always materialize. Boyes-Watson was also part of the team behind Starlight Square, a temporary pandemic-era space that opened in 2020 to host performances and small business markets on a municipal parking lot in Cambridge’s Central Square. Cambridge later awarded the team $500,000 in American Rescue Plan Act funding to go toward developing a permanent civic space modeled on Starlight.

“That would have been another Bow Market,” said Mark Boyes-Watson, Matthew’s father and the architect behind Bow and Starlight.

But asa 2024 city report recommended the Starlight site be developed into “a mixed-use building” — with housing, retail, a public plaza, and performance space — Cambridge reallocated Starlight’s funding to another arts-focused applicant. Starlight’s temporary structure soon shut down.

Later that year, the city put out a “request for information” seeking redevelopment ideas for the site. It got six responses, but progress has since been quiet.

“The City remains deeply committed to activating Central Square and making it a place the community gathers,” City of Cambridge spokesperson Jeremy Warnick said in an emailed statement.

A new project in Lowell is a testament to what can happen when all the stars align. After the owners of Mill No. 5, an eclectic indoor bazaar, announced in late 2024 that the market would close, some of the vendors banded together to find a new home.

“We didn’t know what it was called yet, we didn’t know where it was going to be, but we were very excited to do it on our own, because we knew we could manage it and we could make it happen,” said Jennifer Simone, who ran the artist collective Hive & Forge in Mill No. 5.

The business owners turned to the city, which offered funds and other support. In November, within a year of Mill No. 5’s closure, the newly formed Hive Public Market debuted in a 13,775-square-foot space on the ground floor of Lowell’s historic Hildreth Building. The market’s dozen or so shops — selling everything from video games to stationery to kitchenwares — are a mix of vendors from Mill No. 5 and new entrants.

“The owners are really the people that were making this happen,” said Thomas Golden, Lowell’s city manager. “We, the city, stood behind getting to ‘yes.’ ”

Back at Bow, many vendors, along with other observers, said the market’s special sauce is Baum and Boyes-Watson themselves.

“They’re a uniquely determined group of people, both to set this up and to continue to run it for all these years,” said Proakis.

Vendors said the pair are near-constant fixtures at Bow, as likely to work with entrepreneurs on a storefront expansion as they are to shovel snow in the courtyard.

“They really wanted, I think, to create a space that felt like a place that they wanted to be at,” said Brittany Lajoie, general manager at Remnant Brewing, the market’s anchor. “An owner, operator, developer who actually has a personal stake definitely feels different.”

The pair said people occasionally reach out looking for advice on developing similar concepts in other neighborhoods. More often, though, they’re approached by people who want them to helicopter into a new area and create Bow 2.0. It’s a request that, the pair must break to them, is futile.

“The folks that are going to be able to do this are the people that exist already in a community,” said Baum. “Don’t call us to come down to Dorchester and do it again. That doesn’t work. We don’t live there.”

From Carson Beach to Charles River Esplanade and Boston Common, people ditched puffer jackets for tank tops, shorts, and T-shirts to take advantage of the unseasonably warm weather.

Some were out biking, strolling, running, or reading a book under the sun; others sat around with friends or just by themselves.

“I am definitely enjoying the sunshine and the lack of clouds,” said Christina Fleisch, 26, who recently moved to Dorchester and sat near Carson Beach.

For many, the day truly felt like spring break after a long winter in which 61.5 inches of snow fell in Boston. Much of the snow has melted, but there are still piles and patches left on city streets.

“It’s very funny to be outside when it’s very warm, and there’s still snow on the ground,” said Kiran Hinze, a 30-year-old housing counselor at the Boston Common.

Nyx McDougle, 25, said the winter was really hard this year compared to the past couple years. McDougle said they wanted to come out to enjoy the first few strong rays of sun.

“Just wanted to get out, get my feet in the sand, get my skin exposed to the warm air,” McDougle said as they were lying down on a mat at Carson Beach.

They planned on spending the afternoon at the beach and brought a few books and a LEGO set.

For others, the sunshine was an excuse to slow down and spend time together.

Kerry Byrne, 39, who works for the City of Boston, sat near Carson Beach, with her parents, enjoying a lunch by the water while recovering from a broken leg.

“I’m almost two months into recovery, so [I] figured just to get down here and get some fresh air,” Byrne said as she planned on having chicken salad and tuna fish prepared by her mother for lunch.

Nearby, at the University of Massachusetts Boston campus, students also took advantage of the spring-like day between classes.

Liz Prochazka, a 21-year-old biology major, and her boyfriend, Ethan Rickard, a 20-year-old history major, walked hand-in-hand along the waterfront before classes.

“It’s very nice compared to the heavy snow and cold breeze, except for the giant mountains of dirty snow,” Prochazka said as she pointed out to a few lingering snow piles.

“Drove into school kind of late, but then we just went on a walk, because it’s just a nice day,” Rickard said.

Skie Manda, a 22-year-old graduate student, had been waiting for a sunny day to start training for the Boston Marathon.

“It was really hard for me to practice because it was really cold for the past couple of months,” Manda said. “This is my first run of the season. I’ve been doing pretty good so far.”

Downtown, workers stepped away from their offices for a quick dose of fresh air and sunshine at the Charles River Esplanade and the Boston Common.

Mike Lavin, 31, an auditor, spent his lunch break on the esplanade, which is just a 15-minute walk from his workplace. He usually comes down there around three times a week during the summer.

“The vitamin C feels so good, and guess that it’s definitely a mood booster,” Lavin said as he sat on a bench near the river. “I definitely feel a difference in my day when I’m able to get out here.”

Hinze walked through the Common during their lunch break. They planned to spend their entire break at the park and try to step on the grass if it isn’t very muddy.

“I’m very glad that we have the 70-degree weather,” they said. “I hope we have a few more days.”

Julia Klopfer, 27, a nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, met a friend for a five-mile run along the river on her day off. In the morning, she enjoyed the sun along with a cup of coffee on her front porch.

“It’s nice to feel the sun on my skin and just have a little bit of a respite from all the cold weather and watching all the snow melt,” Klopfer said as she waited for her friend near the river.

Northeastern students Perris Fisher, 24, and Elise Turner, 24, decided to have a picnic. They got coffee and EL Jefe’s and came to the Common.

“It was a beautiful girl’s day,” Turner said.

Some brought their pets outside to enjoy a rare warm day in March.

Jeff Neale, 37, came down to the esplanade with his mother’s cat, Jack Jack.

“This little guy’s been inside all winter and crying to get out,” Neale said, looking down at the fluffy grey cat he’s been looking after. “The dock here is not too much noise, so I figured [I’d] give it a try.”

At the Public Garden, Paul John, 38, played baseball with his five-year-old son, Harry, on his day off.

“He’s kind of been cooped in a little bit because of the storms and the weather, but we’re enjoying the weather and have some fun today,” said John, who works as an accountant. “Hopefully it holds up. I think we’re going to have a fantastic summer this year.”

While many embraced the warmth, most knew they could not be fooled by Mother Nature. Forecasts show colder temperatures returning next week. Still, for one day, Bostonians were happy to forget about winter.

“You better get it before it’s gone,” said David Byrne, 71, who was out having lunch with family near Carson Beach.

About a month ago, Wu also signed an executive order that prohibited federal immigration officials from detaining people on municipal property, proposed ways to protect protestors, and stated that law enforcement would investigate allegations of agents breaking local or state laws.

On Tuesday, more than a dozen leaders from community organizations stood next to Wu and other city officials, including City Council President Liz Breadon, Councilor Enrique J. Pepén, and Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune.

Louijeune, the daughter of Haitian immigrants and the first Haitian American elected to Boston municipal government, greeted the crowd in English, Spanish, Haitian Creole, Chinese, and Portuguese. The funding announced on Tuesday, Louijeune said, would be essential to protecting immigrant groups in Boston — particularly when communities are on high alert.

“Vigilance requires resources,” Louijeune said. “People’s livelihoods are at stake, people’s families are at stake, and we have to use the resources to the social capital that we have, to make sure that we are standing up for those who are most vulnerable.”

Louijeune specifically reference the case of Emmanuel Damas, a Haitian immigrant who was living in Boston when he was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year. In early March, he died in ICE custody at a hospital in Arizona, near the detention center where he had been held for months. He had a toothache which led to a deadly infection after being left untreated, his family said. The Department of Homeland Security has contended that Damas received adequate medical care.

Damas leaves behind several family members in Dorchester, including his 13-year-old son, the Globe reported. Louijeune extended condolences to Damas’s family, and said she had recently met with them.

“There is absolutely no reason why someone should be dying from a toothache,” Louijeune said. “This statement of us all standing together in solidarity, is showing that we stand with people like Emmanuel Damas and his family — and we stand up against the harms that are being created by this administration."

Groups who would be distributed some of the funding included the Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition, the Mattapan-based Immigrant Family Services Institute, the Chinese Progressive Association, and the Mabel Center for Immigrant Justice, which provides immigrants with pro bono legal representation.

And the Foundation would continue to do so, especially under the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies, Pelton said.

The federal government’s actions in places like Chicago, Los Angeles, Minneapolis, and Maine, Pelton said, have made it clear that this moment calls “for truth telling, for mutual aid, for courage, and for resolve.”

“Moments like this remind us of something critically important,” he said. “Boston has always been a city shaped by immigrants. When our immigrant neighbors are threatened or vulnerable, we do not stand aside. We step forward. They are us, and we are them.”

Andrew Collins, who is the identical twin brother of state Senator Nick Collins, spent years assembling the Dot Ave. parcels and pitching the concept of a life-science campus there. That vision stayed abstract; Andrew Collins never formally proposed a project to the city. Senator Collins has said he has no connection with his brother’s real estate business.

Now the Dot Ave. land, and its ownership, is at the heart of the legal imbroglio facing Andrew Collins and his various business entities that the Globe first reported last year. A dozen suits in state and federal court allege Collins owes investors a combined $149 million; Collins has denied wrongdoing.

Together, the Dot Ave. parcels set for auction have an assessed value of $20.4 million. Just who owns the property, however, depends on who you ask.

The foreclosure auction notice heralds the land as a “major Boston development opportunity” being sold at the behest of those that own its mortgage, a partnership connected to New York real estate firms J.T. Magen & Co. and Extell Development. The companies and their development adviser, The HYM Investment Group, previously told the Globe that Collins has no financial interest in the South Boston property.

Collins disputes this, maintaining that his stake in the LLCs that the city assessor lists as the property’s owner gives him a cut of whatever happens to the property.

“I know we’re used to rushing, but this is a mind game. So we want to slow down and think,” Shaheed said. “Don’t move off of impulse.”

It’s a message that extends far beyond the chess board.

Organizers of Boston’s new Chess for Peace program are using one of history’s oldest board games to teach kids important life skills, including strategic thinking and conflict resolution. Their goals are to reduce youth violence and address the negative impacts of technology.

The program offers free chess classes Sunday afternoons in the basement of the Madison Park High School gym in Roxbury. It’s affiliated with a Boston Public Schools initiative that also includes basketball, boxing, yoga, rugby, and more, an effort to support families and keep students engaged throughout the week.

The 6-WON-7 program, which has grown significantly over the past couple of years, is about to mark its 100th Sunday, said Cory McCarthy, director of student support at Boston Public Schools. School administrators launched the program partly in response to reports about unruly teenagers causing chaos at the South Bay shopping center and elsewhere on weekends, McCarthy said.

“School should feel like a community,” he said. “It’s the forgotten piece in the academic journey. It’s a safety issue. It’s violence prevention, it’s youth development, it’s all part of student wellness.”

While violent crime has decreased overall, youth violence remains a concern in Boston, largely concentrated among small groups of teenagers and sometimes fueled by gang affiliations. Social media often plays a role, experts say, with kids posting threats or bragging about crimes they’ve committed.

As technology shortens our attention spans, encourages rash decision-making, and limits in-person interactions, playing chess can be a robust kind of antidote, said Renee Callender, a retired Boston police detective who spearheaded the program.

“It’s more than just a game. It actually mirrors life,” she said. “In the game of chess, like life, every action comes with consequences.”

During more than three decades on the police force, Callender saw firsthand how cycles of violence start and end. She also founded a nonprofit called Promoting Conflict Resolution, Inc.

She said the idea for the program came from watching a youth chess tournament on TV; she was impressed by how poised and attentive the players looked. Maybe this could help kids in Boston stay out of trouble, she thought.

“It’s not only about how to play but how to lose,” she said. “How to gracefully lose. How to be humble.”

Indeed, it’s all fun and games until your king is in check.

Jacquami eventually lost to his opponent, 7-year-old Filip Rancic, who said his winning strategy involved steadily advancing his pieces toward the middle of the board.

“Sometimes he wins, sometimes he loses. So that’s good for him,” said Filip’s dad, Milan Rancic.

“They need to learn to be patient enough to develop a strategy, and obviously avoid a tantrum when they lose — pretty much everything we want our kids to learn,” he added.

During the class, three sets of players sat across from each other at classroom desks, with Shaheed monitoring their games and offering instruction. Sometimes the clink of plastic chess pieces was the only sound in the room.

“I think I got checkmate,” exclaimed Henry Lee, 10, bouncing excitedly in his chair.

Shaheed inspected the board and confirmed — checkmate, indeed.

“Good game,” Lee said, reaching out to shake hands with his opponent, 11-year-old Jesus Beltran.

“Can you believe you just lost to a 10-year-old?” he asked, grinning.

Beltran laughed, rolled his eyes, and started setting up the board again; he had won the previous match. In addition to chess, the boys play soccer together. They agreed their friendship can easily withstand some lighthearted competition.

A few turns into the next game, Lee made a move he instantly regretted.

“Can I have that turn back?” he asked Beltran, who smiled and shook his head no.

“So often, they’re focused on just one piece,” said Rhodes Pierre, another instructor with the program. “I tell them to examine the entire board.”

Pierre, who grew up in Mattapan, has experienced firsthand the impacts of violence. His older brother was shot and killed in 1994 near their childhood home, about two weeks after he inadvertently witnessed another daytime shooting nearby. The case was later linked to a neighborhood drug gang, according to news reports at the time.

Pierre said he started playing chess in college and quickly came to appreciate the life skills it teaches.

“Giving people another outlet to express themselves without having to revert to violence, that’s a good thing,” he said. “Making people sit down and think. It’s a better avenue than what we have right now.”

While sprinkling in the basics of chess strategy, Shaheed sends a similar message.

“It’s about seeing the moves behind the moves,” he told the class. “It takes paying attention, hearing your own self think. Most games are won or lost because of focus.”

It’s something he personally learned the hard way, Shaheed said.

Now 45, he spent much of his youth caught in a cycle of poverty, crime, incarceration, and mental illness. From foster care and psychiatric institutions to jails and prison, he ended up playing a lot of chess.

The game took on a central role in his life, an overarching metaphor that changed the way he approached decision-making, Shaheed said. Especially when he found himself in a hostile environment, he would think about the moves available to him and their potential consequences. That finally helped him leave the streets behind and forge a new path.

“The easy money, it wasn’t working. It was almost like a setup — nothing made sense anymore,” he said. “I needed a better move.”

He still plays chess regularly with various partners he’s befriended around Boston. He said he hopes younger generations will find some of the same benefits he’s experienced.

“Chess is a game of distress, tribulations, defeat, obstacles, resistance, competition, sorrow, and conquest,” Shaheed wrote in his recently published book, “Games Over: The Real Story About Chess and Life.”

“And that’s what life is all about — overcoming barriers and making progress.”

“I’m not saying I can change the world,” Price told the Globe in 2012. “But I’m planning to make a difference one child at a time.”

He also coached basketball, first as an assistant coach at Roxbury Community College and University of Massachusetts Boston, and later as a head coach at Brooke High School.

In March 2019, Price was settling into his new job at Cristo Rey Boston High School and getting ready to move into a new apartment in downtown Boston when he was killed on Greenwood Street, the street he grew up on in Dorchester.

He was 32.

No one has ever been charged with his killing.

His mother, Carol Price, remembers the last time she saw him.

It was Friday night, and she cooked him one of his favorite dishes for dinner: sauteed chicken with onions, green peppers, rice, broccoli, and cheese.

“That day, he came home, he said he was tired. ‘But it’s a good tired,’ he said,” she recalled.

Price told his mother he was going to stay in and take it easy that night.

“He said he was not going out at all,” she said.

But for some reason, after his mother went to sleep, he changed his mind and decided to stop by a garage at 12A Greenwood St., just down the street from his mother’s house. The garage was a known party spot,according to Globe reports at the time.

“It was a party, an after-hours type of thing,” she said.

That’s where he was when gunfire broke out shortly before 3 a.m.

Officers found his body riddled with gunshot wounds, according to police. A police report did not indicate that anyone else was wounded.

For a long time, Price kept thinking that if she had only been awake, she could have stopped him before he went out the door.

“I beat myself up for a long time,” she said.

She still wonders who was at the party when her son was shot.

After her son was killed, many people came to her to show their support while she was grieving, she said. But no one spoke about what actually transpired that night, leading her to assume that witnesses did not come forward and “no one told the police anything.”

When she spoke to investigators right after his death, she pleaded with them to find out what happened and arrest whoever was responsible for taking her son’s life.

“Please do not let this become a cold case,” she said. “I want justice for my son.”

Seven years later, she is still waiting.

“I’d love for someone who knows something to please come forward,” she said. “This perpetrator has probably killed other people since. He needs to be held accountable.”

Carol Price doesn’t like using the word “anniversary” to describe the date of her son’s death. For her, March 2 is a “trauma-versary,” a day she relives the pain and anguish she felt when she learned she had lost her son.

Price had so many opportunities ahead of him and should have had a bright future, she said.

She recalled how busy he always was with school, sports, and other extracurricular activities. And that’s exactly what she wanted: for him to pursue his interests and stay out of trouble.

“I always thought, I don’t ever want the streets to get my son,” she said. “And unfortunately he went to a party, and that’s what happened.”

Carol Price still lives on the same street where her son was murdered and has to pass by the garage where he spent his last moments.

She can’t help but wonder what could have been.

“Kendric came back to Boston,” she said. “He chose to come back and help those who were left behind.”

So she tries to turn her pain into something productive, by giving back to the community like Price did.

She continues to run Big Business Network because it helps people and “reminds me of him,” she said.

Boston police say they continue to investigate Price’s murder.

“It’s an open and active investigation,” said John Boyle, a spokesperson for the Boston Police Department. “We urge anyone to come forward with information, no matter how little they think it is.”

He and his wife regularly send money to relatives so they can afford food, something he says many Cuban families abroad must do.

“We feel so sorry for them, and we cannot do anything for them other than help them out,” said Tarano, a retired financial officer.

The United States volatile relationship with Cuba dates to 1959, when Fidel Castro overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist state. That prompted a long-standing US trade embargo and triggered a massive exodus of Cubans.

Multiple US presidents have tried and failed to topple the regime. But many believe Cuba is facing one of its most vulnerable moments as the Trump administration pursues an aggressive posture in Latin America.

Alejandro de la Fuente, chair of the Cuba Studies Program at Harvard University, said the country imports more than half of the oil it needs to generate electricity, and disruptions in supply are causing the widespread blackouts and transportation breakdowns.

“This has a direct impact on ordinary people and on their daily lives,” de la Fuente, an educator who came to the United States from Cuba in 1992, said about the embargo and the pressure the government is facing from the United States.

He warned that the crisis could prompt a new wave of Cubans to flee. Punitive economic policies could ultimately create challenges for the United States by increasing migration flows.

Boston College student Armando Gonzalez, 20, grew up in Miami in its predominantly Cuban community. Gonzalez said that family friends who had visited Miami from Cuba told stories about food insecurity and the toll of rolling blackouts. While he sympathizes with those suffering, he believes the situation reflects the failure of the Cuban government and the need for political change.

“What the [United States] is doing is hard, but I think it’s needed,” said Gonzalez, treasurer for the Cuban American Student Association at BC. “The regime has to fall and fully be crushed.”

His father was born in Cuba and fled from the country in 1978. He and his family have chosen not to travel to Cuba because they believe tourism spending ultimately benefits the government rather than everyday people.

“We agreed never to support that,” he said. “We’d only agree to go to Cuba once the regime has fallen.”

For older members of the Cuban diaspora, the crisis is part of a much longer saga that began with the Cuban Revolution.

Miriam Gorriaran, a 78-year-old retired professor living in West Roxbury, left Cuba as a child in 1961 as part of a program that brought thousands of Cuban children to the United States when families feared government control over their children’s futures. She challenged the idea that international sanctions alone explain Cuba’s economic collapse, arguing that internal policies and government decisions have had a greater impact.

“The people [who] are in power don’t lack any goods,” she said. “The Cuban government is the one that has restricted the people from getting what they need.”

Gorriaran emphasized that Cubans in the United States have played a major role in keeping families on the island alive through money and supplies sent from abroad.

Alberto Calvo, a 79-year-old Newton resident, and his wife have been helping out relatives in Cuba. He said everything there is rationed, and now with the electricity and oil crisis, the situation is only worsening.

“It’s very dire,” Calvo said, a retired engineer and member of the Cuban Cultural Center in Boston, referring to the current situation. “People are struggling. It’s not getting better; it’s getting worse by the day.”

Calvo, who came to the United States in 1962, recalled experiencing shortages during his time in Cuba. But he blames the economic collapse on the failures of the Cuban system, rather than external pressure. The people, he said, have a “fear of retribution” if they speak up.

“People cannot protest because repression is there,” he said. “Not by the police but even by Cubans [who] are in favor of the government.”

De la Fuente said that beyond political outcomes, one of the most overlooked consequences of the economic pressure may be the growing inequality within Cuban society.

“A situation like this has fairly negative impact over all of Cuba, and Cubans,” he said. “The impact tends to hit disproportionately those who are at the bottom of the ladder.”

He said this crisis magnifies social differences in Cuba and generates an even greater “social polarization.”

Tarano, the Southborough resident, said he is uncertain what would happen if the government falls. He believes any future regime must ultimately come from within Cuba rather than imposed from outside.

“Cubans like Cuba for Cubans,” he said.

But, as we all keep hearing, freedom isn’t free. Just how not-free has been difficult to pin down so far. There have been higher estimates, but most experts seem to agree that, in addition to the loss of seven US service members, we’ve been burning through at least $1 billion a day since we joined Israel to attack Iran on February 28. Pentagon officials told Congress on Tuesday that the first six days alone cost $11.3 billion. Wheeeeeeee!

It can be hard for anyone not named Musk or Bezos to understand numbers that big.

Here, Richard Kogan, a budget expert at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, was helpful. According to his math, a billion a day is more than the federal government spends on all State Department, embassy, and foreign aid programs. He said it’s about what we spend on programs for NASA, scientific research, natural resources, environment, agriculture, commerce, and transportation infrastructure put together. A billion a day is more than double what we spend on all federal education and job training programs, including Pell grants and federal K-12 school aid to states. It is twice our daily spend on all VA hospitals and health care for veterans.

For perspective closer to home: The city of Boston’s entire operating budget was $4.6 billion for 2025. A few days’ worth of Iran spending could cover it.

It costs $60 million per year to run the Codman Square community health center, which serves 23,000 patients each year, and $33.6 million to operate the Food Bank of Western Massachusetts. You could fund them both for 10 years with what we’re spending in a day to level Iran. One billion dollars could buy school lunches for 1.8 million American children for a year.

Poof go the billions. Down come the bombs. Up come the body counts.

Congressman Jim McGovern has been working these numbers, too, and he hates them.

“What the [expletive] is wrong with us,” he said. “It’s just all screwed up.”

The Worcester Democrat has devoted his career to making sure hungry people get fed in the richest country on the planet. Year after year, he pushes for more funding for food stamps, school lunches, and food pantries, and year after year, Congress refuses to do enough. So it’s especially galling for him to see money that could be feeding American children being used to kill Iranian ones.

Reached between stops delivering Meals on Wheels to seniors in Millbury on Wednesday morning, McGovern rattled off the figures: The United States has already spent in Iran more money than the federal government spends on our 1,500 community health centers, more than it spends on Head Start programs for preschoolers each year, and three times what it spends on fuel assistance for low income households annually. McGovern said we have already spent enough in Iran to fund the entire Meals on Wheels program for a decade.

“We spend pennies on everything else, yet when it comes to war, there’s no limit,” he said. “How is this America First?”

The congressman points out that everybody was all “America First” when it came to slashing global food aid and lifesaving USAID health programs designed to uplift poor people around the world. Now, however, “We hear not a peep,” he said.
