What’s more, the price was right. Tuition was thousands less than top-flight private schools — and Given was known to offer steep discounts to families of more modest means.

What Given had created seemed almost too good to be true: A private school without exorbitant costs or moral compromises. And somehow he had managed to do it for a fraction of the price of his competitors.

Families flocked to the school. Given opened in 2018 with 20 kindergartners in Providence. Nownearly 600 students ranging from preschool to middle school are enrolled in Boston and Providence.

Demand was so high by late last year, the school was hiring for a dozen new positions and looking to open a new school in Cambridge and expand in the South End. Details about how Croft would afford the growth were scant, but Given assured parents in a September email that the school’s “financial performance” was “strong.”

Just over five months later, Croft’s board dropped a bombshell.

It was not.

Given had mismanaged the school’s budget for years, keeping two sets of books, and hiding $13 million in debt, the board said. He allegedly forged a $500,000 letter of credit, meant to be a security deposit for a South End lease. And with so much debt, Given sold bonds to parents, promising they could invest in their children’s school while also earning a virtually guaranteed investment return. Then, according to one lawsuit, Given sold a second set of bonds to cover payments from the first — the very definition of a Ponzi scheme.

Croft’s board members say they didn’t know anything was amiss until Given alerted them in early March, after the school’s bank detected a forged document and called the police.

Boston police have said they are investigating. The school’s four-member board, which did not respond to a Boston Globe interview request, suspended Given and has suggested federal and state investigations are underway. Along the way, The Croft School was effectively left broke, facing closure in a matter of weeks.

Given, 45, hasn’t been charged with a crime and, in a statement released last month through his lawyers, said he’s cooperating with the school’s investigation. Given, who did not respond to an interview request, “has never used any school funds for his own personal benefit,” the statement said. When a reporter knocked on his door Tuesday, no one answered.

Many parents remain devoutly loyal to Croft and its teachers, and leapt into a fund-raising campaign to keep the Boston schools open. But parents — in conversations and text chats, over coffee, and waiting to pick up their kids from school — have also been grappling with another topic.

Why would Given risk it all? His reputation, the schools he built, the futures of hundreds of students.

Allison Cox, whose 8-year-old son attends Croft, said Given clearly believed in the school’s mission, but somehow got in over his head.

“Scott conflated hope with facts. I feel like he really believed that it would work,” Cox said. “I think it was hubris.”

Given, a graduate of Dartmouth College and a Harvard Business School alum, was already a prominent education entrepreneur when he was in his thirties.

The nonprofit he started in 2010, UP Education Network, took over failing schools in Boston and Lawrence. It raised millions of dollars from prominent Boston foundations and philanthropists.

In some cases, the organization pulled off remarkable turnarounds. Josh Angrist, an MIT economist and Nobel laureate who studies public education, said his research showed that UP’s first school, which replaced the Gavin middle school in South Boston, was “outstanding.” In its first year, UP nearly doubled the percentage of students who demonstrated math proficiency on the state’s annual test.

Given’s reputation grew beyond education circles. The Dartmouth Class of 2002 honored him with an award for distinguished alumni. Given told the alumni newsletter at the time that he planned to quadruple the size of his UP Education Network, growing it to 20 schools by 2020.

He acknowledged the challenge of running turnaround schools inside big, bureaucratic school districts. “It can be brutally difficult and this requires thick skin and a relentless work ethic,” Given said.

Ultimately, he did not quadruple UP, and some of the schools’ methods were controversial. Like many charter schools of the 2010s, UP’s schools were strict about discipline. Given resigned in 2016 after a WBUR report showed that one of his success stories in Dorchester had issued 68 suspensions to kindergartners, more than any other Massachusetts school.

That controversy may not have been all that pushed Given out. People who know him say he seemed burned out after more than a decade working in public education.

He also became a father and has said he launched Croft, in part, because he wanted to create a school where he would like to send his own children. After opening the Providence school in 2018, he founded the Jamaica Plain location close to his family’s current home in Wellesley, and enrolled his children there.

He named it in honor of Harold Croft, a respected teacher and track coach in Reading.

Croft was going to be different than UP. Instead of a nonprofit aimed at turning around failing schools, this new institution would be a for-profit company, and its financials would remain largely private.

Given told parents and employees the enterprise was backed by private funders who believed in the mission — as well as what he described as sizable, low-interest loans from himself and his father.

Rebecca Ullman, a parent of two Croft students, said Given was a constant presence at the Jamaica Plain location.

“Scott was very present in the life of the Croft school,” Ullman said. “He was an engaged school leader, absolutely.”

At the beginning, Croft’s annual tuition was $18,000 a year, lower than the cost of some day-care centers. Financial aid made it even more affordable for many families.

But Croft also managed to provide offerings that a large, sprawling school district like Boston simply could not match.

One section on Croft’s website, titled “Convenience,” reads like a wishlist for work-weary parents: Hourlong drop off windows, extended day programs, and child care on holidays. At the Jamaica Plain location, there was also a “family cafe” with free Wi-Fi, coffee, tea, and snacks.

The website said Croft strove to be “the most-parent centric school in the world.”

Edith Bazile, chairperson of the Boston Special Education Parent Advisory Council, said schools outside the traditional public system can promise the kind of personalized engagement many parents seek.

“It’s the seductive pull of a school that says, ‘I’m going to give you a different experience, I’m going to celebrate you by not just educating your student in a certain way, I’m going to address your needs as family,’ “ Bazile said. “They market family and community engagement.”

For loyal Boston Public Schools parents like Jennie McDonald-Brown, Croft’s resources were just too appealing to pass up. She was heavily involved with Boston schools before moving her son, now in the fourth grade, to Croft two years ago.

“Most of my dear friends are BPS school leaders and educators, and some of the most talented, passionate educators I’ve ever met still. And so this was a really, really difficult decision for us,” she said. “And I think what it boils down to is, my son was in a class with 26 kids, and at Croft, he was in a class of 13.”

Many Croft parents had once been committed to keeping their children in public schools. But for one reason or another, they’d decided to change course. Some found it difficult to develop relationships with their children’s public school teachers, who generally managed much bigger classes than teachers at Croft.

Josiane Martinez, whose 8-year-old son attends Croft, is married to another woman of color. Martinez said other members of the LGBTQ community sent their children to Croft because the school cultivated a nurturing environment.

“I felt comfortable sending my son there, knowing that he was going to be embraced for everything that he is,” Martinez said, “and he’s been thriving.”

The school advertised an ethos aligned with many parents’ worldview. It was committed to inclusion and billed itself as reflecting the diversity of its community. The school said that 39 percent of its students were nonwhite, although that is a lower share than almost all of Boston’s public elementary schools.

Maria Fernandes, whose son is enrolled in Croft’s third grade, said the school’s staff work with his learning style.

“I knew Black educators who are sending their kids here [and] that for me was a gold stamp, and I said, ‘That’s where I want to send my kid,’” Fernandes recalled.

In time, some parents began to wonder how Croft could afford to be so generous.

Although tuition eventually climbed to $35,000, that is still some $14,000 less than the Park School in Brookline. Croft also charges qualifying families less, including discounts for siblings.

“I don’t see how that translates into an extractive, profit making model,” said Eileen Connor, a Croft parent who runs the Project on Predatory Student Lending, which represents student borrowers at for-profit schools. “It would be a miracle if it broke even.”

In the summer of 2024, Given emailed Croft parents with an unusual pitch. He wanted parents to put up a million dollars to fund improvements, characterizing it as a supplement to the school’s traditional financing. Given offered to sell bonds with a 12.5 percent annual return and virtually zero risk.

In his email, Given told families a $100,000, four-year loan would be repaid along with $50,000 in interest.

The bonds were a “‘win-win’ for Croft and for our families,” he wrote.

Paul Crockett responded to the offer, according to court records. “[C]an you pencil me in for $100k?” he wrote to Given. Crockett would eventually invest $160,000 in the bonds, according to a lawsuit he filed last month.

Then, beginning late last year, Given made a series of financial maneuvers that would lead to his downfall.

In late October, Given began selling a second round of “Croft Bonds” to parents. Two months later, as the school’s debts mounted, Given forged the $500,000 bank letter of credit, according to Croft’s board — using Leader Bank letterhead to make it appear legitimate.

The day after Christmas, he made another move to raise cash fast. He moved up the deadline for the next year’s tuition payments, forcing parents to cough up thousands of dollars five weeks ahead of schedule.

Despite the infusion of cash, the cracks soon began to show.

In January, Given notified families that Croft would abandon its plan to expand into Cambridge. The next month, he attempted to back out of the lease for Croft’s new South End building, according to a lawsuit filed by the landlord.

The landlord, Washington Associates, tried to cash in the allegedly forged letter of credit Given had offered as a security deposit. According to the landlord’s lawsuit, Leader Bank discovered the forgery, and called the Boston Police Department.

In early March, Given confessed to a member of Croft’s board that he had forged the letter of credit and concealed the true amount of the school’s debt, according to statements issued by the board. The board has not answered questions about its oversight, leaving parents to wonder how it could all go wrong.

“How does one person manage to keep two sets of books and get this far down what appears to be a fraud without anyone raising an alarm?” said Croft parent Matt Donohue.

In the end, many families remain baffled that Given would put the school’s survival and so much else at risk.

Croft’s immediate future remains uncertain.

Parents at Croft’s Jamaica Plain location said they have raised enough money — more than a million dollars — to keep their school running through June. In the South End, parents were confident they’d reach a similar fund-raising goal.

Providence parents have raised enough to stay open through April and were optimistic they would find the money to stay afloat until summer.

But those are all short-term fixes. Keeping the school running permanently will be the next challenge. The parents’ groups that organized the fund-raising say they will be exploring options like turning Croft into a nonprofit.

Cox, like many parents, has been left with the challenge of explaining the crisis to her children. She settled on a simple lesson of right and wrong.

Don’t lie to solve a problem, Cox told her 8-year-old son.

“You have to ask for help instead,” Cox explained to him. “That’s what Scott didn’t do.”

Christopher Huffaker and Steph Machado of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

No, I don’t have celiac disease (I was tested already), so it’s just a sensitivity. But it’s one that makes you feel tired, bloated, and a little sick after eating gluten. It affects everything: My face was puffy when I ate gluten, brain fog and migraines made concentrating difficult, and my tummy would hurt for days.

I tried eliminating everything else first, in denial that it would ever be my favorite foods that made me feel this way. Was it the dairy? The sugar? No, it was the gluten.

In theory, keeping gluten out of my diet might sound manageable. Just a little lifestyle tweak, right? A minor inconvenience? In practice, it’s a full-time mental exercise.

Every meal now begins with reconnaissance. I scan menus differently, looking for clues: Could there be hidden flour in that sauce or gravy, breadcrumbs in a meatball, soy sauce in a marinade? I’ve learned that gluten is less an ingredient and more a lifestyle choice that the food industry made on my behalf long ago. It’s everywhere. It’s sneaky. It’s rich and decadent. It is, frankly, a little rude.

Dining out, which used to be the easiest and absolutely most fun part of my job, has become a series of negotiations.

“Is this fried? Do you use a shared fryer?”

“Do you have gluten-free pasta?”

“Can you not bread the eggplant?”

“Do you have Tamari for my sushi?”

There’s a moment that I feel like every gluten-free person knows when the waiter has to go “check with the kitchen.” That’s when you realize dinner just got complicated.

Oftentimes, I find myself staring into the depths of the bread basket on the table, watching others frost their slices with copious amounts of butter. At many places, I desperately ask the server the question – “what here is gluten free?” – and I get a finger over the menu, circling around the salads. Great, I’m a rabbit for the day.

There is also the humiliation of realizing how much of your personality was built on bread. I make my own pasta at home, and even bought a shirt that says “HOT GIRLS EAT BREAD.” I’m an adventurous eater, who will try anything and everything once, who never met a carb she didn’t like, and who believed the best way to get to know a place was to eat your way through it, and speak to the staff who run their eating establishments.

Now, I am the person asking if the tortilla chips are truly gluten free, or just in spirit.

By no means am I perfect with this new diet. Will I happily suffer after eating my favorite cacio e pepe at Oberlin, the roni island pizza (pepperoni, cherry peppers, and hot honey) from Pizza Marvin, bahn mi from Asian Bakery, a stack of pancakes from a diner, mole, dumplings around Boston’s Chinatown? Yes, yes I will.

But I’ve found some great spots that cater to these new needs: Verveine Cafe & Bakery in Cambridge is an entirely gluten-free bakery, and their bread and ube brownies make me feel like I’m not missing out on anything. Nicks on Broadway in Providence has gluten-free crostini and biscuits that taste just as good as his “real” ones (no, really, they do). Eataly, thankfully, has the best selection of gluten-free pastas I can find to make at home. And I’ve been gravitating a lot toward Vietnamese food, much of which is naturally gluten free. Le Madeline in Quincy and Gao in Dorchester have been seeing a lot more of me. I’m ordering poke bowls, crudo, and sushi, my true comfort food, more than ever.

But it’s different now.

I obviously still love going out, and trying new food. But these days, before I take a bite, I find myself doing something I never used to do. I have to hesitate.

In “Deer prudence” (March 26) the Globe’s editorial board argues that liberalizing hunting laws, and in particular authorizing Sunday hunting, is necessary to help control Massachusetts’ deer population. This is a plausible story, but with nearly 35 years’ experience engaging with communities on suburban deer issues, I think it’s probably wrong.

Massachusetts’ deer population has been growing steadily for the past 60 years. Also growing steeply have been the deer populations in most Northeastern and mid-Atlantic states and in suburbs clustered around cities in the South and Midwest. As the Globe notes, all of them have Sunday hunting and more liberal hunting rules. It hasn’t helped there, and it won’t help here.

Loosening hunting laws will improve recreational opportunities for the hunting 1 percent but will do nothing to ease public concerns surrounding deer. The Commonwealth should instead empower towns and cities to apply alternative deer population control and mitigation solutions to the problems associated with deer in their backyards.

The tedious legal battles to halt decades-overdue renovations reveal a profound lack of perspective on what a public-private partnership of this scale actually requires.

Polls have shown greater public support for the city’s plan than opposition. Advocates are right to push for cost accountability and community input, but the conservancy has drifted far from its own mission, steered by out-of-touch board members who don’t live near the park and a president with shallow roots in Boston.

It’s high time the conservancy abandon its protracted legal battle, wasting both its own money and that of taxpayers. The group is standing in the way of Boston’s students, a well-supported mayoral administration, and long-overdue progress for one of the city’s most neglected public spaces.

Denying a fund-raiser permit may be petty. Denying a generation of Boston’s students a stadium they deserve is shameful.

“What’s great here is to see people who can give a legitimate voice of what [Black] culture is like,” said Davis, who owns a comic bookstore in Harvard Square.

More than 200 people attended this year’s festival, which featured several dozen Black artists who set up booths, spoke on panels, and advocated for an art form that has not always incorporated diversity into its milleu.

“The whole goal and premise of Comics in Color is to provide a space for people of color ... to tell their own stories in their own voice, so that their identities, their stories, and their experiences are represented,” said Marisa Luse, an organizer of the event.

According to Luse, Black representation in comic books and superhero tropes experienced a surge when Marvel released the first “Black Panther” movie in 2018, leading many people of color to embrace the art form for the first time.

“There’s definitely been people of color trying to get their stories out ... but it’s no longer a secret, right?” she said. “It’s not underground.”

Omari Malik, a 29-year-old artist from Brooklyn, N.Y., who owns a comic book publishing company, said he originally couldn’t envision a career for himself in the industry.

“A lot of Black people naturally gravitate to entertainment or even sports, because it’s a place where we can see ourselves easily,” he said. “I was seeking, wanting to find people like myself.”

Eventually, Malik discovered artists like David F. Walker, who helped create the DC Comic character Naomi McDuffie, a Black teenage superhero who becomes friends with Superman.

Malik said he could see “myself in those guys,” adding that it was “inspirational and let me know it was really possible.”

The original version of Black Panther, the superhero hailing from the mythical African nation of Wakanda, debuted in 1966 and was created by Marvel creative leader Stan Lee and artist Jack Kirby, according to the Smithsonian Institution.

Though it was groundbreaking at the time to have a Black superhero enter a pantheon typically reserved for white, transatlantic-sounding characters, Davis said the creators, who are both white, ultimately failed to accurately portray the hero as authentically Black.

“[They were] trying to have somebody write Black vernacular who had never spoken Black vernacular and didn’t know it,” said Davis.

Since then, major superhero companies like Marvel and DC have made strides in hiring Black artists to create Black characters.

In 1993, for example, DC signed a partnership with Milestone Media, a group of four Black artists who created new Black superheroes with progressive storylines.

For Davis, who grew up in Los Angeles, the first representative comic book he read was called “Love and Rockets,” a fictional series about punk rockers from Southern California.

“It was the first time you really saw a reflection of the non-white Los Angeles in a comic book,” Davis said. “I felt like I could know some of the people in this, or I’ve listened to some of the music that’s in the background of these stories.”

For younger artists, such as 24-year-old Zac Scandura, a Boston University student, diversity has always been par-for-the-course in comic book writing.

“Comics have always been about community,” he said. “There’s plenty of events like this everywhere in Boston.”

Scandura is part of a BU visual narrative program where students workshop their comic strips with professors and industry professionals.

The program is run by Joel Christian Gill, a leading Black artist in comics who in 2014 published “Strange Fruit,” a comic book about untold stories of African American history.

In a description of his 2023 BU College of Fine Arts exhibition, Gill wrote: “Comics have never been just for kids. Comics have never been only about superheroes.”

“Comics are a vessel for expression,” he continued.

In Roxbury on Saturday, Luce, the event organizer, said her 12-year-old son Coleman started making comics during the pandemic and has since finished six books.

“He’s got his latest book out there now, and so I just see the power in it and how enthusiastic people are,” she said. “That, to me, is inspiring.”

Prosecutors are asking US District Court Chief Judge John J. “Jack” McConnell Jr. to sentence O’Brien to four years and eight months in prison, the maximum allowed by the plea deal. But O’Brien’s defense attorney, Todd A. Spodek, is asking the judge to give O’Brien just three years behind bars.

According to federal authorities and defense attorneys, “traveling conmen fraud” cases reflect an increasingly familiar scheme also seen in New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania.

In a sentencing memorandum, interim US Attorney Charles C. Calenda’s office said O’Brien told his parents he was moving his young family to the United States in the summer of 2021 to “seek out better financial opportunities.”

“But from the very beginning,” Assistant US Attorney Taylor A. Dean wrote, “his version of the ‘American dream’ relied on deceit and exploitation.”

O’Brien entered the United States under a tourist visa that authorized him to remain in the country until Oct. 19, 2021. But he overstayed that visa and “engaged in a complex scheme of deceit” over the next 3½ years, according to the sentencing memorandum.

Prosecutors said O’Brien used a “charming demeanor” to convince homeowners to drain their savings and retirement accounts to pay for unnecessary home repairs. He often approached victims outside their homes, claiming he had noticed some small repairs he could fix, but those minor fixes quickly mushroomed into major projects, prosecutors said.

Many victims reported that O’Brien used “scare tactics” to convince them to pay larger and larger sums. He warned victims that their homes would collapse if they didn’t act fast, and in some cases, he and his crew caused the damage he offered to fix, prosecutors wrote.

O’Brien admitted to defrauding at least 80 homeowners in Rhode Island and Massachusetts between July 2021 and March 2025. But prosecutors estimate that number is “significantly greater,” and they submitted a list of more than 110 victim names to probation officials.

O’Brien used the proceeds to “feed a lavish lifestyle filled with luxury vehicles, expensive vacations, pricey beauty treatments, and an extravagant monthly entertainment budget, the likes of which most Americans can only dream,” prosecutors wrote.

O’Brien not only harmed homeowners, he also “engaged in labor exploitation,” using day laborers who often did not speak English and who were reluctant to complain about his supervision, according to prosecutors. One victim reported that O’Brien’s laborers did not wear respirators while performing work in her basement, and one laborer said he had not been paid in three weeks.

As the fraud grew, O’Brien used a check-cashing company in Dorchester, Mass., to cash victims’ checks rather than deposit them into his bank account. He then used that cash to buy Rolex watches from known money-launderers to conceal the proceeds, prosecutors said.

“He is a man who knew what he was doing,” prosecutors wrote, “a man who had contacts around the world who could help him pull off the fraud and who had a network of like-minded colleagues who were similarly engaged in this type of scheme across the United States.”

Prosecutors described O’Brien as “an organizer or leader of criminal activity involving five or more participants,” saying he directed multiple money launderers to assist him with his crime and used other suspected members of the “Traveling Conmen Fraud Group” to defraud his victims.

The FBI said groups of Irish or United Kingdom nationals have been entering the United States illegally or overstaying tourist visas, soliciting construction work, and overcharging homeowners. They go door-to-door, introducing themselves to homeowners — who are often elderly individuals — claiming to notice damage that needs to be repaired immediately.

In addition to 56 months in prison, prosecutors asked the judge to order O’Brien to forfeit $5,565 in cash, plus property described as Rose Cottage in Telford, England, and to make restitution to victims.

But the defense asked the judge for a sentence of 36 months, challenging the prosecution’s sentencing guideline calculations.

For example, the defense challenged the calculation of how much victims lost. “Regardless of O’Brien’s fraud, the fact remains that there were real crews performing real construction and providing measurable value to homeowners,” the defense attorney wrote.

Also, supporters submitted letters offering a starkly different portrayal of O’Brien.

“My son is not a criminal,” wrote his father, John O’Brien Sr. “John is the type of man who goes to church every Sunday, who hugs and kisses his kids goodnight, who tells his wife and kids he loves them before he goes to work every morning, a man who goes above and beyond to help complete strangers in [their] hour of need.”

O’Brien is married and has three children, ages 7, 4, and 2, according to court documents.

His father said O’Brien grew up in a part of Ireland that had “gangs of youths always looking for young lads to bully into the drugs dealing and dangerous life-threatening situations.” But he said he kept his son away from that life.

His brother, Thomas O’Brien, wrote that, “Putting him in prison is like putting a goldfish in a shark tank.”

His aunt, Margaret Ann O’Brien, wrote that he collected money in a bucket in Dublin to help her raise funds for homeless people in Ireland and Ethiopia. “I am sure he will get back to this selfless work after this bridge is crossed,” she wrote.

The Rev. Stephen Monaghan wrote to the court, saying, “I have only ever known John to be a very reliable and very hard-working man. While he may have acted outside the rules and regulations of his visa, I have only ever known him to be a decent young man.”

Senator Eileen Flynn, a memberof the upper house of the Irish Parliament, described O’Brien as “a man whose kindness and strength of character have been evident throughout his life.”

“John went to America with the best of intentions and to create a new life for himself,” Flynn wrote. “Given the current circumstances, it would be best, if possible, to have John O’Brien back in Ireland for the support of his community and for the benefit of his young family.”

Can I share a secret?

When I was younger, I wanted to be someone who was behind a microphone or in front of a camera. I dreamed of hosting my own TV or radio show.

But then, reality set in. ​The people I saw on TV were nothing like me. As a tomboy from Dorchester, a total Dot Rat at heart, I didn’t see where I would ever fit in.

I didn’t look or sound like a news anchor. And I certainly didn’t want to dress like one.

So I set those ambitions aside and just concentrated on doing good journalism.

Over the years that I’ve worked at the Globe, I’ve always jumped at the chance to work on videos. Whenever I had an opportunity to be on camera, I gladly took it, and cherished every moment.

Such was the case last Tuesday, when I was asked to do a video about a story I was working on: a mansion in Beverly that had been robbed.

I happily agreed, and my colleague Raphael Chinca, one of the Globe’s Emmy Award-winning multimedia producers, set up a camera in the newsroom and filmed me talking about the robbery. The video was posted on social media, and by the next day, it had been viewed over a million times.

Comments — about my voice, and how I pronounced certain words, and how I was wearing an Adidas track jacket while delivering a serious news report — were pouring in. And they haven’t stopped.

I had no idea that my Boston accent and choice of fashion would spark so much discussion online. Honestly, I was shocked ... by both the sheer volume of comments, and how overwhelmingly positive they’ve been.

Lots of people commented that my voice reminded them of home. Others said my casual demeanor made it feel like they were listening to a friend telling them a story.

Many people messaged me privately, saying that they had given up on the news and no longer trusted mainstream media, but they felt like they could trust me.

I was so happy to hear that. It’s given me a lot of hope, and it’s making me realize that there could be a place for this Dot Rat after all.

I hope to continue to do more video reports for the Globe, and I hope you’ll join me by following our social media accounts.

Blue Hill Avenue has remained largely unchanged for the past 60 years, since the streetcar tracks that once ran down the center were removed. The roadway starts at Warren Street in Roxbury, bisects Dorchester and Mattapan, and is as wide as a highway, with four lanes of driving, two parking lanes, and an intermittent median strip. Double-parking, especially for businesses receiving deliveries, is an endemic problem with little enforcement.

City planners and designers have known for years that the most important upgrades for pedestrian and transit infrastructure just wouldn’t be feasible if buses remained reliant on curbside bus stops; there’s too much demand with double-parked cars, buses, pedestrians, cyclists, and businesses all vying for space — which is why the federal grant process has focused on the center-running approach.

Now, bolstered by federal money, it all boils down to those center lanes. Mayor Michelle Wu can either push forward with those plans, helping unclog some of the most high-traffic bus lines in the city and unlocking tens of millions of dollars for other improvements; or keep the roadway largely as it is, pecking at its problems through small initiatives like fixing sidewalks, adding lighting, and resurfacing the street.

Facing those two options, this editorial board stands where it did in 2022: in support of center-running bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue. While this project will never reach unanimous community support, the center-running bus lanes maximize pedestrian safety, preserve the most amount of parking, and cut down the truly disastrous wait times for public transit during rush hour. Keeping Blue Hill Avenue largely unchanged would be its own form of failure; a crash requiring a Boston EMS ambulance happens every three days along the road, according to the city.

The most recent community feedback regarding the project was collected by the MBTA in 2024; while a sizable portion of community members strongly disagreed that the project would meet its goals, they were outnumbered by those who either somewhat or strongly agreed that the project would improve the roadway. The margins were slim, but those in agreement made up the majority.

In Denver, a former highway called Colfax Avenue is facing a dilemma similar to Blue Hill Avenue. Just like Blue Hill, Colfax Avenue is a major city thoroughfare hosting some of the highest-trafficked bus routes in the city. It suffers from clogged lanes, a lack of pedestrian infrastructure, and very little greenery. It also once hosted streetcar tracks and was left with little investment after they were torn out.

That 10-mile project began its buildout in 2024, giving Boston a model. The project in Denver includes small-business relief grants to offset the harms that ongoing construction can cause. With a new pot of cash, Boston should look into ways to support the small businesses that would face direct impacts during the most intensive construction phases.

Construction on the corridor will be a necessary disruption for meaningful change. Luckily, these impacts are something that smart city planning can mitigate. Understanding seasonal high times for businesses, factoring in Boston Public Schools transportation schedules, and even knowing the dates of special community events that provide bumps for local business can help mitigate the damaging impacts of construction.

There are other, local projects that provide a guide as well. The center bus lanes on nearby Columbus Avenue did drastically improve transit times for bus riders at a modest negative cost to drivers.

Any decision the city makes now is going to disappoint someone. Local City Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell, as well as other leaders, say the constituents they represent are against this plan. They believe their constituents deserve large-scale investment on their terms, and this project, like a previous attempt to rework the avenue under former governor Deval Patrick, is a mandate from outside the community.

But many residents do support it — the majority, if the T’s survey is to be believed. As the Dorchester Reporter has noted in its recent coverage, young people are largely in favor of improving this stretch. And while construction will strain the businesses that are the beating heart of this corridor, if they are supported, they will be able to benefit from an influx of investment, customers, and community growth brought by a safer main street.

Today’s Globe editorial urges Mayor Michelle Wu to go forward with the bus lanes, over the objections of some local lawmakers and businesses who worry about losing street parking:

“While this project will never reach unanimous community support, the center-running bus lanes maximize pedestrian safety, preserve the most amount of parking, and cut down the truly disastrous wait times for public transit during rush hour. Keeping Blue Hill Avenue largely unchanged would be its own form of failure; a crash requiring a Boston EMS ambulance happens every three days along the road, according to the city.”

If the city goes forward with the bus lanes, expect to hear complaints about Wu ignoring the neighborhood. Conversely, if the city pulls the plug, expect to hear complaints about Wu… ignoring the neighborhood.

So here’s an idea: hold a vote. Let the precincts Blue Hill Avenue bisects have a yes-or-no say on whether to accept the federal money for the bus lanes.

After all, if the question is, what does the neighborhood really want, then wouldn’t voting be the surest way to find out? Surveys and public meetings do not necessarily capture community sentiment reliably.

Neither does a vote, you say. And yes, turnout would likely be low.

But it would provide some needed resolution. And elected officials — almost all of whom owe their own positions to low-turnout municipal elections — would hardly be in any position to question the validity of the verdict.

There is some precedent for deferring questions to voters. In 2019, the city put a question on the ballot asking whether to rename Dudley Square as Nubian Square, then made the switch when majorities in that neighborhood backed the change.

Now, when I’ve written before in favor of referendums on transit projects, some readers felt it was a terrible suggestion to put engineering decisions to a popular vote.

I would agree if the question on the ballot were how to build a bus lane — experts should guide those details. But whether to build one is a public policy decision that seems legitimate for voters to decide.

There’s also an objection that in our interconnected road and transit system, nobody should be granted an absolute veto on what goes through their own backyard. Major roads and train lines have to go somewhere, but if every community could vote on individual projects within their borders, the result would be a smaller, poorer system for everyone. In this case, whatever happens on Blue Hill Avenue will affect people in Milton, people in other Boston neighborhoods, etc., so is it really fair to let just direct abutters have the last word?

Those are all interesting questions for political scientists to ponder. But in this case, voting wouldn’t just be a way to let residents have a say — it would be a way to at least reach a conclusive answer after so many years of dialogue that never have, and likely never will, yield a consensus.

It said Grier on the evening of Nov. 30, 2008, had encountered Barboza inside a Dorchester store, where the two exchanged words, leaving Grier “upset.”

The ruling didn’t detail what was said between the two.

The following day, the decision said, Grier and Barboza encountered each other again as Barboza exited a store on Washington Street.

Barboza and Grier walked toward a street corner, and when Barboza reached the corner, Grier shot him, causing the teen to fall to the ground, the ruling said.

Grier, the board said, “continued to fire” at Barboza, striking him once in the head and twice in his legs. Barboza was later pronounced dead at an area hospital.

The four board members who voted to free Grier were moved by his progress behind bars, according to the ruling.

“Mr. Grier presented with insight into the causative factors that led to his gang affiliation and offending behavior,” the ruling said.

It said he began “to invest in self development” before the 2024 court ruling made him eligible to seek release as a convicted killer.

“Mr. Grier also invested in education - earning his associates degree,” the board said, without naming the institution that conferred the degree.

He also “developed occupational skills” in an effort to prepare himself for reentry into society, the decision said.

“Mr. Grier also has a support system to assist him with his transition,” the ruling said.

It said the board heard testimony in support of parole from a social worker and from Grier’s relatives, as well as testimony opposing his release from Barboza’s family.

Once he’s out, Grier will have to abide by several conditions including maintaining a nightly curfew, submitting to electronic monitoring for six months, staying off drugs and booze, having no contact with Barboza’s family, and enrolling in “mental health counseling for adjustment,” the ruling said.

A cousin of Barboza’s, Deja Anye, had posted a tribute to Facebook to the slain teenager in 2014, writing that he was shot the day before his birthday.

“The next day was his 17th birthday, but instead of celebrating with his friends and family, he was lying in a hospital bed with a bullet in his head,” Anye wrote. “He was gone. Nobody told me, but I knew. I heard the late-night crying and talk of family deaths, I couldn’t believe it. The person I grew up with, shared laughs with, was gone... No goodbye, no nothing. Matter of fact, the last time I [saw] him I said, ‘Hey De’Andre!’ ... My aunt, De’Andre’s mom, is one of the strongest women I’ve ever met. She is my hero and her son is my family’s guardian angel. I will make them both proud.”

In the wake of a recent police shooting that resulted in a manslaughter charge against the officer involved, some Boston city councilors are dissatisfied with the department’s protocols governing the release of body camera footage in such cases.

Top police leaders didn’t attend a council hearing on the topic Tuesday afternoon, but the department’s legal adviser answered the council’s questions at length.

“The absence of Boston Police Department leadership raises a broader concern,” said Councilor Miniard Culpepper. “If we cannot have these conversations openly … with the people responsible for decision-making, then it becomes harder to build the very trust that body cameras were meant to strengthen.”

He called for a defined timeline and public-facing framework that would help standardize the process, among other changes.

The hearing came just three days after the latest deadly police shooting in Boston, which took place Saturday afternoon at an apartment building near Northeastern University’s campus. Police shot and killed a man experiencing a mental health crisis after he attacked first responders with a sword, officials said.

Last month, a Boston police officer fatally shot a carjacking suspect in Roxbury. Local prosecutors later charged the officer with manslaughter, saying his actions were unreasonable and unjustified.

In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, Councilors Culpepper and Brian Worrell called for the bodycam footage to be released. That hasn’t happened.

But Suffolk County prosecutors have repeatedly cited the footage, along with witness accounts, in support of the manslaughter charge against Officer Nicholas O’Malley. He’s charged in the death of Stephenson King, 39, who was shot March 11 while allegedly fleeing a traffic stop.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden has said his office isn’t releasing the video because it would “clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and the future prosecution of this most serious matter.” Prosecutors plan to present evidence to a grand jury as the case proceeds.

Dave Fredette, general counsel for the Boston Police Department, told councilors that state public records laws forbid release in this case, even though department policy gives the commissioner discretion under other circumstances. That’s partly because of the pending criminal charge and anticipated grand jury proceedings, Fredette said.

“Massachusetts statute will always trump a Boston police rule,” he said.

The council also recently adopted a resolution, without any specific recommendations, calling on the Police Department to update its policies governing bodycam footage release. Councilors reiterated that demand during the hearing.

Other cities across the country have established clear timelines, Worrell said. Oversight bodies, including Boston’s Office of Police Accountability and Transparency or OPAT, should also have faster access to the footage, he added.

OPAT Executive Director Evandro Carvalho, who also testified during the hearing, said the agency is closely monitoring the case. He previously said OPAT would suspend its review of the shooting until the district attorney’s prosecution is complete.

“If we’re going to rely on body cameras as a tool to build public trust, then the public needs to understand when footage will be released, who makes that decision, and what standards are being applied across the board,” said Councilor Erin Murphy.

Local officials have taken a different approach in the past, which councilors pointed out. After the 2015 fatal police shooting of Angelo West, a group of local clergy was allowed to view the footage while the shooting was still under investigation. In that case, West shot a police officer in the face before other officers opened fire, killing him.

But that situation differed from King’s death in that no officers were criminally charged, Fredette noted.

“Again, the public records request has to take a backseat to the criminal process,” he said.

Attorney Ben Crump, who’s representing the King family, said they’ll continue calling for more transparency.

“This family deserves the full truth, real accountability, and justice that is not delayed or denied,” he said in a statement Monday. “We will not stop fighting until they get it.”

YmaNini LaCourt wouldn’t know what she would do without her dog Mizzo, a small Chihuahua-mix with an adorable underbite.

But after losing her job during the pandemic, LaCourt has been working part time for less than $20 an hour, not nearly enough to cover her expenses, including food for a pet she describes as “part of me, part of my life, part of my world.”

LaCourt, 65, is among hundreds of pet owners increasingly turning to local pet food pantries to make ends meet. As the cost of living in the Boston area continues to climb, and with recent federal cuts to programs that help low-income Americans, including SNAP and Medicaid, more people would be forced to give up their furry family members without this kind of assistance, according to the food pantries.

“Pets are part of people’s families, and we’re really focused on keeping families together,” said Edward Schettino, president of the Animal Rescue League of Boston, which runs the Keep Pets SAFE program. SAFE stands for Supporting Animals and Families Everyday and its pantry serves pet owners in Dorchester, Mattapan, and Roxbury.

“When people struggle, pets struggle,” Schettino added.

Demand for the SAFE program and a statewide equivalent run by the Massachusetts Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (MSPCA) has surged this year compared to 2025, according to the nonprofits.

When money is tight, many pet owners sacrifice their own needs to buy a bag of kibble, animal advocates said. Some may feed their pet before eating a meal themselves.

Like LaCourt, many people in Massachusetts got pets during the pandemic to keep them company while spending more time at home.

Alyssa Krieger, director of community outreach for Boston’s MSPCA, said the group distributed 2.8 million pet meals across Massachusetts in 2024. In 2025, the number jumped to 3.5 million, she said.

Krieger said their clients typically get half of their pet’s monthly food from the program, visiting sites such as the Lawrence YMCA, Hyde Park’s Helping Plates and the Falmouth Service Center to pick up a bag of kibble provided by the MSPCA.

Pet owners seek out the program about two to four times per year, she said, and receive around $50 worth of food each time.

“People are using it when they really, really need it because life is nearly impossible in Massachusetts right now,” Krieger said.

Over the past several years, Krieger has talked to hundreds of pet owners at distribution sites in parks and parking lots. Often with their dogs in tow, the owners tell Krieger how thankful they are for the help.

“Those conversations really have taught me that pet ownership shouldn’t just be a privilege for people with a lot of money,” Krieger said.

In Boston, the ARL makes more than 25 deliveries per month, both to people’s homes and the offices of Action for Boston Community Development, a social services nonprofit, Schettino said.

The program focuses on dog and cat food, as well as cat litter. It also honors requests for food for birds, rabbits, guinea pigs, and other less common pets.

Monthly deliveries of about $80 worth of cat food and litter have helped Dorchester resident Betty Strickland pay off her 2019 Toyota Yaris, she said.

Strickland’s husband died in 2018 from health problems that began more than a decade earlier when he was shot in the stomach when their home was robbed, she said.

A friend decided Strickland needed a pet for company and gave her Leah, a long-haired white and tabby.

“She’s such a good kitty, I mean she’s so good, there’s certain things she knows not to do," said Strickland, adding that Leah provides “so much” company for her.

Because Leah had several teeth removed because of dental problems she developed as a kitten living on the street, she only eats canned cat food, said Strickland, 73.

Leah’s expensive taste, as well as her well-mannered behavior, leads neighbors to address her using a royal honorific.

The cat has her own kitchen chair, the only piece of furniture she’s allowed on.

“She really is a princess,” Strickland said.

Strickland’s monthly income, from her pension and Social Security, amounts to less than $2,000. Without the rescue league, she’d be spending nearly $100 a month on canned cat food and litter, she said.

“It makes it easier for me to spend money someplace else,” Strickland said.

Both Strickland and LaCourt receive housing assistance, which covers roughly two-thirds of their rent. A set percentage of their monthly income covers the final third.

LaCourt could work full time now, but she’s hesitant. The more she earns each month, the greater percentage of her income must go toward her rent. She already pays $1,000 toward the monthly cost of her two-bedroom apartment.

LaCourt’s 20-year-old daughter would contribute more to the household budget, but her hours at T.J. Maxx were recently cut to one day a week after her store on Newbury Street shut down and she was moved to another location.

That means that for now, the assistance is giving LaCourt’s family some much-needed peace of mind.

“I’d be lost without them, they’re so helpful,” she said.

A Jamaica Plain man, arrested in connection with a Hyde Park stabbing incident on Monday, was awaiting trial on a separate assault and battery charge and serving probation for violating a restraining order, according to court records.

The new year has brought significant changes to the housing market. The Warren Group reported an over 10 percent dip in Massachusetts single-family home sales, while the war in Iran has increased mortgage rates nationwide.

As house hunters face higher property price tags, here’s how three Boston-area buyers navigated the market.

Tara Flotta, her husband, and their three children recently moved from their house in Medway to a townhouse in Newton. They had a budget of $1.8 million.

Q: What was your house hunting experience like?

Tara Flotta: We were looking to cut down on my husband’s commute and my son’s commute. We had a budget in mind, but we had to increase it.

We really wanted to be in Newton because we wanted enough space. We’re at a stage of life where we have three older kids — one is graduating college, one is in college, and one is in high school in Brookline. So in five years, we may not need so much space, but we still need space for the time being. We thought Newton would probably give us the option of buying a single-family home, but we actually ended up buying a town house.

Probably the trickiest part of house hunting for us was the parking because you can’t park overnight in the winter in Newton, and we have five cars, so that really limited our options.

Q: What else were you looking for?

TF: We’ve lived through a lot of renovations. For our price point, any single-family homes that we came across required almost essentially a full renovation, and I wasn’t interested in living through more renovations. So finding something that was updated to our taste was important.

Q: How long did you search?

TF: We put our house on the market, and it sold in one weekend. We probably looked for houses for maybe six to eight weeks.

Q: How are you feeling about the space?

TF: The space is fantastic. It has a fully finished basement with a bedroom and a bathroom. My high school son loves that. If you asked my husband, he would say, I wish we did this much sooner, because he commuted an hour and 20 minutes each way for 25 years.

Originally from New York City, Ardelin de Jesus is a nurse who used to live with her two teenage children in the South End. She worked with the Boston Housing Authority’s First Home Program and the City of Boston’s Downpayment Assistance Program to purchase a house in Roslindale in October.

Q: What brought you to Boston?

Ardelin de Jesus: I came from the Bronx. It’s was very different. I mean, all my family is in New York. [Boston] was more calm, and when I got pregnant, I said, “Do I want to go back and raise my child over here?” I was thinking of moving to Puerto Rico because my mom was there, or staying in New York because my sister was there. But I said, No, let me just start by myself in a different place.

Q: When did you start to consider buying?

AJ: I came to Boston, I started from zero, and I had two children. I decided to work and go to school. When I finished school, I said, “OK, now I’m in a better place. Now is the time.”

My daughter is going to medical school, so I had to stay in Boston.

Q: What was the process like?

AJ: Everything was really expensive. We started looking for houses in December 2024, and we finally closed the deal on Oct.15.

Q: Were there any challenges?

AJ: The difficulty was mostly the budget.

There was a house that I did go for, and I put more money down than the person that got the house. I got upset. That was a setback that really broke me in the moment. My realtor, she told me, “That sort of thing can happen ... maybe they knew the buyer, maybe they knew the other realtor.”

Q: Were there certain features you were looking for?

AJ: The thing I said wasn’t negotiable was the parking. I wanted a two-bathroom because my daughter takes a whole hour in the bathroom.

Lakia Chambliss was born and raised in Roxbury but moved to Canton, where she lived for 11 years. With help from the City of Boston’s down payment assistance and the Family Self Sufficiency program [Section 8], she was able to move back to Boston in June and bought a home in Hyde Park, where she’s raising her 11-year-old daughter.

Q: When did you start to consider buying?

Lakia Chambliss: It’s always been a dream for me, but I started during the pandemic time back in 2020, that’s when I decided. Since we were stuck indoors and things like that, I was able to really buckle down and save more. And just keeping my credit in good standing.

Q: What was important to you?

LC: Neighborhood was a big one. I wanted to be somewhere where the environment was nice, the school systems, low traffic.

Q: What was your budget?

LC: I wasn’t sure of what I was going to be approved for. But when I finally got the OK through Boston Housing, I went to a lender, they gave me my ballpark, and that’s what I worked around, but I didn’t know going into it what my budget would be. I knew my credit was pretty good, my income wasn’t really up there, so I knew that was going to be like a little setback.

Q: How did the Boston’s programs come onto your radar?

So when I saw the FSS program. I signed up for that because they put a certain amount of money into an account for you, and it builds over five years, and then you work with them towards your goals, like, if you want a new home, a new car, a new business, things like that. That was a big help, right there, that program. And then I always heard about Boston Housing having the homeownership program. I had to have a certain credit score, make a certain amount of money, and have a certain amount of money saved — I met all of those. So then I just went forward.
