The two stores — joining other budget-conscious neighbors like Primark, TJ Maxx, and Old Navy in the city’s stalwart shopping district — reflect an often-counted-out neighborhood learning to play to its strengths.

The COVID-19 pandemic wounded the real estate market in the downtown corridor — a key slice of the city’s property tax base. But that financial blow ended up giving the neighborhood an edge over pricier enclaves like the Back Bay or the Seaport in courting buzzy brands like Uniqlo and Teso Life. And those coups, observers said, are helping infuse the whole neighborhood with fresh energy.

“There’s this temptation to talk about the revitalization of the neighborhood . . . I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s kind of like, we’re already there,” said Noam Ron, of Hudson Group, one of the firms that bought 399 Washington last year. “We find ourselves no longer having to sort of apologize for Downtown Crossing.”

To be sure, downtown is still in recovery mode, with office vacancies well above pre-pandemic levels and foot traffic well below — though both appear to be steadily improving. Retail has been a notable bright spot, with a “single-digit number of vacancies” on Washington Street between City Hall and Chinatown, according to Michael Nichols, president of the Downtown Boston Alliance.

In addition to Uniqlo and Teso Life, Washington Street, a main downtown artery, is soon slated to welcome a new Skechers store, a hot pot restaurant, and an Italian sandwich shop. The retail vacancy rate in the greater downtown neighborhood was 1.6 percent in the last quarter of 2025 — down a tick from the same quarter in 2019, according to city data.

“I’m delighted it’s come as far and as fast as it has, given where we were two years ago,” said Nichols.

The rebirth of 399 Washington St. is a saga 20 years in the making. Once home to a string of clothing stores stretching back to the 1880s, the space has been without a retail tenant since Barnes & Noble moved out in 2006, unable to negotiate a new lease with its landlord. Out-of-state firms LaSalle Investment Management and L3 Capital purchased the building for $63 million in 2017, undertaking a major renovation as it prepared to court new tenants. Then the pandemic hit, robbing the neighborhood of much of its sought-after foot traffic.

That’s how, last year, the building ended up in the hands of Boston-based Hudson Group and New York-based Assembly Investments and Time Equities, for a cool $13 million — just a fifth of its previous price tag.

It was that rock-bottom rate that allowed the new owners to woo a tenant like Uniqlo “pretty immediately,” with an attractive rent price, said Ron. (Ron declined to specify what Uniqlo was paying for rent for the 10-year lease, citing confidentiality.)

“People constantly ask about the 20 years of vacancies, but it’s not rocket science,” he said. “We were fortunate enough to buy it at the right time, at the right basis, and we can pass that lower rent along to folks like Uniqlo.”

The retailer, which specializes in minimalist wares, handled much of the build-out of the 20,000-plus-square-foot space, taking care to preserve the brick ceilings, ornate columns, and central staircase linking the two levels.

“I just feel like bringing it to the area is going to bring a lot of traffic back,” said Alvin Spinkston, 29, a passerby who stopped by the almost-open store this week, wearing a tan Uniqlo trench coat. Growing up in the Roxbury area, he said, he used to go downtown frequently — not as much anymore. But that will change after the opening of the store, he said, which he patronizes often for its “great silhouettes.”

“This definitely got my attention,” he said, knocking on the store window, where mannequins posed in pastel ensembles.

From Uniqlo’s point of view, 399 Washington presented the opportunity to open up what Tomo Yasuda, director of real estate for Uniqlo North America, called a “key store” in Boston — larger than its Newbury Street and since-closed Faneuil Hall outposts, and more central than its other suburban Massachusetts locations. He said a flagship like this one, which will employ about 120 people, has the room to offer a wider selection, plus other services, like the Re.Uniqlo Studio, which can repair or recycle customers’ old Uniqlo duds or spruce them up with embroidery, and UTme!, a program that partnered with local artists to put their Boston-centric designs on T-shirts and tote bags.

“It was a perfect mix,” said Yasuda of the downtown area, pointing to the blend of office workers, tourists, and students. “The people are there, and there’s actually big spaces that we can really operate and show what we have to offer.”

It was a similar story over at the retail space in 459 Washington St., which also stood barren for years after the closure of former tenant Forever 21. In 2024, to avoid foreclosure, the property was taken over by the owner’s private lender. Marc Samwick, the founding partner of that lender’s New York-based parent company, said he connected with Teso Life “within days” of putting the approximately 20,000-square-foot, three-floor space up on the leasing market.

“We think this is really, almost, essentially, at the corner of Main and Main,” he said. “This is where you want to be.”

Like Uniqlo, securing a tenant like Teso Life, he said, required “a more flexible approach” compared to the previous owner. Part of that approach was setting a too-good-to-pass-up asking rent price — $37 per square foot, well below market value.

CY Kwok, general manager at Teso Life, said the brand had been looking to set up shop in Boston for three years, but had “never found the perfect site” before the Downtown Crossing space opened up.

“It has a lot to offer at that location,” he said. “We were looking at Newbury Street, but that area — it’s good, but it’s out of our budget, it’s way too expensive in terms of rent.”

For some consumers, the two retailers are more than just big-box stores.

“I like how it’s getting a lot more Asian representation,” said Kenzie Mao, a 20-year-old Suffolk University student, of the downtown neighborhood with Uniqlo and Teso Life moving in. “It makes us have more of a community.”

Last month, with the 10-year lease secured, Samwick decided it was time to sell the retail space, putting it on the market for $13.7 million. But that wasn’t an easy decision.

“We’ve thought about this longer and harder than others, because we really think that Downtown Crossing is — it has a very bright future in front of it," Samwick said.

That bright future is likely to come sooner because of the splash Uniqlo and Teso Life will make, said Whitney Gallivan, senior managing director and partner at Boston Realty Advisors, who helped broker the latest sale of 399 Washington.

“When a tenant comes to town, historically, they may say to us, ‘We only want to look in the Back Bay, in the Seaport,’ ” she said. “But if we can say, ‘Well, Uniqlo just opened up, and Teso, why don’t you take a look at this block on Washington Street, there might be a spot for you, and plus, you’re paying a lot lower rent than you are in the Back Bay,’ that’s going to help.”

The 39-year-old King had allegedly committed an unarmed carjacking the night of March 11 and was fleeing a traffic stop when Boston police Officer Nicholas O’Malley fired his service weapon, killing King.

Suffolk prosecutors quickly charged O’Malley with manslaughter, saying he wasn’t justified in shooting at the moving vehicle.

Several Boston city councilors and community leaders have also called on police to release the bodycam footage. But prosecutors and police have resisted, saying that would jeopardize the ongoing criminal investigation.

Crump, a civil rights attorney who also represented the family of George Floyd, said King’s mental health declined after his mother died from cancer in 2009.

Family members say they had been trying to get him adequate long-term treatment. They said he would cycle through the criminal justice system, sometimes receiving psychiatric medication while he was incarcerated, only to lose access to regular care after his release.

Recently, he was hearing voices and showing signs of intense paranoia, relatives said. Convinced that he was under surveillance, King would put tape over cellphone cameras, electric outlets, and even the emblems on his sneakers.

“That’s how bad it was,” said his father, Stephenson King Sr., a retired state corrections officer. “That’s why I was trying to get some help for my son.”

Hours before the shooting, King asked his father to call an ambulance because he’d been injured in an assault days earlier. Medics arrived and said they were taking him to the hospital.

“That’s the last time I saw my son,” said Stephenson King Sr., his voice strained with emotion.

Several family members, including two of King’s sisters, addressed the media during the news conference. They displayed a photo of King, smiling widely in a navy sweater and baseball cap, the way they want to remember him.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed the carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Mission Hill. About 15 minutes after the reported carjacking, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away, at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

King then ignored verbal commands as officers approached the car on foot and then he tried to drive away, according to police. A nearby resident who witnessed the shooting told the Globe the situation escalated extremely quickly.

According to a police report, King opened the car window at the command of police officers, but did not turn the vehicle off. Positioned outside the driver’s side window, O’Malley drew a department-issued Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” according to the police report.

At that moment, King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

“Even though he wasn’t perfect, even though he struggled with mental illnesses, he did not deserve to be killed like this,” Crump said. “He did not deserve to be killed just because an officer had a rush to judgment.”

King’s family said they weren’t sure what happened after he was transported to the hospital earlier that day. If only his condition had been stabilized before being discharged, said his sister, Ebony King Gibson.

“He has been in and out of the system for a very long time, battling this thing, battling his demons,” she said.

When King was arrested in 2024 after police found him asleep in a stairwell with a loaded gun in his sweatshirt, he was drunk and suicidal, Gibson said.

“He wanted to take his life,” she said.

King’s death adds to a growing list of recent police shootings in Massachusetts that raise questions about whether mental illness played a role. On Saturday afternoon, a man experiencing a mental health crisis was killed by Boston police after he attacked first responders with a sword, officials said. He was identified as Jacob Graves, 29, a former student at Berklee College of Music.

Police in Weymouth and Westminster also reported deadly officer shootings last month.

Attorneys for the King family praised the district attorney’s quick decision to charge O’Malley.

But leaders of the department’s largest union have expressed outrage, saying it’s a slap in the face to law enforcement officers risking their lives every day. They pointed to King’s criminal history, which includes assault and firearms charges.

Also on Thursday, Boston attorney David Yannetti, who recently represented Karen Read, announced he’s been retained to represent O’Malley.

In the Read case, Yannetti said in a written statement, he “spent nearly four years zealously fighting a district attorney’s office that protected bad police officers while prosecuting an innocent woman.” Now, he plans to “zealously fight another district attorney’s office that is apparently choosing to protect criminals while prosecuting good police officers,” the statement said.

“Officer Nicholas O’Malley has always maintained a stellar record as a sworn Boston police officer,” Yannetti said. “He is an exemplary family man, a husband and a father to young children. He chose to become a police officer for all the right reasons.”

O’Malley told investigators he fired into the vehicle because he thought another officer was in danger of being run over by King, court records show. Moments later, O’Malley called over his radio that officers were involved in a shooting and the suspect “tried to run us over,” according to the police report. King was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

Releasing the bodycam footage would allow people to see for themselves how the tragedy unfolded, Crump said. He questioned whether the video would have already been made public if it exonerated the officer and implicated King.

“We shouldn’t have two justice systems,” Crump said. “We should have equal justice for every citizen. Is that so much to ask?”

Boston City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who has repeatedly raised the issue, called on Police Commissioner Michael Cox to at least let the family view the video.

“This is about whether Boston is serious about transparency when it matters the most,” said Councilor Brian Worrell. “We can’t have trust in the law without accountability.”

But just a short time before close of business Wednesday, Rollins sent everyone back to their original talking points when she took out nomination papers to run for her old Suffolk County position.

The comeback, it seemed, was on — though she would not comment Wednesday or Thursday on whether she actually was running.

Rollins’s sudden return is, in a way, not dissimilar to the five years the brash but calculating former progressive star prosecutor spent in the limelight.

This is a politician who won the district attorney’s office as a relative unknown, grabbed national attention with liberal policy platforms, and was appointed the top federal prosecutor in Massachusetts in 2022, making her the first Black woman to hold the post.

But she also was dogged by a series of escalating scandals, from allegations she inappropriately exerted her influence in a road-rage incident, to threatening to file a police report against a TV reporter outside her house, to her eventual downfall: trying, but failing, to influence the election to succeed her as DA by leaking confidential material to the press, and then lying about it, according to federal investigators.

And now, after three quiet years in which she took small steps toward rebuilding her reputation, Rollins is back — or so it appears. But how the voters of Suffolk County receive her remains to be seen, and a contest against incumbent District Attorney Kevin Hayden, a political foe, could answer weighty questions about the status of progressive policies in the current political moment, as well as the willingness of Boston voters to forgive.

First and foremost for Rollins, said former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, there must be a reckoning — a “public mea culpa.” Wilkerson, who herself went from Beacon Hill to federal prison for a bribery conviction, said Rollins would have to explain her past behavior, apologize, and take ownership of what happened — and be genuine and contrite while doing so.

”People have to see that it’s real," she said. But if she can connect with people, Wilkerson said, Rollins still would be a force. “I wouldn’t count her out.”

Rollins has drawn headlines since she splashed onto the Boston political scene in 2018, winning the DA’s office on a platform that drew national attention because she publicly cited a list of lower-level crimes that she would not prosecute. She was among the crop of staunchly progressive candidates across the country who won in major cities that year. Rollins drew pushback from police unions and some more conservative politicians, but while she was DA, some of her problems were more self-inflicted.

On Christmas Eve 2020, a woman said Rollins threatened her with a ticket and flashed the blue lights on her vehicle as they were both trying to exit the South Bay shopping center. She was ultimately cleared of allegations of a civil rights violation, but it garnered negative headlines, including after Rollins confronted a TV producer who went to her house to ask her about the incident.

Rollins also was a dynamic politician and communicator who made well-placed allies. In 2022, with the support of both of Massachusetts’ senators, then-President Joe Biden appointed her US attorney.

But in a twist that would prove to be her undoing, she was unable to leave local politics behind. Just a few months after her elevation, she attempted to meddle in the election to replace her in Suffolk County.

The Republican governor, Charlie Baker, had appointed Hayden, a moderate Democrat, as her interim replacement, and Hayden later sought a full term against Ricardo Arroyo, a progressive Boston city councilor. Rollins preferred Arroyo, an ally who promised to run the office in the vein she’d run it.

By late summer 2022, the campaign had devolved rapidly into one of the nastiest contests in recent local memory. And ahead of the Democratic primary that would effectively determine who won the seat, Rollins used her office to try to swing the election for Arroyo by leaking damaging information about Hayden, according to reports from federal investigations into her conduct.

By the next spring, she resigned a day before the release of two federal ethics probes, including one that found she sought “to create the impression publicly, before the primary election, that the DOJ was or would be investigating Hayden for public corruption.”

Investigators said Rollins also accepted two free tickets from the Celtics and solicited 30 free tickets from the team for a youth basketball program.

Rollins had maintained a fairly low profile since. She fought to maintain her law license, agreeing to a public reprimand from the Massachusetts Board of Bar Overseers in the wake of the DOJ investigation. In 2024, she took a part-time role at Roxbury Community College leading a program for formerly incarcerated people. As of February, she was still on the school’s payroll making roughly $110,000 a year, according to state data.

For some, including her predecessor as district attorney, the misdeeds of her past are disqualifying. Dan Conley, the county’s longtime district attorney, said Rollins is “unfit to hold an office that demands truthfulness, fairness, and public trust.”

“Through her actions, Rachael Rollins has shown that she lacks the two most fundamental qualifications for serving as district attorney: honesty and integrity. That’s not up for debate,” he said Thursday.

But Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a longtime political strategist based in Boston, warned she could be “a formidable foe.”

“As far as Rachael goes, I think there’s still a lot of love for [her] here,” she said, noting that Rollins has “a core group of supporters who still like her style and commitment.”

Rollins would enter the race with almost $43,000 in her campaign account, more than the $29,000 Hayden reported on hand in March. She also needs to collect at least 1,000 certified signatures by April 28 to appear on the Democratic primary ballot, no small feat in less than three weeks.

The dynamics of the race are complex. Hayden, who personally and professionally has kept a lower profile than Rollins, faced his own issues in 2022, eventually having to pay a $5,000 ethics fine for a press release the office sent attacking Arroyo.

Rollins is to the left of Hayden politically, but the political lanes in this race are not entirely clear. The incumbent, for example, is fending off criticism on his right after he charged a Boston police officer with manslaughter in the fatal shooting of a man during a traffic stop. He’s increasingly allied himself with Mayor Michelle Wu, the most prominent progressive in the city, who hosted a fund-raiser for him last month.

The decision to charge the officer, Nicholas O’Malley, sparked swift backlash from the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the city’s largest police union, which took to social media to call on “Anyone interested in running for Suffolk County District Attorney should start collecting signatures ASAP.”

Rollins is the second possible challenger to emerge: Linda Champion, a former Suffolk assistant district attorney, pulled nomination papers last week.

The range of candidates may offer voters a choice between progressive and more-moderate policies, “and we have to see if the electorate has changed in the last few years,” said state Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who has pledged his support to Hayden. “Anybody in the race has a chance to win.”

Worldwide, prefabricated construction is booming in part driven by increased demand for sustainable homes. In Massachusetts, which has set steep, legally binding targets to reduce greenhouse gases that drive climate change, housing is responsible for about 30 percent of the state’s total energy use.

For their project in Somerville, Buntel and Graber reached out to the New Hampshire firm Bensonwood to build their dream home, which would include two home offices, a second living area upstairs, and striking, exposed New England timber-framing. And the kicker: the home would generate enough electricity to power itself, a big incentive in a state where residents pay the highest electricity rates in the continental United States.

When the various pieces of the couple’s home — walls with windows and doors and a roof — arrived on a truck, they were fixed together like Legos. The design and internal wiring made it extra easy for the couple to add solar panels, cork floors that retain heat, and a heat pump, to both generate power and cut their energy consumption.

“We were delighted to discover that we produce way more energy than we use,” Graber said of her new home.

Bensonwood’s brand called Unity Homes, is run out of a factory in Keene, N.H. Homebuyers can choose from one of five models, then make modifications. The models all have Swedish names, acknowledging that country’s leadership in offsite construction.

Other local prefab designers with an environmental bent include Green Staxx, which turned to a factory in Quebec to construct modular units for installation in a Newton apartment building, and BrightBuilt Home, which offers net-zero design options.

Bensonwood founder Tedd Benson said his company aims to “make a building you could eat” by using organic materials such as wood and cellulose, a recycled insulation product. He added that factory building significantly reduces waste.

“We’re not filling up a dumpster on a job site,” Benson said.

Elsewhere in Greater Boston, Bensonwood also recently designed 12 affordable housing units in Dorchester and three student residences at Tufts University and the Wellesley College Science Complex.

For consumers, prefab homes can be significantly cheaper, though plenty of variables affect the bottom line. For Buntel and Graber, a prefab was more affordable than a deep energy retrofit would’ve been. Plus, they got a brand new home.

The real cost gain for prefabs, though, is time saved.

“Monday, there was a hole in the ground. Thursday, I could walk up to the second floor,” Graber said.

But John Ferrante, CEO of the Associated General Contractors of Massachusetts, noted some downsides. Meeting building codes can be difficult when shipping components to various cities, and the local workforce may feel jobs are being taken away, Ferrante said.

There are also limits to how architecturally ambitious or creative you can get with a preset menu of design choices.

Still, Ferrante says the growing prefab trend will keep growing because “everybody in the industry is looking for ways to control the cost of construction.”

And if people can dramatically cut their energy bills through a prefab design, all the more incentive.

Between their solar panels and energy efficiency upgrades, the Somerville couple is generating a surplus of electricity. Eversource gives them credits for excess energy production, which they can dip into during the winter months if they use more than they produce. The couple also gifts some credits, essentially free energy, to the Somerville Homeless Coalition.

“Imagine if everyone was giving some electricity to people who needed it,” Buntel said.

Environmentally conscious homeowners can also retrofit existing homes. John Sterman, a professor at MIT’s Sloan School of Management and director of the school’s sustainability initiative, took that approach when he did a deep energy retrofit on his 1920s Lexington home. He replaced all the windows and installed a heat pump and solar panels, among other renovations, to turn his home into a personal “power plant.”

Sterman concedes: this took a lot of time and money. While he wasn’t about to rip down his historic home, Sterman adds that in many cases “you’re better off doing a tear down and a rebuild.”

Buntel and Graber hold on to the memory of the fixer upper they started with. A framed illustration of the original house is displayed over a collection of potted plants, and on a nearby bookshelf sits a wooden sign with a heartfelt message to their teardown on Trull Street: “Old Ugly Trull. Mourned not missed.”

Graber said maximizing sustainability and lowering their carbon footprint is a responsibility they take seriously.

“This isn’t just a nice-to-have,” she said. “This is truly a need-to-have. ... It’s just how to make it more accessible.”

We’re a soccer family. It’s our thing. We watch all the big Champions League games (and every Manchester City game). We put up a bracket on the wall and meticulously track the scores of each World Cup game. We have a fish named after Norwegian striker Erling Haaland.

So when it was announced that the World Cup was coming to Boston, I promised my kids there was no way the world’s biggest sporting event was coming to our backyard without the Bakers showing up. Whatever it takes.

Here’s what it has taken: an absurd amount of money and uncertainty, and dealing with the criminal organization that calls itself the soccer governing body FIFA. I would ask the state to investigate this crime ring, but now they’re in on it!

Just the facts

To even have the opportunity to buy tickets to a game, you had to enter a lottery. Which I did, way back in the summer, and lost. I entered again and lost. The third time was a charm. I won! What did I win?

I was offered the opportunity to purchase four tickets to each of the games throughout North America (except the final). The problem is the actual draw had not yet happened. So your options were “Match 005” at “Boston Stadium.” And the seats were beyond expensive, even for the early group stage games featuring “who knows” against “TBD.” And you were not buying seats, you were buying tiers.

After going back and forth with my wife, discussing promises and overusing the phrase “once in a lifetime,” we basically said, “This will be the Christmas gift for the whole family, for the rest of time.” I closed my eyes, entered a credit card number, and bought four tickets for the first game in Boston, in Category 1 — which on the map was the entire lower bowl at Gillette Stadium — for the absurd price of $410 per ticket. Once in a lifetime. Once in a lifetime.

Complications ensue

Then we watched the match draw in December, kept our fingers crossed, and wound up with Scotland vs Haiti. Which, to translate that, is the #43 team in the world vs the #83 team. For $1,640. But hey, I’m sure the Scottish fans will show up in kilts and be drunkenly funny, and we’ll have good seats since we bit the bullet and paid for the top tier.

Wrong! News broke this week, to worldwide ire, that FIFA lied to everyone and reserved all the good seats for obscenely expensive “hospitality packages.” This was discovered when they finally released the seating assignments and put us lowly people, who paid what felt like Rockefeller money for Category 1, into the corners or behind the net.

In some cases, FIFA actually changed the stadium maps and put people who purchased Tier 1 tickets into what had been labeled Category 2 when they bought the tickets. And the ire also noted that none of the good midfield seats, which were on the map we were buying into, had appeared on the resale market, which meant no one had them. This was confirmed when FIFA on Thursday announced new hospitality packages featuring those exact seats.

Who ya gonna call?

I would call the state to file a criminal complaint, but they’re in on the gouging. They just announced the commuter rail to Foxborough will cost $80 per person. That ticket from South Station typically costs less than $20 round trip. Instead, I paid $175 for a parking spot, which is absurd, but is basically half what it would cost us to take public transportation.

When I had the chance to buy tickets in the lottery, I actually reached out to a few buddies and asked if they wanted some. “Who’s playing?” they all asked, and wisely passed when I told them I didn’t know, and then told them the price.

Except one friend, who bought four tickets to the second game. Which turned out to feature Norway. Which has Erling Haaland. Which is the name of our fish. And my wife dressed as him for Halloween.

And … he didn’t even make me go through it. He knew all this, and offered to switch games with us. You’re a good man, Kevin. Sorry I got you involved with FIFA.

Once in a lifetime, indeed.

The bankruptcy of Steward Health Care walloped the Massachusetts health care landscape. Six of its hospital campuses in the state were taken over by new operators, while two others — Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer — closed their doors after Steward’s financial implosion. Meanwhile, in Rhode Island just last month, the Centurion Foundation took over Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital, two safety-net hospitals that had become cash-strapped under Prospect Medical Holdings ownership.

The renewed strain also underscores a broader problem in the hospital industry: bankruptcy is often proving to be less a reset than a handoff. Distressed facilities are being passed to new operators, often with lease relief, asset sales, or emergency financing to keep them open. Even as overall health care Chapter 11 filings fell in 2025, hospital bankruptcies rose, according to Gibbins Advisors, suggesting many hospitals remain financially fragile even after leaving court.

Some of the former Steward hospitals taken over by Michael Sarian and Faisal Gill — two executives chosen by MPT to run the facilities — have been hit in recent months with lawsuits from vendors and service providers, court filings show. The unpaid bills span a wide range of basic services, including medical staffing, physician coverage, plumbing, fire protection, and security systems.

HSA and NOR recently removed Sarian as chief executive officer and replaced him with Gill, even as the hospitals themselves were dealing with growing operational and financial strain. The two executives are now fighting in court, trading accusations of improper fund transfers and a conspiracy to replace Sarian at the helm of the companies.

MPT has said it expects the former Steward and Prospect hospitals sold to HSA and NOR Healthcare Systems Corp. — another company created by Sarian and Gill to take over several Prospect hospitals in California — to resume paying full rent by the end of this year and that Sarian’s companies would be better operators than their predecessors.

MPT didn’t respond to requests for comment.

“Under Mike’s leadership we had issues which right now I am working with vendors to correct,” Gill said in an email, adding that he’s secured an additional $30 million for new equipment at the HSA hospitals.

Trane Technologies plc, Johnson Controls International, and other service providers have filed liens against some of the hospitals, according to court records. Equipment lessors are trying to recover their machines. Several vendors and health care companies have said they stopped providing services altogether.

The strain extends beyond vendor disputes. In Texas, hospitals run by Healthcare Systems of America, or HSA, one of the operating companies tied to Sarian and Gill, are also behind on tax payments owed to two counties, court papers show. In Florida, meanwhile, an employee at one HSA hospital alleged in a whistleblower lawsuit that managers told him to mislead government regulators about building-safety violations and refused to pay to repair an elevator. HSA denies the allegations, Gill said in an email, and has moved to dismiss the complaint. The company argues the plaintiff failed to show that the relevant statute was violated.

For patients and the communities around these facilities, the risk is that mounting financial stress starts to show up in everyday care. When hospitals miss payments to vendors and service providers cut back, they can struggle to maintain equipment, staff departments, and keep up with repairs, basic building operations, and other routine functions essential to patient care.

Medical staff at some HSA hospitals in Florida continue to contend with broken equipment and lack of supplies, but HSA has been more responsive when they raised concerns than Steward had been, DeQuasia Canales, a union official who represents workers at a number of HSA facilities, told Bloomberg in an interview. “That’s a low bar,” said Canales, referencing deterioration in facilities run by Steward.

The management dispute has added another layer of uncertainty. In February, MPT sent HSA a notice of default over unpaid rent and other obligations, including delinquent Texas taxes. In a California lawsuit filed in February, seeking to remove Sarian as chief executive officer, NOR alleged that it bounced $4 million of checks to health care providers in January and had built up about $20 million in unpaid payroll taxes over time. In response to questions from Bloomberg, Gill said NOR is now current on the payroll tax liability, which he said had built up under Prospect’s ownership.

A spokesperson and a lawyer for Prospect didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Gill, in court papers, has accused Sarian of improperly moving more than $50 million out of NOR and another company the two manage and transferring the funds to HSA, which is solely owned by him, since 2021. Sarian, in an email, said claims that he siphoned money out of the businesses are false, and his lawyer said he has been the victim of deceptive colleagues.

Sarian, in his own court filings, has accused Gill and a minority investor of working together to force him out and take control of part of his ownership stake in the companies.

Those accusations remain contested, and the executive feud may take time to sort out in court. But the more immediate problem for MPT is that the hospitals it helped rescue are again facing missed payments and questions about day-to-day operations. The turmoil is another test of whether the operators it backed can stabilize the facilities and restore rent.

Leslie founded two nonprofits — Dorchester Community Center for the Visual Arts, better known as DotArt, in 1998, and Living Art, in 2015. They were small, even by local nonprofit standards — not the type of organization you’d typically read about in the business section.

They had an outsize impact, but Leslie rarely got the recognition she deserved for bringing art to communities, even as schools cut back on such “extras.” No matter. For her, teaching artmaking was a labor of love. And she helped make Boston a better place to live and raise a family.

Today’s newsletter is my way of honoring Leslie, who died March 24 at her home in Stoneham, where she had moved to be closer to family. She was 90.

Welcome to Dorchester

My wife and I met Leslie in December 1989. We’d just moved to the Ashmont section of Dorchester. Leslie knocked on the door, welcomed us to the neighborhood, and offered an invite to her annual New Year’s Day party.

Leslie lived a few houses away, and she was thrilled we’d landed from New York with two small children in tow. She and her husband at the time had a young son and were members of a babysitting cooperative. She was quick to recruit us into the co-op — and we were glad she did. We met people who became longtime friends and introduced us to other Dorchester families.

An unstoppable force

The essential thing to know about Leslie: She was a fighter — determined, unyielding, never one to take no for an answer. Even those who loved her knew she could be a pain in the butt.

That strong will was evident when she battled tuberculosis as a young girl in Dublin. She was bedridden for four years and spent most of that time in a body cast.

During that period, “drawing became a crucial way to realize her ideas about herself and the world,” her ex-husband, Paul Dobbs, said in an email. “This was quite possibly the crucible that created her passion for teaching, or, more specifically, for advocating artmaking as a tool for self-realization.”

Leslie was accepted at Ireland’s National College of Art and Design at 14, and later attended the famed École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. When she returned to Dublin, Leslie taught art while establishing herself as an acclaimed painter.

Coming to America

Leslie came to the US in 1973 to become a graduate student at Boston University. She taught undergraduate art classes at BU and Massachusetts College of Art and Design, where she was later appointed an assistant professor.

It was at BU that Leslie met Dobbs, an archivist, whom she would marry in 1977. A decade later, they adopted an infant, Adam, from Honduras. Leslie lived for several months in a Honduran Mennonite colony while the adoption papers were completed. She was already in her 50s.

In 1992, Leslie created The Children’s Studio in Dorchester, where she and others taught young children to draw, paint, and sculpt. That led to the formation of DotArt six years later.

Leslie focused on portrait paintings, done on hollow-core doors, and figurative sculptures in papier-mâché on simple armatures.

“Leslie also made the creation of these portraits a ‘paying job’ by securing funding from the city of Boston and charitable foundations (including the Boston Foundation) to create and manage summer jobs for teens,” according to an obituary by family friend Mark Farrington.

Moving on

Leslie left DotArt in 2012 after a consultant recommended the organization hire a new executive director with better organizational skills. Leslie was notoriously late for everything. (I would kid her about operating on “MacWeeney Time.”)

While a persuasive fundraiser, Leslie didn’t care much for the paperwork that many institutional donors wanted to see detailing how their grant money was spent and the results achieved, said Evan Hershenson, DotArt’s executive officer and treasurer.

A few years after leaving DotArt, she started Living Art, which recruited police officers, firefighters, EMTs, and veterans to pose for portraits.

Her genius was the ability to provide “new art opportunities in so many mediums,” Hershenson said. “She knew how to bring art into a lot of different spaces. And the one constant was creating a safe space where you wouldn’t be judged on your work.”

A Funeral Mass for Leslie will be held April 25, 10 a.m., at the Paulist Center, 5 Park St. in Boston, with an informal gathering afterward to celebrate and appreciate Leslie’s remarkable life.

After taking responsibility for his actions, Hayden left it at that. Rollins is still trying to equivocate and deflect responsibility, and that’s a mistake.

As the first Black woman elected as Suffolk County district attorney and the first Black woman to become the region’s top federal prosecutor, she broke ground in many important ways. She pivoted away from punishment toward fighting the societal causes of crime and released a list of nonviolent crimes she said she wouldn’t prosecute. But over time, she gave critics of that approach too many weapons to use against her.

During her first run for Suffolk County DA in 2018, the Boston Herald first reported she had been charged with receiving stolen property while she was a college student. In response, her campaign said that the “minor” arrest did not affect her career as a prosecutor but has “informed how she views criminal justice reform.” The misdemeanor charge, which dated back to 1991, was eventually continued without a finding and dropped.

A stint as chief legal counsel at Massport from 2013 to 2015 ended with what CommonWealth Beacon described as “a puzzling coda” — a $175,000 severance agreement and a $45,000 education benefit that have never been explained to the public.

When Rollins was Suffolk County DA, a Dorchester resident filed a complaint alleging that Rollins threatened her and inappropriately flashed blue lights at her during a 2020 Christmas Eve confrontation at the South Bay shopping center. Then-Attorney General Maura Healey launched a review that found no civil rights or criminal violations, which is not the same thing as saying nothing happened. The matter was referred to the state Ethics Commission, which ultimately cleared her.

In January 2021, Rollins yelled at a television news crew that approached her in front of her home, seeking comment about the traffic incident. Telling them to “get out of here,” she added, “You know what I’ll do? I’ll call the police on you and make an allegation and we’ll see how that works out for you.” That from a prosecutor who listed trespass as a crime she wouldn’t prosecute in the name of criminal justice reform.

Some will say that because of race and gender, she was judged more harshly for reactions such as those connected to the alleged road rage incident. But I think she was also granted leeway because of her progressive agenda. The Globe, for example, endorsed her for DA, describing the charge of receiving stolen property as “a minor brush with the law as a college student” and emphasizing her ability to “push the office in new directions.”

With backing from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey, who hailed her as a national leader in transforming the criminal justice system, Rollins was nominated by President Biden to be the region’s top federal prosecutor. Then came the scathing reports by two watchdog agencies about her conduct in that job.

The Massachusetts Board of Bar Overseers voted to publicly reprimand Rollins, with three of the 12 members finding the punishment too lenient and a fourth member recusing herself, the Globe reported at the time. When Rollins agreed to the public reprimand, she admitted to improperly disclosing confidential information to a Herald reporter about an investigation into Hayden. But still, according to the Globe report, she told the board she “erroneously thought she had discretion to disclose the matter without prior authorization pursuant to DOJ manual.”

She has been working at Roxbury Community College as executive director of a program focused on helping formerly incarcerated people for an annual salary of $96,000.

Does she deserve a second chance as a prosecutor? That’s up to the voters.

But she did mess up. Better to just admit that.

Like so many formerly gritty spots throughout the region, the building’s interior has become something else entirely. It’s dominated by a mural of people being baptized in a river, flanked by screens welcoming worshipers to the church. The carpet is purple, as are the seats. During one recent Sunday service, about 20 people were in attendance.

The Rev. Collin Green led them in prayer and song. After the service, he acknowledged the sordid history of the property, bringing up the prior owner and longtime leader of the Winter Hill Gang, the late Howie Winter, unprompted. He said the neighborhood is no longer a place where people need to look over their shoulder.

“It’s changed,” he said. “It’s not that way. God is in the building.”

But not all the changes from how it was to how it is are for the better. He mentioned the local housing crunch, saying one congregant, who grew up in Somerville, travels to attend services from Worcester, where housing is more affordable.

It’s a transformation playing out across the region. As Greater Boston has gentrified, it has become less of a backdrop for working-class, clannish noirs that hinge on loyalty and limited life choices directed by Ben Affleck or Martin Scorsese. It’s now more of a hub of gentrifying young professionals, skyrocketing housing costs, and concerns about displacement.

Holly Simione, 56, grew up a short walk away from the former Somerville garage-turned-church. When she was a kid, she knew who the “bad guys” were in the neighborhood. While she was in middle school, a man on the run from police hid in her yard. Simione was on the porch, she recalled. He pointed a gun at her but didn’t fire. That was the neighborhood back then.

“I remember being mindful of people but not being afraid of them,” she said.

Now, Marshall Street itself has two dozen properties assessed at more than $1 million, according to city records. Winter Hill, according to some residents, may be home to some of the last slices of un-gentrified Somerville, but is not immune to the market forces that have seen rents skyrocket locally. Others say, no, Winter Hill has already been gentrified, just not as much as, say, Davis Square. They all agree the neighborhood is not what it used to be. And it’s hardly alone.

Down Interstate 93 in South Boston is the former location of Triple O’s Lounge, a hive of misdeeds. In another age, here is where James “Whitey” Bulger held court, a bookmaker disappeared, at least one bar fight led to a gangland slaying, and a Bulger protégé worked the door. It is now a joint called Fox & the Knife, where you can order $38 scallops. Not your grandfather’s Southie, to say the least.

In the same neighborhood, the so-called Haunty, a notorious cottage where mobsters killed and buried bodies in the basement, has been razed. In its stead, there are condominiums, all of them assessed at more than $1.7 million. (One of the units sold for $1.9 million in 2022.)

“It was always going to be replaced by something like this,” said Joshua Lown a post-doctoral research associate at Boston University’s Initiative on Cities, as he stood next to the building that replaced the Haunty.

A mob associate of Bulger’s once testified that he said he stood guard as Bulger killed Arthur “Bucky” Barrett, 45; Deborah Hussey, 26; and John McIntyre, 32, on separate occasions inside the Haunty. Their bodies were buried in the dirt cellar. When the house was being sold, they were exhumed and buried on Halloween night 1985 near Florian Hall.

Now at the address, there is a new building featuring a bump-out on a corner, an architectural flick to historic housing in Boston, Lown said in an interview.

“There’s some nod to the triple-decker look,” said Lown.

Gentrification, he said, can be a squishy term.

“Nobody is saying ‘I don’t want nice stuff,’” he said. “What they’re saying is we resist nice stuff because it often brings displacement.”

In the Seaport, the pier where Bulger gunned down two people has become a testament to Boston’s nouveau riche. Nearby are gleaming towers of glass housing biotech companies, trendy cocktail places, and expensive apartments to house the people who work, eat, and drink around there. Much of the neighborhood used to be parking lots.

In Dorchester last year, one restaurant found out what can happen when you fail to account for the grimmer chapters of the city’s history. The owner of Savin Bar and Kitchen was forced to take down a photo of Bulger after local outcry. Neighborhood residents had said the Bulger photo was especially inappropriate considering the mobster brutally killed Eddie Connors, who owned Bulldogs, a restaurant on the same site in the early 1970s.

Farther north, the North End’s Prince Street was once home to the Mafia in Boston. There, federal authorities raided and bugged what was the headquarters of the Angiulo family in the early 1980s. Some things haven’t changed; the building remains in the Angiulo family to this day, according to records with the Suffolk Registry of Deeds. But much has. For one, the North End is considerably less Italian than it was in the heyday of the Boston branch of the Mafia. And the neighborhood, like so much of the city, has been battered by gentrification.

The biggest crime on Prince Street nowadays may be a $19 espresso martini.

Six miles away, there is a house on Guild Street in Medford where a Mafia induction was recorded by federal agents decades ago — a singular coup for American law enforcement.

Here, on Oct. 29, 1989, blood was drawn from each of the inductees’ trigger fingers, a holy card with the image of a family saint was burned, and gangsters recited an oath: “As burns this saint so will burn my soul. I enter alive into this organization and leave it dead.”

There are no indications of that past nowadays, as the neighborhood is a solidly middle-class, suburban enclave just off the Fellsway. Here, gangsters may have come and gone, but real estate remains a good investment. The house where the induction ceremony took place was sold in 2019 for $600,000 and is now likely worth more.

“It comes down to the money,” said Joe Leeman, a retired Boston police lieutenant who is a historic tour guide in Boston. “Everything is so expensive to live here ... so there’s not a lot of nonsense anymore.”

Leeman grew up in Charlestown but has lived in South Boston for years. Both neighborhoods, once home to the more rough-and-tumble elements of the city’s milieu, have evolved. His property value has gone up drastically over the past 10 years, he said.

While Boston’s cost of living is a chief deterrent for organized crime, there may be other factors at play. Namely, the government has legalized some sectors that were key for organized crime for decades. Sports betting is legal in Massachusetts, which cuts into illicit loan sharking and betting operations. Recreational marijuana is also a legal reality in the state, although Leeman acknowledges that the market for harder, still illegal drugs is still very much there.

If the paths for a neighborhood are between remaining intertwined with organized crime and gentrification, Leeman said, without question, the latter is better.

But, nowadays, he said, “There’s no organized crime to speak of.”

Back in Winter Hill, so much has changed for long-term residents like Simione.

“As it should,” she said.

Still, she said, “I was OK with ‘Slummerville.’”

She paused for a moment.

“That’s where I grew up.”

“We were kind of dead in the water,” Evans said in an interview. “I didn’t want to keep staff in the lurch not knowing how long it would take before the hold would be lifted off.”

Evans said he faced a vortex of troubles. A bill that recently passed in the Legislature would double the marijuana stores companies can own, which he said will give an advantage to large, well-funded, out-of-state corporations. A well-heeled competitor who can afford to undercut his prices recently got approval for a downtown store neighboring his. And persistent economic woes caused by dwindling customer spending, plummeting prices, and oversupply in the weed market forced a tough decision to close, Evans said. Pure Oasis has also faced a slew of lawsuits over alleged unpaid debts, court records show.

“I kind of felt like the landscape of cannabis, especially for equity and small operators, was changing,” Evans said. “At one point, equity operators were celebrated, and now we felt like there was no one to turn to.”

Pure Oasis’ problems came amid broader industry turmoil. Thirteen stores shuttered last fiscal year, more than all previous years combined, state data show. A record 24 cannabis companies in January were in receivership, a process similar to bankruptcy, the latest reports show.

Pure Oasis was also working to open a third store in Brighton, a move Evans said could still be possible through loans. Financing the expansion in 2025, he added, strained the business, causing a cascade of missed payments.

Evans, a real estate agent, and his business partner, Kevin Hart, a hospital administrative director, had entered the pot business because of the state’s pioneering marijuana legalization law. Massachusetts was the first in the nation to require that communities hit hardest by marijuana arrests be given full access to the industry. Many states followed suit.

Now, six years after opening his first store, Evans said he feels “abandoned by lawmakers.”

On March 25, the Boston Cannabis Boardgranted approval for Curaleaf, a large national cannabis chain, to open a block and a half from Pure Oasis in downtown, contingent on Curaleaf’s plan to offer downtown equity businesses discounts, officials said. A sweeping cannabis reform bill recently passed by the Legislature would ultimately increase the number of pot shops any entity can own from three to six.

Evans said large companies will now consolidate and wipe out “all the small mom-and-pops.” Attempts by equity operators to lobby for a smaller license cap increase “fell on deaf ears,” he said.

Evans is still looking to reopen his Dorchester store, likely with the help of an operating partner. The top priority remains lifting the tax lien and paying staff, he said.

If Evans and Hart couldn’t succeed, that’s a bad sign for others in the state’s social equity programs with less education and business experience, said Laury Lucien, a social equity advocate who advises the Cannabis Control Commission.

“These guys from Pure Oasis, they’re very intelligent human beings,” Lucien said. “That’s what’s so heartbreaking about it.”

Marissa Reese, a budtender at Grove Hall, said customers asked if a closure was coming in recent months.

“But we thought because they were the first dispensary, they would be protected,” Reese said. “Nobody expected this.”

Pure Oasis was part of the state’s economic empowerment program. That program fast-tracked license approvals for entrepreneurs from disproportionately Black and Latino communities with high rates of marijuana arrests.

In 2025, the company was selected to receive $50,000 through the state’s social equity fund, despite applying for more than $1 million to cover costs for its third dispensary in Brighton, Evans said. To make up the remaining funds, Pure Oasis diverted money from daily operations last year, Evans said. In February he also told the Globe he had taken out a high-interest loan.

Last month, the social equity fund awarded Pure Oasis another $300,000, the maximum amount allowed.

Evans said he planned to use that money to pay the taxes owed.

But the grant money has yet to arrive, with no clear timeline, he added. (A spokesperson for the Executive Office of Economic Development said awardees were notified that the contracting process to be able to receive the money is set to start soon.)

The company has tried unsuccessfully to set up a payment plan with the Department of Revenue, Evans said.

The Department of Revenue declined to comment, citing taxpayer confidentiality.

Last year, Pure Oasis owed another $178,000 in state taxes, which was paid, records show. The company had a different federal tax lien for $4.1 million filed in August 2024, records show, but the company structured a payment plan to resolve it, Evans said.

Still, taxes represent just the beginning of the cannabis seller’s financial woes.

On April 8, a judge ordered Pure Oasis to pay nearly $2.3 million to resolve defaulted mortgage payments on an industrial space in Dighton, outside Taunton, court records show.

That day, signs appeared in the downtown store’s windows saying “closed temporarily,” and Evans emailed employees to say the business had exhausted “every option” and needed to shut down immediately.

“It was totally abrupt,” said Josue Soto Lora, an inventory worker at the Grove Hall store. “It was just an email saying, ‘Hey, we’re closed.’”

Many workers are trying to file for unemployment and get their final paychecks. Some have sent complaints to the attorney general’s office over the money they’re owed, former employees said. A spokesperson for the attorney general said the office was aware of the matter.

The company also faces four pending lawsuits over alleged debts totaling more than $320,000 for cannabis products, construction costs, and contractor services. Separately, in recent months, courts have ordered Pure Oasis to pay roughly $120,500 in unpaid rent and $66,000 for pot product debts, records show.

The company had paid its bills on time for years, but beginning in June 2025 debt issues escalated, with more than $1 million in unpaid debts accumulating in the past six months, said Mike Blumenthal, executive director of Cannabiz Credit Association, which collects self-reported invoice data from more than 130 businesses in Massachusetts.

Across the state, unpaid debt issues among cannabis companies have ballooned in recent years. The recently passed cannabis reform legislation, currently awaiting Governor Maura Healey’s signature, would ramp up debt enforcement by publicizing delinquent companies and restricting their activities, though not until 2028.

Joe Baker, who worked the front desk at the downtown Pure Oasis, said the company was served lawsuits multiple times in his eight months there.

“I honestly didn’t see it coming as far as getting closed down because in my head, I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you probably just didn’t pay some money,’” Baker said. “I didn’t know the depth of how crazy it was.”

Pure Oasis’grand opening in Dorchester in March 2020, with state officials in attendance and lines around the block, was heralded as a proud milestone for the state’s social equity programs.

Lucien, the advocate for social equity in cannabis, said she hopes the state doubles down on its efforts to support disadvantaged businesses, even if these remedies didn’t work in time to save Boston’s first equity retailer.

She said multiple social equity companies are being “kept afloat” by the state’s social equity fund, a recent measure aimed at bolstering these businesses amid high federal taxes and a lack of bank loans. She said the fund is helping address financial pressures for equity operators, though regulatory strains remain. Some, such as Pure Oasis, may not have gotten their financial lifeline soon enough, Lucien added.

“It might have been a little bit too late for them, perhaps,” she said. “So long as marijuana is federally prohibited and banks are not making loans available to people, we’re going to see this happening quite a bit.”

It’s not just gas stations where Massachusetts consumers are seeing erratic prices. It’s also in the produce section at Boston-area supermarkets: Some raspberries now cost as much as $18 a pound and blueberries as much as $14 a quart.

According to the USDA’s Consumer Price Index, food prices nationwide in February rose 3.1 percent over the previous year. Fruit decreased in price by 0.3 percent but is expected to rise 0.3 percent in the coming year.

President Trump campaigned on a promise of delivering cheaper groceries. Now, more than a month into a war with Iran, the United States is blockading the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices higher and driving up the cost of transportation.

Even when more New England produce becomes available in the coming months, buying local may not be a workaround, as farmers rely on oil products in their operations, from tractors to fertilizer.

Fruit is different from other foods, with price changes that can be more turbulent. Experts said a trio of factors — oil costs, labor shortages, and tariffs — could drive prices up.

Basically no fruit is in season in Massachusetts right now, so at the big stores, everything’s been shipped.

In a 13-store survey over the weekend, the Globe took a snapshot of Boston-area fruit prices. Trader Joe’s charged 23 cents per individual Chiquita banana. Sounds like a deal, but let’s do a little napkin math. A 6-ounce banana will cost 61 cents a pound at that price. If that banana weighed 4.16 ounces, as the USDA estimates it might, that would be around 88 cents a pound. The national average hit 67 cents in September. You could do better at Wegman’s, Market Basket, and Milton’s Fruit Center Marketplace, where bananas cost 49 cents per pound.

At a Brookline Stop & Shop, Cosmic Crisp apples cost 77 cents per pound with a coupon. The same apples were $2.99 per pound at the Roche Bros. in West Roxbury. Somerville’s Market Basket had Cortland apples for 99 cents per pound, while boutique grocer and wine shop Momma’s in Cambridge priced them at $6 a pound.

You can find the trademarked variety “Cotton Candy” green grapes for anywhere between $4.99 and $6.99 per pound, the latter at Milton’s Fruit Center. (There was a taste test, and yes, that name is descriptive.) The cheapest seedless grapes were at Brookline’s Stop & Shop for $1.69 per pound, and the most expensive at Formaggio Kitchen in Cambridge, where green table grapes were $10.95 per pound. (Nobody goes to Formaggio to bargain shop.)

With bags of grapes typically weighing in at 1.5 to 3 pounds, those prices mean that Massachusetts shoppers can expect to see their grape purchases ring up to almost $10 a bag at many local stores.

Formaggio is also where you can get a pound of anjou pears for $7.75. Move a decimal point and a few miles, and you’ll pay 79 cents for one at Trader Joe’s, or about $1.40 per pound depending on weight.

It may sound like cherry-picking, but pay attention to unit price.

At Roche Bros., a package of premium Oishii strawberries is just a dollar more than a clamshell of Driscoll’s, but by weight they’re considerably more: almost $15 per pound for the Oishiis compared to $5.99 for the conventional berries. A cantaloupe costs 99 cents at Star Market, but you’ll need $5 to take one home from the West Roxbury Roche Bros.

Fruit prices are more susceptible than those of other foods to fluctuations in supply and demand, said William Masters, professor of food economics and policy at Tufts University’s Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy.

“Whole fruit is mostly the price of the fruit itself,” said Masters. “It’s one of those rare grocery prices that actually goes up and down.”

Across all grocery items, Masters said, the more complex the packaging, the more expensive. “Shopping in the center aisles of a grocery store, it’s mostly brand costs, whereas when you’re shopping the periphery of the store, it’s mostly the product price,” he said.

People have taken for granted a substantial decline in the retail cost of produce, which since 2016 has dipped about 10 percent on average compared to the Consumer Price Index, as well as improvements in quality and variety, said Masters. From genetic innovation to improvements in distribution, we’ve come a long way from the days of the maligned Red Delicious apple.

“This has been a golden age for fruits and vegetables in America,” he said.

Rising labor and oil prices, plus tariffs, could bring that period to an end, said Masters. Labor shortfalls will make their mark by summer as the seasonal farm work gets underway, and oil prices are already having an impact.

The changes could hit Massachusetts’ mighty cranberry industry hard.

No one besides Wisconsin grows more cranberries than Massachusetts, which produces about 2 million 100-pound barrels annually (compared to 5 million in Wisconsin). Farmers contract with wholesalers for processing and distribution, who set prices based on supply and demand.

Most cranberries are made into juice, sauce, and nutritional supplements, said James Ross, a Cape Cod cranberry farmer. About 98 percent of his crop is sold wholesale, with just 2 percent sold direct to consumers.

“We had to pay a significantly higher price to fill up our tanks this spring compared to even six months ago,” said Ross. “If we had filled up midwinter, we would have been probably a little bit happier than where we’re at today.”

His operation uses diesel fuel and liquid propane to run pumps and motors, which power his irrigation system and guard against temperature fluctuation.

While Ross said he has some anxiety about fertilizer costs, one benefit to the cranberry being a native fruit here is that the peat bogs where they grow naturally contribute nitrogen, saving up to 50 percent in that type of fertilizer cost, compared to corn, soy, or wheat.

Unlike wholesale growers, local farmers have more flexibility to set their own prices, which could sway some shoppers to buy local instead.

“If supermarket fruit is coming up [in price], the prices might be coming closer to what’s being sold at your local farm stand,” said Karen Schwalbe, executive director of the Massachusetts Farm Bureau Federation. “Farmers are price sensitive. Their crops are perishable, and they want to move them so they can be competitive.”

For large-scale growers, higher retail prices do not necessarily mean bigger profits. In 2025, rising fuel costs, land costs, and weather contributed to a second consecutive year in which US apple growers failed to break even on production costs, reported US Apple, a national apple production association, this month.

“What the retailers charge is entirely up to them,” said Jon Clements, an extension fruit specialist at UMass Amherst. “I will say the apple growers are getting less and less of it.”

It costs more to farm here than in other parts of the country, said Claire Morenon, communications manager for Community Involved in Sustaining Agriculture, a nonprofit based in Deerfield. Oil costs impact heated greenhouses and refrigeration, she said. For farms that recently built new barns or added solar panels, tariffs added to the pain. It seems likely, she said, that locally grown food costs will increase.

Still, Morenon said, consumers can only bear so much.

“Shoppers are pretty price conscious, which makes a lot of sense, because obviously, everyone’s expenses are increasing in the current moment,” she said. “It’s not like wages are rising to meet them.”

As the New England growing season gets underway, Morenon said it’s worth it for fruit consumers to do a price comparison — taking into consideration that local farmers are stewards of the ecosystem — as they decide which apples and blueberries to buy.

“Money that goes to [farmers] circulates within our local economy,” Morenon said. “Locally grown food, especially when it’s picked fresh and it doesn’t have to travel as far to the grocery store, is really a special thing to be putting on your table.”

But critics are skeptical, arguing that the discrepancy raises questions about whether authorities are picking and choosing when to be transparent.

Other cities have issued guidance and timelines to promote consistency. And the public has largely become accustomed to seeing the footage in high-profile cases nationwide, from the recent DUI arrest of Tiger Woods following a crash last month, to George Floyd’s death under an officer’s knee in 2020.

But without a specific policy dictating when bodycam footage is released following police killings, experts say, Boston is behind the curve.

“The reason we have policies is to eliminate decision-making in the moment of crisis. It’s hugely important to building public trust,” said Christine Cole, a Boston-based public safety consultant who’s advised police reform efforts across the country. “Policies also convey your values, your habits, your philosophy — to people inside and outside the department.”

Boston police said they’re committed to building and maintaining public trust while protecting “the integrity of investigations and prosecutions.”

“We are always reviewing our policies to ensure they include clear explanations of our processes,” department spokesperson Mariellen Burns said in a statement. “The goal is to demystify how and why we do things within the criminal justice system.”

Several Boston city councilors have recently raised concerns about the inconsistencies, calling for more transparency. On Wednesday, the council passed an order seeking bodycam footage in a host of cases, including King’s death and other police shootings.

“Why is footage shared in some cases but not others? Is that decision being driven by law and procedure, or is it influenced by pressure, timing, or public reaction?” Councilor Erin Murphy said during a recent hearing. “Because from the outside, without clear and consistent standards, it can start to feel selective.”

In an interview, Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune said other jurisdictions have addressed the issue through policy.

In New York, officials announced last month that they’d codified the practice of releasing bodycam footage within 30 days. The Milwaukee Police Department generally allows up to 15 days. In Baltimore, the police commissioner typically releases video roughly within a week.

Boston police were relatively late to roll out body cameras, which is probably why they’re lagging behind, criminal justice analysts said. The department began a widespread implementation of bodycams in 2019. Since then, police shootings and in-custody deaths have been a rarity in Boston; a higher volume of such tragedies has sometimes spurred policy changes elsewhere.

Dave Fredette, general counsel for the Boston Police Department, told city councilors last week that state public records laws forbid release in the case of King’s death, even though department rules give the commissioner discretion under other circumstances. That’s partly because of the pending criminal charge and anticipated grand jury proceedings, he said.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden has also declined to immediately release the video, saying it would “clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and the future prosecution of this most serious matter.”

But it’ll happen eventually, officials said last week.

“The body camera footage is subject to public records law, and will be released,” Mayor Michelle Wu told reporters. “It is a matter of at what point in the legal process is that appropriate.”

She said that generally the family would be allowed to view the footage before it becomes public.

In 2015, after the Boston police killing of Angelo West, a group of local clergy was invited to view surveillance footage of the shooting. West shot a police officer in the face at point-blank range before other officers opened fire.

Prosecutors and police then decided to release the video publicly while the investigation was still ongoing. Officials said they planned to continue that practice moving forward because it helped tamp down speculation and quell potential rumors.

Then-police commissioner William B. Evans said he supported the decision despite the difficult precedent it could set. “You can’t have it both ways,” he said at the time. “It can’t only happen when things are good. We’re going to have to do it when things are bad, too.”

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper has repeatedly cited the case in support of his recent demands for increased transparency.

“They have set a precedent,” he said during a news conference last week with the King family and their attorneys. “We’ve been pressing the Police Department because of the precedent they’ve already set.”

In addition to filing the order for bodycam footage passed by the council Wednesday, Culpepper proposed officially summoning Police Commissioner Michael Cox and his top deputies before councilors to discuss the department’s protocols, in what would be a rare flex of council authority. Culpepper withdrew the proposal, though, saying he recently spoke to Cox, who agreed to appear voluntarily.

King had long struggled with serious mental illness, according to family. He allegedly committed a carjacking about 15 minutes before police pulled him over. He tried to flee the traffic stop, which is when Officer Nicholas O’Malley fired at the moving vehicle, prosecutors say.

King’s father, Stephenson King Sr., said he wants to watch the video to see his son’s face and learn “what really happened.”

Attorney Ben Crump, who represents the family, questioned why Boston leaders aren’t being more transparent.

“I wonder if . . . they’re afraid of what’s going to be revealed once the body camera video is released,” he said.

Less than a month after King’s death, Boston police shot and killed another man, Jacob Graves, after he stabbed an officer with a sword during a mental health crisis at his apartment, officials said.

The Police Department also declined to release bodycam footage in that case, citing a state statute that says local prosecutors should “direct and control” death investigations. In response to a records request from the Globe this week, police said the Suffolk district attorney’s office “has said not to release the records.” The DA’s office hasn’t responded to a similar request. No criminal charges have been filed in that case.

A report released last year from the Police Executive Research Forum, a Washington-based think tank, recommends that law enforcement agencies proactively release bodycam footage from officer shootings and other serious incidents whenever “they can legally and ethically do so.” That “sends a powerful statement about their commitment to transparency,” the report reads.

However, there are many factors to consider, especially when criminal charges are involved, said PERF executive director Chuck Wexler. It’s never a decision to be made lightly, he said.

“You have the tension here between the public’s right to know and the district attorney’s investigation,” he said. “That puts the police department in a very difficult position.”

But a written policy would be a good start, analysts said.

“There needs to be a rule, something solid,” said Sam Harold, a youth public defender and chair of the city’s Civilian Review Board, which evaluates police misconduct complaints. “I don’t know the answer, but I think there has to be some clarity.”

A Boston man was arraigned Monday for allegedly attacking MBTA Transit Police officers last week, gouging one lawman’s eyes during the tumult, officials said.

Fritznel Jean, 28, pleaded not guilty in Roxbury Municipal Court to charges of assault and battery on a police officer causing serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery on a police officer, and mayhem, legal filings said.

He was ordered held on $100 cash bail, and his bail in a prior case out of Quincy was revoked for 60 days, records show.

His lawyer didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The violence erupted around 8:20 a.m. Friday at Transit police headquarters, where officials were trying to process Jean before his court appearance on the Quincy case alleging shoplifting, said Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office in a statement.

Jean, who’d been arrested the night before, shouted that he wanted to go free when a police officer opened the cell door to escort him to the fingerprinting station, the statement said.

The officer told Jean he had to be booked and then brought to court for the Quincy case, but he remained uncooperative and was told to get back in his cell, authorities said.

“As the officer turned his back to open the cell door, Jean lunged toward the officer, jumped onto his back and bit him on the back of his head,” the statement said.

Hayden’s office said additional cops tried to intervene.

“During the struggle, Jean began to scratch and gouge the first officer’s eyes, causing significant facial injuries,” the statement said. “Another officer witnessed Jean grabbing the first officer’s face while driving his thumbs forcefully into the officer’s eye sockets.”

Jean allegedly tried to bite another officer’s hand before he was restrained, according to the statement.

Paramedics responded and evaluated all the injured officers.

“The first officer suffered severe bruising, burst blood vessels to both eyes, and a cut on his left bottom eye, requiring two stitches,” the statement said.

Hayden in the statement decried Jean’s alleged maelstrom of violence.

“This was an extraordinary burst of violence that hurt one officer and endangered all the others involved,” Hayden said. “I thank the officers for restraining this defendant before he could inflict more injuries and I wish the wounded officer a full and fast recover.”

Jean’s next hearing in the attack case is scheduled for May 12, records show.

What do Mattapoisett, Milton, and West Roxbury have in common?

One has strong Cape-Cod vibes, another is nestled into Blue Hills Reservation, and the third is home to a decadent gelato shop that appears on the Globe’s Best of the Best list.

The answer? They’re all among the 47 communities in Greater Boston that appear on another big list, the 2026 edition of the Globe Magazine’s Top Spots to Live.

How does a town make this tally of the hottest places to call home? We hone in on communities where median home prices have increased the most over a five-year period, through analyzing data from The Warren Group and Redfin. Boiled down, it’s supply and demand: These are the places where people are lining up to live, driving up the prices. Rounding it out is our “May We Suggest” category, selected more subjectively by a small panel of experts.

The deep dive

We took a deep dive into each community to understand what’s driving the interest. There are the usual suspects: highly-rated schools, beaches or green spaces, public transportation.

We found some things rang true across all four pricing tiers, which started at under $750,000. There was a strong desire for community: places where neighbors jump in to help shovel during a snowstorm, or parents can gather as children romp on the playground.

Each has its own allure. “The entire town turns out, and it’s like a little bit of Norman Rockwell,” one resident said of their town. Another raved about theirs: “The community vibe is really strong.” And another: “We’ve tried to keep it a quiet little gem.”

Finances intrude

Sounds great, but anyone who’s peeked at Zillow or Redfin in the last year knows the market feels stuck in a frustratingly familiar place. Mortgage rates are still more than twice what they were in 2021. Owners paying low rates aren’t eager to jump back into the market. Low inventory is keeping competition — and prices — high. To acknowledge these realities, we added a new pricing tier — over $1.25 million.

Add in economic fallout from the Iran war, oil prices, and tariffs, and prospective home buyers are faced with daunting prospects. Still, experts and our data say there are reasons for guarded optimism. Inventory is one: The number of properties coming onto the market edged up in 2025. And the MBTA communities act may be starting to have an impact.

Woven with insights from experts and residents, Top Spots to Live 2026 guides buyers through this admittedly uncertain market. And even if you’re not house hunting, you may learn something about your own town — and the neighbors you may soon be welcoming in.
