As recently as two years ago, the department’s effort torecruit more women and people of color was still struggling through fits and smarts: 71 percent of that academy class was white and 93 percent were men. Demographic data the city posts online show that 73 percent of the department’s employees is white, even though 44 percent of the city population is.

“We’re going to make this a job that’s equal for everyone,” Marshall said Thursday. “Men, women, people of color — whoever wants this job is going to have the opportunity.”

He pointed to the department’s efforts to recruit new firefighters from all of the city’s neighborhoods through the cadet program, as well as its Teen Academy — a paid summer job program for 14- to 18 year-olds that introduces youth to fire services.

The mayor’s office did not immediately provide updated demographic data for the department or its most recent fire cadet class.

“It’s important that we reflect who we are in public safety, in our schools, in the cabinet, and wherever there’s positions of power in the city,” said state Senator Lydia Edwards of East Boston, who has previously criticized the department for its handling of reports of racial and gender discrimination.

But while Marshall’s appointment marks a turning point, Edwards said, she is most impressed by the Boston native’s decades of service, which has earned him the deep respect of his peers.

Wu on Thursday thanked Burke for his leadership, calling him “a shining example of what it means to be a public servant.” She said it is an “honor” to appoint Marshall as his successor.

“He served all across our city in East Boston, Back Bay, Brighton, South Boston, and has seen firsthand the needs of our neighborhoods and the people who call them home,” Wu said of Marshall. ”Rodney has earned a reputation as someone who earns trust, and that’s the kind of leadership this department, the oldest and the best, deserves."

Burke also celebrated Marshall’s promotion, saying he has personally witnessed Marshall’s “steady leadership, sound judgment, and commitment to our mission” over his four years as fire commissioner.

“My title might have been Commissioner, but Chief Marshall and myself were equals,” Burke said. “We did everything together. His instincts were unbelievable when things got tough, ... and I’m proud that it’s him. It couldn’t be a better day.”

Marshall first joined the fire department in 1991, before rising through the ranks to become deputy fire chief in 2022. He was recognized by the department in 1998 for saving several lives during a six-alarm fire, and earned another commendation for rescuing people trapped in a bus in 2013, according to Wu’s office.

Marshall also designed and launched the fire department’s cadet program, which aims to recruit young Boston residents.

Marshall is a Grove Hall native and graduate of Boston College.

Joined by his family, friends, and colleagues on Thursday, Marshall emphasized his commitment to prioritizing the health and safety of Boston residents and his fellow firefighters.

“It takes a team to assemble a 50-foot ladder and stand it up; it takes a team to stretch a two-and-a-half hose line down the hallway; and it’s the strength of that team that makes the difference between life and death on this job,” Marshall said. “I take this job very seriously. I love this department, and I love this city.”

Marshall’s appointment comes after Wu has seen the departure of several high-profile Black officials from her administration in recent months. Jessicah Pierre, Wu’s former chief of communications, left the administration last November after Wu resoundingly won a second term. Segun Idowu, the city’s former chief of economic opportunity and inclusion, resigned from his job in January.

Then last month, Wu’s tourism chief, John Borders IV, stepped down for a role with Boston’s new women’s professional soccer team, Boston Legacy FC.

The Boston Fire Department has long faced criticism for its purportedly change-resistant culture, and lack of diversity, as well as reports of racial discrimination, and sexual harassment and assault.

In early February, 12 elected officials of color, including City Councilor Brian Worrell, sent a letter to Wu urging her to name the city’s first Black fire commissioner.

Marshall’s appointment is well-deserved based solely on his resume, Worrell told the Globe, but it’s also “an inspiration, and it continues to show that Boston will not be a city that sets barriers on any of their residents.”

“This is us continuing to take that step in the right direction, making sure that we create a fire department that is reflective of every neighborhood in the city and that every resident could see themselves in,” Worrell said.

The city hosted the announcement of Marshall’s appointment Thursday at the Berkshire Partners Blue Hill Boys & Girls Club in Dorchester, where his two children attend after school programs.

Whenever he picks them up while in uniform, Marshall said it sparks the curiosity of other kids.

“I love these questions because they present an opportunity to have a conversation about this job, this profession, and this department,” Marshall said. “These conversations open kids’ eyes to what’s possible, and to considering a path” they didn’t know existed.

Marshall said that, as a child growing up, he didn’t know what firefighters did, and remembers walking past a fire house on Washington Street that always had its doors closed. This summer, he said he plans to issue a directive for all fire stations to keep their doors open during the warm months.

“I want city kids, kids from every neighborhood, to be able to walk in, see the trucks, talk to the firefighters, and experience the wonder and excitement of seeing this job up close,” Marshall said.

His hope, he said, is that one of those children will grow up and land the department’s top job — like he did.

School daze: Hampshire College, a small liberal arts school that has been under financial pressure for years, said it would close after the fall semester.

Enrollment at the Amherst campus has declined by half since the early 2000s to about 625 students, according to Hampshire president Jennifer Chrisler.

Its closing is part of a broader trend within higher education, in which smaller private colleges in particular have struggled, while the soaring costs of tuition have prompted more families to question the value of a four-year degree, write the Globe’s Brooke Hauser and Diti Kohli. By one new estimate, more than one-quarter of all private colleges in the US could close or be forced to merge within the next 10 years.

Fewer high school graduates are choosing to go to college amid a “public discussion in this country about the value of a liberal arts education,” Chrisler told The New York Times.

Moreover, higher education is facing an enrollment cliff. The number of college-age students will fall about 15 percent through 2029, according to Carleton College economist Nathan D. Grawe.

The implications for Massachusetts are large. Fifty-nine private, nonprofit colleges and universities contributed $71.1 billion to the state’s economic output, supported more than 320,000 jobs, and generated $2.4 billion in annual tax revenue, according to a 2023 study by Econsult Solutions for the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts.

Texas toast: When it comes to venture financing, Austin is hot on Boston’s heels.

Texas startups gathered $5.8 billion from venture capital investors in the first three months of the year, topping the $5.3 billion for Massachusetts startups, according to research firm PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association.

My colleague Aaron Pressman says it’s likely the first time ever that the Bay State has fallen behind the Lone Star State. In the previous four years, Massachusetts held an average quarterly advantage of $2 billion quarterly over Texas.

Though it may just be a slip in the rankings, and Massachusetts startups could pull back ahead for the rest of the year, the news comes as the state is dealing with several major challenges, Aaron reports. And it continues the narrative of decline for the state that invented venture capital investing and ranked behind only California as recently as 2013, when New York’s position as a capital of finance and media helped it pull ahead.

Trump administration policies, including research cuts and hostility to climate-change initiatives, have hurt the biotech and green-tech industries. The state hasn’t been a player in AI, which is sucking up hundreds of billions of dollars in investments. Texas, meanwhile, has emerged as a power in defense tech, robotics, and energy.

The financing slowdown matters because venture capital is the lifeblood of the life sciences, biotech, and technology sectors at the heart of the state’s high-end economy. Jobs, workers — and tax revenues — will go where that money flows.

Rent ruckus: Sky-high housing costs put the state at a competitive disadvantage to lower-cost rivals, and that disadvantage is getting worse.

A statewide rent control initiative likely headed to the November ballot is being sold as a fix. It isn’t.

The proposal would limit annual rent hikes to the rate of inflation, with a cap of 5 percent. But controlling rents won’t build a single new unit. And by capping landlord returns, it discourages the new construction that is the only real path to keeping rents in check. It would also depress property values, straining municipal budgets.

Last month I argued that the measure is a bad idea. This week, a group of mayors made their case against the initiative.

“What is especially ominous about the proposed ballot question is that it applies not just to the red-hot Boston housing market, but everywhere else in the Commonwealth,” New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell warned. “In Greater New Bedford and other regions where housing developers at times struggle to make their numbers work, it would effectively shut down housing production.”

Mayors from Worcester, Lawrence, Quincy, and Revere also oppose the initiative.

The solution to Massachusetts’ housing crisis isn’t a limit on what landlords can charge. It’s a combination of development incentives and zoning changes that make it easier and more profitable to build.

Final thought: None of this week’s developments — one soft quarter for venture capital, one college closing, one ballot initiative that hasn’t passed — is fatal on its own.

But the trends continue to move in the wrong direction.

In the April 6 editorial, “Bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue still make sense,” the Globe contends that the new center bus lanes on Columbus Avenue “drastically [improved] transit times for bus riders at a modest negative cost to drivers.” This statement is only partially true, since this busway currently ends at the Jackson Square MBTA station and its northern half is yet to be built.

The unreconstructed mile or so from Jackson to Ruggles is a six-lane raceway with traffic often zooming by at speeds well beyond the posted limit, and with multiple accidents over the years, some fatal. As one who lives a block up Cedar Street, I have had a front-row seat to the frequent crashes in front of Roxbury Community College — one of them just after I had crossed Columbus Avenue on foot.

I was eager for the construction of the final mile of this busway and was frustrated to see its originally projected 2025 completion date come and go. Then I was appalled to read in StreetsBlogMASS last month that this project appears to have been indefinitely postponed.

Given what I have witnessed here over more than four decades, I find this delay inexcusable.

I write to you with some updates on a crucial measure that currently shields some 350,000 Haitian nationals across the US from deportation.

The Trump administration since last year has worked to terminate this special class of legal protections granted to Haitians — as well as Hondurans, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans. Formally called Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, the program shields immigrants whose home countries are undergoing armed conflict, environmental disasters, or other extraordinary country conditions, from deportation.

President Trump’s effort to end TPS protection, part of his wider crackdown on legal immigration, has faced mounting legal challenges. The Supreme Court is expected to rule on the case this summer.

Haitians in this country, however, potentially have another lifeline on the horizon. On Thursday, the US House passed bipartisan legislation to extend this status for Haitians through 2029, my colleague Julian E.J. Sorapuru in Washington reported. In a somewhat surprising move, 10 Republicans sided with Democrats, breaking party lines.

In Boston, Haitian American advocates and community leaders were heartened. “It’s a wonderful moment,” said Geralde Gabeau, the executive director of Immigrant Family Services Institute Inc., a Mattapan-based nonprofit and one of the leading groups supporting Haitians in Boston.

Greater Boston has the third largest Haitian diaspora in the country, following Florida and New York. An estimated 45,000 Haitian TPS holders live in Massachusetts, where many work in health care, across nursing homes and hospitals in the region.

Many Haitians in Massachusetts have been living in the region for decades, with some relying on TPS since 2010, when the US government designated Haitian nationals for these protections after an earthquake devastated the country. Now, deadly violence grips the country, with gangs controlling as much as 90% of the country’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

Many Haitians have told me it is too unsafe for them to return, and as the Trump administration has tried to roll back their deportation protections, they’re not sure what comes next for them. The House vote seemed to offer some comfort.

“Knowing all the pain, all of the anxiety and all of the issues that our community is facing – to me, it’s such a big relief for them to know there is hope,” Gabeau told me on Thursday after the House voted on the legislation.

Massachusetts Representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat who is the co-chair for the House Haiti Caucus, has been a staunch advocate in Washington for Haitians under TPS. She pushed forward despite many obstacles, using a procedural measure called a discharge petition in order to get a vote.

Gabeau has been collaborating with Pressley and others to drive the discharge petition forward, even as many people initially had doubts. But they had to try anyway – and now, she said: “We’re going to do everything in our power to get to the finish line.”

On Thursday, Carline Desire had been watching the results of the House vote closely. She leads the Association of Haitian Women in Boston, a Dorchester-based group that works to advance social and economic opportunities for Haitian women across the area. Desire said that Thursday’s vote represented a major step forward for a community that has spent the last year “really on edge.”

She was especially reassured to see that the legislation had bipartisan support. “We are a nation of immigrants. Most immigrants have just been phenomenal in enhancing so many different aspects of our society,” she told me. “There are some who really meet across the aisle to make sure that we do the right thing as a nation.”

Still, the bill faces difficult odds in the Senate, where the legislation needs 60 votes to pass. Advocates in Boston are pushing for the momentum to continue.

“The urgency remains clear: Haitian families cannot wait,” said Ruthzee Louijeune, an at-large city councilor in Boston and the first Haitian American elected to Boston municipal government. “We call on the Senate to move without delay and deliver protections that reflect the realities on the ground.”

It’s time to get back home. ... I’ve really always put my family first."

Powder was one of 400 runners who participated in 26.TRUE on Saturday, a racing event designed as a more inclusive option to the Boston Marathon that takes the runner through the “real” city.

The event, which features a half and full marathon, was held for the first time during the COVID-19 pandemic when PIONEERS Run Crew, Boston’s first Black and brown-led running community, put together a race for runners who’d registered for the canceled Boston Marathon. It was supposed to be a one-time event, but garnered so much interest that it’s now in its sixth year.

Aliese Lash, an event organizer, said 26.TRUE is dedicated to celebrating predominantly Black and brown neighborhoods including Dorchester, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan, which are usually overlooked during marathon weekend.

“These [neighborhoods] are historically underrepresented in running culture,” Lash said. “Something we care a lot about is how to make running more equitable and accessible to people of color and people who may not see themselves as elite, strong runners.”

Unlike traditional road races, 26.TRUE does not receive city-mandated road closures. Participants run on sidewalks and are encouraged to follow pedestrian rules. The marathon requires no qualifying standards, and runners register on a first-come, first-served basis and pay a $100 fee to cover overhead costs. Runners are able to complete 26.TRUE’s full or half-marathon options at their own pace without fear of having nobody left at the finish line.

This year 400 runners participated, the largest number in the event’s history, Lash said.

“We’re really centering it to be a tour of the city as opposed to a competitive race,” Lash said. “26.TRUE is so beautiful because the course itself gives runners a chance to really see the sights, smells, sounds, and culture of the parts of the city that we really love. This is what we call home.”

At the finish line, a block party was in full swing with a DJ, food trucks, and a recovery tent. Runners embraced family and friends and congratulated one another.

Near the finish line, Kelvin Velez stood holding a sign that read, “Jackie! Free tacos at the finish line!”

Velez said that Jackie is his “amazing” younger sister. While she’s not a regular runner, she always tries new things, he said.

“I’m the older brother, so I have her back, of course,” Velez said.

Later, when Jackie Velez crossed the finish line, she said completing the half-marathon was a personal goal of hers that she wanted to make by the time she turned 40 next month.

“This opportunity came, and I just signed up and started training,” she said.

Elsewhere at the block party, Whitney Polich greeted her friend Dylan Reyes, who had just completed the full route, with a sign reading, “Dylan runs on Dunkin!”

Reyes, of Boston, began running two years ago after reaching a low point in his life. He joined PIONEERS Run Crew and said the community helped carry him through.

The 26.TRUE route had excellent energy that kept him and other runners going, he said.

“You get to see so much of the historic parts of the city and so many people are out on their porches cheering,” he said. “It’s just a good vibe, everyone’s happy.”

Reyes is a fan of his friend’s poster, but he swapped Dunkin’ for a Modelo.

“No coffee now, but alcohol is great!” Reyes said, lifting his glass.

Volunteer coordinator Molly Ryan said the event’s 150 volunteers were essential to make 26.TRUE happen. Volunteers handle everything from bib pickup and registration to medal distribution and crowd support.

“Nothing would happen without the volunteers,” Ryan said. “It’s definitely a community effort.”

Powder said she plans to run the full marathon next year. Part of the reason she ran 26.TRUE was for its empowering community. Within the group, she’s seen runners become motivated to take risks like starting businesses and finishing school.

“Running is just the starting point, but the finish line is endless,” she said.

In Massachusetts, roughly 1,300 slots for children across Head Start’s 28 agencies have been eliminated in the last three years because federal funding has plateaued over that time, while the cost of running the program continues to rise, according to the Massachusetts Head Start Association. Nationally, Head Start enrollment dropped from 1.1 million kids in 2013 to around 785,000 in 2022, according to research by the Annie E. Casey Foundation.

“If they didn’t get into a Head Start program, they would be sitting at home,” said Brittany Acosta, a Head Start parent in Dorchester.

It’s teachers are drastically underpaid, and there’s a serious need for a rainy day-type fund should the federal government shut down again, the association says. As they’ve done in years past, state lawmakers have offered to provide financial relief, but the Massachusetts Head Start Association’s request for 3 percent above the amount it received last year, an additional $4.6 million to help its staff keep up with the state’s rising cost of living, so far has not been allocated.

Last year, President Trump’s leaked budget proposal revealed he considered eliminating Head Start entirely. Then, in the summer, he cut off Head Start enrollment for immigrants without legal status. And during the fall’s government shutdown, four Head Start centers in Massachusetts closed because they couldn’t access their funding.

Trump’s latest budget proposal shows a fourth year without increasing funding for the program, which was established in the mid-1960s.

Michelle Haimowitz, executive director of the Massachusetts Head Start Association, said the program doesn’t want to eliminate more child slots than it already has, but paying teachers a competitive salary is equally important in order to keep them from leaving for higher paying jobs. Head Start teachers make under $50,000 annually compared to over $85,000 for the average Massachusetts kindergarten teacher.

“It’s an impossible choice,” Haimowitz said. “When we reduce the size of our programs, we’re not reducing the size of the need.”

Massachusetts is one of few states that supplements federal funding for Head Start, and last year it increased the program’s state grant from $5 million to $20 million, adding to the $189 million in federal aid it receives in this state.

“We can’t run a program without giving staff a raise for three years,” Haimowitz said. “Our next fight now is not just for survival, but it’s for thriving and growth.”

The Massachusetts House Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday released its budget, which doesn’t grant Head Start’s request of a 3 percent boost. But state Representative Christopher Worrell filed an amendment for additional funding. Worrell, whose district covers parts of Dorchester and Roxbury, said he loves Head Start’s embrace of culture, recalling one visit to a center where he could smell staff cooking stew chicken, a traditional Caribbean dish.

“I’ve been to dozens of schools throughout the district, and you don’t get that home-cooked meal,” Worrell said. “[The state is] stepping up and doing the best we can with what we have.”

At the Action for Boston Community Development’s Head Start and Early Head Start center in Dorchester, the children of Classroom 7 arrived one Monday morning and dove into bins of magnetic tiles before their teachers, Paola Polanco and Leolina Rasundar Chinnappa, served breakfast. Acosta dropped off her 4-year-old daughter, Violeta, before reporting to her teaching position at the center, where several other Head Start parents also work.

“It’s important for all Head Start parents to have the opportunity to give their child an experience in a learning environment before they actually start kindergarten,” Acosta said.

Beyond providing early education and care to children of low-income families, from birth to age 5, the program helps them access other resources, including mental health services, SNAP benefits, homelessness assistance, and employment opportunities.

It also serves as daycare for parents who might not be able to afford it, while they’re at work.

Research has shown the importance of preschool in a child’s development with one 2023 study, focused on Boston public preschools, finding that it improves student behavior and increases the likelihood of high school graduation and college enrollment.

For Rickencia Clerveaux and Christopher Mclean, the Dorchester Head Start center is the only place they feel comfortable sending their 3-year-old son, Shontz, who is on the autism spectrum. Shontz’s stimming — repetitive movements that stimulate the senses — has reduced, and his speech has improved since he joined the center in 2024, Clerveaux said.

His parents say he’s also come out of his shell. Mclean now drops his son off and gets a simple “bye” as Shontz joins his classmates, he said.

He and Clerveaux said they appreciate the specialized attention Shontz can receive from teachers, such as when staff identified that Shontz might have hearing issues. His parents were able to follow up with their doctor and get Shontz to have surgery to improve his hearing.

“It’s a safe net for parents,” Clerveaux said. “There’s so many ways that him being here helps him grow better.”

Without Head Start, Clerveaux said a lot of pressure would be put on parents to find care for their children, “knowing that they’re already struggling or not getting the ends to meet.”

“That’s a burden for everybody in the community,” she said. “If there’s no funding, there’s no daycare and parents cannot work.”

“I’ve done a lot of different things in my life, but there’s no question in my mind that the youth development aspect of what I’ve done with kids and tennis in Boston is the most important work I’ve ever done,” said Crane, who has dedicated the last 30 years of his life to youth tennis.

Once upon a time, Crane served as a sports journalist for the New York Post, the defender general of Vermont, and the executive director of the Massachusetts State Ethics Commission.

He has been the head boys’ tennis coach at Latin Academy since 2009, and last season led the Dragons to their first Division 3 semifinal appearance in program history.

This season, the Dragons are trying to repeat that success, and are doing so with players from five Boston high schools (Latin Academy, O’Bryant, Josiah Quincy Upper, East Boston, and New Mission).

Sophomore Mayfre Moreta, a New Mission student, has never crossed paths in the school hallways with his doubles partner, Gio Waterman, who attends Latin Academy, but the pair still managed to rally from a set down to clinch the deciding No. 2 doubles point in last year’s D3 quarterfinals.

“I think [that win] speaks to our identity as a program,” said Waterman. “It’s so nice to play with all these new guys from other city schools. We share that bond of representing the city of Boston.”

Along with the unique co-op structure, Crane runs a no-cut program that carries roughly 35 kids ranging from seventh to 12th grade every year who vary from beginners to experienced tournament players.

“We don’t cut because we want to teach kids from all over the city how to play the game,” said Crane. “We want to give them a sport that they’ll play for the rest of their lives.”

Matteus Washington, a Latin Academy senior, is in his sixth, and final, year with the program. Although Washington has dueled the state’s top players at No. 1 singles this season, he is just as proud that he gets to lead his teammates every day.

“It’s really cool to see how the seventh-graders of this generation look so much like I did in seventh grade,” said Washington, who has posted a 3-3 record this year. “It’s super eye-opening and enriching to be a part of their development.”

Crane recognizes that the team’s makeup is unique and oftentimes difficult to manage.

“Logistically, it’s difficult. The kids are coming from all over the city, and they can’t all show up at the same time because their schools get out at different times,” said Crane.

But above all, Crane is thankful he can give his kids — many of whom come from low-income situations — the chance to play tennis, as well as offer them summer jobs at Tenacity, Sportsmen’s, Franklin Park Tennis Association, and other tennis facilities around the city.

“What motivates me the most is getting to know these kids, building relationships with them, and figuring out how I can be of help to them. I want to help them grow, help them succeed on and off the court, and help them get ready for the rest of their lives.”

Lancaster first responded to the ad at 7:21 a.m. on Nov. 14, 2024, initiating a back-and-forth conversation that continued into the afternoon, according to court records. He repeatedly asked undercover agents for reassurance that they weren’t with the police, then confirmed his intentions.

“I’ll be there at 3:15,” he wrote.

While in the hotel parking lot, Lancaster expressed nervousness about the transaction and sought further assurances that an undercover agent wasn’t working with law enforcement, according to an affidavit that prosecutors filed with the court. Then he confirmed he was ready to follow through with the planned encounter, and was arrested.

Lancaster was placed on administrative leave immediately, and the New Hampshire Department of Education suspended his credential eligibility within a week of his arrest.

Lancaster was convicted at the conclusion of a jury trial in May 2025 and detained pending sentencing.

Lancaster’s defense attorney, Charles J. Keefe, urged the court to impose a sentence of five years in prison followed by five years of supervised release, along with a $5,000 penalty. He argued the government had “enticed” his client to commit a crime that didn’t involve any actual children.

In the defense’s sentencing memorandum, Keefe wrote that a search of Lancaster’s phone and laptop “revealed that he had no demonstrated prior interest in underage girls” and that it was an agent who “pushed the conversation” at the hotel when Lancaster expressed reservations.

“Although the jury convicted him in this case, the evidence revealed someone appearing not to be fully committed to going through with the actual act,” Keefe wrote.

Lancaster’s wife and 10 other people, including fellow parishioners from a church in Lancaster, Mass., submitted letters of support ahead of his sentencing.

“The situation that led to his incarceration does not reflect who he truly is,” wrote his wife, Tamires Lancaster.

“Our family stands fully prepared to support him by providing a stable home, guidance, and encouragement as he moves forward,” she added.

The US attorney’s office in New Hampshire argued that a 15-year mandatory minimum sentence applies in this case. The prosecutors recommended that Lancaster be sentenced to nearly 20 years (235 months) in prison, followed by five years of supervised release.

In their sentencing memorandum, assistant US attorneys Matthew Vicinanzo and Anna Krasinski wrote that Lancaster’s plan was egregious, and the actions he took offer strong indications that he believed a real child was at the hotel awaiting his planned abuse.

“The conduct is all the more flagrant when considering that the defendant was employed as a teacher at Manchester West High School, that he worked with children every day, and that he was trained as a mandatory reporter of child abuse in his role as a teacher,” Vicinanzo and Krasinski wrote. “The defendant was in the process of negotiating to abuse a child that day while he was at work in a school building.”

Lancaster had testified that he intended to rescue the 12-year-old girl, but prosecutors said that testimony was inconsistent with his chat messages, his actions at the hotel, and his decision not to report the situation to law enforcement. The jury concluded his testimony was false, so a sentencing enhancement should apply, prosecutors said.

Judge Paul J. Barbadoro, at the federal court in Concord, N.H., ultimately imposed a sentence of 13.5 years (162 months) in prison, followed by five years of supervised release, according to a statement from prosecutors.

Prior to his job at Manchester West High School, Lancaster held a similar position at the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science in Roxbury, Mass., according to court records. He served in the US Navy from 1999 until 2023, has a master’s degree, and had been enrolled in graduate coursework at Northeastern University when he was arrested.

A man died and a police officer was wounded during an exchange of gunfire during a traffic stop in New Hampshire Monday night, authorities said.

The fatal shooting in Ashland, a small town in the Lakes Region, is the latest in a series of officer-involved killings in New England in recent weeks.

During the Monday incident, officials said the man produced a gun when officers from the Ashland Police Department stopped his vehicle and “engaged in an exchange of gunfire with the officers,” New Hampshire Attorney General John M. Formella said.

There is no known threat to the public at this time, Formalla said in a statement.

One officer was shot and is being treated at an area hospital, he said.

The suspect died at the scene. His identity was not disclosed pending notification of next of kin.

An autopsy will be conducted by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

Ngọc-Trân Vũ is a Vietnamese artist, cultural organizer, and strategist based in Dorchester who leads the “1975: A Vietnamese Diaspora Memorial” public art initiative.

I came to Boston as the daughter of a Vietnamese refugee family, including a South Vietnamese veteran, who arrived in 1992 through the US Humanitarian Operation Program. My family first resettled in Dorchester’s Neponset-Port Norfolk neighborhood with support from the International Rescue Committee. Over time, the seven of us also lived in Columbia Point and South Boston’s Old Colony Housing Project before eventually finding our way to Fields Corner, the heart of the Vietnamese community in Boston and New England.

Like many in our community, I grew up in the aftermath of war. I inherited stories of rupture, migration, survival, grief, and rebuilding that were not always spoken but were transmitted through gesture, silence, sacrifice, ritual, and love. Those histories shaped how I understand family, community, and what it means to build a life after displacement. They also shape how I understand public memory.

Boston often speaks of being a “city of belonging.” I believe that aspiration matters. But belonging must be felt in the places we shape, the histories we honor, and the stories we choose to make visible on public land.

For all that Vietnamese families have contributed to the city, there is still no permanent public marker in the heart of Boston’s Little Saigon Cultural District that honors the Vietnamese diaspora and the refugee journeys that brought so many families here.

That is why the proposed “1975: A Vietnamese Diaspora Memorial” at Town Field Park in Dorchester matters so deeply right now.

This is not just a public art project. It is an offering. It is a call to remember, to repair, and to root a history in the public landscape of the city we now call home. It is also a chance for Boston to recognize the Vietnamese diaspora not as a footnote but as part of the living fabric of this city, a community whose labor, memory, resilience, and presence have shaped Dorchester across generations.

The absence of such a marker matters.

The year 1975 marked a profound rupture for Vietnamese people around the world. It marked loss, forced displacement, separation, and the beginning of rebuilding under painful conditions. More than 50 years later, that history still lives in our bodies, our homes, our small businesses, our places of worship, our memories, and our intergenerational relationships. In Fields Corner and throughout Dorchester, Vietnamese families have built lives with resilience and care. We have created culture and community even when public recognition has lagged behind.

A memorial at Town Field Park would help change that.

Public memory is never neutral. What a city chooses to mark permanently on public land reveals whose lives are seen, whose histories are valued, and who is recognized as belonging. For immigrant and refugee communities, especially in this political moment, visibility is not symbolic alone. It is deeply civic. It tells our elders that their journeys matter. It tells younger generations that their histories deserve space. And it tells the broader public that Dorchester’s story is incomplete without the Vietnamese community.

Town Field Park is the heart of a neighborhood where our families have built businesses, raised children, organized community life, and sustained cultural traditions over decades. Our story is rooted here. The “1975: A Vietnamese Diaspora Memorial” would be a public site for remembrance, reflection, learning, gathering, and intergenerational connection in the very district where our histories continue to unfold.

This matters not only for Vietnamese families but also for our neighbors in Dorchester and across the city.

A permanent cultural marker would help recognize Boston’s Little Saigon as an arts and cultural destination in a part of Dorchester that is too often overlooked. It would invite residents, students, and visitors to spend time in the district, learn its history, and support local businesses. It would strengthen neighborhood identity, deepen civic pride, and contribute to the kind of place-based cultural vitality that helps communities thrive. This is what happens when public art is community-driven and grounded in real histories. It becomes more than art. It becomes civic infrastructure for belonging.

Over the past three years, community members, coalition partners, artists, small-business supporters, and cultural organizations have helped shape this vision. What is needed now is for the city of Boston to make room for it on public land, yet so far the city has been largely unresponsive.

If Boston truly wants to be a city of belonging, this is the moment to take action.

Clinton, 46, the daughter of former president Bill Clinton and former secretary of state Hillary Clinton, took on the Boston Marathon for the first time.

When she completed the race, she was greeted by her famous parents at the finish, who gave her a Marathon medal.

Chelsea Clinton is an author, advocate, and the vice chair of the Clinton Foundation, a philanthropic organization aimed at addressing global problems. Clinton has run several marathons and ran as a qualified participant at Boston.

Smith Foundation, an organization dedicated to advancing comprehensive and compassionate care for people affected by paralysis.

Chara finished in 3:18:00.

The Needham native and trailblazing astronaut fell in love with the Boston Marathon as a child and has run it multiple times, including unofficially as a 17-year-old, and on a treadmill while aboard the International Space Station, where she became the first human to complete a marathon in orbit.

A former Navy captain and longtime runner who now lives in rural Maine, Williams, 60, ran from Hopkinton to Boston more than a year after her space mission unexpectedly stretched from weeks into months. Retired from her nearly three-decade-long career with NASA, Williams recently spoke with the Globe about the race.

This year, he raced alongside three of his children — Max, Luke, and Elle — to support his Finish Strong Foundation, which aims to inspire youth through running, reading, and kindness.

Vishal Thapar and Rohini Sen know chai. Combined, the couple estimates they have made about 500,000 cups of the spiced tea in their lives.

However, after emigrating from India, Thapar and Sen noticed the lack of what they considered high-quality chai in the United States. They took matters into their own hands and in 2015 launched Boston Chai Party, selling chai concentrate made from authentic Indian spices.

According to Thapar and Sen, Boston Chai Party is the first East Coast company producing unsweetened chai concentrate without preservatives or additives. In addition to its being sold online, the tea has become a staple in popular Boston-area establishments like Café La Paz, Davis Square Hand Crafted Donuts & Bagels, Goldilox Bagels in Medford, Third Cliff Bakery in Jamaica Plain, and The Mill Cafe in Arlington. Recently, the tea became available at all Flour Bakery locations.

While starting their business, the couple learned that most products in the tea industry come from large international brokers and distributors. As a result, “by the time the tea comes to you, it’s gone through four or five different channels and hands, and most of it is two or three years old,” Thapar explained.

With Boston Chai Party, Thapar and Sen streamlined this process by working directly with tea estates, bypassing the wholesalers. They began to make trips to India to meet with farmers and pluckers, who harvest tea leaves.

They now primarily work with a farm in Assam, India, a location they chose because of their connection to the workers.

“They’re just wonderful, lovely people. The owner of the farm, he takes such good care of them.” said Sen. “It just resonated with us, the environment and the atmosphere and the sense of belonging and the sense of pride that they take in each and every tea leaf that they grow.”

The couple and their children now make regular visits to the farm. Over the course of these trips, Thapar described the workers becoming “part of [their] extended family.”

“It’s a huge motivation for us to run this chai business, to basically go back every year, give them updates, show them how their hard work is translating to actual consumption over here,” said Sen.

Thapar and Sen work to help the Assam community through initiatives like donating feminine hygiene products and distributing supplies to a school that many of the pluckers’ children attend.

While they source their ingredients in India, they make the concentrate itself in Boston. In both places, the couple prioritizes working with businesses and organizations they feel a connection with.

“The center of everything is the relationship[s] that we build as part of this,” said Thapar. “To me, that is more precious than the business itself.”

Using Thapar and Sen’s recipe, the company produces its chai with CommonWealth Kitchen, a nonprofit in Dorchester. It also works with Community Work Services, an organization that helps people find employment opportunities, to fulfill orders.

Even before they launched the company, chai was a big part of the couple’s lives.

“Growing up, our neighbors would come over at the drop of a hat — not appointment based, very spontaneous — just to come have chai,” said Sen. “Chai would signal, ‘OK, put everything aside, time for a break.’”

For the business owners, chai serves as an icebreaker and creates a simple, informal occasion for people to come together. In their own household, Sen and Thapar even use it as a peace offering after arguments.

The couple met in graduate school at the University of Connecticut, and both work in the health care industry doing cancer research. Their medical background taught them about the health benefits of chai, which has been shown to support gut health and boost immunity.

Currently, Thapar and Sen are expanding the business to sell other types of tea, including varieties designed for health benefits like Chamomile Lavender Sleep Support and Honey Lemon Cough & Cold Relief. Since most tea estates specialize in one particular variety, they have begun working with other farms across India to source these new ingredients.

In the future, Thapar and Sen hope to continue expanding their selections and work with tea farmers from other countries like Sri Lanka and Japan.

“It’s inconceivable that somebody would put a bomb in a public place like that,” Narine, 88, said at his Brockton home.

The bombing, which investigators later linked to a broader series of attacks across New England in the months that followed, came at a volatile time in Boston, as the city grappled with racial tensions from school desegregation, economic decline, and deep uncertainty about the future.

Nearly two dozen people were injured in the blast, and while the attack has largely faded into history, for victims such as Narine the consequences have lasted for decades.

The explosion, fueled by at least six sticks of dynamite, ripped apart the courthouse’s second floor, just feet away from where Narine was in line.

“I was close to it . . . too close,” he said, sitting in his living room alongside his wife, Samali Kajubi.

Narine lost his left leg, and his left elbow was shattered so badly it no longer has a joint, he said. He suffered severe burns on his right leg that left deep scars.

Narine was rushed to Massachusetts General Hospital, where he awoke to find his right leg suspended in traction. His other leg was wrapped in bandages that were soaked in blood. A surgeon later told him he only survived the blast because he was in good physical shape.

The explosion knocked down parts of the ceiling, smashed walls and office partitions, and brought down large sections of marble.

In the immediate aftermath, authorities searched for a man who was seen running from the building after leaving a package, but the search was later called off after investigators were given conflicting descriptions of the suspect.

Narine said there was no sign of danger before the blast. He said he later learned that a warning call had been made to the courthouse before the explosion, but the building was never fully cleared, a lapse that Robert Allison, a history professor at Suffolk University, said reflected the lack of coordinated security protocols at the time.

The Globe reported that a courthouse operator had answered a telephone call from a woman who warned that a bomb would go off in 20 minutes. Allison said courthouse officials struggled to determine how seriously to take the threat, or how to respond, and did not order a full evacuation.

“Today, there would be a way of tracking where the phone call was made and who made it,” Allison said. “You couldn’t do that then.”

Court officials believed that if there were a bomb, it would be on the upper floors near a courtroom, and people on those levels were warned of the threat, according to Allison. But people on the lower levels were not notified.

“There was much less of a coordinated response,” he said. “These are things we learn through painful experience.”

Narine said there was no indication of a threat when he entered the courthouse and bounded up the steps to the second floor.

“One or two phone calls had been made, but nobody took the opportunity to say, ‘No, you can’t come in,’ ” he said.

Boston in the mid-1970s was a different city than it is today. Still reeling from the turmoil of court-ordered school desegregation and years of economic stagnation, the city “hadn’t yet figured out what it was going to do next,” Allison said.

The bombing happened just a day before a planned “March for Peace,” part of a broader effort by Mayor Kevin White to mark the nation’s bicentennial and project a sense of unity and renewal.

But the courthouse attack was only the beginning.

In the weeks that followed, radical groups launched a series of attacks across New England against symbols of authority, violence that investigators later connected to the courthouse bombing.

Explosions hit a power facility in Maine in May, and another courthouse in Lowell was bombed in June, injuring a custodian. On a single day in early July, bombs struck an Eastern Airlines plane at Logan Airport, a National Guard armory in Dorchester, and a courthouse in Newburyport. A post office in Seabrook, N.H., was also hit.

Over time, investigators focused on a group that included three figures who were allegedly tied to a radical underground network called the Sam Melville/Jonathan Jackson Unit, later to be known as United Freedom Front. The group allegedly carried out bombings and robberies along the East Coast in the 1970s and early 1980s.

“There was a proliferation of these left-wing groups that wanted to overthrow the government, and they didn’t have a whole lot of coordination among them,” Allison said.

For years, no arrests were made in the courthouse bombing. But more than a decade later, federal authorities launched a sweeping prosecution that charged the three with seditious conspiracy and racketeering tied to a string of bombings, including the attack on the courthouse.

The federal trial in Springfield lasted months, becoming the longest and most expensive trial in state history, the Globe reported. It seemed like a long-awaited chance for justice, but the jury was unable to reach a verdict, and a mistrial was declared in November 1989.

Prosecutors considered trying the case again, according to Globe reports from the time, but the defendants were already serving lengthy federal sentences for other bombings. A retrial would be costly and, in the government’s view, unlikely to change the outcome in a meaningful way.

The lack of a resolution is one reason the bombing has faded from modern memory, Allison said.

“You really can’t write history until you know the end,” Allison said.

Narine tried to find justice another way.

A jury found that courthouse officials had been negligent in their response to the threat and awarded Narine $1.5 million. But the state appealed and the award was overturned, apparently because Narine had not established which government entity at the city, state, or federal level was ultimately responsible.

“The court found that there was negligence,” he recalled. “But who was responsible for negligence? I didn’t prove that.”

Narine turned to state politicians for help, and at one point he was offered $100,000 by the Legislature, he said. But he refused, believing it did not properly compensate him for his loss.

The bombing changed the course of Narine’s life but didn’t diminish his ambition. At the time, he was attending Roxbury Community College at night while working days at Tufts University. He finished his degree and later continued his education at Boston University, where he studied creative writing and discovered a love for writing stories. He published a couple of books and built a life around reading and creativity.

Narine learned to walk with a prosthetic, but has faced chronic pain since the attack. He raised a family and has grandchildren now. He still drives; a few years ago he drove alone from Massachusetts to Philadelphia to visit a dying friend.

He said that he rarely thinks about the bombing, and that he “didn’t sustain anger over it.”

But Narine remains frustrated that what happened to him and others in the courthouse that day was never fully explained and over time largely forgotten.

“I lost my leg for no good reason,” he said. “Changed my life, absolutely, with a lot of pain behind it.”

It’s tricky to pinpoint the exact moment that Noah Kahan became Vermont’s poster boy. The Strafford-raised folk artist’s timeline is a blur of earth tones: the verdant mountains on the cover of his breakthrough album, 2022’s “Stick Season”; the camo-colored apparel of his L.L. Bean collaboration; the Kelly green walls surrounding him at Fenway Park, which he sold out twice in 2024 (and returns to for four nights this July).

Consciously or not, Kahan’s been signaling his role as the Green Mountain state’s latest music star, following in the footsteps of acts like Phish and Grace Potter. (The fact that he’s since pulled up stakes for Watertown, then Nashville, is beside the point — you can’t scrub the “Vermont woods” look off that hirsute mug.) His latest album, “The Great Divide,” arrives Friday, and includes material written “next to a pond” in the town of Guilford.

Kahan’s not the only one drawing inspiration from placid surroundings. With Vermont in the national spotlight once again, here’s a handful of performers from the state who’ve recently released new music and have upcoming performances in Greater Boston.

King Tuff, a.k.a. singer and guitarist Kyle Thomas, was enmeshed in Los Angeles’ 2010s music scene, churning out rock tunes that ranged from kaleidoscopic psychedelia to fuzz-coated rippers. But in recent years, the Brattleboro native returned to his home state, where he crafted his latest LP, March’s “MOO,” a sun-streaked collection of garage rock.

“Vermont is full of furniture makers, weavers, dyers, stonemasons, luthiers, quilters, blacksmiths, sign painters, popcorn farmers — tradespeople with very specialized skills who are just doing their own thing and making it work,” Thomas, who plays the Middle East Upstairs May 22, tells the Globe. “I find it really inspiring to be surrounded by people like that. I think of music as a trade as well.”

Another March offering from Vermont’s music scene is the latest LP from Burlington duo Dwight + Nicole, the longtime partnership of Dwight Ritscher and Nicole Nelson (who appeared on season 3 of “The Voice”). The group’s album “Day or Night” is a rich sampler of their pop-tinged blues and soul; perhaps their genre-blending flair is best described by saying that Mavis Staples and Melissa Etheridge are fans. In late June, the pair returns to Greater Boston — where they first linked up in the early aughts — to take the stage at Club Passim.

Another Burlington transplant is Lily Seabird, a Pennsylvania-raised artist who moved to the area “on a whim” when she was 19, not intending to stay past a season. That was eight years ago.

In the last three years, Seabird began putting all of her energy into her music career, yielding the albums “Alas,” and “Trash Mountain” (previously praised in this column as “heart-swelling alt-country”) and most recently, a frenzied folk single called “Demon in Me.”

“Burlington is a small town, and Vermont is pretty far from a lot [of things] — I’m not a skier or anything so I think being bored a lot has lent itself to making a lot of music,” says Seabird, who performs with Saintseneca at Lowell venue Taffeta May 16. “People here really like supporting the arts, too, I think more than the average place, so I’m really grateful for that.”

The tight-knit community is another advantage, she says, citing the satisfaction of witnessing the success of fellow VermontersRobber Robber, as well as Dari Bay, the project of Robber Robber’s drummer, Zack James. The acts are two sides of the same alt-rock coin. Robber Robber, who perform at Deep Cuts in Medford on May 23, streamline turbulent post-punk on the April album “Two Wheels Move the Soul,” while James’s latest work, the singles ”The Joke” and “We’re Gonna Be Okay,” can barely contain their mushrooming fuzz-rock riffs.

That’s just the tip of the Green Mountains’ music scene. Here are a few more artists to add to your palette of Vermont sounds: the liquid dream-pop of Acqua Mossa; Latin psychedelia by Sonido Mal Maïz; Burundian, Somalian, and Tanzanian musical traditions marbled with hip-hop from A2VT; and punchy post-punk delivered by THUS LOVE, my longstanding bet for Vermont’s “next big thing.”

Two Boston men were sentenced to serve 18 to 22 years in state prison for a 2024 shooting in Dorchester that killed a man and injured his son, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Wednesday.

Manuel Guerrero, 19 and Luis Perez, 18, pleaded guilty to manslaughter, armed assault to murder, and home invasion on Tuesday ahead of their trial, which was scheduled to begin next week, prosecutors said in a statement.

Both teenagers were charged with shooting the father and son though it is unclear who actually fired the shots.

On August 12, 2024, Guerrero and Perez were seen on surveillance video getting out of a Kia Forte at the intersection of Trent and Clarkson streets, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said Guerrero and Perez walked up to the third floor of a home on Trent Street and knocked on the door. Leudis Concepcion, 20, opened the door, saw the two masked men with guns, and quickly closed it.

Prosecutors allege that one of the men fired two shots through the door, striking Concepcion in the arm.

Hearing the shots from outside, Concepcion’s father, Leudis Mejia Sanchez, 49, ran up the stairs as Guerrero and Perez ran down, and was shot in the chest at close range, prosecutors said.

Guerrero and Perez ran back to the Kia and drove to Inwood Street, where they got out and walked toward Geneva Avenue, prosecutors said. They were caught on video without their masks, leading investigators to identify them, according to prosecutors.

A few days later, the Kia was found in a Zipcar parking space. Police traced the men’s location through GPS information from the rental car and a GPS monitoring bracelet Perez was wearing for an unrelated armed robbery, prosecutors said.

“The combination of surveillance technology and strong investigative work led to the identification and arrest of these defendants and their eventual confession,” Hayden said. “I extend my deepest sympathies to the family and friends of Leudis Mejia Sanchez, whose last act in life was a valiant effort to help his son.”

In court on Tuesday, Mejia Sanchez’s family remembered him for his “kindness and spirit,” prosecutors said. They described him as a “community leader, a person who touched countless lives with selflessness, always prioritizing others.”

“We’re not seeing a replacement of traditional amenities; we’re seeing an expansion of expectations,” said Shengchao Ying, a senior associate of research and analytics services at Greystar, one of the country’s largest apartment developers. “What’s changing is that residents increasingly want spaces that support how they live and connect day to day.”

Greystar’s 2025 Design Survey found that fitness centers and covered parking remain must-haves for more than 80 percent of renters. But layered on top of those basics is a growing appetite for amenities that blur the line between residential and hospitality.

At Gibson Point Apartments in Revere, developer Redgate transformed a former junkyard into a wellness-forward complex complete with outdoor saunas, cold plunges, a recovery room stocked with compression sleeves and vibrating massage guns, and a treatment room for massages and facials. The inspiration has roots that are more than a century old: the site once hosted a wellness retreat in the late 1800s.

“We don’t think it’s trendy,” Damian Szary, a principal at Redgate, said of the increasing emphasis on wellness. “We think it’s going to stick around for a while.”

What makes Gibson Point’s wellness program function, Szary said, is technology that eliminates friction points. Through a resident app called Elevate Living, prescreened service providers (physical therapists, personal trainers, and even estheticians) are bookable directly from a phone. Residents check availability and schedule an appointment in minutes, while the building avoids carrying the cost of full-time staff. The transaction happens directly between residents and providers while Redgate supplies the space. Apartments lease for $2,300-$4,400 a month.

But the wellness philosophy extends beyond equipment. At 273 Highland in Roxbury, Studio G Architects took a materials and design-driven approach.

“We think about wellness holistically — how a building is experienced, functions, and supports everyday life,” said Gabriela Shelburne, principal at Studio G. “That comes to life through healthier materials, abundant natural light, and shared spaces like the gallery-style gathering area that foster connection just as much as comfort.”

The affordable housing building serves households earning 30 percent to 60 percent of the area median income.

Coworking is another front in this amenities race, but the old model is dead. The conference room with a video setup that inevitably got colonized by one person has given way to something more intentional. Gibson Point features 13 individual glass pods with varied seating — including walking workstations — for a 300-unit building. They’re utilized all the time, Szary said.

Ying at Greystar echoed the shift: “Residents aren’t just looking for a desk, they want spaces that support real productivity, whether that’s private areas for focused work, strong connectivity, or adaptable layouts.”

For luxury condo buyers, the bar is higher still. At The EchelonSeaport, Cottonwood Group built out a PGA golf simulator and tech-enabled sports spaces that became a cornerstone of the sales pitch. The building is now 99 percent sold out. Units range from about 500 to 2,000 square feet and are priced at about $1,700 to $2,400 per square foot with fees ranging from $1.50 to $1.77 per square foot monthly. So, as an example, a 500-square-foot condo could be priced at $850,000 with a monthly fee of $750.

Angelica Nouhi, Cottonwood’s vice president of asset management, sees multisport simulators like those offered at The St. Regis Residences Boston as the next benchmark for residential amenities, alongside fully furnished guest suites that owners can book for visiting friends and family.

As for the broader trajectory, Greystar’s Scott Berka, senior managing director of brand and customer experience, sees amenity design evolving from individual features into something closer to community infrastructure.

“Overall, it points to a broader shift; amenities aren’t just about convenience anymore, but about supporting a more engaging, lifestyle-driven experience,” she said.

“The country is better when we invest in our children,” Ocasio-Cortez, who is joining Pressley in Boston for a fireside chat Friday evening, told reporters after story time. [We’re] ”trying to make sure we invest in child care to every American, health care to every American, and making sure our teachers and our educators are dignified.”

Pressley singled out the Trump administration, which has requested raising defense spending to $1.5 trillion in its proposed 2027 budget, the largest such request in decades.

“We have an occupant in the Oval Office that says we have to fund a war that we don’t even know why we’re there, but we cannot afford to pay for child care,” Pressley said.

Trump’s budget proposal keeps funding to federal early education programs, including Head Start and the Child Care and Development Block Grant, the same as recent years, even as those programs struggle with rising costs. The proposal also eliminates the Preschool Development Block Grant Birth through Five program.

“We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of day care,” Trump said at a private White House event April 1 ahead of a national address about the war in Iran, reported by the Associated Press.

“It’s not possible for us to take care of day care, Medicaid, Medicare — all these individual things,” Trump said. “They can do it on a state basis. You can’t do it on a federal.”

In Massachusetts, state and federally-funded early education programs support more than 111,000 children and families.

Head Start, a federal program founded in the 1960s, has eliminated 1,300 child slots in Massachusetts over the past three years as its federal funding has plateaued, and last year Trump threatened to eliminate the program. Head Start has looked to the state for additional support, and is advocating for an extra $4.6 million in grant funding this year to raise wages and adjust to the rising cost of living.

“I don’t think that the president’s administration right now is friendly to Head Start,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “There are some things that should not be on the table [to be cut], and Head Start should not be off the table.”

The state’s Commonwealth Cares for Children program supports more than 8,000 children, according to the Healey administration. At the local level, Boston Public Schools’ Universal Pre-K program offers free early education through partnerships with home- and community-based centers.

Research shows that investing in early childhood development results in significant gains in children’s health, cognition, and long-term learning.

Pressley said centers like Horizons, an independent, Massachusetts-based nonprofit, support some of the country’s “most vulnerable” families.

“So often, the children that have the greatest need are provided the least amount of support,” Pressley said. “Families are experiencing greater financial hardship and economic anxiety and vulnerabilities each and every day, because of the hostilities of this administration that are not focused on the things that matter most.”

Beyond the impacts on childhood development, Wu, Pressley, and Ocasio-Cortez said early education strengthens the workforce: Parents can leave their kids in good hands while they go to work, thus spurring the economy, they said.

Wu reminisced on a visit to Horizons that she and Pressley made as city councilors in 2017 to discuss the importance of providing child care to homeless families. She said Boston has seen increased public school enrollment since Boston Public Schools expanded its Universal Pre-K program, bringing in home- and community-based centers.

Wu said they don’t view early education, housing, and workforce development as separate issues.

“It’s really one in the same,” Wu said. “By taking care of what matters most, the impact then also ripples out across all of these areas.”

During the story time, young students bounced on their lily pad cushions as the elected officials took turns reading from “Ambitious Girl.” Pressley told the children what her mother always told her, “Don’t let anyone tell you who you are.”

“I am valued. I am loved. I have purpose, hope, and power,” the children said, affirming the words in the book.

“You have power,” one boy told his teacher in turn.

“We’ve got a number of things accomplished,” Jefferson said in an interview. “It was more of a celebration than it was inauguration.”

That approach was echoed by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who described Jefferson as a leader focused on action before recognition.

“[He] didn’t want to get celebrated until he’d actually done the work and could bring us all together with proof of that vision,” Wu said in her remarks.

Since taking office in July 2024, Jefferson has overseen a time of institutional change. Data from the state Department of Higher Education show the college’s enrollment grew 21 percent, from 2,694 students in fiscal 2024, to 3,281 students in fiscal 2025, which ended on June 30.

The college has also secured millions in grants, completed its reaccreditation process, and expanded programming in workforce development, STEM, health care, and clean energy.

Jefferson highlighted the completion of 22 projects in 16 months as a key milestone.

“That is a tremendous achievement,” he said with a smile. “We looked at where our college was and where it needed to go and what projects we need to do to get them there.”

Other initiatives include RCC Connect, a centralized “one-stop shop” for student services. The college has promoted dozens of staff members and improved IT systems.

In his inaugural address, Jefferson outlined a vision of RCC where students gain both academic credentials and practical experience.

“Our vision is to transform Roxbury Community College into a career-ready work college,” Jefferson said, talking about a model for students where every student has at least one paid learn-and-earn opportunity.

That vision is part of the college’s “Roxbury 2030″ strategic plan, which focuses on five priorities: purpose, people, place, programs, and partnerships.

“That’s what we’re doing, students at the center, faculty and staff are around that,” Jefferson said in an interview. “We just want to make sure that we’re providing economic mobility to our students.”

He said they are working on 18 projects following the theme, “transforming today for a better tomorrow.”

At the event, Israul Marrero, the interim chair of the college’s board of trustees, lauded Jefferson’s leadership and focus on student outcomes.

“I know that you will continue to prioritize student experience and will continue to work diligently to provide every student with personalized support needed for long-term success,” Marrero said.

RCC’s origins trace back to community activism in the 1960s when residents opposed the construction of Interstate 95 through Roxbury and instead advocated for an institution that would serve local educational needs.

Jefferson referenced the college’s history in his remarks, describing it as a college built on decades of community effort.

In 2021, RCC was recognized as a Predominantly Black Institution by the US Department of Education, the only one in the Northeast.

Much of the ceremony focused on RCC’s role in expanding access to higher education, particularly for minority students.

“Educational attainment and the economic mobility that comes with it is still too often determined by zip code, income, and race,” Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll said. “It’s exactly why institutions like RCC are so critical.”

For many attendees, the inauguration represented a sense of renewed stability after years of leadership turnover.

Jumaada Abdal-Khallaq Smith, a community volunteer with deep family ties to the college, said she admires Jefferson’s commitment.

“He promised not to leave,” Smith said, talking about the history of unstable leadership. “His consistency is very important ... people are feeling positive about that.”

Jefferson framed the college’s trajectory as a shift from instability to sustained growth, emphasizing long-term leadership and institutional trust.

“We want people to know that we’re here to stay,” he said.

Two years ago, the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce Foundation whipped the city into a frenzy by reporting that a fourth of 20- and 30-somethings were looking to leave here in the next five years.

An update to the study this week offers as much good as it does bad.

Today, 26 percent of the region’s youngest adult cohort are looking to move away from Boston. It’s a “distressing number,” the study says, though at least the outlook has not gotten much worse in the last few years.

Students, single people, and newer residents less than two years from their arrival to Boston are the most likely to leave. That said, fewer people (79 percent in all) are satisfied with their day-to-day lives in town.

Tell me why

The 600 people surveyed ranked job availability, the cost of rent, and safety as the most important factors when deciding whether to stay in Boston. And, shocker: They said local leaders should prioritize creating affordable housing and accessible health care options.

It follows a seemingly endless string of disheartening research about the ways Boston often delays adult milestones, which the Globe has covered over and over and over. Young people in Massachusetts have the fourth-lowest homeownership rate of anywhere in the country. And Bay State couples are typically older than those in all but one state when they get married and have kids.

Anna Giles, a self-certified “city girl” with no plans to leave, said “being in a central location for me is worth paying a little more in rent.” But she feels the same financial pressures as most other 28-year-olds who sacrifice financial security to keep pace with the cost of living.

“I make more money than I’ve ever made in my life,” she said, “but I still cannot save as much as I want to.”

Where are they going?

What is surprising from the Chamber survey is that the South is scooping up Boston’s leftovers. Of the respondents planning to leave Massachusetts, almost half are looking to the southeast and southwest. By comparison, 15 percent are looking to other Northeast states, and 11 percent are eyeing areas in New England.

Warmer and often cheaper, “the South seems to be an attraction these days,” Chamber President and CEO Jim Rooney said. Amber Haskell, the Chamber executive director, quipped that “the worst snowstorm we’ve had in years” might’ve also nudged people towards more tropical climes.

And yet...

There is some good news: Because of the sheer volume of young adults here, Boston still has the highest proportion of people under 34 of the largest American cities. They are having an easier time building community today than a few years ago, the study found. More and more are seeking on-the-job training to advance their careers, or exploring starting their own businesses. And even though complaints about the T abound, most people said they have an easy enough time getting around.

On Monday evening, I’ll be chatting with young Bostonians about how the city can slow outmigration and tackle its biggest challenges. They’ll be refreshments, a prize wheel, and a live art installation. If you care about people staying, or think about leaving yourself, RSVP here.

As Governor Maura Healey put it last month, “there’s work to do, certainly, but there are assets that this state has that other states just don’t.”
