Wu, who ran as a champion for climate issues, faced criticism early in her tenure for not moving faster on climate policy, and did not release a climate plan until her second term. Wu allies said Monday the new plan delivers the comprehensive agenda they had been waiting for, and lays out a clear path to achieving the city’s long-held emissions targets.

“We need to do more than just envision,” Wu said at a news conference, standing before a view of the city from the East Boston Waterfront. “We are taking action.”

The city plans to achieve these cuts primarily by curtailing emissions from buildings and transportation, which account for almost all the city’s greenhouse gas emissions. As the city implements BERDO — an ordinance that requires large buildings to reduce their emissions — officials said they will expand programs supporting building owners as they come into compliance. To reduce emissions from smaller buildings, the city will convene a task force to decarbonize restaurants and consider expanding a program that helps residents switch to electric stoves.

On transportation, the city wants to shift Bostonians away from driving toward walking, biking, and public transportation, while increasing the share of electric cars to about 20 percent of all vehicles. The city will expand electric vehicle charging stations in municipal lots and curbside locations with the goal of ensuring every resident is within a five-minute walk of a station by 2030.

Officials also plan to secure permanent funding for three existing fare-free bus routes and study parking fees, tolls, and congestion charges to dissuade private vehicle trips.

While Wu’s plan offers few specifics, she is all but certain to face resistance to any proposal for congestion pricing or increased fees.

“The economy of Boston is struggling,” said city Councilor Ed Flynn. “Now is not the time for an expensive expansion of city regulations.”

In particular, charging drivers more to use the roads has long been a hard sell in Massachusetts. In 2024, former state transportation secretary Monica Tibbits-Nutt caused an uproar when she mentioned the possibility of tolling vehicles at the state’s borders. Governor Maura Healey promptly walked back the idea and rebuked the secretary for a “very poor choice of words.”

While the plan suggests further study, some said the city should take stronger steps.

Joan Fitzgerald, a Northeastern University public policy and urban affairs professor, noted that Boston has struggled to reduce its transportation emissions. Though she supports congestion pricing, she said the measure would likely face political headwinds and require state approval.

“The city should start enforcing actions that make the things that they have, such as the bus rapid transit, work better,” she said.

The plan also includes previously announced initiatives such as studying the feasibility of harnessing thermal energy from the Boston Harbor and the Charles and Mystic rivers. And the city intends to join a FEMA program that officials say will reduce flood insurance premiums.

Officials said Monday they believe this plan will put Boston on track to reach its 2030 target of cutting emissions in half — an encouraging, and perhaps unexpected, finding given the dismantling of federal climate policy under the Trump administration. In 2022, NU researchers, including Fitzgerald, concluded that the end-of-decade emissions goal was out of reach, barring a dramatic pivot from the city and other leaders.

City climate officials on Monday, though, projected a more optimistic tone. Since 2005, Boston has already reduced its emissions by about 20 percent, the report said. Officials said if they successfully implement existing policies and programs, the city will slash emissions by about 48 percent by 2030 without adding new requirements.

Not everyone was convinced that Boston is on track for those targets.

“Very similar to the Commonwealth and the nation, I think that we are going to be challenged to hit our goal,” said John Walkey, director of climate justice and waterfront initiatives at GreenRoots, an environmental justice group.

He said the initiatives could face funding challenges, especially if the economy takes a turn for the worse. And, he added, the city’s bureaucracy sometimes needs to “get out of its own way.”

Brian Swett, Boston’s chief climate officer, acknowledged implementing existing initiatives successfully will be “a big lift.”

The city has already taken most of the easy steps to decarbonize, Wu said.

“The first steps are the easiest ones, and then every additional percentage towards the end gets harder and harder and harder to do,” she said.

The plan also maps out a strategy for Boston to combat the accelerating impacts of climate change on residents, including worsening heat waves, heavy downpours, and coastal flooding. These impacts aren’t felt equally across the city, officials noted, disproportionately burdening the most vulnerable communities.

By 2030, the city is targeting a 25 percent reduction in heat-related emergency room visits during heat waves. Wu said she will advocate for the state to set a “maximum indoor temperature” during heat emergencies, including preventing utilities from disconnecting customers during periods of extreme heat. To assess how best to combat flooding of basement units, the city has launched a pilot program in Dorchester.

Wu was elected in 2021 on a promise to deliver Boston a “Green New Deal,” a proposal to decarbonize while boosting economic opportunity and combatting inequities. Her campaign plan, from before her first bid for mayor, set far more ambitious targets: zeroing out municipal emissions by 2024 and powering Boston fully on renewables by 2030.

When asked about those earlier ambitious targets, Swett said the city had sought to set goals that are “both ambitious but achievable.”

“There are tweaks to goals over time based on things that may be outside of our control,” he said.

Nonetheless, some climate activists praised the plan as ambitious and credited the mayor for her leadership. They said Boston needed an actionable plan to meet its goals, not additional future targets.

Larry Chretien, executive director of the Green Energy Consumers Alliance, a climate nonprofit, said Wu’s plan creates opportunities for Boston to put “put points on the board,” and keeps the door open for more ambitious targets in the future.

“She’s not backing away from climate commitments,” he said of the mayor.

Lindsey Butler, the executive director of the Boston Green Ribbon Commission, said at the news conference, “At a time when so many leaders have failed us on climate, we continue to be pushed forward.”

Police in Boston are investigating two armed bank robberies less than two hours apart on Tuesday morning.

Doubling down on an appealing communal experience starts with stories an artist feels must be told.

For Psych Drama Company, which produces only one or two plays each year, “theater offers a communal place to talk about complex emotions so we don’t act on them,” says Wendy Lippe, Psych’s producing artistic director and a practicing therapist. Psych Drama’s mission is to integrate theater and psychology, encouraging audience members to share their observations during post-show discussions.

“We choose plays that explore the dialectical tensions we live with every day — light and dark, love and hate. They are better tolerated when we hold them collectively,” she says.

Small theater companies also serve as petri dishes for experimentation — allowing playwrights to try out ideas or push the boundaries of the form. By nurturing new work, they invest in the next generation of theater and prevent the art form from getting stale.

“We’re interested in creating new hybrids of theater and performance,” says Charlotte Meehan, cofounder and executive artistic director of Sleeping Weazel, which is known for multimedia performances.

To accomplish this, Meehan says her company works in “increasing iterations, with workshops and cabarets” as the piece develops.

Investing in the development process is also fundamental to Punctuate4 Productions, says president and artistic director Myriam Cyr.

The company’s projects range from historic dramas, including “Saltonstall’s Trial” and “The Abolitionist’s Refrain” to a musical, “Thru Hike,” based on Appalachian Trail adventures, and adaptations of stories by Agatha Christie and Arthur Conan Doyle.

“We like to be incubators for new work, but we’re also committed to seeing these works have a life beyond us,” says Cyr, who as a freelance director and with Punctuate4 Productions collaborates with a wide range of playwrights, theaters, cultural organizations, and international artists willing to participate in the development process. This iterative, collaborative journey is, says Cyr, “an investment in the next generation of theatrical expression, allowing the form to meet the moment.”

Some companies meet the moment by rooting their work in Boston neighborhoods.

Even with a 30-year track record, Company One’s commitment to community and to nurturing new work keeps them producing stories that resonate within those communities.

“Our loyalty to neighborhoods transcends specific spaces,” says Summer L. Williams, associate artistic director and cofounder of the company. “We’ve developed deep partnerships with the City of Boston, the Boston Public Library, and the BCA, and we are thoughtful about looking at who’s left out of the conversation, what issues community leaders are interested in, and then what story is the best fit for a particular venue.”

Small and fringe companies lack anchor venues and move from one available space to another, adding another pressure to their decision making.

“I am grateful to produce at the BCA, and have a ‘summer home’ at Club Café,” says Lauren Elias, founder and producing artistic director of Hub Theatre Company, “but the space dictates the kind of play that will work.”

“I like to balance thought-provoking plays with theatrical Cheetos,” Elias says. “[The late] Spiro Veloudos taught me that you have to earn the audience’s trust. When you do good work, they are more likely to come to something less well known.”

Danielle Fauteux Jacques founded and has served as Chelsea-based Apollinaire Theatre’s artistic director for 30 years, and is currently co-directing “Dido of Idaho” through May 10. Fauteux Jacques says that when they’re considering titles, the question is simple: “Would we want to see it?” But rather than rely on her own taste, Apollinaire invites a group of people currently involved with the theater to suggest play titles, and then meet and talk about them.

“It tends to be about eight to 10 people who meet two, three times a week for six weeks,” she says. “It’s not a fixed group, but can include actors, designers, anyone involved in behind-the-scenes work. Having different minds in the room opens the discussion up to different viewpoints or ways to stage things within the fringe aesthetic.”

Other small and fringe companies have a culturally specific focus, while understanding how to amplify their stories by partnering with other, more established organizations. Front Porch Arts Collective, CHUANG Stage, and Teatro Chelsea each emerged in response to a desire to tell the stories of communities whose voices haven’t been heard.

“Boston doesn’t get enough credit for how diverse it is,” says Maurice Emmanuel Parent, cofounder and producing artistic director at Front Porch, Boston’s only professional Black theater company. “It’s healthy that Boston is now home to three theater companies telling stories about the specific cultural fabric of the community.”

Hernandez says Teatro Chelsea pays attention to other Latino stories being produced across the country. “Our goal is to produce two full-length shows and the [New Play] Festival each year,” Hernandez says. “We are driven by the stories. The right partners allow us to do more than what we could do on our own.”

Alison Yueming Qu, CHUANG Stage’s executive director, says her company is New England’s first Asian-American theater company to focus on pan-Asian narratives.

“We have our eyes out for bilingual and multilingual stories, and our choice of plays reflects our commitment to producing Asian-American playwrights with a passion for community and locality.”

CHUANG Stage also produces a very intentional roster of events at PAU Arts in Chinatown; last year, it partnered with Company One and Umbrella Stage for “Learning How to Read by Moonlight,” reaching the large Filipino population in Metro West.

“As we grow, we are looking for other neighborhoods where we can produce culturally specific work,” says Qu. “We’d like to reach the Vietnamese community in Dorchester, the Korean community in Allston.

“The city relies on commercial development to provide funding for affordable housing,” said Matthew Kiefer, a land-use attorney for Goulston & Storrs in Boston who frequently represents developers. “The effect of the recent fall-off in construction is that there is just going to be less money available for affordable housing.”

Construction of both commercial development and market-rate housing — two of the top funders of new subsidized units in Boston —has slowed to a crawl as broad shifts in the economy have made it more difficult for developers to build. Few new office and lab projects, which provide millions of dollars in payments to the city’s affordable housing fund, filed plans with the city in 2024 and 2025. And while the city has shoveled money from the COVID-era American Rescue Plan Act funding into subsidized housing projects, that money, too, is running out.

City housing officials are bracing for the possibility that they will be able to fund fewer affordable housing projects in the years to come if the development slowdown persists, dimming one remaining bright spot of Boston’s construction industry.

Development has long been a key economic engine for Boston. The city boasts one of the most valuable markets for new construction in the US, and officials over the years have increasingly sought to take advantage of that status, charging fees to builders to help finance other policy priorities.

That includes affordable housing.

The city’s inclusionary development policy, for example, requires developers of market-rate housing to set aside 20 percent of the units in their projects at affordable rents, or pay a sum equivalent to what it would cost to build that many affordable units.

And Boston’s “linkage” policy requires commercial developers to pay a fixed amount based on the size of their project. A 200,000-square-foot lab project, for instance, would owe the city a little more than $4.6 million in linkage payments.

Those two policies will account for around one-third of the city’s nearly $95 million in funding for subsidized development and preservation in the 2026 fiscal year, and around 42 percent of that budget in the 2027 fiscal year.

Tying so much funding to affordable housing construction can be a highly effective strategy in times of plenty.

In 2022, at the peak of a lab building boom, developers in Boston filed applications for dozens of new projects that were due to pay the city an estimated $61.4 million.

In 2024, buoyed by that surge, the Neighborhood Housing Trust — the city’s fund for affordable housing development — received around $17 million in payments.

All of that money — as well as the $91 million in COVID recovery funding Mayor Michelle Wu allocated for new affordable housing development — helped pay for one of the most prosperous periods for affordable housing development in recent memory.

Between 2021 and 2023, the city permitted 3,488 new income-restricted units, the most in any three-year period since at least the late 1990s. And more is on the way, with some 4,504 units in the pipeline as of December 2025.

“It has been a wonderful couple of years,” said Sheila Dillon, the city’s housing chief. “We have been able to fund a lot of really excellent projects that our residents need.”

In 2023, the city looked to lean even more on commercial development for affordable housing money, raising the proportion of affordable units required in market-rate developments under the IDP from 13 percent to 20 percent, and doubling linkage payment requirements for lab projects.

The idea was to tap into the prosperity that developers were enjoying. When building boomed in Boston, city officials said, money should be set aside to help build homes for low- and middle-income residents, not just those who work in fancy new lab buildings or who could afford luxury condos.

“Developers are making money from these periods of economic prosperity, and it makes sense that that prosperity should be used to benefit people who need it,” said Kiefer. “As a taxpayer in the city of Boston, I would much rather you tap development to fund affordable housing than raise my taxes.”

But those policies “effectively tie this essential public benefit to the health of the macroeconomy,” Kiefer said.

While the city still received around $16 million in 2025 in payments from projects permitted in previous years, payments to the Neighborhood Housing Trust are expected to decline in 2026, as new housing and commercial development in the city have fallen to their lowest level in recent memory.

Only a few projects with linkage obligations filed applications with the city in 2024 and 2025, with $3.6 million in payments expected from projects filed in 2024, and just $2.1 million from those filed in 2025, a drop off of over $59 million compared to 2022.

The decline comes at a time when affordable developers need more money from local and state governments than ever to get their projects off the ground.

Generally, affordable housing development is an expensive endeavor — even more so than market-rate construction — because projects have to meet rigorous energy, accessibility, and design standards. These days, developers of those projects are also grappling with the same factors that have driven the market-rate development decline lately, namely the rising cost of materials.

“There is a lot that goes into building affordable housing,” said Emily Haber, CEO of the Massachusetts Association of Community Development Corporations. “It’s a balance because you want to make the best use of limited funds, but you want to make sure you’re building something high quality with that funding that is going to last for decades.”

The West End library project, for instance, was projected to cost more than $835,000 per unit when it was first proposed in 2023, without factoring in the cost of building the library on the bottom floors. Those costs have since gone up.

Meanwhile, competition is increasing, because some developers who are struggling to finance their market-rate housing projects are these days considering using subsidies to make their projects work. In Dorchester, Samuels & Associates rearranged the two-building second phase of its nearly 500-unit mixed-use DOT Block project. Both buildings were initially planned to be market-rate with a small number of affordable units, but the developer instead made a deal with the city to make one building entirely market-rate to make it easier to finance, and the other entirely affordable so it could tap federal, state, and city subsidies.

While affordable developments utilize a mix of subsidies from the local, state, and federal governments, Boston’s network of small nonprofit developers that build many of the city’s neighborhood-level projects leans hard on city money.

After receiving money from the state, Fenway Forward, a community development corporation in Boston’s Fenway neighborhood, still needed roughly $3 million from the city to break ground and begin building 24 homes for low-income families on the site of a vacant commercial building on Queensberry Street last year.

“When you’re building 24 units of deeply subsidized housing . . . it is expensive and complicated . . . because of the discounted rents,” said Suneeth John, Fenway Forward’s deputy director and head of real estate. “Without both the city and the state contributing, we don’t have a project.”

Her trial finally began earlier this month, and on April 17, a jury found Woods guilty of four counts of assault and battery and two counts of assault in connection with the incident, according to Hampden District Attorney Anthony D. Gulluni’s office.

“I feared intensive medical intervention,” she said. “And as a Black woman, I worried about being pushed into a C-section.”

Nationally, research shows, Black women are far more likely than white women to have C-sections and, in Massachusetts, twice as likely to die during pregnancy or within one year of giving birth.

Gaps in maternal health care, and the disparities associated with them, have grown wider in the past decade, a period during which 13 hospital maternity units have shut down across Massachusetts. State leaders, including Governor Maura Healey, have pointed to birth centers as a lower-cost, lower-intervention alternative, and have allocated millions of dollars in funding to support them.

But even as policy makers devote cash and attention to birth centers, there’s one lingering problem: They’ve been disappearing. And even Seven Sisters, the last freestanding center in the state, teeters on the brink.

Three birth centers in Massachusetts have closed in recent years, largely due to financial strain. A facility at Holyoke Medical Center shut down in 2020, and the North Shore Birth Center at Beverly Hospital closed in December 2022. Cambridge Health Alliance closed its center in mid-Cambridge in 2020, though it is planning to reopen in July.

Elsewhere in New England, options are similarly dwindling. There is one freestanding center in Connecticut, and three in Maine. Of the three remaining in New Hampshire, after two recently closed, Gentle Landing has had to launch a GoFundMe campaign to stay afloat.

Freestanding birth centers offer a different model from hospitals: a home-like setting where midwives — licensed providers trained to support patients through pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period — lead care for low-risk pregnancies. The centers typically offer longer appointments than hospitals, and many patients work with doulas, nonmedical professionals who provide physical and emotional support.

Freestanding birth centers have been associated with lower rates of C-sections, episiotomies, preterm births, and use of labor-inducing drugs like Pitocin, along with higher rates of breastfeeding and patient satisfaction.

These outcomes are often attributed to birth centers’ focus on not using medications during birth and a culture of shared decision-making that empowers patients and contributes to lower stress levels.

At the same time, the centers have limitations. They are designed for low-risk pregnancies and do not typically include physicians or OB/GYNs as part of routine care. They also have restrictions on the procedures they can offer, including the use of epidural anesthesia and surgical interventions. If complications arise during childbirth, patients are transferred to a hospital that is likely to have a neonatal intensive care unit and specialized staff.

In time, Johnson-Nagy, the mother from New Hampshire, would need to face a decision about going to a hospital. And Kim Vongbunyong, a 36-year-old from Conway, also had one of those births that didn’t go as planned.

Vongbunyong and her husband, Craig Christian, spent more than four years trying to get pregnant. When she finally conceived, she chose Seven Sisters for its longer appointments and more attentive personalized care. When she had a brief scare early in her pregnancy, the facility saw her right away.

“I was scanned the same day here. You don’t get that in most places,” Vongbunyong said.

But after her water broke in June and it was time to have her baby, her cervix stopped dilating due to swelling. She eventually needed to transfer to a hospital, as around 15 percent of Seven Sisters patients do.

“One of the nurses came with me and stayed through the transfer process. We didn’t do any paperwork in between,” Vongbunyong said. “She advocated for me and explained everything. I never felt alone.”

Their healthy daughter, Vera, was born the next day.

“It wasn’t the birth I imagined,” Vongbunyong said. “But they knew exactly when to pivot. They gave me the option. That’s what made me feel safe.”

Modern birth centers grew in the 1970s as people sought more control over their health care and explored holistic practices. Today there are more than 400 in the US, though they handle only about 0.5 percent of births. Standards established by the American Association of Birth Centers guide best practices, and each center is nationally accredited and licensed by its state.

When Ginny Miller and her late business partner Kirsten Kowalski-Lane founded Seven Sisters in 2020, it was the first independent, midwife-run birth center in Massachusetts. Miller’s husband constructed the building, and they bootstrapped the operation themselves. Since opening, more than 950 people have received care there, many of whom stay for other services.

“We’ve seen an uptick of people who want to continue here with GYN care,” said Miller, a certified nurse midwife who previously spent 17 years at the now-closed Holyoke Medical Center. “We also do infertility treatments, contraception, hormone replacement, and full scope care.”

On a recent day, three people were in active labor while others were there for prenatal visits, postpartum checkups, and gynecological appointments. Some weren’t patients at all, but friends and neighbors. They were stopping by to drop off clothes or simply to say hello.

On the second level, a weekly postpartum group gathered: 15 parents with a dozen babies, talking through everything from colic, to the high cost of rent, to dealing with grief. In a quieter room, pregnant couples practiced hypnobirthing, a meditative approach that includes visualization to relax and manage pain.

Jennifer Milikowsky of Westhampton first came to Seven Sisters after a miscarriage during the pandemic.

“It was a confusing time on how to interact with the health care system,” said Milikowsky, 38, who was at the clinic recently for a Pap smear. She said the center supported her through infertility treatments and mental health care. Even after her “two dream births there” — Calvin, now 2, and Camden, 1 — she still comes back for care.

Despite demand — Seven Sisters has a months-long wait list even though it doesn’t advertise — birth center leaders say the business model is fundamentally strained.

Reimbursement remains the biggest barrier. Midwives are often paid less than physicians for the same procedures, and insurance billing can be inconsistent and difficult to navigate.

Nearly half of Seven Sisters’ patients are covered by MassHealth, the state Medicaid program, yet reimbursement rates lag behind those of hospitals — the center now gets about $6,000 per birth compared to $7,700 for hospitals. Miller credits MassHealth for increasing the rate by over 60 percent in 2023, but says it’s still not nearly enough.

Miller, 71, doesn’t take a salary. She says she’s saved enough in her previous roles, and many staff members work second jobs to sustain themselves. The center spends significant time negotiating each insurance rate separately, appealing denials, correcting coding issues, and pursuing insurance payments that are delayed and may, in the end, never come.

“A lot of times it just gets lost, and we never get paid,” Miller said. “We’ve been running in a deficit since we started.”

Insurers say hospitals are reimbursed at higher rates because they handle higher-risk deliveries and surgeries, and have to be ready to respond 24/7.

“The higher reimbursement reflects those additional services, as well as their immense overhead and the cost of maintaining a constant state of readiness,” said Amy McHugh, a spokesperson for Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, the state’s largest private insurer. “Birth centers are designed for low-risk pregnancies and have a lower cost structure.”

McHugh declined to discuss reimbursement rates, but said that most claims are processed within 30 days and that Blue Cross is not aware of systemic payment issues.

Still, advocates argue the reimbursement gap is too large and threatens the model’s survival. If a patient at Seven Sisters is transferred during labor to nearby Cooley Dickinson Hospital in Northampton, the birthing center sees its reimbursement cut, despite having already invested time and labor in the birth.

“Something’s gotta give,” Miller said. “We should be paid the same.”

MassHealth, which covers nearly 40 percent of births in Massachusetts, said birth center rates are 70 percent of hospital rates to reflect higher hospital operating costs. They’re lower, but the state still provides one of the highest reimbursement rates in the country.

In recent years, Massachusetts officials have been working hard to expand access to birth centers. In 2024, Healey signed the Maternal Health Law, which removed some barriers. It also created a nine-member maternal health task force that is studying birth centers and disparities and is expected to deliver recommendations this spring.

Last year, the state distributed $2 million in grant payments to Seven Sisters and two centers in the planning stages: Worcester Community Midwifery and Neighborhood Birthing Center in Roxbury.

The state expanded maternal health access to postpartum home visits, and MassHealth began covering doula services and providing equal reimbursement for midwives, whether they work inside or outside a hospital.

Still, workforce shortages persist. The extra time of the midwifery model — which emphasizes hour-long prenatal visits — requires more staffing. There is a limited supply of midwives nationwide, particularly diverse midwives, a gap that advocates say also contributes to disparities in maternal care.

To increase the number of centers, the Department of Public Health has modernized licensure rules, eliminating requirements that freestanding birth centers operate under the supervision of hospitals.

Massachusetts also created a Board of Registration in Midwifery to establish a licensure pathway, and has moved to license lactation consultants.

Meanwhile, new centers have been in development for years. Neighborhood Birth Center in Roxbury hopes to open in 2027, and permits for Worcester Community Midwifery were conditionally approved in October. Two other birth centers are in the early stages of planning. It’s a path forward, but many leaders question whether it’s actually sustainable.

“It feels like we’re trying to redress a system that has historically advantaged obstetrics over midwifery,” said Nashira Brail, founder of the Neighborhood Birth Center and member of the state’s maternal health task force. Neighborhood, a nonprofit, has already raised more than $6 million but still needs additional funding.

As for Miller, she worries about what will happen to her patients if she retires. She hasn’t been able to line up a successor to lead Seven Sisters. “We simply don’t have that money,” she said.

Back in February, Johnson-Nagy and her husband, Aaron, arrived at Seven Sisters from New Hampshire at 1:30 a.m. She labored for eight hours, much of it in the birthing tub, but her son wouldn’t descend.

By early afternoon, after nearly 12 hours of active labor, the decision was made to transfer her to Cooley Dickinson.

“When we transferred, everyone at the hospital knew this wasn’t part of my plan and tried to get me settled and comfortable quickly,” Johnson-Nagy said.

Her midwife aided in the transition and paperwork, and within an hour, Johnson-Nagy had an IV followed by an epidural. By the hospital’s transfer agreement policy, her midwife wasn’t allowed to stay.

By 9 p.m., doctors recommended a C-section, the last thing Johnson-Nagy wanted.

“I cried. I was upset,” she said, beginning to cry at the memory, “but we literally tried everything.”

Her son, Royal, was born at 9:51 p.m., after 24 hours of labor.

Royal was healthy, but her recovery was harder than she expected. Nothing had gone according to plan. But the next day, she felt she had to go back to Seven Sisters to thank them for all that they did. The family would continue to go to the center for checkups and other post-natal care.

When she walked in with Royal, Miller wrapped her in a hug, and the two sank to the floor in tears.

“Nothing went right,” Johnson-Nagy said. “But I’d still choose them. I’m forever grateful for Seven Sisters.”

A Boston Fire Department spokesperson told the Globe on Thursday that Marshall, who was born and raised in Dorchester, was referring to his family and community ties when he answered the question of where he lived. The Globe requested an interview with Marshall, but Wu’s office did not make him available.

For decades, the city’s municipal code has required that city workers live in Boston as a condition of their employment, but the rule is often disregarded or only selectively enforced. There are also various exceptions to the rule: State law exempts teachers from the mandate, and many of the city’s union contracts — including those of the fire department and Boston’s largest police union — allow members to move out of the city after 10 years of service.

The code also exempts firefighters who are appointed to senior management positions, subject to the residency rule, if they are promoted from a union-covered role and have already met the 10-year residency requirement. That exemption means Marshall does not appear to have been in violation of the rule in recent years, as he served as one of the fire department’s chiefs of operations.

The residency requirement does apply, however, to the city’s department heads and cabinet chiefs, including the fire commissioner, but allows for a grace period of six months for appointees to move within city limits, according to the city code.

Veronica Yoo, the city’s chief of communications, emphasized that timeline in response to questions from the Globe about Marshall’s residency, though she did not answer questions about when Marshall plans to move.

“Like his two immediate predecessors before him, incoming Commissioner Marshall will comply with the [residency] requirement,” Yoo told the Globe in a statement Thursday.

Marshall is far from the only senior mayoral appointee to face the prospect of moving upon their promotion. Many officials in former mayor Martin J. Walsh’s administration — including former Boston Redevelopment Authority director Brian Golden, top aide Joseph Rull, and former corporation counsel Eugene L. O’Flaherty — kept homes outside the city during their time at City Hall.

Current Fire Commissioner Paul Burke, who was slated to retire from the role Thursday, moved from his home in Norwell to Roslindale when he was appointed to the job in 2022.

The city’s residency requirement has also been the subject of debate as Boston’s cost of living has skyrocketed, with officials questioning whether the rule places too heavy a burden on city workers, particularly those making lower wages. Wu issued hundreds of waivers of the requirement in her first term in a bid to fill chronically vacant, essential positions — including for lifeguard roles at city pools.

Marshall is set to earn an annual salary of $318,000 per year as Boston’s fire commissioner, according to his employment contract.

Public property records show that Marshall purchased a four-bedroom home in Canton in 1993 and, in December 2020, signed a homestead declaration stating that he and his wife live in, or intend to live in, the home as their primary residence.

According to state campaign finance records, Marshall also made two donations to former Suffolk County district attorney Daniel Conley in 2013 and 2015, listing his Canton property as his home address.

Marshall, 58, is listed under a Dorchester zip code in the city’s payroll records from 2025. Boston property records list Marshall’s parents as the owners of a home in Dorchester, and court documents show Marshall and his two siblings inherited the home when his mother died last year. Those court documents, which Marshall signed last summer, list his address as his Canton home.

At the announcement of his appointment, Wu, other elected officials, and many of Marshall’s colleagues praised him for his decades of service to the city, saying he is widely and deeply respected in the department for his leadership.

The city hosted the event at the Berkshire Partners Blue Hill Boys & Girls Club in Dorchester, where Marshall said his two children attend after-school programs.

Marshall first joined the fire department in 1991, before rising through the ranks to become deputy fire chief in 2022.

He was recognized by the department in 1998 for saving several lives during a six-alarm fire, and earned another commendation for rescuing people trapped in a bus in 2013, according to Wu’s office. He also designed and launched the fire department’s cadet program, which aims to recruit young Boston residents.

His appointment as the city’s first Black fire commissioner marks a historic moment for the department, which has long struggled to diversify its ranks and faced years of allegations of sexism and racism.

Andrew Ryan of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

When he was 16, Richie Parsons, a Dorchester native, flipped through a copy of the Boston Phoenix and spotted an ad for the $8.95 double LP.

Too young to get into the clubs, Parsons bought the record instead. He played it to death, falling through a portal into Boston’s underground.

The bands on the album became Parsons’s “local rock ’n’ roll heroes,” a model for the path that would turn him into one of Boston’s punk rock veterans.

Today, Parsons said, the album functions as a period piece that “really captured the whole scene.” He looks back on the album fondly, crediting it with his first exposure to Boston bands.

Jim Harold, the club’s tough but protective owner, curated the album’s track list, selecting the hardest-working bands. Among them was The Boize, with their song “I Want Sex,” an accurate portrayal of the club’s seedy underbelly.

Another was “Who Needs You,” on which The Real Kids angrily sing about a former lover who has moved on.

“The best thing I ever did was get rid of you,” lead singer John Felice growls into the microphone.

Songs like “At the Rat” and “Boy from Nowhere” name-drop Kenmore Square to enthusiastic screams from the crowd.

At the time, Parsons was working in Filene’s department Store in Downtown Crossing. A co-worker’s boyfriend played in one of The Rat’s bands, and Parsons gathered stories.

“I used to come home and tell my guitar player, ‘I heard about this band and this guy, and they’re playing at this club,’” Parsons said. “It was all the different people from the ‘Live at the Rat’ album.”

On March 16, 1977, The Runaways, the all-female rock band featuring Joan Jett, played their final night at The Rat. An advertisement noted reservations would be held until 8 p.m.

Parsons was desperate to go. Still underage, he called the club and promised he wouldn’t drink. Somehow, it worked.

His English teacher lent him his 35-millimeter camera. Equipped with a roll of slides and a roll of black and whites, Parsons had his first Rat night.

“It was all Boston rock ’n’ roll from there on for me,” Parsons said.

The club itself was a fire hazard. The floors were sticky with beer. The air hung thick with sweat and smoke. The bathrooms were layered with grime. At one point, a urinal was ripped from the wall. Instead of fixing it, men simply used the hole left in the floor.

It was disgusting and beloved.

“That was the charm of it all,” one clubgoer said.

When Kathei Logue, who would later become an influential booking agent for the club, first heard the live album, she was electrified. She remembers playing it at home as her daughter danced to its rhythm.

“I discovered there’s music happening that doesn’t sound like all this stuff I don’t like,” Logue said in an interview. “That wasn’t what was being played on the radio.”

By 1978, she was booking local bands and chasing the newest sounds.

The energy preserved on “Live at the Rat” extended beyond the stage as bands tried and failed to break into the industry, moving without shame.

Across the city in Boston’s long-gone Combat Zone, Elizabeth Brawner danced at the Naked I Cabaret, under the name Kendra Wild. She and another dancer shared an apartment in Kenmore Square, a 2-minute walk from The Rat.

When they weren’t working, they were at the club: dancing, partying, bringing musicians back to their apartment.

“It was the most incredible time of my life,” Brawner said in an interview.

The same recklessness and defiance pulsing through the album’s tracks spilled into Boston’s streets.

Brawner found power in the spandex, leather, and the women who came in to get drunk and find someone to go home with.

“They were outside of the box, didn’t follow the script,” she said. “It was a bubble of creativity.”

The Rathskeller closed in November 1997, after decades of fueling not only punk rockers but lovers of new wave, hardcore, and ska.

In its place now stands Hotel Commonwealth, which pays homage with its Rat Suite. Initially, the hotel hired a specialty firm to locate memorabilia from The Rat.

After six months, the team found nothing, and the suite plan was almost scrapped. Then Henry Santoro, a GBH radio producer and host and an avid member of The Rat community, stepped in.

Santoro secured Willie Alexander’s sticker- and graffiti-covered keyboard that was practically glued to the stage. Any band could play it.

Once word spread that the “godfather of punk” had donated his signature piece, artifacts began pouring in.

“It got to the point where we amassed so much stuff that they had enough [to] switch stuff out,” Santoro said in an interview.

Ken Casey of the Dropkick Murphys donated a signed guitar. Parsons handed over photographs. Dicky Barrett of The Mighty Mighty Bosstones contributed a plaid suit.

Santoro even tracked down the club’s comically ugly 2-foot-tall papier-mache rat, once perched at the end of the bar. An Ohio homeowner had it, and he agreed to sell the sculpture for a few thousand dollars, the only item the hotel paid for.

In 2013, Peter Rinnig, former owner of QRST, a screenprint shop, teamed up with Jim Harold to remaster “Live at the Rat” on CD. They sold around 1,000 copies.

“Somebody was smart enough to roll tape and get these bands to perform,” Santoro said. “It really meant something.”

Nearly five decades since The Rat’s start, longtime rockers remain enthralled. A Facebook group dedicated to The Rathskeller keeps the memories alive, and members scavenge for new scraps of shared histories.

“It was like a home for misfits,” Santoro said. “And we were the misfits.”

“In a time of rapid gentrification and displacement of Black spaces, our fight is not just for survival, but for the right to remain and thrive in the community we have always called home,” Kai Grant said in the video. “We must act quickly to not be uprooted from the ecosystem we have worked so hard to build.”

Their campaign’s aim was to raise funds. But it also raised some eyebrows — and questions.

Many were surprised to learn that the Grants didn’t already own the building outright; they simply had an option to buy it for $1.3 million. Others asked why an organization that had recently been awarded an $823,000city contract for “creative placemaking” would struggle to keep its doors open. And some wondered why Madison Park, a Roxbury nonprofit of long standing, was at odds with a small business that seemed to share its mission.

While the two parties have now reached a tentative detente, the conflict highlights the tenuous status of Black-owned businesses and spaces in Boston, six years after the outpouring of support in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in 2020. And it renewed focus on the persistent challenges facing Nubian Square, a Black commercial hub in the heart of the city that has never quite reached its potential.

In an interview, Kai Grant said their lease agreement with Madison Park “was supposed to be about becoming a model for equity and antidisplacement” that ensured artisans, founders, and microbusinesses could stay in Roxbury. She feared Black Market would lose its space just as the neighborhood begins its long awaited metamorphosis.

“We’ve always had the mindset of creating this idea of Nubian Square as this premiere destination for the city of Boston,” she said. “Are we going to be able to see ourselves in the future that we created?”

But Monica Dean, a longtime community development executive who became Madison Park’s chief executive in February, said that Black Market “has not been able to uphold their end of the bargain,” and that Madison Park would put its own finances at risk if it continued to subsidize their lease. According to documents reviewed by the Globe, the Grants owed $124,229.12 in unpaid rent accrued over 32 months between 2021 and 2023 — a time when Madison Park also covered the cost of repairs, insurance, and real estate taxes.

“We’re a nonprofit, and we’re committed to working with small businesses, entrepreneurs, and those aspiring to become entrepreneurs,” said Dean. But in the case of Black Market, she continued, “we’ve not been able to confirm exactly what their business model is.”

The Grants opened Black Market Nubian in 2017, envisioning a launchpad for Black-owned businesses in the center of the city’s Black core. For years, they hosted a marketplace out of the first floor of the 4,300-square-foot building on Washington Street, offering space to food, fashion, and craft vendors they hoped would plant roots and grow in Nubian Square.

Post-COVID realities and the changing nature of the neighborhood made the Grants rethink that business model, pivoting to position Black Market more as a cultural space — an arts and events venue, and even for a time offering co-working. They’ve partnered with the city on mural installations around Roxbury and for five years have hosted an annual block party, which last year featured artists like Slick Rick and Doug E. Fresh.

Black Market’s work to create space for artists in Roxbury has been formative for creatives like Cedric Douglas, whom the Grants commissioned to paint a massive mural of Donna Summer on the side of the Black Market building in 2024. Douglas said their annual block party not only promotes a message of Black-ownership in the neighborhood, but strengthens community ties and helps inspire the next generation of artists.

“It would be a big loss if they were to leave,” Douglas said.

But the Grants say a confluence of external factors has thwarted their ability to raise enough money to buy their building: rising retail vacancy in Nubian Square; ongoing construction; the migration of the opioid crisis from nearby Mass. and Cass.; and a retreat of civic and philanthropic commitments made during the racial reckoning of 2020 and 2021.

The Grants have also struggled to fulfill their own vision. They were awarded a prized city liquor license in the hopes of hosting more events, but don’t yet have the operating capital to afford the $110,000 it would cost to install a new fire alarm system and meet city codes. And while the city helped them with a $50,000 grant from its Cultural Space Fund toward the purchase of their building in 2023, Kai Grant said the local bank they had partnered with to help complete the deal backed out of the agreement.

“We weren’t able to get the traction we needed to get to the finish line,” she said.

Still, Black Market has received considerable outside support.

In 2024 the city awarded the market the $823,000 contract to implement placemaking efforts in the Roxbury arts corridor along Massachusetts Avenue, Columbus Avenue, and Grove Hall. According to city records, those funds have been paid out regularly for the past two years. The money is now being funneled to contractors to develop Ascension, a performing arts pavilion that’s been proposed for a vacant lot next to Black Market. It is scheduled to open in late summer or early fall.

“In order for us to be a thriving city we need an ecosystem of multicultural business,” said Imari Paris Jeffries, president and chief executive of Embrace Boston. “I’m rooting for all parties involved to get what they need in order to be sustainable.”

The dispute comes at an inflection point for Nubian Square, Jeffries notes. Franklin Cummings Tech last year opened a new campus in the neighborhood, bringing long-sought foot traffic in the form of hundreds of students. After years of delays, the Jazz Urbane nightclub last month secured $2.6 million in financing and is scheduled to open in May.

At the same time, some in the neighborhood are rankled by Mayor Michelle Wu’s recent move to scrap plans to build lab space and affordable housing on a long-empty parcel along Tremont Street, and look at putting a new Madison Park vocational high school there instead. The canceled project was to include a museum and cultural center for Embrace, Jeffries notes, and the lab space would have brought good jobs.

Now, he said, the potential loss of Black Market has drawn additional concerns.

“[The Tremont Street project] was de-designated,” he said, “and to see this other viable commercial space in trouble is disheartening.”

That sentiment is shared by others who want to ensure that longtime local institutions don’t fall through the cracks of Roxbury’s hoped-for resurgence.

The Black Economic Council of Massachusetts recently purchased its own building on Roxbury Street in Nubian Square for $1.5 million. With the neighborhood on the upswing, said executive director Nicole Obi, ownership is key to building wealth and providing stability, for residents and business alike. But no one group can solve the challenges that have plagued Nubian for generations.

“It’s bigger than one organization, it’s really about the whole area,” Obi said. “There is no lack of interest and ideas and plans, but there needs to be coordination.”

Some argue that while the mission of Black Market is well-intended, its execution has fallen short. In the last few weeks their fund-raising effort raised hackles among some locals like Joao Zezito DePina, who took to Facebook asking why in a moment of broad economic hardship, people should be asked to contribute to a “fiscally irresponsible” organization.

“If you have all those resources and you haven’t paid your rent in three years,” said DePina, a florist and community activist who ran for City Council in 2021, “why should we come in and bail you out?”

After hosting a series of events at Black Market over the past two weeks, the Grants were able to raise over $33,000 toward the purchase of their building — one-tenth of what they needed. But for now, it seems they’ll be able to stay put for a little bit longer.

They have come to terms with Madison Park to remain open.

On Thursday, Kai Grant said that they now need to reach a goal of $80,000 instead of the $369,000 they’d set out to raise in their original campaign.

“I just want to respect the process and stay grateful for all the support for the past two weeks, it was incredible and overwhelming,” Grant said. “It’s important to know there’s an opportunity for us to make it to 10 [years].”

Dean said she was disappointed by the narrative that Madison Park was somehow pushing out Black Market. This week, she sent a statement to the Globe saying Madison Park was providing Black Market “with an additional opportunity to fulfill the terms of the original agreement.”

“We’re bound by confidentiality not to discuss the means of such opportunity,“ Dean said, ”but we wish Black Market the best."

Hi there, and welcome back to Immigration Unmasked. Today I have an update for you from my perch on Beacon Hill.

For those or you who’ve been following along, there’s been a months-long push for lawmakers to do more to protect immigrants in Massachusetts from the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

The State House has already passed a bill aiming to do so, and Governor Maura Healey proposed language of her own.

Now, the last piece of the puzzle — the state Senate bill — has been unveiled, and will likely go up for a vote on Tuesday. (My colleague Kelly Garrity has the full story here.)

The wide-ranging proposal hews closely to the version that House lawmakers already passed. That’s a good sign for the chances of a package landing on Healey’s desk, because both chambers have to agree on a final bill before it can become law.

Senators are expected to vote on their bill next week, and then both chambers will hash out their differences before voting on what’s called a “conference report,” or compromise version of the bill.

Once both chambers approve that compromise version, it gets sent to the governor.

From that point, she can sign, veto, or amend parts of the bill.

Here are the highlights of what is inside this time around:

Similar to the House’s so-called PROTECT Act, the Senate bill would ban ICE agents from detaining people in state courthouses. The senators also go further than their House colleagues — they want to extend those protections to other sensitive locations, like child care centers and public schools.

The bill would limit local police’s ability to collaborate and communicate with ICE. They also want to ban local law enforcement from asking people their immigration status.

The legislation would allow residents to sue federal immigration officers, language that Senator Will Brownsberger, from Belmont, proposed earlier this year.

The proposal also pitches banning other states from sending members of its National Guard into Massachusetts without consent from the governor. The idea is to prevent what happened in Chicago, Los Angeles, and Minneapolis, when the federal government deployed the National Guard to help carry out immigration enforcement.

Like Healey’s bill, the legislation would allow parents to set up a pre-arranged guardianship plan for their children in the event that they are detained.

It also seeks to ban government entities from entering into new agreements between ICE and local enforcement. The Massachusetts Department of Correction currently is the only state agency with one of those contracts, also known as a 287(g) agreement.

The bill got the seal of approval from state Senator Adam Gómez, a Springfield Democrat and member of the Legislature’s Black and Latino Caucus, who helped draft an early version of the House’s bill.

“To those immigrant families forced now to live in fear we tell them: We are standing with you. You are not alone. Fear will not win,” Gómez told my colleague in a statement. “We will keep leading and protecting our neighbors from any kind of abuse.”

Other notable votes (er, quotes!) of confidence:

Elizabeth Sweet, executive director of the Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy (MIRA) Coalition and Lenita Reason, executive director of the Brazilian Worker Center: “This bill sends a powerful message to ICE that their illegal actions and harmful tactics are unwelcome in Massachusetts. To keep our communities safe, individuals must be able to trust local officials and law enforcement. When people are afraid to report crimes, seek medical care, or engage with public institutions, entire communities are put at risk.”

Carol Rose, executive director, ACLU of Massachusetts: “We are deeply appreciative of the Senate’s dedication to pushing back on the worst excesses of the Trump administration and ICE’s lawless and brutal tactics in Massachusetts. The Commonwealth needs the PROTECT Act and we need it now.”

Maroni Minter, political director, MIRA Coalition: “Our immigrant neighbors must be able to move safely to work, school, doctors appointments and more without fear that they will never see their loved ones again. The grim reality is that we must pass legislation to protect civil rights and due process from the militaristic actions of our federal government, actions that are incompatible with democratic values.”

“We want to be witnesses to what is going to happen to our futures. ... The future of my family depends on this.”

The Legislature is exploring procurement of wind and solar energy equal to our needs, increased solar panel installation by cities and towns, and ways to support these developments. Massachusetts residents should express their support for these options, which are possible, climate friendly, and produce no nuclear waste.

Donna Trainor

Sherborn

Kate Selig’s front-page article on a possible “nuclear renaissance” in New England points to a vital shift in our regional energy strategy. While the debate often centers on historical safety fears vs. climate goals, the engineering requirements for grid reliability are often overlooked.

According to the ISO-NE 2024 Economic Study, achieving a fully decarbonized New England grid by 2050 is not just a matter of building more wind and solar. Relying solely on renewables would require a massive, arguably unfeasible overbuild of capacity to ensure reliability during the extended overcast and windless periods in winter. The study found that incorporating small modular reactors is a more cost-effective way to meet these reliability needs than relying solely on long-duration battery storage.

When it comes to Boston neighborhoods, using the definite article is far from definitive. For some, adding a “the” before the neighborhood name is only natural, a nod to its unique character and historical identity. It’s always “the” North End. “The” South End. God forbid you drop the “the” from the West End. Someone will want a word.

But bump into someone on the street, and you might well hear them dropping the “the.” I live in Fenway. They work in Back Bay. Let’s grab a drink in Seaport.

“It’s just Back Bay,” Marianne Zemmes, a graduate student at Boston University, said while sitting on a park bench on Commonwealth Avenue. “I’ve never heard of ‘the’ Back Bay, actually.”

Tell that to some residents, and they’ll give you a strange face.

“We always say ‘the’ Back Bay, when somebody asks us where we live,” said Kathy Ennis, 76. “I have no idea, really, why we do that.”

Her husband, David Ennis, 75, took a moment to roll the words over in his mouth.

“‘Back Bay,’” he considered. “I live in ‘Back Bay.’”

After a few seconds, he shook his head. “It doesn’t work,” he said.

For some residents, the distinction is lost completely.

“I’ve never heard the term ‘Seaport,’ except on the signs that I see on the way to the airport,” said Anthony Sammarco, a local historian. “I guess it’s the official name. But do you hear people saying it? No!”

But reality is not so cut and dried. In a poll of a neighborhood Facebook group, 68 percent of respondents said they lived “in Seaport,” versus 32 percent “in the Seaport.” (The sole point of agreement, it seems, is that barely any residents use “South Boston Waterfront,” which is the neighborhood’s official name.)

If residents are split, what does the city have to say?

Official sources aren’t much help. The city website lists every neighborhood without a “the” — even those, like the South End, where the presence of a definite article is hardly controversial. And even those names aren’t “official,” since city planners work in terms of zoning districts rather than traditional neighborhood boundaries.

(For the record, the Globe’s senior copy editor recommends “the” for all relevant neighborhood names.)

So there’s not much agreement one way or the other. Sounds about right for Boston, where seemingly trivial issues can spark sharp debate.

“I think it has a lot to do with the longevity of exposure to the city of Boston, and to the Back Bay neighborhood, specifically,” said Meg Mainzer-Cohen, president of the Back Bay Association. “Whether you grew up here, or whether you more recently came here. I think that’s where the distinctions lie.”

In her experience, longer-term residents typically default to including the definite article, while more recent arrivals “may not have fully adapted the same vernacular.”

That checks out: most histories of the area use “the” Back Bay, dating back to 1857, when city planners first began filling in the marshy water to build housing. So does Henry James, in his Gilded Age novel “The Bostonians,” describing the newly built neighborhood as “a row of houses, impressive ... in their extreme modernness.” (“Don’t you hate the name?” one character quips.)

Ever since, though, “Back Bay” has closed the gap; a review of Google Books data shows that, in written use at least, the two are now virtually neck-and-neck.

For proponents of “the Back Bay,” the article makes a small but crucial distinction; like “the” Ohio State University, it signals something special and unique.

“There are other Back Bays,” Mainzer-Cohen said. “I don’t think the shopping is as good in Back Bay, Antarctica, as it is in ‘the’ Back Bay.”

Calling it “the Fenway,” some say, also helps distinguish the neighborhood (formally a part of Fenway-Kenmore) from the ballpark. That would make sense if it weren’t for a recent social media poll where nearly 90 percent of people said that plain old “Fenway” is just fine.

What to call the waterfront neighborhood with luxury condos and high-end restaurants is a pricklier question, entangled in decades of redevelopment and local squabbling. First proposed as “the Seaport District,” it was officially named “the South Boston Waterfront” — a concession by Mayor Thomas Menino to South Boston politicians that has not stood the test of time.

Developers, for the most part, have ignored the official name in favor of the standalone “Seaport” branding — itself a matter of legal dispute in some cases.

Neighborhood advocate Steve Hollinger said, from his perspective, dropping the “the” is something of a branding scheme. Developers have long sought to establish the neighborhood as “its own thing,” he said, and plenty of residents feel the same way.

“There’s probably more of a hip crowd that calls it ‘Seaport,’ and that’s sort of the target audience of WS Development,” he said, referring to the firm responsible for much of the neighborhood’s transformation. “Whether they’re transplants or not, I don’t know, but [they are] definitely skewing younger.”

WS Development runs bostonseaport.xyz, the all-but-official neighborhood website which almost exclusively uses just “Seaport.” (The domain for bostonseaport.com is still held by Hollinger, who said he “didn’t want them suggesting they own the rights to that word.”)

Hollinger, 63, said that while he probably refers to the neighborhood both ways — “It kind of depends on the context,” he said — most people he knows tend to use the definite article.

But, as Google Books data shows, “the Seaport” loyalists may soon be a minority — if they aren’t already.

So if most neighborhood residents call it “Seaport,” does that make it right?

Maybe, said Margaret Thomas, a linguistics professor at Boston College.

“In each community, people are innovating, unconsciously or self-consciously, to create new forms,” she said. “[Some] people are attracted to new forms. Others are repelled by new forms.”

And it’s the collective “speech community,” she said, that ultimately decides what to call things.

Usually, Thomas said, place names are more stable than other elements of language, which often shift over time.

But that doesn’t mean they can’t evolve as well. We may think of Roxbury as an opaque proper noun today, but the name comes from its stony ground (“Rocksborough”). Other names are even stranger contractions: the original Boston, in Lincolnshire, England, was once St. Botolph’s Town.

“It was [once] a description, but it’s just become a label, like a nonparsable label,” Thomas said.

Perhaps like Seaport.

It’s no surprise, she added, that young people seem to be more likely to drop the “the,” given the generational habit of experimenting with language.

“Young people, teenagers, college students, are kind of a dynamo of linguistic change,” Thomas said.

Look no further than Thomas’s own students. In an informal survey, most indicated they would never say “the” when talking about [the] Seaport, [the] Back Bay, or [the] Fenway. Even those raised in the Boston area said they would drop the definite article at least sometimes.

“The whole system is constantly undergoing change, erosion,” Thomas said. “Like the dunes, they never disappear; they just move around, century after century.”

Hollinger has lived in the Seaport for more than three decades, but said he doesn’t get riled up over a three-letter word. He remembers the naming tug-of-war between Menino and South Boston, something that’s better off in the past.

There are bigger things to be worried about in the neighborhood, he noted.

“I don’t see the world as binary,” Hollinger said. “Whatever you want to call it, call it.”

The MSPCA-Angell is asking for the public’s help to learn more about a hypothermic, severely underweight stray dog found in Dorchester in late April.

Animal control officers brought the dog, a Cane Corso mix, to the Angell Animal Medical Center in Boston on April 22.

Veterinarians said the dog, which staff has named Balboa, arrived in critical condition.

“When Balboa first arrived at our emergency room, he was weak and significantly underweight — to the point that his ribs and hip bones were clearly visible,” Dr. Emily Hussey said in a press release on Friday.

The dog’s body temperature was very low, according to veterinarians.

A dog’s normal body temperature ranges from 101 to 102.5 degrees, and hypothermia can set in when that drops below 95 degrees, officials said.

Balboa’s temperature was just 94.4 degrees upon arrival.

“Thankfully, Balboa came to us when he did,” said Mike Keiley, MSPCA-Angell’s vice president of animal protection. “Our veterinary staff were able to begin stabilizing him by providing heat and offering supportive care.”

Now stable, Balboa has been transferred from the medical center’s intensive care unit to the organization’s animal care and adoption facility, where he continues to recover.

Keiley said it will take time for the dog to regain its health, and food must be reintroduced slowly to avoid refeeding syndrome, a potentially dangerous condition caused by rapid intake of nutrition after being malnourished.

Before becoming available for adoption, Balboa will enter foster care so staff can monitor his recovery and understand his behavior in a home environment. He will later return to the shelter for neutering before being placed for adoption.

The organization’s law enforcement officers are working with Boston Animal Control to determine how the dog came to be malnourished and potentially abandoned. The MSPCA-Angell is asking anyone with information about the dog’s background to come forward. Officials also urge pet owners to seek assistance through MSPCA programs.

“There are still a number of unanswered questions about Balboa’s past. It’s possible his former owner was struggling to care for him,” Keiley said. “If that’s the case, we want them — and anyone else facing a difficult time — to know that we’re here to help connect them with resources.”

Rai’s breakthrough came in 2023, when he co-launched Dorchester’s five-star Comfort Kitchen along with his wife, Nyacko Pearl Perry. Together, they now run Pearl & Law Hospitality, striving to create restaurants that feel like extensions of home. Their latest projects are inside Allston’s Atlas Hotel: There’s Ama, serving global comfort food, and the brand-new Foxglove Terrace, a rooftop sanctuary with live music and glittery city views. We talked about his hospitality philosophy, his opinion on Boston diners, and his most-loathed sushi roll.

What appealed to you about opening in a hotel?

We were definitely thinking of opening a second location and were looking for the right partner. Tishman, the developer, actually reached out to us about this project, and it really made sense.

To be candid about opening restaurants, it’s a very heavy undertaking financially. This project made sense to us because it was already built into a hotel. It’s also serving the Harvard Business School community. It’s a built-in economy. On the internal side, we have a very talented team that needed growth in a different capacity, and this felt like the right fit.

How would you describe the new restaurants to a friend?

Ama, in its literal translation, means mother in Nepali. The whole concept is built on motherhood and caregiving. My mother works at Comfort Kitchen as a prep person, and she really sustained [my wife]’s health during pregnancy by making Nepali chicken soup, a recovery soup. It was very deep and meaningful on that level. And we have a lot of female leadership in our company.

In our world, caregiving is usually not really the front and center in our conversations, but it’s a very meaningful act. The whole point is: We should start seeing this industry as a caregiving industry versus just a service industry.

Foxglove is named after a flower. It’s both medicinal and poisonous. It flowers every other year. It just happened to be in our driveway one summer, and we liked it. Foxglove is definitely a younger version of motherhood, the fruit of caregiving: excitement and joy. Our food is focused on local, sustainable seafood. It’s on a rooftop overlooking Cambridge and Boston. Once we get our entertainment license, we’ll have live music.

What inspired you to enter this industry?

I was born and raised in Nepal, and I have family in Cambridge, and they invited me for Thanksgiving, Christmas, summer vacations.

My very first job was working at Darwin’s, which is no longer in operation. I worked in places like Charlie’s Kitchen and Hi-Rise. I liked the culture. It was really young and vibrant.

What was your first impression of Boston?

I gravitate toward walking cities, where everything is close. It really drew me in, more than any other city in the States. And I really felt that people in Boston are straightforward. They will not mince their words. I’m the same way: very straightforward, very kind, and hospitable.

What’s missing from the Boston food scene, and what does Boston do well?

This one is going to be a little spicy.

I like spicy, and salty.

When I travel to hospitality conferences and summits, one thing that I really see that’s missing is people showing up for you. We have so many great restaurants and concepts. When I [say] showing up, you have to be there in person. You’ve got to bring your body there. You cannot just like a post or share with friends. We have to be present, we’ve got to partake, and it can’t be in silos. And Boston is in many ways, just in geography, very segregated, and I think that makes it a little more difficult. For instance, Cambridge and Dorchester: It might as well be South Carolina and New York. But they’re like a mile apart.

I won’t name the restaurant we went to in Connecticut. It’s a James Beard winner. It was good: really good food and service. I feel like Boston has that but does not get the accolades or exposure.

What’s the hang up? What’s going on?

Maybe it’s this story of Boston itself being an old city and stale. It just pulls us back. And I really think our branding for Boston needs a little update. We’ve got such good seafood here, but that’s rarely mentioned.

How do we fix that?

I think it’s a collective effort. When I think of media in general, and now also influencers, social media folks, I think we spend a lot of time just talking about how beautiful this restaurant is … I think it’s a collective effort, talking about what makes Boston unique, and what really puts us out there. How can we compete with South Carolina, New York City, LA? We have our own brand. We have our own uniqueness. We do things well; we have great chefs.

How would you describe Boston customers?

Loyal during summers and not very loyal during winters. You know, this is something that I’ve been studying for a while. It’s the start of May. Now, restaurants are gearing up for patio season. Everyone is going to get their guests in.

There’s something about the winter in New England. I lived in Minnesota for a couple years. I feel like people there have ways to engage even during the harshest of winters. I’m talking about myself, too: I don’t like getting out during the dead of winter, and I think that’s the time restaurants really need support because it’s so slow.

Where do you like to eat when you’re not working?

It’s changed over time, just because now we have a 3½-year-old. It’s: Where can we take our toddler and be OK? We like the Dumpling House in Central Square. They’ve been there forever. My son loves to eat dumplings, rice, and noodles. We love it, too.

We live in Hyde Park, and Exodus Bagels is one place we love. And then we have Midnight Morning, a brunch restaurant space in Roslindale. It’s really dependent on our lifestyle at the moment.

Is there a restaurant that you really miss that no longer exists?

Yes, where Nyacko and I went for our very first date: City Girl in Inman Square. They had really good brunch and pasta. I don’t remember what we ate. Obviously, they had great food, but it’s just the space, the emotions that we had at that time, how they made us feel. It was such a small, intimate space. I love small, intimate spaces: two servers on the floor and three in the kitchen. You can really feel the energy. But I think they’d been running that restaurant for 15 or 16 years, and it’s taxing.

Speaking of taxing, what’s your advice for someone contemplating opening a restaurant?

For someone not in the industry and who wants to open a restaurant: You should work in a restaurant for at least three months. There’s a very romanticized version of what this business is. It’s a lot of hard work, raw emotions, and the industry itself is very fickle. No holidays.

For someone already in the industry, my advice would be to start with something small, like a pop-up that really would test their concept.

What do you like about this business?

I think this really grounds me in many ways. I don’t imagine myself working 9-to-5 in front of a desk. I come across so many people. I get to work with people from all different backgrounds. It really fuels my passion.

I was raised by a community, and that’s where I feel safe. It’s in my DNA. It’s a very natural thing for me to be in a space like this, meeting chefs, farmers, purveyors, all on a single mission of serving friends and family.

What would you eat for your last meal?

That would have to be my mom’s cooking. Rice, pork belly curry, and mustard greens.

Is there any food that you cannot stand?

My wife and I have this joke. Whenever we go to a sushi place, my wife loves California rolls. And if I were to pick any sushi roll, that would be the last one. They just do not vibe with me. There’s something off-putting about California rolls. I’d rather spend money on something different.

Avra Estiatorio

Nick Tsoulos grew up in coastal Nafpaktos, Greece, fishing with his family and grilling what they caught for dinner. The Avra restaurants he runs with partner Nick Pashalis are inspired by his hometown — loosely. Avra Estiatorio is an export from New York, with branches in Beverly Hills, Dallas, and Miami, and now here in the Lyrik development at the burgeoning intersection of Newbury Street and Mass. Ave. Expect white tablecloths, spiraling stairs, faux olive trees, and fresh seafood — on the grill, in sashimi and ceviche, and on display over ice in the “fish market.” After feasting on oysters and Greek-inspired small plates, choose a whole fish to be grilled and dressed with lemony ladolemono sauce. Boston seems to have an insatiable appetite these days for modern, stylish Greek fare — see: Kaia, Kava, Krasi, and a few that don’t even start with “K” — so there’s an audience here. Is there such a thing as too many? Maybe a good question for the city’s 86,000 steakhouses.

400 Newbury St., Back Bay, Boston, 617-592-8888, www.theavragroup.com/avra-boston

Dalia

The decor is the star at this South Boston stunner from chef Nicholas Dixon and Broadway Restaurant Group (Capri, Prima). No detail has been overlooked, from the retractable glass ceiling in the dining room to the gallery of pet portraits in the fireside lounge. But the heart of this Spanish restaurant is the open kitchen, where a team of chefs cooks octopus tendrils and wagyu beef over live flames. If you can get a reservation at all right now, aim for a seat overlooking the show, where you can sip sherry and sangria while gobbling potato chips with jamon, garlicky shrimp, mini burgers, and hamachi crudo. If Dalia is all about Being Here, the food is a fine supporting player.

429 West Broadway, South Boston, 617-752-0429, www.daliaboston.com

Foxglove Terrace

Earlier this year, Pearl & Law Hospitality Group — behind Comfort Kitchen in Dorchester — began to grow, opening Ama at the Atlas Hotel in Allston. Now they’ve found a way to top it, literally, with Foxglove Terrace, a rooftop cocktail bar open Wednesday through Sunday. Exit the elevator on the 16th floor and find yourself in a space with panoramic views, works by contemporary artists, and dishes and drinks that draw from world influences. It’s open now, so the secret is out, but Pearl & Law has tried to protect its sky-high baby — and you — from the omnipresent, mystery-wrecking gaze of devices. They want this space to be intimate, and visitors to be present with one another. Is this a nice thing we can still have in the year 2026? Please approach with buy-in, for the sake of your experience and ours. We all have to just disconnect and dance, sometimes.

40 Western Ave., Allston, 617-675-8881, Instagram @foxglove.terrace

La Tavernetta

This is the latest chapter in the evolution of chef Douglass Williams, who cooked at Radius and Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and Paris before opening MIDA, first in the South End, then all over town, including East Boston. Wave from its pier to La Tavernetta, Williams’s new wharfside Italian tavern across the way, open 11 a.m. to midnight (1 a.m. Fridays and Saturdays). Find a make-you-a-regular menu with an it’s-an-occasion view: oysters, skewers, wings with caramel-chile sauce, sandwiches like a porchetta Reuben, plus a little pasta and some proteins from the grill with sides. The filling for the house stromboli changes on the regular. There’s plenty of crisp white wine for summer drinking, plus a full cocktail program with low- and no-alcohol options. 45 Lewis St., East Boston, 617-600-8922, www.latavernettaeastie.com

Find me the market report that says Boston should be the next destination for your schmancy steakhouse. So many of these are opening. 131 Seaport Boulevard, Seaport, Boston, 617-362-8881, www.mapleandash.com
