The project is receiving $8.4 million from the city’s Accelerator Fund and $2.1 million from the state Momentum Fund — money that will be repaid once the project is built. (MassHousing is also offering a loan for the project from mortgage lender Berkadia.) The idea is that the funds will eventually be circular. Once the city and the state are paid back, the money can be reinvested in new developments.

The city’s Accelerator Fund for stalled private sector projects is part of a larger $110 million investment in 2024: $50 million was set aside to jump-start stalled apartment projects, $50 million was earmarked for the Boston Housing Authority’s $1.4 billion overhaul of Charlestown’s Bunker Hill public housing complex, and $10 million was set aside for a pilot program targeting new homeownership developments.

Both the Accelerator Fund and the state Momentum Fund, which is also $50 million, are administered by MassHousing, a quasi-state housing agency. While the funds are separate and financed by the state and city, respectively, deploying them together on projects in Boston increases the equity that stalled developments can tap into.

Prior to the Nubian Square project, the Momentum Fund had been used to help launch two projects outside of Boston, with more to come. The Residences at East Milton Square will total 92 apartments on a prominent street in Milton and is under construction with the help of $5 million from the Momentum Fund. The other is a 233-unit mixed-income project near the commuter rail station in Grafton, which received $9 million in equity from the state.

MassHousing eventually hopes to help finance the creation of more than 1,000 new multifamily units through the Momentum Fund.

Several developers have explored using Boston’s Accelerator Fund before the Nubian Square project, to no avail. One project, the 170-unit redevelopment of the former US Postal Service branch on Harvard Avenue in Allston, received approval to utilize the Accelerator Fund before the developer, Eden Properties, eventually landed on a different financing model.

And while builders have at times struggled to use the fund, the Nubian Square developers said it was critical to moving forward their project, which will also preserve the historic former Roxbury Boys Club building on the site.

“The takeout financing provided by the MassHousing Momentum Fund and Boston’s Housing Accelerator Fund is integral to the success of the project, and we are proud to be the first to put this state-city partnership to work,” said Jacob Vance, principal of SV+Partners.

Brown, who lives in Dorchester, was confronted by a state Trooper and an armed Marine veteran, who shot him several times in the extremities. Brown is in custody at a Boston hospital.

The shooting in broad daylight appeared to confirm the worst fears police had about Brown, according to testimony from his sentencing hearing nearly five years ago.

“Mr. Tyler Brown [couldn’t] care less if innocent people get hurt,” Boston police officer Edward Gately III said at Brown’s sentencing in Suffolk Superior Court on Aug. 18, 2021.

During his delivery of an emotional victim impact statement, Gately recounted how Brown fired an estimated 17 rounds at four officers on a Saturday afternoon on May 16, 2020, as they responded to reports of a man threatening people with a gun.

Gately said he was “a firm believer” that when Brown gets out, “he will hurt or … kill someone," according to a recording of the hearing obtained by the Globe.

Gately implored Superior Court Judge Janet L. Sanders to give Brown the maximum sentence, calling him “a very dangerous individual who doesn’t care who he hurts.”

Brown was on probation at the time of the May 2020 shooting. He had been released from prison in January 2020 after serving six years for the stabbing.

“He has shown us how well he has done while he was out on probation for his stabbing,” Gately said, his voice cracking with emotion. “Probation apparently means nothing [to] Mr. Tyler Brown, nor does the value of life.”

Brown has a long criminal history in the Boston area. He took a deal in the May 2020 shooting case, pleading guilty to eight charges.

Prosecutors asked for at least 10 years behind bars, but Brown received a maximum of six years, with credit for about 18 months time served.

The sentence immediately was criticized by both the Suffolk District Attorney at the time, Rachael Rollins, and Boston Police Superintendent-in-Chief Gregory Long. They said the sentence did not reflect the magnitude of the offense.

Judge Sanders said she felt a decade in lock up was too harsh.

Speaking from the bench, Sanders told Brown she was taking a chance by sentencing him to six years, especially since he was admitting to shooting at officers. She also acknowledged Gately’s emotional plea.

Sanders considered a number of factors before announcing her decision, according to an audio recording of the hearing obtained by The Globe.

First, there was a consequential change to Brown’s criminal record after prosecutors moved to vacate his 2009 conviction for cocaine distribution. Brown was among the thousands of defendants whose cases were compromised in the state drug lab scandal involving Annie Dookhan, a former state chemist who admitted to tampering with samples.

Without that conviction on his record, Brown could no longer face a sentence enhancement for armed career criminals; he also no longer qualified for a mandatory 10-year sentence, prosecutors said.

Sanders said many criminal defendants have terrible childhoods during which they experienced abuse — as did Brown. Many also have psychiatric issues, the judge said.

She listed letters of support for Brown , including from then-Acting Mayor Kim Janey’s Office of Returning Citizens, which helps formerly incarcerated people. She said that Despite being incarcerated for much of his adult life, Brown still forged a strong relationship with his two children, the judge noted. He had reached out for mental health treatment just days before the May 2020 shooting, when resources were scarce because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What set Brown apart to her, Sanders said, were the letters of support from family members, from Kevin Sibley, who then worked for the mayor, along with two other self-help organizations for incarcerated people Brown was involved with.

Sanders quoted the letter from the mayor’s Returning Citizens Office: “We believe that Tyler, if he’s provided with reliable opportunities for personal growth, he will be a valuable contributing member of our community.”

“I don’t see letters like that,” the judge said.

But a Superior Court probation officer also called for a lengthy sentence, saying Brown had an eight-page criminal record in Massachusetts, as well as convictions in New Hampshire and Michigan for drug charges, possession of a dangerous weapon, armed robbery, escape through violence, and assault of a prison employee.

“What’s most concerning,” the probation officer said, were the similarities between the stabbing and the May 2020 shooting.

“They both involve Mr. Brown approaching a group of individuals unknown to him and asking, ‘Where are you from,’ followed by the showing or use of a weapon,” the probation officer said. “Probation believes that Mr. Brown is a danger to the community due to his random acts of violence towards strangers.”

Sanders said she was going to rely on her own intuition and trust Brown to make positive decisions in the future.

“While it’s certainly incredibly serious to be shooting at a police officer, there is a difference between shooting at a police officer and shooting a police officer, and the reality is that nobody was injured,” Sanders said.

“I do think that he was out there wildly shooting,” she said. “But I’m not so sure that he was really intending to hurt any particular person, particularly when one understands or takes into account the fact there are mental health issues.”

Sanders reiterated to Brown, “I’m kind of taking a chance on you.”

“I can’t look into a crystal ball and figure out what’s going to happen once you get out. But I do understand that I am taking on risk here, and I just pray that, you know, my intuitions are right and that you have the ability, the smarts, the will, the support, not to go out there and endanger other people like you have in the past.”

Sanders ordered that all of Brown’s charges, including his probation violation, run concurrently with the six-year sentence, and that he serve three years of probation after his release.

The Massachusetts Parole Board agreed to Brown’s prison release on March 26 last year, and Brown was released from MCI-Shirley on May 21. He was allowed to serve the remainder of his sentence under parole supervision.

Members of the parole board noted that while Brown was incarcerated, he had completed a violence reduction program and other classes through a Tufts University program.

Brown is “remorseful about the part he played in the offense, and realizes that this offense could have worked out,” according to a copy of theboard’s ruling.

Brown suffers from mental health disorders, including PTSD, depression and anxiety, and takes medications daily, the ruling said.

Upon release, Brown was ordered to attend classes at Tufts University, attend mental-health counseling, take his medications, and undergo testing for alcohol and illegal drugs, the ruling said.

Now, less than a year later, Brown is facing two counts of armed assault with intent to murder and firearms offenses for Monday’s shooting. His arraignment date has not been scheduled yet.

O’Malley shot and killed a suspect in a carjacking in March. The swift decision to prosecute prompted outrage by the police union and law enforcement officials.

O’Malley, 33, has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter for the death of Stephenson King, 39, who was shot March 11 while he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car. Prosecutors determined that O’Malley had no justification for shooting at a moving vehicle.

“It is disappointing that the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office is choosing to second-guess an officer whose only goal was to protect the public,” O’Malley’s lawyer, David Yannetti, said in an email to the Globe. “We will continue to vigorously defend this officer and this case.”

“The main issue in this case will be who the aggressor really was and whether Officer O’Malley acted in lawful defense,” Yannetti wrote in court filings.

On Wednesday, Yannetti filed several defense motions in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court, in an effort to illustrate “King’s mayhem and reign of terror,” spanning nearly two decades and resulting in more than 17 criminal cases across Massachusetts, court records show.

Over the years, King has been charged with strangulation, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, carjacking, breaking and entering, gun charges, and resisting arrest, according to court filings.

At the time of his death, King was free on bail for at least three separate felony cases, and had active warrants for his arrest, court records said.

O’Malley is seeking King’s mental health, criminal, and court records from all of his past cases, recordings from police body-worn and dash cameras, the medical examiner’s file on King, along with statements taken from O’Malley and witnesses at the scene of the shooting.

O’Malley told investigators that when he shot King, he feared for his own life and for the life of another officer on the scene, believing his colleague was about to be run over.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood. About 15 minutes later, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away, at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

The driver ignored “multiple verbal commands” as officers approached and tried to drive away, police said.

King opened the car window, but did not turn the vehicle off. O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” the police report said.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley fired three shots through the driver’s window, striking King, the report said.

King’s family has contended that he was experiencing a mental health crisis in the hours leading up to the deadly encounter.

In court filings, O’Malley’s lawyer, Yannetti, said King gave “O’Malley no choice that night.”

“Any suggestion that this shooting was precipitated by simply a ‘mental health crisis’ completely misses the point,” Yannetti wrote. “When facing an extremely dangerous threat, there is no time for a police officer to hold a counseling session on the street or to sit down to discuss the feelings of a menace who is intent on using a motor vehicle as a deadly weapon.”

“If a man is going to assault and carjack an innocent woman, then threaten the lives and safety of the public and a police officer, that man needs to be stopped — whether he is in his right mind or not,” according to O’Malley’s motion.

O’Malley’s next court date, a probable-cause hearing, is scheduled for May 21.

Brown was released on parole last year for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in 2020. He was reportedly suicidal in the hours leading up to the Memorial Drive shooting. Brown was released from a psychiatric hospital Friday and was reportedly using crack cocaine, court filings show.

A parole officer called 911 Monday and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester.

The Boston Police Department issued an internal bulletin warned that Brown was “in possession of an assault rifle and stated that he intended to use it.” The memo also referenced the 2020 incident when Brown opened fire on responding law enforcement officers.

Brown was taken into custody with gunshot injuries after a state trooper and an armed civilian intervened.

Brown has a long criminal history in the Boston area. He had been released from prison, after serving time for stabbing two people in 2014, just four months before the May 2020 shooting in the South End.

Brown took a plea deal in the shooting case and received a six-year sentence, well below what prosecutors had requested, despite a Boston police officer testifying that he was certain Brown would eventually “hurt or ... kill someone.”

The judge, Janet L. Sanders, who sentenced Brown acknowledged she was taking a “risk” with the lesser sentence.

At the sentencing hearing in August 2021, Boston police officer Edward Gately III delivered an emotional victim impact statement and implored Sanders to give Brown the maximum sentence of 10 to 12 years.

Gateley told Sanders he considered Brown “a very dangerous individual who doesn’t care who he hurts.”

“I am a firm believer that when Mr. Tyler Brown gets out, he will hurt or … kill someone,” Gately said, according to a recording of his testimony.

Sanders said she would rely on her intuition in fashioning Brown’s sentence.

“I can’t look into a crystal ball and figure out what’s going to happen once you get out,” Sanders said. “But I do understand that I am taking on risk here. And I just pray that … my intuitions are right and that you have the ability, the smarts, the will, the support — not to go out there and endanger other people like you have in the past.”

The state Parole Board found that Brown was “remorseful about the part he played in the offense.” He was ordered to attend classes at Tufts University, attend mental-health counseling, take his medications, and undergo testing for alcohol and illegal drugs, the parole board ruled.

Brown, 46, of Dorchester, is on dual parole and probation for a host of violent offenses, including armed assault to murder. His criminal history means it was illegal for Brown to possess any gun whatsoever, never mind the multi-caliber BCI-Defense Model FF-15 authorities allege he used in the shooting, according to court documents.

“The state and federal laws are straightforward: if you have a felony conviction, you cannot legally purchase, possess, or carry a firearm,” said Elisabeth Ryan, the Boston-based policy counsel at Everytown for Gun Safety, in a statement. “This individual should never have had access to a gun.”

George W. Vien, a former federal prosecutor, concurred, saying that federal law prohibits someone with a felony conviction from possessing any firearm or ammunition, regardless of the style of gun.

“It’s really clear cut,” he said.

Additionally, Massachusetts law prohibits sale and possession of assault weapons, such as a Colt AR-15 or an AK-47. The law also bans weapons that have internal functional components that “are substantially similar to the construction or configuration of a weapon that is expressly banned under the law.” But there are exceptions, including grandfathering clauses.

Massachusetts law bars specific military-style weapons and their duplicates and any semiautomatic weapons with at least two identifying features — such as a folding or telescoping stock, a bayonet mount, a grenade launcher, or an ammunition magazine that attaches to a pistol.

But could a local resident who is not a convicted felon buy this particular gun in Massachusetts? Given carveouts the state has in its gun laws, the answer remains unclear. Messages left with the Middlesex district attorney’s office, State Police, and the governor’s office were not returned Wednesday.

The gun also has a serial number, according to court documents, raising the possibility that it could be traced. A Globe review of two decades worth of state data for gun dealer transactions, personal transfers, and gun registrations in Massachusetts turned up no results for a firearm with the gun’s serial number.

According to a statement of facts from a State Police trooper, Brown’s parole officer called Boston police shortly after noon on Monday to report concerns with Brown.

Brown had previously served multiple stints behind bars, including one for a May 2020 shooting in the South End that involved four Boston police officers.

The trooper noted in the report that Brown’s parole officer spoke to him through a video call on Monday, during which the parole officer saw Brown waving a round a “semi-automatic rifle” while in a kitchen that was not his own.

The State Police report offers other details to the immediate run-up to the shooting, noting that Brown had been released from a local psychiatric hospital on Friday, and that he had been previously diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, and depression.

Brown, who has a history of crack cocaine use, according to authorities, had a drug test scheduled for Monday and told his parole officer that he had relapsed and was ready to end his life.

Massachusetts is considered to have among the most stringent gun laws in the nation. According to Everytown, the state is one of a few to bar gun purchases by people with outstanding warrants and one of a few to require secure storage for any firearm not in the owner’s immediate control.

Still, violence in Massachusetts can be affected by weaker gun laws elsewhere, said Ruth Zakarin, chief executive for the Massachusetts Coalition to Prevent Gun Violence.

“We’re impacted by weaker gun laws in other states,” she said. “We’re impacted by the fact that what we have in Massachusetts is not what we have on the federal level.”

If someone can’t legally purchase a gun, there are myriad ways to illicitly possess one. They can be stolen, straw-purchased, where someone purchases a gun legally, attests that the gun is for them, but in reality they are buying it for someone else, or guns could be trafficked in from somewhere else, perhaps a location that has more lax gun ownership laws, according to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

Untraceable, 3-D printed guns have also been on the uptick in the US.

Brandon del Pozo, a medical professor at Brown University and a member of the Regional Gun Violence Research Consortium, said the weapon Brown used “appears to be a variant of the AR-15, a lightly modified version of the US military’s standard combat rifle.”

“Despite stricter laws in Massachusetts, they are easy to purchase throughout the country, including in the region here. Convicted felons are precluded from buying a weapon like this, but the background checks that would prohibit it aren’t required at private sales or gun shows many states, or when the system takes too long to return the results,” he said.

Such loopholes, said del Pozo, “mean that nearly anyone, including convicted felons and people with severe mental illness, can buy one of these weapons designed for combat.”

Warren Eller, a professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice, lamented that “the gun legislation that we pass doesn’t really affect the causal reasons of why people go out and shoot.”

“Anyone in our country can get a hold of any thing they want to depending on the amount of effort you put into it,” he said. “The question is what kind of impediments can we put up now to stop these sorts of things. The day and age to stop illicit use of firearms through simply banning purchases is long, long gone.”

Super, historic, record-setting.

Those are just some of the words meteorologists are using to describe what is expected to develop across the Equatorial Pacific in the coming months.

Quick refresher: El Niño develops when winds weaken and sea surface temperatures surge across the Equatorial Pacific near South America — and this one may affect us bigtime.

Here are the four biggest things you need to know:

1. This could be one of the strongest El Niños on record

Nearly every major forecast model shows a significant El Niño developing by late 2026, with ocean temperatures potentially rising around 3 degrees Celsius above average. That would place this event among the strongest ever observed, rivaling the legendary 1877-78 El Niño.

Why does that matter? El Niño acts like a giant atmospheric heat engine. It tends to bring wetter conditions to the Southern US, leading to floods, while the northern tier often turns warmer and drier, increasing drought and wildfire risks out West.

2. New England may feel the effects by late summer

There’s usually a delay between El Niño forming and its impacts reaching New England. But by late summer and fall, we could see hotter, more humid weather settle in.

That may translate to more heat waves, sticky nights, and an increase in heavy downpours and thunderstorms. Coastal storms could also become more frequent later in the year as the jet stream grows more active.

3. Winter could turn warmer and wetter

Historically, strong El Niño winters favor milder temperatures across New England. That doesn’t eliminate snow, but it often means more mixed precipitation and rain events, especially near the coast.

At the same time, El Niño winters can still produce major nor’easters. Some of New England’s biggest storms have occurred during strong El Niño years.

4. Hurricane season may quiet down

Strong El Niño patterns typically increase wind shear over the Atlantic, making it harder for hurricanes to organize and strengthen.

That could lead to a slightly quieter-than-average Atlantic hurricane season overall, although, as always, it only takes one storm to make it memorable. After all, Hurricane Bob did make landfall in New England during an El Niño year (1991).

So, quieter hurricane seasons, maybe? Hey, you wanted a silver lining, right?

“In relocating bus operations to the center of the roadway, the proposed project will greatly improve the travel experience for bus riders,” the report concluded. “The anticipated increases in vehicle travel time will encourage drivers to consider other modes of transportation and will ultimately help the City of Boston reach their mode shift targets.”

It’s not unexpected that the redesign plan — which is not final — would add time for drivers while reducing waits for bus riders. But the analysis puts numbers to a neighborhood concern that has been roiling for years. The data would have been helpful to see before the numerous hearings and meetings held on the project over the last few months, public officials and activists said. Two city councilors and one state representative who have been closely involved in the project said they had not seen the analysis until the Globe shared it with them on Thursday; some officials were not even aware it was conducted.

“To have to get it from you, it’s amazing,” said City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who alongside many of his constituents has been a vocal opponent of the center-running bus lane. “We didn’t even know it was in existence.”

“I can’t say” there was an effort to hide it, Culpepper added, but “I can certainly say there wasn’t an effort to make it public.”

In response to Globe questions, MBTA spokesperson Joe Pesaturo said Thursday that “highly technical work products such as this early analysis are not generally posted publicly.” He added that the MBTA is still working with city officials to improve the Blue Hill Avenue design “with the goal of minimizing traffic impacts as much as possible.”

For years, transit planners have been pitching a center-running bus lane along Blue Hill Avenue from Mattapan Square to Grove Hall, a design they say would free up the bus to move faster and allow for badly needed safety improvements while having minimal impact on drivers. But that plan has never proven popular in the surrounding neighborhoods. Communities along the avenue rejected a similar plan, called the 28X, in 2009.

For Mayor Michelle Wu, the Blue Hill Avenue project has become a political quagmire, particularly as a vocal segment of Black voters expresses disappointment with her tenure. Critics from Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester worry it would slow traffic and hurt businesses along the corridor.

“No one is disputing that it would be a good idea if the 28 would go faster,” said Dianne Wilkerson, a former state senator who has been actively opposed to the project. “We just think that there are some other ways to do it, rather than destroying the entire economic underpinning of the avenue.”

Some, however, particularly young transit riders, say a faster bus would be life-changing, allowing them to get to work, school, and recreation more quickly. Transit activists say the corridor, which is home to some of the city’s most diverse neighborhoods, deserves faster and more reliable ways to get around.

“This is about equity,” said state Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who supports redesigning the avenue. “The road has been designed primarily for car drivers. ... But you’re trying to balance 40,000 car drivers and 40,000 transit riders.”

He acknowledged there might be some “tradeoffs” in the plan, including slower commutes for drivers, but said he is advocating for a design that will preserve two traffic lanes in each direction to keep cars moving. Holmes said he was aware the report was being done but had not seen it until this week.

“What’s driving our decisions is data and not emotions,” he said. “The existing conditions are horrible.”

City Councilor Brian Worrell, who also had not seen the report until Thursday, said government officials should be “as transparent as possible.”

“The fact that they’re not releasing the traffic study is telling me that the traffic study’s not good,” Worrell said. “We don’t know the plan because you’re not releasing all the information.”

Both the city and the MBTA had the report in their possession; both provided the report to the Globe on Thursday in response to separate public record requests. The project “has been a joint effort of the MBTA and the City of Boston in terms of community engagement, key design elements and traffic impacts,” said Pesaturo, the T spokesperson. He said the analysis cost the MBTA approximately $300,000.

Marcela Dwork, a spokesperson for Wu, said the report — which was dated Aug. 29, 2025, and received by the city in December — was “not yet vetted” and emphasized that “the design will continue to evolve.”

She did not respond to questions about whether the mayor supports the center-running bus lane as currently designed. At a council hearing last month, city transportation officials sounded noncommittal about the project’s future and said they would meet with the MBTA to discuss next steps.

“The City supports investing needed resources to deliver the highest quality of life throughout every neighborhood,” Dwork said in a statement Thursday. “The Mayor is in regular contact with and working closely with [MBTA General Manager Phil Eng] to incorporate community concerns into design details and get this important project right for the people who rely on this corridor every day.”

But as a report by the Globe’s Niki Griswold detailed this week, a recent community meeting at Roxbury Community College was heavy on criticism of Wu on a range of issues confronting Black Boston — some current, some grievances years old.

Former state senator Dianne Wilkerson headlined the event last month billed as a challenge to hold Black elected officials “accountable” for failing to aggressively advocate for the community’s concerns. City Council members who support Wu were put on notice that they should expect contested elections, or worse, if they continue to support Wu’s agenda.

The list of complaints included longstanding criticism of the renovation of White Stadium, as well as more recent concerns like the proposed center bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue.

But high on the list was Wu’s supposed sabotage of Brian Worrell’s bid to become president of the City Council. Worrell would have been the council’s fourth black president. But the council’s progressive wing — Wu’s usual allies, including several former aides — lined up behind Councilor Gabriel Coletta Zapata and didn’t back Worrell, even after Coletta Zapata’s bid fell apart the day before the election.

The machinations behind council president elections are mostly inside baseball, and the last election was no exception. Still, the bitterness behind Worrell’s defeat has shown staying power.

But more interesting complaints are the ones playing in the background. That Wu isn’t receptive enough to community input. That her inner circle doesn’t include enough Black voices. And that Wu isn’t the mayor some in Black Boston wanted in the first place.

In an interview, Wu said she believes some of the criticism comes with leading a city confronting major issues.

“We’re in a complicated moment with big challenges, and we’re in a smart, engaged city where all the easy solutions have already been implemented,” she said.

“So the problems that are left have bigger and harder issues to sort through, and it’s up to us to have those hard conversations and choose the places where we are going to decide to press forward together, even if it means doing something differently.”

Certainly, some of the criticism is deserved. Wu and her team botched the decision to change direction of the development of Parcel 3 in Roxbury, abandoning a longstanding community-backed plan in favor of designating that land for a new Madison Park High School. Building a new Madison Park is a great idea that will have a huge community benefit, but surely there was a better, more inclusive, way to navigate the neighborhood politics of the decision.

It played into the perception that many of Wu’s decisions are imposed, rather than reached through consensus.

White Stadium is also viewed by Wu’s critics as a community project the community never asked for, driven by a professional women’s soccer team — though Wu insists the driving force was the desire to create a first-class athletic facility for Boston Public Schools students (when they can use it).

Does the neighborhood really oppose it? Wu carried every precinct that borders Franklin Park, mostly by wide margins. If this project is so unpopular, why didn’t it have any traction as a campaign issue?

For some people, the biggest issue with Wu is one they are reluctant to air publicly: that they believe Boston’s first elected mayor of color should have been Black. Her supposed lack of responsiveness is especially galling, critics whisper, because there should be more solidarity.

I would argue Wu should be measured by what she does, especially as her second term unfolds. If her administration can deliver on its promises to spur development in Roxbury, improve the schools, and continue to drive down crime, that will be a great record on the issues that matter in Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan.

And in that sense, it’s good to know that Wu’s critics have no plans to stop pushing her. Landslide victories have been known to breed complacency. That’s something Black Boston rightly has no time for.

A number of the state’s biggest umbrella unions have yet to hand out their endorsements, even as Healey faces little, if any, competition for their support. They include the Massachusetts Teachers Association, the Massachusetts Nurses Association, and the SEIU Massachusetts State Council, all of which endorsed her four years ago.

While Healey is likely to ultimately earn a slate of labor endorsements over one of her Republican opponents, it will come weighed down by behind-the-scenes tension and a lack of enthusiasm among many labor folks for a reelection bid that’s largely become a referendum on the state’s economic health, according to interviews with more than a dozen labor leaders.

“It feels like the fox is in the hen house, and it’s hard to think of her as a potential partner,” said one union leader, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak freely about the union’s relationship with the Democratic administration.

To be sure, some powerful union leaders have publicly embraced Healey and say their members strongly back her for a second term. She earned their endorsement, labor leaders said, because of her staunch support of project labor agreements, her appointment of experienced leaders to run the MBTA, and her availability to unions who want the governor’s ear.

“We were silenced and kept outside the door by the [Charlie] Baker administration for eight years,” said Frank Callahan, president of the Massachusetts Building Trades Council, which endorsed Healey at its convention in March. “Working with this administration has been a breath of fresh air.”

But that view isn’t held in all labor circles. Those who have not endorsed in the race cited a litany of grievances, including Healey’s 2025 attempt to close a residential hospital for disabled children in Canton, which would have put some 225 jobs in limbo and, workers said, separated patients from their families.

Some lament a dormant labor advisory council she created, or cringe when she touts being the first governor to cut taxes in decades.

Others have been rankled by the administration’s approach to reining in health care costs, particularly a move by the Group Insurance Commission — which covers nearly 500,000 public sector employees and their families, and is made up of gubernatorial appointees. The changes would hike premiums and scrap coverage for items like GLP-1 weight loss drugs.

“We want to be partners with anybody who is going to find a solution,” said Katie Murphy, president of the Massachusetts Nurses Association. “We still feel like there is a long way to go.”

Harris Gruman, a leader at a community coalition known as Raise Up Massachusetts and a top SEIU official, said Healey has met with local unions individually, including after her administration sought, and then backtracked on, a plan, to close a beloved children’s hospital. The attempt spurred an uproar among labor leaders and was admittedly a “hard moment,” Gruman said.

“The next six weeks are going to be very important,” Gruman said of the ongoing SEIU’s endorsement discussions. “Hopefully, they will strengthen our relationship with the governor, but you never know.”

Recently, Healey nabbed an endorsement from the North Atlantic States Regional Council of Carpenters, which hosted her at its state-of-the-art training facility in Dorchester for an event announcing its support on April 30. The 30,000-worker union said it would “greatly benefit from another four years” of Healey in office.

When asked at the event about her campaign’s relationship with other, larger unions this cycle, Healey was circumspect. “You have to talk to the campaign about that,” she told the Globe.

In a statement, Healey campaign spokesperson Kerry Lyons said her track record with workers is “unmatched,” citing her time fighting wage theft as attorney general, support for project labor agreements to bargain with unions for public works projects, and legislation that proposed new investments in job-creating public infrastructure projects on college campuses. Lyons also said the state funneled hundreds of millions of dollars into research and development jobs.

“Workers recognize her commitment to lowering costs for working families, and it’s why she is the only candidate in this race to earn the endorsement of organized labor,” Lyons said.

Healey, of course, has long enjoyed support from powerful unions as the state’s de facto Democratic leader. During her 2022 gubernatorial run, she quickly accumulated labor endorsements amid what was then a still-competitive primary against Senator Sonia Chang-Díaz.

By late April that year, the SEIU Massachusetts State Council, one of the state’s largest umbrella unions, threw its support behind Healey, marking the first time in 20 years that all six SEIU local unions under the council had collectively endorsed a single candidate in an open gubernatorial primary.

Healey’s endorsements do include a list of building trade-focused unions, including those who represent carpenters, bricklayers, ironworkers, plumbers, and pipefitters.

Jim Evers, president of the Boston Carmen’s Union Local 589, said Healey’s hiring of general manager Phil Eng has benefited his members. He also citeda bill Healey signed into law that increased penalties for those convicted of attacking transit employees.

“She fully staffed the T and gave workers the tools to do their jobs,” he said.

Jim Durkin, the legislative director at AFSCME 93, pointed to a recent visit Healey made to Cape Cod, where she met with human services workers for more than 90 minutes, taking questions until there weren’t any left, he said.

“We are able to pick up the phone and call her directly, that is very important to us,” said Durkin, whose union will take up endorsements at its meeting in late June. “We have had some battles with the governor, but it’s no different than any other administration, Democratic and Republican.”

But some union members said they have a long memory for ways in which the administration has let them down.

Last year, Healey proposed saving $31 million by closing the Pappas Rehabilitation Hospital for Children and transferring many residents to another facility in western Massachusetts, more than 100 miles away. The proposal caused an uproar, and the administration ultimately walked back its plans.

It still left bad feelings. In March, workers belonging to three unions representing Pappas staff members announced an overwhelming vote of no confidence in Dr. Robbie Goldstein, Healey’s appointed public health commissioner.

Nancy Silva, president of AFSCME Local 1517, said at the time that admissions were declining at the facility because of DPH officials and “their inaction, neglect, and shortsighted policy changes.” Healey’s office said the accusations “represent an inaccurate, unhelpful escalation.”

Healey was also at odds with the state’s top teachers union, which once roundly supported her, when she came out against a successful 2024 ballot question that eliminated the MCAS exam as a high school graduation requirement.

The Massachusetts Teachers Association is finalizing its questionnaire for candidates, union president Max Page told the Globe.

Other union leaders said they haven’t had the communication they’ve hoped for from Healey. Healey’s 20-member Labor Advisory Council, the first convened in more than 50 years, hasn’t met in nine months, said members, who feel that they are sometimes the last to know about major policy decisions or budget actions affecting unions.

For example, last year the governor weighed offering buyouts of up to $20,000 to state employees — her administration ultimately never did — and prolonged an existing hiring freeze across the executive branch, setting state employees on edge.

Others felt that the use of AI in state agencies, such as the state’s sprawling Health and Human Services secretariat, should have been bargained over, including employing AI to summarize health care benefits or help process Medicaid claims. There are also active requests for information, or RFIs, out for liability programs and AI data consulting services that could focus on the health care sector that go beyond Healey’s plan to roll out a ChatGPT-powered AI assistant for state workers.

“We can’t bargain the future,” said one union leader, who requested anonymity to speak because of ongoing contract negotiations with Healey administration officials.

Tatishe Nteta, a University of Massachusetts Amherst political science professor and director of the UMass poll, which regularly gathers voter viewpoints on state issues, said the reticence on the part of unions — and, perhaps, other voters — could be felt most acutely when Healey tries to marshal supporters this fall against either Republicans Mike Minogue or Brian Shortsleeve, the former of whom has already poured more than $13 million into this campaign.

“One of the things that unions do really effectively is mobilize,” Nteta said. “When they are noncommittal, that becomes a fundamental problem.”

Catherine Carlock of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

An 18-year-old was ordered held without bail after his arrest in connection with a double shooting in Dorchester on Sunday that left a man and woman wounded.

On Wednesday, police arrested Jaynell Sumler, of Dorchester, on two charges of assault to murder, and single charges for unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition and discharging a firearm striking a building, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said Thursday.

Prosecutors allege that Sumler was inside 69 Kingsdale St. in Dorchester around 6:45 p.m. on Sunday when he shot a 42-year-old woman in the head. He then allegedly shot a 42-year-old man in the arm and leg, prosecutors said.

Witnesses identified Sumler, the boyfriend of the woman’s daughter, as the shooter, prosecutors said.

The woman remained at a local hospital on Thursday with life-threatening injuries, police said. The man’s injuries were not life-threatening, officials said.

Wednesday’s arrest marks the first apprehension in a series of shootings over the weekend. Across four days beginning Saturday, there were five shootings in Boston — three in Dorchester, one in Roxbury, and one in Mattapan.

MEDFORD — The man accused of gunning down motorists in heavy traffic on Memorial Drive in Cambridge earlier this week pleaded not guilty Thursday from his hospital bed, where’s being treated for injuries suffered in a shootout with State Police and an armed former Marine.

Tyler E. Brown IV, 46, appeared heavily medicated during his arraignment, which he participated in via video conference. Officials said he was shot in the “lower extremities.”

The shooting unfolded around lunchtime Monday, not long after a Massachusetts parole officer called 911 to report that Brown was suicidal and armed with an assault rifle. The officer said Brown had a long criminal record, including a 2020 shootout with Boston police in the South End, and a history of crack cocaine use and mental health problems; he had recently been discharged from a psychiatric hospital.

Brown didn’t speak during the 18-minute proceeding Thursday afternoon. He nodded once to confirm he could hear the judge, but spent most of the time with his head bent down and his eyes closed. With a blanket pulled up to his chin, Brown periodically opened his eyes for brief seconds, appearing exceedingly drowsy.

He was flanked by Carolyn I. McGowan and Josina Raisler-Cohn, Committee for Public Counsel Services attorneys appointed to represent him.

Brown was charged in Cambridge District Court with six felony and two misdemeanor charges, including two counts of assault to murder, two counts of attempted assault and battery with a firearm, and gun and ammunition charges.

In the Medford courthouse, not guilty pleas were entered on his behalf by District Court Judge David E. Frank.

Middlesex Assistant District Attorney Nicole L. Allain asked the court to hold Brown without bail under the state’s dangerousness law, noting that his criminal history dates back decades. Brown was arrested as a teenager in 1994 in Michigan and charged with armed robbery. His other convictions include drug and gun offenses in Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

A bail hearing was set for next Thursday; McGowan did not challenge the issue.

Allain summarized Brown’s alleged actions Monday, including three phone calls with a parole officer during which he repeatedly said he wanted to end his life, displayed the assault rifle he allegedly later used, and talked about crimes he committed but was not prosecuted for.

“These people are going to pay,” she quoted Brown as telling his parole officer not long before the shooting rampage. “I’m not going back to prison.”

In their final conversation, Brown displayed the firearm during a FaceTime conversation, standing in a kitchen the officer didn’t recognize, Allain said.

The officer called 911 and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester but he wasn’t home when officers got there. Boston police pinged his phone and tracked him to Cambridge.

Less than two hours after the 911 call, Brown allegedly began randomly shooting while walking down Memorial Drive. Motorists ran for cover, some hiding under their cars.

Brown was taken into custody after a state trooper and a Marine veteran returned fire.

Allain said two bullet holes were found in the driver’s side door of the Marine’s car. She said at least 70 spent shell casings were recovered from the scene.

Without identifying them by name, Allain said one victim was shot four times in one leg and the second was shot in the back of the head.

The shooting victims have been identified by family members as Casimir Bangoura, a Cambridge resident who was driving to the car wash, and another man whose first name is Felix, and is a father of eight. The family declined to provide his last name, but they said he was an MBTA Ride Services contract driver who drove himself to the hospital.

Brown was on parole for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in the South End in 2020, a case that has repeatedly raised questions about the relatively lenient sentence he received after a judge was persuaded by his intellectual gifts and his commitment to keeping his life on track.

When Brown was released from prison in May 2025 after serving that sentence, he was accepted into the Tufts University Prison Initiative’s yearlong re-entry program, which combines college coursework with housing, employment, and other wraparound services. According to university officials, Brown stopped attending the program in February.

Wearing a military cap, Lusardi, who served as an Army medic on Okinawa Island during World War II, sat at the table with his daughter and niece.

“He never bragged about it, he is just a great family guy,” said his daughter, Ann Hadayia, 65. “He is a hard worker, he never complained, always willing to help people, just everything that makes you live to 103.”

Hadayia and her cousin, Diane Butler, 73, joked that it was probably all the “red wine and salami” that helped Lusardi live so long.

For DeSantis, a longtime member of the Brookline Garden Club, it’s her love for gardening that “always kept her mind sharp,” her grandson, Nicolas DeSantis, said.

“She would always be going and doing stuff,” said DeSantis, 51. “It’s like mind over matter. It just overcomes your body. I am hoping some of those genes get passed down.”

State Senator Mike Rush, State Representative William MacGregor, and Emily Shea, head of the city’s Age Strong Commission, handed out citations to the residents for reaching the century milestone.

In Massachusetts, about 1 out of 3,000 people are 100 years or older, meaning there are around 2,200 centenarians living in the state, according to Dr. Thomas Perls, a geriatrician and director of the New England Centenarian Study at Boston University.

The right combination of genes plays an important role in longevity and becomes more important the older you get, Perls said.

“Interestingly, it isn’t really lacking genes that are associated with age-related diseases, but rather protective genes that slow down aging and decrease your risk for age-related diseases,” Perls said. “That’s not to say that some habits don’t play a strong role, for example, finding a centenarian who has a history of smoking is extraordinarily rare.”

Massachusetts residents have a much better chance of living to 100 than those in other parts of the country, thanks to better health care, education, and overall socioeconomic conditions, he said. But within that success are enormous disparities.

“Average life expectancy in Back Bay is 93, and you go three miles southeast to Dorchester, and it’s 26 years less,” Perls said. “I attribute that to structural and systemic racism, and all the things that go along with that in terms of determinants of aging-related diseases and disability.”

While some people might not want to live so long, assuming their health will be in decline at that age, getting older is worth celebrating, Perls said.

“Instead of it being the older you get, the sicker you get, I think it’s much more the case of the older you get, the healthier you’ve been,” Perls said. “I think it’s a very optimistic and enabling point of view about aging.”

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the May 14 episode of the “Say More” podcast.

Shirley Leung: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Shirley Leung. I’m in the studio this week with Globe reporter Chris Serres, who just released a reporting project on gambling in Massachusetts. Chris and a team of reporters looked at how casinos target Asian communities with their marketing, kind of like how big tobacco pushed another addictive product, menthol cigarettes, onto Black customers.

The Globe team also explored how illegal gambling dens are flourishing in Chinatown, and how the Boston Police, the Suffolk District Attorney, and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu have all looked the other way. Welcome to the studio, Chris.

Chris Serres: Thank you, Shirley. I appreciate it.

Leung: So Chris, this reporting project started with some simple observations. You saw a shuttle bus. Tell me what you saw and what questions you had.

Serres: Sure. It was about a year ago, I was just spending time in Boston’s Chinatown neighborhood and noticed these shuttles with the big Encore logo across the windows, and noticed that these shuttles were packed to the gills.

And that just had me wondering, “Well, why are these shuttle buses coming to this neighborhood?” And I just started riding the shuttles and talking to folks that were going to Encore. And then I learned that there were other shuttle routes and that they were going through other neighborhoods around Greater Boston with high concentrations of Asian residents, and so I started riding those shuttles.

Leung: Probably like Quincy, right?

Serres: Like Quincy, Malden, Dorchester. You could draw a map, and we actually did that, which shows the route and how it goes directly through specific Asian neighborhoods and skips over neighborhoods like the one where I live in Medford.

Leung: So Chris, you don’t speak Chinese, right? Most people spoke English? Or is English the second language? How did you...

Serres: No. In fact, that became a barrier. Several months into it, spending time on the shuttles as well as spending time in the casinos, I said, “Look, we need to have some help here. We need to have someone working on this who actually speaks Chinese, who knows Cantonese, who knows Mandarin.”

And so that’s when Mable Chan got on board, and she’s terrific. She’s done work for The New York Times, and she was just fantastic in terms of building relationships with people and talking to people, and especially people that were struggling with gambling disorders, pretty severe ones.

Leung: You and I talked a little bit about this. Asians like to gamble. It’s not new, right? But what I appreciate about your series is that you uncovered that these casinos disproportionately targeted Asians, and you found that a lot of Asian customers were more likely to be in serious debt as a result of going to these casinos. What other surprising things did you find in this series?

Serres: I guess one thing that really struck me was we went through thousands of pages of lawsuits that had been filed against casino patrons, and these were lawsuits against people that had gotten deeply in debt.

I was really struck at the lavish amount of credit lines that they had been given, in some cases over $300,000. I was also struck by the high percentage of those borrowers who were being sued who happened to be of Asian descent. I think in Encore’s case, more than 80 percent of those that they were suing were people of Asian descent.

And so you could start to see the connection between the way they were being targeted through the shuttles and the billboards and the freebies that were being offered at the casinos, and the credit lines, but also the damaging effects where the casinos were using these hardball tactics to go after them, suing them, in some cases getting judges to issue arrest warrants for them to collect on those debts.

So that was one really alarming finding from the legal documents. The other was that there’s illegal activity happening in plain sight within the casinos.

Mable and I made many trips to the casinos, and we witnessed that there were loan sharks that were circling the Asian card games and ducking into restrooms outside of the surveillance systems to give people chips so they could continue gambling. We learned from others that know some of these loan sharks that some of the interest rates on some of those loans are just exceedingly high. And all of it’s illegal. I was really struck that all of this activity that we could witness was being allowed to happen by our regulators.

Leung: One of the people you focused on in the series, Kim Chung Ma, can you tell me where you met him and what happened to him?

Serres: Sure. So Kim Chung Ma is someone we came to know really well. He’s really a gentle human being. He came from Hong Kong, an immigrant.

We met him at a mahjong party in Quincy, and he was sitting in the corner. I still remember this vividly. He was sitting by himself in the corner while other people were playing mahjong. Shirley, you probably have played...

Leung: Yes, I’ve played a lot of mahjong. It’s very loud. There’s the clacking of tiles.

Serres: Yeah. So there’s a lot of activity. And I was really struck at this older gentleman that was in the corner, and so approached him and we started talking, and he revealed to me that he didn’t want to be there. Where he really wanted to be was at a casino. And he couldn’t go to a casino because he had no money left. He just seemed really sad and despondent. He started to talk about how he had thoughts of suicide, and that began this journey where we started to spend more time with him and better understand his situation.

Tragically, during the time in which we had come to know Kim Chung Ma, he had resumed his gambling, and it got so bad that his partner that he loved ended up leaving him. And so we kind of witnessed this whole tragic rupturing of the love of his life happen during real time as we were reporting on this.

But Kim Chung Ma really stood out as somebody that I found as a really sympathetic figure. He had issues with loneliness. He was cut off from much of his support network. He was isolated from his family members, and we found that to be some of the recurring themes or underlying factors behind why so many people get caught in this vicious cycle of gambling.

Leung: And he had worked in the restaurant industry and basically retired, right? And so in retirement, he gambled away all his money. Because he’s lonely and maybe bored.

Serres: I mean, that’s a big factor behind this. Here’s the thing. I really don’t think that there’s any reason to believe that Asians have more of a predisposition toward gambling than anyone else. I happen to be of Italian descent. A lot of my relatives gambled.

I do think that there’s some truth to the idea that gambling fills a void for some people if they’re cut off from social networks, especially if they’re new to this country, and I think that’s the case with many people in these neighborhoods. I think the casinos know that, and that’s why they’re specifically sending those shuttles and putting those billboards in those neighborhoods.

Leung: You and I have talked about this series before it ran about, “Where is that line?” Asians like to gamble. You found out Italians like to gamble.

But where is that fine line where you’re giving customers what they want, but then maybe you’re exploiting them for profit? Can you talk about the range of opinions you encountered talking to people about this series? Where is it just fun and where is it exploitation?

Serres: Right. That’s a great question, and I don’t think we ever really untangled it entirely. We did talk to casino executives who were quite open about the idea that it’s good business to target these communities because, quite frankly, one of the executives just came right out and said, “Asians love to gamble and we send shuttles to those communities for a reason.”

Leung: So they’re “giving them what they want,” right?

Serres: We’re giving them what they want, and they’re popular. That was one thing they kept saying. The shuttles are used frequently, so that is evidence enough that this is justified.

And as you said, we’re giving people what they want. At the same time, we have to acknowledge that this is an addictive product and has major public health implications. I like the fact that you mentioned menthol cigarettes at the beginning of this, because the parallel there is really strong between what was happening in previous decades with big tobacco targeting Black neighborhoods with billboards for menthol cigarettes — extremely addictive, extremely dangerous. Gambling also has major public health implications. I just think a lot of that is missed when we talk about gambling and casinos and online betting and everything else because we’re so caught up in the glamour of it?

Leung: Well, yeah. It’s exciting. In your own series, why did people go to the casinos? It felt important.

Serres: It is kind of exciting. Just on that note, I remember starting the Lunar New Year in Chinatown, and Chinatown can be a tight-knit neighborhood as you know. It can be a little rough. And getting on that shuttle and coming to Encore, there they were shooting off fireworks, and there were the dancers, and they were handing out hundreds of these envelopes with $2 bills in them. They were hanging them on the plants in the casino, and children were taking them.

It just occurred to me, where else are these folks going to get this kind of experience? There’s the daily grind of working and living in that neighborhood, and then you come to Encore, and you’re being given red envelopes with $2 bills and there’s a celebration around you. Of course, it’s going to look glamorous. It’s exciting. So I see the attraction.

Leung: Chris, you’ve been on this addiction beat. You cover everything from the opioid crisis to now gambling. Maybe you could talk about this addiction science as it relates to gambling. Is it really similar to how people get addicted to opioids? How does gambling become addictive?

Serres: Sure. I mean, it’s absolutely analogous.

Gambling plays on the same receptors in the brain that activate the reward system in the same way that opioids do, that alcohol does, that pretty much any addictive product does. So I don’t view it as its own separate category. Just because it’s a behavioral addiction as opposed to a substance-use addiction doesn’t make it, in any way, less harmful.

It’s part of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, the DSM, which is the bible of mental health disorders, and it’s there for a reason. It’s there because gambling disorders are correlated with all kinds of serious health effects, from high anxiety to chronic stress to high blood pressure, to depression, and suicide. There have been studies that have shown that people with gambling disorders have five to 10 times higher rates of suicide as the overall population, and that its correlation with suicide is higher than any other type of addiction.

It’s a serious public health issue. I’m not saying I’m against gambling, because I’m not. I view it as a public health issue, and that’s the prism in which I look at it. And so when I see those shuttles going specifically through Asian neighborhoods, that raises alarm bells for me, and it should for everybody else.

Leung: I was surprised to read in your stories that Massachusetts spends more per capita than any other state on helping people with their gambling problems. Maybe you could talk about what kind of things that is spent on, and do they spend more of it on the Asian community if there are a lot of us gambling with addictive gambling issues?

Serres: Absolutely. And I think it’s important to put that statistic in context. We may spend more per capita than any other state, but I don’t think that’s saying a lot. We’re still spending just a very small fraction of the overall amount of money that’s being brought in through casino gambling, which is something on the order of $2.6 billion. Only a tiny percentage of that, less than 1 percent, actually flows to Asian community groups that are working to mitigate the effects.

And up until 2019, there was not a single dollar spent specifically that went to Asian community groups to help address the problem in those communities.

Leung: Wow. Even though there’s a disproportionate amount of Asians gambling, right?

Serres: Right. The casinos have indicated that up to a quarter of their customers are of Asian descent, and there have been surveys that suggest that’s the case. Yet that’s about three times their share of the population in our state. You would think that this would be more of a focus. And it’s not a new problem.

This has been an issue ever since Foxwoods Resort Casino and Mohegan Sun in Connecticut were sending shuttles to Boston’s Chinatown neighborhood 20 years ago. In 2021, there was a big study that came out known as the Asian CARES Report, which laid out the problem and called for tighter regulation and called on the Massachusetts Gaming Commission to actually fund investigations into whether the shuttle buses were ethical and whether the marketing practices were predatory.

And here we are five years later, none of that has happened. The recommendations have been ignored. But we’re starting to hear more and more from community members that they’re just taking matters into their own hands. They’re not going to wait for state regulators. They’re going to address it and build resilience in their own communities.

Leung: Sometimes the money is spent on TV ads, they do advertising. And aren’t there people... is it called GameSense? They’re walking through the casinos trying to look for people who might be struggling with a gambling addiction. Where does this money go? What do they do with it?

Serres: Well, one of the struggles I hear from public health experts is that a lot of the money being spent to address gambling addiction is going toward ideas and programs that aren’t really evidence-based. It may look good to see a problem gambling billboard at a MBTA stop. It may look good that there’s a gambling helpline, and there should be. And it may look good that there are these GameSense agents walking the casino floors with green shirts.

But what’s the evidence that those actually work?

I asked the state repeatedly for any evidence that GameSense, which costs the state over $3 million a year, actually on a statewide level has helped to reduce problem gambling, and they couldn’t come up with any. And so I just think that there’s a whole body of thought that this money would be better spent if it went directly to the communities that are being targeted and are being harmed.

There are incredible community organizations, the Boston Chinatown Neighborhood Center and others, that are doing great work on this topic. There’s a whole argument that instead of putting all this money toward flashy billboards and whatnot, give it directly to the people to address the problem in their communities so that there are people that can help them.

There are clinicians in their communities who speak their language, who speak Mandarin and Cantonese, who can help them. Because that was one thing I kept hearing over and over again, which was, “I have a loved one, I have a parent, I have a brother, I have a sister who has a gambling problem, and we can’t find anyone who can help them who actually speaks their language.” So we as a state need to grow the ranks of folks who can help people in their communities and who speak their language.

Leung: So Chris, if money were given directly to more Asian community groups to address problem gambling, what should they do with the money?

Serres: Wow. Those groups I think would be able to come up with some creative solutions. Some already have. There’s an organization out of Quincy, the Civic Education Alliance, that has started to organize these community events closer to home so people don’t get on the shuttles.

Leung: Like the mahjong clubs.

Serres: Like the mahjong gatherings, which are great. I don’t want to speak for these community organizations, but some of them have talked about how they could use that money to hire more clinicians, more mental health counselors who could address some of the underlying issues in their communities and move upstream from the problem.

But I think there are very creative, dynamic people who understand the problem specifically within their communities that could address it in a way that might be better than people on Beacon Hill.

Leung: What has been the reaction to your series?

Serres: I gotta say that the initial reaction from community groups within the Asian communities was overwhelmingly positive. I think there was a lot of frustration that their story had not been fully told. So they appreciated that. There’s been some talk of calling on the State Gaming Commission to actually follow through on some of the recommendations that were made five years ago to look into these marketing practices and the shuttles.

A city councilor, Ed Flynn, filed a resolution for a city council hearing specifically on the marketing practices and the prevalence of gambling in Chinatown, including the issue of the underground dens, which are prevalent. We counted at least 30 to 40 of these illegal dens in the Chinatown neighborhood. So the important thing is for the conversation just to keep going, and I appreciate the fact that you’re willing to continue it.

Leung: Chris, it was a great series. I know I’ve heard a lot from the Chinese community about it, and Chinese leaders. I hope The Globe stays on it. I hope you stay on it.

Serres: I really appreciate it. We will. Thank you.

Leung: Chris Serres is The Globe’s addiction reporter. [Here is the] link to his series, “A Losing Bet.” The series is also available in Chinese. Thanks, Chris, for coming in.

Serres: Thank you. I appreciate it.

“Over 50 years ago, this campus rose from land once intended to divide a community,” Jonathan Jefferson president of the college, told the crowd, referring to the expressway that was originally meant to be built on the land but was halted because of community activism. “Today, it does just the opposite. It connects, uplifts, and transforms.”

The commencement, the second of Jefferson’s tenure, seemed to indicate the school appeared to be recovering from some of the problems that marked his predecessors’ terms and returning to its mission of supporting students through challenges both in and out of the classroom. In addition to having its largest number of graduates since 2019, Jefferson said nearly three-quarters of the graduating class earned honors, while more than 70 percent planned to either transfer to a four-year university or enter the workforce immediately.

Christelle Jean Louis, 27, who graduated with degrees in biological science and laboratory animal care, called Jefferson “a blessing for the school.” Other graduates spoke about how the college allowed them to accomplish their goals of earning a higher education degree later in life or preparing them for a four-year school.

Louis, a first-generation college student from Haiti who plans to transfer to Simmons University to pursue a nursing degree, credited tutoring services, advising, and campus resources with helping her succeed. She had always wanted to attend college but was unsure if she would ever get the opportunity.

“It’s a dream come true,” Louis said.

Hanuel Corbitt Jr., 20, who majored in health careers while also being a member of the college’s basketball team, said balancing athletics and academics required discipline and sacrifice.

“There were times where I had to sacrifice extra workouts for studying,” Corbitt, who maintained a 4.0 GPA throughout his time in college, said. “It was definitely strenuous, but it was worth it.”

Roxbury Community College was opened in the ’70s after years of activism by local community members to provide higher education to the Roxbury community. It was recognized as a Predominantly Black Institution by the US Department of Education in 2021.

Jefferson described the school as “a true highway for economic mobility,” and highlighted programs such as RCC Connect, a centralized one-stop shop for student services, along with workforce training opportunities and the school’s food pantry, known as the Rox Box, which helps students stay enrolled and to graduate despite financial and personal hardships.

“These are not just programs, these are your struggle,” he said. “They are part of the reason that you are here today, and they reflect a broader commitment to ensure that every student has the support they need.”

Suzanne Walsh, the commencement speaker and the president of City University in Seattle, talked about her failures in college and in her career and encouraged students to embrace uncertainty. She described the modern world as volatile, uncertain, and ambiguous, and argued that Roxbury Community College students were uniquely prepared to navigate those challenges.

“You are more than resilient,” Walsh said. “You are anti-fragile. You are uniquely ready to give back to your family, to your friends, and to your community.”

For many families in attendance, the ceremony represented generations of sacrifice and support.

Minister Brenda Womack, 72, attended to celebrate her niece, Zandra Banks, a Roxbury resident who earned her liberal arts degree after years of stopping and restarting college because of financial struggles and family responsibilities.

“She’s showing us that it’s never too late,” Womack said. “Once you set your mind to it, stay focused, you can achieve it.”

Banks, who is in her late 50s, paused her own education while raising her son, who graduated with a bachelor’s degree in business administration. Now, Womack said, he is supporting his mother as she reaches her own milestone.

Brandon Kelly, 32, attended the ceremony to celebrate his wife, Dawntayia Kelly, 31, who graduated with high honors in criminal justice while raising two young children. She is pursuing a career as a corrections officer.

“Whatever she needed, whatever I had to do, we got it done,” Kelly said, while wearing a “Proud husband of the class of 2026″ T-shirt. “That way, she’d be able to be here two years later.”

Mattingly didn’t join the Phillies as bench coach in January with any expectation of becoming their manager. Rob Thomson, who had the job, is one of his best friends in baseball.

His only aim was to offer advice to Thomson when needed and spend more time with two of his sons. Preston, 38, is Philadelphia’s general manager under president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. His youngest, 11-year-old Louie, also loves being around the game.

Then Thomson was fired late last month after a 9-19 start, and now Mattingly is managing again for the first time since he was with the Dodgers and Marlins from 2011-22.

“I’m enjoying it,” he said. “As a player, at the end of my career, it’s something that I felt like I wanted to do. The way it happened is not something you want, right?”

The Phillies started 12-4 under Mattingly and are working back into contention.

The schedule helped. After Mattingly took over, the Phillies played the Giants, Marlins, Athletics, Rockies, and Red Sox and won all five series. They had played their previous 13 games against the Braves and Cubs, winning twice.

The Phillies, who are loaded with lefthanded hitters, also faced righthanded starters in 12 of Mattingly’s first 16 games.

“Our guys are playing better now than they were before,” said Phillies major league field coordinator Mike Calitri, a Canton native. “I think we’ll be battling for something. There’s some excitement because we’re all going in the same direction.”

It helps that Mattingly’s stature as a player resonates in a clubhouse that includes Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner, Zack Wheeler, and other stars.

“When they make the decision to make the change, you look at Donnie and the resume, that he played at such a high level and managed some good teams,” Schwarber said. “He knows what it takes. There were no drastic changes in what we’re doing. We know the group we have and what we’re capable of. We needed to start playing better, no matter who the manager was.

“But with him at the helm and having trust in us, there’s going to be some different things we’re going to try to do. There’s a lot of trust in him, and he has trust in us.”

Mattingly played 14 seasons in the majors, all for the Yankees, and has coached or managed at the highest level since 2004. He has yet to earn a World Series ring. This season may represent his last, best chance.

“I feel fairly comfortable,” Mattingly said. “Early on, it felt fast. Since then, it’s been pretty good. It helps when we’re winning. I’m glad to be in this seat.”

Pardon my cynicism, but it was refreshing — and a bit surprising — to hear interim Red Sox manager Chad Tracy say last week that he decides the lineup, not the front office.

“The final pen to paper is my call,” he said.

Tracy said he generally sits with bench coach José David Flores to come up with the lineup.

“I get ideas and hear other people’s thoughts about where will be a good day [to use] this guy or that guy,” he said. “That will always be the case. I have really good people around me that I trust to cover your blind spots.”

It can’t be easy. The Sox went into the weekend with the worst offense in the American League, a product of their lack of power and poor seasons from, among others, Caleb Durbin, Jarren Duran, Carlos Narváez, and Trevor Story.

Tracy had seven-plus years of experience managing in the minors before he was promoted. He said the level of information in the major leagues is far deeper, and there’s more video to use when making decisions.

“Similar information but a much wider [range] of what is actually available to you,” he said.

Minor league lineups are focused on development, not necessarily winning games.

“In the minor leagues, the construction of a lineup is who’s on the 40-man [roster] that’s immediately going to help us? Who are the top prospects that we need to see get in the batter’s box a lot?

“A guy hitting first vs. sixth could be the difference of 100 plate appearances in a year. All of that stuff is considered for getting guys the reps they need; making sure that 40-man guys who are going to come up the next day are ready to go.”

A few other observations on the Red Sox:

▪ Speaking of the lineup, how long do the Sox keep Duran batting leadoff? He has a .304 on-base percentage batting first over the last two seasons, with 100 more strikeouts (142) than walks (42).

That’s a 127-game sample size, too.

▪ Wilyer Abreu is off to a start that could merit down-ballot MVP votes.

The 27-year-old right fielder has a team-best .860 OPS and leads all American League outfielders with 11 defensive runs saved. Only Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong (13) has more.

Abreu won his second Gold Glove last season and has been even better this year.

“It’s hard to believe because he was so good before,” Tracy said. “Balls get hit, and it looks like he’s already taken four steps by the time you glance at him.

“He’s moving before the ball even comes off the bat. He’s just become very, very good.”

▪ You may have noticed Sox players on second base seeming to signal the batter what pitch is coming. With PitchCom, there are no signs to steal, but some pitchers give it away by how they waggle their gloves or if they show their grip too early.

That said, the Sox are mostly pretending, according to several opposing teams.

“Some of it’s real, and some of it’s just to make you think they know something,” Mattingly said. “We saw a lot of the same [signals] on different pitches, so it tells you they didn’t really have anything.”

▪ If the Sox wanted to fire Jason Varitek as game planning and run prevention coach, fine. That’s their right. Varitek was traded as a prospect and became a part-time player at the end of his playing career. He understands how the game works.

But the Sox claimed, “he has been reassigned to a new role within the organization.” Was that supposed to mollify the fans who have fond memories of Varitek from his playing days?

That wasn’t true. Like manager Alex Cora and the rest of the coaches who were fired, Varitek is a free agent and can join another team if he chooses.

In a NESN appearance, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said Varitek has an “open invitation to stay in the organization as long as he wants.”

It would be out of character for Varitek to take some phony job and pretend all is well. If he wants to stay in baseball, there are teams that would value what he has to offer.
