Ryan Flynn is a baseball evangelist, bringing the game to places such as Australia, Guam, and New Zealand, undeterred by any obstacles.

He arrived in New Zealand in 2009 and helped build the national team to the point where it fell a game short of qualifying for the 2013 World Baseball Classic.

“It would have been one of the greatest upsets in baseball history had we advanced,” Flynn said.

Now he has taken on another big challenge: building up the baseball culture in Ireland.

Flynn was named chief executive officer of Baseball Ireland earlier this month. He is tasked with growing a grassroots program from the tee-ball level up while finding or developing players for the national team.

There are eight baseball clubs in Ireland, home to about 500 players. Gaelic football, soccer, hurling, rugby, and a few other sports are far more popular.

“That’s the kind of challenge I like,” Flynn said. “I want to go head-to-head and go after the best athletes and show a vision for the future.”

Beyond his Irish roots, the 55-year-old Flynn has an eclectic background that makes him a perfect fit for the job. He was born in upstate New York and played third base for St. Rose College. He has since visited 80-plus countries and lived in England, Hungary, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and Palau, a small island nation in the Pacific.

Flynn has a playbook for fundraising, building awareness, and engaging people. He has already spoken to Yankees general manager Brian Cashman and scheduled a meeting with Red Sox team president Sam Kennedy, among others.

“You have to work with the diaspora and raise awareness,” Flynn said.

Italy offers an example of what is possible. The Azzurri beat the United States in pool play during this year’s WBC, then knocked off Puerto Rico in the quarterfinals before losing 4-2 to Venezuela in the semifinals.

Most of Italy’s players were major leaguers of Italian heritage. But there were three natives on the roster, and baseball gained previously unprecedented attention in the country.

“Why can’t Ireland do that?” Flynn said. “The WBC had a huge impact in Italy in terms of interest in baseball.”

There have been 48 major leaguers born in Ireland, most of whom played in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The last was righthander Joe Cleary, who was born in Cork and raised in New York City. He appeared in one game for the 1945 Senators and allowed seven runs in one-third of an inning against the Red Sox at Washington’s Griffith Stadium.

If there’s a next one, it could be a player Flynn helps to discover.

The large Irish community in the Boston area could be a resource for Baseball Ireland, and Flynn is eager to hear from would-be supporters. Contact him at rflynn@baseballireland.com.

“It doesn’t seem like the sentence matches the seriousness of the offense in any way, shape, or form,” Cox said Sunday. “Now the person comes out and almost does the exact same thing with a bigger gun and more bullets. It is troubling and the lack of accountability around that.”

Cox, who was not the Boston police commissioner in 2020, stopped short of directly criticizing the judge or parole authorities involved in the earlier case but repeatedly questioned whether the criminal justice system had adequately addressed the danger Brown posed.

“My job is not to criticize other people in their roles,” Cox said. “I don’t know all the factors that were considered, but clearly this person was really willing and able to offend again, and it didn’t really take long.”

The commissioner, who said he has been shot at before, described the emotional toll such cases take on police officers, particularly when suspects accused of violent crimes are later released and allegedly reoffend.

“It is disheartening,” Cox said. “You feel as though I’m putting my life on the line for what, when this person can get out pretty easily.”

On Monday, Brown’s alleged attack sent motorists fleeing from their cars and triggered a chaotic police response near Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Prosecutors say Brown fired 50 to 60 rounds from an “assault-style” rifle into traffic, striking two bystanders, before he was shot and apprehended by a Massachusetts State Police trooper assisted by an armed former Marine.

Brown pleaded not guilty Thursday from his hospital bed on video conference. He appeared heavily medicated during his arraignment. Officials said he was shot in the “lower extremities.”

Authorities said he had been reported suicidal and armed shortly before the shooting began. Brown, who suffered from mental health problems, was recently released from a psychiatric hospital and was reportedly using crack cocaine, according to court documents.

Cox said the Memorial Drive attack was “extremely scary” and praised both the responding troopers and the civilian who intervened.

“It’s a nightmare for the community, it’s a nightmare for law enforcement that has to respond to that as an active shooter,” he said.

The Memorial Drive shootout occurred during a recent spate of shootings in Roxbury, Mattapan, and Dorchester. Five shootings in just several days, including one fatal attack.

Cox defended the city’s public safety record while acknowledging public concern, maintaining that Boston remains among the nation’s safest large cities.

“Any act of violence is too many,” Cox said. “But our city is a safe city... sometimes we have a rush of things that happen, and then we do what we can and hold those folks accountable.”

Cox said Boston police have already made arrests in two of the recent shooting cases and are continuing efforts to identify and prosecute those responsible.

During Sunday’s interview, Cox also defended the department’s body camera policy, which received public criticism after Officer Nicholas O’Malley shot and killed a suspect in a carjacking in March. Under the current policy, bodycam footage is subject to public records laws but is exempt from release during an active investigation.

O’Malley was charged over the fatal on-duty shooting, meaning bodycam footage of the incident is not available to the public. He is the first officer charged with shooting and killing a suspect on duty in more than 30 years.

Some police departments across the country have adopted timelines requiring footage to be released within 30, 60, or 90 days, regardless of the status of an investigation. But Cox said those policies often contain exceptions that ultimately allow departments to withhold video anyway.

“There are certain things I think that we should do in the future, as far as transparency, as far as making sure people understand what our investigative processes are,” he said. “Putting things on the website so people can know what happens when someone is involved in a shooting, things of that nature, which we’re working on.”

O’Malley has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter for the death of Stephenson King, 39, who allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car.

Many local business leaders know Jim Brett as the New England Council’s longstanding chief executive.

Some are familiar with his work on behalf of those with disabilities, and others remember his political career: a state rep from Savin Hill who went on to run for mayor and lose to Tom Menino.

But it was another side hustle of Brett’s that was recognized on May 8 at the annual gala for the United South End Settlements, an anti-poverty nonprofit. There, Brett received the Philip Dushku Changemaker award (named after the late school teacher). The honor is meant to recognize Brett’s efforts helping USES and mentoring USES chief executive Jerrell Cox, along with the food and holiday toy donations he provides to USES from the Mary Ann Brett Food Pantry in Dorchester. (Also honored that night: Gary Bailey, program director for Simmons University’s school of social work, received the Mel King Social Innovator award.)

Brett first started helping Cox and USES about five years ago, after Becca Gould, senior vice president of public affairs at American Tower, introduced the two of them. Brett took Cox under his wing and showed him around Boston’s business community. The food pantry also gives dozens of toys to USES kids at Christmastime, and provides meals to families served by USES.

Brett’s food-pantry work goes back even further, around 20 years — to when Father Paul Soper, a pastor in Dorchester at the time, started the pantry at St. Margaret’s Church. Seventeen years ago, when Brett planned his 60th birthday, he threw a party to raise some $40,000 for the food pantry, prompting church leaders to name the pantry after his mother. Now he helps out almost every Saturday at the pantry, along with his wife Pattie, and two-dozen other volunteers who prepare and pack food for around 200 families.

“The reward is so great, knowing you are helping your neighborhood,” Brett says. “I get a lot out of it, to say the least.”

“It’s not a lifetime achievement award,” Thorndike said. “It’s the opposite of that.”

Thorndike wants to support scholars near the start of their research career, similar to how he invested in first-time chief executives. His 2012 book, “The Outsiders,” covers this ground, too, exploring what makes a successful CEO. He learned younger, successful chief executives are more open to new ideas and more likely to learn from different industries.

Similarly, he said, scientists who do the most groundbreaking research usually make discoveries at relatively young ages, before becoming more risk-averse.

Thorndike cofounded Housatonic Partners in 1994 with two partners in Boston, and they expanded to San Francisco several years later. “We backed really early-career CEOs, and we had a terrific record of doing that over time,” Thorndike said.

Thorndike had read a book by Tracy Kidder about Paul Farmer and his nonprofit Partners In Health and told himself he would devote money to help the next generation of Paul Farmers pursue their dreams if he became financially successful.

Thorndike has retired from the PE firm, though Housatonic still lists him as a senior adviser. His focus is primarily on Cromwell Harbor and its Chrysalis Prize project. With academic research facing funding cuts lately, he figures this new prize is more important than ever. There will be a particular emphasis on researchers willing to look outside of their core fields for insights.

“We’re trying to break the general trend in academia toward increasing specialization,” Thorndike said. “We like this broader idea of providing resources to extremely talented, very early-career people, at the time when it’s most difficult to attract resources.”

As Boston and Massachusetts prepare to celebrate the country’s 250th birthday, Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce chief executive Jim Rooney wants to remind us that businesspeople made it all possible.

The birth of the country, that is, not the birthday celebration — though Boston’s business leaders are playing a big role in that as well.

At the chamber’s annual meeting last week, Rooney focused on the pivotal role Boston’s business community played in the nation’s independence. The colonists who revolted against the British, he said, shared a common belief in the importance of free enterprise.

“The American free enterprise story that started here in Boston is a story of growth and opportunity, a story of collective hope and optimism, not division and fear,” Rooney told the crowd gathered in the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center ballroom. “It is no exaggeration to say that the America we will celebrate this summer was born right here in Boston. As I always remind my friends from Philly, Boston shed the blood. Philly filed the paperwork.”

Rooney implored those in the room to tackle today’s economic challenges — including affordable housing, energy prices, and transportation — with the same revolutionary mindset. He concluded: “To support these efforts, we should be embracing growth and free markets, as we have in the past, when they are most needed.”

Rapid7 chief executive Corey Thomas said Rooney shows no sign of slowing down, as evidenced by all the late-night phone calls he got from Rooney during his tenure as board chair. (Thomas hands over the role to Bank of America executive Miceal Chamberlain this summer.)

That prompted Mayor Michelle Wu to joke, as she stepped to the podium: “I’m glad to hear I’m not the only one who gets the late-night Jim Rooney phone calls.”

Wu also echoed one of the points Rooney made in his speech.

“Boston has always been on the leading edge in reinventing the next wave of innovation,” she said. “We’re doubling down on making Boston the ‘human capital’ capital of the globe.”

Governor Maura Healey, in her speech, offered personal stories about the three businesspeople honored by the chamber as “Distinguished Bostonians”: Paul Ayoub, chair of Nutter McClennen & Fish; Kevin Churchwell, chief executive of Boston Children’s Hospital; and Catherine D’Amato, retiring chief executive of the Greater Boston Food Bank.

“Amazing things are happening in our city and our state,” Healey said. “But none of it would be possible without the leadership, the creativity, and the generosity of our business community.”

Massachusetts Senate President Karen Spilka is promising energy legislation in the coming weeks that offers companies and consumers significant savings. But she’s being coy, for now, about how she plans to pull it off.

Last week, speaking at an Associated Industries of Massachusetts meeting at the New England Aquarium, Spilka told the business-oriented crowd that the Senate’s upcoming energy bill will balance “climate leadership, economic competitiveness, and cost savings.”

Speaking with AIM chief executive Brooke Thomson, Spilka emphasized the last of those three elements. She said her team, led by energy committee co-chair Mike Barrett, will produce an energy bill not long after the Senate’s budget debate ends this week.

The House of Representatives has passed its version, which would trim $1 billion from the Mass Save energy efficiency program’s three-year budget. The House bill would also require refunds of payments that electricity suppliers make if they miss the state’s renewable energy goals, estimated at $388 million over 10 years.

The Senate is expected to leave Mass Save largely intact, so it’s not clear where Spilka and Barrett will turn for savings. (Barrett has said he has his eyes on an expensive natural-gas pipe replacement program, known as “GSEP.”)

Still, Spilka promised rate relief is coming.

“There will be savings in our energy bill, I don’t want to say specifically where at this point, stay tuned,” Spilka said. “It will, no surprise, be different than the House [bill]. We have savings, significant savings as well.”

More than 4,400 undergraduates and graduate students dressed in black caps and gowns and multicolored hoods and cords celebrated with cheers and big waves for their family and friends seated in the stands.

“You Boston College graduates of 2026 are more needed than ever,” said Leahy, who did not mention his planned retirement in his short remarks. “I pray that you strive to be forces for good and powerful examples for those around you, and that you bear fruit that will last.”

Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, encouraged graduates to work for justice, promote dialogue, and never forget the poor and marginalized.

“Human dignity is granted or ceded, be it by the state, or government, or even popular consensus,” said Gallagher, a native of Liverpool, noting the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. “But rather arises from truths about the human person that precede all those things.”

He referenced the writings of theologian John Henry Newman, emphasizing the importance of community and human connection in education. Gallagher said Newman believed universities were shaped not only by classrooms and lectures, but also by relationships students build with one another.

“I would like to dwell briefly on the three verbs Newman highlighted: to respect, to consult, and to aid,” he said.

Gallagher and five others received honorary degrees from BC, the nation’s seventh-largest Catholic university.

After the ceremony, students retreated to other parts of campus to receive diplomas from their individual colleges, including arts and sciences, business, education, nursing and theology.

“We’re walking with all our friends in the sunshine, and that’s what BC has felt like for me,” said Charlotte Caine, 22, who received a degree in English and classics. “I’d like to continue feeling that way.”

Zaria Carter, a 21-year-old math major, teaches third- and fourth-graders at a local school and plans to continue doing so. She said a few years ago, she would have said she wanted to be an accountant, but she discovered a different path at BC.

“I’m really excited about the thought of being a teacher, and I was never really excited about being an accountant,” she said while walking to the ceremony. “BC has taught me to follow what makes me excited and passionate.”

The pride and emotion of the day extended to faculty and family.

“Today’s our 150th commencement ceremony, and so our [Messina College] students are part of that long, proud legacy,” said Thomas Wesner, a professor of business law who taught at Messina College.

Stefano DeZerega flew from San Francisco to watch his son, Nico Tomlinson DeZerega, get his bachelor’s degree in economics.

“I’m really grateful for all the experiences he had,” DeZerega said. “It’s a moment of optimism and exploration. I am very proud.”

Nancy Beltran was a proud aunt, there to see her niece, Katy Elena Meza, graduate with a nursing degree.

“She is the first grandchild in the family who is graduating,” Beltran said as she sat with their entire family. “We are all immigrants from Honduras, and honestly, I think we’re just very proud.”

About 100 Messina College graduates were welcomed into the BC alumni ranks during a ceremony on its campus in Brookline.

“Not many people can say that they were the first for their class,” said student speaker Truns-Winslie Paul. “We created a community where there wasn’t one yet, and we made it our own.”

Family members clutched balloons and cheered as students walked across the stage to collect their degrees.

About 40 students who earned a 3.4 grade point average or better will continue at BC for bachelor’s degrees. Others will head off to one of six colleges with which Messina has enrollment agreements: Bryant University in Rhode Island, Endicott College, Regis College, the University of Massachusetts-Boston, Worcester State University, and Albertus Magnus College in Connecticut.

Students took pride in being the first graduates of a program still finding its footing.

“We were the first class,” said Jose Builes Lemus, 19, a data science major who is from Colombia. “We were building everything together.”

Lemus, who is continuing at BC, said coming to the United States three years ago and entering a brand-new program was intimidating. But students learned to advocate to address some logistical challenges, such as transportation and campus resources, he said.

“Being able to help others that are coming behind me,” he said, “that was a good part of it.”

Brianna Amado, who graduated with an associate degree in applied psychology, said that they’re “setting the tone” for the upcoming classes.

“I’m happy to move on to bigger and better things,” said Amado, who will continue her education in psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

Other Messina graduates reflected on how much they had changed since they first arrived on campus.

For Hodan Ahmed, a 20-year-old who will continue her education at BC’s nursing school, balancing demanding coursework with summer classes tested her.

“This semester specifically was really difficult for me,” Ahmed, who is from Roxbury. “But I have professors who were genuinely willing to help me outside of class time.”

Families who attended the ceremony at Alumni Stadium and at Messina are excited for their students’ future educational journey.

“They’re very excited,” Ahmed said about her family sitting in the stadium. “They’re really proud of me, which I see as obviously an accomplishment.”

Family meant everything to Ryan Pina Gonzalez, who graduated with a business degree.

“Without them I’m nothing, so it’s amazing having them here,” Pina Gonzalez said as he stood surrounded by his family after graduation.

“I’m so proud of him,” added his sister, Gianna Pina Gonzalez, “because I know how hard he’s worked to get to this point.”

With less than a month to the kickoff of the games in Foxborough, the finger-pointing has added further tension to what have become underwhelming preparations and event-planning for the international tournament.

“I really don’t know how we got here. This is a major international event, this should’ve been sorted out a long time ago,” said City Council President Liz Breadon.

Last Friday, Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority general manager Phil Eng sent a letter to Boston officials that serves “as notice that the MBTA intends to acquire the temporary right to occupy this portion of Summer Street.” (The T says it has legal authority to take public property, so long as it is temporary.)

The city says not so fast, painting the letter as an “eminent domain” power move.

“The City opposes this inappropriate use of eminent domain to bypass the permitting process for roadways under local jurisdiction, and we urge the Commonwealth to withdraw the filing while plans are being reviewed,” a spokesperson for Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration said in a statement.

The spokesperson said Boston has ”proposed alternatives to meet the safety and security needs of the World Cup while preserving access to this area for residents, visitors, and local commuters.”

The T, for its part, said through a spokesperson that it continues to work with the city, with talks taking place as recently as Tuesday.

The MBTA expects about 20,000 fans to take trains from Boston to Gillette Stadium for each of the local Cup matches. The T asserts that given the crowds, the “security posture” around South Station should mirror that of Gillette on match days.

But Boston officials argue the street closure would further snarl traffic in an area already heavily congested during rush hour. They worry that planned detours for the closure don’t accurately account for driver behavior and that the proposal is underpinned by old data.

The city says it has proposed alternatives to shutting Summer Street that include utilizing Dewey Square and the Rose Kennedy Greenway Station as staging areas for passengers.

But the T nixed that counter-offer, saying it needs the space for security screenings, and that the threat a vehicle poses to the crowd is a legitimate concern. Staging crowds across the street from South Station at the Greenway or in Dewey Square could create unsafe bottlenecks at crosswalks and would disrupt Atlantic Avenue traffic anyway, according to the T.

World Cup matches will be held in Foxborough on June 13, 16, 19, 23, 26, and 29, as well as July 9. The T wants to close down the street for up to 10 hours on game days, according to the letter. Previously, the T and the city agreed to close only a portion of Summer Street on June 13 and 19, but Eng declared in the letter that “equal public safety needs exist for the other five matches.”

Only one of the seven matches is slated for a weekend day, with the rest scheduled for kickoff in the afternoon or evening during the work week.

Summer Street is a busy thoroughfare that runs through the Financial District into the Seaport and South Boston. The portion that would be closed on Cup game days is about one-fifth of a mile to just before the intersection with Dorchester Avenue on the west side of the channel.

For City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, the spat represents a larger issue: how the T deals with the city.

“The MBTA is so insensitive to the needs of the city,” he said. “If the city says, ‘You can’t shut down the street,’ the MBTA should come back and say, ‘How should we do it?’ ”

“They’re not listening.”

Breadon, the council president, pointed to an international friendly match between France and Brazil in late March, when so many fans mobbed South Station for the 20-plus-mile train ride to the stadium that some pedestrians were forced to walk in the street. For that friendly, the T set aside 5,760 roundtrip tickets, and only about 2,600 were sold, far fewer than the 20,000 riders expected for each World Cup game.

Given the anticipated crowds, removing cars from that portion of Summer Street would be a prudent move, said Breadon.

“With that amount of people, it seems to make sense that closing Summer Street is the proper way to go,” she said.

At the T’s most recent board of directors meeting on April 30, Erika Mazza, chief enterprise development officer, said the queuing of train riders on just the sidewalk for the Brazil-France friendly did not work out. In short, there was inadequate space, pedestrians who were simply trying to pass through on the sidewalk did not have enough room, and emergency access to the station was compromised, as was accessibility for the disabled.

Moving the queue off the sidewalk and onto a closed-off Summer Street would allow the T to relieve reduce crowding and access issues by giving fans a larger space.

As part of its security preparations, the T is viewing the large crowds in a different light from those who flock to Red Sox, Celtics, Bruins, and Patriots games. For example, there will be far fewer English speaking fans and many of the international fans often celebrate their teams with exuberant and lengthy marches.

Keeping them safe outside and inside South Station, and on each of the 14 trains making the express round trips to the stadium, requires a different approach than the usual Boston sporting events, T officials said.

The dispute over crowd management around South Station is the latest sign of broader dysfunction surrounding Boston’s preparations for the Cup, now just three weeks away.

For months, doubts have swirled in Greater Boston business circles about whether celebrations will have to be scaled back due to a lack of money from private and public sources.

Earlier this year, a protracted dispute between Boston Soccer 26 and the town of Foxborough briefly cast doubt over whether the event would proceed when Foxborough threatened to withhold an entertainment license. (The bitter feuding ended when the town received the assurances it sought.)

But that embarrassment could pale in comparison to what would happen if the region does not get crowd management right for the tournament.

Brian Higgins, a former police chief for Bergen County, N.J., and a lecturer at John Jay College of Criminal Justice, said good crowd management is crucial to the success of a large event such as the World Cup. Local public safety authorities will want to consider a multitude of measures to safeguard the crowd from vehicles, to ensure safe egress and ingress, all the while keeping the queue moving so that fans don’t grow frustrated and tense.

“We’ve seen example after example of crowded situations that end in tragedy,” he said. “It’s a key to the whole event.”

In an interview on Saturday, Councilor Christopher A. Iannella Jr., of Boston, said DeMore’s nomination wasn’t put to a vote because he didn’t have enough support for confirmation. Nominees need a majority of the eight elected councilors, though Healey can tap Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll to break a tie.

Iannella said he opposes DeMore’s nomination, saying he’d prefer a nominee with expertise in mental health and substance abuse.

Councilor Paul DePalo of Worcester said Tuesday he would also vote against DeMore because he lacks expertise to evaluate whether a prisoner would be a good fit for parole.

Councilor Tara Jacobs, who represents Western Massachusetts, told State House News Service she would vote against DeMore and hoped Healey, a Democrat, would withdraw the nomination.

Yet Healey held firm, and then last week Tyler E. Brown IV, a parolee, allegedly shot and wounded motorists on Memorial Drive. The violence triggered fresh scrutiny of the Parole Board and harsh criticism of its performance from the state Republican Party and two GOP gubernatorial candidates hoping to unseat Healey in November.

When the Governor’s Council reconvenes on Wednesday, councilors voting on DeMore’s nomination will have to weigh unusually vocal opposition to his candidacy alongside public alarm over parole decisions at levels not seen since a parolee shot and killed a veteran Woburn police officer in 2010.

Late Monday, Healey’s office sent a letter to the Governor’s Council urging it to confirm DeMore’s nomination, saying it’s important that the Parole Board has diverse representation.

“It is imperative that — in all its functions — the Parole Board carefully evaluate the requests of its incarcerated individuals, the voices of victims and their family members, and public safety,” the letter reads.

DeMore is a cofounder and defense attorney at Henning Strategies, a Boston law firm, and a former prosecutor for the Suffolk district attorney’s office. He serves as a US Army Reserve captain who represents crime victims in the Judge Advocate General Corps. Reached Friday for comment, DeMore referred the Globe to Healey’s office.

The Parole Board has had a vacancy since last September when Tonomey Coleman, the panel’s acting leader, was nominated for a District Court judgeship.

The other Parole Board members confirmed for five-year terms during Healey’s tenure are Angelo Gomez Jr., a former parole supervisor who took charge of the panel in October; Rafael Ortiz and Edith J. Alexander, both former probation officers; and Sarah B. Coughlin, a licensed clinical social worker.

Healey also renominated Charlene Bonner, a forensic psychologist who joined the board in 2011 and was confirmed for a fourth term in 2023. Her credentials satisfy a state requirement adopted by the Legislature in 2014 that the board have at least one member with “experience in forensic psychology.”

Board members hold thousands of parole hearings annually, mostly in state prisons and county jails, and parole officers supervised nearly 3,000 people in 2024, the latest data available.

The institutional hearings resulted in votes for release for two-thirds of applicants from 2021 to last year, board figures show.

In 2024, the board’s workload grew significantly after the state Supreme Judicial Court banned life without parole for people who were convicted of crimes they committed when they were between the ages of 18 and 20.

Overnight, 210 offenders became eligible for parole for the first time, leading to closely watched hearings as people sentenced to life terms as far back as the 1960s lined up seeking release.

The board has issued decisions in 89 of those cases and granted parole to 65, or 73 percent, according to figures tracked by the Globe.

The parole rate between 2021 and last year for people serving life sentences was 59 percent, though the figures exclude six pending cases from 2025, the board said.

At DeMore’s hearing last month, six people, including a social worker and parole lawyer, testified against his nomination, arguing his prosecutorial background is at odds with the panel’s mandate to decide whether offenders have rehabilitated themselves and can safely rejoin the community.

More than 400 people have signed a letter urging the Governor’s Council to vote against DeMore, opponents said.

Among DeMore’s detractors is Stacey Borden, founder of New Beginnings Reentry Services, Inc. in Roxbury.

In an interview Saturday, Borden said the Parole Board needs a member who was previously incarcerated to provide more balance and insight into what parole candidates face.

She also took exception to DeMore’s testimony that his prosecution work was not a law enforcement role.

“The DA is absolutely law enforcement,” said Borden, who testified against DeMore’s nomination at his hearing.

Borden ran unsuccessfully in 2024 for the Governor’s Council, sharing her story about serving prison time for drug and financial crimes, and later earning a master’s degree.

“We do not need another punitive law enforcement person sitting on the Parole Board,” Borden said.

A former prosecutor hasn’t served on the Parole Board since 2022 when Gloriann Moroney resigned and became a District Court judge, Healey’s office said.

DeMore told the Governor’s Council that as a prosecutor, he worked in juvenile courts and collaborated with community partners to reach just outcomes for people with mental illness who were accused of crimes.

He highlighted his role in litigation before the SJC that led to the dismissal of more than 21,000 cases tainted by disgraced chemist Annie Dookhan. He also noted his work addressing drunken driving prosecutions undermined by unreliable breath tests.

“Service on the Parole Board represents an opportunity to use my diverse experience and marshal the many voices I’ve heard through the years to positively impact my community and to continue to lead with empathy and respect,” DeMore told the council.

A retired state judge and a formerly incarcerated person who now runs substance abuse and mental health programs for the city of Chelsea testified in support of DeMore.

Councilors Terrence W. Kennedy, of Lynnfield, and Tamisha Civil said they intend to vote for DeMore.

In the case of Brown, the alleged Memorial Drive shooter, Kennedy said DeMore might have scrutinized his parole request more closely.

“I fully support the governor in terms of not withdrawing the nomination. I think that would be a shame,” he said.

Councilor Mara Dolan, of Concord, said in an interview that “public safety must come first” but declined to comment on how she would vote on DeMore.

“When it can cost over $200,000 a year to keep someone in jail, we must be careful not to err on the other side and keep people in custody who do not pose a danger and have paid their debt to society,” she said.

Liam Lowney, executive director of the Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance, said the Parole Board would benefit from a member well-versed in survivors’ experiences, though he said neither he nor his agency is taking a position on DeMore’s nomination.

Here’s another tale about the gang that can’t shoot straight: Our vaunted World Cup host committee, Boston 26.

Last summer officials from Airbnb met with Boston 26 about sponsoring World Cup festivities as soccer fans descend upon the region for seven games this summer. The short-term rental giant, which is an official FIFA partner, had set aside $5 million to spend on World Cup programming at 16 host cities in North America.

On the same Zoom call, Airbnb brought up something they’re hoping to see happen in host cities: Relaxing short-term-rental regulations during the World Cup, to make it easier for people to rent out their homes, or what’s known as a special event exemption.

The meeting put Boston 26 on edge and they didn’t pursue a deal with Airbnb, for reasons that fairly sum up why local World Cup organizers can’t seem to get out of their own way.

According to a person knowledgeable about the call, the rationale went something like this: No way we’re approaching Mayor Michelle Wu. She was in the midst of a re-election fight against Josh Kraft, son of Robert Kraft, the driving force behind bringing the World Cup to Boston. Asking her to do a favor to help the World Cup? Awkward. Not only that, Wu, back when she was a city councilor, was the lead author of the short-term rental rules that Airbnb wanted to relax.

Then there was Meet Boston. The tourism agency is one of Boston 26’s biggest funders, and is itself largely funded by taxes on Boston and Cambridge hotels. Those hotels see Airbnb as a major competitor, and while Meet Boston CEO Martha Sheridan has touted the World Cup as an economic boom for the region, she presumably wants that boom to flow to hotels, not Airbnb hosts.

Moreover, at the time, Boston 26 was focused on securing seven-figure sponsorships. So its leaders, according to a person familiar with their thinking, decided it wasn’t worth alienating key allies for a slice of $5 million from Airbnb.

But Airbnb is keen on raising its profile this summer because soccer fans need a place to stay. Of the 164,000 tourists projected to visit Boston for the tournament, about 17,000 will stay in short-term rentals, according to a Deloitte study the company commissioned. Add in the nation’s 250th birthday on July 4, and Sail Boston’s parade of tall ships, and it’s shaping up to be a big summer.

In other words, Boston had leverage. And other cities, including New York, turned down Airbnb’s request to change their rules, yet still got Airbnb’s money for World Cup events.

It’s my understanding that Boston 26 did not think it was incumbent upon them to come up with a deal that would work for all involved. Meanwhile Airbnb was confounded by Boston 26’s tepid response, and moved on.

In the months since, Boston 26 has struggled with fundraising, securing a little more than $20 million in private donations from just a handful of companies.

Airbnb, meanwhile, has been delivering gifts to host cities like Santa Claus: more than $1.2 million to refurbish soccer pitches in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Oakland, over $1 million for festivals and fields in New York and New Jersey, and over $1 million to Houston to expand green infrastructure and increase youth access to soccer. Philadelphia cleverly used Airbnb money to fund free subway rides home from its games (compare that with the $80 round-trip gameday fare on the commuter rail between South Station and Foxborough).

Airbnb even sent $250,000 to Rhode Island to help fund a summer of soccer celebrations. With Gillette Stadium about as close to Providence as it is to Boston, Ocean State 26 organizers gladly took Airbnb’s money.

Airbnb’s largesse makes me wonder if the company would take another look at supporting Boston’s World Cup festivities. After all, co-founder Nathan Blecharczyk, is a West Roxbury native and went to Boston Latin Academy. He’s still with Airbnb as its chief strategy officer and likes to support his hometown like the time he presented a $1 million gift to BLA.

So I asked an Airbnb spokesman, who said the company continues to look at ways to support host cities and is “open” to what more it can do in Boston.

Meanwhile, Boston 26 spokeswoman Julie Duffy said the committee welcomes partnership conversations and “our commercial team has reached out to explore what may be possible here.”

As for Meet Boston, Sheridan says she has no issues with a potential Airbnb sponsorship.

“Original discussions with Airbnb involved a Boston 26 staff member who has since departed the organization,” she said in a statement. “Meet Boston’s priority is to fill hotel rooms and we are confident that bookings are solid, so that is not influencing current discussions with Airbnb about a Boston partnership.”

This feels like the latest in a long string of misunderstandings around the World Cup, from who pays for security in Foxborough to FIFA holding up applications for local watch parties. But maybe there’s still time to make this relationship right. Perhaps it’s a chance to lower our cost of transportation to the games. Why should Philly be the only one?

Sounds like something we should pursue. Just don’t leave the negotiations up to Boston 26.

What do Raffles Boston general manager Carlos Bueno, Comfort Kitchen cofounder Biplaw Rai, and event planner extraordinaire Rose Staram have in common? They are all being honored Tuesday night at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center for being among the “50 Most Influential People Of Color in Hospitality & Tourism.” We got a sneak peek of the list, compiled by Colette Phillips’s Get Konnected! networking group, as the region prepares to host a throng of tourists for the World Cup, a historic Fourth of July, and a parade of tall ships. We’ve heard from Associated Industries of Massachusetts that local employers have been downbeat for the past year. Now we have a new poll out today from the Retailers Association of Massachusetts showing consumers aren’t too happy, either. A pollster surveyed 608 registered voters a few weeks ago, via a web poll, and found only 36 percent believe things in Massachusetts are headed in the right direction, compared to 48 percent two years ago, and 59 percent in 2023. RAM president Jon Hurst says his business members regularly complain about taxes, health insurance requirements, and electric utility mandates, and he suspects consumers are starting to feel the pinch, too.

The Boston-based autonomous aviation startup Merlin has been banking on defense contracts, such as its work retrofitting a military transport jet made by Lockheed Martin. But now the publicly traded firm, led by entrepreneur Matt George, is branching out into commercial business as well, with a new collaboration with freighter lessor World Star Aviation. Merlin’s tech specializes in flying a plane with one pilot instead of two, or maybe someday, no pilot at all. So far, though, the pilots who fly our passenger airlines – Delta, JetBlue, and the like – seem to be safe from Merlin’s magic.

You-Do-It Development? One of the last vestiges of mid-century Americana along Route 128 will be preserved by developer Onyx Partners, which has acquired the former You-Do-It Electronics building in Needham, the one with the distinctive sign, to use as its headquarters. After more than 70 years of being run by the Achigian family, You-Do-It sold its last receivers and speaker wire in 2024. Onyx is redoing the building’s interior but has pledged to keep the You-Do-It billboard that sits atop its roof, a reminder of simpler times.

It was bound to happen: NIMBYs coming for data centers.

Municipalities all over the country, including in Massachusetts, are itching to pass ordinances to ban the hulking structures, which can be the size of a Walmart or even bigger, as our colleague Hiawatha Bray reported. A recent Quinnipiac University poll confirmed just how unpopular they are, with 65 percent of Americans saying they oppose the building of a data center in their community, citing concerns about electricity costs and water use, as well as noise.

The truth is, the data center boom has pretty much bypassed New England. Electricity is simply too expensive here. Still, we can understand why some towns are apprehensive about so-called hyperscalers coming here, even as other locales roll out the red carpet.

But the dearth of data centers has its downside: These are massive construction projects at a time when that sector is hurting locally. Harvard University economist Jason Furman has estimated that data center investment accounted for 92 percent of GDP growth in the first half of 2025.

And Governor Maura Healey knows the economic stakes are high for Massachusetts. In late 2024, she signed a measure that would exempt proposed data centers from state sales tax. And in April she pledged not to sign a moratorium on new data centers like one recently proposed in Maine. “That’s not going to help our economy,” Healey said at a New England Council meeting. “That’s not going to help our future.”

In the two years since Carney Hospital shuttered amid the collapse of its former owner, Steward Health Care, Dorchester residents have grappled with both grief over the loss of a community institution and with longer trips to receive emergency medical care.

Now, the real estate firms tasked with revamping the nearly 13-acre health care campus on Dorchester Avenue near Lower Mills are kicking off the city’s formal development process.

The HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace, led by veteran developer Thomas N. O’Brien and the Rev. Jeffrey Brown, respectively, this week expect to notify the city’s planning department of their intent to demolish the now-empty hospital and build a five-building, $850 million campus with a health care facility, apartments and senior housing, and an education center. That process will kick off a series of community meetings and eventually a vote by the Boston Planning and Development Agency board.

If approved, the project would be built in phases, with the health care facility coming first, Brown and O’Brien said this week. They are in talks with a number of health care networks to lease the expected 350,000-square-foot property, among them Mass General Brigham, Beth Israel Lahey Health, BMC Health System, and Brown University Health, O’Brien said.

Brown and O’Brien stressed the health care facility would not be a hospital. Its final uses will be determined in collaboration with the future tenant, along with the state and city, and could include offerings such as an emergency room, MRI and X-Ray machines, and behavioral health beds. A 2025 community health report cochaired by Boston Public Health Commissioner Dr. Bisola Ojikutu and Michael Curry, chief executive of the Massachusetts League of Community Health Centers, recommended that a redeveloped property incorporate emergency services, primary care, and behavioral health services, among other suggestions.

“The community wants this to be a robust health facility,” O’Brien said. “We feel an obligation to make sure that we work to deliver on the aspects that the community has asked for.”

New York-based investment firm Apollo Global Management owns the Carney campus, and last year tapped HYM and My City at Peace to redevelop the property. Beyond the health care facility, the campus is expected to include 50,000 square feet of retail, a 50,000-square-foot educational facility — possibly for hands-on nursing or health care training — and 500 residential units.

The housing would include at least 200 apartments, along with another 100 units that could be either apartments or condominiums. The campus would include a separate senior living building, with 200 units of independent and assisted living and memory care. There’s a demand for senior housing that includes different methods of care under one roof, Brown said.

“I live in Dorchester, and I know that the residents of Dorchester are getting older,” he said.

Since last year, Brown and O’Brien have been to 35 community meetings, including more than a dozen civic associations and neighborhood councils. The meetings so far have been filled with emotion, they said, as the Dorchester community has collectively grieved the loss of the Carney. Beyond people losing jobs and access to health care, losing the Carney also meant losing a community institution where families gathered for meals and the legendary 15-minute Mass held in the hospital’s chapel.

The meetings were rough but necessary, Brown said.

“We thought it was an important part of the process to listen and to hold all of that, so that we can get to what we can do now as a result of the loss of this hospital,” Brown said. “The goal is to revive the sense of community that was lost in the old Carney.”

If one of the health care systems signs on board, O’Brien said, the project’s first phase could be ready to start construction by the end of next year and be ready to open by mid-2030.

“We think the window is now,” O’Brien said.

The now-suspended officer was released on personal recognizance following his March arraignment in Roxbury Municipal Court. The indictment moves the case to Suffolk Superior Court, where O’Malley will be arraigned at a later date, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

King was shot while he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car. Prosecutors determined that O’Malley had no justification for shooting at a moving vehicle.

“It is disappointing that the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office is choosing to second-guess an officer whose only goal was to protect the public,” O’Malley’s lawyer, David Yannetti, previously said in a statement. “We will continue to vigorously defend this officer and this case.”

Yannetti, best known for his successful defense of Karen Read, added in court papers that the “main issue in this case will be who the aggressor really was and whether Officer O’Malley acted in lawful defense.”

Yannetti filed several defense motions in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court in an effort to illustrate “King’s mayhem and reign of terror,” spanning nearly two decades and resulting in more than 17 criminal cases across Massachusetts, court records show.

Over the years, King has been charged with strangulation, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, carjacking, breaking and entering, gun offenses, and resisting arrest, according to court filings.

At the time of his death, King was free on bail for at least three separate felony cases and had active warrants for his arrest, court records said.

Yannetti is seeking King’s mental health, criminal, and court records from all his past cases, recordings from police body-worn and dash cameras, the medical examiner’s file on King, along with statements taken from O’Malley and witnesses at the scene of the shooting.

O’Malley told investigators that when he shot King, he feared for his own life and for the life of another officer at the scene, believing his colleague was about to be run over.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood. About 15 minutes later, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

The driver ignored “multiple verbal commands” as officers approached and tried to drive away, police said.

King opened the car window, but did not turn the vehicle off. O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” a police report said.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley fired three shots through the driver’s window, striking King, the report said.

King’s family has said he was experiencing a mental health crisis in the hours leading up to the deadly encounter.

In court filings, Yannetti said King gave “O’Malley no choice that night.”

“Any suggestion that this shooting was precipitated by simply a ‘mental health crisis’ completely misses the point,” Yannetti wrote. “When facing an extremely dangerous threat, there is no time for a police officer to hold a counseling session on the street or to sit down to discuss the feelings of a menace who is intent on using a motor vehicle as a deadly weapon.”

“If a man is going to assault and carjack an innocent woman, then threaten the lives and safety of the public and a police officer, that man needs to be stopped — whether he is in his right mind or not,” a defense motion stated.

But Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum said in court in March that investigators determined O’Malley’s explanation wasn’t reasonable, citing witness testimony and footage from police body cameras.

The other officer, Polumbaum, said, “was in greater danger of being struck by those bullets than he ever was by the car.”

While the law affords police officers deference for split-second decisions, “we keep in mind the law and common sense,” he said.

Immediately after firing the shots, O’Malley called over his radio that officers were involved in a shooting and the suspect “tried to run us over,” according to the police report. He later told investigators he believed the other officer “was going to be crushed by the suspect’s vehicle,” according to the police report.

However, investigating officers concluded that O’Malley’s statement “was not factually true.” State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

In March, responding to a question from reporters about whether the officers should have allowed the suspect to drive away, Hayden said that “in this circumstance, that might have been prudent.”

Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney representing King’s family, said he welcomed the indictment.

“For months, Stephenson King Jr.’s loved ones have been grieving the devastating loss of a son, a family member and a man whose life mattered deeply, while also fighting for the transparency and accountability they deserve,” Crump said. “The arrest, manslaughter charge, and now this indictment against the officer involved sends a powerful message about the seriousness of this case.”

Crump said the family “knows that accountability cannot stop here. They deserve the full truth about what happened to Stephenson and a justice system willing to fully examine every decision that led to his death. We will continue standing beside them and demanding transparency, truth and justice every step of the way.”

“I never thought coffee could taste like that,” the 35-year-old said.

He’s been trying to convince Boston of the same ever since.

Katisomsakul is part of a new generation of immigrant and Asian American entrepreneurs rethinking the traditional cafe with scrappy pop-ups and temporary concepts inside bars, gyms, and galleries across Boston. Together, they’re trying to transform a city long defined by convenience coffee into one driven by craft and cultural identity, even as the economics of Boston are increasingly stacked against them.

Even as independent operators like Katisomsakul are multiplying, commercial rents are soaring and chains are quickly adapting to trends.

But while Boston may still run on Dunkin’, its next generation of coffee drinkers increasingly wants something else.

Nearing closing time at Newbery, there was hardly an empty seat. Customers sipped light roasts, lingering over them like tea. Next door, Dunkin’ didn’t have a single customer sitting inside.

“The coffee scene is changing,” said Katisomsakul. “The industry has been ready for it. Finally, so is Boston.”

Whether Boston’s new wave of independent operators can survive may be another question entirely.

“At this rate, it’s going to be a whole lot of major corporations versus an army of independents,” said Tam Le, owner of Càphê Collective, a new Vietnamese cafe attached to a Cambridge art gallery. “National brands are knocking on Boston’s doorsteps. Those players will always have the marketing budgets, consultants, and ability to quickly add new items.”

Boston’s current coffee boom didn’t emerge out of nowhere. The city’s most recent coffee movement arrived in the 2000s and early 2010s, when specialty shops such as George Howell Coffee, Thinking Cup, Pavement Coffeehouse, and Barismo introduced single-origin beans and meticulous pour-overs.

But while craft coffee has long flourished in other Northeast cities, these previous spurts struggled to penetrate beyond Boston’s affluent neighborhoods. Some locals viewed $8 pour-overs as elitist and for yuppie newcomers, while Dunkin’ remained synonymous with the city’s working-class identity.

Today’s wave reflects a broader shift toward Thai beans, Vietnamese coffee, Japanese matcha, and social media-driven aesthetics where bright colors, white fluffy cold foam, and sweeter flavors reflect the tastes of a younger, more diverse Boston.

“Starbucks created coffee culture. But Generation Z and millennials don’t know anything other than coffee culture,” said Brian Warrener, director of the Center for Beverage Education & Innovation at Johnson & Wales University.

He said the region’s younger generation isn’t ashamed to swap the “difficult to consume” drinks such as bitter black coffee, hoppy IPAs, and dry wine with lots of tannins, for lighter, smoother, and sweeter choices.

“Starbucks and Dunkin’ now represent a commoditization of that culture. These generations expect more, and want everything to be an experience,” he said.

Americans are drinking more coffee, with 66 percent of adults reportedly drinking a cup every day. A recent Toast analysis found a bump in barista-crafted drinks that many people don’t have the skills or time to make at home. Latte orders rose 4 percent in 2025, while regular drip coffee sales fell by nearly the same amount.

Many of the same trends driving Boston’s indie coffee boom are also being rapidly adopted by the chains the newcomers are taking on.

Blank Street Coffee, the venture capital-backed chain that’s expanding rapidly, has embraced Gen Z-focused matcha drinks, now accounting for 50 percent of its business.

Starbucks and Dunkin’, which is attempting to go public for a third time, still dominate the market. But both chains have recently closed underperforming stores, are reconsidering their retail footprint, and introduced trendier items, such as dirty soda and protein-rich drinks.

Many of Boston’s newest coffee businesses don’t have a permanent address as owners avoid costs of traditional storefronts. Even established operators said Boston is becoming increasingly difficult.

“The challenge is finding locations and rents that actually can sustain an independent business,” said Andy LoPilato, CEO of Pavement Coffeehouse, a local chain still owned by its founder.

For many entering Boston’s coffee scene, the math behind opening a traditional cafe no longer works.

“We looked at different places all over Boston and surrounding areas, and it all ranges from $6,000 at the lowest to $22,000 a month,” to rent a retail space, said Najma Mohamed, who cofounded Espresso East, a yellow coffee truck that’s parked along the Neponset Greenway Trail, behind a CrossFit in Dorchester. It’s not visible from the street, but customers line up for lattes with flavors like maple sea salt, pistachio, Dutch cookie, and even baklava.

The coffee truck also serves a fig matcha that uses tea from a Japanese farm the owners have traveled to. That’s a menu that would have been considered nearly unthinkable at an indie shop two decades ago when French vanilla, mocha, and hazelnut were largely the only flavors. Then, being an aficionado meant being a purist.

Mohamed and her sister, who were born in Kenya, started planning Espresso East in 2023, in their early 20s. They pulled personal loans, credit cards, and their savings to make it happen. Opening a truck dramatically lowered the barrier. The sisters now own the truck debt-free. A brick-and-mortar would have required a weightier upfront investment between rent, build-outs, utilities, permits, and staffing.

“We stopped doing the math as soon as we saw the monthly lease amount alone,” said Mohamed.

On a recent Saturday, Simon Ngo and Tiffany Zheng were in Kenmore Square at The Handle Bar, vigorously whisking matcha powder to serve dozens of sweaty young people who had just finished a workout class. This spring, they launched Nomu, a roaming pop-up cafe serving ceremonial-grade Uji matcha, after traveling to Japan and learning about the tea.

Sarah Chan, 25, snagged one. “It’s nice to get matcha from an Asian-owned business by people who know what they’re doing,” said Chan.

Young Bostonians “see rising prices and want to actually know where the ingredients are coming from,” said Ngo, an East Boston native whose parents immigrated from Vietnam. “If they’re paying seven to eight dollars for a drink, they want to know it’s one of the best things they’re going to find in Boston.”

Le, of Càphê Collective, also owns Lê Madeline in Quincy. He remembers a moment after opening his first shop in Dorchester a decade ago where “typical blue collar Dunkin’ customers” first tried Vietnamese coffee.

“They were converted,” said Le.

Back at Merai in Brookline, Katisomsakul will soon take Newbery Street down a more traditional route, poised to open a storefront this summer. It’s a feat he never could have imagined — or afforded — when he started hosting pop-ups last year.

“I got my start selling coffee bags on a corner,” said Katisomsakul. “I think this is the beginning for coffee in Boston. I’m just a small piece of the movement.”

During the hearing Thursday morning in Cambridge District Court, Middlesex prosecutors played a short video showing Brown allegedly opening fire on Memorial Drive. The popping of gunshots rang out in an otherwise silent courtroom.

Citing the video and Brown’s criminal history dating back to his teen years, Assistant Middlesex District Attorney Nicole L. Allain argued he should be held without bail under the state’s dangerousness law.

District Court Judge David E. Frank agreed.

Brown’s public defender Carolyn I. McGowan didn’t challenge the dangerousness request.

But McGowan said there would be a vigorous defense at trial.

“There are miles to go in this case,” she said, also appearing via video conference from Brown’s bedside.

From the hospital bed, Brown wore a face mask and kept the covers pulled up to his chin. He didn’t speak during the hearing but appeared somewhat more alert than during his arraignment last week. He’s being treated for gunshot wounds to his “lower extremities,” officials have said.

Speaking from the bench, the judge said the information provided by prosecutors led him to conclude that Brown poses a danger to the public.

The shooting unfolded around lunchtime on May 11, not long after a Massachusetts parole officer called 911 to report that Brown was suicidal and armed with an assault rifle. The officer said Brown had an extensive criminal record, including a 2020 shootout with Boston police in the South End, along with a history of crack cocaine use and mental health problems. He had recently been discharged from a psychiatric hospital.

His long and complicated history with the criminal justice system includes a 2021 sentencing decision that has repeatedly drawn criticism for its apparent leniency. After the 2020 shootout with Boston police officers in the South End, now retired Superior Court judge Janet L. Sanders sentenced him to six years in prison, less than the 10-year sentence prosecutors had requested. Sanders had said she was persuaded by Brown’s intellectual gifts, his commitment to fatherhood, and promises to keep his life on track.

When Brown was released in May 2025, he was accepted into a yearlong re-entry program through the Tufts University Prison Initiative, but officials said he stopped attending in February.

In the hours preceding the Memorial Drive shooting, Brown repeatedly told his parole officer he was suicidal and displayed the assault rifle he allegedly later used, according to police and prosecutors.

The officer called 911 and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester, but he wasn’t home when officers got there. Boston police pinged his phone and tracked him to Cambridge.

Less than two hours after the 911 call, Brown began randomly shooting while walking down Memorial Drive, according to prosecutors. Panicked motorists ran for cover, some hiding under their cars.

Brown has been charged in Cambridge District Court with six felonies and two misdemeanors, including assault to murder, attempted assault and battery with a firearm, and gun and ammunition charges.

He pleaded not guilty last week, also from his hospital bed, appearing heavily medicated during a relatively short arraignment hearing.

In court on Thursday, prosecutors cited Brown’s long criminal history, including convictions from other states. Records show he was charged with armed robbery as a teenager in 1994. In 1999, he was charged with assaulting a Michigan corrections employee and escaping from jail. His other convictions include drug and gun offenses in Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

The May 2020 police shooting unfolded after someone called 911 and said a man was “talking crazy” and carrying a gun, according to court records. The caller and three other people were moving stuff into an apartment on Northampton Street when the man approached them, asked where they were from multiple times, then told them to “call your boys” and reached into his bag — where he had a firearm, a police report says.

When Boston police responded and found Brown a block away in the South End, he “appeared agitated,” leading officers to believe he could be an “emotionally disturbed person,” according to court records. He then pushed one of the officers, threw his backpack, and started running, according to police. During the ensuing chase, he started shooting at officers, who fired back. No one was injured and Brown was taken into custody.

In the immediate aftermath of the shootout, one of the responding officers, who said he was in shock, wondered aloud how he’d escaped uninjured, court records say. Brown responded with something to the effect of: “I don’t know, I can’t shoot,” according to the records.

That was a few months after Brown had been released from prison after serving time for a 2014 stabbing.

Brown “had been keeping up with his mental health conditions during his initial months on probation, but with the COVID outbreak, had lacked the ability to maintain services and had suffered from a deteriorated mental state as a result,” the records say.

Police reports describe somewhat similar circumstances in the stabbing case, which also took place in the South End. Brown approached a group of people and asked them: “Where you boys from,” according to a police report. He stabbed one man in the stomach, chased them with a knife, and then stabbed another man in the chest, police said.

When the Grants opened Black Market Nubian in 2017, it was hosted out of the first floor of a building on Washington Street and featured fashion, food, and craft vendors they hoped would gain traction in Nubian Square and help it grow. After COVID, they changed their business model, positioning Black Market as more of a cultural space and an arts and events venue. For five years, they have hosted an annual block party.

Earlier this spring, the Grants revealed they were in a dispute with their landlord and asked for community help raising $369,000 by the end of this month to buy the two-story building at 2316 Washington St.

Many were surprised the Grants didn’t own the building outright and instead had an option to buy it for $1.3 million. Others wondered why an organization that had recently been awarded an $823,000city contract for “creative placemaking” would struggle to keep its doors open. And some wondered why Madison Park, a longstanding Roxbury nonprofit, was at odds with a small business that seemed to share its mission.

In a statement Friday, Monica Dean, Madison Park’s chief executive, said the nonprofit was notified Friday afternoon that “the tenant had chosen to nullify the terms of the agreed-upon extension and vacate within the coming week.”

“This is an unfortunate turn of events,” Dean said. “Madison Park Development Corp. has worked diligently and in good faith to provide a path forward for Black Market.”

Dean said the nonprofit remains committed to its Nubian Square tenants and wishes the Grants “the best.”

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, whose district includes the market, said in a phone interview Saturday that though the market is closing “physically,” it’s not closing “emotionally.”

“We’ll all work to keep it emotionally open,” he said. “The spirit of Kai and Chris will never stop.”

Nevertheless, he said the closure of the market is a loss of “an engine of economic development” for Boston’s Black community.

Imari Paris Jeffries, president and chief executive of Embrace Boston, a nonprofit dedicated to racial equity, said Saturday that the market likely struggled financially because the surrounding area lacked enough complementary businesses to generate consistent foot traffic.

“You can’t be out there by yourself,” he said. “We need multiple businesses at the same time happening, and ... that hasn’t happened yet.”

Jeffries said Nubian Square’s soon-to-be-opened Jazz Urbane Cafe, a jazz club with an attached restaurant, would have provided foot traffic that could have helped the market.

“It’s just sad,” he said of the market’s closure. “You need those types of things to make Nubian Square an attraction for people to go to as a tourist hub.”

Kai Grant told the Globe last month that their lease agreement with Madison Park “was supposed to be about becoming a model for equity and antidisplacement” that ensured artisans, founders, and microbusinesses could stay in Roxbury.

Dean told the Globe that Black Market had not upheld “their end of the bargain,” and the nonprofit would “put its own finances at risk if it continued to subsidize” the market’s lease.

The Grants owed $124,229.12 in unpaid rent accrued over 32 months between 2021 and 2023, according to records reviewed by the Globe.

The closure of the Black Market also highlights the tenuous status of Black-owned businesses and spaces in Boston.

A 2024 report from the Donahue Institute at UMass Amherst found that “business owners of color struggle to find capital,” particularly in Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and East Boston.

Culpepper said the closure is “a product of this economy,” and emphasized that the venture was never intended as a “money-making venture.”

“If you look at the cuts in the city’s budget financially, the city is having challenging times. It’s not just Black Market, it’s even the city government,” he said, referencing Mayor Wu’s proposed budget cuts.

Jeffries said that although the loss of the market is a hit to the local culture and economy, there is still hope for the area.

“We’re pinning a lot of hope on Jazz Urbane to be successful,” he said.

Boston firefighters removed a man who was apparently trapped inside an elevator shaft at the Fields Corner MBTA station, officials said Saturday.
