Over the last decade, Rapo’s charity,Giving the Glam, has helped over a thousand Massachusetts students afford the dance of their dreams. She gives high schoolers free ballgowns and suits expertly fitted by seamstresses; a glam squad for hair, nails, and makeup; and even a ride in a Ferrari with a police escort to the party.

As prices surge on everything fromtomatoes to coffee to beef, more parents can’t dish out the $1,000 it typically costs for a storybook prom. Teens are left scouring for gowns, borrowing outfits from relatives, and embellishing old dresses with tricks from TikTok. But people like Rapo are stepping in to fill an increasing need because they believe every student deserves that fairy tale.

Last week, prom festivities kicked off at midday at Rapo’s sprawling house in Dover, about 15 miles outside Boston. It was the big night for seniors at Cristo Rey, a Catholic high school in Dorchester that serves families with limited economic means.

In Rapo’s living room, two long tables were covered in an array of high heels, designer clutches, and men’s dress shoes. More tables held a rainbow of nail polish, lipsticks, and enough makeup to fill a stand at a Sephora. One at a time, 45 high school seniors rushed into the pop-up dressing room to try on bow-ties and necklaces covered in rhinestones.

“I never thought prom day would be like this,” said senior Abdiel Reyes. “It feels like I’m in the movies.”

Upstairs in a guest bedroom, Acosta had a fresh manicure and hair blowout when she slipped into a $600 gown that had been altered just for her. Like all the other teens, she will get to keep the dress.

“I feel like I’m glowing,” Acosta said.

Her mother, a social worker named Aracelis Acosta, was relieved when the school announced it was partnering with Giving the Glam.

“With everything being so expensive,” Aracelis Acosta said, “I wasn’t sure I could give her the prom she always deserved.”

One of the charity’s volunteers, who all wore black T-shirts with the nonprofit’s logo, knelt down before Acosta to help her adjust the straps on her black heels. Another volunteer, Josias Barbosa, closed his Loov Concept salon in Medford to curl and style students’ hair for the big night.

They were part of an army of 25 helpers who had traveled from as far away as Fall River and Nashua, N.H., to give students the royal prom treatment. Most of the volunteers grew up struggling in Brazil and want to help those who need a lift.

That’s what inspired Rapo to launch her charity. She grew up in Favela do Aço, a dense, low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, and she sees herself in today’s urban high schoolers.

“I want them to feel like a million bucks,” Rapo said.

The cost of prom has nearly doubled over the last 16 years, according to research by Jay Zagorsky of Boston University’s Questrom School of Business. The big ticket items include outfits, accessories, salon visits, and limo rides. Tickets to the dance can range from $30 to $150 in Massachusetts.

A number of local organizations work to make prom memorable on a budget. Anton’s Cleaners helps spearhead Belle of the Ball, which provides used prom dresses and accessories free of charge to higher schoolers.

Hundreds of girls referred by their schools flock to Hynes Convention Center every year to sift through thousands of donated gowns. A swarm of volunteers act as personal stylists, helping them find the perfect dress, shoes, and bag.

Demand has surged since the pandemic, according to Anton’s marketing director, Stephanie Littefield. They now invite 1,800 students to participate, up from 1,200 in 2019.

“Everything is expensive today,” Littlefield said.

The issue goes beyond cost, said Shauna King, a marketing teacher at Plymouth South High School. Students are spending more because they want their photos to meet the impossible standards they see online, King said.

King runs the Massachusetts chapter of Becca’s Closet, a national initiative that helps students find gowns. A dressing room built into Plymouth South High School allows students from all over the state to make an appointment and browse through donated dresses.

Rapo at Giving the Glam doesn’t rely on used outfits or do-it-yourself projects. The charity provides brand new gowns and celebrity quality makeovers. Rapo typically spends between $700 and $1,000 on each student, she said, and raises between $150,000 and $200,000 every year to make it happen.

“Helping kids afford the prom of their dreams isn’t about the money,” Rapo said. “It’s about teaching them to give back to the community.“

Earlier this month, Giving the Glam helped teens at Brockton High School, many of whom have lived in homeless shelters or were in foster care.

Marc Laviolette, 19, walked into the dance in a shiny pink suit that Rapo’s team helped him pick out. He said he never felt “so loved” by his classmates.

“They told me I should have been nominated for prom king,” Laviolette said. “I got my dream prom.”

The fire broke out about 8 p.m. Saturday, and five residents were home at the time. All residents escaped safely without injury, though all were displaced.

The blaze spread through all three floors and burned through the roof, according to the Boston Fire Department, which said firefighters deployed “multiple ground and aerial ladders” to keep the flames from spreading to neighboring homes. Video posted to social media showed flames shooting from the roof of the building.

By 8:32 p.m., officials said the heavy fire had been “knocked down,” with crews continuing an aggressive interior and exterior attack to contain the blaze.

A mayday call went out for an injured firefighter. Minutes later, a second alert reported that the firefighter was being transported to a hospital under police escort, where he was later pronounced dead.

Fire officials said they could not provide additional details because an investigation into the fire and Kilduff’s death remained ongoing.

Early Sunday, rows of firefighters, police officers, and other personnel stood at attention as Kilduff’s body was loaded into an ambulance and taken from the hospital to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

On Sunday night, despite steady rain, dozens of firefighters and police officers lined Albany Street outside the medical examiner’s office to honor Kilduff during a dignified transfer to a funeral home in West Roxbury. Flashing blue police lights and red firetrucks illuminated the street as a hearse carrying Kilduff slowly pulled away under escort.

Kilduff, a father of two, was a third-generation Boston firefighter and a US Marine veteran. He was remembered not only for his 24 years with the Boston Fire Department, but also for the compassion and energy he brought to volunteer work supporting families of fallen service members and first responders.

Kilduff — known as “BK” — was assigned to Rescue Company 2 and was a “quintessential rescue man,” Kelly said. He is the first Boston firefighter to die in the line of duty in more than a decade.

“He’s probably been to more fires than any firefighter currently employed by the Boston Fire Department and in this region,” Kelly said, adding the crew hasn’t slept since the fire.

On Sunday afternoon, firefighters at the fire station in Egleston Square hung black drapes from the bay doors and laid flowers on the ground.

The crew described Kilduff as the lifeblood of the station — “the guy that took care of everything” — who even kept retirees looped in to firehouse events.

On the floor near a fire rig was an outline of Kilduff’s shoes where he had left them the night of the fire, his initials “BK” inside.

“We gotta write ‘too big to fill’ on them,” Kelly said.

Inside the Rescue 2 break room on Sunday, the men who worked alongside Kilduff described him as the kind of rescuer who was either already at a trapped firefighter’s side, or sprinting toward them.

“That would be the only two modes BK would be in,” Kelly said.

Rescue 2 is a specialized company that responds to dangerous situations involving firefighters in distress. Kelly said Kilduff was among the few firefighters appointed directly to the unit because of his skill and experience.

Victor Gaybor, another Rescue 2 firefighter who was at the fire Saturday night, recalled his final interaction with Kilduff.

“We were on that fire floor in the back porch and like we always do, we take a moment and just bust each other’s chops a bit, we’d lighten the whole situation,” Gaybor said. “I went back downstairs to report to my lieutenant at the time, and what happened, happened. We just went out to see what we can do for BK.”

As they traded stories about Kilduff’s jokes and his “excellent” cooking, members of Rescue 2 team said they considered themselves family and felt as if they had lost a brother.

Kilduff’s two children were traveling and unable to reach the hospital Saturday night, Kelly said, adding that Rescue 2 would fully support the family.

Funeral arrangements were still being finalized Sunday, but union officials said services would likely take place this week.

“He’ll be buried with the highest honors available in the city and within our union,” said Sam Dillon, president of the Boston Firefighters Local 718.

On Saturday morning, before the fatal blaze, Kilduff helped rescue a homeless man “who was trapped in a confined space of an MBTA yard,” Kelly said.

Kilduff was also credited with helping save the life of a fellow firefighter who suffered cardiac arrest while battling a fire more than a month ago. Dillon said Kilduff rode to the hospital with the firefighter and performed CPR.

Michelle Caroline, a former volunteer coordinator for the Gary Sinise Foundation, said Kilduff became one of the organization’s core volunteers helping families of fallen military and first responders.

“He never backed down from a challenge and stepped in whenever or wherever needed,” Caroline said.

By Sunday afternoon, a small memorial had begun to take shape along the metal fence outside the home on Treadway Road. A photo of Kilduff smiling in his firefighter’s uniform sat above flowers, candles, toy firetrucks, and American and Irish flags.

Katelyn McCabe, 33, who lives across the street, said she spent much of Sunday helping build the memorial, including printing and framing a photo of Kilduff at a nearby Walgreens.

“Sometimes people say, ‘That’s what they signed up for,’ but you still expect them to come home,” McCabe said. She said her late grandfather served as a district fire chief in Boston.

McCabe said she came outside soon after the fire broke out and was there when Kilduff fell.

“I heard the impact, and then I heard ‘Mayday,’” she said. “I just can’t get it out of my mind.”

Nearby, a lone firetruck remained stationed outside the three-story home, where the charred interior was visible through shattered upper-floor windows.

Phat Dao, 56, was visiting a friend when he stepped outside Saturday night to find Treadway Road crowded with firetrucks as flames and smoke poured from the building.

Standing in the rain near Kilduff’s memorial Sunday, Dao said the firefighter’s death hit him hard because “he died helping people.”

“He’s a hero,” Dao said.

Kilduff’s father, who served as a Boston fire lieutenant, died in 2008, according to his obituary. The elder Robert Kilduff served as Local 718 vice president and founded the local’s Children’s Fund.

“Boston lost a hero,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement Sunday morning. “The Kilduff family has given everything in service to this country and this city. ... Boston will forever honor Firefighter Kilduff’s dedication and service with the most profound gratitude.”

Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall said Kilduff was a “firefighter’s firefighter.”

“It’s going to stick with us for a long time,” he said. “There’s no routine fire, there’s no routine call. And you’re never truly safe until you get home.”

On Sunday morning, Governor Maura Healey ordered US and Massachusetts flags lowered to half-staff at all state buildings in honor of Kilduff.

“His death serves as a reminder of the dangers firefighters face every day when they put their lives on the line to keep our communities safe,” Healey said in a statement.

Edward Kelly, general president of the International Association of Fire Fighters, called Kilduff the union’s “unsung hero.”

“He did everything behind the scenes for our union,” Kelly said. “He mentored fire unions all throughout the state. He was just someone that left an indelible mark.”

The last two Boston firefighters killed in the line of duty were Lieutenant Edward J. Walsh Jr. and Michael R. Kennedy, who died in 2014 while battling a nine-alarm blaze in the Back Bay.

At the time, Kilduff spoke to the Globe about the somber rituals held to honor fallen firefighters, including the black shroud draped across uniform badges, the honor guard, and the bagpipes.

“It’s a show of respect for the family, and it’s a tribute from us as firefighters,” said Kilduff, then the director of operations for the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts. “It’s really hard to explain, except to say that our job, if you break it all down to the bare bones, [is that] we show up at somebody’s really bad day and try to make it a little better.”

Scotland opening World Cup play against Haiti in Foxborough on June 13 will act as a reminder of the country’s influence on soccer in the United States and New England.

In the first World Cup in 1930 in Uruguay, the US team was coached by Scotland-born Bob Millar, who moved to the United States to play for J&P Coats and the Fall River Marksmen in the American Soccer League. The lineup included Scotsmen Andy Auld, James Brown, Jimmy Gallagher, Bart McGhee, and Alexander Wood. They were among more than 80 Scotland-born players to compete for the US men’s national team, from Neil Clarke (1916) through Stu Holden (2008).

The Scottish accent on the US game goes back to its origins in the late 1800s. According to Iain Campbell Whittle of The Scots Football Historians Group, textile magnate William Clark can be considered the “father” of soccer in the United States. Clark founded the Clark ONT (Our New Thread) team in 1883 in Newark, and served as captain in its inaugural game. Clark’s team won the first three editions of the American Football Association Cup, forerunner of the US Open Cup, and several of its players competed for the first United States national team in 1885.

By the turn of the century, Scots probably outnumbered the English in soccer management positions and on the playing fields in New England. They kept the game alive year-round, setting up five-a-side games that emphasized precise passing at the Caledonian Games ($125 to the 1915 winner) in West Roxbury. They provided the backbone of the American Soccer League from 1921-31. The Boston & District League, one of the country’s top semi-pro leagues, listed 200 Scottish players on 1922 rosters, according to a Globe story. That’s along with the Boston area’s 10-team Scottish Clans League.

But the Scottish contribution — Whittle calls it “the Scottish inheritance” — transcends numbers. The Scots refined soccer, using subtle maneuvers to counterattack the direct, physical style of the English. Creativity and skill were emphasized, opening horizons for the game to expand. And the Scots didn’t just get style points — they outplayed England in the early years of the British Home Championship.

“There was disagreement over the best way to play,” said Tom McCabe, history professor at the University of Notre Dame in London. “You see the word scientific being used, and that means using geometry, angles, combination play, and, for that, it is the Scottish influence. Passing and moving, their particular brand of soccer. They were working class, in the mines, so they weren’t big, didn’t have the nutrition, didn’t do training on the side like English gentlemen, who were men of leisure and had a better diet, time to train. It’s an interesting turning point in the evolution of the game. Scots even talk about Enlightenment ideas of community and work. Where the English game was more dribbling and violent, Scots have to show up for work, so they’re passing and moving.

“They’re on to something there. They saw the game differently. It was not just played on festival days, but a weekly thing. You’ve got to go to work the next day. So, there’s that element, and it’s more beautiful, a game with a kaleidoscope of options, constantly changing — rather than boot it and chase it, and dribble till you lose it. Scots see passing and moving, that’s our innovation, we brought that to the global game.”

Soccer might not be the same without Scottish influence. The game, Whittle said in an email, “was invented in England but raised by us to what we know today, a global phenomenon. No Scots, no soccer.”

On the brick wall of the Rescue Co. 2 firehouse in Roxbury, five plaques commemorate the lives of Boston firemen from that unit who have died in the line of duty. The newest plaque remembers the oldest tragedy, the death of Charles Buchanan in 1947. Buchanan only got a plaque in 2022 after a modern-day fireman dove deep in the archives and asked the fire commissioner to honor him.

What that modern-day fireman didn’t know then was that in just a few years his own plaque would be the sixth to be mounted on that brick wall.

Robert Kilduff Jr. died Saturday after suffering severe injuries working to extinguish a blaze on Treadway Road in Dorchester. On Memorial Day, residents and firefighters stopped by the firehouse to pay their respects, leaving flowers, American flags, and even a firetruck toy.

Kilduff’s colleagues say they are devastated by his loss, remembering him as a model citizen who went above and beyond his duties. A third-generation Boston fireman, he knew all the dates and details of historical fires in the city and acted as the firehouse’s informal historian. Serving the community was his calling, his colleagues said.

“We’re going to need four people to replace him,” said Lieutenant Glenn McGillivray. “His character is extremely difficult to replace. We can get another body in here, but it’s not going to be BK.”

Among his colleagues, the 53-year-old West Roxbury resident was known as BK or Bobby.

McGillivray said Kilduff was going back to school to get a degree in fire science. He was constantly learning, “trying to better himself, better the job, better the firehouse. That was BK,” McGillivray said.

Kilduff was admired for being an excellent problem solver, finding simple solutions for complicated situations, said Lieutenant Gilbert Quinchia. Most firemen aspired to be like him, he said.

“This is where he wanted to be,” Quinchia said. “This was his calling. He was happy to be here every day.”

At the firehouse Monday, Quinchia welcomed community members who wanted to show solidarity to the men currently working. A mother with her daughters carrying American flags. A couple with their son carrying flowers. Residents who knew Kilduff.

Quinchia said a resident who stopped by the firehouse remembered Kilduff from a time he helped her with a car fire. Quinchia said people don’t usually remember firefighters’ names and faces. That’s how special Kilduff was to the community, he said.

While the firehouse is open and serving the community, its members are mourning.

“If you can somehow relate to losing a close family member, that’s how we feel,” Quinchia said. “Not losing a coworker, that’s a very different thing. We lost family.”

In 2022, when Kilduff honored Buchanan, Kilduff told The Boston Globe firefighters’ work is “unique.”

“We show up on people’s really bad days, and try to make them a little bit better,” Kilduff said then.

What does it all mean for Boston dining and Kenmore Square? Let’s discuss. — Devra First

Kara: So it seems there’s finally a replacement for Blue Ribbon Brasserie, and it’s from Tuscan Brands. On one hand, it’s nice that a respected local operator with a solid track record is moving in. Devra: I think it’s deeply symbolic of where this city (and many a city) is at. Where the great, grimy Rat once ruled, there’s now going to be an upscale Old Spaghetti Factory. Kara: I think this is a safe choice. And I think safe choices can certainly make for bland dining — or they can provide reliability and comfort. In an ideal world, where liquor licenses are handed out like candy and rent was affordable, it would be amazing to have a down-and-dirty pub or a lovely Persian restaurant at that address. Devra: A Market Basket.

Kara: You and me both.

Devra: I know neither of us is kidding. Or how about a classic Hong Kong dim sum palace with exquisite service and handmade everything?

Kara: I wish it were a dim sum parlour.

Devra: Oh wow, we really just said that at the same time. How much would that a) kill and b) rule? Or if we’re doing salutes to New York, how about Balthazar Boston? Keith McNally, where are ya? Wait, Eastern Standard was already kind of Balthazar Boston. How about a Horn & Hardart? Bring back the automat!

Kara: Or what about salutes to Old Boston? Growing up here, I have fond memories of places like Anthony’s Pier 4, The Pewter Pot, and Bailey’s. If we’re harking back to days of yore, why not hark back to days of local yore? And local lore?

Devra: Yes! But if we can’t have a Bailey’s (which would be amazing), I would love to see anything independent, chef-owned, risk-taking, experimental, interesting, envelope-pushing, different, driven by vision and passion. Buitoni Spaghetti Bar could be some of those things. It could turn out to be a lot of fun. Owner Joe Faro is a local guy, who happens to now own pasta company Buitoni, and this will be Buitoni Spaghetti Bar. If you’re going to make a product, it makes perfect sense to create a restaurant to showcase, prepare, and sell that product. There’s an old-school pride in that. Kara: I do worry when nostalgia becomes a marketing technique. Eastern Standard was very much of its place and time. So was the Rat. It wasn’t trying to recreate anything. Why are we trying to summon a bygone era in New York City, in a Boston neighborhood? I enjoy old-timey New York as much as the next person, and that’s why I like to visit New York. Devra: It’s like Vegas or Disney. I can enjoy those things in an ironic way, with a perpetual awareness of the ersatz-ness of it all. In a sense, Eastern Standard did it: It was an homage to the French brasserie. Devra: And its time and place are so expensive. The cost of that real estate alone would be prohibitive to many of the concepts you and I might choose to see there. Tuscan Brands operates on that scale successfully in neighborhoods like the Seaport. It’s a realistic tenant for the Kenmore Square space. Is creative, risk-taking, independent dining dead in expensive American neighborhoods? And do you think Buitoni Spaghetti Bar will be a hit? What will be important as the plan moves forward is ensuring the right mix of medical services — services that residents need and can access.

Carney Hospital sits on 12.8 acres of land in Dorchester owned by Apollo Global Management, a New York-based private equity firm.

The developers plan to demolish the existing hospital buildings. They would build a new 350,000-square-foot health care building, an education building geared toward training nurses, 200 units of senior housing, and 300 units of family housing, in addition to retail and open space. The senior housing is expected to include a memory care unit, assisted living units, and independent living units. The project is estimated to cost around $850 million, with at least the health care facility completed by 2030.

To their credit, the developers have been actively engaging the local community, holding around 35 community meetings before taking the first step in the city of Boston permitting process by filing a letter of intent on May 20. Although Apollo hasn’t garnered much local good will, due to its role in Steward’s operations and bankruptcy, HYM CEO Thomas O’Brien is a longtime Boston area developer and civic leader, while the Rev. Jeffrey Brown of My City at Peace also has deep roots in Boston city affairs.

Many of the decisions about the health care center will be made by its eventual operator. O’Brien told the editorial board he expects it will be run by a major local health system — he’s talking to Mass General Brigham, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Boston Medical Center, and Brown University Health. According to the developers, the health care center would not be a hospital but would include a yet-undetermined mix of services, potentially including emergency and urgent care, behavioral and mental health care, imaging services, primary care, or specialty care. (The housing on the site will be managed by HYM, who would hire an outside operator to run the senior housing.)

As the health system — and state health care regulators — considers any proposal, it should take into account the recommendations of a Dorchester Health Planning Working Group report and ensure that the site offers the services the surrounding communities need the most: namely, primary care, behavioral and mental health care, and emergency and urgent care.

When Carney Hospital was open, it had 50 inpatient psychiatric beds. Although the hospital also had medical-surgical beds, the most common reasons patients were hospitalized at Carney were for mental health disorders, including bipolar disorders and schizophrenia. Carney’s emergency department had around 30,000 visits a year, although the data suggest many of those could have been avoided with timely access to urgent or primary care.

Since Carney closed, the working group found, other local hospital emergency departments have been increasingly crowded while community health centers have had longer wait times. Codman Square Health Center is reporting a 4.5 month wait for a primary care physician.

The lack of those services today is a reason Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s office says any development must include health care uses that fill the gaps left by Carney’s closure. “Any proposal must include a committed health care partner with the capacity to deliver and sustain these critical services in the long term, so that residents and families have the care they deserve and are not left without options again,” a Wu spokesperson said in a statement sent to the editorial board.

Importantly, the health care system should also commit to ensuring that the services are accessible to patients with a variety of Medicaid plans. More than 70 percent of Carney Hospital patients had government health insurance, often MassHealth.

There may be community pushback on the size of the housing development. David Keenan, a member of the Dorchester Lower Mills Civic Association, told the editorial board he worries about traffic based on the number of family units being proposed. Tributes flowed last week for Baker, a Roxbury-raised resident of Dorchester who died May 17 of complications from an April stroke. He was 88.

Friends remembered him as a local basketball star, a community icon, a champion of the city’s young dreamers. One of Boston’s best all-around athletes of the 1950s and ’60s, he spent the following decades showing others how to be great.

“People called him the unofficial mayor of Boston,” said his daughter, Jillian Baker. “He was a tall guy with a big personality who really cared about his students, the community, the homeless, and how sports can be an avenue for youth to excel.”

Baker was a multisport star at Roxbury Memorial High, as a basketball guard, football quarterback, baseball pitcher, and track athlete. He led Delaware State basketball in scoring as a senior in 1961. Upon returning home, he filled it up for the semi-pro South End Bruins, coached by Jack Crump.

“Roscoe was a legend,” said teammate Ray Flynn of South Boston, the future Boston mayor. “I admired him. It was his sportsmanship on the court.”

Baker became a player-coach and a referee, working hundreds of college games over 50-plus years (including as one of the first officials in the Big East). In 1974, he did a Celtics-Bulls game at the Garden next to friend Ken Hudson, the NBA’s first Black full-time official.

Those two also combined, with others including Harris, Clarence “Jeep” Jones, Wayne Embry, and Rudy Cabral, in 1969 to create the Boston Neighborhood Basketball League. In a time where the city was torn apart by racial strife, the BNBL brought together different neighborhoods to compete on the outdoor courts.

“It took away the negativity of the busing era,” Harris said. “If you rode around the city at night, you’d see kids playing under the lights, teams of mixed races, making friendships that lasted for life.”

That group in 1972 formed the Boston Shootout, which quickly became America’s premier grassroots basketball tournament. Over the decades, it attracted the likes of Adrian Dantley, Tree Rollins, Patrick Ewing, Chris Mullin, Grant Hill, Kobe Bryant, Antoine Walker, and Paul Pierce.

In the hottest summer days, “it had a calming effect,” said Albert Holland, former principal at Burke High (now Holland Tech). “It really helped Boston move from a point where we were angry at each other to a point where we could sit together and watch great basketball.”

Baker was born in Thomasville, Ga., on July 29, 1937, to Edwina Baker Curtis. He grew up in the Roxbury home of Barbadian immigrants Gustavus and Edna Haynes, whose four sons each answered their callings. Vincent was a journalist and jazz historian. Roy was a world-renowned jazz drummer. Douglas was a musician and World War II veteran.

Michael, the oldest, served 40 years as the pastor at Twelfth Baptist, and was a friend of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He was in high school when he invited Baker, then a grade-schooler, to live with the family. Baker’s mother, a singer, was moving out of the area. “He wanted to stay and play sports,” said his daughter, Jessica Moore. “I think he saw a future and an opportunity for himself, even at a young age, in Boston.”

The community leader Mel King once told the Globe that Rev. Haynes constantly challenged him and other Black men around him to serve the community and understand their power, to “recognize our capacity to make a difference.”

Baker, who taught at Timilty Middle School after graduating college, in 1968 became the first Black director of the Roxbury Boys Club. Among those he guided were two young girls from Roxbury, Andrea Swain and her sister, Lisa.

Hanging out at the club in the early ’70s, they wondered why they were not allowed to swim. Baker encouraged them to speak out. Girls soon joined various activities at the club. In 1981, the Roxbury Boys Club allowed girls as full members, and changed its name to reflect that — the first Boys Club in the country to do so. Soon, other affiliates did the same.

“He gave me a voice,” said Swain, 61, now chief impact officer of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston.

In the early ’80s, Burke High was in dire straights. Drugs and gangs rattled the pillars on its facade. Its academics were crumbling. In 1986, Holland brought in Baker as a teacher and dean of discipline to help him turn the school around.

“Encouraging kids to go to class and to do the right thing, he was just a special person that cared about individuals, and everywhere he went, he’d make you laugh or put a smile on your face. He left such an imprint on your heart,” said Brandy Cruthird, a late-80s basketball star at what is now the Dr. Albert D. Holland Technical High School.

The original plan at Burke, she added, was to dedicate the school gym to Holland, but Baker’s passionate speech about Holland’s impact helped convince decision-makers to rename the entire school.

Charlie Titus, 76, grew up in Columbia Point, and later Roxbury, in the ’60s. He remembered a community that was united in its struggle for progress, and pushed forward by leaders such as Baker.

Titus listened, staying in school and on the court. He wound up becoming UMass Boston’s first athletic director, founding the men’s basketball team, and coaching for 29 years. He is in the St. Michael’s College and UMB Halls of Fame.

“That doesn’t happen to me without people like Roscoe Baker, Mike Haynes, Jeep Jones,” he said. “They were 24/7 youth workers. Their days never ended. They were always around, taking us places, taking us down south to the HBCUs, to jobs. They were just there — they were a part of your life.”

Baker leaves behind his daughters, Jessica Moore, of Boston, and Jillian Baker, of Los Angeles; a son, Roscoe Baker Jr., of Kissimmee, Fla.; three grandchildren; and numerous family members and friends.

A funeral will be held Friday, May 29, at the Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury, with a viewing from 9:30-11 a.m., and a service from 11 a.m.-noon.

The guidance was promised by an executive order Healey signed in January, which sought to prohibit ICE agents from making arrests in nonpublic areas of state facilities and barred the use of state property for immigration enforcement staging.

Healey unveiled that order when she filed legislation that would ban federal immigration enforcement from entering churches, schools, courthouses, and other locations. The Massachusetts House and Senate have each passed differing versions of wide-ranging immigration bills designed to be a bulwark against the Trump administration’s deportation operation.

The guidance spells out how schools, child care centers, health care facilities, and places of worship have the right to require federal immigration officials to present any warrants before entering a facility, and deny access to nonpublic areas without a valid judicial warrant. It also recommends that facilities have lawyers on call and train staff on how to respond if federal immigration officers show up at their places of work.

Healey said she hopes the guidance will help restore any drops in school enrollment, attendance at places of worship, and patients seeking medical care, which she said have taken a dip in communities with high immigration populations.

“These are the noble care professions that society depends on each and every day,” the Rev. Mariama White-Hammond, founding pastor of the New Roots AME Church in Dorchester, said at the State House on Thursday. “This advisory gives practical guidance on how we honor the laws of this land.”

The guidance outlines the kinds of signage that places can post to clearly designate nonpublic areas, as well as advice on adopting written visitor policies and procedures.

It also urges employees and staff to “remain calm” and to “never attempt to physically interfere” with ICE agents, and instead contact the highest-ranking staff member on site, who should call an attorney.

The guidance asks that staff members document their actions, as well as information about the ICE agents, and contact the families of children who may have witnessed the interaction.

The state also offers examples of what are considered public and nonpublic spaces. Offices, classrooms, stairwells, and nursery and play areas are all nonpublic, according to the guidance. So are storage areas, athletic fields, parking lots, dormitories, research labs, and exam rooms.

Katie Murphy, a Brigham and Women’s Hospital nurse and president of the Massachusetts Nurses Association, said her colleagues have for months seen patients skipping regular appointments while others wait to go to the emergency room for care to avoid potentially being detained by ICE.

The guidance from the Healey administration offers extra comfort, she said, though health care providers are more concerned with patients deferring care than ICE showing up.

“They are not going to their appointments, [and] they are not going to the emergency department until they are really sick,” she said. “This puts even a greater strain on a failing system.”

Gladys Vega, the head of Chelsea-based La Colaborativa, said the guidance is a welcome step in her community, which she said has seen ICE agents show up in a school parking lot, grocery store, and food distribution line.

La Colaborativa also runs a health clinic in collaboration with Mass General Brigham, which sees patients with varying immigration statuses.

“As an organization that serves thousands of residents and operates a small practice, we have been deeply concerned about the privacy, the dignity, and the health of our community members,” said Vega, who worked with the administration on the guidelines. “We are constantly very nervous about it.”

Lauren Cook — chief executive of Ellis Early Learning, which operates three child care facilities in Boston — said the guidance is helpful, though she worries about child care centers like hers that don’t have ready access to legal counsel.

Nonprofits often rely on pro bono help, which can take days to find, Cook said.

Even so, “it’s helpful to be able to use this as . . . a guidepost against what we have already established,” she said, noting that her team had stitched together a hodgepodge ICE response plan from a variety of sources.

Ellis lost two beloved teachers in recent months because their work authorizations weren’t renewed.

Healey on Thursday said she couldn’t say how this guidance would be enforced in a situation where federal agents clash with, say, a faith leader or a school employee.

“I expect this to not be an issue, because I expect them to actually follow the regulations,” she said of federal officials. “Should they not do that, and I would be very disappointed if I saw that . . . that will be immediately reported to the attorney general’s office and to our office, and appropriate action will be taken.”

Healey’s taken other steps to push back on ICE operations, including creating a portal with the AG’s office where residents can report alleged misconduct by ICE. She’s publicly demanded ICE stop deportation flights out of Hanscom Field, called for an extension of temporary protected status for Haitian immigrants, and opposed a since-scrapped plan for an ICE detention center in southern New Hampshire.

Earlier this year, the governor also prohibited the state from entering into any new agreements with ICE unless there is a public safety need. Her own Department of Correction is the only entity in Massachusetts that has an existing deal with ICE. It allows local law enforcement to act as deputized immigration agents for the purpose of identifying noncitizens who could be eligible for deportation once they complete their sentences.

She said at the time that she supported the existing agreement, which was implemented in 2007, because if someone is incarcerated in a state prison, they’ve “done something pretty bad.”

The DOC’s agreement is among 12 such arrangements between federal immigration agents and state prison systems around the country, and Massachusetts is one of only two of those states — Arizona being the other — that are currently led by a Democratic governor.

The Randolph man accused of stealing millions of dollars worth of jewelry from a basement safe in Jamaica Plain had solicited and accepted a $10,000 loan from the homeowners to buy a new vehicle, because he was having car troubles.

But, after deposting the money, Cory Kisakye “never once returned to their home to work for them, nor has he ever spoken to them or reached out in any capacity,” authorities said in a police report, which offered new details on the alleged jewelry theft.

The police report and court records describe Kisakye, 27, of Randolph, as an apparent longtime fraudster. He was arrested in Miami this week after previously fleeing to Uganda.

Kisakye was arraigned Wednesday in West Roxbury District Court, and was ordered held without bail. He pleaded not guilty, and a hearing is slated for Thursday to determine if he is a danger and flight risk who should remain jailed pending trial.

Kisakye started working for the homeowners as a home-care assistant in December 2023, according to a police report. He helped change the batteries to the basement safe last summer, the report says.

And he had intimate knowledge of the property, including the safe’s combination, police said.

On Nov. 19, the homeowners called 911 because their dog started barking nonstop and they were worried someone was lurking around the property, located inside a gated community on Allandale Road, according to police. Officers responded to the address and searched outside the home, finding nothing amiss. But later that morning, they discovered the back door was unlocked and the safe had been emptied.

The police report contains a long list of stolen items, including a 17-carat diamond ring worth an estimated $850,000.

On Dec. 9, Kisakye bought a one-way ticket to Uganda and departed the same day, declaring $54,000 in cash, according to the report.

Detectives later obtained surveillance footage showing two hooded figures leaving the Jamaica Plane property around midnight Nov. 19, according to the report.

Police said the suspects gained access to a locked safe room and emptied its contents, including diamond rings, luxury watches, gold bracelets, and designer pieces from brands such as Tiffany and Co., Piaget, and Chopard — worth several million in total.

They ultimately zeroed in on Kisakye, noting his long history of “thefts, check fraud and pawning jewelry.” Police reports in Randolph had already linked him to a stolen diamond ring and a residential burglary where an Xbox gaming system was stolen. He had also made 14 pawn transactions between December 2024 and August 2025, according to the Boston police report.

A fingerprint at the crime scene was identified as belonging to Kisakye, police said, and GPS data placed him in the area of the home around the time of the burglary and on a suspected scouting visit about a month prior.

Boston police allege that after breaking into the Jamaica Plain home, Kisakye tried to sell the stolen jewels in various states, including Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Florida, before fleeing to Uganda “upon learning that investigators were inquiring about him.”

He started communicating with and visiting a local jeweler less than 48 hours after the break-in, police say. Within days, he traveled to Miami, where he allegedly sold a stolen gold bracelet for $11,000, according to police.

Detectives found suspicious activity in his financial transactions dating back years, including evidence he had opened accounts “in the name of a deceased individual for whom he had previously served as a caretaker,” according to the report. His criminal record includes fraud charges in Florida and Michigan, according to the report.

Police also noted his extensive gambling activity, including at the Encore in Everett.

It’s not clear when Kisakye returned to the United States from Africa or how police finally tracked him down in Miami. On Tuesday, Boston police brought him back to Suffolk County.

He faces felony charges of unarmed burglary, breaking into a depository, and larceny from a building, court records show.

An attorney representing Kisakye declined to comment Thursday.

Graduation caps decorated with glitter flashed in the bright sun Thursday morning as the University of Massachusetts Boston celebrated its 58th commencement with graduates hailing from more than 133 countries.

The campus overlooking Dorchester Bay teemed with families as some 2,740 undergraduates accepted their diplomas and began the next chapter of their lives. As speakers addressed the crowd, references to the diversity of the graduating class emerged as theme.

Madeeha Masroor Syeda, who delivered remarks on behalf of the class of 2026, told her fellow graduates that her achievement was rooted in the sacrifices of her immigrant parents. She used her moment at the podium to highlight those who have been denied similar opportunities.

“There are young people around the world with the same dreams and potential, who do not have the safety or freedom to sit where we are today,” Syeda said. “Many may never get to experience a day like this.”

Students, some shaking with enthusiasm, lined up for their turn to walk across the stage.

“I feel very excited to be done, but also slightly nervous for the real world,” said graduate Olivia Hill, who studied nursing. “I hope to get a really nice job that I enjoy.”

The campus grounds were lined with flower bouquets as parents beamed with pride.

“It’s very emotional,” said Jen Clark, mother of a graduating senior. “You’re proud of yourself and you’re proud of your son, and it was everything. I just had a great day.”

The ceremony began with a welcome from chancellor Marcelo Suárez-Orozco.

“Beacons, you did it. You made it. You earned it,” Suárez-Orozco said. “Take everything that UMass Boston has offered you, go out with it into the world fiercely, boldly.”

Students radiated joy as they crossed the stage to collect their diplomas, many donning graduation stoles embroidered with the flags of the countries they represented.

The celebration came against a backdrop of growing uncertainty about whether that global reach can be sustained for schools like UMass Boston, which saw about 250 fewer international students arrive on campus last fall, a 17 percent drop from 2024.

“UMass Boston is the most diverse public university in New England, and the third most diverse university in the United States of America,” said Senator Edward J. Markey, who received the Chancellor’s Medal.

Like at other commencements this season, the mention of Artificial Intelligence drew jeers and boos, highlighting the unease that looms over a class entering the workforce at a time of heightened uncertainty.

“We live in a world of growing disinformation, distrust of science, devaluing of higher education, of your degrees and of overpromises of AI without a full reckoning of its threats,” Suárez-Orozco said.

Syeda, the class speaker, received the John F. Kennedy Award for Academic Excellence, which is given to the graduate who best exemplifies academic excellence, commitment to service, and good citizenship.

“As we step into this next chapter of our lives, we are no longer just the ones being guided; we are becoming the ones others will look to for guidance,” Syeda said. “We will be the ones who will mentor, who will teach, who will give people a place to belong.”

A drizzle began to form as the ceremony neared its end and families embraced their graduates.

“It is an honor for me to see her graduate, because she worked hard, she worked full time and she went to school full time,” said Elmire Guillaume, cousin of a graduate. “She made it through and we’re very proud of her.”

With city and state officials tight-lipped, tens of thousands of World Cup fans remain in limbo as they seek a clearer picture of traffic and pedestrian plans outside South Station when the Cup kicks off, with the first game at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough slated for June 13. T officials expect as many as 20,000 fans could ride trains for each of the seven games slated in Foxborough.

Two weeks ago, state transportation officials informed City Hall that they intend to take the unusual step of temporarily occupying part of Summer Street — between South Station and Fort Point Channel — and closing it off to vehicle traffic for 10 hours at a time on match days, according to a May 15 letter from Eng.

But Boston officials said in a statement last week that the plan is an “inappropriate use of eminent domain to bypass the permitting process for roadways under local jurisdiction.”

A spokesperson for Wu did not respond this week to multiple requests for comment on the dispute.

The stalemate is the latest in a string of coordination breakdowns and other missteps surrounding Boston’s World Cup preparations. It began early this year with a months-long standoff between Boston Soccer 26, the host committee, and the town of Foxborough over security costs at Gillette. The dispute was eventually resolved to Foxborough’s liking, but not before drawing unwanted international attention and briefly casting doubt over whether the event would even proceed.

Meanwhile, dozens of Massachusetts towns and cities that were awarded $10 million in state grants in March to support local watch parties and other celebrations spent months waiting for vital permits needed to move forward. Without the public-viewing licenses from FIFA, soccer’s global governing body, communities could not finalize their plans. As the tournament neared, some municipalities began considering scaling back or canceling events altogether.

FIFA officials finally issued most of the licenses within the past week. As of Thursday, all but one of the 17 organizations that received state grants had obtained the licenses for the roughly two dozen watch parties or confirmed they didn’t need one, according to state officials.

Even so, the approvals came so late that many communities say they are now scrambling to finalize important details, including hiring local food vendors and musical performers.

“It’s crazy that an event this large would not have more organization behind it and more forethought,” said Jackey West Devine, executive director of a nonprofit, Fields Corner Main Street, that finally received a license from FIFA on Tuesday for a watch party on June 21 in Dorchester. “This is history in the making, after all.”

Speaking at the T’s board meeting Thursday, Eng called the World Cup “an unprecedented event” and said he expected the state and city would reach a resolution, though he offered no timeline.

“I’m confident that with the ongoing dialogue that we have with the city, we will find a resolution to how to balance the needs of our riders, the visitors, the enhanced service that we intend to ride the thousands of people that we are ready to carry, as well as the users and the people that live around our system at South Station,” Eng said.

Yet two Boston city councilors said this week that they were surprised crowd control measures at South Station had not been resolved by now.

The lack of preparation is particularly jarring, they said, given that most host cities resolved transportation issues months ago. Other cities have also shown greater willingness to block off streets for Cup-related events. Houston, for instance, plans to designate some 30 blocks of streets near its soccer stadium. In New York, officials are planning significant traffic disruptions to accommodate Cup-related traffic, with multiple streets and lanes in Manhattan closed on game days.

Talks over how to manage crowds at South Station have stretched on for months. The question of closing Summer Street surfaced as early as February, when Eng toured the station with local law enforcement officials. The urgency grew after an international friendly game in late March between Brazil and France, what was seen as a test run for the tournament. Officials concluded South Station needed an “additional footprint” to handle the crowds.

Among the problems: there was not enough space, pedestrians trying to pass through were obstructed, and access for emergency vehicles and personnel was compromised.

“The friendly match is where we saw . . . the crowds did end up on the streets, so we know from that perspective the sidewalks were insufficient,” Eng said in a short briefing with reporters after Thursday’s board meeting.

As of Wednesday, more than 37,000 train tickets had been sold across the first five games of the tournament, which is about a third of the total tickets on sale.

Of those sales, some 11,500 tickets were for the first game on June 13 between Scotland and Haiti.

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper said Wednesday that the city and the T should be able to “strike a happy medium” between fully shutting down a busy thoroughfare for 10 hours on match days and restricting traffic during peak crowd periods. He said the agency should identify those hours when the largest numbers of fans are expected to use South Station to travel to the games, and focus traffic restrictions around those times to minimize disruption for commuters.

Boston has already agreed to allow the T to close a portion of Summer Street to traffic for the first match on June 13, and the third match on June 19 between Scotland and Morocco. However, the two sides remain at odds over whether — and when — traffic restrictions should be imposed for the remaining five games.

“No matter what, it’s going to be difficult,” Culpepper said of crowd control efforts at South Station. “Here’s the question: Do you cut off the street for those who depend on it and use it every day, just for the World Cup? Or do you look at the times when it’s most used for the games? Why close the street in the mornings, when there won’t be games?”

Ed Flynn, the South Boston district councilor, said he was frustrated that negotiations between the T and city officials have taken place behind closed doors, with little transparency and no clear resolution in sight.

“This should have been resolved five or six months ago,” Flynn said. “But it wasn’t resolved, so here we are, just days from the World Cup, and we don’t have a clear public safety and logistical plan in place for getting people to and from the games.”

Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police blotters in our communities.

The Massachusetts State Police bomb squad traveled to Nantucket earlier this month after some World War II-era rockets turned up on the island off the Cape. The rockets, which were once used in military training exercises, were discovered in an eroding sand dune. State fire officials said that although the rockets were “old and degraded,” they were still potentially dangerous, so the State Police, along with the Nantucket Fire Department and the US Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit 12, “conducted a controlled explosion to mitigate the hazard.”

Police recently rescued a rabbit that was stuck in a fence in back of a home at 132 Beacon St. in Chelsea. “The little guy was having a real hare emergency and needed some-bunny to help,” police wrote on social media. “Our officers hopped into action, carefully cut the fence, and freed the furry friend without any further bunny business. At the Chelsea Police Department, we answer all types of calls for service. Whether it is a serious emergency, a community concern, or a rabbit rescue that needed a little hop-eration, every call matters.” Police shared video of the rescue and publicly thanked Officer Jonathan Maldonado and the caller who notified them that the rabbit needed help. “No bunny gets left behind!” police wrote.

At about 3:30 p.m. on May 2, the Groton Fire Department was dispatched to assist a pregnant woman who was going into labor in the parking lot of a local business in town. With the help of Groton Fire Lieutenant Tyler Shute, Firefighter-EMT Chris Braun, and EMT Gibson McCullagh, the baby was safely delivered in the mother’s vehicle, according to Groton Fire Chief Arthur Cheeks. The woman and her newborn boy were then taken to UMass Memorial Medical Center in Worcester. “The Groton Fire Department would like to congratulate the family on their new addition, and commend Lt. Shute, Firefighter Braun and EMT McCullagh and all other responders, who helped ensure a safe birth in challenging circumstances,” said Cheeks. “We are pleased to hear that mom and baby are recovering well. It is an honor to be able to provide care to people in the most pivotal, positive moments of their lives.”

The Boston Police Department’s auto theft unit recently teamed up with Milton police to investigate the theft of off-road vehicles that had allegedly been sold — and then promptly stolen — through fraudulent Facebook Marketplace sales. Police say the alleged scam worked like this: The buyers allegedly wrote bad checks to purchase the vehicles, and by the time the sellers realized they couldn’t cash the checks, it was too late, because their ATVs were long gone. As a result of the investigation, police arrested two males on charges of larceny of a motor vehicle, forgery of a check, and uttering a false check. Police also said a search warrant for a home on Woodgate Street in Dorchester led to the recovery of three allegedly stolen ATVs, and a search warrant at a home on Sprague Street in Dedham led to the recovery of a dirt bike.

Advocates say the loss of funds could threaten the state’s mandate to ensure its most vulnerable residents are protected from environmental pollution and the harms of global warming. Amid the Trump administration’s dismantling of federal environmental justice programs, some advocates worry that the Healey administration is stepping back its commitment.

“We were hoping for a bit more backbone,” said John Walkey, director of climate justice and waterfront initiatives at GreenRoots, an environmental group based in Chelsea.

Danielle Burney, a spokesperson for the Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs, said the state remains committed to leading on environmental justice.

“Like other states and agencies, we are experiencing fiscal constraints driven by federal rollbacks,” she said. She said the budget would allow the Office of Environmental Justice and Equity’s work “to continue while ensuring fiscal responsibility and protecting taxpayer dollars.” Burney added that environmental justice has become part of the work of every state agency.

Healey created the office early in her administration and appointed the first-ever environmental justice undersecretary. During her first year, she signed a budget that increased the line item for environmental justice initiatives from $1.3 million to $8.8 million, an amount the state touted as “historic.”

That budget was roughly maintained for a second year. But the 2026 budget — the first Healey signed after President Trump returned to office — reduced these funds to $6.2 million. This year, facing headwinds of large cuts in federal funding and an uncertain economic outlook, both the governor’s office and the Legislature have advanced deeper cuts. The House passed a budget allocating $4.6 million, and the Senate proposed $4 million. Lawmakers are now negotiating the final bill.

One of the environmental justice office’s major achievements last year was developing statewide standards requiring developers to assess the cumulative impact of large energy projects on vulnerable communities, rather than evaluating projects in isolation.

The environmental justice funding also supports the state Environmental Justice Council, which meets in libraries, schools, and other community spaces across Massachusetts to hear residents’ concerns and gather input on decisions being made by state agencies. At a meeting in Taunton, for example, community members spoke to the health and traffic repercussions of nearby industrial plants. In Lowell, residents shared the environmental consequences of living next to hydropower facilities.

Dwaign Tyndal, executive director of Alternatives for Community and Environment, a Roxbury-based nonprofit, acknowledged that the work funded by the line item may seem modest compared to the scale of injustices across the state — including rising asthma rates, devastating flooding, and extreme heat.

“When you have generational issues like air quality, and you point to the siting reforms, it sounds not as important,” he said. “But it’s literally the foundational step of changing environmental justice in frontline communities.”

State Senator Lydia Edwards, who represents East Boston, filed an amendment to maintain last year’s funding level. She said that growing environmental threats and a hostile federal government called for more investment, not less.

Sean Fitzgerald, spokesperson for Senate Ways and Means Chair Michael Rodrigues, said funding would still remain “substantially higher than several prior years.” He said this priority could also receive support in a $3.9 billion environmental bond bill known as the Mass Ready Act, which the Senate passed in April.

Other agencies working on climate and environmental issues are also poised to take a financial hit. The funding levels in the budget resolutions could result in the loss of dozens of jobs at the Department of Conservation & Recreation and Department of Environmental Protection, according to the Green Budget Coalition, which represents environmental organizations.

Several members of the Environmental Justice Council said that despite the budget proposal, they hadn’t seen the Healey administration’s commitment to the issue diminish.

“If anything, we’ve been continuing to invest time and effort into building out the policy infrastructure to make it a regular part of government,” said Marcos Luna, a geography and sustainability professor at Salem State University.

Still, some nonetheless worried about the consequences of the loss of funds.

“I don’t want to attribute concerns around the general budget to a moral retreat from environmental justice,” said Miles Gresham, policy director for Neighbor to Neighbor Massachusetts. “But that’s the impact it’s going to have.”

The 54th annual Boston Shootout is taking place this weekend at Catholic Memorial in West Roxbury, welcoming three prominent Northeast-based travel programs for two days of competition.

In the event’s opening game Saturday, the Boston Amateur Basketball Club’s 16-under squad rolled to a 115-64 victory over the 18-under Connecticut HoopWave.

“It’s fun to play at home and have a good crowd, play a good team and just show who we are,” said BABC forward Malachi Odugbela, a 6-foot-5-inch sophomore guard at St. Andrew’s (R.I.) who led BABC with 24 points. “We know it’s a very big event for us, and we try not to lose when we’re playing in it.”

The Roxbury Boys & Girls Club sponsored the Shootout until 1999, but financial challenges led the organization to cease overseeing the event.

BABC founder and director Leo Papile — then also a senior member of the Celtics front office — stepped in to preserve the Shootout, and the BABC has run it each year since.

As the youth basketball landscape has evolved, the Shootout has transitioned from a national all-star event with graduating seniors to a regional event with younger players competing for their travel teams. Still, many of New England’s top talents take part.

“In those days, it was critical for the graduating seniors to play in the springs,” said Papile, now in his 49th season leading BABC. “It’s different now, but we [take pride] in keeping it going.”

On Papile’s mind during this year’s Shootout is Roscoe Baker, a local basketball legend who passed away May 17 at age 88. Baker was among the many community leaders who had a role in founding the event.

The conversations follow a period of marked decline in new housing and construction citywide, even as rents continue to rise, and come as developers fear a successful rent control ballot question would effectively freeze new residential construction. Wu has said she would vote in support of the rent control question but favors the conditions set in her own, more modest, proposal, which languished at the Legislature after she filed it in early 2023.

That development slowdown is due in large part to high costs for both materials and construction financing, though some developers also point to more stringent rules that Wu implemented around affordable housing and energy efficiency as driving costs upward. Reducing property taxes could help developers meet the investment return demanded by residential investors, such as pension funds and insurance companies.

Either way, the city counts more than 20,000 units that have been approved, but where construction has not yet started, and hopes to ease some of that backlog.

“With construction and borrowing costs reflecting interest rates that show no signs of abating soon, otherwise viable housing projects get stalled before groundbreaking,” said city spokesperson Marcela Dwork in an email. “Targeted, short-term tax abatements are one tool among many that the city has made available to help viable developments break ground and deliver much-needed housing for residents.”

The city declined to specify how many development teams have been offered possible tax abatement deals or estimate the number of units that could be built if those offers were successful. Developing housing in Boston can cost between $600,000 and $1 million per unit, if not more, depending on a project’s size and location.

Officials in the Boston Planning Department have for years worked one-on-one with developers in an attempt to get city-approved projects out of the permitting pipeline and into construction. This spring, the city provided $50 million from its $110 million Housing Accelerator Fund to help fund a 266-unit building at the Bunker Hill public housing community. The city and state are also jointly funding $10.5 million for 110 apartments in Roxbury’s Nubian Square.

In 2023, the Wu administration announced deep tax breaks for projects that would convert defunct offices into apartments, with developers eligible to reduce property taxes by up to 75 percent for as long as 29 years. While a handful of those projects have started construction, others have had a difficult time making financing work, even with a tax break in hand. In June, three downtown office buildings that the city approved to convert into 95 apartments will hit the auction block.

Still, it has been years since the Wu administration weighed the idea of direct tax breaks for traditional market-rate housing. In fall 2023, Wu told business leaders she was “strongly considering” such a tax break alongside plans to revamp the city’s outdated zoning code. Developers eagerly awaited a formal announcement at Wu’s state of the city speech the following January, but her prepared remarks did not include any mention of a policy shift. Only after the speech, in conversation with reporters, did Wu make a surprise statement: The city was backing away from abatements amid feedback from developers that the breaks would not go far enough to make the economics work on a stalled project.

“We have spent a tremendous amount of time and energy really engaging with the real estate community, with academics, with just about every source of data, to understand the financials and what it would take to get our pipeline going,” Wu said then. “The scale of resources that it would take to close the gaps, to make these projects actually move forward — and at scale, to start to bring rents down — is simply not something that the city could afford.”

In the years since, the city’s budget has only gotten tighter; Boston Public Schools in January said it may need to cut as many as 400 positions. Wu has also proposed cuts to grant programs and department budgets, and the city recently forecast the lowest amount of revenue from new construction than at any point in the past decade.

Officials in the Planning Department have asked developers whether they could make various financial plans work, including a break on taxes during construction with a five- or 10-year abatement on real estate taxes after that. Those breaks would be available only if a project’s developer could commit to breaking ground relatively quickly — a tall order these days, developers say, with many investors holding off on committing any funding to Massachusetts projects ahead of the November vote on rent control.

While developers appreciate the renewed conversations, six industry sources told the Globe that a five- or 10-year tax break was too short a period to have a meaningful impact on a project’s finances.

“It’s too incremental to make much of a difference,” said one Boston developer who has spoken with the city about abatements. “This is revenue they don’t have today. And they haven’t got a chance of getting it, because these projects aren’t starting.”

Several pointed to Boston’s office-to-residential abatement program, which grants tax breaks that last nearly three decades, and a New York City tax exemption that extends as long as 40 years.

Still, developers said, it’s a positive sign that Wu is entertaining the idea of abatements for market-rate projects — even those with a 20 percent affordability requirement.

“It’s been a long process,” said another Boston developer who has spoken with the city about abatements. “It seems like there’s some movement in City Hall, but it’s snail’s progress.”

Powell received the award “for protecting the independence” of the Fed despite Trump’s aggressive efforts to try to force him to lower interest rates and to get him to resign when he would not.

The people of Minnesota’s Twin Cities also received the award for “peacefully defending” human rights and immigrants in their community during a Trump administration immigration enforcement surge that included federal agents killing two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during protests there in January.

Four Twin Cities community leaders — Iman Yusuf Abdulle, Natalie Ehret, Carolina Ortiz, and Zena Stenvik — accepted Sunday night on behalf of the residents of Minneapolis and Saint Paul.

“Joining Chicago, Portland, and other communities, their compassion and unwavering commitment to the ideals that sustain our democracy inspired communities across this country and forced the federal government to back down,” Caroline Kennedy, honorary president of the JFK Library Foundation, told the crowd. “We especially remember the courage of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who gave their lives for their community and our country.”

The award choices led to unusually strong demand for this year’s award ceremony, which was moved to a tent outside the library for capacity reasons for only the third time. The other occasions were in 2017, when former President Barack Obama received the award, and in 2019, when the recipient was then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Among the attendees Sunday were Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, and three members of Renee Good’s family — her father, Tim Ganger, brother Brent Ganger, and sister Anna Ganger Collins.

Powell was an unusual choice for the award, created in 1989 to recognize “public servants who have made courageous decisions of conscience without regard for the personal or professional consequences.” Many past recipients, such as Obama, Pelosi, and last year’s honoree, former Vice President Mike Pence, were elected officials.

“He is not an elected official, and these are not ordinary times,” Jack Schlossberg, Caroline Kennedy’s son and a member of the Profile in Courage Award committee, said in introducing Powell. “His commitment to the public interest never wavered.”

A lawyer and former investment banker who served President George H.W. Bush’s Treasury Department, Powell is a soft-spoken government official who led the nation’s central bank for eight years ending May 22. Despite initially appointing him to the job, Trump quickly turned on Powell in mid-2018 when the Fed began inching up its benchmark interest rate to head off potential inflation.

Then, as in Trump’s second term, Powell refused to give into the pressure.

While the Fed has made mistakes in the difficult task of monetary policy, the public expects “we will make our decisions based only on our best economic analysis of what would most benefit the people we serve.

“We do not take into account the fortunes of any political party or politician in making those decisions,” Powell said.

The Fed was created by Congress as a uniquely independent federal agency so that it would make decisions based on what’s good for the economy and not for short-term political reasons. Interest rate decisions are made by a 12-member board, but the chair is highly influential and publicly explains the Fed’s actions.

Powell was reappointed to a second four-year term by President Joe Biden in 2022. When Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he wanted the Fed to significantly lower rates to spur more economic growth. But Trump’s high tariffs led to concerns among economists about price increases, and the Fed moved cautiously.

Trump was infuriated. He publicly derided Powell as “stupid,” a “knucklehead,” and a “stubborn moron” while calling on him to resign and musing about firing him. But Fed board members can only be fired “for cause,” not for policy disputes.

So Trump tried to find a reason last year, focusing on the rising cost of renovating and expanding the Fed’s Washington, D.C., headquarters.

He increased the pressure on Powell and the Fed by attempting to fire another member of the central bank’s Board of Governors, Lisa Cook, because of mortgage fraud allegations she denies. Trump’s unprecedented move was put on hold by a federal judge pending Cook’s legal challenge, which the Supreme Court is deciding. Cook attended Sunday night’s ceremony.

Then in January, Powell revealed that the Justice Department was conducting a criminal investigation into whether he had lied to Congress about the renovation.

Still, Powell refused to resign as chair before his term ended May 22. Trump nominated his replacement, Kevin Warsh, who was recently sworn in to succeed him. But Powell broke with tradition and opted to remain on the Fed board until the criminal investigation is over, denying Trump another seat to fill. His separate 14-year board term doesn’t end until 2028.

Powell described President Kennedy as “an inspiring public servant” and “a towering figure in my early life.”

“Partisan political differences are normal — indeed essential — in a thriving democracy,“ Powell said. ”But we ought to be united in our commitment to the higher principles that define our nation. Chief among them is respect for the rule of law."
