A 24-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department and third-generation firefighter, Kilduff was killed May 23 when he fell from a third-story window during a three-alarm blaze in Dorchester. He was 53.

Kilduff — or “BK,” as he was affectionately known at the firehouse — died as he lived: helping others, his family and colleagues said during the service, which was held at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross in the South End.

“My dad is my hero. He’s the hero everyone says he is, and I’ll miss him forever,” said his son, Mason Kilduff. “He taught us all how to live, and now he’s taught us how to die.”

Kilduff served in the Marines before becoming a firefighter, coached youth football, and mentored younger first responders. Above all, he showed up for his family, loved ones said.

When Kilduff responded to that Dorchester fire, he unwittingly answered the final call, a call from above, summoning him home for good, said Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall.

Kilduff served with the department’s Rescue Company 2, a specialized unit that responds to particularly dangerous situations, including firefighters in distress.

“While Bobby is worthy of the title hero many times over, he would never want you to call him that,” Marshall said. “He would prefer to be known for being a great dad, a great partner, a mentor, a brother firefighter, a friend. He was truly a light in this world.”

Just moments before his fatal fall, Kilduff alerted other firefighters to tenuous conditions as the engulfed structure became unstable, said Lieutenant Greg Kelly. Five residents of the house also escaped without injury.

“His very last act was to push two firefighters out of the dangerous area,” Kelly said.

In the 48 hours preceding that call, Kilduff likely saved two other lives, officials have said. One was a young woman threatening to jump off a building in the Fenway. The other was a homeless man who became trapped in a confined space in a Dorchester MBTA yard. Kilduff was also credited with helping save a fellow firefighter who suffered cardiac arrest while responding to a call several weeks ago.

“My dad represents everything our world can be if we look out for each other,” said his daughter, Hanna Jane Kilduff, 24, who’s pursuing a master’s degree in education. “Nobody was outside the bounds of his compassion.”

She said he consistently encouraged her to take risks and prioritize her own joy.

Always a diehard Boston sports fan, Kilduff shared that passion with his son, a Marine currently stationed in North Carolina.

“We’re both Boston guys forever,” said Mason Kilduff, 22. Their common interests led to frequent phone calls, discussing “the most recent news in Boston sports, what we would do to fix the Red Sox,” and other pressing issues.

Mason Kilduff said he still has the dozens of letters his dad sent him during bootcamp.

Later during the service, Richard G. Henning, archbishop of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Boston, addressed the Kilduff children directly.

“We heard you speak so beautifully about the ways in which your father, your beloved, shaped you. But I think it’s fair to say that in a very real sense you shaped him as well,” Henning said. “He knew what he was fighting for. It was ever and always you.”

Shortly after Henning spoke, fire officials rang a ceremonial bell to commemorate Kilduff; his helmet rested on the coffin.

He was a prankster during downtime, said firefighter Vic Gaybor, but the “one I wanted by my side” during emergencies.

At the Rescue Company 2 firehouse in Roxbury, Kilduff was known as the company’s informal historian. He could recite dates and details of historical fires in the city, and he was often the first to honor those killed in the line of duty.

It just doesn’t feel right to honor a fallen brother without him, said Sam Dillon, president of Local 718, the Boston firefighters’ union.

“I hope we got it right,” he said. “Brother, I hope we made you proud. And we’ll never stop trying.”

Hours before the funeral was set to begin Monday morning, throngs of firefighters parked in a Dorchester lot and boarded buses that brought them downtown.

“Rest in peace firefighter Robert Kilduff,” read the bus marquees.

A giant American flag hung over Washington Street, suspended between two firetruck ladders. Bagpipe music echoed through the neighborhood on an unseasonably cold, dreary morning. When Kilduff’s casket arrived outside the cathedral, some of his closest colleagues served as pallbearers, proceeding carefully up the church steps.

It was a level of fanfare Kilduff would have found excessive, said his longtime partner, Jess Spruell.

“He probably wouldn’t want us standing here, focusing on what he did. Because for him, helping people wasn’t about being called a hero,” she said. “It was about caring. It was about showing up, being there for others. It was about doing what was right.”

Kilduff embodied the spirit of Boston, a city built on the principle “that our people will show up for one another,” Mayor Michelle Wu said during her remarks.

“Boston has never lost the faith that when we call, someone will come,” she said. “When one of our protectors lays down their life in service to our city, every heart in Boston feels the pain of that loss.”

Members of the public also came to pay their respects.

“It’s very emotional,” said Mary Reardon, 61, whose late father worked alongside Kilduff’s grandfather in the department. “I have a lot of respect for firefighters, for what they do and what they sacrifice.”

After the service, Kilduff’s casket was transported down the church steps and loaded again atop Engine 42. The clouds had dissipated as morning turned to afternoon, giving way to bright sunshine. It was time for one last ride.

So what’s happening?

Costs have been skyrocketing, to start, particularly for housing. In Massachusetts, home prices have increased more than in any other state; housing-related costs more than doubled over the past two decades, MassINC data shows. Rents are now often more than a mortgage payment. And health care expenses shot up more than 150 percent.

These rising costs are causing those in lower and middle income brackets to pull back on spending, while wealthy households keep opening their wallets: The top 10 percent of earners now account for nearly half of consumer spending — a record high, according to Moody’s Analytics.

This is significant because the consumer price index — which determines the inflation rate — weights different types of spending in proportion to their share of overall spending. And with lower-income households pulling back and largely limiting their spending to essentials such as utilities, which have gotten more expensive, and higher-income people shelling out a lot more on extras such as clothing, where prices have remained stable, the published inflation rate does not fully reflect ordinary spending patterns.

And that means the increasing cost of living for all but the highest earners is being vastly underestimated.

This is especially true in Massachusetts, one of the most expensive states in the country for families raising children and trying to maintain a middle-class standard of living, according to MassINC.

And Black and Latino residents feel the squeeze even more. In two-earner households with children, the share meeting the middle-class threshold is more than 30 percentage points lower than for whites.

It’s no wonder that, despite the soaring stock market and a steadily growing economy, “affordability” has become a buzz word.

“When there was really high inflation, and then it slowed down, people in the news and in political circles were frustrated that people were still complaining about the cost of living,” said Elise Rapoza, a senior research associate at MassINC Policy Center. “Part of that is just the prices were stuck high. They never came back down. But part of it is because that inflation rate underestimated the extent to which ordinary households were experiencing cost of living increases.”

And that can be confounding for people who make decent money and aren’t getting ahead.

Candice Watch and her husband make a comfortable living and are able to pay their mortgage and go out to dinner when they want. But saving is harder than it used to be, and spending money requires more planning than she’d like.

“It’s not as easily accessible as you would think for someone whose income has been increasing,” said Watch, a program director at Children’s Services of Roxbury, a behavioral health provider that arranged funding for the master’s degree in counseling psychology she just received at Framingham State University. “Things are just tight.”

Watch and her husband, a regional property manager, live south of Boston but would love to move back to the city where they both work and grew up. But buying a house here isn’t in the cards right now.

“In Boston, you can get, like, a parking spot for how much we would want to spend,” she said.

The middle-class budget used for MassINC’s analysis includes items that are often left out of standard budget assessments, such as higher education, retirement savings, and modest leisure activities. Housing and child care accounted for the largest increases in cost between 2020 and 2024, but the roughly 30 percent rise in dining out and recreation prices may disproportionately contribute to the “economic malaise” people feel because these purchases are highly visible and frequent, according to the MassINC report, one of a series from the group focused on the state’s middle class.

In the last few months, the Framingham food pantry Daniel’s Table has seen a marked uptick in English-speaking residents who’ve never needed food assistance before, said founder David Blais. Many are older, most have jobs, some even own homes, but the increase in food and gas prices has put them in precarious situations. Some clients are paying 80 percent of their income on rent; others have fallen behind on their mortgage or taxes.

“Middle class on the edge,” Blais calls them. “They were just barely making it, and now they’ve kind of toppled into the abyss.”

When most of a family’s budget is going toward bills, there’s often nothing left for birthday presents or trips to visit relatives — decisions that cut into quality of life, said Melissa Dimond, executive director of Wellspring House, a North Shore economic mobility nonprofit. “It’s part of what makes us human,” she said.

Nationwide, only 26 percent of middle-income caregivers, who make between $50,000 and $100,000 a year, say they are living comfortably, according to a new Bipartisan Policy Center poll.

Incomes have been rising, but part of that is due to people working more hours, according to MassINC, driven by a growing reliance on both parents working full time. For households in lower income brackets, nearly all of their increased earnings is due to working more.

More sticker shock may be on the horizon.

Rising gas prices are projected to tack on more than $1,000 on average per Massachusetts household by the end of the year if prices don’t go down, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. Health insurance premiums are set to increase by up to 220 percent for residents who relied on now-expired federal health tax credits, Massachusetts Budget and Policy Center data show.

But the cost of living doesn’t appear to be a focus for the current administration.

On the day gas hit more than $4.50 a gallon last month, and the Labor Department announced that the inflation rate was accelerating at its fastest rate in three years, President Trump said he wasn’t motivated by people’s economic hardships — “not even a little bit” — to end the war in Iran.

“I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation,” he said.

The growing divide between the haves and the have-nots is clear in Massachusetts, where the median household income is roughly $104,000 but more than a quarter of households make less than $50,000 a year. A small percentage of people are making a lot of money, while a lot of households are barely able to afford basic needs, said Viviana Abreu-Hernandez, president of the Massachusetts Budget and Policy Center.

The expense of living in Massachusetts is driving many people away. Nearly nine out of every 10 households leaving the state made less than $200,000 a year, according to MassBudget.

“We are saying that the economy is working,” Abreu-Hernandez said. “The question that I always ask is: For whom?”

But even if he were to try to run again … would Republican voters still want him?

A new Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll found that, at least in Massachusetts, they’re literally split. Close to 47 percent of the 465 likely GOP primary voters surveyed said they would vote for Trump again, while another 47 percent said they wouldn’t.

The virtually dead-even divide reflects some cracks in the president’s support within his own party, said David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center.

“We’re back to a divided GOP regarding Trump,” he said. Half of likely GOP voters “are solidly loyal, while the other half either want to move on from Trump, or oppose the hypothetical because they know it’s not possible by law.”

Even some of the loyalists aren’t holding their breath for a third Trump term, though.

“I would vote for him again,” said Heather Zimmerman, a Republican voter from North Hatfield. “But it’s illegal, so he can’t do it.”

Charles Sweeney, 68, of Merrimac, said he would support Trump for another term — if the Constitution allowed.

“Which is kind of debatable at this point,” Sweeney, an independent voter, said.

Trump mused for months about seeking a third term in the White House — a proposition likely to run him smack into the 22nd Amendment (the one that says that no one can be elected president more than twice). At least one ally, podcaster and former Trump White House aide Steve Bannon, hinted at “a plan” to help elect Trump to the White House in 2028, and last year, Trump told NBC News that he was “not joking” and “there are methods” for him to seek another term.

But he’s since backed off the rhetoric, at least publicly, telling reporters last fall that it’s “pretty clear” he’s termed out.

Massachusetts might not be the most apt place to gauge the Republican president’s popularity, but he still has a grip on the party’s grassroots here. More than 63 percent of those surveyed in the Suffolk poll rated his job performance as good or excellent.

“I’ll take Trump, just because I like a lot of the things he does,” said Craig Lane, a Republican from Newburyport. “But I think the talk of a third term is more just theater.”

Here are some other notable numbers from the poll:

— 32 percentage points: How much Mike Minogue, the former medical device company executive, leads former MBTA chief administrator Brian Shortsleeve in a head-to-head matchup in the party’s gubernatorial primary. Around 45 percent of likely GOP primary voters — both Republicans and independents — said they would vote for Minogue, compared to roughly 13 percent who are backing Shortsleeve.

Another 40 percent are still undecided, but the race is Mingoue’s to lose, Paleologos said.

“To use an MBTA analogy, it’s like Minogue is one stop away from Government Center, and Shortsleeve is stuck on the platform in Braintree,” he said.

— 46 percent: The percentage of voters who said they had never heard of the GOP’s de facto US Senate nominee John Deaton. That’s gotta be a bit of an ego hit for Deaton, who isn’t a total newcomer to the Massachusetts political scene. He challenged US Senator Elizabeth Warren in 2024, who defeated him 60-40 percent.

— 61 percent: Former GOP Governor Charlie Baker’s favorability among the likely primary electorate. That’s not far off the 69 percent who view Trump favorably.

— 36 percent: The percentage of voters excited about Secretary of State/Trump administration multi-tool Marco Rubio as a potential presidential candidate in 2028. Rubio generated the most excitement among those surveyed in the poll, followed by Vice President JD Vance (28 percent).

The poll, conducted between May 26 and May 29, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Live callers reached respondents via mobile and landline phones.

In Boston, an 1,800-square-foot house for $579,000 is a rare bargain, especially an attractive, free-standing house in a nice neighborhood.

The structure at 8 Pine Street in the Mount Neponset neighborhood of Hyde Park is just that — but there’s a catch. It’s completely unfinished on the inside.

As is, artists could use it as a spacious and private studio; antiques dealers and interior designers would find it useful for furniture storage; it could serve as grand place to keep a collectible vehicle. Or, given permission by the City of Boston (and with some TLC), you could even live here.

“It can’t be a commercial enterprise, like a store,” said Christopher Lydon, the realtor with Milton’s William Raveis Real Estate, who is listing the property. “Its legal designation is as a barn. But, if you got a variance from the Zoning Board of Appeals, you could turn it into a really nice residence.”

While it is a solid gambrel-roofed building with a lot of historic charm, it’s just a shell. The interior contains little more than four walls, studs, rough flooring, ceiling joists, and rudimentary plumbing and wiring.

“Often, buyers are seduced by an attractive purchase price. But they need to know that it will involve effort, and they have to have a plan,” said Robb Cohen, a long-time real estate broker with Engel and Völkers in Boston.

In April, a heavily burned Dorchester house that would need to be mostly gutted or torn down sold for $776,000.

That being said, it does present the possibility for the next owners to make it their own. “They can put their own stamp on it, whether as a residence or as a work place,” said Cohen.

The barn that is for sale is a condominium with a monthly fee of $110.

Laid out in 1858, Maple, Oak, Pine, and Walnut Streets were part of a new development named for the area’s various kinds of trees by the Real Estate & Building Company. This barn, unit 4, was built in 1884. By 1912, Hyde Park had become the southernmost part of Boston, but traces of its history remain, including this building. The house it once served is long gone and the surrounding land was subdivided and filled with newer construction. One of those newer buildings is a classic Boston triple-decker; it and the old carriage house now comprise a four-unit condominium complex.

“This property has proved attractive to a lot of people,” Lydon said. “This is a free-standing condominium with a deeded off-street parking spot.”

He believes that the building’s original use was as a horse stable and that it became a carriage house when the population moved from horse-drawn to automotive transportation. Over the years, it retained its wide barn doors and entrance ramp, a side door, and a substantial rubble stone foundation. But it never became a studio or a home.

For a person who needs work or storage space, or who wants to build a home of their own, this could be a rare opportunity.

“But you do have to know what you are doing,” Cohen warns. “You don’t want to build a million-dollar kitchen in a half-million dollar house.”

Embrace Boston, the group behind the landmark monument to Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King on Boston Common, says it has acquired two buildings in Downtown Crossing that it plans to transform into a vibrant social and cultural hub for racial justice.

The buildings, next door to one another at 33 and 41 West St., will be redeveloped as a 35,000-square-foot complex for civic and cultural endeavors, the group said. The new location is a half block from Boston Common and a stone’s throw from “The Embrace,” the towering bronze sculpture of the Kings’ arms locked together in a triumphant hug after Martin was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

“Embrace was always built on the theory that the built environment — monuments, buildings — can either harm or help,” said Imari Paris Jeffries, Embrace Boston’s president and chief executive. “Being in the center of the city, having a permanent, physical presence, will allow us to help that in a way we maybe haven’t been able to before.” It hopes to be able to open its doors in 2030, in time for Boston’s 400th anniversary.

Embrace Boston was founded in 2017 as the nonprofit King Boston, with the express purpose of conceiving and funding the King memorial for the last available spot on the Common. When “The Embrace,” by the artist Hank Willis Thomas, was unveiled in January 2023, the group changed names and expanded its mission to become a broad-based organization that hosts festivals, organizes events, and conducts research on the city’s civic life from a social justice perspective.

Its new home, conceived in the spirit of a New England meeting house — and to honor Frederick Douglass — will include exhibition space, a podcast studio, and theater space for films, performances, and lectures, the group said. Plans also include gathering space for community groups and a cafe and restaurant. In the coming weeks, a public call will go out to artists for a commission to transform the two buildings’ facades into a single work of public art that represents the organization’s priorities.

For the West Street project, Embrace has enlisted the Boston-based firm Model of Architecture Serving Society (MASS), with which it worked to commission the King memorial and to build the 1965 Freedom Plaza on which it stands, honoring dozens of local civil rights leaders from 1950 to 1970.

“I think the idea of the actual memorial was kind of an opening act,” said Jonathan Evans, a principal at MASS. “The idea now is, ‘How can we help them extend this idea of art, architecture, and design into something that has an active role in making the city better?’ We want it to be part of a constellation of ideas about belonging and place-making.”

The acquisition is a welcome turnaround from the organization’s years-long quest to take up residence in a proposed multipurpose development slated for Parcel 3, a nearly 8-acre lot of city-owned land in Roxbury. But the city canceled the project in January and announced that it would instead use the site to build a new campus for Madison Park Technical Vocational High School.

Jeffries said Embrace Boston is still planning for a presence in Roxbury, calling it “an imperative” for the organization. “We will still need that commitment, and we’re actively working on that,” he said. In the meantime, the West Street properties came within reach, and Embrace seized the opportunity.

While much remains to be seen as Embrace fund-raises to execute its vision, its potential is tantalizing. In a statement, Governor Maura Healey said the move is “about more than a building. It’s about creating a space where people from every neighborhood and background can come together to connect, reflect, create, and leave a meaningful impact on our communities.”

Jeffries hopes to capitalize on that potential with an open-door approach. “The excitement, I think, is that it’s stone soup,” he said. “We want to use this moment to get people talking about and engaged with the possibilities here, and to contribute,” Jeffries said.

The project emerges in a radically different political environment than the one that greeted the unveiling of “The Embrace” in January 2023. A large-scale emblem of a nationwide racial reckoning that exploded from the murder of George Floyd amid the early days of the COVID pandemic, the sculpture helped reconfigure public space in a city largely reserved for historical icons of the country’s founding, like George Washington or Paul Revere.

“The Embrace” anchored more recent, fractious elements of American history in its oldest public park, the Common, in a moment receptive to the public blossoming of those stories. Now, with a federal administration openly hostile to Embrace’s mission of equity and inclusion, the group’s growth is remarkable.

“Back then, I felt kind of like we were in ‘Star Wars: A New Hope,’” Jeffries said. “Now it feels more like ‘The Empire Strikes Back.’ But that’s the fight we’re built for.”

Along with the facade commission, Embrace is also in discussions with the city to create an open call to artists for the empty plinth in nearby Park Square, vacant since the removal of Thomas Ball’s “The Emancipation Group“ in 2020 after a public outcry over its portrayal of Abraham Lincoln seeming to bestow freedom on an enslaved man crouched at his feet. The organization hopes to be able to put out a public call for proposals by fall.

The buildings are currently largely occupied by commercial tenants, Jeffries said, who are welcome to remain as the organization begins raising capital to renovate both buildings. But an unoccupied portion of the building is slated to host a kickoff as soon as this fall.

But Novo Marketplace is about more than food, Chen says: People are welcome to spend time here without buying anything. “We are building more of a community,” he says. “We want people to come out. We have board games, free WiFi, places to sit and hang out, and a stage for events.”

The space is large and airy, with tables to seat more than 250 people. Pop music plays in the background. This isn’t a fast food court; although the food is casual, many of the dishes and drinks are made to order. Customers take buzzers or numbers, then wander while they wait. Although a few stalls aren’t open yet, including Molly Tea and Noodle Lab, most of Novo is in business.

Here is what you’ll find — along with the best things to order — when you visit.

You’re not imagining things: There was previously a branch of this California-based Hong Kong-style cafe just a few steps away from Novo Marketplace. Now it’s inside the food court, serving rich beef stew, shredded chicken, and other specialties.

What to order: Hainan chicken ($14.99) is an excellent starting place, the slices of tender-skinned poached chicken served with yellow rice, cucumbers, and ginger-scallion sauce. Add on a milk tea for $3 more for the full Hong Kong cafe experience.

This chain started in China in 2022 and has expanded to more than 30 countries. It’s new to Allston, one of its latest landing spots. Sure, you could get something classic, like an Americano or flat white, but why would you when Cotti also offers honey-lemon sparkling cold brew, matcha-mango-coconut drinks, and blue-tinged cloud mousse lattes? Adjust the sugar level to your liking when you order. There are Hong Kong egg puffs and other baked goods, too.

What to order: The pandan coco latte ($6.49) is a layered drink of pale green and creamy brown, with pandan-flavored coconut milk on the bottom, and Cotti’s Gold Dark roast coffee and espresso on top. The coffee is satisfyingly bitter against the pandan and coconut sweetness.

Tall, airy souffle pancakes became an Internet trend a few years back, and they are Fluffy Fluffy’s specialty. Pancake makers whip egg whites, then cook the cakes low and slow and serve them in stacks topped with whipped cream and fruit, Nutella and banana, Oreos and cream, and more. There are also breakfast sets, Basque cheesecakes, and drinks — but it’s the fluffy, fluffy pancakes you’re here for.

What to order: Light, eggy matcha tiramisu pancakes ($16.50) come with whipped cream, a sprinkle of matcha powder, and strawberries, with a side of matcha cream for pouring.

If Hangover’s name obscures the fact that this business serves Istanbul-inspired street food, the Turkish flag and evil-eye talisman on the wall tip you off. You can build your own bowl with rice, beans, chicken or beef gyro, and other toppings. (Or get your fries loaded with gyro meat and sauces.) Panini come with egg and cheese, and also the spicy sausage sujuk. There are American classics like chicken salad sandwiches, and baklava for dessert.

What to order: Hangover’s specialty is the juicy bun burger ($6.99), or islak (wet) burger, a Turkish street staple for staving off regrets from a night of drinking. The seasoned beef patties are served on buns soaked in tomato-based sauce, a messy, squishy flavor bomb. Think of it as a Turkish dip.

This corner of Novo Marketplace is a Korean twofer. Park’s Kitchen previously gained a following at its takeout kitchen in Roxbury. This is the next chapter for the business, specializing in tteokbokki (rice cakes), fried chicken, fish cake skewers, and assorted snacks. Mumu’s Kimbap and Ramyun, as you might guess, offers kimbap (rice and seaweed rolls with various fillings) and popular varieties of instant ramyun, packaged noodle soups customers prepare themselves at the special ramyun machines on the counter.

What to order: Rosé tteokbokki ($17.99), a rich, smoky, spicy bowl of chewy, oblong rice cakes in creamy pink sauce with fish cake, bacon, and snappy little sausages, the whole thing topped in melted cheese. Pick a heat level, from mild to “insane.” Pair it with bulgogi kimbap ($11.99), stuffed with barbecue beef and vegetables.

Now, from the folks behind Hangover, something completely different: Liv serves smoothies, juices, and acai, mango, and coconut bowls. This is for the day after you stuffed yourself full of wet burgers. A healthful reset is just the thing, sometimes.

What to order: It’s hard to resist a juice called Better Than Botox (apple, cucumber, celery, spinach, and lemon, $13). But if you’re craving something more substantial, try a Hawaii bowl, with acai, blueberry granola, pineapple, banana, coconut flakes, and honey ($13).

A sister business to Lumi Vietnamese Bistro at the South Shore Plaza and Lumi Wok & Roast in Randolph, this branch specializes in fresh and fried spring rolls, vermicelli bowls, rice plates, pho, and banh mi. There’s also an alluring roster of Vietnamese coffee drinks.

What to order: Shrimp fresh rolls ($6.95) and a grilled pork banh mi ($10.95), filled with savory meat, pickled veggies, cilantro, and (if you want them) sliced chiles. Don’t forget a coffee topped with sweet egg or ube foam ($6.45).

At Mi-Nori, assorted push pops can be purchased and eaten — but they’re not ice cream push pops. The TikTok-trending tubes hold pre-sliced sushi rolls of your choice, from California roll to seared salmon truffle roll. The handle, a hollow plastic tube, is filled with soy sauce; pop open the cap at the end, sprinkle some on your sushi (careful not to spill), then use the handle to push the sushi out, bite by bite. It’s more than a gimmick; the sushi is fresh and delicious. You can also get sashimi, nigiri, regular rolls, and hand rolls.

What to order: A Lava Crunch push pop ($16), filled with rice, shrimp tempura, spicy crab, avocado, and fish roe, a satisfying mix of flavors and textures.

The smell of intermingling spices draws you to this Indian restaurant, related to Tabla outlets in Florida and beyond. Burnt-orange metal casseroles are on display, filled with butter chicken, palak paneer, Hakka noodles, and more; a friendly staffer is happy to offer samples. The Tabla chicken curry is rustic and fragrant, the vindaloo has real heat, and the biryani is studded with cardamom pods. I couldn’t tell you about vegetable korma, because the fellow behind the counter didn’t think it looked quite right and sent the batch back to the kitchen. Expect generous paneer in your palak, lively spicing, and pride of craftsmanship.

What to order: Tabla’s chicken tikka masala is more nuanced than many versions, and shrimp Madras curry is lively with mustard seeds and tamarind. If you like heat, try the vindaloo, with a mango lassi ($4.49) to cool the burn. Order in combos, from bowl ($10.99) to family feast ($54.99): The Royal Plate ($21.99) gets you three entrees, biryani, naan, and sweet gulab jamun (syrup-soaked fried dumplings) for dessert.

Indonesian food isn’t easy to come by in these parts. Tasya’s Kitchen changes that, serving Indonesian street food by way of New Hampshire. (The original Tasya’s, in Somersworth, is temporarily closed while this one gets up and running.) Come for fragrant, beautifully spiced dishes thrumming with lemongrass and coconut, as well as the ministrations of kind staffers who want to know if you like spicy food and where you might have eaten Indonesian cooking before. You’ll find Tasya’s signature nasi goreng, spicy fried rice with chicken or salted fish, egg, and toppings; variations on light, crisp fried chicken; and gado-gado, a salad of tofu and more that comes with thick, spicy peanut sauce.

What to order: Soto ayam ($17), chicken and glass noodle soup that’s bright yellow with turmeric, is a comforting elixir; apply lime and sambal sauce as you wish. Lontong sayur with chicken ($18) or beef rendang ($20) is a rich, spicy coconut curry with rice cakes and hard-boiled eggs.

This Chinese chain specializes in chicken, with nary a steak in sight. It comes in sandwiches, on skewers, as nuggets, and more. Skewered squid, fries, and other snacks are here, too. It has a following; this stand was doing numbers on a recent Friday night, the staff hoarse from calling out orders.

What to order: The signature spicy fried chicken breast ($6.99), flavored with your choice of sweet plum, chile, or fragrant, salty cumin. After the chicken is fried, staff cut it into bite-size pieces, then serve it in a bag with several long wooden picks to use for stabbing and eating.

122 Brighton Ave., Allston, www.novomarketplace.com. Open 10 a.m.-10 p.m. daily.

But in the speakeasy of Hue, it is sung with gusto, an outpouring of joy. The patrons were there to celebrate Haiti at the World Cup and toast a sporting hero who has roots in both Haiti and Massachusetts: a forward for the national team, Frantzdy Pierrot, 31, who went to high school at the northern end of the Orange Line.

The World Cup can have this effect on people — national pride, mixed with bittersweet history, and a heavy dose of delight. And yes, there is discussion of the soccer, or football, as pretty much the rest of the world calls it. The tactics, the predictions, the strengths and weaknesses of the various squads.

But the sheer scale of the tournament is so culturally impactful that the talk inevitably turns to the personal. Ostensibly, people are talking about soccer, but really they’re talking about their childhood, their country’s history and culture, and how it fits in with the game. The tournament is simply a rhetorical entry point to all that.

For Haitians of a certain age, their Dave Roberts moment came in 1974, when their country qualified for the Cup. They were playing Italy, a European footballing superpower. The goal came shortly after halftime via Route 1 football: there is a clearing header from the Haitian central defense, then a straightforward through-ball that Haitian forward Emmanuel “Manno” Sanon latches onto.

He rounds the renowned Italian goalkeeper, Dino Zoff, and puts the ball in the net. Haiti 1, Italy 0. It broke Zoff’s lengthy string of scoreless games.

In Port-au-Prince, there was bedlam, Lucien, 62, recalled. He can still remember walking to his friend’s house to watch. Televisions were a relative rarity at the time in Haiti, and his buddy had the appliance that conveyed the match in real-time. He remembered that on the walk, all the radios in the street were tuned to the game. After the goal, there was the shouting and jumping. General elation.

The result of the game is typically a footnote in these recollections. (Italy won 3-1.) As is the case with the rest of the tournament for the national team. (Haiti failed to earn a single point and was cumulatively outscored 14 to 2.) But for Haitians, Sanon’s goal was enough proof that they belonged on soccer’s global stage.

More than half a century has passed since that goal. Haiti has failed to qualify for every World Cup since. Until now.

And there is, of course, a Massachusetts connection that goes beyond the team’s June 13 clash with Scotland at Gillette Stadium and the local diaspora’s jubilation at the upcoming tournament. Frantzdy Pierrot spent his formative years here in Massachusetts, attending middle school and high school in Melrose, before a stop playing college soccer at Northeastern University.

Ten miles north of Boston is where Pierrot’s family sought a better life.

“Melrose gave me everything,” Pierrot said at Hue.

When they moved from Haiti, the focus was education for him, not athletics, said Pierrot. His father drove a bus and worked other jobs, including one at Logan Airport, sometimes only sleeping four or five hours a night to make ends meet.

Nowadays, his father, Destine, is sure that uprooting his family to Melrose was the right move. Asked what he will feel when his son walks onto the field, and the Haitian national anthem is played before the first World Cup match, he answers simply, “Happy.”

The meet-and-greet at the Back Bay bar came shortly after Pierrot was feted as a sporting hero during a ceremony at the State House. Governor Maura Healey said he represented “the very best of” the Commonwealth, all the while declaring a statewide day in his honor. Former coaches recalled his dogged determination and unshakable self-belief. The Melrose High School marching band struck up a version of “Sweet Caroline.”

He fielded questions in English and Haitian Creole from the press and posed for photos with admirers decked out in Haiti jerseys and signed autographs.

Pierrot’s soccer journey has taken him overseas, with stints in Belgium, France, Israel, Greece, and, most recently, Turkey. He has played Champions League soccer against some of Europe’s biggest clubs, including Juventus, Paris Saint-Germain, and Benfica.

It’s a long way from Bas-Limbé, a community on Haiti’s northern coast, about 140 miles away from Port-au-Prince. That is where his family’s roots are. It’s where he recalled playing soccer in the streets barefoot, using whatever was around as a ball, including spherical fruit.

“Football gave us happiness,” he told the State House crowd.

Nowadays, Haiti remains a nation rocked by turmoil, with gangs controlling much of the capital. In recent years, the national team’s home stadium was overrun by gangs and vandalized and the national soccer training center was set ablaze. The violent instability has also meant that the Haitian national team had to qualify for the World Cup, all the while playing their home games abroad.

The Haitian diaspora, too, has weathered hardship, namely federal hostility toward immigrants. Greater Boston, which is home to the third-largest Haitian community in the United States, has not been spared the pain, as tens of thousands of immigrants in the state wonder whether they will be deported to a country riven by chaos.

For Pierrot, the Cup offers him and his teammates an opportunity to show that there is more to Haiti than horrific headlines and news dispatches. For Haitians, both at home and abroad, the Cup offers a respite.

“It means so much,” said Boston City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune, a Haitian American.

After the event at Hue and the State House ceremony, Lucien hosted a local access television program to discuss Haiti at the World Cup inside an Egleston Square media studio.

Among his guests was Donnet Desilus, a 65-year-old Dorchester resident who once captained the Haitian national team.

He spoke about what the United States has given his family: four college educations for his children, three of whom went to Ivy League schools. And like everyone else in the local Haitian community, he talked glowingly about what the competition means for Haiti.

“It’s the best thing for the country,” he said.

But he is measured when talking about the team’s chances.

Haiti’s initial opponents include Brazil, which has won more World Cups than any other nation. Morocco made it to the semifinals of the most recent Cup four years ago and was recently — and controversially — crowned champion of Africa. Scotland earned its trip here through the gauntlet of European qualification.

“It’s a tough group,” he said.

Wu on Wednesday said Gayle would be a “powerful, principled voice” in the Senate who “has stood with our families even when state legislators have not.”

She went even further at a news conference trumpeting her support, commending Gayle’s years of grass-roots advocacy work in Boston while criticizing the Senate for “offloading their elected power to unelected corporate interests to negotiate against Boston families.”

“We are tired of our own senators blocking solutions that came out of a vote of the City Council and the House of Representatives, town halls, meetings, organizing unions, faith leaders — everyone coming together to say we need relief and we need help now,” Wu added. “We’re tired of feeling like ballot initiatives are the only way to get anything to happen up there.”

Collins represents the First Suffolk District, which is anchored by Dorchester and South Boston. He is the second Democrat in the Senate to face a challenge with roots in Wu’s City Hall: Will Brownsberger, who also opposed Wu’s tax shift proposal, is being challenged by Daniel Lander, a former Wu aide.

While Wu has not yet weighed in on that race, on Wednesday she signaled she would be active in Gayle’s campaign effort and encouraged voters to rally behind her.

“This is going to be a fun election cycle,” Wu said.

Vanessa Woo, a spokesperson for Collins’s campaign, said the incumbent has built a record of fighting for Boston’s underserved populations, saying he’s addressed mental health and substance use crises and helped provide “working families tax relief,” among a series of other priorities.

“He will continue to do what he does every day,” Woo said, including “partnering with community leaders to address the challenges residents face.”

Brownsberger, meanwhile, is from Belmont but his district includes part of Boston.

“I’m just focused on serving the people in my district and making sure that people are aware of the hard work we’re doing,” Brownsberger said Wednesday. “And that’s about all I have to say.”

Wu’s decision to directly align herself against a fellow Democratic incumbent could test both her sway among city voters who overwhelmingly gave her a second term, and her standing in the State House, where she has trusted allies in the House but fraught relations with Senate leaders.

Senate President Karen Spilka declined to comment on Wu’s remarks after appearing at a Pride flag-raising event at the State House.

“I’m not here for politics,” she said.

Collins, considered a conservative Democrat in the Senate dominated by progressive voices, once weighed a run for mayor in 2021. Wu went on to win the office that fall.

A married mother of four, the 47-year-old Gayle has lived in Dorchester or the South End for more than 20 years, according to her campaign, and currently works as the senior director of advocacy and family partnerships at Neighborhood Villages, a Boston-based early education and child care nonprofit.

Wu’s entrance into the race aside, Collins appears to be operating from a position of strength. An internal poll circulated by his campaign showed that 82 percent of the roughly 800 people surveyed said they would vote for Collins in the primary election, compared to 10 percent for Gayle and 9 percent for Juwan Skeens, who is also running in the Democratic contest.

Collins also had $92,000 on hand at the end of last month — Gayle had about $15,600 at the end of April, according to her most recent filings — giving him a cash advantage in a contest where tens of thousands of dollars can be a major difference-maker.

As South Boston’s senator, he also hosts the annual St. Patrick’s Day Breakfast, one of the city’s most hallowed, if sometimes awkward, political traditions. Wu skipped the breakfast in March, prompting Collins to joke about Wu’s absence that “she found it just a little bit too taxing.”

Gayle on Wednesday said that she is “honored” to have the mayor’s support and cast Collins as prioritizing the needs of “the wealthiest residents.”

“When I talk to folks across this district, the number one thing they bring up is housing and affordability,” Gayle said. “I’m on your side.”

Wu’s endorsement could offer a much-needed boost to Gayle as she challenges Collins, an established sitting lawmaker who has served in elected office on Beacon Hill for more than 15 years.

Wu’s influence on Gayle’s campaign is already apparent. Gayle’s campaign manager, Maccon Bonner, worked for two years as Wu’s liaison to the Back Bay, Beacon Hill, Fenway, and Mission Hill until Gayle hired him this year.

Wu’s endorsement, particularly for first-time candidates, has proven powerful and influential in the past.

In the 2023 municipal election, Wu backed four new City Council candidates, all of whom won council seats that November.

In 2024, Wu endorsed longtime public defender and first-time candidate Allison Cartwright in her successful bid to be clerk of the Suffolk County Supreme Judicial Court against sitting city councilor Erin Murphy. Cartwright also had the backing of US Representative Ayanna Pressley and Attorney General Andrea Campbell, bringing an unusually high level of attention to a race typically far below the average voter’s radar.

Then last fall, as Wu easily rolled to reelection, her close allies on the council again held onto their seats by fairly wide margins with her support, including Councilor at Large Henry Santana, who was seen as the most vulnerable incumbent in last year’s election.

Six years since the pandemic began, most people have tested positive at least once.

It’s become a near-universal experience — a shared disruption that reshaped daily life, work, family, and health. And yet, there’s a group of people who say they’ve managed to avoid it entirely. No positive test. No unmistakable illness. Nothing.

Who are these so-called COVID “superdodgers”?

Responses from more than 500 of you revealed a wide spectrum of experiences and beliefs. Some of you described taking rigorous precautions long after others relaxed — still masking, avoiding crowds, carefully managing risk. Others said you eventually returned to normal routines but somehow never got sick. A number of you credited luck. Some pointed to faith. Others shared detailed personal regimens: UV lights for disinfecting mail, multiple daily showers, vitamin stacks, nasal sprays, strict isolation, or giving up travel altogether.

Reading through your messages, one thing became clear: There isn’t a single story here. There are hundreds.

Still, how?

I began digging deeper by speaking to many of you, but also with a coalition of international researchers and local scientists who have spent years trying to answer the same question. Why do some people seem to escape infection, even after repeated exposures?

Is it behavior? Biology? Timing? Or something we don’t fully understand yet?

It turns out, the answers are complicated and may challenge some assumptions. In some cases, what feels like certainty may be less clear-cut. In others, emerging science offers intriguing clues about immunity, genetics, and how the virus interacts with the body.

This is just the beginning of that exploration. I’ll share what I’ve learned from your stories and from the science about what it really means to be a “superdodger” of COVID-19.

What started this?

For a while, I thought I might be a “superdodger” myself. I was living in Detroit, one of the hardest-hit cities by the pandemic, reporting from COVID units while also caring for my parents in in-home hospice. I also quarantined with my husband three separate times when he had the virus, and I never tested positive. It felt impossible.

That changed after I moved to Boston. In October, I felt the worst sickness of my life. I remember the disbelief when the urgent care provider told me I was positive with COVID… I actually asked them to run the test again. I resonate with many of your stories and do believe there’s something special here.

This Saturday, at least four Massachusetts communities will host a Porchfest of their own, including Newton, Medford, Franklin, and Dorchester (“Dorchfest”). Arlington and the Fenway neighborhood are coming up on June 20, and the second annual Cambridge Porchfest is set for July 11.

Greene keeps a spreadsheet listing all the Porchfests she’s aware of.

“I like to track things,” she said. By her count, seven states haven’t hosted one yet, but there have been two in Australia.

Cleveland was the second place to host a Porchfest, in 2009, after a couple who’d been living in Ithaca brought the idea with them. In 2011, Somerville became the first city in Massachusetts to embrace Porchfest. That one has grown so large — more than 500 bands performed this year alone — that many Bostonians assume Somerville is where it all started.

Elle Marrone is executive director of Greater Ashmont Main Street, a nonprofit that supports Dorchester’s economic viability through pop-ups and other “activations.” After serving as fiscal sponsors for Dorchfest for a few years, Greater Ashmont Main Street became the host organization last year.

Marrone grew up in Arlington, and her husband, Matt Weinburg, is from Sudbury. They embraced Dorchester’s diversity from the moment they moved in.

“We really did fall in love with the neighborhood hanging out on porches,” she said.

In Norfolk County, the Town of Franklin (as it’s officially known, though it now has city government) will host its third Porchfest this weekend. Mixing private residences with municipal spaces in Franklin’s Cultural District, this Porchfest is another example of local leadership combining neighborliness with civic boosterism.

“What’s unique about us is we’re not only on porches but on town property,” said John Lopresti, chair of Franklin’s Cultural District Committee. They’ll have music on the Franklin Town Common, at the Historical Museum, and on the steps of the Franklin Public Library, the nation’s first.

“We wanted to expand it, really bring the beauty of Franklin [by] showcasing these historical assets,” Lopresti said.

On the last Sunday of May, the North Shore city of Beverly — one of the latest communities in Massachusetts to adopt the Porchfest model — celebrated its second annual event a day later than originally planned, after Saturday’s wind and rain necessitated a postponement. In the residential neighborhood of Ryal Side, the Danvers River provided the backdrop for the Jonee Earthquake Band, a trio that played a rowdy mix of punk, rockabilly, and surf-rock while perched atop a garage.

The band’s piratical namesake, Jonee, who alternated between electric and pedal steel guitar, noted that the band didn’t expect donations but would be glad to sell anything from their merch table.

“And if you can’t afford anything,” he joked, “enjoy windowshopping!”

A few blocks around the corner, a crowd of at least a few hundred people mingled behind police tape to listen to Wood & Bone, a professional soul and Americana band with traces of Van Morrison and Ray LaMontagne in their original songs. A tangle of bikes of all sizes rested on the street at the edge of the crowd.

Amid that throng, Ace and Alan Foulds wore shirts advertising their own Porchfest, in Reading. The town will host its eighth annual Porchfest on June 27.

The Foulds try to visit as many Porchfests as they can, for inspiration. They helped bring the concept to Reading in 2019 as part of the town’s 375th anniversary celebration. During the COVID-19 pandemic, they organized a Porchfest online.

One of the joys of Porchfest is learning which of your neighbors make music, said Alan, who serves as Reading’s town moderator.

“It’s like, ‘I didn’t know you played the pennywhistle!’” he said.

In Ithaca, Greene worked for many years at the Kitchen Theatre Company, where the tagline was “Important conversations happen in the kitchen.”

“I’m very soaked in that philosophy,” she said. To her, Porchfest is a prime example of community building through the arts: “Not that it was a conscious plan, but I do like things that bring people together.”

After Greene’s initial Porchfest partner, Gretchen Hildreth, stepped aside, she recruited another neighbor, Andy Adelewitz, to pick up the slack. He was in a heavy metal band that played an acoustic set at an early Porchfest in Ithaca. By now, they’ve amassed a group of around 100 volunteers to help organize each year.

The Ithaca group is still surprised at how far the concept has traveled. There’s a store in Ithaca that now sells “Porch Fest” summer lager, produced by Framingham’s Jack’s Abby brewery.

Back in Beverly, a high school rock band led by guitarist Silas Bellino held court from the front porch of his family’s home. They played a loose, spirited set ranging from covers of Neil Young and the Allman Brothers to Mountain’s “Mississippi Queen.”

“Anybody have a cowbell, or any cowbell-adjacent items?” Silas asked the crowd, as a group of younger kids played hacky sack in the street.

Erin Cherry, who teaches in the city’s elementary school music program, was on hand to support Silas, who has been volunteering in her classroom.

She introduced herself to Silas’s father, Guy Bellino, who teaches political science at nearby Salem State University. Silas has been a joy to have in the music room, Cherry said.

“That makes me feel so good,” said Bellino, beaming.

Dozens of Boston police officers filed into the courthouse Thursday morning to support their colleague. Several of King’s family members also attended the hearing, watching silently from the gallery; one of his sisters wiped away tears.

The swift prosecution marks the first time in more than three decades that a Boston police officer has been criminally charged under similar circumstances.

Prosecutors allege the officer wasn’t justified in shooting at the moving vehicle.

O’Malley, who joined the Boston Police Department about six years ago, told investigators he believed his partner was in danger of being run over.

State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

“Mr. O’Malley was not acting in reasonable defense of either himself, the other officer, or the general public,” said Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum, calling the shooting excessive.

O’Malley’s supporters have accused Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden of pursuing the prosecution to make a political statement.

“It is truly unjust that Nicholas O’Malley was forced to walk to a courthouse today, when he instead should be walking his beat in Roxbury — meeting, greeting, interacting with, and hearing the concerns of residents there as he always does,” his defense attorney, David Yannetti, told reporters after the arraignment.

In brief remarks during the hearing, Yannetti accused prosecutors of presenting a sanitized version of the facts. He sought to malign King, saying his violent behavior “left officer O’Malley with no choice.”

In recent court filings, Yannetti also documented King’s long criminal history, which includes assaults, breaking and entering, and gun charges.

Police pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood; officials say he punched a woman in the face, forced her out of the car, and took off.

A short time later, a Boston police officer was heading to get dinner in his personal vehicle when he spotted the stolen car, prosecutors wrote in the court documents filed Thursday. Instead of broadcasting a message via dispatch radio, the officer called O’Malley’s cellphone, prosecutors said. O’Malley picked up that officer, and together they located the stolen car parked on Linwood Square in Roxbury. O’Malley then made a radio call saying as much.

Approaching on foot, the officers repeatedly told King to show his hands, turn off the car, and unlock the doors.

“King held up his empty hands and appeared to be speaking to O’Malley through the closed window, but did not unlock the doors or douse the engine,” according to prosecutors. He opened the driver’s side window slightly.

O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” according to prosecutors.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back, essentially completing a three-point turn to get away, according to records. As he started to drive forward again, O’Malley “switched from the Taser back to his handgun and rapidly fired three times,” prosecutors wrote. The whole encounter lasted just 84 seconds.

In the moments that followed, O’Malley said over the radio that King had “tried to run us over,” according to the records.

“By this time sirens were audible from approaching police units that would have converged on the stolen car minutes earlier had they received timely word of its location,” prosecutors wrote.

King’s family has said he was experiencing a mental health crisis, hearing voices and showing signs of intense paranoia in the hours leading up to the shooting. Relatives said they’d been trying to get him adequate long-term treatment. They said he would cycle through the criminal justice system, sometimes receiving psychiatric medication while he was incarcerated, only to lose access to regular care after his release.

Along with some Boston city councilors and other community leaders, the family called on police to release bodycam footage of the encounter. But prosecutors and police have resisted, saying that would jeopardize the ongoing criminal investigation.

In an interview with homicide detectives during their investigation, O’Malley said he “did not know King or anything about his history, other than the reported carjacking described in the radio call,” prosecutors wrote in court documents. He said he initially planned to discharge his Taser through the small window opening, but he realized that wouldn’t be effective. He said he ultimately fired his gun to protect the other officer, who was positioned on the other side of the car, according to the records.

“I was fearing the worst,” O’Malley told detectives, believing the officer could get run over or crushed between vehicles, according to the records.

Prosecutors disputed his reasoning. They said the street was well-lit and the second officer was safely positioned.

“In fact, the second officer had holstered his own firearm” and tried to grab the car’s door handle, prosecutors wrote. They argued that when O’Malley opened fire, his partner was “at greater risk of being struck by the bullets than by the vehicle.”

They said that even if O’Malley thought his partner was in serious danger, “such a belief was not objectively reasonable.”

Police union leaders, however, are continuing to back O’Malley, reiterating claims that the prosecution is politically motivated.

“Make no mistake about it, he was treated differently because he’s a police officer. He is being scapegoated because he’s a police officer,” Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, told reporters after the hearing.

De-escalation requires compliance from the suspect, he said. “It’s unfortunate and horrible that we lost a life, but Nick O’Malley did what he should have done as a police officer.”

But to the supporters who packed an Italian restaurant near Ashmont Wednesday morning to watch Wu offer her endorsement, Gayle offers more than just an opportunity to unseat a foe.

To her supporters, Gayle is viewed as a candidate who will fight for residents they say Collins ignores.

“My experience has been he’s unserious,” said Kate Warren Barnes, a longtime community advocate and college lecturer. “He’s unserious, he’s unresponsive, and he hasn’t been the solutions-focused leader that this district needs.”

Gayle, 47, has spent years as an advocate for families and young children. Currently, she works as director of advocacy for a nonprofit called Neighborhood Villages, pushing for changes in the state’s child care system.

Like a surprising number of influential Black Bostonians, Gayle grew up in Springfield, as the youngest of seven sisters. She has raised her own family of four children in the South End and in Dorchester, where the family now lives.

Her parents migrated to Massachusetts from Alabama, seeking refuge from the oppressive racial politics of the Deep South. She said her run for office has been inspired, in part, by a feeling the progress her parents’ generation fought for is slipping away.

“I think people my age grew up and we were taught so many things that we’re dealing with today were behind us,” Gayle told me. “And not that the world is perfect, but that we weren’t gonna go back. And it seems like we’re on a backwards trajectory right now.”

For years, friends had casually suggested she think about running for office, but she had always brushed the idea aside. She was already involved as a Boston Public Schools parent active in educational issues and raising her family. But this year she finally came to believe that she had reached the right moment in her life to go for it.

That was largely driven by her feeling Collins was too conservative on many issues, among them rent stabilization and driver’s licenses for undocumented immigrants. She’s running to be a more progressive, community-centered voice.

The First Suffolk district has an interesting history. For years the domain of legendary powerbroker William M. Bulger, it was redrawn long ago to reflect a changing population. Bulger was followed by Linda Dorcena Forry, a Haitian American, who held the seat for five years, until being succeeded by Collins in 2018.

In perception, it has reverted to being a seat identified with South Boston because of Collins. But the district also includes part of the South End, Chinatown, downtown, and much of Dorchester, making it one of the most diverse in the Massachusetts Senate. That’s a big part of the reason Collins, who gradually become a darling of the downtown business establishment, is viewed as perhaps more vulnerable than his supporters assume.

As for the mayor, the mutual contempt between Collins and Wu is hardly a secret. Not only did he expend every possible ounce of political capital to kill Wu’s attempts to raise revenue by shifting more of the property tax burden away from residential homeowners and onto commercial property, he relentlessly attacked Wu in the process.

That played well behind closed doors at the State House, where cities and towns are often treated like pawns. But Wu is clearly betting that it will prove less popular with voters.

In endorsing Gayle Wednesday, she openly accused Collins of siding with corporate interests at the expense of his constituents in a sleazy backroom negotiation.

“We are tired of the state Senate saying no to everything,” she said. “We are tired of our state Senate offloading their elective power to unelected corporate interests to negotiate against Boston families.”

Gayle is a definite underdog in a race against a well-known and well-funded incumbent. But Wu’s support is beyond valuable. And underdogs sometimes win.

Gayle said this moment demands change. And she believes she can be that change.

“If there’s ever a time to do it, now is that time.”

But the state Senate race she waded into Wednesday may be her biggest gamble yet — one that’ll test the bounds of her influence in the city, and, win or lose, could have damaging side effects on Beacon Hill.

Wu escalated her long-running feud with South Boston Senator Nick Collins, endorsing child care advocate Latoya Gayle in her primary bid to unseat him. Wu and Collins’ long-running beef hit its peak late last year, after the conservative Democrat (again) blocked her attempts to get property tax legislation passed on Beacon Hill. (You can catch up on the drawn-out drama here, here, here, and here.)

The endorsement wasn’t exactly a surprise. Those in Wu’s political orbit have for months been quietly supporting Gayle, a first-time candidate who lives in Dorchester and whose campaign manager, Maccon Bonner, served in Wu’s administration before joining the campaign. But in putting her name — and fiery criticisms of the entire Senate — behind the effort to oust Collins, the mayor officially opened a new front in her battle with the upper chamber. It was a moment she seemed to revel in.

“This is going to be a fun election cycle,” she said.

Gayle faces an otherwise uphill battle. Collins is well-known in the district, and has a significant cash advantage. He had $92,000 in his campaign account at the end of last month to Gayle’s $15,500. Shortly after Wu’s endorsement, his campaign began circulating an internal poll that showed that 82 percent of the roughly 800 people surveyed said they would vote for him in the primary, compared to 10 percent for Gayle. (Collins’ campaign didn’t respond to questions about details of the poll, including its margin of error or how it was conducted).

It’s not the first time Wu has backed apparent underdogs and won. She helped install several allies on the City Council in 2023, and aided political unknown Allison Cartwright in her defeat of sitting City Councilor Erin Murphy in a 2024 race for the oft-ignored role of clerk Suffolk County Supreme Judicial Court.

Still, this one will test her clout in some of the less-friendly areas of the city toward her. Seven of the nine precincts where her opponent, Josh Kraft, outperformed her in last year’s preliminary election were in South Boston.

“Mayor Wu is arguably the most influential figure in Boston politics right now, and this is about whether that popularity translates into influence in a state legislative race,” said Kate Norton, a political consultant who previously worked for former mayor, Martin J. Walsh. “By weighing in against Collins, she’s putting her political capital on the line. He’s a well-established incumbent who has really strong support in the neighborhood.”

Collins isn’t the only one caught in the mayor’s crosshairs. State Senator Will Brownsberger, the other member of the Senate’s Boston delegation who spoke out publicly against her property tax shift bill, is facing a challenge from former Wu aide, Daniel Lander. Though Wu has yet to weigh in directly on that race, Lander’s campaign finance reports are peppered with donations from those in the Wu-inverse.

Senate President Karen Spilka declined to address the Gayle endorsement at an unrelated event Wednesday. But she’s been quietly helping Collins and Brownsberger, one of her top deputies, by making calls to union leaders to rally their support for them, according to two people with knowledge of the calls.

Taken together, the races have the feel of a revenge tour, a risky game for a mayor who needs buy-in from both chambers of the state Legislature if she wants to get some of her biggest priorities passed.

Then again, many of those priorities already seem stuck in neutral.

“The question really is,” Norton said, “what does she have to lose?”

Unlike traditional nature paths, the walking trail network uses “green spaces, built environments, and walkable connections between them,” said Miles Howard, the group’s founder and director.

“Our hope in launching this trail is encouraging people to think beyond arbitrary lines of demarcation,” Howard said. “This whole area is far more interconnected in a physical and geographic sense than one might realize, and walking is a fantastic way to discover that firsthand.”

Howard gained national attention for his work designing two other trails that run through Boston — the original Walking City Trail and the City on the Hills Trail.

Official maps and guides for the Boston Boundless Trail will launch online on June 6, which is National Trails Day. The maps can be downloaded from BostonTrails.org and will be compatible with Google Maps and the popular map platform AllTrails, Howard said.

Other than turn-by-turn instructions, which can be used on smartphones or printed out, hikers will be on their own, Howard said. There are no signposts.

“We recommend pairing one of the maps with the turn-by-turn directions, so that you’re not constantly looking at your phone on the trail,” he said.

Howard recently answered a few questions about the new urban loop trail.

What is an urban hike?

One of the key differences between just going for a walk and going for an urban hike is that you’re really prioritizing interesting scenery over efficiency and directness.

An urban hike can be any place where you know the features are more built up, but where you’re constantly looking around and thinking, ‘I have an inclination to walk through here.’

I would guesstimate that the trail is about 60 percent paved and 40 percent dirt.

But some of the dirt sections are really going to have a lot of rustic elements, like roots and rocks.

How did you come up with the Boston Boundless Trail?

When you look at a map of the Boston area, you can see parks and conservation lands and gardens that could be interesting features for a route.

But you really can’t get a sense of how all this is going to feel as a curated sequential experience until you actually go out and try walking it.

One of the most fun planning elements happens in areas where there are no obvious walkable connections in sight. I have to think, like, ‘OK, how do we do this? Is it even possible to do this?’

That element of discovering how a map translates to real life is part of the fun. It kind of feels like you’ve stumbled across something that’s been lost or forgotten when you find a walkable means of getting somewhere.

So there’s the theoretical phase, which is mapping it out, and then there’s the translation to real-life phase, where you’re actually going out and walking it.

How long is the trail?

It is going to be an 80- to 90-mile loop.

The longest section of the 12 is going to be the third section that goes from East Milton to the Trailside Museum in the Blue Hills, and it’s also going to have the most elevation gain by far.

How hard is it to navigate the trail?

The number of junctions and turns one will encounter is comparable to what you might experience on a backcountry trail. There will be more of them in residential areas though.

I can’t really say how hard or easy it is to follow the route because it’s subjective for each person, but we have found that offering multiple navigation resources makes this wholly doable for most trail users.

Can you walk me through the 12 sections?

Section 1: Long Wharf North to Savin Hill Beach in Dorchester

Section 2: Savin Hill Beach to East Milton Square

Section 3: East Milton Square to Blue Hills Trailside Museum

And hikers can take the MBTA ferry from East Boston back to Long Wharf if they want to complete the full loop.

What are some highlights?

The trail is going to utilize the core of the Skyline Trail in the Blue Hill Reservation, which will definitely be the most challenging part by far.

To get out of the Blue Hills, on the west side, to get into Hyde Park and Dedham, we’re actually going to be utilizing the lost highway of the I-95 connector that was partially built that exists in those woods now. You can basically link up to it via the west end of the Skyline Trail, walk the old overgrown highway through the woods for a bit, and then follow the green corridor where the rest of it was supposed to be built to get out of the woods. It’s such a cool piece of Boston history.

The trail will utilize paths along the Malden River in Everett and also take you past the Potato Shed Memorial in Charlestown.

The trail also takes people through marshes and over water crossings.

Can cycling enthusiasts bike the trail?

There are more stretches of this trail than prior Walking City Trails that can be thoroughly biked, and we are going to be including an overlay with the finalized Google map of the route that will show stretches where you can bike.

But there are definitely portions where biking is not going to be feasible.

How would you recommend amateur hikers tackle the loop?

For beginner hikers approaching this with cross-trainers, a bag, and a couple bottles of water, most of the trail is going to be very natural territory.

The 12 segments range anywhere from just under 5 miles to almost 10 miles in length, so they’re going to want to ideally cut most of those trail segments in half. We do designate a suggested halfway point for each segment in case people want to divvy it up into shorter hikes.

We also list connections to public transit.

This is going to be something that, while great in distance, has a lot of outdoor territory that will feel very entry level for a lot of people.

What if someone wants to tackle the whole trail in separate chunks?

It’s obviously very subjective, but I’m going to estimate that the average person might want to do under 5 miles in a day. Basically, my guess is that it would probably take them somewhere between 21 to 24 sectioned hikes to do the whole thing.

A handful of races have the potential to get interesting this September and November — whether a result of unfinished business, intra-party combat, or a rare open seat. Here are a few we’re watching in a cycle where, as CommonWealth Beacon’s Chris Lisinski reported, three out of five seats are otherwise going uncontested:

THE REMATCHES: A pair of Democratic candidates who nearly pulled off primary upsets in 2024 are running it back this year.

In Cambridge, union leader Evan MacKay, who lost to six-term incumbent state Representative Marjorie Decker by just 41 votes, is giving it another go. MacKay, who made transparency a central issue in their last campaign, is once again trying to carve out space to Decker’s left. Decker and her supporters, meanwhile, have already been active. The Massachusetts Teachers Association was sending out mailers backing her a full year before the general election in November.

And in Springfield, public school teacher Johnnie McKnight is spoiling for a rematch against state Representative Bud Williams after Williams defeated him by 245 votes in their 2024 primary. Nicole Coakley, a mental health clinician, is also running in the Democratic contest.

THE OPEN SEATS: State Senator Patricia Jehlen’s impending retirement set off a game of musical chairs in the Camberville/Medford area.

The race to replace her in the district that covers all of Somerville and parts of Cambridge, Medford and Winchester has attracted a crowded Democratic field: state representatives Erika Uyterhoeven and Christine Barber, Somerville City Councilor Matt McLaughlin, Cambridge City Councilor Burhan Azeem, and Tom Hopcroft of Winchester.

That race has opened up competition down-ballot, too. Somerville City Councilor Ben Ewen-Campen and Olivia Gilligan-Corsetti, a former staffer for Governor Maura Healey, are both vying for Uyterhoeven’s seat. And three Democrats — Somerville City Councilor Will Mbah, software engineer Paul Ruseau, and Chris Oates, founder of the data analysis startup Legislata — are competing to fill Barber’s spot.

On the Cape, Brewster Democrat and school committee member Steve Leibowitz and Dennis Select Board vice chair Chris Lambton, who once appeared on “The Bachelorette,” are both seeking the Democratic nomination in the race to fill the seat currently held by state Representative Chris Flanagan, whose name isn’t on the ballot as he faces federal fraud charges. Joe Glynn, whose party is listed as “Gulf War Veteran” on the state’s candidate list, is also in that race.

In Western Mass., where former state Representative Natalie Blais’ seat has been open since she resigned for a job at UMass Amherst, unenrolled Whately Town Clerk Amy Lavallee will face whoever wins the Democratic primary between Corinne Coryat, Blais’ chief of staff at the State House, and Greenfield City Council President Lora Wondolowski.

THE PARTY CRASHERS: There are others looking to oust members of their own party.

Three Boston-area state senators are facing primary challenges. In addition to Nick Collins and Will Brownsberger — whose contests have drawn no shortage of attention amid disputes with Mayor Michelle Wu — incumbent Mike Rush is facing a challenge from Persis Yu, a non-profit executive running to his left.

In Plymouth County, Republican Mark Townsend, the chair of the Carver Select Board, is looking to take out first-term GOP state Representative John Gaskey, one of the Legislature’s most conservative members.

THE DEBATE DEBATE: A sign the US Senate primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Seth Moulton is finally entering a new phase: Markey is finally mentioning Moulton by name.

After Moulton spent the last handful of months hounding Markey for a debate, the 79-year-old senator threw down his own gauntlet Thursday. In addition to a mid-August debate and another that’s still to be scheduled, Markey is challenging Moulton to meet him on stage in western Mass. in late June or early July — about two months out from the Sept. 1 primary.

The challenge came with some trash talk. Markey targeted Moulton for “giving airtime to a MAGA multimillionaire in a fake debate,” an apparent reference to the mid-June debate scheduled between Moulton and GOP Senate hopeful John Deaton (and to which Markey was also invited but declined).

Moulton quickly accepted and hit back — hard: “No more hiding in Maryland,” Moulton wrote on social media. “I am ready to debate you every single week until the primary in September — if you can keep up.”

The former housing and economic development secretary jumped back into the Republican governor’s race Thursday — this time as a surrogate. Kennealy endorsed former Abiomed chief executive Mike Minogue, calling him “the only remaining Republican with a chance to defeat Governor Healey.”

The endorsement itself was a backhand to former MBTA chief administrator Brian Shortsleeve, a fellow Baker administration alum also running for the GOP nomination.
