The local real estate industry is facing the most consequential decision it may make for a long time: Deal or no deal?

So far there’s no consensus among developers, landlords, and real estate agents, as they stare down a July 1 deadline for a compromise that would keep what would be one of the nation’s strictest rent control policies from reaching the ballot this fall.

That’s because the proposed compromise would usher in something industry leaders have long resisted: limits on annual rent increases. They have the money and the motivation to go all the way to defeat the measure in November, which would ensure it can’t be brought back to the voters for another six years.

But sensing that might be too risky of a path, a small faction broke off this spring to work on an alternative that could prompt rent-control supporters to drop the ballot question. The faction includes several prominent developers: WinnCompanies CEO Gil Winn, HYM Investment Group managing partner Tom O’Brien, Lupoli Companies CEO Sal Lupoli, and The Builder Coalition executive director Dave Madan.

The proposed compromise they’ve crafted would allow rent control in Massachusetts for the first time since the 1990s, but it’s a more modest version than what’s headed for the ballot. The new proposal would allow towns to opt in to a program capping annual rent increases at 5 percent plus inflation, up to 10 percent, and exempting new construction for 15 years. It’s far looser than the ballot measure, which would mandate a statewide cap limiting rent increases to the rate of inflation, or 5 percent, whichever is lower.

Advocates sent the new language to Beacon Hill on Tuesday, offering to withdraw their ballot measure if it’s passed into law by the end of the month. That’s going to be a tough sell. House Speaker Ron Mariano is no fan of rent control, and he and Senate President Karen Spilka are unlikely to get on board without buy-in from key real estate groups – NAIOP Massachusetts, the Mass. Association of Realtors, and the Greater Boston Real Estate Board.

Now the ball’s in their court.

NAIOP chief executive Tamara Small says her members and advisers spotted a number of red flags in their review of the proposed legislation, and they’re “digging into it to understand what it means.” When might NAIOP decide? All Small would say on that: “Relatively soon.”

The Greater Boston Real Estate Board is an umbrella group, with five boards it needs to satisfy. Greg Vasil, GBREB’s chief executive, knows time is of the essence. But proffering a deal at the eleventh hour, he says, shows no consideration for the steps an organization like his must take to review. His projection: “It may take us a couple of weeks.”

Then there’s the Realtors group. While they will consider the proposal, general counsel Justin Davidson said his group remains committed to fighting rent control.

These groups have been the financial backbone of the “no on rent control” campaign, and they have been confident, deciding just three weeks ago not to cut a deal with rent control supporters. The no campaign is well on track to raise the $30 million pledged to fight the ballot measure, and has viewed any compromise offered by rent control supporters as a sign of weakness.

But not everyone agrees. Early polling suggests a majority of voters support rent control, and the stakes are huge. That has some in the real estate industry wondering if cutting a deal is better than risking defeat.

That’s why Winn decided on his own to seek an alternative proposal that the real estate community could live with. Winn, whose company builds and manages affordable housing projects, first began reaching out to nonprofit partners, such as community development corporations, with ties to tenant groups. More recently, he called developers O’Brien, Lupoli, and Madan.

Winn’s goal, we’re told, was to craft a framework that could jumpstart a meaningful conversation with the rest of the real estate industry and lawmakers. Talks began to ramp up between the CDCs and the rent control supporters in March, and by the end of last week, Winn helped facilitate compromise language that tenant advocates have signed off on, transforming the debate.

The real work begins now, as the industry groups review a proposal that they would have dismissed out of hand not that long ago. Will the clock run out on everyone? Tick, tick, tick.

Teachers and staff at the Croft School in Jamaica Plain have been fighting with the board over getting fully paid as the for-profit private school prepares to shut its doors on June 12. No good deed goes unpunished. You know the feeling. And it’s a good bet that Corey Thomas does, too. As chief executive of Boston cybersecurity company Rapid7, he took on a number of leadership roles in local civic circles. Notably, Thomas sits on the board of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (after a stint as chair), and he’s wrapping up his role as chairman of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, a two-year term that ends this month as BofA’s Miceal Chamberlain takes over.

Rapid7’s stock took a tumble in 2024. That prompted activist investor JANA Partners to start buying up shares and shaming management. In particular, JANA criticized Thomas’s prominent board service, calling it a distraction from the all-consuming job of a public company chief executive.

JANA and Rapid7 settled their differences last year, and put three JANA-backed directors on the board. The fallout became clear this week when the company announced Thomas had been replaced as CEO by one of the new board members, Wael Mohamed. Thomas will remain with the Rapid7 board as executive chairman.

The idea that a CEO who is civically engaged is somehow harming shareholders is silly. These extracurricular activities help develop networks and valuable relationships in communities where their companies are located. Conversely, public company CEOs provide an important voice in civic conversations. It was even more essential for Thomas, one of the few Black CEOs of a public company, to hold prominent civic posts because it showed how Boston welcomes diverse leadership. It would be a shame if JANA’s attack discourages other C-suite types in Boston from taking on these time-consuming but critically important roles. We shouldn’t let activist investors dictate what’s important for building a better Boston.

Soccer Field Day was part of a series of events surrounding the city’s Fiesta de Fútbol: From June 11 to July 19, Chelsea Square will transform into an outdoor watch party, complete with local food vendors, music, and other community programming. Unlike other watch parties in the Boston area, the broadcast feeds in Chelsea will feature Telemundo broadcasts with Spanish-language commentators. The programming is partially funded by a $175,000 state grant, one of a number of grants for World Cup watch parties across the state. The city will also host a free alumni tournament for graduates of Chelsea High School and Chelsea charter schools at Veterans Stadium on June 27.

“Soccer is so simple, it’s one ball, two nets, and if you don’t have two nets, you can use anything, and it speaks to the whole world, and so that’s why I think soccer connects to everybody,” Giuffrida said. “It’s accessible.”

Home to a diverse immigrant community that is largely from Latin America, Chelsea cherishes a strong soccer culture. Several youth programs, including Matias Soccer Club, founded by players from Colombian club Envigado, and the Escuela de Fútbol Infantil, work especially, though not exclusively, with immigrant children. And at a time of increased immigration enforcement in the Boston area, youth soccer programs in Chelsea and elsewhere can act as a refuge for children and parents alike.

Saturday’s Field Day event included players from the city’s youth soccer teams, Chelsea High School, and the nonprofit Soccer Without Borders, which uses soccer as a vehicle for positive change.

Alejandro Lopez, a parent and coach, played soccer as a kid in Highland Park over 30 years ago, and he’s been impressed with the growth of youth soccer in the city.

“Growing up in Chelsea, my whole life, we really didn’t have events like this for soccer,” he said as he looked across the turf. “It was a lot different, was real grass, and wasn’t maintained like it is today.”

Lopez said his daughter, Valencia Lopez, competed in her first-ever tournament through Soccer Without Borders, and the organization has even offered her a chance to escort one of the players onto the field during one of the games and to watch the match. She is already a soccer fan.

“My favorite team is Costa Rica, [El] Salvador and Puerto Rico,” she said.

The larger community is gearing up for the games, with excitement and some trepidation. As Soccer Field Day drew to a close, on Broadway, a main thoroughfare brimming with retail stores, restaurants and bars, Jaredy Ramirez, who was eating at Curly’s Restaurant, worried that the immigration crackdowns of the last year might sap the World Cup of some of its joy. The Trump administration has said those in the country legally have nothing to fear.

“A lot of people, from out of the country, they’re not coming because they see what is happening right now,” Ramirez said.

William Tejada, who said he watches 10 or 15 soccer games a weekend, said he was nevertheless excited for the upcoming matches. He got to go to a World Cup match in person back in 1994, when the US last hosted the games. Back then, he said, soccer wasn’t such a popular sport here.

“But now it is,” he said. “I think that was the beginning.”

He had free tickets then. Not this time, though, and with sky-high ticket prices starting in the thousands, he plans to watch the games from his TV.

The 120th-annual Dorchester Day Parade caps a weekend of festivities that included Dorchfest, a porchfest-style music festival, and the Dorchester Day 5K, which raises money for local charities and youth programs. Together, the events serve as a reunion for residents and a tribute to the community’s history.

Dot Day’s genesis dates to 1905, when organizers launched a parade to commemorate the founding of Boston’s largest neighborhood, according to the Dorchester Reporter. More than a century later, what began as a single procession has grown into a multiday tradition.

On Saturday, hundreds of people packed Ashmont and Adams Village for the fifth year of Dorchfest. Bands and solo performers played from porches, driveways, and front yards as crowds wandered from block to block, stopping to listen and dance.

“We come every year,” said Carla Alvarez, swaying to salsa music near Bushnell Street. “The music is amazing.”

As he held his 2-year-old son in his arms on Saturday, Winston Jones, of Lower Mills, spoke of Dorchester’s diversity. He said events like Dorchfest and the parade celebrate the mix of communities that has long defined the neighborhood.

“Music is a great organizer, a great way to bring different cultures, families, all sorts of levels of age together,” said Jones, 38. “You walk up a block, and you see people you see at the park or people you go to the gym with.”

Dorchester is home to large Cape Verdean, Latino, Black, Vietnamese, and Irish communities. Though the neighborhood has seen less luxury development than other corners of Boston, some longtime residents say new condominium projects and rising housing costs have reshaped parts of the area.

“We’ve lost a lot of folks because of displacement and gentrification,” said T. Michael Thomas, founder of The People’s Academy, a nonprofit that trains underserved youth and adults for trade careers. “The parade means everything because it highlights diversity, community, and family. It promotes it and it shows it.”

Matthew Milhomme, 42, has witnessed a different side of Dorchester’s evolution. Sitting along the parade route as traditional Vietnamese dancers glided past, he said he’s watched new businesses open and public infrastructure improve since moving into the home where his wife has lived since 2013.

He said the parade serves as a showcase for local groups and organizations, giving his family a chance to reconnect with the locality.

“I love looking at all the different parts of our community,” Milhomme said. “But our neighborhood hasn’t changed, it’s been the same people that were there before us.”

As marching bands blared and dancers twirled past, Edward Bordenave clapped from the sidelines alongside his wife and daughter, who recently traded their Dorchester home for one in Milton. Having spent nearly a decade in the neighborhood, Bordenave said celebrating local changes is one reason he’ll keep coming back for Dot Day.

“It’s good to be back seeing familiar faces and seeing the parade again,” said Bordenave, 40. “I just hope that the cultural fabric of Dorchester still remains.”

Dorchester crowns an honorary mayor each year. The title goes to the community member who raises the most money for the parade, with every dollar donated counting as a vote.

This year, that honor belonged to Nolan, a Dorchester native and lifelong resident who spent Sunday atop a float surrounded by friends, family members, and children from the youth sports teams she coaches. Near the Ashmont fire station, a large group of supporters cheered as her float passed by.

“If you’re not from here, you might not get it, but if you come and stay a bit, you learn that everyone feels a deep sense of pride to be from here,” said Nolan, who raised more than $18,000 for the parade committee. “There’s so many different groups and people that make Dorchester so special, so it’s awesome to be able to see that represented through the parade year in and year out.”

Among them was Myles King, who bounced excitedly on the curb as a pack of motorcycles roared past.

At 8 years old, King hasn’t lived through the decades of change that older locals describe. But somehow, he expressed the same pride in Dorchester that so many lifelong residents share.

“My neighborhood is kind, weird, and peaceful,” King said. “I just like living here.”

Boston Globe correspondent Aayushi Datta contributed to this report.

But Dr. Coles’s thoughts came with a quiet passion and a stunning velocity that shook the worlds of medicine and education, civil rights and American civic life.

“He added greatly to our understanding of children and the world they live in,” said Judith Palfrey, chief of the division of general pediatrics at Children’s Hospital Boston for more than two decades and a professor of pediatrics at Harvard Medical School. “He taught students of all ages through his books, and he studied the social determinants of health long before it became an important topic in popular conversation. He made these issues very accessible.”

Dr. Coles did so while helping to reinvent the professions of psychiatry and pediatrics and elementary and undergraduate education.

“His combination of brilliance and humility is what provided his lasting insights,” said David Greene, an expert in human development and psychology who is the president of Colby College. “He was open to hearing others and learning from them, not simply being the teacher or the expert. Seeing value in others and in their experiences seems to be a lost art, but he kept it very much alive and helped countless others recognize the power of the stories in us all.”

Dr. Coles’s acolytes and onetime teaching fellows are scattered across the country, a kind of diaspora sustaining the principal precepts of his teaching: the thoughts of children are significant; the lives of adults are empty without introspection and intervention in social problems; and people of all ages can profit by, as he would counsel his students, “putting your neuroses to work.”

One of Dr. Coles’s own neuroses — he might have called it his preoccupation — was to fill each moment not only with purpose but also with reflection.

“In an environment where everyone was ambitiously rushing around,” said one of those Coles graduate fellows, Gene Corbin, Harvard’s former dean for public service, “he created a space for students to reflect on who they were and their responsibilities to others and to society.”

When Corbin headed Harvard’s Phillips Brooks House Center for Public Service and Engaged Scholarship, he created an annual Robert Coles “Call of Service” Lecture and Award, a play on the title of a book Dr. Coles wrote that examines motivations for service.

Dr. Coles’s life ricocheted into unconventional, unpredictable, and unconnected directions. He was outspoken on issues of race and faith. He strayed into areas such as music (a book about Bruce Springsteen) and social activism (a book on the Catholic Worker leader Dorothy Day). He was as interested in the victims of polio as in the victims of racial discrimination (among the topics in the multivolume “Children of Crisis” that was awarded the Pulitzer in 1973). He published two volumes about the psychoanalyst Erik Erickson and one book illustrated by Norman Rockwell. He joined the poet-physician William Carlos Williams on medical house calls and hid the antiwar priest Daniel Berrigan from the FBI in his Concord home and the two produced “The Geography of Faith: Underground Conversations on Religious, Political, and Social Change.” He taught the novels of Dickens to law students and campaigned with Senator Robert F. Kennedy.

But his most evocative and enduring encounter may have been with a 6-year-old Black girl in segregated Louisiana, the best example of Dr. Coles’s devotion to what he called “in medias res,” Latin for “into the middle of things,” or, as he defined, it, “’in the midst of trouble,’ right in the midst of it.’’

Dr. Coles was an Air Force psychiatrist stationed in New Orleans when he learned about the integration crucible of Ruby Bridges, whose entry into the all-white William Frantz Elementary School in the autumn of 1960 triggered street protests and led the white parents to withdraw their children from the premises. He approached the local branch of the NAACP and asked to consult with the child, who was taught — in an otherwise empty first grade classroom — by an inspiring teacher from West Roxbury, Barbara Henry.

Henry said she did not know until years later the role Dr. Coles played for Ruby.

“A teacher told me there was some doctor involved with Ruby,” she said in an interview for this obituary. “I thought it was some kind of physical doctor.”

But Ruby surmised what Dr. Coles was up to.

“Every week Dr. Coles would come to my house with his tape recorder,” Bridges said in “Through My Eyes,” a book she wrote about her early life. “He would ask how I was doing, and I mostly told him I was doing fine. Then he would pull out crayons and asked me to draw pictures of myself or the school or some of the people in my life.”

She said she enjoyed the time with Dr. Coles, who also would write a children’s picture book about Ruby, “because an important man was coming to visit and color with me, and that made me feel special.”

Separately in “The Moral Life of Children,” Dr. Coles wrote, “Ruby had a will and used it to make an ethical choice; she demonstrated moral stamina; she possessed honor, courage.”

Moral stamina, honor, and courage were the touchstones of the creed of Dr. Coles, who was awarded a MacArthur “genius” award in 1981 and the Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor America bestows, by President Clinton in 1998.

“From Dr. Coles I learned the importance of staying committed to the things you love, the things you cared about, along with your professionalism,” said Brian Buckley, who took the Coles course in 1989, became a Coles teaching fellow a decade later, and eventually became executive director of the Southwest Native American Foundation. “He constantly told me how I could put my thoughts, insights, and ideals into action in practical daily life.”

For Dr. Coles in his own life, that meant a lifelong commitment to understanding how children thought and acted.

“There weren’t that many people around who were looking at the lives of children in such an open and deep way and who didn’t restrict the role of a doctor to just practicing medicine,” said Richard Goldstein, a pediatric palliative care doctor at Boston Children’s. “He really wanted to think about the insights a doctor might have for the world. He particularly cared about the moral lives of children.”

That inevitably drew him into religious waters. In his influential 1990 “The Spiritual Life of Children,” he argued that the seeds of religious practice were planted by parents who “talked about faith with them as children and practiced the faith in their presence.”

That constituted another break with the conventional thinking of the academic and medical milieu that Dr. Coles inhabited.

“Because he was a psychiatrist, he wrestled with the antireligious bias of his own profession,” said J. Bradley Wigger, a minister who teaches at Kentucky’s Louisville Presbyterian Theological Seminary and whose research was inspired by Dr. Coles’s work. “But he understood that religion could be a deep and powerful resource in the lives of children, particularly if they were in the hospital or going through trauma or other difficult circumstances.”

Though he possessed some of the instincts and methods of a reporter, Dr. Coles was not a journalist but a scholar, trusting the insights a child would share over an ice cream cone or in a school bus.

“He was an amazing listener,” said Goldstein, another Coles student who became a Coles teaching assistant and eventually a Coles collaborator, “and this technique started with Ruby Bridges.”

Dr. Coles was a rebel in a blue Oxford dress shirt, an iconoclast with a heterodox ideology.

“You mention his name to people in his field, and the word ‘maverick’ always comes up,” said Clark Power, a professor of psychology and education at Notre Dame. “He was at war with the establishment.”

In the days of rioting following the 1968 assassination of the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., Dr. Coles challenged students who demanded institutional change through violence, suggesting that women in Black sections of Boston might not recoil at the presence of a white Irish-American police officer in their neighborhoods. He railed against what he called the “carefully well adjusted and certified” mandarins of his profession, arguing in “A Young Psychiatrist Looks at his Profession,” a 1961 broadside later collected in his 1995 “The Mind’s Fate,” that his colleagues — complacent if not burned-out — trafficked in “wordy and doctrinaire caricatures of life” with their “habits of talk [becoming] cluttered with jargon or the trivial.”

That was not the Coles way, though his upbringing was as conventional as his teachings were unconventional.

Reared in the Back Bay and Milton by a Jewish father from Leeds, England, and a mother from Iowa, he attended Boston Latin School and majored in English at Harvard before abandoning his dream of becoming a high school teacher, switching to the pre-med track, and, after graduation, enrolling in the Columbia College of Physicians and Surgeons.

The man who influenced so many was himself influenced by several people he encountered.

Before there was Ruby Bridges — whose passage in front of what he called in a later video “200 people waiting at 8:00 in the morning telling her they wanted to kill her” moved him deeply — he was shaped by childhood visits to the Museum of Fine Arts. There he encountered the Gauguin triptych: “D’où venons-nous? Que sommes-nous? Où allons-nous?” three searching questions (translated into “Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?”) that his father told him was “the human story.” That notion would lead him to the conviction that the purpose of higher education was learning “how to live an honorable, a caring, and a decent life.”

Walker Percy was another important influence. Dr. Coles read Percy’s 1961 novel “The Moviegoer” — about a young man’s search for meaning — at a time when, Dr. Coles wrote, “I was somewhat lost, confused, vulnerable, and, it seemed, drifting badly.”

Dr. Coles credited Percy, who died in 1990, for giving focus to his life, saying, “I can scarcely imagine how I would have thought about either my own life or the lives of the children, parents, teachers I have met (in order to write “Children of Crisis”), were he to have decided, long ago, to keep his important and instructive thoughts to himself.” Dr. Coles would write Percy’s biography.

Dr. Coles was a constant presence in classrooms nationwide where psychiatry was taught.

“No one who studied psychiatry in the past half century failed to encounter Robert Coles,” said Charles Raison, a prominent psychiatrist and professor at the University of Wisconsin Madison and Emory University. “He realized the importance of childhood in adult development and the needs of children, and he knew that the things they thought about needed to be understood and studied. That was really a big deal, and it influenced the entire profession.”

His wife, the former Jane Hallowell, whom he married in 1960 and with whom he wrote the 1978 book “Women of Crisis: Lives of Struggle and Hope,” died in 1993.

In addition to Michael Coles, he leaves two sons, Daniel and Robert, and four grandsons, according to the Post.

In a 2008 article in the Journal of Catholic Legal Studies, Widener University Commonwealth Law School professor Greg Randall Lee wrote that Dr. Coles “would say that he has not so much performed research throughout his career as he has been a student of life,” adding, “He is not so much an author as a storyteller, which, in his own words, makes him a healer, because ‘healers make sense of stories.’ ”

Indeed, Greene, the Colby president, said that Dr. Coles’s book “The Call of Stories” “taught me to listen for stories instead of just to them.”

“Now my son can write his name for the first time without guidance,” Whyte said.

The Henderson was once hailed as a model of inclusive education, drawing scholars from as far as Germany and Brazil to observe how students with and without disabilities learned side by side. But soon the kindergarten-through-12th-grade school will stop serving as a long-term destination for Boston’s most vulnerable students.

After next year, the city plans to eliminate Henderson’s high school grades amid declining enrollment and a budget crunch. A similar institution in Brighton, the Mary Lyon, is shutting its high school this year.

The closures come as Boston Public Schools is in the final stages of a once-in-a-generation transformation of special education. The plan includes a shift away from high schools like Henderson that specialize in teaching students with disabilities. Instead, city officials envision making all classrooms inclusive environments.

Some parents and educators worry that with Boston schools poised for layoffs, there won’t be enough staff in every classroom to meet the needs of children, like Julian, with more severe disabilities.

Boston Public Schools agreed in 2022 to overhaul special education after the state found that services for students with disabilities were in “systemic disarray.” Another audit determined that too often children with disabilities were being segregated from their classmates and taught in separate classrooms.

When Superintendent Mary Skipper presented a solution in 2023, she outlined an urgent plan to fix longstanding problems.

“We can no longer be a district where students need to travel to a certain school with a certain program in another neighborhood, sometimes far away from home, to get the services they need,” Skipper said. “All Boston Public Schools must be inclusive.”

The goal was to educate students with disabilities in general education classes whenever possible by 2027. Boston has made progress, but about one of every three students with disabilities is still mostly learning separately from other children, according to state data.

And many of these children are still struggling. More than 90 percent of students with disabilities from third to fifth grades are not meeting expectations in reading on the most recent state MCAS tests.

Some studies have found that general education students perform just as well in inclusion classes, but others found negative effects on students who are struggling academically.

City officials say the new approach to special education is designed to meet the needs of all children.

“This is a student-centered approach,” said Simone Wright, Boston’s deputy superintendent of academics.

Parents welcome a system built around individual kids, but they fear there won’t be enough staff to make it work, especially for students with more severe disabilities. Across Boston next year, schools are slated to eliminate 147 full-time special education positions as the city faces growing financial challenges.

The cuts are due in part to the closure of a handful of schools, and city officials downplayed the repercussions.

“We feel really confident saying student services and supports will not be impacted by any staffing reductions,” Wright said.

The Roosevelt K-8 school in Hyde Park is set to lose four special education teachers and four classroom aides, according to Noah Patel, a sixth-grade math and science teacher. Staff have been told, Patel said, that next year they will group most children with disabilities from kindergarten to fourth grade in the same classroom.

“It feels like we are going backwards,” Patel said.

In Jamaica Plain, the Curley School used to have two teachers at all times in core classes such as English and math. With the cuts, third-grade teacher Kafunda Banks said three teachers will have to divide their time between two classrooms.

That sentiment was echoed at 15 schools surveyed by Megan Murray, a third-grade special education teacher at the Holmes School in Dorchester who is writing her dissertation about the overhaul of special education.

“Teachers felt like they are tasked with the impossible mission of providing instruction to all students without the resources they need to make it work,” said Murray, who is studying at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

Across the country, more students are being diagnosed with disabilities. In Boston, 24 percent of public school students had one this year, up from 21 percent in 2020, according to state data.

Given that rise, advocates expressed concern about the planned closure of the two specialized high schools.

“If you take the Henderson and the Mary Lyon away, we won’t have many schools that can handle” students with more severe disabilities, said Elaine Meehan, a Mary Lyon board member.

At both high schools, students with disabilities make up over a third of the population. For decades, they have learned alongside their typically developing peers. The model had a simple secret: They had more staff.

In core subjects such as math and English, two teachers work together in a classroom at all times and at least one of them must have a degree in special education.

However, a budget shortfall driven by raises for staff, rising special education costs, and other factors prompted administrators to propose cutting up to 400 jobs districtwide next school year, including more than 100 classroom aides.

At the same time, enrollment across the city has steadily dropped, a trend that officials said has had an acute impact on the Henderson.

Over the past three years, 45 percent of eighth-graders did not continue there into high school. The Henderson had the smallest ninth to 12th grade population in the entire city, according to Boston Public Schools.

Some parents blame the Henderson’s enrollment drop on the school’s inability to recover after a 16-year-old student brutally assaulted its principal in 2021. The city increased security and added more social workers, but some thought more could be done.

Some parents say they have no choice but to go elsewhere. Mae Colanti, a lively third-grader with Down syndrome, is leaving the Henderson, according to her parents, Cristina and Michael Colanti. Currently at the school, one aide is bouncing among three classrooms and Mae, who has a hard time transitioning to new activities, needs more support, her parents said.

Mae’s parents made the difficult decision to move her next year to Roslindale’s George Conley School. She will be taught in a separate classroom where children with disabilities are grouped together.

Other parents fear that the changes will force them to seek placements outside of Boston. Under the law, if local public schools can’t meet a child’s needs, the city must pay the tuition to send them to a private institution.

This year, Boston Public Schools budgeted $49 million to send 450 students to private schools. Rising tuition costs have become a significant strain on the city’s school budget, officials have said.

If children with more severe disabilities can’t find a placement under the new special education model “out of district costs are only going to grow,” said Victoria Crisp, a special education advocate and former administrator at Boston Public Schools.

That includes Deanna Webb, a former Henderson teacher, who said that for eight years the school has been the best place for her daughter, who has Down syndrome and autism.

“A student like my daughter,” Webb said, “would be learning in a separate environment if she weren’t at the Henderson.”

Walsh, the former Boston mayor and current executive director of the NHL Players’ Association, has been leaning on local labor leaders as their members weigh which candidate to endorse to replace US Representative Seth Moulton. And in many cases, it seems to be helping.

Koh has endorsements from more than 30 unions, and can now add another one to the list. Members of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, the umbrella organization representing more than 700 unions and labor groups around the state, voted to endorse him Friday.

In announcing the group’s backing Monday, AFL-CIO president Chrissy Lynch highlighted Koh’s history with Walsh overseeing “a City Hall in Boston that brought in historic economic development that secured tens of thousands of union jobs,” as well as his work in former president Joe Biden’s labor department. (Koh followed Walsh there when the then-mayor left City Hall).

Walsh — whose labor credits include a stretch as the head of the Building and Construction Trades Council — insists he’s not twisting any arms.

“I’ve definitely made some calls for Dan, but most of it’s been him,” he said in a phone interview Sunday.

Walsh has been poking his head into the state’s political scene since he left for (er, started commuting to) D.C. He endorsed Boston City Councilor John FitzGerald in his successful 2023 campaign, and got behind former city councilor Frank Baker’s comeback bid and Alexandra Valdez’s council campaign last year, though both fell short in November. The Dorchester native pounded the pavement for Koh in 2018, when Koh was running for the open seat in the Third Congressional District.

“The first time he ran for Congress, obviously, I was helpful there because people didn’t really know who he was at the time, other than being my chief of staff,” Walsh said. “This is a whole different ball game. This one is really about Dan’s relationships.”

But not all labor groups are breaking Walsh’s Koh’s way.

The SEIU State Council, a coalition of 1199 SEIU, SEIU Local 509, SEIU Local 32BJ and the SEIU Committee of Interns and Residents, announced Monday it’s backing state Representative Tram Nguyen in the Sixth District primary, a move that Harris Gruman, the SEIU State Council’s executive director, acknowledged might ruffle Walsh’s feathers.

“I think [Walsh] would like us to respond to what he did for us in the past, which was very good,” and Gruman, nodding to Walsh’s record when he was a state representative for nearly 17 years. “But he wasn’t at the forum because he wasn’t a candidate. People were judging the candidates, not judging who is supporting the candidates.”

Nguyen has also nabbed support from United Auto Workers International, three local affiliates of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, the Boston Carmen’s Union Local 589, and all four local United Food and Commercial Workers chapters in the state. And Mariah Lancaster, a veterinarian and former congressional aide also vying in the Democratic primary, scored support from the influential Massachusetts Teachers Association.

The SEIU council backed Nguyen, Gruman said, because she has been at the State House for years “making sure that our members are protected and get fair treatment and livable wages and benefits.”

LABOR INTENSIVE: The AFL-CIO also voted to endorse Governor Maura Healey and US Senator Ed Markey, who’s facing a primary challenge from Moulton. The picks weren’t totally surprising, but it’s a big deal for both campaigns — particularly Healey, by whom some union officials have felt a little let down. For Markey, it’s one more thing to help quell any momentum for Moulton.

NO SMALL PARTS: Attention suburban dads with a little free time! You could star in a campaign ad for John Beccia, the Lynnfield Democrat and fintech executive running for Moulton’s Sixth District seat.

Beccia’s campaign put out a call for actors to perform in three ads it’s set to film this week. Roles include:

— “Waitress in a diner,” who has what the casting call describes as “one line in conversation with John Beccia,” for a spot titled, “Scam Likely.”

— Male and female roles in an ad dubbed “You Beccia,” where a couple, in front of their home, speak one line to the camera. (His campaign has used the slogan so voters know to pronounce his last name as “betcha.”)

— Or, this Oscar-worthy assignment: “A suburban Dad at a gas station filling up his tank. No dialogue.”

The gigs pay between $500 and $750 for about five hours of work, according to the listing. Though the casting call says it’s for “non-union” actors — after the AFL-CIO asked Democratic campaigns this year not to hire non-union actors, per an email viewed by the Globe — a spokesperson for Beccia’s campaign said it’s paying actors through the Screen Actors Guild, and that the production company posted the ad without giving the campaign a heads up.

Across the academic spectrum and around the state, education leaders are rolling out initiatives to prepare students for a world where the pace of change is accelerating rapidly. That will demand more flexibility, sounder judgment, and greater entrepreneurial energy from today’s graduates. It will also challenge academic and government leaders to ensure that more of those graduates build careers and companies in the Boston area and Massachusetts.

“The superpower has always been the university system,” says Aman Narang, CEO of restaurant-tech company Toast and an MIT alum. “The best thing Boston can do is keep these people around.”

For its part, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology is working to drive artificial intelligence forward in sectors where the region is strongest, from biotechnology and robotics to defense and clean energy. It’s also trying to broaden entrepreneurship through a “dorm-to-startup” push, creating a pipeline of support services — from hack-a-thons to venture funding — to help students to start companies between classes.

“We’re in the race, and we can dominate in some areas,” says Anantha Chandrakasan, provost at MIT, who is leading several of its new initiatives.

Trade schools are also stepping up. Franklin Cummings Tech, for example, is hosting “skills showcases” at its new Roxbury campus, inviting Boston-area employers seeking tech-savvy students who can operate high-tech machinery.

“Front-line hiring managers, CEOs, industry leaders, they get a sense of what our students know,” says Aisha Francis, the school’s president. “And we give students a chance to show their skills.”

Colleges and universities across the state are ramping up training and collaborations with employers in a range of fields as companies adapt operations and business models to artificial intelligence. Some schools in Massachusetts, including MIT, are carving out a specialty in applied AI — sometimes called “AI+X” — deploying the technology to help businesses, hospitals, and research institutions to supercharge productivity, innovation, and scientific breakthroughs.

But too few leading artificial intelligence companies are based in the Boston area, says Boston venture capitalist Jeff Bussgang, who teaches a Harvard Business School course on launching technology ventures. The region’s universities still act as talent magnets and launchpads for entrepreneurs, Bussgang says, but too many of the brightest students launch companies in other states.

“Let’s get back in the arena,” Bussgang says. “Let’s fight for the talent, not sit back on our laurels.”

One local company fighting for talent — and winning — is Blitzy, a Cambridge startup that raised $200 million in May to develop AI apps that help businesses revamp old software programs and write new ones.

Brian Elliott, the founder of Blitzy (which is backed by Bussgang’s Flybridge Capital Partners), says he finds it easier to recruit talented graduates of local colleges and universities for his 80-person company without having to hire in the shadow of Silicon Valley giants such as Google, ChatGPT developer OpenAI, and advanced chipmaker Nvidia.

Blitzy’s pitch, in part, is to offer people a chance to build careers with a growing company rather than jump from one California goliath to another.

“We think there’s a competitive advantage to being one of the most interesting companies to work for here versus trying to compete with the headquarters of Nvidia, the headquarters of Google,” says Elliott. “There are so many brilliant engineers and [commercial talent] here in Boston that we can attract. That’s allowed us to have a very loyal employee base.”

The innovations fueled by local universities aren’t limited to AI. Coming out of the MIT lab of scientist and engineer Yet-Ming Chiang, for example, are new products that are allowing batteries to store more electricity over longer periods, creating more opportunities for wind, solar, and other clean energy sources.

Students at Chiang’s lab and other MIT research centers are also working on innovations in microchips, critical minerals, fusion technology, and defense tech. All are examples of “tough tech” projects combining science and engineering, which Chiang says “are in the sweet spot of the Boston ecosystem.”

At Worcester Polytechnic Institute, meanwhile, student researchers are recycling batteries and transforming bamboo and other non-food plants into fuel. The school is tailoring its research, along with its undergraduate and master’s programs, to align with the needs of Central Massachusetts industries such as data storage, medical gear, and biomanufacturing.

Grace Wang, WPI president, says the state’s companies and research universities are creating a lane in Massachusetts for using AI to make robots, drug development, manufacturing, and supply chains more efficient.

But that can only work, she says, if colleges and universities instill the broad knowledge, curiosity, flexibility, and open-mindedness students will need to thrive in a fast-changing technological world.

“We educate our students purposely on the human skills,” Wang says, “the skills to work in a team, communicate effectively, critical thinking, dealing with the pace, ambiguity, and complexity of this world.”

Three MBTA bus routes will remain free to ride through the end of the year, Mayor Michelle Wu and the MBTA announced Tuesday, just weeks before the fare-free pilot program was again set to run out of funding.

Spokespeople for the Wu administration and the transit agency did not immediately make clear Tuesday how much the program’s temporary extension would cost.

City and state officials indicated that money used for the MBTA’s reduced fare program would cover the plan to temporarily extend the program for bus routes 23, 28, and 29, which go through Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury. Wu’s office said in a statement that the reduced fare program “resulted in cost savings that are being applied to deliver this extension through the end of the year.”

City officials also said that they plan on “working this summer and fall on options for the fare free program in 2027.”

“There’s no such thing as free,” said Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board. “It just means someone else is paying for it, and every trip on the MBTA is already significantly subsidized.”

Wu’s office on Tuesday touted the program’s success, saying riders have taken nearly 23,000 fare-free trips every weekday on the three bus routes since the start of the year. All-door boarding on the buses has cut times at stops by 20 percent, according to the city.

“We’re proud to partner with the MBTA to extend this successful program as we continue building a more reliable, accessible, and affordable transportation system across Boston,” Wu said in a statement.

Wu first eliminated fares on the three bus routes in March 2022, when she used $8 million in federal pandemic relief dollars to fund the program.

Then, in February 2024, Wu again used federal COVID-19 funds to reimburse the MBTA and continue the pilot program for an additional two years.

That money was set to run out at the end of February, but roughly a week before, city officials announced that enough of those funds remained to pay for the program through the end of this month.

Transit advocates have fretted over the program’s long-term future and from where officials could pull money to keep rides free on the three bus routes.

Seth Gadbois, a transportation attorney for the Conservation Law Foundation, applauded the extension of “this essential program.” But Gadbois said it feels “a little like we’re driving in circles when it comes to long-term solutions.”

“We bought four months of this back in February, and here we are buying six months more now,” Gadbois said. “Especially at a time when many transit advocates see the administration’s commitments to climate safety and justice missing from the budget, this is a promising and important step, but riders need and deserve more long-term certainty.”

Reggie Ramos, the executive director of the nonprofit Transportation for Massachusetts, said she was not surprised officials wanted to extend the fare-free routes through the end of this year, calling it a “wildly popular program that has proven to be a lifeline for that corridor.”

“Beyond the extension of this program, the real and critical questions are: How do we make programs like this sustainable and how do we ensure that the service these buses provide are at a level that is dignified and truly reliable?” Ramos said in a statement.

Transit advocates have pushed Wu and city officials to find a long-term, sustainable funding source to continue the program. In February, Wu’s office said the city is discussing the future of the program with the MBTA.

Supporters of the three fare-free routes have pointed to city statistics that show more than one-quarter of riders on the routes save $20 or more per month, savings they can put toward other expenses.

City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune said the routes are used “ heavily by our working-class and Black and Brown residents.”

“We’re helping families save money, making it easier for people to get to work, school, and essential services, and continuing to build a more equitable and connected city,” she said in a statement provided by Wu’s office.

For Governor Maura Healey, there’s been an important piece missing in World Cup planning: How to get free tickets into the hands of kids across Massachusetts.

Healey knows the power of sports and how it can change young lives. She lived it. Basketball took her from a small town in New Hampshire to Harvard University, and opened a whole new world for her.

So with the world’s biggest sporting event coming to town, Healey has been reaching out to see if any local organization would donate tickets, which easily cost several hundred dollars apiece. No dice. That just shows how hard it has been to drum up local support for the World Cup. Not even the governor could convince anyone to pony up for kids.

Then along came Airbnb. Three weeks ago, I reported how the short-term rental company had set aside millions of dollars to support World Cup programs in 16 host cities. Last summer Airbnb met with the local host committee, Boston Soccer 26, about a potential sponsorship here. Let’s just say it didn’t go as planned. Airbnb moved on, spreading their largesse from San Francisco to New York refurbishing soccer pitches and sponsoring festivals.

But my piece set off a flurry of calls from leaders wondering how much Airbnb wanted to play ball. And on Monday, Airbnb found a big way to help Massachusetts when Healey announced that the company is donating 1,104 World Cup tickets to local kids.

The agreement came together quickly. If the state could come up with a distribution plan, Airbnb would foot the bill. Community partners were lined up with the Massachusetts Alliance of Boys & Girls Clubs taking the lead on dispersing tickets to Foxborough’s seven games.

“I’m just really grateful to Airbnb for stepping up … when we asked them to do this, they said yes right away,” Healey told me. “This is just something I wanted to do from the beginning. It’s a big deal having the World Cup here. We know that not everybody’s going to be able to afford to get to these games.”

To be clear, this isn’t charity for Airbnb. It’s good business. Soccer fans need a place to stay, and Airbnb anticipates that the World Cup will be its biggest hosting event yet. A Deloitte study commissioned by Airbnb projected that 164,000 tourists would come from around the world for the tournament, and close to 10 percent would stay in a short-term rental.

Airbnb spokesman Ivan Valladares would not say how much the company is spending on the tickets other than it is a “significant investment.” But Airbnb, as an official FIFA partner, does get a little break because it can buy tickets at face value. The company has also given away tickets in bulk to youth in other host cities — Mexico City and in New Jersey and New York.

Valladares said Airbnb has been looking for ways to support host cities but ultimately relies on each region to tell them what’s needed. In Philadelphia, for example, the city prioritized free subway rides home from games, so Airbnb underwrote the cost for that.

“We have taken the lead of the host cities on these investments,” said Valladares.

Airbnb isn’t quite done with showing love to Massachusetts. After all, Nathan Blecharczyk, the company’s cofounder and chief strategy officer, grew up in West Roxbury and is a proud Boston Latin Academy graduate who gifted $1 million to the school.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has needs too. And despite Airbnb’s history of beefing with the now mayor, the company is expected to announce it will fund a $200,000 microgrant program for small businesses and neighborhood organizations to support their activities during our very busy summer of tourism.

So on the eve of the World Cup, the news is getting good.

“It is a tough time in higher education, and we are not immune to the slings and arrows that are being aimed at so-called elite colleges,” Francis said. “It’s a call for us to be as creative as possible, as nimble as possible, and as collaborative as possible. Those are the hallmarks of our transformation over the past five years.”

In the latest episode of Bold Types, Francis sat down with Globe business reporter Janelle Nanos to talk about how her English PhD led her to lead a vocational school, why the job feels like part of her family history, and whether she’s managed to get any shut-eye lately. This interview was condensed and edited.

You became president of the then Benjamin Franklin Institute of Technology in 2021. Since that time, you’ve doubled enrollment, exceeded a $60 million campaign fund-raising goal, and established or expanded several majors. I’m curious if you’ve slept at all in the last few years.

I have slept [laughs]. I became president at a time when things were very different for the world and things were very different on campus. We have been very engaged here in this prospect of making trade and tech education accessible since 1791. When you do that work with folks who are first-generation and people who are not necessarily financially wealthy, it’s always work that can be precarious.

You have a PhD in literature. From an academic perspective, you may not expect someone with that sort of a background to lead a vocational school. I wanted to know more about what has driven you to this role.

Education, and education access, has always been a throughline. I come from a family of educators. And through some genealogy that I’ve been doing, I learned that I have a great-great aunt who actually was running a voc tech one-room school in the 1940s.

I do believe that there are things that you are called to do in this life. It’s really fate in some ways. I felt compelled by the mission of Franklin Cummings Tech at a point in my life when I wanted to work in higher ed administration and put the skills that I’ve amassed over my lifetime to bear for a community that I cared about.

Americans’ faith in higher ed is fading, with a recent Newsweek poll showing that nearly 60 percent of respondents said it wasn’t worth the cost. What’s your pitch for why vocational education can make a difference?

We were established as a college for people who were working and wanted to get an apprenticeship. But what we realized is that the work the students were doing to pay their way through college was completely disconnected from the automotive associate degree or from the cybersecurity degree that they were pursuing. That then made it such that their work and their degree were in competition. And we need work and the pursuit of education that leads to a good job to be complementary.

We can create more incentives for companies to create career exposure opportunities for students who are learning at all different levels. Our piece of that puzzle is to provide education that embeds industry-recognized credentials and to do our level best to make sure folks get in and get out in a very timely fashion.

Can you tell me more about the opportunities you’ve been able to introduce in your new building?

We teach HVAC and refrigeration and are making sure that our education is as comprehensive as possible and is as embedded with sustainability as possible. So our students are also learning about installation of heat pumps as well as traditional furnaces.

We are mostly focused on delivering certificate and associate degree education that leads to wonderful careers in our region and beyond. We have 10 tech and trade majors. These are the makers. These are the folks that help to operate and maintain our infrastructure, our built environment, our homes, and the buildings where we conduct our daily life.

Everyone I’ve talked to has said that this school exists because of the sheer force of your will. Tell me about the behind-the-scenes — the networks you’ve created and the relationships you’ve developed — to get some of Boston’s biggest names to look here and say: “This is where my money should go. This is where my emphasis should go. This is where my heart should go.”

There are a few ways to answer that question. First of all, I do believe that it is important to bring all of yourself to a big project, to an assignment if you will. And I think of my professional roles as an assignment. And so if I’m going to commit to something, I’m all in.

And I do think that the mission of the college is one that absolutely deserves to be championed from the rooftops. That the city on a hill should be as much about the folks who are educated at a Franklin Cummings Tech as it is about an MIT. Because these two are synergistic. One should not exist without the other.

Aerodynamics applies not just to airplanes, rocket ships, and race cars, but even the subtle design of soccer balls that makes the inflated orb behave in ways we don’t always expect. If you’re in Seattle this week for a World Cup match or other adventures, don’t miss a presentation by sports physics expert John Eric Goff about what makes each World Cup soccer ball new and unique — and why some have generated controversy. “Soccer Science: Beautiful Physics in the Beautiful Game!” takes place June 14 (2-3:30 p.m.) at Seattle’s Museum of Flight (allow a couple of hours to take in this fascinating museum, which includes the original Boeing barn, old warbirds, artifacts from Apollo missions, and a flight hangar with historic Air Force One and Concorde planes). Goff, a visiting professor at the University of Puget Sound’s physics department, focuses his research on the aerodynamics of World Cup soccer balls. He’ll explain how the design of each World Cup soccer ball has subtle differences in surface texture and construction that affect how the ball moves through the air, and how experiments help connect ball design to what players experience on the field.

“The experiments are essentially the soccer-ball version of aircraft testing,” Goff, author of “Gold Medal Physics: The Science of Sports,” told the Globe. “We mount a ball in a wind tunnel, blow air past it at game-like speeds, and measure the aerodynamic forces on it. From those forces, we determine how much drag and lift the ball experiences and then use computer simulations to predict how the ball will fly.”

Soccer balls don’t come with smooth surfaces; they have surface textures (slightly raised patterns), seams, grooves, and a varying number of panels. The official 2026 FIFA World Cup match ball, the Adidas Trionda, has just four panels — the fewest number of panels for a men’s World Cup ball, said Goff. Air density also affects how a ball flies through the air, meaning it will behave differently at a higher-elevation stadium in Mexico City, for instance, versus near sea level in Boston, Seattle, or Vancouver. Goff will also explore AI’s role in modern ball technology and soccer officiating. Museum admission, which includes the presentation: Free for children up to age 4, $21 ages 5-17, $25 for age 65 and older, and $29 for age 18 and older. www.museumofflight.org

Festival shines spotlight on diverse people whose stories risk being erased

New England’s largest film fest celebrating people of color worldwide returns this week, running June 18-26 in person and June 26-July 2 online. The Roxbury International Film Festival (RoxFilm), now in its 28th year, helps amplify underrepresented voices and provide a platform for diverse stories. It opens with a screening of “Transforming the Beautiful Game: The Clyde Best Story,” directed by Dan Egan, a documentary that highlights the journey and impact of Clyde Best, the first Black soccer (or “English football”) superstar of the modern TV era who became a legend in the North American Soccer League; it runs June 18 at 7 p.m. at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, with Best in attendance to field questions after the screening.

RoxFilm includes more than 100 narrative, documentary, animated, experimental, and student-produced films from across the country (and from Boston Public School students and Lynn’s Raw Arts Program). Add to that question-and-answer sessions with filmmakers, panel discussions, networking opportunities, and filmmaker hangouts. Other film highlights include “Finding Your Laughter,” which follows Chicago comedian Arlieta Hall who uses stand-up comedy and improvisation as tools to support her mental health while caregiving for her father with Alzheimer’s disease (June 25), and “She Dared to Dream,” a portrait of US Representative Ayanna Pressley as part of a series of short films on June 21. “This historic marker is going to be dropped on a very well-traveled street,” said Lew Finfer, cochair of the Boston desegregation and busing initiative, during the event. “In 50 years, maybe somebody will say, ‘What was going on there?’”

One of the 14 demands presented in 1963 was the acknowledgment of unintentional segregation in public schools. The demand was fulfilled in 1974, when a federal judge recognized the segregation and ordered Boston Public Schools to begin busing students between predominantly white and predominantly Black communities. The ruling sparked protests and violence, and Black students faced harassment as they entered previously all-white schools.

Leola Hampton, a former student bused in 1974, described the fear and trauma Black students endured.

“For us, education was secondary to survival,” Hampton said.

She recalled bricks thrown through bus windows, shouted slurs, and the uncertainty of entering hostile schools.

“We were the casualties of desegregation,” she said, garnering supportive reactions from the audience. “In spite of all the ugliness we endured, we continue to persist, to dream, to thrive.”

Vernita Weller, daughter of Rev. Vernon Carter, a civil rights leader and pastor at a South End church, described his 114-day vigil for the Racial Imbalance Law in 1965. Carter launched the vigil outside the headquarters and spent over a hundred days sleeping on the sidewalk, demanding that officials address racial segregation and inequality in the public schools.

She recounted his endurance through harassment, exhaustion, and harsh weather to demand action from school officials.

“I’m so proud of what he contributed to this story,” Weller said.

Susan Batson, daughter of Ruth Batson, the late chairperson of the public education committee of the NAACP, who delivered the 14 demands, reflected on her mother’s role in challenging segregation in Boston’s schools. During the ceremony, she recalled accompanying her mother to committee meetings and watching her relentlessly push for change.

She called her mother a “tour de force” whose persistence brought attention to injustices officials ignored.

The growing recognition of Boston’s civil rights history feels like a continuation of her mother’s legacy, she said.

“For me, it’s a very, very powerful evolution of my mother,” Batson said in an interview. “I think she is working like crazy in heaven, or wherever she is, to make all of this happen.”

For some attendees, the marker represented a chance to recover a history that was often overlooked.

Klare Shaw, 71, was a kid when she saw her mother, Sarah-Ann Shaw, Boston’s first Black female television reporter, actively participate in Boston’s civil rights movement. She was glad she came to the ceremony to celebrate the movement’s unsung heroes.

“I’m glad that we are lifting up today’s history and keeping it relevant,” Shaw said, standing in front of the marker. “I hope that people will continue to be involved in advocating for the education they want for their families.”

Jeri Robinson, 77, chair of the Boston School Committee, now headquartered on Washington Street in Roxbury, said the event was both personal and professional for her. Robinson participated in desegregation-era demonstrations as a student and now oversees the same institution that activists once challenged.

Looking back at the demands made by civil rights advocates in the 1960s, Robinson said Boston has made progress but still faces inequality.

“We know there still are many inequities,” Robinson said. “We can continue to work to create an equitable opportunity for all.”

As Rachael Rollins launches her improbable political comeback, her best defense may be a good offense.

At least that seems to be her modus operandi as she sat down for her first lengthy media interview since resigning as US Attorney three years ago amid two federal probes detailing “egregious” and “flagrant” ethical breaches.

“I will own that this entire situation when I was US Attorney was incredibly messy,” Rollins told me in a joint interview with GBH News’s Jim Braude. “I feel profoundly embarrassed. I feel shame, like remorse, about what happened.”

Yet Rollins can’t bring herself to say she did anything wrong — at least without knowing more about how the Department of Justice Inspector General and the Office of Special Counsel drew their conclusions that she violated the Hatch Act, which bars federal workers from partisan political activity, by attending a 2022 fundraiser with Jill Biden, and, separately, used her office to influence a Suffolk County District Attorney’s race.

“I concede they don’t think I was truthful,” said Rollins. “I believe I was.”

The 55-year-old Roxbury resident is emerging out of exile because she’s running for Suffolk District Attorney again – a role that catapulted her into political stardom in 2018. She was among the first in the nation to run as a progressive prosecutor, pledging not to pursue low-level crimes like shoplifting.

Today, Rollins likens herself to two defendants she had a hand in exonerating as DA and as US Attorney: Sean Ellis, who was found guilty of murder, and Gang Chen, an MIT professor accused of concealing ties to China. Both professed their innocence, and were ultimately vindicated.

She knows she’s asking a lot of voters to look past her transgressions — both of which involve improper use of political power. Keep in mind, all of this took place under friendlier times with President Joe Biden, who had appointed her to the role.

Still, Rollins remains characteristically defiant. She argues that scandals may not derail candidates the way they used to, drawing a parallel with Graham Platner, who easily won the Democratic senate primary in Maine on Tuesday, despite having a Nazi tattoo and allegations that he mistreated women.

“There’s righteous indignation that’s happening … that doesn’t mean I shouldn’t be held accountable,” said Rollins. “It’s just some of these things before used to be nonstarters, and now we’re in a world where they aren’t.”

So if Rollins — who blazed a trail as the first Black woman to serve as Suffolk DA and as US Attorney from Massachusetts — maintains she didn’t break the rules, then why did she resign her post as federal prosecutor? Why not stay and fight?

Rollins, who has spoken before about receiving death threats, said she had made up her mind to step down a couple of weeks before the federal probes were released in May 2023. Rollins said she had lost confidence that the US Marshal Service — assigned to protect her and her family — could provide adequate security, and another death threat was the last straw.

“Why am I fighting to stay in a place that does not care literally whether I live or die?” she recalled thinking.

Since leaving public office, Rollins has been teaching at Roxbury Community College and holding classes for incarcerated youth at Suffolk County House of Correction. Supporters urged her to run for Suffolk DA, she said, with momentum building after incumbent Kevin Hayden came under fire from the patrolmen’s union for filing a manslaughter charge against a Boston police officer for the shooting death of a carjacking suspect. The race has also recently drawn another Democratic challenger and local attorney Linda Champion.

“We were the most innovative and exceptional DA’s office in the country, hands down, and I believe we’ve lost that,” Rollins said. “We are lacking inspiration, we are lacking leadership, and we’re lacking transparency.”

And in what will likely be a familiar refrain as the campaign heats up, Rollins took a swipe at Hayden’s own ethical breach in the 2022 race. He paid a $5,000 fine after the state Ethics Commission found that he violated the conflict of interest law when used his official position to release information related to his opponent, then-Boston city councilor Ricardo Arroyo.

Rollins has always played by her own rules, and now she’s running on her own terms. Whether voters are ready to forgive and forget remains to be seen. But she’s ready to try again.

“When you ascend to the levels that I have, when you fall, it’s far,” Rollins said. “What I want is my daughter and my two nieces, who I’m the guardian of, to know that if you make a mistake, it’s okay … but you will pick yourself up, and you will continue moving forward.”

The prosecution is asking that Kisakye be detained until trial, or held on $250,000 cash bail, fitted with a GPS, and confined to his home because of the size of the amount allegedly stolen. Kisakye’s defense attorney, Andrew Stockwell-Alpert, asked that bail be lowered to $2,000 because the alleged incident involved no weapons and $2,000 is the maximum amount Kisakye’s mother, who is experiencing financial struggles, could pay.

He said Kisakye was no longer a flight risk.

“I would suggest to the court that he would not dishonor his commitment to his mother to not run away with the $2,000 bail, particularly with the GPS and home confinement,” Stockwell-Alpert said.

Kisakye was arrested in Miami last week and brought to Suffolk County, where he pleaded not guilty at his arraignment in West Roxbury District Court and ordered held without bail.

The alleged incident was reported on Nov. 19, when the homeowners called 911 worried that someone was lurking around the property, located inside a gated community on Allandale Road, according to the police report. Officers originally found nothing amiss, but discovered later that morning the back door was unlocked and the safe had been emptied.

Numerous items, including a 17-carat diamond ring worth an estimated $850,000, were allegedly stolen.

Detectives later obtained surveillance footage showing two hooded figures leaving the property around midnight, and began investigating Kisakye, according to the report.

Kisakye bought a one-way ticket to Uganda on Dec. 19 and departed the same day, declaring $54,000 in cash, according to the report. He later traveled to Miami, where he allegedly sold a stolen gold bracelet for $11,000, according to police.

On Thursday, Flaherty also approved a protective order to prevent Kisakye from accessing any evidence that involves personal and financial information about the alleged victims.

Prosecutor Alexander Jones said during the alleged incident, Kisakye knew the victims’ safe passcode because he knew their dates of birth.

He also alleged that Kisakye has, on at least two occasions, altered checks from the victims to be a higher amount than intended, and that there is evidence showing that Kisakye has done this with another alleged victim.

“The defendant has shown a pattern of targeting and victimizing elderly victims using financial information,” Jones said.

Kisakye started working for the homeowners as a home-care assistant in December 2023, according to a police report. He helped change the batteries in the basement safe last summer and has intimate knowledge of the property.

Kisakye had solicited a $10,000 loan from the homeowners to buy a new vehicle, but after depositing the money, Kisakye “never once returned to their home to work for them, nor has he ever spoken to them or reached out in any capacity,” the report says.

The police report said Kisakye has a long history of “thefts, check fraud and pawning jewelry.” Randolph police reports had already linked him to a stolen diamond ring and a residential burglary where an Xbox gaming system was stolen.

He had also made 14 pawn transactions between December 2024 and August 2025, according to the Boston police report.

A fingerprint at the crime scene was identified as belonging to Kisakye, police said, and GPS data placed him in the area of the home around the time of the burglary and on a suspected scouting visit about a month prior.

Boston police allege that after breaking into the Jamaica Plain home, Kisakye tried to sell the stolen jewels in various states before fleeing to Uganda “upon learning that investigators were inquiring about him.”

Detectives found suspicious activity in his financial transactions dating back years, including evidence he had opened accounts “in the name of a deceased individual for whom he had previously served as a caretaker,” according to the report.

“The Wu administration’s unwillingness to listen to its most vulnerable residents continues a pattern of racist governance that Black Bostonians are all too familiar with,” Reggie Stewart, a Dorchester resident and chair of the Environmental and Climate Justice Committee of the Boston NAACP, said at a press conference Friday morning about the Blue Hill Ave. project. “We support better public transit, safer streets, and real investments in communities that have been neglected for generations, but investment does not mean forcing a harmful project onto Black neighborhoods after the people who live, work, worship, and run businesses there have said no to it.”

Residents are concerned the road redesign will decrease parking along Blue Hill Avenue, limit travel to one lane in spots, and remove trees along the thoroughfare, which could lead to more pollution and add to an already heightened rate of respiratory ailments among nearby residents.

What the community needs, according to the Coalition for Responsible Transportation Policy, which requested the revocation of federal funding, is for the city to lobby the MBTA to extend the Orange Line to Mattapan Square as well as beyond Forest Hills into Roslindale.

A light rail was supposed to be installed after the elevated Orange Line was taken down in the 1980s, coalition members said, but the Silver Line bus route was eventually added instead — one of many transportation-related “broken promises” to the Black community, they said.

Federal money for Blue Hill Avenue has been scrapped before. In 2009, the state withdrew an application for a federal grant for the 28X rapid transit bus line following significant opposition from the community.

In a statement, the Wu administration said the plan for roadway improvements would continue to evolve during the ongoing community process.

“The city is working closely with community leaders, residents, and the MBTA to deploy federally-awarded funds to make much-needed improvements to Blue Hill Avenue, beautify the roadway, speed up commutes, and expand opportunities for small businesses along the corridor,” city officials said in a statement.

The US Department of Transportation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russell Holmes, the state representative from Mattapan who supports the proposed developments around his neighborhood, pushed back against the idea that they were being built on the backs of the Black community.

“All of these developments are being done for Black people,” he said. “The rest of this city, it’s exploding in development, and for so long it felt like there was … nothing happening in the communities that I represent."

“Black people need to also be a part of this development and a part of this economic change that’s happening in Boston.”

But on Thursday night, city officials got an earful during a contentious meeting in Dorchester about the transportation plan for the White Stadium redevelopment in Franklin Park. Residents were upset at the plan to restrict parking on game days and require visitors to Franklin Park to request parking passes, according to the Dorchester Reporter, while people in surrounding neighborhoods would have to get resident permits to park in front of their homes.

“People like me, particularly Black people like me, who are homeowners, who pay taxes, cannot be anywhere around here celebrating birthdays, a regular cookout, a Little League team ... on game days,” one woman at the meeting said.

The city’s $325 million bid to redevelop White Stadium for a professional women’s soccer team is facing a legal challenge over whether it’s an impermissible use of a public park. The question before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court is whether the project is a renovation of an aging facility or a new arena altogether.

Dorchester residents are also up in arms about a proposal from the state to build a campus for hundreds of people dealing with mental illness and addiction at Shattuck Hospital, adjacent to Franklin Park. One resident called the plan “a new form of geographic redlining” that would concentrate social burdens in the city’s majority-minority neighborhoods.

Speaking at the press conference about Blue Hill Avenue, Louis Elisa, president of the Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association said all those projects would be built “on the backs of the Black community.”

“Stop trying to fool people that this means anything to the residents of Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan,” Elisa said of the bus lane. “This proposed project, which will bring a lot of money to the city of Boston for construction, will do very little to improve the quality of life along Blue Hill Avenue.”

“Stop trying to destroy the Black community,” he added. “Stop the aggressive takeover.”

A project to improve sidewalks and add bike lanes to Cummins Highway in Mattapan, which has taken years and caused major disruptions, has added to worries about construction projects in the area.

The coalition opposed to the bus lane said the “last straw” was a meeting Mayor Michelle Wu held a few weeks ago about the Blue Hill Avenue revitalization without inviting community advocates or two city councilors, Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper, who have been critical of the project.

The coalition said Wu hasn’t met with residents or business owners in person about their concerns, despite the city holding 100-plus meetings about it in the past several years.

“I just want you to understand the extraordinary moment that we’re in, where a predominantly Black community … out of sheer frustration, have thrown up their hands and decided to prevail to the Trump administration for relief,” Dianne Wilkerson, a Dorchester resident and former state senator, said at the press conference.

Asking for the federal funds to be withdrawn, she said, is the only way to get the city to the table to discuss a plan that will help the community.
