For CEOs and dignitaries all over the globe, the World Cup is the Super Bowl and Davos rolled into one.

Before, during, and after the games in Foxborough, business and political leaders from around the world are converging on Greater Boston to network, strike deals, and forge partnerships. But how important is it, really?

Consider the itinerary of John Swinney, First Minister of Scotland (the country’s top elected official). He spent Saturday in a kilt and soccer jersey for the FIFA Fan Festival on City Hall Plaza and Scotland’s match against Haiti that night. The day before? He was all business — wearing a shirt and tie to visit Harvard, meet with Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and Governor Maura Healey, and participate in a roundtable on artificial intelligence.

“Sporting tournaments of this type are really significant ... they bring us all together,” Swinney said at the AI event held at Goodwin Procter’s Seaport office.

“It gives us the opportunity to construct a number of opportunities to develop partnerships and cooperation.”

That’s not lost on Jeevan Ramapriya, executive director of the Massachusetts Office of International Trade and Investment, and state economic secretary Eric Paley, who moderated the AI roundtable with two dozen business and government leaders. They’ve spent months scouting out the VIPs who are coming to Massachusetts for the World Cup. The playbook is a familiar one — highlight Massachusetts as a destination for innovation and startups — and then play the long game.

“Let’s build these relationships because nothing’s going to happen overnight,” said Ramapriya. “This is a process.”

Like the Scottish, the Norwegians are mixing soccer and business. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre arrived in Boston Sunday night for a round of meetings ahead of tonight’s match against Iraq, according to Hege Vibeke Barnes, managing director of Innovation Norway USA, the Norwegian trade and promotion agency.

Vibeke Barnes, who is based in New York, will also be at the Norway game, entertaining nearly a dozen American tour operators. “We have very good seats,” she noted.

And the economic opportunities between Massachusetts and Norway go well beyond tourism — extending into clean energy, life sciences, and the maritime industry. Norway is becoming a leader in electric boats; Vibeke Barnes thinks there’s a market here for that, too. Convening over the World Cup, she said, brings a bit of “joy” to “our business meetings and creates stronger relations.”

For the Ghanaians, soccer comes first — a match against England next Tuesday, followed by the Ghana–Boston Trade & Investment Summit in downtown Boston on Wednesday and then the Ghana Worcester Trade Fair in Worcester on Thursday.

The idea for the gatherings grew out of a March visit from a Ghanaian delegation to Worcester, which is home to one of the biggest Ghanaian populations in the US, said Rita Adubra Asante, a global business consultant who is organizing the events.

Kicking off the Ghana-Boston summit will be Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, Victor Emmanuel Smith. He’s based in Washington, D.C., but has been spending time in Rhode Island where Ghana’s soccer team is practicing at Bryant University. Since becoming ambassador last year, strengthening economic ties with the US has been a top priority, in particular drawing investment to create jobs in the African country so that more young people will stay there.

“I’ll talk to anybody who wants to do business,” said Emmanuel Smith. “We need to help our country progress. We don’t want to go around cup in hand looking for help every time. Come, and let’s partner.”

Too often the economic payoff of hosting a World Cup is measured by the number of tourists, hotel rooms filled, or beers sold. Edinaldo Tebaldi, an economics professor at Bryant, thinks we’ve been using the wrong metric.

“The World Cup is much more than just this massive sports event,” said Tebaldi, who also serves as the university’s vice president of strategy and partnerships. “It’s a platform for global collaborations and partnerships … a catalyst for economic development.

That World Cup energy Boston is feeling? It just might be the spark our economy needs these days.

That’s because Conley has strong feelings about Rachael Rollins running for the office she succeeded him in eight years ago. Conley called up Shirley last week to dispute Rollins’s recollection of how she first entered the DA race in 2018. In a lengthy interview last week with Power Play and GBH’s Jim Braude, Rollins said her candidacy prompted Conley to resign. Conley said he chose not to seek re-election after 16 years – which was publicly announced weeks before Rollins declared her candidacy. Who cares at this point? Well, Conley, who today serves as special counsel at Mintz Levin, said it’s important to set the record straight, given that Rollins resigned as US Attorney amid two federal ethics probes. “It’s just another example of shooting from the hip and not being truthful with the public,” Conley said. “This is about her fitness for office.” (Rollins said she stands by her chronology.) When Governor Maura Healey announced a deal to save a group of former Steward hospitals two years ago, she said the fate of the shuttered Norwood Hospital would be dealt with at a later date. Norwood was different, after all. It was being rebuilt after a flood. Meanwhile, the need for health care services in that area remains great. You can’t blame local leaders if they’re restless.

Our colleague Jonathan Saltzman just reported that Mass General Brigham was in talks months ago with property owner MPT to buy the unfinished hospital — to no avail. (The price that MPT sought seems ridiculously high.) Meanwhile, Representative John Rogers and others are trying to build support for a bill that Rogers filed to help the Healey administration take it by eminent domain.

Healey may not need that bill. Reopening a half-finished hospital should fit the definition of a public purpose that’s needed for Healey to seize it. (Healey did it once before, with St. E’s in Brighton, now part of Boston Medical Center‘s health system.) What she does need is some money on hand to reimburse MPT for the value of the property, and a hospital operator willing to invest in this turnaround project and cover those site acquisition costs. Healey should consider calling up MGB to hash out some kind of deal that works for everyone.

“Standing here today, we didn’t know years ago whether this would happen,” said Decker, a former Birth Center patient, during an open house Wednesday. “During COVID, there were real questions about whether the center would reopen. But many people remained committed to the mission and making it equitable.”

More than 200 people attended the celebration , waiting in line for a tour. The building was operational for 22 years before closing, and since then, they’ve expanded to three delivery rooms, designed to resemble bedrooms rather than traditional hospital rooms. Two rooms have soaking tubs for water births, an option that medical professionals say can help with pain management and relaxation during labor. The facility also has exam rooms, cribs, a kitchen, a waiting room, an elevator, and a wheelchair ramp.

Birth centers offer a different model from hospitals: a home-like setting where midwives — licensed providers trained to support patients through pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period — lead care for low-risk pregnancies. The centers typically offer longer appointments than hospitals, and many patients work with doulas, nonmedical professionals who provide physical and emotional support.

Midwives and doulas gave tours, many answering questions of expecting parents like “Do you have a birth stool? And a certified lactation consultant?” They replied yes.

Birth centers tend to have fewer patients, provide more personalized care, avoid medications during birth, and foster a culture of shared decision-making that empowers patients and reduces stress. They can administer IVs, but it’s not routine, midwives say. It’s also normal to be discharged 4 to 6 hours after giving birth with frequent follow-up visits. Patients who need to stay for 8 hours or longer will need to be transferred to the hospital.

At the same time, the centers have limitations. They are designed for low-risk pregnancies and do not typically include physicians or OB/GYNs as part of routine care. They also have restrictions on the procedures they can offer, including the use of epidural anesthesia and surgical interventions. If complications arise during childbirth, patients are transferred to a hospital.

The reopening comes as Massachusetts faces growing concern over maternal health access and outcomes. Hospitals across the state have shuttered 13 maternity units, totaling more than 100 beds, over the past decade. Maternal health inequities are widening despite years of state investment, with Black families disproportionately affected by complications and unequal access to care.

State leaders, including Governor Maura Healey, have pointed to birth centers as a lower-cost, lower-intervention alternative for people with low-risk pregnancies and have allocated millions of dollars in funding to support them.

Care will be led by certified nurse-midwives, supported by a team of 19 doulas who collectively speak 13 languages. Doula services are covered by MassHealth.

The Birth Center expects to deliver 100 babies in its first year, ramping up to about 300 by the fourth year. Hospital leaders said the center will be open to all patients but will place particular emphasis on serving vulnerable and underserved populations.

Samya Singletary of Boston, whose son is due on Halloween, enrolled at the CHA Birth Center when she was six weeks pregnant in March. She had some initial uncertainty about whether the facility would reopen in time for her delivery, but after touring the center Wednesday, those concerns had disappeared.

“I love my midwife here. I love that there’s no pressure, no monitors all over the place, and that I can feel relaxed and at home with good support,” said Singletary, 33. “I especially like the tubs and not feeling like I’m on a time crunch to push a baby out. I’m excited to come back when it’s time.”

Massachusetts currently has only one operating freestanding birth center, Seven Sisters in Florence, after a handful closed due to financial strain. The reopening of CHA’s Birth Center is expected to expand access to midwifery-led care in Greater Boston and comes as advocates push to grow the model statewide, with new birth centers planned in Roxbury and Worcester.

Neighborhood Birth Center, opening next year in Roxbury, and members of the Mount Auburn Midwifery Program also joined the open house to show their support.

During the last six years, CHA officials said they hired consultants to study whether the facility could safely resume deliveries and said it took several years to implement operational and infrastructure recommendations.

“I think this is a beacon of hope, not just for Cambridge, but for all of the other communities,” said Claire Laporte, vice chair of the Cambridge Health Alliance’s board of trustees.

CHA chief executive officer Dr. Assaad Sayah welcomed state and local leaders, including Decker, Representative Katherine Clark, whose congressional district includes part of Cambridge, Massachusetts Department of Public Health Commissioner Dr. Robbie Goldstein, and Cambridge Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui.

Goldstein said the Birth Center is special as it’s the oldest in the state.

“For decades, it had been a place where families have welcomed new life into the world,” Goldstein said. “Like so many institutions, this center faced enormous challenges during the pandemic, but today is not the story of a closure. Today is the story of renewal.”

Ballot question campaigns face one of their last checkpoints Wednesday before they can officially get their proposal before voters this fall. Whether they actually do may be another matter entirely.

Campaigns have until the end of the day to turn their final batch of 12,429 signatures into local clerks, a hurdle most campaigns say they will clear.

But several questions are still tangled up in court. Others could get negotiated away on Beacon Hill before voters ever see them. One has already been knocked off completely. As of Wednesday morning, here’s the potentially record lineup of 11 measures currently barreling toward the ballot:

💸 Income tax cut: The business leaders behind a ballot question that would slash the state’s income tax from 5 percent to 4 percent say they have the signatures to get the question before voters.

It already seems to be popular with voters: 66 percent of the 500 registered voters in a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll conducted last week said they support the question, compared to 21 percent who were opposed.

Not so much with labor unions or on Beacon Hill. House Speaker Ron Mariano expressed some interest in negotiating to keep the question off the ballot, where if approved experts estimate it could cost the state $5.1 billion in tax revenue. But lawmakers also passed legislation that would hold some other tax changes hostage if the question passes.

📈 Tax cap rewrite: It’s mostly flown under the radar so far, but this proposal, also pressed by business groups, could significantly reshape how the state crafts its budget.

The question would change the formula for Chapter 62F, the automatic tax refund rule you might remember from 2022 for delivering $3 billion back to taxpayers. That includes by counting revenue from the so-called millionaires tax in calculating what tax collections would be capped at before triggering a refund to taxpayers.

In other words, the law would likely be triggered more often — delivering taxpayers more money, but muddying the state’s budget-writing process.

🏠 Rent control: Supporters of a proposal to bring back a form of rent control say they’ve collected 33,000 signatures this round — more than twice what they would need — but two outside factors could still keep the question from going before voters this fall.

First, the courts: Opponents filed a lawsuit earlier this year claiming that the question was too ambiguous and the summary of it drafted by Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office was misleading.

There’s also the possibility that proponents could strike a deal to keep the question off the ballot. The Globe’s Andrew Brinker has more on where those conversations stand.

🗳️ All-party primaries: After vowing to increase ballot access on her way out of the governor’s race in 2022, former Democratic hopeful Danielle Allen is back with a proposal to scrap traditional party primaries and replace them with a “top two” system for state elections in which every candidate runs in the same preliminary election, regardless of party affiliation.

The campaign says it has submitted 20,000 signatures this round, though the Supreme Judicial Court is still weighing a challenge from Democratic Party leaders on whether the proposal is constitutional.

📂 Public records: State Auditor Diana DiZoglio says the campaign she’s leading to subject the governor’s office and the state Legislature to the public records law has cleared the signature hurdle.

Don’t submit your records requests just yet, though. There’s no formal opposition to DiZoligo’s latest crusade, but the state Senate sought an advisory opinion from the SJC that left the door open for the Legislature to amend the ballot proposal if it passes.

And House lawmakers have already passed legislation intended to cut the ballot question off by subjecting the Governor Maura Healey to the current public records law while carving out new requirements for themselves that would allow the public access to a specific set of “legislative” records.

🌿 Marijuana legalization repeal: The state’s highest court cleared this one for the ballot late last week, and supporters say they’ve got the signatures needed to advance.

If it reaches the ballot, voters would decide whether Massachusetts should reverse course on recreational marijuana legalization a decade after it passed a separate ballot question creating the multibillion-dollar industry here.

☑️ Same-day voter registration: Secretary of State Bill Galvin is backing a proposal allowing voters to register on Election Day. No organized opposition has emerged so far, though the concept is not popular in the House.

🏘️ Starter homes: This is another measure that appears to be cruising toward November. The proposal would make it easier to build so-called starter homes across Massachusetts by changing zoning law to allow for development of single-family homes on smaller lots. Supporters say they’ve collected about 16,000 signatures and are already gearing up for a major advertising push after Labor Day, according to the campaign’s committee chair, Andrew Mikula.

🌊 Land and water conservation: We forgive if you totally missed this one. If passed, the proposal from the “Protect Water and Nature” campaign would redirect some of the sales tax on sporting goods into a conservation fund. So far, there isn’t any formal opposition campaign.

⚖️ CPCS collective bargaining: Another deep cut on the list.

The measure would give employees at the Committee for Public Counsel Services — the state’s public defenders agency — the right to collectively bargain. SEIU Local 888 Tom McKeever, whose union is one of two locals supporting the question, said the campaign is poised to clear the next signature hurdle.

📝 Gun law repeal: There’s also a measure targeting the state’s firearms law that is heading to voters through a slightly different process and doesn’t need to clear Wednesday’s signature deadline. That measure would give voters the final word on whether to keep or toss the sweeping gun-control law lawmakers approved last session.

For most of this century, Massachusetts officials have been debating whether, and how, to move the sprawling US Postal Service annex next to South Station. Now the future of the massive complex is once again up for discussion among state and federal leaders.

Representative Stephen Lynch this week told The Globe that US Postmaster General David Steiner has expressed willingness to sell the 1.3 million-square-foot mail sorting facility and relocate its operations. Such a move would clear the way for even more large-scale development alongside the region’s busiest transportation hub, and perhaps an expansion of South Station itself.

Steiner assumed the top position at the US Postal Service last year, following Louis DeJoy’s resignation, and his openness to a sale came as a surprise to the congressman. Lynch said he and Steiner have even visited a property in South Boston near the Reserved Channel that could hold the vast sorting center.

When Texas development giant Hines last year opened its 51-story South Station Tower, the project included a refurbished train platform and larger bus terminal that expanded capacity by 50 percent, but no expansion of train tracks. Compared with the $1.6 billion expansion and renovation of New York City’s Moynihan Train Hall — a head house for Penn Station — and a similar “multibillion” dollar redevelopment at Washington, D.C.’s Union Station, Boston’s South Station is something of “the stepchild on that whole process,” Lynch said.

“If we had that extra land and that opportunity, we could really, really increase the amount of train traffic and people traveling by rail,” Lynch said, adding that an expansion could also hold space for cargo trains.

The Postal Annex has long hemmed in South Station. Government leaders for decades have discussed relocating the facility, a low and long property that stretches across 15 acres along Dorchester Avenue and Fort Point Channel across from former Gillette parking lots.

Moving the mail-sorting facility would open up space for more tracks at South Station, expanding from 13 tracks to as many as 21, and would likely include air rights to develop commercial or residential buildings above that expansion. The South Station Tower stretches 690 feet above the station’s existing tracks, and there would likely be room for another skyscraper above a track expansion, Lynch said.

Still, there is a long, and expensive, road ahead before any of this becomes a reality. The South Station Tower took around half a century to develop, from discussions in the 1970s until the tower’s opening last year. And moving the sorting facility to South Boston would likely require the support of the Massachusetts Port Authority, which owns large stretches of land off Summer Street beyond the Menino Convention and Exhibition Center.

The land long considered to be an option for a relocated mail-sorting center is tucked between E and Summer streets near the Reserved Channel heading into South Boston. Massport acquired a four-acre parcel at 525 E St. in 2022 and owns a combined 22 acres along that stretch, according to Boston assessing records.

The property is currently something of an industrial no-man’s-land and sits adjacent to the 42-acre site where developer Oxford Properties has pitched an eight-building, 1.7 million-square-foot mixed-use development. Oxford has leased 38 acres from Massport for the project, which the city is reviewing.

Massport chief executive Rich Davey said the organization is keeping a close eye on any discussions around South Station. In the 15 years since he started his tenure as the state’s transportation secretary under Governor Deval Patrick, Davey has watched the South Boston waterfront transform from dirt parking lots into a neighborhood that powers 10 percent of Boston’s property-tax base.

“The neighborhood’s changed dramatically,” he said.

It’s important USPS find a suitable site for mail sorting and distribution, he said. And while Massport would support a postal service facility on its South Boston land, Davey wonders whether it’s the highest and best use for the property.

“We’ll be prepared to support [a mail-sorting facility] if that’s the best use, but I also think we’re starting to really think about, for the first time, what would it be if it wasn’t a post office?” Davey said. “We’re going to keep a close eye on it.”

But, in my defense, nobody told me about the Tartan Army.

It wasn’t until last week, when I saw downtown invaded by men in kilts and felt the energy that hit our town like a hurricane, that I suddenly began to get it.

No Scotland No Party!

But of course, it isn’t just the Scots infusing the city with this badly needed energy. The huge Fan Fest installation on City Hall Plaza reflects the breadth of the revelry.

It’s Haitians cheering an unexpected strong performance against Scotland Saturday night. It’s been Cape Verdeans across Dorchester celebrating perhaps the greatest day in the history of Cape Verdean football Monday, a scoreless draw against mighty Spain.

It’s fans from Norway “rowing” up escalators at South Station.

In perhaps the most unexpected development, there were even alarming reports of Boston running out of beer given the thirsty onslaught of revelers — or at least running low.

If you really want to see a city, it doesn’t hurt to see it through the fresh eyes of people who don’t live here. It’s easy for us to forget that we live in a really fun city. Our new international friends have made it easy to remember, whether they intend to or not.

Ask anyone who was in Fenway Sunday night, watching thousands of Scots who probably know as much about baseball strategy as I know about offsides in soccer, having the time of their lives, singing along to “Dancing Queen.”

Their Boston has been warm and welcoming, and full of newfound friends. Not the version of the US that had led many people, especially on social media, to urge foreign travelers to think twice about coming to America.

This comes at an interesting moment. We’ve spent years now listening to our xenophobe-in-chief demonize people from outside the country.

What started out as a purported push for stronger borders was quickly revealed for what it is. It was never just a bid to curb “illegal” immigration. It was about the systematic denigration of people who don’t fit President Trump’s notion of who deserves to come here.

Sure, I recognize that people here for the World Cup are tourists, not immigrants. Even so, they are demonstrating on an hourly basis how much better letting people in is than shutting them out.

Turns out building a big tent is a lot more fun than building a wall.

Not to be overlooked, even for a second, is that some of the most passionate revelers in Boston are people who have been here all along.

Massachusetts has among the largest Haitian and Cape Verdean communities in the United States. And that Haitian community, in particular, has been literally fighting for its existence in the time of Trump.

For those communities, this is a moment of pure joy.

John Barros, the interim executive director of the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority, hosted a watch party at the Menino Center for the Cape Verde match, joined by “a couple thousand of my closest friends.”

Like most Cape Verdeans, he’s still glowing with pride from his team’s performance.

“Most of our talent plays for other countries,” he noted. “We had hard-working dreamers on our team representing the American story: If you work hard and work together, you can achieve the impossible. People are riding high on that narrative that the little guy can get it done.”

You could argue that immigration policy and the World Cup have nothing to do with one another. But there is no way to reconcile the images of vibrancy and joy that have gripped all of us this past week with a constant message that people from outside are almost always a problem.

Not that facts seem to sway these people, but part of me wishes that some of the so-called immigration hard-liners in Washington could be in Boston this week to see what the people they denounce actually bring to a city.

For that matter, to a country.

Created by the architectural firm CambridgeSeven, “Where’s Boston?” was the city’s contribution to the Bicentennial celebration: a visual tour of the Cradle of Liberty. Forty projectors showed 3,100 slides of contemporary Boston. The audio was in quadrophonic sound (very ’70s). In addition to Manos, photographic contributors included such prominent local photographers as Lou Jones and Jerry Berndt and a not-yet-famous Susan Meiselas. Manos’s work took pride of place: 154 of his photographs lined the outside of the pavilion. Blown up to 4 feet by 6 feet, they served as declaration and invitation both.

“Where’s Boston? 50 Years Later” celebrates the installation and Manos’s part in it. The exhibition runs through Dec. 12 at the Boston Athenaeum. The Athenaeum’s Lauren Graves curated.

The heart of the show is 53 of Manos’s black-and-white photographs. They’re a less imposing size than the ones outside the pavilion: either 8 inches by 12 inches or 11 inches by 14 inches. Over the course of nine months in 1974, from March to December, Manos made 19,000 exposures, producing 534 contact sheets. A dozen are in the show.

Along with Manos’s work, there are two color photographs of the pavilion, taken by Steve Rosenthal, and also a mini-slide show with 20 color images from “Where’s Boston?” taken by other, unidentified photographers. Excerpts can be heard from a dozen interviews with people photographed for “Where’s Boston?,” including the late Barney Frank. It’s good to hear again that familiar yammery growl.

The Manos photographs are a Boston visual gazetteer. They present neighborhoods (the South End, Mattapan, South Boston, Charlestown, East Boston, Roxbury, the North End, Beacon Hill). Also seen are Faneuil Hall, the Old State House, Franklin Park, White Stadium, Durgin Park, Locke-Ober, the Elma Lewis School, the Museum of Fine Arts, the Combat Zone, Haymarket, Boston Common, the Public Garden, the Boston Ballet, and, it’s only fitting, the Athenaeum.

Two photographs of City Hall Plaza show demonstrators with American flags. One of the protests is against court-ordered desegregation: “busing,” a word that defined, and haunted, Boston in the mid-’70s in a way that’s barely imaginable half a century later. Another photograph shows a middle-aged couple sprawled on the sand at Castle Island. Visible in the background are no fewer than 11 school buses. The caption is “Couple and buses at an outing.” The innocuous situation makes the image no less unsettling, taken in that particular year, in that particular place.

Ultimately, these photographs aren’t about geography or institutions or politics. They’re about people. Manos said he didn’t take a single photograph without a person in it. “The people were great and helpful everywhere I went,” he explained. “My wish is that seeing these pictures will help them to understand each other and their city.” They help us do that today, as a reminder of both how much Boston has changed and how much it hasn’t.

Deeply human and humane without ever being sentimental or touristy, the photographs remain so alive now because the photographer was so alert then. The title of “Where’s Boston?” was a rhetorical question. But Manos’s camera offered an answer: Who’s Boston.

Manos photographed many subjects during his career: the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Greece (his parents were Greek immigrants), Florida, Southern California, Mardi Gras, and a large 1993 protest in Washington, D.C., featuring the AIDS Memorial Quilt.

The quilt, as part of demonstrations in both Boston and Washington, figures in “Sal Lopes: Living with AIDS.” It runs at Leica Gallery Boston through Aug. 9. The show comprises 28 black-and-white photographs taken between 1988 and 1993. In addition to the quilt images, there are three of a Boston couple who adopted a young child with AIDS, and seven of participants in the Buddy Program organized by the AIDS Action Committee. In their own way, they are as much about a particular time as Manos’s are. Certainly, they, too, are focused on people and deeply human and humane.

Lopes will be giving a talk at the gallery and signing books on Saturday June 27 from noon to 2 p.m.

“We have a lot of work to do,” said Scott Prince, one of the partners in the venture. “But so far, the experience has been really great. I’m very hopeful that our vision will become a reality.”

Prince, 40, knows his way around a bar; he’s poured drinks at The Banshee in Dorchester for the past eight years. Before that, he lived on Mission Hill and worked at another neighborhood staple, the Puddingstone Tavern.

The original Flann O’Brien’s, known for its rusting statue of its Irish poet namesake (since auctioned off), closed in December 2020 after being open since at least the early 1990s. But Prince said his memories of it are still strong.

“It was a place where you kind of got lost in,” he said. “You would go in for a brunch, right, and you’re hanging out, you’re watching whatever, and before you know it, it’s 6 o’clock.”

That getaway feel is “kind of what we want” to bring back, he said.

Prince said that after he found out that Yellow Door was closing, he brought the idea of bringing Flann’s back to Ray Butler and Michael Vaughan, who run The Banshee as well as Brick & Beam Tavern in Quincy. Butler and Vaughan agreed to partner with Prince to resurrect the bar, which they too had frequented in the 1990s.

“It was nostalgic to them, so it was kind of the perfect opportunity for all of us,” Prince said. “When that opportunity came up, you know, we kind of pounced on it.”

Since Flann’s heyday, Mission Hill has seen plenty of change. But Prince said the bar will reflect both the old and the new.

“Flann’s brought a ton of people together,” he said. “You would get Irish immigrants, hospital workers, college kids, Mission Hill [locals]. Sharon Butler-Charles, an author, was showing off books she had written and her wellness products at the festival. Butler-Charles said people should use the day to understand their “beginning and how blessed we are to be separated from that.”

“Not to the extent that we’ve forgotten, but to celebrate the blood, sweat, and tears of our ancestors and what they went through, so that we can stand on their shoulders and be here today talking about it and celebrating what they went through,” Butler-Charles said.

Bernadine Kirkland, 63, of Dorchester said she was using the day to honor “our rich cultural heritage.”

“I love the celebrations. I love ... the significance of them, and just being out here and being able to celebrate,” Kirkland said.

Dixon, the artist, said events like the one in Franklin Park allowed people to “see us in the light that we always are in.”

A few updates on the Sad Six:

Astros: Outside of 2020, they haven’t had a losing season since 2014. Trading players such as shortstop Jeremy Peña [a free agent after the 2027 season] or first baseman Christian Walker won’t be easy for owner Jim Crane.

With Peña represented by Scott Boras, the Astros have to listen to offers.

It still feels like there’s a deal to be made with the Red Sox because Jarren Duran fits their roster, and the Astros have righthanded hitters.

Blue Jays: Toronto would not be afraid to add to its $307.5 million payroll, having witnessed what last season’s World Series berth meant to the franchise and the city. The Blue Jays are a financial giant at this point.

But there is no specific need beyond better health. Shane Bieber is due back from the injured list Monday. Outfielders Addison Barger and Daulton Varsho are close to returns, and reliever Yimi Garcia has started a rehab assignment.

Their inner-circle leaders — particularly Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer — do not lack confidence.

“We’re going to be fine,” Springer predicted. “Once we get everybody back, we’ll be a lot more consistent.”

Giants: It was funny to hear the “news” that the Giants are open to offers on Rafael Devers. Predictably, he has clashed with new manager Tony Vitello , a former college coach.

It was only a year ago that the Giants welcomed Devers with a splashy press conference and proclaimed him their missing piece. Now it’s fair to question how president of baseball operations Buster Posey has built the team.

If the Giants trade a prominent player, it’s likely to be second baseman Luis Arraez.

Mets: Francisco Lindor is close to a return from the injured list, and Bo Bichette has started to hit. Getting Lindor back at shortstop with Bichette returning to third base will help.

Their rotation has underachieved, but the Mets could hit their way into contention. If not, manager Carlos Mendoza won’t be around much longer.

Red Sox: The question is not whether the Sox will be sellers — they have to be at this point. It’s whether ownership will allow chief baseball officer Craig Breslow to make more than minor moves at the deadline.

If the Sox see themselves as contenders in 2027, which is not unreasonable, they could elect to retain Aroldis Chapman and other veterans under team control beyond this season.

Then you hire a new manager and coaching staff — presumably one with vastly more major league experience — and see what the offseason presents.

Tigers: Ace lefthander Tarik Skubal knows what is coming if Detroit doesn’t turn its season around.

“The reality is we need to play better baseball or else. Come the deadline, you give the front office an option to reassess where this team is,” he told the Detroit News. “And if they don’t think what we have is a World Series — or playoff-caliber — team, then the whole team is going to look different.”

The Tigers faced the same decision with Skubal that the Angels did with Shohei Ohtani in 2023: Trade him now or risk losing him to free agency after the season, and nothing in return except for a draft pick.

A prospect-laden team such as the Brewers could see Skubal as their chance to win the World Series now. The Phillies, resurrected under Don Mattingly, also would be suitors. The Braves need a starter, too.

For president of baseball operations Scott Harris, the job is to create as much of a bidding war as he can for Skubal.

Tyron Guerrero appeared in 112 games for the Marlins from 2018-19. He struck out 111 over 104 innings but also walked 66, hit nine batters, and threw 17 wild pitches.

“I had velocity but not the command,” said Guerrero, who spent 2020-25 pitching in Japan, Mexico, the Dominican Republic, and in Triple-A for the White Sox, Reds, and Angels.

Guerrero signed as a minor league free agent with the Red Sox on Jan. 9 and started the season in Triple-A. He had not appeared in a major league game for six years and nearly eight months when he debuted with the Sox on May 22.

He is now a late-inning option after a series of strong outings. Starting on May 28, he allowed one run over 6⅔ innings in eight games and struck out nine without a walk.

Guerrero has averaged 99.9 miles per hour with his two-seam fastball and topped out at 102.9.

At 35, his career is back on track.

“It’s been very gratifying to be back in the big leagues and be able to perform when the team needs me,” said Guerrero, a native of Colombia.

Guerrero credits Chapman for his revival.

“I met him during the offseason,” Guerrero said. “We have the same agent [Adam Katz], and I asked him to call Chappy when I signed with Boston to see if I could train with him. He invited me to his house, and I started working with him.

“To learn from him, somebody who has had all that success, has meant a lot to me. He has passed on a lot of knowledge. He knows about throwing hard and being able to throw strikes.”

Epstein lived that life for the better part of 18 years and isn’t interested in going back.

But if the Sox fire Breslow, Epstein is the best candidate to lead the search for a replacement, if only from behind the scenes. Nobody knows that job better than Epstein, or knows who the best candidates would be.

▪ Wes Gardner, who died June 10 at 65, is the last Red Sox pitcher who worked as many as 8⅓ innings in relief.

It happened on July 22, 1987, at Fenway Park. Oil Can Boyd allowed four runs in the first inning and was taken out by John McNamara. Gardner, then 26, finished the game and allowed only two runs in a 6-5 loss.

Gardner had pitched 4⅔ innings only three days earlier. At the time, he was a nondescript reliever with a 6.91 ERA.

“I’m surprised I’m not tired,” Gardner told Jackie MacMullan of the Globe after the game.

The crusty McNamara gave Gardner some grudging respect.

“You couldn’t ask for a better relief job than that,” McNamara said. “Unless, I guess, he shuts them out.”

Gardner was in the majors from 1984-91 with the Mets, Sox, Padres, and Royals. He appeared in 189 games, 142 of them with the Sox. He worked as an electrician after leaving baseball.

▪ There was a little bit of a Red Sox connection to the Knicks winning the NBA championship.

Knicks radio voice Tyler Murray did some Red Sox games on WEEI during the 2024 season and play-by-play for Worcester on television and radio from 2002-24.

Murray also called Hockey East games on NESN from 2021-24.

▪ Orioles owner David Rubenstein made an interesting gift to the Red Sox: a framed replica of the Declaration of Independence.

The replica was made earlier this year based on a copper-plate engraving made in 1823 at the behest of then-Secretary of State John Quincy Adams, who was concerned that the original document was showing signs of aging.

It will be displayed at Fenway in the Royal Rooters Club through July 4. If you attend a game, go to the Gate B fan services booth, and you’ll be escorted to the club.

Keith Beauregard went from Leominster High to St. Anselm and was an All-Northeast Conference player from 2002-05. That led to playing three seasons for Worcester in the independent Can-Am League under manager Rich Gedman.

He hit well for the Tornadoes, but not enough to draw the attention of major league scouts. That led to a coaching position at UMass Lowell under coach Ken Harring.

A lifelong New Englander, Beauregard then took a leap of faith to California to coach at Santa Clara University in 2013.

“Packed a suitcase and that was it,” the 43-year-old Beauregard said. “I had no idea what I was getting into. I just knew it would be a good move for me from a career standpoint.”

Little did he know how good. Beauregard landed with the Dodgers in 2019 as a minor league hitting coach. Then he became a field coordinator in 2021. That led to Beauregard becoming the hitting coach of the Tigers from 2023-25 and now the Twins.

Minnesota is second in the American League with 4.78 runs per game and fifth in OPS at .725. That’s significantly better than last season.

“It’s been a great experience. Every day gets a little bit better,” Beauregard said. “Trying not to look too far ahead.”

Beauregard’s time as a coach has coincided with the advent of teams using technology and data to improve player development. The four years he spent with the Dodgers gave him a foundation on that side of the game.

“That opened my eyes. They gave me a lot of freedom,” Beauregard said. “A lot of the guys I worked with at that time are major league coaches now. It was a good group.”

Baseball is the family business. Beauregard’s father, Jim, was a high school coach for 32 seasons at Bromfield, Saint Bernard’s, and North Middlesex Regional before announcing his retirement this past week.

“I’ve been on the dirt as long as I can remember because of my father,” Beauregard said. “The times I’ve come back to Fenway Park as a coach, it’s special. I saw so many games here watching players like Manny [Ramirez] and Dustin [Pedroia]. Coaching at this level now, it’s incredible.”

So MLB’s recent proposal to the Players Association to completely remake how amateur players enter the professional ranks has to be viewed through that prism. Still, what MLB suggested was radical: cutting the draft to 12 rounds, denying draft eligibility to high school players, and having set signing bonuses. MLB also wants an international draft. So many star players — Ken Griffey Jr., Bryce Harper, and Bobby Witt Jr. are just a few examples — came directly from high school. Making them wait two years after graduation to play professionally makes little sense. Ultimately, it’s about keeping players from becoming free agents when they are younger and worth more. MLB promoted the idea by suggesting players would develop best in an “elite development environment.” But college coaches are paid to win, not develop. Still, it’s understandable that owners want to restrict bonus payments to amateurs, given how much money is wasted on prospects who don’t pan out. An international draft for players 18 and older [as opposed to 16] would solve much of the corruption in that process, but it would also be a cost-cutting measure. A body covered with a white sheet lay in the street outside a lawyer’s office and a pizza shop. The scene, King said, left her rattled.

“It’s really devastating, and it’s scary because it’s close to home,” said King, 31, who works at a sneaker store across from the scene of the crash.

“We are devastated by the senseless act of violence on Blue Hill Avenue that took a woman’s life, left others injured, and has shaken the Mattapan community and our City,” Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement. “Our hearts are with the victim’s family, friends, and loved ones, as well as everyone impacted by this terrible tragedy.”

Saturday’s episode began unfolding with a crash just up the road.

Matos was driving near Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street when he collided with another vehicle, police said in a statement Sunday. He then abandoned his damaged car and fled to a nearby car wash, where he allegedly pulled a woman out of her vehicle, got behind the wheel, and drove the wrong way on Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square.

Matos allegedly sped down the avenue, driving on the sidewalk before hitting the female pedestrian and crashing into another vehicle at the intersection of Blue Hill Avenue and Fairway Street, according to police.

Police said Matos allegedly drove away from that collision and continued down Blue Hill Avenue before coming to a stop after striking an MBTA bus.

“The suspect was then forcibly removed from the vehicle and restrained by several community members until officers arrived at the scene,” police said.

Genara Peters, 56, was working in Super Dollar on Blue Hill Avenue when she heard a commotion outside. People, Peters said, were “running up and down the street.”

“I asked my customers what’s going on. They say someone got hit,” she said. “I was sad, and I was scared, because it’s right by the store.”

When police arrived around 2 p.m., they found the woman and a vehicle crashed into the side of an MBTA bus. Matos was taken into custody.

He is expected to be arraigned in Dorchester District Court Monday.

The woman’s name was not immediately released pending notification of her family, police said.

Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan said in an email that the MBTA will not “make any statements and/or comments which may interfere with an active and ongoing investigation,” citing the “seriousness of the incident and the tragic loss of life.”

Police said they made another arrest Saturday night after a man was seen entering the taped-off crime scene and recording video of the area while laughing. The man, identified Sunday as Robert Monestime, 21, of Braintree, will be arraigned in Dorchester District Court on charges of disturbing the peace and interfering with a police officer, authorities said.

Other local officials decried Saturday’s murder.

Boston City Councilor At-Large Erin Murphy said the death was the result of “a violent and reckless chain of events.”

“No one should ever be put in danger simply walking through their neighborhood,” Murphy said in a statement.

Boston City Councilor Enrique Pepén, who represents the district that includes Mattapan, praised the bystanders who rushed to help in the aftermath of the crash.

“Their actions reflect the care and concern so many of our community members have for one another,” Pepén said in a statement.

Some people said the crash left them worried for their own safety.

“When I heard it was really sad and really horrifying,” said Mia Mahhan, 26, who works at Finest Int’l Market on Blue Hill Avenue. “We need to have more security. I’m just hoping we can walk safely and move around safely.”

On Sunday afternoon, the busy road lined with stores, food markets, and restaurants showed little sign of the fatal car collision. A few people strolled on the sidewalks as cars and motorcycles streamed down both sides of the six-lane avenue.

While there wasn’t a piece of police tape in sight, King said she felt “a little bit traumatized.”

“That could’ve been me,” she said.

Dybantsa is at the top of most experts’ lists entering Tuesday’s NBA Draft, and if his name is called first, he’ll join Patrick Ewing in 1985 and Jimmy Walker in 1967 as the only Massachusetts products to be selected No. 1 overall.

What makes Dybantsa different from Ewing and Walker, though, is that he’s the only one of the three who was actually born here. Ewing’s mother moved their family to Cambridge from Jamaica when he was 12. Walker spent most of his childhood in Roxbury after his family moved there from Amherst, Va., when he was an infant.

Dybantsa seemed to understand his position in the time and lineage of Massachusetts basketball even as he navigated a unique path that took him from Massachusetts to California to Utah and now to the NBA.

“The last guy that we had besides Terrence was, like, Patrick Ewing — and that was 40 years ago,” Dybantsa said when his Utah Prep team made a tour stop at Emmanuel College in 2024. “I just want to be a guy that people know where Brockton is on the map. Everybody talks about the New Yorks of the world, the Cali’s of the world. But Mass. got some hoopers.”

If anything, Dybantsa’s path to draft night shows how much the road has changed.

For more than a half-century — from 1947, when Springfield native Bob Hubbard was drafted by the Providence Steamrollers to 1999 when Fall River’s Chris Herren was drafted by the Denver Nuggets — the pipeline from Massachusetts to the NBA essentially went through high schools.

Ewing was the type of player that shifted the NBA once he arrived — the league’s television deal with CBS nearly quadrupled in value in 1985 — but he earned his reputation at Cambridge Rindge and Latin.

Walker was an anomaly in his era.

He was discovered by Celtics legends Sam Jones and Satch Sanders, and Jones guided him to play high school ball at Laurinburg Institute in North Carolina. He thrived there, then returned to New England and became an All-American at Providence, then the Detroit Pistons took him with the No. 1 overall pick in 1967.

But in the 2000s, the landscape shifted.

Massachusetts became a pipeline for NBA talent — but it wasn’t necessarily churning out players from the area.

Dan Gadzuric came from the Netherlands to The Governor’s Academy in Byfield to a second-round pick in 2000. Jarrett Jack left his home in Maryland to play at Worcester Academy and became a first-round pick in 2005. Antoine Wright traveled from California to play at Lawrence Academy in Groton and became a first-round pick in 2005. Michael Beasley went from Maryland to Notre Dame Prep in Fitchburg and was taken with the No. 2 overall pick in 2008.

The state became known more for developing NBA talent from around the country than producing homegrown players itself.

Since 2001, nearly 30 players were drafted with ties to Massachusetts, but only 11 — Bruce Brown, Jake Layman, Georges Niang, Pat Connaughton, Noah Vonleh, Shabazz Napier, Nerlens Noel, Michael Carter-Williams, Demetris Nichols, Will Blalock, and Michael Bradley — were actually born or bred here.

Dybantsa’s time at national prep schools has become par for the course for prominent prospects. But his roots in Brockton matter the same way that his predecessor’s did.

“I think it’s, No. 1, a source of pride for Brockton and the greater Boston community to see one of their own gain stature like that,” said Leo Papile, who’s been tapped into the area’s basketball talent for nearly a half-century as founder and director of the Boston Amateur Basketball Club. “Whenever someone from your area distinguishes themselves nationally or internationally, I think everyone that saw him in the corner store or taught him or had him in youth sports, they all kind of share in that success. So it’s a great thing. It’s a day everybody raises the AJ flag and says hey, another one made it.”

From Walker to Ewing to Clarke, that baton for Massachusetts basketball is now in Dybantsa’s hands, and he’ll hold it as high as it’s been in more than four decades.

“It’s great for the region,” Papile said. “It’s inspirational to younger kids. It’s great for the families. When you’re a pro athlete now, you’re a worldwide brand ambassador. And part of your brand is where you’re from.”

On Sunday, the Roxbury International Film Festival held a screening of “She Dared to Dream,” a short documentary offering a behind the scenes look at the life and career of Massachusetts congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, the first Black woman elected to Boston’s City Council, and later the first Black woman elected to Congress in Massachusetts.

Sunday’s screening, which Pressley attended, was part of the festival’s Dreamers series, which focused on short films highlighting Black women stories involving human rights and their contributions to modern day activism.

“Dreaming is not only powerful, it is necessary.” Pressley said at the event.

Detailing her first influences, such as her late mother (Sandra Pressley), and her journey in living proudly with alopecia, “She Dared to Dream” shows the congresswoman in vulnerable moments.

Director Abby Ginzberg, a Peabody and Emmy winner, followed Pressley for several days as she worked to free Rümeysa Öztürk, a Tufts University doctoral student who was detained by ICE agents in Somerville last year.

The two were introduced while Ginzberg was working on “Speaking Truth Into Power,” a documentary about Oakland, Calif., mayor Barbara Lee, who mentored Pressley. But Pressley initially declined Ginzberg’s request to document her own story.

“To be Black and a Black woman, everything I do is political,” she said at the screening, explaining that she feared her transparency could be weaponized against her in future campaigns.

But in the lead-up to the country’s 250th anniversary, as she worked to push back against the policies of President Trump’s administration, she had a change of heart. Pressley said more stories like her own need more light among citizens. She also said that attitudes of distrust toward the government among the electorate call for elected officials to pull back the curtain and tell their stories.

“She’s been on the front lines essentially trying to save our democracy, and I think people should know more about her,” Ginzberg said in an interview before the screening.

From Lee to Pressley to Maxine Waters(who’s featured in the film talking about Pressley), bringing the stories of Black women in Congress to screens across the country is Ginzberg’s mission.

“She Dared to Dream” has been on quite the screening tour since it premiered at the Martha’s Vineyard African American Film Festival in August 2025, with 11 events in the last year, including in Cambridge during Emerge Massachusetts. Ginzberg said she hopes the documentary will be available on streaming services no later than February 2027.

The film speaks to voters and community leaders, but Pressley is also hoping the events depicted resonate with her fellow liberals active in Congress.

“I need Democrats to name and acknowledge that this [Trump] administration is anti-Blackness on steroids,” she said.

As Ginzberg works to get “She Dared to Dream” on screens at home by next Black History Month, Pressley said she wants her story to serve as a “love letter” to activists and politicians throughout the nation.

“I want to make sure anything I’m doing is going to advance the greater cause,” Pressley told The Boston Globe.

“There are shifting priorities for the City of Boston around what to support at this time,” said BAMS Festival founder and executive director Catherine T. Morris. “We maintain that our communities deserve access to the arts.”

A fund-raising message posted to the BAMS Festival website said that both “reductions in municipal funding and corporate investment have left a gap in our financial resources.” It noted that the organization considered canceling the event entirely, but instead was able to reduce some production expenses with this year’s move.

Morris explained that Play Playe is built “around the art of play. We don’t do enough of that.”

“It was born to center games, opportunities to activate creativity, and to try something new and meet someone new,” she added. “It’s important that we know each other and don’t forget the core elements of our humanity.”

That means board, card, and hand games as well as team challenges. Returning to the event are BAMS Festival staples such as dance lessons — which range from crumping to bachata to the Black line dancing of Boston Rhythm Riders — small business and arts vendors, and a “Soul Food Row” of food options. The indoor KidChella stage, curated by several area organizations, will showcase local youth talent.

Morris said that holding the event at The Record Co. will bring new visitors to that branch of the Boston music nonprofit, which rents out practice and creative spaces to local artists. The building, located at 55 Morrissey Blvd., is slated for redevelopment.

The event’s entertainment will be centered around DJs, who Morris said are “the lifeblood of any party. They help to mobilize communities. These are DJs who are community-centered and play music for the people. They’re not about ego.”

Topping the bill is hip-hop royalty DJ Jazzy Jeff, who will be appearing the week before he reunites with Will Smith as part of Philadelphia’s celebration of America’s 250th anniversary. The DJ will also participate in a June 25 “Artdacity: Check Ya Self” conversation at Converse’s headquarters on Lovejoy Wharf, which will discuss issues related to health and wellness in the creative community.

Also appearing will be Junior Rodigan, who for decades has been the region’s leading reggae and Caribbean music selector. Rodigan told the Globe that he is excited to be part of a “concept of bringing top DJs from various genres together, so we can showcase what we do at nightclubs in front of family audiences.”

A wide spectrum of house and dance music will be represented by Kelvin Sylvester, a Boston DJ, artist, songwriter, and producer whose soulful approach has earned him overseas tours and airplay for his deep, infectious grooves, which include collaborations with fellow Bostonian Lee Wilson.

“For the BAMS Fest set I am going to take people on a musical journey with different time stamps,” said Sylvester, who is excited to see younger house DJs adopt the all-vinyl approach that he’s long championed. “It’s good that a new generation is discovering music that’s not overstimulating, keeps your attention, tells a story and still slaps!”

Some additional Momentum events include a tribute to pioneering hip-hop producer J Dilla at City Winery, multiple events co-produced with the poetry and open mic organization FreeVerse, and a roller skating party at the venerable Chez Vous roller rink in Dorchester, the kind of community institution that Morris said BAMS Festival tries to partner with.

Another such institution is the Community Art Center in Cambridge. On Thursday the center will, as part of Momentum, celebrate the opening of the photo exhibit “A Place Called Home | Our Voice, Our Stories, Our Legacy,” at the Street Theory Gallery & Collective in Central Square. CAC executive director Erin Muirhead McCarty said the exhibit collects images taken in Cambridge’s Port neighborhood between the 1970s and early 2000s by youth photographers.

While most art exhibits involve a handful of curators, McCarty said that the CAC “invited the community into the building to help us curate the images,” resulting in an exhibit of “photos that seemed to resonate with the largest swath of people.” The attendees of those sessions are included in the list of 18 co-curators.

BAMS Festival is seeking to raise $95,000 to make up for its current shortfall. As for whether BAMS Festival will be back in Franklin Park next year, Morris encouraged the community to “stay tuned.”

“We don’t know where the city will be next year, but our goal is to maintain the integrity and the scale and the offering of BAMS Festival, as well as year-round programming.”

He abandoned his damaged Acura and ran to a nearby car wash. There, he allegedly yanked a woman out of her vehicle, got behind the wheel and drove off again, traveling the wrong way on Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square shortly after 2 p.m., authorities said.

Encountering traffic, he then “intentionally drove up on the sidewalk, which was pedestrian-filled,” Knight said.

Meanwhile, Janneh was stepping off the bus.

When she saw Matos speeding down the sidewalk, she and other pedestrians desperately tried to get out of the way, ducking into doorways and otherwise seeking cover, the prosecutor said.

“Unfortunately, however, she could not outrun the defendant’s car,” Knight said. “She was overtaken by him.”

She said Janneh was dragged “several hundred feet” as Matos continued driving — “until her lifeless body was ultimately dislodged.” He ultimately ran into another vehicle and then a bus, which stopped his rampage, she said.

That’s when a group of bystanders forcibly removed Matos from the vehicle and restrained him until officers arrived.

“It’s impossible to overstate the peril posed by this man’s actions when so many people were out and about enjoying a beautiful summer Saturday,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement Monday.

Matos is charged with murder, carjacking, and leaving the scene of two crashes.

Janneh’s family members declined an interview Monday. Tributes poured in on social media, from loved ones in the US and her native Sierra Leone.

“Mabinty was a beautiful soul whose kindness, love, and hardworking spirit touched everyone who had the privilege of knowing her,” the family wrote on a GoFundMe page seeking donations for burial and other costs. “She was a devoted family member, a loyal friend, and someone who always put others before herself.”

Records show Matos has a long criminal history in the Boston area, including assault charges. Prosecutors said the previous charges are largely domestic in nature, with several restraining orders against him.

A court-appointed mental health professional testified Monday that a preliminary assessment led her to recommend further psychological evaluation. In terms of his factual understanding of the charges he faces, Matos seemed confused and became “overwhelmed and tearful” during their interaction, she said.

She said he reported suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. She also mentioned possible schizophrenia and past hospitalizations.

Judge Erika Reis ordered Matos to undergo evaluation at the state-run mental hospital in Bridgewater. She set his next court appearance for July 10.

In Mattapan Monday afternoon, Fernandez X-Press Car Wash was busy; cars filled the small parking lot where Matos allegedly terrorized customers Saturday.

Owner Yancarlo Fernandez, 36, said he wasn’t there at the time but saw videos circulating online.

“The staff called me when it happened,” he said, describing how the carjacking victim screamed when Matos accosted her. He had initially tried to steal a different car, but switched gears after realizing it was locked, Fernandez said.

Mattapan resident Michelle Vargas, 48, said the fatal crash has traumatized the neighborhood, but she took comfort in the fact that Matos was quickly arrested.

“He needs to be held accountable for what he did,” she said.

With just over 10 weeks until the primary against US Senator Ed Markey, Moulton’s campaign has turned to a practice known as “red-boxing,” a wink-and-nod communication tactic campaigns use to legally get around rules barring coordination between campaigns and super PACs.

Moulton’s messaging plan is all laid out in a discreetly placed section of his campaign website, and framed in a tidy red box. And if the reader happens to work for a super PAC backing Moulton’s bid, who knows, that message could pop up in ads in the run-up to the Sept. 1 primary.

Anyone can access the page, though you’ll have to dig around to find it. Scroll past a section titled “Meet Seth Moulton,” his policy platform, a donation button, a section for news clips, and another highlighting the campaign’s social media platforms, and underneath directions for how to donate by mail, alllllll the way at the bottom on the webpage, there is a “media info” link — tucked right next to the campaign’s privacy policy — that has the game plan.

Moulton’s campaign wants messages targeting Democratic primary voters in the last six weeks of the election, letting them know about his stance to abolish ICE, his plans to “make life more affordable for working people,” and his views on President Trump’s foreign policy. A month out from election day, the campaign wants to convince unenrolled voters to know that Moulton is on a mission to “stop the gerontocracy in Washington,” and that it’s vital they pull a Democratic primary ballot.

The page also includes a link to an unlisted YouTube video stocked with silent B-roll footage of Moulton shaking hands with and greeting people at an anti-war rally, marching in a Pride parade, and working delegates at the state Democratic convention — ready-made material for any outside group looking to cut an ad.

A spokesperson for Moulton’s campaign pointed out that it “can’t control what our supporters do.”

“[We] hope that they stay focused on delivering a positive message about Seth and his progressive vision for Massachusetts and the country,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Red-boxing gets its name from the literal red boxes campaigns use to highlight information they hope outside groups will notice. It’s a practice that has become increasingly common among Democrats who also tend to spend a fair amount of time arguing that campaign finance laws need tightening. There aren’t any federal laws explicitly barring the practice, but groups like the Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Campaign Legal Center say it’s a no-no.

Unlike campaigns, where donors are limited in how much they can give a candidate, super PACs can raise and spend unlimited funds. Advance Progress, the super PAC backing Moulton, has spent nearly $1.5 million so far this year. Some of the largest donations came from David Peeler, a senior advisor at the Boston-based private equity firm Berkshire Partners, and Richard Wells, a director at the tech investment firm, Insight Partners, who each donated $250,000, records show.

A separate group, MA Progress Action, has also jumped into the race with ads that bear a striking resemblance to the PAC’s anti-Markey campaign messaging. Because the organization is a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, it isn’t required to publicly disclose its donors — and technically has to serve a public purpose beyond politics, something campaign watchdogshave argued it isn’t doing.

Blue Hill Avenue is one of Boston’s main arteries, traveling from Milton into the city through predominantly Black neighborhoods. Situated between the existing Orange and Red Lines, the neighborhoods are predominantly served by bus service, not rail.

“What we are proposing is to remedy this train desert ... so that we can enjoy the same kind of transportation that everyone else in the state enjoys,” Culpepper said.

Worrell and Culpepper said they met with State Transportation Secretary Phil Eng on Tuesday morning to present the idea. They said Eng committed to studying the proposal. A spokesperson for Eng said state officials are committed to looking at the proposal through the Program for Mass Transportation, the MBTA’s long-range capital plan.

Culpepper also said he had presented his idea to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who he said “does like it.”

In a statement Tuesday afternoon, a spokesperson for Wu said she was “open to discussing potential future rail options.” A second statement later Tuesday evening, however, sounded a more skeptical note.

“Digging new miles of subway tunnel under City streets would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment,” the spokesperson said. “Today, Boston has an opportunity to deliver more immediate improvements and beautification of the Blue Hill Ave corridor.”

Culpepper and Worrell did not present a timeline or a cost estimate for their proposal, saying they want to work with state transit experts to determine both. In a mock-up the councilors distributed Tuesday, they proposed adding a branch of the Orange Line that would head south from Ruggles Station and make several stops along Blue Hill Avenue, including Grove Hall, the Franklin Park Zoo, and Mattapan Square.

The pitch for a new, longer Orange Line that would bring rail service to more Black Bostonians comes as many in the Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester neighborhoods that branch off Blue Hill Avenue reject a longstanding plan to add dedicated bus lanes up the center of the congested street, alongside trees, lighting, shortened crosswalks, and bike lanes. Proponents of the plan say it will speed up bus travel and bring critical safety improvements, while critics argue it will add to traffic and threaten small businesses along the corridor. Earlier this month, some neighbors who oppose the plan went so far as to ask the Trump administration to rescind $80 million that had been allocated for the project.

Decades ago, a street car ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square, but it was ripped out in the mid-20th century. In 2009, the state proposed, and residents rejected, an earlier plan for “bus rapid transit.”

Worrell and Culpepper said they did not explicitly discuss the bus lane proposal with Eng on Tuesday, but they have been clear that they oppose it.

The energy in fighting the bus lane proposal makes now a good time to pitch something else, Worrell said: “We’ve always needed it, and I think this is the time.”

With the Orange Line idea, Worrell said, “we are trying to bring a new idea and a new proposal to the table.”

“And a better proposal,” Culpepper added. “A more efficient proposal. It might cost a little bit more, but this is the best way the community will get the best and efficient transportation, just like the rest of the state.”

Milton town and school officials are hurrying to analyze the potential purchase of Labouré College, a private nursing school closing this summer, with an eye toward converting it into a prekindergarten and kindergarten.

The School Committee voted earlier this month to explore design options to build an early education center at the school in time to potentially bid on the campus when it goes up for sale in August.

If the School Committee determines it wants the property, the Select Board would have to decide to buy it by early August to get any needed financing on the town ballot in November, School Building Committee Chairman Sean O’Rourke told the School Committee June 3.

“I think it’s a great asset for the town. That’s my personal opinion,” O’Rourke said. “Does it work for a school? That’s kind of what we’re all trying to figure out.”

The 134-year-old Catholic college is set to close this summer amid financial headwinds, with its nursing programs to be absorbed by nearby Curry College. Like many small private colleges across the region, the school’s enrollment has dropped rapidly in recent years.

Earlier this month, the Quincy City Council rejected Mayor Thomas Koch’s plan to buy the campus of the former Eastern Nazarene College, which closed in 2025. Koch had proposed paying $22.5 million for campus, but several city councilors expressed concern about Quincy’s existing debt.

Milton is one of relatively few Boston-area school districts with a growing enrollment, causing space constraints across the district. Its student population has grown by about 200 over the last decade, to more than 4,350 students, while Massachusetts as a whole recently reported its lowest enrollment in 30 years.

That means that while many Massachusetts districts are considering school closures, Milton is now simultaneously pursuing two options to add classroom space: the potential Labouré purchase joins an existing process of seeking state funds for a new elementary or middle school.

The town was accepted into the state school building agency’s pipeline in December 2024 with a goal of getting partial reimbursement for a new or renovated school. Other than Labouré, the main option officials are considering is an all-new school near Milton High School.

The Labouré site could be renovated with the same state assistance, but only for the previously proposed elementary or middle school project, unless the town restarts the long process to get state funds.

District leadership recommended considering the site for an early education center, which would free up space at every elementary school and potentially save on operating costs, according to a presentation to the School Committee.

“If the schools can make it work, then great,” said interim Superintendent John Phelan. “If not, it can be a town asset that can be utilized by the town in another way.”

Buying and renovating Labouré without state help could cost Milton some money — the state may reimburse about 28 percent of the district’s costs on a new project — but could also be completed much more quickly. A year and a half after being accepted into the Massachusetts School Building Authority pipeline, the district is still in very early planning stages, as construction with state funding can take years.

The Labouré campus has three buildings, with both classrooms and office space. O’Rourke recommended renovating just one building for students, in the hopes of not triggering costly energy code upgrades in the other two structures.

On June 15, the School Building Committee voted to hire contractors to evaluate potential costs and design options. Little design work could be done before the Select Board would have to purchase the buildings, one member noted. That means the town will have little information on how costly renovations might be.

The district will continue to pursue state funding in parallel to the Labouré purchase, O’Rourke told the School Committee.

Labouré College itself purchased the Milton site, formerly home to Aquinas College, in 2012. The nursing school had previously been located in Dorchester.

“It was not a hard decision to close,” said Cherag Selhi, who co-owns 19 McDonald’s franchises in Boston, along with his dad and brother. “We don’t want to create noise where there doesn’t need to be noise.”

Despite the lost revenue, it seemed like a simple solution to what had become a serious safety issue for employees and guests. So the dining room was off limits to patrons from 1 to 5 p.m., though the drive-through and takeout window remained open.

That arrangement lasted until Monday — when a team of local law enforcement and youth service providers convened for a grand reopening, presenting a united front against the unruly crowds of afternoons past.

“We want this to be a beacon … not under-appreciated and undervalued,” said Selhi, pointing out mismatched upholstery on the restaurant’s leather booths, the result of repairing frequent damage.

Perhaps an unlikely coalition, the groups share a common goal: helping Boston kids stay out of trouble.

That requires addressing a host of challenges facing young people and their families, organizers said, from the lasting impacts of pandemic school closures to rampant social media use, economic instability, and other barriers to educational and job opportunities.

The approach echoes messaging from city leaders, who often tout their holistic conception of crime-fighting that includes investing more in heavily impacted communities. Mayor Michelle Wu recently announced her latest summer safety plan, offering paid summer jobs to Boston Public Schools students.

Among the organizations supporting the McDonald’s reopening are the Roxbury YMCA, the nearby nonprofit Center for Teen Empowerment, and Project R.I.G.H.T. Inc., which focuses on anti-violence and neighborhood stabilization in Boston’s Grove Hall community. The groups plan to establish a regular presence during afterschool hours, offering resources, assistance, activities, and mentorship.

“We’re refocusing on what this space can actually do, trying to re-engage and re-establish relationships,” said Michael Kozu, co-director of Project R.I.G.H.T.

It was the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office that spearheaded the effort.

Migdalia Nalls, who oversees the agency’s juvenile unit, said she recently learned about the closure at a community meeting. She immediately reached out to the franchise owners, hoping to find a solution.

“Because this should be a community issue, not a private business issue,” she said. “Let’s bring the youth services where they’re most needed.”

During the reopening Monday afternoon, a few teens trickled in and made themselves at home.

“It feels good to be back,” said Angel Martinez, a sophomore at Boston Latin Academy. But he found the timing a little suspect, coinciding with the end of the school year.

Organizers said they plan to ramp up their efforts before school starts again next fall.

Martinez was there with two classmates, all longtime regulars before the closure. Jhostin Feliz, a football player, was showing off his new championship ring.

They acknowledged how chaotic things had gotten in the past, saying they saw people smoking marijuana and throwing frozen drinks. But they also took issue with how some restaurant staff handled the situation.

“Like not everyone was causing problems,” said sophomore Cindy Alves, biting into a crispy chicken nugget.

She said plenty of teens, herself included, help support the business. It was a place to socialize, meet new people, and have an afterschool snack.

At another table, Boston Police Deputy Superintendent Juana Hernandez talked to two high school girls about opportunities they could consider checking out.

Selhi said similar closures have been necessary at other McDonald’s locations in the city. He hopes the Roxbury initiative can eventually be expanded to those franchises.

McDonald’s runs in Selhi’s family. His father started working at its Somerville location after immigrating to the United States from India in the 1980s. He worked his way up from maintenance to management, and in 2015, he became a franchise owner. His sons later joined him in the venture. They now own most of the McDonald’s restaurants in Boston.

Selhi said the fast food chain loomed large in his childhood, the source of many happy memories. He later worked at the Somerville McDonald’s in high school. Ultimately, the golden arches became a symbol of opportunity, his family’s path to the American Dream.

“Our purpose right now is giving our dad a legacy,” Selhi said. “So for us, family culture is at the forefront of all our decision-making.”

He wants their restaurants to be community hubs where Boston teens can access the resources they need to succeed.

Izzy Marrero, chief of safety for Boston Public Schools, said the goal is getting kids to understand that “they’re also members of the community” who can bring about positive change.

Marrero, who served as a Boston police officer for over 20 years before moving to his current role, said addressing youth violence often requires looking beneath the surface and figuring out what’s causing kids to act out. It could be food insecurity, financial problems at home, petty disagreements that escalate on social media.

The restaurant reopening provides an opportunity for young people to turn a new leaf, he said.

“Hopefully they take ownership and protect the peace in here.”
