In the 2010s, new schools dedicated to educational equity were posting striking results. When the Center for Research on Education Outcomes at Stanford University examined student outcomes from 2015 to 2019 in 29 states as well as Washington, D.C., and New York City, it identified some 200 charter school networks serving urban areas that were closing — or even reversing — longstanding achievement gaps in reading, math, or both.

“More critically,” the authors wrote, “there is strong evidence that these gap-busting schools can be scaled.”

Indeed, the Charter School Growth Fund, a nonprofit organization that funds high-performing charter networks, reported in 2021 that the schools in its portfolio were together adding 50,000 students annually — equivalent to opening a new district larger than the Boston Public Schools.

Boston’s charter schools were among the best of them. A 2016 report from the Brookings Institution found that “test-score gains produced by Boston’s charters are some of the largest that have ever been documented for an at-scale educational intervention.”

Longtime education reformer Orin Gutlerner remembers visiting one of the high-fliers, Roxbury Preparatory Charter School, as a young middle school math teacher in 2001. He’d received state commendations for his own teaching, but when he stepped into a seventh-grade classroom in the school he was astonished. “I thought I held a high bar for teaching,” he said in an interview. “But what these students were doing, their engagement, the pace of the teaching — it absolutely blew me away.”

But it wasn’t to last.

From 2019 to 2023, the percentage of students in Boston’s charters that met or exceeded expectations on the state’s 10th-grade math exam fell by 19 percentage points. In the Boston Public Schools, the drop was only 8 points.

Why did charter achievement tank? To be sure, charter teachers struggled with COVID-19 pandemic-related learning loss, increased screen time, and rising mental health concerns. But so did educators everywhere. It was not external challenges that derailed charters. It was forsaken commitments.

The racial reckoning that followed the 2020 police murder of George Floyd could have accelerated the transformation of urban public schools, where most of America’s historically marginalized students are educated. Instead, it dealt reform a body blow.

For two decades, teachers at Boston’s high-performing charters had pledged never to make excuses for low achievement. They would do “whatever it took” for their students to succeed. Safe and orderly classrooms, high expectations, engaging curricula, precisely crafted lessons, and more time to learn set every child on the path to college and career.

But in the 2010s, as identitarian ideology reached its apex on college campuses, newly minted teachers questioned the schools’ practices. Were white teachers who ensured disciplined classrooms and expected all students to go to college engaging in a neocolonialist project that enforced “whiteness”? A pamphlet widely circulated among the charters seemed to offer the answer. It held that the “worship of the written word,” “perfectionism,” and “objectivity” were all toxic “characteristics” of “white supremacy culture.”

The charter schools’ longer school days, disciplinary systems, and standardized testing to gauge student progress were similarly cast as racist. Academic expectations were lessened and curricula, even in math, rewritten to foreground social inequities. Before holding students to behavioral expectations and delivering a rigorous curriculum, teachers needed to address students’ “trauma” from growing up in a racist society. The approach was an inexhaustible excuse for failure.

Racism is real and learning about it must be part of every child’s education. But antiracist programming (also known as social justice education) turned instruction therapeutic and political, robbing students of the essential tool of influence — a richly academic education.

One experienced Boston educator reports that many of the foundational practices that drove the highest-performing Boston charters have been removed. In one school, for instance, where homework was once given daily and its timely completion tracked, teachers were told not to assign homework more than twice a week.

Yet one charter network stood firm in its belief that the surest route to social justice was to provide its students with a rigorous liberal arts education.

Boston’s Brooke Charter Schools in Roslindale, Mattapan, and East Boston have become a haven for charter educators dismayed by the changes at their schools. They offer rich curricula, exceptional professional development, and high salaries. In 2023, 70 percent of the network’s eighth-graders were proficient in math, compared to a quarter of students in the Boston Public Schools. Brooke’s 2023 results actually improved from 2019, before the pandemic struck.

Education reform has taken a grievous wrong turn. It’s time for Boston’s charter schools — once at the vanguard of reform — to again ensure that every student is afforded effective instruction, high expectations, and a vibrant curriculum. It’s time to stop telling students what to think and to invite them to spar with ideas not their own.

To at last build an equitable and inclusive society, we must afford every American the leg up long granted the privileged: an expansive liberal arts education.

For me, gun violence is not an abstract issue. Day to day, I work with survivors of gun violence from Boston and New England, who can never fully escape the memory of those lost to gunfire.

Gun violence in America is all too common, and shootings often spike in the summer. Cities, like Boston, are successfully fighting gun violence with violence-prevention programming, but the crisis remains urgent. Despite a decline in homicide rates in Boston compared to this time last year, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan saw five shootings in four days in May.

Meanwhile, the gun lobby has been working to dismantle Massachusetts’ critical public safety laws. An alliance of political operatives, a gun shop owner, and the state’s gun lobby, operating as the “Civil Rights Coalition,” gathered enough signatures to force the upcoming statewide referendum to repeal the “Act Modernizing Firearm Laws.”

This landmark legislative package addressed critical gaps in the state’s laws by outlawing build-it-yourself, unserialized firearms; empowering clinicians and school administrators to file Extreme Risk Protection Orders to remove a gun when a person poses serious danger; and strengthening the state ban on the possession, transfer, and sale of assault-style firearms.

If this law were to be repealed, communities would be less equipped to stop shootings. Without a comprehensive legal framework to remove a gun from a dangerous situation, school officials and doctors, who are using Extreme Risk Protection Orders for deescalation, would have their hands tied even when they see clear warning signs.

The act also created a public dashboard to track the state’s landscape of gun-related incidents, supported the state’s firearm registration system and violence prevention infrastructure, and required evidence-based firearm safety courses for gun owners. Now, for example, the Basic Firearms Safety Course covers secure gun storage, suicide-prevention education, disengagement tactics, and live-fire training.

These changes are already yielding tangible results. Local law enforcement report that the law has given them tools to curb gun violence by dismantling the supply chains for unserialized guns and Glock switches that transform pistols into automatic weapons. Research by the National Policing Institute has found that unserialized guns are the weapons of choice for those barred from purchasing firearms, from high schoolers to people with violent histories.

This referendum is bigger than Massachusetts. The gun lobby is using the state to test a new strategy to erode gun safety laws across the country. If it succeeds in rolling back good public safety laws here, it will probably push other states to follow, putting even more Americans in more danger.

Major Michelle Wu jumped on the trend eight years later, presenting the city of Boston’s first “Dear Summer” project in 2023. “Berklee does a good job at creating some programs where they reach out to the community, so we just wanted to be more of a conduit as well, to really open doors for the Berklee kids,” he says. “Like, ‘Hey, come to Hibernian Hall and do a show, connect with these artists that are really pushing the culture in the city,’ and vice versa. ‘[Boston] artists, now take advantage of some of the resources that are at Berklee. On a street where everyone is battling for space, and every inch is contested, this barren strip sits right in the center of everything, in most places entirely useless. The cracked concrete is a reminder of the inaction and disinvestment that’s made this crucial artery through Black Boston so frustrating and dangerous to navigate.

“Cambridge has beautiful streets and bike lanes, beautiful bus stops, all that,” said Glorian Lee, 18, who lives near Franklin Park and takes the 28 bus down Blue Hill Avenue every day. “Why can we not have the same thing?”

City and state officials say they finally have a plan to make things better. They see the neglected median as the key to transforming Blue Hill Avenue into something like the functional, even pleasant boulevard it was 80 years ago. The pitch is this: Take the beleaguered buses out of the side lane of traffic, where they get stuck behind the double-parkers and right-turners, and put them in the exclusive, unencumbered center, in new dedicated bus lanes. There, they can move more swiftly, ferrying the people of Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester — who are some of the heaviest users of public transit, but suffer through some of the least reliable service — to and from their schools, jobs, and dentist appointments. It’s the anchor of a larger plan for the avenue that also includes trees, crosswalks, streetlights, and new sidewalks.

After decades of stops and starts, the money for improvements is finally there. The federal government has come through with grants totaling $95 million, while the state and city are set to kick in $51 million and $18 million, respectively. But Mayor Michelle Wu has gone quiet on the center bus lane proposal, caught between competing pressures to remake the city’s streets for the better and to avoid alienating the Black voters already frustrated with her.

The trouble is, many people in the neighborhoods branching out from Blue Hill Avenue are deeply opposed to this plan, a skepticism wrought by decades of broken promises and worse. They fear that adding a bus lane and removing some dedicated travel lanes would slow car commutes that are impossible already, or that street improvements could limit parking and gut the local businesses that are the spirit of the corridor. Alongside promises of better lighting and safer crosswalks, the latest version of the plan also includes bike lanes — which to many represent the first, galloping horseman of the gentrification apocalypse. Some neighbors have gone so far as to ask the Trump administration to rescind $80 million in federal funding, an effort to halt the project.

Supporters say they do not anticipate any harmful effects on businesses, and officials intend to preserve as much as 90 percent of parking. But those assurances do little for communities that have every reason to doubt what the government says. The MBTA in 2025 spent $300,000 on a traffic analysis, but never released it to the public, adding to worries about what officials have planned.

When a corridor is neglected for so long, promises to improve it can feel like something nefarious. Many in Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester say they feel like the plan for a center-running bus lane — along with other government efforts to increase housing and boost businesses along the avenue — is being forced on them despite protests.

Which is to say, the current debate is about much more than a bus lane. It’s about trust, and what happens when the government has done so little to help and so much to harm a neighborhood that it has little credibility left. It’s about who gets a say in Blue Hill Avenue’s future.

“Why are we even here tonight? They already know that we don’t want this,” said West Ward, 25, at a March community meeting on the bus lane. “Why aren’t they listening to the people who live here?”

The story of Blue Hill Avenue is a story of disinvestment. Once home to Jewish neighborhoods, the corridor swiftly transformed in the mid-20th century when racist housing policies funneled Black residents there, as banks refused to give them home loans elsewhere in the city. Now, its neighborhoods are home to some of Boston’s most diverse communities, Black families who trace their roots here back generations and newer arrivals from Haiti or Cape Verde.

A century ago, a streetcar ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square. Families queued up to ride it through a vibrant cultural corridor with meat markets, furniture stores, synagogues, and historic theaters. But in the 1950s, as cars became more prevalent and white families left the city for the suburbs, authorities ripped out the streetcar and redesigned the avenue to add a traffic lane in each direction. The new setup made it easier for commuters to travel in and out from the suburbs in their cars. But it also made Blue Hill Avenue less of a destination for shopping and dining, and did little for the people who lived there.

They “pull the trolleys out, and create this road, that is a huge road, that’s designed to get people through my neighborhood and not to my neighborhood,” said state Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat.

As long ago as the 1970s, city and state transit officials recognized that removing the trolley had condemned the neighborhoods to poor public transit — a “major [factor] contributing to the deterioration of the Blue Hill Avenue community,” according to a city report from that time. Archival documents show officials wanted to restore the trolley and even weighed extending the Orange Line beneath the corridor.

“Fixed-rail trolley service is the preferred technology,” a 1979 report concluded. “It has to be made easy for Corridor residents and others to reach these important destinations.”

The plan for rail was ultimately rejected as costly and infeasible.

As the decades wore on, trains and trolleys expanded elsewhere in the MBTA system, including an extension of the Green Line into Somerville that took three decades and cost $2.3 billion. But rail never returned to Blue Hill Avenue.

It was not the only time such transit was taken from Boston’s Black communities.

“When they took the Orange Line away from Nubian Square, we were supposed to have a replacement, and we never got that,” said City Councilor Brian Worrell, who argues his constituents deserve subway service, not just buses. “It’s like we’ve been redlined out of the rapid rail infrastructure — and you’re talking about one of the highest transit rider corridors. Why doesn’t Blue Hill Ave. get what Dorchester Ave. has?"

By 2009, when at last federal funding was available for a project to refurbish the street, the proposal was for “bus rapid transit” called the 28X, after the 28 bus route that ran up the corridor.

Rail “was never feasible,” said Jim Aloisi, who shepherded the effort as transportation secretary under Governor Deval Patrick. “I heard those voices back then, and we had plenty of discussions about it, but I just had to politely say, ‘I know that’s what you think you want, or what you want, but that’s not feasible.’”

Instead, Aloisi said, he wanted to prove to residents of the corridor that the 28X bus could be “really, really, really good, and function as well as light rail.”

Skeptics in the neighborhood felt like they were being presented with a fully formed plan — one with no room for their feedback to shape it, said Vivien Morris, a longtime community leader in Mattapan who recalled the opposition.

“That’s been our history — being treated negatively and pushed around town,” she said. “That’s why if the initiative came through the city, then people feel like, first we have to push back in order to make sure that our voices are heard.”

The 28X quickly fell apart. Facing widespread opposition from neighbors, Massachusetts turned down the federal money, leaving Blue Hill Avenue’s problems to fester.

Not everyone in the community was happy to see the 28X project die. Its collapse inspired Holmes to run for state representative. Now, he keeps a rendering of the rejected route in his office.

“I’m still just in disbelief that we made that decision,” Holmes said. Elected officials had turned down tens of millions of dollars, he said, when “what we should be doing is bringing resources back to our Black neighborhood that has been under-resourced and under-delivered to for decades.”

In 2019, Boston officials decided to try again. Recognizing the failures of the previous, state-run effort, the city under Mayor Marty Walsh took a more active role in planning the bus project, hoping to rebuild trust in the skeptical communities around Blue Hill Avenue.

“This is a part of the city that has been underserved over the last several decades,” Vineet Gupta, the city Transportation Department’s planning director, told GBH News at the time. “We really want to start learning from people who live in the corridor.”

But after seven years, hundreds of survey responses, and thousands of public comments, trust is still frayed, and residents remain dubious that the plan will help them. Meanwhile, the consequences of inaction on Blue Hill Avenue plague everyone who lives near it.

The corridor is one of Boston’s most dangerous, with a collision requiring EMS transport every three days on average, according to city data. For pedestrians, crossing the wide street can be treacherous. And driving it is a singularly maddening experience.

“I do whatever I can to avoid Blue Hill Ave.,” said Ihioma Breneus, 42, who lives in Mattapan.

Residents and commuters complain about the traffic, particularly during peak times; they gripe about double- sometimes triple-parking; they fear for their safety, and their kids’ safety, when they cross the street or, God forbid, ride a bike.

“Blue Hill Avenue is as unsafe today as it was 50 years ago,” said Tiffany Cogell, who grew up in Roxbury and now heads the Boston Cyclists Union. As a kid, she recalled, she was never allowed to cross the wide street — meaning though she lived just a few minutes away, she couldn’t get to Franklin Park on foot. “There is no reason in the world that I’m about to be 57 years old, and Blue Hill Avenue doesn’t feel any different or safer than it did when I was a little girl.”

If there is consensus on the problems, though, there is still no consensus on the solution. Neighbors are sharply divided on, if not overwhelmingly opposed to, the center-running bus plan. An analysis prepared for the MBTA found the plan would speed up the 28 bus by as much as 15 minutes at peak times, while slowing down cars by as much as six minutes during the morning rush, in part because the latest version of the plan would get rid of some traffic lanes. Critics fret over that increase, and argue officials should make other improvements — more trees, safer crosswalks, better lights — without changing the bus path.

“Nobody’s asking for it,” Breneus said of the center lane. Many fear the revamp could bring gentrification, and say the city isn’t doing enough to prevent that.

Two city councilors who represent Dorchester and Roxbury are still pushing for rail, not bus service, along Blue Hill Avenue. Worrell and Councilor Miniard Culpepper on Tuesday unveiled a plan to extend the Orange Line beneath the corridor. Officials owe their neighborhoods faster, better transit, they said.

“We want them to live up to their promise from 40 years ago,” Culpepper said.

But even if political leaders were to embrace the idea — and Wu has already sounded skeptical — any rail expansion would be costly and time-intensive. For some, the bus lane at least offers a quicker answer to Blue Hill Avenue’s problems.

Lee, the 18-year-old, lives in Dorchester, just a few miles from his part-time job in Mattapan Square. The bus ride should take about half an hour, but one recent Thursday, Lee left home two hours early, knowing he could be delayed. Once, he said, he was so late for work that he missed his two-hour shift entirely.

At his stop near Franklin Park, Lee tracked the bus on an app, knowing that the schedule is merely a suggestion.

“Another bus bunching!” he lamented, referring to delays that made his bus arrive at the same time as the one scheduled for 15 minutes later. That day, he made it to work before his shift started. But he often thinks about all the things he could do with the luxury of a bit more time.

There is a clear generational divide between younger transit users who take the bus and want a better one, and older commuters who drive. At a public meeting this spring, former state senator Dianne Wilkerson described the center bus lane as yet another unwanted change that officials were inflicting on her community.

“Nobody takes a bus to go pick up the pizza,” she said. “Nobody takes a bus to go pick up their kids. … That’s not how anybody lives. So we will not have this forced on us.”

It hasn’t helped that the Blue Hill Avenue plan is being debated alongside two other controversial developments nearby. Wu is pushing to turn Franklin Park’s White Stadium into a professional soccer venue, and the mayor also caused uproar when she shelved a plan for a life sciences and affordable housing project in Roxbury in favor of building a new high school on the site.

“You have three projects affecting a really marginalized community, and at this point they feel really unheard,” said Chevanese VanDyke, 46, who lives in Dorchester. “No bus is going to make up for that.”

For transit officials who want the project to go forward, the next few months will be about persuading people like VanDyke. The MBTA has promised more public engagement, and planners emphasize the design is far from final, meaning some of the more unpopular features in early sketches may change. The MBTA won’t go ahead with the project if Wu doesn’t want it, and for the mayor, there are landmines everywhere. Elected with the support of Boston’s Black communities and its transit advocates, she has now alienated swaths of both. Any choice she makes on Blue Hill Avenue could further incense at least one group.

Aloisi blamed critics for exaggerating how much parking might be lost, and how much businesses might suffer.

“Do you want to condemn those bus riders, those transit-dependent residents of the city, to a lifetime of substandard transit access on the altar of false information?” he said. “This is really a moral responsibility to make something like this happen and not to let it fail again.”

For Blue Hill Avenue to get better, Holmes said, it has to change. Beautifying the streets and leaving the traffic setup as is will not solve the problems, he said.

Alongside the bus lane, he’d like to see two traffic lanes in each direction, and as much parking retained as possible. He can live with losing some trees from the plan.

“We’re not going to have any bike lanes,” Holmes added. “Forget that.”

Those tweaks could assuage some fears about congestion and gentrification.

“So much of this is the Black community saying, ‘We don’t trust that this is for our community,’” Holmes said. “‘Is this for us?’ And I say the answer is, ‘Yes. Don’t move.’”

The distrust is hard to get around. But if the city and state don’t have a record of doing right by Black neighborhoods, Holmes said, “at least I do.”

He can see a future where the government, with the support of the neighborhood, fixes a problem it helped create. “You’re going to see young folks going to and from school on the buses,” he said. “You’re going to see those who are in most need.”

That’s who the improvements are for, Holmes emphasized. “We’re looking to serve the people who live in our community.”

Now, he just has to convince them, too.

Last year, I wrote a story about Kevin Boyce, a loving husband and new grandfather who died in 2024 of Powassan virus, a rare tickborne illness. His hospital stay had been torturous; the story warned of a lack of awareness of the virus by health care professionals.

Afterward, other families of people who’d contracted Powassan virus reached out. Lisa Boyce, Kevin’s widow, connected me with even more. This is a virus that just two decades ago was so rare that maybe one case would be reported worldwide every couple years — if that. How was it that I was suddenly in contact with so many families hurt by a virus that basically shouldn’t exist?

Powassan virus is one of several tick-borne illnesses that’s seen a dramatic rise over recent decades in the Northeast. Lyme disease is on the rise along with anaplasmosis, babesiosis, alpha-gal syndrome … and the list goes on. It’s hard to comprehend just how fast this shift has occurred. The numbers tell part of the story: In less than a decade, the case rate for babesiosis, a tick-borne parasitic disease, tripled in Massachusetts. Lyme disease alone is now estimated to put up to a $1 billion strain on the health care system each year.

For hundreds of thousands of New Englanders, tick-borne illness has become one of the most life-altering impacts of climate change — a rapid shift that for many, has occurred within our lifetime and upended our relationship with the outdoors. How did we get here?

My Boston Globe Magazine story today explores how climate change, our biodiversity crisis, an out-of-control deer population, and sprawling suburbs combined to create a dangerous explosion of tick-borne illness across New England, including the often deadly Powassan virus.

I track down the history of Powassan virus to its namesake, a small farming town in northern Ontario. I traveled there to speak with the sister of the very first person, a 4-year-old boy, reported to have died from the virus almost 70 years ago, leading to the discovery of the virus. I also trace the environmental history of New England to find out why exactly this part of the US has become so hospitable to ticks and the dangerous germs they can carry — and what, if anything, we can do about it.

I hope you’ll read the piece, but more than that, I hope that you please, please remember to do your tick checks.

But all good runs come to an end, whether you’re Ted Williams, Elma Lewis, Arthur Fiedler, Tom Menino, or Casimir “Chip” Zigulis.

And so, this week, Chip’s run comes to an end. He put in his papers and, after 38 years as a State House page, he is officially retired.

“I had a blast,” he told me, sitting in his chair, second from the right, under the rostrum in the House chambers, where he outlasted a half-dozen speakers and not a few chairmen of Ways and Means.

He was an institution within an institution.

“Chip,” House Speaker Ron Mariano said, “represents so much of what is great about this institution — a place where folks from all walks of life can come together to better the Commonwealth that we all love."

Chip Zigulis came from a walk of life very different than all the pages who preceded him.

He was the first person with an intellectual disability, with any disability, to serve as a State House page.

Many moons ago, Jim Brett, then a state rep from Dorchester, and probably the best mayor the city of Boston never had, was shooting the breeze with then Speaker George Keverian about the state’s efforts to help the disabled community.

“I was telling George, you know, we spend all this money on programs for the disabled, why don’t we hire some of them?” Brett recalled. “And George was like, ‘What kind of job are you thinking?’ ”

Brett, whose brother Jack had an intellectual disability, had thought about it long and hard.

“A page,” he told the speaker.

The pages sit in four chairs under the rostrum in the House, Brett reasoned, facing the 160 legislators in the chamber.

“When they’d look at the page,” Brett explained, “they’d see he or she is no different than anybody else. It would take the ‘dis’ off the word, and all you’d see is their ability.”

Then Keverian asked, “Do you have anyone in mind?”

Brett had Chip Zigulis in mind.

Shortly before meeting with Keverian, Brett had met with Chip and his mother after he was mugged, not far from their home in Dorchester.

“My mother sent me to the store,” Chip said. “Some guys jumped me. They took 23 dollars off me.”

They punched Chip so hard his hearing aids popped out.

Brett, whose brother Jack’s intellectual disability made him especially empathetic toward those like Jack, was moved by Chip’s story, a guy just trying to make a living, trying to help his mom.

Chip had been working for the Marriott Long Wharf but jumped at the chance to work at the State House in 1988.

It was the same year he represented Massachusetts in the Special Olympics, in figure skating. Ten years later, he represented the state in tennis. He also got to play a friendly match against Monica Seles.

“She said I was pretty good,” he said. “She’s a nice lady.”

Chip Zigulis is the Forrest Gump of the State House, one of those guys who just happens to be there when famous people are about, and they gravitate to him. He got an uncredited role in “Good Will Hunting” and met Robin Williams and Matt Damon.

When he met Williams, he imitated the actor’s catchphrase from “Mork and Mindy,” the old sitcom that made Williams famous.

“I said, ‘Nanu, Nanu.’ And he said, ‘I don’t do that anymore.’ But he couldn’t have been nicer to me.”

Before he became governor of California, Arnold Schwarzenegger was pushing physical fitness when he visited then Governor Bill Weld. Not long after, Schwarzenegger was hugging Chip and they went over to the Common and did pushups together.

Chip met his wife, Janet, at Bible study, and when they got married 25 years ago all the big shots from Beacon Hill showed up.

“Jim Brett was there,” Chip said. “George Keverian, Tom Finneran. They all came.”

He says Charlie Flaherty was the funniest speaker, Finneran the sharpest, and Keverian the kindest.

“Charlie would tell me, ‘I’m gonna tell you something but you can’t tell anybody’,” he said. “George was a very nice gentleman. The one thing I didn’t appreciate was them making fun of George for his weight. It was very disrespectful to George. If you can’t say something nice, don’t say anything at all.”

That kind of sums up Chip Zigulis. If he can’t say something nice, he just doesn’t say anything.

He loves Jim Brett.

The feeling is mutual. Brett left the Legislature and went on to become, very appropriately, a member and then chairman of the President’s Committee for People with Intellectual Disabilities under three presidents. He did the same, heading the state’s commission on those with intellectual disabilities, under governors both Democrat and Republican. He has spent his life trying to help disabled people into the mainstream and independence, a living, active memorial to his brother Jack.

Brett gets emotional talking about Chip Zigulis.

“Like all people with disabilities, all he wanted was a chance,” Brett said. “He got the chance, and he did the job, he lived a life of independence, and made a difference, and just by being who he was, he made people happy. Every day, the public and the members met Chip’s smile.”

It’s not been all sunshine and roses.

About five years ago, Chip finished work, crossed Beacon Street, and walked down through the Common to Park Street Station, to take the Red Line home. Some guys mugged him near the station.

“They were not nice,” he said.

But Chip Zigulis is, and that’s the difference.

He is 63, and could have worked longer, but he’s had some health problems, was hospitalized for a while, and it led him to take retirement sooner than me might have wanted.

“I’m really gonna miss this place, the people here,” he said, looking around at the chamber where names of the great and good watch over those who make laws. “Not just the speakers and the big guys, but the little guys. They were good to me, and I tried to be good to them.”

Chip Zigulis was better than good.

He was the best.

Instead of getting full makeovers, the four buildings in Worcester and Pittsfield still had myriad problems: rickety stairways, deficient siding, peeling paint, nasty refrigerators and toilets, and a possible bedbug infestation, according to post-renovation inspections. Some low-quality kitchen countertops had been inexplicably painted over.

The lone tenant in the Worcester triple-decker targeted for renovation, 76-year-old Stephen Jenkins, called the modest improvements to his unit “some half-ass [expletive],” saying the developers relied on “sidewalk Willies,” or uncredentialed handymen.

Fraud is also at least partly to blame for the disappointing outcome, the Globe Spotlight Team found. At least nine subcontractors flatly denied doing the work attributed to them, for which the state paid nearly $580,000. Another two said they suspected the invoices the developers attributed to them were inaccurate. Only two subcontractors reached by the Globe confirmed they did the work on the invoices attributed to them and got paid for it.

Those misrepresentations were missed by officials at MassHousing, a quasi-state agency with a critical role in addressing the Commonwealth’s housing affordability crisis.

The agency executive who awarded the grants to the developers in Worcester and Pittsfield had a connection to them: He had purchased a home in West Roxbury from the same two men just six months before, paying $204,000 less than the original listing price, records show.

That executive, Tony Richards II, did not file a written disclosure about his relationship at the time, in apparent violation of state ethics laws. Asked about that lapse, MassHousing’s top lawyer initially told the Globe that Richards belatedly discovered the connection more than a year after making the grant awards.

But a Spotlight review of Richards’s emails shows he was corresponding with the developers about real-estate financing opportunities around the time of the home sale. After initially defending Richards, the agency’s lawyer, Colin McNiece, announced MassHousing would be hiring an outside firm to audit the entire matter.

In the meantime, Richards, who earns $255,000 as MassHousing’s vice president of strategic community investments, remains in his position, the agency said, though oversight of grants has been taken over by the legal department while the review is underway. The agency is also reviewing several grant programs under Richards’s purview.

Richards served as a deputy chief of staff to then-Governor Charlie Baker before joining MassHousing in 2021, just over a year before Baker left office. Shortly after taking office, Governor Maura Healey named him vice-chair of her Advisory Council on Black Empowerment.

Richards declined to speak with the Globe. He has retained a lawyer, Payal Salsburg of Smith Kane, according to MassHousing officials, but she did not return multiple messages seeking comment.

The developers who left a trail of shoddy work and bogus invoices, Gary Acquah and Reggie Woods, also did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the Globe.

Two ethics experts who reviewed the matter for the Globe said MassHousing did not properly address Richards’s conflict of interest when he made his bosses aware of it. Despite a number of red flags, including Richards’s conflict, the agency also failed to recognize the depth of the problems in Worcester and Pittsfield until after the Spotlight Team dug into the matter.

At first, the agency downplayed the Globe’s findings.

On June 9, MassHousing officials said Richards told them that when he was awarding the grants in 2023, he did not realize that four of the first seven went to the same people who had just sold him his house. He said that was why he failed to report the apparent conflict.

In that interview, Richards had made an innocent mistake, MassHousing said.

But the agency’s position changed after the Globe sought emails between Richards and the developers, which cast serious doubts on his claims. The messages make clear that Richards knew Acquah and Woods.

For instance, less than three weeks after Richards closed on the home, Acquah emailed him about an upcoming meeting of industry professionals to discuss obtaining pre-development capital, referencing a previous conversation between the two.

“Hey Tony, was this event the one you mentioned would be remote?” Acquah wrote. “Or is this one in person and where? Thanks, Gary.”

Days before, Richards had emailed MassHousing CEO Chrystal Kornegay asking for her approval of a list of 12 professionals under the heading “Equitable Business Kitchen Cabinet,” apparently a group of unofficial advisers. Acquah and Woods were included on that list.

MassHousing officials initially urged the Globe to drop its request for emails from the time period of the home sale. The Globe declined, and the agency subsequently turned over most of the emails.

Along with the emails, MassHousing released a statement saying the agency would hire an outside firm to audit the matter. About two dozen emails were withheld as privileged.

“Our initial review indicated that all grant award decisions were made in a manner consistent with grant criteria and aligned with the program’s stated objectives,” said McNiece, the agency’s chief legal and operating officer. “However, we have recently learned additional information that warrants further investigation.”

This week, when the Globe notified MassHousing that several subcontractors denied doing the work attributed to them, the agency said in a prepared statement it “takes allegations of potential fraud and noncompliance seriously and will thoroughly investigate any allegations brought to our attention.”

“MassHousing is committed to taking all necessary steps to respond to these allegations, including cooperating with law enforcement as appropriate,” the statement added.

Today, most of the 13 units the state paid Acquah and Woods $1.4 million to fix up are still in rough shape.

Jenkins, who lives on the second floor of the three-family in Worcester, said his unit has hardly been improved. While the first- and third-floor units are in better shape, the only occupants in the last three years have been squatters, Jenkins said.

Worcester officials had given Acquah a separate grant of $134,750 to fix up the triple-decker. The city now wants its money back because of his failures; the building was sold at a foreclosure auction in late March.

“It is definitely disappointing seeing the units not come to fruition, and seeing that opportunity not delivered to Worcester families that need affordable housing,” said Peter Dunn, the city’s chief development officer.

In both Pittsfield and Worcester, officials expressed concerns late in the process about whether the apartments will be able to be rented to people with Section 8 vouchers because of their condition, a frustrating outcome for a program that aims to help low-income residents.

Emily Baird, a tenant in one of the Pittsfield properties, recently showed reporters around her place. She pointed out how the porch is “really rickety,” while many doors don’t close right and “the floor is tilted every which way” because nothing is plumb.

But Baird, who said she struggled with homelessness before moving in, said she’s thankful for the place, imperfections and all.

Baird and her neighbors got a new landlord last year when Acquah and Woods sold the three Pittsfield properties.

The developers were supposed to retain control of the buildings under the terms of the Gateway Housing Rehabilitation Program — which ultimately gave away about $2.3 million, more than half of it to Acquah and Woods. The program had several aims: to boost “emerging” developers; to address blight in Massachusetts cities with weak markets; and to add quality affordable housing at a time when people are leaving the Commonwealth in droves over the cost of shelter.

While MassHousing mostly functions like a bank, selling billions of dollars in bonds to subsidize affordable projects, the agency has also been overseeing a growing array of state grant programs. It disbursed more than $100 million in grants last year.

Records show agency officials did not realize there were problems with the Pittsfield renovations until the grant money was gone. They had relied on photos and invoices from Acquah and Woods and signoffs from local officials.

But in the summer of 2024, they inspected the Worcester triple-decker and were appalled at what they found. The agency visited Pittsfield next.

“We are very disappointed with the quality of this construction and are concerned that these issues could affect your ability to successfully access MassHousing funding in the future,” wrote Richards, in a letter to Acquah.

It was shortly after those problems surfaced, in the fall of 2024, that MassHousing officials say they learned of Richards’s potential conflict.

McNiece, the agency’s lawyer, said Richards told Kornegay, the CEO, in October 2024 he had just realized the people who sold him his home were also the grant recipients in hot water over the sloppy renovations.

Richards told them he realized the connection when he was going through paperwork in preparation to have his private mortgage insurance canceled, officials said.

Kornegay referred Richards to McNiece, the lawyer said. McNiece said he determined that a formal written disclosure by Richards would have been “basically moot” at that point, since the grants were already awarded. So none was filed.

Typically, homeowners whose equity stake in their home is under 20 percent must carry mortgage insurance. Records show Richards put only 5 percent down when he bought his place. To increase his equity stake, Richards would likely have had to do one of two things: Put down more money or commission an appraisal showing his house was worth significantly more than he paid for it.

Regarding the Pittsfield properties, some of the invoices the developers submitted were “sloppy,” even amateurish, McNiece said, but officials eventually considered the issues closed in late 2024 after a back-and-forth with Acquah and Woods.

“We did dig into the invoicing and the work that was done,” McNiece said on June 9. “At the end of the day, the scope of work was completed. The quality of work was lacking.”

Had the agency dug a little deeper, officials might have noticed many obvious discrepancies on the invoices: Two different subcontractors were invoiced for installation of a roof on the same Pittsfield property. In another case, $20,000 appeared to have been added to materials costs on a receipt, without explanation. Another invoice catalogued repairs to a garage on a property that didn’t have one.

That puzzling contradiction was on an invoice purportedly prepared by contractor Michael Biancaniello. Contacted by the Globe, he was happy to clarify.

“I never set foot in Pittsfield,” Biancaniello said flatly.

Records show Acquah and Woods collected about $125,000 on invoices bearing Biancaniello’s letterhead. He said he never saw a dime of it.

Biancaniello said he does know the pair. He did a job for them in early 2022, fixing up a Colonial single-family house in Pascoag, R.I., he said. He vowed not to work for them again because they took so long to pay him, he said.

The invoice from the Rhode Island job, which Biancaniello shared with the Globe, was almost identical to one Acquah and Woods sent to MassHousing — the one that listed work on a phantom “garage” in Pittsfield.

Eight of the nine contractors who told the Globe they did not do the work attributed to them all said they had worked with Acquah and Woods in the past on smaller jobs.

“I’m super upset,” said Bruno Balles, who was shocked when the Globe showed him invoices for $160,000 worth of work on the Worcester property attributed to his company. He didn’t get paid nearly that much, he said, and the scope of the work was far smaller.

He said the documents Acquah gave MassHousing were “fake,” and he shared real invoices totaling $56,000. Balles’s signature did not match the ones on Acquah’s paperwork.

“It’s not only fake invoices and using my name,” Balles said. “He pretended that I signed those papers.”

Even after he revealed his relationship to the developers in late 2024, Richards continued to serve as the agency’s contact with Acquah and Woods. In letters to the two, Richards requested a series of fixes.

In December 2024, Richards said in a letter to the developers the grants for the three Pittsfield properties would be considered “closed.” He also suggested the developers might want to sell to someone more experienced — even though the terms of the grant program had envisioned long-term stewardship.

Asked why Richards continued to interface with Acquah and Woods, McNiece called the letters Richards sent out “miscommunications.” He added: “Tony was a signatory, but he didn’t have any involvement in any transactions at that time.”

Two ethics experts who reviewed the matter at the request of the Globe both criticized the agency’s handling of it. They said Richards should have filed a disclosure as soon as he made the conflict known — even if it was late — and that he should have been kept away from the matter after that.

“As soon as he recognized having had a commercial transaction with the grantees, that was the time to recuse and disclose,” Thomas Susman, a Washington-based lawyer and lobbyist who has written and lectured extensively on ethics, said by email.

Even a late disclosure has real value, Susman said, envisioning a scenario where ”an agency employee notices the disclosure and says, ‘Wait a minute. I saw Mr. Official at the Capital Grille having steaks and wine with the grantees right about the time the grants were made.’”

A situation like that, Susman said, would “suggest that maybe the ‘basically moot’ conclusion was premature.”

By June 2025, the developers had flipped the three Pittsfield properties. The $780,000 they received was enough for a profit in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, though that sum was $320,000 less than what the Commonwealth had invested into the properties.

In addition to the money they made on the Pittsfield sales, Acquah and Woods collected at least $139,000 in developers’ fees from MassHousing, a typical amount in such deals.

In July 2025, several months after the Globe began filing public records requests related to the Gateway Housing program, MassHousing officials started taking a harder line with Acquah and Woods.

An agency lawyer notified the developers they were in default on their Pittsfield grants because they had failed to get the city’s permission to sell the property.

On Sept. 2, McNiece sent a letter ordering the developers to return the $1.1 million that MassHousing invested in Pittsfield.

Acquah and Woods have not done so, and MassHousing officials conceded they’re unlikely to recover any of it.

Richards is well-known in local and state political circles.

He spent six years working for the local nonprofit Action for Boston Community Development, better known as ABCD, after graduating from Clark Atlanta University.

He left for a job in the Baker administration, where he spent four years, working his way up to deputy chief of staff. While working for Baker, he attended night school at Suffolk, earning a master’s in public administration.

Richards’s social media posts frequently highlight his connections to Baker, Healey, and other boldface political names, from Representatives Ayanna Pressley and Steven Lynch to Mayor Michelle Wu.

In 2017, the same year Richards went to work for Baker, Acquah and Woods started a development firm, Flex Investments, and focused on flipping small residential properties in and around Boston.

The duo had played football together at Holy Cross. Both then worked for technology firms and went on to get MBAs from Cornell, according to their resumes.

A Flex Investments slide deck from 2023 showcased various projects completed and under way in Boston, Worcester, and Western Massachusetts. Starting in late 2020, the pair went on an acquisition spree in Pittsfield, the largest city in the Berkshires. They soon owned nearly two dozen multiunit buildings, far more property than they had anywhere else.

The properties were cheap and rundown. It’s not clear if Acquah and Woods had a grand vision, but in the short run, many of their apartments were rented out, despite their bedraggled condition.

Closer to home, Acquah and Woods were trying to flip a five-bedroom, 2.5-bath house near Catholic Memorial, a prep school in West Roxbury. They’d bought it for $590,000 in early 2022 and taken out permits for $68,000 of improvements, according to records. The listing boasted of a “beautifully renovated” home with “granite, upscale cabinets and stainless appliances.” The asking price was $989,000.

Around the same time, Acquah bought himself a glitzy new condo in Boston’s upscale Seaport District for $2.2 million.

The West Roxbury house languished on the market, and Acquah and Woods reduced the price several times.

Eventually they relisted the property with Acquah as the seller’s agent, saving them from having to pay a commission. It eventually sold for $785,000, with the deal closing on Dec. 23, 2022.

The purchaser was Richards.

About seven weeks later, MassHousing announced the new grant program, to be overseen by Richards. Acquah and Woods, who had been corresponding with Richards, quickly became its biggest beneficiaries.

Days after Richards closed on his house, Baker named Acquah to the board of the Community Economic Development Assistance Corp., a quasi-public nonprofit known as CEDAC.

It is a prestigious appointment in the affordable housing world. It was one of Baker’s final acts as governor – in fact, the news was announced by Healey, who kept Acquah in the role.

Baker, now president of the National Collegiate Athletic Association, told the Globe through a spokesman that he doesn’t know Acquah.

The governor apparently got a recommendation via Chris Collins, a onetime rainmaker for Baker. Collins, a partner at First Atlantic Capital, which manages a large portfolio of multifamily housing, said through a spokesman that he had “offered a favorable impression” of Acquah when asked by the Governor’s Office of Boards and Commissions.

Several months after Acquah’s appointment to CEDAC, he and Woods applied for the Gateway Cities grants. On a slide deck, they listed Collins as a “partner and advisor” of Flex Investments, along with Collins’s business partner, Margaret Wagner.

Wagner, who was on the CEDAC board when Acquah joined, also said through the First Atlantic spokesman she had no involvement in Acquah joining the board.

The spokesman said Collins and Wagner “are not, and have never been, financially, formally, or programmatically affiliated with Flex Investments. They provided informal advice on a friendly basis, some of which was viewed as helpful and some of which was ignored.”

In addition, the spokesman said, the two “were not aware they had been listed as partners or advisers” to the firm. They did not lobby MassHousing or any other agency on behalf of Acquah and Woods, he said.

Acquah’s name recently disappeared from CEDAC’s website. Its executive director, Ethan Handelman, confirmed Acquah resigned June 5 without elaborating why, days after the Globe first sought comment from him about the MassHousing grants.

While Flex Investments is still listed on Acquah’s LinkedIn page, his profile now shows him as chief executive of a “cutting edge travel planning application” called Let’s Go Plan.

By late 2023, Flex had lost nearly all of the remaining properties in its Pittsfield portfolio to foreclosure. Acquah also is facing foreclosure at his Seaport condo, records show.

Woods has continued to buy property periodically, including a two-story home in Winchester he acquired for $965,000 at a foreclosure auction in early 2025.

When the Gateway Housing grant program was announced, Acquah and Woods were at the head of the line. Behind them were a young couple who saw the grant as a lifeline.

Taylor Dickerson and her then-fiance applied for funding after they bought a home in Brockton that badly needed repairs, including major electrical updates, plumbing, and new stair railings. MassHousing applications required local support, and theirs was backed by the Brockton Redevelopment Authority.

The couple seemed to check every box.

As children, Dickerson — who asked the Globe to use her middle name — and her husband moved frequently. Home is precious to the couple, and when they bought their first house, they were ecstatic. “I want stability,” Dickerson said. “I want to know there’s a space that’s ours, that we’re not going to get kicked out of.”

The couple went through a “rigorous” vetting process with MassHousing that took more than a year and included a binder full of contractor bids that they shared with the Globe.

Agency officials assured them they would be funded, they said, and the couple wound up spending roughly $90,000 on repairs. They took on sizable credit card debt and borrowed from family and friends, largely because of the promises they’d been made, they said.

In late 2024 — around the time the problems in Pittsfield and Worcester were discovered — they learned the program had been paused and they were out of luck. Dickerson was upset and let officials at MassHousing know it. Her husband, an optimist by nature, cried, she said.

“I had let myself be hopeful,” Dickerson said. “Then I was just really angry.”

“For people who are interested in whaling history, or interested in Black whaling captains, Absalom just sort of stands out,” Karttunen said in a phone interview Wednesday. “And of course, that’s why a lot of people come to Nantucket.”

Absalom Boston’s story is recorded in the first segment of “Nantucket’s Historic Coloured Cemetery: Stories Told by Nantucketers,” a documentary made by Karttunen and local historian Barbara Ann White.

The film was screened at the Roxbury International Film Festival on June 19.

Born in 1785, Boston made history for captaining an all-Black whaling crew on a six-month voyage in 1822, according to the filmmakers.

“That’s not common in Nantucket history — or in any history,” White said in a phone interview Thursday. “People here know about Absalom Boston. If you ask people on the street who they know from history that’s of African American descent on Nantucket, his would be the first name that would come to their lips.”

Boston was known for other deeds as well. Two decades after his trailblazing voyage, he sued Nantucket’s segregated public schools to comply with a statewide integration law so that his daughter, Phebe Ann Boston, could attend.

The Massachusetts Legislature in 1845 passed a law prohibiting discrimination in the state’s schools. But the Nantucket school committee still refused to admit Black students to two of the island’s grammar schools, the filmmakers said.

An overhauled Nantucket school board integrated the island’s school system in 1846, after more than a year of Black residents boycotting the segregated school system, and Boston dropped his lawsuit. Still, there are no records of Phebe Ann, then 18, attending one of the schools to which her father fought for her admission, Karttunen said. She died only a few years later.

Just three of Absalom Boston’s seven children survived him. The four that predeceased him and his first two wives are all buried in the Historic Coloured Cemetery on Nantucket, according to Karttunen.

“Unlike some families who have family plots with well-defined corners, the Bostons are a little bit scattered,” she said.

The cemetery commission put the new monument to Absalom and Hannah near Phebe Ann’s grave marker.

Absalom Boston was born to a family that figures prominently in the history of Nantucket’s Black community. His father, Seneca Boston, worked as a weaver. Seneca Boston’s house still stands on Nantucket and has been owned by the Museum of African American History, or MAAH, since 2001. His mother, Thankful Micah, was Wampanoag.

Meanwhile, Absalom Boston’s uncle, Prince Boston, was the first enslaved person on Nantucket to successfully sue for his freedom.

Hannah Cook Boston, the whaling captain’s third wife, was born to a prominent Black family in Dartmouth in 1795, according to Karttunen. After her husband’s death, she became the first woman to be a steamship stewardess on the S.S. Island Home, which traveled between Hyannis and Nantucket.

“That was a pioneering job because following her, at least four other women from Nantucket’s Black neighborhood, called New Guinea, also found employment as stewardesses on the steamships,” Karttunen said.

Hannah Cook Boston died in 1857.

In 2022, Absalom Boston was inducted into the National Sailing Hall of Fame. The Nantucket Whaling Museum has featured Boston in its tours for years, helping preserve his legacy on the island, White said. The Nantucket Historical Association owns an oil portrait of Boston believed to have been painted around 1835.

“There are not many portraits of African Americans before the Civil War, and the fact that we have one that was made of Absalom Boston speaks to his prosperity and his being well-known locally,” White said.

Neville Richen, a Nantucket resident since 1987, attended the Juneteenth ceremony at the cemetery. An actor, Richen has forged a special connection to Boston: He has portrayed him in reenactments and performances based on the whaling captain’s life. He helped narrate the story of the Boston family at the ceremony.

Richen said in a phone interview Thursday that he was glad the Bostons now have a headstone in the cemetery, but he believes more can be done to memorialize the couple and other figures of Nantucket’s historic Black community.

“I would have liked to have a pedestal and a plaque, but the headstone was good,” Richen said. “I like the acknowledgment.”

Karttunen hopes that the headstone will attract new visitors to the cemetery.

“People who come looking for something will be happy to find that there is a tangible monument there now,” she said.

It didn’t take long, though, for observers to notice a few problems with the map the councilors presented.

For one thing, it’s missing the Charles River, and locates Aquarium station on a brand-new island in Boston Harbor. (Maybe the Zakim Bridge was dammed to flood the Financial District?)

That’s to say nothing of the lines themselves; the Green Line’s B branch has somehow added two Kent Street stops (the third, and the original, still marked correctly on the C branch), while the E branch seemingly runs express from Hynes Convention Center all the way to Heath Street. The Mattapan Line runs in reverse, and the Red Line’s Braintree branch has disappeared altogether.

Even the Orange Line seems somewhat bare bones, skipping three stops between Chinatown and Ruggles, and then running straight on (or rather, dipping slightly) to Forest Hills.

The slapdash mistakes pointed clearly to one culprit: artificial intelligence.

And as with anything that seems AI-generated, social media commenters were quick to poke fun.

“Green line stop consolidation has gone too far,” one commenter wrote on X.

“They evaporated Boston University,” another mused.

(Northeastern University, for the record, was also “evaporated.”)

The slapdash map has also raised more serious questions about the proposal. Caitlin Allen-Connelly, executive director of advocacy group TransitMatters, told WBUR that commuters on Blue Hill Avenue “deserve better than a concept that appears to have been assembled over a weekend.”

On Wednesday, Culpepper’s office acknowledged the map was produced by a large-language model, based on various hand-drawn proposals drawn up over the past several months.

Both councilors said the mistakes on the map did not detract from the merits of the proposal.

In a joint statement Wednesday afternoon, the two councilors characterized the map as a “conversation starter” with the MBTA “to make a case for why this should and could be studied.”

“The map we shared is just an initial vision of what’s possible, not a final plan,” the councilors wrote. “We leveraged AI to combine a number of iterative, hand-drawn maps to bring a vision to life during our meeting.”

Culpepper’s office said the proposed Orange Line stations in the mock-up were not randomly generated by AI, but deliberately selected over the course of several months of discussions.

The map, the councilors suggested, was just a visual aid. Only a formal prospectus from the MBTA, they said, would be able to “properly show constituents what rapid rail transit could look like in a corridor that has only ever been given bus options for half a century.”

“We left that meeting with an alignment from the MBTA that this was indeed possible,” they said.

In a social media post earlier Wednesday, Worrell acknowledged the map had been “upgraded” by AI, while sharing an earlier “handmade” proposal.

“No matter the map, the point remains the same: There is a gaping hole for rail in this section of Boston that aligns with economic, environmental and educational inequalities,” Worrell wrote.

The map shared by Worrell also gives a clearer idea where the proposed Orange Line stations would go: following Warren Street to MLK Boulevard and Grove Hall, before cutting down Blue Hill Avenue to Mattapan Square. (The Talbot Avenue and Morton Street stops, at least on Worrell’s map, would be west of the commuter rail stations of the same name.)

An extension of the Orange Line along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor would connect parts of Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, predominantly Black neighborhoods, with the rest of the city. The MBTA said this week it’s committed to exploring the idea further.

Culpepper and Worrell said that a timeline or a cost estimate for the proposal would be available only after consultation with state experts.

The Orange Line pitch comes after fierce debate over plans to add a dedicated bus lane up the center of the frequently congested Blue Hill Avenue,. That plan has sparked deep opposition in certain quarters, with critics arguing it will worsen traffic and threaten small businesses along the corridor.

Culpepper and Worrell have emerged as vocal opponents of the proposed bus lane, although they said they did not explicitly address the issue with Eng on Tuesday.

Decades ago, a street car ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square, but it was ripped out in the mid-20th century. In 2009, the state proposed, and residents rejected, an earlier plan for “bus rapid transit.”

“This ask for rapid rail options has been a core feature of our proposal since day one,” the councilors said in Wednesday’s statement. “The bus should always have been the floor, not the ceiling, for a community that has experienced over 40 years of transportation inequity and broken promises.”

On the biggest night of his life, AJ Dybantsa wore his pride on his chest.

His strikingly modern double-breasted suit — closed with a ribbon, embroidered with delicate florals — was a statement. But the pins adorning his jacket were the message.

Over his heart, connected with silver links, were the flags of Jamaica, his mother’s birthplace, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where his father was born. And on the right lapel, Dybantsa wore a blue-and-white pin with “TC5,” in honor of the late Terrence Clarke.

On a night that was all about where he’s going — Dybantsa became the first Massachusetts-born No. 1 overall pick in the NBA Draft on Tuesday — he showed everyone where he’s from.

Dybantsa’s parents were the guiding forces in his journey, from their home in Brockton to basketball’s biggest stage.

And Clarke, a Dorchester native and projected first-round pick who died in a car crash just weeks before the 2021 draft, was a source of inspiration.

So when Dybantsa walked across the Barclays Center stage to shake NBA commissioner Adam Silver’s hand, it was both a culmination of one family’s journey and a coronation for an entire era of Massachusetts basketball.

“I just try to put on for my state,” Dybantsa said. “Brockton bred, 508. I do everything for them. I like helping back in the community and giving the kids hope.

“There’s a lot of kids that play basketball out there and think that they can’t make it, but once they see me, they can be like, ‘OK.’ They might have some hope. It doesn’t necessarily have to be basketball, but anything they do. If they want to be a doctor, an engineer, anything. I’ll just try to be that role model.”

The fact that Dybantsa is the first born-and-raised Bay Stater to go No. 1 is even more striking when you consider the long list of Massachusetts basketball talent that came before. Most notable among them is Hall of Famer Patrick Ewing — also a No. 1 pick — who was born in Jamaica and starred at Cambridge Rindge and Latin.

A man was convicted of first-degree murder Friday for his role in a 2015 Dorchester home invasion that left one man fatally stabbed and shot, with his fiancée suffering a gunshot wound to the head in the presence of their infant, officials said.

Victor Arrington, 40, whose first trial in 2024 ended in a hung jury, was convicted at his retrial of murder as well as several lesser charges in the slaying of Richard Long, 37, who was killed on March 31, 2015, the Suffolk District Attorney’s office said in a statement.

Arrington’s lawyers didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. He faces a mandatory sentence of life without parole at a June 30 hearing, records show.

All first-degree murder convictions are reviewed by the state’s highest court on appeal.

Prosecutors said Arrington and two other men had planned to assault and a rob a man who lived on Harvard Street in Dorchester but broke into the wrong home and encountered Long, a union ironworker.

They forced Long and his fiancée into their bedroom and tied them up with electrical cords, and then decided to kill the couple to cover their tracks once they realized they were in the wrong residence, prosecutors said.

The assailants stabbed Long and fatally shot him in the head. They also shot Long’s partner in the head in the presence of the couple’s infant child, according to prosecutors.

They doused the couple with bleach and set fire to the kitchen before fleeing, prosecutors said. Long died at the scene, but his fiancée somehow regained consciousness and climbed the stairs to a neighbor’s apartment to get help.

Arrington was arrested in July 2015 but his case moved slowly as both sides fought over whether the jury could view his location history on his iPhone, which a judge ultimately granted, prosecutors said.

A co-defendant, James Boyd, 33, is expected to plead guilty on July 1 to home invasion, assault with a dangerous weapon, and two counts of kidnapping, prosecutors said.

They said the third suspect was identified but never charged since he was killed in April 2015. He wasn’t named on Friday.

“This team effort helped secure a just verdict in an extraordinarily harrowing case, notable not only for its shocking violence against completely innocent victims but also for the precedent it set in the use of advanced digital evidence,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “But most important of all is the opportunity for Richard Long’s family and loved ones to see someone held accountable for this terrible crime.”

An online obituary for Long described him as a devoted father.

“His children were his joy and he took every opportunity to spend time with them, never hesitating to hug them and express his love. Richard made people feel special,” the tribute stated.

While Wu has many allies in the House, her deteriorating relationships in the Senate have led her here, dropping the veil and endorsing first-time candidates running against those she views as thwarting one of her biggest priorities: a plan that would shift more of the city’s tax burden onto commercial real estate.

Perhaps no issue has more strikingly animated Wu’s bitter, nearly two-year-long battle with powerful Democrats in the Senate. It’s also the driving force behind her political moves now. She has endorsed both Lander and Latoya Gayle, one of the Democrats challenging Senator Nicholas Collins, another Wu antagonist.

Her decision to directly insert herself into races against sitting Democrats in her own city, and her unflinching public portrayals of Senate leadership, have prompted even her allies to question her tactics. Wu, fresh from a romp to reelection, is awash in political capital, but she also risks inviting further isolation from the power brokers who pull the legislative levers.

Wu said she isn’t worried about blowback.

“There are a lot of egos in politics,” she said in a recent interview at her City Hall office. “If the top criteria was to make sure that we get along with everyone and prioritize comfort in conversations and relationships, then we wouldn’t do anything at all.”

Wu repeatedly pushed her tax measure through both the City Council and the House, and in 2024 negotiated a compromise version of the legislation with business and real estate group leaders, who had initially opposed her plan.

But those organizations later walked back their support after data showed that residential tax bills would not jump as high as her administration had previously estimated, and feared commercial landlords would bear too much of the burden. Senators then killed the bill amid staunch opposition from Collins, and then the chamber denied it again this past winter as Collins and Brownsberger pushed alternative proposals.

“We were all disappointed by how that all played out,” said Representative Aaron Michlewitz, a North End Democrat, close Wu ally, and the House budget chief, who said his own property taxes have gone up the past two years. “What was very frustrating was that the bill could not even be advanced.”

That fight informs Wu’s new one. The mayor said that she personally didn’t recruit Lander or Gayle, but that the chamber’s moves to block her bills — and their “comfort of maintaining the status quo” — are driving why she’s targeting two sitting Democrats who represent her city.

“The question for all of us who are in leadership roles is: Are we going to throw up our hands and say this is bigger than we can manage? Or are we going to roll up our sleeves and try to find any and every way to make a difference for our constituents,” Wu said. “That’s what every election cycle is about.”

Senate leaders dispute that they’re the problem. Brownsberger said he is a collaborative partner on many issues, and pointed to endorsements he’s gotten from Governor Maura Healey, Attorney General Andrea Campbell, and several state representatives and officials.

“Most other local officials are endorsing me because they know what a great partner I am,” said Brownsberger, a Belmont Democrat who represents parts of Boston.

A spokesperson for Senate President Karen Spilka said lawmakers have delivered a myriad of progressive policies that benefit Boston and other residents, be it funding for tuition-free community college or free school meals.

“The question isn’t whether Boston should have a voice. It already does,” said Gray Milkowski, the Spilka spokesperson. The question, he said, is “whether every proposal that emerges from City Hall should become state law, or whether legislators have a responsibility to weigh different perspectives and sometimes take a different approach.”

Multiple efforts to reach Collins were unsuccessful.

Wu is not the first mayor to run into speed bumps on Beacon Hill, nor is she the first to pick political battles at the State House, where local officials are reliant on legislative approval for changes big and small.

While Wu has had some success, such as helping realize a dramatic expansion of liquor licenses in the city and getting her own appointee on the MBTA board, Boston has far less control over its own fate in the State House than other major cities across the country.

Tom Menino, the late and longest-serving Boston mayor, used to call members of the city’s legislative delegation to the mayor’s residence at the Parkman House or into his office overlooking Faneuil Hall to talk through his legislative agenda.

In his memoir, Menino recounted “haranguing” resistant state legislators to support in-district charter schools: “I put on my hot-under-the-collar act.”

“Hanging up on one rep, I told my press secretary Dot Joyce, ‘I’ll bet I gave him brown pants!’ " he wrote.

Former mayor Martin J. Walsh, who served in the State House from 1997 to 2014, ran a similar ground game as mayor, with the insider knowledge of a veteran legislator. But even he had setbacks, too, fighting unsuccessful battles to secure ambitious tenant protections, protect seniors from being displaced due to rent hikes, and move revenue to help fund Boston Public Schools.

Neither Menino nor Walsh played their cards like Wu has, however, in backing upstart challengers to sitting Democratic state lawmakers.

“You can point a finger at the Legislature and say, ‘I tried my hardest, but these people wouldn’t budge.’ You can work back channels and find a compromise,” said Keith Mahoney, who served as City Hall’s director of state relations under Menino. “Or you can stick to your guns and refile the bill and try a different approach.”

Boston lawmakers also view Wu differently than they did Menino or Walsh, said Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who was first elected in 2010. Menino and lawmakers had a “father-son” relationship where he “pushed hard on us” to pass his legislation, he said, while Walsh felt like more of an “older brother” with the experience on Beacon Hill.

“She is making things harder in the Senate by running people against senators. It puts us all in the box when she does that,” he said. “The culture in the Legislature isn’t to go against your colleagues. . . . She doesn’t understand that.”

Senator Lydia Edwards, a Wu ally and former Boston city councilor, openly wondered if Wu’s endorsements constitute “normal politics” or “a division that can’t be mended.”

To be sure, the mayor’s not writing off all Beacon Hill incumbents being challenged in their primaries this year.

In January, she endorsed Senator Mike Rush, a moderate West Roxbury Democrat facing a progressive primary challenger in Hyde Park attorney Persis Yu. The race marks Rush’s first primary challenge since 2008.

While Wu has faced uphill battles in the Senate, the House is a different story. Speaker Ron Mariano, a Quincy Democrat; Michlewitz of the North End; and the chamber’s majority leader, Mike Moran of Brighton, all live in Greater Boston, and have had longstanding relationships with the mayor. In the Senate, Spilka is from Ashland in the MetroWest region, and Senate budget chief Michael Rodrigues is from Westport, near the Rhode Island border.

Wu said that in her experience, it’s not geography, but added that House lawmakers have shown more interest in collaborating. On the property tax issue, she said she personally called all 40 state senators.

“There was outright rejection or silence,” she said.

For the first time in years, a vast majority of Boston’s public pools will be open this season, providing a free space for families to cool off as the summer heat approaches.

This comes as the city has spent millions in recent years to fix and clean up neighborhood pools — some of which closed for multiple summers — and as the Wu administration expands free youth swim lessons.

“This has been a major project over the last five years. When our administration started, there was a lot of work that we had to dig out from,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Monday at the Hennigan Community Center Pool reopening. “Some of them, the pools had been kept going much longer than they should have been.”

Last year, nine of the city’s 20 pools were closed for repairs or renovations. This summer, six of them will be closed: Mirabella Pool, Blackstone, Holland, Curtis Hall, Leahy-Holloran, and Mildred Avenue.

Among the six closed pools, operated by Boston Centers for Youth and Families, four — Mirabella in the North End, Blackstone in the South End, Curtis Hall in Jamaica Plain, and Holland in Dorchester — are closed for unspecified repairs.

Leahy-Holloran in Dorchester is closed during construction at the adjacent Richard J. Murphy K-8 School, and the Mildred Avenue pool in Mattapan is expected to open sometime in July.

For residents not close to a city pool, Boston currently has some 70 splash pads spread throughout the city for kids to cool off.

Prompted by concerns over some of the city’s public pool conditions, the Boston City Council is holding a virtual hearing Monday on the “conditions, operations and access” to BCYF pools.

Last month, the city reopened the Hennigan pool in Jamaica Plain, which had been closed for years due to maintenance issues and renovations. Its nearly six-year closure sparked community protests, as residents pushed for the repair and reopening of the natatorium, which primarily serves the largely Latino and Black Hyde Square community.

On Monday, Mayor Wu took a dip in the refurbished pool, which was fitted with new gutters, ventilation systems, and floor tiles, among other improvements.

“It’s really because of years of advocacy, feedback, and community participation in shaping all the different parts of this that now, the Hennigan is back and better than ever,” Wu said at the pool’s reopening celebration.

Two years ago, Wu also attended the opening of Clougherty pool in Charlestown — a pool that had closed for a two-year renovation. Before its remodeling, the pool had a faulty filtration system, sizzling concrete that burned to the touch, and a leaking tank. Post-renovation, residents likened it to a country club.

Reaffirming the mayor’s commitment to expanding access to swimming, the city announced in June a collective grant of over $100,000 to 11 nonprofits to cover free swimming lessons for Boston’s youth.

Expanding access to swimming lessons and free community pools could be a matter of life or death for some children. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, drowning is the leading cause of death for children under 5.

Eryn-Ashlei Bailey of the Jamaica Plain Neighborhood Council said community pools are especially important in disadvantaged communities.

“Other students are advantaged in that they have access to private swim clubs where they can practice during school breaks, school vacations, summer vacations,” Bailey said.

And then there’s the matter of the sweltering summer weather, Bailey said.

“The question becomes, if we didn’t have this pool, if we didn’t have this resource, how would people cool off in the really, really hot weather?” Bailey said.
