The Spotlight report revealed that MassHousing executive Tony Richards II awarded the bulk of the $2.4 million available in the Gateway Housing Rehabilitation Program to developers Gary Acquah and Reginald Woods just months after the duo sold Richards a house in West Roxbury. Records show Richards purchased the home for $204,000 less than the original list price.

Richards, a former aide to Governor Charlie Baker who serves as vice chair of an advisory council created by Healey, failed to disclose his relationship with the developers when he doled out the grants, a likely violation of state ethics laws.

MassHousing officials initially told the Globe that Richards wasn’t aware the grants were going to the same men who sold him his house. They said he alerted his bosses to the conflict when he realized it about a year later. But emails reviewed by the Globe Spotlight Team showed Richards interacting with Acquah and Woods in the months before and after the home purchase.

MassHousing officials have acknowledged the contradiction but have not said whether they believe Richards lied to them.

The developers’ work on properties in Pittsfield and Worcester had come under scrutiny from MassHousing officials in 2024, after inspections revealed that repairs had been poorly done or, in some cases, not done at all. The agency asked the developers to make several fixes and warned them they might no longer be eligible for grants.

But the Globe found Acquah and Woods submitted fake invoices bearing the names of at least nine contractors who told the Globe they never did the work attributed to them — apparent fraud that MassHousing failed to detect when it paid the bills. Following questions from the Spotlight Team, the agency announced an internal investigation by the Mintz firm into the Gateway Cities program and others under Richards’ purview.

Agency officials have declined to offer a timeline for when that review will be complete. Lawyers from the Mintz firm have already begun interviewing MassHousing employees at the agency’s Beacon Hill offices.

The Globe has repeatedly sought comment from Acquah, Woods, Richards, and Richards’s attorney. To date, none has responded.

Richards remains employed at MassHousing, where he earns a salary of $255,000 as vice president of strategic community investments. A spokesperson for the agency said the oversight of grants in his department has been taken over by the legal department while the outside review is underway.

Acquah, meanwhile, resigned from the board of the Community Economic Development Assistance Corporation when the Globe began asking questions about his dealings with MassHousing. CEDAC is a quasi-state nonprofit housing agency whose members are appointed by the governor.

Healey declined to comment on whether she will keep Richards as vice chair of her Advisory Council on Black Empowerment, a position she named him to shortly after she took office.

The Globe’s findings alarmed Representative Rodney Elliott, a Lowell Democrat and sponsor of pending legislation that would reshape the board at MassHousing and trigger a review of the agency’s spending of public money on affordable and low-income housing in the Gateway Cities. Elliott filed his bill before the Spotlight Team published its findings, but said the Globe report highlights an urgent need for “more oversight of the processes at MassHousing.”

“A full audit is required of all programs,” he said. “The more open, the more transparent the programs are, the better.”

Mintz, the firm conducting the review for MassHousing, has its own longstanding connections with MassHousing. Colin McNiece, the agency’s chief legal and operating officer, worked at Mintz for 11 years before joining MassHousing in 2019. Mintz has also served as bond counsel for the agency’s multifamily housing programs for more than 30 years, according to the firm’s website. Mintz helped the agency issue more than $1.3 billion in bonds over the last two decades.

For the Mintz audit to have real value, DiZoglio said, it’s important it be truly independent and open to public inspection, not subject to attorney-client privilege — citing as an example of the latter the report the Baker administration commissioned on the mismanagement at the Holyoke Soldiers Home that led to 76 deaths amid the pandemic. In that case, Baker’s office was the client of the firm of lawyer Mark Pearlstein, raising questions about whether Pearlstein was working for the governor or the public.

The Globe has requested a copy of MassHousing’s contract or letter of engagement with Mintz, but has yet to receive it. A spokesperson for the agency could not provide information about the cost of the contract, the timeline, or whether any of the firm’s findings would be privileged.

“Better late than never, I guess you could say,” said Ben Hires, chief executive of the Boston Chinatown Neighborhood Center, a group that helped spearhead that 2021 report.

Hires is among the advocates who feel that casinos have an oversized marketing presence in Asian communities in the state. He hopes the audit will provide data that will shape policymaking around the issue.

“Let’s get it out on the table,” said Hires. “A report versus an opinion is obviously very powerful.”

Thomas Mills, a spokesman for the Gaming Commission, said the agency is “committed to advancing knowledge through its annual research agenda, which has produced nearly 100 pieces of research to inform Massachusetts policymaking.”

Regarding the audit, Mills said, “The goal of this research is to produce an independent examination of how operators advertise and what role the Commission may have to regulate these practices.”

Locally, the marketing push from casinos includes huge billboards in the heart of Chinatown advertising pop stars from Hong Kong and Taiwan performing at local casinos. Casino shuttles also stop frequently near Boston’s Chinatown Gate to whisk residents away to gamble.

Other casino outreach includes sending regular postcards to their frequent customers, buying large advertisements in local Asian-language newspapers, and setting up booths at cultural festivals.

A Globe investigation published earlier this year found that 52 times a day, Encore’s 32-seat buses arrive like clockwork near the Chinatown gateway. And several times a day, a 60-seat bus operated by Bally’s Twin River snakes through Chinatown and four other Greater Boston areas with high percentages of Asians — Dorchester, Quincy, North Quincy, and Malden.

An analysis of shuttle routes with Census tract data showed that the Encore and Bally’s shuttles stop in areas with some of the highest concentrations of Asians, including neighborhoods where more than 40 percent of the population is of Asian descent.

Messages left with Massachusetts casinos, Bally’s in Rhode Island, and Foxwoods and Mohegan in Connecticut were not immediately returned on Wednesday.

Previously, an Encore spokesperson said in a written statement that its “shuttle program is deployed based upon demonstrated ridership demand,” and each shuttle posts information on responsible gambling.

The Globe also reported that casinos entice Asian patrons to gamble more by offering free and frequent transit to the gambling halls and often bait patrons with loans, sometimes in excess of six figures. They then use hardball tactics to squeeze those who fail to pay up.

Specifically, Asian Americans represent a disproportionate share of casino patrons being sued by casinos for unpaid debts, the Globe found. For instance, more than 80 percent of those sued by Encore since its opening in 2019 for gambling debts are people of Asian descent.

For their part, casinos in New England said they cooperate with state and local law enforcement to ensure their properties comply with all gaming regulations. And though they declined to elaborate on their marketing strategies, casino officials said courting Asian customers is simply a smart business strategy.

The Gaming Commission’s audit request was posted on July 1. After a researcher is identified, the study will be conducted and a report, subject to peer review, developed. That report will ultimately be presented to the commission, according to officials.

The commission does not have jurisdiction over operators licensed in other states, and some of the casino gambling outreach and marketing in Boston’s Chinatown is from out-of-state operators, such as Bally’s, Mohegan, or Foxwoods. It’s unclear what the commission could do to curb such marketing efforts that originate from outside the state if they were found to be problematic.

Mills, the commission spokesman, said the agency is “mindful of the First Amendment” when it comes to policymaking.

It’s also unclear how much the audit could cost the commission. The agency’s research agenda for fiscal year 2027 is estimated to be $2.7 million.

There are already rules in Massachusetts restricting in-state casino operators from advertising false and misleading information, from advertising directly to minors, as well as people who have excluded themselves from gambling marketing.

The enforcement of illegal gambling, which flourishes in Boston’s Chinatown and in other Asian communities like Quincy, is outside the commission’s jurisdiction. The scope of the audit would not feature the underground gambling dens that the Globe found are commonplace in those communities.

On this second episode of PATRIOTISM IS A VERB, Pressley discusses the verbs that are most patriotic to her: things like lawmaking, protest, and dissent. She also talks about the ways Black people have pushed America to be better since its founding.

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the July 9 episode of “Say More.”

Anna Kusmer: On Friday, two New Yorkers, two stark messages about the country on its big birthday.

Mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani, and U.S. President Donald Trump. It’s like these two guys are having a boss battle for the soul of America. And it does feel like a battle, doesn’t it?

That’s the mess and the majesty of American democracy. It is the battleground for America’s soul, and the battle can be between the left and the right, but it can also be between activists and lawmakers.

I think at its most robust, democracy is rife with engaged activists reacting to the ways the country is falling short of its ideals.

This is “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Anna Kusmer. This three-part series is called “Patriotism is a Verb.” It’s a journey through my feelings of despair for my country to something else, some version of patriotism.

When thinking about the verbs of patriotism, democracy encapsulates so many: voting, lawmaking, campaigning. It’s so cliché, but I really try to remember not to lose sight of how lucky we are to have this system, as imperfect as it may be. And voting is important, but I think activists are the real engine of change.

There’s this moment from 2013 when President Barack Obama was giving a speech about immigration reform in San Francisco. From the risers behind the president, a man was yelling about record-high deportations happening under Obama. Obama asked security to let the protesters stay.

In the end, the immigration bill Obama spent years trying to pass died in Congress, and Obama shifted entirely to executive action, including more protections for Dreamers, undocumented people who came to the United States as kids. So I think those protesters were right to shout at Obama, and I’m glad he let them stay. I think Obama was right that reform takes more than shouting. But I also think the shouting helped push Obama to do more.

And of course, activism exists on the left and right side of the political divide, and within parties. I may not agree with the values of the right, but I do respect their right to protest. I want to believe that in a robust, self-realized society, the values of justice and equality will win out. For the second episode of “Patriotism is a Verb,” I knew I wanted to talk to a lawmaker who also embodies the spirit of activism.

Ayanna Pressley: We should hold elected officials accountable, but it’s not for us just to make demands. We have to do our part, too. And so part of that relationship, that symbiotic partnership, begins at that ballot box, but it doesn’t end there.

Kusmer: When I told Massachusetts Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley the idea for my series, she got it right away.

Pressley: I do believe it is a practice. It is a verb. Patriotism ultimately is something that exists not because of the legacy and history of this country, but in spite of it.

Kusmer: Pressley lives and breathes the values of democracy. She literally sells T-shirts on her website that say, “Policy is my love language.”

Lucky for her, she grew up in Chicago in the 1970s and 1980s, a hotbed of inspiring politicians.

Pressley: Growing up in Chicago exposed me to the likes of the Rev. Jesse Jackson and Harold Washington, the first Black mayor elected in the city of Chicago.

Female mayors to Black mayors, to ultimately Illinois’ election of the first Black woman elected to the United States Senate in Carol Moseley Braun.

Kusmer: But like so many children, her number one political role model was at home.

Pressley: If I’m being honest, my president was always my mother.

Kusmer: Pressley’s early worldview swirled around her mom, Sandra Pressley, and her neighborhood in Chicago, which was centered around mutual aid and Black pride.

Pressley: My first coloring books, my first flag that I ever had a relationship with was the Pan-African flag. My coloring books as a child were produced by “The Chicago Defender,” our Black newspaper. I was coloring in the images of children with Afros with solidarity fists raised.

Kusmer: Pressley says she got a great education at one of the best schools in Chicago, despite being one of the only Black students there. In U.S. history class, it was hard to feel proud of the country, considering nearly all the Founding Fathers owned slaves. When Pressley got a bit older, she developed her own ideas about what patriotism was all about.

Pressley: One of the most patriotic things I’ve ever bore witness to, that nearly brings me to tears every time I think about it, was Black custodians cleaning up the mess left behind by a white supremacist mob in the Capitol on the day of the insurrection.

We could not return to the House Chamber to finish our work. These so-called patriots that seized and stormed the Capitol to interrupt a peaceful transfer of power—so-called patriots, so-called. Those Black custodians cleaned up the mess left behind by this white supremacist mob, so my colleagues and I could return to that chamber and finish what we started. They’re patriots.

This is what it is to be in a relationship with America, which is why it feels like more of a situationship, that your heart breaks and in the same minute is made whole.

Because I can be laudatory about that, and acknowledge, that Black people have been the defenders of democracy, the architects of progress. They’ve been the patriots. Every time Black people are more free, everyone else benefits. Even when Black folks have not enjoyed our full citizenship, we have fought to liberate others. That is a fact. So I can stand on that history, on that business, and be patriotic and prideful about that.

But also, why did they have to clean? Why was the mess created in the first place? What those Black custodians did is as literal as it is metaphorical for our relationship with this country. We have been cleaning up the mess left behind by violent white supremacists, for everyone’s benefit. Their action made it possible for us to do our job, for everyone’s benefit.

Kusmer: One of Pressley’s favorite lines is, “Dissent is patriotic,” and I find her love of country completely sincere. And with that, I wondered how it must have felt when President Trump specifically called her out, along with other members of “the Squad” in Congress, accusing them of hating America. [He] never used any names, but we all knew who he was talking about.

Pressley: Of course I love this country, which is why I reserve the right to criticize it.

Again, patriotism is dissent. Because I agitate, because I organize, because I mobilize, because I litigate, because I legislate to get us closer to the promise and the ideals that we’ve espoused, to make them an actual practice.

See, people misunderstand righteous indignation, especially when it is coming from a bald Black woman. The righteous indignation that I display is rooted in a patriotism. It’s rooted in a radical love for humanity.

Kusmer: Yeah. For a lot of people who are on board with you about the idea of patriotism as dissent and these ways that you’re expressing patriotism, I think it’s still specifically really hard to celebrate July Fourth, a holiday that remembers the signing of the Declaration of Independence, which was only agreed upon because Northern states tabled the issue of abolition and let Southern states keep the institution of slavery.

I just think that’s really hard to celebrate. Do you struggle to celebrate July Fourth? Do you think about it differently?

Pressley: I didn’t need the federal government to make Juneteenth a federal holiday to celebrate it. I’ve been celebrating it for decades. We’ve been celebrating it for generations in Franklin Park, in Roxbury, which has its own patriotic history.

So I think Juneteenth has always been more, from a celebratory standpoint. [It’s been] my, our, July Fourth.

It’s a celebration of emancipation and freedom, and acknowledging the history of my ancestors and a more accurate telling of our history. I think against the backdrop of what’s happening right now, that is especially true.

Kusmer: You’re saying that Juneteenth is much more of a celebration for you than July Fourth. That makes me wonder what your relationship is with America 250 as even a milestone. Is that something that—

Pressley: Well, I told you I’m in a situationship with this country. So what happens when you’re in a situationship? We’re not gonna all sit here and pretend we’ve never been in a situationship. We thought it was a relationship, but it was a situationship. And so when people would ask you, ‘Are you in a relationship? Are you dating anyone?’ What would you say? ‘It’s complicated.’

So when it comes to America 250, it’s complicated. It’s complicated. The fact that I can, again, practice dissent is in and of itself a tribute to the freedoms I enjoy in this country, that I’m the beneficiary of. It is a testament and a celebration of the founding of our country that I can do that.

But that’s why I can say I’m “free-ish.” The fact that I can vote, the fact that I can own property, the fact that I can open my own bank account, the fact that I do have bodily autonomy, the fact that I could run for public office. That is proof of a level of freedom.

But I’ll say I’m “free-ish” because of the attacks on Black bodies, Black workers, Black voters, Black power, and Black progress. The way to undo centuries of harm, to disrupt that, is through lawmaking. We know what it is to experience in real time, in a residual way, legislated hurt and harm. I know we can legislate equity, healing, and justice. So the next 250 have to look different.

Kusmer: I’m trying to put this all together. Tell me if I’m wrong, but it seems like America 250 for you is not necessarily gonna be this big happy party, but it is a time to reflect on the country and on this complicated relationship you have with American patriotism, American history, the American project. Is that right?

Pressley: Though my first introduction to a flag was a Pan-African flag, because of my mother and that coloring book produced by “The Chicago Defender,” a Black newspaper, I also am a Fannie Lou Hamer Democrat who said, “The blood of my ancestors is drenched in that American flag,” that red, white, and blue. So I also deserve to claim that.

Little piece of history if you didn’t know: The Juneteenth flag was created by a Boston Roxbury artist, Ben Haith. Boston Ben.

And it was controversial to some that he chose to use the colors red, white, and blue in that flag. It’s a star to represent Texas, the Lone Star. It’s bursting. It’s like a nova to speak to a new horizon, freedom and a future. But he uses red, white, and blue in that design because this is stolen land, a country built by stolen hands. So we have every right to that flag, to that patriotism.

Kusmer: When you say, ‘Stolen land, stolen hands,’ that is so upsetting. It’s such an upsetting, true, but upsetting framing of American history.

But there’s so much to celebrate, too, in terms of the freedom fighting and the progress. So are these moments for you all about sort of not turning away from either truth about America in these moments of reflection?

Pressley: Yeah, I mean, embrace the whole truth, our whole history, as complicated as it is. And we shouldn’t shy away from that, not at all. Again, what is controversial about the truth? That is the truth. This is the season of “call a thing a thing,” if nothing else.

The thing is, violence is not something that can be contained. The harm in this moment is coming for everyone, and that is exactly why the path forward to survive and for the work of reconstruction is solidarity.

You cannot see attacks on majority-Black seats being represented by Black members of Congress or the defense of voting rights — all of this that we’re managing when it comes to the racial gerrymandering of districts, the attacks to disenfranchise and silence Black voters and voices — as just a fight for Black people to take on or just for Black people in the South to take on.

You can’t see the fight to extend temporary protected status as just a fight for immigrants’ rights advocates and our immigrant neighbors to take on. You can’t see attacks on bodily autonomy as just something for women to take on. It must be the work of all of us. We have to have a stakeholder in one another’s freedom.

That is the ultimate patriotism: to be in pursuit of each other’s collective safety, dignity, and the centering of each other’s humanity so that we can all experience our full citizenship. I want everybody to be free. And I am audacious enough in my radical dreaming to believe it is possible. And that is patriotism. That’s how I show up with it. That’s how I practice it.

I love this country, and so I reserve the right to criticize it and to do the work and to agitate to get it to live up to its promise.

Kusmer: Yeah. It’s an act of love.

Pressley: It is an act of love. It is an act of patriotism.

Kusmer: Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley is the U.S. representative for Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District.

Pressley: That’s right. Respect on my name. The MA 7th.

Kusmer: Congresswoman Pressley, it is such an honor to speak with you about this topic. Thank you so much for coming in and for taking the time.

Pressley: Thank you.

Kusmer: Next week on “Patriotism is a Verb.”

“The next morning we woke up, and our phones were red hot,” said Fergus, who, along with the rest of the crew, hails from Kilmarnock in southwestern Scotland. Back home, friends were feverishly sending them the viral video and laughing at their newfound internet fame.

Perriello, who lives with his wife, Karen, his daughter, and their three grandchildren in Dracut, only became aware that his houseguests were blowing up on social media when his son called him.

“He says, ‘Have you seen social media?’ I said, ‘No, why?’ And he says, ‘Your guests in Wakefield are all over social media right now,” Perriello, who works as the Wakefield Highway Supervisor, recalled.

Perriello has had the Wakefield Airbnb for nine years, and also has rental properties on Lake Winnipesaukee and in Old Orchard Beach, Maine. Airbnb bookings around Boston have seen a boom this summer thanks to the World Cup and Tall Ships event. Some neighborhoods in and around the Boston area, such as East Somerville, Dorchester, and downtown Newport, recorded the largest year-over-year growth in bookings — with Dorchester up 122% as of early June, according to Airbnb.

Perriello said Fergus and his group were the only guests who told him they booked his Airbnb specifically for the World Cup.

Recognizing that it was Morrison who made them go viral, the Scots soon spotted him across the street, and invited him over for an 8 a.m. beer. He had to work, but ended up joining the crew later. The next morning, he fired up the grill and welcomed them over for sausage, peppers, and onions. In the days that followed, neighbors would stop by with beer and Rice Krispies Treats and knock on the door to say hello to the visitors, asking questions about Scotland and their heritage. The men handed out small Scottish flags and hats to the neighborhood children and welcomed the residents to the yard. And whenever they left the house, they were welcomed everywhere they went.

“Anywhere we went — into a coffee shop, a cafe, a restaurant, a bar — it was just a complete welcome from everybody. The best part about it is that once they got to know us in the Tartan Army and that we were actually just here for a good time, they all started joining in,” said Lewis.

Across Greater Boston, the Tartan Army’s presence was met with joy and enthusiasm, leading Mayor Michelle Wu to sign a letter of intent to establish Boston and Glasgow, Scotland, as sister cities.

The crew attended the Scotland-Haiti game in Foxborough, which they called an “electric experience.” But when they weren’t watching the matches, they immersed themselves in the intricacies of Massachusetts life. They drank coffee at Dunkin’ and were shocked by the size of the SUVs on the roads. (“We don’t have cars that size on our roads over here,” said Neil.) They discovered that a trip to the grocery store didn’t mean you could buy any alcohol you want. And when it came to Massachusetts haute cuisine, they were particularly enthralled with the delicacy that is North Shore roast beef sandwiches topped with American cheese.

As for Morrison, who works in communications for an academic health system, opening up his home to the visitors across the street was just the beginning of a journey. After going viral online, a generous member of the Tartan Army messaged him and shared she was in town for the game and wanted to gift him a ticket to the Morocco-Scotland match in Foxborough. The morning of the game, the Scots again came over for breakfast and visited with Morrison, his wife, and their three sons. He later found himself sporting a kilt in Miami after Airbnb thanked him with a trip to the Scotland-Brazil match.

“The last two weeks have just been absurd,” said Morrison.

Perriello didn’t get to spend any time with the Scots. But seeing his Wakefield neighborhood come together still makes him smile.

“Especially where the world is right now, it’s nice to get everybody together in a happy moment,” he shared, noting that the Scots left a sweet parting gift in the Airbnb.

“They did leave me a nice bottle of Scotch,” said Perriello.

▪ A recent change by the National Federation of High School State Associations that expands the permitted bat weights for high school players is sparking controversy. The NFHS unveiled several major rule changes for baseball and softball, including an oversized (18 inch) bag for first base that can be used instead of the double bag, which will be required in 2027, and softball pitchers can now wear one-way communication devices to hear from coaches in their dugout.

But the most controversial is allowing bats with a “drop weight” of minus-4, minus-5, and minus-6 starting in 2028, which means a bat can weigh up to six ounces less than its number of inches. For example, a 31-inch bat can weigh as little as 25 ounces. Previously, the drop weight was only minus-3.

“Expanding the available drop-weight options provides younger and developing players with additional opportunities to build proper mechanics, confidence and skills while maintaining the safety and performance standards expected in education-based athletics,” said Elliot Hopkins, director of sports and liaison to the NFHS Baseball Rules Committee.

While the MIAA plays under NFHS rules for the most part, it does allow sports to make their own modifications. Look for the new bat weights to be discussed at the next MIAA baseball committee meeting in the fall.

All the hard-earned wisdom of his elders wasn’t enough to save him. Neither was his own hard work and ambition. He had a college degree, a well-paying job, and a legion of supporters rooting for his continued success.

Despite decades of progress placing Boston among the safest major cities in the country, a violent Fourth of July weekend reopened old wounds. Two young men died and 11 other people were injured in five separate shootings, prompting immediate outcry from elected officials and community leaders alike. The holiday served as a painful reminder that gun violence remains a devastating force, its impacts heavily concentrated in historically underserved communities.

“When you look around, you’ll see soldiers that have done a lot of time, that have a lot of experience. And we’re the ones we need to turn to in these times,” said Stanley Greene, a longtime friend of Washington-Conway’s father who addressed a crowd of mourners Wednesday night in Dorchester’s Grove Hall neighborhood.

“We can’t allow these losses to take the fuel and allow us to self-destruct,” he said. “When we talk about breaking generational curses, this is how it starts.”

A therapist who earned a master’s degree in social work after struggling with addiction and other challenges, Greene had a clear message for the younger generation: “The antidote can’t be revenge” — even when hopelessness starts to creep in, even when it seems like you’re fighting a losing battle in an environment you can’t escape.

While he encouraged peace and healing, Greene said it’s no coincidence that violence is still concentrated in Boston’s Black neighborhoods, where tragedy so often hits close to home.

“Policies are the reason behind a lot of the challenges we’re dealing with,” he said.

Shootings in Boston used to be a lot more common. Between 1985 and 1995, the city recorded on average 97 homicides per year, with a peak of 143 in 1990, according to federal crime data analyzed by the nonprofit Murder Accountability Project.

Overall, the city has experienced a drastic drop in gun violence since then. Police have recorded nine fatal shootings so far in 2026, compared to 12 at this time last year.

But the numbers lose meaning in certain neighborhoods where crime is more common, residents say.

The other weekend homicide victim was Washington-Conway’s cousin, according to relatives. Police identified him as Travis Deonard Washington, 24, who was killed after gunfire broke out in the 500 block of Blue Hill Avenue shortly after midnight Sunday. Attempts to reach his immediate family were not successful.

“A lot of problems in our community are systemic. They put us in the condition that we’re in,” said Randy Muhammad of the Dorchester-based group 10,000 Fearless Peacemakers, also speaking during the memorial.

In the aftermath of the violence, local leaders quickly demanded a comprehensive response, including additional police officers on the streets and increased funding for anti-violence organizations.

While more affluent neighborhoods benefit from robust public safety resources and ample attention from local media and other stakeholders, residents of Dorchester, Roxbury, and Mattapan often find themselves overlooked, said Renee Callender, a retired Boston police detective who now runs the nonprofit Promoting Conflict Resolution, Inc.

“That’s the perception,” she said. “It feels like a lot of lip service, but what are we actually doing to help these families?”

Leaders of the city’s largest police union have long complained they’re hundreds of officers short. They said the events of last weekend exposed a full-blown staffing crisis as officers found themselves “outnumbered on the street.”

The police were facing a heavy call volume, especially after midnight Sunday.

Police Commissioner Michael Cox described a series of large late-night gatherings “involving both fireworks and firearms,” which he said have “no place in our city.”

The first shooting was reported around 12:30 a.m. in Dorchester, where four people were injured, one fatally. About an hour later, officers were trying to gain control of an unruly crowd, also in Dorchester, when disorderly revelers threw fireworks at them, according to a police report.

The Roxbury shooting unfolded around 3:15 a.m. Neighbors described a festive, raucous block party that devolved suddenly into chaos and terror as people ran for their lives. One resident told the Globe that she had previously called the police multiple times about noise complaints as the party continued into the early morning hours, but a dispatcher responded that officers were busy.

No arrests have been announced in the shootings, and police haven’t publicly identified any motives.

While the area around downtown and the Charles River Esplanade was adequately staffed for the Saturday night fireworks show, other districts needed more officers, said Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association. Instead, the strategy was “gambling that they can borrow officers from another station when they run out,” he said.

Calderone argued that recent reductions in overtime spending have exacerbated the problem. Department leadership has refuted that claim, saying there’s “no correlation between overtime and crime.”

During an appearance Wednesday on GBH’s Boston Public Radio, Mayor Michelle Wu said she and Cox believe the department is appropriately staffed. She also noted that homicides are down compared to last year. But, she said, “no matter how low a number is, any incident of violence is unacceptable in our city.”

“The hardest and heaviest part of my job is speaking to families who have gone through unthinkable loss,” she said.

City officials often tout a holistic approach to crime-fighting, which means addressing the root causes of violence and investing in impacted neighborhoods.

Washington-Conway was doing his part to change the narrative, making his community proud, loved ones said.

He played basketball at Charlestown High School, where he made lifelong friends. He later graduated from the College of St. Joseph, a small Catholic school in Vermont that’s since closed. He was among the last graduating class in 2019. A photo in the Rutland Herald newspaper features Washington-Conway waving to his family during commencement, looking sharp in a black cap and gown, his beard freshly trimmed, glasses perched on his nose.

After college, he started working for the MBTA, helping to monitor and maintain the tracks. He was making good money and enjoyed the work, his family said.

An amateur rapper, he recently released a music video under the rap name BIG BABY 6IIX.

He was most at home on the basketball court. He joined a local men’s summer league several years ago. His enthusiasm and dedication quickly made him stand out, said Coach James Webb, who helped establish the John Winthrop Basketball League in Dorchester.

“He was our gentle giant,” he said. “Some guys you just don’t see God taking away.”

Well over 6 feet tall, Washington-Conway was always easy to spot in a crowd, loved ones said.

“He was tall but soft,” said Jacque Jackson, a (notably shorter, he admitted) friend from high school. Smiling at the memory, he tilted his head skyward to demonstrate their difference in height. The two had recently reconnected in the neighborhood and enjoyed reminiscing about old times, Jackson said.

“Sometimes our environment gets the best of us,” Washington-Conway’s father, Chris Conway, said at the memorial.

Conway, a substance abuse counselor who runs a behavioral health nonprofit, also grew up in Grove Hall. He said his own father was killed before he was born. He spent his youth “running these streets,” before turning his life around and going back to school. He wanted to set a positive example for his son.

House lawmakers are now looking to sweeten the deal in an effort to bring more blockbusters (and the jobs they create) to the Bay State.

Tucked into the policy-packed economic development bill the House approved Wednesday night is a provision that would give filmmakers more breathing room to get some of their costs covered through the program, through which the state offers a 25 percent payroll credit for any project that spends more than $50,000 within Massachusetts.

Under current law, productions can only claim the payroll credit for work completed within a 12-month period. The proposal would extend that window by an additional year, a technical change with real recruiting value, industry experts say.

The current 12-month limit “has created issues for some productions who want to do post-production or visual effects here, who may choose not to because of the strict timeline,” said Chris O’Donnell, the business manager for IATSE Local 481, the union representing New England motion picture and studio mechanics. Extending the window to 24 months, as the House passed, could be particularly helpful for projects with longer timetables. (Think documentaries or TV series.)

Plenty of productions have already capitalized on the program in the past. Massachusetts has handed out millions in subsidies to multiple Academy Award nominees — a record-breaking $46.4 million tax credit to apocalyptic satire “Don’t Look Up,” in 2021 — and more than a few clunkers. The superhero flop, “Madame Web,” was made with the help of $23.7 million from Massachusetts taxpayers.

The pace appears slower in 2024, at least for now. The most recent available data show the state issued about $22.5 million in film tax credits for 2024, including roughly $4 million for “The Collaboration,” a yet-to-be-released drama about artists Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat, plus more than $2 million for the movie “Aftermath,” which was filmed in Chelsea and Weymouth. That number could jump, however, since there are often applications still pending when the state releases its annual tax credit transparency report.

Supporters say the tax credits help pay for themselves by keeping production crews — and their paychecks — in Massachusetts. Extending the eligibility window would “enable projects to get finished and keep people here employed,” said Gary Crossen, the general manager of New England Studios.

There have also long been detractors of the program, charging it’s an inefficient use of taxpayer money. A state commission agreed in 2021, finding that the film tax credit program cost the state $100,000 per job created and concluding it was “not the best use of the state’s money.”

Lawmakers moved to extend it permanently that year, however, with some changes: The program also makes productions that spend more than 75 percent of their total budget in Massachusetts, or film at least 75 percent of the time in the state, eligible for a production credit and a sales tax exemption.

There’s no annual cap on the credit, and it’s transferable, allowing a production company to sell it to insurance companies, corporations, or even individuals.

State lawmakers now also want to credit where credits are due. The House also adopted an amendment during Wednesday’s debate that would require qualifying films to include a closing credit noting that the movie or show was “Proudly Made in Massachusetts,” alongside a logo designed and approved by the Massachusetts Film Office.

By Chloe Craft, Globe correspondent

Across from the iconic USS Constitution, a humble blue tent housed a wealth of maritime history curated by the Naval History and Heritage Command, much of it highlighting the rich seafaring culture of New England.

“A lot of people don’t know that all the wood [of the USS Constitution] is all grown in its own forest in Indiana. Those trees are still used to make repairs or replace any deteriorating or rotting wood,” said Kim Ortega, 34, outreach coordinator for the Museum of the American Soldier in Chicago, one of 10 official Navy museums operating under the Naval History and Heritage Command.

“Seeing the ship today reminds me how the Navy works so hard to maintain the structural integrity and the beauty and majesticness of the Constitution for folks in the community of Boston, if not internationally, to enjoy,” she said.

Along with engaging the old salts — an affectionate term for sage elder mariners — Ortega said she has had plenty of memorable interactions with younger visitors.

“We had two boys, maybe 4 or 5 years old, come over and start spitballing questions left and right,” she said, pausing to laugh and pointing to postcards bearing vintage images of tall ships set out on a table. “They took one of each and asked, ‘Why do the ships look like this? Where are they going? What happened to them?’”

One of the postcards is a grainy black-and-white photograph from a World War II era PT boat, featuring the crew and the particularly famous commanding officer posing shirtless. That officer? Then-Lieutenant John F. Kennedy.

“One of our very popular images on our free postcards has been shirtless JFK, back when he was on the PT 109,” said Navy conservator Isabel Lobley, 30, from Maine.

“We’ve been giving a lot of these out, especially as it relates to Boston and Massachusetts. Everyone is like, ‘Is that JFK?’ And I say, ‘Yes, yes it is.’ You ought to take one too.”

The Naval History and Heritage Command pop-up will be in Charlestown Navy Yard, across from the USS Constitution, through Thursday.

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

For Robert Graves, 16, who sails for Nantucket High School, getting the chance to work on — and even steer — the 122-foot schooner Lynx is definitely a major upgrade.

The Lynx is a 2001 wooden ship that regularly commutes between its home port in Nantucket and Georgia, her crew said. Compared to some other ships in this year’s lineup, the Lynx doesn’t need assistance to be moved by another vessel and largely does all of its own sailing.

That means it needs more hands, too, like Graves.

He is part of a program through Egan Maritime Institute that helps get students on board sailing vessels like Lynx. It’s an interpretation based on a 19th century privateer that evaded the Royal Navy during the War of 1812.

“Part of our main mission is getting kids out on the water and getting them to see what they can do with their own two hands,” said crew member Nina Schiefelbein, 23.

Grave will be joining the crew for the next few days, his third time working on the Lynx, he said.

“It’s a great experience. I never thought I’d see this many tall ships all at once,” he said. “It’s kind of like a surreal moment.”

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe staff

Passengers at Boston’s Logan International Airport got their own taste of the tall ships.

The height of some of the ships passing the end of major runways at the airport caused “temporary” delays, said a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Port Authority, the quasi-public agency that runs the airport.

“The delay program has ended,” the spokesperson said just after 4:30 p.m.

There were 325 delays at Logan as of 4:30 p.m., according to the flight tracker FlightAware.

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

As a volunteer liaison, Pat Cogan, 62, of Milton, will spend this week helping the crew of the tall ship Virginia settle in their Charlestown Navy Yard port.

He boarded the Virginia just after it docked to tell its passengers where they could go in the Navy Yard to use the bathroom or do laundry. He will also help control how many people board the ship at once when it opens to visitors.

Cogan said he retired a couple of years ago and has been looking for opportunities to take part in interesting events.

“I thought it was going to be a historic event and I just wanted to be a part of it,” he said. “I tried to volunteer for FIFA in Gillette, but didn’t make it. I’m trying to find things that I find interesting.”

Cogan does not consider himself a “boat person,” and clarified that he has no sailing experience.

“But I’ve always found these tall ships so beautiful, so I just thought it would be fun to be part of.”

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

On the Virginia, a recreation of a 1608 ship of the same name, the crew gathered to debrief the morning’s sail.

“Everything worked out,” said JB Smith, the ship’s 82-year-old captain. “We didn’t hit anything, nobody hit us. We did what we came here to do: Boston 250.”

The ship’s journey from its home port of Bath, Maine, to Boston for Sail Boston 250 is the farthest it has traveled since its launch in 2022, according to Matt Blazek, the interim director of Maine’s First Ship, which operates the Virginia.

Now docked in the Charlestown Navy Yard’s Pier 6, the ship’s crew left Gloucester Friday morning and arrived in Boston last night, docking in the Seaport.

While most of the crew plans to stay overnight in an Airbnb in the North End, Smith plans to stay on the ship, sleeping on his air mattress in the hull, he said.

Sailors wore clothes designed to imitate what a 17th-century crew might have worn.

They donned linen shirts and short pants, handmade by volunteers for the ship’s operating organization, Maine’s First Ship. Frances South, 69, also wore a colorful sash and a small satchel, in which she kept a rigging knife that she said a “guy in Maine” also handmade for the crew.

For South, the clothes and the knife testify to the ship’s ability to bring volunteers into the fold. The Virginia, whose home port is in Bath, Maine, was launched in 2022 after an 11-year volunteer-led recreation project.

“There’s always a guy in Maine, a woman in Maine, who does these amazing things,” she said.

By Chloe Craft, Globe correspondent

“Fiți bineveniți!” shouted 30-year-old Christina Goran from Romania, grinning as she hoisted a billowing Romanian flag. In an aside, she added, “That’s ‘welcome’ in Romanian.”

More than 100 people crowded at the end of Pier 4 in Charlestown Navy Yard at 3:30 p.m. to celebrate the arrival of the Mircea, a towering tall ship which is designated the official vessel of the Romanian Navy. As a tugboat carefully guided it towards the landing, a line of around 50 sailors in crisp white uniforms raised their hats with a shout, met with a chorus of cheers from those gathered on shore.

“We are very eager to welcome our friends from Romania who took a six-month-long trip to come here and celebrate 250 years of America with us,” said Liliana Oniță-Lenco, 62, of Revere.

Oniță-Lenco explained that she led a group representing the Association of Romanians in New England to welcome the Tall Ship.

“We are very excited for this beautiful ship to join us,” she said, pausing to speak a few words in Romanian to a nearby friend, who handed her an American flag that she unfurled with a smile. “Romania and America, together today!”

Before Oniță-Lenco could say another word, some of the ship’s crew members waved, drawing out another enthusiastic cheer from the crowd.

By Chloe Craft, Globe correspondent

A crew of enthusiastic Polish cadet sailors turned Pier 4 at Charlestown Navy Yard into the port city of Gdynia, as they exchanged words in their native language from aboard the tall ship Dar Młodzieży with Boston’s Polish diaspora, who were standing on the shore.

The ship, which will be open to boarding starting Sunday, is based at Gdynia Maritime University, where it serves as a training vessel for Poland’s future sailors.

“I am very pleased they’ve come over, and I challenge any non-Pole to pronounce the name of their ship,” said third-generation Polish immigrant Jan Tkacz, 81, of Charlestown, who pointed to the letters on the side of the vessel and sounded out, “Dar Mwohd-zee-jey.”

Tkacz said he previously taught English in Gdansk, a city not far from Gdynia, but that it was “heartwarming” to hear Polish spoken between the crew and their supporters in the states.

Second-year cadet Frank Gepner, 20, said he was pleasantly surprised to meet so many Polish diaspora after preparing to put his English lessons into practice.

“We prepared to visit something different since United States is quite far from us, and especially for me, since it is the first time here,” Gepner said. “But it’s really nice to see our Polish brothers and sisters over here.”

By Bryan Hecht, Globe staff

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

With outstretched arms, Vivian Sanchez, 34, held up a red and white Peruvian flag as it unfurled with the breeze.

“Of course, we want to see all the tall ships, right? But me, especially, I want to see the one from my country, which is Peru,” Sanchez said. “I’m experiencing this amazing show [for] the first time in my life.”

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe staff

Between the foghorns and cannonades, spectators at Castle Island were treated to a non-stop parade of nautical themed music, booming from speakers mounted on the fort’s ramparts.

There were the obvious “sailing” hits: “Sailing” by Christopher Cross and “Sail On, Sailor,” by The Beach Boys. By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

Andrea Pinilla, 52, and her family watched as crew members of the Chilean ship Esmeralda prepared the vessel for visitors on Commonwealth Pier in Seaport.

She said they regularly visit the ship whenever it is in Boston, where she lives, as well as at its home port in Valparaíso.

The Esmeralda was part of multiple previous Boston tall ships festivals, but has a controversial history in Chile, said Pinilla, who runs the local group Comunidad Chilena de Boston.

According to Amnesty International, Esmeralda was used to imprison and torture political prisoners under the military dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet in the 1970s.

However, for Pinilla, the ship carries happier memories. Over the years they have gotten to know much of the crew. With her was Lynette Trujillo, whose husband Carlos Pizzaro works as a machine repair technician on the Esmeralda.

“[For us] it’s a beautiful thing,” Pinilla said.

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe staff

Once the tall ships make the turn into Boston Harbor, Ryan Stranz has roughly a minute — maybe two, if he’s lucky — to put his impressions of their sails down on paper. Dipping his brush into a vial of black ink, his split second brush strokes are like trying to catch lightning in a bottle.

“It’s only here for a second, so you’ve got to make a decision and put the ink down in the way that makes the most sense to you,” he said. “Otherwise the boat’s gone.”

Stranz, who runs an art studio in Somerville, said he’s used to large-scale oil paintings and figure drawing. But with black watercolor ink, he said he’s able to work quickly and capture “all of the expressive gestures exactly as I mean them.”

“This is the stern of one of these large boats, the three-masted giants,” he said, the sea breeze whipping through the canvases in his hands. “And then this is one of those smaller ones. It just has some beautiful lines to it. It kind of steals the show from the large one.”

After running out of canvas, Stranz turned to anything else he can put his brush on — cardboard boxes, printer paper, even a greasy Sullivan’s lobster roll wrapper.

“My soul feels full being out here,” he said.

By Bryan Hect, Globe correspondent

Dozens of ship watchers flocked to the observation deck on the top floor of the Institute of Contemporary Art in Seaport — away from the heat — taking in the vistas of ships passing and docking, and crowds on Fan Pier.

For David Moy, 67, of Wellesley, the deck offered a nice place to rest while waiting for the American ship Elissa to pass through Boston Harbor.

“That’s my daughter’s name, so we’re excited to see that one,” Moy said as he adjusted his binoculars.

Admission to the ICA is free for all on Saturday, and hundreds more people thronged the grandstand steps behind the museum to watch the parade in the building’s shadow.

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

Lou Jones, 80, had the picture perfect spot off the pier in East Boston. His camera, fit with a massive 600mm lens, was fixated right on the spot where the ships would emerge to the backdrop of the city.

Seeing that this is his fifth time visiting the passage of the Tall Ships, this is business as usual for Jones.

“I think it was more exciting then,” Jones said in reference to the 1976 Tall Ships event. At the time, he sailed on one of the ships from New York City to Boston.

“This is the first time I haven’t been on a ship for the Tall Ships’ visit,” Jones said. The Washington, D.C., native has been a photographer in Boston for the last 50 years. “I’ve done it so many times. I’m not going to say it’s boring, but I wanted to do it from a different kind of perspective.”

And a different perspective he got. The passing ships shored up memories from his experience back in 1976. Having seen the labor that crew members put into pulling the ropes as they tamed the wind with their sails, Jones thought back to his ancestors 300 years ago.

“It really shoved me back into history, and I think that that’s probably the most interesting part,” Jones said. “Literally having people sailing me, transporting me hundreds of miles on a ship that my forefathers sailed on just like that, that many years ago.”

By Thai Theodoro and Jaden Perry, Globe correspondents

Many spectators the Globe interviewed talked about how memorable the summer’s been, especially with the rareness of events such as the World Cup and, now, Sail Boston 2026.

“The history, the city, the charm with the World Cup and just everything all coming together — this is the coolest place to live,” Marissa Riveira, 40, of Winthrop, said at the Massport Marine Terminal.

Riveira attended Sail Boston in 1992 and 2017, but this year marks a first: bringing her two daughters, ages 5 and 11, to experience it for themselves. Riveira said she was most excited to introduce them to a piece of Boston’s history.

The scramble got us wondering: What happens if a major-party nominee exits at the last minute in Massachusetts?

The short-answer is, nothing quite like Maine. When lawmakers passed a law last year moving up this year’s primary date to Sept. 1, they also rewrote the timeline for replacing candidates who withdraw after the primary, at least for this specific year.

Under the 2025 law, candidates have until noon on Sept. 4 — the Friday after the primary — to withdraw or file an objection against a nominee with the secretary of state’s office. If a vacancy opens up, the nominee’s party can fill it through an executive committee whose membership is determined by its state committee. That committee then has until 5 p.m. on Sept. 8 — just a week after the primary — to submit a new certificate of nomination to the secretary of state.

Part of the compressed timeline is because of Massachusetts’ notoriously late primary date. With just nine weeks between the primary and the general election, there simply isn’t enough time to remake the November ballots before they have to go out to voters.

“There is a limited window to replace people, because it’s about ballot printing now,” Secretary of State William F. Galvin said.

The timeline has also only gotten tighter as Massachusetts has expanded voting by mail. Applications for mail-in ballots go out to voters 45 days before each statewide election.

“It’s a very tight window,” Galvin said.

Massachusetts just doesn’t have much room for the kind of replacement campaign now unfolding in Maine, where primary voters had their say in early June.

Still, that doesn’t mean parties in Massachusetts have never had to improvise.

In 1986, Republicans pushed businessman George Kariotis to enter the race for governor after two other candidates — Royall Switzler and Gregory Hyatt — ended their campaigns amid separate scandals. Switzler admitted to lying about his military record, while Hyatt was accused of “bizarre behavior” in the workplace, submitting fraudulent nomination signatures, and accepting cash from an organized crime figure.

But because the deadline to qualify for the ballot had already passed, Kariotis was left to run a write-in campaign. Kariotis advanced to the general election, despite earning fewer votes than both Switzler and Hyatt, according to records from Galvin’s office. The Republican State Committee then had to hold a post-primary vote to solidify his position as the nominee, the Globe reported at the time.

Such a mess, unsurprisingly, didn’t do the GOP any favors. Kariotis got trounced that November by incumbent governor Michael Dukakis.

Two decades earlier, Democrats faced an even more unexpected vacancy after state Auditor Thomas Buckley died of a heart attack on the eve of the 1964 primary while running unopposed. Members of the Democratic State Committee voted to replace him with Thaddeus Buczko, who won that November.

BALLOT WHIPLASH: That’s not to say Massachusetts isn’t having its own ballot turmoil this year, too.

Michael Walsh, the state Republican Party’s endorsed pick for attorney general, could end up on the GOP primary ballot after all despite “substantial evidence” that he submitted forged signatures to qualify, reports the Globe’s Chris Van Buskirk.

Walsh owed his technical court victory to snail mail. Judge Jeffrey T. Karp wrote in a court ruling Friday that the state Democratic Party official, Adam Roof, who originally challenged Walsh’s place on the ballot did not correctly submit his objection under state law, which requires it to be sent via registered or certified mail.

Roof instead sent it by email and through first-class mail.

Karp, however, ruled that Anne Manning Martin, another statewide candidate facing allegations of submitting fraudulent signatures, should not be reinstated to the ballot. Shawn Oliver, a fellow lieutenant governor candidate who challenged her place on the ballot, had “complied” with state law in submitting his objection, Karp wrote.

Walsh’s spot on the ballot isn’t official yet. Lawyers for the State Ballot Law Commission — which issued the initial ruling removing him from the ballot after determining that hundreds of signatures he submitted were likely fake — filed an appeal with the Supreme Judicial Court late on Friday, according to David Mackey, an attorney for the commission.

Any decision will have to happen fast. Galvin’s office had asked the lower court to rule by Wednesday to give officials enough time to prepare Republican primary ballots for local clerks to send to overseas and military voters by Saturday.

SIX-TH PAC: Outside money is officially starting to flow into the race to replace US Representative Seth Moulton in the Sixth District.

The New Leadership PAC, a super PAC with a stated mission of “electing Democrats who fight,” spent nearly $270,000 on digital advertising and “media production” in support of former White House aide Dan Koh, one of six Democrats running for the seat.

The PAC started spending in the race Thursday, according to federal campaign filings, the same day Koh’s campaign last updated its red box to suggest supportive groups run ads “starting immediately.” (A red box is a public webpage that allows the campaign to whisper to a super PAC while circumventing campaign finance rules barring coordination between the two.)

Boston-based Sports betting giant DraftKings is the New Leadership PAC’s top donor with a $250,000 donation from late May. James MacKay, a construction company owner who maxed out to Koh’s campaign last year and gave another $3,500 this year, also donated $25,000 to the PAC, and Peter Palandjian, the CEO of Intercontinental Real Estate Corp., and another Koh donor, gave $50,000.

New Leadership PAC has spent some money in other races, too, running ads opposing Texas Representative Julie Johnson, a Democrat, who lost the party’s nomination to former Representative Colin Allred in a runoff election in one of Texas’s newly redrawn districts in May. It also supported Brooke Pinto, who lost the race to become Washington, D.C.’s delegate in Congress.

JOB INSECURITIES: For Boston’s City Council staff, their jobs carry few protections or guarantees. by Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: For most employees of the city of Boston, the vast majority of whom are unionized, sick time, vacation days, and set salary ranges for their positions are a given. But for Boston City Council staffers, almost none of those basic employment conditions apply.

First, they are all technically considered temporary workers; both their employment and biweekly pay must be publicly reauthorized by the council roughly every three months. The 13 councilors are not required to provide even a minimum amount of paid time off. Staff also are not eligible for overtime. There are no salary minimums or set pay ranges for council staff.

That leaves nearly every aspect of each staffer’s job to be dictated by the personal preferences and priorities of the individual councilor, which current and former council staffers say can lead to deep disparities, open staff to mistreatment, and, in rare cases, create an environment for criminal wrongdoing.

We have been left without the permanent rapid rail transit infrastructure that other communities take for granted. A look at the MBTA map shows a wide swath of Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury with no rapid transit.

One can overlay maps of economic, environmental, and even educational inequality over this gap in the MBTA system. The lack of transit access has limited economic development and created more pollution for our residents.

Improvements to Blue Hill Avenue should never be conditional. Yet that is the choice being presented: Accept a plan for a center-running bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue, or continue waiting for long-overdue safety improvements. Routine infrastructure upgrades should not be used to pressure a community into accepting a proposal it has repeatedly opposed.

The absence of rail along Blue Hill Avenue is not an accident of geography. It is the product of decades of public policy that consistently underinvested in Boston’s Black and brown neighborhoods. In 1979, the MBTA studied expanding rapid transit to Nubian Square and along Blue Hill Avenue. Rather than advancing the project, planners prioritized investments elsewhere, such as Red and Green Line extensions and commuter rail expansions. Whether judged by the standards of the day or today’s understanding of equity, the result is unmistakable: Generations of residents were left without the rapid transit service other communities received.

An Orange Line branch, beginning at Ruggles, traveling down Blue Hill Avenue, and terminating at Mattapan Square, would cost billions of dollars and take years to build. That much is certain. But so is the need for that branch. Today, more than 30,000 riders depend on buses along Blue Hill Avenue every day. Imagine what that demand could become with true rapid transit. The Commonwealth invested roughly $1.1 billion to extend commuter rail to Fall River for a projected 2,500 riders. If that investment is justified, what is the appropriate investment for a road already serving more than 10 times as many people every day?

This is a double standard. When communities of color raise these transportation inequities or push for transformative investment, the conversation begins and ends with cost. Rail is too expensive, too ambitious, unnecessary because a bus already runs there. Some communities are told to dream big. Others are told to settle.

Rail serving Nubian Square and Blue Hill Avenue is not a fantasy. For decades, state and regional planners have examined major transit concepts for this corridor. The 2012 Roxbury-Dorchester-Mattapan Transit Needs Study evaluated rapid transit options linking Dudley (now Nubian Square), Grove Hall, Blue Hill Avenue, and Mattapan. The Urban Ring planning process envisioned rail connections through Ruggles and Nubian Square. The 2014 Fairmount Indigo Corridor Plan called for expanded rail service and expanded subway integration.

These studies were never intended to provide final engineering designs. But they did show something important: that residents and stakeholders had already done the work to build consensus around the need and that rail deserved serious consideration.

Yet, despite decades of planning and repeated acknowledgment of the corridor’s importance, the Commonwealth has never commissioned a comprehensive feasibility study to determine how a rail-based rapid transit replacement could actually be built, what it would cost, or what benefits it would deliver. Instead, those questions remain unanswered — not because rail was proven infeasible, but because the analysis needed to answer them was never completed.

Residents deserve to see a comparison of enhanced bus service, center-running bus lanes, and surface and underground rail. They deserve to understand the costs, construction impacts, effects on businesses and parking, travel time improvements, and displacement risks associated with each option.

That comprehensive comparison has never been presented.

Many residents along Blue Hill Avenue have said they do not support the current center-running bus lane proposal, and more than 2,100 residents signed a petition opposing the plan. Their concerns should not be dismissed as resistance to change or a misunderstanding of transit policy.

Today, policy makers are actively discussing the possibility of extending the Orange Line to Roslindale. If that corridor merits a study for rapid transit expansion, it is reasonable to ask why Blue Hill Avenue, one of the region’s busiest bus routes, has not received a comparable modern evaluation despite decades of existing plans.

The nearby Fairmount Line does not resolve the challenge. While it provides valuable commuter rail service, it does not directly serve the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, operate at true rapid transit frequencies, and, without the North-South Rail Link, cannot provide seamless through-service across downtown. It is an important part of the region’s transit network — but it is not a substitute for high-capacity rapid transit serving Blue Hill Avenue.

The next step is straightforward: The state should commission a comprehensive rail feasibility study; establish a timeline for funding, environmental review, and preliminary engineering; and allow the public to evaluate the alternatives based on evidence rather than assumptions.

Massachusetts is entering a new era of transportation investment. Service has improved, and Fair Share revenues have created billions of dollars for transit. That gives us the opportunity to think beyond incremental improvements, especially in communities that have waited generations for the investments others take for granted. After decades of deferred upgrades, Blue Hill Avenue deserves more than another bus debate. It deserves the same vision, analysis, and ambition that Massachusetts brings to every major transit investment.

That was the first of many trips to Mattapan Station, many rides on the 28, many breakfasts at Brothers Deli, and many meetings about how the MBTA could improve the bus rider experience in a meaningful way. We proposed the 28X project, a plan for center-running bus rapid transit, or BRT, from Mattapan Station to Grove Hall, with bus priority features for the rest of the trip to Nubian Square. Using federal American Recovery and Reinvestment Act funding that had to be spent quickly, we had no time for meaningful public engagement. This gap in the engagement process was irreconcilable, and the effort failed that same year, but the idea remained alive.

Fast forward to today. Fast and reliable BRT along Blue Hill Avenue is finally within reach, with a strong federal funding commitment and active support from the MBTA, the city of Boston, bus riders, local youth groups, and transit advocates. Each day more than 30,000 riders use one of the bus routes using Blue Hill Avenue, and each day they collectively lose 3,000 hours of precious time due to traffic congestion and impediments like double parking. Bus rapid transit will change all that in this decade.

It puzzles and pains me to see two members of the Boston City Council, after several years of robust public engagement by the city and the T, actively oppose the project now, jeopardizing both the federal funding and the rare opportunity to significantly improve bus transit along this route. The councilors have proposed an alternative, their vision for a new Orange Line subway extension. The danger is that local residents may mistakenly believe that BRT conflicts with a future Orange Line extension. It does not.

A subway is a blunt mobility instrument, taking you from point A to point B with speed but none of the inherent flexibility provided by surface bus routes. Riders using the 22, 28, and 31 buses are reaching different destinations — each with different points A and B — and they will all be well served by the BRT corridor. The BRT plan would complement any future subway extension because each would serve different journey needs and patterns.

More than half the people traveling along Blue Hill Avenue during rush hour are bus riders. They are among the most transit-dependent passengers on the system. There is therefore substantial upside to benefiting bus riders in the short term while a subway vision wends its way through the lengthy, complex, and uncertain process of community engagement, design, engineering, and environmental review. Funding uncertainty is also inherent to the subway vision, because the federal money committed to the BRT project cannot be used for any other project or purpose.

How tall a mountain is this to climb? By comparison, the relatively simple and inexpensive Red Line/Blue Line connector has taken decades to advance to 30 percent design, and there is still no funding plan or construction commitment from the MBTA despite the economic and environmental justice benefits the project will provide. The Green Line Extension Project cost $2.3 billion and took nearly two decades to complete — and that is a surface and elevated light rail system built largely on existing or abandoned rail rights of way, not a complex subway project in the middle of a dense urban neighborhood.

There has never been an urban subway extension on the scale proposed by the councilors that has come to fruition in either a short period of time or at a politically feasible cost. We know little to nothing about the right path for an Orange Line subway extension (a 1978 study looked superficially at what were termed “generalized alternatives”), about soil or utility conditions, about constructability and potential property impacts from excavation, about surface street disruptions, about the right number of stops, or about an all-in cost estimate. Those issues will require decades to sort out, with no guarantee of success.

I assume the councilors are acting in good faith, but they are giving their constituents false hope. Their vision is not achievable in a reasonable time frame and faces many substantial challenges. In contrast, their constituents will benefit in the short term from the joint MBTA/city BRT plan. The bus riders who lived with suboptimal bus trips in 2009 continue to experience poor transit conditions. These riders have suffered long enough. BRT along Blue Hill Avenue will measurably improve transit access and pedestrian and vehicular safety along the route. The time has come.

The MIX tries to do its theme nights a little differently, Samedi said. Boston has one of the country’s largest Cape Verdean communities, for instance, and the Ashmont bar went all-out for Cape Verde’s World Cup matches.

Then there’s Love Island. Samedi said he had no idea the competition dating show was so popular. A customer suggested he open the bar up for devotees to watch, so he put a social post out to see if people would be interested. Since then, “Love Island” nights have been a mainstay at The MIX.

As bars try to find new and creative ways to get customers in the door, they’re capitalizing on other things that draw a different demographic, like reality TV and shows with a larger female audience.

“Whatever the new hot trend is, we’ll try to get behind [it],” said Paul Bruno, operations and beverage manager for Glynn Hospitality Group, which manages Dillon’s in Back Bay. The bar is big on Premier League soccer, college basketball, and college football.

And it’s not just sports, he said. Anything of public interest is fair game. Dillon’s has hosted nights dedicated to Amazon Prime’s “The Summer I Turned Pretty,” Bravo’s “Summer House,” and HBO’s “Heated Rivalry.”

“We’re always just looking for different ways to bring in guests,” Bruno said. “We try not to be too pigeonholed in doing one thing.”

For sports bar Game On! in Fenway, ideas to expand its typical customer base started with “Love Island USA” watch parties in 2024. The show builds a nightly audience by releasing episodes six times a week. It’s one of a few competition series shot in close to real time (The episodes are aired to the audience about two days after filming, according to Peacock. This compares to shows like CBS’s “Survivor,” which air episodes months after a season wraps filming).

“We are so deeply rooted in being known as a sports bar, but we also try to have a lot of fun with reaching out to a different audience,” said Tyler Hall, marketing manager at Lyons Group, which operates Game On! in Fenway.

Watching “Love Island USA” blow up on social media each night, Hall said Game On! wanted a part in that.

“There’s clearly a community looking to watch this thing and experience it together,” he said. “So, we figured, let’s give it a shot.”

Game On! has even hosted former “Love Island USA” contestants, including last season’s winner, Bryan Arenales of Everett, as part of bigger themed events.

Hall said events like these have made a difference for the bar’s slower nights.

Even this past weekend, Game On! was a destination for Noah Kahan fans who may not have gotten tickets to his Fenway Park residency.

With post-pandemic shifts in both foot traffic and nightlife, the last few years have been challenging ones for bars, said Tyler Raymond, the general manager of Lulu’s Allston.

For about 10 years, the bar was open until 2 a.m. every night. They’ve trimmed down their hours since the pandemic, though Raymond said World Cup games are bringing back the late-night crowd.

“Around here, it’s been tough to come back after COVID,” he said. “Pre-COVID or whatever … people just were naturally out. Now, [it’s become] how do we get them out?”

So on Mondays, Lulu’s hosts a “Bar Jeopardy” league. They’re packed on Tuesday nights with trivia. The bar even bought a projector to open up their patio space for movie nights.

Loco Taqueria & Oyster Bar in South Boston has been experimenting with big events, too. It’s played host to several reality TV trivia nights and watch parties beyond “Love Island USA.” This summer has been especially busy on World Cup match days, said manager Julia Spugnardi. The bar uses its TVs and projectors to “naturally” bring in a crowd.

“It’s cool to fill the space on a night that we might not,” she said.

But the bar goes all-out for its reality TV events. The energy is just different, Spugnardi said, more “hyped” for those shows.

“People are specifically coming for that show that they’ve spent so many months watching,” she said. “I also feel like, with the demographic, girls are just so into it.”

So this weekend, after cleaning up from two World Cup matches Saturday night, the Loco staff turned a Sunday night in Southie into the Fijian villa. They decorated the place with island-themed balloons, passed around leis, and gave each ticket holder a commemorative champagne flute in “Love Island”-themed Loco insignia.

“Normally, we just watch at one of our apartments,” said Clara O’Connor, a customer with a prime spot in front of one of Loco’s many TVs. “We’d all be in our PJs and eat ice cream, very chill vibe. This is fun to be in a bigger area with a much larger group of people.”

Last night’s watch party sold around 150 tickets for $25 each — not to mention drinks and food.

“When you’re gasping, at the same time, so are, like, 50 other people,” said Stephanie Lignos during the commercial break, of course. “It’s like a little community.”
