But despite more coming on time, some buses still came more than an hour late, or not at all.

In May, nearly 500 of these “blown trips,” triggered $184,000 in damages, even as combined on-time percentages hit 90 percent that month.

The fines, first reported by WBUR in April and again last week, have led parents and local officials to call for the state to increase its oversight of Massachusetts’ largest school district, just years after local officials narrowly averted a state takeover of BPS following reports of “entrenched dysfunction,” extending from staffing issues to the districts’ tardy buses.

That compromise created a remedial improvement agreement with the district, which the state let expire last summer even as the city failed to hit other goals beyond reliable buses, including improving special education and ESL programs.

Cheryl Buckman, a BPS parent and advocate, created a petition this week calling for the state to again intervene on busing and for BPS to consider terminating service with the company, which has been its sole busing provider since 2013.

“Why weren’t [these] guys fined a long time ago?” said Buckman, whose petition on Wednesday had 20 signatures. “I believe it’s time to drop the hammer on them.”

Per their contract, the district can charge Transdev $500 for any no-show or overly late trips, district transportation director Daniel Rosengard told City Council members in a March session discussing bus lateness. Transdev can also secure bonuses by being on-time.

Using this price calculation, the district likely left millions on the table by not enforcing fines across previous years.

Last fiscal year, BPS allocated $189 million to transportation, at least $21 million of which went directly to Transdev for management expenses, Rosengard told the Council members.

Following ramped up enforcement, Transdev’s end to last school year was among its strongest ever.

In June, the company achieved a month of bus service that was on time 95 percent of mornings, for the first time satisfying the minimum target BPS promised state officials they would realize along all routes in their now-expired improvement agreement from 2022.

June also had the smallest number of blown trips at 197. For reference, district buses complete roughly 3,000 total routes each school day, according to a 2025 progress report.

In a statement, Transdev spokesperson Mischa Wanek-Libman said the company has made various improvements over the past year, including hiring 40 additional drivers and training 750 drivers in safety and defensive driving courses.

“While we recognize there is more work to do, these improvements reflect our continued investment in safety, service, and accountability,” Wanek-Libman said.

In a statement Monday, a district spokesperson said the fines “address an uptick we were seeing in the number of uncovered trips even as overall [on-time performance] was continuing to improve.”

But some in the community said they haven’t felt like performance is improving, and see the fines as proof of that.

Theresa Delehanty, 66, who helps two of her elementary-age grandchildren catch the bus in South Boston each morning, said the bus didn’t arrive at all five times last school year, more than ever before.

Transdev service began to seriously regress around last December, necessitating the start of fines, Rosengard also told city councilors in March.

In an open letter to state education officials published Friday, City Councilor-At-Large Erin Murphy expressed frustration with BPS officials.

She said she has repeatedly received the same kind of “local assurances,” about transportation but without “sufficient answers and meaningful change,” and now wants the state to do its own review.

“The need for these fines,” Murphy added, “confirms that the district and its contractor are still failing to meet basic expectations.”

In a statement on Monday, a district spokesperson wrote that BPS, “continues to work closely with Transdev to ensure that during the 2026-27 school year we build on the record high on-time performance seen this past school year.”

Addressing why fines only began this year, the spokesperson said that “while our experience has shown that non-performance damages are not always the most effective tool at our disposal, we use them strategically when necessary to maintain accountability.”

So far, “this targeted use of damages” had led to “a significant reduction in uncovered trips,” the spokesperson added.

The district’s busing protocols and its relationship with Transdev have come under intensified scrutiny over the last year, following the death of Lens Arthur Joseph, a 5-year-old Hyde Park student who was struck by Transdev driver Jean Charles shortly after afternoon drop-off in April 2025. It was later revealed that Charles, who tried to flee the scene of the crash, was also driving with an expired state certification.

A WBUR and ProPublica report released last month exposed further issues at Transdev. According to their investigation the company did not properly identify its role in 42 fatal crashes, including the one that killed Joseph, in federal databases.

In Boston alone, they identified 71 serious school bus crashes involving the company which weren’t reported using its name.

An independent probe last year revealed a collective failure by BPS and Transdev to properly document and track training requirements and accident reports.

New safety recommendations were adopted at the start of last school year, but parents like Buckman said they don’t trust that Transdev is being held accountable.

“Sorry just does not cut it anymore,” she added. “There is [a] huge fracture between BPS families and BPS itself.”

BPS is also Transdev’s only school bus client, and the company was the only bidder for the district’s most recent five-year busing contract, signed in 2023.

According to a district spokesperson, multiple vendors were invited to bid in 2021, but only Transdev submitted an offer.

First Student, which provided district busing before Transdev, was also plagued by chronic delay issues. In 2012, the Globe reported 37 percent of its buses were arriving up to an hour late and the firm was fined $800,000 as a result.

The Governor’s Council, the elected panel that must vote on her nomination, scheduled a hearing to question O’Leary for Aug. 12. O’Leary was not available Wednesday for an interview, Healey’s office said.

By nominating another former prosecutor, Healey signaled she remains committed to adding that perspective to the Parole Board after the Governor’s Council in May rejected her last nominee, Vincent J. DeMore III, a former Suffolk County assistant district attorney turned defense lawyer.

Healey wants the seven-person board to include a lawyer who has handled complex criminal cases and worked with victims — experience she says is missing from the panel, her office said Wednesday.

In a statement, Healey praised O’Leary for dedicating her career to state government service and public safety.

“As both a leader at the Parole Board and a former prosecutor, she understands the importance of making thoughtful, fair decisions that protect public safety while supporting successful reentry,” Healey said. “I know she’ll be a tremendous asset to the Board.”

O’Leary’s nomination must be approved by the Governor’s Council, a relatively obscure group of elected officials who represent eight districts from across the state.

The body rejected DeMore’s nomination by a 4-3 vote after some council members said they wanted a candidate with more experience evaluating prisoners’ fitness for integrating back into society.

Some criminal justice reform advocates also argued that adding DeMore would give the Parole Board a majority of members with a law enforcement background, given three others previously worked in probation and parole services. One councilor, Eunice D. Zeigler, didn’t attend the meeting when the vote was taken.

About a week before the vote on DeMore, a parolee allegedly shot and wounded motorists on Memorial Drive in Cambridge, generating fresh scrutiny of the Parole Board. But the incident didn’t shift opinions enough among councilors to secure his nomination.

On Wednesday, two opponents of DeMore’s nomination criticized Healey for tapping another former prosecutor.

“Why is Governor Healey doing this? Why does she think it’s OK to put a former DA on the board?” asked Stacey Borden, founder of New Beginnings Reentry Services in Roxbury and a former Governor’s Council candidate.

Borden said she prefers a nominee with a background in psychology or social work, or a person who was previously incarcerated.

“Maura Healey is not hearing the community,” she said.

Olivia Dubois, a social worker with a background working with public defenders, said she was also disappointed with Healey’s nomination.

“The Governor’s Council made it pretty clear they wanted a Parole Board member who had a deep understanding of reentry, mental health, substance abuse, and trauma,” she said.

A former prosecutor hasn’t served on the Parole Board since 2022 when Gloriann Moroney — who had been nominated to the board by Healey’s Republican predecessor, Charlie Baker — resigned to become a District Court judge. If confirmed, O’Leary would fill a vacancy left by Tonomey Coleman, who was nominated last year by Healey, and approved by the Governor’s Council, for a District Court judgeship.

O’Leary on Wednesday drew praise from others, including Julie J. Bernard, chief executive of the Flaschner Judicial Institute, who said O’Leary in 2014 helped to establish a drug court in Brockton District Court.

O’Leary was open to alternatives in incarceration and sentencing, said Bernard, who was the presiding justice in Brockton District Court when she met O’Leary.

“She’s fair-minded, reasonable, and I think she’d be an excellent choice for the Parole Board,” Bernard said Wednesday.

Criminal defense lawyer Michael A. Bergeron said O’Leary has a “unique ability to listen and look at the other side’s perspective and evaluate what was appropriate for each defendant.”

“She is more than qualified to make reasonable and fair parole decisions,” said Bergeron, a former supervising attorney for Pilgrim Advocates, Inc., a nonprofit organization that provides lawyers to indigent defendants.

Robert Sheketoff, a criminal defense attorney who has faced O’Leary in court, said she is smart, detail-oriented, and was attuned to his clients’ circumstances.

The Parole Board holds thousands of hearings annually, mostly in state prisons and county jails, and parole officers supervised nearly 3,000 people in 2024, according to data released by the panel in May.

Four people have joined the Parole Board under Healey, with three getting unanimous votes: Rafael Ortiz and Edith J. Alexander, both former probation officers; and Sarah B. Coughlin, a licensed clinical social worker.

The fourth, Angelo Gomez Jr., a former parole supervisor, was confirmed on a 6-1 vote. He took charge as chairperson of the board in October.

Healey also renominated Charlene Bonner, a forensic psychologist who joined the board in 2011 and was confirmed for a fourth term in 2023. Her credentials satisfy a state requirement adopted by the Legislature in 2014 that the board have at least one member with “experience in forensic psychology.”

Representative Ayanna Pressley said Tuesday that she’s “devastated” by the death of a teenager who was found in a Mattapan rental property owned by her husband.

“I am devastated about the death of Yoseliani Marte, an 18-year-old with so many dreams ahead of her, her life cut short by domestic violence,” Pressley said in a statement.

The Democratic lawmaker said that as a parent of a teenager herself, “the thought of a young person violently losing their life in this way is beyond crushing.”

Pressley said she stands with “our community and everyone who loved Yoseliani as we grieve this deep loss. May we all honor her life and humanity and extend compassion to her loved ones as they navigate this heartbreaking tragedy.”

Police haven’t publicly identified Marte as the victim in the case, but her mother, Elenie Ocasio, told Boston 25 News on Monday that an assailant had “put a gun to her head, took my baby in that house, and left her to die.”

No arrests have been made.

Police said there’s “absolutely nothing that indicates any connection to the owners of the property.”

Property records show the seven-bedroom home where Marte was found is owned by Pressley’s husband, Conan Harris. Pressley and Harris live in the Hyde Park section of Boston, according to the lawmaker’s website.

Shortly before 2 p.m. on Saturday, two officers responded to a radio call for a person shot at 25 Malta St., according to the report.

Another officer working the front desk of a police station in Hyde Park “took a walk-in report” of a person shot at an apartment in the building.

The victim was found in a bedroom inside that unit, the report said.

Shea Butter Smoothies, a Dorchester juice bar where Marte worked, posted a heartfelt remembrance of her to Facebook on Monday.

“Liani was a brilliant and motivated young lady whose passion and dedication had a profound impact on our team and the work we do,” the business said. “Her innovative ideas, particularly in enhancing Shea Butter Smoothies, brought a unique touch that our customers adored. She approached every project with enthusiasm, creativity, and an unwavering commitment to excellence.”

She also “brought joy and positivity to our workplace. Her infectious laughter, kindness, and willingness to help others made her not just a colleague, but a cherished friend to many,” the post said. “She will be missed immensely, and her legacy will live on in the hearts of those who had the privilege of knowing her.”

To honor her life and support her relatives as they grieve, the business said, “we will be donating 50% of the proceeds from every purchase of the Big Papi smoothie to assist with her funeral costs. We encourage our community to join us in this effort, as we remember the beautiful person she was. ... Rest in peace, Yoseliani. You will always be remembered.”

SIGN NOT OF THE TIMES: Spotted at Rachael Rollins’s campaign headquarters in Roxbury: a campaign sign touting an endorsement from the Boston Globe’s editorial board, per a photo obtained by the Globe.

NUMBERS GAME: The order of the record-tying nine(!) ballot questions Massachusetts voters will weigh this fall are officially set after a last-ditch effort to strike a proposal that would repeal the law that legalized recreational marijuana failed Tuesday.

The questions run the gamut:

Question 1: Expanding the public records law;

Question 2: Giving collective bargaining rights to Committee for Public Counsel Services employees;

Question 3: Overhauling the state’s primary elections system;

Question 4: Instituting Election Day voter registration;

Question 5: Changing the state’s tax-cap law;

Question 6: Creating a new conservation fund;

Question 7: Changing single-family zoning laws;

Question 8: Repealing legal recreational marijuana sales;

Question 9: Repealing a 2024 gun control law.

Get ready to spend some time in the ballot booth this November. Secretary of State William F. Galvin’s office said some ballots could be three pages long, depending on the district.

Gross and Anjali Huynh, The Boston Globe: Massachusetts Democratic leaders said they expect to pass a bill Wednesday that would dramatically loosen the state’s already-liberal abortion laws by making it easier for women to terminate late-term pregnancies.

Given that sequence, it seems fair to conclude that politics played some role in Wu’s retreat from unabashed champion of bus and bike lanes to something less ardent and more politically pragmatic — a retreat that is now drawing harsh criticism from cycling advocates after the tragic death of Louisa Gag, a city transportation planner who was killed while riding her bike on July 9. In Gag’s memory and honor, Wu has pledged to review safety designs for the section of Tremont Street where Gag was killed and greater enforcement of laws regarding bike lanes that are blocked by illegally parked cars.

What should not be lost in the emotion of the moment is the need for balance and openness to different points of view when it comes to creating safe streets for everyone. The perception that both were lacking under Wu gave Kraft an opportunity on the bike lane issue. While he was never able to capitalize on it beyond the loud cheers he got for mentioning it at his announcement, he did force Wu to acknowledge there is more than one side to the bicycle lane debate. It’s the side of businesses that say they lose customer parking spaces to bike lanes as well as the side of pedestrians who dodge people on bicycles, e-bikes, and scooters who ignore red lights and other rules of the road.

To cycling advocates, those are fighting words. From where I sit — which is usually not on a bicycle — they see no other side to the issue, just energy-hogging barbarians. While I respect those who believe cycling is the best way to save the planet, an all-or-nothing perspective defies the reality of Boston’s jumble of streets and the need to share them with cars and trucks because everyone can’t or won’t ride a bike. Unless the city somehow builds protected tunnels for cyclists, they are going up against vehicles that weigh thousands of pounds. That’s inherently unsafe. Speed limits and attention to traffic signals should be enforced on the motorist side, but risk is part of cycling.

Of course, the city should also do what it can to address roads that are especially unsafe. For example, in 2023, the city said that section of Tremont Street in Mission Hill where Gag was killed needed improvements, such as wider sidewalks, more protections for cyclists, and measures to slow traffic. Whether it simply got lost in a bureaucratic shuffle, or was put off because of election year politics, the project has not advanced.

Kraft never posed any real threat to Wu. Early polls showed she was ahead of him by 14 points. She beat him by a 49-point margin in the September preliminary election and he dropped out shortly afterward.

Yet despite her big political win, the perception that Wu does not listen to all sides persists and continues to fuel criticism of the way she pursues transportation policy. That’s the case with her $135-million proposal to add center-running bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue. The pushback is now so strong that opponents asked the Trump administration to withhold $80 million in federal funding that’s allocated for the project.

Bill Forry, executive editor and co-publisher of The Dorchester Reporter, recently wrote that complaints from opponents about a lack of public input on the Blue Hill bus project don’t “pass the sniff test.” His review of news articles in The Reporter chronicled 18 forums, open houses, and hearings over the past four years, plus pop-up workshops and “street team” engagement.

Yet quantity doesn’t trump quality. If people don’t feel they are being listened to, that’s a problem for a mayor. For Wu, it’s a consistent problem on any number of issues, from bike and bus lanes to renovating White Stadium.

From a personal perspective, this has to be a difficult moment for Wu. Gag worked for her as a policy fellow and intern when Wu was a Boston city councilor, then took on a role as a city transportation planner who oversaw bike-share policies and road safety improvements.

She will want to do the right thing for the cycling community. But she shouldn’t make the same mistake she did before and shut out Bostonians with a different point of view.

Some may have cheered Kraft’s words about bike lanes. But like it or not, she’s their mayor, too.

In late June, the Spotlight Team showed that MassHousing had awarded $1.4 million to two developers who submitted invoices bearing the names of at least nine subcontractors who later told the Globe they did not do the work attributed to them. The apparent fraud, for which developers Gary Acquah and Reginald Woods were paid more than half a million dollars, left the multi-unit buildings in Pittsfield and Worcester they were supposed to be fixing up in poor condition.

Acquah and Woods had a secret connection to Tony Richards II, the MassHousing executive who awarded them the money. Months earlier, he purchased a home in West Roxbury from the same developers for $204,000 less than the original asking price. Richards did not disclose the connection at the time, a likely violation of Massachusetts ethics laws.

When the Globe brought the matter to light last month, the agency paused Richards’s authority to disburse grant money and launched an internal review of grant programs he oversaw, though he remained on the payroll.

Last week, Richards voluntarily resigned from MassHousing and from his seat on one of Governor Maura Healey’s advisory councils. Neither he nor his attorney has responded to the Globe’s repeated requests for comment.

Healey, who appoints the members of the board that oversees the quasi-state agency, declined to comment on the scandal at first. When a reporter approached her three weeks later at a public event, she said the matter should be “fully investigated.”

For its internal review of programs under Richards, MassHousing tapped the Mintz law firm, which has done legal work for the agency for decades. The agency’s top legal officer, Colin McNiece, worked at Mintz for 11 years before joining MassHousing.

Last month, McNiece told the Globe that when Richards finally told his bosses about his relationship with Acquah and Woods, more than a year after giving them the grants, McNiece determined that there was no need to file a written disclosure because the matter was “basically moot.”

That decision was criticized by some ethics experts, who said a late disclosure would have been preferable to none at all.

A MassHousing spokesperson told the Globe last week that McNiece arrived at his opinion after he consulted with outside counsel for the agency. The spokesperson declined to comment about whether Mintz or some other firm offered that advice.

In part because of the close relationship between MassHousing and Mintz, State Auditor Diana DiZoglio has called for an independent government investigation. Earlier, she said her office might take it on, but on Thursday, she said her auditors will not get involved because federal auditing standards require her to defer to the attorney general’s investigation.

The controversy has sparked outcry from labor unions who seek to organize MassHousing’s workforce as a means of combating what they see as poor leadership. The activists called for reforms at the agency, including the passage of proposed legislation that could shake up the agency’s board and trigger a review of its spending in Gateway Cities.

“Pastor Chris has left an indelible impact on our city and state that will be felt for generations to come,” Wu said. “I am grateful to have called him a partner and friend. May we carry forward his legacy, and may he rest in peace.”

Throughout Mr. Sumner’s life, family and friends said, he seemed to fill more hours than each day held, and that carried on to the end.

“Everyone has been amazed at how well I am doing,” he said at the April gathering. “God has had plenty of chances to take me home, but I believe I am still here because he has much more work for me to do.”

Along with having held leadership positions at various organizations, he devoted endless hours to being a father to his three daughters and a father figure to more people than he could count.

That was a role to which he had always aspired. He was raised by a single mother and never knew his own father.

His wife, Katani Eaton Sumner, recalled that when they were high school seniors — long before they began dating — she asked him one day as they walked home from basketball practice “what he wanted to be, and he said, ‘I want to be a good dad and a good husband.’”

In a Father’s Day tribute this year in The Bay State Banner, his oldest daughter, Kandice Sumner, president and chief executive of the Metco program, wrote that “my dad was everyone’s Dad, and there was enough of him to go around.”

“All of my friends wanted my dad for their dad,” she added in a phone interview. “My dad was our superman. I feel like I’m cutting it short by calling him a superhero. He was a magical human being on earth.”

Born on Nov. 9, 1961, Byron Christopher Sumner was the son of Annie Blanche Sumner, who raised him and his two sisters — one older, one younger.

The family moved a few times, but Mr. Sumner spent some of his youth in Roxbury and was delighted to have a view, from his Melnea Cass center office, of an area where he had lived.

A powerful athlete who grew to 6-foot-2 and 250 pounds, Mr. Sumner competed in baseball, track, and hockey, and later in life took to lengthy bicycle rides.

But he particularly loved basketball and played for the Titans, a Boston Neighborhood Basketball League championship team coached by the legendary Al Brodsky.

Having struggled with dyslexia, Mr. Sumner left English High School without a diploma but still landed basketball scholarships in Canada, playing for the University of Prince Edward Island and Acadia University in Nova Scotia, and garnering hoops honors.

Returning home after his college and semi-pro basketball career, he fell in love with Katani Eaton, proposing while she was a Brown University student. She was impressed by his intelligence and surprised he wasn’t bookish — due in large part to his dyslexia. At her encouragement, he pored through “The Autobiography of Malcolm X,” cover to cover.

“That’s the first book he ever read,” she said, laughing as she recalled that he’d tell people: “My wife made me read a book before she would go out with me.”

They married in 1985. He then earned his general equivalency diploma and went on to graduate with a bachelor’s degree from Springfield College and a master’s in social work from Wheelock College.

“I told him: ‘You’re going to be a role model for so many young Black men. You’ve got to go back and get your degree,’” his wife recalled.

Mr. Sumner went on to hold leadership positions at places including the Blue Hill Boys & Girls Club and the St. Stephen’s Youth Programs.

His reach exceeded his titles, though, the Rev. Ray Hammond of Bethel AME Church said in a video message played in April 2025 at a night of prayer at Jubilee Christian Church in honor of Mr. Sumner.

Hammond said Mr. Sumner was a mentor to many young people “who saw in you the living proof that early adversity can be a steppingstone to a great destiny.”

“His whole life is a miracle,” Katani Eaton Sumner, who worked for three decades in education, said.

In addition to his wife and his oldest daughter, Kandice, Mr. Sumner leaves his two younger daughters, Kortney of Pawtucket, R.I., and Kristian of Hyde Park; a sister, Cheryl of Jacksonville, Fla.; and two grandchildren.

Family and friends will gather for a visitation at 5 p.m. Friday in Jubilee Christian Church in Mattapan, where a celebration of Mr. Sumner’s life will begin at 6.

“One of my dad’s lasting legacies is the sacredness of joy,” Kandice said. “He would make everything joyful. And it wasn’t an effort. It was just him.”

Through Mr. Sumner’s own example, informed by his spirituality, he showed all he met how to navigate their own inevitable mortality, said Ron Hoffman, founder and chief executive of the nonprofit Compassionate Care ALS.

“Here was this extraordinary man, who was dancing his own dying,” Hoffman said. “That’s an unseen gift that Chris has given everyone who knew him and saw him — a gift to his family, his friends, his community, his church.”

September 23, 1994, Burke, Virginia. After a high school football game, a fight broke out in a nearby park. Someone fired a .38-caliber handgun into the crowd. A stray bullet struck me in the throat. I was 17 years old.

I remember the warmth of blood soaking through my white shirt before I understood what had happened. I remember trying to speak and realizing I couldn’t. I remember my surgeon, Dr. Robert Ahmed, unlocking my gurney himself because he was dismayed at how long it was taking to get me to the operating room. I remember him leaning over me and saying, “Joe, I have to do this to save your life.” And I remember thinking about the pack of cigarettes in my pocket that my parents would kill me for if they found out — the kind of small, ordinary thought a teenager clings to in the middle of something enormous.

I survived. My windpipe was rebuilt. A vein from my leg was used to repair the carotid artery the bullet had torn open. In the hospital bed where I recovered, I made a decision that would shape the rest of my life: I was going to spend my life on the other side of the operating table. And for nearly two decades now, I have.

I am a trauma surgeon at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. I have spent much of my career caring for victims of violence and sitting with families as they learn that their son, daughter, husband, or wife is not coming home. I know what a gunshot wound does to a windpipe because it happened to mine. So when I say that a new round of federal deregulation could cost lives, I am not speaking from a policy brief. I am describing what I have lived through and what I now spend my days trying to repair.

What should stop every American cold is this: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is eliminating more than three dozen federal firearms regulations in what amounts to the broadest rewrite of its rules in agency history, and by its own admission, some of the changes could result in harm, “including potential mass casualty events.”

Note that that warning did not come from gun safety advocates or political opponents. It came from the agency itself. In its proposal for rule changes, the agency acknowledged risks in loosening restrictions on firearm access for people with documented histories of serious mental illness and in restoring access to stabilizing braces that allow pistols to be fired with greater accuracy and control, so that they function more like rifles. Devices of this type have been used in some of the deadliest mass shootings in recent years.

At the same time, the Justice Department has gone after states that have tried to curb gun violence. In May, Virginia banned the sale of AR-15-style rifles and capped magazines at 15 rounds; California barred the sale of handguns with a trigger design, common to Glocks, that makes them easy to convert into machine guns using aftermarket devices. Within weeks, the DOJ sued to overturn both laws, arguing they violate the Second Amendment. It is part of a pattern: Since September, the department has filed seven lawsuits challenging state and local gun laws designed to keep the most dangerous weapons off the streets. This is precisely why the legal defense work of organizations like Brady, where I serve as board chair and chief medical officer, matters as much now as the laws themselves: When the federal government turns litigation into a weapon against public safety statutes, someone has to be in court pushing back.

Enforcement against firearm dealers most likely to arm dangerous individuals has also sharply declined. After the Trump administration ended a zero tolerance policy for lawbreaking gun dealers earlier this year, federal license revocations for dealers who falsified records or failed to conduct background checks dropped dramatically.

Meanwhile, the public health infrastructure designed to understand and prevent firearm injury is being dismantled. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Division of Violence Prevention has been hollowed out by layoffs. Government-funded reports on strategies to reduce firearm injuries have quietly disappeared from federal websites. And Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary, recently told Congress that he does not consider gun violence a public health issue at all, calling it “a law enforcement issue and not public health.”

As a physician, I can say plainly: He is wrong. Nearly 60 percent of firearm deaths in America are suicides. You cannot arrest your way out of a mental health crisis. Public health is the framework that has helped reduce deaths from smoking, motor vehicle crashes, and infectious diseases. It works by identifying risk factors and implementing interventions before tragedy occurs, rather than simply responding to it afterward. Eliminating our ability to study gun violence does not eliminate gun violence. It only makes us less capable of understanding what works and less able to save lives.

I want to be precise about what these policies mean because policy language has a way of becoming abstract. A revoked license means a dealer can no longer sell guns illegally or irresponsibly. A restored license means that the pipeline may reopen. A stabilizing brace increases control and makes a weapon more deadly. For me, none of this is abstract. It is a Friday night in my trauma bay.

A couple of years ago, I operated on a 19-year-old with the same injury I survived at 17. I stood with his mother and delivered the devastating news that Dr. Ahmed never had to give mine. Those are the stakes of licensing rules, enforcement decisions, and regulatory exemptions. They are not abstractions. A specific family in a specific room on a specific night. And then another family. And another.

Although I did not grow up in a household with firearms, I’m not opposed to responsible gun ownership. And over the years of caring for patients, engaging with responsible gun owners, and working on firearm-injury prevention, I have come to understand both the culture surrounding gun ownership and the constitutional protections afforded by the Second Amendment.

But there is no interpretation of the Second Amendment that requires making it easier for someone in acute crisis to obtain a weapon or that demands we stop holding dealers accountable when they falsify records or ignore background check requirements. These are not questions about gun rights. They are questions about public safety.

We were building policies that were beginning to work. The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, passed one month after 19 children and two teachers were murdered in Uvalde, Texas, was followed by declines in firearm deaths from their 2021 peak. States added their own protections on top of those federal measures — Illinois, for instance, banned assault weapons and high-capacity magazines in 2023, directly in response to the mass shooting at a Highland Park Fourth of July parade. (The Justice Department has since filed briefs in federal court arguing against that law’s constitutionality.)

For the first time in years, the trajectory was moving in the right direction.

Now the federal government is dismantling that progress on multiple fronts at once, even as its own experts warn of the consequences.

I did not need a government memo to understand what a bullet does to a body. I carry the scar. I have spent every year since my injury trying to ensure fewer families have to experience what mine did. I am asking Secretary Kennedy to walk through my trauma bay before deciding that this is not a health issue. And I am asking the officials who authored those warnings in the ATF’s report, and the members of Congress who can still act on them, to take those warnings as seriously as I take every patient who comes through my doors.

ANOTHER CHAPTER FOR 62F: Massachusetts’s tax cap law — and the refunds it can deliver taxpayers — will live to see another day.

State senators on Thursday night pulled back an amendment to their sweeping economic development bill that would have repealed the decades-old law known as Chapter 62F — not a totally surprising move given the tough election-year optics of blocking money from potentially flowing back into taxpayers’ pockets.

But lawmakers didn’t leave the 1980’s-era law untouched. Senators instead passed a redrafted version of the proposal from state Senator Jason Lewis that is designed to effectively blunt the impact of a ballot question going before voters in November that would make it easier to trigger refunds to taxpayers.

The law, as it currently stands, is intended to limit state tax revenue growth to the growth of total wages and salaries and return any excess to taxpayers. That’s calculated by looking at the previous year’s cap, and then adding the adjustment for wage and salary growth, according to an analysis from Tufts University’s Center for State Policy Analysis.

The ballot question would reshape the law by setting the cap each year based on the actual revenue collected — a tweak, the analysis found, that could trigger three to five times as many refunds and return as much as 15 times as much money to taxpayers.

To taxpayers, that could be very appealing. To lawmakers who must build the state budget each year, not so much.

Enter the Senate’s 11th-hour proposal. The new version senators embraced Thursday adds what Lewis called “an additional test” to determine if and when refunds can start flowing. It would prevent tax givebacks if net tax revenues in the fiscal year are less than 7.5 percent of the total statewide personal income for the calendar year.

In other words, before voters weigh whether to make it easier to get a refund, the Senate wants to make it that much harder.

Though it’s a step down from the full-on repeal senators first floated, the ballot question backers weren’t placated.

The amendment as passed “would weaken the law months before voters consider a ballot question to strengthen it, undermining the ballot process and further eroding public trust in state government,” Taxpayers for an Affordable Massachusetts, the campaign behind the question, said in a statement late Thursday night.

Implemented last August, the rules have radically upended the routines of some RIDE customers, people with disabilities who have few options to get around otherwise. They used to be able to stow all their shopping either in the rear of a van or the trunk of a RIDE sedan, but patrons must now fit their folded carts and belongings within their own sitting area, often jammed in by their feet or resting on their stomachs.

So widespread is the frustration over the rules that more than 50 RIDE patrons showed up at an MBTA board meeting this month wearing T-shirts and carrying signs that read, “Secure Our Dignity.”

T officials argue the limitations make the RIDE safer and faster for the roughly 4,000 weekly riders who use the shared door-to-door service. Fewer bags, T officials said, leave more space for wheelchairs and walkers and prevent the possibility of produce and eggs shifting around in traffic.

Yet dozens of riders and transit advocates argue the policy has resulted in inconvenient and painful consequences. Seniors who can only carry so much say they are going without heavier items such as milk or laundry detergent; some disabled riders stack grocery bags on their stomachs and feet, leaving them in an uncomfortable, if not, embarrassing position.

“It cuts off your circulation if the bag is heavy and sitting on your legs,” said Valerie Best, a 77-year-old RIDE customer who lives in Mattapan. “Once the bag fell and my packages were rolling up and down the aisle. Just talking about it — it almost brings me to tears.”

While RIDE drivers are still allowed to assist riders, they are limited to items up to 15 pounds that can be carried “in one arm and in one trip.”

The Massachusetts Senior Action Council met with MBTA officials several times and demonstrated how the policy leaves riders cramped. But advocates say their calls to reverse the most restrictive rules had largely gone unheard.

After the demonstration at the July T board meeting, general manager Phillip Eng said the policy will be reviewed in the coming weeks. T board member Chanda Smart said the potential worst-case scenario for RIDE customers — being left without a ride home — is “unacceptable.”

Maya Bingaman, a T spokesperson, said in a statement the agency is “exploring several options that strike a balance between transporting customers and their items, maintaining safety, and operating a high quality, efficient transportation system.”

The RIDE charges either $3.35 or $5.60 for eligible riders from 58 communities. Its service has long been plagued by issues with contractors and staffing shortages, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic. Wait-times were long, and drivers often arrived late or canceled altogether, the Globe reported.

T data show that on-time performance has improved and now is up to 98 percent. The RIDE last summer also rolled out a new online booking service the T says will help make it more efficient.

“It’s never been a perfect service,” said Carolyn Villers, an organizer with the Massachusetts Senior Action Council. But, she said, the RIDE is a lifeline for its riders who need to get to senior centers, dialysis appointments, and social visits to friends and family, especially as many food assistance programs and other welfare benefits face federal cuts.

“People were blindsided by this rule,” Villers said. “At a time when there are cutbacks on safety net programs, the T making it impossible for people to care for themselves in this way is especially troubling.”

Federal paratransit guidance requires drivers to assist people getting on and off vehicles, but whether they should also help with packages and carts is “not specifically addressed,” said Kenneth Shiotani, a senior staff attorney at the National Disability Rights Network. While he “understands” the T policy, he thinks it’s “a little too stringent.”

“Paratransit is by definition slow getting on and slow getting off. They may need extra time and help with even minor levels of packaging,” he said of riders. “Being more flexible” — and allowing riders to carry on larger grocery orders — “makes more sense,” he said.

For Katherine Stearns and her husband, the policy change has quadrupled the Lynn couple’s transportation costs.

She uses a wheelchair, and he has health issues of his own. They take the RIDE to the nearby Market Basket to stock up: They typically fill one foldable cart with food they can store in two freezers and feed them for a month. Now, she said, they have to ride the service about once a week and pay all four times in order to stay within the bag limits. The couple is on a limited income of under $1,200 a month.

“It’s terribly unfair,” Stearns said. At the local Lynn senior center, “everyone is complaining that the RIDE is useless now.”

Nika Lea Tomicic — a transit advocate at the Riders’ Transportation Access Group, a T advisory group — said the policy contradicts the core promise of the RIDE: providing dependable transit service for older and disabled people.

“It’s about not understanding the RIDE user and their perspective as someone who uses this service to have an independent-living style,” she said. The T is “thinking instead that this is some van that scoops folks up and can take as many as possible to maximize efficiency.”

In extreme cases, riders have reported being refused RIDE service for having too many bags, advocates and three riders told the Globe. The T policy says “any customers violating policy will be no-showed and will not be sent another vehicle.”

Elizabeth Gillaspie saw that almost happen. She frequently accompanies a friend suffering from a heart and stomach aneurysm and said they were once turned away from a RIDE vehicle outside a Revere grocery store in September for having too many items — five grocery bags in all.

The T ultimately sent another ride, when her friend “was crying and in tears,” Gillaspie said.

Daniela Depina, who is visually impaired and has been a RIDE user for 22 years, said limiting herself to two grocery bags per ride is difficult for her family of five.

But what’s worse, she said, is that the people who were impacted were scarcely consulted about the policy changes.

“I wish that when this decision was made, they had included persons with disabilities and our seniors,” Depina said. “To eliminate shopping carts and say this is a safety issue, without hearing from us, is wrong.”

“Seeing the families and the friends, they all come out and enjoy … It’s like a family reunion,” said Hector Pantoja, 40, a warehouse worker who has come to the event all his life. “[We] love each other.”

The parade is put on every year by The Puerto Rican Festival of Massachusetts, an organization founded in 1967 to promote belonging and cultural affirmation for Puerto Ricans in the area. It serves as the culminating event for the organization’s annual two-day Puerto Rican Festival, which in the past attracted more than 50,000 attendees, according to the organization’s website.

Massachusetts has the fifth-largest Puerto Rican population in the United States, according to 2023 data from the Boston Planning and Development Agency.

Near the front of the parade, just behind a group marching with a welcome sign, a tow truck decorated for Lulu’s Barbershop threw bags of candy towards the crowd. Elsewhere, a man dressed in Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl outfit waved at the crowd. Throughout the procession, several young dance groups, whose members wore long flowing skirts and cheer uniforms, twirled and jumped.

“It is a big deal. It feels like we’re back home,” Christina Colon, 34, a freelance UX/UI designer from Dorchester, said. “Honestly, it’s rough because I feel like Boston is slightly segregated … It does feel good because we don’t see this on a regular basis, especially when you’re at the inner, inner city like, let’s say, downtown.”

She added that this year, the parade seemed to include “more of our culture” such as “the dances, the history of it, some of the up-and-coming artists.”

Local politicians and activists attended the event, too. One group encouraging young people to consider a career in law enforcement marched in black shirts reading “Injustice everywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.”

Another group, standing on the back of a junk removal truck, carried red and black signs reading “No human being is illegal” and “No one is free when others are oppressed.”

Other groups walked in support of political candidates up for election, including a group for Massachusetts treasurer candidate Elizabeth Dionne and a group for Suffolk County district attorney candidate Linda Champion.

For community coordinator Veronica Bowens-Wiggins, 52, from South End, it was nice to see representatives in person rather than through a flier.

“They’re actually trying to give you a small token of who they are personally. And I think that’s important,” she said.

But for Myrna Santana, 50, who has been coming to the parade since childhood, the event was less about politics and more about community enjoyment.

“We always keep politics on the side when it’s [time] to have fun as family, as neighbors. … You just have to have fun as a community,” she said.

As the parade continued, a group of men on horses trotted by. One man pulled his horse to the side to greet three women with their iPhones out, filming, the horse’s nostrils getting up close to the cameras.

At the end of the procession, dozens and dozens of cars drove by, their doors opened or removed entirely— many balanced large speakers on their roofs.

But, even after the parade ended, festivities felt far from over. On building stoops, people sat, blasting music, waving flags, and chatting.

“People are going to be calling out of work tomorrow because it’s going to be a good night,” Jason Rodriguez, 30, from Jamaica Plains, said. “Puerto Ricans are very prideful people, so the fact that the community is this loud and this proud makes sense.”

The swimmer who drowned over the weekend at a Milford quarry was identified Monday as a Boston teenager.

Yanick Rodrigues, 17, drowned at the Shadowbrook Quarries, while swimming with a friend Saturday, officials said.

His body was recovered on Sunday.

After immigrating from Cape Verde in 2016, Rodrigues attended Madison Park High School in Roxbury, where he was a star soccer player, according to a report by WCVB-TV.

His death comes less than a week after local officials issued a warning about the dangers of the quarries, a popular spot where swimming is forbidden.

On July 19, an 18-year-old woman fell about 12 feet from a ledge onto jagged rocks. The woman, who said she briefly lost consciousness after the fall, was found bleeding in several places, police said. She was flown to UMass Memorial Medical Center for treatment.

“While we’re thankful this incident did not have an even more tragic outcome, it serves as an important reminder that the Quarries are not a safe place for recreation,” Milford’s police chief, Robert Tusino, said in a statement last week.

“The steep rock faces, unstable terrain, and limited access for emergency responders create an extremely dangerous environment where a single misstep can have life-altering consequences for civilians and responders,” he said.

Other swimmers have drowned at quarries in Milford over the years.

In 2014, an 18-year-old from Providencejumped into Fletcher’s Quarry and did not resurface. The teen’s body was found a day later about 70 feet down and 10 feet away from the cliff. At the time, the death was the second at a local quarry since 2007, and the fourth in almost two decades.

Last summer, police said they would be cracking down on trespassing at local quarries by threatening thousands of dollars in fines.

These high-profile openings reflect a larger shift in Boston: Concepts that once held appeal mostly among East Asian immigrants, Asian Americans, and other cultural enthusiasts are becoming mainstream.

The new entrants to Boston retail have been urged on by landlords who are eager to revive empty storefronts. And they’re finding an eager audience among a young generation of consumers raised on social media, anime, K-pop, and international cuisine.

“Boston’s retail market definitely needed some new blood,” said Peng Jia, who owns MoreFun, a toy mecca, in Back Bay and Cambridge, with a third location on the way in Allston.

Amy Pei, a Northeastern University marketing professor, said social media has meant global trends travel much more quickly. Instead of encountering skincare from Korea through friends or while traveling abroad, shoppers now see them through influencers — watching videos of skincare regimens, product reviews, and house tours. By the time retail shops open, the demand already exists, she said.

The trend began in Boston, as it has in other cities, with dining. In the late 1800s, an early wave of immigration from China began, establishing Boston’s Chinatown. There, restaurants served familiar dishes to the mostly men who lived and worked in the neighborhood, marking one of the earliest examples of food trends making their way from Asia. Over the past several decades, immigrants and international students have expanded the market for new concepts.

“Food is always the conduit,” said Arnold Byun, the co-founder of MAUM Market, a pop-up featuring dozens of Asian-owned small businesses. “Then comes the retail.”

In recent years, broad consumer curiosity has expanded from food to fashion, art, beauty, and other products. Landlords and retail brokers see it as an opportunity.

“Generally speaking, the retail market is starved for new concepts. So everybody’s very excited to see these new retailers coming to the market,” said Sara Taylor, a partner at Newton-based Blackline Retail Group. She helped broker the deal to get Teso Life to sign a 10-year lease for downtown.

The appetite extends well beyond Boston. Asian food alone in the US is now a $37 billion market, and it’s growing annually, outpacing the broader food sector, according to BDA Partners, a research investment banking advisory firm. Sales of Asian food products in the US are expected to reach $51.3 billion by 2031.

H Mart, which opened its first Boston-area store in 2014 and has become a $2 billion powerhouse, now it has five area supermarkets stretching from Burlington to Quincy. In 2020, 99 Ranch Marketopened in a former Quincy Big Y space, where shoppers can now find about 100 different kinds of soy sauces and live goby fish. Newcomers such as Hashi Market are expanding into Cambridge and Brookline this year, while products that were once considered speciality items — from chili crisp and seaweed snacks to kimchi — have become everyday staples.

Boston’s embrace of Asian cuisines including Vietnamese, Thai, Taiwanese, and Japanese now spans from neighborhood restaurants to Michelin-recognized dining, helping transform areas around Quincy, Cambridge, and Dorchester’s Fields Corner (which is sometimes referred to as “Little Saigon”).

Chef Peter Nguyen is reimagining Vietnamese food at Lê Madeleine in Quincy, while Laurence Louie transformed his family’s Hong Kong bakery into Rubato, a modern café inspired by Cantonese comfort food. Last year, 10 of the 26 local restaurants recognized by the Michelin guide served Asian-inspired food or were Asian-owned.

Boston’s growing appetite for Asian food is what convinced Byun that the city was ready for MAUM Market. The idea first started in 2022 in Los Angeles and then later New York, coming off the pandemic as Byun said he noticed many Asian businesses bubbling up.

At MAUM’s first Boston pop-up last summer, about 6,000 attended in just a few hours. On a recent Sunday, MAUM hosted its second annual market in the Seaport, where 45 local vendors participated, selling goods such as gaming accessories, jewelry, art, plushy anime characters, and ceramics.

Because of the turnout, the company is expanding in Boston, and it is poised to host three pop-ups in 2027, putting it in scope with MAUM’s plans for New York City and Los Angeles.

Pei, at Northeastern, said some consumers associate Korean and Japanese products with quality and innovation, helping explain why demand has persisted beyond fleeting social media trends. “If they weren’t good, this wouldn’t have lasted,” she said.

Cy Kwok, a general manager of Teso Life, said that’s led to a natural broadening of the target market. “People are curious about this culture, and we’re bringing it into the community and educating them.”

Demographic shifts are also expanding the customer base. From 2010 to 2020, Massachusetts residents identifying as Asian grew from 307,000 to 504,000. In recent years, they’re also moving to wealthier suburbs, such as Lexington, where Asian Americans account for a third of the population. Students from Asia also make up a large share of Boston’s international student population. Nationally, Asian Americans represent one of the country’s fastest-growing consumer groups, with roughly $1.4 trillion in buying power, according to global data firm Nielsen.

That growth has also expanded the customer base for businesses selling Asian products, even while retailers are drawing shoppers far beyond Asian immigrant and Asian American communities.

What many of these concepts share is that they ask customers to do more than just shop for goods. At Memory Shop, visitors spend 20 to 30 minutes posing for photos, decorating prints, and hanging out, even though a single photo session itself lasts less than three minutes. At Anime Zakka, also on Newbury Street, rows of gacha toy machines that dispense mystery prizes like quirky miniatures or anime figures encourage customers to linger.

“I think that’s exactly where retail is slowly moving towards,” said Brian Cheung, Memory Shop’s owner. He has two stores now, and is opening a third on Harvard Avenue in Allston, known for its retail options, this summer. “Making shopping feel more like an experience is just something that Asian retailers do the best.”

For years, Boston was an afterthought for many of these concepts, said Byun. Today, entrepreneurs and national chains alike see Boston as a city worth investing in.

“You always heard about LA and New York, but that’s it,” said Byun of MAUM. “Now people are looking way outside of New York.”

“For us,” he added. “We’re doubling down in Boston.”

“We didn’t really need another restaurant around here... We needed a market like this,” said Kerrigan, who opened Steel & Rye in an old and largely empty auto dealership in 2012.

Perched up on a hill overlooking Dorchester’s Lower Mills, Two Pence Market will be part café, part neighborhood grocer where shoppers can pick up prepared meals, local produce, pantry staples, and fresh pasta. Or they can linger over breakfast, lunch, coffee, or scoops of Toscanini’s Ice Cream before browsing through a collection of wine and spirits to bring home. But behind shelves of groceries is a broader bet that the locally-owned businesses — not the highest-paying commercial tenants — can help revive Milton Village.

Wild, who lives in Milton and owns the building as well as several others that surround the market, said he purchased the property not knowing initially what would go in it.

“Certainly, I have a vision for everything in the Village, and knew that this [building] was kind of the cornerstone, a really important piece,” said Wild, who lives in Milton with his wife and three young children. His vision stretches beyond the market itself; he imagines closing some streets to cars for pop-up markets and other neighborhood events overlooking the Neponset River and Mattapan trolley tracks.

Buying the building before settling on a tenant, he said, was partly about “avoid[ing] it getting in the wrong hands.” He wanted an independent operator, not a national chain.

Instead, they’ll sell goods from local farms, like seasonal greens from the historic Allandale Farm, which dates back to the late 1700s in Chestnut Hill; and strawberries, blueberries, and peaches from Ward’s Berry Farm, a family-owned 175-acre farm in Sharon. They’ll have a self-serve coffee station using coffee from Fazenda Coffee Roasters of Dedham, along with black iced tea, a peach iced tea, and a lemongrass lemonade on draft.

Floral arrangements from Vow & Vine, whose owner creates arrangements out of her home in Dorchester, will line outdoor shelves next to the market’s front door and throughout the market. Fruits and vegetables will be piled up inside an old banking cart the owners found inside an old vault in the basement.

That same vault has been redeveloped into a workable, professional kitchen where they had to cut through 14-inch concrete walls. And they reused as much as they could from the original bank, such as the chandeliers and other lighting that were refurbished and hung from the ceiling.

Banking statements, a flyer advertising safe deposit boxes, and money bags from the early 1900s are framed in a hallway by the bathrooms. The fireplace has been reactivated, and people can lounge around it with coffee or a lunch. An upstairs vault has become “the bottle shop,” where shoppers can browse more than 200 wine labels, some local beer, and 120 spirit brands.

“We’re not looking to be a package store,” said Kerrigan. “We’re really looking to say: Here are three IPAs we love, three pilsners we love, a few non-alcoholic brands... showcasing stuff that’s local or small production.”

While shoppers can grab meals and bring them home, they can also order off the menu — filled with smoothies, breakfast sandwiches, farro bowls and poke, soups, and more — and eat them inside or outside on the market’s patio.

And there’s been plenty of buzz and anticipation for Two Pence to open. During a Globe interview with the three owners, neighbors pressed their faces against the front doors while peering inside, trying to catch a glimpse of when it might open. At one point, Larry Moulter, the former chairman of Boston Garden, strolled into the market wandered in with the same question.

Standing outside the restored bank and overlooking Milton Village, Wild gestured toward the market behind him.

“I had another [tenant] that would have paid more in rent... But it’s not about that,” said Wild, while standing outside of the market and looking over the neighborhood. “I believe in building up this Village for the long-term, and I know what’s possible.”

He pointed toward the front doors.

“Opening this,” said Wild, “Is the next step in that vision.”

“We’re both very optimistic,” Rush, a West Roxbury Democrat, told the Globe, referring to himself and Rogers. “We’re both committed to rebuilding a hospital in the town of Norwood.”

A spokesperson for the Healey administration wasn’t immediately available for comment.

For roughly two years, the massive skeleton of the hospital has stood unfinished in Norwood, an unsightly symbol of the spectacular downfall of its disgraced and bankrupt former operator, Steward Health Care.

The bill would authorize the state Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance to take the 11-acre property from its owner, Medical Properties Trust, an Alabama real estate investment trust, to ensure public access to health care.

“We’re ecstatic that the Legislature is taking the lead in making this happen,” said Tony Mazzucco, Norwood’s longtime town general manager. “It finally feels like we’ve reached a turning point and we’re on the other side of this long journey to get a hospital back.”

A spokesperson for MPT said the company had no comment. MPT’s website said the company wants to set the record straight on Norwood Hospital, although it did not address the possibility of the property’s seizure. MPT says it did not abandon the construction project and that it “has finished the building as much as possible without having a new hospital operator in place.”

“MPT Built the Hospital with its own funds when it could have walked away,” its website reads. “Massachusetts Must Work with MPT to Finish the Job.”

Under the bill heading to the House, the process to use eminent domain would begin on Nov. 1. It would involve the state assessing the value of the unfinished hospital and soliciting bids from nonprofit hospital operators who would seek to buy or lease the property.

The Globe reported last month that Mass General Brigham held talks late last year and early this year with MPT to buy the construction site in the hopes of finally completing the project and reopening the hospital.

But MPT sought “flagrantly unreasonable” sums from Mass General Brigham, and the negotiations fizzled out, according to Rogers, who said he had personally encouraged both sides to make a deal. A Mass General Brigham spokesperson declined to comment on the latest development Wednesday.

Norwood Hospital has been closed since June 28, 2020, after a storm in the area dumped nearly six inches of rain in 90 minutes. Flooding destroyed the facility’s electrical room, cutting off power and forcing the evacuation of all patients. The damage was so severe that the hospital, which had about 200 beds, had to be razed.

Steward paid for that, then launched a $375 million project to rebuild the century-old institution. The steel framework of the hospital went up.

But in 2024, Steward, a for-profit national chain, ran out of money, stopped paying its bills, and collapsed in a bankruptcy that made headlines across the country. MPT paid to build a roof, install a heating and cooling system, and add windows and metal panels to seal the structure before winter, the Globe reported last year. Then the work stopped, local officials say. (MPT on its website said, “Construction has never been ‘paused.’”)

Because Norwood Hospital was closed when Steward declared bankruptcy, and its doctors and nurses had moved elsewhere, it wasn’t among the 31 hospitals nationally that Steward put up for sale. Norwood Hospital’s travails were overshadowed by the broader crisis provoked by Steward’s collapse.

It is the only one of eight former Steward hospitals in Massachusetts whose fate remains unresolved. It served an estimated quarter of a million people in a dozen nearby communities, and residents say they still intensely feel its absence.

MPT had bought Steward hospitals’ land and buildings in a sale-leaseback deal in 2016. The arrangement left the hospitals on the hook for excessively high rents, weakening them financially before life-threatening lapses in care occurred, a Globe Spotlight Team investigation reported.

The Spotlight Team in 2024 found a pattern of overpayment in MPT purchases of Steward real estate. Asked at that time about what appeared to be inflated hospital valuations, MPT’s then-spokesperson Drew Babin called the Globe’s findings “false and misleading” and said, “MPT stands firmly behind our rigorous underwriting process.”

Judge William F. Sullivan has a delicate path to walk.

He’s presiding over the high-profile trial of Lindsay Clancy for the killings of her three children. And he does so with the unenviable task of navigating between the public’s long-held right to view court proceedings and the necessity to avoid a circus that could upend them.

Clancy, of Duxbury, does not deny she killed her children, but is pleading not guilty under what’s commonly known as the insanity defense. Her lawyer maintains she should not be held criminally responsible because she was so deep in the throes of postpartum depression and psychosis.

The case has drawn intense attention for the unfathomable crime alleged, and also what it may spotlight about the way the health system treats women and, in particular, mothers.

Harrowing listening

The trial is expected to run as long as two months, and already Sullivan’s balancing act faces two tests. The first is expected to come this morning, when the court will hear the 911 call that Clancy’s husband, Patrick Clancy, made when he arrived home from getting take-out. He found his three children strangled in their basement and his then-wife severely injured following a suicide attempt outside the home.

From prosecutors’ statements and court records, we know the broad strokes: Patrick Clancy stayed on the phone as he first saw Lindsay Clancy, and then still as he discovered his children dead or dying. It will be harrowing listening, if admissible evidence that will give the jury more information about what happened that night in January 2023.

So Sullivan is allowing it to be played in court — but not livestreamed and widely broadcast, as much of the rest of the trial is. Only those present can hear it. The media can report on it, but not record it.

A controlled crime scene

The second test of balance is the jury’s viewing of the Clancys’ former home, expected later in the week. On Tuesday, Sullivan deemed it to be limited to lawyers on both sides, court staff, and the 18-person jury, six of whom will be designated as alternates when deliberations start.

Sullivan also ordered that Duxbury and State Police will be responsible for securing the area before jurors arrive, and for keeping unauthorized “third parties” off the premises during the view. He also decided jurors will be allowed “to visually inspect the outside of the property as well as . . . the basement, all rooms on the first floor, and all rooms on the second floor of the premises.”

They won’t be permitted to “open closet doors, touch any items within the premises, or disturb items,” Sullivan wrote.

This can work. Two years ago, I covered the first trial of Karen Read, the Mansfield woman who was tried twice and ultimately acquitted of the death of her boyfriend, Boston Police officer John O’Keefe. That trial was, if anything, even more closely watched and controversial than this one, driven by claims of police corruption and a coverup.

A break in the circus

In spring 2023, those of us in the media cohort covering the Read trial followed the jury as they were bused to the scene of O’Keefe’s death outside of a Canton home. Police kept us — and some of the non-media spectators who regularly attended the trial — down the street, probably a few hundred feet away as the jurors, attorneys, and even the judge milled about outside the home where O’Keefe’s body was found. A crowd watched from afar, but didn’t interfere.

The trial was a circus, but the crime scene view went fine.
