There used to be a homicide in Boston, on average, every 58 hours. A man was found beaten and strangled to death in Savin Hill Park one Saturday afternoon in July, a pregnant woman found shot in the face on Neponset Avenue a few hours later. The year was 1990.

And at the forefront of fighting this vicious scourge of violence were Black clergymen, working with residents, advocates, and police to help bring about a huge dip in street violence, in what was eventually dubbed the Boston Miracle.

Now, more than three decades later, homicides in Boston are down nearly 80 percent from 1990, with fewer shootings and assaults than comparable American cities.

Those statistics beg the question: What makes a city safe?

It’s an inquiry with a multifaceted — and sometimes elusive — answer that keeps local ministers out on the streets on hot July evenings, talking to any stranger who will listen and some who won’t, and meeting with local police and other community leaders to dissect the problem in granular detail.

For Randy Muhammad, the solution to street violence in every era starts with being out on the streets. So on a recent Monday, he approached the type of crowd plenty of people would walk by and avoid eye contact. He sees an opportunity.

The group of men and women were hanging outside Ashmont T station. Some drank beers in brown paper bags, others nips of liquor. One guy rolled a joint. Another wore a balaclava obscuring his face despite the July heat.

Muhammad, senior minister for the Nation of Islam’s Muhammad Mosque No. 11 in Grove Hall, was on an hour-long peace walk through this section of Dorchester with about 30 others. The group walks the streets every Monday night.

“More unites us than divides us,” Muhammad tells those who are here. “We’re an example that we can come together, regardless of what neighborhood you come from.”

Boston, strictly by the numbers, is a safe American city. In 2024, The Economist declared it the safest major city in the nation, a distinction some, though not all, advocates scoff at. After all, if there are still shots being fired on your block, what good is that label?

Muhammad is acutely aware of this.

“It don’t feel safe to everybody,” he said, “but numbers don’t lie.”

This year, those numbers look like this: total shooting incidents in Boston for the year, as of July 19, were at 53, the same tally for the same time frame last year, but below the five-year average of 68. Homicides are down, both year over year and when compared to the five-year average: 13 so far this year, compared to 21 last year over the same period. The five-year average is 17. Those are a fraction of the killings that gripped so many neighborhoods decades ago.

While homicides are also down elsewhere in the US, the number of slayings in Boston is much lower than in cities of comparable size, like Baltimore and Washington, D.C., and much lower than smaller cities like New Orleans.

Among the Black ministers who have done this street-level outreach work, there is little consensus over what has kept street violence in Boston down.

Some credit police engagement with various communities, and the willingness of city officials, nonprofit advocates, and clergy to collaborate and identify shooters and would-be shooters and try to encourage them to choose a different life path.

Some church leaders offer a simple explanation: maybe a critical mass of the really bad guys are locked up or have been rehabilitated.

Others, among 10 clergy interviewed, hail the impact of after-school and extracurricular programming. Some highlight the importance of summer jobs.

“It takes a job to stop a bullet,” said City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, senior pastor of Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church.

Yet others point to gentrification, suggesting that the escalating cost of living may have pushed out some would-be shooters. Some even cite the quality of hospitals, in keeping some gunshot victims from being another murder stat.

Or maybe it’s a combination of all of those factors.

* * *

It was not always this way. In 1990, Boston saw a record-breaking 152 homicides. The driver of that bloodshed was the introduction of crack cocaine in the late 1980s. As that market developed, so did turf-based gangs and the wars that went along with them, according to research from Christopher Winship, a sociology professor at Harvard University.

Boston had a street violence problem, and some people wondered aloud if that level of bloodshed was going to become a permanent reality.

It didn’t. Between 1990 and 1996, homicides in the city dropped about 60 percent. Many city stakeholders believe the decline in violence was driven, at least in part, by Black clergy, according to Harvard research, specifically a consortium of churches known as the Ten-Point Coalition.

Some faith-based leaders participated in Operation Ceasefire, an initiative from the mid-1990s that saw a “fully institutionalized collaboration” among various agencies, including Boston police and outreach workers. It focused on offering gang members ways out, and threatening them with federal sentences in prisons far from their families if they continued to be violent, according to past Globe coverage.

The dip in street violence during the 1990s was eventually called the Boston Miracle, and underpinning it was the street outreach work of Black ministers, who, in working with at-risk youth, “projected a sense of fairness.” Because people trusted them, the Black clergy created “an umbrella of legitimacy for fair and just policing.”

“The police cannot be effective if their activities are not perceived as legitimate by the community,” one of Winship’s research publications stated.

An outgrowth of that effort in the 1990s can still be seen in the basement of Roxbury’s Charles Street AME Church, every Wednesday morning. There, police, including members of the city’s gang unit, probation officers, sheriff’s deputies, representatives from the district attorney’s office, nonprofit staffers, and clergy convene to discuss crime in the city. These weekly meetings have continued since 1998, and some credit the collaboration fostered by such regular communication as helping prevent and mitigate street violence.

“That level of collaboration had never existed anywhere,” said the Rev. Eugene F. Rivers III, pastor at Azusa Christian Community, who founded the weekly meeting during the 1990s and was a leader in the Ten-Point Coalition.

Bishop John M. Borders III, of Morning Star Baptist Church in Mattapan, agrees that cooperation between the political, law enforcement, and pastoral classes of Boston is key. He recalls years in the early 1990s when he would preside over funerals for 25 to 30 murder victims.

“It was a way of life for me,” he said this summer. “It became personally exhausting and I suffered depression as a result of grieving with those families for so many years. So many deaths.”

One of those funerals would become the flashpoint for action and the partnerships lauded by so many in the city. In 1992, a funeral on a Thursday night for a 20-year-old victim of a drive-by shooting was interrupted when a group of young men stabbed a mourner.

Globe coverage of the violence paints a picture of hysteria and chaos: one person was chased through a parking lot and fired several shots from a handgun, one of which went through the open church door and lodged in a wall. Another mourner was pursued by youths up a church aisle toward the altar, almost tripping over the casket before being cornered in an alcove, where the assailants mauled him.

The funeral violence shook Boston, and prompted hundreds of clergy to come together. That spirit of collaboration continues to this day.

“It was the tipping point for the city,” Borders said.

Like Borders, Bishop William E. Dickerson II, senior pastor for Greater Love Tabernacle in Dorchester, has done hundreds of funerals for homicide victims. He grew up in Boston. He knows the city’s history of racism, including a stark racial wealth gap. One doesn’t have to be a scholar to see the link between affluence and reduced levels of street violence.

He has done street-level outreach and is not above getting confrontational to drive his points home, particularly during funeral services.

“You see your boy lying in the casket?” he demonstrated during an interview. “What y’all going to do? Go right back to the block?”

The Rev. Jeffrey Brown, associate pastor at Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury and a leader of the Ten-Point Coalition in the 1990s, did street-level ministry work throughout the worst violence of past decades and understood that locking people up was not going to be enough.

Collaboration was key. Sometimes, it meant police allowing clergy to work with gang members to get them on a better track rather than arresting them. Other times, it was city officials securing a job for a young person who was at risk of making some terrible choices.

Brown acknowledged that some people, no matter how they are approached, “are going to do what they’re going to do.” But he estimates that cohort to be a small percentage of those wrapped up in the criminal underground, say 2 to 4 percent.

His message to those embedded in street life was always the same: “The potential of your worth has yet to be seen.”

* * *

Back on the streets of Ashmont, Muhammad, the Nation of Islam minister, is handing out fliers promoting a mediation and conflict resolution hot line.

He’s wearing a bright orange T-shirt emblazoned with a quote from Louis Farrakhan, the Nation of Islam leader who attracted controversy in years past for antisemitic, homophobic, and misogynistic rhetoric. The quote itself is unobjectionable: “Making our communities safe & decent places to live.”

The idea behind events such as the peace walk is to build a rapport with community members, he said. That way, when it comes to disputes that could end in violence, his group can act as a neutral third party.

“We offer an exit ramp,” said Muhammad. Oftentimes, he said, “we’re the only voice of deescalation.”

Muhammad and others will talk to everyone they come across in their walks: men and women, old and young, Black and white. Some cajole strangers to join them on Mondays for the peace walk.

“We have to be vigilant, stay on it,” he said of street violence in Boston. “If you’re not out here being proactive, it just takes an instant . . . it can change.”

Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

The state medical examiner on Thursday ruled that the death of a teenager who was found July 18 in a Mattapan rental property owned by Representative Ayanna Pressley’s husband was a homicide, police said.

Police also formally identified the victim as Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio, 18, of Boston.

No arrests have been made; police officials have said there’s “absolutely nothing that indicates any connection to the owners of the property” on Malta Street.

Pressley and her husband, Conan Harris, live in the Hyde Park section of Boston, according to her website.

“The Boston Police Department Homicide Unit is actively investigating the facts and circumstances surrounding this incident,” officials said in a statement Thursday.

Ocasio’s mother, Elenie Ocasio, previously told Boston 25 News that a perpetrator fatally shot her daughter in an act of domestic violence.

“He put a gun to her head, took my baby in that house, and left her to die,” she told the station.

She had identified her daughter at the time as Yoseliani Marte.

Pressley said in a recent statement that she is “devastated about the death of Yoseliani Marte, an 18-year-old with so many dreams ahead of her, her life cut short by domestic violence.”

Police have released no information about a suspect.

Pressley said that as a parent of a teenager herself, “the thought of a young person violently losing their life in this way is beyond crushing.”

The lawmaker said she stands with “our community and everyone who loved Yoseliani as we grieve this deep loss. May we all honor her life and humanity and extend compassion to her loved ones as they navigate this heartbreaking tragedy.”

Shea Butter Smoothies, a Dorchester juice bar where Marte worked, posted a heartfelt remembrance of her to Facebook on July 20.

“Liani was a brilliant and motivated young lady whose passion and dedication had a profound impact on our team and the work we do,” the business said. “Her innovative ideas, particularly in enhancing Shea Butter Smoothies, brought a unique touch that our customers adored. She approached every project with enthusiasm, creativity, and an unwavering commitment to excellence.”

She also “brought joy and positivity to our workplace. Her infectious laughter, kindness, and willingness to help others made her not just a colleague, but a cherished friend to many,” the post said. “She will be missed immensely, and her legacy will live on in the hearts of those who had the privilege of knowing her.”

To honor her life and support her relatives as they grieve, the business said, “we will be donating 50 percent of the proceeds from every purchase of the Big Papi smoothie to assist with her funeral costs. We encourage our community to join us in this effort, as we remember the beautiful person she was. ... Rest in peace, Yoseliani. You will always be remembered.”

Since Wilkins took over leadership, the orchestra has tried to attract audiences through what he calls a “strategy of participation,” he said.

“Partnerships, and collaborations, and invitations to communities who wouldn’t ordinarily think of symphonic music are very much front of mind.”

In other words, Landmarks is equally as likely to collaborate with the likes of the New England Aquarium, Brazilian drumming project Grooversity, and Haitian and Armenian dance companies as they are to pull in a Boys and Girls club or a local music education program such as Boston Strings Academy. American Sign Language interpreters are present at most Landmarks events. Some concerts even make haptic vests available, to provide a tactile experience of the music for deaf and hard of hearing attendees.

“We tend to program backwards. We first think of who we can get involved, and then we think, ‘What can we program to support that collaboration?’” said Wilkins. “I think it’s been really effective, and fun, and…the orchestra’s stretched artistically, because it’s playing some music orchestras don’t usually play.”

In the earliest years, concerts were slightly more formal and standard-repertoire driven “after the Arthur Fiedler model,” explained Paula Oakes, a violinist who has been in the ensemble since its second season.

Landmarks started regularly performing at the Hatch Shell in 2007, a handful of years after the Pops Esplanade Orchestra (in which several Landmarks players also play) scaled back its summer concerts in the city.

“It’s not a situation where it’s high-falutin’ classical music,” said trumpeter Dana Oakes, another longtime Landmarks player and Paula’s husband. “It’s a really good vibe out there.”

There’s little separation from the sights and sounds of the city, with cars driving along Storrow Drive on one side and joggers and dog walkers taking the Esplanade path on the other. Anyone can leave the concert and come back without consequence. It perhaps follows naturally that there’s barely any enforcement of the usual rules of orchestral concert hall etiquette, even those some might take for granted, such as sitting quietly while the orchestra plays.

It’s not unusual to see young children with batons in hand “conducting” the orchestra from a music stand near the Hatch Shell (cutely dubbed the “Maestro Zone”) or patrons wandering to a nearby ice cream truck mid-concert; or people listening while they play card games. With a much different atmosphere than Boston’s temples of music like Symphony Hall, the Hatch shell during these concerts feels like a gathering place, where people can choose to socialize in parallel with the music.

And that’s not even getting into the music Wilkins chooses. “With all due respect, Charles had a great concept for the orchestra, but this is something Charles would not have done: reach out to what would not be considered classical by any stretch, and somehow weave it into a program that’s seamless,” said Paula Oakes.

Landmarks’s repertoire mixes symphonies and other large-scale works from the standard repertoire with some film music, the Leroy Anderson-esque fare sometimes called “light classical,” orchestrations of genre-crossing modern tunes, and the occasional world premiere, such as 2018’s “Pegasus Promenade,” which was collectively composed by Gonzalo Grau and four students and alumni of East Boston arts program ZUMIX.

Paula Oakes admitted she doesn’t adore every piece she plays with Landmarks, but that’s not a negative in her reckoning. “It stretches your imagination, it stretches your technique,” she said.

Wilkins “made the programs we play much more challenging, and he just included so many different types of music as well,” Dana concurred.

Because Landmarks’s outdoor season is confined to the short New England summer, the orchestra has been making overtures towards performing more indoor concerts as well during and outside its standard performing weeks. This weekend, the orchestra brings a program including Mozart’s Symphony No. 40 and Max Richter’s recomposition of Vivaldi’s “Four Seasons” to churches in Jamaica Plain and Roxbury; next week, it’s back to the Hatch Shell for Verdi’s massive “Requiem” on the evening of August 5 with the One City Choir and Cantata Singers.

So far, the indoor audiences haven’t been as large as the lawn crowds on the Esplanade, but Wilkins sees it as “not as much about the numbers,” that being more important that people attend in the first place, he said.

“I think for the most part, people understand what our mission is,” he said. “I think it’s pretty obvious that we’re using great music to create community connection.”

Though a summer rainstorm soaked the Esplanade a few hours before showtime on July 22, that community connection seemed to be in abundance at the first concert of the season, which was performed to an all-ages crowd including a handful of multigenerational families and even a few dogs. Many brought sandwiches and other picnic fare; one ambitious group even brought their own table and spread out a Thai takeout feast. A young musician who had performed in the prelude concert happily added a Landmarks Orchestra sticker to the collection of Sanrio characters on her cello case. Couples wandered down the path holding hands, some lingering for a few minutes to listen, some content to enjoy the music as they passed by. A tattooed man in all black ate popcorn out of a plastic bag with chopsticks.

Landmarks season ”is one of my favorite times of year,” said state representative Jay Livingstone from the stage, naming the most crucial key to Landmarks’s success. “Anyone can come down the Esplanade and enjoy it.”

Legislators slapped a lot more on the table Thursday. The House added bills covering road safety, prosthetics, and licenses to the docket for Friday. The Senate passed its version of public records legislation Thursday, and teed up a likely vote on Friday for a bill that supporters say would furtherexpand abortion access. And negotiators checked other items off of their to-do list, striking deals on legislation that would set new standards and protections for home care workers and reshapechild welfare laws.

House Speaker Ron Mariano struck an optimistic-ish note Thursday. “There’s less of a potential for us to be here at 3:30 in the morning like we were last [session],” he told reporters. (The House actually adjourned at 9:19 a.m,. on Aug. 1 in 2024 after an all-night final formal session.)

Still, no one really knows how the day (and night) will go. So for the lobbyists, staffers, lawmakers, and assorted State House denizens settling in for whatever Friday turns into, we put together a list of do’s-and-don’ts to survive the last scheduled formal session.

Do lower your expectations. Waiting on a deal to finally pop on the Legislature’s energy affordability bill? Hoping to see movement on the policy-packed economic development bill? Don’t hold your breath. Lawmakers could reach agreements and vote to pass bills that are already being negotiated behind closed doors, but it’s more likely they spend the next 17 hours (and maybe beyond) getting bills into so-called conference committees instead of pulling almost-finished products out of them.

Don’t lower your caffeine intake.

Do take your time getting to the State House. You probably have time to see a matinee of “The Odyssey.” In IMAX. In Rhode Island. Most of the real action probably won’t start until later in the day.

Don’t make any Friday night plans. Even if they don’t drag things out until 3:30 a.m., on Saturday, Beacon Hill lawmakers have a tendency to start late and end late. And with that in mind …

Do remember that time is an illusion. Technically, legislators have to finish moving things into closed-door negotiations by midnight to keep them in play for the remainder of the two-year session. But time often works differently on the last night of the session, and lawmakers can extend the clock for as long as they want, technically keeping it July 31 until, say, 9:19 a.m. the next day.

Don’t panic if the bill you’re watching doesn’t land on the governor’s desk by Friday night. Lawmakers have until early January to finish work on anything that survives Friday’s deadline — though with the November election looming, there’s plenty of incentive to wrap things up sooner.

Do keep an eye on the more than 1,000 bills that were awaiting action from the House and Senate budget committees as of Thursday.

Don’t expect most of those to pass. While legislative leaders likely will try to get a range of legislation into conference committees so they have more fodder to trade for things they actually want to pass, most of the bills that aren’t already on the move face long odds of surviving this session.

Do take some comfort in knowing the session has to end at some point. Right? RIGHT???

Don’t hit The 21st Amendment until that actually happens.

In the Vanderburgh case, a sprinkler installer told the Globe that Foote had done something similar, using a legitimate invoice from when the contractor previously did work for Foote to create phony ones for other locations where he did little or no work.

Steven DeLiberto of WAM Fire Protection said the bogus invoices on his letterhead featured his electronic signature — which he disavowed — and specified that various payments were due “forthwith.”

“I don’t use words like ‘forthwith,’” DeLiberto said, calling himself “just the sprinkler guy, moderately intelligent. … Nope, I leave that for reporters and highly educated college guys like Hunter. That’s for people who are smarter than I’ll ever be.”

After consulting with DeLiberto and conducting inspections in late 2024 and early 2025, MassHousing determined Foote “misrepresented” the extent of work completed at seven sober homes and told him to return the agency’s money. In three cases, inspectors found no work at all had been done, according to the letters, though the grants had been almost fully paid out based on invoices submitted by Foote and his associates.

All told, the agency demanded Foote and the associates give back more than $430,000. None of it has been returned to date.

Paul McMorrow, a MassHousing spokesperson, said the agency “takes allegations of potential fraud and noncompliance seriously.” He noted staffers took “immediate action” after identifying discrepancies in the sprinkler program in 2024, demanding the return of the money and referring the matter to the attorney general.

The sprinkler program and the problems with Gateway Cities grants were both referred to the Massachusetts attorney general, whose office confirmed to the Globe it is investigating both matters.

In an interview with the Globe, Foote denied any wrongdoing and said he doesn’t believe he owes the state anything. He acknowledged preparing the disputed invoices, but said if there were any inflated claims of progress, they were based on assertions from DeLiberto, whom he trusted at the time. He said he paid DeLiberto for all of the work listed on invoices and then billed the state.

Foote said he eventually completed all of the jobs, except for two where he determined sprinklers weren’t needed under local law, and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars of his own money to do it.

He said he submitted voluminous paperwork to MassHousing documenting compliance more than a year ago, but, “it’s been radio silence for a long time.” He did not share the paperwork with the Globe, which requested it.

The fire sprinkler grant program is the second program overseen by a now-former MassHousing official in which grantees have been accused of submitting — and receiving payment for — bogus invoices for work that was not performed.

The Globe Spotlight team reported in June that developers Gary Acquah and Reggie Woods, who received $1.4 million in grant money from MassHousing to rehabilitate blighted apartments in Worcester and Pittsfield, submitted invoices claiming more than $500,000 in work was done by at least nine subcontractors who said they didn’t do the jobs and weren’t paid for them.

Many of those subcontractors had done other work for Acquah and Woods, and they believed the pair used their earlier invoices as a template for fake ones.

Both programs were overseen by Tony Richards II, who resigned July 17 as vice president of strategic community initiatives for MassHousing. His departure came three weeks after the Globe reported he had steered the Gateway Cities grant money to Acquah and Woods months after they sold Richards a home in West Roxbury for $204,000 less than its original list price.

For the sprinkler program, MassHousing would not provide the Globe with contractor invoices and other records related to payments to Foote and his affiliates, citing an exemption in the public records law for documents that are part of an open investigation.

The Fire Sprinkler Safety Program was designed to cover most or all of the cost of installing sprinklers at sober homes around the state amid new regulations. The program offered up to $80,000 to sober homes that had been in operation for at least a year and certified by a nonprofit association.

But as with the grants in the Gateway Cities housing program, MassHousing did not inspect the sprinkler installations before it paid for the bulk of the work, a setup one watchdog group criticized.

“Any system of internal controls that relies on trust is not a system of internal controls,” said Mary Connaughton, director of government transparency at the Pioneer Institute, a right-leaning think tank. “Onsite inspections would obviously be the best solution.”

Connaughton added, “It would make sense for MassHousing to take a really close look at their policies,” especially because “this is the second kind of incident where this has happened.”

The seven homes where the state is disputing the payments are all linked to Foote, a Worcester entrepreneur who operates sober homes in Springfield, Taunton, New Bedford, and other locations and also offers franchising arrangements.

Foote acknowledged challenges with getting sprinklers installed at the nine properties for which he received grants. Ultimately, he told the Globe, work was completed at all but two, at a cost of more than $900,000 — significantly more than what he received from MassHousing. He said the scope of work at the two incomplete jobs had been scaled back for valid reasons.

Foote denied knowingly submitting fake invoices. He said the requests for payment he made on DeLiberto’s letterhead reflected the contractor’s assertions of how much work had been completed at the time. However, he declined to say how much he paid DeLiberto for work that he now alleges the contractor did not do. Foote has not filed a lawsuit seeking to recover money from DeLiberto.

What really matters, Foote said, is that the sprinklers were eventually installed.

“We’re ready to address any concerns,” Foote said. “But we need to know what they are and what we need to do about them. If it’s a permit closeout, we’ll close it out. We spent more money than was disbursed to us by a significant factor. It did take a long time, and it was very frustrating. But it all got done.”

DeLiberto, for his part, flatly denied Foote’s claims.

“He’s a worthless piece of [expletive] who continues to lie about everything,” DeLiberto said.

Moreover, in at least three cases, public records raise questions about Foote’s assertion that the work was completed satisfactorily. In Taunton, Deputy Fire Chief Robert Bastis told the Globe the city has not approved any sprinkler systems at two properties for which Foote received grants.

“From our perspective, there are no fire sprinklers, no building permits, no fire inspections” on record for those properties, Bastis said.

Likewise, in New Bedford, a permit application for a sprinkler system at a Vanderburgh sober home was rejected by inspectors with the city’s Department of Public Infrastructure in late 2024. No permit was ever approved, officials said.

Foote provided the Globe with documents showing a private firm had inspected those three systems in July 2025 and said there were “no deficiencies observed.” MassHousing’s contract with grant recipients says all jobs must be inspected and approved by municipal authorities. Foote did not respond to a question from the Globe about why some of the Vanderburgh jobs lacked such a designation.

Records show the firm that did the inspections, Tristar Fire Protection, has taken out a lien on Foote’s New Bedford sober home over unpaid bills of more than $16,000.

Since the problems were discovered in 2024, MassHousing has made some changes, according to agency officials, including “immediate re-inspection” of all fire sprinkler projects and new protocols requiring multiple inspections of such projects in the future.

Originally, the sprinkler program imposed no deadlines. The program’s current rules require work to be complete in 12 months, with the possibility of a six-month extension.

It does not appear MassHousing’s board, which is appointed by the governor, was made aware of the problems its staff discovered in either the sprinkler program or the Gateway Cities program. The Globe could not find records of any discussion in board minutes. Board Chair Jeanne Pinado declined to comment, deferring questions to the agency’s communications office. A MassHousing spokesperson also declined to comment.

Six of the board’s nine members were appointed by Governor Maura Healey, who has said little about the problems at MassHousing.

An internal audit by MassHousing published late last year made cryptic reference to recent “control improvements” to some programs under Richards’s oversight after management had “self-identified” shortcomings. McMorrow, the agency spokesperson, said it “has revamped grant application intake and evaluation processes, clarified design standards, created new grant closing checklists, improved invoicing and disbursement processes, and instituted mandatory third-party construction inspections.”

War in Iran, and the high gas prices it has brought, is one place to start. ICE killings and general uncertainty about the direction of the country under President Trump is another. Democracy is being threatened and violence is condoned. Bad news streams 24/7.

Then again, things have been worse. The country was fiercely divided by the bloodshed of the Civil War and the politics and lives lost in Vietnam. The Great Depression brought bread lines before the New Deal.

And, more recently, the COVID-19 pandemic claimed 1.2 million American lives and radically changed how we live and work.

In an unscientific survey, the Globe interviewed folks relaxing outdoors. Maybe something someone says here can help reduce our stress.

Chris Cuddy is barefoot, sitting on a park bench in Marblehead’s Crocker Park reading a book on a Sunday afternoon.

He says that last night he got in a long debate in a café with a friend about Trump and he regrets it.

“He’s just going on and on about Trump and I’m like, ‘dude, I just want to read a book now,’” he says.

“Whether you like him or not, it’s too much,” says Cuddy. who calls the president “a clown.”

But even the book he’s reading “The Typewriter and the Guillotine” by Mark Braude, makes him think of Trump.

It’s about Janet Flanner, a New Yorker writer in Paris sounding the alarm about the rise of fascism before World War II. She profiles German Chancellor Adolf Hitler as a megalomaniac with mystical tendencies and no common sense.

“She starts seeing that this Hitler guy is coming up and he’s up to no good, but no one believes her, so don’t worry about him,’' he says.

Sound familiar?

“I wish he would just go away,” he says of the president.

With that off his chest, he pauses, and gazes out over spectacular Marblehead Harbor.

“I like the children’s laughter and watching the birds. It calms me down,” says Cuddy, a creative director and author of children’s books. “And I like random conversations like this. It makes you realize this is what life is about.”

Mark Kahn, strumming a guitar at nearby Devereaux Beach, says he watches the news, “as little as possible. I play the guitar, I bike, and I swim.”

Instead of doing an interview, he sings a Frank Zappa song, “Take Your Clothes Off When You Dance.”

He smiles when he sings the lyrics: “There will come a time when every evil that we know will be an evil that we can rise above!”

Joining in the impromptu jam is Joseph Edwin Downy, 2, playing the cymbals. “He’s obsessed with music.” says Emilie Flores, his mother. “He literally will dance to any beat.”

They keep the music turned up and shield him from the bad news on the tube.

“I’m just taking it one thing at a time, one day at a time. Trying to make sure he sees the positive,” she says. “It’s kind of impossible not to have him see something dark but even if he does, we try to at least make sure he’s understanding of it.’’

On Revere Beach, when people ask Richard Salvo, 80, how he reduces stress, he tells them to go fly a kite. Literally.

Salvo, a retired building supply salesman from Saugus, had just launched a half dozen bright kites. He gets them airborne and anchors them in a stake buried in sand. Then relaxes in a beach chair.

“I bring my book, but then I get antsy after a while, so I get up and check my kites … then I go back to reading my book.”

It’s a Chase Fulton spy novel. He’s also a big Trump supporter, one of the 77 million Americans who voted for him in 2024. Salvo still supports him.

“The only thing I blame the president for is he’s not a politician, but he proved that a businessman could run the country better than a politician.”

“What’s ruining the world is social media right now. People will say things they would never say to your face.”

His advice to relax is simple: “Enjoy life,” he says. “And it doesn’t hurt to pray once in a while.”

At Skaket Beach in Orleans, Brian Convery crafts a pair of fire breathing sand dragons with his friend, Ed Foisy. It takes them three hours and then they place flares inside the sculptures’ mouths and light them at sunset.

Convery deliberately sculpts them below the high tide line, so they get swallowed by the ocean. That’s a life lesson, he says.

“Everything is temporary,” he says.

The art encourages conversations and keeps kids away from their iPhones.

“It’s just people saying, ‘wow, I never saw anything like this before.’ It’s fun. And what we are missing is fun.”

In Quincy, Erica Norman, a jewelry store manager, runs through a tunnel of trees along the city’s riverwalk next to the Neponset. She’s listening to Billy Joel sing “We Didn’t Start the Fire” with its chorus, “It was always burning since the world’s been turning.”

But she believes people are nastier these days.

“There’s terrible people out there getting brainwashed left and right, and you just want to find people that are like-minded. You can’t get away from it so running is just a way to clear my head.”

Keith Jones, 61, of Concord loves to bike to Walden Pond and swim in its warm, gentle waters.

He says he channels the pond’s onetime neighbor, Henry David Thoreau, but is not very optimistic for our future.

“I don’t think human beings can fix a broken world,” he says.

He is also concerned about AI. “We evolved from an agrarian society to an industrial society. Now we’re a technical society where machines are starting to do work for us and think for us. And what will that do to the human species is a complete unknown.”

A recovering addict, he’s gone back to school to be an addiction counselor “to offer people hope,” he says. “Life is stressful. It’s ebbs and flows. And I’ve lived long enough to know that with every trough, there’s going to be a peak. … It’s one of life’s lessons,” he says.

Restaurants close, as surely as they open. The closing of these particular restaurants feels notable. They are successful. They helped turn their corner of the South End into a dining destination. They’ve been open for a decade, with loyal followings. And they are run by one of Boston’s strongest, most-experienced hospitality teams — the kind of people who pay back investors and give back to the community.

If the bottom line doesn’t work for them, who can it work for?

Boston dining feels as if it has reached a tipping point. This is a city where a liquor license can sell for more than half a million dollars. Rent and other expenses keep rising while thin margins narrow further. The cost of ingredients fluctuates so dramatically, restaurants can’t update their menu prices fast enough to keep up. And well-known, well-funded out-of-town businesses — Cactus Club Cafe (Canada), Hawksmoor (London), Major Food Group (New York), Union Square Hospitality Group (New York) — are moving in at a rapid rate, replicating concepts that already exist elsewhere.

They see Boston as an opportunity. Developers and landlords see them as a good bet. Small, local, independent restaurants keep fighting. Over the last year, in fact, they’ve noticeably upped their game — perhaps in response to the presence of the Michelin Guide, which included Boston for the first time in 2025. But the landscape is much more challenging than it was when places like Biba, Clio, Hamersley’s Bistro, L’Espalier, Olives, Radius, Rialto, and so many others flourished here.

In March, I received a message from the team behind Nine, the restaurant that took over the former No. 9 Park space in Beacon Hill. “Since opening, we’ve had our share of ups and downs in this economy, but we’re so proud of the team that’s stuck with us through it all,” it read. “It would mean everything to be able to reward that loyalty with a busy, thriving restaurant — especially before the bigger city chains start moving in.” That was not to be. Nine closed in June, after less than a year in business.

A month later, Seaport restaurant Chickadee followed, after eight years at the industrial end of the neighborhood. Another excellent independent restaurant with experienced operators, gone.

“It’s an expensive city to live in, so people are tightening the belt. People are leaving, unfortunately,” said Chickadee chef and co-owner John DaSilva. “The labor shortage, too . . . . With the talent gap and lack of training, it’s almost like we as operators are hiring line cooks as sous chefs and sous chefs as chefs de cuisine.”

Just above us is Portland. Just below us is Providence, home to culinary school Johnson & Wales. Both cities have excellent, interesting dining scenes where independent businesses can thrive. Both offer a lower cost of living and operating.

“We see articles comparing Boston [dining] to Portland and Providence. Often people are putting us at No. 3,” DaSilva said. “Maybe you’re a young cook who went to Johnson & Wales. You used to come to Boston. Now it’s, why would you, when they’re doing cool and interesting [things] in Providence or Portland — or New York? If Boston is almost as expensive, you might as well move to New York and work for the best chefs in the country.”

This doesn’t scream “world-class city.”

When the Michelin Guide announced its results for Boston, 311 Omakase received one star; six restaurants received a Bib Gourmand designation, connoting good value; and 19 restaurants were “recommended.” Even just a decade ago, Michelin would have found many more restaurants to consider. Tourism marketing bureau Meet Boston reportedly spent $1 million to bring the prestigious dining awards here for three years. But if the city isn’t friendly to the kind of restaurants that win those awards, why bother? This year, there wasn’t a single Boston nominee for the James Beard Awards.

Things need to change, before it is too late. Boston’s character is at stake.

That’s not hyperbole. The flavor of a city’s restaurant landscape helps determine the flavor of the city itself. A diverse, risk-taking, high-quality dining scene — a “cool” dining scene — brings in visitors and their dollars. More important, it attracts residents and keeps them here. It makes a city a desirable place to call home. It makes our high residential rents seem more worth it. Restaurants are where we gather, what we line up for, what we follow (almost) as closely as sports. They are the center of our weekend plans and social lives.

It won’t feel like Boston anymore if we can’t say: Hey, want to meet for dim sum in Chinatown, tacos in East Boston, pho in Fields Corner, Haitian food in Mattapan, Italian food in the North End, cocktails in South Boston, dinner in the South End? It won’t feel like Boston anymore if the hot new restaurant is always an outpost of a chain, or another iteration of a dominant restaurant group’s aesthetic, just with different spices.

There are many good landlords in this city, and Lynch and DaSilva stress their strong relationships with theirs. But we cannot count on landlords to prioritize local, independent restaurants without incentive or requirement. We cannot make it solely diners’ responsibility to keep their favorite restaurants in business — especially as dining grows ever more expensive, and diners’ dollars dearer.

We need intentional, concerted plans and policies from the city itself in order to reverse course.

Easier said than done, and Boston is certainly working on it — creating free liquor licenses, starting entrepreneur training programs like the new BizUnlocked, which graduated its first class this summer, and more.

I recently had a rich and lively conversation with City Councilor Brian Worrell about what might help. He spoke of streamlining the notoriously onerous permitting process, making restaurant and transportation hours later, connecting more neighborhoods by rail, including skills like culinary arts in the public school curriculum, creating more cultural districts like Little Saigon in Dorchester, and creating pathways for business owners to purchase their spaces, thus keeping expenses more predictable.

There is a will. There are ways. But the restaurant scene needs to be someone’s priority. Boston has had a food czar and a nightlife czar. It needs a dedicated person to drive change and find solutions, and to work with and coordinate all of the city’s stakeholders, in the name of creating the rich, diverse, soulful, ambitious, exciting, and uniquely Boston restaurant scene the entire city deserves.

Boston needs a restaurant czar.

Suman Shah’s journey has taken her from Bihar, India, her hometown; to Bombay; to Boston. And as of this month, she’s setting up shop at the Boston Public Library’s Nutrition Lab, where she has been named the new chef-in-residence.

Shah, the latest appointee to the BPL’s two-year-old program based out of the Shaw-Roxbury branch in Nubian Square, is the founder of Fork On a Road, an Ayurvedic-inspired maker of spice blends and vegetarian meal kits rooted in the ancient Indian practice of using herbs, spices, and food to support overall wellness. She’s also spent years teaching cooking classes that show people how everyday meals can nourish the body and even play a role in healing.

Her experience will carry over into this role, where she’ll lead conversations about cultural food traditions, and help community members build confidence in the kitchen and learn more about nutrition. Shah considers the work deeply personal: Her belief in food as medicine grew while caring for her aging parents, and became even more meaningful during her own recovery from cancer. Her classes will feature plant-based and vegetarian recipes, with an emphasis on making healthy cooking simple, flavorful, and culturally relevant.

Prosecutors released more details about the circumstances of the shooting in court, describing how investigators identified Derima in graphic videos that showed how a physical altercation escalated suddenly to shots fired. But some key questions still remain unanswered, including how many shooters were involved and what started the preceding fight.

The violence took place outside Little Haiti International Cuisine, which has recently drawn noise complaints and other concerns from neighbors.

One video showed Reynolds fighting with another unnamed person, who was apparently holding a gun and bleeding from his back, according to a police report. Sometime during the altercation, the gun was discharged into the air, and Reynolds fell to the ground, Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ben Sabol said during the arraignment. While Reynolds was lying there on his back, Derima approached him, brandished a gun, and fired it “at least twice at his chest and torso area,” Sabol said. He said Derima’s clothing matched what the shooter was wearing in the videos.

Both Reynolds and Derima later arrived at Boston Medical Center for treatment of gunshot wounds, according to the police report.

Derima was arrested after being discharged from the hospital. During a brief interview with police, he admitted he was outside the restaurant when a fight broke out, according to prosecutors. “He did concede that there was gunfire that resulted in him also being shot that evening,” Sabol said.

Derima said his memory wasn’t clear because “he had been drinking and … lost a lot of blood since being shot,” the police report said.

Derima’s defense attorney, Anthony Ellison, firmly disputed the prosecution’s account and questioned where the fatal bullet came from.

“They got the wrong guy,” he said during remarks to reporters after the arraignment. He said more information will come out as the case proceeds.

“This is a live case. A lot of witnesses and a lot of evidence is going to be turned over, and we’ll get to the bottom of it,” he said.

Ellison noted some of Derima’s family members attended the hearing. Derima was allowed to hide behind a partially open door, meaning he wasn’t visible from the courtroom gallery.

In a statement Monday morning, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden thanked investigators “for such quick and effective work leading to this arrest of the man directly responsible for the killing.”

“Heinous acts like what happened a few days ago in Hyde Park show an utter disregard for the sanctity of life and tear at the fabric of our communities,” he said. “This investigation is continuing and we will hold anyone involved in this multiple shooting accountable for their actions.”

Police responded around 12:40 a.m. Monday to 1184 Hyde Park Ave., the address of Little Haiti International Cuisine. Boston police had been stationing officers outside the club on weekend nights around closing time because of complaints from the surrounding residential area.

City records show Little Haiti has also been brought before the Boston Licensing Board several times in recent years, including for allegations of operating after hours and over capacity.

The business expanded its operations in May 2025 to close at 1 a.m., records show. Posts on its Instagram account advertised a party starting at 4 p.m. Sunday with DJs, Haitian food, and no cover charge for women before 11:30 p.m.

In addition to Reynolds and Derima, three other gunshot victims were transported to local hospitals via ambulance, with one person “possibly being both stabbed and shot,” according to the police report.

At the scene Tuesday afternoon, a Boston police cruiser was stationed outside the restaurant and its entrance remained roped off with yellow crime tape. A bouquet of blue and white hydrangeas lay wilting on the sidewalk nearby.

In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, some local leaders have called for increased police staffing and more public safety resources.

“These complex cases require significant resources to investigate and prosecute,” leaders of the Boston Police Detectives Benevolent Society said in a statement Monday. The union called on department leadership to hire more detectives, saying the bureau is significantly understaffed.

“It is long past time to move on from campaign slogans and accept the reality for many Boston residents who no longer feel safe in their own neighborhoods,” said City Councilor Ed Flynn, also in a statement released Monday.

Similar demands also surfaced after a violent Fourth of July weekend that left two people dead and 11 others injured in gunfire.

While city officials have acknowledged the recent tragedies, they’ve also pointed to crime stats showing that violence remains relatively rare, especially compared to other major cities.

Boston has recorded 18 homicides so far in 2026, compared to 22 at this time last year, according to police data.

State court records show Derima has a criminal history that includes assault and domestic violence charges, most of which were ultimately dismissed by prosecutors. A warrant was issued last month for failure to appear in a credit card forgery case from 2024, records show. His next scheduled court date in the murder case is Sept. 4.

Black students accounted for 12 of the 15 Tucker students investigated during the school year that began in fall 2024.

Across all Milton schools, nearly half the children investigated that year were Black in a town where Black students account for less than 12 percent of enrollment.

And in the previous academic year, more than half of students expelled from Milton schools over residency issues were Black, including nine from Tucker.

Milton’s tactics stand out compared to other school districts. In some cases, the town pays police officers to conduct surveillance of children’s homes, going so far as to inspect the student’s bedroom, as part of residency investigations.

By contrast, officials from seven other local school districts said they do not use police for residency checks.

Milton interim schools Superintendent John Phelan said the town does not target families because of their race but acknowledged that some students have been scrutinized more than others.

“The School Committee and I have considered that there may be any number of factors that contribute to overrepresentation of some groups in residency investigations and removals,” Phelan said in an email.

Camille Sanabria-Cooper, a Black Milton resident with two children in the schools, said the disparate enforcement made her question the town’s commitment to all children.

“Do they really have investment in our Black and Brown kids?” Sanabria-Cooper said. “They deserve the same treatment that other kids have.”

Even a Milton school official questioned the fairness of the town’s tactics after noting that one-quarter of the students expelled during one school year were allowed to reenroll.

“If 25 percent of removals come back to the system,” Vy Vu, Milton’s director of data and analytics, asked in a September 2024 email to then-superintendent Peter Burrows and others, “then is our removal process efficient, accurate, equitable?”

That same month in an email to school officials, a parent whose son was expelled that same month expressed disbelief.

“I am a tax paying resident of Milton,” the parent wrote. “What does this say about the culture of our school?”

Massachusetts schools are funded in part by local taxes and state law allows officials to expel children who do not live in a school district, which are generally defined by municipal boundaries. In Milton, the residency requirement is enforced by the school registrar and two Milton police officers who work as school resource officers during the academic year.

Phelan and School Committee Chairperson Mark Loring declined interview requests. In a statement, Phelan said he would not address how residency investigations were handled prior to his appointment in June 2025.

In his statement, Phelan said he has been personally involved in every residency case during his tenure to ensure fairness.

The records provided by the town show that since Phelan took charge, officials stopped tracking the race and other characteristics of students investigated. That made it impossible to determine whether children were scrutinized equitably.

Better data collection is a top priority, said Phelan, adding that a staffer was hired to help families navigate the process and avoid unnecessary investigations.

During Phelan’s first year, Milton conducted at least 32 residency investigations, five involving police. Ten students have been expelled. And since 2022, Milton police officers have been involved in at least 33 residency investigations, according to town records.

Police Chief John King also declined to be interviewed and would not make his officers available for comment. In an email, King said the two officers work full time for schools when they are open and are otherwise assigned to the Police Department. The officers are each paid roughly $125,000 annually, which includes almost $15,000 to serve as school resource officers, according to King and Milton payroll records.

When assigned to the schools, the officers conduct surveillance and home visits for residency investigations. But King said that for that work they do not wear police uniforms or drive cruisers.

“They do not use police equipment,” King said. “They identify as working for the schools.”

But a Black mother of a Milton student disputed King’s account. The mother resides outside Milton, but her child lives with a grandparent in town and attends Milton schools. She spoke on the condition of anonymity because she feared retaliation.

In 2022, a Milton police officer in full uniform arrived in a marked cruiser to conduct a home residency check at the grandmother’s house, she said.

It lasted less than five minutes: She showed the officer her son’s bedroom, and the officer left, she said. The officer never presented a warrant, but the mother felt she had no choice but to consent to the search.

“It’s an intimidation tactic,” said the mother, adding, “you feel almost like you’re a criminal, and you haven’t done anything wrong.”

Another former Tucker parent, Jean Ambroise, who is Black and grew up in Milton, said a town police officer searched his home in 2018 to confirm his three children lived there.

Police may surveil families at their homes repeatedly at mealtimes and on weekends, records show. Home visits are typically scheduled with families in advance, according to Superintendent Phelan.

Civil rights watchdogs were alarmed by the practice.

“The district should not be sending an officer to a private home to investigate a civil violation unless they have a warrant supported by probable cause,” said Katy Naples-Mitchell of the American Civil Liberties Union.

The state education department doesn’t track how schools enforce residency requirements, but most districts require parents to submit documents to prove where they live. Many school systems, including Boston and Milton, have tip lines to allow anonymous report violators.

However, school superintendents in the suburbs of Newton and Wellesley said they don’t use police officers to investigate school residency complaints.

And in Needham, Superintendent Daniel Gutekanst estimated his town has had up to 25 residency cases over the last two decades. Police were involved in perhaps two of them, he said.

Like Needham, Newton, and Wellesley, the high-performing schools in Milton have long lured parents of means to the suburbs.

But unlike those communities, Milton does not belong to Metco, a 60-year-old program that buses Boston kids to schools in 33 suburbs. A lawsuit filed in May seeks to expand Metco into more communities as a way to reduce racial segregation, arguing that municipal school district boundaries have created an inequitable education system.

Black Milton parents say it is widely known that enforcement of the residency policy focuses in the vicinity of Tucker Elementary near the Mattapan border.

“Black people are being followed, and it’s happened for many years,” said Somaneh Bouba Diemé, founder of Milton Reckoning. “It’s more harassment for people than anything.”

This fall, Milton schools will begin using new software to match the addresses of enrolled students against current public records. The goal is to ensure that local tax dollars are only paying to educate students who live in Milton.

It was not clear how this change would affect the town’s broader investigative efforts.

Milton, which was once part of Dorchester, has a population of more than 28,000. The town remains inextricably linked to the city: It is home to 4,500 commuters who work in Boston, including more than 300 city employees.

In response to a record request about the school residency policy, Milton released nearly 180 pages of documents, which included emails between administrators and parents, and spreadsheets tracking the cases of individual students. Large sections of the documents were heavily redacted.

The level of detail and the type of information varied widely by year, making it difficult to assess whether the investigations were equitable, according to the records.

When officials did track race, disparities were apparent. In the school year that began in fall 2024, officials scrutinized the residency of 103 students, 47 of them Black and 18 white.

The prior academic year, a spreadsheet tracked characteristics of expelled students that included race, gender, income level, whether they were non-native English speakers, and whether they had special education plans.

That year officials kicked out two dozen children for residency violations: Records show 14 were Black and five white.

Emails suggest the investigations caused tensions among staff and administrators.

“It is certainly difficult enough to do this job and to also have to deal with school personnel upset that I am doing my job,” wrote Sarina Burke, the schools registrar who takes the lead on investigating families, in a January 2022 email.

In an email later that year, then-acting superintendent Janet Sheehan wrote it was a “red flag” that a child whose family had immigrated to the United States was living with an aunt in Milton. A police officer conducted a home visit: The child and her mother both had bedrooms, Burke reported.

The family would be placed on a “residency watch,” wrote Burke, who vowed to “keep this on my radar.”

In November 2024 an investigator for the state Education Department contacted Milton about a parent’s complaint over its residency enforcement. Milton’s director of student services, Danielle Wetmore, objected in an email to a colleague.

“Residency is a local issue, so they should not be interfering,” Wetmore said, writing that the state investigator “is particularly difficult and pushes all complaints through.”

In recent years, school administrators have been under pressure to more vigorously screen students to ensure they are Milton residents. One official, Timothy Lyons, demanded in 2024 that all families face a residency audit.

“I would volunteer time to come and do it myself,” said Lyons, then a member of the Warrant Committee, which helps oversee town finances. “That’s how much I believe we have a problem.”

In 2025, Milton added another verification, so now families must prove residency at the third grade, as well as when they enter the school system and before grades 6, and 9. The town can require documentation from families beyond a signed lease or mortgage statement, photo identification, and a current utility bill.

Historically it has been up to families to establish that they live in town.

“It’s not our job to prove what community the kids live in,” then-superintendent James F. Jette, who is Black, told a colleague in a February 2022 email. “On the contrary, it is their job to prove that the kids live in Milton.”

Katie Johnston of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

The man was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead just before noon, police said.

“We’re very early on, less than two hours from that time and still doing a very active investigation,” McLaughlin said. He asked anyone with video or information about the shooting to contact police.

“We have witnesses,” he said. But “We’ll be out here for a while canvassing.”

McLaughlin said the shooting does not appear to be random.

“I don’t believe there’s a danger to the rest of the community,” he said. “This was a situation where [the] parties are known in one way or another.”

Investigators appeared to focus on the steps of an apartment complex, where yellow evidence markers were placed.

Police tape blocked off the road in front of the complex and a liquor store next door.

Hector Acevedo, 47, said he was friends with the person who was shot. He described him as a young man who had emigrated from the Dominican Republic less than two years ago.

Acevedo, who lives in nearby Grove Hall, said that he had hung out with the victim in front of the apartments just a few hours before the shooting.

When Acevedo came back later, he was shocked to learn what had happened.

“I heard a lot of noise, but I didn’t think it was my friend,” Acevedo said as he sat with other neighbors a few doors down from the crime scene. “Maybe they [went after] the wrong person, because [he was] not the kind of person to be a big criminal.”

The man’s death, if ruled a homicide, would be the 19th slaying in the city this year, compared with 22 at this time last year, police said.

On Monday, a person was killed and four others were injured in a shooting outside a Hyde Park restaurant. Oliver C. Derima, 27, of Randolph, has been charged with murder and was ordered held without bail Tuesday.

“Clearly, we’ve had a few incidents recently. We have a lot of detectives assigned to this, and we’ll be looking to put this case together as quickly as we possibly can,” McLaughlin said, referring to Wednesday’s shooting.

“The biggest thing that we look at, especially when it comes to retaliatory violence, is we look to try to get that shooter off the street as quickly as we can,” McLaughlin added.

The shooting occurred not far from the Franklin Park Zoo, one of the city’s most popular destinations.

At the entrance to the zoo , people said the daytime violence was unsettling.

Kathy Foote, of Gloucester, said she was driving to the zoo with her family a few hours earlier when she had to pull over as police cruisers passed by on their way to the scene of the shooting.

Add those to the list of at-risk incumbents Healey is backing this cycle. None of those candidates are obvious underdogs, and most are the more moderate picks (relatively speaking) in their respective races. Backing them over insurgent newcomers is also reflective of the realities the Healey is facing in her role as governor. Even if lawmakers occasionally drag their feet on (or ignore) some of her legislative priorities, Healey needs like-minded allies in office in order to get her priorities passed — a circumstance she nodded to in statements Wednesday announcing several of the endorsements.

We are members of Shared Spaces, a coalition convened by the Boston Center for Independent Living with WalkMassachusetts, MassBike, Boston Cyclists Union, Transportation for Massachusetts, and individual disability and deaf-blind advocates. Our mission is to promote collaboration and understanding of the challenges associated with shared spaces, such as bike lanes, sidewalks, crosswalks, and bus stops statewide. We are committed to advocating for safety and accessibility in the design of these spaces, focusing on the unique experiences of individuals with disabilities.

As we work to improve street safety in honor of Boston transportation planner Louisa Gag, who was killed last month when she was hit by a truck while cycling, we affirm that our streets must serve and protect everyone, especially the most vulnerable. That includes people walking, rolling, biking, using mobility devices, taking transit, and traveling by other forms of micromobility.

Safe, accessible street design is not a choice between disability rights and bicycle infrastructure. Protected bike lanes can and must be built while considering the need for accessible van ramps and accessible parking spaces, accessible sidewalks, safe crossings, accessible transit stops, and accessibly designed curb space.

By advancing solutions that reflect the principles of universal design and mobility justice, we can build streets that expand independence, improve safety, and ensure that everyone can travel with dignity. This work would honor Gag’s legacy.

The victim was identified Thursday as Victor Armani Arias Rivera, 20. According to a police report, Huynh showed up outside the house on Blue Hill Avenue asking about a stolen bike. Detectives interviewed his friend, who accompanied Huynh to Blue Hill Avenue on Wednesday morning after he “received a phone call stating that his stolen bike” was in that area, the police report says. The person told police that Huynh turned himself in because he “made a bad decision,” the report says.

During a brief interview with detectives, Huynh admitted to the shooting, according to prosecutors. He told police: “I guess I shot somebody ... I just snapped, blacked out,” Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ashlee Mastrangelo said in court.

At least, that’s one tongue-in-cheek theory from Secretary of State William F. Galvin, who suggested that voters may have more on their minds than September primaries.

“I don’t sense that there’s any great excitement about the election in September,” Galvin said in an interview Thursday. “Now, you can offer a lot of other reasons for that. … There are other things people are paying attention to. First, we had all the World Cup stuff. Now we’re getting the revival of the Red Sox. There are a lot of distractions.”

Whether baseball is actually siphoning off attention from politics is another question. But Galvin’s broader point reflects a reality of this year’s campaign season: With just weeks until voters head to the polls, there hasn’t been the same buzz that accompanied previous statewide primaries despite a handful of contested congressional races and a (sort of) nationally watched US Senate Democratic primary at the top of the ticket.

It’s an election cycle that feels “pretty flat,” Galvin said — and an unusually early pre-Labor Day primary that aligns with the annual Sept. 1 move-in rush across Greater Boston doesn’t help. That said, Galvin said he expects participation to land roughly where it has in past mid-term election cycles, which also didn’t set ballots ablaze.

As of Thursday morning, more than 570,000 voters had requested mail-in ballots, and roughly 46,000 had turned them in, according to Galvin. The number the state sent out is similar to 2022, the last statewide election year, when nearly 480,000 people ultimately voted by mail, accounting for nearly half of the 1 million ballots cast in those September primaries, according to data from Galvin’s office.

Galvin expects Republican and Democratic primary turnout this year is likely to resemble that year and 2018, despite the calendar shuffle. Lawmakers regularly move up the state’s primary to address logistical concerns tied to overseas and military ballots or to avoid primary day landing on religious holidays — a maneuver that this year is creating a campaign calendar that’s compressed even further.

Past primaries also featured marquee races that naturally drew more attention. In 2018, Senator Elizabeth Warren’s reelection campaign doubled as an unofficial preview of her eventual presidential bid. Four years later, while the governor’s race was largely settled before primary day, competitive contests for attorney general, lieutenant governor, and state auditor gave voters additional reasons to tune in.

Of course, in 2020, the US Senate primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Joe Kennedy III drew national attention and helped juice turnout, which topped 1.7 million that Sept. 1. The COVID-19 pandemic also prompted lawmakers to expand — and voters to embrace — mail-in voting that year.

The ballot this year is filled with challengers, but relatively few races have emerged as true toss-ups. None of the state’s six statewide constitutional officers, Galvin included, face any primary challenge, and even for the high-profile incumbents who do, voters say they’re having a hard time getting jazzed about their choices.

Take Markey’s challenge this year from Representative Seth Moulton. More than a dozen voters told the Globe’s Anjali Huynh and Samantha J. Gross that they’re either turned off or largely disinterested in the contest.

“People are just sick and tired and exhausted from the last couple of years,” said Lynn Chenevert, 65. “You just put your head in the sand and pretend it’s not happening.”

Republican gubernatorial hopeful Brian Shortsleeve spent the opening stretch of his campaign putting some distance between himself and Charlie Baker — the popular former governor who elevated Shortsleeve to lead the MBTA, but who some Massachusetts Republicans view as a liability in a GOP primary.

Now, with less than four weeks until the Sept. 1 primary against fellow GOP hopeful Michael Minogue, Shortsleeve is embracing the Baker brand.

Shortsleeve’s campaign on Friday rolled out an ad leaning hard on the candidate’s ties to the former governor, whose approval ratings routinely topped national rankings.

The spot, dubbed “Roll Up,” packs in nearly as much Baker as it does Shortsleeve, featuring photos of the duo shaking hands at a press conference, standing shoulder-to-shoulder for the camera, and sitting around a conference table looking suitably serious. (Baker, to be sure, hasn’t endorsed Shortsleeve nor has he gotten involved in the gubernatorial primary.)

“The T was in crisis and Charlie Baker called me,” Shortsleeve, a venture capitalist who served as the MBTA’s chief administrator, says in the 30-second spot.

It would be an obvious general election pitch; Baker left office four years ago still broadly popular with Massachusetts voters. But in a Republican primary, the calculation is trickier.

Baker spent his final years in office openly feuding with the conservative wing of the state GOP and breaking with the national party as President Trump’s rise reshaped it. He ultimately opted against seeking reelection and fighting through a primary against a Trump-aligned Republican. And even out of office, he’s continued to dabble in Massachusetts politics — and not always on the Republican side.

Which may help explain why Shortsleeve wasn’t always eager to campaign as Baker’s political heir. Pressed earlier this year on whether his politics more closely aligned with Baker or former Governor Mitt Romney — another moderate Republican whom Shortsleeve long supported — Shortsleeve told WBUR that he was his “own man.”

His new ad, which Shortsleeve’s campaign says it’s putting $1 million behind, also milks Shortsleeve’s last name for all it’s worth. It includes the phrases “long sleeves” and “no sleeves,” and Shortsleeve says he’s a guy who’s been “rolling up [his] sleeves.” It then pivots to his a résumé reel: He pitches himself as a Marine veteran and MBTA budget-slasher who Baker recruited to help get the T’s finances under control.

In 2017, JET Boston started with a few machines, many dumbbells, and a hope that embracing personal training, not a traditional gym model, would allow the business to boom.

Now, after a pause for COVID-19, that plan seems to be working. The original JET location in the Back Bay has closed, but facilities in the South End, Nubian Square, and Brooklyn have opened. The South End studio expanded in May to include pilates and strength conditioning equipment, costing $25,000 and aiming to retain hundreds of members.

Five years after the pandemic decimated health clubs, the industry has come roaring back to a point where many owners say they are on the verge of turning new applicants away. In Massachusetts, more than 150,000 more people were gym members last year than in 2021, according to industry data.

The reasons for the rebound are many. The fading of COVID-era sensitivities helped propel many fitness enthusiasts from home treadmills to public clubs. Employers’ return-to-office plans have led many employees to look for spots near work. And health-conscious young people are bringing a whole new generation of customers into the gym.

Geoffrey Janey, founder and owner of JET Boston-Brooklyn, said some of his young gym-goers are intermingling expensive lifestyle choices like high-end workouts with weekend nights out on the town.

“It’s almost like the new club is working out,” Janey said.

Since 2019, membership has grown 20 percent at Healthworks, GymIt, and Republic Fitness, making it the highest on record, according to Mark Harrington Jr., president of Healthworks Group, which operates the three gym franchises.

Healthworks has been trying to construct new gyms and expand its current locations, but it’s a difficult feat, he said, pointing to how a successful gym should be in a pedestrian-dense district and tends to require a large, costly build-out.

Even when gyms make their best attempt to persuade people to switch, loyal gym-goers often won’t leave.

Selhadin Yasin, 25, doesn’t plan on leaving any time soon from the Planet Fitness in Downtown Crossing. Yasin, an accountant, pays $15 per month for unlimited access to gym equipment.

“It’s all I need,” he said.

A few blocks away, Jeff Bissinger, a 33-year-old who works in finance, frequents Equinox for an hour or two most mornings for amenities like a steam room and personal trainer. Bissinger pays around $500 per month and lives nearby.

“It’s stupid. It’s very expensive,” Bissinger said. “But I value investing in health and wellness, and this is incredibly convenient for me.” (Equinox, a premier gym chain with five clubs open in Boston, declined to comment.)

In 2025, there were 1.9 million fitness-facility members across Massachusetts. That number is the same as in 2019, according to the Health and Fitness Association, a trade group that represents gyms. Meanwhile, the number of commercial health clubs and studios remains around 1,700 — about the same as in 2019.

Buoyed by such high demand, some of Boston’s priciest gyms cost hundreds of dollars per month even for memberships that don’t include all amenities.

Bene Stroud, a 29-year-old who works in marketing, did deep research on Equinox’s fitness instructors and their techniques before putting down almost $300 per month.

A private fitness instructor, Stroud moved from Florida around two months ago and has tried other Boston gyms. Those she frequented didn’t open early or have savvy instructors, she said.

But other operators may have somewhat lower prices, niche workout classes, and special events — providing a middle ground between low-cost and higher-end gyms.

“We’re not running it like a [private equity] firm,” said Giampaolo Nicosia, managing partner of SoWa Health and Wellness, referring to some ritzy high-end gyms.

When SoWa opened in September 2023 in the South End, it had 400 memberships. Now, it has more than 2,000 gym-goers, each paying $190 per month — the same rate as when it opened. But management will cap memberships when lines for equipment become too long, Nicosia said.

Nicosia has noticed that there’s almost no space for large gyms to come to town, and attracting customers from small boutique studios is difficult. “Most of Boston is pretty saturated right now,” he said.

Elsewhere, Planet Fitness gyms recorded $1.3 billion revenue in 2025, up 12 percent from 2024. Memberships also grew by a net 1.1 million, according to a report from February. Now, it has over 21 million members worldwide.

New York Sports Club, formerly operated as the chain Boston Sports Club, has three locations in Greater Boston after a whirlwind of legal headaches and bankruptcy erupted in 2020.

At six of Beacon Hill Athletics Clubs’ seven locations, around 35 percent of gym-goers are Gen Z, and referrals grew 10 percent year-over-year from 2024 to 2025.
