“The system wasn’t broken before,” said Robert Mellion, executive director of the Massachusetts Package Stores Association, which represents alcoholic beverage retail stores headquartered in the state. “A better way doesn’t mean that you necessarily do it.”

Bracken said he doesn’t expect all lottery players to migrate to the app, which was built with some $2.5 million the state approved in 2024 for start-up costs. Instead, he believes online-exclusive users will make up a subsection of players, with the rest playing online and in person.

More than 24,000 players have made bets on the app, according to Mass. Lottery officials. The new platform offers just over 7 percent of all Mass. Lottery games online, including draw games like Mass Cash, Powerball, and a number of slot machine-style instant win games. All lottery games are still found in stores.

“Retailers in the commonwealth, obviously, they are the cornerstone of our lottery operation. They’ve been with us since the start,” Bracken said. “We value our partnerships and our relationships with our retailers.”

Before launching online, Massachusetts residents spent more on the lottery per capita than any other state. On average, Bay Staters spend about $839 a year on the lottery.

“We’ve been there for them since the beginning, and now they can simply just bypass us and sell direct to consumers,” said Joe Dion, owner of Dion’s Fine Wine in Newton and Waltham. “It’s just not right.”

Retailers that sell lottery tickets get a small cut from every sale: a 5 percent commission from every ticket sold, and a 1 percent commission from winning tickets.

Because they only receive a modest commission, ticket sales aren’t what most retailers are worried about. Instead, it’s the foot traffic the lottery brings to their stores. A pack of chips, a few drinks, maybe a bottle of alcohol. All of that contributes to a retailer’s profit when customers walk in to play the lottery.

“Those loss of sales are going to have negative impacts on our members, not only lottery sales but on their ancillary sales,” said Ryan Kearney, vice president of the Retailers Association of Massachusetts, a retail advocacy nonprofit.

Some business are already struggling, said Mellion with MassPack, as consumers are spending less in stores partly because of the Trump administration’s tariffs on goods, less alcohol consumption, and the affordability crisis.

“Whatever those reasons may be, the state just decided that they’re gonna give [shoppers] one more reason not to step into a brick and mortar store,” said Ryan Maloney, owner of Julio’s Liquors in Westborough.

Ying Huang, a marketing professor at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, said it’s reasonable for store owners to be nervous about the digitization of lottery sales.

“This is like a typical concern in the retail industry over the past decades,” Huang said. “Even with Walmart going to Walmart e-commerce, of course, that will take some sales from the Walmart physical store.”

Huang’s solution: create an omnichannel marketing system, in which products are promoted both online and in stores. For the lottery, this could look like exclusive events for in-store players that are promoted online.

To ensure sales are sustained both online and in stores, Bracken, of Mass. Lottery, said his team is considering the omnichannel model along with other exclusive in-person games. Wellion agrees with the solution, but said it should have been rolled out in tandem with online gaming to avoid retailers’ possible profit loss.

Meanwhile, Bracken said the state continues to onboard new retailers. At present, Mass. Lottery has over 7,200 locations selling lottery games across Massachusetts, making it the state with the most ticket sellers per capita, per square mile in the country.

“Access to the lottery has never been greater as it is in the commonwealth,” Bracken said.

For some, easy access is the concern.

On a recent Wednesday at Fort Point Market in Seaport, Moses Shin, 39, held a stack of Numbers Game tickets in his hand as he fed them to a machine.

Shin said he spends a moderate $10 a week in tickets. With the lottery now available at his fingertips, he said he’s choosing to avoid the app out of fear of catching an addiction.

“[I would] not be able to control myself,” Shin said.

Janelle Patrick, 48, stood in Mission Hill Liquors in Roxbury zoned in on the more than 15 red Numbers Game tickets strewn across the counter. She crossed out numbers to place her bets. Slip by slip, she handed them over to the cashier for scanning.

“I mastered this [expletive], man. It’s sickening,” said Patrick, who has played since 2016 and is studying for a masters in psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston. She hopes to one day use her experiences to help others addicted to gambling, and is set to graduate next May.

“I picked up one of the worst addictions,” she said. “One of the worst addictions, meaning this is worse than drugs.”

Because of the easy accessibility, Patrick warned that online gambling would exacerbate addiction, especially in lower-income communities.

There’s no definitive data on whether online lottery will increase addiction, said Marlene Warner, CEO of the Massachusetts Council on Gaming and Health. But she understands the concern, considering the rise of other gambling sites.

“They go online and now they have more access, and you can gamble faster,” said Warner, whose nonprofit helps residents overcome addiction to consumer activities, including gambling. “There’s the ability to just place wagers that much faster, and that does become problematic rapidly.”

To avoid the pitfall that is 24/7 access to the lottery, Bracken of Mass. Lottery said the app has integrated a number of safeguards. An on-screen timer counting play time, a 30-minute pop-up and mandatory cool down time are just some of the ways Mass. Lottery is trying to curb addictive habits.

There’s also voluntary self-exclusion, which blocks people from using the app. So far, Warner said more than 20 people have self-excluded.

Dr. Timothy Fong, a psychiatrist and co-director of the gambling studies program at the University of California Los Angeles, said such safeguards could help people become aware of how much they’re spending.

“That’s a very different experience than going to the gas station five times a day,” Fong said, “and it’s highly unlikely that vendor is gonna say ‘This is the fifth time you’ve been here this week or today, I’m not selling you a scratcher.’”

When Steward Health Care closed Nashoba Valley Medical Center outside of Ayer on Aug. 31, 2024, residents clamored to save it, pushing for its purchase by another hospital operator or for the state to take it over by eminent domain and transfer it to another operator. Some nearby homes still have signs reading “No hospital 2024, No Healey 2026,” expressing the frustration many felt that Governor Maura Healey let it close. But ask many in the region today what should happen to the vacant building, and the response tends to be a shrug. Health care providers and community-based organizations have largely moved on to seeking other ways to fill the health care gaps.

“It’s owned by Apollo,” said Chelsey Patriss, executive director of the Health Equity Partnership of North Central Massachusetts, referring to the New York-based investment firm that acquired the property during Steward’s bankruptcy. “We don’t get to decide what happens with it.”

The loss of the hospital was felt in myriad ways by residents of small towns like Ayer, Pepperell, Shirley, and Groton. It was Ayer’s biggest employer, with around 500 employees, according to Ayer Town Manager Robert Pontbriand, and its closure left the town with between $250,000 and $300,000 less in annual property tax revenue because a vacant hospital is worth less than an operational one. Patriss said residents lost further trust in the health system, with the hospital closure coming less than a year after UMass Memorial Health HealthAlliance-Clinton Hospital in Leominster eliminated its maternity unit.

The biggest concrete impact is on emergency services. Ambulances now have to travel to UMass hospital in Leominster or Emerson Hospital in Concord, each about 15 miles from Nashoba Valley Medical Center. A report by the Nashoba Valley Health Planning Working Group found that as of February 2025, the median emergency medical services transport time in the region had increased from 12 minutes to 17 minutes.

But that metric understates the actual impact in the most affected communities. Ayer Fire Chief Timothy Johnston said the typical time ambulances took between leaving for a call and returning to the station in Ayer went from between 20 and 40 minutes when Nashoba Valley was open to one to two hours after the closure. Johnston said the department had four people working 24/7 before the closure, but as calls took longer, the department relied more on on-call firefighters and mutual aid. Since the closure, the department has received about $1 million in state aid, which it used to buy a paramedic vehicle and hire two more firefighters to work each day shift.

Another lingering impact is the loss of primary care and specialty doctors. While Bookmark Medical, formerly Revere Medical, acquired Steward’s physicians, Patriss said some doctors retired or took jobs elsewhere.

Jenna Montgomery, public health educator for Nashoba Associated Boards of Health, a regional health department that works on behalf of 15 towns’ boards of health, said her father, who lives in Townsend, had a Steward primary care doctor in Townsend. It took him six months to find a new doctor in Sudbury, nearly an hour away.

Montgomery said the boards of health, working with consumer health care advocacy group Health Care for All, held focus groups with residents after the hospital closure and found people were delaying or skipping care. Montgomery said a common refrain was, “I’m not going to doctors’ appointments because I couldn’t be bothered to deal with the logistics to figure it out.”

Providers are working to address these shortages. A big improvement should come when UMass Memorial Health opens a satellite emergency facility in Groton in February 2027 with 16 treatment rooms, imaging, and a helipad and private ambulance to transport people to area hospitals. “A big piece of what we’re doing is to support local EMS crews so they don’t have to make long travel times to other area hospitals,” UMass Medical Center President Justin Precourt said.

Emerson Health President and CEO Christine Schuster said Emerson is rotating more specialists through its Littleton office and adding five new clinicians plus mammography services to a Groton primary care office.

One ongoing problem is transportation. The region has minimal public transit, and most people have cars — but not everyone. Patriss said senior centers that provide rides to older adults have had to turn down requests or eliminate rides to social events or grocery stores to accommodate the need for medical transportation.

A lingering reminder of the hospital loss still sits in Ayer: the hospital’s vacant shell. Although parts of the campus were sold and remain in use as a nursing home and doctors’ offices, the main building is empty. Both UMass Memorial and Emerson Health considered buying the hospital but couldn’t make it work financially.

At the other hospital Steward closed during its bankruptcy, Carney Hospital in Dorchester, developers are advancing a proposal to build housing and a medical building.

The Ayer site is zoned for medical services, and Pontbriand, the town manager, said he hopes the site can be used to serve the region’s growing, aging population. Nashoba Valley Medical Center had a geriatric psychiatric ward, which hasn’t been replaced. It provided medical care to the region’s three prisons. A report by the Nashoba Valley Health Planning Working Group identified an ongoing lack of mental health and addiction services.

The challenge will be finding an operator that can make money there given the cost of removing or renovating the hospital building. “In Boston, there are many more people you might be able to bring to the table to finance a big project like that. It’s hard the farther you get from Boston,” said Amie Shei, president and CEO of the Health Foundation of Central Massachusetts.

Shei said the region’s residents are accustomed to traveling far distances and struggling to access health care. Even before the hospital closure, a Community Health Needs Assessment by the Nashoba Associated Boards of Health found, based on 2022 data, that there are far fewer primary care physicians and mental health providers per capita in the region than in Massachusetts overall. The closure of Nashoba Valley Medical Center made those problems worse. Two years later, finding solutions to help the most vulnerable residents remains a work in process.

Darryl Whiting was 71. He died of natural causes on Aug. 1, according to a one-page letter notifying US District Judge Denise J. Casper, chief judge of federal courts in Massachusetts, of Whiting’s death.

The letter was entered into Whiting’s court record on Monday.

Whiting had been serving out his life term at Federal Correctional Institution Schuylkill, a medium-security men’s prison in Minersville, Pa. He died at the Geisinger Medical Center in nearby Danville, Pa., the letter signed by Warden A. Cruz said.

“Despite being incarcerated for more than three decades, Darryl was deeply loved by his family,” Sandra Ganz, Whiting’s former federal assistant public defender told the Globe in a telephone interview Tuesday night. “He had six kids, and he’s a grandfather who’s incredibly close to his niece, his sister, and his brother.”

“Daryl’s life sentence, imposed in 1991, was a relic of draconian and mandatory sentenching schemes,” Ganz said.

Whiting ruled the crack trade in the Orchard Park housing project in Roxbury in the late 1980s and early ‘90s, grossing millions of dollars. His group, known as the New York Boys, forcibly removed residents from the project and used their apartments to store and sell drugs, prosecutors said.

Whiting had been locked up since his arrest Dec. 21, 1990.

He was sentenced Oct. 21, 1991 to life without the possibility of parole for running a criminal cocaine enterprise.

A decade ago, Whiting made a bid for early release, arguing that sentencing laws for drug crimes had changed, making it so that a life term was no longer the mandatory penalty for his convictions.

Whiting lost his bid largely due to his self-published e-book, “Takin’ It to Another Level.” The novel came out in June 2013.

Federal prosecutors initially supported Whiting’s request for a reduced sentence, as part of the office’s general support of shorter sentences for drug crimes, but later withdrew support after learning that Whiting had written a novel that glorified his life of crime.

Prosecutors said Whiting’s book showed a likelihood that he may return to criminality. The main character had the same name as Whiting and was serving a life term for running a continuing criminal enterprise. The fictional Whiting was released from prison after 20 years because of a change in the law and took revenge on former associates who testified against him.

At a February 2016 hearing on his release, Whiting choked back tears as he pleaded for mercy.

“I’m sincere in trying to be, in wanting to be, a productive member of society,” Whiting told the judge. “I just want a chance.”

Whiting also inspired a 1999 movie called “In Too Deep,” starring rapper LL Cool J as a Cincinnati gang lord who goes by the alias “God.”

Whiting renewed his bid for release in December 2024. His federal assistant public defenders wrote in court filings that during Whiting’s three decades in prison, he had embarked on a journey of personal growth, completing courses in history, economics, business, and screenplay writing, as well as vocational courses in barbering, Spanish, and computer skills.

US District Judge Patti B. Saris on Dec. 1, 2025, reserved ruling on Whiting’s release until after the US Supreme Court issued its opinion on a case with similar issues. Saris still had not issued a decision at the time of Whiting’s death.

“He died still in the fight,” Ganz said, adding that she believes “that had he been sentenced today, and had the court had the full and complete picture of his life history, and the benefit of expert opinions related to his work of fiction, Daryl could have died free.”

If released, Whiting had hoped to live with his sister, an ordained minister, her husband, and their adult children in Corona, N.Y. He had plans to revive his relationship with his six children and live out his remaining years, peacefully and free, his lawyers wrote.

Whiting was born in New York, the youngest of seven children. His father died when he was an infant, leaving his mother, maternal grandmother, and aunt to raise him, according to court filings.

Whiting was the adored baby of the family with few restrictions and little discipline. A pattern of incarceration began when Whiting was 12 with a stint in juvenile detention that was repeated into his teens and adulthood and eventually saw him imprisoned at Rikers Island, court records said.

Whiting arrived in Boston in 1987. He was flamboyant and known for his stylish dress, diamond rings and luxury cars. He portrayed himself as a role model and treated the children who worked for him to new sneakers, leather coats, and motor scooters, the Globe reported.

Whiting also owned and ran several business in Roxbury, including a barber shop, video store, and the Crown Social and Recreational Hall which were used to recruit youth to work for him and as fronts for his drug deals.

Whiting was convicted by a Boston jury after a month-long trial in which former colleagues testified to being recruited by Whiting when they were young. They also testified about the violence Whiting used to discipline those within his organization. A single mother who relied on welfare told jurors that Whiting supplied her with drugs so he could use her apartment to sell drugs.

Whiting testified too, telling jurors he considered himself a community-minded entrepreneur and role model for young people who came to his social hall, barbecues, rap concerts and outings to amusement parks. Whiting said he knew some of his associates were dealing drugs, but he wasn’t involved in it.

A 12-year-old boy was seriously injured after he climbed onto the roof of a Red Line car and attempted to “subway surf” while the train was moving around 1 a.m. Tuesday, according to MBTA Transit Police.

The child boarded the train at the JFK/UMass station in Dorchester just before 1 a.m., said Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan in a statement. He fell off the car and onto the ground shortly after.

The boy sustained a serious but not life-threatening head injury, Sullivan said.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with this child, and it is our sincere hope he makes a full recovery,” he said. “This incident underscores the inherent extreme danger of ‘train surfing.’ It could literally cost you your life.”

Transit Police are continuing to investigate.

Train surfing is a dangerous practice that involves riding on top of speeding trains. In 2014, a teen faced criminal charges after he was seen surfing — and doing a handstand on — the roof of an Orange Line car. More recently, in 2023, a young man was captured on video standing on top of a Red Line car heading toward North Quincy Station as it moved across a bridge.

The thrill-seeking act has risen in popularity among young people in cities nationwide in recent years, spurred on by sensational videos shared on social media. And it has proven deadly. In New York City, five people were killed while subway surfing last year, and a 14-year-old boy was fatally injured in May, ABC News reported.

A stray puppy that was hit by a car in Dorchester last week had one of her back legs amputated this week and is recovering at a veterinary facility, MSPCA-Angell said.

Lark, a 5-month old Siberian Husky, was hit on Friday evening on Geneva Avenue, officials said. The driver did not stop or report the accident, the animal welfare group said in a statement Tuesday.

Boston Animal Control is investigating.

After the crash, animal control officials brought the dog to Angell Animal Medical Center in Jamaica Plain, where it was treated for severe injuries, including an extensive fracture and “degloving” of her back leg, officials wrote.

After cleaning the dog’s injury, taking X-rays, and putting it on pain medication and antibiotics, officials determined the damage was “too significant for her leg to be saved,” and performed an amputation on Monday, officials said.

Mike Keiley, vice president of animal protection for MSPCA-Angell, said officials are trying to identify Lark’s owner as well as the driver who hit her.

“It’s possible Lark has a family out there who’s been searching for her,” he said. “If that’s the case, we want them to know she’s safe and receiving the care she needs.”

If the dog isn’t claimed within seven days, officials will begin searching for an adopter after she receives medical clearance, Keiley said.

Anyone with information regarding the driver who hit the dog is urged to contact Boston Animal Control at (617) 635-5348, while anyone who thinks they recognize her or may be her owner can contact MSPCA-Angell’s Boston Adoption Center at (617) 522-5055.

Updates on her adoption will be posted to the organization’s website and social media, and interested adopters can contact officials there.

The puppy has “shown us what a fighter she is,” Keiley said. “We’re grateful to give her a chance at the long, happy life she deserves.”

This summer, there’s no “tune in” or “turn on.” For politicians of all stripes, it’s just the third element of that 1960s hippie catchphrase:

Drop out.

Dropping out, or calls to do so, seems like the defining characteristic of the 2026 midterms, the Globe’s James Pindell writes. Many reasons have prompted the calls for the candidates to quit.

“Some of it was based in political strategy. Several exits were caused by a male candidate’s unacceptable past behavior toward women,” Pindell writes.

And some calls to quit, such as dueling efforts to oust Democratic and Independent Senate candidates in Montana, were based on polling that said one or the other could possibly defeat the Republican candidate — but both would lose to the GOP if they both stayed in.

Who’s gone?

North Carolina’s Representative Chuck Edwards gave up his Republican seat after an ethics report detailed widespread — and very cringey — sexual harassment events on his own staff, Pindell writes.

Maine Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner dropped out over allegations that he raped a former girlfriend. Allegations of sexual misconduct prompted Democrat Eric Swalwell to leave the California gubernatorial race.

Ahead of yesterday’s contentious race for Wisconsin governor, three Democratic candidates had dropped out. Then one of them resumed the campaign.

Who’s still in?

In choosing to stay in, Ohio Representative Max Miller pointed to Trump’s persistence in running despite Trump’s negative publicity — over his infidelities, 34 criminal convictions, and reported sexual assaults. Miller’s contentious divorce comes with allegations he broke the collarbone of his 2-year-old daughter and committed significant domestic abuse.

Also not quitting: Kentucky’s Mitch McConnell, despite the fact he hasn’t been seen in person or even heard by voice since he went to the hospital in June.

As Pindell writes, there are three more months to November’s general elections — so dropout season could roll deep into fall.

Mysterious Skin returns

Scott Heim’s “Mysterious Skin” was published in 1995 and quickly became a gen X cult classic, treasured for its honesty, empathy, and eerie beauty. Following two Kansas boys as they mature into adulthood and reckon with the legacy of sexual abuse, the novel established Heim as a master of unsettling landscapes and disturbing events: Kansas, UFOs, New York, AIDS. The movie version, directed by Gregg Araki and starring Joseph Gordon-Levitt, came out in 2004 to rave reviews (the New York Times’s A.O. Scott called it “a gorgeous, heartbreaking and utterly convincing work of art”).

Now the film is being re-released in a 4K restoration, and the book has both a newly released paperback edition and a new unabridged audiobook. Heim, 59, a Kansas native who lives in Roslindale, says the experience is “Surreal! I started writing the book when I was 25, and it’s a huge honor to even have the book in print still, let alone have the film get produced and make an impact. So now to see this ‘new generation’ of fans seeing the movie and making TikToks about it — a lot of whom are younger than I was when I wrote the book — is especially wild, and humbling.” The film opens Friday at the Seaport Alamo, and Heim will introduce it at an event August 25 at Coolidge Corner. — Kate Tuttle

In July, the one-year anniversary was celebrated at the more capacious, newly opened Opera + Community Studios in Boston’s Fort Point neighborhood. The series moves back to the Burren Aug. 18.

“Which Side?” began when Joyce Linehan found herself confronting a second term of President Trump. The famously proactive Linehan — former chief of policy and planning for Mayor Marty Walsh and longtime community organizer with deep roots in the Boston rock scene — faced questions from her set: “What are we gonna do?”

She realized, “For the first time in my life I had absolutely no idea.” (Linehan was recently appointed chief of staff at the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority.)

Linehan now jokes that, in the midst of these discussions, a book fell off its shelf and hit her on the head: “Which Side Are You On? 20th Century American History in 100 Protest Songs,” by James Sullivan, a regular Globe contributor and Emerson College teacher. She had presented Sullivan and his book in the ongoing series of readings in her Ashmont living room.

She had her answer: organize protest-music concerts.

One of the truths that Sullivan and Linehan hold self-evident is that, contrary to common perceptions, protest music is not dead. That, yes, protest songs are still being written. The “Which Side?” events are organized around songs old and new. Six acts are asked to perform two songs each, one cover and one original.

Sometimes, as Sullivan said at July’s event, the “protest” content of a particular song is a matter of context. The first “Which Side?” show opened with guitarist Jon Butcher playing Jimi Hendrix’s hellacious arrangement of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

It’s also a matter of interpretation. At the Fort Point show, Sullivan pointed out that the Falmouth-born Wellesley grad and professor Katharine Lee Bates wrote the poem that became the lyrics to “America the Beautiful” as a patriotic protest, citing the line “God mend thine ev’ry flaw.” There’s also the malleable meaning of “Born in the USA,” depending on who is singing it and for what.

One of the hallmarks of the event has been Sullivan’s role as an ad hoc talent scout. He found the OG’s — four formerly incarcerated men — through his work with Emerson’s prison education program at MCI-Norfolk.

As for performers that Sullivan booked in previous months, he saw the singer Salyse portray Coretta Scott King in the play “Stokely and Martin” at the Multicultural Arts Center in Cambridge, where she sang Billie Holiday’s “Strange Fruit.” At “Which Side?,” she sang “Dog Days Are Over” by Florence + The Machine. He heard the Guatemalan singer-songwriter Mercedes Escobar sing the Staple Singers’ “Freedom Highway” at a Folk Americana Roots Hall of Fame event at the Boch Center. Escobar in turn brought along the octogenarian Kossoy Sisters, identical twins Irene and Ellen, whose involvement in the folk scene goes back to Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie. They sang a haunting a cappella version of the Guthrie favorite “Hobo’s Lullaby.”

Linehan, meanwhile, has drawn on her years as club wrangler to recruit echt-Boston indie artists like the Bags, the Cavedogs, Barrence Whitfield, and Thalia Zedek. The “Which Side?” house band — comprising Boston music scene ringers — is the wryly-named Paid Protestors.

So, what’s the good of singing protest songs in the face of the Trump administration?

“I see this as an organizing exercise,” Linehan told the crowd at Fort Point last month, in keeping with her feelings about the social uses of music. “I don’t know what we’re organizing for, but one of my labor activist friends says, ‘We need to keep that muscle limber, because we’re going to need it at some point.’”

The “Which Side” events include speakers in the breaks between songs. At the July event, those included Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, the ACLU’s Kade Crockford, and Boston lawyer, public policy expert, and civil rights activist Ted Landsmark. There are often less established but nonetheless important speakers, like one man who talked at a previous event about his experience of being unhoused for 14 months. Guests can offer inspiring words of solidarity, or, in the case of Crockford, specific paths of action, like enrolling in the ACLU’s program for training election poll monitors.

At the July event, Linehan allowed that much of the effect provided by “Which Side?” is “therapeutic.”

But the event also gives each attendee a specific “assignment.”

“I want you to meet two people [tonight] that you’ve never met before and talk to them a little about what brings them joy and what makes them anxious,” Linehan said. “Because at some point you’re going to need to know where everybody is; you’re going to need to know who has help to give and who needs help. Because we are a community.”

The final speaker of the night was Landsmark, famously known for a Pulitzer Prize-winning photo by Stanley Forman of Landsmark being attacked by a flag-wielding anti-busing protestor on City Hall Plaza.

Throughout the night, images of the American flag had been shown on a video screen above the stage. At one point, the screen showed the infamous image of the attack on Landsmark.

Landsmark talked about how that photo had embarrassed the city and inspired action, and he talked about the importance of the arts in building community. The image changed to Landsmark smiling on his couch at home with his prize collection of American banjos — “the definitive American musical instrument,” he said — from a recent Globe story by Sullivan.

He told the audience, “All the organizing power we need is in this room.”

“But with Abby, she was my one constant person for nine years that I could depend on,” McKenzie said, referring to Abigail Judge, a clinical and forensic psychologist who cofounded the nonprofit, the Boston Human Exploitation Advocacy Team, or HEAT.

Other groups designed to support housing needs and substance use recovery oftentimes don’t address trauma from sex trafficking, advocates said. Meanwhile, organizations helping trafficking victims frequently don’t have the bandwidth to address drug use, according to social workers.

Flying under the radar of clinics meant to help homeless Bostonians, unhoused women who are trafficked and use opioids, as was the case for McKenzie, are exposed to overdose risks and physical violence from abusers. Since 2024, nine women trafficked around Mass. and Cass died from homicide or overdose, according to data collected by HEAT.

The intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard has long been a hub for sex trafficking because unhoused people who use drugs there are in survival mode, said Katie Koh, a street psychiatrist with Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program.

“A lot of people use drugs in the first place to cope with the adversity and pain they’ve experienced throughout their life, and their addiction can lead them to make decisions they wouldn’t make in the absence of using substances,” Koh said.

Women who use intravenous opioids at Mass. and Cass become targeted by traffickers who exploit their basic needs for shelter, substances, and food. Victims who work with HEAT said they’ve also used fentanyl and heroin to numb the trauma of being sexually exploited.

Without safe housing and facing criminalization and stigma surrounding their drug use and the commercial sex trade, the women become trapped in a coercive web, said Jessica Loftus, a clinical social worker who helps trafficked women at two Boston hospitals.

“When you have a criminal history and you have really complex medical and mental health needs, you get ruled out of accessing services, which perpetuates the problem and prevents you from getting to a place where stabilization is possible,” Loftus said.

Judge and Sandra Andrade, a Roxbury District Court senior peer advocate, launched HEAT in 2020 after working at a Massachusetts General Hospital clinic helping women like McKenzie. After they realized that only a sliver of women from Mass. and Cass checked in, they took their work to the streets. Via sidewalk outreach, they invite women to HEAT’s nighttime safe space, called “the spot,” which feels like a cozy, underground bunker.

Relying mostly on grant funding, including a recent anti-trafficking grant from FIFA, Judge provides victims with psychotherapy, and Andrade navigates them through legal obstacles.

“The ‘spot’ isn’t only temporary respite and safety, it‘s a community based on what I know from a clinical perspective about trauma recovery and what Sandra knows in her bones from lived experience,” said Judge, who has remained on the faculty at MGH.

When a woman calls the phone numbers on her wristband, Judge and Andrade accompany her to the hospital in the middle of the night, meet her at the police station, or shepherd her through a court hearing.

“I go to court with them, because a lot of them don’t like to walk in, there’s a lot of anxiety, or fear of [withdrawal] because they’re in active addiction,” Andrade, 46, said.

When the Boston Police Department Human Trafficking Unit refers victims to resource groups, HEAT is their first call, according to Sergeant Detective Marc Sullivan. Since 2024, the unit has sent more than 120 victims to Judge and Andrade.

South End residents formed a group to build community buy-in for HEAT, which has quickly become Boston’s most effective advocate for commercial sexual exploitation victims, said Jim O’Connell, founder of Boston Health Care for the Homeless.

“We knew about the drug trade, but we were not aware of how many people were really being trafficked,” O’Connell said. “What Abigail and Sandra did on Mass. and Cass quietly and under the radar was really astonishing.”

Like many women who work with HEAT, McKenzie said she was first trafficked as a teenager, at age 15, after meeting the son of a local “pimp” in downtown Boston.

For the next 15 years, McKenzie said life was a blur of paid “dates,” physical abuse, and a “full-blown” drug addiction.

She met Judge at MGH in 2017 while receiving treatment for endocarditis, an infection of the heart, which she suffered from using intravenous drugs.

“I’d probably be dead if it wasn’t for Abby,” McKenzie, 39, said in an interview.

Now, McKenzie is on Sublocade treatment and other medications for PTSD.

“Abby has been the most essential part of my health care,” said McKenzie, who lives about seven miles northwest of Boston with her father and son. “With the trauma and PTSD, it’s really hard to not live in the past, but Abby’s helped me focus on the present.”

Another woman who accesses HEAT’s resources said in a written testimonial filed to city officials last year that she was first sexually trafficked as a child by her own mother.

“The amount of support and understanding I feel from Abigail and her team is something I have never experienced in my life,” wrote the woman, who signed her initials, “SM.”

Women such as SM can also find support at Boston hospitals that have social workers trained to help.

But many victims avoid health care settings, said Amy Farrell, director of Northeastern University’s School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.

Women describe feeling a “very static” underlying stigma from doctors and nurses, she said.

“They are often treated as people who are not worth helping or somehow responsible for their own victimization,” Farrell said.

Social workers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Brigham & Women’s Hospital can help, usually when a patient checks in for more than one day.

“I think we do, unfortunately, miss folks who come through the emergency department,” said Loftus, the clinical social worker.

When many women return to the streets after a medical crisis, they find themselves in the situations that landed them in the hospital.

But on Tuesday and Friday nights, women who work with HEAT come inside at “the spot,” which has an address that isn’t listed online.

The space has a large dining table, a soft couch, a kitchen, and a clothes closet. Women can shower and get daily essentials such as deodorant, toothpaste, and hair ties.

During recent evenings, women laughed as they ate watermelon cubes, green grapes, and frosted sugar cookies while blasting hip-hop music on their phones.

When they’re with Andrade and Judge, women are surrounded by pastel portraits painted by a former client who is now an accomplished artist. They vent about drama that’s unfolded on the streets and reflect on their relationships, both good and bad, as well as deaths in the community.

Andrade and Judge are on track to help more women this year than last, to expand weekly hours at “the spot,” and to acquire a mobile van. They hired a third staff member in June.

“People seem to help women a lot when they’re clean, but what about when they’re actually going through things?” Andrade said. “Our women sustain being clean and being in housing because they have support now, when things are really shady.”

The press conference, which Cox said is the first to be held before one of these events, comes just two years after five people were shot at the same festival.

Officials said that disorderly behavior won’t be tolerated at the parade , which regularly draws tens of thousands of visitors. The route goes from Hyde Square in Jamaica Plain to Franklin Park. It will begin around noon and result in various road closures along Centre Street, Perkins Street, Columbus Avenue, and Walnut Avenue, city officials announced.

Various other festival and parade gatherings in Boston have been marred by violence.

Just last month, a teenager was arrested for opening fire at a Puerto Rican Festival also held in Franklin Park, though no one was injured, police said.

At the Caribbean Carnival heritage festival in 2023, eight people were shot when gunfire broke out between two rival groups, catching civilians in the crossfire. This year’s festival is set for next month.

In 2022, a man was fatally shot at the same event, and the early morning hours before the parade were the backdrop for fatal shootings in 2015 and 2014 as well.

Cox said that Sunday’s parade route is “part of the area where we have had discharged firearms, certainly over the summer,” but that “this year we’re looking to improve.”

He said that lessons have been learned from past incidents and the upcoming festival was planned with a focus on addressing safety “blind spots.”

More officers will be on the ground this year, Cox added, and visitors are asked to leave the area immediately following the event.

Last year’s Dominican Parade was held without any violent incidents.

“We do a lot in general to try to curtail” violence, he said. “For the most part, we’ve probably done a decent job doing that, but … anytime violence happens, it’s not a good thing. It’s not something we plan for, but the fact is that it does occur."

Sunday’s event also comes as community concerns have mounted following a string of various shooting and stabbing deaths in the city.

A man was fatally stabbed during rush hour Wednesday at South Station, while various fatal shootings have occurred throughout the city in recent weeks.

In July, Jonathan Sanon of Norwood was also fatally beaten outside an MBTA Green Line station on Boston Common, prompting civic leaders to hold a forum on improving safety.

In total there have been 20 homicides in Boston this year, police data show, compared with 24 at this time last year.

Cox emphasized that the South Station stabbing, which police have said was not a random incident, like a domestic violence stabbing that also took place near North Station on Thursday, follow a pattern that is true of most of the recent violence in Boston.

“Usually it’s related to people who know each other and choose to engage in some type of altercation,” he said, adding that violent crime is “down in every category except for two, which is aggravated assaults and domestic assaults.”

So, “we don’t have an uptick,” in violence, Cox added. “What we have is an uptick of reported events ... [and] isolated incidents in different parts of the city.”

Most of the public debate around the pending NextEra-Dominion megamerger is happening in the Southeast, where the companies have extensive electric utility operations.

But now it’s taking shape here, too. Rebecca Tepper, Governor Maura Healey’s energy secretary, is speaking out about the Healey administration’s concerns, saying the merger could result in serious cost impacts for New England ratepayers. As if we didn’t have enough reasons to worry about our utility bills.

She raised her concerns in a statement to me, as requests pile up to intervene in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s merger review. In recent days, the state Department of Public Utilities, the state attorney general’s office, and the New England States Committee on Electricity all filed motions to be included in the case — and those are just the ones representing Massachusetts. Then, on Monday, Senator Ed Markey urged FERC to reject the merger outright, citing affordability and antitrust concerns.

NextEra and Dominion aren’t household names in New England. Neither company owns a utility here. But they do have something that’s quite valuable: our last two nuclear power plants.

Dominion owns Millstone in Waterford, Conn., the region’s biggest power plant. Guess who is number two? NextEra’s Seabrook, in New Hampshire. Together, they provide a quarter of New England’s electricity.

Should the merger go through as planned, a single company (NextEra) would control the region’s two biggest power stations — also its last remaining nuclear plants.

It’s easy to see why Tepper is concerned. She is calling on FERC to “heavily scrutinize the impacts this merger may have on ratepayer bills, market power, and reliability.”

The merger lands on our doorstep as New England warms up to nuclear power again, thanks to its reliability and low carbon emissions. In 2018, Connecticut officials orchestrated long-term contracts to financially support the two power plants, after Dominion threatened to close Millstone.

Those contracts expire in 2029 — right around the corner in infrastructure-planning terms. As a result, Governor Ned Lamont’s administration is knocking on Healey’s door, looking for help in a new multi-state procurement of green energy; the contracts will likely again support one or both nuclear plants.

Meanwhile, Beacon Hill lawmakers have embarked on closed-door negotiations to resolve differences between two sprawling energy bills. Among the disputed items: the House wants to end a state law that requires a statewide vote before nuclear construction happens — effectively a ban on new nukes — while the Senate version doesn’t lift the requirement. No one expects a new reactor similar in scale to the shuttered Pilgrim or dismantled Yankee Rowe, near the Vermont border. Local fights would be too fierce. But maybe the bill opens the door for compact “microreactors,” like ones being sold by Radiant, to supplant backup diesel generators.

Of more importance to the New England grid: the future of Millstone and Seabrook. Ensuring they stay open for the long haul is crucial to keeping our lights on.

The Conservation Law Foundation’s Caitlin Peale Sloan worries about the negotiating power the new company would have for future contracts. “When Millstone first put its hand out to Connecticut, they had a lot of leverage,” she said. “And now that leverage is going to grow.”

There’s another reason for concern with NextEra at the helm. The Florida-based company became Public Enemy No. 1 on Beacon Hill as it fought a power line from going up through western Maine — first quietly, then quite publicly. NextEra didn’t want the competition from Canada’s hydropower that would come along the new line for Massachusetts. The project officially finished in January, but its cost grew by more than 50 percent, to $1.6 billion, because of the delays. Massachusetts ratepayers picked up the tab.

Could NextEra use its increased might in the region to thwart other competitors? Boston energy consultantRichard Levitan says it’s likely. “They have a history,” he says, “of not playing well in the giant New England sandbox.”

Others in the industry speak in more favorable terms, echoing the two companies’ talking points. One insider suggests to me that NextEra might be more likely to invest in New England, such as with a new small modular reactor at one of the existing sites, if it has a bigger scale here. NextEra, per its usual MO, didn’t respond to my request for a comment; a Dominion spokesperson reminded me that Connecticut ratepayers are saving a ton of money now with those nuclear contracts.

On balance, though, the NextEra-Dominion combo is generating skepticism around here. With no local regulated utility involved, state officials here have no say in ultimately deciding the merger’s fate. But they’ve got a voice. And, as the documents piling up at FERC show, they plan on using it.

The White Stadium waiting game is going to take a little longer now. In case you are living under a Roxbury puddingstone boulder, a revamp of the Franklin Park fixture is being pursued by Mayor Michelle Wu and the Boston Legacy FC soccer team but also challenged in court by the nonprofit Emerald Necklace Conservancy. The issue, now before the Supreme Judicial Court, could hinge on whether the stadium site should be deemed parkland, which would require Wu and the soccer team to get approval from the state Legislature to host a business there. The SJC heard oral arguments back on April 8. But this week, lawyers for all sides were informed that the court is waiving its standard “130-day guideline” to resolve the White Stadium debate. What’s taking so long? Are the judges closer to shutting the project down, too busy with stopping ballot questions, or just spending a little extra time on the Cape?

The consensus at a summer economic roundtable convened Wednesday by Mayor Michelle Wu was clear: Make 3 a.m. last call and social districts permanent. Those were measures the Legislature temporarily passed to help bars and restaurants take advantage of the throngs of tourists and fans visiting for World Cup, Fourth of July, and Sail Boston. We hate to be a party pooper, but only social districts – allowing municipalities to create designated public drinking areas – made it to a conference committee as part of the Senate’s “fun agenda.” That means extending last call for an extra hour is dead until next session, according to state senator Julian Cyr. While lawmakers were not enthused, business leaders and bar owners who gathered at Roundhead Brewing in Hyde Park for the mayoral roundtable – including Apex Noire’s Tito Jackson, The Haven’s Jason Waddleton, Meet Boston CEO Martha Sheridan and Downtown Boston Alliance president Michael Nichols – value the 3 a.m. option.

Think it’s hard getting homes built in Boston? Sometimes, it’s even harder in Newton. Just ask Brian Golden. The former head of the Boston Planning & Development Agency is now on the Newton City Council, and he gave his first speech to the full council the other night. The issue in question: whether the council should approve replacing a two-family house with four attached single-family homes in Newtonville. Golden said he agrees with some arguments on both sides, but in the end favors more housing: “It is impossible for me to lose sight of how important it is to grow the number of units not just in Newton but in the commonwealth,” Golden said. “All along the socioeconomic spectrum, we need more units.” A passionate plea, but apparently it wasn’t enough. The special permit didn’t get the two-thirds majority vote that city officials say it needed.

It’s an email no restaurateur wants to write: “I Don’t Want This To Become Our Farewell Letter.” But that’s what Suya Joint founder and chef Cecelia Lizotte sent Wednesday to a local food email group run by Jen Faigel’s CommonWealth Kitchen. Lizotte revealed she has considered closing her West African restaurant with locations in Roxbury and Providence due to rising food and labor costs and heightened fears about ICE that have kept immigrant customers home. (Her brother Paul Dama, who works with her, was detained and released by ICE last year.) Suya Joint also bet big on the World Cup, staffing up and activating its food truck, but it didn’t pay off. The poignant letter was Lizotte’s way of telling her network that she needs help to survive – including booking catering, hiring the food truck, and hosting private events. “We are not looking for a handout. We are looking for opportunities, partnerships, resources, and a bridge through an extraordinarily difficult period.”

The Federal Reserve Bank of Boston released this week its much anticipated follow up to its landmark “Color of Wealth” report from 2015. The new analysis, years in the making, takes a deeper dive into family wealth by surveying more than 5,000 Massachusetts residents. One data point that caught our attention because it wasn’t studied last time: About one in six families expect to receive an inheritance in the future. It’s another way to look at generational wealth and the ability for families to pass on their assets. The study found that only 3.7 percent of Latino families and 4.3 percent of Black families expect to receive one, compared to 18.6 percent of white households and 13.1 percent of Asian American households.

It didn’t take long for the progressive Massachusetts Budget & Policy Center to seize on that part of the Fed study as a reason to keep the estate tax. Their argument: proceeds from the tax — which is expected to bring in more than $700 million a year — could be used to address economic disparities. MassBudget will have a fight on their hands: Major business groups say the estate tax is driving wealthy people out of the state, and they want it eliminated. This issue could be the next big tax-related showdown when lawmakers start their new two-year session in January.

“I’m going to be honest with everyone here, we need the most help with this song,” Koh, clad in a sweat-soaked “Harvey Milk Supervisor” shirt, told the smattering of spectators, who gamely clapped along to the popular folk-country song “Wagon Wheel.”

This is the sort of humbling exercise that only a candidate for office — and perhaps only a particularly thirsty candidate for office — is willing to endure. And Koh, in the closing days of a six-way race to replace US Representative Seth Moulton may be among the thirstiest.

After narrowly losing the open Third District Democratic primary in 2018, Koh once openly considered challenging US Representative Lori Trahan, the Westford Democrat who edged him in that 2018 race. He ultimately passed, and his hometown of Andover was later carved from the Third and pushed into the Sixth District amid the state’s 2021 redistricting process.

That shuffling proved serendipitous this year. After Koh quietly considered challenging Moulton, the seat opened up when the Salem Democrat mounted his own challenge to US Senator Ed Markey. A chance for Koh’s thirst to be quenched.

This time around, is there anything he wouldn’t do to win?

“This is going to sound corny, but compromise Democratic values against Trump,” Koh said in a post-performance interview.

There’s plenty that he is willing to do — beyond, literally, playing to the crowd.

The former Biden administration official and Boston City Hall alum has leveraged his connections, big and small, to build a dominant war chest, topping the field in fundraising at roughly $4.5 million through June. The next closest candidate, Lynnfield fintech executive John Beccia, ended June having raised about $3.5 million, though nearly $3 million of that has come from his own pocket.

The next closest fundraiser, state Representative Tram Nguyen, isn’t in the same financial stratosphere. Three other candidates — Topsfield’s Jamie Belsito, a former state lawmaker; software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck; and Mariah Lancaster, a veterinarian and former Congressional aide — are also running in the Democratic primary.

Add Koh’s own fundraising to the more than $700,000 a super PAC has already spent to send mailers and air digital ads on his behalf, and he’s enjoyed a huge cash advantage.

Whether that means he also has a huge advantage in general . . .

“There is definitely some anti-Dan sentiment,” said Essex County Register of Deeds Eileen Duff, a Democrat who has yet to endorse in the race. “But I think how non-stop he is shows tenacity more than just blind ambition.”

Koh has been here before. He looked, at times, like the favorite in the 2018 race before he fell to Trahan by razor-thin margin, losing the Democratic nomination by 145 votes after a recount. Which may be why the second-time candidate spent a sweltering Sunday in Salem, performing for just a handful of people.

For at least one Sixth District voter, it worked.

“When my husband told me Dan Koh was performing, I was like, ‘He’s actually playing music?’” said Tanya Shallop, a Salem resident who was, until Sunday, undecided on who she would back.

“I mean, I wouldn’t hire him as my wedding singer,” she said. “I had actually been on the fence, but it was so endearing and kind of vulnerable, and I really like that about him.”

Shallop then added. “I know that sounds ridiculous.”

A Dominican flag soared through the air Sunday, leading a parade through Jamaica Plain to celebrate Dominican heritage and culture in New England.

Thousands gathered to cheer on the floats, praise the dancers, and wear Dominican flags as capes at the annual Dominican Parade and Festival. The parade, which ended in Franklin Park, was created to showcase the “vibrant culture and traditions of the Dominican,” according to the website of Casa de la Cultura Dominicana en Boston, the nonprofit that organized the event.

“We’ve been celebrating this event for 40 years,” said Alejandro Guzmán, a youth coordinator for Casa de la Cultura. “Now, we’re trying to develop it and make it a safe place for the community.”

Before the parade officially began at 11 a.m., the celebration was already underway. Loud music played from cars waiting to join the procession, and people danced on the sidewalks.

The streets were draped in the Dominican flag, and people arrived decked out in red, white, and blue. Several people pushed carts selling red, white, and blue items. Others waved beaded necklaces, flags, hats, and towels.

Floats, dancers, advocacy organizations, and cars adorned with bass boosters proceeded along the parade route, winding through the streets. Several groups attended Sunday’s event, including the Consulate General of the Dominican Republic, MeetBoston, a visitor services organization that promotes events around the city, and America’s Food Basket, a grocery store chain co-op. As the groups passed by on their floats, members threw beads and candy into the crowds, while the Boston Public Schools float tossed beach balls that some people bounced along the sidewalk.

“This means a lot,” Guzmán said. ”Not only because I’m part of [Casa de la Cultura Dominicana en Boston], but because I’m Dominican."

He explained that the two main goals for this year’s festival were to enjoy the festival and keep everyone safe.

In recent years, violence has erupted at the festival, and in 2024, five people were shot as the celebration wound down. Ahead of this year’s event, city officials pledged to keep the festival safe.

Scattered among attendees, Boston police could be seen walking around during the event, periodically stopping by the force’s booth and chatting with attendees.

At the festival’s stage, performances throughout the day featured dancers from Latin dance schools, several DJ sets, and Toño Rosario, a Dominican merengue artist.

Rosario was Nicolas Gonzalez’s favorite performance of the day. Gonzalez was behind a booth selling flavored drinks in cups that resembled pineapples and skulls.

“We’ve been doing [our business] for almost 10 years,” said Gonzalez, who runs Tropicana Prestige, a frozen juice vendor. This year’s festival was his sixth time selling the drinks, which come in four different flavors.

“My mom and dad used to make these drinks,” he said. “And then it was my turn to work.”

Just a few booths down, Juan Marte was selling a variety of tequeños, arepas, and hot dogs. Marte owns Don Tequeño y Doña Arepa, a Venezuelan and Dominican Latin restaurant with locations in Dorchester and Jamaica Plain.

The couple started their business from their home during the COVID-19 pandemic, and Sunday’s event marked the restaurant’s first time selling food at the festival.

“We were so surprised to see how much the community was welcoming of something new in the city,” he said.

As the day carried on, Latin music filled the air while people relaxed on the grass. Near the front of the stage, some people danced to the music as a few kids kicked a soccer ball around nearby.

When a new performer took the stage, the crowd erupted in cheers, coupled with the revving of motorcycle engines as people popped wheelies and raced down a side street.

“When you see all the people, not just the Dominican people, when you see everybody on the streets, appreciate the culture that makes you feel something on the inside,” Guzmán said.

Thank you for highlighting the contributions of Boston’s ministerial community to public safety (“Decades on, a constant voice for peace,” Page A1, Aug. 2).

As the mother of Louis D. Brown, my 15-year-old son murdered in Dorchester in 1993, I lived this history. Boston recorded 152 homicides in 1990. By 1996, that number had fallen to 61, and juvenile homicides declined dramatically. This progress grew from partnerships among clergy, police, prosecutors, probation, public health officials, community organizations, youth, and families, and included implementation of the Louis D. Brown Peace Curriculum in Boston schools.

That history matters today.

But numbers tell only part of the story. Every homicide creates a ripple effect, expanding the circle of trauma to parents, children, spouses, siblings, grandparents, friends, neighbors, and others whose lives are forever changed.

Our response to violence must include a survivor-centered focus that recognizes healing — of individuals, families, and communities — as essential to interrupting cycles of violence that plague our neighborhoods. This involves faithfully supporting those affected by violence throughout the criminal justice process and beyond, engaging community members to discourage retaliation, and showing survivors that their loved ones’ lives mattered.

Prevention, intervention, enforcement, and faith partnerships matter. So does healing. A survivor-centered homicide response is a necessary component of public safety.

President and chief executive officer

Several sponsors that had approached the Fed made it happen. The Barr Foundation kicked in $1.3 million, while The Boston Foundation provided $450,000 and handled the contract with Mathematica, according to Keith Mahoney at TBF. The Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce and Eastern Bank each chipped in $250,000. Mahoney also said a city resiliency fund established by then-mayor Marty Walsh with private donations during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic provided another $65,000.

The bottom line: Things haven’t changed all that much from 2015. The wealth gap remains huge between white ($549,000 in net wealth) and Black families ($7,800), though it’s even more pronounced when comparing homeowners ($790,000) to renters ($1,500), or households led by Latinos ($1,200) to white families.

“We were not expecting the report would yield different results in terms of inequity,” said Eastern executive chair Bob Rivers. “I’m fine with updating the study ... to give it more credibility but believed the answers were going to be fundamentally the same.”

Jim Rooney, chief executive of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, said the report’s findings reinforced that homeownership is a big driver of wealth here, and making it easier for people to achieve that should remain a chamber priority. “Do we need yet another reason to double down on housing production?” Rooney said.

The work, to some extent, can be traced back to a 2015 meeting at McKenna’s in Savin Hill between Rooney and Walsh. Over breakfast, they lamented Boston’s racial wealth gap and vowed to put City Hall and the chamber to work to address it. Walsh, for example, then brought on Karilyn Crockett as the city’s first chief of equity. And Rooney later launched the Pacesetters program connecting small-business contractors with large enterprises in need of their services.

Separately, the 2015 report spurred civic leaders to create the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts and prompted Eastern to launch a business equity fund through its foundation.

Through it all, though, the hope for more thorough research continued. Finally, following the racial reckoning and the Black Lives Matter protests early in the pandemic, the Boston Fed and the report sponsors got to work in 2022. By that point, Crockett had left City Hall to teach at MIT, and was working with the chamber on a consulting basis.

The initial budget for the report was set at $1.5 million. But costs grew as the parameters expanded, and both the Barr and Boston foundations kicked in more money.

“The fact there were more than 5,000 households that participated in this, that’s a great indication of people’s willingness to share their personal and financial data,” Crockett said. “We now have a snapshot of how households are doing in terms of their wealth, in terms of their economic status.”

Lee Pelton had also made a push for the 2015 report to be revisited after he became president of The Boston Foundation in 2021. The timing of the report’s release is good for Pelton, as he plan to retire at the end of this month, though Mahoney says it’s purely a coincidence.

The big question hanging over everyone: What’s next?

Rivers, for one, can’t help but admit frustration that more hasn’t been done to address wealth inequity since the 2015 report. He hopes this time will be different.

“I think the last time we missed the moment,” Rivers said. “We shouldn’t miss the moment again.”

The expansion comes as Boston’s Italian restaurant scene is getting bigger and more corporate, while Quaresima is purposefully small and entirely self-funded. The new restaurant is also the product of an unusually community-driven process, with the landlord asking neighbors to weigh in on what should fill a vacant storefront.

“I really want to create a space outside with some tables and chairs, like a small bistro you’d find in Paris. That’s the picture I’ve had in my mind,” said Quaresima in an exclusive interview with the Globe.

The empty storefront wasn’t simply another vacancy that Quaresima happened to stumble upon, despite looking for the past year for the right space for a second location. Its landlord, developer and Dorchester resident Travis Lee, saw an opportunity to bring in another local operator when his longtime tenant closed in June. Over the years, he’s made a practice of asking community members and neighbors what they want in the storefronts he owns, and, in some cases, letting them help him decide who actually moves in.

When the roughly 1,000-square-foot storefront became available, Lee said he circulated the opportunity among people in his network and heard from five interested parties, including Quaresima and a mother-daughter team behind the concept of Café Bleu. After interviewing the candidates, he narrowed the field to Quaresima and Café Bleu and asked people to weigh in.

Lee’s approach is unusual in a city where commercial real estate is often a costly numbers game, and where many independent restaurants can’t survive — let alone open a second location — because of the high rent costs for a business that already has such thin margins.

“I think it’s the right thing to bring people that live and have invested themselves into a specific geographic community into the process,” said Lee. “But I also think it’s good business.”

Lee’s model has produced a string of neighborhood businesses, which included the now-shuttered 50 Kitchen, Fresh Food Generation, the store Just Bookish, and more.

For this prominent corner location in the historic Lenane building, the neighborhood’s newest restaurant will be a second outpost from one of Dorchester’s most exciting culinary names. For Lee, that meant betting on a chef whose first restaurant had already demonstrated that the neighborhood would show up for him and fill his seats.

Over Easter weekend in 2023, Quaresima opened Via Cannuccia, naming it after his childhood street just south of Rome in the seaside town of Anzio. He’s built a career working in restaurants in Italy and France and came to the United States in 2013 to work at Petit Robert Bistro, a Parisian-style bistro in the South End.

Since striking out on his own in Dorchester — a neighborhood with a food culture shaped by generations of Irish, Cantonese, and Vietnamese immigrants — Quaresima quickly developed a particularly loyal following among restaurant professionals. On their days off, chefs, servers, and bartenders from across the city regularly fill the tables at Via Cannuccia, eating Italian food that hasn’t been Americanized. “I don’t put meatballs on top of spaghetti, and I won’t ever put chicken parmesan on the menu,” said Quaresima. “We serve traditional Italian dishes.”

Quaresima said Bottega Cannuccia will be a place where guests can stop in for fresh pastries, like butter croissants, cookies, muffins, scones, cinnamon rolls, sfogliatella, and his favorite pastry, zeppola, which is a rich Italian cream puff that’s served warm, filled with pastry cream and dusted with powdered sugar. He’ll serve sandwiches with Cannuccia’s homemade bread, salads, Italian espresso, and tea from Mariage Frères, a French tea house from Paris that was founded in 1854.

At night, the Bottega will serve cheese and charcuterie boards, crostinis, fresh soups, and dishes like bruschetta with smoked trout and sweet potato and saffron aioli, and a crocchetta di pasta alla carbonara. The wine list will focus on Italian grapes, such as Montepulciano d’Abruzzo, Vermentino from Sardegna, and Nero d’Avola from Sicily. There will be a handful of cocktails, Italian and American beers, ciders, and a selection of Italian amari, cordials, and digestifs.

While restaurant groups are spending millions opening sprawling Italian-focused concepts around the city, Quaresima is taking a very different approach, funding the 30-seat neighborhood shop entirely by him and his wife, Tsedenia Kiros.

“I think parts of the restaurant scene in Boston has lost some of its charm with these really big spaces,” said Quaresima. “It’s why I went with little spaces. They’re unique here. And you have to be attentive [to] all the details.”

The suspect in a domestic violence incident near North Station last week stabbed his girlfriend repeatedly and only stopped when a Good Samaritan pulled him off the victim, authorities said Monday.

Daudy B. Martinez was arraigned Monday from a Boston hospital where he is recovering from self-inflicted injuries sustained Thursday in a building on Causeway Street, according to Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office.

Martinez, 51, was ordered held by Judge James W. Coffey pending a dangerousness hearing sought by Hayden’s office. He faces multiple charges, including armed assault with intent to murder and domestic violence, subsequent offense.

Hayden’s office provided new details during the arraignment. Martinez, prosecutors said, got into an argument with a woman identified as his 44-year-old girlfriend.

The woman was rushed to a Boston hospital where officers learned she had stab wounds to her forehead, her left hand, her chin and neck area, and behind her left leg, the prosecutor said.

On-scene officers reviewed surveillance video that captured Martinez’s alleged assault, the prosecutor said.

Martinez “doesn’t stop until an unidentified female comes up behind him and pulls him off the victim,” the prosecutor said.

The victim is hospitalized for treatment of her multiple injuries, the prosecutor said.

Officers pursued Martinez, allegedly still armed with a knife, into a nearby restaurant. When police ordered him to drop the knife or be tased by them, Martinez injured himself with the weapon, the prosecutor said.

Martinez pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges in West Roxbury Municipal Court in 2021 and was sentenced to two years in Suffolk County House of Correction, court records show.

He completed a two-year probation period last October, records show.|
