“I’m not a romantic; at the end of the day, his legacy is [expletive] crack cocaine,” said Jamarhl Crawford, who grew up in Roxbury and dealt drugs as a teenager, before becoming a community activist and organizer. “He was just a crack dealer.”

Whiting, for all his imprint locally, was not from Boston. He came here from New York in the 1980s and took over the Orchard Park housing development in Roxbury, eventually turning it into his personal trap house. There, he preyed upon the weaknesses of drug-addicted mothers surviving on government assistance to gain the use of their apartments to move significant amounts of narcotics.

“Basically, he came into Orchard Park, got rid of the old dealers, and either you were buying from him or selling for him,” said Crawford.

The operation was 24-7, with Whiting’s organization eventually becoming the largest supplier of cocaine in Roxbury, authorities said at the time.

By the time his New York Boys organization was dismantled by law enforcement in the early 1990s, the group was grossing more than $6 million a year in drug sales and controlled about $11 million in local real estate, according to federal court testimony. Whiting owned and operated a video store, sneaker shop, and barbershop, all on Warren Street in Roxbury, as well as the Crown Social and Recreation Hall on Geneva Avenue in Grove Hall.

At one point, Whiting’s organization had about 75 members, according to court testimony from someone who worked for him, including women who acted as drug mules, bringing hard drugs from New York to packing houses in Boston. There were also people who processed and packed cocaine, runners, and street-level sellers, all ultimately answering to him.

His rise in the Boston underworld inspired LL Cool J’s character in the 1999 crime thriller “In Too Deep.” And some of Whiting’s tale has become blurred with fiction locally.

Some observers from his era have suggested that Whiting was the one person most responsible for bringing wholesale amounts of crack cocaine to the streets of Boston. Others are adamant that that is an urban myth, a reductive oversimplification, and a fundamental misreading of Boston street life during the 1980s.

Whatever the reality, a Boston police commissioner once described him as “an evil person.” To the head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration office in Boston, he was “a piece of trash.” A different investigator labeled him “a city’s worst nightmare.” Newspapers dubbed him a criminal mastermind.

The head federal prosecutor in Boston once gave his case higher priority than that of New England Mafia boss Raymond “Junior” Patriarca.

His larger-than-life story sometimes had elements of a Hollywood noir script.

During one court appearance, he announced to the gathered press, “Call this the second trial of Jesus Christ!” He once struck a cop with a ring shaped like a ram’s head. Police said he went by many names: God, G, Rah.

Taking down his operation was a massive undertaking: In 1990, 250 federal agents and police raided locations in Roxbury, including Orchard Park, Dorchester, and Mattapan, arresting 18. Whiting was already behind bars when that happened, serving an assault and battery sentence at the Deer Island House of Correction.

Ultimately, Whiting became the first person in Massachusetts to receive a life sentence for selling narcotics.

The Rev. Eugene F. Rivers III has worked on street violence prevention and mitigation in Boston for decades. To him, Whiting was among the dominant underworld forces that circulated hard drugs throughout Black Boston, ripping apart families and ruining lives.

“There wasn’t anybody comparable to what he was doing,” Rivers said this past week.

Whiting’s rise to the top of the Boston drug trade corresponded with a historic spike in street violence in the city. In 1989, there were 100 homicides in the city. The next year, the number was 152. Such street violence, according to researchers, was fueled by the crack cocaine trade and the turf-based conflicts it fostered.

Rivers said Whiting’s organization was part of the milieu that increased the bloodshed on the streets of Boston.

“There was no question about that,” he said.

Like so many underworld figures, he leaned into the Robin Hood trope, projecting an image of someone who cared about Black communities in a city that had a very real history of racism.

He once put on a free rap concert for more than 1,000 teenagers at Dorchester’s Strand Theatre. There were also free trips to amusement parks for youths, Christmas parties, Easter egg hunts, barbecues, weekend brunches, and gifts of sports equipment. One registered nurse testified in court that his Grove Hall club doubled as a day care center for homeless mothers and offered youth programs and health care counseling.

But for one retired Boston police officer who grew up in Orchard Park, Whiting’s legacy is no different from James “Whitey” Bulger, the mobster who lorded over South Boston’s underworld for years and corrupted the local FBI office. Crack turned their home into a “zombieland,” they said.

Speaking on the condition of anonymity because they feared reprisals on their relatives, the former cop said it’s true that Whiting would buy people groceries and pay their bills when they were tight on money. But once he did someone a favor, that meant they owed him. For the Orchard Park native, Whiting was a “wolf in sheep’s clothing.”

“He did all that, but he had his own agenda,” said the retiree. “He was helping himself. He was making his money.”

Court testimony painted an even darker and more violent picture. One former member of his organization said under oath that discipline was instilled with violence, saying he was beaten on Whiting’s command at least three times.

A woman testified she became addicted to crack after agreeing to let Whiting’s gang use her apartment to set up a drug-dealing operation. The woman said she earned $350 a week for allowing drugs to be processed and packaged in the apartment she shared with her two small children. She also admitted to torturing a suspected informant on behalf of Whiting’s gang, saying the person was burned on the forehead with a curling iron “for a long time.”

Boston political consultant Joyce Ferriabough Bolling recalled feeling “horrible for the Orchard Park community” during Whiting’s heyday, which was marked by rampant and brazen drug peddling in and around the development that was colloquially known as “OP.”

“I wondered why the police or somebody in authority didn’t move on closing down God’s in-your-face operation,” she said.

His legacy is a dark one, according to Ferriabough Bolling, as it took at least two generations to clean up the crack scourge in Boston.

“I hope he made his peace with the real God,” she said.

Jeremiah Manion of Globe staff contributed to this report.

Bill helped him land a good job with a good pension.

Whitey cost him that pension, enlisting him in a harebrained scheme to help Whitey stay out of prison after Whitey went on the lam in 1994.

In 1938, Jack was a newborn when his family moved into the Old Harbor development at 41 Logan Way, just around the corner from St. Monica’s Church.

He will, as his family noted in his obituary, “be remembered for his generosity, humor, and fierce loyalty.”

If that last quality defined him, it also helped and cost him in equal measure.

In 1964, Jack accompanied their father, James, for whom Whitey was named, to visit Whitey after he was transferred to the federal prison in Lewisburg, Pa. It was the last time the elder Bulger would see his wayward son.

Bill Bulger said his father never had a good day after Whitey went to prison. James Bulger did not live long enough to see his son emerge from prison and become the city’s most powerful, and lethal, gangster.

Bill Bulger became a powerful figure himself, on Beacon Hill, ascending to Senate president in 1978.

With his politician brother’s considerable influence, Jack became clerk-magistrate of the Boston Juvenile Court in 1982, a job that he held until his retirement in 2001.

But even as an officer of the court, Jack Bulger didn’t hesitate to help his gangster brother after Whitey went on the lam in 1994. He paid the monthly rental fee for a safe deposit box Whitey kept at a bank in Clearwater, Fla., and he spoke with Whitey twice in prearranged telephone calls while Whitey was on the run.

Jack Bulger lied twice before federal grand juries investigating Whitey, insisting he hadn’t spoken to his fugitive brother since Whitey took off, and that he didn’t know where he hid his money.

During one of those phone calls, Jack agreed to help Whitey obtain phony IDs to use on the run.

Even though Jack was nine years younger than Whitey, they bore enough of a resemblance to make the scheme somewhat plausible. Whitey instructed Kevin Weeks, his top lieutenant, to go to Jack’s home in Southie to take photos with Jack wearing a fake mustache.

When Weeks delivered the fake ID to Whitey at the Water Tower in Chicago, Whitey frowned. The photo was all wrong. Whitey’s mustache was pencil thin. Jack’s was big and bushy. It looked like he had a caterpillar on his lip.

The task force trying to find Whitey put traces on the phones of Bill and Jack, but a corrupt state cop told Whitey’s partner in crime, Stevie Flemmi, about it. Flemmi, whose parents were Bill Bulger’s neighbors, gave them the heads up.

What the cops couldn’t do Whitey did unwittingly, using traceable phone cards to call his brothers, which put them in compromising positions.

In a letter to a friend after he was captured in 2011, Whitey acknowledged he screwed up.

“I put the heat on people,” he admitted. “My brother Jack was trapped.”

After it emerged that he had admitted to a grand jury that he had spoken to his brother while Whitey was on the run, Bill was forced to resign as president of the University of Massachusetts, the sweet sinecure he had secured after his tenure as Senate president.

But Bill was able to keep his annual $274,539 pension.

Jack wasn’t as lucky. In 2003, Jack was sentenced to six months in prison and six months of house arrest for lying to two grand juries and thwarting efforts to capture his brother.

He was stripped of his pension, which was not even a quarter of Bill’s. Loyalty to Whitey had cost Jack his freedom and his income, and it cost Bill his job and, in the eyes of many, his good name.

It was a heavy price to pay for the Bulger credo of family above all else.

While Whitey was willing to forgive Teresa Stanley, his longtime companion who spoke to the authorities after deciding she didn’t want to spend her life on the lam with him, Jack was less forgiving.

During an interview for the book Shelley Murphy and I wrote about Whitey, Stanley told us that Jack Bulger confronted her once while walking on Castle Island and snarled, “I wish you were dead. Look at what you’ve done, all the trouble you caused.”

That was pretty rich, because Teresa Stanley didn’t cause any trouble. Whitey did.

That was something that neither Jack nor Bill were able to fully acknowledge. They remembered the funny, fiercely loyal, and protective brother who stuck up for little kids and carried the groceries of older neighbors.

But it was Whitey who murdered people. It was Whitey who made millions by allowing drug dealers to operate freely in Southie as long as they paid him tribute, while his family perpetuated the myth that Whitey was the Robin Hood of Southie, that he kept the drugs out of Southie.

It was Whitey who made their lives difficult, not the State Police and DEA agents who finally held Whitey to account, not the reporters who wrote about his exploits, not the big bad world outside of Southie.

They were enthusiastic purveyors of Southie exceptionalism, the myth that Southie was God’s country, the best neighborhood in the city, while Whitey’s criminal activity rotted the neighborhood from within, like termites.

When Whitey was convicted of murder and myriad crimes in the courthouse on the waterfront named for his old neighbor, Joe Moakley, he gave a thumbs up to Jack as he was led out of the courtroom.

Whatever you think of them, the Bulger brothers had longevity in their genes. Whitey was 89 when he was murdered in a West Virginia prison in 2018. Jack made it to 88.

Bill is, at 92, the last one standing.

The Bulger brothers lived long, long lives, a blessing not afforded to so many of Whitey’s victims.

A new poll — commissioned by Leaders We Deserve, the progressive group putting its firepower behind Eighth Congressional District candidate Patrick Roath and other younger, progressive challengers — shows a tightening race in Roath’s primary against US Representative Stephen Lynch.

The survey of 469 likely Democratic primary voters in the district found Roath, a 39-year-old Jamaica Plain attorney, trailing Lynch by seven percentage points, 43 percent to 50 percent. The remaining 7 percent were undecided.

As with any internal survey, caveats apply. The poll, which was conducted on Aug. 5-6, had a margin of error of plus-or-minus 4.53 percent, according to a polling memo shared by Leaders We Deserve. The PAC, founded by gun control activist David Hogg, also has a vested interest in boosting Roath, a first-time candidate trying to unseat a more well-known, moderate incumbent in Lynch, 71.

A poll Roath’s campaign paid for from February found him lagging Lynch by 26 percentage points. There’s been no independent public polling of the race so far.

Still, if the latest numbers hold, those results paint a picture of a race that’s far closer than the matchup between US Representative Seth Moulton and US Senator Ed Markey in the party’s US Senate primary, according to a new University of Massachusetts Amherst/WCVB poll.

Of the 445 Democratic primary voters surveyed, 54 percent said they would vote for Markey, 80, compared to 28 percent who said they’d back Moulton, 47, if the Sept. 1 election were held today. Another 17 percent were still undecided. Throw in those who said they are leaning toward one candidate or another, and Markey’s lead grows wider: 60 percent for the incumbent, versus 32 percent for Moulton.

Markey’s edge in the new poll is far wider than the one he had in a University of New Hampshire poll conducted in late June that showed the Malden Democrat leading Moulton by just 6 percentage points.

“We’ve seen primaries across the country where you have the establishment candidate versus the progressive challenger or upstart, but in this instance, we have a little bit of a different story,” said Tatishe Nteta, the UMass Poll director. “The incumbent [Markey] is viewed as a more progressive candidate. The challenger is viewed, at least by the electorate, as a much more moderate candidate.”

Moulton, he added, “is going to need a miracle or a Hail Mary to really change the dynamics of this race.”

In the Eighth District, it’s a different story. Roath has positioned himself to Lynch’s left on an array of issues from healthcare to immigration.

Still, Lynch holds several advantages in the race. He ended June with a $1.2 million war chest, more than doubling the $460,000 Roath had on hand. Lynch has also fended off progressive challengers in the past, defeating Robbie Goldstein, now the state’s public health commissioner, in 2020, and Democrats Brianna Wu and Christopher Voehl in 2018.

Lynch is also running — literally — at least in his latest digital ad, a 15-second spot that shows him jogging along the beach in South Boston.

I see you honking at me with your New York plates, guy, but I know how to drive on a rotary. Trust me, pal. Born and bred. Rotaries are our state bird, probably.

So I don’t know what you’re getting at leaning on your horn there. Relax, guy, I’m in the right lane ‘cause I’m getting off the second exit. That’s how it’s done around here. I know the sign just says something like “yield” or “enter if you dare.” But I assure you there are rules because right after you flipped me off I immediately looked ‘em up in the state driving handbook because I will not stop trying to win an argument even if all parties are no longer present.

Don’t worry, I didn’t Google ‘em while I was driving. As soon as it was safe, I double-parked.

Why us?

“Rotaries are much more common in Massachusetts than in other parts of the country,” the section of the official Massachusetts Driver’s Manual begins, a clear dig at you and your stupid yellow license plate. And if the rotary has multiple lanes, like that one where we exchanged fingers, then “for a quarter-turn, or to continue straight ahead, enter the rotary from the right lane.”

Boom. Roasted. I need to bang a U-ey and go find that clown. Tell me how to drive on a rotary? Listen pal, lemme explain how it works, cause it’s so simple even someone from a place where you can’t make a right on red will follow it.

If you’re gonna be blocking anyone in the inside lane from getting off, you can’t be in the outside lane. You still with me? So if you’re getting off the first exit, no problem. Ain’t blocking no one, and youse can both exit together.

‘Simple manners’

Same if you’re going straight and hopping off the second exit, like you seen me doing. Not sure if your little brain can follow along here, but same logic applies. I’m gettin’ off, so anyone in the inside lane is either exiting with me, or continuing around to I-don’t-care-because-I-ain’t-in-their-way. It’s simple manners.

“For a three-quarter-turn, or a U-turn, enter the rotary from the left lane. Travel through the middle or inner lane.” So you ain’t blocking anyone from getting off!

It’s a perfect system, pal. So where was you coming from that you dare honk at me like I was blocking you? I’m not a blocker, buddy. That’s you clowns. You and Connecticut. Gotta be on your toes around them blue plates.

I seen you coming around the rotary on the inside, but the right lane was open so I hopped in. Pretty sure that’s the definition of “yield.” There’s no way I could be blocking you from getting off, because if there’s one thing we know in this state, it’s how to drive.

Since I know you’re too dumb to follow this, I’ll draw you a picture.

Now that I look at it, I suppose that if you was getting off the third or fourth exit, and if that happened to be my first exit but I was going to the second, there might be a moment where those rules don’t make sense. Am I a blocker? That can’t be right. My mother didn’t raise no blockers.

‘Wicked confusing’

Hold up, is that why the state is doing that thing where they paint a million lines all over rotaries when no one’s looking? Don’t know if you’ve seen these, but they’re wicked confusing unless you’re in the right lane, cause then they just make you get off the first exit.

Wait a sec. Is that why they done that? Are we trying to paint our way out of a corner? Just sneak in with a Statie detail and a paint roller and quietly pretend like they didn’t raise an entire state of blockers?

Did I just lose an argument to a New Yorker? This ain’t right; I never lose arguments in my head.

But hey, maybe next time use your blinker, huh? I’m not a mind-reader, guy.

Rollins is trying to make a political comeback after resigning in disgrace three years ago as the top federal prosecutor in Massachusetts, and she seems to be betting that there’s enough dissatisfaction with Wu that yoking the current Suffolk DA, Kevin Hayden, to the mayor might be enough for Rollins to win her old office back.

In Rollins’s telling, the problem isn’t Wu’s policies — it’s just that she has too much power.

“I support Mayor Wu. I think she can be a great mayor,” Rollins said. “I just don’t want her to be in charge of my Boston City Council, or my DA. She controls everything right now. So, for me, I just feel like we need an autonomous DA.”

If the Trump administration decides to launch an immigration enforcement operation in Boston, she wondered, “Who do you want at a podium? Do you want Kevin Hayden, who can’t make a decision without speaking to Mayor Wu, who, by the way, is now about to control all three branches of municipal government?” (Rollins argues that because DAs are the gateway to the judiciary, controlling the DA amounts to controlling the judicial branch.)

Rollins’s loaded, hyperbolic attack seems, on its surface, like a cheap political calculation. But the attack has an identifiable audience.

A vocal network of Black neighborhood and civic leaders have clashed with Wu over the redevelopment of White Stadium in Franklin Park and Parcel P3, and the redesign of Blue Hill Avenue, as well as other projects, often accusing her administration of asking for communities’ feedback only after decisions have effectively been made. Rollins appears to be betting that frustration with Wu can be converted into votes against Hayden.

Boston political strategist Jacquetta Van Zandt told me there’s “something distinctly Trumpian” about Wu’s tactical approach to opposition, though not about her ideology. Van Zandt served as a senior communications advisor to Josh Kraft, whose 2025 bid for mayor collapsed after Wu trounced him by a stunning margin in the preliminary election — 72 percent to his 23 percent.

“I think Rachael is making a legitimate political argument when she is asking people to examine Kevin Hayden’s relationship with Mayor Wu,” Van Zandt told me. But “having the mayor’s support and being controlled by the mayor are two different things,” she said. If Rollins can show that Hayden made prosecutorial decisions at Wu’s request, Van Zandt noted, “that’s serious.” But if the two elected officials merely agree and partner on public-safety policy and work together, “that’s not being a puppet, that’s government.”

Reggie Stewart, a director of the Roxbury Neighborhood Council, called Black civic opposition to Wu “a coherent, real thing,” animated by multiple projects and a shared belief that the mayor simply does not listen to critics.

And yet, Rollins’s Black political base exists independently of that opposition, according to Stewart, who is not supporting any of the Suffolk DA’s candidates publicly as of now. “Maybe the anti-Wu sentiment is the icing on the cake, but I don’t believe that’s what makes Rachael popular,” Stewart said. “Her Black supporters support her because they support her, not because they oppose Wu. Those two things just happen to intersect.”

To be sure, Rollins has offered no evidence that Hayden is controlled by Wu, and none emerged in my reporting. In an interview, Wu didn’t directly respond to Rollins’s accusation but she defended her partnership with Hayden by citing the city’s falling crime and violence.

“I’m proud to support District Attorney Hayden because he has been steady, thoughtful, and innovative in his work,” Wu said. “He’s built relationships, is competent, drama-free, and has been leading that office in a way that has helped achieve the results that we’ve seen.”

As for an anti-Wu constituency in Black Boston, the mayor’s defenders point to her decisive victory over Kraft in last fall’s preliminary to rebut those claims: The mayor won three out of four votes in Wards 12 and 14, which are regarded as the heart of the city’s Black community.

True, but that is not necessarily proof that the underlying frustration is imaginary. Elections measure choices and voters were choosing between Wu and Kraft, a challenger whose campaign never really gave dissatisfied Black voters a compelling reason to defect.

“It was like, ‘anti-Wu, okay, great. We agree. What will you do differently?’ And the [Kraft] campaign just couldn’t answer that question,” Stewart said.

There’s actually a lesson for Rollins in Kraft’s failure. Anti-Wu sentiment may give her an audience but it can’t substitute for evidence that Hayden has surrendered his office’s autonomy. Rollins has found a provocative way to frame the race: If Wu is Boston’s Trump, then she is running as the resistance. But calling Hayden a puppet is not the same thing as proving that he is one. And running against Wu is not the same as making a strong case for Rachael Rollins.

It all adds up to a big win for Wu, who has faced more than a year of allegations that she was stuffing an unpopular and possibly illegitimate idea down the throat of a community that didn’t want it. The prospect of losing must have been nightmarish for her.

It’s fair to say that White Stadium was an unlikely choice for a crusade. The stadium has been a mess for years, but somehow it became a mess everyone had learned to live with. Plans to improve it had been floated and discarded without fanfare or outrage. It was as though everyone had decided it wasn’t great, but it was good enough.

Politically, it didn’t help Wu that the catalyst for this project was bringing a women’s professional soccer team to Franklin Park. Though Boston Legacy FC has committed to paying $190 million of the cost of the $325 million project, the claim the city was somehow selling out the community around Franklin Park resonated in some quarters. Many would argue that Wu could have chosen a more worthy cause for a 2 ½ year dogfight.

For my part, I became an advocate for restoring White Stadium years ago. Unlike some so-called advocates, I’ve toured White Stadium multiple times and was shocked by its decrepitude. I supported construction magnate John Fish’s idea of renovating it in 2013 - which died a quiet death after Mayor Thomas M. Menino left office before it could be realized. And I’ve never changed my mind that a new White Stadium would be a great benefit for the young people of Boston.

I give Wu’s courtroom adversaries, the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, great credit for its deep concern about Franklin Park. It fought this battle for principled reasons, and the finished product will be better for its advocacy.

Of course, no ruling will change the fact that a large and vocal contingent of neighboring residents are uneasy with the White Stadium renovation.

It’s up to the city to prove the many remaining issues of access can be resolved without placing an undue burden on residents. Wu should expect to be held to her promises this will be an economic engine for Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, beginning with the awarding of contracts to renovate and operate it. And that this will be a facility for Boston Public School students first, and for a soccer team second.

Those are the reasons this project is worth it.

As for Wu, it’s fair to say the start of her second term has been a slog. After her resounding victory in the mayor’s race last year, Wu immediately became the target of criticism. Black activists have argued that she is both too inaccessible and too inflexible. Progressives say she isn’t going far enough in pushing their issues. Even cyclists are bitterly critical, even though Wu is literally the first champion of their causes to occupy the mayor’s office.

But wins like Tuesday’s offer an opportunity to reset. Instead of debating what happens if Wu loses the White Stadium case, the conversation can now move to what the renovation can bring to Boston. It can dampen the talk that she’s damaged politically, or headed to some other work opportunity.

The truth is that Wu, for better or worse, is the same person who destroyed Josh Kraft a year ago, the same person who has never, in fact, had a single close race in her political career.

We might not know for years whether White Stadium was a visionary idea or a lousy idea. But what we know today is that Wu took a considerable political risk, stuck to her guns, and won.

The SJC’s decision eliminated the final legal hurdle for the controversial project, effectively clearing the path forward for construction to continue. The redeveloped stadium, which the city is partnering with the professional women’s soccer team Boston Legacy FC to deliver, will be the new hub for Boston Public Schools athletics and the home stadium for the women’s soccer team.

The city committed to covering $135 million of the project’s estimated price tag. Boston Legacy FC is expected to pay about $190 million.

Officials from Boston Legacy FC, top City Hall staff, and local and state leaders joined Wu on Thursday to celebrate the SJC’s decision.

“We are charting a course that teams and cities around the country are already looking to,” Wu said at a news conference behind the William J. Devine Golf Course clubhouse, situated on the other end of Franklin Park from the stadium.

The project has generated substantial scrutiny and opposition over the past three years, as critics raised concerns about the project’s rising price tag, the city’s partnership with a private entity, and the decision to locate a professional sports complex in Franklin Park.

Wu has framed the project as an extraordinary opportunity to overhaul the more than 75-year-old dilapidated stadium and give Boston Public Schools students and city residents access to a professional-grade sports facility, without taxpayers having to shoulder the full cost.

She said “generations” of Boston Public Schools families have been asking the city to renovate the aging stadium. “Our Boston kids deserve the very best, and as a city, we can never apologize for fighting to give it to them,” she said.

But the project’s opponents, who filed the initial lawsuit to stop the project in February of 2024, argued it violates constitutional parkland protections, and that the neighborhoods around Franklin Park are not an appropriate place for a professional sports stadium.

The Supreme Judicial Court ruled Wednesday that the stadium site is a school facility, not parkland, and therefore not subject to those protections.

Still, even with that legal victory in hand, it remains unclear when the stadium will be finished and ready to host games and practices, either for students or professionals.

Wu did not directly answer questions Thursday about the project’s timeline and target completion date, but said construction work is happening on the site six days a week and meeting planned milestones.

She indicated that the lawsuit over the project had caused some delays.

“It’s undeniable that the litigation process has been a distraction and took significant resources and time and energy,” Wu said. “So we are evaluating closely, and we’ll be working to really fully assess what that means for the remainder of the schedule.”

Wu and Boston Legacy FC owner Jennifer Epstein on Thursday also did not answer questions about whether the professional women’s team plans to host any home games at White Stadium during the 2027 National Women’s Soccer League season, which begins in February.

The team is currently playing all of its home games this season at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

Work on the stadium began in early 2025 with the demolition of the old facility, and on Thursday, construction appeared to be back in full swing.

The sound of clangs, beeps, and crashes filled the air as excavators rumbled across the site. Two red cranes towered over dozens of laborers in hard hats and fluorescent T-shirts and vests, helping lift long metal rods.

As construction continues, a group of elected and community leaders that make up the White Stadium Neighborhood Advisory Council will finalize transportation plans for the 20 Boston Legacy FC game days, Wu said.

Residents can share their input on traffic management plans, including game-day parking restrictions, at four community meetings the city is planning to host in Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, and Dorchester this fall.

A Roslindale woman was charged with felony home invasion after allegedly breaking into the home of a former boyfriend wielding a baseball bat and assaulting his parents, authorities said Wednesday.

Alyssah G. Harrison, 19, pleaded not guilty in West Roxbury Municipal Court on Wednesday to single counts of home invasion, assault with a dangerous weapon, assault and battery, and malicious destruction of property, court records show.

She was released on personal recognizance by Judge Maureen Flaherty, ordered to comply with a restraining order, and stay away from the home, the alleged victims, and witnesses, records show. A pretrial hearing is scheduled for Oct. 2.

Harrison’s lawyer, Patrick Kelly, declined to comment on Thursday.

Prosecutors allege that Harrison used a baseball bat to smash through the door of her former boyfriend’s house before trying to steal money from a safe on the second floor, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said.

“It’s not hard to imagine the fear these homeowners must have experienced when their peaceful day at home was suddenly turned chaotic and violent by an armed intruder,” Hayden said in a statement.

Around 1 p.m. on July 22, police responded to a call from a security office for a property near Highcrest Road and Highcrest Terrace stating that a distressed resident had reported a woman was inside his home vandalizing the property, prosecutors said.

The resident said that he was home with his wife when the woman whom they recognized as their son’s former girlfriend, came to the front door and swung an aluminum baseball bat, shattering a glass screen and entering the home.

When the man and his wife tried to approach Harrison, she allegedly pushed the woman and punched her in the face. Harrison then threatened the couple, holding the bat in “a cocked position,” and proceeded upstairs to a second-floor bedroom where the couple said they heard her rummaging through drawers.

At that point, the husband left the home to contact security, while the wife tried to remove Harrison from the bedroom.

According to a police report, the husband appeared at the security desk holding a baseball bat, though it is unclear whether it was the same bat Harrison allegedly used or when he may have gained possession of it.

Upstairs in the house, the wife told police she got into a fight with Harrison, causing her to flee, prosecutors said. The couple declined medical attention, police said.

The wife told police she didn’t know if Harrison had stolen anything, but didn’t see anything in her hands as she ran off. Harrison’s former boyfriend told police he believed she had targeted the upstairs safe, prosecutors said.

When speaking to police, the wife said Harrison only entered one of two upstairs bedrooms, although her husband later told officers that she had told him she’d seen Harrison enter both bedrooms.

When police told the husband that his wife only reported seeing Harrison entering one room, he became “visibly upset” and walked away.

When the Supreme Judicial Court heard oral arguments in the White Stadium fight in April, it looked like opponents might have a shot.

The questioning at times seemed more antagonistic to the Wu administration and Boston Legacy FC than to the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, the plaintiff aiming to stop their stadium project.

However, the justices ended up siding with Mayor Michelle Wu this week. They decided rebuilding White Stadium to share with a pro sports team — as well as related work nearby in Franklin Park — won’t violate the state constitution’s parkland protections.

Their ruling will affect many constituencies, in and outside of the city. Here’s a rundown of where they stand.

The mayor: It’s a big vindication for Wu — who staked considerable political capital on this — and her advisers from the Rose, Goulston & Storrs, and WilmerHale law firms. Wu plowed ahead with the controversial $325 million project despite the litigation. (The price has gone up a bit in two years.) The city committed to an eye-popping $135 million, to rebuild one grandstand area. Boston Legacy is covering the rest.

The Kraft Group: Boston Legacy has played at Gillette Stadium in the team’s first year, and theoretically could use the Everett stadium that Robert Kraft and Jonathan Kraft are pursuing for the Revs once that’s done. But the Kraft Group actually rooted for Wu’s project by filing a surprising legal brief in support in March. A stated reason: generating more interest in soccer. The Krafts need Wu on their side, as they build their own stadium on Boston’s doorstep.

Emerald Necklace Conservancy: Guess who is not on Wu’s good side? The conservancy, led by Karen Mauney-Brodek. The nonprofit sees itself as a city partner in supporting Emerald Necklace parks. But the city recently denied a permit for its spring fundraiser. Could its home at the Curley House (another George White legacy building) be next?

Boston Legacy/Able Co.: Team lead owner Jennifer Epstein calls the ruling a “tremendous victory” for the city’s schools, “the Franklin Park community,” and pro women’s soccer in Boston. Left unsaid: It’s also a win for Able Co., the firm led by Bill Keravuori, Epstein’s husband. Able is developing the team’s portion of the stadium, and is involved with another city project in Nubian Square.

Bank of America: Miceal Chamberlain and other local BofA execs can breathe easy. They agreed to a $100 million-plus financing deal for Boston Legacy’s portion a year ago. (The team has not said whether the bank will chip in more after the costs shot up.)

The governor: Maura Healey steered clear of this imbroglio — until this summer. Several of her top aides, such as Rebecca Tepper and Phil Eng, recently met with a group of stadium opponents. Among them: former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, who took to social media on Wednesday saying: “This doesn’t mean the City can do anything they want. Much more to say later. For now, just know we’re not done!”

Environmental groups: Several expressed concern the project could weaken the constitution’s Article 97, which requires state legislative approval for changing the use of parkland. (The SJC ruled this was fulfilled with votes in 1947 and 1950.) However, many prominent environmental organizations — including Mass Audubon and the Conservation Law Foundation — sat this one out.

Mass. Municipal Association: The group representing cities and towns essentially had an opposite fear, that a ruling against Wu could make it harder for municipalities to convert their own land for different uses. “We feel strongly it protects all cities and towns,” executive director Adam Chapdelaine said of the ruling.

Local businesses: How much of the stadium business will trickle down to the neighborhoods abutting the park? Ed Gaskin, executive director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets, says now is the time for a plan ensuring an economic benefit comes to his area, and not just congestion from soccer fans passing through.

Olmsted Network: The national coalition that supports the work of famed landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted lodged an amicus brief supporting the conservancy, an ally. “Disappointing is not a strong enough word,” said president Sue Breitkopf, adding that the real losers are neighbors whose use of Franklin Park will be interrupted, particularly on game days.

George White: Speaking of historical figures, it’s hard not to wonder what White — a philanthropist and “antibacterial soap magnate,” to quote the SJC — would think of all this fighting over the stadium that bears his name. Maybe it’s time for the “Angel of Peace,” as the memorial to White in Forest Hills is known, to get to work.

The Poor Clare Nuns aren’t the only ones anxiously waiting for the city of Boston to approve the long-stalled redevelopment of their Jamaica Plain monastery – so are the sisters of the Monastery of Christ the King. The order, located in Florida, merged last month with the Boston nuns so they can retire together in Westwood, where the Poor Clares have relocated. But there’s no room at the inn. As our colleague Catherine Carlock wrote earlier this year, the nuns can’t expand their Westwood home until they finalize the sale of the old monastery on Centre Street, which is contingent on the Boston Planning Department approving developer John Holland’s plan to build 158 apartments and condos. The big hang-up: Concerns over how new housing would impact the Arnold Arboretum next door. But after three years, patience is wearing thin. Michael Perry, Minister Provincial of the Franciscan Friars — a bishop-like figure for the sister orders – asked for the project to move “as expeditiously as possible” in an Aug. 11 letter addressed to sister leaders Mary Veronica McGuff and Leanna Chrostowski, with Boston Archbishop Richard Henning copied in.

In the 2010s, CSR adopted a program called Beats Rhymes and Life (BRL), an initiative that uses hip-hop clinics to address mental health and community wellness for children and young adults. These clinics, which last about 10 weeks each semester, involve writing workshops, hip-hop education, and other exercises that build communication skills.

CSR currently uses the program to work with clients between the ages of 14 and 24 who may not want to receive treatment through traditional therapeutic services.

Artist coordinators and registered local clinicians create programming that is hip-hop inspired and addresses issues students might be experiencing at home, such as substance abuse and depression. Staff use tools like a visual “hip-hop timeline” and songwriting exercises to teach students how the genre has been used to address oppression in Black and brown communities for decades.

The program is the first of its kind in Massachusetts, and similar programs are extremely uncommon in other parts of the country. Representatives from CSR say that shouldn’t be the case.

According to Stephanie Sabins, the lead clinician for BRL, the creative process in therapy creates opportunities for “healthy risks” and helps people understand themselves.

“Some of the best conversations I’ve ever had with youth are in these groups,” she added.

Sabins, who has worked in the program for five years, thinks hip-hop therapy is still making its case as a respected approach to improving mental health.

“We are actively decolonizing therapy,” said Candice Watch, BRL’s director. “Storytelling is actually what hip-hop has always been, and that is an actual form of therapy.”

Therapy doesn’t have to look like the traditional medical model, Watch explained. She said using an already known form of cultural expression — such as hip-hop — is sometimes more effective than talk therapy or other clinical treatments.

Each cohort is encouraged to write about whatever they want in their songs. Heartbreak, stress, and grief are among the many topics. That creative autonomy helps participants develop social skills, creativity, and self-assurance.

Students like Luis “Louie” Colon are reaping the benefits.

Colon, a 22-year-old Roxbury native, started the program in the spring. He struggled with public speaking and, at times, connecting with and relating to his peers. BRL changed that.

He said BRL is one of “the only things I really had where I can be with my peers, laugh, joke, and have fun.”

When Colon’s not in BRL sessions, he’s pursuing a career in photography and visual art. Making time for his personal life is difficult. Dwindling support for artistry leaves Colon feeling like he’s fighting an uphill battle and often alone.

“We all go through the same stuff, but being here, I was happy,” he said.

Clinicians say that relatability is crucial in participants’ mental health.

Alan-Michael Chest is a Massachusetts-licensed mental health counselor and musician. He incorporates music and culture into his practice.

“Music offers vulnerability without judgment,” Chest said.

At age 7, Chest wrote his first rap: a song about struggling to understand crime in America. He said the creative process must be a part of therapy: “It’s really meeting a client where they’re at, and it’s really changing the framework for therapy altogether.”

BRL reaches participants through local grassroots organizations and city programs that work with youth at risk, such as Spoke Art and You Got This Center. Several programs can’t pay for partnerships with CSR, or can’t give kids stipends to participate, which makes getting people to participate in the clinics more challenging. When BRL loses participation numbers, the program itself is at risk; a portion of BRL’s grant funding is based on the number of young people it serves.

In 2021, BRL built a studio in a van to bring the program to prospective artists’ backyard. Budget cuts have kept the van off the streets because it needs repairs.

For staff, demonstrating to the public that BRL offers an important model for therapy is a challenge, but one that keeps them inspired.

Michael “Big Mike” Mendes, BRL’s main teacher-artist, has been making music and drawing since he was a kid. Growing up in Dorchester and coming from a Cape Verdean family, art has always been how he communicated best.

Mendes said BRL’s mission isn’t making artists, but introducing a new channel of healthy expression. He believes hip-hop is a key path to inspire new leaders.

“Through rapping and teaching people how to rap, we’re getting them to find their confidence, have conversations that they’re not having, and develop healthy relationships with adults,” he concluded.

In America, by law, everyone has a mall. That accident of proximity you are referring to when you utter the phrase: “My mall.”

Mine is the Liberty Tree Mall in Danvers, and I feel some duty to defend its weirdness as it has become much-maligned in recent days, thanks to a new song about it by Phoebe Bridgers that is called, simply, “Liberty Tree.”

Bridgers is from California, though it is no great mystery how she was introduced to my mall, for she is in a relationship with the comedian and filmmaker Bo Burnham. And the Liberty Tree is also his mall, which I know because back in 2009, when Burnham was an 18-year-old who’d become a YouTube sensation singing funny songs in his childhood bedroom in Hamilton, I spent quite a bit of time with him for a Globe Magazine profile.

When I asked him to show me around his life, he took me to the Liberty Tree Mall. “This is where I was conceived,” he told me in the parking lot.

So what on earth is this song about? To understand, I did the unthinkable. I went inside the Liberty Tree Mall, which most people avoid unless they are going to the movie theater or going to church. (See: my story from last year about Netcast, the mini-megachurch that is slowly taking over the mall.)

Clue No. 1: Beyond Dippin’ Dots

Long ago, the mall transitioned to big-box retailers positioned along its periphery, leaving the inside as some sort of strange ghost town with a Marshalls. I don’t like the way it feels. No, I love it.

Liberty Tree Mall… Bridgers sang as I inserted my earbuds just inside the main entrance.

In the photo booth… Ok, I see it right in front of me.

This place is dying…

Wrong! I pause the song and approach a man fixing an iPhone at a workbench overlooking the photo booth.

Who you calling ‘dying’?

“I’ve been here 15 years now, and I wouldn’t say it’s dying,” Kyle Barvaro, the owner of Tech Center, tells me. “It’s been dead the whole time.”

Correct. And that’s the eerie magic of this place, I tell myself as I take a deep breath and walk to the start of the dystopian Kohl’s corridor. What is the opposite of claustrophobia? That’s what I feel as I look at the hangar-sized hallway, with exactly zero storefronts, that leads to a Kohl’s you need binoculars to see.

You know what, I’m not going down there. I’ll just stop and take a photo.

This place is dying… We don’t care if we’re living proof...

Wait, am I dead? I think I’m already dead. When I stopped to take that photo, I swear there was no one in the corridor. But is that a figure in the distance? I’m definitely dead. This is awesome, but I’m going back to the photo booth.

I’m sticking out my tongue/And liftin’ up my shirt

Not gettin’ any younger, honey/But if we don’t try, how can we be sure?

Wait, is this a love song? What happened in that photo booth? Is this really where Burnhams are made?

You were made in the image of God

But you look like your mom in this picture of us

Fallin’ in love that night after our fight

This is a song about falling in love at the Liberty Tree Mall? Then why has the Internet been using it as an excuse to pile on my mall, making all these easy jokes about how creepy it is. Bridgers has it right; this is a love mall. There are deep emotions in this place, a palpable feeling of yesterday, of the time before malls were turned into these Disney-fied small towns.

And the past is lookin’ brighter all the time

See! She gets it. And while one should never read song lyrics literally, this California girl wrote the perfect song about my mall. Or at least the first half of the song is. I didn’t quite follow the second half about running through an airport.

Is that the Kohl’s corridor? I could see how it feels like an airport, but I’m not going down there.

Báez started his high school career at Cristo Rey High in Dorchester, then transferred to Snowden International School in the Back Bay.

His emerging baseball talent led Báez to Dexter Southfield in Brookline for the 2020 season. That season was canceled by the pandemic, but Báez continued to improve.

Báez played summer ball for The BASE in Roxbury and embraced their commitment to academics, ultimately committing to play for Vanderbilt.

There weren’t many ballfields in the greater Boston area that Báez didn’t play on at some point.

“The first time I saw him take batting practice, my jaw dropped,” said Dan Donato, who coaches baseball and hockey at Dexter Southfield and is the brother of former Bruins winger and Harvard coach, Ted Donato. “He had massive power. He was somebody who could hit 20 home runs in his sleep.”

And a powerful right arm, too. Major League teams saw Báez as almost a perfect draft pick because if he didn’t hit, he could move to the mound and take advantage of his 98 mile-per-hour fastball.

Craig Breslow, then working for the Cubs, was among the scouts and team officials who came to watch Báez play in 2021. But he fell into the second round after an inconsistent senior season.

The Red Sox were interested, but had the fourth pick that season and used it on Marcelo Mayer. Their mistake was taking University of Florida outfielder Jud Fabian early in the second round. He didn’t sign.

The Cardinals took Báez with the 54th pick. His apprenticeship in the minors was longer than expected — 452 games over parts of six seasons — because of injuries and a high strikeout rate. But Báez had a strong 2025, and it continued with Triple-A Memphis this season.

“[The Cardinals] told him a few weeks ago that he was a big part of their future. And once he was called up, they wanted him there for good,” Donato said.

Donato played in the minors for the Yankees, Mariners, and Rays from 1995-98, reaching Triple-A. He knew a five-tool player when he saw one, having shared the field with Derek Jeter and Bernie Williams, among others, during spring training.

“Josh ran a 6.31 60 [yard dash], and Bernie Williams was 6.7. In the outfield he’d go the gap as smooth as Ceddanne Rafaela and make a throw right to the bag,” Donato said. “He had all the skill, and he worked harder than anybody I had ever watched.”

Báez came of age at a time when baseball talent in the Boston area was at a high level. Boston College outfielder Sal Frelick was a first-round pick in 2021. Maryland’s Sean Burke, who played at St. John’s (Shrewsbury), was a third-round pick that year.

Future All-Stars Ben Rice, Cam Schlittler, and Shane Smith also emerged during that period.

“There were always pitchers from the Northeast, but there are more indoor facilities now, and players can work on baseball all year. For somebody like Josh, that was huge,” Donato said. “It’s different now than when I was coming up. It’s super competitive now. In our league, we have pitchers throwing 88-93.”

Landmark days are nothing new for Báez. He hit four home runs for Memphis on June 16, the third anniversary of his father’s passing. His mother, Yris, was at the game.

José Manuel Báez, known as “El Bronco” in the Dominican Republic, was an accomplished semi-pro baseball and softball player known for his power. His son promised him he would make it to the majors, and he did.

Without fail, new Red Sox catcher Adley Rutschman makes it a habit to meet the pitcher as he’s coming off the mound at the end of an inning to offer a few words of encouragement.

The exchange usually comes along the baseline and lasts only a few seconds.

“I really don’t know when it started, but I’ve always done it,” Rutschman said.

It’s a habit he picked up from his father. Randy Rutschman was a catcher at Linfield University in Oregon who later coached and played semi-pro ball in the West Coast League.

“He kept playing after college just because he liked baseball so much,” Rutschman said. “I think I was 6 when he stopped playing, but I remember him doing that with the pitchers.”

Rutschman said his message is usually something along the lines of, “Great job, let’s keep it going,” or “We’re going to get through this,” if it’s a rough inning.

Rather than wait until they get to the dugout, Rutschman says what’s on his mind right away.

The passing of Tommy John earlier this month sparked a discussion about if he should be in the Hall of Fame, given the combination of a successful career and having ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction surgery named after him.

Everybody in baseball, from the amateur ranks on up, knows about Tommy John even if they aren’t familiar with all the details of this career.

But when it comes to the Hall of Fame, less is more.

Only players, managers, team or league executives, and umpires can be Hall of Famers. Broadcasters and writers are honored by the Hall every year with awards voted on by their peers but aren’t inducted.

Still, they are recognized on the stage and have their moment in the spotlight. It’s special.

The late Dr. Frank Jobe changed the course of the game in 1974 when he performed what was revolutionary surgery on John by replacing his elbow ligament with a tendon from his left wrist.

Jobe was recognized by the Hall during the 2013 induction ceremony with John in attendance. One of Jobe’s proteges, Dr. Neal ElAttrache, spoke. Jobe passed away less than a year later. They had their moment.

The Hall has also given out the Buck O’Neil Lifetime Achievement Award since 2008, “to honor an individual whose extraordinary efforts enhanced baseball’s positive impact on society, broadened the game’s appeal, and whose character, integrity and dignity are comparable to the qualities exhibited by O’Neil.”

O’Neil was a player and manager in the Negro American League, and later a revered scout and coach. He was the first recipient of the award, which is given every three years.

Roland Hemond (2011), Joe Garagiola (2014), Rachel Robinson (2017), David Montgomery (2020), Carl Erskine (2023), and Bill White (2026) have been honored in the years since.

Ballpark architect Janet Marie Smith should also be on that list, along with notable coaches — Dave Duncan, Leo Mazzone, and Ron Washington come to mind — scouts, and others in the game who don’t fit neatly into a particular category.

It’s been almost a week since Karen Solomon, last pictured in grainy surveillance video shared by police, walked around the corner of an animal clinic in Worcester’s Columbus Park neighborhood and disappeared into thin air.

The 58-year-old mother of two is wanted by police for the slaying of her husband, 57-year-old Kurt Solomon. The veteran Worcester police officer was found dead at the couple’s Wildwood Avenue home early last Tuesday.

Solomon, police said, is armed, dangerous, and still at large.

Her mysteries also run deeper than her disappearance.

From founder to fugitive

Before she wound up the target of a massive police manhunt, Solomon spent decades as a highly respected law enforcement advocate.

She’s the founder of a nonprofit advancing police and first responder mental health awareness and suicide prevention, and wrote two books detailing the personal struggles officers face on the job.

For former colleagues, friends, and neighbors, the turn of events has been hard to reconcile with the woman they said they knew.

Yet Solomon’s work leaves a trail of interviews and collected writings offering clues.

In a 2023 interview with The Guns & Yoga podcast, she described her husband as being initially hesitant about her advocacy work, describing him as reserved and not wanting the spotlight.

Describing her work, she implored anyone feeling lost to seek help.

“You can fix anything … please don’t think suicide is your only option,” Solomon said on the podcast. “I know it’s incredibly difficult to ask for help ... but it’s going to make everything easier after that.”

In an interview last year commemorating a new memorial for first responders and military veterans who died by suicide, Solomon described her own mental health struggles, saying she sought counseling for “compassion fatigue,” brought on by her advocacy work.

She said she had previously attempted suicide three times.

“Every time I’ve said, ‘No, no, I’m not going to hurt myself,’ and I did,” Solomon said.

The morning of

Investigators have declined to comment on whether Solomon is believed to be alive or when she was last seen.

Kurt Solomon died from injuries inflicted by a “sharp object,” police said, but officials have not shared more details. Karen Solomon is wanted on charges of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, police said.

Dispatch recordings show that Karen Solomon made the 911 call to police, reporting a “male laid out in her backyard, unknown breathing,” around 5:30 a.m. When officers arrived, she was not there.

Worcester District Attorney Joseph Early has said other people were “involved at the house” during the incident, but he hasn’t elaborated.

Combing the pond

The manhunt so far has brought battalions of law enforcement down on a residential Worcester neighborhood where neighbors said tight community bonds are common and violence is rare.

Officials spent days canvassing the animal clinic and local woods and combing the waters of Coes Pond, a reservoir near where security video spotted Solomon on Tuesday morning.

For the community, the investigation has turned life upside down, particularly in the secluded neighborhood where Kurt Solomon grew up and lived his life, according to a family obituary.

“I just want it to end,” neighbor Karen Avedian said.

So there I was, with neither a boatload of money nor sufficient sleep, weaving between pedestrians on Bennington Street, desperate to fill out an application before someone else did.

This is what it takes to find an apartment around here.

As The Boston Globe’s housing reporter, I spend my professional life writing about Massachusetts’ intractable housing problem, and how it warps the lives of so many people in this state — especially renters.

But the ever-rising cost of housing is big in my personal life, too. Countless friends have moved away because rents are too high; others complain about the city’s notorious Sept. 1 shuffle — when about two-thirds of all the leases in Boston turn over.

Finding a new apartment is, in a word, a nightmare. Every decent listing seemingly has 50 interested applicants. Some brokers still try to charge steep (and mostly now-illegal) fees. And the rent itself soars higher every year.

For years, I have managed to avoid the anguish of a housing search here by staying put in my charming-if-slightly-tattered apartment in an East Boston three-decker. But I have finally outgrown that place, and my partner — Globe transportation reporter Diti Kohli — and I decided in March that it was time to look for somewhere new.

I initially dismissed the seriousness of this endeavor, and volunteered to head our search. As someone who writes about housing for a living, I figured I would be uniquely equipped to navigate Boston’s frenetic rental market.

I had no idea what lay in store.

The apartment in Magoun Square was a great find — a first-floor unit in a little multifamily building steps from the Green Line extension.

It met much of what we were looking for: Outdoor space, a good kitchen, plenty of windows for our cat, Mittens. With friends nearby, Somerville was our preferred neighborhood. And at $2,700 a month, it was in our price range.

The challenge, of course, would be beating out dozens of other applicants.

Half the trouble of apartment hunting here — if you want to avoid a several-thousand-dollar broker fee, that is — is poring through the sheer volume of listings online. There are dozens of websites, from local brokerages to national sites like Apartments.com, with thousands of apartments to choose from.

It’s no simple feat to figure out what is a real, available apartment, and what isn’t. It requires backgrounding landlords and brokers, finding an actual person to set up a tour, ensuring move-in timing works — all while hoping that some better-financed renter doesn’t beat you to the punch.

As it turned out, shockingly few of the thousands of apartments listed online were available on our timeline, or fit even a few of our criteria we had established. For those, competition was fierce. And many landlords and brokers didn’t return messages.

When they did, there were often issues, like that some were charging broker fees, which was a nonstarter. (Massachusetts mostly outlawed tenant-paid broker fees last year, but some brokers still charge them, sometimes through a loophole with so-called “open listings” that are shared by multiple brokers, or in apparent violation of the law in other instances.)

“Does the landlord have any flexibility on the broker fee?” I had asked the broker of one Somerville apartment.

This broker actually wrote me back.

“No.”

Before long, apartment-hunting became something of a full-time job. I turned on Zillow notifications for new listings in our preferred neighborhoods — Somerville, Jamaica Plain, perhaps Dorchester.

Each buzz of my phone sent my heart rate soaring. Maybe this was the place? But our search quickly fell into a tiresome pattern: Either a listing would be for a place that wouldn’t work for us, or it would be somewhere that looked right, but the landlord would already be swamped with applications. March drifted into April, and apartments available for Sept. 1 move-ins were quickly getting scooped up.

So when Bethany, the owner of that apartment in Magoun Square, messaged me back to set up a tour, the stakes suddenly felt very high.

It may sound ridiculous, but I spent two days rehearsing what I would say to her.

The night before the tour, I could barely sleep.

When we arrived at the apartment, a woman who looked to be around 30 and had clearly just finished her own tour was outside chatting with Bethany, laughing and looking very personable. I muttered something to Diti about her apparent charm offensive, and offered the woman a smile as we walked in. She did not smile back.

Without a word, it felt like she was telling us: “This place is mine.”

Bethany, a kind woman whose arms were full of tattoos and appeared very much like the sort of person who would own a building in Somerville, explained that she already had more than a dozen tours lined up, with more to come.

We tried our best to be charming. We asked questions and chatted about Bethany’s impending move to Portugal. I sprinted home from the Blue Line and returned our application as soon as it landed in our inbox.

But I just had a feeling that we weren’t getting this place. And sure enough, three days later, Bethany wrote back.

Good afternoon,

Thank you for the application. We just signed a lease.

Good luck in your search!

Ouch.

I realized at that point that I had probably let the search process get to me more than was reasonable. But this is an experience shared by many Boston 20-somethings, including those who make significantly more money than Diti and me.

There is an argument to be made that a tight housing market is a good thing — a sign that, despite the region’s recent struggles, demand to live here remains high. Indeed while rents have been dropping in some other high-cost rental markets lately, they’re still rising in Greater Boston.

At the same time, when 20- and 30-somethings with professional jobs can’t find an apartment, it’s a clear sign the region simply doesn’t have enough homes for the people who want to live here. When young professionals struggle to find housing at their tier of the housing market, it puts even more pressure on working-class families, who are leaving the region due to cost pressures in increasing numbers.

I decided after the Magoun Square debacle that I needed to shift my strategy away from Zillow searches, and perhaps focus on Jamaica Plain, where I hoped competition might be less intense. I started wandering neighborhoods hunting for “for rent” signs, and even turned to a platform I had previously shunned: Craigslist.

There, small landlords were advertising units in old multifamily buildings — the sort of buildings that Diti and I love.

After a few failed attempts, I stumbled upon a broker who seemed to exclusively work with small landlords. I perused her portfolio and found a unit that almost seemed too good to be true: A 1,000 square-foot two-bedroom in an old triple-decker near an Orange Line station. It had a front porch, a walk-in pantry, and some interesting built-in quirks like a stained-glass window.

The broker answered her phone after one ring, and offered to show us the place the following day. On the tour, she said the apartment had been on the market for a few weeks, and while a couple of people had liked it, no one had yet applied.

She handed us a paper application form and told us to email the completed version to her as soon as possible.

Driving home, Diti and I talked about how much we both loved the place. So we pulled over at a Dunkin’, filled out the application by hand, and emailed it back.

A few days later the broker texted.

The owner wants to meet you on Sunday . . . to go forward!

A few days later, we met our new landlords — a couple who have lived in Jamaica Plain and owned the triple decker for decades — at JP Licks on Centre Street, and signed the lease.

We recently got the keys, and though we aren’t moving for a few more weeks (to avoid the peak Sept. 1 moving costs), we stopped by the other day to plan and clean.

As we sat there munching on a pastry from what will be one of our new neighborhood cafes, I realized that there was still one thing I had forgotten to do.

I pulled out my phone and deleted the Zillow app.

The Boston Public Health Commission (BPHC) has lifted an advisory on a cyanobacteria algae bloom in the West Roxbury part of the Charles River but another warning on a bloom downstream near the Massachusetts Avenue Bridge is still effect.

On July 21, the BPHC warned residents to avoid contact with the West Roxbury area of the Charles River, from Kendrick Street in Needham to Spring Street.

As of Tuesday, officials announced that the advisory for this West Roxbury part of the Charles River had been lifted.

“The concerns were originally raised, as all of these start, because somebody looked at the water and said, ‘My, that looks green’,” said Shoemaker.

Testing in the West Roxbury part of the river revealed that cyanobacteria had been growing as mats on the riverbed, said Shoemaker.

According to the advisory put out by the BPHC, contact with cyanobacteria may cause a plethora of serious health problems, including gastrointestinal issues, respiratory irritation, and in very severe cases, death.

The state continued monitoring the site and conducted two water tests, which as of Monday, showed that the bloom had cleared, said Shoemaker.

A separate health advisory, announced August 20, still remains active for the cyanobacteria bloom located near the Massachusetts Avenue Bridge, in what is called the Charles River’s “lower basin,” said Paul Shoemaker, Director of the Environmental and Occupational Health Division.

“We have not yet reached the stage where things have started to look visually clear for the state to even begin to take the first of its tests,” said Shoemaker.

Shoemaker said that it will be at least another week and a half to two weeks before he could see the advisory being lifted for the lower basin.

According to the Charles River Watershed Association (CRWA), this is the third consecutive year that the Charles River has experienced a cyanobacteria bloom.

“Cyanobacteria blooms are fueled by excess phosphorus from stormwater runoff and warmer water temperatures,” Carly Sherman, communications manager at the CRWA, wrote in a message to the Globe.

“There’s concerns there around climate change and shifting weather patterns that give us more of those long, dry, hot summer days with bright sunshine,” said Shoemaker.

“As the climate changes and average water temperature gets warmer, the rate at which cyanobacteria reproduces increases,” Amanda Darby, a fellow at the CRWA, wrote in an email to the Globe.

The coming fall season, with cooler temperatures, should bring the river some reprieve, said Shoemaker.

Her appeal — not necessarily her music, but the whole ouvre of her as a human being — cut across all sorts of cultures and divides, in all sorts of countries.

It was often said that at her concerts, it wouldn’t be unusual to see a drag queen and a guy wearing a trucker’s cap with a Confederate flag on it in the same audience.

And yet she was intuitively sensitive to how some of her down-home themes came across. When she learned that the word “Dixie” made some folks, especially Black folks, uncomfortable because of its connection to the Confederacy and slavery, she ordered it removed from the Dixie Stampede dining spots at her theme parks in Tennessee and Missouri.

“There’s such a thing as innocent ignorance, and so many of us are guilty of that,” Parton told Billboard in 2018 after the name change. “When they said ‘Dixie’ was an offensive word, I thought, ‘Well, I don’t want to offend anybody. This is a business. We’ll just call it ‘The Stampede.’ As soon as you realize that [something] is a problem, you should fix it. Don’t be a dumbass.”

“That’s where my heart is,” she added. “I would never dream of hurting anybody on purpose.”

In saying that, she offered a life lesson as profound as anything Jesus, Mohammed or the Buddha ever said: Don’t be a dumbass. And don’t hurt people on purpose.

Like many women of her era, she was wildly underestimated while rising in a music industry dominated by men.

She had a great line when people suggested she was just a dumb blonde: she said she wasn’t dumb, and she wasn’t a blonde.

She grew up, one of 12 children, in a one-room cabin in the Great Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee. Her father, a poor farmer, paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal.

Her father never learned to read or write. She considered him the smartest man she ever met, but recognized that his illiteracy made his life very difficult.

That is why she threw so much of her passion and her money into promoting children’s literacy, not just in this country but in several others.

In a country where class divisions are often dismissed, lest it contradict the myth that every American is born equal and has the same chances in life, Dolly Parton knew that was, as she’d put it, pure bunk.

She never forgot where she came from, or that poverty did the same thing to the human spirit whether it was in Appalachia, the Bronx, Dorchester, or the slums of Calcutta.

Deprivation wasn’t the worst part of being poor, she said; the worst part was the shame.

It was her humble roots, and being constantly underestimated, that seemed to drive her most, and there’s nothing more American than that.

Her embrace of any and all others was also quintessentially American. She embodied the words that united the 13 original American states, the words that remain on US currency, e pluribus unum: out of many, one.

She believed deeply in the American concept of identity, the idea that Americans can maintain diverse identities while sharing a common, collective identity and purpose.

That’s why she wouldn’t hurt anyone on purpose. Because if you hurt another person on purpose, she believed, you were hurting yourself.

And that’s why she was so loved and respected by such an array of different people, from not just this country, but all over the world.

She was never fond of the word feminist, but her ability to build a successful career in an entertainment industry dominated by men made her a role model, especially for American women.

How many people, men or women, would say no to Elvis?

Dolly did.

In 1974, at the height of his fame, Elvis Presley wanted to record the song she wrote, “I Will Always Love You.” Parton was thrilled, because she admired Presley so much.

But when, right before the recording session, Presley’s manager insisted he would record it only if he was entitled to at least half of the publishing rights, Parton walked away.

She cried, but she stuck to her principle.

When Whitney Houston covered “I Will Always Love You” in 1992, it became an international hit, and in the end Parton collected some $10 million in royalties from that rendition in just the 1990s alone.

She used some of that money to build an office complex in a Black neighborhood in Nashville.

She did it to honor Whitney Houston, telling an interviewer, “I just thought, ‘This was great. I’m going to be down here with her people, who are my people as well.’ ”

My people as well. How American is that?

Parton’s embrace of the LGBTQ+ community was similar in outlook. If her Christian faith was central to her own identity, she couldn’t understand how people who call themselves Christian could hate queer and transgender people.

“I try to love everybody,” she said.

It is probably not news that Americans are not especially popular around the world these days. It’s easy to blame it all on Donald Trump, who insults other countries and projects the kind of American exceptionalism that denigrates others.

But for all its great achievements, for all its many great people, this country has done plenty of things around the world that aren’t good and have nothing to do with Donald Trump.

In more recent times, we’ve become a more cruel country, a bad neighbor, a place less serious and taken less seriously abroad.

That in and of itself is a reason to celebrate Dolly Parton’s life, and to mourn her passing. She was loved because, as she put it, she tried to love everybody.

She reminded us what it means to be a good American, a good person, a good soul. She was all that, and more.

What do President Trump and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu have in common?

Both have a zeal for endorsing candidates of their choice to try to control election outcomes — and with that zeal, the confidence to test their own clout.

State Senators Nick Collins and Will Brownsberger, both Democrats, now face Wu-backed primary opponents because they did not support the mayor’s proposal to shift some of Boston’s property tax burden from residents to commercial property owners. Daniel Lander, a former Wu aide, is taking on Brownsberger, while Latoya Gayle, a community activist and first-time candidate is challenging Collins with Wu’s blessing.

While these contests do test the power of insurgency against incumbency, because of Wu’s involvement, the debate has focused more about the role that Boston lawmakers should play in pushing the mayor’s agenda. There is palpable tension between Wu and the two senators, especially Collins, who during the fight over her property tax legislation accused Wu of using “fear and manipulation” in her ultimately unsuccessful bid to get the proposal through the Legislature.

After serving eight years in the House, Collins won election to the state Senate in 2018 and now represents a district that includes South Boston, Dorchester, the South End, Chinatown and parts of Roxbury, Mattapan and the Back Bay. Brownsberger, a 20-year veteran of the Legislature, is a key part of Senate leadership, and represents a district that includes parts of Boston and Cambridge, along with all of Watertown and Belmont. Sounding less than eager for this fight with Wu, Brownsberger recently told the Globe editorial board, “I’m not quarreling with the mayor. The minute we can have peace in the valley, I will embrace peace in the valley.”

But peace does not seem to be Wu’s priority right now and, in a way, that’s understandable. Her power is at its height. She ran unopposed in her 2025 reelection campaign, after she bested challenger Josh Kraft by 49 points in the preliminary election and he dropped out. She has a track record of success when it comes to endorsing Boston City Council candidates. Watching congressional candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sweep to victory may have also encouraged her to test her own political muscle.

Yet the stakes are different for Wu than they were for Mamdani. If either Gayle or Lander win, she gets credit. But that credit won’t win Wu any more friends in the Senate or any more support on Beacon Hill for her tax proposal. Indeed, it may produce the opposite.

But she’s all-in with Lander and Gayle, just like Trump is all-in with Darline Graham, naming her interim US senator in South Carolina after her brother, longtime Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly last month. Trump then backed her in Tuesday’s special run-off election.

At least Trump’s backing of Darline Graham is motivated partly by his loyalty to her late brother. Wu’s backing of Lander and Gayle is strictly a matter of payback politics.

Is there no way to build bridges instead? Wu seems to share Trump’s view that there isn’t.
