But she also views them as “two sides of the exact same coin.”

AND THEN THERE WERE FIVE: Mariah Lancaster, a veterinarian and former congressional staffer running in the Sixth Congressional District, dropped out of the Democratic primary on Saturday and endorsed state Representative Tram Nguyen, lending another last-minute jolt of momentum to the Andover Democrat’s campaign to replace Representative Seth Moulton.

It’s unclear how Lancaster’s exit might sway the outcome of Tuesday’s election, given Lancaster’s name will remain on the ballot. But the Salem Democrat’s departure is the latest in an 11th-hour surge of support for Nguyen, and could add some clarity to a field where Nguyen has positioned herself as the progressive alternative to other two other perceived front-runners, former White House aide Dan Koh and Lynnfield fintech executive John Beccia.

ONE VOTER WHO’S STILL UNDECIDED: Which candidate is the highest profile pol in the Sixth District voting for on Tuesday?

That’s a secret Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll isn’t ready to tell.

“I’m still considering all the choices,” the former Salem mayor said (after a long pause) when we caught her on the campaign trail Sunday. “I haven’t endorsed in that race officially, but I’m looking forward to voting.”

Driscoll isn’t alone in staying out of the race. Nguyen picked up a string of endorsements last week from US Representatives Ayanna Pressley and Lori Trahan and Attorney General Andrea Campbell. But with just days to go, much of the state’s congressional delegation — Moulton included — still hasn’t taken a side. Neither has Driscoll’s partner in state government, Governor Maura Healey.

A Hyde Park man will serve at least 16 years in state prison for a 2025 shooting that wounded a Boston police officer, officials said Tuesday.

Daiquan Rice, 32, was convicted by a jury last week of assault and battery with a firearm, carrying a firearm without a license, and carrying a loaded firearm without a license, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Judge Mark Hallal Tuesday sentenced Rice to 12 to 13 years in state prison for the assault and battery and four to five years for firearm possession, to be served consecutively, the statement said.

Hallal also sentenced Rice to two years of probation for carrying a loaded firearm without a license with the conditions that he obtain a GED or equivalent degree and complete a violence prevention program, the statement said.

“This is an appropriate sentence for such a reckless and dangerous action,” Hayden said. “I’m so grateful that the officer survived and was able to overcome his injuries. We will never relent in prosecuting anyone who harms or attempts to harm our law enforcement officers.”

Rice was convicted of several prior firearm-related offenses out of Suffolk Superior Court, where he received a seven-to-10-year prison sentence with three years of probation to follow, the statement said.

Rice was on probation and parole at the time of the 2025 shooting.

On Sept. 12, 2025, at about 12:45 a.m., officers were patrolling the area of Washington and Dudley streets to address complaints about quality-of-life issues in Nubian Square, including complaints of people congregating in and around the African American Veterans Memorial Park, the statement said.

Officers reported several people in the park and one person standing away from the group smoking, the statement said. The park has posted signs indicating it closes at dusk and prohibits smoking.

Officers approached the person smoking, later identified as Rice, and he began walking in the opposite direction. Rice fled down Washington Street when officers exited their cruiser, the statement said.

Officers followed as Rice turned right onto Archer Terrace toward Kenilworth Street. Rice shot an officer in the arm during the pursuit, which prompted police to return fire, the statement said.

Rice and the officer were taken to hospitals with wounds that were not considered life-threatening, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox told reporters near the scene on Sept. 12, 2025.

Police recovered a loaded firearm with a large-capacity magazine, the statement said.

Three additional officers were treated for non-life-threatening injuries at local hospitals, according to past Globe coverage.

“This is another example of the amount of guns that are out there,” Cox said. ”We’re very lucky and fortunate that there was no loss of life here."

With the results of the GOP now in hand, the general election will likely be as much about Trump as it will be about Healey’s first term in office.

At her own primary night party at a union hall in Dorchester, Healey was quick to cast blame on Trump for the high cost of living in Massachusetts, telling supporters the president put in place harmful tariffs, cut funding and access to health care, and slashed funding for science, research, and local universities.

“We see the damage Trump is doing every day. He’s raising your costs, he’s terrorizing our communities, he’s taking away your health care and your rights,” Healey said, warning that her Republican opponent “will bring Trump’s agenda to Massachusetts.”

The primary comes as Massachusetts faces challenges on multiple fronts: a housing crunch that is driving many residents to consider leaving the state, for example, and a higher cost of living that is straining household budgets across the economic spectrum.

Healey is running for a second term alongside Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, a former mayor of Salem who was also unopposed in the primary.

The results on Tuesday are expected to kick into high gear what has already become an expensive gubernatorial election. Minogue has poured more than $15 million of his own money into his gubernatorial bid while Healey had $6.6 million in her campaign account as of the end of July.

At his primary night party in Medford, Minogue did not name Healey in his victory speech, but said “our opponents will choose division” in the race for governor.

“They will choose to dishonestly attack me with political ads, and in fact, they already have begun,” the Hamilton Republican said. “Well, we’re choosing something different. We’re going to go down a different path. Our opponents know what happens when we stand united. They know when we put aside our differences and join together, we will defeat the one-party system.”

The general election battle over the next several months is likely to generate intensified attacks from Democrats on Minogue for his ties to Trump and congressional Republicans.

Unlike in the 2022 election, in which the Republican nominee openly embraced Trump, both Minogue and Shortsleeve had sought to distance themselves from the White House in an apparent bid to make themselves more appealing to unenrolled voters who make up a majority of Massachusetts’ voter rolls.

Trump had not endorsed either candidate in the GOP primary.

Still, Healey and the state Democratic Party have attempted to paint Minogue as “MAGA Mike,” pointing to the hundreds of thousands of dollars he donated to national Republican causes and a super PAC that backed Trump’s successful 2024 bid for the White House.

“In this election, we’re going to send a message that if you support Donald Trump, if you funded him, if you endorse the bad things he’s done to our state, then you cannot be governor of Massachusetts,” Healey said Tuesday night.

Minogue, 59, is a businessman making his first overture into politics after earning a fortune in the medical device industry, where he oversaw the sale of the Danvers-based heart-pump maker Abiomed to Johnson & Johnson in 2022 for $16.6 billion.

He was little known outside the medical field before entering the political fray last year, but has since spent millions of his own dollars to boost his name recognition and catapult himself to the top of the GOP ticket.

He is a “pro-life” Catholic who has said he would “uphold” reproductive rights laws in Massachusetts if elected governor. And he has promised to help deport “illegal immigrants” in the state and reform safety-net benefits for migrants who arrive in the state.

Laureen Goodhue, 64, said she voted for Minogue on Tuesday in Allston because she “aligned with everything that he believed.”

“I feel that he’s more Republican than Shortsleeve,” she said. “Plus, I think he’s pro-life.”

Minogue has also largely pitched himself as a “new kind of governor,” or a political outsider intent on using his business acumen to run the state. He drew heavily on his experience in the military and health care field in his pitch to voters Tuesday night, and labeled himself an “outsider.”

“I am beholden to no special group. I go into this role knowing I will work for you,” he said.

But Minogue faces a steep uphill battle in his campaign to unseat Healey. Polls have shown that Healey led by double digits in a hypothetical head-to-head matchup with Minogue, including in a Suffolk University/Boston Globe survey from June.

Shortsleeve, 54, was also making his first foray into elected politics. But he is best known for leaving venture capital more than a decade ago to serve as acting general manager and chief administrator of the MBTA after a series of major snowstorms in 2015 crushed the transit system.

Shortsleeve conceded the Republican primary to Minogue shortly after 9 p.m. and endorsed his opponent.

“I have been a fighter my entire life, and we fought hard throughout this campaign for the future we believe Massachusetts deserves. Mike Minogue is a fighter, too, and I know he will bring that same fight on behalf of the taxpayers to Beacon Hill,” Shortsleeve said in a statement.

Shawn Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor and Shortsleeve’s running mate, locked up the Republican nomination for lieutenant governor after two other candidates were forced out of the race amid a signature fraud controversy earlier this summer.

That means Oliver would pair with Minogue after months of his and Shortsleeve’s campaigns criticizing him as un-electable in a head-to-head matchup with Healey.

Healey, 55, swept into office four years ago as the state’s first woman and first openly LGBTQ elected governor, riding a progressive reputation built over eight years as attorney general when she emerged as one of the state’s most notable Trump antagonists, filing nearly 100 lawsuits against the Republican’s administration during his first term in office.

But since succeeding Baker, Healey has cut a more moderate tone. Healey has regularly touted a $1 billion-a-year tax package she signed in 2023 as one of her signature achievements and has sought to firm up her public safety credentials this year.

She has also leaned into Democratic calls to counter Trump on immigration. In her speech Tuesday, Healey pointed to her past work as attorney general.

“I’m the only one in this race who’s actually prosecuted and put away bad guys, drug traffickers, human traffickers. We can agree that we want violent criminals off the streets and deported. What we can also agree on is that none of what ICE is doing is making us safe,” she said.

Markey spoke to a jam-packed ballroom at the Omni Parker House in Boston, where supporters and Democratic stalwarts, including Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, packed in to celebrate the incumbent.

Against a backdrop of high school and college-age students, Markey promised the crowd a future chock-full of progressive priorities, from abolishing federal immigration enforcement to passing universal child care to cementing abortion rights in law.

He said the race is “all about the American dream” in Massachusetts and in states where he has backed other successful progressive Democrats this cycle.

“That fight is in our hands here in Massachusetts, in Maine, in Michigan,” he said. “Our progressive movement knows how to fight. We cannot surrender tomorrow.”

About an hour after polls closed, Moulton took the stage at his own election night watch party at a union hall in Dorchester to tell supporters he called Markey to congratulate him on his victory.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary,” he said. “We started conversations that needed to happen, and I will never stop pushing the Democratic Party and our country to look toward the future.”

With a win in November, Markey would return to Washington for a third full six-year term as the junior senator and extend his time in Washington into a sixth decade.

Markey’s primary victory tells the story of a race in which, despite Moulton’s attempts, age appears to have played little role in many voters’ decisions about whether to back an incumbent who will be 86 by the time his next term would end.

The dynamic complicates the emerging national narrative of Democratic politics in this year’s midterm elections, during which a historic number of incumbent lawmakers have lost primary challenges due to perceptions they had been in office too long, were insufficiently progressive — or both.

Markey ran well to the left of his 47-year old rival, embracing staunch progressive policies — Medicare for All being his most common talking point — as national left-wing figures like Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez embraced him. Markey said shortly before their first debate in July that, should he win, his next term would be his last, saying he needed “to finish this progressive agenda, and then I will step down.”

Moulton repeatedly hammered his argument that Markey’s age was a liability and that new leaders were needed to tackle contemporary problems. Still, many voters said they were skeptical of his liberal bona fides.

This contest did not come close to attracting the national or statewide energy, fund-raising, or media attention that Markey’s battle with Joseph Kennedy III did six years ago. Amid general voter indifference and relative lack of enthusiasm for the candidates, Markey’s ability to rally the progressive faithful was enough to hand him another term this time around in what was expected to be a low-turnout contest.

Much of the race involved both Markey and Moulton vying to prove their progressive credibility to primary voters, as well as their desire to stand out in a race where both candidates often landed on the same side of national issues.

With few genuine policy differences between them, the race was contentious and, sometimes bitter. In their second debate, Moulton unveiled a narrative that Markey was somehow implicated in the Epstein files, a claim that the congressman pushed with little to no evidence and that Markey called “reprehensible” and “character assassination.”

Markey, meanwhile, criticized Moulton as beholden to his financial supporters in the private equity sector. The senator’s supporters went harsher, with Representative Ayanna Pressley in the final weekend calling Moulton’s past comments on trans youth in sports “disqualifying” and saying that Democrats cannot afford “mediocre” representatives.

Moulton had suggested in 2024 that identity politics were to blame for the party’s electoral losses, saying he would not want his two young daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”

Moulton has since, and repeatedly this campaign, apologized to the trans community for his comments, saying “he was sorry if my comments hurt you.”

“We don’t accept a younger politician with older politics,” transgender activist Tyler Hack, who founded a political action committee to elect pro-trans candidates to federal office, said at Markey’s election night party. “Throwing trans kids under the bus is . . . a dealbreaker.”

Even as the snipes became sharper, public opinion polls showed a largely consistent race, with Markey often in the lead by double digits. After a Suffolk/Globe poll showed Markey with a double-digit lead last month, Moulton dismissed polling in this election cycle as being “wildly off.”

But the factors that contributed to polling misses elsewhere — like significant consolidation for one candidate or onslaughts of outside spending — weren’t present in Massachusetts. Markey enjoyed far more support from the party establishment and key groups throughout the entire campaign. Moulton also had comparatively few backers in local offices around the state, and zero public supporters among his Massachusetts colleagues in Washington.

While Moulton was the beneficiary of the lion’s share of outside spending in the race, largely through a super PAC funded by his supporters, it was not enough to make the contest closer.

Moulton, a six-term congressman, swept into office 12 years ago by topping a longtime incumbent. But Markey’s ability to cast himself as the ideological choice among a primary electorate that disproportionately leans left paid off.

Doug Rubin, a senior adviser to Moulton’s campaign, told the Globe that “we had a theory of the case that voters were looking for change,” but that “clearly voters in Massachusetts were looking for the future that Markey provided.”

“So credit to them. They ran a very effective campaign,” Rubin said. “The senator has already obviously had a very long and good career, and people really like him.”

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday night in Medford, Deaton, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, indicated he would put up a spirited fight in the general election. Deaton ran for the Senate two years ago, losing to Senator Elizabeth Warren.

“I want people to get past labels and look at who’s the best candidate in each race,” he said. “In the race between me versus Ed Markey, I’m the better candidate, not because of age, not because of how long he’s been in office, because I have real solutions to the problems that people face.”

As Moulton supporters and staff continued to mingle at the Plumbers Local 12 union hall after he conceded the race, several expressed hope he would remain in politics.

“I hope he would” run for office again, said Lei Huang, 59, a Brighton consultant whose teenage daughter volunteered for Moulton. “He has good clarity on what he wants to achieve.”

Melissa Woods, 39, voted for Markey in Allston Tuesday, citing her perspective that he is “just the more seriously progressive candidate.”

Markey’s age, however, was also top of mind for voters, regardless of who they ultimately supported. Betty Ellis, 76, said her decision to vote for Markey was a tough one.

“I really do feel like after 80, you know, age is really a factor,” Ellis, of Cambridge, said. “But I wasn’t thrilled with Moulton, and I thought, ‘Well, I feel like Markey has done a great job.’ I feel like he’s a man of integrity, and if he’s feeling too old, he will step down.”

Norah Burch, 53, said in Allston that she voted for Markey because he’s “doing a great job for however long he’s been doing it.”

“People are like, ‘Oh, he’s so old.’ But I don’t think Moulton’s got what it takes. I don’t care how old he is,” Burch said.

Some older voters were turned off by Moulton’s closing attack on Markey: hammering him for stumbling over details about artificial intelligence programs in their final debate. Moulton’s TV ads highlighting the flub blanketed the airwaves in the closing weeks of the campaign — which Cheryl Hassan, a retired chiropractor from Lynnfield, said she “personally hated.”

“I don’t know either what [AI programs] I use,” Hassan said. “And I’m not stupid.”

The results on Tuesday should settle the question: Did the 2024 razor-thin margin reflect momentary dissatisfaction with Decker or a more durable demand for change?

No Republican or independent candidate is officially running in any of these four contests. That means a relatively small share of the electorate will decide four consequential questions about ideology, political power, and experience.

“We cannot change the circumstances of the burial, but we can change what happens now,” said Diana Lam, president of the Boston Women’s Heritage Trail. “We can speak their names, we can honor their lives, we can tell their stories, and we can ensure the future generations know that these women were here.”

The project began when Joyce Linehan, a former aide to ex-Boston mayor Martin J. Walsh who lives in Dorchester, walked her dog past the burial site and noticed it was marked only by a stone inscribed with the name of the Home for Aged Colored Women. She wondered who was buried there and started asking questions.

Linehan’s friend Karilyn Crockett, also a former city official and a professor at MIT, then launched a multiyear research project that led to the discovery of the buried women’s names and shed light on a mostly forgotten chapter of the city’s history.

“These women were building a city for us and with us at a time [when] they were not given credit or recognition for that at all,” Crockett said.

The women lived in a segregated elder home on Beacon Hill between 1860 and 1944. They were domestic servants and suffrage activists. They were congregants at Twelfth Baptist, then known as the Fugitive Slave Church. Some had been born into Southern slavery and moved north after the Civil War.

They were not welcome at the nearby Home for Aged Women, where the residents were white and mostly Protestant. The homes were only a few blocks apart. Their burial sites were even closer — literally adjacent plots at Cedar Grove. But only one had headstones. The residents of the Home for Aged Colored Women were buried, and then their names — or at least their burial sites — were largely forgotten.

In 2024, Rita Steele, a data analytics professional and avid genealogist, was trying to trace her family tree to its Native American roots. She thought her fourth great-grandmother, Sarah Smith, who died in Boston in 1890, might provide the link.

“So I used one of my successful research strategies (reverse address search) of the address on her death certificate,” Steele said by text message. She assumed the Beacon Hill address was a family home. But instead, “it came back with the name for the Home for Aged Colored Women.”

That discovery led her to a blog post by Linehan about the Dorchester burial site. She got in touch with Linehan and Crockett and has been involved in planning the memorial ever since.

Crockett’s research has proceeded on a parallel track. After learning of the burial site from Linehan, she assigned her MIT graduate students to research the home. The cemetery had handwritten note cards listing the women’s names in its archives. Then they found the home’s records in the archives of the Massachusetts Historical Society.

What emerged was an unusually intimate portrait of the women’s lives. The records showed “who was an avid reader, who was a vegetarian, who didn’t like who,” Linehan said. “There was gossipy stuff in there.”

For Crockett, the research also challenged the assumption that Black Bostonians, especially elderly Black women, must have been isolated, only marginal participants in the life of the city. Eliza Gardner, who received financial assistance from the home, was a prominent public speaker and member of Black political organizations, Crockett said. She was once featured in The Woman’s Era, a newspaper founded in Boston in 1894.

Other women were part of migrations to New England. Some came from Canada, others from the American South.

Annie B. Merrick was born into slavery in North Carolina in 1848, according to Crockett. She moved north and then lived in the Home for Aged Colored Women beginning in 1923. She died at Boston State Hospital in 1941.

Smith, Steele’s ancestor, was born in Newport, R.I., around 1799. Her father had been enslaved and fought in the Revolutionary War. Two of Smith’s brothers were abolitionists who worked with Frederick Douglass. Steele and Crockett are still trying to learn more about Smith herself.

Steele traveled from her home in Maryland to attend the ceremony. “There’s tons of work to be done,” she said. “I hope this is a flicker of light for someone.”

The women, including her ancestor, Smith, are buried in two plots — the one next to the white women’s burial ground and a second one that was used when the first filled up.

The temporary memorial is a “collage” of flowers and women’s portraits formed into a single figure to “reflect both the individuality of each woman and her presence in a greater community,” artist Ekua Holmes said.

The Roxbury-born artist entered the chapel to applause. She drew inspiration from Ellis Wilson’s “Funeral Procession” painting, she said.

The installation will remain there for a year while the nonprofit Boston Women’s Heritage Trail raises money for a permanent memorial that includes all of the women’s names.

Robert MacEachern, who runs the cemetery, estimates the memorial will cost more than $100,000. The past two state budgets earmarked $45,000 combined for the project. A grant from the city of Boston paid for Holmes’s work but is not funding the permanent memorial.

When Steele first learned of Smith’s burial place, she found the circumstances “very disturbing and disappointing.”

“No one knew who they were walking by,” she said. “Like they didn’t mean anything to anyone. . . . But I am so proud that their names are finally being restored.”

Wu downplayed the outcome of the primary in an interview Wednesday, noting that she backed two first-time candidates who took on entrenched incumbents.

“Every election matters, and every year matters for getting things done, and that’s what we saw in the results from yesterday,” Wu said. “We had first-time candidates who started with no name recognition, taking on incumbents, and really outperforming expectations.”

In addition to Lander, Wu backed education activist Latoya Gayle, also a first-time candidate, in her unsuccessful bid to unseat state Senator Nick Collins of South Boston.

Wu has publicly clashed with both Collins and Brownsberger in recent years, and her endorsement of their challengers raised eyebrows as an attempt to oust her political adversaries on Beacon Hill.

Wu also endorsed state Senator Michael F. Rush of West Roxbury, an eight-term incumbent who lost to attorney Persis Yu in a district that includes Dedham, Norwood, Walpole, Westwood, and parts of Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, and Hyde Park.

On Tuesday, Gayle lost to Collins by roughly 10 percentage points. And Yu unseated Rush by winning 51 percent of the vote to Rush’s 49 percent.

Lander and Brownsberger, though, remain neck and neck. As of 6:30 p.m. Wednesday, Lander had 12,132 votes — a mere three votes ahead of Brownsberger, who tallied 12,129 according to the Associated Press.

The candidates have until 3 p.m. Thursday to request a districtwide recount, in a race where more is riding on the outcome than just who will represent a district that covers swaths of Boston, Cambridge, Watertown, and Belmont, in the state Senate. Neither candidate responded Wednesday for comment.

Wu took a risk spending her political capital backing newcomers against well-established incumbents, said Erin O’Brien, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

“People are going to do the tally,” O’Brien said. “If you endorse and the person loses, it goes against your tally.”

Still, O’Brien argued it would be premature to assume that the losses are a reflection that the mayor’s influence or popularity are waning.

“Wu’s a variable,” O’Brien said. “She’s not a determining force.”

But on a night where most incumbents across the state retained their seats, Rush’s loss, especially with Wu’s endorsement, was a notable outlier.

The result reflected the broader trend across the country as Democratic voters showed an increasing appetite for generational change and progressive leadership, according to David Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College. Yu, who defeated Rush, ran to his left.

“There is clearly this increasingly mobilized progressive vote in Democratic primaries here in this state, as well many other places around the country,” Hopkins said. “Some Democratic incumbents are facing serious competition, sometimes for the first time in many years, or the first time in their career.”

On Wednesday, Rush’s campaign did not respond to a request comment. Wu defended her endorsement of the West Roxbury Democrat, who faced a progressive challenger who espoused many of the same talking points as Lander and Gayle.

Still, Rush “has often been the first to call and ask what Boston needs in the state Senate,” Wu said. “He has moved issues and funding for us quietly and effectively, and I wish he would still be in a position to help serve our community, [but] the voters have spoken.”

In an interview in the wake of her loss against Collins, Gayle said that the 10-point margin in her race shows that Boston voters’ are scrutinizing incumbents’ records and demanding urgency from elected leadership.

“The people are watching,” Gayle said. “It’s important that when you show up to the State House, when you volunteer for this job, that you are listening to the people and and pushing the policies, the budget, the things that the people actually need and want.”

“Because your seat won’t be safe,” Gayle said, ”if you’re not.”

Insurance reimbursements, labor, and real estate costs have squeezed margins as drugstores have lost market share on everyday retail to competitors, including Amazon. Meanwhile, executives have said shoplifting has become an increasing concern.

CVS isn’t alone in experimenting with a smaller drugstore footprint. Walgreens has also tried smaller-format stores that are about 20 to 25 percent of the size of their typical stores, said Neil Saunders, managing director at GlobalData Retail, a retail consulting agency.

At the same time, drugstores’ basic retail business has also weakened, Saunders said. Dollar stores have eroded their convenience advantage, while Amazon and Walmart have made it easier to have goods delivered. Meanwhile, drugstores often charge more than Target and Walmart for the same everyday items.

Pharmacy chains “have kind of have lost the battle on retail,” said Saunders. “They don’t really want to do that on pharmacy.”

In Roxbury, CVS tried a new path: bringing back the pharmacy without the drugstore. It’s one of roughly 20 such concepts that CVS plans to roll out in cities nationwide. The Boston move triggered mixed feelings, with some arguing it represents an inequity.

Rahsaan D. Hall, president and CEO of The Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts, said CVS should be praised for returning a pharmacy to the community, but added the company was “creating a two-tier retail experience.”

“Residents in one community can browse products, compare ingredients and prices, and purchase ordinary household necessities while residents in another community, made up of a completely different racial and socioeconomic demographic, cannot,” said Hall. “That difference deserves a level of scrutiny.”

The new format comes after a string of pharmacies, including Walgreens and CVS, have pulled out of the neighborhood over the last decade. In fact, the community lost five drugstores since 2017, with only one family-owned shop — Kornfield Pharmacy — left standing.

Renewed pharmacy access fills one major gap in Roxbury. But CVS isn’t filling another: the loss of a local drugstore where residents can pick up toiletries, food, and other everyday necessities. For a neighborhood that has lost pharmacies and drugstores, is it enough?

“I’m glad there’s a new pharmacy here, but I wish they sold retail goods,” said Alex DiMario, 38, who lives near the new store. “There’s not enough real convenience stores in the neighborhood.”

CVS, headquartered in Rhode Island, calls this model a new answer to an old problem of how to put pharmacies back into communities where access has become increasingly challenging.

“People [have been] taking the bus to go pick up their prescriptions,” said Siddharth “Sid” Tenneti, the senior vice president and interim president of CVS’s pharmacy and consumer wellness division. “This is our attempt to be a health care answer to the community.”

The first pharmacy-only CVS opened earlier this year on Chicago’s West Side, a dense and diverse neighborhood. Others opened in Houston, Detroit, Birmingham, and Washington, D.C. CVS is also opening a dozen new traditional stores and more than 30 pharmacies inside Target stores across the United States.

Chris Ribeiro, the founder of retail strategy firm Starlight Analytics, said this format signals a broader shift in the economics of retail drugstores, particularly in places with high rents.

“The question to ask is whether prescription revenue alone is enough to justify even these smaller footprints,” Ribeiro said.

Michelle Fenstermaker, the executive strategy director of consulting firm Landor, is blunt about the industry’s future: “The era of the monolithic, one-size-fits-all, 14,000-square-foot corner drugstore is officially over.”

Rite Aid, which operated more than 5,000 stores at its peak, is now defunct after filing for bankruptcy twice. To survive, Walgreens has also closed underperforming stores, cut corporate positions, and invested in technology such as prescription-filling robots.

Walgreens’s small-format stores, which the company first began testing in 2019, mostly offer Walgreens-branded health-related products. As of 2024, Walgreens had reportedly opened about 100 mini drugstores nationwide.

At the same time, pressure from competitors seems to be coming from everywhere: Club chains, such as Costco, have continued to grow and compete with drugstores’ convenience-based demand for beauty and hygiene products, said Jeremy Bowman, a retail analyst for investment research company The Motley Fool. Online pharmacies, such as Amazon, GoodRx, and Hims & Hers Health Inc., have also exploded, said Bowman.

The vast majority of Roxbury has long qualified as a pharmacy desert — meaning a poorer, urban area with low car-ownership rates, where the nearest pharmacy can be at least a half-mile away. In contrast, many white and wealthier residents in the Back Bay can walk to two or three pharmacies within a half mile.

The disparities extend beyond convenience. Pharmacy access is among the factors that health experts say can worsen health disparities. The average life expectancy in Roxbury is 68, 23 years fewer than in the Back Bay. And the neighborhood has higher rates of chronic diseases.

At 3,000 square feet, the new CVS store is less than half the size of the company’s urban stores in the area.

The format comes as CVS has restructured its portfolio in recent years: Coming out of COVID, the company closed 900 stores, while theft is one complication in “certain markets,” CVS CEO David Joyner has said. Merchandise is often locked behind glass to deter theft, a practice Joyner has acknowledged creates a “horrible customer experience.”

For years, customers of CVS, and its competitors, have complained about having to wait for employees to unlock everything from toothpaste to deodorant. Some analysts have warned that the practice has undermined the convenience factor that’s supposed to be the stores’ selling point.

Joyner didn’t want security guards in every store where there’s a high theft rate, he said during a talk at the Boston College Chief Executives Club in June.

One solution, he said, was to roll out pharmacy-only stores like the one in Roxbury — “where we can still meet the clinical needs of the population, but not feel like you’re constantly trying to deal with the safety of running a front store.”

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, a longtime Roxbury pastor, said he disagrees with Joyner. When he protested against Walgreens closing in Roxbury, Culpepper presented data that showed theft wasn’t as high as executives made it out to be.

“I challenge the CVS executive to cite the data that supports his statement,” said Culpepper.

Hall said while he understands theft is an issue broadly, CVS’s response to “the behavior of a small number of people should not be to punish an entire neighborhood by removing resources from everyone.”

The new Roxbury store can order products for customers and deliver them to their homes free of charge.

Lauren Beitelspacher, a Babson College marketing professor, said she expects dollar stores to try to fill the in-person retail void.

“However, I do think that establishing yourself as a leader in the health care and wellness space in a neighborhood that doesn’t have access is a way to really build up brand loyalty,” said Beitelspacher.

The clock is ticking for the MBTA to put the finishing touches on an unusual financing deal within the next few weeks — one that could help determine the entire commuter rail system’s future.

The T is in final negotiations with several private-sector partners to finally redo the Fairmount Line, with battery-powered cars to replace the diesel dinosaurs that rumble through the heart of the city.

They’re working with the familiar faces at commuter rail operator Keolis, and some new ones at the table. This will be the first time the T has relied on a third-party financier — in this case, British infrastructure firm Rock Rail — to buy new commuter rail vehicles on its behalf.

The T board blessed this in June, agreeing to spend $765 million over 15 years to cover the cost of leasing and maintaining seven four-car trainsets that run on electric batteries. The cars will be made by Stadler in Utah, and start showing up for testing in late 2029.

This isn’t only about righting a wrong for Boston’s poorer neighborhoods, by offering trains that arrive at 20-minute intervals. The ramifications go well beyond the Fairmount’s nine-mile corridor through Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park.

General manager Phil Eng sees this as a model that could be replicated as he looks to put the entire commuter rail system on track for electrification, another long-awaited change. What works in Boston’s urban neighborhoods might also work in suburban outposts. The Fairmount purchase is a test run; the deal includes options to procure as many as 96 more new cars, the equivalent of 24 trainsets, for other lines.

Another reason to watch Fairmount: politics. Keolis is in a race to keep its coveted job as the commuter rail operator. By coincidence, bids for the new contract are due later this month. It was once thought delivering an electric train in time for Governor Maura Healey’s reelection campaign in 2026 would give her bragging rights — and maybe help Keolis with its case that it should stick around.

That timing turned out to be wishful thinking. But at least Healey can brag about the financing, right?

Whether this helps the French company’s bid, we may never know. T officials structured the Fairmount financing so a different operator, or even the T itself, can take over the lease.

The more traditional route would be issuing bonds for new trains. But the T says it would have had to cancel or reschedule other critical projects to do so. Plus, Rock Rail takes on some of the risk; lease payments don’t start until these machines are in service.

An upgraded Fairmount has been on the arrivals board for years, thanks to pressure from neighborhood advocates and politicians, along with the Conservation Law Foundation that fought for mitigation to offset Big Dig impacts.

The T did add four stations to Fairmount’s three preexisting ones and its South Station and Readville terminals. And the cost to ride was also cut, to the same price as the subway.

What about subway frequency? A plan from Deval Patrick’s administration to buy self-propelled diesel-powered units was scuttled after Charlie Baker took over, though the T did trim headways in 2020 under Baker.

Finally, we have a plan to go electric — even though it will take four more years to see it in action. T officials decided each car should be wheelchair accessible (in part to adhere to a 2006 legal settlement), not just one per trainset. That drove up costs, and delayed delivery.

In June, board member Mary Skelton Roberts chastised T executives for the delays, and a failure to keep the community apprised. Folks, she said, have been waiting for these trains for ages.

Some still won’t be fully satisfied. City councilor Brian Worrell says the neighborhood might be better served by overhead wires the whole way, instead of batteries, making the line even more like a subway. (The trains will use overhead lines to recharge, but for only a small section.) Worrell has been in the news along with councilor Miniard Culpepper pushing their own transit proposal for the area, an Orange Line extension along Blue Hill Avenue; he says it could augment, not replace, the electrified Fairmount trains.

Kimberly Lyle, head of the Dorchester Bay Economic Development Corp., says she’s just happy to see meaningful progress. Her neighbors deserve a quick commute downtown, and cleaner air, as much as anyone in Boston.

Now, finally, the T is poised to deliver on that promise — and put the wheels in motion for bigger changes down the line.

If only lawyer David Lurie were still here to savor this victory. The town of Nahant just won big at the Supreme Judicial Court today, in its years-long fight with Northeastern University over the fate of East Point. The town has a waterfront park there, including an easement over land Northeastern owns. In 2018, the university unveiled plans to expand its marine science campus there, to the chagrin of those in the town. The town then used its eminent domain authority to seize access rights, essentially blocking the expansion. Northeastern sued, saying this was an illegal use of the authority simply to block a project, and a Superior Court judge agreed. But the SJC today overruled that decision: Protecting a park fits as a public purpose for eminent domain. Lurie represented the Nahant Preservation Trust in the case, but died in 2024 before he was able to see it through fruition; former colleague Harley Racer kept the fight going.

About 350,000 Haitians have sought refuge in the United States since an earthquake devastated their island in 2010, and violent gangs make it so unsafe that the US has banned flights to its capital. Nearly 45,000 Haitians have settled in Massachusetts, and received tens of millions of dollars in federal and state funding for job training and other assistance over the past three years.

But the Trump administration revoked Haitians’ temporary protected status in July and started deporting them.

The damage goes far deeper than the workforce. A Haitian college student in Springfield, Ohio, walked in front of a truck barreling down the highway, an apparent suicide. He had been forced to wear an ankle monitor by immigration authorities and had written an Instagram post a few weeks before about the “shame and humiliation” this caused.

To Canada

Some Haitians who lost their TPS status have fled north to Quebec, a French-speaking province where many have family members and know the language. State officials and local employers say the loss of an estimated 10,000 workers will be devastating for an economy where the skills they have, including caring for elderly and disabled residents, are sorely in need.

One Haitian man I talked to, who went to Canada in July, already had four jobs lined up, including one at a branch of the factory he worked at in Massachusetts. A Haitian woman who had been trained by JVS Boston as a certified nursing assistant, and landed a job at Mass General, also went to Canada. So did her husband, who trained here as a carpenter.

‘Dollars go out the window’

Labor force growth in Massachusetts has come almost exclusively from immigration, the leader of a workforce development program told me, and now that the border is essentially closed, things are going to get “desperate” if new strategies aren’t put in place.

The Guild for Human Services in Concord had to let go of eight Haitian employees with TPS who assisted people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. These workers developed relationships with people, chief executive Amy Sousa said, working nights and weekends for relatively low pay, trained by the nonprofit with more than $240,000 in state funds.

“All those training hours and dollars go out the window,” Sousa said. “We are in desperate need of exemplary employees, and I had to fire eight of them.”

Peres said a medical evaluation for Nuñez was not completed, and a required medical certificate was never filed.

“In the future, if they ever got a certificate, they can come back,” Peres said.

Court filings state Nuñez, who was listed as living in Dorchester, now resides in Utah. Attorneys for Nuñez and Greenhalgh did not return requests for comment.

Her insurgent campaign flew largely under the radar outside of the district stretching from West Roxbury into Boston’s southern suburbs, despite Mayor Michelle Wu coming to the moderate incumbent’s defense in the very district in which she lives.

That was due, in part, to Wu’s other electoral pursuits: The second-term mayor backed two first-time candidates who were trying to take down sitting senators, including one of Rush’s fellow Senate leaders.

“People outside the district didn’t know what was happening,” said Rob Orthman, a Yu backer and co-director of Progressive West Roxbury/Roslindale. “And we were perfectly fine keeping it that way. We did not want to raise attention to this to suddenly start seeing, you know, all the money and support for the incumbent start to flow in.”

Yu was one of a tiny percentage of candidates Tuesday to successfully take out an incumbent by running to their left.

With no Republican on the ballot in November, she effectively clinched the Norfolk and Suffolk seat with her primary victory, taking out not just an eight-term incumbent but also Senate President Karen Spilka’s handpicked majority whip.

So who is this first-time candidate turned (likely) senator-elect — and how did she turn a quiet primary challenge into Tuesday’s biggest down-ballot shocker?

Yu jumped into the race last year, motivated in part by President Trump’s reelection in 2024. In the current political climate, “we need to have steadfast leaders who are protecting our rights, especially on abortion access, especially on LGBTQ+ issues, and especially on immigrant rights,” she said.

But the campaign wasn’t simply a referendum on social issues. Much of her pitch centered on affordability concerns, and, according to Yu, frustration with what voters saw as a Legislature that wasn’t getting enough done. Lawmakers’ resistance to a voter-approved law giving the state auditor the authority to probe the Legislature often came up organically on the trail, Yu said.

“There was a dissatisfaction with the status quo,” the Hyde Park Democrat said. “And people want to know what is actually happening in the Legislature.”

Yu, a Boston Public Schools parent and mother of two, had been active on Boston’s Ward 18 Democratic Committee, but first popped up on Orthman’s radar last spring, he said, as she met with progressive groups around the district to test the waters on a potential state Senate bid.

A consumer protection attorney, “she always likes to say [that] she’s sued the last few presidential administrations on behalf of student loan borrowers, both Democratic and Republican,” Orthman said.

Her campaign was up against some early headwinds. While Rush started off with a cash advantage, Yu outraised him during the campaign, pulling in a little over $156,000 since the start of last September, compared to Rush’s roughly $148,000.

Rush, an Iraq War veteran who first won his seat in 2010, also had some serious institutional support from both Wu and Governor Maura Healey.

The mayor’s support for the more moderate Rush normally would’ve been somewhat surprising. But Rush helped shepherd Wu’s closely watched property tax shift legislation on Beacon Hill, pushing an amendment that the Senate ultimately rejected in January.

That denial prompted Wu to put her political power on the line by backing challengers to Senators Nick Collins and William Brownsberger, and turning those races into something of a proxy war. But her presence was less notable in Rush’s region — and ultimately, didn’t seem to sway voters in her city.

Yu outperformed Rush in Boston, according to unofficial results, earning 57 percent of the vote in the city while Rush carried parts of the district beyond.

“The kind of voter who is highly engaged and supports Michelle is unlikely to be swayed to vote for Rush by her endorsement,” said Matt McCloskey, a Yu volunteer focused on elections data. The district itself changed as well when state lawmakers crafted new maps in 2021, McCloskey said.

“It’s definitely an easier district for a progressive to win now than it would have been in 2020,” he said.

Then there was another notable moment days ahead of the election: When Rush skipped a debate set up by the Dedham and Westwood Democratic town committees, apparently to present a check for state funding in another town in the district.

The move handed Yu and her supporters a ready-made cudgel to hammer Rush heading into the home stretch of the campaign.

Rush has not commented publicly since the loss, and efforts to reach him Thursday were not successful.

Yu, however, said she spoke to Wu briefly Wednesday, and the mayor “was very gracious.”

“It’s a good place-starting conversation, and I definitely look forward to having further ones in the future,” Yu said.

Wu, in a statement, said she offered Yu her “full partnership and support,” and that she looked forward to “working with her as my new state senator to deliver on a shared agenda for the district and the city.”

Notably, Yu isn’t pitching herself as some type of Wu agitator. Case in point: She said that she, too, is supportive of the mayor’s tax shift proposal.

About a year ago, I opened Zillow and started messing around with the website’s interactive map. I stumbled upon one street in particular, in Roxbury: Montrose. The home valuations were noticeably varied, from several hundred thousand to over $1.2 million. What was going on?

Using land records, I learned that the $1.2 million home had been sold just about two years before, for $525,000, by a long-term resident to two Boston restaurateurs, who had turned it into a freshly renovated, gleaming duplex.

I wanted to know more: About the seller, the buyers, and what the home’s reincarnation might tell us about Boston’s overheated housing market.

So I headed to Montrose and started knocking on doors. I met older residents who said they were struggling to hang on, amidst rising taxes and constant pressure from real estate agents. And I met newer residents who were thrilled to gain a foothold in a vibrant, diverse community with a rich history and new, attractive amenities.

Something different in play

It soon became clear that this wasn’t a classic story of gentrification as it’s often told: Some white people were moving in, but so were people of color, who worked in academia, business, for non-profits. And some of the long-term residents were thrilled they could get up to a million bucks on old properties that were becoming onerous to care for.

But there was a real sense of loss, too. The woman who originally sold the $1.2 million house told me she couldn’t afford to hang onto it, even though she had planned to pass it down to her children, and felt pressured by developers who didn’t give her a fair price.

I learned that many of the older residents had faced liens, foreclosures, and debt. Our data editor, Yoohyun Jung, pointed out that this part of Roxbury faces one of the highest risks of displacement in Boston. As one long-term resident, Silvery Richardson, told me: “Each time something sells, the calls and the paperwork start coming.”

How it happens

Everyone talks about gentrification. But you rarely get the backstory of how it actually happens. This week, we offer you an intimate portrait of one block facing drastic change, told through the people who have lived there.

There are tensions here, but there’s also humor — one resident told me, “you’ve gotta be careful about juice places!”

You’ll also get a real sense of the stakes. One woman, who first moved to the neighborhood, stopped in the middle of our interview. “I’m not going to talk it up,” she said. “I don’t want even more people to move here.”

Yu’s account of the upset — in which Democratic primary voters ousted a senator who has served on Beacon Hill since 2003 — is not a magic formula. But it does show how a credible challenge to entrenched power gets built: You show up early and often, you give voters a compelling reason to fire the incumbent, and you run against him on purpose, and not simply because the seat opened up.

Yu, the deputy executive director and managing counsel for Protect Borrowers, a national nonprofit group that fights predatory debt, was clear-eyed about how she made an invisible race visible. “We had an incredible ground game. We were everywhere, we were out in every single community multiple times a week,” Yu told me. “I connected with families of all kinds across the political spectrum.”

Yu treated campaigning as a conversation rather than a pitch, she said. “Once you connect with people as people, and as families, the labels kind of disappear.” It’s why she believes “Democrats as a whole” need “to get better at just talking to people.”

It sounds embarrassingly basic, but this is Massachusetts, the land of the low-competition political culture. In those conversations, Yu drew a contrast between her stances and Rush’s record. For example, Rush voted against expanding access to reproductive health care in 2020 (although he has voted for the major reproductive-rights bills since.) And he was perceived as absent from the district: He declined Yu’s debate requests, skipped a town hall in August, and canceled a Dedham-Westwood forum by email the day of, citing a scheduling conflict.

She was also gathering intelligence from voters. On doorsteps, at community events and parks, Yu kept hearing about an issue she had not expected to carry much weight: the stalled audit of the Legislature.

Lest we forget, in 2024, 72 percent of voters in the state approved Question 1, granting state Auditor Diana DiZoglio explicit authority to audit the Legislature. House and Senate leaders spent the year and a half that followed refusing to comply, until a Supreme Judicial Court order this past May forced the Senate to hand over a narrow set of financial records while still reserving its constitutional objections. As Senate majority whip, Rush was part of the leadership that dragged its feet on the audit.

“People were really worked up about it. ‘The only thing I care about is the audit. I’m a single-issue voter. Where do you stand on the audit?’,” Yu said, recalling what she heard from voters. Yu had entered the race talking about transparency as a principle, but door-knocking taught her that the state auditor fight had given some voters a concrete way to understand it. “They said, ‘I voted for this, and you haven’t done it,’ and that felt unfair.” And Rush’s seniority and leadership post meant he had “more unique ownership of this issue.”

In a way, the audit was a symbol of the deeper dysfunction of the Legislature: Lawmakers answer to leadership because they so rarely face a challenger at the ballot box. That dysfunction was part of why she decided to challenge Rush in the first place.

“One of the reasons why I ran against an incumbent is because I think it’s important to show that it can be done,” Yu said. “Even if I lost by [the same] margin, it’s still a huge statement … by voters here of a desire for change — but also, it’s the change that they want.”

Yu ran on the proposition that competition moves power “out of the hands of leadership and back into the hands of voters,” as she put it. Winning proved that an entrenched incumbent could be beaten. Governing will test the harder part of her argument: whether a candidate elected by challenging Beacon Hill can enter it without becoming insulated from the voters who sent her there.

Yu offered one measurable promise: “I can always put my votes [out]. I can be transparent about where I stand on things. I can hold town halls in my community and provide feedback about the process. People will know what’s happening because we’re going to tell them what’s happening.”

Vera DeVito, a 78-year-old Democrat who packed into one of Newsom’s eight public events across South Carolina, said she didn’t know much about him or his policies — except that he’s from the Golden State. On that basis alone, she suggested that supporting Newsom could be “risky.”

“It’s going to be hard for him to appeal to the whole country,” she said in the town of Summerville. “Everybody thinks California is different — especially in the South. They’re not crazy about California.”

Newsom’s home state stands in stark contrast with likely primary competitors who hail from battlegrounds like Michigan’s Pete Buttigieg and Pennsylvania’s Gov. Josh Shapiro. Should they run, which is likely, all could make credible claims that they are in a better position to win over the moderate and independent voters ultimately needed to win the presidency.

Newsom’s team acknowledges that “California derangement syndrome” is real. In the almost half-century since former California Gov. Ronald Reagan first won the presidency, the state has produced a long list of failed White House contenders, including Gov. Pete Wilson, Gov. Jerry Brown, businessman Tom Steyer, and most recently Vice President Kamala Harris.

Despite such daunting history, Newsom is not hiding his interest in the presidency. In an interview, he left open the possibility of announcing his decision before the end of the year.

“It’s the right question. Honestly, I don’t know,” Newsom told The Associated Press. “I think this thing’s happening. I mean, you already feel it, right? There are folks out here — they’re saying they’re already starting to interview state directors. So this thing is going to happen very, very quickly.”

Newsom’s breakneck pace in South Carolina — which included a handful of private engagements in addition to his public events — mirrored or even exceeded that of a presidential campaign.

His visit was billed as part of his “take it back tour” across states in the Deep South where he argues that President Donald Trump and his Republican allies are rolling back civil rights.

He opened the trip on Wednesday with one day in Alabama and finished on Saturday with two stops in North Carolina. But the overwhelming focus was South Carolina, which will host the Democratic Party’s opening presidential primary contest in little more than a year. It was Newsom’s third trip to South Carolina this midterm season.

The voters who crowded into community halls, courthouses and a university lecture hall talked openly about Newsom’s presidential ambitions, even as Democrats try to keep the focus on November’s midterm elections.

“He has strong potential,” said Kirk Bovill, a 65-year-old semi-retired actor and former Los Angeles resident who now lives in Summerville. “The question is how he’s perceived outside of California. People might think he’s too Hollywood.”

“The one thing he does very well: He doesn’t have a problem standing up to Trump,” Bovill continued. “He’s not intimidated.”

Indeed, Newsom’s message this past week was overwhelmingly focused on attacking Trump and rallying Democrats to stand up against him.

“We cannot do business as usual. We need to fight fire with fire,” Newsom told roughly 150 people gathered inside a Lexington, S.C. community center on Friday. “We’ve got to meet this moment and recognize what we’re up against. We’re up against an invasive species in the name of Donald Trump.”

At every stop, Newsom highlighted the hundreds of millions of dollars Trump and his family have made from crypto currency and other private business dealings since the 2024 election; Trump’s decision to dispatch the National Guard to Los Angeles and other major U.S. cities; the federal immigration agents that have descended upon Los Angeles and other cities under Trump’s direction; and Trump’s push to disrupt the midterm elections, including his recent move to limit mail voting.

“Donald Trump is ruthless. He’s ruthless. He’s going to try to steal this election,” Newsom charged. “He is not screwing around. Neither can we.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Republican activists protesting outside of some of Newsom’s stops focused largely on his connection to California.

CJ Westfall, the Republican chairman of Dorchester County, described Newsom as “a far-left extreme Democrat who’s probably the front-runner of this (presidential) race right now.” He was surrounded by protesters who waved signs that read things like, “Wrong Coast” and “Clean Up Your State First.”

“We don’t want Gavin Newsom to California our South Carolina,” Westfall said.

Newsom’s team acknowledges widespread dislike for California, even among some Democrats, but argues that the California governor is gifted and experienced at fighting back against such criticism on the national stage. Newsom is a regular on Fox News, he faced Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in a debate and he was the most prominent national surrogate for former President Joe Biden’s campaign.

Newsom acknowledged that California is both a political liability and “the greatest opportunity” because the California story has only been told on the national stage by “people that have ‘California Derangement Syndrome.’” He said it would play far differently if he’s able to reframe the conversation in 2028.

“In a Democratic primary, in particular — we’ve got the receipts, things that the party is arguing for, we’ve delivered across a spectrum of issues,” he told AP.

Indeed, some of the achievements that Republican critics attack him for are the same issues that might play well among Democratic base voters.

California under Newsom’s leadership has enacted progressive priorities such as expanded healthcare coverage regardless of immigration status, expanded paid sick leave, universal free school meals, a $20 minimum wage for fast food workers, protections for women from other states seeking abortions, aggressive climate change and gun control laws and a death penalty moratorium.

California also remains the nation’s most populous state and the world’s fourth-largest economy, even as critics decry the state’s high taxes that have pushed some businesses and residents alike into other states. The population has been growing since a COVID-era dip, however.

While South Carolina voters may have had mixed views on California, several said they were drawn in by Newsom’s celebrity image. The 58-year-old Democrat certainly looked the part of a made-for-TV president as he charmed voters in his plain white dress shirt with his sleeves rolled up and no tie.

“We don’t get that many famous people here in Aiken. He’s pretty famous,” said 73-year-old Monty Fetterolf, who attended one of Newsom’s Friday events in Aiken, S.C.

DeVito, the 78-year-old Democrat from Summerville, said Newsom still has work to do.

“He’s a little slick — not a lot of meat,” she said after listening to his speech in Dorchester. “But he’s good looking, which helps.”

But at the same time, property owners and residents cleared roughly 120 acres of urban forest from residential land, where officials often have little say over the fate of the trees.

Boston has been working hard in recent years to expand its urban forests, including launching a forestry division and prioritizing plantings in the neighborhoods that need them most. But if the city wants to grow more trees, it has to solve a thorny problem: how to stop residents from cutting them down.

“We’re not going to plant ourselves a robust and vibrant urban forest,” said David Meshoulam, the executive director of Tree Boston, an advocacy nonprofit. “We need to preserve those trees that we have.”

According to Boston’s latest tree assessment, the tree canopy — the branches and leaves that cover the ground when viewed from above — grew modestly by 0.5 percent between 2019 and 2024, covering 28.5 percent of the city when excluding the airport. This marked an improvement from the previous five-year period, when there was no net change in canopy coverage. But the city’s gains on open space and rights-of-way land were largely offset by removals on residential properties, which contain the largest share of tree canopy.

Behind those losses are everyday decisions made by developers and residents: Trees are cut down to make room for housing, meet the stipulations of an insurance company, or create a better view. The problem comes when these collective choices constitute a significant loss of trees.

“There is no regulation, no ordinance, or state protection in place over private trees,” said Diana Fernandez Bibeau, the city’s parks and recreation commissioner, though she noted that Boston’s antiquated zoning laws give the city some room to engage with private landowners about their trees.

Some Massachusetts cities and towns have implemented local laws that regulate the removal of trees on private land, including Somerville and Lexington.

In Cambridge, the City Council passed strict protections for private trees in 2019. The city’s most recent tree report, spanning 2018 to 2024, found that residential properties experienced the most canopy growth, increasing by 4.5 percent.

“That difference is hard to ignore,” said Nasser Brahim, the Mystic River Watershed Association’s director of climate resilience, noting that Boston saw a roughly 1 percent decrease in residential tree canopy around the same time.

Cambridge requires residents to seek a permit to remove a tree that has a diameter of 6 inches or more at roughly chest height. Barring special circumstances, such as if the tree is dead or threatens a nearby home, residents must plant replacement trees or pay into a city fund if they want to cut one down.

David Lefcourt, the city arborist, said the private tree protections required extra staff time but did not necessitate standing up an enforcement division. Cambridge hired an assistant city arborist who is responsible for managing removal permits from private property owners and handling the tree planting side of the program.

Lefcourt said residents help keep an eye out for anyone trying to skirt the law: “It’s pretty tough to get away with,” he said. He tells contractors: “It’s going to be the next-door neighbors, it’s going to be the person walking their dog down the street, saying, ‘Hey, something doesn’t look right in this parcel.’”

An effort to pass a similar measure by Boston’s City Council did not gain traction. In 2023, an ordinance was filed that would have included protections for both public and private trees. The language regarding private trees did not make it into the final policy.

The city said at the time that it was adopting a “phased approach,” allowing it to “lead by example before engaging with the community to extend regulations to trees on private property.”

But Brian Swett, Boston’s chief climate officer, said a private tree ordinance is no longer being explored as a solution in the near term.

Instead, officials said, Boston is looking at other approaches, such as “pedestrian easements” that would allow homeowners to plant trees that the city then takes care of. It is also working with community partners to plant more trees on private land.

“We’ve turned the corner where before 2019, the previous decade, we lost canopy coverage,” Swett said, adding, “We’ve shown the art of the possible in the last five years.”

In the meantime, tensions have flared between landowners seeking to remove trees and some residents who say city regulations on these trees are overdue.

In Hyde Park, several trees were cut down behind an apartment complex in June, including one so large that Becky Shuster, 64, couldn’t get her arms around it.

Shuster, who has lived in a house behind the apartment complex for nearly three decades, said, “I sat there and wept.” She said her deck and home are hotter and sunnier, but she is more concerned about the citywide consequences of trees on private property.

“They destroyed a piece of the tree canopy in Boston, and there’s absolutely no accountability,” she said.

Oleg Uritsky, director of Advanced Property Management, which manages the apartment complex, said the company does not want to remove healthy trees, but the trees that were removed were in bad shape and dropping branches on neighbors’ yards.

Uritsky said new regulations on removing private trees would add bureaucracy, expense, and delays to cases when property owners need to move quickly to protect safety and homes.

A few years ago during a winter storm, a tree fell on Uritsky’s home in Newton, narrowly missing a window by his young son’s crib. He has since sought to have a large branch removed from a second “dangerous” tree in front of his house, but he said a company refused to do it, saying a city inspector “would not be happy.” Newton requires residents to seek a permit to remove trees that have a trunk diameter of 6 inches or more.

“Safety comes first, and to have additional red tape — I don’t think it’s a good idea,” Uritsky said.

While Boston figures out its next steps to protect private trees, advocates said the city’s gains on public land, aided by community partners, are nothing to scoff at.

Life as a city tree is an uphill battle, fought against depleted soils, pollutants like car exhaust and dog urine, and sometimes even vandalism. Planting the tree, by comparison, is the easy part.

Tree Boston plants trees and cares for them for two years before turning them over to the city. On a recent weekday morning in Harambee Park in Dorchester, two watering trucks staffed by a crew from the nonprofit moved from tree to tree, pumping 30 gallons into watering bags. Despite temperatures hovering in the mid-70s, the team was sweating. The park has very little tree cover, even along the pathways that run between playing fields.

Marco Lomax, the tree care coordinator for Tree Boston, knelt by a young London plane tree and gave it a shake to check how well it had rooted in the rocky soil. He pointed to the nearby roadway, where cars spew pollutants that coat trees’ leaves and send toxic runoff into the ground. One time, he said, the nonprofit visited a tree it planted to find a pile of beer bottles and the stakes keeping the tree upright torn out and flung across the grass.

“We’re throwing these trees in the deep end,” he said.

Re “Here’s how to get your son to vote” (Opinion, Aug. 31): John Della Volpe’s excellent op-ed is a subject close to my heart. I have taught government and civics in high school, at a community college, and at a county jail. I urge all of my students to vote, but I emphasize that it is not about the national political circus that they see on TV, where so much is just for show and power. Rather, I advise, pay heed to the local and state elections, where you and your vote can make a real difference.

For my men in jail — and indeed for the jail itself — politics is local, as is government. For example, educational and reentry programs are directly important to them and their situation, as is the district attorney race this fall.

I also tell my students that city councilors and state lawmakers are based nearby and that students can get to know them, work on their campaigns, get involved in other ways, and become an agent rather than an object of politics and government. I tell them that candidates seeking office may be their neighbors and that, for the most part, they are good men and women trying to do their best for the community.

Remember that in 2019 Julia Mejia won her Boston City Council seat by a single vote. Voting and participation do matter at this level.
