Since moving, he’s earned six Grammy nominations and released six albums. He’s on a cross-country tour and has 120,000 monthly listeners on Spotify.

Lacossade is one of many Boston musicians who felt they had to leave town to seek fame and fortune. Artists say the music industry in Boston has always been tough — and is only getting tougher.

Since the pandemic, the obstacles for local musicians have multiplied. A slew of performance venues have recently closed, including Thunder Road, ONCE Lounge, and Hennessy’s Bar. At a time of tight budgets, government funding for arts programs has also been slashed.

One of the largest cuts in Mayor Michelle Wu’s $4.9 billion spending plan for the next fiscal year was to the Mayor’s Office of Art and Culture fund, which supports programs for local musicians and artists such as Beat the Odds, Boston Music Project, and the Roxbury Concert Series.

In January 2023, Allston’s Sound Museum, a studio and rehearsal space, was bought out to be turned into biotech labs, displacing hundreds of musicians. The organizers of this year’s BAMSFest, an annual arts festival, decided to save money by getting rid of music performances. That closed a huge door for rising local artists, as each year around five music acts were selected to perform.

Lacossade started in local Boys and Girls Clubs’ studios and studied audio engineering at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. He’s lived in New York and Atlanta and said his fan bases are stronger in those cities than in Boston. With the cost of living here continuing to soar even as resources and opportunities erode, it’s increasingly difficult to make it in Boston as a creative.

“As much as I would love to live in Boston full time, it’s just not realistic,” he said.

His first Atlanta apartment, which he shared with two roommates, only cost him $550 a month and allowed him to save money while trying to make it in the industry. (That would be much tougher in Boston; the average rent for a three-bedroom apartment is now nearly $5,800 per month.)

City officials say the issue isn’t a shortage of artists, but a dearth of infrastructure — performing venues, affordable housing, and grants — to support them.

“We are producing talent, but it’s seemingly hard to keep them here,” said Kenny Mascary, a member of the Boston Art Commission. “We have a $15 billion sector here in Boston, but it’s invisible.”

He told the Globe that less than 1 percent of the new construction approved by the Boston Planning & Development Agency in the last decade was for creative or cultural uses. Meanwhile, over a quarter of Boston residents say they earn their main income from creative work, according to a 2026 city-conducted report.

Sophia Perez, a recent Berklee College of Music graduate, faces a similar dilemma to Lacossade’s. She likes Boston, but constantly tosses around the idea of moving to New York or even Spain to break into the music industry. She moved here with dreams of becoming an R&B singer-songwriter, and thought she’d get a jump-start from attending a renowned music school.

“I left with my degree not knowing what to do,” she said. “I studied songwriting, and I don’t think there [were] any opportunities for songwriting or singing.”

It’s been over a year since Perez graduated, and she spends most days balancing work at a coffee shop with performing gigs, booked through an agency, playing with a band at weddings and corporate events. Those jobs help pay her bills, but after factoring in costs for her music — studio time, engineers, and musicians — it’s hard to make ends meet.

To record her upcoming album, Perez has been seeking grants and searching for venues where she can perform her music. She also wants to build a community with rising musicians. She feels stuck.

Several local artists say that since there’s little of the pie to go around for them, Boston has developed what some refer to as a “crabs-in-a-barrel” mindset, where there’s less camaraderie and mutual support and more unhealthy competition.

Lisa Bello, Boston’s 2009 Female Vocalist of the Year, is a member of the Recording Academy, the nonprofit responsible for Grammy selections. She has been working as an artist for over two decades, and over that time, as an artist and mentor for rising acts, she has witnessed Boston’s music industry change.

“We complain because the OGs that have been in [the industry] 15-plus years know that there were pockets of time where we were fully supported in the city,” Bello said. She believes that time is over.

She said a main turning point was Live Nation’s increasing domination of some of Boston’s most prominent performing venues over the past 20 years through ownership or other management agreements.

When major entertainment corporations control key spaces like Brighton Music Hall, MGM at Fenway, and Citizens House of Blues, getting booked is harder for smaller local artists who may not generate the revenue an out-of-towner could.

“If you’re a new artist here, you’ve got to go through a gamut to even get on stage,” Bello said.

The closures of performance venues heighten competition in ways that ripple beyond the community of area musicians.

Clay Ferno, the publicist and event producer for the Cambridge rock club Middle East, said he prioritizes local acts for the club’s five venues in Central Square, but space is still tight.

“When venues close down, it hurts us because it increases the demand on the room,” he said. “We don’t have enough rooms to sustain those bands.”

As city leaders and nonprofits take stock of the challenges, they are hopeful that Boston can still be a home for musicians.

Mascary said the city is partnering with the Boston Housing Authority to develop new affordable housing and rehearsal space for artists by the end of 2026. He also wants to restore funding to the Mayor’s Office of Art and Culture.

The Record Co., a nonprofit that offers low-cost studio and rehearsal spaces in Dorchester and Roxbury, is working against what many artists see as bad vibes in Boston’s industry. When the Sound Museum closed, many of those artists found new homes with The Record Co.

The nonprofit has also received city grants, but after watching such support fluctuate, CEO Bobby Boyd said the organization hopes to be sustainable without government assistance.

A Dorchester native, he thinks Boston can be like New York and Los Angeles as a place to start a successful music career. Boyd said support for local artistry “should be critical infrastructure,” not an afterthought.

“When we exercise our creative genius,” Boyd said, “that’s when we’re at our best.”

UMass Boston chancellor Marcelo Suárez-Orozco announced on Tuesday that he plans to step down on Feb. 1 and join the school’s faculty to focus on issues related to climate change and artificial intelligence.

Suárez-Orozco will wrap up a six-and-a-half-year tenure leading the public university on the Dorchester waterfront that serves 15,000-plus students. He stabilized the school’s leadership, oversaw the completion of major campus construction, drew big donations from the business world, and helped elevate the school’s status as a research university. He also raised its profile on the world stage though his work with the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences.

In an interview, he described how he felt it was time to make a change with his 70th birthday approaching this month. His wife, Carola Suárez-Orozco, has also retired, and is working as a senior fellow at Boston College.

As an immigrant to the United States from Argentina at age 17, he related to many of the challenges faced by students at UMass Boston, a school known for the diversity of its student body. (In-state tuition is under $17,000 a year for residents, a fraction of what most schools charge.) He credits them for showing “ganas,” the Spanish word for desire or enthusiasm, to get ahead and make a difference.

“This has been the honor of a lifetime,” said Suárez-Orozco, an anthropologist by training. “We’ve achieved everything we set out to achieve [and] our relationship with the city and with the commonwealth has never been better.”

Suárez-Orozco plans to take a sabbatical before focusing on AI and climate change, and their societal impacts — dual issues that already have been the focus of his efforts at the pontifical academy. He said he doesn’t know yet which UMass Boston department he’ll join.

“I have enough energy to really focus on what I believe are, from a scholarly and a humanistic perspective, the big challenges of our time,” said Suárez-Orozco, who came to UMass Boston as chancellor in the summer of 2020.

At that point, UMass Boston had been without a chancellor for three years, following Keith Motley’s departure.

The school had two interim chancellors before UMass president Marty Meehan recruited Suárez-Orozco for the job.

Suárez-Orozco was working as a dean at University of California Los Angeles at the time, though he was familiar with Boston in part because of time he spent on the faculty at Harvard, where he codirected the Harvard Immigration Project with Carola. His wife was also eager to return to the Boston area.

“I love this city. I think it’s an iconic city,” Suárez-Orozco said. “We have tremendous challenges and tremendous opportunities.”

Early on, Suárez-Orozco worked to build bridges between the school and the city’s business community. Those efforts helped lead to partnerships such as an expanded New Balance sponsorship of a sports management program, Paul English’s launch of an AI program at the school, and millions from Robert and Donna Manning to endow the school’s nursing program. In 2023, the school, with the prodding of dean Venky Venkatachalam, launched what would become BEST Boston, a program that aims to harness students’ brainpower to help small businesses.

Meehan said he wasn’t surprised by Suárez-Orozco’s decision to step down; they had discussed it last year, and Suárez-Orozco talked about wrapping up on June 30 this year. Meehan says he persuaded Suárez-Orozco to consider staying in the role for another six months.

“He’s raised [UMass Boston’s] national and global profile as a top-tier research university,” Meehan said. “While I would have loved to keep him [in that position] longer, he was up front with me and said he wanted to do some other things.”

During his six-plus years, Suárez-Orozco was responsible for raising more than $180 million, Meehan said, a new philanthropic record for a UMass Boston chancellor.

Meehan hopes to name an interim leader later this month. Eventually, he’ll assemble a search committee to vet candidates. He expects that committee will submit three candidates to him, and then he’ll pick a top choice to bring to the board of trustees for approval.

While Meehan said he expects a smooth transition, Suárez-Orozco will leave a lasting legacy.

“He’s credited with turning UMass Boston around in many respects,” Meehan said. “He has brought charisma, leadership, and academic credentials that have made UMass Boston and Massachusetts a better place.”

A draft of the Wu administration’s new plan, obtained by the Globe, indicates the city hopes to permit 3,000 new housing units annually over her second four-year term. That’s fewer than the 13,000 she set out to build over her first four years in office, but roughly on pace with construction over the last 18 months.

Boston officials stressed the plan is preliminary — drafted by the city’s top housing officials, it has not been finalized by the mayor herself. But a draft was shared with developers and advocates last week, and it outlines how Wu might address one of Boston’s thorniest challenges in her second term.

The new goal of 3,000 units per year is a relatively low bar for a city with more than 675,000 residents that built far more than that just a few years ago. The goal would, though, mark an uptick from the deep lull of the last three years, the slowest period for new development in Boston since the Great Recession.

That modest target is an acknowledgement of the broad market forces that are slowing housing construction across the country, officials said, as well as the lagging growth in the population in Boston itself.

“Our discussions have been framed by: how do we stretch our goals because production is such an important piece of the puzzle?” said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “But we also don’t want to put out a big round number that we couldn’t achieve in these economic headwinds. We’re trying to thread that needle of something that’s ambitious but possible.”

The high cost of housing is a major issue for Boston, warping the lives of residents across the income spectrum. And the biggest factor keeping prices high and driving them upward, many economists agree, is that there simply aren’t enough homes for everyone who wants to live here.

Rents have declined in cities such as Austin, Texas, that have added a significant number of new units recently. But in Boston, where the rate of building has slowed, rents are still going up.

Wu has, at times, been hesitant to set targets for new construction, citing a commitment to what she describes as a more holistic approach that prioritizes housing for everyone — targeting all the “different stages of life we’re trying to house,” as Bok put it — instead of numerical goals for market-rate building.

This plan follows that same tack.

But developers have frequently complained Wu’s policies — particularly around affordable housing and energy efficiency requirements — have driven up the cost of building and slowed development.

To that end, the draft housing plan includes measures the city hopes may lower costs and boost production, including short-term tax breaks for “high-priority” projects that have been approved but are not financed due to prohibitive construction and borrowing costs.

One challenge is making incentives, such as property tax abatements, meaningful for developers without undermining city finances.

“Tax revenue is what our city runs on, so we have to be really careful about how any abatement is given out,” said Sheila Dillon, the city’s housing chief. “But we are working seriously on using that tool in a targeted way to advance specific, high-quality projects that are truly ready to go if they get that relief. We need housing now, and we need to grow as a city.”

The draft also says City Hall would consider “offering flexibility for how projects meet” Boston’s requirement that 17 percent of units in most new buildings be set aside at affordable rents, plus another 3 percent for Section 8 tenants. Importantly, it stopped short of saying officials would lower the 20 percent target, as some developers have urged. (Wu increased the affordable threshold from 13 percent under her predecessor, Martin J. Walsh.)

Boston would also continue to rework stringent zoning rules to allow for taller and denser housing developments near key transit nodes and in major squares and corridors, the draft plan says, though details were limited. While Boston has moved forward rezoning efforts in some neighborhoods recently, progress has been gradual, and at least one such effort in the Codman Square section of Dorchester was delayed due to pushback from residents.

Wu’s more measured approach to housing development is a shift from Walsh, who preferred to set high long-term goals, at one point saying the city would need to add 69,000 units over a 16-year period, citing population trends.

But growth in Boston has slowed significantly since the COVID-19 pandemic, and when Wu has set housing production goals, they have been more modest.

Her Boston Housing Strategy 2025 said the city would aim to build 13,000 units — 8,300 market rate and 4,700 income-restricted — during her first four years in office.

Those years coincided with rising interest rates and higher materials and construction costs that discouraged construction nationwide; Boston missed its goal by about 1,200 units, permitting 11,804 new homes during that period.

Indeed, 2023 and 2024 were the two slowest years for new housing permits since 2011, with fewer than 2,400 in each. Last year was slightly higher, but still slow, while the first half of 2026 was better yet, with 1,643 units permitted.

That is roughly in line with the goal outlined in the administration’s draft plan, which says that while it’s harder to build now than before, Boston continues to remain ahead of its neighboring communities.

“Boston has far exceeded its share of housing production, while so many others in the region have fallen short,” the plan says.

Much of the strategy focuses on affordable housing, which has been Wu’s top housing priority.

Under her tenure, Boston has built a wave of new subsidized units — funded in part by hundreds of millions of dollars of federal pandemic relief funds. That money is running out, and affordable housing funding generated by new commercial and market-rate housing development is dwindling amid the broader development slowdown.

To offset those losses, the plan says, the city may consider an effort to boost the Community Preservation Act levy it charges property owners. It will also consider tax breaks for affordable housing projects and plans to tweak its Housing Accelerator Fund, a $100 million effort to unlock stalled projects that has not been widely utilized.

The plan also suggests citywide zoning for affordable housing, allowing projects that meet certain affordability requirements in designated locations to build at higher densities. That idea is modeled on a policy Cambridge adopted in 2020 allowing fully-affordable buildings up to 12 and 15 stories tall in key corridors without special approval from a zoning board. And officials said the Boston Housing Authority will continue expanding its affordable housing footprint in the city.

While Boston has policy levers it can pull on its own, many of the Wu administration’s preferred housing solutions — namely, rent control and a small fee on high-dollar real estate transactions to fund affordable housing — hinge on approval from a Legislature that has thus far been skeptical.

Winning over lawmakers and moving forward a broad array of new housing policies, the plan said, is essential to the city’s long-term vitality.

“Boston needs additional market rate housing, but it’s more than this,” said Dillon. “We need a more nuanced, comprehensive plan that also focuses on increased affordability and making sure that all of our populations — including seniors, families with kids, and students — are safely and appropriately housed.“

When she finally returned to Boston last week, the city made sure she knew how much she meant.

Roxbury Prep, one of the launching pads that lifted Mair from Dorchester to the WNBA, hosted a homecoming last Friday, filling the gym with everyone from starstruck students to proud former coaches.

Mair’s mother, Mercy Pineda, sister Trayana, and brother Talik shared emotional messages. Her mother and sister held back tears. Her brother couldn’t.

“She always said, ‘Ma, I’m going to go out there and I’m going to do what I need to do,’ ” Pineda said. “And that’s what she’s doing. And I’m proud.”

State Representative Chris Worrell presented Mair with an official citation and award. Then City Councilor Brian Worrell declared Sept. 4 “Taina Mair Day” in the city.

Mair was overwhelmed, but also honored to be an example for kids who were sitting where she once sat.

“I don’t even know the word for it, but I’m so grateful,” she said. “This is something that, as a kid, you dream of. When you go away and you do great things, and you come back home and the city shows you nothing but love.

“It’s a top-tier feeling. I’ve never felt like this in my life and I’ve won plenty of championships, I’ve won a lot of things in my life, but this is something different.”

Emma Simmons, principal of Roxbury Prep’s Dorchester campus, coached Mair in middle school and remembered the packed gyms for middle school games. She also remembered Mair working as relentlessly in the classroom as she did on the court — the combination set her apart at an early age and sets an example to this day.

“If you ask, I’d say, 25 percent of our kids right now, what do you want to be when you grow up, they’d say basketball player, football player,” Simmons said. “And she’s one of the only ones that I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re going to get there.’

“I just feel grateful that she’s coming back to Roxbury Prep and she sees us as a home and that my current students can look up to her and see her as a real inspiration.”

From AJ Dybantsa, who took Brockton everywhere he went on his journey to becoming the NBA’s No. 1 pick in June, to Veronica Burton, a star at Newton South who’s now the reigning WNBA Most Improved Player and the engine for the Golden State Valkyries, Mair joins a growing list of players carrying Boston-area basketball onto the sport’s biggest stages.

The closest example Mair had when she was growing up would’ve been Roxbury native Shey Peddy, but Mair was 15 by the time Peddy made her WNBA debut in 2019.

“I feel like I didn’t really have anybody, to be honest,” Mair said. “That’s why me coming back is pivotal for the youth. Just being able to be the person that they can look up to and see they can reach these heights.”

Mair signed a player development contract with the Storm in May that allows her to practice and travel with the team, but limits her to 12 regular-season games. She’s played nine this season, six since late July, putting up her most productive night on Aug. 23 in a loss to the Dallas Wings (6 points in 13 minutes).

With the WNBA season coming to a close at the end of the month, Mair said she already has plans to sharpen her game in the offseason in Poland.

“There’s really levels, and you can see it,” she said. “When you get to the pros, there’s a bigger gap because these girls have been playing for 20-plus years and they know their role, they know what they have to do.

“But I think just coming in, figuring out how to adjust my play style, just being a little more physical, understanding that when you get a shot it needs to be knocked down. You’ve just got to be sharper.”

But on a day dedicated to her, Mair was proud to be an example of what’s possible.

“I wear Boston through and through,” Mair said. “Everywhere I go, I’m like, ‘I’m from Boston.’ You can’t tell me nothing. This is the city where I came from, I grew up here, born and raised.

“So to be able to have that is a special gift for what I’ve done for my city. Just being a role model — or trying to be one — I think having that kind of solidifies me as who I am as a person and who I’m trying to be.”

The dispute followed a previous plea discussion before retired Superior Court Judge Mary Ames, who had indicated she would sentence McDermott to three years of probation, prosecutors said.

Wall said he is not bound by the previous discussions and told the two sides the proposed sentences were too far apart for effective negotiations.

He advised prosecutors and McDermott’s defense that if they want to resolve the case with a plea, they should try to reach a joint sentencing recommendation.

“If you don’t have a joint recommendation, prepare for trial,” Wall said.

A trial date is currently scheduled for Sept. 28. The two sides are due back in court on Monday for a status conference.

“We just came forward to try to resolve the case today, and that didn’t happen,” Seed told reporters outside the courtroom. “We do have a trial date for the end of the month, but we’re still working on that.”

McDermott was indicted in 2024 on charges of witness intimidation, seeking criminal record information under false pretenses, and maintaining a gambling nuisance.

His certification to serve as a police officer remains suspended with the state’s oversight board, the Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission. McDermott also remains suspended without pay from the Boston Police Department, according to Sergeant Detective John Boyle, a department spokesperson.

Prosecutors alleged McDermott and Luigi D’Addieco, a suspended campus police officer for the Boston Public Health Commission, operated the unlicensed nightclub at 360B Centre St., where they offered liquor bottle service, hookahs, and a DJ booth.

The operation caught the attention of law enforcement after a 4:30 a.m. shooting at the club in 2021, according to prosecutors. Evan Velez, of Dorchester, allegedly shot at a bouncer several times during a dispute with the club’s promoter.

Police who responded to the shooting recognized McDermott, who was allegedly armed with a gun and among the last people to leave. McDermott allegedly told officers he did not know what was happening and had merely been attending his brother-in-law’s party.

Prosecutors said security video contradicted McDermott’s account, showing him looking out through the club’s front door and stepping over blood and broken glass before police arrived.

Prosecutors also alleged that McDermott later used a police database without authorization to search for information about the shooting and witnesses.

McDermott and D’Addieco had originally rented the basement to run a heating, ventilation, and air conditioning company, according to court records. Prosecutors alleged that during the pandemic they converted it into a nightclub where patrons could buy full bottles of liquor for more than $100.

McDermott pleaded not guilty to all charges at his October 2024 arraignment and was released on personal recognizance.

He sought dismissal of the witness intimidation charge, arguing there was insufficient evidence. A judge denied the motion on June 25, court records show.

Trial dates for both McDermott and D’Addieco have been postponed multiple times, court records show.

D’Addieco has pleaded not guilty to charges of withholding evidence from a criminal proceeding and maintaining a gambling nuisance. He is due to appear in court Sept. 21 for a pretrial conference, court records show.

The Aug. 25 indictment moves the high-profile case to Middlesex Superior Court, where Brown will enter a plea Thursday to an array of charges, including six counts of armed assault to murder, a sole count of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery with a firearm, and four counts of attempted assault and battery with a firearm.

The shooting unfolded around lunchtime on May 11, not long after a Massachusetts parole officer called 911 to report that Brown was suicidal and armed with an assault rifle. The officer said Brown had a long criminal record, including a 2020 shootout with Boston police in the South End, and a history of crack cocaine use and mental health problems; he had recently been discharged from a psychiatric hospital.

Middlesex Assistant District Attorney Nicole L. Allain asked the court to hold Brown without bail under the state’s dangerousness law, noting that his criminal history dates back decades. Brown was arrested as a teenager in 1994 in Michigan and charged with armed robbery. His other convictions include drug and gun offenses in Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

At his arraignment, Allain summarized Brown’s alleged actions, including three phone calls with the parole officer during which he repeatedly said he wanted to end his life and talked about crimes he committed but was not prosecuted for.

“These people are going to pay,” she quoted Brown as telling his parole officer not long before the shooting rampage. “I’m not going back to prison.”

In their final conversation, Brown displayed the gun during a FaceTime conversation, standing in a kitchen the officer didn’t recognize, Allain said.

The officer called 911 and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester, but he wasn’t there when police arrived. Police pinged his phone and tracked him to Cambridge.

Less than two hours after the 911 call, Brown allegedly began randomly shooting while walking down Memorial Drive. Motorists ran for cover, some hiding under their cars.

Brown was taken into custody after a state trooper and a Marine veteran returned fire.

Allain said two bullet holes were found in the driver’s side door of the Marine’s car. At least 70 spent shell casings were recovered, she said.

Allain said one victim was shot four times in one leg and the second was shot in the back of the head.

The shooting victims have been identified by family members as Casimir Bangoura, a Cambridge resident who was driving to the car wash, and another man whose first name is Felix, a father of eight. The family declined to provide his last name but said he was an MBTA Ride driver who drove himself to the hospital.

Brown was on parole for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in the South End in 2020, a case that has raised questions about the relatively lenient sentence he received after a judge was persuaded by his intellectual gifts and his commitment to keeping his life on track.

When Brown was released from prison in May 2025 after serving that sentence, he was accepted into the Tufts University Prison Initiative’s yearlong reentry program that combines college coursework with housing, employment, and other services. According to university officials, Brown stopped attending the program in February.

A development team behind one of New York’s tallest residential skyscrapers intends to build 1,945 homes on a prime South Boston site — property where Southie native Andrew J. Collins long dreamed of building.

New York-based J.T. Magen & Co. and Extell Development in March successfully bid $75 million at a public foreclosure auction — held on St. Patrick’s Day — to buy a collection of industrial property along Dorchester Avenue where it splits from Old Colony Avenue. The site, located midway between the Broadway and Andrew MBTA Red Line stations, is at the heart of a decade-old city plan that called for a corridor of dense, tall development in what is now a low-slung industrial zone.

Now the group has kicked off the city’s formal development-review process, with local partner Thomas O’Brien of The HYM Investment Group this month alerting Boston officials of the plan to build 1.8 million square feet of residential and retail space at 314-420 Dorchester Ave. In terms of space, that’s just a tad larger than the former John Hancock tower in the Back Bay, though the Southie project will be developed as multiple buildings.

Collins, the identical twin brother of state Senator Nick Collins, spent years cobbling together multiple parcels along the Dot. Ave. corridor and pitching a life-science campus there. Despite persuading a number of investors to funnel money toward a project, Andrew Collins never got a development off the ground. Collins has faced a number of lawsuits in state and federal court from investors claiming he owes them around $150 million.

The J.T. Magen, Extell, and HYM development is one of the largest new housing projects proposed in Boston in years. The group envisions a collection of four 200-foot residential buildings with about 45,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and is exploring the potential to bring a grocery store to the site.

None of the buildings would rise higher than 200 feet, O’Brien said. At that height, the buildings would be roughly 18 stories. The project would have underground parking, which costs about $350,000 per space to build.

O’Brien, who last year briefly considered challenging Mayor Michelle Wu’s reelection, declined to share an estimated total development cost. However, new high-rise residential construction in Boston these days can cost more than $1 million per unit to build. The development team hopes to have all permits in hand by early next year.

“The idea is to build as fast as possible,” O’Brien said. “Not much housing is being built right now. ... You’d be delivering those units into a market that has not had much new product, and that’s a really important consideration.”

The anemic pace at which Boston is permitting and constructing housing is a top concern for many residents and the regional real estate development community, many of whom have sought to build outside city limits given the expense of developing in Boston. Approving 2,000 units would help the Wu administration’s preliminary goal of adding 3,000 new units annually over her second four-year term, which started in January.

Capping the buildings’ height at 200 feet aligns with the city’s adopted plan for the Dot. Ave. corridor. Still, because the plan’s guidelines were never incorporated in Boston’s zoning code, the J.T. Magen, Extell, and HYM partnership would need additional approval in order to build anywhere near that high.

The first building would likely be situated on a triangular-shaped parcel, currently home to a parking lot and vacant Castle Self Storage facility. The distinctive shape gives Boston-based architecture firm CBT “an opportunity for a really beautiful design,” O’Brien said.

Extell has built in Boston before, but not for decades. In 2006, the firm built the waterfront Intercontinental Hotel and Residences in downtown.

“These are two groups who are very familiar with Boston, and they understand the basic dynamics of what makes our city great,” O’Brien said.

As for the drive-through Dunkin’ located at 75 Old Colony Ave. in the center of the site, the Extell, J.T. Magen and HYM team intends for it to “stay for as long as possible,” O’Brien said.

“Everybody always says, ‘Hey, the T is a good job. They have good benefits, pension, all that,’ ” he said.

After a training class to learn the ins and outs of operating the light rail, Conveniencia took to the tracks. “It’s muscle memory now,” he said.

Conveniencia bounces between the line’s branches on an often-changing schedule, which is how he likes it. “You’re always seeing something different,” he said, including the cast of characters that boards his trollies. He strives to be the friendly face of an often-unfriendly transit system, taking pride in helping riders navigate diversions, giving tourists directions, and holding the doors for people he sees running to catch the train.

“I know I’m helping everybody get to where they need to go,” he said.

The earnings: Last year, Conveniencia earned about $73,000. Without a college degree or a professional passion, “I didn’t think I would be making this much,” he said. “I’m grateful to be in the position that I’m in.”

And he will soon get a raise. At the end of the month, he said, his roughly $36 hourly wage will grow to about $41, a pay bump built into the MBTA’s union contract. Under the current bargaining agreement, he can expect to make about $49 an hour after he’s been with the T five years.

But those numbers are just on paper. Conveniencia’s biweekly paychecks currently come out to around $1,700 to $1,800, depending on overtime, he said. Deductions for health insurance (about $230), union dues (about $50), and the MBTA retirement fund (about $300) each cut into his take-home pay.

The steady pay, plus the promise of a pension, means Conveniencia is inclined to stay with the MBTA for the long haul. Plus, he knows the job has stability in a topsy-turvy labor market.

When it comes to the T, “I don’t think AI is going to take over,” he said.

The expenses: Conveniencia pays $1,500 a month in rent for an income-restricted studio apartment in Mission Hill, which he found through Metrolist, a city database. It’s a big discount, with the normal rent for such a unit topping $3,000, he said. Utilities, meanwhile, are all on him. He tries to budget at least $300 a month for gas, electricity, Internet, and water.

As for transportation, he sticks to riding the T — his badge gets him free rides — and the occasional Bluebike. Until late last year, he drove a Honda Civic, which cost $800 a month between the car payment and insurance, he said. But in November, he got into an accident, and decided to give it up.

About once a month, Conveniencia goes to Stop & Shop or Price Rite for a big grocery trip, and his last one cost about $200, he said. On workdays, he tends to eat fruit or toast for breakfast, bring leftovers or fruit to work to avoid buying lunch, and turn to simple dinner recipes.

“My meals will pretty much always consist of rice, some type of meat, and beans,” he said.

One more regular expense? “I work in the public, and I just want to make sure I look my best at all times,” he said, so he spends $35 on a weekly barbershop visit.

The debt: While Conveniencia now tries to keep his regular expenses to a minimum, he wasn’t always so prudent.

After getting his first credit card at 19, he began swiping with abandon, recalling dropping “like, $1,000″ on hauls of trendy clothing, or high-end sneakers, his kryptonite. “When I do shop, I kind of go crazy,” he said.

Eventually, he said, he racked up close to $10,000 in credit card debt. “The bulk of it was really just pointless purchases,” he said, plus the ensuing interest and late fees. When his cards maxed out, he turned to the “buy now, pay later” service Klarna, which breaks up purchases into smaller installments. Earlier this year, for instance, he paid for an $860 laptop in four $215 chunks.

“Everything’s at your hands,” he said. “It’s hard to break out of the habit.”

But, finally, he did, once he realized he wanted to buy a house one day, and with the milestone of his 25th birthday approaching.

He made it his mission to free himself of credit card debt by his March birthday, promising himself a trip to the Dominican Republic, where his family is from, if he could do it. Once he no longer had his car to pay for, he began funneling around $1,500 a month to dig himself out of the financial hole, he said.

“I had to cut down on everything,” he said — and he means everything. “I was dating at the time, and basically, I just had to say, ‘I can’t afford to be in a relationship right now,’ ” he said.

In the end, he pulled it off, and booked the Caribbean getaway — on a debit card.

Now that Conveniencia is back in the black, “I feel like a weight’s been lifted off my shoulders,” he said. But the experience left its mark. He limits using credit cards and removed them from his phone’s Apple Pay — while still trying to improve his credit score — and resists Klarna.

“I kind of scared myself,” he said. “I’m still kind of recovering from that.”

The outlook: For Conveniencia, that recovery means unlearning the bad habits that he observed growing up, where “everybody around me maybe drives a really nice car, but might not have enough money to afford the really nice car,” he said.

Don’t get him wrong — he still splurges occasionally, such as on a $220 pair of Nike Jordan shoes or, yes, on a date, where he always expects to spend at least $100. But these days, he tries to follow a simple maxim: “If you don’t have the money to do what you’re trying to do, just don’t do it,” he said.

Beyond that, he’s taking steps to improve his financial literacy, such as reading up on starting a Roth IRA account.

“I was living reactively,” he said. “Now I’m trying to live proactive, so I don’t have to react to my bad decisions.”

The goal: Like so many Boston residents, “my goal is to buy a home,” Conveniencia said. No one in his family owns their home here, he said, and he wants the security of knowing he won’t “get priced out of my city.”

He took one of Boston’s homebuyer classes, which qualifies him for financial assistance programs. “After a year of saving, I want to see how much I’ve saved and see where I can go from there,” he said.

He currently has about $2,500 in his savings account, he said, and he is currently trying to set aside $1,000 a month — money that once went toward paying off debt — with the hope of accumulating at least $12,000 by next September. “Is that possible? I’m not sure,” he said.

It’s something he feels good about working toward. The idea of taking out a mortgage? Not so much.

“I worked so hard this year to get rid of my debt, to now get into a debt of 30 years,” he said. “Granted, at the end of those 30 years, I’ll have something, but I’m like, ‘Man, does it ever end?’ ”

A vocal movement of opponents warned Thursday: “This is not a done deal.”

Roughly three dozen people called for the elimination of the proposed center-running bus lane in a protest march down Blue Hill Avenue before the meeting. Business owners at the meeting raised concerns that changes to the street, and parking, will spell doom for their storefronts. And dozens of public commenters accused public officials of, once again, not listening to the people of Black Boston, arguing that changes to the avenue will be the harbinger of gentrification.

When Bishop John Borders III asked opponents of the project to stand, half the room rose.

“They have a meeting, but they don’t really listen to us,” said Cynthia Grant Carter, 54. “What’s wrong with what we got?”

The $163 million trove of public money set aside for Blue Hill Avenue would not only go toward adding the bus lane, but also narrowing pedestrian crossings, planting 200 trees, and replacing street lighting — beautification and safety improvements many agree are sorely needed.

The latest proposal preserves roughly 11 of the existing 14 miles of car-travel lanes from Grove Hall through Mattapan Square and increases the total number of parking spots to 717 from 675. It separates some parts of the thoroughfare for car travel during rush hour and parking in off-peak periods.

In the meeting, Wu cited conversations with more than 3,000 people, saying they informed how City Hall and the T created the latest redesign, block by block.

“This is part of a big-picture plan to put dollars where they need to be to ensure we have equity throughout the city and opportunity in every neighborhood,” she said.

In the meeting, just five residents spoke to say they back the plan; two others raised concerns about the pullback of some proposed bike lanes in the latest design.

Carmen Blyden, director of community organizing at Bikes Not Bombs, said she “supports the project” but asked for additional bike parking on the avenue. Tony Baez, a cycling advocate, made the final remarks before public comment was cut off nearly an hour after the meeting’s scheduled 8 p.m. end time.

“I support this project today, just like I did a year ago,” he said. “We are asking drivers to give up 20 seconds, so that bus riders can get 15 minutes.”

But few meeting attendees were otherwise on board.

City councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper called for “real alternatives” to the plan, including a feasibility study on bringing rail back to the corridor. The two councilors have proposed extending the Orange Line subway beneath the street, though Wu’s office has warned it “would take many years ... and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment.”

There’s been long-standing frustration among residents about decades of neglect on the avenue dating to the 1950s, when the streetcar trolley along it was eliminated.

The MBTA previously committed to looking into a rail expansion, and Eng — serving as both the leader of the T and the state’s interim secretary of transportation — said on Thursday that the bus lane “does not preclude future discussions of rail.”

Public officials said Thursday the changes announced last week would immediately make the corridor safer. Blue Hill Avenue is frequently congested and accident-prone, with a crash requiring emergency medical services every three days on average, according to city data.

Justin Rodriguez, a 33-year-old Dorchester resident, said the center-running bus lane would be an “interference” to his commute as a regular bus rider. And frankly, he said he isn’t inclined to trust public officials, even when it comes to repaving sidewalks.

“If the idea didn’t come from people who are here every day, where did it come from?” Rodriguez asked. “These projects happen. We are never asked.”

Muhammed Uddin, owner of American Food Mart on Blue Hill Avenue, said the congestion and parking impacts he believes the center-running bus lane would hurt his business, which opened in 2024.

“It’s going to slow down everything,” Uddin said. “You want the street widely open.”

Dana Dowell, a lifelong Mattapan resident, said she’s “for beautifying our neighborhood and better infrastructure.” But not like this.

“This decision is being forced down our throat,” she said.

Still, some residents hope City Hall backtracks entirely and leaves their neighborhood untouched.

Gwendolyn McLaurin lives around the corner from Blue Hill Avenue and regularly takes the 28 and 31 bus. She believes the city and state should simply back off. No bus lane, no new rail line, no touching the sidewalks.

“There’s already not enough room for everybody. It’s not fair,” she said. “It should stay the way it is.”

Two open houses where public officials plan to share the block-by-block redesign will take place on Monday and Sept. 22 in Dorchester and Mattapan respectively. A final town hall is planned for Sept. 30, which Wu also plans to attend.

There were, according to court documents released Thursday, many close calls on May 11 when Tyler E. Brown IV allegedly opened fire seemingly at random on cars and buildings on Cambridge’s busy Memorial Drive. The mayhem injured two people but, despite the hail of bullets fired in multiple directions, did not kill any of the scores of drivers, pedestrians, or neighbors in harm’s way.

“His actions created chaos, confusion and fear in the motorists, pedestrians, workers, residents and shoppers who were in that area,” Assistant District Attorney Nicole Allain wrote in a court filing released Thursday.

The documents offer the most detailed picture yet of the events leading up to the violence, a portion of the path taken by the high-powered weapon he is accused of using in the attack, and just how close the shooter came to causing more harm than he allegedly did.

Brown, 46, of Dorchester, pleaded not guilty Thursday to 43 counts against him for the shooting, including assault to murder. He appeared in Middlesex Superior Court in a wheelchair and said “hello” and “not guilty,” but nothing else, during a brief hearing.

Brown’s attorney, Carolyn McGowan, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Prosecutors had previously said in court filings that Brown, who had a long rap sheet, had been released from a psychiatric hospital days earlier and was reportedly using crack cocaine.

The outbreak of violence had come with a warning. His parole officer had called 911 to report Brown was suicidal and armed.

Shortly after, investigators said, Brown took an Uber to Kelly Road in Cambridge, before walking to the parking lot of a Dunkin’ Donuts on Memorial Drive.

There, the document says, he approached a man and asked “how he felt about law enforcement and told him that he had ‘served 25 years’ and was ready to ‘take anyone out.’”

Shortly after, the gunman fired bullets at a different car, striking its driver several times. That victim has not been publicly named but has been identified by family members as Casimir Bangoura, a Cambridge resident. He is expected to recover from his injuries.

The other man who was injured was the driver of an MBTA Ride van, who had made a U-turn to flee the shooting when one or more bullets traveled through a rear window, a plastic shield, and a seat before hitting the driver in the back of his head.

The man, previously identified by family as Felix, a father of eight, reportedly drove himself to the hospital and was released that same day.

The bullet fragment, which caused “no serious physical injuries,” was later removed, the document said.

At one moment, the court document said, as the gunman shot into cars stopped at a red light on Memorial Drive, a bullet sailed into the rear lift gate of a USPS truck and through a metal divider, grazing a jacket draped over a driver’s seat before flying through the windshield, only narrowly missing the driver.

At another, the gunman approached a car and smashed its driver-side window with the firearm — but only after the driver had already fled.

Meanwhile, it described how two women inside a school bus van managed to flee as the gunman fired at their vehicle, hitting a side mirror, but missing them. The women, who earlier described their harrowing experience to a reporter, were not injured.

The frenzy ultimately came to an end when a Marine veteran who happened to be driving by pulled a gun from his own car and began firing at the suspect, subduing him.

The unnamed Marine and a state trooper who also traded fire with the gunman were unharmed, even as two bullets penetrated the Marine’s driver-side door.

It was still not clear in court documents how Brown may have come to own the firearm he allegedly used. As a convicted felon, he would not have been allowed to possess it legally.

Records showed the gun, a BCI-Defense Model FF-15, was first bought legally in 2015. Its owner then transferred the gun’s receiver to someone in Maine, who sold it two years later to another person in Maine, who “built an AR pistol from the receiver,” then sold it online in either 2018 or 2019.

The firearm sold again in 2019, either online or at a gun show, prosecutors said. That owner died, and there was no other record of how the gun exchanged hands after.

The charges against Brown include six counts of armed assault to murder, a sole count of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery with a firearm, and four counts of attempted assault and battery with a firearm.

Brown had been held without bail since an earlier arraignment on eight gun-related counts following the May 11 shooting.

Brown had been on parole for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in the South End in 2020, a case that has raised questions about the relatively lenient sentence he received after a judge was persuaded by his intellectual gifts and his commitment to keeping his life on track.

When Brown was released from prison in May 2025 after serving that sentence, he was accepted into Tufts University Prison Initiative, a yearlong reentry program that combines college coursework with housing, employment, and other services. According to university officials, Brown stopped attending the program in February.

He is due back in court for a dangerousness hearing set for Oct. 8.

Featuring: Gogi Gupta, John Civello, Ben Heller, Bryan Sparkes, Mike Simonelli, Don Chiofaro, Rachel Flor, Danny Lewin, Tom Leighton, Brooks Tingle, Seow Hui Lim, Maggie O’Toole, Edwin Tong, Lui Tuck Yew, Sumbul Siddiqui, Jesse Baerkahn, Mike Minogue, and more.

For one night each year, the Boston skyline takes on a shade of sky blue.

John Civello witnessed it a year ago after leaving work late. The drive across the Longfellow Bridge was one he will never forget. Civello heads up real estate at Akamai Technologies, which had just put up blue lights atop its Cambridge headquarters as a tribute to those who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. He stayed after hours to make sure the installation went OK.

While crossing the Charles, Civello was struck by what he saw in that postcard-perfect view. Tower after tower, lit up with blue. Only then, Civello recalls, did he realize how many others were participating.

This will be the third year Boston hosts our own version of the “Tribute in Light” that takes place in Manhattan each September. There will be more buildings aglow on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the attacks, than there were during Civello’s drive in 2025 — more than 30, in total.

It all began with a pitch from Boston marketer Gogi Gupta two years ago. The founder of Gupta Media emailed business leaders with an idea. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum in New York sends up two beams of blue light every year, an ethereal evocation of the World Trade Center towers, and nearby skyscrapers are lit up in solidarity. Boston, Gupta suggested, should join in.

Gupta was inspired after rereading an excerpt of Garrett Graff’s “The Only Plane in the Sky,” an account of the fateful day. Also, a college classmate from Cornell, Allison Blais, was then the 9/11 Memorial’s chief strategy officer. Mostly, Gupta worried the painful memories were fading as a new generation that only knows 9/11 from history books reached adulthood.

To find real estate contacts, Gupta turned to his leasing brokers at JLL, Ben Heller and Bryan Sparkes, and Mike Simonelli of Structure Tone, the firm that outfitted his Back Bay office.

That first year, it was short notice, less than two days in advance. Many companies need time to hire a contractor; it’s not like flicking on a switch for them. But several prominent tower owners, including BXP and the Chiofaro Co., made it happen.

For Don Chiofaro, there was no question he would light up International Place. He thinks about the firefighters who rushed into the burning World Trade Center, with 70 pounds of equipment on their backs, knowing they might not make it out. That kind of public service doesn’t get appreciated, he says, until it’s needed the most.

This year, the JFK Library illuminates its nine-story atrium overlooking Dorchester Bay. The blue lights went on at dusk on Tuesday, and are being rekindled each night through Friday. Foundation executive director Rachel Flor says it’s an important reminder of the service and sacrifice that we witnessed 25 years ago.

Many of Boston’s tallest office towers will be lit up. Among them: One Financial, South Station, the Pru, One Congress, 100 Federal. At 200 Berkeley St., aka the “Old Hancock Tower,” home to insurer John Hancock, the famous weather beacon at its tip will be lit in blue. CEO Brooks Tingle hopes it can remind people of the resilience, unity, and spirit of service that emerged that day.

For Akamai, it’s personal. Cofounder Danny Lewin, then 31, died in one of the two commandeered planes that took off from Logan. He’s considered the first 9/11 victim, believed to be stabbed after trying to stop the hijackers on American Airlines Flight 11. Lewin remains revered at Akamai; its highest employee award is given out each year in his honor.

Last year, Gupta emailed chief executive Tom Leighton, Lewin’s mentor when they were at MIT, asking Akamai to join. Leighton told Civello: Let’s see if we can make this happen. Civello got to work, and building owner BXP gave its blessing. Contractor Stagedge assembled 90 lights around the roof, echoing the blue shade that would appear on so many buildings across the Charles.

Word is getting out to other cities, too. More than 50 buildings outside of Manhattan — around half of them here — will be lit with blue on Friday night. The next highest concentration? Hartford, where Blais, Gupta’s college friend, now leads The Wadsworth museum.

Every July 4, fireworks light up the night sky in Boston.

Gupta hopes for something similar every Sept. 11, with building crowns alight in blue, sending a simple but powerful message: We remember.

Singapore is the latest country to put down roots in Massachusetts, announcing on Wednesday that it has opened a trade office at the Cambridge Innovation Center in Kendall Square. It’s the fifth US outpost for Enterprise Singapore, the economic development agency that helps Singaporean companies grow globally. The agency also signed an agreement with the Massachusetts Office of International Trade and Investment to encourage collaboration in key sectors including life sciences, climate tech, advanced manufacturing, robotics, and artificial intelligence. Singapore companies already operating here include defense firm MAK Technologies and air cargo handler Worldwide Flight Services. Because Singapore is geographically smaller than Rhode Island, businesses must look abroad to expand. “It’s a survival instinct,” explained Seow Hui Lim, who oversees Enterprise Singapore’s US division. Leaders gathered at a reception at Raffles Boston to celebrate, including Singapore Minister for Law Edwin Tong, Singapore’s Ambassador to the US Lui Tuck Yew, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, Cambridge Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, Massachusetts economic secretary Eric Paley, and Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce CEO Jim Rooney.

We’ve been as disappointed as most Bostonians to see Faneuil Hall Marketplace struggle with an identity crisis and a backlog of repairs. But here’s some good news: The marketplace’s ground-floor retail occupancy is now 85 percent, up from 76 percent in 2024 when new owner J. Safra Real Estate took over. First, OpenAI raised a stink about the state Senate’s proposed crackdown on artificial intelligence. Now, the complaints are coming from a giant trade group representing most of the biggest names in tech (Amazon, Google, Meta, et al). That group, NetChoice, published a 1,100-word treatise to Beacon Hill conferees on Tuesday about a measure under consideration for an economic development bill that would require large AI companies to undergo third-party evaluations of possible catastrophic risks every 120 days. NetChoice says this frequent testing, which is supported by AI developer Anthropic, is untenable — particularly with another provision spelling out the state attorney general’s enforcement powers. The group says it’s ready to work with lawmakers as they finalize the bill on guardrails that don’t put these big “AI labs” in legal jeopardy or harm innovation. Not the best timing for Big Tech: A day after NetChoice’s testimony came out, an Anthropic researcher announced to the world that he believes there’s more than a 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade.

The rap on Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue is that he has been light on details about his agenda. On Thursday morning, as he attended a rally at Shea Concrete in Amesbury, Minogue unveiled his much anticipated “Blueprint for a Better Future.” What caught our attention: the focus on energy costs, which is a big concern for residents and businesses alike. Minogue wants to cut state mandates from utility bills (which represent as much as a third of the cost of electricity), expand natural gas capacity, and evaluate nuclear energy options. He also would support enacting a gas tax holiday whenever prices at the pump exceed $4 a gallon, which they currently are. How to pay for these policies? One way: Cancel the state’s “net zero” mandate, a sustainability goal that he says costs taxpayers billions of dollars.

Producing more housing is another priority, and Minogue says he would incentivize towns to eliminate energy-efficiency “stretch” codes for buildings and reduce permitting times for single-family homes to 45 days or less. He also would not enforce the MBTA Communities Act, and instead work with municipalities that worry about the strain from new housing on infrastructure and schools.

The upshot: Minogue is staying on the Republican message of cutting taxes and government spending. Appealing to voters on affordability is a textbook political move, but we still don’t have enough details about how the math works out.

As I approached my own 15th birthday more than a decade ago, I thought having a quinceañera meant following all its traditions or not having one at all. If only I could’ve seen my niece’s celebration — eight years later — which began with her in a lilac gown and soccer cleats, and ended with her and her cousins playing soccer behind the outdoor dance floor.

The quinceañera’s roots trace back centuries to the Indigenous civilizations of the Maya and Aztec people; the ceremony honored a young woman reaching maturity. In the 1500s, Spanish missionaries and colonizers settled in the Americas and adapted the ceremony to reflect Roman Catholic beliefs and European court traditions, which led to the addition of a Mass, crowns, and elaborate gowns.

Evolving to celebrate the broader sense of womanhood, the event gained in popularity, spreading farther into South America, the Caribbean, and, eventually, the United States. Over time, different countries developed their own unique practices.

Even within my family, the associated traditions have changed since we came to the United States from Peru nearly 40 years ago. Nine years after Angelica’s magical quinceañera, I got my chance to be part of another prima’s court celebration in Connecticut.

The birthday girl (who, like the event, is also called the quinceañera, or quince), traditionally has a court of 14 girls, called damas, symbolizing each year of her life so far. Each dama has a gentleman escort, or chambelán.

Today, though, traditional courts are rarer. “Back in the day, when we had our quinces...it was still a thing to have 15 damas,” says Karla De La Rosa, founder of the Quinceañera & Sweet 16 Expo of New England, an annual Rhode Island trade show attended by about 250 people. “Now, some [people] don’t even have them.”

Madrinas (godmothers or female sponsors) and padrinos (godfathers or male sponsors) act as mentors to the quince, participating in the ceremony and helping out financially with specific items for the event. A relative or close friend gives the brindis (toast), paying tribute to the relationships within the quinceañera’s life and the community she has built.

In my family, there’s a moment during the celebration where we form a line to dance with the birthday girl and offer her our congratulations. However this custom came to be, it’s our way of expressing togetherness.

Pedro Aguirre and Raúl Garcia II had dreamed about what their daughter’s quinceañera would be like since she was born. The couple, who live in Roxbury, began saving for the celebration when she was still an infant.

This past June, they hosted Luna Garcia Aguirre’s long-awaited celebration, themed “A Night Under The Moon,” at The Cedars Center in Jamaica Plain. The ballroom, decorated in glittering black and gold, featured an elaborate throne at the front. Pedro and Raúl watched their daughter glide across the ballroom in a gold and black gown, greeting their friends and family as mariachis played. “It does truly become a celebration of the woman you see her becoming,” Pedro says.

“As Guatemalan and Mexican men, we knew that it was important to continue that with her in front of our family that maybe didn’t expect us to hold certain traditions,” Raúl tells me. “And sometimes, when we do some things, they end up being a little different — because we are different also.” Some relatives who chose not to attend Pedro and Raúl’s wedding 22 years ago were there to watch them present their daughter — to celebrate Luna and share their story as a family with this loving community they built together over the years and across regions.

“It meant so many different things to me,” Luna says. “Being Latina, it was such a good moment for me to really feel that aspect of myself and my community” — including, she emphasizes, “family” not related by blood.

Luna’s chosen madrinas — Pedro’s eldest sister and Raúl’s cousin — gifted her traditional Mexican accessories from Veracruz: a headband, hairpiece, and skirt. In Spanish, both women spoke about what an honor it was to watch her become the wonderful young woman she is. “It just made me feel so thankful,” Luna says. “I was so emotional.”

Although more than half of the guests were not Spanish speakers and had never attended a quince before, the emotions behind the speakers’ words were evident. Pedro says there was not a dry eye under that sparkly moon.

“I know there’s a lot of history attached to the quinceañera. It’s probably a little antiquated, but we just thought, Let us make it our own, let’s have a party, let’s pass on a tradition,” Pedro says. “We get to redefine it.”

For their father-daughter dances, both dads surprised Luna with pop songs they chose — orchestral covers of “Complicated” by Avril Lavigne and “The Only Exception” by Paramore — and they each got a turn to waltz with their daughter.

Luna’s quinceañera included a court, and the traditional ceremony of the changing of her shoes (more on that later). But she personalized moments to reflect herself at this stage in her life and omitted parts, including the Catholic Mass before the celebration, that she doesn’t identify with.

She chose to focus on female empowerment: An all-women mariachi band performed, and her court consisted solely of six damas (no chambelanes). “She wanted it to be about her and her girls,” Pedro says.

Across the country, designated themes for quinceañeras have become a big trend, industry professionals say, though some stick with the more traditional quince, including a white gown and simpler, classic decor.

Jynia Laury, who goes by Nia, transported guests to the world of Alice in Wonderland in Holyoke in 2024. After watching the Disney movie as a child, she’d fallen in love with the character of Alice. Vivid flowers and butterfly decorations created an enchanting garden setting in the ballroom, and “drink me” potions and “eat me” cookies set the scene for Nia to make her appearance in an Alice-inspired, shimmering, sky-blue gown.

Born in Colombia, Nia’s mother, Lori Goshea, was adopted by an American family and raised on Long Island. She didn’t get to have a quinceañera, but hoped to continue Colombian traditions with her daughter.

It took Lori and Nia eight months to plan the whimsical celebration for more than 150 guests. Nia, now 17, had a specific vision and talked it through with her mother — which traditions to keep and what she wanted to do differently.

Nia and her mom danced to “Blue” by Beyoncé — the artist’s tribute to her own daughter — in a meaningful parent-child moment. For the father-daughter dance, Nia glided across the floor holding a photo of her father, who is incarcerated, adorned in a gold frame. “She came up with the idea,” Lori says. “The father-daughter dance was really sad, touching. ... She looked up to him, growing up.”

Nia says she felt a powerful sense of “being celebrated ... getting a little bit older, maturing, and surrounding myself with family.”

On the morning of July 20, 2024, my mother’s backyard in Connecticut metamorphosed into an outdoor ballroom for my niece Kayley Rodriguez’s Sweet 16. The ivory tents were set up, the glossy dance floor in place; all that was left were the decorations. Then the torrential downpour began. We all rushed outside to hold the tents down, working together for about 40 minutes. It was some true family bonding.

Kayley was the first in our immediate family to have such an event; my mother, sister, and I were either too shy or couldn’t afford a quince or Sweet 16. And we had waited an extra year to save up for Kayley’s celebration, which is why it included numerous quinceañera traditions. We weren’t going to let rain get in the way.

The sky was completely clear the rest of the day. Family and friends watched tearfully as Kayley waltzed with her father, then her mother and sister, and participated in the changing of the shoes and the crowning ceremony.

During the “changing of the shoes,” the father or a father figure ceremoniously replaces the quinceañera’s slippers with high heels, symbolizing her transition into womanhood. Now, young women are swapping their slippers for sneakers — or exchanging their high heels, as everyone looks on, for a customized, bedazzled pair of Jordans or Nikes.

Surrounded by soccer fans in my family and circle of friends, it’s no surprise that I know not just one but two young women who traded in their soccer cleats for glittering high heels at their parties. For the crowning, as the tradition goes, a tiara or crown is placed on the quinceañera’s head by her parents, godparents, grandparents, or another close relative. Kayley got a traditional tiara from her dad, but at my cousin Angelica’s celebration, she received a necklace and ring from her madrina and padrino.

After the formal waltz by the court and the father-daughter dance, there’s el baile de sorpresa (surprise dance), choreographed and performed by the birthday girl along with her court. This tradition usually includes modern dance styles chosen by the quinceañera. At the quince for another one of my cousins, the surprise dance included hip-hop moves and ended with two of her damas waving the Peruvian and Puerto Rican flags in honor of her heritage. Luna’s blended disco, R&B, pop, norteño, and other genres.

As special as quinceañeras are to many young Latina and Hispanic women, plenty of us never had one. The most common reason I’ve heard is the cost. But financial barriers are nothing new. Like Pedro Aguirre’s sisters, who longed for a quinceañera, none of my aunts was able to have one. None, that is, except my tía Gladys Salcedo, who had hers in Lima in 1976. Growing up, Gladys felt excitement at turning 15. With 10 children to provide for, my grandparents postponed Gladys’s event until they had enough savings for a modest dress, a cake, and plenty of food. At 17, she celebrated her quince in a short-sleeved, baby blue dress, surrounded by her friends and family.

Here in the States, today’s price tags range from about $2,000 for a small-scale celebration to as much as $60,000 for something extravagant, according to New Dawn Photo, a quinceañera photography and videography business based in Dallas -Fort Worth that analyzed 80 actual budgets. New Dawn Photo is also behind a Facebook group called Quinceañeras on a Budget, set up for people to exchange planning advice and tips.

In New England, quinces usually run from $8,000 to $15,000, De La Rosa estimates. Catering, venue, and photography expenses add up quickly on top of formal wear for the family.

Operations specialist Celeste Ribeiro Hewitt at Spinelli’s, a popular venue with branches in East Boston and Lynnfield, says she has noticed quinceañeras becoming smaller in size in recent years, after peaking before COVID. “I would say, post-COVID, the way people celebrate things in general are a little bit different,” she says. The East Boston location services about 24 to 30 quinceañeras a year, either in-house or for catering. “They happen almost as frequently as weddings, and that’s multiple per month.”

Instead of a party, some parents offer a trip as quieter way to celebrate. My mother and I drove along California’s coast for my 15th birthday — the most meaningful trip I’ve taken to this day.

Maybe when I reach 50, decades from now, I’ll decide to have a cincuentañera, like some women who didn’t get a big celebration of womanhood in their teens are doing now.

I asked my cousin Angelica what her quince means to her, over a decade later. “What stands out [was] the unity I was able to have with my family, the experience alone, how beautiful everything was, and how beautiful I felt,” she says. “And how I was able to enjoy that with friends and family.”

Michael T. Minogue, that is.

The eponymous donor popped on the Republican candidate’s latest campaign finance report after he donated $75 in mid-August. Sure, that’s not going to buy a whole lotta airtime, but it prompted us to wonder, just who is this other Mike Minogue?

Well, Minogue’s New York namesake is a 25-year veteran of the New York Police Department who retired in 2020. The 56-year-old was born and raised in Brooklyn’s Windsor Terrace neighborhood, a residential enclave near Prospect Park where he lives with his family, including a 16-year-old son named — you guessed it — Michael R. Minogue. (His middle name is Rourke; the gubernatorial candidate’s is Roger).

The retired dad of two stumbled across his Massachusetts doppelnamer late last month, when he met up with a friend for a Mumford & Sons concert at Madison Square Garden.

That friend had just moved to Massachusetts, Minogue said, “and she goes, ‘You’re not going to believe this, but there’s a guy running for governor named Mike Minogue.’ I go, ‘Get the hell out.’”

Naturally, he looked him up.

“I’m sitting at the concert and I find his site,” he said in a phone interview this week. “I go, ‘Holy [expletive]! There is a guy, Michael Minogue.’ And so I got some of his merch.”

In addition to adding the $75 worth of Minogue gear to his cart that doubled as his campaign donation — he bought a “Mike Minogue” hat and a “Minogue for Governor” shirt, and a hoodie is on the way — he said he’s also toying with buying a campaign flag for a property he owns by the water in Breezy Point, Queens. He then promptly started spreading the news.

“I started sending it out to my buddies, like, ‘Hey, look, I’m running for governor’ — you know, as a joke,” he said.

But the joke took off in his close-knit community, and Minogue and his buddies — mostly friends he’s known since kindergarten who still live in the neighborhood — have been lightly following the race since.

“My friends were like, ‘Wow, he just destroyed his opponent over in Massachusetts,’” he said, after Minogue (the candidate) handily beat Brian Shortsleeve in the GOP primary last week.

The merch is already getting a lot of use. The New York Minogue spent Labor Day weekend at his Queens beach property, where the neighborhood celebrates the end of summer with an annual “Mardi Gras” parade (Who cares when the actual holiday is!). He showed up decked out in the full Mike Minogue for Governor ensemble.

One piece in particular is already becoming a wardrobe staple. “This will be my main hat going forward,” he said. “It’s actually a pretty nice hat.”

Massachusetts’s political scene has seen its share of same-named pols and political figures over the years. There’s Charlie Baker, the Democratic operative, and Charlie Baker, the Republican former governor. There are multiple people named Marty Walsh, too — Martin J. Walsh, the former Boston mayor and former US Labor Secretary; his cousin,Martin F. Walsh, a local labor leader; andMarty Walsh of Natick, who once served as an aide to former US Senator Ted Kennedy (and once got an accidental call from Joe Biden looking for Marty Walsh, the mayor).

And state Representative William C. Galvin’s retirement announcement earlier this year caused some confusion. Secretary of State William F. Galvin, who once hinted his current term would be his last, is indeed back on the ballot this fall.

But Minogue, the one from New York, is far less likely to be mistaken for the ultra-wealthy GOP gubernatorial nominee who lives hundreds of miles away.

The New York Minogue, admittedly, is “not the most political individual in the world,” he said, but he is involved with his local Knights of Columbus chapter and, when he does tune into the political realm, leans right.

“People did say to me, you better make sure he’s a Republican before you put his shirt on,” he said.

As for his take on President Trump, the Republican president who Democratic Governor Maura Healey has sought to center in the gubernatorial race here?

“I do agree with a lot of his stuff,” the New York Minogue said. “Maybe not his personality, right? He’s a little aggressive at times. But I do agree with his policies.”

But it wasn’t the Massachusetts Minogue’s policies or past support of Trump that drew the Brooklyn native to the candidate.

No, his reason for his interest in the race was simple: “My name, and his name.”

SAFETY NET: Healey got a fresh boost Thursday in her effort to shore up her public-safety bona fides as she faces a challenge from her right, landing endorsements from four of the state’s major law enforcement unions.

Leaders of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, Massachusetts Coalition of Police, State Police Association of Massachusetts, and State Police Commissioned Officers Association of Massachusetts gathered in Dorchester to encourage voters to cast their ballot for the former attorney general in November. Healey cast herself as the “cheerleader-in-chief for law enforcement.”

McLaughlin joined the company’s accounting department in 2002, back when Cabot was one of the few major businesses with offices in what is now known as the Seaport. The biotech industry is in full swing, with deals activity happening at a breakneck pace and investors’ dollars pouring into new treatments. But there’s one important segment getting left behind: early-stage firms.

That’s why Governor Maura Healey and her economic development secretary, Eric Paley, huddled with a few dozen chief executives of young biotechs last week at MassBio’s headquarters in Kendall Square. Also on hand: Kirk Taylor, chief executive of the quasipublic Mass. Life Sciences Center, through which many of the state subsidies for the biotech sector flow. Healey later told reporters that state officials should consider increasing the state assistance available for early-stage biotechs, given the financial challenges they face.

Paley and Taylor are updating the strategic approach for the Mass. Life Sciences Center, and want to use the input they gleaned to tweak its incentives. The hope is to come up with more grants for these younger biotechs, in particular to support them through expensive clinical trials, as well as working with another quasi-public, MassVentures, to help commercialize more university research.

“Massachusetts has an unbelievable pipeline of research,” Paley said. “We’re not getting enough of it out of the labs.”

For Ben Pope, founder of MelliCell, a Newton biotech working on a pill to treat the Fragile X syndrome that can cause autism, it was refreshing to hear state officials so engaged on these issues. “I really appreciate them recognizing,” Pope said, “that our success is what will drive Massachusetts to continue to dominate in this space.”

When brothers Ronn Garry and Randy Garry started chatting about a succession plan for Tropical Foods, their grocery store near Nubian Square in Roxbury, they thought about selling to a competitor. They worried, though, about what might happen to Tropical’s 100 workers if a chain bought Tropical. So the two brothers decided to sell it to the employees instead.

To help line up financing, Tropical turned to Apis & Heritage, a foundation-backed investment firm that specializes in arranging employee buyouts to protect blue-collar jobs. Now the company’s newly created Employee Stock Ownership Plan holds a majority stake, with a trustee overseeing the shares for the ESOP.

Tropical’s new board will feature two seats for Washington-based Apis & Heritage, one for Ronn Garry, and one for an outside adviser. Ronn Garry said his brother will exit in six months, while he’ll leave in around 18 months, after helping to find a general manager to replace him. He plans to stay on the board for five years.

Choosing the ESOP route gives employees a stake in the company’s future while also ensuring stability after the brothers’ departure.

Rumors had circulated that the brothers had put the business up for sale, so employees were nervous when they headed over to the nearby Residence Inn in waves for meetings on Aug. 31. The relief, Garry said, was palpable when they were told not only was no one losing their job, but they’re now going to be owners in the company.

“By the end of the day, when the last group came in, and they heard from the previous groups what was going on, . . . it was a very different feeling,” Garry said. “This is such a great solution, and such a great thing for us and the community. This is real wealth-building in Roxbury.”

Boston Casting worked with casting director Allison Jones, a Needham native who made it big in Hollywood.
