The state’s Parole Board is releasing another “emerging adult” first-degree murderer who killed a hated rival in a brazen broad-daylight shooting in front of a bustling post office.

Patrick Grier was 20 years old in 2008 when he gunned down 16-year-old De’Andre Barboza in Boston.

Grier two years later was convicted of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

But in 2024, Grier became eligible for parole after the state Supreme Judicial Court’s decision in Commonwealth v. Mattis. The court ruled that “emerging adult” offenders who were 18 to 20 at the time of the offense could not be sentenced to life without parole.

As a result of the SJC’s decision regarding his first-degree murder conviction, Grier was re-sentenced to life with the possibility of parole after 15 years.

Grier is now 37 years old, and the Massachusetts Parole Board has OK’d his release.

The deadly shooting

Back on Nov. 30, 2008, Grier and his co-defendant — a 16-year-old girl — were at a store in Dorchester, where they saw Barboza.

Grier talked with Barboza, and afterwards Grier appeared quiet and upset.

The next morning, Grier met up with his co-defendant in Dorchester. As the pair were passing a market on Washington Street, they spotted Barboza inside.

Barboza then left the market, and both Grier and Barboza walked toward the Codman Square street corner. When Barboza reached the corner in front of a busy post office, Grier shot him — causing him to fall to the ground.

With Barboza on the ground, Grier continued to fire at him from point-blank range. One shot struck Barboza in the head, while two shots wounded his legs.

Barboza was transported to Boston Medical Center, where he died two days later from the gunshot wound to his head.

Right after the shooting, Grier and his co-defendant fled the scene. Grier threw the gun he used to shoot Barboza at his co-defendant, telling the 16-year-old girl to take it.

She caught the gun, a .22 caliber revolver, and tucked it in her waistband before continuing to flee.

Police officers then apprehended Grier and the 16-year-old girl, and recovered the gun. Samples were taken from their hands, which tested positive for gunshot residue.

Grier and Barboza came from different neighborhoods, and the homicide stemmed from an “ongoing feud,” according to the Suffolk DA prosecutor during the arraignment years ago.

Parole decision

Last year, Grier appeared before the Massachusetts Parole Board for an initial hearing.

“Mr. Grier presented with insight into the causative factors that led to his gang affiliation and offending behavior,” the Parole Board wrote in its ruling. “Mr. Grier began to invest in self-development prior to the Mattis decision, and furthered his rehabilitation by participating in and completing programs related to his need areas.

“Mr. Grier also invested in education – earning his associate’s degree,” the Parole Board added. “In an effort to prepare himself for re-entry, Mr. Grier also developed occupational skills… The Board concludes that Patrick Grier has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society.”

The Massachusetts Parole Board has released dozens of “emerging adult” first-degree convicted murderers who were 18 to 20 at the time of the offense.

The Mattis ruling in 2024 made more than 200 convicts eligible for parole hearings.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said the city’s new plan to tackle the open-air drug market at and around Mass and Cass this summer could be funded by a new $4 million boost in the state House budget, but the Senate has yet to get on board.

Wu joined House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz at a press conference in Roxbury Thursday to announce that the House of Representatives budget for next fiscal year will include $4 million to fund various city and state initiatives aimed at tackling homelessness, addiction and related crime at Mass and Cass.

The funding is aimed at supporting a three-pronged plan put forward by a South End, Roxbury, and Newmarket community working group in February that focuses on getting addicts off the streets, out of jail, and into recovery to avoid the chaos and crowding that worsens there each summer.

“These practical initiatives need the right resources and we felt it was time for the Commonwealth to step up even more, and help us with the city financially throughout this upcoming year,” Michlewitz, a North End Democrat and Wu ally, said. “Our commitment from the House is being made because we are confident in the city’s commitment to this issue, particularly under Mayor Wu’s leadership.”

The working group, led by state Rep. John Moran and City Councilor John FitzGerald, was tasked by the mayor last year with putting forward recommendations for a new Mass and Cass plan that builds on the city’s work.

“Boston has made meaningful progress toward the goal of ending outdoor drug use in our neighborhoods through a sustained and coordinated effort grounded in public health, safety, and accountability,” Wu said. “I’m grateful to Chairman Aaron Michlewitz and Representative John Moran for their leadership in including significant funding in the House budget that would support even more of this critical work.”

The mayor said violent crime at Mass and Cass is down 33% year-to-date compared to last year, and quality-of-life service calls are down 20%. Violent crime decreased 7%, property crime fell by 6%, and arrests increased by 54% for 2025 compared to 2024.

No members of the state Senate were present at the press conference, and Michlewitz said that while the funding was guaranteed in next week’s House Ways and Means budget, it wasn’t necessarily a lock to make it into the Senate or final state budget.

“We’ll see where it goes as far as the funding process,” Michlewitz said, in response to whether he anticipated support from the Senate for his proposal.

Michlewitz also said the House is not committing to annual funding for Mass and Cass.

“I think we’re going to take this … one step at a time, one year at a time, one season at a time, in essence,” Michlewitz said. “This discussion continues to evolve. The city and state officials have all tried doing different things over the years to varying degrees of success, and I think we need to keep trying different things until we get it completely right.”

Michlewitz said $2.24 million would go directly to the city to distribute grants to organizations, contracted or otherwise, providing recovery housing for up to 200 people for up to a year.

Another $650,000 would allow for at least three contracted nurse practitioners, a psychiatrist, and two additional mental health specialists, Michlewitz said.

He said $500,000 would be earmarked for the Suffolk District Attorney’s office to create and operate a pre-arraignment diversion program, or “recovery court,” that builds on the DA’s services-over-sentences initiative, which seeks to divert drug users and other low-level offenders to treatment rather than incarcerate them.

“Let me be clear, if we are talking about predators, if we are talking about drug dealers, and if we are talking about people that are driving cycles of human trafficking and that sort of thing, then we want to hold them accountable in our criminal legal process,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said.

“But when it’s someone in the throes of addiction and homelessness and joblessness and in need of recovery, we want to help them with that,” Hayden added. “We’re always doing the best we can to minimize the damage that the criminal legal system has on people who are caught up in these circumstances.”

The Boston Public Health Commission would receive $460,000 to provide an additional 30 transitional treatment beds, 20 for women and 10 for men, for up to 60 days to “cover shortages,” Michlewitz said.

The remaining $150,000 would go to the city’s coordinated response mobile vehicle operation program to provide services to the addicted and homeless.

Mayor Wu, who plans to file her warm-weather plan for Mass and Cass with the City Council next week, would not confirm that her administration’s shift in strategy is a move away from harm reduction, which critics say incentivizes drug use by handing out needles and other paraphernalia.

“I think people use terms to sometimes suggest things that may or may not actually be true,” Wu said. “For us as a city, harm reduction means finding ways where we are providing services to people who need them, and trying, wherever possible, to remove barriers to accessing that kind of life-saving treatment.

“Some people suggest that harm reduction means eliminating accountability or letting anyone do whatever they want, wherever they want, at any time,” Wu said, “and that has never been what that term has been.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is reviewing a plan to transform warehouses across the U.S. into detention facilities for tens of thousands of immigrants.

So far immigration officials have spent a total of $1.074 billion for 11 warehouses. They’ve mostly faced fierce opposition. And days after Mullin was sworn in, the Department of Homeland Security paused the purchase of new warehouses intended to house immigrants. The department is scrutinizing all contracts signed under his predecessor, Kristi Noem.

A look at some of the locations:

Arizona

Local officials were told nothing before ICE purchased a 418,000-square-foot warehouse in the Phoenix suburb of Surprise for $70 million, the state’s top prosecutor, Kris Mayes, said in a letter to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Documents later provided by ICE said the Department of Homeland Security plans a processing site with an average daily capacity of 1,000 to 1,500, and a contract worth at least $313.4 million was awarded to transform it.

DHS is now planning something more modest, starting out with 250 people per week and capping occupied beds at 542, according to Surprise Mayor Kevin Sartor.

Florida

A TV reporter in Orlando spotted private contractors and federal officials in January touring a 439,945-square-foot industrial warehouse. ICE senior adviser David Venturella told a WFTV reporter the tour was “exploratory.”

As of April, the city still hadn’t heard anything, a spokesperson said in an email.

Georgia

ICE bought a massive warehouse in Social Circle for $128.6 million. The city said the federal government informed it that the facility is expected to house from 7,500 to 10,000 detainees.

The city is so concerned about the strain on its water supply that it put a lock on the warehouse’s water meter. DHS has suggested trucking in drinking water and trucking out waste, according to a letter from Georgia Democratic Sens. Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff, who said the plan was unworkable.

DHS also bought a 540,408-square-foot warehouse in Oakwood for $68.2 million, a deed shows. City Manager B.R. White said his first inkling that a deal was imminent came when a warehouse supervisor told a city inspector he’d been instructed to clear the job site to make way for the new owners — the federal government.

Indiana

After the town of Merrillville raised concerns about ICE touring a new 275,000-square-foot warehouse, owner Opus Holding LLC sent a letter stating it isn’t negotiating with federal officials for the property. The letter said Opus was limited in what it could share because of legal issues.

Maryland

ICE purchased a warehouse about 60 miles northwest of Baltimore in Washington County for $102.4 million and signed a contract worth at least $113 million to renovate it. But work is on hold after Maryland’s attorney general sued.

The warehouse has divided the community. County commissioners passed a resolution in support of ICE during a contentious meeting.

Michigan

After DHS paid $34.7 million for a 250,000-square-foot warehouse in Romulus, the state and city sued. The suit said the warehouse is in a flood plain, and that the sewage system couldn’t keep up if 500 people are detained inside. It also faults DHS for not considering any of the state’s empty prison facilities and for not talking to state or city officials.

Minnesota

The owners of warehouses in the Minneapolis suburbs of Woodbury and Shakopee pulled out of possible ICE deals after public outcry, according to local officials.

Mississippi

Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Wicker posted that Noem agreed to look elsewhere after local elected and zoning officials opposed a possible detention center in the town of Byhalia.

Missouri

After weeks of public pressure, development company Platform Ventures announced it would not move forward with the sale of a massive warehouse in Kansas City.

New Hampshire

New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte said in March that DHS would not move forward with a proposed ICE facility in the town of Merrimack.

Ayotte, a Republican, had sparred with federal officials after ICE disclosed plans to spend $158 million to convert a warehouse in the town into a 500-bed processing center.

The issue came to a head after an ICE official testified that DHS “has worked with Gov. Ayotte” and provided her with an economic impact summary. Ayotte said the summary was not sent until hours after that testimony.

The document erroneously refers to the “ripple effects to the Oklahoma economy” and revenue generated by state sales and income taxes, neither of which exist in New Hampshire.

New Jersey

After DHS bought a 470,044-square-foot warehouse in Roxbury for $129.3 million, the township and state sued, alleging that federal officials kept them in the dark.

“State and local officials might not have a veto over DHS’s decisions, but this utter lack of communication and consultation flies in the face of federal law,” the suit said.

New York

ICE said it made a mistake when it announced the purchase of a vacant warehouse in Chester. New York state Assemblyman Brian Maher later said ICE was no longer considering the facility.

Oklahoma

Oklahoma City Mayor David Holt announced in January that property owners had informed him they are no longer engaged with DHS about a potential acquisition or lease of a warehouse.

Pennsylvania

DHS purchased a warehouse in Tremont Township for $119.5 million and one in Upper Bern Township for $87.4 million. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has said his administration will fight DHS’ plans. The state’s Department of Environmental Protection has barred water and sewage from being supplied to them for now.

Tennessee

ICE mistakenly announced it had completed the purchase of a warehouse in Lebanon, Tennessee.

The sheriff, Robert Bryan, wrote that a facility of the size and scope being discussed — 14,000 to 16,000 detainees — would “significantly impact local law enforcement resources.” And the mayor, Rick Bell, wrote that as a conservative Republican, he supports a secure border but that his town “is not the place.”

Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn later announced that the deal was dead.

Texas

In the El Paso suburb of Socorro, ICE paid $122.8 million for a trio of warehouses that span 826,780 square feet. ICE also paid $66.1 million for a 639,595-square-foot warehouse in San Antonio. The mayors of both cities are opposed. Socorro officials — like others — have questioned water supplies. As of April, San Antonio still had heard nothing from DHS.

However, another deal in the state was scuttled following community backlash. In the Dallas suburb of Hutchins, a real estate company confirmed that it was contacted about one of its properties but wouldn’t sell or lease any buildings to DHS for use as a detention facility. California-based Majestic Realty Co. provided no explanation in its statement.

Utah

DHS bought an 833,280-square-foot warehouse in Salt Lake City for $145.4 million without notifying the city’s Democratic leaders or the state’s Republican governor or congressional delegation. Mayor Erin Mendenhall said in a statement released in March that ICE officials later told her that the facility will house 7,500 to 10,000 people.

The city has moved to cap water use at just a fraction of what would be needed to operate the warehouse as a detention site.

The sale of the warehouse came two months after the owner of another Salt Lake City warehouse announced plans not to sell or lease to the federal government amid protests.

Virginia

Following boycott threats, Jim Pattison Developments announced in January that it would not proceed with a planned sale of a warehouse in the suburbs of Richmond, Virginia. It said it was not aware of the intended use until after it agreed to the sale.

Associated Press reporters Holly Ramer, Isabella Volmert and Marc Levy contributed to this report.

The family of a man killed by a Boston Police officer during an alleged carjacking last month said he was suffering from mental health issues at the time of his death.

Stephenson King’s family held a press conference at Grant African Methodist Episcopal Church Thursday to discuss the circumstances surrounding King’s death and to ask for the release of body camera footage of the incident.

“My son wasn’t perfect but he was a great son. He did a lot of things that made me happy and made his family happy,” King’s father Stephenson King Sr. said. “However, he had a lot of mental issues going on.”

Boston Police Officer Nicholas O’Malley shot and killed 39-year-old King during an encounter on March 11.

King allegedly assaulted a woman and stole her vehicle, and when O’Malley and another officer approached him parked in Roxbury, he didn’t fully comply with their orders, according to police reports based on the footage of the incident.

According to O’Malley, after King backed into their cruiser, the officer feared his partner would get hit, but according to prosecutors, King was only trying to flee the scene.

O’Malley was charged with manslaughter, and Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said his office has brought the matter to a grand jury.

In the wake of his death, King’s family is asking for justice and calling on footage from that incident to be released.

“He shouldn’t be dead,” King Sr. said. “I worked in the system… it’s very broken-hearted for me.”

King Sr. said that he worked as a state correctional officer.

“I apologize if I seem a little angry, I am,” King Sr. said. “One of the things officers are taught: you think before you do.”

King Sr. and Ebony King Gibson, King’s sister, said they’d both tried to get King help — even on the day he was shot. Previous attempts at court intervention failed, they said, even though King was exhibiting odd behaviors like covering outlets, camera lenses, and even the branding on his shoes, telling family members that people were watching him.

King Gibson said after the death of their mother in 2009, “he’d been in and out of the system battling these things for years.”

King struggled with alcohol, she said, but when he was put on medication in prison (the family did not disclose a particular diagnosis) he did better.

King Sr.’s fiancée Tina, who has known the family for 11 years, said that despite his mental health, King was still a person deeply loved by his family, who attended every family function and always brought gifts for his nieces and nephews.

“He came in like Santa,” she said. “I’ll miss Stephenson on Christmas.”

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump who has been retained to represent the Kings said video of the shooting should be released or at least shown to the family as it has in other officer-involved deaths.

When asked if Crump would be filing a suit against the city, he said, “We intend to explore every possible legal remedy available to the family to get justice.”

In response to the presser, both DA Hayden and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said the video would be released but not at this point in time.

Roxbury Community College, where Rachael Rollins is on staff, should give her an honorary doctorate. In spin.

After the disgraced former U.S. Attorney pulled papers to run against Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden for her old seat late Wednesday, she shared this post on X:

“I always tell my daughter and nieces that circumstances don’t define you,” Rollins wrote. “Every moment in life — whether victory or defeat — is temporary. What endures is who you become in the face of that hardship and what you do moving forward. Dare greatly.”

At the heart of Rollins’ fall from grace in 2023: a pair of federal reports that found she abused her position, in part, by leaking non-public information to the media in an attempt to influence the outcome of the Suffolk DA’s race in favor of her preferred candidate, ex-Boston City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo.

Rollins agreed to a public reprimand for misconduct by the state board that oversees her law license last June, two years after her resignation.

Hardship, or consequences? They mean the same in Massachusetts’ political circles, which is why Rollins’ re-bid for Suffolk DA isn’t a complete surprise.

The Bay State is kind to wayward elected officials. Former House Speaker Charlie Flaherty plead guilty in 1996 to felony tax evasion as well as violating the state conflict of interest law for taking free vacation housing from lobbyists.

He got two years probation, then became a lobbyist on Beacon Hill.

Subsequent House Speaker Tom Finneran pleaded guilty to lying under oath in 2007 and left the Legislature. He later returned as a lobbyist. No harm no foul.

Even running for public office post-scandal has a Massachusetts precedent: the late Sen. Ted Kennedy. Chappaquiddick would have demolished the career of most, but not Ted, and not in Kennedy country. He was elected seven times since the 1969 accident that claimed the life of Mary Jo Kopechne.

So Rollins returning to the campaign trail is certainly “daring greatly,” but she’s no outlier.

But addressing the reason she is a former US Attorney will take some finesse. Rollins is running for a job in justice, ostensibly to uphold the law and hold lawbreakers accountable. Abusing her position, as the federal reports revealed, is the antithesis of that mission.

While it doesn’t define the sum of her life, it does offer a snapshot of Rollins’ character in office, a picture that may give voters pause.

Or not. Rollins is a progressive, and that means a lot in Massachusetts. Her policy memo from 2019 spelled out her views on justice: “I don’t believe accountability has to equal incarceration. There are many ways that we can hold people accountable without putting them in jail.”

That idea still has legs here, as does Rollins’ take on ICE, this from 2020: “I am troubled by the actions of federal Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents, heavily armed and wearing body armor, who stopped a United States citizen and Massachusetts resident earlier this week for no other reason apparently than the color of his skin.”

Can Rollins’ message erase past violations in the eyes of Suffolk County voters? Or will the scandal, just three years gone, put off fans of her progressive policies?

In Massachusetts, you never can tell.

Disgraced former U.S. Attorney Rachael Rollins insinuated that her past transgressions have been judged more harshly than her male counterparts, like Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden, after drawing backlash for joining the DA’s race.

“Funny, men can have a state ETHICS violation, PAY A $5K FINE for using their ‘official position as Suffolk DA to secure … the substantially valuable and unwarranted privilege of the … DA’s Office to their own personal political advantage’ to win their 2022 election & have integrity,” Rollins wrote Friday on X.

In April 2024, Hayden agreed to pay a $5,000 civil penalty for violating conflict of interest law by allowing his office to issue an official press statement aimed at discrediting his primary opponent, former City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo, days before the election. Rollins’ post references the violation issued by the state Ethics Commission.

The post came two days after Rollins pulled papers with the Secretary of State’s office to run for Suffolk DA, a position she held for three years before being appointed as U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts by President Biden.

Hayden, when asked for comment about Rollins’ move to join the race by a Herald reporter on Thursday, said he had none. His office did not respond to a request for comment about Rollins’ post about him on Friday.

Rollins’ decision to run for her old Suffolk DA post came after weeks of speculation, and has drawn criticism, given her past transgressions.

She reacted to the criticism on Friday, by not only ripping into Hayden, but also former Suffolk DA Dan Conley and ex-Lt. Gov. Tim Murray. Rollins succeeded Conley as DA.

“And Dan Conley talking about Integrity & Honesty is like Lt. Gov. Tim Murray lecturing us on safe driving,” Rollins wrote on X. “Of the 500+ years of wrongful convictions (& counting) undone during my tenure as DA — each approved by the Court — Dan ignored police corruption and prosecutorial misconduct.”

Conley likely set Rollins off through an interview he gave to the Boston Globe on Thursday about her following her decision to join the DA’s race. He described her as “unfit to hold an office that demands truthfulness, fairness, and public trust.”

“Through her actions, Rachael Rollins has shown that she lacks the two most fundamental qualifications for serving as district attorney: honesty and integrity,” Conley told the Globe.

Rollins resigned as U.S. Attorney in May 2023 amid an ethics scandal revealed during a federal investigation. She had been sworn into the role just a year prior after Congress narrowly confirmed Biden’s appointment, with then-Vice President Kamala Harris casting the tie-breaking vote.

Her progressive policies had given some federal lawmakers pause in Congress, including the controversial “do-not-prosecute” list she implemented during her time as Suffolk DA for low-level crimes like shoplifting.

She resigned as U.S. Attorney after being scorched in two federal reports that found she abused her position, by improperly disclosing sensitive Department of Justice information to the media about a possible investigation into the Suffolk DA, Hayden, while he was running for election — to try to influence the race in favor of her preferred candidate, Arroyo.

After a nasty race, Arroyo lost the 2022 Democratic primary to Hayden, who then ran unopposed in that year’s general election.

The two federal reports stated that Rollins faced further discipline from the feds if she did not promptly quit.

Rollins was later issued a public reprimand for the ethics breach cited in the two federal reports by the state Board of Bar Overseers, which oversees her bar license, last October. The board voted to accept the reprimand Rollins agreed to last June — for leaking the sensitive DOJ information to the media — but three members of the board dissented, preferring to reject the penalty as “too lenient.”

Disciplinary proceedings by the board are generally triggered by allegations of misconduct against an attorney, which could lead to disbarment, resignation, or suspension by the court, public reprimand by the board, or admonition by the bar counsel, according to Supreme Judicial Court Rule 4:01 for Bar Discipline.

Rollins is the second candidate to pull papers to challenge Hayden for DA this year. Linda Champion, an attorney who ran for Suffolk DA in 2018 and finished fifth in a race that Rollins eventually won, has also pulled papers to run.

Hayden drew challengers after his decision to charge a Boston police officer with manslaughter last month in connection with a fatal police-involved shooting that led to the death of a carjacking suspect. He’s drawn criticism from the city’s largest police union for the rare move to charge the officer, which has led political insiders to speculate that he may be suddenly vulnerable in the race.

The federal investigation against Rollins that led to her resignation as U.S. Attorney was sparked by her appearance at a Democratic National Committee fundraiser headlined by then-First Lady Jill Biden, in potential violation of the Hatch Act, after it was first reported by the Herald.

The Herald has since reported that Rollins tore through her taxpayer-funded credit cards during her time as Suffolk DA, spending lavishly on travel accommodations, posh hotels, and fancy restaurants.

Rollins — who works now as an executive director for a program at Roxbury Community College — positioned her move to try to reclaim public office as a comeback story.

The Boston City Council may issue a rare subpoena to compel Police Commissioner Michael Cox to testify on BPD’s protocols for releasing body camera footage after a fatal police-involved shooting led to a manslaughter charge.

Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell filed the summons request for a potential vote by the Council on Wednesday, after expressing disappointment that Boston Police leadership did not accept the body’s invitation to testify at a hearing held last week on the department’s protocols for releasing body cam footage.

“In the aftermath of fatal Boston Police Department officer encounters, elected officials, oversight bodies, and the public have a vested (interest) in viewing this footage,” the Council order states. “The Boston Police Department at the discretion of the Boston police commissioner, maintains custody and control over body camera footage and related records that are essential to understanding the circumstances surrounding incidents involving the use of deadly force.

“The public deserves to see body camera footage related to the Roxbury incident in order to protect transparency, support community healing, and ensure accountability in the administration of justice. Given the seriousness of this matter, the impact on public trust, and the failure of the Boston Police Department to appear before the Council, it is necessary to compel testimony and the production of relevant information,” the Council order states.

BPD sent its attorney, Dave Fredette, to last week’s hearing. Fredette said release of the footage is within Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden’s jurisdiction, rather than the police commissioner, due to it being a death investigation. Fredette also said all public records requests for the footage, including from the Council, would be denied by BPD, due to an investigatory exemption under the public records law.

“This particular case, (Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden) came out and he said in public that this case is going to go before a grand jury and no body camera video is going to be released prior to that,” Fredette said. “We need to abide by that.”

Culpepper disagreed, arguing that under BPD rules that govern the department’s body-worn camera program and state statute, the police commissioner is not required “to follow the direction of the district attorney” as it relates to releasing footage tied to public or Council records requests.

Culpepper plans to ask his colleagues to approve his 17F request for body camera footage tied to fatal police-involved shootings over the past five years on Wednesday. If approved, the mayor would have a week to respond.

The two orders are sparked by a March 11 police-involved shooting that led to the death of Stephenson King, a carjacking suspect, and a rare manslaughter charge filed against the involved officer, Nicholas O’Malley.

Hayden has been criticized by O’Malley’s attorney for charging the officer before waiting for a grand jury indictment, and has faced blowback from the local police community.

After King’s family held a press conference last week calling for the footage to be released, Hayden and Cox both said the video would be released but not at this point in time.

Cox said he would defer to the DA. With the case before a grand jury, Hayden said withholding the footage is a choice “in accordance with making sure that rights and due processes are preserved.”

The City Council voted to issue a subpoena to USPS Boston Postmaster Joshua Balcunas in October 2024, after the USPS blew off a Council hearing on mail delivery delays in the city.

The USPS then dismissed the subpoena, saying that the Council likely had little to no legal authority to pursue enforcement action for its failure to comply with the summons, such as fines or penalties for defaults.

BPD did not respond to a request for comment on whether the police commissioner would comply with a Council subpoena.

Boston City Council President Liz Breadon said the people she represents in Allston-Brighton are “enraged” over the mayor’s decision to exclude funding for a new community center from the city’s $4.4 billion capital plan.

Breadon said Monday she’s been advocating for the city to fund a new community center to replace Allston-Brighton’s current facility — which is so run down that it can’t even operate on weekends or as a cooling center in hot weather — for six years to no avail.

This year represents a breaking point for the Allston-Brighton community, however, as Breadon said she “was assured that we were moving forward” as a city on building a new Boston Center for Youth and Families facility, given that a number of studies have been conducted and a site has been tentatively agreed upon.

“I was disappointed,” Breadon said after seeing that the project was not included in the five-year capital plan proposed by Mayor Michelle Wu last week. “We had the site, we had these different studies down and the indications where we were moving forward.

“The crazy thing about it is that we are the second largest neighborhood in the city of Boston. We’re approximately the same size as the City of Somerville by population and area, and we have one severely depleted community center that needs to be replaced, and it’s not been given any level of urgency,” Breadon added.

Breadon said the city broke ground last year on two new community centers in the North End and Dorchester, at an anticipated cost of $110 million and $65 million, respectively. She estimates that a new Allston-Brighton community center would cost $70-$80 million.

She said the Allston-Brighton community center is located in the Jackson-Mann Educational Complex in Allston’s Union Square, a campus that housed two schools that have either closed entirely or moved to a new neighborhood.

Breadon said the community favors building a new facility on the same site. She said no further studies are needed. The city’s capital budget allocates $10 million to develop a building program and assess siting options for a new BCYF center, but no funding for new construction, which has angered residents, she said.

“I think people are really disappointed — they’re enraged basically because we have really been scraping together to keep … our youth programs going,” Breadon said. “I’ve been talking about this for six years as a city councilor. Sooner or later, the city has to step up and support our neighborhood.”

The lack of funding for a new Allston-Brighton community center has led Breadon to vote against the city’s capital plan for the past two years — despite being seen as an ally of the mayor. She doesn’t see the $10 million commitment by the city in this year’s capital plan as a “meaningful commitment from this administration to construct a new” facility.

“As with many things in Allston-Brighton, we have lots of studies and not a lot of action,” Breadon said.

She said the center has been operating since the 1970s. Its dilapidated state and lack of funding — just $25,000 was budgeted for programming by the city last year — prevents the facility from offering a full slate of services for residents.

Breadon said the gymnasium and dance studio have failing roofs and floors. The heating, ventilation and air conditioning system doesn’t work, which prevents the center from operating as a cooling center as it should. It is closed on Saturdays, which prevents weekend programming, she added.

“It’s really a very sad situation,” Breadon said. “It’s a very poor reflection on our ability to serve our community here in Allston-Brighton.”

Allstonia reported Wu’s chief of civic engagement Brianna Millor as citing the city’s $48.4 million budget gap and need to prioritize other capital projects like the contentious $325 million White Stadium pro soccer rehab and the $700 million Madison Park high school rebuild as reasons for excluding funding for a new community center.

Breadon said she sees the city’s historic lack of investment in Allston-Brighton as being due to the district’s lack of political connections compared to other neighborhoods, along with a fundamental misunderstanding about its demographics.

“It’s like the neighborhoods that have got the most continue to get more, and those that are left behind are getting less,” Breadon said. “We have been consistently under-invested for decades. I just think that there’s a gross misunderstanding of who we are out here as a community.

“We’re probably one of the most diverse neighborhoods in the city. We don’t have a predominant Hispanic community. We don’t have a predominantly Black community. We just have a lot of different people living out here,” Breadon said. “At this rate, it’ll be a long time before we get the community center we need.”

The Council president plans to hold a “protest rally” with Allston-Brighton elected officials and community members on Tuesday.

Mayor Wu’s office walked back Millor’s reported remarks in a statement on Monday, saying that no project has been “bumped” in favor of another — the current funding authorization simply reflects the different stage that the Jackson Mann project is in.

“The city is working to make Boston the most family-friendly city in the country, and our public assets are especially critical to making our city a home for everyone,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said. “Significant resources to advance the Jackson Mann Community Center project are set aside in this year’s capital budget and will move the project closer towards design even amid the difficult choices required in this economic environment.

“This particular project will not be a simple rebuild, as the former combined school and community center uses must be evaluated in the context of changing school enrollment in the neighborhood and the BPS long-term facilities plan, as well as community desires for housing to potentially be incorporated into the site. We look forward to working closely with residents and elected officials so that the future of this community hub reflects the neighborhood’s evolving needs and priorities.”

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s warm-weather plan for tackling the open-air drug market and related crime at Mass and Cass puts a heavy focus on diverting drug users breaking the law into addiction treatment programs.

The plan was laid out by the mayor’s coordinated response team Monday in a memo filed with the City Council. It calls for expansion of the Boston Police Department’s new Neighborhood Engagement Safety Team, or NEST, strategy citywide to “enhance diversion and co-response efforts on the ground.”

The memo states that the coordinated response team and NEST diversion model will “be the primary frontline engagement strategy” this year, as the city aims to curb the crowding and chaos that is seen each summer at and around Melnea Cass Boulevard and Massachusetts Avenue, commonly referred to as Mass and Cass.

“In the warm-weather season of 2026, the CRT/NEST diversion model will lead on-the-ground proactive outreach, ensuring that individuals engaged in unlawful conduct are not permitted to remain in the area and are directed into treatment pathways,” the city memo states.

The memo states that CRT and NEST began the city’s warm-weather initiative for Mass and Cass on March 30. Since that time, the coordinated response team has engaged with more than 200 people in the area, and diverted 125 “into a recovery pathway” for addiction.

“This initiative aligned additional BPD resources under NEST’s leadership, alongside coordinated support from State Police and Transit Police partners from the MBTA,” the memo states. “This cross-sector initiative works across two shifts, alongside CRT recovery specialists, and is producing measurable results on our city streets.”

The police department’s new NEST initiative launched by the Wu administration last September, as part of the mayor’s shift in approach for Mass and Cass that is aimed at ending outdoor congregate drug use.

This week’s memo states that the BPD initiative will be expanded and deployed citywide this year “to support CRT-led diversion, enhance quality of life, strengthen community-focused policing, and respond to community feedback.”

Since March 30, NEST has supported the city’s coordinated response team in engaging more than 160 people and directing 90 people into recovery, the memo states.

The NEST deployment expansion will target “designated impact zones,” for Mass and Cass, the memo states, likely referring to hot-spot spillover neighborhoods that have been identified in the past as the South End, Nubian Square in Roxbury, and Andrew Square in South Boston, among other areas.

“The BPD will supplement dedicated (Street Outreach Unit) deployments by expanding training in the NEST strategy for officers in districts throughout Boston, ensuring more consistent, neighborhood-based application of NEST/CRT practices across the city, fostering sustained community engagement, trust, and improved public safety and quality of life outcomes,” the memo states.

The mayor rolled out her warm-weather approach for Mass and Cass after announcing last Thursday that the state House of Representatives budget for next fiscal year will include $4 million to fund various city and state initiatives aimed at tackling homelessness, addiction, and related crime in the troubled area.

The funding is aimed at supporting a three-pronged plan put forward by a South End, Roxbury, and Newmarket community working group in February that focuses on getting addicts off the streets, out of jail, and into recovery to avoid the chaos and crowding that worsens there each summer.

House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz, an ally of the mayor who joined her for the announcement, said that while the funding was guaranteed in this week’s House Ways and Means budget, it wasn’t necessarily a lock to make it into the Senate or final state budget.

“We’ll see where it goes as far as the funding process,” Michlewitz said, in response to whether he anticipated support from the Senate for his proposal.

The open-air drug use, dealing and related crime that has long plagued Mass and Cass and surrounding neighborhoods has worsened in the past several summers, officials have said, leading to a shift in the city’s response to the problem.

Wu said last Thursday that the city’s “sustained and coordinated effort grounded in public health, safety, and accountability” has led to “meaningful progress toward the goal of ending outdoor drug use in our neighborhoods.”

The mayor said violent crime at Mass and Cass is down 33% year-to-date compared to last year, and quality-of-life service calls are down 20%. Violent crime decreased 7%, property crime fell by 6%, and arrests increased by 54% for 2025 compared to 2024.

“As Boston enters the warm weather season of 2026,” the city memo states, “residents, businesses, health providers, and partners in government continue to work with the city to address the serious impacts on public safety, public health, quality of life, and business sustainability stemming from outdoor substance use and addiction.”

A Boston City Council subpoena for the police commissioner to testify on body camera footage release protocols after a fatal cop shooting led to a manslaughter charge was withdrawn following pressure from the mayor, the Herald has learned.

Councilor Miniard Culpepper went forward with his 17F, or public records request, for body camera footage tied to fatal police-involved shootings for 2025 and this year to date at Wednesday’s meeting, and received unanimous approval. The mayor now has a week to respond.

But Culpepper then withdrew a more contentious and specific request that, if approved by the Council, would have compelled Police Commissioner Michael Cox to testify and produce “relevant information” tied to the March 11 fatal officer-involved shooting in Roxbury.

The wording of the order, co-sponsored by Brian Worrell, indicates that the summons was not only calling for testimony but for the release of body cam footage tied to that shooting, which Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden is withholding. Culpepper said he withdrew the subpoena after speaking with Cox.

“I’ve had conversations with Commissioner Cox,” Culpepper said. “He’s assured me that he’s ready, willing, and able to work with us to set a date to come before the Council to provide the testimony that we need in this case.”

Cox agreed to appear at a future Council hearing on body camera release protocols, in exchange for dropping the summons request, but there was more going on behind the scenes to set that deal into motion, a City Hall source told the Herald.

Mayor Michelle Wu called city councilors on Tuesday night and Wednesday ahead of the noon Council meeting to request that councilors vote against the proposed order to subpoena the police commissioner, a City Hall source said.

The mayor’s calls to councilors put pressure on Culpepper to withdraw the subpoena request, the source said.

The City Council’s “power to summons and subpoena” residents, effectively treating them like witnesses compelled to testify in court who are subject to the same fines and penalties for defaults, is enshrined in state law and among its strongest tools.

The subpoena authority is spelled out in both the Boston City Charter and City Council rules.

Culpepper and Worrell filed the summons request after expressing disappointment that Cox and other Boston Police leadership did not accept the Council’s invitation to testify at a hearing held last week on the department’s protocols for releasing body camera footage.

“In the aftermath of fatal Boston Police Department officer encounters, elected officials, oversight bodies, and the public have a vested (interest) in viewing this footage,” the withdrawn summons order stated. “The Boston Police Department at the discretion of the Boston police commissioner, maintains custody and control over body camera footage and related records that are essential to understanding the circumstances surrounding incidents involving the use of deadly force.

“The public deserves to see body camera footage related to the Roxbury incident in order to protect transparency, support community healing, and ensure accountability in the administration of justice. Given the seriousness of this matter, the impact on public trust, and the failure of the Boston Police Department to appear before the Council, it is necessary to compel testimony and the production of relevant information,” the withdrawn order stated.

BPD sent its attorney, Dave Fredette, to last week’s hearing. Fredette said release of the footage is within Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden’s jurisdiction, rather than the police commissioner, due to it being a death investigation. Fredette also said all public records requests for the footage, including from the Council, would be denied by BPD, due to an investigatory exemption under the public records law.

“This particular case, (Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden) came out and he said in public that this case is going to go before a grand jury and no body camera video is going to be released prior to that,” Fredette said. “We need to abide by that.”

Culpepper disagreed, arguing that under BPD rules that govern the department’s body-worn camera program and state statute, the police commissioner is not required “to follow the direction of the district attorney” as it relates to releasing footage tied to public or Council records requests.

The 17F request and withdrawn summons were sparked by a March 11 police-involved shooting that led to the death of Stephenson King, a carjacking suspect, and a rare manslaughter charge filed against the involved officer, Nicholas O’Malley.

Hayden has been criticized by O’Malley’s attorney for charging the officer before waiting for a grand jury indictment, and has faced blowback from the local police community.

After King’s family held a press conference last week calling for the footage to be released, Hayden and Cox both said the video would be released but not at this point in time.

Cox said he would defer to the DA. With the case before a grand jury, Hayden said withholding the footage is a choice “in accordance with making sure that rights and due processes are preserved.”

Wu added last week, “Whenever there is a death investigation such as this one, the district attorney’s office has jurisdiction over that process, and they have determined that releasing the footage prematurely could have the potential to undermine the grand jury process or next steps.”

“We, at the city level, are always complying with public records law … but in this case, because of the active investigation, statements that this would potentially undermine and compromise that process, we are respecting that,” Wu said. “That’s why at this point the footage hasn’t been released, but it certainly will be.”

A Boston man was charged with mayhem after allegedly attacking an MBTA Police officer and trying to gouge out his eyes, the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office announced.

Fritznel Jean, 28, was also charged with assault and battery on a police officer, causing serious bodily injury, and an additional two courts of assault and battery on a police officer.

He was arraigned in Boston Municipal Court in Roxbury Monday and held on $100 bail, although Judge David Breen revoked his bail on other pending charges out of Quincy District Court.

T Police had arrested Jean last week on an outstanding warrant for the Quincy court charges, which included resisting arrest, disorderly conduct, and shoplifting.

While in custody Friday morning, officers responded to his holding cell after he allegedly attacked an officer who was trying to escort him to get fingerprinted, the DA’s office said.

“Jean shouted at the officer that he wanted to go free,” the DA said in a statement, and when the officer said that he was being booked, Jean continued to shout and refused to comply with the officer.

The officer then told Jean to go back into the cell.

“As the officer turned his back to open the cell door, Jean lunged toward the officer, jumped onto his back and bit him on the back of his head,” according to the statement.

Other officers responded and “a violent struggle ensued,” the DA’s office said, in which Jean allegedly began to scratch at and gouge the officer’s eyes. One witnessing officer said Jean also tried to press his thumb into the other officer’s eye sockets.

Jean also allegedly tried to bite a different officer’s hand during the incident, the DA said.

The officer who was initially attacked had severe bruising, burst blood vessels in his eyes, and a cut on his face that required two stitches.

“This was an extraordinary burst of violence that hurt one officer and endangered all the others involved,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “I thank the officers for restraining this defendant before he could inflict more injuries and I wish the wounded officer a full and fast recovery.”

Jean is expected back in court on May 12 for a probable cause hearing.

Mayor Michelle Wu has appointed Rodney Marshall, a 35-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department, as the city’s first Black fire commissioner.

Wu announced Thursday that she has appointed Marshall as the fire department’s 45th commissioner. He replaces Paul Burke, who retired this year, and will take over the leadership position later this month after he is sworn into his new role.

“As a distinguished and deeply respected 35-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department, Deputy Chief Rodney Marshall is exceptionally qualified to lead the brave men and women of Boston Fire who put their lives on the line to keep our communities safe,” Wu said in a statement.

“As a lifelong Bostonian, he knows our communities, has demonstrated his leadership on the job and has dedicated his career to serving and protecting our residents,” Wu added.

The mayor also mentioned that she is “deeply grateful for Commissioner Paul Burke’s strong and steady leadership over the past nearly four years, and knows that his legacy in the department and city will continue to have an impact on our neighborhoods.”

Marshall joined the Boston Fire Department in 1991. He is currently the department’s chief of operations for support services.

Upon joining the department, he was assigned to Engine 56, and rose through the ranks to become a fire lieutenant in 1998. That same year, he was awarded the commissioner’s unit citation for saving the lives of multiple residents during a six-alarm fire, the mayor’s office said.

Marshall was later promoted to fire captain in 2005, district fire chief in 2014, and deputy fire chief in 2022. He has been chief of operations since 2022.

His second commissioner’s unit citation came in 2013, for rescuing several people trapped in a bus with severe roof damage, the mayor’s office said.

Marshall, a Dorchester native and Boston College graduate, thanked the mayor “for the privilege of leading the department that has shaped my life and career.”

“As a proud son of Dorchester, I joined the Boston Fire Department because I wanted to give back to the communities where I grew up, and I’m committed to supporting the firefighters and staff who work every day to keep Boston’s neighborhoods safe,” Marshall said in a statement.

Marshall cited his efforts to design and oversee the launch of the fire department’s cadet program, which is aimed at helping city kids become firefighters, as one of his proudest career accomplishments, per the mayor’s office.

Wu’s office did not immediately provide salary information for Marshall’s new position. Burke was paid a base salary of $311,382 as fire commissioner last year, per city payroll records.

The mayor’s decision to appoint a Black fire commissioner came after pressure from city and state elected officials of color.

Boston City Councilor Brian Worrell sent a letter to Wu on Feb. 3 calling for her to “promote from the qualified Black and brown firefighters in leadership that are representative of our city’s diversity.”

“The Boston Fire Department’s 175-year history has not fully reflected the diversity of the communities it is sworn to serve,” Worrell wrote. “Over the past five years, the city has undertaken efforts to make the Boston Fire Department more equitable, through efforts such as the fire cadet program and the hybrid residency model, but leadership representation remains a critical missing piece.

“Our firehouses should reflect the full strength, talent and diversity of Boston, and that reflection must extend to the highest levels of leadership. Appointing Boston’s first Black fire commissioner would send a clear message to current and future firefighters that opportunity is real and leadership is within reach for everyone willing to serve,” Worrell wrote.

Signing onto Worrell’s letter were City Councilors Miniard Culpepper, Ruthzee Louijeune, Julia Mejia, Enrique Pepén, and Henry Santana; state Reps. Russell Holmes, Brandy Fluker Reid, Chynah Tyler, and Christoper Worrell; state Sen. Liz Miranda; and Suffolk Register of Probate Stephanie Everett.

On Monday, Drudys Ledbetter will be turning the tragic loss of her brother into a cause for good for others experiencing their own grief.

The Sharon resident will set off from Hopkinton and conquer her second straight Boston Marathon, but unlike last year, she says she’s running with her brother, not for.

Ledbetter’s brother, Wolf Ruben Valmond, died at the age 37 in December 2019, when he was shot and killed outside of a bar in Georgia. He had his eyes set on becoming a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent.

Wolf’s death weighs heavy on Ledbetter’s mind.

The Boston native, in her early 40s, is raising $25,000 for the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, a city-based nonprofit that supports families and communities impacted by murder, trauma, grief and loss.

Ledbetter told the Herald that she felt last year that she had tried to run for her brother. That has changed this year, as she feels like she’s running with him.

“In those long runs, you’re by yourself, in your head, and I was very intentional about just moving through whatever grief was left in my body,” Ledbetter said, “and letting it go, and moving into that place of acceptance.”

“I feel when we cross that finish line,” she added, “it’s going to be me and him, going, ‘This is our new normal. This is how we connect. This is how we engage as siblings. This is a beautiful way to bond.’”

Ledbetter, a nurse by training, founded Project Destigmatize Healthcare, a nonprofit that advances research and public education on cannabis and health.

Ledbetter said she remains heavily active in Boston, where she remembers seeing, as a teenager, someone shot and attending funerals for 15-year-olds.

“That’s real in the city of Boston. That trauma is real, Ledbetter said. “Half of the crimes in the city of Boston are not solved. These moms, these families, everyone left behind is carrying this grief forever and ever and ever.”

Last year, while looking to participate in the Boston Marathon, Ledbetter reached out to the Peace Institute to see whether it had any racing bibs since she wanted to run for a “really good reason.”

The institute did not have any bibs.

That changed this year, though, as Ledbetter is captaining a four-member charity team, the institute’s first ever crew of marathon runners.

She said she is getting close to her fundraising goal of $25,000, which she added will make a real difference for the institute.

The institute’s programming is supported through donations, sponsorships and relationships. To further its cause, the institute is constructing a new headquarters, on Westville Street in Dorchester.

“That’s going to be a pillar of peace in the community,” Ledbetter said of the new building. “It’s going to need programming to support the community, the children, the families.”

“We want to make sure that they cannot only build the building,” she added, “but can also support the programming that will come out of that building, as well.”

Ledbetter is an active member of Heartbreak Hill Running Company, attending the club’s weekly Saturday morning long runs in Newton.

“You master the hills,” she said.

Two MBTA Police officers were wounded, one having his eyes gouged and his head bitten, when an arrestee attacked them during booking, according to the agency.

Fritznel Jean, 28, a resident of Boston, faces a count of causing mayhem and three counts of assault and battery on a police officer — one causing serious bodily injury — for the melee that took place at Transit Police headquarters the morning of April 10.

Jean, who has the reverse of his actual name as a listed alias on his probation file, has a criminal record in Massachusetts dating back to March 2017 when he was charged in Brockton District Court with trespassing, disorderly conduct and disturbing the peace. His record continued with arrests in December 2021 for destruction of property and assault with a dangerous weapon.

Jean was at the time of this new incident about to go through booking after Transit officers arrested him on warrants for three charges from October 2024: disorderly conduct, shoplifting, and resisting arrest.

Jean, whose custody report warns of “mental health violent tendencies,” was being held in Cell 5 at the Transit Police headquarters at 240 Southampton St. in Roxbury when an officer who can speak Haitian Creole — Jean’s native language — removed him from the cell for booking.

But, according to the police report, Jean didn’t have much interest in getting booked.

“Jean began to shout at (an officer) saying that he wanted to go free,” the police report states. And his shouting continued as the officers continued to try to get him to comply: “Jean continued to shout in an aggressive manner and not cooperate … Jean became non-compliant and refused to be fingerprinted.”

Each outburst prompted the Creole-speaking officer to explain how the booking process worked and that Jean had no choice in the matter. But,after continued non-compliance, an officer told Jean he needed to go back into his holding cell, the report states.

As the officer turned his back to the open cell door, the report states, “Jean lunched toward (the officer) from behind, jumping onto his back and biting him on the back of the head.”

Other officers jumped into the fray and “a violent struggle ensued in which all parties fell to the ground trying to place Jean into handcuffs,” according to the report, which detailed that the melee became even more violent.

“Jean began to scratch and gouge (one officer’s) eyes … driving his thumbs forcefully into (the officer’s) sockets,” the report states, adding that Jean then “attempted to bite (another officer’s) hand.”

Finally, the officer who would file the report says that he “delivered 2 strikes with a closed fist to Jean’s face” and that this tactic “proved effective, stunning Jean” and allowing officers to handcuff him, put leg irons on him, and stuff him back into his cell.

Jean was charged in Boston Municipal Court’s Roxbury division on Monday, where he pleaded not guilty. The new offenses caused his bail to be revoked from his Quincy District Court cases until at least June 12.

The Boston School Committee is advancing a plan to the state school building authority seeking funding for a new facility for the Melvin H. King South End Academy.

“We are very excited about this opportunity to provide Melvin H. King South End Academy students with a state of the art therapeutic school building that is designed to meet their academic, social, emotional and mental health needs,” said Superintendent Mary Skipper. “This will bring the district another step closer to our long term goal of giving our students with different abilities the supports they need and the high quality educational experience they deserve.”

The school committee approved sending a statement of interest for a new facility for the Melvin H. King South End Academy to the Massachusetts School Building Authority (MSBA), aiming to kick off construction for the facility with state funding.

The Boston City Council also approved the MSBA application for the South End school earlier Wednesday, allowing the city to narrowly meet the April 17 deadline for MSBA applications this year with both approvals ready.

If the project gains state approval and moves forward, construction would likely begin around 2031, BPS officials stated Wednesday. The district said they will likely hear back from the MSBA about whether the project will move into an eligibility period in December.

The new application joins three BPS projects currently in the pipeline to receive MSBA funding for facility construction; the Shaw-Taylor Elementary School currently in the design selection process, the Ruth Batson Academy seeking a project manager in May, and Madison Park Vocational Technical High School entering an eligibility period in July.

The small K-12 school, which serves students who require a high level of academic and/or therapeutic support, was previously split across three buildings but will consolidate into only the Warren Ave. location in the South End in the 2026-27 school year.

“If this project advances into the eligibility phase, the MSBA will evaluate the Warren Ave. site, along with other potential locations,” said BPS Chief of Capital Planning Delavern Stanislaus. “The current facility was not designed to be a therapeutic school, and it is in poor condition. According to our facilities condition assessment, across every domain the building at Warren Ave. falls well below the district’s average. We are confident in this application to invest in this community.”

The academy has seen shrinking enrollment since COVID and the rollout of a district-wide inclusive education plan, said the academy’s Assistant Superintendent Harold Miller, shrinking from 300 students in 2020 to 160 in 2023 and a projection of 65 next year.

“Melvin H. King South End Academy is now in an active rebuilding phase, grounded in the Melvin H. King way,” said Miller, “asking ourselves, ‘What would Melvin H. King do?’ and our core values of safety, respect, responsibility, perseverance, kindness and a clear commitment to equity-driven transformation.”

The Boston City Council is considering a measure that would eliminate parking requirements for new residential development.

Councilors Sharon Durkan, Henry Santana and Liz Breadon, the body’s president, put forward an amendment to the city’s zoning code that would eliminate off-street parking minimum requirements tied to residential development in Boston.

The councilors said the amendment is aimed at reducing development costs that are exacerbating the city’s “housing crisis” by stalling production.

“We know that it is harder than ever to build,” Durkan said at last Wednesday’s Council meeting. “Housing production is at historic lows. Costs are rising and people are being priced out of the city. We know we need to do everything we can to increase affordability and expand the housing pipeline.

“This text amendment eliminates costly parking mandates from our zoning code,” Durkan added. “Most of Boston’s housing was built before these rules were made into law. These rules were established in the 1950s out of the false thinking that parking would reduce congestion. Instead, they made it harder to build housing and force developers to build more parking than we actually need.”

Durkan, who represents Beacon Hill and Back Bay, cited a report from the Metropolitan Area Planning Council that found more than a third of all parking in Boston sits empty overnight.

She said her proposed amendment would not ban parking from being built with new residential development, but would allow for flexibility.

“Developers will be able to build parking based on the needs of each project, rather than the outdated rules of the zoning code,” Durkan said.

She said the policy has worked in other Massachusetts cities, like Cambridge and Somerville, which eliminated parking requirements in 2022 and 2024, respectively. Similar reforms have been implemented outside of the Bay State, including Austin, Seattle, Minneapolis, San Francisco, Buffalo and Portland, her amendment states.

Boston eliminated parking minimums for affordable housing projects that include at least 60 percent income-restricted units in 2021, the amendment states.

“For Boston residents, this reform is a common sense, immediate step we can take to lower housing costs, support housing production and build a stronger, more sustainable city,” Durkan said. “The real question is whether we actually have the political leadership to get this done.”

Breadon said there’s been efforts over the last decade to eliminate parking requirements in her district, Allston-Brighton, which has led to “huge projects being approved with little or no parking.”

Developers seeking to build underground parking garages pay between $75,000 to $100,000 per parking space, at roughly one space per housing unit, Breadon said.

“This inevitably is added on to the cost of the housing and makes it more and more difficult for developers to make the numbers work,” Breadon said.

The proposal appears to have divided the Council. Six of the 13 councilors did not sign onto the zoning amendment order, indicating early resistance.

Two councilors who didn’t sign onto the order, Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy, confirmed Friday that they are opposed to the proposed parking changes.

Flynn said developers are not citing parking minimums that he said are disregarded by the Boston Zoning Board of Appeals and Transportation Department “on a routine basis as the reason why we’re not building anything in Boston anymore.”

“It’s that we added increased affordable housing and energy requirements on top of high interest rates, increased construction costs, and tariffs,” Flynn said in a statement to the Herald. “The focus should be on economic development, not parking purity tests.

“District 2 has absorbed as much or more housing as any part of the city,” Flynn said. “With the MBTA needing over $30 billion in repairs and school buses routinely late, working families in Chinatown and South Boston rely on a car to meet their needs. When we don’t include parking in new buildings, those cars invariably wind up on the street and exacerbate our existing parking crisis.”

Murphy, an at-large councilor who lives in Dorchester, said the proposal is not for a “small adjustment to zoning,” but rather, a “sweeping change” that would eliminate parking requirements citywide and create situations where residents won’t have the ability to park their cars at home.

“The language is explicit — no off-street parking shall be required,” Murphy said in a statement to the Herald. “That means housing can be built anywhere in the city with no parking at all. Supporters say the market will decide. But when that decision is wrong, the market does not absorb the impact. Residents do.

“People still own cars,” Murphy said. “They still need to park them. And when there is no off-street parking, that demand spills onto already crowded neighborhood streets. That is not theoretical. That is exactly what residents are already experiencing.”

Murphy said parking is the No. 1 concern cited at community meetings for new development proposals. The proposed amendment, she said, would not work as a “blanket policy” for all Boston neighborhoods.

“What works in Back Bay or the South End does not work the same way in neighborhoods like Mattapan, Lower Mills, Adams Corner, or Orient Heights, where residents rely on their cars as part of daily life,” Murphy said. “Parking in those communities is not optional. It is infrastructure.

“We can build more housing,” Murphy added. “But we should not adopt a citywide policy that removes all parking requirements and leaves our neighborhoods to absorb the consequences.”
