Josh Kraft, the son of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, officially announced his bid for mayor of Boston on Tuesday morning.

“I’m asking the city of Boston to set aside any ideas they may have about me based on my last name and let me tell you about the path of service I’ve forged,” he said at the event at Prince Hall in Dorchester.

He flagged housing and transportation improvements, as well as responsiveness at City Hall, as some of his key concerns for the city. He described himself as an underdog in the race.

"I'm excited for this challenge," Kraft told supporters.

Kraft released a video on YouTube on Monday in which he outlines his reasons for seeking the mayor's office and his top priority.

"There's a saying we had at the Boys & Girls Club. I care," Kraft says in the video. "I care that Boston is heading in the wrong direction. I care that our region continues to leave many people behind. I care that middle class families are being squeezed by the cost of housing, and I care that City Hall puts politics and ideology ahead of impact. That's why I'm running for mayor."

Kraft says in the video that his number one priority is to lower the cost of housing by building more of it in Boston.

"Strong leadership starts with listening," he says. "I will continue listening to people in every part of Boston, because my life has taught me that you can learn form anyone. True change comes not from orders from City Hall but by empowering people and communities."

The video ends with a slate that reads, "Democrat for Mayor Josh Kraft. More housing. More opportunity."

Kraft's entry into the mayoral race sets up a high-profile battle with incumbent Michelle Wu, who said in an interview last year that she expects to make her official announcement in 2025. Wu gave birth to her third child last month and has already returned to work.

Kraft took aim at Wu's administration in his announcement.

"On the number one challenge facing our residents, access to housing that regular people can afford, production under Mayor Wu has ground to a dead halt," he said.

More than 20,000 planned housing units are shovel-ready but are "stuck due to regulations imposed by the current administration," Kraft said. His plan includes one-time incentives to spur construction of new units at a price-point that middle class and first-time buyers can afford, he said.

Kraft's housing plan also includes a form of rent control that he said would be acceptable for renters and landlords alike. Under his leadership, Kraft said, Boston would cut a building owner's real estate taxes in exchange for the landlord capping rent increases for a 10-year period. "Luxury rentals" would be excluded from the program, he added.

"Mayor Wu promised us rent control three years ago. We will deliver it," Kraft said.

A former CEO of the Boys and Girls Clubs of Boston and leader of Kraft Family Philanthropies, Kraft is president of the New England Patriots Foundation. He lists his primary residence as a Battery Wharf condominium on Boston's waterfront purchased in 2023 by a Foxborough-based LLC.

Wu has run into brick walls on Beacon Hill as state lawmakers have batted aside proposals to allow a return to rent control and to shift some of Boston's tax burden onto commercial property owners.

Lawmakers did advance a measure to open up a swath of land on the Mystic River where the Kraft family aims to build a pro soccer stadium, despite Wu voicing concerns from City Hall. Kraft told reporters Tuesday that he would recuse himself from any soccer stadium negotiations if he wins the mayor's office.

Kraft said he could succeed with the solons of the State House where Wu has met resistance, because "I feel like one of the things I'm good at is listening to people, connecting with people, understanding what makes them tick or what they need."

Kraft also focused on the city's budget, public schools system, and transportation woes.

Taking aim at city spending, Kraft said Wu has overseen increased payrolls and boosted spending, while not finding "a single penny to be cut."

"That this is not only irresponsible, it's just not believable," he said.

The North End resident bemoaned high spending on Boston Public Schools while the system "regularly fails our kids on virtually every measure" including the timeliness of school buses.

One of the biggest cheers from the crowd came in response to a knock on Wu's effort to build more bus and bike lanes around the city, which Kraft said has increased congestion. He said he would immediately pause all bike lane construction.

"We have a leader that just does not listen. Too often, Mayor Wu acts as if she alone has all the answers. Whether it's housing, schools, neighborhood services, or bike lanes," he said. "Instead of listening to community voices, trying to understand what families and businesses need, too often they're being tuned out. On issue after issue, the mayor has become less and less receptive, and more and more disconnected from the communities, their feedback, and their needs."

He also took a shot at the Wu administration's handling of 3-1-1 complaints for issues like broken streetlights or potholes in need of filling. Constituents get voicemail recordings and unresponsive phone apps, he said, rather than timely results.

Being responsive to residents was a theme during the remarks, and former Boston Police Commissioner William Gross, who stood in the crowd of supporters behind Kraft, struck a similar note in his comments to reporters after the event.

"Talk to the people. Some people feel left out. Some people feel as though they're not listened to. I know, man, the seniors still come to me about bike lanes and transportation. I'm like, I'm retired, go to your politicians. And they feel as though no one's listening to them where they live," Gross said.

Gross said he personally knows Kraft and believes he is "a listener" who would fill that void.

"He takes constructive criticism. He'll never retaliate against you if he doesn't agree with you, or you don't agree with him," the former commissioner said.

Other familiar faces popped up in the crowd from the political scene of yesteryear.

Anisha Chakrabarti, Gov. Charlie Baker's deputy communications director until he left office, was handling press at Kraft's event. She works for Kraft Sports + Entertainment as director of corporate communications and strategy. Will Keyser, who worked on Baker's winning campaign, stood behind Kraft during the media scrum. And retired State Trooper Nathan Thomas, who served on the protection detail for Baker and other governors, stood watch at the edge of the stage area.

Hampden County District Attorney Anthony Gulluni, who prosecutes crimes in the state's third-largest city of Springfield, was on hand to show his support. He met Kraft through their service on the state Hate Crimes Task Force, both originally appointed by Gov. Baker.

"[I] immediately realized how passionate Josh is for any sort of public service and working to better our communities. And we became very good friends," Gulluni told the News Service. "And I believe in him. I think he's a tremendous leader. I think he has so much to give to public service. And I think in this case, he's going to be a tremendous leader for the City of Boston."

Kraft has already faced questions about his positions on national politics, particularly given his father's high-profile support for President Donald Trump, but he was unabashed Tuesday in his rejection of Trump and his identification as a Democrat, telling reporters he supported Kamala Harris in 2024.

"This campaign is not about ideology. It's about getting results," Kraft told his supporters in Grove Hall.

A voicemail left at a Wu campaign number was not returned. An email to Wu's campaign press address, seeking comment on Kraft's remarks, triggered an auto-reply directing the media to instead contact City Hall. There was no response to a followup email sent to Wu's City Hall press office.

A number of events have been happening across Massachusetts this week and they'll continue over the long weekend to celebrate Juneteenth, which commemorates the end of slavery in the U.S.

The holiday officially marks June 19, 1865, when Union troops arrived in Galveston, Texas at the end of the Civil War with an order declaring the state's enslaved people to be free with “absolute equality.” By then, 2 1/2 years had passed since the Emancipation Proclamation declared the freedom of enslaved people in the South.

There was a unity walk Thursday night at Harambee Park in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, marking a meaningful opportunity for neighbors, faith leaders, and public safety officials to come together and walk side-by-side for peace in the city's neighborhoods.

Earlier Thursday in Boston, city and state leaders attended flag raising ceremonies ahead of the Friday holiday.

Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll attended the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus’ Juneteenth flag raising ceremony at 11 a.m. at the State House.

Mayor Michelle Wu gave remarks at Boston's Juneteenth flag raising ceremony at City Hall Plaza Friday afternoon.

"It just stills gives me goosebumps to know that we are living in a city that takes care of our history, preserves the moments and memorials and spaces, so that we can learn from what's happened and plan for our best possible future," Wu told NBC10 Boston.

Another Juneteenth celebration and flag raising ceremony was held in Beacon Hill, hosted by the Museum of African American History. Joy Street transformed into a community festival featuring live music, spoken word performances, local Black-owned businesses, food vendors, family activities, storytelling, and free admission to the African Meeting House and Abiel Smith School.

On Tuesday, education advocates read aloud a famous Frederick Douglass speech in the shadow of the State House. Delivered 174 years ago, "What to the slave is the Fourth of July" is meant to highlight hypocrisies in the Declaration of Independence because rights in the document, like freedom, did not extend to enslaved people.

While freedom was guaranteed to Americans 250 years ago, for enslaved people, that written guarantee didn't come until almost 100 years later on Juneteenth.

The Center for Law and Education put on the reading with funding from Mass Humanities. On Friday, Mass Humanities will fund about 10 more free public readings from Amherst to Fall River to Salem.

Also Friday in Cambridge, the Black Response hosted its second Juneteenth Festival from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the Cambridge Common in Harvard Square. It will be a fun-filled event with activities for the whole family including bouncy houses, arts and crafts for all ages, school supply giveaways, free ice cream, pizza, fruit salad and empanadas, sensory play spaces, face painting, and lawn games.

The City of Framingham was hosting its third annual Juneteenth flag raising ceremony at noon on the Memorial Building Plaza. There were scheduled to be remarks from the city's diversity, equity and inclusion officer, as well as a presentation on the significance of Juneteenth from a Framingham High student.

“Juneteenth is an opportunity for our community to reflect on our nation’s history, honor those who fought for freedom and justice, and recommit ourselves to building a more inclusive future,” Mayor Charlie Sisitsky said in a statement ahead of the event. “I encourage all residents to join us as we celebrate this important day and the values that unite our community.”

“Juneteenth reminds us that freedom, equity, and opportunity are ideals that require ongoing commitment,” said Jesse Edwards, the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Officer for the City of Framingham. “This event brings our community together to honor the past, recognize progress, and continue the work of creating a more equitable and welcoming Framingham for all.”

Residents were encouraged to attend the event, which was free and open to the public. There is also a community Juneteenth event at Farm Pond on Saturday, June 20, from 1 p.m. to 6 p.m.

Also Saturday in Boston, the public is invited to Franklin Park's Shattuck Picnic Grove for Juneteenth Freedom Day 2026. The event is free and family friendly. It runs from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.

This day has been celebrated even before it was officially recognized as a federal holiday in 2021. Government buildings, banks, schools and some stores are closed in observance.

The history of Juneteenth

This is the fifth year since Juneteenth was designated as a federal holiday by former President Joe Biden, who served as Barack Obama's vice president. But the celebrations, which began in Texas and then spread across the country, have a rich and long history in Black America, with the day often spent gathering for picnics and cookouts.

The holiday — a combination of “June” and “nineteenth” — marks the day when U.S. Maj. Gen. Gordon Granger and his troops arrived in the Texas port city with the declaration of freedom in General Order No. 3.

As the third year of the Civil War neared, President Abraham Lincoln had issued the Emancipation Proclamation declaring the freedom of “all persons held as slaves” in the still rebellious states of the Confederacy. Though, for many, it did not mean immediate freedom but a promise of liberation, to be secured with a Union victory.

About six months after Granger's arrival in Galveston, the 13th Amendment abolishing slavery nationwide was ratified.

Celebrations across the nation this year

Juneteenth’s birthplace is celebrating with a daylong gathering at a Galveston park with music and fireworks, a parade and a worship service in a historic Black church. Nearby Houston lined up of musical artists and a domino tournament at Emancipation Park, established in 1872 by a group of formerly enslaved men.

Hundreds of other cities across the U.S. announced events over the long weekend, including a parade in Atlanta, a bike ride in Los Angeles and a festival on Martha’s Vineyard.

Several cities across the U.S. will host walks named for Opal Lee, the Texas woman who pushed for years to make Juneteenth a federal holiday. Participants will walk 2 1/2 miles to symbolize the 2 1/2 years it took for the Emancipation Proclamation to be enforced in Texas. Lee, known as the “grandmother of Juneteenth,” turns 100 this year.

The 250th anniversary of Henry Knox's "Noble Train of Artillery" continued Saturday in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood.

A gathering was held at the First Parish Church of Roxbury where a commemorative program recognized all of the communities along the Knox trail who aided Knox in 1776. There were also outdoor activities beside the Dillaway-Thomas House including a procession of 1776 militia units, horse-drawn sleds, and fife and drum groups.

The Noble Train of Artillery was one of the most extraordinary achievements of the American Revolution.

The next event will be held on March 17 in South Boston, honoring the 250th anniversary of Evacuation Day -- Washington's first victory of the Revolution. It will begin with a memorial service in St. Augustine's chapel on Dorchester Street, followed by a short procession up to Dorchester Heights for a commemorative program featuring political and community leaders from around the Commonwealth as well as reenacting units such as the Lexington Minute Men and the 2nd Massachusetts Regiment.

Revolution 250 is a collaborative initiative uniting more than 70 organizations across Massachusetts to plan and promote the Semiquincentennial — the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.

A water main break flooded Tremont Street in Boston on the Roxbury-South End line overnight – spawning a sinkhole that swallowed an SUV.

And believe it or not – the same exact thing happened in the same spot just last Tuesday to a transit van.

“But the second time it’s like, 'Wow, what’s going on?'” said Robert Morgan, whose car narrowly escaped the giant crater both times but was completely surrounded by sediment as the water started rising.

“So me and a firefighter were shoveling it out at 1 a.m., while water’s all around," Morgan said.

“This whole area was flooded,” said Erik Grau, president of Piano Craft Gallery.

Water rushed right down the stairs and into his business.

The nonprofit was still cleaning up from the last water main break when this break caused significantly more damage Friday morning.

“We’re going to have to replace our walls, we lost artwork in the backroom, we lost all of our pedestals,” Grau said.

“Unfortunately, it’s the same pipe that broke a week and a half ago and we don’t know the cause, why it broke,” Boston Water and Sewer Commission spokesman Tom Bagley said.

It’s a 150-year-old, 20-inch pipe that was relined more than half a century ago, with a 16-foot section replaced after last week’s break.

“Unfortunately these things do happen," Bagley said. "Again, we apologize and we’re going to try to ensure that this will never happen again in this location.”

City officials say they’ll keep the water shut off for now because it’s not affecting the water supply to any buildings while they do temporary repairs here to hopefully reopen the street later in the day. Then engineers will determine whether this entire stretch needs to be replaced.

Prosecutors say a Massachusetts man is facing numerous assault charges after he allegedly knocked a pregnant woman to the ground and kicked her several times in the stomach, resulting in her being told by doctors that she will not be able to carry her child to full term and it might suffer brain damage.

Dana Young, 33, of Randolph, is charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, assault and battery in violation of a restraining order and assault and battery on a pregnant victim, the Suffolk District Attorney's Office said.

The 23-year-old victim told police that on April 29 at about 6:30 p.m., she was walking along Winthrop Street in Roxbury after getting off an MBTA bus when a man, later identified as Young, approached her from behind and slapped her across the head, knocking her to the ground. He then kicked her in the stomach several times and fled toward Blue Hill Avenue.

The victim was 17 weeks pregnant at the time of the attack,. She refused medical treatment immediately after the assault, prosecutors said, but the next day visited Tufts Medical Center out of concern for her unborn child. Doctors informed her that she would not be able to carry the child to full term, and that the child might suffer brain damage due to ingesting blood because of the kicks to her stomach.

Young was arraigned Thursday in Boston Municipal Court. A judge revoked Young's bail from an earlier case and ordered him held for at least 60 days. He also set $2,000 bail on the new charges and ordered Young not to have any contact with the victim if he is released. He is scheduled to be back in court on June 3.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said the incident was not a random attack and additional charges are possible as the investigation continues.

“The allegations here are shocking in their brutality and violence," Hayden said. "We’ll provide this victim with all the help and support she needs as the case moves forward, but our first thoughts are with her health and the health of her unborn child."

A man was arrested three weeks after another man was shot to death in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood.

The shooting happened shortly before noon on July 15 on York Street. The victim, 29-year-old Breidy Martinez of Dorchester, was pronounced dead at the scene.

Boston police said that 32-year-old Hensly Dominique Jeanty of Dorchester was arrested around 4 p.m. Wednesday.

He's charged with A straight warrant out of Dorchester District Court charges Jeanty with murder, discharging a firearm within 500 feet of a dwelling, carrying a loaded firearm without a license and carrying a firearm without a license.

At the time of the shooting, police said Martinez was believed to have been riding a motorized scooter found at the scene.

Investigators recovered ballistic evidence in the area of Glenway Street.

Traffic in the area was affected during the investigation.

Anyone with information is asked to call 617-343-4470.

On the day of the shooting, Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said it was too early to say if the shooting was random or targeted, but that there was no reason to believe that the larger community should have any concerns for their safety and welfare.

"As is always the circumstance of a situation like this, we need the help and support of the community. If you know something or have information regarding this matter, please reach out to the Boston Police Department," Hayden said at the time.

The shooting was the second of the day in the city, following a 5 a.m. shooting near Boston Common that left one person injured.

The man convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting of a teenager in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood in 2022 was expected to be sentenced Wednesday, but the case was continued to November.

Zontre Mack, of Canton, opened fire on a group of people on the evening of July 27, 2022, killing 15-year-old Curtis Ashford Jr., the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office said.

Curtis' family has said that the recent eighth-grade graduate was on his way to the park to meet up with some friends when the shooting broke out on Ellington Street.

Another man charged in the shooting, Dominick Gavin, has pleaded guilty to a count of accessory after the fact and was sentenced to three to four years in prison.

Mack, who was 18 at the time of the shooting, was identified after investigators found DNA and fingerprints that matched to his in a vehicle that was seen carrying the shooter, prosecutors said.

Mack, now 21, was originally scheduled to be sentenced at 9:30 a.m. Wednesday. The case was continued to Nov. 13.

"Losing someone so young to violence is a blow to the entire city. Every person who cares about the health of our neighborhoods and the safety of our young people—and that should be all of us—should be shocked, saddened and motivated to make things better. But nowhere is Curtis's loss felt more profoundly than by his family and friends, and they will always have our sympathy and our support," Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement.

A man was convicted of murder nearly three years after a deadly shooting in a Massachusetts mall.

Dijoun Beasley, a 26-year-old from Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, was fatally shot at South Shore Plaza in Braintree on Jan. 22, 2022.

Julius Hammond-Desir of Maynard, who was 19 at the time, was arrested on a murder charge. The Norfolk County District Attorney's Office said Tuesday that a jury had convicted him of first-degree murder.

Prosecutors say Hammond-Desir is due to be sentenced Thursday in Norfolk Superior Court.

State and local police responded to a call of shots fired with a person down at South Shore Plaza around 3 p.m. on a Saturday. The mall was evacuated and those still inside were ordered to shelter in place until it was safe to come out.

Emergency personnel found Beasley on the ground with at least one apparent gunshot wound. He was taken to a Boston hospital with life-threatening injuries and died several days later.

According to Braintree police, there was an "encounter" between the two men inside a store on the first floor of the mall. Hammond-Desir allegedly approached Beasley, pulled out a firearm and shot him. Police believe Hammond-Desir immediately fled the mall.

Police said at the time that it appeared this was a targeted shooting and not a random event and insisted there was no danger to the community at large.

A man convicted of killing a taxi driver outside a Boston hotel nearly six years ago has been sentenced to life in prison, the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office said Friday.

Phillip Foy, 40, was found guilty Monday of first-degree murder in the June 4, 2019, shooting of Luckinson Oruma, the DA said. The sentence carries a mandatory life sentence, with no chance for parole.

Oruma, a 60-year-old from Dorchester, was a father of five, his boss told NBC10 Boston at the time of the shooting. Several family members attended the sentencing. His son delivered a victim impact statement, describing his father as a “hardworking, devoted, loving dad,” and that “he was doing what he always did, working hard to provide,” when he was killed. He noted that his father put five kids through college while working as a cab driver.

Oruma was parked in front of the Colonnade Hotel on the day of the killing, when Foy got in and asked to be taken to Mansfield. When Oruma declined, Foy got out, opened Oruma's door and attacked him, then shot him multiple times, including while he was lying on the ground, directly underneath Foy, prosecutors said.

Foy then drove the cab down Huntington Avenue and parked, ditched the gun and sat down, without his shoes, in front of a Starbucks. When officers arrived, he grabbed a pedestrian in an attempt to shield himself from them, but was taken into custody, when he claimed the shooting was a case of self-defense.

“The shooting death of Luckinson Oruma was shattering not just for his family and friends, but for anyone who goes to work each day expecting, as they should, to be in a safe environment," Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a media statement after the verdict. "This defendant turned Mr. Oruma’s environment into something tragically different, and I’m very grateful that the jury held him accountable for his devastating actions."

Transit police are investigating after a man's neck was slashed Friday evening at an MBTA station in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood.

The incident happened just after 8 p.m. at Nubian Square Station, which serves the Silver Line and other buses.

Police said two men were in a verbal dispute before one of them slashed the other with an unknown instrument.

The attacker fled the scene.

Transit police officers treated the victim before he was taken to an area hospital with a serious neck wound, police said.

The attack is under investigation.

Nearly two years after violence unfolded near Boston's J'ouvert Parade, the man charged in the case was held without bail, accused of fleeing the state before his original trial was set to start.

It was the first time Gerald Vick has been in a Massachusetts court after allegedly running from authorities the night before he was set to go on trial — and it was a longtime effort by police to capture the man.

The multi-month search began in December of 2024 and ended 13 days ago when 31-year-old Vick, a Dorchester resident, was apprehended by U.S. Marshals in Lithia Springs, Georgia.

Vick appeared in Suffolk Superior Court on Tuesday to answer to a handful of charges, including eight counts of assault and battery with a firearm, unlawful possession of a machine gun, as well as others.

Police said they found him with a pistol, equipped with a Glock switch — a device that makes the gun fire automatically and erratically — as well as a lot of ammo, shortly after shots rang out the morning of Aug. 26, 2023. That was the day of the annual J'ouvert Parade, which is part of the city's Caribbean Carnival Festival.

Investigators believe an argument between two "rival groups" played a role in the incident.

Residents voiced their concerns as city councilors considered whether to declare the situation at the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, and the impacted neighboring communities, a humanitarian crisis and public health emergency.

The neighborhood has been a hot bed of drugs and mental illness for years.

Residents say they're tired of meetings and want something done.

Promising to "fix" Massachusetts, Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue will spend the next nine weeks trying to convince voters that he can serve them better than Gov. Maura Healey has for almost four years.

The 59-year-old former CEO of Danvers-based medical device company Abiomed, Minogue on Tuesday night defeated businessman and former MBTA head Brian Shortsleeve in the Republican primary for the corner office, per the Associated Press. The AP called the race for Minogue at 8:44 p.m. As of 9:10 p.m., the AP said about 7% of votes had been counted, with 73.6% in favor of Minogue.

"The good news is it's going to be a little bit of an earlier night. The better news is we won," Minogue said during his election night party, vowing to bring an outsider's approach to shake up state government.

"Because of you, this is more than a campaign, this is a movement," Minogue told his supporters. "And because of your courage and your willingness to say, 'it's time to do something different, it is time to put people before politics.' Because of that, we are going to make history in 63 days."

The Republican ticket is now poised to feature Minogue with Shawn Oliver, who ran unopposed but also in tandem with Shortsleeve.

"This primary is over. Now it’s time to come together," Shortsleeve said Tuesday night, endorsing Minogue.

Republican candidate for treasurer Elizabeth Dionne and GOP contender for U.S. Senate John Deaton also attended the election night party. Both Dionne and Deaton ran unopposed in their primaries, coasting to their nominations.

The contentious race between Shortsleeve and Minogue featured both infighting revolving around the soul of the state's Republican Party and cohesion among candidates about issues including state's cost of living, economic competitiveness, immigration, job growth and government accountability.

Spending heavily from his own pockets, Minogue held few media events and also refused to debate Shortsleeve during the primary cycle, electing only to say that he would win the primary and debate Healey in the leadup to the general.

Minogue describes himself as pro-life Catholic who would "uphold" current abortion laws; believes the state should lean on natural gas — not "disruptive" and "expensive" offshore wind; and says he would "repeal or cancel all unfunded mandates," among various other proposals.

When signature fraud woes derailed and disrupted the campaigns of two other statewide Republican candidates, Minogue condemned Oliver for filing complaints about fraudulent signatures submitted on behalf of GOP candidates. Standing by Oliver, Shortsleeve in June called the party "incompetent and ineffective" and said "the hypocrisy being demonstrated by Minogue and his MassGOP minions will do lasting damage to the Republican Party's attempts to improve election security and generate more confidence in election outcomes."

Now Minogue and Oliver are ticket mates.

"Together we will unify the party," Oliver said Tuesday night as he congratulated Minogue on his win.

Republicans face an uphill battle to win the corner office and if he is elected Minogue would face Democratic super-majorities in the Legislature. Minogue and Healey are mindful that voters here have a history of electing Republican governors, from William Weld to Paul Cellucci, Mitt Romney and Charlie Baker.

Complaints over fraudulent nomination signatures sunk Minogue-backed lieutenant governor hopeful Anne Brensley and Anne Manning-Martin. Brensley ultimately opted to run as a write-in for secretary of state and Manning-Martin chose the same avenue to continue her campaign for lieutenant governor.

Minogue has funneled $15.8 million into his campaign since last October, and has repeatedly said he has the resources to win the primary and general elections. Shortsleeve had significantly less cash on hand than Minogue during their primary contest. At the end of July, Shortsleeve had roughly $526,800 cash on hand compared to Minogue's $8.1 million.

A graduate of West Point and Operation Desert Storm veteran, Minogue grew up as the youngest of four in New Jersey. After returning home from his military service, he spent 11 years working for GE HealthCare before leading Abiomed, which Johnson & Johnson reportedly bought for $16.6 billion in cash. Minogue's government experience is limited to the time he spent on the Governor's Advisory Council on Veteran's Services under former Gov. Charlie Baker, according to his LinkedIn. He also founded MedTechVets, a nonprofit helping military veterans find careers in the medical device industry. Minogue and his wife, Renee, created the Michael & Renee Minogue Foundation in 2015 to support faith-based education, healthcare innovation, children and veterans. His religious, military and healthcare backgrounds underpin his profile.

"From leading soldiers in combat to pioneering the field of heart recovery, Mike Minogue has spent his life serving others. A man of faith, husband, and father of five, he’s committed to serve Massachusetts with integrity and heart," his website says.

Minogue has run on the slogan "AAOK," which stands for Accountability, Affordability, Opportunity and Keeping communities safe.

While Minogue has been a prolific donor and supporter of President Donald Trump and other national Republicans, he said in July that he has a different outlook on tariffs than Trump, specifically opposing tariffs on medical device companies. Minogue also said he doesn't support cuts to the National Institutes of Health, that he thinks "everyone that's entitled to Medicaid needs to get it," and that he doesn't agree with Trump's assessment that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is doing a "great job."

After Healey signed a bill loosening abortion restrictions in August, Minogue's campaign said he'd "rather see the people of Massachusetts voice their opinion and decide this - not the politicians." Shortsleeve has called himself a "pro-choice Republican," and his campaign said he would have also signed the abortion law.

Minogue has also said that he would uphold the state's "common sense" laws regarding LGBTQ+ protections.

A Trump-aligned candidate in a state where Trump is unpopular, especially among Democrats, Minogue will look to entice the block of unenrolled voters who collectively outnumber registered Democrats. Both Minogue and Healey will compete over which candidate is better suited to address the high costs of energy, housing and healthcare.

Maura Healey calls for Minogue to agree to debate

The general election had already begun by the time Healey took the stage at her election night party in Dorchester, shortly after the AP called the race for Minogue. She was unopposed in the Democratic primary, and officially won the nomination shortly after polls closed at 8 p.m.

She jabbed at her new opponent, drawing a connection between the Republican candidate and President Donald Trump, as well as Minogue's documented personal anti-abortion stance. Healey will likely try to draw attention to Trump and abortion on the campaign trail over the next few months, as the state has consistently voted against Trump in presidential elections and even many independent voters support pro-abortion policies.

"Mike Minogue? He’s given more than a million dollars to Trump. He held a fundraiser for JD Vance at his waterfront mansion. By the way, that means Mike Minogue saw what Donald Trump did in his first term and said - sign me up, I want more of that!" Healey said in her prepared speech.

According to the written speech, Healey also planned to point out Minogue's financial support for conservative media organization PragerU, which she called on Thursday "a right-wing propaganda machine that promotes racist and anti-gay views, denies climate change, and spreads extremism and misinformation."

She continued, "Mike Minogue supports Donald Trump’s agenda that is raising your costs and killing Massachusetts jobs. He’s pro-ICE and anti-choice. Look, Donald Trump is gonna be president for two more years. Who your governor is right now matters more than ever."

Healey cast the general election in the terms of "whose side you're on" which she described, "Mike Minogue stands with Donald Trump, I'll always stand with you."

Wednesday morning the Healey-Driscoll campaign called on Minogue and Oliver, their Republican opponents, to accept debate invitations to provide voters with a clear picture of the race this fall.

Healey has agreed to participate in two statewide live, televised debates in the general election. The first debate is scheduled to be aired live on Oct. 8, followed by a second debate later in October.

“This fall, voters deserve to see the clear choice in this election on the debate stage,” Healey-Driscoll Campaign Manager Katie Prisco-Buxbaum said in a statement. “While Governor Healey works every day to lower costs and stand up to Donald Trump, Mike Minogue is dodging debates and questions about his extreme views and his support for Donald Trump’s pro-tariff, pro-ICE, and anti-choice agenda.”

Brian Shortsleeve

Shortsleeve, a former Marine and Harvard College graduate, just barely made the September ballot in April at the state GOP convention, where he raked in 15.5% of delegate votes to Minogue's 70.38%. The threshold to survive was 15%.

Just before 9 p.m., Shortsleeve, his wife and their three sons gathered on stage to again address supporters.

"While we came up short tonight, I believe that our message was heard, and I am proud of the campaign we ran," Shortsleeve said, drawing a round of applause from supporters who held up Shortsleeve campaign posters.

Shortsleeve also quickly endorsed his opponent, saying he would do everything he could to get Minogue elected.

"However, you supported me, I'm asking you: Join me in supporting Mike Minogue," Shortsleeve said. "Let's unify this party. Let's bring Independents and Democrats into this movement, and most importantly, let's defeat Maura Healey."

Without explaining how he would do it, Minogue has said he intends to initiate the voter-approved legislative audit on his first day in office. Shortsleeve said he would veto the Legislature's budget appropriation until lawmakers comply with the audit law.

Shortsleeve promised to "audit every state agency for waste, fraud, abuse and inefficiency"; to "conduct independent performance audits to evaluate whether programs are producing measurable results"; and implement a front-end identity and eligibility verification for SNAP recipients.

The party's two gubernatorial candidates were also largely aligned on immigration. When Healey signed the long-awaited PROTECT Act, an attempt to protect immigrants in Massachusetts from ICE, Shortsleeve said that Healey "prioritizes politics over public safety."

Minogue's platform outlines that Massachusetts will not be a "sanctuary state" and that "illegal immigrants will not have free Right to Shelter." Minogue's website also says that "girls need fair and safe sports."

In the showdown over local property taxes, the Massachusetts Senate on Thursday advanced a relief bill and delivered a formal rebuke to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's tax shift plan.

Senators voted 37-1 to pass the so-called tax shock bill and rejected an amendment that mirrored Wu's home rule petition on a 33-5 vote. The majority of the Boston delegation supported the amendment.

The bill, sponsored by Sens. Nick Collins of South Boston and William Brownsberger of Belmont, allows cities and towns to offer targeted rebates and credits to taxpayers during years when the residential property tax levy increases by more than 10%. Supporters framed it as a way to protect "vulnerable" homeowners from sudden spikes in tax bills without altering the state's existing property tax classification system.

The Senate rejected a version of Wu's proposal, offered as a Sen. Michael Rush amendment, which would have temporarily shifted a greater share of Boston's tax burden to commercial property owners in fiscal years 2027 through 2029. Voting in favor were Sens. Rush, Lydia Edwards, Liz Miranda and Sal DiDomenico, all of whom represent parts of Boston, along with Sen. Pat Jehlen, who is not seeking reelection and whose district includes Somerville and parts of Cambridge, Medford and Winchester.

Wu's amendment would have allowed Boston to adjust its property tax classification if residential properties were set to bear a higher share of the total levy than in fiscal year 2025, with maximum shift levels capped at 181.5% in fiscal 2027, 180% in fiscal 2028, and 178% in fiscal 2029.

The vote marked the Senate's first formal rejection of the mayor's tax shift plan after over a year of opposing the measure without taking a recorded vote.

Brownsberger and Collins have been the leading voices behind the Senate's opposition to Wu's proposal, with Brownsberger — whose district includes parts of Boston — speaking for more than 15 minutes during debate on the amendment.

Brownsberger said it was "about time" the Senate held a full debate on the issue so lawmakers could "move on past this issue to work with our municipal partners on all the goals we truly share." He emphasized that his opposition was not personal, saying he respects Wu and the Boston City Council and understands the motivation behind the proposal.

The vote comes amid escalating political tensions between Wu and Senate leadership. The mayor is backing a challenger to Brownsberger in the 2026 Democratic primary — her senior aide, Daniel Lander — and is also supporting a primary opponent to Collins.

Brownsberger argued that the tax shift proposal risked producing unintended and inequitable outcomes.

"One narrative, one example, would be, well, I've got a struggling homeowner that's benefiting from it. That's good, and I've got an office tower whose private equity owners are paying more taxes. Maybe that narrative makes sense in some cases," Brownsberger said. "But on the other hand, the truth is, we're lowering… taxes for your very wealthy single family homeowner, perhaps living in something of a mansion in the most tony neighborhood of the city. And you're raising taxes on your little garage owner trying to make things work."

Rush, a West Roxbury Democrat, framed the amendment as a direct response to what he described as a mounting affordability crisis for Boston homeowners, particularly seniors and working families.

Rush said the amendment was filed at the request of Wu and the Boston City Council and closely mirrored a home rule petition approved by the council and first filed with the Legislature in 2024. He pointed to rising residential values, lagging commercial property values and statutory limits on municipal tax increases as drivers of recent spikes in Boston tax bills.

Rush said the average tax bill for a family home rose by more than $500 in 2025 and is expected to increase by more than $700 in 2026, while commercial tax rates have continued to decline. He said those increases have disproportionately affected seniors on fixed incomes, particularly in his district, which he said has the highest density of senior citizens of any Boston Senate district.

The amendment, Rush said, would give Boston temporary flexibility to blunt those increases while state and city officials work on longer-term solutions.

Brownsberger responded by placing the debate within a broader discussion of the Legislature's role in regulating municipal finances for what he described as the "common good" of a single, interconnected state.

He argued that the state's property tax classification limits function as guardrails, rooted in decades-old reforms aimed at ending politically driven and inequitable assessments that once favored certain neighborhoods and disproportionately burdened businesses.

Allowing Boston to exceed those limits, he said, would invite similar requests from more than 100 other communities that use classification, undermining what he described as a carefully balanced statewide system.

Edwards, an East Boston Democrat and former city councilor, pushed back on that framing, saying the amendment reflected the immediate reality facing Boston residents and the calls city councilors continue to receive from constituents struggling with rising tax bills.

"I think it's very important that we, or someone in this body, address the fact that Boston does have unique needs in this time," she said. "And I'm not just talking about fiscal needs... I don't know too many other cities and towns whose housing authorities were denied hundreds of millions of dollars from the Trump administration. I don't know, but you can correct me, too many cities and towns that are facing lawsuit after lawsuit from this Trump administration."

Addressing concerns raised about impacts on small businesses, Edwards said the amendment was narrowly focused on shifting tax burden in the short term and not on economic development policy, while noting that the city has deployed a range of other tools — including grants, planning initiatives and licensing reforms — to support neighborhood businesses.

Edwards also argued that Boston's challenges extend beyond fiscal pressures, pointing to what she described as heightened scrutiny and legal challenges facing the city at the federal level. She said it was important for the Legislature to acknowledge those pressures even while disagreeing on the tax policy question.

She urged colleagues to view the amendment as consistent with instances in which lawmakers have granted Boston flexibility and autonomy in decision making through home rule petitions, including on liquor licenses, development policy and linkage fees, and questioned why the city should be treated differently in this case.

Despite the amendment's defeat, Edwards thanked colleagues for what she characterized as a respectful debate, while reiterating her support for the city's request. Later, Edwards delivered gifts to some senators in the chamber who opposed the amendment, including Senate President Karen Spilka.

The bill heads to a House that has previously been more receptive to the mayor's proposal. Wu's home rule petition won support in the chamber last session, and lawmakers have sparred over the competing versions of tax shock relief, setting the stage for another potentially contentious debate over the measure's fate.

Even homes destroyed by fire can attract strong interest from buyers across the Boston area, highlighting just how competitive—and unconventional—the Massachusetts housing market has become.

In Dorchester, a burned and condemned multi-family property recently went under agreement in just two days, according to the listing agent.

“It’s not your typical buyer,” said Anthony Bruno of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty. “You’re dealing with contractors, developers—people who know what it takes to bring something like this back.”

Why fire-damaged homes are still selling

Despite significant damage, these properties are drawing investors eager to take on major renovation projects. Bruno says the current buyer is looking to keep the existing structure and rebuild, possibly adding additional units depending on zoning.

“There’s only so much land,” he said. “Opportunities like this attract developers who are ready to move quickly.”

In a tight housing market like Boston’s—where inventory remains limited—these types of properties can offer rare opportunities for expansion or redevelopment.

A Melrose homeowner’s different path

In Melrose, one fire-ravaged property tells a different story about what happens after disaster strikes.

Paul Schille has owned his property since 1982. The original house, built in the mid-1800s, was destroyed in a fire that displaced his family and forced a series of difficult decisions.

“It was very, very stressful,” Schille said. “We were looking for homes almost every night.”

At one point, the property was listed for $650,000, drawing attention for what appeared to be a burned-out home selling at a high price. But Schille says the real value was in the land.

“This happens to be a quarter acre—and that’s big for Melrose,” he explained.

Developers expressed interest, with some considering multi-unit construction, but zoning challenges and timing issues slowed the process. Ultimately, the deal didn’t come together.

Starting over after losing everything

After months of uncertainty—and ongoing battles with insurance—Schille made a major decision.

“I said, this is way too stressful… I’m going to build the house myself,” he said.

With no prior construction experience, Schille stepped in as his own general contractor, overseeing the demolition of the damaged home and starting from scratch.

“When it happened, I had to really get in gear,” he said.

The rebuilding process took 19 months and required more money than his insurance coverage provided. Schille says he put everything he received from insurance back into the home, ultimately spending about $775,000 on the rebuild.

Now worth nearly $1.8 million

Today, the property has been completely transformed into a new two-family home—now valued at around $1.8 million.

“I couldn’t be happier with the way the house turned out,” Schille said.

He credits the Melrose community for helping his family through the crisis.

“The community was outstanding,” he said. “We had so many offers for help.”

Lessons for homeowners

Schille says the experience taught him important lessons—especially about insurance.

“You should talk to your insurance agent almost every year,” he said. “Make sure it’s insured at the proper value—because prices go up quickly.”

He also recommends homeowners consider working with a public adjuster when navigating insurance claims after a disaster.

A sign of the times in Boston real estate

From Dorchester to Melrose, these cases underscore a broader trend: even severely damaged homes can attract serious interest in Greater Boston’s competitive housing market.

For developers, agents say the appeal is clear—limited land, strong demand, and the potential to build equity. For homeowners like Schille, the journey is far more personal—one of loss, resilience, and rebuilding from the ground up.

“I love the place,” he said. “I love the community.”

U.S. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark of Revere, the highest ranking woman in the U.S. House, was the victor of a three-way Democratic primary in the Fifth District that also included Tarik Samman of Cambridge and Jonathan Paz of Waltham. No Republican sought the seat this year, setting Clark up to return to her leadership post in D.C. The AP called Clark's primary around 9:30 p.m. when about 10% of the vote was in, with Clark carrying about 75% of it.

U.S. Rep. Bill Keating of Bourne, a former county prosecutor and state senator, is set up to face Republican candidate R. Tyler MacAllister of Mattapoisett in the general election after outpolling primary challenger Craig Swallow of New Bedford on Tuesday. Keating has represented the Ninth District for eight terms. When the AP called the race for Keating at 9:50 p.m., about 7% of votes had been counted and 77% were for Keating.

U.S. Rep. Lori Trahan of Westford is lined up to compete with Republican Gary Grossi of Acton in the general after neither had a primary contest. U.S. Reps. James McGovern of Worcester and Ayanna Pressley of Boston faced no opponent in Tuesday's primary and also have no Republican opponent in November.

Legislative incumbents

Many legislative incumbents facing primary challenges appeared to have survived Tuesday's elections, but several of the night's most closely watched contests remained unresolved as ballots continued to be counted, leaving open questions about the strength of the anti-incumbent and progressive currents that animated campaign season.

The races will not determine control of Beacon Hill. Democrats currently hold 166 of the Legislature's 197 filled seats, compared with 30 Republicans and one independent, and will mathematically retain overwhelming majorities heading into 2027. Instead, the contests offered a series of tests of individual incumbents, and in several open seats, the ideological and political direction of districts that are virtually certain to remain Democratic.

In the Senate, four Democratic incumbents were facing primary challengers, including two members of the chamber's leadership ranks. Two of those contests remained too close to call around 10:30 p.m. Tuesday. The incumbents held substantial leads in the others.

In the Suffolk and Middlesex District, Senate President Pro Tempore William Brownsberger led Democratic challenger Daniel Lander, 55.7% to 44.4% according to the Associated Press, with 59% of the vote counted as of roughly 10:30 p.m. The race has carried broader significance because Lander, a former senior policy adviser to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, framed his challenge around generational change to the status quo and the divide between Brownsberger's suburban Belmont base and Lander's Boston home in Fenway.

The contest has also been a proxy for tensions between Wu and Senate leadership.

A second leadership test was even tighter. In the Norfolk and Suffolk District, longtime Sen. Michael Rush held 53.8% to civil rights attorney and consumer advocate Persis Yu's 46.2%, with 52% of ballots counted. The AP had not declared a projected winner.

Rush had not faced a primary or general election opponent since 2012, making Tuesday's contest an unusual test after more than a decade without an electoral challenge.

Sen. Nick Collins was also leading in the First Suffolk District, where he held 59.4% to Latoya Gayle's 38%, with 20% of votes counted. Gayle, who is aligned with Wu's political orbit, has made the race another closely watched contest involving an incumbent and a challenger associated with the mayor's supporters. Collins had not been declared the winner as of the latest count.

In the Norfolk, Plymouth and Bristol District, Sen. William Driscoll led Tony King and Michael Zullas with 65.1% of the vote, compared with 27% for Zullas and 7.9% for King, with 22% counted according to the AP. The race remained uncalled.

The most consequential Senate races for the future of open seats were also still developing.

In the Second Middlesex District, Rep. Erika Uyterhoeven led fellow Rep. Christine Barber, 38.5% to 30.9%, with 81% counted. Cambridge City Councilor Burhan Azeem had 14.7% and Somerville City Councilor Matt McLaughlin had 13.8%. No winner had been called.

The four-way contest is taking place for the seat being vacated by longtime Sen. Pat Jehlen and has attracted candidates from the district's progressive political base. Uyterhoeven has pushed for greater openness in the Legislature's processes.

In the Fifth Middlesex District, Rep. Kate Lipper-Garabedian held a considerable lead as of 10:30 p.m., claiming 73.5% of the vote with 56% counted in the Democratic primary for the seat being vacated by Sen. Jason Lewis. Malden City Councilors Carey McDonald and Ryan O'Malley were also competing.

The House picture was similarly mixed, with several incumbents declaring victory or being called winners while other races remained unsettled.

Rep. Lisa Field declared victory in the Third Bristol District after facing Taunton Police Chief Edward Walsh in the Democratic primary. Field won a special election to the seat last year by just 15 votes after a recount and is now preparing for another November contest against Republican Larry Quintal. Walsh entered the primary after legislation concerning his mandatory retirement age stalled on Beacon Hill.

The AP called Rep. Andrew "Dru" Tarr's victory in the Fifth Essex District at 10:21 p.m. Tarr, who won the seat in a spring special election following the death of Rep. Ann-Margaret Ferrante, was leading Democrat Sarah Wilkinson. Tarr could face Republican Christina Delisio in November.

Rep. John Lawn was also declared the winner by the AP at 10:20 p.m., defeating Newton City Councilor Alison Leary, 63.6% to 36.4%, with 99% counted. Lawn is the chairman of the Health Care Financing Committee and a longtime ally of Speaker Ron Mariano.

Rep. Angelo Puppolo Jr. declared victory in the 12th Hampden District over younger progressive challenger Michael Lachenmeyer. With 49% counted, Puppolo had 68.9% to Lachenmeyer's 31.1%. Lachenmeyer had sought to make housing and affordability central issues and portrayed the longtime Springfield-area lawmaker as part of an entrenched establishment. Puppolo's campaign said it won every precinct, except for one.

Rep. Mike Connolly also declared victory in the 26th Middlesex District. With 21% counted, Connolly held 81.6% to Neil Miller's 18.4%. The Cambridge representative is himself considered a member of the Legislature's progressive wing, making the race less a traditional moderate-versus-progressive contest than a debate over transparency, accountability and generational change.

Another closely watched Cambridge contest remained unresolved. In the 25th Middlesex District, challenger Evan MacKay led Rep. Marjorie Decker, 53% to 47%, with only 8% of votes counted, according to the AP. MacKay nearly defeated Decker in the 2024 Democratic primary, losing by just 41 votes after a recount. House leadership has rallied behind Decker this year.

An open House seat in Cambridge also changed hands, after Barber gave it up to run for Senate. The AP called the 34th Middlesex District race for Somerville City Councilor Will Mbah at 10:09 p.m., with 54.1% and 99% counted.

In the 27th Middlesex seat Uyterhoeven left open, the AP called victory for Ben Ewen-Campen.

In western Massachusetts, the open First Franklin District remained too close to call. With 37% counted, former Rep. Natalie Blais aide Corinne Coryat led former Greenfield City Council President Lora Wondolowski, 54.2% to 45.8%. Independent Amy Lavalle has already secured a place on the November ballot.

In the 19th Suffolk District, Rep. Jeffrey Turco led paramedic LeeAllen Meyer, 60.1% to 39.9%, with 62% counted. The contest had pitted one of the House's more moderate Democrats against a challenger campaigning on a progressive agenda and abortion access.

At least two other House primaries had no publicly available vote totals at the time: the Democratic and Republican contests for the open 9th Bristol District, where Democrats Edward Pacheco and Stephen Medeiros were competing and Republicans Chester Tam and Henry Bousquet were also seeking their party's nomination. The district is the only one in Massachusetts where both parties had contested primaries, setting up a November race in one of the Republicans' better potential pickup opportunities.

The Republican primary in the Second Plymouth District, where first-term Rep. John Gaskey faced Carver Select Board member Mark Townsend, also had no publicly available vote totals.

The night's results thus far largely reinforced the broader picture that had defined the campaign: Massachusetts remains a state where most legislative incumbents face little or no electoral competition, and Tuesday's contests were unlikely to alter the basic partisan balance on Beacon Hill.

But the races that remained unsettled will offer a more nuanced measure of voter sentiment.

Governor's race

Promising to "fix" Massachusetts, Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue will spend the next nine weeks trying to convince voters that he can serve them better than Gov. Maura Healey has for almost four years.

The 59-year-old former CEO of Danvers-based medical device company Abiomed, Minogue on Tuesday night defeated businessman and former MBTA head Brian Shortsleeve in the Republican primary for the corner office, per the Associated Press. The AP called the race for Minogue at 8:44 p.m. As of 9:10 p.m., the AP said about 7% of votes had been counted, with 73.6% in favor of Minogue.

"The good news is it's going to be a little bit of an earlier night. The better news is we won," Minogue said during his election night party, vowing to bring an outsider's approach to shake up state government.

"Because of you, this is more than a campaign, this is a movement," Minogue told his supporters. "And because of your courage and your willingness to say, 'it's time to do something different, it is time to put people before politics.' Because of that, we are going to make history in 63 days."

The Republican ticket is now poised to feature Minogue with Shawn Oliver, who ran unopposed but also in tandem with Shortsleeve.

"This primary is over. Now it’s time to come together," Shortsleeve said Tuesday night, endorsing Minogue.

Republican candidate for treasurer Elizabeth Dionne and GOP contender for U.S. Senate John Deaton also attended the election night party. Both Dionne and Deaton ran unopposed in their primaries, coasting to their nominations.

The contentious race between Shortsleeve and Minogue featured both infighting revolving around the soul of the state's Republican Party and cohesion among candidates about issues including state's cost of living, economic competitiveness, immigration, job growth and government accountability.

Spending heavily from his own pockets, Minogue held few media events and also refused to debate Shortsleeve during the primary cycle, electing only to say that he would win the primary and debate Healey in the leadup to the general.

Minogue describes himself as pro-life Catholic who would "uphold" current abortion laws; believes the state should lean on natural gas — not "disruptive" and "expensive" offshore wind; and says he would "repeal or cancel all unfunded mandates," among various other proposals.

When signature fraud woes derailed and disrupted the campaigns of two other statewide Republican candidates, Minogue condemned Oliver for filing complaints about fraudulent signatures submitted on behalf of GOP candidates. Standing by Oliver, Shortsleeve in June called the party "incompetent and ineffective" and said "the hypocrisy being demonstrated by Minogue and his MassGOP minions will do lasting damage to the Republican Party's attempts to improve election security and generate more confidence in election outcomes."

Now Minogue and Oliver are ticket mates.

"Together we will unify the party," Oliver said Tuesday night as he congratulated Minogue on his win.

Republicans face an uphill battle to win the corner office and if he is elected Minogue would face Democratic super-majorities in the Legislature. Minogue and Healey are mindful that voters here have a history of electing Republican governors, from William Weld to Paul Cellucci, Mitt Romney and Charlie Baker.

Complaints over fraudulent nomination signatures sunk Minogue-backed lieutenant governor hopeful Anne Brensley and Anne Manning-Martin. Brensley ultimately opted to run as a write-in for secretary of state and Manning-Martin chose the same avenue to continue her campaign for lieutenant governor.

Minogue has funneled $15.8 million into his campaign since last October, and has repeatedly said he has the resources to win the primary and general elections. Shortsleeve had significantly less cash on hand than Minogue during their primary contest. At the end of July, Shortsleeve had roughly $526,800 cash on hand compared to Minogue's $8.1 million.

A graduate of West Point and Operation Desert Storm veteran, Minogue grew up as the youngest of four in New Jersey. After returning home from his military service, he spent 11 years working for GE HealthCare before leading Abiomed, which Johnson & Johnson reportedly bought for $16.6 billion in cash. Minogue's government experience is limited to the time he spent on the Governor's Advisory Council on Veteran's Services under former Gov. Charlie Baker, according to his LinkedIn. He also founded MedTechVets, a nonprofit helping military veterans find careers in the medical device industry. Minogue and his wife, Renee, created the Michael & Renee Minogue Foundation in 2015 to support faith-based education, healthcare innovation, children and veterans. His religious, military and healthcare backgrounds underpin his profile.

"From leading soldiers in combat to pioneering the field of heart recovery, Mike Minogue has spent his life serving others. A man of faith, husband, and father of five, he’s committed to serve Massachusetts with integrity and heart," his website says.

Minogue has run on the slogan "AAOK," which stands for Accountability, Affordability, Opportunity and Keeping communities safe.

While Minogue has been a prolific donor and supporter of President Donald Trump and other national Republicans, he said in July that he has a different outlook on tariffs than Trump, specifically opposing tariffs on medical device companies. Minogue also said he doesn't support cuts to the National Institutes of Health, that he thinks "everyone that's entitled to Medicaid needs to get it," and that he doesn't agree with Trump's assessment that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is doing a "great job."

After Healey signed a bill loosening abortion restrictions in August, Minogue's campaign said he'd "rather see the people of Massachusetts voice their opinion and decide this - not the politicians." Shortsleeve has called himself a "pro-choice Republican," and his campaign said he would have also signed the abortion law.

Minogue has also said that he would uphold the state's "common sense" laws regarding LGBTQ+ protections.

A Trump-aligned candidate in a state where Trump is unpopular, especially among Democrats, Minogue will look to entice the block of unenrolled voters who collectively outnumber registered Democrats. Both Minogue and Healey will compete over which candidate is better suited to address the high costs of energy, housing and healthcare.

The general election had already begun by the time Healey took the stage at her election night party in Dorchester, shortly after the AP called the race for Minogue. She was unopposed in the Democratic primary, and officially won the nomination shortly after polls closed at 8 p.m.

She jabbed at her new opponent, drawing a connection between the Republican candidate and President Donald Trump, as well as Minogue's documented personal anti-abortion stance. Healey will likely try to draw attention to Trump and abortion on the campaign trail over the next few months, as the state has consistently voted against Trump in presidential elections and even many independent voters support pro-abortion policies.

"Mike Minogue? He’s given more than a million dollars to Trump. He held a fundraiser for JD Vance at his waterfront mansion. By the way, that means Mike Minogue saw what Donald Trump did in his first term and said - sign me up, I want more of that!" Healey said in her prepared speech.

According to the written speech, Healey also planned to point out Minogue's financial support for conservative media organization PragerU, which she called on Thursday "a right-wing propaganda machine that promotes racist and anti-gay views, denies climate change, and spreads extremism and misinformation."

She continued, "Mike Minogue supports Donald Trump’s agenda that is raising your costs and killing Massachusetts jobs. He’s pro-ICE and anti-choice. Look, Donald Trump is gonna be president for two more years. Who your governor is right now matters more than ever."

Healey cast the general election in the terms of "whose side you're on" which she described, "Mike Minogue stands with Donald Trump, I'll always stand with you."

Shortsleeve, a former Marine and Harvard College graduate, just barely made the September ballot in April at the state GOP convention, where he raked in 15.5% of delegate votes to Minogue's 70.38%. The threshold to survive was 15%.

Just before 9 p.m., Shortsleeve, his wife and their three sons gathered on stage to again address supporters.

"While we came up short tonight, I believe that our message was heard, and I am proud of the campaign we ran," Shortsleeve said, drawing a round of applause from supporters who held up Shortsleeve campaign posters.

Shortsleeve also quickly endorsed his opponent, saying he would do everything he could to get Minogue elected.

"However, you supported me, I'm asking you: Join me in supporting Mike Minogue," Shortsleeve said. "Let's unify this party. Let's bring Independents and Democrats into this movement, and most importantly, let's defeat Maura Healey."

Without explaining how he would do it, Minogue has said he intends to initiate the voter-approved legislative audit on his first day in office. Shortsleeve said he would veto the Legislature's budget appropriation until lawmakers comply with the audit law.

Shortsleeve promised to "audit every state agency for waste, fraud, abuse and inefficiency"; to "conduct independent performance audits to evaluate whether programs are producing measurable results"; and implement a front-end identity and eligibility verification for SNAP recipients.

The party's two gubernatorial candidates were also largely aligned on immigration. When Healey signed the long-awaited PROTECT Act, an attempt to protect immigrants in Massachusetts from ICE, Shortsleeve said that Healey "prioritizes politics over public safety."

Minogue's platform outlines that Massachusetts will not be a "sanctuary state" and that "illegal immigrants will not have free Right to Shelter." Minogue's website also says that "girls need fair and safe sports."

Sen. Ed. Markey prevails over Rep. Seth Moulton

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey secured the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts’ Senate primary Tuesday, once again fending off a push for generational change as he seeks a third term.

Markey, 80, defeated U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who had attempted to argue that it was time to do away with the “status quo” in his pursuit to oust the octogenarian.

Yet Markey successfully pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it was Moulton — not the older incumbent — who was out of touch with the state’s voters. Perhaps no other issue defined the race more than transgender rights, and Markey repeatedly hit Moulton for previously saying he would not want his daughters to play against transgender athletes.

“Massachusetts needs a senator who stands up and fights back, a senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey said during his victory speech. “That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”

In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle, where Democratic winners are expected to prevail in the general election in November. Markey will face Republican John Deaton, who who lost to Sen. Elizabeth Warren by about 20 points in 2024 and was unopposed in his primary Tuesday.

Markey has been a fixture in Massachusetts politics since the 1970s, prompting Moulton to make his “status quo” arguments on the campaign trail and to question Markey’s accomplishments during his lengthy time in office.

“Generational change isn’t about compromising, to do the small things better,” Markey said Tuesday. “It’s about fighting to do the big things best.”

In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”

“We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn,” he added.

The Senate race was not the only generational challenge for Democrats on the ballot. Similar dynamics played out in several congressional races, but ultimately, the older incumbents won Tuesday. In the 8th Congressional District, longtime incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch defeated Patrick Roath. And in the 1st Congressional District of western Massachusetts, Rep. Richard Neal defeated public school teacher Jeromie Whalen to advance to the general election.

During the campaign Markey repeatedly pointed out that Moulton, in 2024, raised eyebrows among some in the party for saying he did not want his daughters playing sports against transgender girls.

Critics said he was echoing President Donald Trump’s talking points against allowing transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.

Moulton later apologized for his remarks, saying it was not his intention to hurt the transgender community and stressing his support for other transgender rights bills.

“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”

Moulton, who enlisted in the Marines after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and served four tours of duty in Iraq, was first elected to Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in 2014. He launched a 2020 presidential campaign but dropped it after a few months.

Markey was elected to the Senate in 2013. Before that he represented Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District from 1976 to 2013.

Markey notably fended off a challenge in 2020 from Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a younger rival from one of the nation’s most famous political families. Markey did so by aligning himself with the liberal wing of the Democratic Party.

Antoine Hilaire, a 76-year-old Democrat who voted for Markey in Brockton on Tuesday, said being older can be a positive because it offers people experience and wisdom.

“If the older one is doing the better job, I don’t know,” he said. “He’s doing a good job. It’s not a big, big, big problem.”

Longtime Democratic House incumbents also defeated younger challengers

Lynch, 71, has held the 8th District seat in south Boston since 2001. He won Tuesday’s primary against Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer who contended that it is time to end “wait-your-turn” politics. Lynch stressed the value of experience inside Congress.

Lynch has fended off other youth challenges in the past, but Roath’s campaign hoped for a boost of excitement after longtime Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. John Larson was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in August in neighboring Connecticut. Like Roath, Bronin called for the need for generational change while running against an establishment politician.

In the 1st District Democratic primary in western Massachusetts, Neal, 77, bested Whalen, 39.

Neal, known as the dean of the New England House delegation, was first elected in 1988. Whalen ran to the left of Neal, calling for Medicare for All and questioning whether Neal has done enough to oppose Trump’s agenda.

Whalen was endorsed by Our Revolution, a progressive organization founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

District Attorney races

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden secured renomination in a race against two challengers, including his predecessor, Rachael Rollins.

Democrat Djuna Perkins claimed victory in a tight primary race for Norfolk County District Attorney. With 98% of the vote in, Perkins was leading with 28.95%, followed closely by Adam Deitch at 26.28%.

"We did it! Yesterday, we finished first in a field of 7 candidates running to be the Democratic nominee for Norfolk County District Attorney. I am so grateful for the countless volunteers, tens of thousands of voters who supported us, my dedicated campaign team and endorsers, and my family who supported me every step of the way in this 23-month long campaign," she wrote in a statement.

Perkins ran a campaign based on calls for reform in the office in the wake of the Karen Read and Sandra Birchmore trials.

"This campaign has never been about me. It has always been about restoring justice and integrity to a broken criminal justice system here in Norfolk County; ensuring that no one is treated differently under the law due to political connections, money or privilege; protecting victims of crime; prosecuting those who prey upon or harm others; and keeping every resident of Norfolk County safe," the statement continued.

Deitch conceded on Wednesday, saying he'd called Perkins to congratulate her.

"A new administration will take office in a few months, and our job does not end with this election — it continues. We must keep fighting for a justice system defined by fairness, trust, and accountability and where, at its core, everyone is treated the same," he said in a statement.

There are no Republican challengers. Independent Joe Pagliarulo advanced straight to the ballot.
