A $10,000 solid-wood mahjong table made its debut at Art Basel Miami Beach last winter. At the push of a button, the center of the table sank, tiles rose automatically from within and walls assembled around the edges.

The display left local mahjong instructor Elyse Kremins in awe. Mahjong had become art, she said.

From living rooms to offices, bistros to bars, mahjong is everywhere in South Florida. While it never disappeared, the centuries-old game has far outgrown its reputation as a grandmother’s pastime. In Miami, it’s now considered “cool” to play, Kremins said.

Some players stand in swimming pools and play for hours using floating mahjong sets and tiles. Kremins's students include women in their 30s, young mothers who bring their babies to lessons, where the little ones often end up playing together themselves, and a growing number of men.

“The guys don't flinch when their wives or girlfriends just say, why don't you learn?” she said.

The game is having a major pop culture moment. A-listers like Julia Roberts, Meghan Markle, and Blake Lively have all been seen slapping tiles. So has Cindy Crawford, who in an interview with NBC described mahjong as "a great excuse for women to get together” and an incredible mental exercise. The model rarely turns down a chance to play, she added, and she often practices on the Real Mahjong app.

Mahjong’s explosion in popularity appears to be linked to a post-pandemic desire for connection. Players say they crave sensory, analog experiences in an age of digitization and AI. For others, the allure is in the beauty of the tiles themselves — the most coveted sets can easily fetch up to $600.

In South Florida, American mahjong is the overwhelming local favorite. For those who aren’t familiar with the rules, mahjong is loosely a tile-based cousin of gin rummy. Most Asian styles like Hong Kong let players assemble winning hands freely. Meanwhile, American mahjong relies on a standardized card of preset hands and eight additional joker “wild cards.”

But when someone says “mahjong,” they could be referring to any one of over 40 distinct variations, each with its own rules and traditions, all demanding some combination of strategy, skill and luck.

Mahjong's evolution means some players gather around vintage sets passed down through generations. Some play for cash. Others compete in tournaments where mahjong is treated as a sport. Along the way, the game has also become the center of cultural debates over appropriation vs. appreciation.

How did mahjong come to the US?

Mahjong emerged in 1800s China near Shanghai, where it was mainly a male gambling game. Its path to America is largely credited to Joseph Park Babcock, a Standard Oil representative who returned home from China in the 1920s and helped market the game to an American audience.

Aided by Hollywood stars, similar to influencers today, the game fueled a nationwide craze. Soon, President Warren G. Harding and first lady Florence Harding were playing in the White House. So were wealthy families like the Vanderbilts. Glossy magazines featured players gathered around ornate sets, while department stores filled display windows with mahjong tiles. At the height of the Roaring Twenties, mahjong was a marker of cosmopolitan taste.

Nearly a century later, entrepreneurs like Kremins say COVID fueled mahjong’s resurgence in South Florida. An influx of newcomers from out of state wrote to her saying they were looking for ways to meet people, Kremins said.

That’s when she began hosting weekly lessons and open games at the Shelbourne Hotel in Miami Beach. Nearly 100 players ranging from their late 20s to 80s came to play American mahjong, she said.

Recently, Kremins bought her grandchildren “Mini Mahjer,” an interactive board game specifically designed to teach children American Mahjong. The four-year-olds already love shouting mahjong, she said, and she’s confident they’ll continue to play when they’re older.

"Miami is cutting edge, and mahjong fits right in,” Kremins said.

Jewish American women forged American mahjong culture

By the 1930s, a new mahjong tradition was taking shape in the United States.

American mahjong, formalized by the National Mah Jongg League in 1937, revolves around an annually updated card of preset winning hands. This version of the game has developed its own rituals and vocabulary, from tile racks and coin purses to table snacks and a distinctive shorthand.

American mahjong culture was shaped by Jewish women in the New York area during and after World War II. The game spread through predominantly Jewish social networks that had formed due to antisemitic exclusion. As Jewish families moved to the suburbs after the war, mahjong moved with them, becoming a fixture of suburban life and a lifeline for many young mothers adjusting to new communities.

The current revival has been fueled in part by those same networks, making mahjong more diverse than ever, historian Annelise Heinz said. Heinz began researching the game and its “virtually forgotten historical record” in grad school, after a question she always had growing up — "Why do the mothers of my Jewish friends all play a Chinese game?" — yielded mostly theories and misinformation online, she said. She has since authored a book narrating the history of the game, “Mahjong: A Chinese Game and the Making of Modern American Culture.”

Heinz said that many baby boomers are now passing down mahjong, while their daughters, who often grew up around the game without learning it, are returning to it later in life and teaching friends, spouses and neighbors how to play.

Dara Collins, co-founder of Modern Mahjong in Broward County, is one of them. She grew up in New York, where she remembers her mother hosting games at home with friends and serving traditional Jewish foods as they played.

Her mother was only 36 at the time, but as a kid, Collins considered mahjong an old women’s game, she joked.

Today, mahjong extends far beyond living rooms. Along with her business partner, Donna Kassman, Collins travels to teach classes across Florida and the U.S. The game has also found a surprising place in corporate offices, she added. Companies have invited Modern Mahjong to lead educational programs and lunches, partly due to the fact that its visibility has exploded online.

“When we first started in 2019, you did not see as many mahjong accounts,” Collins said. “Now, you can’t go on Instagram without seeing mahjong sets.”

Pop culture has helped fuel interest, with players recognizing the game from films like “The Joy Luck Club” and “Crazy Rich Asians.” But Collins said mahjong’s appeal goes beyond mere nostalgia. Players often use online groups to find games while traveling, and strangers regularly welcome newcomers into their homes to play.

“Mahjong is like having a dog,” Kassman said. “If you’re walking by yourself, no one talks to you. But if you’re walking with a dog, people stop and connect. The same thing happens when you’re playing mahjong in public. People come up and say, ‘My mother played. My grandmother played.’”

For Collins and Kassman, mahjong is a social pastime and a connection to their heritage. Both women are Jewish, and they recently hosted a mahjong festival at the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York.

The event drew around 500 participants and featured open-level lessons and competitive tournament play. Experts spoke on panels about the history of the game, and players of all ages faced off while munching on food from a Manischewitz food truck.

At the event, Collins could make out the Statue of Liberty in the distance. It appeared to her as a symbol of the game’s enduring legacy, she said. The National Mah Jongg League was founded by eight Jewish women in New York City. Eighty years later, she was at the largest Jewish mahjong festival ever, and it was sold out. The game continues to bring people together, she added.

Learning mahjong for the first time

I didn’t grow up playing mahjong, even though both of my parents are from China. So I turned to one of the best options out there: New York’s Chinatown.

At the Phoenix Palace on Bowery, young men and women sipped drinks at the bar, ate popcorn chicken catered from Potluck Club, one of the city’s hottest Cantonese-American restaurants, and kindly annihilated me at the mahjong table.

That was partly my fault — I hadn’t gone on a beginner night — but I did manage to get a Hong-Kong style rundown from Chris Kumaradjaja, a staffer at the Green Tile Social Club. As he explained the different suits, I asked him why he started playing.

The social aspect of the game was a big motivator. “It’s a bit of a catalyst for conversation,” he said. Basically, he clarified, a round could mean the start of a new friendship, or a silent, focused battle between “life or death.”

I really liked the sound of the former, and not so much the latter. Most beginners start off with “chicken hands,” or mahjong in easy mode. After an hour, you can graduate to scoring hands.

But I soon found out that I wouldn’t have the luxury of puttering around the kiddie pool. As I took my seat among seasoned Gen Z and millennial players and constructed my tile wall — my puny line of defense against the sharks — an atmosphere of concentration settled over the booth. Players crossed their arms and leaned back to read the table, scan discards and update their strategy.

For experienced players, tile counting and decision making goes by fast, albeit with great deliberation. I slowed them down by grabbing the wrong tile here and there, mistakes my table graciously corrected. Fingers tapped rapidly against felt mats. Around us, exclamations over a rare hand, accompanied by the rhythmic cascading of tiles, created a comforting chatter in the background. The noise made by the shuffling tiles is similar to a flock of sparrows, the bird after which the game was named.

To nobody’s surprise, I didn’t win any of the four sets, each taking around 15 minutes. But by the third round, I felt something click. I was getting better — I’d managed to form four sets of three — but was beaten by the young woman to my left, who managed to snag a pair and call mahjong.

Many players told me the game is an addiction. I didn’t believe it, until I went home and started practicing online. I won my first game against bots, then a second, then a third. I was in love.

For the rest of the week, I kept practicing. I even booked a ticket to play in another mahjong league for the following week. This time, I made sure my opponents were beginners.

Mahjong’s high-glamour rebranding in the South

Mahjong is a particularly adaptable game. “The tiles themselves are a canvas,” historian Annelise Heinz said, and they allow for endless variations in imagery and symbolism, often related to local identity.

That flexibility has sparked cultural controversy, particularly in the South.

In Texas, a hub of the mahjong boom, companies founded by entrepreneurs who are neither Jewish nor Asian American sell tiles with designs that stray from the game’s traditional iconography. One Dallas-based company, The Mahjong Line, aligns the tile suits with the theme of each set. In the $485 Ranch Line, for example, tiles with Chinese characters become horseshoes, bamboo become cacti, and circles become sunsets.

The glitzy sets often cater to a distinctly Southern aesthetic of hosting and femininity, Heinz said. Game runners coordinate their sets, tabletop décor and even the cocktails they serve, adding an aesthetic, material element to the game.

The breakthrough came during the COVID-19 pandemic, when three players in Highland Park, Texas, decided to redesign mahjong’s classic white tiles with Pantone colors and custom artwork. The Mahjong Line is part of a group of businesses founded in Dallas over the last six years that have become many of the country’s leading mahjong companies.

Brands like My Fair Mahjong, Oh My Mahjong, and Bespoke Mahjong all sell tile pushers, floating game mats, and a wide array of tile sets. There are mahjong-themed hats, cups, and carrying cases, as well as mahjong mats and racks in teal, hot pink or cheetah print.

Many of The Mahjong Line’s most popular themed sets are sold out online. That includes the Foodie Line, whose joker tiles feature playful illustrations of martinis and pizzas. Who is the foodie gal? The “consummate host and connector” whose “unofficial amuse-bouche is a game of trivia” and whose “post-dinner palate cleanser is karaoke,” according to the product description on the brand’s website.

The redesigned sets quickly sparked controversy. Critics were outraged when the brand coined the Pantone-colored tiles as a “respectful refresh” of traditional tiles — which, “while beautiful, were all the same,” the website once read. The original tiles contained “unnecessary” Chinese symbols, and the brand aimed to replace them with “minimal designs” for new players, according to the site’s FAQ section before it was updated.

Members of the Asian American community, including Grace Meng, New York’s first Asian American member of Congress, took to social media to air their frustrations.

"Please put the Chinese characters BACK onto the Chinese game," Meng wrote in a January 2021 post on X with a Mahjong Line hashtag. "Don't change my culture and history to make it more palatable to you."

The Mahjong Line founders have since apologized for their “failure to pay proper homage to the game’s Chinese heritage" and updated their website and social media to include educational content about mahjong’s origins. LaGere said she has received death threats, two of which were so alarming that local law enforcement was involved. Her only concern at that point was her family and their safety, she added.

The use of the words “modern” and “refresh” when talking about the tile redesign was unintentionally "loaded," LaGere told NBC. She comes from the advertising industry, where those kinds of words are used daily to say you are changing something established, she said, describing the experience as "a learning moment."

The feedback from the Asian and Asian American community over the tiles was mixed, she added.

"I received countless emails from Asian Americans and Asians that expressed their support of our highlighting the game and growing the game," she said. "Many thought it was great and were encouraging us to keep going."

The comments LaGere received condemned the “misplaced anger and ugliness” directed toward her, she said. One player wrote to her, “I don’t take any offense; I love the product you have created,” while another said, “Please keep going; this will mean there will be more people to play with," according to LaGere.

Today, the co-founder of The Mahjong Line emphasizes the importance of learning the history of the game in China. At the same time, there is a large market for the products that the company designs, she said.

“We unabashedly use creativity and originality and color to a game that we love,” LaGere said. “We have grown this game and brought more women into the fold of American mahjong, and we're super proud of that contribution.”

Heinz remains hopeful that mahjong can open broader conversations about racism and growing up Asian American in the United States. The game’s complex history continues to unfold at a moment of heightened attention toward China, she said, both as a geopolitical concern and a point of cultural objectification.

“Mahjong retains its really valuable place in American culture as a bridge across difference, and I think it can play that role,” Heinz added.

Mahjong isn’t going anywhere

Players and league organizers believe the signs are clear: mahjong is here to stay.

Part of its lasting power is built into the game itself. Mahjong is played with four people, creating a recurring reason to gather.

Mahjong’s recent surge in popularity has invited comparisons to pickleball. But Kassman joked that many Floridians sign up for pickleball without realizing just how tough the humidity can be. Sooner or later, they discover mahjong and its air-conditioned appeal, she said.

Mahjong’s cultural power extends beyond its current moment. It has long served as a way for newly formed or displaced communities to build community, Heinz said. During and after World War II, for example, the Air Force Officers' Spouses Club developed its own variant, Wright-Patterson mahjong, which is still played by officer spouses on Air Force bases around the world.

One of mahjong's greatest rewards is the unlikely groups of people it brings together, league organizers say. Every game needs four players, and strangers often become regulars.

“I just love that we're there at everyone's mahjong meet cute,” Kassman said. “At the end of the event, players take out their phone, and they give each other their numbers. It’s so much fun to be able to give people a social hobby.”

Arlington officials are eyeing efforts to extend the MBTA's Red Line in an effort to help residents frustrated by traffic congestion. But first, Massachusetts lawmakers will need to address a 46-year-old law.

"We'll choke in traffic if we don't get better transit in town," said Paul Schlichtman, an Arlington Town Meeting member who is part of the community group "Extend the Red Line."

Schlichtman said officials in Arlington — a suburb that sits about 10 miles northwest of downtown Boston — have been working to build more homes, making it crucial for the town to boost public transportation.

"The town has done a lot in terms of housing density. And if we're going to pull that off, if we're going to build more housing in town, we can't do it with the current infrastructure," he said.

Reps. Sean Garballey and David Rogers and Sen. Cindy Friedman — who all represent Arlington — filed legislation (HD 6313) this month repealing a section of a 1980 law barring the MBTA from planning or building any Red Line extension further into Arlington "unless specifically authorized to do so by law."

The bill is a home rule petition approved by Arlington Town Meeting in May, Garballey said, and something he's "strongly" in favor of as a way to offer traffic relief for residents.

"It's a goal to provide more services to our constituents. You know, the town of Arlington, is made up of around 45,000 people. We are a massive population right outside Boston and there is no train service that goes through the town of Arlington. There's been a lot of conversations within our community for decades about why that is," Garballey said.

According to town records, Arlington's Town Meeting voted 145-54 in May, with 11 members abstaining, authorizing the Select Board to file a home rule petition to repeal the 1980 law.

Schlichtman, who is also a School Committee member, said he hopes it will help revive once controversial 1970s plans to extend the Red Line through Arlington Center to Arlington Heights, with the possibility of stretching it further out to Route 128.

"So, the plans have been drawn, once upon a time, and we're trying to get them to dust them off and move it forward," Schlichtman told State House News Service.

In the 1970s, the MBTA sought to extend the line but ran into opposition from Arlington and Lexington residents.

The Red Line has 22 stops running from Braintree and Dorchester through Boston and ending in Cambridge at Alewife Station, a few miles from the Arlington border. Depending on the month, the line's daily ridership averaged between 107,000 to 146,000 riders in 2025, according to state data. While there is no subway or commuter rail service in Arlington, the MBTA runs several bus lines through the town.

Ahead of the Town Meeting, Arlington's Select Board voted 4-0 to recommend that no action be taken on the home rule petition. The Select Board presented several reasons for recommending no action in its report to the Town Meeting that State House News Service obtained. One of these reasons is that the board believed the law's specific reference to the "northwest rapid transit extension" to mean it expired when the MBTA completed the Northwest Extension in 1985. Also, the board felt there were several other more pressing pending home rule petitions and the MBTA didn't view the law as a restriction to its planning. Schlichtman presented a substitute motion to repeal the 1980 law that the Town Meeting passed.

"MBTA is looking forward to working with the legislators who filed this amendment to discuss their goals as we explore possible options for future transit to support this region," MBTA communications manager Maya Bingaman said in a statement referencing the bill and responding to State House News Service inquiries about agency's plans for extending the line.

The MBTA's 2027-2031 Capital Investment Plan (CIP) specifically states it does not include funding to support extending the Red Line to Arlington, along with other projects brought up during a public comment period for the plan. The MBTA's 2026-2030 CIP also references public support for extending the Red Line but allocates no funding for the project.

"I sponsor the home rule petitions of each community I represent as long as there are no moral, ethical, or legal issues with the proposed legislation," Friedman said in a statement responding to State House News Service's inquiry. "That said, I supported a law to remove similar restrictions on the extension of the Red Line in 2024 and am proud to do so again. While we may not see an extension project in the near future, I don't believe our laws should prohibit it."

A 2024 law stemming from legislation filed by Garballey, Rogers and Friedman repealed a 1976 law prohibiting the MBTA from building a mass transportation facility — including a parking garage or rapid transit station – within 75 yards of Arlington Catholic High School.

The bill repealing the 1980 law has yet to be assigned to a committee and the Legislature concluded scheduled formal sessions in July. Still, Garballey says he's hopeful it will get passed before the end of the year.

Repealing the 1980 law doesn't guarantee the Red Line will be extended. Before any plans can move forward, Garballey and Schlichtman say studies are needed to better understand how much the project would cost.

Garballey and Rep. Michelle Ciccolo of Lexington, which borders Arlington, secured a $50,000 earmark in the fiscal 2027 budget for the MBTA to "study the financial feasibility and department capability" of extending the Red Line and/or creating a Bus Rapid Transit line from Alewife along Route 2 to the Concord Rotary. Garballey and Ciccolo say they have had initial conversations with the MBTA about the earmark, with the last discussion taking place around a month ago.

Garballey also said a more comprehensive feasibility study is needed. He and Ciccolo have co-sponsored legislation (H 3666) creating a commission to assess the feasibility of either extending the Red Line or creating a new Bus Rapid Transit service in Arlington and Lexington. The bill has been in front of the House Ways and Means Committee since January and cleared the House side of the Committee on Transportation in November on a 12-0 vote.

"I think Arlington demands adequate public transportation, and I think it was a real missed opportunity decades ago when the Red Line was not extended through Arlington, and I would like to see a comprehensive study in terms of what are the future transportation options from Alewife to better service the constituents of Arlington, Lexington, Concord and the Route 2 corridor," Garballey said.

For spots like Ula Café in Boston's Jamaica Plain neighborhood, a small slip of paper is cause for celebration.

"I was like, 'Finally, we have it in our hands,'" said General Manager Jon Sanchez. "I'm so happy a little one-café business like ours has an opportunity like this."

The eatery will soon add beer and wine to its menu providing an economic boost that in the past has been tough to come by. In 2024 state and local leaders sought to change that creating 225 new liquor licenses intended for neighborhoods that were previously passed over.

"It's rolling out, and it's a tremendous, tremendous thing for this community," said Massachusetts Rep. Chris Worrell, a Boston Democrat.

"It's giving an opportunity to entrepreneurs," said Democratic state Rep. John Moran of Boston.

In the two years since the legislation passed, Boston officials have slowly rolled out many of the licenses into communities throughout the city.

"We've gotten out close to maybe 100 licenses across the city," said state Sen. Liz Miranda, a Democrat in Boston.

"We just released a slew of 11 new licenses that just came out," said Boston Director of Nightlife Economy Corean Reynolds.

But how immediate has that economic impact been? Andre Williams owns Cool Shade, a Jamaican restaurant, and says he's had his license for over a year.

"We see a little change, but not significant yet, because a lot of people don't know we have it. People are surprised to hear we have a full liquor license," said Williams.

Part of the struggle is a small space that largely serves takeout orders. Williams says he is pursuing a bigger space where the license can have a bigger impact.

"Right now, I'm on the verge of getting a bigger space so we can do more sit-down dining," said Williams.

"If there isn't enough commercial property, they actually can't build that restaurant in Mattapan, or in Roxbury or Dorchester, like they want to," said Miranda.

Meanwhile, spots like Ula are preparing to unveil their new menu and are hopeful customers new and old will embrace their added offerings.

"We're launching beer and wine next week with the JP Porchfest," said Sanchez. "Are we going to be packed? That's our hope."

One final hurdle to issuing the new licenses is getting the word out to businesses that applications are open. Boston officials encourage small business owners throughout Boston to apply on the city website.

In a debate-style conversation, Ahmed and Culpepper, who advanced from the preliminary election in September, each weighed in on the controversy and how they would bring credibility back to the role if elected.

"When you show the community how you are transparent, then folks will trust you," Ahmed said.

Beyond restoring trust, the candidates were focused on the issues that will impact those living in the district long-term. White Stadium is high on that list, with concerns growing over traffic impacts associated with a professional women's soccer team becoming a tenant of the stadium.

"The process that took place wasn't one that included the community," Culpepper said.

"It's not clear if our football teams can still play at White Stadium. It's the only facility that Boston Public Schools see as a home," Ahmed said.

Boston voters will narrow the field of candidates for mayor on Tuesday in a municipal preliminary election that pits incumbent Michelle Wu against a deep-pocketed challenger with one of the most famous last names in New England.

Wu seeks a second term as President Donald Trump has threatened federal intervention in some of the nation’s largest cities, following his deployment of National Guard troops and federal officers to Los Angeles and Washington for local law enforcement matters. Since Trump took office in January, Republican leaders have excoriated Wu and other big-city mayors for immigration policies they say undermine the president’s mass deportation efforts.

Wu faces a challenge from Josh Kraft, son of billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and the former head of both the New England Patriots Foundation and the Boys & Girls Club of Boston. Wu and Kraft are Democrats. Also on the ballot are former Boston police officer and frequent candidate Robert Cappucci and community organizer Domingos DaRosa.

As of the end of August, Kraft had outspent Wu, $5.5 million to about $1.1 million, thanks in large part to more than $5 million in loans from the candidate to his campaign. But Wu entered the final days of the campaign with much more cash in the bank, $2.4 million to about $1.3 million for Kraft.

Although Democrats have exclusively occupied the Boston mayor’s office for nearly 100 years, the position is officially nonpartisan, with all candidates running on the same ballot and the top two vote-getters advancing to the November general election.

Wu placed first in the crowded 2021 preliminary election with 33% of the vote against seven other candidates, including Cappucci in his third mayoral bid. She went on to win the general election with 64% of the vote, carrying 19 of the city’s 22 wards.

She lost Wards 6 and 7 in South Boston and Ward 16 in South Dorchester in that race and in the general election. These were the three wards where Trump posted his best performances in the city in the 2024 presidential election, receiving about a third of the vote. In the preliminary, Wu lost some additional wards in North and South Dorchester, the South End and West Roxbury.

The Associated Press does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidates to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

There are no automatic recounts in Massachusetts, but candidates for Boston offices may petition for a recount by obtaining signatures from 50 or more registered voters from each ward. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Here’s a look at what to expect on Tuesday:

Election day

Boston’s preliminary mayoral election will be held Tuesday. Polls close at 8 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The AP will provide vote results and declare winners in Boston’s mayoral election. Cities and towns across Massachusetts will also hold primaries for various municipal offices, including Boston’s city council, but only Boston’s mayoral race will be included in the AP’s vote tabulation.

Who gets to vote?

Any voter registered in Boston may participate in the election.

What do turnout and advance vote look like?

As of Feb. 1, there were nearly 422,000 registered voters in Boston. Of those, about 39% were Democrats, 4% were Republicans and 56% were not enrolled in any political party.

In the 2021 mayoral preliminary, turnout was just shy of 25% of registered voters. Roughly a quarter of votes in that election were cast early or by mail. Early and absentee voting was considerably higher in the last two even-year primaries, with 46% of 2022 ballots and 60% of 2024 ballots cast before preliminary Election Day.

As of Tuesday, more than 25,000 ballots had been cast before the preliminary, about 54% from Democrats, 3% from Republicans and 42% from voters not registered with any party.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the 2024 presidential election, the AP first reported results from Boston at 9:44 p.m. ET. The election night tabulation ended at 2:24 a.m. ET with about 93% of total votes counted.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 56 days until Boston’s mayoral general election on Nov. 4.

Boston's mayoral hopefuls made their case to Black voters a week before the preliminary election.

At the Bethel AME Church in Jamaica Plain, incumbent Mayor Michelle Wu and two of her challengers — Josh Kraft and Domingos DaRosa — spoke about Madison Park Technical Vocational High School in Roxbury. The candidates addressed long-standing concerns about the school's condition and reputation.

Wu pledged a massive investment.

"This will be more than a $700 million project," she said. "That is a big chunk of the city's capital budget, and we will need some supports to figure out how we get there, but we will get there."

Kraft promised to make Madison Park the top vocational school in the state.

"Under my watch, we will finally fix and give Madison Park High School and what every student, teacher, and alumni there deserves — the best vocational school in Massachusetts."

DaRosa, a community advocate, argued that it's about more than just funding.

"For me, it's not just the funding. It's about giving our young people the inspiration to go to Madison, to get rid of the stigma that Madison is the worst school in Boston," he said. "Because it's not."

The candidates also addressed housing concerns and immigration.

Wu and Kraft will take part in "The Final Word," a forum hosted by NBC10 Boston and Telemundo Boston in partnership with Embrace Boston and the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts, at 7 p.m. Wednesday.

Gov. Maura Healey signed legislation Wednesday giving Boston 225 more alcohol licenses, the majority of which are expected to boost economic development in 13 targeted ZIP codes.

Sit-down restaurants in Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, East Boston, Roslindale, West Roxbury, Hyde Park, Charlestown, Jamaica Plain and the South End now stand to benefit from the restricted licenses. The steep price tag for existing licenses, which can cost around $600,000, has been a major obstacle for businesses looking to turn a profit, including in underserved neighborhoods.

"Neighborhood restaurants play such an essential role in our communities and our economy," Healey said in a statement. "This bill will lower barriers for Boston restaurants to provide the services that their customers are looking for and help them succeed, while also supporting local nonprofits, theaters and outdoor spaces. I'm grateful for the leadership of Mayor Michelle Wu, the Boston City Council, the Boston legislative delegation, the Legislature and restaurant owners who advocated for this change that will have long-lasting positive impacts."

The idea is encouraging for business owners like Andre Williams, the owner of Jamaican restaurant Cool Sade, who's previously told NBC10 Boston he hopes to claim one of those initial licenses, which he thinks will bring more customers in.

“We’ll build a bar, have a licensed bartender,” said Williams, “We love mixed drinks. I’m from Jamaica so we do a lot of mixed drinks.”

As thousands of residents drop coverage or hunt for higher priced plans through the Massachusetts Health Connector, Gov. Maura Healey said Tuesday that officials are exploring how to connect residents with other insurance options.

"We've seen premiums expected to increase two or three times," Healey said on GBH News' Boston Public Radio. "Now the good news — and I hope to be out with more word on this soon — we're working to see how we can come up with ways to cover people."

Tuesday marked the Health Connector's deadline for Bay Staters to sign up for plans that start on Jan. 1. It's been a tumultuous open enrollment cycle, with more than 10,000 people already dropping coverage as they grapple with sticker shock from premium spikes.

In the aftermath of the country's longest government shutdown, Congress couldn't reach a bipartisan deal to extend enhanced premium tax credits, which are slated to expire on Dec. 31 under a 2022 federal law.

Healey said Tuesday that the loss of subsidies will translate into "upwards of 350,000" Massachusetts residents losing their health insurance. GBH co-host Jim Braude asked Healey to clarify whether her administration is examining whether those people "could be covered by the state in some fashion."

"Well there are other programs, Jim. There are other health insurance plans," Healey replied. "And we just want to make sure that, you know, those people, if they qualify for a different plan, that we're able to get them into that."

Analysts say Massachusetts residents will face additional health insurance losses in 2027, as new Medicaid work requirements take effect under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A recent report advised the state to develop a model similar to the "COVID-era command center" to thwart coverage losses and ensure compliance with forthcoming federal regulations.

Massachusetts is expected to lose $3.5 billion annually once all health care components of that federal law take effect, according to Audrey Shelto of the Blue Cross Blue Shield Foundation of Massachusetts.

Healey did not directly answer a question from a caller who asked the governor to use her power and tap into the state's more than $8 billion rainy day fund to stave off federal funding cuts. The caller, identified as Chris in Boston, said he has a disability and relies on MassHealth.

"I will say I am focused as we move into this budget season on making sure that we do what we need to do to protect the most vulnerable among us," said Healey, who must file her fiscal 2027 budget proposal by Jan. 28.

Later in the interview, Healey lamented that "health care is broken in this country."

"And we're seeing it every day with what's happening with escalating health care costs for people and businesses around this country," Healey said. "You know in Massachusetts, we can only work with the money that we have. And you know, you see the reports of hospitals struggling."

The governor's comments came after a veteran nurse called in to reflect on the closure of Carney Hospital in Dorchester during the Steward Health Care bankruptcy crisis. The caller, identified as Susan in Milton, told Healey Massachusetts has a "dearth of hospitals" and that she "had never seen health care so bad in my life."

The state seized another Steward hospital, St. Elizabeth's Medical Center in Brighton, by eminent domain in September 2024. Nurses at the facility — since renamed Boston Medical Center-Brighton — voted to authorize a three-day strike depending on how contract negotiations unfold, the Massachusetts Nurses Association announced Monday.

BMC Brighton nurses are concerned about potential plans to eliminate certain positions, curtail access to a pension plan, reduce paid time-off benefits, increase health insurance costs and not raise pay for the majority of nurses, the union said. The MNA said it represents 650 nurses at the hospital.

"To do this to our members, who already sacrificed so much during the turmoil of the Steward crisis and stuck with this hospital to ensure the safety of our community just adds further insult to the injury we have already suffered," said Kate Cashman, a BMC Brighton nurse and bargaining committee co-chair.

Josh Kraft is suspending his Boston mayoral campaign, days after finishing a distant second to incumbent Michelle Wu in the preliminary election, and rerouting funding he would have spent on the race to causes close to him.

"After careful consideration, I have decided to suspend my candidacy for mayor of Boston," he wrote in a post on social media. Read the full statement to supporters below.

Kraft advanced to November's general election from Tuesday's preliminary, but his second-place finish was nearly 50 percentage points behind Mayor Michelle Wu's.

The move effectively clears the way for Wu to be reelected, and she released a statement Thursday night thanking "him for caring about our city deeply enough to want to make it better."

Kraft is the former CEO of the Boys and Girls Club of Boston and a son of Patriots owner Robert Kraft. When he entered the race in February, he said he was running because he saw the city being run the wrong way.

"I care that Boston is heading in the wrong direction. I care that our region continues to leave many people behind. I care that middle class families are being squeezed by the cost of housing, and I care that City Hall puts politics and ideology ahead of impact," he said.

On Thursday, he said he was dropping out because "political mudslinging" wouldn't help Boston "during a time in America where we need to come closer together despite all our differences, instead of igniting divisiveness that pulls us further apart."

Kraft also announced that he was putting $3 million — "resources I had committed to this race and additional funds" — toward organizations tackling the homelessness situation at Mass. and Cass and a job training organization for people who've spent time in prison that he's previously supported. He also said he'd announce details about "setting up a recovery campus."

In her statement on the suspension of Kraft's campaign, Wu said she respected the decision and vowed to keep engaging the community.

"I respect Josh’s decision and thank him for caring about our city deeply enough to want to make it better. We are going to continue over the next two months and beyond to keep engaging our community members about the critical work in front of us and how we keep making Boston a safe, welcoming home for everyone," Wu said.

Battle lines continue to form around a ballot question to change a key component of the education reform law that some say made Massachusetts the best educated state in the country, separating politicians who are used to standing on the same side of most issues, and simultaneously creating strange allies.

The day after U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, declared during a televised debate against Republican John Deaton that she would be voting in favor of Question 2 to eliminate the requirement that students pass the MCAS exam to graduate from a Massachusetts public high school, a triumvirate of constitutional office holders from her party planted their flags firmly in the camp against the measure.

Gov. Maura Healey, Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll and Attorney General Andrea Campbell headlined a press conference hosted by the "No on 2" campaign on Wednesday afternoon in Roxbury.

Campbell had only publicly stated her position on the question for the first time the day before, as a guest on GBH's Boston Public Radio. Healey had previously said she did not believe in removing the requirement when asked, but speaking at Wednesday's rally seems like a shift in tone for the governor to perhaps a more proactive role against the initiative.

At Wednesday's press conference, Healey attributed the state's standing as the oft-ranked best public education system in the country to its teachers and to its statewide standards.

"A way to assess performance and how kids are doing, that is through the MCAS exam," she said. "Massachusetts has the best public schools in the country because of our high standards, not in spite of them, and Question 2, in our view, would eliminate a tool that we know works in terms of our ability to assess how our young people are doing."

Question 2 supporters say scrapping the standardized MCAS exam's use as a high school graduation requirement would allow educators to stop "teaching to the test" and instead focus on student needs. Districts would gain more autonomy over establishing graduation requirements that reflect students who have mastered competencies in the state's academic standards, proponents say.

The Massachusetts Teachers Association and other supporters say the measure would bolster equity among students from marginalized communities, and they often point to 700 students each year who are unable to graduate because they failed MCAS but met all other requirements.

Critics warn the measure's passage could lead to a patchwork of education standards and ultimately harm the state's future workforce.

"We'll have different standards in Randolph than we will in Reading, and that's a system that I don't believe sets us up for success," Healey said.

Late Wednesday afternoon, the "Yes on 2" campaign released a statement from MTA President Max Page and Vice President Deb McCarthy calling Healey's comments "disappointing."

"It’s disappointing that Governor Healey has chosen to side with the few corporate donors opposing Question 2 and against Massachusetts educators, parents and students," the statement says.

Wednesday's press conference could be the beginning of a more active opposition effort on behalf of some of the state's top elected officials. In addition to Healey, Driscoll and Campbell, House Speaker Ron Mariano and Senate President Karen Spilka -- the two most powerful people in the Legislature -- have also come out against Question 2.

"I, too, have real concerns about Question 2 because it would not just remove our only statewide graduation standard, it would remove the state standard and offer no replacement," Campbell said. "This would result in over 300 different and unequal standards for high school graduation across the commonwealth and potentially lead to haphazard assessments of student readiness for college and careers, and even wider inequities in student achievement and, of course, opportunities."

As more electeds take official positions as the election inches closer, another line has been drawn -- former Education Chair Rep. Alice Peisch has declared for "No on 2" while current Education Chair Sen. Jason Lewis has declared in favor of the question. Neither campaign has claimed the endorsement of House chair of the Education Committee Rep. Denise Garlick.

The initiative puts some top Democrats at home in Massachusetts at odds with a Bay State Democrat in D.C., and in line with the state's Republican party on the issue. The MassGOP has said they recommend voting against the question, and Tuesday night the GOP challenger for Warren's Senate seat also said he's casting a "no" vote.

"We can't have 351 standards," Deaton said during the debate on Tuesday. "Our school system is still recovering from COVID. There's statistics of fifth graders can't even read. And there's people being graduated, if you don't have the MCAS and you have no standards, you're going to get people graduating from high school that can't fully speak English now in the state. And that puts them at a disadvantage."

English language learners are disproportionately represented in the roughly 1% of students who do not graduate due to the MCAS exam.

In 2019, of 702 students who did not earn a diploma due to the exam, 281 were English language learners, according to data provided to the State House News Service by Board of Elementary and Secondary Education Vice Chair Matt Hills.

However, of those 281 students, fewer than 30 failed the exam just due to a language barrier alone and not other academic challenges, according to Hills' analysis of the data, which considers that the math and science sections of the test are available in Spanish at the high school level.

Warren, leaning on her past experience as a special education teacher, said a single test is not a good measure for every child's ability.

Warren said that the yes campaign is being driven by the state's teachers, and the voters should listen to those who are in classrooms with kids. The campaign is being bankrolled by teachers unions, who also wrote the ballot question and have been knocking doors and collecting signatures for the initiative.

"Our teachers are telling us that the consequence of this test is actually to teach our kids less, because we're teaching them more about test-taking skills, taking them out of the classroom. They want an opportunity to help shape a broader view of which children get a high school diploma, and that's something that we should support our teachers who have helped us build the number one education system in the country," Warren said.

At Wednesday's press conference, Campbell said that voting no on Question 2 does not equate to not supporting educators.

"Parents and students don't have unions, which sadly can leave their voice and perspective out of some of the most important policy discussions and decision making," Campbell said.

During a radio debate Wednesday on GBH's Boston Public Radio, co-host Jim Braude asked MTA Vice President McCarthy why Healey, whom the MTA endorsed for governor, is at odds with the teachers union over the future of MCAS.

McCarthy said Healey is not standing with educators and labor, including the Massachusetts Association of School Committees, the Massachusetts Parent Teacher Association, and Massachusetts AFL-CIO, who have all voiced support for the question.

"This ballot measure is being supported by parents, educators, community activists and students," McCarthy said. "We met for more than seven weeks with Patrick Tutwiler, and we came pretty close to almost having a legislative solution. And there was a lot of alignment and agreement that we are not doing things right."

The special legislative committee tasked with reviewing initiative petitions decided against taking action on any of the ballot questions this spring. In a report, the committee said the MCAS question removes the state's uniform graduation requirement without establishing a "uniform alternative."

"Simply eliminating the uniform graduation requirement, which will allow students to graduate who do not meet basic standards, with no standardized and consistent benchmark in place to ensure those standards are met, will not improve student outcomes and runs the risk of exacerbating inconsistencies and inequities in instruction and learning across districts," the report said

Rattling off the growing list of names of top elected officials who are against Question 2, McCarthy's opponent in the radio debate -- Keri Rodrigues, founder of the National Parents Union -- said those leaders understand the "significant impact" of scrapping MCAS, namely students will be "handed a piece of paper at the end of 12 years of education that is almost meaningless because it's a participation trophy; it is a certificate of attendance."

"Moving forward, the idea that we are going to fly blind and hope, based on vibes, that our kids are going to be ready for the jobs and the economy of the future -- what is going to happen to the workforce?" Rodrigues said.

Healey, who also appeared on GBH Wednesday, told Braude and co-host Margery Eagan that she "actually listened to the debate that you had earlier" but still thinks Question 2 is a bad idea.

"For me, Question 2 is one of these, to me, unfortunate creations of this ballot process," Healey said on the radio Wednesday, before going to the Roxbury press conference. "Sometimes, I don't think that the ballot process is always the best way to make policy here in the state. And the reason that I oppose Question 2 and the elimination of MCAS as a graduation requirement is because, as a matter of education policy, I think ... it's better for us as a state to have a statewide standard graduation requirement."

Healey noted that she is "the daughter of two union teachers, my mom was a longtime school nurse and health educator, and my stepdad was actually president of his teachers' union."

"Without a replacement for a uniform standard statewide, I don't think it makes sense to go this way," the governor said. "And I think that there's a better way to achieve this."

Three candidates for Boston's top prosecutor faced off in a tense forum Thursday in Roxbury.

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden, former Suffolk County District Attorney Rachael Rollins and former Suffolk County Assistant District Attorney Linda Champion made their cases to voters ahead of the Democratic primary.

Rollins was elected to the position in 2018 and held it until 2022, when she became U.S. attorney for Massachusetts under then-President Joe Biden. She resigned the following year after reports from watchdogs, including the Department of Justice's inspector general, outlined a litany of misconduct allegations against her.

Among the allegations was that Rollins leaked information aiming to sabotage Hayden, then acting district attorney, in his campaign to succeed her, favoring his competitor, then-Boston City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo.

"You only know Kevin because I left to become your U.S. attorney," Rollins said Thursday.

"This person left her job, and now she wants it back, cause nothing else worked out for her, and it didn't work out for her because of her lack of ethics and integrity," Hayden fired back.

Champion, a former assistant district attorney in Suffolk County who ran unsuccessfully against Rollins in 2018 and later served as a legal counsel under Hayden, criticized both candidates who have led the office.

"I don't care who has held the seat, there has been no change," Champion said.

Rollins pointed to crime in the city since her time in office.

"In Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, we've seen an uptick in shootings and homicides," she told NBC10 Boston in an interview.

"The number of people shot and not killed in the city of Boston, last year, was at an all-time recorded low of 103," Hayden told the station.

"All they're talking about and doing is personal attacks on each other," Champion said. "It's about making sure every child in our community has safe streets and safe neighborhoods."

While Hayden highlighted lower crime rates, Rollins said he had lost progress made under her leadership, saying people with multiple open gun cases are getting arrested again.

Champion said it's time for a new face altogether.

"I think we deserve more than people who want to weaponize the legal system," she said. "Let's go in a new direction."

The candidates also addressed bodycam footage in the deadly shooting of Stephenson King by Boston Police Officer Nicholas O'Malley, who has been charged with manslaughter. A civil rights group has sued the police department and district attorney's office for the footage, which Hayden has said will not be released.

Hayden stood by that decision, while Rollins and Champion said it should be made public.

A day after announcing she would plead guilty to federal corruption charges and resign from the Boston City Council, Tania Fernandes Anderson returned to City Hall Wednesday.

The councilor, who represents District 7, spoke with NBC10 Boston about the months since her December arrest.

"I'm not just a mom to two boys, as you know, I have actually four sons, with my stepsons. I'm soon to be a grandma," she said. "How do I do the right thing to ensure that my family is safe, is stable?"

Fernandes Anderson, 46, represents Dorchester, Roxbury, Fenway and parts of the South End. She is accused of pocketing $7,000 in a kickback scheme that unfolded in a city hall bathroom with a relative who works on her staff.

She is pleading guilty to a count each of wire fraud and theft involving federal funds, according to a copy of the plea agreement shared by prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney's Office for Massachusetts. Four counts are being dropped.

Prosecutors are recommending that she serve a year and one day in prison, with three years of probation. They also recommended that she pay $13,000 in restitution.

Fernandes Anderson told NBC10 Boston why she returned to work Wednesday.

"You shouldn't avoid conflict," she said. "You should face it, you should grow, you should take accountability."

NBC10 Boston asked Fernandes Anderson if she's concerned that the trust of her constituents may have been violated.

"Of course," she responded.

She said that due to the ongoing case, she was unable to answer questions about why she is pleading guilty and whether she views this as an error she brought on herself.

Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune said she would help fill the void caused by the scandal and the pending resignation.

"We're going to continue working in partnership, as well, with the mayor's office to make sure that Roxbury residents, and the residents of all of District 7, have their representation during this challenging time," she said.

"We're going to make sure to reach out to community leaders, to residents, and be on the ground to make sure that their concerns and issues are still represented," added Councilor-at-Large Henry Santana.

"It's an incredibly unfortunate situation," Mayor Michelle Wu said Tuesday. "Residents of District 7 and across the city rightly should have representation, and public officials rightly should be held to a high standard. So I called initially for resignation months ago."

Louijeune explained that, if Fernandes Anderson's resignation comes prior to May 8, there would be a special election for the seat, but that certain steps must be taken first.

"When that notice is given, the charter is very clear that the city clerk must notify the city council of the vacancy, and the provisions of the special election will then come into effect," Louijeune said.

Fernandes Anderson says her attention is now shifting to life beyond this moment.

"I've been through many changes and many hardships," "Ugly circumstances, beautiful ones, all make up a part of your journey. I'm optimistic and I humble myself."

Fernandes Anderson issued the following statement Tuesday:

I have decided to plead guilty and resolve the case brought against me. I would like to apologize to my constituents, supporters, and all who have been impacted.

Please forgive me.

I will be resigning. It is the right thing to do. In coming days, I will evaluate transition plans and timeline with the District 7 Advisory Council. I will do everything possible to make an orderly exit to ensure my constituents’ needs are met.

I will have more to say at the appropriate time in court but I will not be commenting further beyond this statement. I pray that the press will respect my privacy, as well as the privacy of my family.

A series of street closures will be in place around South Station starting Tuesday morning, and the Massachusetts Department of Transportation is telling drivers who will be in or passing through the Foxborough area to expect delays.

More than 19,000 people took the Commuter Rail to Saturday's game, according to the MBTA. "The queue was really bad but people were so amazing," said Colin Craig, who attended the game.

According to Caitlin Allen Connelly, the executive director of public transit advocacy group TransitMatters, "operationally, things were a success."
